Section 3: Ekalasañcikā (Varḍa).
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*—*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 1.
[Author: Chapter 2 → Salutations to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ. Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, the third section: The Continuation of the Dvāpara Age.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Oṃ, salutations to the glorious Supreme Brahman, who transcends the imperishable, the wielder of the discus;
to the Supreme Lord, whose emblems are the banner, the trident, and the bow, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow.
Salutations to the beloved of all, the Beloved One, the inner controller of all.
Salutations to the one who has cast off all bonds, who is dear to the heart, and who descends in every incarnation.
Salutations to You, the Beloved, from whom all this has been born, by whom it attains growth, and in whom it shall finally abide.
Salutations to You, the Beloved, from whom all incarnations such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa arise, and of whom Time and Māyā are but portions.
She who is indeed Lakṣmī, the bestower of happiness, and the daughter of Viśveśvara, is Yours.

Having become beloved, you became Nārāyaṇī, the Śrī of Nārāyaṇa; salutations, salutations to you! (5) Infinite maidens were born as Nārāyaṇīs, dear to Hari; salutations, salutations to you, Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! (6)
Salutations to You, the beloved of Lakṣmī; salutations to You, the beloved of Rādhā.
Salutations again and again to You, the Lord of Ramā, who wears a ruby. Salutations again and again to the Lord of Śrī and the husband of Padmāvatī.
Salutations again and again to you, the lord of the Brahmapriyas, Aśanas, and others;
salutations to you, the husband of the goddess Ṣaṣṭhī who is honored by the mind;
salutations to the lord of the Dīpāvalīs, to the lord of the Talājās.
Salutations to the protector of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) and the lord of the Ārjantī rivers;

salutations to the lord of the Krodhanā rivers and the lord of the daughters of the Earth (Dharā). Salutations to you, the beloved of Sūcīkā and the lord of the progenitors of the forest goddesses (Vanadevīs).
Salutations to you, the lord of Dāmanī, whose hair is like that of a *kaṅkata* bird;
salutations to you, Bālakṛṣṇa, who is beloved by the daughters of the Pitṛs, who are the lords of the progenitors of the people, and who are also the masters of the maidservants of the Pitṛs. 11–12.
Obeisance to you, the beloved of the women dwelling in the subterranean realm; obeisance to you, the lord of the women hiding within the rows of *sāla* trees.
Obeisance again and again to you, the husband of the daughters of the Svastika-nāgas.
Salutations to you, the supreme lord and husband of the *nāginīs*. Salutations to you, the supreme lord and beloved of the female ghosts (*śāvinīs*).
Salutations again and again to you, the husband of the sorceresses (*aindrajālikas*). 14–15.
Salutations to you, the Lord of Knowledge and the Master of Sarasvatī;
salutations to you, the divine Lord of Lakṣmaṇā and the Lord of Nāḍikā. Salutations to you, Jummasemlīśa, the Lord of the Gāndharvīs.
Salutations to you, the lord of Sauratī, who is also the lord of Sāntapanī;
salutations to you, the lord of Mahābālā, the lord of Cailabīlā, and the lord of Dākṣajāvaṅgā; and salutations to you, the lord of Oṣṇī. (17–18)
Salutation to you, the Lord of the Prācīnas; salutation to you, the Lord of the Piśaṅgis. O Lord of the Sāntāṇaris, O Kṛṣṇa, salutation to you, the Lord of the Śaibīs.
Salutation to you, O Lord of Vīrajārī, who dwells in the region of Thārkūṭasthīpra.
O Lord of the Śāktyakṣī women, O Sovereign of the Piśācīs, homage be to you!
O Kālimāśīśvara, O Kṛṣṇa, O Friend of the Wretched, homage be to you!
Homage to the Lord of Auralaka and Kaithavī, and homage to the Lord of Krāthakī! 3.1.20–21.
Salutations to you, the lord of Pṛthuputrī and the master of the herd of camels;
salutations to you, the lord of Hāṃkārī and the sovereign born of the wood of victory.
Salutations to you, O Lord, the master of Tīrāṇī and the husband of Cālvīnārī.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the daughter of Jīnavardhana, the protector of the helpless;
salutations to you, the Supreme Lord whose domain is filled with celestial nymphs;
salutations to you, the beloved of the illusory Ālpa, the Lord of Pārīśānī.
Salutation to Indu, the lord of Āyāsuta, and to Mudrāṇḍīpati;
salutation to Gaṇḍabhūpa, the lord of Suta, and to Līnorṇāpati. Salutation to you, the master of Bārhacchārī; salutation to you, the lord of Bālalīnī.
Obeisance to you, the Lord of Vārasiṃhī; obeisance to you, the Lord of Rāyagāmī.
Obeisance to you, the Lord of Phainatāntavīkānta; obeisance to you, the Lord of Stokahomī.
Obeisance to you, the Lord of Kāṣṭhayānī; obeisance to the Lord of Kolakī.
Salutations to you, my lord who bestows daily honor;
salutations to you, my beloved; salutations to the Supreme Lord, the husband of Rāyakiṇṇaṭī;
salutations to you, the Supreme Self, the sovereign of Rāyakoṭīsvarī. 28.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the daughter of Rāyaraṇajit; salutations to Hari.
Salutations to the Lord of Rāyavākakṣikā, to the Lord of Rāyamārīśaka, to the Lord of Rāyabāleśvarī, and to the Lord of Rāyalambārikā. (3.1.30)
Salutations to you, O Lord of Rāyanavāri, the Supreme Self;
to the Lord of Rāyahūṇḍeśika, to the Lord of Rāyakūpeśika;
to the Master of Kālīmaṇḍī, to the Lord of Vanajaleśika.
Salutations to you, the Lord of the shore and the beyond, the Lord of ten million islands;
salutations to the divine Lord of Satī, whose hair is as fierce as the Tretā age,
the Master of those born from eggs, and the Master of the youthful Rājasī.
Obeisance again and again to you, the Lord of all, the husband of Rāyasomanī;
obeisance to the Lord of Urugavākṣikā and the husband of Parāṅvratanikā.
O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, husband of Rāyasvastrī, obeisance to You!
Obeloved of Aiśānī and Pārvatī, O Lord of Rājārājī, homage to you!
Homage to the one who is the beloved of Maṅgalā and others, and to the Lord of Ajanābhi; homage to the Lord of Kauberikā, and homage to the husband of Māhendrī. 35–36.
Obeisance to you, Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Yamīs and the master of the Vāyavīs.
Obeisance to you, the lord of the Vaiśvakarmīs and the master of the Vārkṣīs. Obeisance to the lord of the Raudrīs and the master of the daughters of Agni.
Salutations to you, the lord of the Śrāvaṇīs and the master of the Khānijīs. Salutations to you, the lord of the Sāṃvatsarīs and the husband of the Gopīs.
Salutations to you, the lord of the Prācīnīs and the master of the Piśaṅgīs. (38–39)
Salutations to you, the Lord of the Rāśiyāṇīs and the Lord of the Romāyaṇīs.
O Kṛṣṇa, salutations to the Lord of the Pāraśī women and the Lord of the Dhīvarīs.
Salutations to the Lord of the Kinnarīs and the Lord of the celestial Apsarases.
Salutations again and again to you, the lord of the Gaurīs, the lord of the Parīpatis.
Salutations again and again to you, the master of the Ābrikts, the lord of the Hāritīs.
Salutations again and again to you, the lord of the Pātālīs, the lord of the Svargīs. 41–42.
Salutations to you, the lord of the Apsarases, the sun to the Brahma-lake,
the sovereign of the Gandharvas, and the master of all auspiciousness. Salutations to you,
the lord of the Vidyādharas and the master of the Bhūmīs.
Salutations to you, the lord of the Dānavīs; salutations to you, the lord of the Śaktis.
(44) O Lord of the maidens of Kāśī, O Lord of the protectors of the cows, salutations to you!
O Lord of the beloved of the beloved, O Lord of all, O Lord of my life-breaths, salutations to you! (45)
Salutations to the son of Śrī Kaṃbharā; salutations to you, the contented younger brother.
Salutations to the inner controller of all, by whom this entire universe is pervaded.
Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, to Viṣṇu, to the Lord, my own master.
You alone are the Lord of Lakṣmī; you are the best of sages and the most excellent of kings.
You are the sacrifice, you are the digestive fire, and you are the giver of satisfaction, O Supreme Lord.
Having attained you, Arbuda and other women have indeed gone to liberation here.
Men who have been liberated and attained liberation become those who reach the supreme limit (*parārdha*).
By worshipping you, they go to heaven; by worshipping you, they go to the realm of truth (*satyaloka*).
And by worshipping you, they go to Vaikuṇṭha and to the earth of Vairāja.
By worshipping you, they indeed go to the immortal realm and to Goloka;
by worshipping you, they surely reach the imperishable, supreme abode.
O Blessed One, everything has indeed been shown to us by you in meditative absorption.
Since then, a desire for inquiry has occupied my mind regarding the scope of time:
you shine forth within the circles of liberated souls during the ultimate dissolution;
yet when a new material creation begins, impelled by time, [you appear] once more. ||51-52||
When Pradhānapuruṣa was born, and likewise when Mahāviṣṇu arose;
when Vairāja was then born, and likewise when Vedhas was born—
tell me, how much time has passed up until now?
O Hari, if there be anything further to be known, tell it to me.
O protector of my life, if I am a fit vessel for knowledge, speak to me;
and tell me, how much time remains now on this earth?
"You alone are the Supreme Person, the omniscient one, and the witness of all;
O Nārāyaṇa, indeed no one other than you is capable of speaking thus.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen with reverence, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the enumeration of time,
which cannot be described by anyone else and is likewise impossible for others to know.
At that time, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), who consists of the three qualities and whose form is creation, did not exist.
When she, whose form is my will, was dissolved in the imperishable state (akṣara-pada);
when Mahākāla did not exist, nor the Puruṣa who has him as his purpose;
and when he too, whose form is my sovereign power, was liberated and dissolved in the imperishable. (58–59)
At that time, there was only my own supreme abode, the Imperishable (akṣara), and nothing else.

That was solely the creation of Brahmā; it was not the creation of Īśvara. How could there be individual souls? O Nārāyaṇī, you should understand this to be the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya) itself.
Then I performed an act of observation: "May I, though one, become many through the power of *māyā*.
At that time, that *māyā*, whose nature is will, came into manifestation;
she is my divine power, Muktānikā, who consists of the *guṇas*.
Furthermore, the person named Kāla was revealed by me;
he is the very nature of my sovereignty, and being liberated, he has entered into union with her.
That couple, however, are Prakṛti and Puruṣa, my two children.
As soon as they were born, I indeed gave them the command for the purpose of creation.
And by those two, as soon as they were born, the commencement of creation was made at dawn;
one excellent pair was created, consisting of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.

By him was created a manifestation consisting of tens of millions and hundreds of millions of Great Viṣṇus; he is this very Pradhāna-Puruṣa, and from that he divided himself. At the end of night, at dawn, through Time and Primordial Matter (Prakṛti), he becomes new again.
Another pair, consisting of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, was indeed created.
Having performed that creation, it perished again at evening;
this day is proclaimed as a Mahākāla-kalpa within the Imperishable (Akṣara).
A thousand Mahākāla kalpas constitute one year for Prakṛti; such a time indeed exists there in every respect.
Fifty such years have indeed passed.
The lifespan of the primordial person (*prakṛtipuruṣa*) is exactly fifty-one years.
From this very day until today, that many creations have passed; fifty thousand such primordial persons have died. (3.1.70–71)
The first Pradhānapuruṣa indeed consists of fifty-one thousand [years];
listen further to the duration of the creation of Nārāyaṇīśrī.
This Pradhānapuruṣa, at the very dawn [of each cycle], [creates] ever anew.
Vairājī gives birth to Mahāviṣṇu, the creator of the emanation;
that Mahāviṣṇu indeed perishes at the end of the day.
In this manner, a year consisting of a thousand days is fashioned by Pradhāna. (73–74)
Fifty years have indeed passed for this Pradhānapuruṣa;
fifty thousand Mahāviṣṇus have died during that time.
And now, in the fifty-first year, on the very first day—
The first Mahāviṣṇu shines forth with fifty-one thousand [years] and so on.
Listen further, O Śrī of Nārāyaṇa, regarding the time of creation:
here, at the very dawn, this Mahāviṣṇu [manifests] ever anew.
He indeed produces the Vairāja, who is the cause of the creation of Brahmā;
and that Vairāja perishes at the end of the day in the evening.
In this manner, a year consisting of a thousand days is known to exist.
Of my father Mahāviṣṇu Gopālakṛṣṇaka—indeed, fifty years have passed there for this Mahāviṣṇu;
fifty thousand sons of that Vairāja have died. (3.1.80)
In the fifty-first year,
on the very first day, the Vairāja, consisting of fifty-one thousand [years] and so forth, shines forth. Listen further, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, to the time of creation.
And here, at dawn, this Vairāja himself generates a new and ever-fresh Brahmā, accompanied by Viṣṇu and Rudra;
yet that Brahmā also always perishes at evening, at the end of the day. (82–83)
In this manner, a year consisting of one thousand days was fashioned by Virāṭ;
and fifty such years have passed for this Vairāja Puruṣa.
Those fifty thousand Brahmās, his sons, have perished.
In the fifty-first year, on the very first day, the Creator,
numbering fifty-one thousand and so forth, shines forth. Listen further, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, to the time of creation as well.
And here, at dawn, this very Creator likewise creates anew,
from the gods, seers, and humans, down to the very limits of heaven;
and at evening, that same world, from the limits of heaven downward, constantly perishes.
Thus, a year of the Creator (Vidhātṛ) consists of one thousand days;
one thousand such [years] are proclaimed to be a single day of Brahmā.
And fifty such years of this Creator have already passed.
Fifty thousand triple-worlds (trailokya) indeed perish;
in the fifty-first year, on the very first day,
the first kalpa of fifty-one thousand years, known as the Vārāha-kalpa, begins.
This very day constitutes the first four yugas.
This four-faced Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, remains;
a day of Brahmā has been designated by me as a *kalpa*.
The day of Vairāja has been made by me the Mahākalpa;
the day of Mahāviṣṇu is the kalpa known as Mahāmahā.
The day of Pradhānapuruṣa has been made the Prākṛtakalpa.
A day of Māyākāla is a kalpa known as Mahākāla.
Upon its destruction, that which is called the Great [Dissolution] occurs; indeed, it is the Mahāpralaya.
Brahmā remains for a hundred years, and Virāj likewise remains for his own [period].
The Lord Mahāviṣṇu lives for his own hundred years;
likewise, Pradhānapuruṣa lives for his own hundred years,
and Prakṛtipuruṣa also lives for his own hundred years thereafter.
A hundred such years indeed constitutes the night of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya).
Again there is creation, and again the great dissolution; it is exactly thus.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇīśrī, this eternal system has been composed by me. (97–98)
Furthermore, the great creation itself is followed by the great dissolution;
and during each single day of Brahmā, fourteen Manus arise and dissolve—what need is there to count them, O beloved? (99)
One thousand kalpas are considered to be one year of Brahmā.
Eight thousand such years of Brahmā are recorded as his one yuga. One thousand such yugas are considered to be one day of Brahmā. (3.1.100–101)
Upon the destruction of one hundred thousand Trailokyas, Brahmā perishes;
upon the destruction of one hundred thousand Unborn Ones (Ajās), Virāṭ perishes;
and upon the destruction of one hundred thousand Virāṭs, Mahāviṣṇu perishes.
Upon the destruction of the marks of Mahāviṣṇu, there is the destruction of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Upon the destruction of the marks of Pradhāna and Puruṣa, there is the destruction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa. O Nārāyaṇī, you should understand the calculation of time in this manner. (1.03–1.04)
In all those various creations, I—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
the Lord of Śrī, and the Supreme Controller— manifest as an incarnation together with you.
Indeed, my incarnations arise there in incalculable numbers.
I know them, and no one else; I am omniscient, and no other is.
Nor do those incarnations themselves know them, for they are aware only of their own previous creations.
"Do not entertain doubt in this matter; my length is endless. Ask further whatever you wish to know, and I shall explain it to you in brief.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Puruṣottama by Śrī Nārāyaṇī, the Calculation of the Time of Creation, and so forth," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: O Creator, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama, O my Lord!
I desire to know the names of these fifty-two years.
From that, a desire has arisen; therefore speak, O Śrī Puruṣottama!
O Blessed One, I wish to know even the mere names of the fourteen Manus in this Vārāhaka Kalpa.

I also wish to know those kalpas that have come to an end during the fifty-first year [of Your manifestation]. O Beloved, tell me in brief about them, if it is not too much of a burden for You, who are the embodiment of manifestation.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: The first year of this Brahmā is the Padma-year;
the second is the Nāla-year, and the third is the Nālordhvaga-year.
The fourth is the Stāvana year, the fifth is Vyomavāṇa,
the sixth is Tapovapsara, the seventh is Yamavatsara,
the eighth is Niyama, and the ninth year is Āsana.
The tenth is called the restraint of breath (prāṇarodha), and the eleventh is the counter-strike (pratihṛti).
The twelfth is retention (dhāraṇa), the thirteenth is the shower of meditation (dhyānavarṣa),
the fourteenth is reflection (manana), and the fifteenth is absorption (samādhi).
The sixteenth is proclaimed as the year of Brahmā known as *prajñāta* (the known);
the seventeenth is *aprajñāta* (the unknown), while the eighteenth is *līnatā* (dissolution).
Then, the nineteenth year is called *sākṣātkāra* (direct realization).
Then the twentieth year is named Sṛṣṭibhānu;
the twenty-first is indeed called Vedavatsara;
and the twenty-second year thereafter is by the name Rudravatsara.
The twenty-third is Sanātana, and likewise the twenty-fourth is Ārṣaka;
the twenty-fifth is Dharmavarṣa, and the twenty-sixth is Anaṅgavatsara.
The twenty-seventh is named Adharma, and the twenty-eighth is Analavatsara.
The twenty-ninth is the year of the Pitṛs; the thirtieth is the year of the Devas.
The thirty-first is called Mānava; the thirty-second is Kalpapādapa.
The thirty-third is known as Sasya; the thirty-fourth is Pāśava.
The thirty-fifth is the Yākṣa year, the twenty-sixth is named Rākṣasa;
the thirty-seventh is called Cāṇḍaja, and the thirty-eighth is Gharmaja.
The thirty-ninth is the Nāga year, while the fortieth is the Yādas year.
Then follows the forty-first year, called Adhvara;
after that, the forty-second is Hiraṇyavatsara;
the forty-third is Rājata, and after that is Kāpālaka.
Then there was the forty-fifth year, Apsarōvatsara;
after that, Brahmāsarovatsara, and then Svardhūnīvatsara.
And the forty-eighth year was named Arcimārga.
Then the year Abdhimantha, followed by the year named Nārada;
thereafter the fifty-first year, Somanātha,
and the fifty-second year shall be known as Vaiṣṇava.
The fifty-third year, Gāyatrī, will commence;
this Kalpa named Vārāha will begin in the fifty-first [year].
By me, in the form of a boar, the earth was lifted up from the waters.
In this [age], fourteen Manus will indeed be the lords of the earth:
first Svāyambhuva Manu, then Svārociṣa Manu,
then Auttami, Tāmasa, Raivata, and Cākṣuṣa.
Vaivasvata and Sāvarṇi are the [seventh and] eighth Manus respectively; the ninth is Dakṣasāvarṇi, and after him is Brahmasāvarṇika. Then follows Dharmasāvarṇi, and after him Rudrasāvarṇika.
Then there is Devasāvarṇi, and after him Indrasāvarṇika.
These are the fourteen Manus, and there are likewise fourteen Indras.
They come into being during the day; the dissolution is considered to last for an equal duration at night.
In age after age, I indeed become the Supreme Person upon the earth. Fifty thousand such kalpas of Brahmā have passed;
O Nārāyaṇī, for that many times have I appeared as an incarnation on the earth.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama—(28)—in every age, my incarnations occur according to what must be done;
there is no end to their number, for neither I nor others know it. (29)
In that regard, there are infinite names according to my qualities and activities;
however, in every kalpa, I appear once as Puruṣottama.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, known as Bālakṛṣṇa.
The Lord of the masters of millions of devotees is the one who descends.
(3.1) In whichever Kalpa my incarnation occurs at its commencement, that Kalpa is indeed made manifest by me after the name of that very incarnation. (3.2)
Therefore, these designations of the kalpas were indeed created by my own consciousness;
it is not possible to state them in their full detail according to their sequence,
because time is beginningless and the creators are innumerable.
For this day and night is known as the dissolution of the elements (ābhūtasamplava).
Whatever beings exist in the three worlds, whether mobile or immobile, they dissolve along with the primary elements;
therefore it is called the dissolution of the elements.
When a thousand cycles of four yugas have passed at the end of a day of Brahmā, the Creator of the universe, desiring to sleep, then makes his own night. Thereafter,
he dwells through that night in the waters of the single ocean of darkness.
At dawn, impelled by the desire to create, he acts just as before.
Whatever Brahmā performs on the first day of the year, that primary act gives its name to the year as well. (37–38)
In the fifty-first Kalpa of Brahmā,
I have been born many times together with you, O Nārāyaṇī—
both in the Brāhma-kalpa, the Pādma-kalpa, and likewise in the Vairāja-kalpa.
I existed likewise in the Śveta-kalpa and the Lohita-kalpa, as well as in the Kṛṣṇa-kalpa;
in the Sanat-kalpa, the Bhava-kalpa, and the Bhuvaḥ-kalpa;
and likewise in the Tapaḥ-kalpa, the Bhāva-kalpa, the Raṃbha-kalpa, and the Ṛtu-kalpa.
In the Ṛtukalpa, the Vahnikalpa, and also in the Havyavāhanaka,
I was then Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the Sāvitrakalpa, the Bhuvaḥkalpa, and the Ūṣikakalpaka, [I was likewise].
In Kuśika, Gāndhāra, Ṛṣabha, and Ṣaḍjakalpaka;
in Mārjālīya, Madhyama, and Vairāja-kalpaka;
and likewise in Niṣāda, Prāṇaka, and Meghavāhya, they were born. (43–44)
They likewise became Cintaka, Akūtika, Vijñāta, and Mānasa; Bhāva, Rathantara, Śvetalohita,
Raktavāsas, Pīta, Sitakalpa, and Viśvarūpa.
And in other kalpas as well, O Nārāyaṇī,
my incarnations have been innumerable, appearing and disappearing according to necessity.
In every single kalpa, you, the illustrious one, are born in many ways and in great abundance.
Just as my wife is to be wed today, so are you born as my wife;
your names are infinite and your incarnations are innumerable.
Yet, O Śrī, consort of Nārāyaṇa, I know all of that in every respect.
O Nārāyaṇī! All this is pervaded by my very splendor—by my Lakṣmī, my sovereignties, my qualities, my manifestations, by my portions, my powers, and by the abundance of my riches. (3.2.49–50)
My energy is present in the firefly and also in the flame of a lamp;
it is in lightning, in the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars, and in the moon and the sun.
Indeed, my energy is everywhere, for all those who possess energy have been infused with it by me.
Indeed, my splendor resides in jewels and medicinal herbs, on the celestial path, in heaven, among the people, and in asceticism;
in Maharloka and Satyaloka, on Mount Meru, on Lokāloka, in Śaṅkara, in Viṣṇu, and in the unborn Virāja. (52–53)
In Mahāviṣṇu, the Lord of Pradhāna, the Lord of Prakṛti, and even in the Imperishable One;
in all liberated souls and in all incarnations as well— in every respect,
those very sovereignties, qualities, and splendors belong to me alone.
Through the rays of my form, they attain nourishment and satisfaction.
(55) Furthermore, the manifold variety of the rays of the form of Puruṣottama nourishes the multitudes of liberated beings by bestowing diverse forms of fulfillment. (56)
Always sixteen years of age, I abide alone in the supreme imperishable;
I nourish the liberated souls by bestowing the gift of great bliss and other such gifts.
Indeed, all my splendors are considered to be great bliss itself.
There exist [realms] filled with the nectar of peace, coolness, and contentment.
Those who enjoy them—the liberated ones and others besides—are indeed eternally satisfied, for they are filled with perpetual bliss along with you. (58–59)
From the form of the hair, rays indeed emerge carrying the essence;
the medicinal herbs of the three worlds are always nourished by that essence.
And the pearls, nourished by that essence, are at all times of uniform size.
The solar splendors of these indeed issue forth from his two eyes.
By their radiance, the embodied beings of the three worlds perceive;
from the rays of the right eye, suns come into being in every direction.
From the rays of his left eye, moons emerge in every direction;
from the circumference of his head, thunderclouds arise;
and indeed, streams of lightning flash forth for the sake of the three worlds.
The sweetness and splendor of Hari’s face radiate forth on all sides.
By the honey of that sweetness, millions of liberated souls are satisfied;
indeed, by those rays which bear fulfillment, the embodied beings of the three worlds are nourished.
From the two cheeks of my form, enchanting splendors emerge;
by them, Īśa and the other gods are released and indeed become infatuated within that form.
From the two lips, rays bearing nectar truly emerge.
By drinking the nectar of its essence, those dwelling in the three worlds are satisfied.
From the corners of her eyes, rays of light emerge, laden with love;
drawn by them, portions of love are born among those dwelling in the three worlds.
Indeed, rays filled with nectar arise from his teeth;
by drinking this nectar, all creations are perpetually satisfied.
These rays of ambrosia indeed emerge from the center of his forehead.
And those dwelling in the three emissions are born satisfied by drinking nectar.
From their two ears, they are produced as the essence of sound and the brilliance of the notes;
through those streams of brilliance, all those with divine ears hear.
On all sides of the body, pleasant touches that bring happiness arise;
touched by the rays of touch, they experience unfailing bliss.
Indeed, from the tongue, rays go forth toward desired and cherished tastes.
By means of those [rays], all created beings are delighted and they consume that essence.
From the nose, fragrant rays go forth;
by means of those fragrances, all who dwell in creation indeed smell that sweet scent.
Indeed, from my heart, O Śrī Hari, rays of bliss filled with eternal joy are surely streaming forth in all directions.
Immersed in great bliss by those rays, all beings dwelling within the three worlds exist.
From the aperture at the crown of my head, known as Brahman and consisting of the space of consciousness, the Great Bliss and the supreme Speech emerge;
indeed, from them, the words of those dwelling in the three worlds are uttered. (76–77)
By my word, all become eloquent and pursue the goals I have set for them;
from my two hands, rays of light go forth, endowed with the power of action.
Through these, those who dwell in the three worlds indeed become diligent in their efforts.
From my belly, rays indeed issue forth in all directions;
by them, all those dwelling in the three worlds live, for they grant life. From my generative organ, rays rich with bliss indeed go forth. (3.2.80)
The embodied beings dwelling within the three worlds possess bliss only in a limited measure; indeed, they reach the playful rays emanating from my form’s feet, and by means of those rays,
the embodied beings of the three worlds attain their movement.
Indeed, rays issue forth from the waist region of my embodied form;
by these, all indeed become powerful.
And from the spinal column, rays proceed, providing support.
By that [light], millions of world-eggs are always supported by pillars;
the radiance of my emission of excrement indeed proceeds through millions of creations.
Through those rays, emissions and births come to be.
And rays proceed from my two hips;
by their power of the mouth, all the worlds become bound to their seats.
The splendors that have entered within me proceed into all creations. (85–86)
By those rays, embodied beings attain reflection, awakening, honor, contemplation, discernment,
and direct realization. Furthermore,
lamps are produced by the radiance of my Kaustubha gem.
By the rays of my beauty, these beautiful women have been created;
and by the rays of my Lakṣmī, the housewives in all creations become the very goddesses of domestic prosperity,
adorned with every auspicious fortune.
For all creations are bound by affection through the rays of my tenderness;
indeed, all creations are endowed with magnanimity through the splendors of my nobility.
Through the rays of my beauty, everything is always possessed of form.
By the rays called *kalpa* from me, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as the power of fulfilling desires (*kāmāvasāyitā*) proceed like the creepers of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpapādapa*).
And by the rays that bestow righteousness (*dharma*) from me, the three worlds are satisfied.
Through those [rays] of mine, the emanations undergo ripening and transformation;
and through my fierce rays, they even go to concealment.
Furthermore, by means of the rays consisting of the power of stability, the entire sphere [is maintained].
The triad of emanations proceeds through the stabilization of their respective sequences.
Indeed, the emanations are filled by my rays of *āpūraka*;
and by my rays of *puṇyaka*, the lords (*īśvara*) and others are purified. (94–95)
By the rays of my consciousness, embodied beings attain omniscience;
by the splendors of my compassion, indeed, embodied beings rise up.
And by the splendors of my beauty, the leaders of creation shine forth.
Through my secret splendors, I am the possessor of hidden sovereignty.
By means of constant meditation upon my form, the virtuous become identical with me; indeed, "Sat" is my name, and those who truly possess that [name] are the virtuous.
Those virtuous ones who have attained absolute union with me are my beloved forms; you ladies,
having performed the circumambulation of the sacred fire in the field of Kāśī,
have become my beloved forms who have attained union with me.
Having propitiated me, they have attained my yoga; they are my very forms.
Liberated lords, gods, brahmins, the virtuous, cows, maidens, youths of Brahmanic character, and those devoted to truth—they are all my forms.
And by the rays of my form, which possess substantial existence, kings are produced throughout the three worlds; through my yoga, they are indeed my own forms.
Indra, Svāyambhuva Brahmā, and his father Vairāja as well.
And his father and even his grandfather—all these are my forms.
Śacī, who possesses a hundred forms, as well as Sāvitrī, Vairājikā, Mahālakṣmī, and Pradhāna—these are my forms. (103–104)
The Vyūhas such as Vāsudeva and others, the forms such as Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others,
as well as the Nārāyaṇas, the virtuous, and the saintly women, are my own forms.
Fire, Viṣṇu, gold, the heart, consciousness, and the spiritual preceptor [are also my forms].
The couple and Tulasī are truly always my forms.
The Veda, the sun, industry, punishment, affection, the guest, happiness, the child, the dependent, the helpless, and the seeker of knowledge are my forms. (106–107)

The King, the Preceptor, the Chief, the Instructor, Vyāsa, the Remover of Suffering, the Protector, the Guardian, and the Lord—these are my forms, the worthy refuge. Sacrifice, ancestral rites, worship, hospitality, and the offering of honey-mixture [are likewise my forms]. 108.
The sacrificial fees, the offerings to the gods and ancestors, and so forth—consisting of me—are my forms.
(109) The grinding stone, the mortar, the hearth, the water jar, and the broom—when employed for my sake, they are purifying and are my forms. (3.2.110)
Whether it be a bed, a vehicle, a mount, wealth such as cattle, or houses and the like—
if these are used for my sake, they are all of the nature of my own form.
O Śrī, consort of Nārāyaṇa, everything is permeated by me, just as you are mine.
"If everything has been done for my sake, it shall grant me union [with the Divine].
Thus have I spoken here regarding food; I am the very form of the Divine Image. Ask me anything else that you may desire to know.
"By reading this and likewise hearing it, O beloved, one shall attain my own state;
one shall obtain liberation after liberation, the fruit of visiting sacred fords, and the fruit of yoga.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fifty-two Names of the Creator’s Years in the Dvāpara Cycle, the Names of the Fourteen Manus of the Current Kalpa, the Forty Names of the Final Fifty-Year Cycle of the Kalpa, and the Manifestation of the Glory of the Threefold Creation Sustained by the Rays of Puruṣottama," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, ocean of mercy, please tell me this which I desire to know:
in which year of Brahmā’s fifty-two-year cycle [did this occur]? (1)
You have appeared as the primary incarnation, endowed with name, action, and qualities;
I desire to hear all of that, since your divine play bestows liberation.
There is no end to your incarnations, yet I do not place that burden upon you.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the manifestation of the nature of the Incarnate (Avatāra) which occurred in that former time, so that I too may have remembrance of it;
O affectionate one, tell me only of the manifestation of Puruṣottama.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! I shall speak; understand it from me.
O beautiful lady, I shall tell you that very life-story of mine which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the year of the Creator, during the eighth kalpa and under the eighth Manu,
from the Nāla-section of the Creator’s [abode], there was indeed born an asura named Rohiṇāṇḍodara,
equal to the cosmic egg in both body and strength.
By his fiery and even his dark power, he became a devourer of the three worlds.
Struck by Rudra with both a mace and a trident, he fled into the midst of the waters; then Rudra pursued him.
Having pierced through the covering of the earth, he entered the sphere of the cosmic egg;
passing beyond the worlds of Satya, Tapas, and Jana, he reached Maharloka.
Thereupon, becoming subtle and remaining hidden, he dwelt within a cave of Mount Meru.
Rudra indeed went to the abode of Mahendra to behold heaven.
The gods, the ancestors, and the great seers also arrived;
at that time, Indra’s assembly hall was filled with the sun, the moon, and the other luminaries.
Then Rohiṇāṇḍodara, perceiving the opportunity,
grew until his belly became equal to Mount Meru; having opened his mouth wide toward that assembly hall,
he encompassed it along with heaven, including the sun, moon, Indra, Rudra, and the constellations.
He suddenly swallowed everything, and heaven came to be within his belly.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the worlds shook;
the realms of Mahar, Jana, and the others trembled all at once.
Then a great and most terrible trembling arose in Satyaloka;
even the Lokāloka mountain shook repeatedly at that time.
Perceiving that the destruction of the heavenly realm was imminent, the deities [were struck with alarm].
Then Rudra, Indra, the Sun, and the Moon, situated within the interior of the cosmic egg of Rohiṇī, overcome with fear, praised me, the Supreme Person:
"O Supreme Brahman, ocean of compassion, protector of all, Mādhava! (16–17)
Salutations to you, O Blessed One, the inner witness of all, the Supreme Lord!
Apart from you, there is no other protector here against sudden dissolution.
O Lord of Life, protect me, protect me from this great dissolution!
"O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Teacher of the World, we do not know where our residence in heaven has gone into this deep abyss;
how could the divine heaven, consisting of all splendor, exist within such a vast cavern? (3.3.20)
"Or perhaps some being has swallowed us who have fallen;
an untimely dissolution has arrived. Therefore, protect us!
Protect us! We gods have come to you for refuge, surrendering ourselves of our own accord."
"Offering themselves to you here, do as you wish for our sake.
Thus was I praised by Brahmā, and likewise praised by you,
O Śrī, consort of Nārāyaṇa, at that time within the belly of Rohitāśva.
I quickly became the mind-born son of Indra, together with Cakra;
[so too did] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
At that time, O beloved, you also became the mind-born daughter of Rudra.
Then the gods, beholding me, the Supreme Person, who had become manifest before their eyes,
were overwhelmed at heart and worshipped me by offering up their hearts.
At that time, I swiftly manifested my great Sudarśana discus.
The tip of my sword, released swiftly from my hand, cut through the body of the demon Rohitāṇḍa— measuring ten million *arats*—
as it had moved about in many directions and whirled repeatedly. (27)
The great fire produced from the discus reduced the fragments of the bodies of the foremost asuras into ten million pieces and turned them to ashes. Then those ashes became gold known as *rohitaka*.
When the destruction of Rohitaṇḍodara had occurred, the gods and others became at ease;
having recognized me as the imperishable Lord, the Master Śrī Mahendra-bālaka,
the Supreme Sovereign and Protector, in the abode of Indra, the dwelling of the gods.
Having performed a supreme great festival in the presence of the gods, Rudra then gave you,
his own mind-born daughter, to me in the pavilion;
and at that time, I too obtained you, that beautiful woman, through the divine rite.
At that time, my perception was that Anādi-Dyumanārāyaṇa existed;
then heaven and the gods were established by me exactly as they are.
By the very power of my yoga, this auspicious transformation was accomplished.
I am that very one who descended; he who I am here, he I have become.
Remember, O Raudrī, my beloved, my divine play there with you, the Yoginīs.
My incarnations there in that year were many, occurring every single day.
Thus has my first mental birth been described;
now hear of my second birth as well, which occurred in the second year,
in the year named Nāla, on the very first day of Brahmā.
At the end of the third Manu, a mountain named Meru was indeed overwhelmed by the great weight of the fourteen *taras*;
it then sank slightly into the depths of Pātāla. (37–38)
Endowed with fourteen tiers and containing the abodes of both gods and asuras,
when Mount Meru sank into a low state, the fourteen worlds,
along with Meru itself, were indeed broken and fell into the depths below.
Bent against the sides of Mount Meru and drawn from every direction,
heaven, earth, and the netherworld (rasātala) truly became filled with offspring;
indeed, everything on all sides came to have its base turned upward.
The Lokāloka mountain, which forms the wall of the cosmic egg on all sides,
was drawn inward toward the interior and took the form of a short ring;
nevertheless, by its power, it remained truly firm even though it was bent.

There, even the worlds were momentarily contracted. And Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others, seeing the destruction of the pillar and perceiving it to be the destruction of the cosmic egg, [approached] the Supreme Lord for the sake of its protection.
They praised me, the Supreme Brahman, Lord Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, with supreme fear for the sake of protecting Mount Meru,
for the protection of this universe, and for the preservation of the worlds.
O Supreme Lord, you are the support of all cosmic eggs.
O Master, the power that sustains the stability of the entire creation resides in you alone;
because everything exists within you, all things remain stable.
O Blessed One, everything produced by you has you as its support;
deprived of you, it would go to dissolution. Save me from the proximity of destruction!
Without a pillar, a house cannot stand, and so too is this [universe] dependent on you.

Without Meru, the worlds could not remain in the sky. Meru, burdened by their weight and covered with stars, sinks into the foundation; we too would go to destruction. Therefore, let us protect Meru, for it is our refuge. (3.3.49–50)
Having thus praised me, the lords of the gods meditated for a moment.
O Lakṣmī!
I quickly departed from the imperishable abode and arrived swiftly in Satyaloka, in the presence of Brahmā.
While the gods were looking on, I became a child in the lap of the Creator (Brahmā).
Resplendent with the brilliance of ten million suns, wearing matted locks and adorned with all ornaments, I laughed and said to the Creator in my lap, "Father."
Addressing me as "son," he accepted me as his son through his illusory power (*māyā*).
The gods, having bowed to Hari and recognizing him as the Supreme Lord, worshipped me with flowers and other offerings;
they offered hymns of praise and said again and again, "Protect us!"
I, too, am your son, named Anādiśrīmerunārāyaṇa.
Having quickly made you my supreme Śakti, the sustainer of Meru, and having very swiftly merged you—who are perfectly endowed with my own form—into myself, [I shall remain]. || 55-56 ||
Having led the gods, beginning with Brahmā, he went together to Pātāla.
There, I worshipped that [form] of yours which is established at the base of Meru on the earth. O Śrī Mahānārāyaṇī, having fully worshipped you, he indeed gave his command.
At that moment, you entered suddenly there in the form of Śakti.
You, the Great Śakti, were created by me and accompanied by me;
then Meru was uprooted from its base by me along with the gods. ||58-59||
Lifted up by the exceedingly powerful ones together with Brahmā and the others,
Mount Meru then attained its height according to their respective requirements;
all the worlds were likewise brought to a level plane.
They became fit for habitation, and the gods and others were made happy.
(61) O Lakṣmī! From that time forth, this Meru has always been supported at its base by you, who are of the nature of your own shadow and are known as Dhṛti (Fortitude). (62)
And I entered there upon Meru in the form of *dhāraṇā*;
as the inner self (*antarātman*) in the form of drawing up the sky, I remained within the interior of Meru.
Thus, having established supreme stability on Meru, [I was then addressed] by the gods and others.

And having observed that the roots of the worlds were attached to Mount Meru, he then made them well-fixed and established them firmly in their proper order. Likewise, from Rasātala, Mahātala, and Talātala... [64–65]
From Sutala, Vitala, and likewise from Atala,
he came toward Bhuvarloka along with you; then, having passed through Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Mahar, and Jana,
and having reached Tapaḥ and Satya, the son of Aja became established.
I am the beginningless Śrī Meru-Nārāyaṇa, the son of Brahmā.
I was married by you, the daughter of Meru, along with the gods and others;
and from that time until the end of the kalpa, I remained for the sake of protecting all beings.
The Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself is the original source of descent;
at that time, as well as in every age and every kalpa, my incarnations have occurred.
Many of them have appeared according to the requirements of specific tasks, for their limit is truly not known.
O Śrī Mahānārāyaṇī! remember that [birth] of yours;
then remember my auspicious birth as Meru-Nārāyaṇa.
Then, O Lakṣmī, in another year, even for the Creator (Brahmā), [there was a birth]. || 3.3.70–71 ||
O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇī, listen as I tell you of my birth here: in the first year of the Nārada Kalpa, during the third Manvantara,
O Nārāyaṇī, at that time the solar orb was in heaven upon the earth.
But that which had not been cast down became the reducer of the worlds to ashes;
it possessed a million rays and was a burner facing in every direction—
[a destroyer] of the cardinal points, the intermediate directions, the worlds, the planets, and all embodied beings.
It was the burner of all the terrestrial realms and the oceans;
indeed, it became the burner of the elemental creations of wind situated upon the earth.
It was the burner of Lokāloka, of Meru, and of those dwelling in the forests.
It became a burner of the constellations and stars for those dwelling among people,
and likewise a burner that reduced to ashes all those residing in Maharloka as well as those living in the worlds above. ||76-77||
Having encountered the pain of that burning, the Manus, the deities,
and all the inhabitants of the worlds then praised the Creator.
Having heard the hymn of praise, Brahmā went for the sake of pacifying the Sun.
He too, being consumed by fire, turned back and then went to Satyaloka.
Śaṅkara indeed went toward the Sun to bring about great peace;
he too, being consumed, offered salutation, turned back, and became inactive.
Then Viṣṇu and the gods,
having assembled, praised me, the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama. To pacify the splendor of the sun, they offered salutations again and again.
O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, you are the leader of ten million suns.
O Eye of the World, Bestower of Light upon the World, protect us from the sun!
We who dwell in the three worlds, as well as others who dwell above, [seek your protection]. (82–83)
We would have been consumed by the sun’s flames spreading across hundreds of thousands of leagues;
yet it is by you that the entire world has been made luminous for the sake of happiness.
If it were instead reduced to burnt ashes, what need would there be for the sun?
"Therefore, O Lord of Gods, protect us; grant us peace, for we are tormented.
Having spoken thus, they offered extensive worship in the form of an oblation to the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then, O Kamalā, together with you, I quickly became Nārāyaṇa;
truly, I went from Akṣara to the supreme abode of Brahman.
Worshipped by the gods, I became the son upon the lap of Viṣṇu.
He was gentle, possessing a thousand arms, adorned with a crown, earrings, and other ornaments;
he was equipped with whetstones, weapons, and the like, as well as jars of nectar and ambrosia.
There, by my power, the Sudarśana discus was instantly transformed into the nature of a whetstone.
"O Lakṣmī, that nectar which extinguishes all fire possesses the power to cut;
therefore, O Goddess, commanded by me, become the Cutter (Śātanī).
Having entered the sun, hold that nectar there, O Śātanī! (3.3.90)
"Act quickly so that the heat may become diminished.
And you, having received my command, swiftly take on the form of fire;
becoming composed of great splendor, you shall be one who causes intense burning."
Taking the nectar, she entered the solar orb;
then, she gradually placed that ambrosia within its interior.
Gradually, the rays of the sun indeed attained a state of tranquility.
And you, gradually and little by little, withdrew your own splendor there.
Then, having placed the sun upon the whetstone of your form as if on a grinding wheel, I sharpened it and even ground away its exceedingly sharp regions.
Having divided all those regions, I then gave them to the gods and others;
they indeed fashioned unimpeded weapons at that time.
There, I made the thousand-rayed sun a bestower of happiness.
O Lakṣmī! Other portions of yourself were absorbed by you into your own body.
From that time forward, that Sun became the bringer of prosperity to the world;
and you, from then on, became his daughter, the daughter of the Sun, known by the name Śātanikā.
I, the son of Viṣṇu and destroyer of the sun, have married that Abhavā; even I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, have wed her.
Remember how you dwelt there with me until the end of the kalpa.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, there was a time when I, the Lord, became Sūryakarmā.
O beloved, I myself, the Supreme Brahman, became Sūryakarmā;
likewise, in that very year, my incarnations numbered in the tens of millions.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma and likewise for the protection of embodied beings,
the primordial Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself is said to have descended as an incarnation.
O Lakṣmī, that was indeed my third manifestation in that year.
O beloved, I know all of that as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of my hand.
Having worshipped me at that time, countless embodied beings have indeed attained liberation.
Likewise, through reading and hearing [this], both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestations," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the second section on the Dvāpara age, concerning the first year of the Creator (Brahmā): the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Dyunārāyaṇa for the purpose of protecting the heavens from the asuras who had swallowed them within the womb of the Rohiṇa-egg; concerning the second year: the manifestation of the beginningless Meru-Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of supporting Mount Meru as it was sinking under its own weight; and concerning the third year: the manifestation of the beginningless Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of cooling the sun as it was burning [the world]. 3.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! This is my fourth mode of conduct, which provides protection for the moon in heaven and bestows supreme liberation upon those who sing it. (1)
Then, in the fourth kalpa of the Unborn One (Aja),
during the twelfth Manvantara,
there arose from the back of Śambhu’s head a most terrible and fierce asura named Dhūmra.
He arose with a body of space, moving through the atmosphere and terrifying to behold.
Seeing the beautiful jewel adorning Śambhu’s forehead,
he felt a sense of rivalry and went into the sky to seize that "jewel of the night" (the moon).
Then he made a great effort to seize the moon;
though restrained by the moon with sharp weapons and missiles,
he then fell from the sky onto the mountain named Śvetaśṛṅga.
Then, for the sake of Śambhu, the son of Śambhu performed penance.
He remained without food for the duration of one yuga; consequently, Śaṅkara became pleased and spoke to that son, Dhūmra, who was born from the back of his head.
"Tell me, what pleases you today? Why do you persist in penance? Speak your desire; I shall surely grant it. Do not perform such fierce asceticism.
Thus addressed, the asura replied, "Grant me a boon that brings victory."
"I wish to conquer the Moon without effort, and nothing else.
"So be it," said Hara; he gave a trident to Dhūmra that was invincible, indestructible, and superior even to the discus in power. (3.4.10)
Taking that [weapon], Dhūmra first went to Mount Meru,
impelled by the thread of craving to achieve universal victory.
Having conquered the gods dwelling on Meru, he went forth to defeat the kings upon the earth.
Having conquered the kings on earth, he then proceeded to the netherworlds (pātāla).
Having defeated the Daityas, Nāgas, tortoises, crocodiles, small fish, and likewise sharks,
as well as having conquered the hooded serpents (phaṇadhr), he went to the Aṭavī forest.
Having conquered the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras,
and having defeated the Guhyakas and Cāraṇas, he proceeded to the city of Saṃyamanī. Then, having defeated the messengers of Yama, he indeed fought with Yama himself.
Yama fought with his staff and the Asura with his trident;
indeed, they battled one another, yet for neither was defeat found there.
Rudra was invoked by Yama, and Hara was invoked by the Asura.
Hara and Rudra arrived and stood between them;
they both tried to restrain him, but he went on, praising [them] as he went home. Then the Asura, filled with pride, went to Indra, the lord of heaven.
Indra, recognizing that the spear given by Mahādeva was invincible,
rose with a gentle disposition and performed auspicious honors;
he gave the Asura a beautiful necklace fashioned from jewels.
And the asura, becoming gentle and free from anger upon seeing that, worshipped Śambhu’s trident in many ways;
he then set out to conquer the sun, but the sun quickly went to its setting.
Then the Asura went forth to conquer the unborn Parameṣṭhin.
Brahmā, recognizing that trident as belonging to Śambhu, worshipped it;
he offered the madhuparka and paid honor to the Asura.
Having reached a highly beautiful golden throne, Dhūmra rejoiced;
becoming humble and bowing to the Unborn One (Aja), he departed for heaven.
Seeing the full-lustered Moon, he went toward it with haste.
There, the moon was always free from disease, complete, and ever-present;
it was uniform, devoid of waning or waxing, eternal, and blissful.
It was free from being eclipsed by planets and the like, and its digits were full on all sides. (24–25)
Having approached that terrifying Dhūmra, who was like full-blown nectar,
he assumed a form as vast as a hundred moons and seized it with his hand.
With the touch of those rays of nectar-like ambrosia, the great Asura—
He indeed attained an unprecedented and supreme bliss filled with great joy.
Consequently, having conceived greed for the moon, he seized the hare-marked one in his mouth. A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose everywhere in heaven and on earth. (27–28)
Indeed, that jewel was a repository of nectar, possessing cool radiance;
yet, without even attaining its moonlight, the medicinal herbs became exceedingly weakened, and the gods, deprived of nectar, became as if dead. (29)
"Indeed, all living beings who possess rays [of consciousness] are subject to death.
(3.4.30) Then the gods who had been born took refuge with their own preceptor; Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods, praised me, the Supreme Lord. (31)
For the sake of protecting the moon, and for the purpose of protecting the world,
salutations to the God of gods, whose eyes are the sun and the moon;
to the Supreme Self, the inner witness of all, who acts as a protector.
Salutations to the one known as Puruṣottama, the bestower of nectar, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
salutations to the great-souled Sun among the planets, lunar mansions, and stars; salutations to the inner altar, the destroyer of those who lack devotion.
Come quickly, O Hari; you must provide protection for the Moon.
Mahādeva, absorbed in meditation, remains there for a long time.
O Śrī Parameśvara, Lord of the Liberated, protect [him] swiftly from Dhūmra!

O Śrī, Nārāyaṇī! Having been thus praised by you at that time, I quickly went with you to the celestial abode of the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati). There, my mental son, though invisible in form, immediately entered his body.
I became Subāla, adorned with all ornaments,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, trident, spear, and arrows as my weapons,
and resplendent with the thunderbolt, bow, staff, noose, sword, and shield.
Then, commanded by me, you entered the belly of the asura.
You became the stable lunar digit (cāndrī kalā) residing within the moon, its protector.
Indeed, O Lakṣmī, it was by your power that the moon did not fall into a swoon at that time.
Nor was he deprived of heat, nor was he bereft of nectar;
nor was he matured within the womb by the smoke-colored fire of the Asura.
In this very way, he remained in the womb exactly as he had been before.
Then, honored by the gods and adorned by the preceptor of the gods, he said:
"Requested for the sake of destroying the asuras, I went against the great asura;
accompanied by the divine army, I fought with Candraghātī. (42–43)
Then, O Lakṣmī! at my command, you assumed the form of a maiden for a moment;
and the asura named Dhūmra, upon beholding you, was infatuated.
Casting aside his trident, he made an effort to seize you for a moment.
Then, by my command, you indeed swallowed that trident of Śaṅkara.
By me, with my discus, that Asura was swiftly struck into a thousand pieces;
Dhūmra met his destruction and was then reduced to ashes.
There, the moon with its full digits emerged from her womb;
and you were the daughter of the Moon, known by the name Kaumudī.
You, the Supreme Goddess, were nourished and worshipped by all the gods and others.
I have been honored, nourished, and likewise saluted by all.
I am the son of the preceptor of the gods, the Blessed One, Puruṣottama.
Knowing me to be Hari, Candra has likewise saluted and honored me.
"O beloved Narayani! At that time, you were a maiden named Kaumudi, and you were given to me;
you were wedded by me, who am the householder of Devaguru, under the name Anadi-shri-deva-narayana."
Then I remembered Śambhu even while in the house of the preceptor of the gods.
Knowing me to be the Supreme Lord, Śambhu arrived quickly;
and knowing that Dhūmāsura had been destroyed, Hara indeed rejoiced.
Śambhu indeed gave the eternal trident to Candra;
your father gave you the eternal, auspicious trident as a wedding gift.
It was given by you to me, and by me, the beautiful-lined [ring] was placed in his hand.

Behold, O skillful one, the trident always held and grasped in my right hand; it remains marked there and manifests at will. Remember, Lakṣmī! Your manifestation occurred, and mine as well, at that very time.
At that time, I myself was Devanarāyaṇa; my incarnations at that time also numbered thousands of crores. And until the end of the kalpa, I indeed remained with you in the house of our guru.
Now, listen to the story of who I was in my fifth year as Ajā, and who you were in the first Manvantara of the first Kalpa.
In the first Manu of the previous Kalpa, during the year named Vyomabāṇa (1000), [I was... 57–58.
While the sons of Brahmā, the great sages who proclaim the Vedas, were assembled in the assembly of the unborn one,
they indeed engaged in deliberation: "In the cosmic egg,
the terrestrial world is the land of action, for it yields fruit."

In that regard, whatever gift—such as a bull or other offerings—has been performed and given by embodied beings while they were on this earth, all of it is obtained as food and so forth by those who have gone to other worlds. Whatever water, food, clothing, and ornaments were bestowed upon the surface of the earth [are likewise received]. (3.4.60–61)
Fields, groves, silver, maidens, gold, houses, and means of subsistence;
oblations to the gods, oblations to the ancestors, ritual offerings, merit, vows, ancestral rites, and assistants—
all this is obtained by the donor and the performer in the other world increased ten-thousandfold.
Just as renunciants (*sannyāsins*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*),

and lifelong celibates live by relying upon the householder stage (*gārhasthya*), so too do the gods of heaven, the ancestors, and the great seers (*maharṣis*) live by relying upon what is performed on earth. (63–64)
That sacrificial rite is well-performed when it provides sustenance for all embodied beings,
wherein the feeding of Brahmins serves as the oblation (havya) for the gods;
and likewise, the ancestral rite (śrāddha) is meritorious as it serves as the offering for the ancestors, the gods, and the sages.
In sacrifice, indeed, everything is obtained: Soma, nectar, ambrosia, and food.
Therefore, sacrifice must be performed—taught as being essentially action—for the sake of maintaining the continuity of ritual for both humans and the gods upon earth.
When the thread of the sacrifice has been commenced, joined, applied,
and completed through the proper performance of sacrifices, life shall be free from affliction.
Therefore, O great sages, let us indeed go to the earth this very day.

"Having brought together the gods and the ancestors, we shall perform the supreme sacrifice. Having thus deliberated, O Lakṣmī, the sages, the ancestors, and the lords of the gods arrived at the earth near Mount Meru for the sake of the sacrifice.
All the Pālāśas and Āraṇyakas were situated on the bank of the Svargaṅgā;
though engaged in different ritual duties, they strove for the sake of the sacrifice. Since this was the first sacrifice, they did not know the proper sequence at all. (71)
No one at that time was a practitioner of all sacrifices within the sphere of ritual action;
for whether it was a god, a father, a brahmin, or a great seer who was designated to perform them in due order, there was no manifestation of the sequence of rituals there.

Then, having fallen into delusion and being ignorant of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), they became obstinate, insisting that "this must come first" and "that must come first. At that time, there was no certainty regarding the sequence of the sacrifice nor even the sequence of its constituent parts.
The son of Vedhas, known as Brahmakumāra, possessed of lifelong celibacy and virtuous conduct, spoke there to the sacrificer, Manu named Jyotiṣmat:
"Indeed, we are all within the sphere of the unprecedented (apūrva) in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa). || 75-76 ||
But when a sacrifice is performed with deficient qualities, the result becomes the opposite.
There is no seer of sacrifice nor speaker of sacrifice other than Nārāyaṇa—
Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the imperishable.
Let us worship him here together for the sake of following the proper sequence;
he, the performer of sacrifice, will come and instruct us in the entire ritual—
he who is the deity of sacrifice, whose essence is sacrifice, who knows sacrifice, and who is the maker of sacrifice.
Thus addressed, Manu and the others accepted those words;
then, having approached the Supreme Lord, they worshipped him with great eagerness.
So too did the great sages, the ancestors, the deities, the brahmins, and the rest.
Oṃ, salutations to the Supreme Lord who has the form of sacrifice, the performer of ritual action;
to the deity of sacrifice, to sacrifice itself, to the knower of sacrifice, the performer of the rite;
to the Supreme Self, the author of the sacrificial scriptures, who carries out the work of the sacrifice.
"Salutations to the Inner Controller, and to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow who grants us assistance"—

thus did the gods and others praise me, the Supreme Person, for the sake of the sacrifice. Then, having heard those meaningful words even from the Imperishable (Viṣṇu), I [responded] together with you.
I went indeed to the bank of the Gaṅgā, to a forest of Palāśa wood on Mount Meru (84).
Near the sons of Brahmā, I was a boy wearing the guise of a sage;
I was composed of all branches of knowledge, a seer of all mantras, and acting under command (85).
To the extent that I am proficient in the ritual procedures, to the extent that I am a twice-born bearer of the sacred vessel,
a knower of all sequences, and possessed of knowledge regarding all substances and so forth—
I have indeed become manifest as a second Brahmā.
But when they all saw me, the brahmin, resplendent like ten million suns, they rose up suddenly and bowed to me; eager, they asked, "Who are you? [I replied:
"I am indeed the Lord Adhvara, the fruit of your worship. (87–88)
Having spoken thus, I, in the form of a child, came to rest upon the lap of the young Brahma;
he likewise meditated upon me as his son.
And you, being exceedingly great, then entered into his luminous mind.

Then, having comforted them all and appointed them to their respective duties for the sake of the sacrifice, I set that ritual in motion according to the sequence. I am the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

Having become the illustrious Yajñanārāyaṇa from time immemorial, I caused that Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, which was fit for a universal monarch, to be performed until its conclusion with the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Therefore, as the Sacrifice (Adhvara), I then requested a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) from Manu.
Then, O auspicious one, you appeared on the sacrificial ground near the pavilion at the edge of the altar as a maiden named Bhūyasī, also known by the name Dakṣiṇā;
indeed, you were a maiden seeking me. (93–94)
Manu’s daughter, Nārāyaṇī, was indeed most excellent;
adorned with celestial ornaments at the sacrifice and endowed with a wealth of ten million gold pieces,
she was bestowed by Manu upon me as I requested her as a fitting bride.
From that time on, throughout that year consisting of a thousand kalpas,
all sacrifices were performed by me according to the manner I had prescribed.
And there, along with you, I performed the great sacrifice for the duration of a kalpa.
I am that very Yajñanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Puruṣottama;
the self-manifested Incarnate Lord, the Supreme Brahman, the Highest Sovereign.
At that time, you became my wife, known by the name Bhūyasī Dakṣiṇā.
Remember that kalpa and that year, O Lakṣmī, consort of Nārāyaṇa!
After those, millions of other incarnations of mine occurred there;
I know them all, O Lakṣmī, but others do not remember even them. (3.4.100)
I am the very form of all sacrifices; all sacrifices abide in Me.
All sacrifices are My manifestations, and I am the instigator of all sacrifices.
I am the enjoyer in all sacrifices and the bestower of the fruits of all ritual offerings.
"I am one who knows the entire collection of ritual acts in the sacrifice;
O Lakṣmī, I do not remain without you in rites for the gods, the ancestors, the sages, or humans, nor in giving, honoring, or worship. (10.2–10.3)
"In recitation, in vows, in ritual sequence, in knowledge, and even in righteousness, I attend upon you, O Queen of Gods! O Sovereign of Śiva! and not otherwise.
Thus indeed has this sacrifice and birth been described together with you.
From reciting or even hearing this, the fruit of a great sacrifice shall be obtained.
O Lakṣmī! From remembering you as well, there shall be the fruit of abundant sacrificial fees;
prosperity and success shall arise here, and liberation shall occur in the hereafter.

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless God Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Destroying the Asura Dhūmra and Protecting Candra in the Fourth Year of the Creator [Brahmā], and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Sacrificial Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Completing the Ritual Threads in the Fifth Year," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-Yuga-Santāna*), Chapter 4.
