Chapter 6 → Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! In your sixth year as an ascetic,
during the second *kalpa* of this Creator (Brahmā) and in the first *manvantara*,
your manifestation occurred through Rudra, and mine likewise through Brahmā.
In every kalpa, the creation of the three worlds occurs therein.
In this regard, Brahmā is indeed the creator, Hara is the destroyer at evening,
and Viṣṇu is always considered there to be the performer of nourishment.
But having set aside that rule, the god Rudra, Maheśvara, said to Brahmā: "Do not perform the creation; I shall do it.
You take upon yourself the task of the evening—the withdrawal of the world."
O Brahmin, that action known as destruction does not please me.
For such a task brings great suffering to discerning yogis like myself;
indeed, this destruction is violent by nature and utterly merciless, and thus it is not fit for me.
The dharma of the virtuous is certainly not violence, which brings suffering to others;
since I am unable to endure the suffering of others, violence does not please me.
Even with my body or my mind, I do not desire the harming of another.
And why? Because of my past actions, I have committed this terrifying deed.
(8) For among those who are without status, violence against those with status is accompanied by greater sin;
and even among those with status, [violence against] lice and flies is even more sinful than that. (9)
Greater than those [of crows] are the [powers] of sparrows, vultures, and Garuḍas;
greater still than those are the [powers] of dogs and the like, cows, buffaloes, camels, and elephants;
and greater than those are the [powers] of nāgas, piśācas, and bhūtas.
The violence of the Daityas and Rākṣasas was indeed great, and that of the Dānavas even greater than that.
It was even greater among the Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins, as well as among servants, Śvapākas, men, Brahmins, and women. (11–12)
It is likewise for maidens, boys, and children;
for yogis, devotees, holy men, and celibate students (brahmacāris);
and it is even greater for pregnant women, those who have recently given birth, and virtuous wives.

The destruction of sacred fords (tīrtha), shrines (caitya), and images is more [sinful] than that; the destruction of temples, sages, and gods is even more so. Likewise, the killing of ascetics who seek liberation is a greater sin. (14–15)
The harming of kings worthy of sacrifice, of gurus, and even more so of the Vedas and the scriptures, is the gravest of all.
And the harming of the manifestations of Hari and Īśa is even greater than that. (16)
Thus, this expansion of evil, characterized by violence, is not pleasing to me.
I shall indeed perform the act of creation, while you perform the act of destruction.
For a long time, I have performed the work of destruction, and you have performed the work of creation.
"In the future, you alone shall perform the dissolution (*visarjana*) and not the creation (*sarjana*);
I, however, shall always perform the creation and not the dissolution.
Thus addressed then, O Lakṣmī, was Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
He said to Śaṅkara, "Do not say such a thing; for I am no one who would commit violence.
Abandoning the most excellent task, what man would enter into a lesser one?
I am a Brāhmaṇa; I can never do such a thing here."
That task belongs to you, Rudra, who are cruel and merciless;
Brahmins, being endowed with compassion, are never indeed Niṣādas.
Even in my mind, I do not consider this work of a Niṣāda to be appropriate for them.
A net, a snare, killing, cutting, and likewise tearing;
splitting, obstructing—that indeed constitutes the work of a hunter (naiṣādika).
Furthermore, burning, piercing, grinding, and the extraction of life-force (prāṇakarṣaṇa). || 23–24 ||
"O Śambhu, this act of killing is an evil deed; it does not please me.
I am not one whose wisdom is fixed upon such a thing, nor do you, O Lord, deserve to perform it.
Thus addressed, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara fell into a state of wrath.
Unable to endure these words, Hara seized the Creator by the throat.
There, Hara threw the Creator face-upward upon the ground;
placing his foot forcefully upon his chest, he drove the trident into his throat.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the inhabitants of the three worlds;
they thought, "Today the destruction of Brahmā will surely occur.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, and even the insentient and sentient beings [were filled with alarm].
They trembled from the wrath of Rudra; not a single person remained neutral.
Even Viṣṇu was seized by fear—what then can be said of others?
There, Brahmā remembered me, the Supreme Lord, as his protector. (3.5.30)
She quickly arrived there from my abode, the Imperishable;
then, O Lakṣmī, she took up the trident with her hand along with you.
You, the virtuous one who brings peace, were commanded by Hari to enter.
O beloved, through your absorption (*āveśa*), my fierce anger was then pacified.
Seeing me bowed down and filled with shame, he recognized that this was indeed an improper act;
[he beheld] the glorious Puruṣottama, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus. (32–33)
He who possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns, adorned with every ornament,
the Lord of all, holding a trident, the Master who provides protection to Brahmā—
him, the peaceful one who dwells within all, who had arrived suddenly.
[He is] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Supreme Lord.
At that time, O beloved, the foot of Śambhu was placed upon the chest of Brahmā by me; and the trident was effortlessly lifted from my two hands. 35–36.
Then Śambhu fell forcefully onto his back by my power.
As Śambhu was falling at my side, the gods provided support for him, crying out:
"Save us! Save us! O Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord!"
"Protect Aja, protect Hara, protect us who have come to you for refuge!
We are all your children; we must always be nourished and protected by you.
Having spoken thus, they then fell at my feet like a prostrate staff. (38–39)
With flowers and other mental dispositions, they worshipped me, the compassionate one— Hari, who is the Supreme Brahman, beyond the imperishable, and seated upon the chest of Brahmā.
Even Śaṅkara, my devotee, offered a prayer for forgiveness.
And I have been awakened by Śambhu; there is no fault in you regarding this act of withdrawal.
You are of the very nature of my power (śakti), and I am the agent possessing your form.
All this has been created by me, who am of the nature of Brahmā, the knower of all.
Everything is nourished by me in the form of Viṣṇu, the Giver;
everything is withdrawn by me in the form of Hara, the Destroyer.
I who am he—Hara, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā—are endowed with distinct designations.
Separateness does not exist for you; my Māyā is difficult to overcome.
Having fallen into a state of duality through that Māyā by my own will, I make everything appear as if divided, just like any other distinct entity.
I act as if ignorant; that is my eternal play (*līlā*).
In that regard, O Śambhu, there is indeed no fault in you consisting of the defect of violence.
For whatever arises must surely perish; such is the very nature of an entity.
In this matter, you, Rudra, shall be the witness for my destruction according to justice.
The signs [of dissolution] are the pralayas and so forth; time consists of the yugas and likewise the nights.
Indeed, the limit of time was established by me as a boundary.
"Therefore, O Śambhu, there is no possibility of refutation for you in the matter of universal dissolution in any way whatsoever.
Thus addressed by me, O Lakṣmī, Śaṅkara attained composure;
having abandoned that quarrel, he became forever intent upon the mind of dissolution.
He indeed serves my yoga and takes it away at the end, as has been described.
Then, having disciplined Śambhu, I became the son of Brahmā;
I am the beginningless, illustrious Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
"And you, Lakṣmī, emerged from the body of Hara as a maiden;
you are indeed the daughter of Rudra and belong to Viṣṇu, having been bestowed upon me by Hara.
Thus did my manifestation occur there, and yours as well."

Then, O Brahman, until the end of the kalpa, I remained as Nārāyaṇa together with you, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, who belong to Viṣṇu; remember that. In this way, millions of other incarnations of mine occurred there.
O beloved, others besides me are not able to enumerate them;
now hear of my manifestation in another year as well.
In the first Kalpa, during the first Manvantara, in the year known as Yama.
A dispute arose among the deities dwelling in heaven regarding their sacrificial seats (dhiṣṇya).
One said, "I alone shall enjoy the position of Mahendra," while another then said, "I am Sūrya; there shall be no other."
The third said, "I am Candra"; the fourth said, "I am Dhanī.
One said, "I am Jaleśa," and another said, "I am Marut.
"I am Vasu," "I am Devaguru," and "I am the deity Īśāna."
I am Agni, I am Gaṇeśa, I am Senānī, and I am Dhruva as well.
Meru is mine, heaven is mine, and I also become Vāyu.
I am Yama, I am Viṣṇu, and I am Śaṅkara too. (3.5.60)
"I am the guardian of the quarters, I am the guardian of the worlds, I am indeed the Sādhya;
I shall enjoy the station of the Viśvedevas, and I shall enjoy the station of the Pitṛs.
As the gods were speaking thus, a mutual quarrel arose among them.
It continued to revolve like a great, unappeasable wheel, governed by no one at all.
O Lakṣmī! At that time, the most powerful of the gods, having completely brought their respective desired domains under their own control, contended with one another by force.
Then they became powerless and without support;
the heaven, though won by strength, became like a kingdom of the blind.
At that time, the sattvic deities, Indra, Vasu, Candra, and the others—
Indeed, in order to prevent blindness, they deliberated in the house of their preceptor;
they conducted an inquiry as to how that blindness might be removed,
considering the words of Brahmā, or Śambhu, or Viṣṇu.
Driven by pride, the gods do not recognize the bounds of propriety;
therefore, a rule must be established here that brings benefit to all.
Just as the Preceptor of the Gods might show the path, we ourselves shall indeed follow it.
Having heard this, the preceptor of the gods himself then spoke to the deities:
"The sky is indeed the eternal mother of the gods; she protects the gods within her womb.
She now stands here in embodied form; let us do as she says."
"Likewise, the Sun-god named Viṣṇu shines here even in this assembly.
'As he shall speak, so shall we all carry out his beneficial word.
Having spoken thus, the two of them paid homage to all the gods who were present.
They both said: "In this matter of final determination, we two are not qualified for blindness;
nevertheless, we shall indicate to you Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the supreme, eternal Brahman.
And we shall worship the Lord right here, who bestows the station of authority."
He alone, the Lord of the Imperishable,
who has sustained everything and by whom this was indeed impelled,
and by whom it moves as it is set in motion— he will surely grant us the final decision. (73)
"He by whom supernatural power was bestowed according to their karma,
according to their merit, according to their station, according to their sovereignty, and according to their celestial abodes—
having approached him who has been propitiated, he will grant us a definitive decision. (74–75)
Thus addressed by those who spoke with force, all the gods, for the sake of instruction, called to mind the eternal Supreme Brahman— the Lord of the Immutable,
the Blessed One among the blessed, the Supreme Sovereign.

And quickly, O Nārāyaṇī-Śrī, I, the Great Lord, arrived together with you from the abode of the Imperishable. At that time, the Supreme Ruler, known as Viṣṇu, was indeed in the assembly of the Preceptor of the Gods in the presence of the Sun. || 77–78 ||
Divine, adorned with celestial garments and ornaments, and endowed with divine sovereignty,
he stood in the midst of the assembly, possessing the splendor of ten million moons and suns.
At that time, O Lakṣmī, you were commanded and remained established within his radiant body.
"You are invisible, the instructor, and the benefactor of all.
(3.5.80) Then all the gods, having beheld me—the Lord of the lords of the lords—bowed down and offered a seat as well as the *madhuparka* offering. (3.5.81)

O Śrī of Nārāyaṇa! Having asked them about their welfare, I too did not inform them [of my own state], even while praying for peace regarding that blindness in heaven for the sake of my station. At that time, indeed, my Sudarśanas— 82. 83ab. *mayā nārāyaṇīśri vai tadā sudarśanāni me* (The first half-verse is part of the preceding line).

O beloved! Capable instruments of that aforementioned form, cruel and indeed armed, were dispatched from all sides into the sky; wherever the gods were stationed in their celestial abodes at that time, [they followed]. 83–84.
Having summoned all of them, those who were devoted to me and possessed of beautiful vision,
they repeatedly held onto the door of the Guru and brought them into my presence.
Then, I questioned those who were indeed the instigators of the blindness.
You were not at all ashamed; you begged me for forgiveness.
Indeed, I have punished them all and restrained them in their own positions;
the gods dwelling in heaven have been established in their respective appropriate stations.
Indeed, I established the respective jurisdictions for all;
at that time, you were appointed by me as the supervisor of everything.
You then became the one who blocks those unfit vessels from entering the supreme abode.
"And my sovereignty, O Lakṣmī, was then entrusted by me to you.
You must always remain there, in every abode, O beloved;
for if one unworthy should forcibly approach that supreme station, [you must protect it]. (3.5.90)
O Lakṣmī! at that time, you must cast another far away from anyone else.
Indeed, from that point forward, among the gods, whenever another person sits in a place belonging to someone else, he becomes subject to being swiftly cast out by the rightful occupant.
In this very manner, O beloved, you were then established within every single word.
At that time, I became the dear son of Viṣṇu Āditya;
you, moreover, were born as a maiden from the womb of the sky, Śrī Nārāyaṇī.
At that time, heaven and earth were entrusted to me; at that time, you were Dyunārāyaṇa.
At that time, in that kalpa, I was Anādyādityanārāyaṇa, the beginningless Śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the infallible Acyuta.
"O son, from that time until the end of the kalpa, I have always resided in the house of the Sun. You were the daughter of Heaven, my wife Devavīthī; at that time you became Devavīthī.
I remember all of that; you too, remember Devavīthī."
I myself am indeed the Supreme Brahman, and I was always present there;
moreover, my innumerable incarnations also appeared there during that year.
Thus, having abandoned their dispute over the celestial abodes as previously described, the gods [departed].
Having returned each to their own respective abodes, they were all freed from the grounds of dispute.
From that time forward, there was never again any quarrel over objects of value anywhere in that realm,
neither during that year nor even throughout other kalpas.
"Everything has been regulated by me and established according to my will;
thus it proceeds with ease, and never indeed in any contrary manner.
O Daughter of Śiva! In this way, my manifestation has been described to you."
"By reading or even by hearing this, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Brahman-Nārāyaṇa for the purpose of instructing Rudra in the sixth year of the Creator [Brahmā], and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Āditya-Nārāyaṇa in the seventh year for the purpose of regulating the abodes of the gods," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya-saṃhitā*.

Chapter 6 [[Author:
→ Chapter 7
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! Furthermore, in the eighth year thereafter, during the fifth kalpa, in the year known as Ajaya.
Furthermore, while the seventh Manu was reigning at that time, I myself appeared there as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
for the sake of the happiness of the Manus and their subjects. (2)
Once in the netherworld (pātāla), O beloved, the nāgas, assuming forms at will,
set out to gratify Saṃkarṣaṇa as Mahārudra.
At that sacrifice to Mahārudra, indeed, the families of the hooded serpents [were present].
Then there were fifty-two thousand gathered together:
black, red, variegated, white, spotted, and brindled;
blue, yellow, green, as well as those with swastikas and moon-marks.
There were also spears with two hoods, three hoods, and four hoods;
likewise, there were serpents with a hundred faces and others with a thousand hoods.
There were serpent-kings, Karkaṭakas, Śītalas, and likewise Ḍiṇḍimas.
The Bhūpiṇḍas and others, the Koḍiphas, the pale Pāṇḍakas,
as well as the Śūlakas and Daṇḍakas, the two-faced ones with divine vision,
the Oṃkāras, the Tilavarṇas, the Pāraḍaṅkas, and the Kaṇāśanas.
The Tiryagdhāras, Sūtradhāras, Mudrapṛṣṭhas, and Dvipṛṣṭhakas;
the Dvijihvas, Bahujihvas, Bahudaṃṣṭras, and Viṣālayas;
the Kālakūṭas, Samaṇayas, Kārdamikas, and Vārśayas. (3.6.9–10)
The Ānalikas, Anilakas, Mārucchryas, Sapakṣakas, Ugrakas, Śāntadāsas, Māhālasyas, and Viḍambins— thus,
many such diverse tribes of Kaṇādhras were then assembled together.

They, being eager, worshipped and gratified Saṃkarṣaṇa, Yajñadeva, and their own beloved Analānana with sweet oblations. For a thousand days, they performed their own sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.
Svastika was their preceptor, and Śeṣa was then the king;
he was the foremost patron, while the others were meritorious officiating priests.
There were sweet foods from the netherworld and savory juices from the ocean.
Fruits growing in the forest, edible roots from the earth, grains produced by crops, as well as tubers from medicinal plants and trees;
various kinds of sacrificial fuel and diverse types of *gundra* grass. (15–16)
In that sacrifice, they offered all kinds of food preparations, oblations fit for the gods, and suitable items for the observance of vows;
and there, the great god Saṃkarṣaṇa, adorned with his own discus, [was present].
Accompanied by the lords of the netherworld, millions of Garuḍas, and celestial women,
he attained supreme satisfaction at the sacrifice.
On the final day, he appeared there in person, assuming the form of Rudra.
During the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation), while it was being performed with milk-rice and other offerings, ghee, sesame seeds, flour-cakes, sweet juices,
and pungent herbs, he said to the serpents, "I am pleased," and again and again, "I am satiated."
"Choose a boon; may you be happy," he said to them again. Then the king, the subjects, and those serpents made this request:
"In the world of men, may we indeed be sharers in the kingdom. (21–22)
"Having performed our duties, we shall go to liberation, heaven, or the supreme dissolution.
O excellent Karṣaṇa, if you are pleased, grant us this boon.
O Viṣṇu, O bestower of one's own desires, we are worthy of a boon, together with Karṣaṇa."
After reflecting for a moment, Saṃkarṣaṇa said to them:
"Let those who dwell in the forest, constantly residing in the great wilderness, become enjoyers of the kingdom on earth, partaking in the pleasures of the gods. (24–25)
"O twice-born ones, I grant you this boon after making this rule: 'May you never at any time cause distress to human beings who dwell upon the earth.
While you conduct yourselves in this manner, there shall be supreme happiness."
"O twice-born ones, may there be happiness and may you always attain prosperity.
Having spoken thus, the god Saṃkarṣaṇa, together with the gods, received the sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) which was the very form of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), and then vanished from sight.
Then, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, even those powerful serpents were not truly eager for the granting of boons,
being instead greedy for human enjoyments and slain by delusion. (29)
Assuming any form at will, all those men, women, and human beings arrived from every direction into the world of mortals through the openings of the wind;
indeed, they possessed no serpent-like forms when they came to the earth.
They exist and dwell among human beings in disguise;
acting as deceitful servants, they seek to seize kingdoms and enjoyments.
Indeed, throughout the entire earth, they possess great beauty of form.
Even the male and female nāgas became intent on performing service for them.
They dwelt among kings, merchants, groups of brahmins, ministers, servants, the virtuous, the eminent, and even among householders. (33–34)
Having become servants, male slaves, and female slaves, they imitated the [four] castes;
indeed, daughters were married among one another by those of human birth.
Human maidens and Nāgas in human form brought them together.

Having thus established their connection and having found their opportunity, they bit men here and there at night while they were under the power of sleep. And the kings and queens died, completely bitten. (36–37)
The merchants, the wealthy, and the most excellent among all the social classes—
having made that empty place their own property—
those lords of the earth, serpents capable of assuming any form at will, then enjoyed it. (38)
Indeed, the words of Saṃkarṣaṇa were not carried out by those of tamasic nature—those intent on their own self-interest, hypocrites, and those secretly devoted to sensual enjoyment.
Thus, the human creation was for the most part destroyed by them. (3.6.40)
Even though she was protected by the Naga race, her own creation was increased by those of the serpent lineage who were devoted to their own self-interest and concealed the faults of biting.
Furthermore, all the activities of human beings were considered as worship of the gods.
The sacrificial rites were repeatedly neglected, as were the twilight prayers and the fire oblations;
the ancestral offerings and the giving of gifts were likewise abandoned, and human self-restraint fell away.
Furthermore, the sages' ritual intentions regarding their lineages were completely lost on all sides.
The ritual acts of men have been lost, as have the movements of the serpents;
the vows have also been lost, and the rites of invocation and so forth have vanished.
The water-offering for the Sun has been lost, and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has gone to destruction.
Likewise, ancestral rites were neglected, and temples were devoid of worship.
Portions of the sacred narratives vanished, and indeed, the Brahmins and kings passed away.
The dwellings of celibate students and the residences of teachers came to an end.
The truthful and virtuous women died, even though they were protected by millions of Nāgas;
the virtuous men also died, as did their dwellings, villages, and cities.
Due to the wrath of the Nāgas on all sides, those people became non-human beings.
The names of the *pravara* ancestors vanished into their quivers;
people did not know this, nor how it had come to pass.
Then the gods were deprived of sacrifice, and the ancestors were denied their satisfaction.
When a hundred years had passed, we remained composed without deliberating:
"From where has this inauspicious atheism arisen on the earth, and how did it come to be?
A full century of human years has already elapsed upon this world. (3.6.50)
How indeed could there be no addressing, summoning, and so forth?
Having seen with divine vision that men had died, the snakes took over the kingdoms, even though the subjects were of the nature of snakes. (51–52)
Snakes assuming forms at will, as well as female nāgas and women who take on whatever forms they desire, enjoy the riches of the earth.
This birth is indeed undesirable and is devoid of righteous action.
The serpents, belonging to the mode of darkness (tāmasa), move horizontally; they act with concealed guile and devour the enjoyments of men, destroying the exalted status of gods and sages.
Indeed, the destruction of human beings has occurred in manifold ways since ancient times.
In dwellings and the like, humans do not exist between [the houses] as do serpents;
in forests and the like, humans are found only rarely in some places.
Therefore, they must be alerted by us regarding death at the hands of the nāgas.
"Even regarding the means of slaying the *nāgas* and those who must be awakened,"—
having thus consecrated the lotus, they returned to the surface of the earth to the central region of Ilāvṛta, which was filled with vast forests. (57–58)
There, in that forest free from serpents, sat pure twice-born ones who were experts in the Gāruḍa and Atharva Vedas and devoted to the performance of fire-sacrifices (homa).
Upon beholding the sages and gods, those twice-born ones offered them a welcome.
Having offered the *madhuparka*, the gods, desiring to know the reason for his arrival, then questioned him; he replied:
"Let all the twice-born and men, along with millions of *nāgas*, come to know [the truth]. (3.6.60–61)
All have died; they perish day after day through the application of poisons.
These serpents exist on earth in human form due to the boon of Saṃkarṣaṇa;
having arrived here, they indeed continue to kill human beings.
Concealing their true nature, they enjoy human pleasures and revel in them.
Their birth-related rites, as well as their duties toward the gods, ancestors, and the sun—including the performance, invocation, worship, and offering of dharma—have all ceased. (63–64)
"O sirs, that you live as forest-dwellers is due to the grace of Hari;
it is by good fortune that you live where there are neither serpents nor arrows. [I shall now describe] the mantras found in the Atharvaveda, which are the means for slaying serpents."
Having performed their recitations, let them bring about the destruction of the Nāga-creations upon the earth.
Let the twice-born kings here perform the Nāga-sacrifice;
likewise, let them propitiate the Lord of the World, the Supreme Lord, during the ritual.
"May the Supreme Brahman, who transcends the imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, the Puruṣottama,
grant us protection and drive away the serpents from here.
Having spoken thus, the divine ancestors departed for their own abode.
The Brahmins dwelling on the island of Ceylon performed a sacrifice.
There, one known as Gāruḍa, who was indeed proficient in the rites of the Atharva Veda,
served as the Hotṛ priest at that sacrifice, while the other Brahmins performed the oblations.
Then the serpents, unable to descend into the sacrifice because they had not been drawn forth,
spoke with focused attention to the brahmins:
"Worship the Lord of the gods, the Lord of lords, the supreme Lord of lords."
"O brāhmaṇas, that Supreme Lord will indeed act for your benefit.
Having been told this, O Lakṣmī, those thousand brāhmaṇas quickly performed a Brahma-sacrifice in the cave of the twice-born named Gāruḍa.
There, the Lord Hari, the sovereign of the syllables, arrived swiftly;
he who is "I am He" appeared together with you, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person,
in the midst of Garuḍa’s abode, while the twice-born and yogis looked on.

Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and attended by mantras, I stood there before him accompanied by the Vedas in embodied form. Seeing me, the twice-born rose and bowed to me, offering words of welcome. (76)
They offered him a seat, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), water for his feet, and respectful worship;
all of them reported the calamity that was destroying humanity.
He said to them, "May it be well with you; your fear has now departed."
"Let them indeed perform a snake-sacrifice; let them employ these mantras!
Thus addressed and impelled by my words, the Garuḍa-brahmins quickly performed the snake-sacrifice and recited the mantras that strike at the hoods [of the serpents].
Oṃ! Those who dwell among mortals and those who dwell among immortals, those who have moved away and those who have not moved away,

those who enjoy the essence of the earth, those who have closed their eyes and those who are free from impurity, those who enjoy the waters and those who do not experience [sensual] enjoyment— [to them I offer salutations].
"Let them scatter the oblations here; let them be consumed! Om!
Those who are malicious, those who bite their lips, those who strike at men, those who walk crookedly, and those who destroy righteousness—let them scatter here!"
Oṃ! May those who possess a hundred streams, those who possess the streams of the ocean, and even those who flow downwards, descend here into these fierce flames;
Oṃ! May those who enjoy immortality, those who enjoy extreme immortality, and those who enjoy the serpents—descend here.
May those who delight in piercing [the darkness],
who delight in protection, who delight in prosperity, who delight in non-violence, who delight in the absence of deceit, and who delight in sovereignty, come here to protect us. (82)
Then the Garuḍa-brāhmaṇas there recited these mantras;
having invoked the nāgas with mantras beginning with cruel seed-syllables, they offered oblations.
Coming again and again from the sky, they arrived from every part of the earth as far as the edge of the ocean.
Then the nāgas indeed fell into the pit, which was fierce with the fire of poison.
Killed and burnt by the thousands, those who remained were bound with ropes;
bound by mantras, they were truly unable even to liberate themselves. (84–85)
Then the bound Ananta-Śeṣa praised me, the Supreme Lord:
"Protect us, O Lord, ocean of mercy! Release us from this great fire.
We shall not remain on the earth, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Lord. (86)
"Protect her who has fallen into this refuge; grant us the gift of life!
"O Janārdana, I am your eternal servant, Ananta Śeṣa. Having been addressed thus, I then spoke to the serpent-bearers dwelling upon the earth: (87–88)
"Having taken all the *nāgas* of every kind, go indeed to the lower realm;
do not establish your abode here again in this world of men.
Thus addressed, having been liberated by me, he accepted everything.
All the serpents were indeed liberated from the jaws of death by means of the Gāruḍa [mantra].
Ananta, my devotee, worshipped me, the Supreme Lord;
at that time, O daughter of Janaka, you became the daughter of Śeṣa.
And you, Ānantī, were indeed offered by Śeṣa as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to me;
then [the boon was granted] to the son of a Brahmin, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
the protector of snakes and serpents, the glorious Lord, the Supreme Self.
Then, when the sacrifice was restrained and turned back by me,
Śeṣa indeed took all the serpents dwelling upon the surface of the earth and went to the subterranean caverns known as Pātāla. ||93-94||
Therefore, this world of humans was made contemptible by me. Then, I settled the humans dwelling in the region of Ilāvṛtaka throughout all lands,
and likewise established them with many lineages.
Furthermore, the human age was gathered from that [human] man.
Through my yoga, all those gods who were devoted to the rites for the gods and ancestors became highly learned and auspicious, O Brahmins.
At that time, I became the beginningless Śrī Garuḍa-Nārāyaṇa;
you, Ānantī, the daughter of Śeṣa, became my wife at that time.
[I am] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
I myself manifested an incarnation there.
Then, in that year, many incarnations of Brahmā came into being.
I know all of this; O Anantī, remember my former existence! (3.6.100)
At that time, I indeed provided protection for the humans on the earth;
thereafter, you remained steadfast with me until the end of the kalpa.
By reading, hearing, reciting, or even remembering this, [one attains the same].
Fear of serpents does not arise at all, and likewise, there shall be both enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Boundless Garuḍa-Nārāyaṇa upon the Earth for the Purpose of Subduing the Serpents in the Eighth Year of Brahmā," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 7 [Author:
Chapter 8 → Now, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, listen to my story.
It is the purifying and delightful [account] of the Daityas dwelling in Sutala,
occurring in the past, during the ninth year known as the *āsana* of Brahmā,
in the first of the fourteen kalpas, in the Manvantara of Sūtalaka.
There was once a king named Calavarman, a sovereign of the entire earth and possessed of great strength;
he was the lord of Atala, Vitala, and Sutala.
Indeed, his celestial vehicle then traveled through the three worlds.
The subjects and people of Atala, Vitala,
and Sutala worshipped King Caladeva as their manifest protector.
The king, too, was righteous and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
O Daughter of Śiva! My devotee is devoted to the worship of the gods;
he is a refuge for the helpless, guests, and women, and is beautiful in his character.
Indeed, half the day always passes for him in the worship of the deity.
Half of that [time] he then spends observing the kingdom, and from that,
the remaining half he always spends in his own worlds while on his wanderings.
As he was acting in this manner, a desire for asceticism arose within him.
"Since asceticism bears fruit ten thousand times faster on the land of action (karmabhūmi),
he reflected that he must go to the earth to perform penance; then, traveling by celestial chariot,
he inquired of a true guru among the sages and subsequently [renounced] his entire kingdom."
Having paid homage to his guru, the king departed while being watched by Mānava.
Reaching Mount Kumuda, in a forest perpetually pervaded by coolness,
he performed austerities without food for a thousand years.
There, while he was performing austerities, that king beheld with divine vision Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the God Śrī Puruṣottama;
having bowed to me alone as the Supreme Self, he spoke what was in his heart.
"Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord, the bestower of the fruits of austerity;
salutations to Hari, the Supreme Self, who fulfills the minds of his devotees.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated himself like a staff and drank the nectar of my feet.
Then, urged by me, King Cala begged him:
"Grant me steadiness here; for that which is unstable surely comes to destruction.
The kingdom is unstable, wealth is unstable, and likewise, the family is unstable."
"O Kṛṣṇa, life is transient, and even the realm of Sutala and others are transient; therefore, I choose immortality from you. I am your devotee; grant me my desire.
Śrī Parameśvara said:
Listen, O King! The entire universe is moving, and it is indeed said to be moving.
Time is moving, Māyā is moving, and the mind as well as the individual soul are moving.
If everything is moving, then tell me: what do you consider to be unmoving?
Śrī Caladeva said:
"The mind is fickle, fortune is fickle, and even royal command is fickle;
but your devotion, O Lord, is indeed steadfast—choose that, grant it to me!"
"O Keśava, may my vessel be as immovable as Acalā, and may I myself be immovable.
Śrī Parameśvara said: "Acalā is my loving devotion; that service is preceded by love."
If you truly desire to become that very vessel which is immovable,
then I shall grant you eternal and certain liberation in my world.
Accept my mantra quickly and go to my imperishable abode.
Śrī Caladeva said:
"By your grace, I, who was moving, have now become unmoving;
likewise, let the lineage of this unmoving one become unmoving—so please ordain for me. (22)
The illustrious Supreme Lord said:
"O King, just as you have become immovable by a portion of my grace, so too shall your lineage attain immovability through my yoga."
"You remain childless, O King; become one who possesses children!
Without me, all that is transient shall be your offspring, and I myself shall become [your] offspring.
Behold here: I, though immovable, shall become your offspring."
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, I then became his mind-born son,
named Ārṣadeva; the king attained great satisfaction,
and having completed his penance, he departed with me.
There, the noble sage, my guru, recognized me as the Lord;
and by my command, O Lakṣmī, you became the daughter of that sage.
The king, according to the prescribed rites, [accepted] you, his own mind-born son, as Ārṣadeva.

He consecrated him in the kingdom; that descendant of the Ṛṣis also gave his daughter to me. You, named Ārṣapadmā, served both me, the Lord of Śrī, and Ārṣadeva, the incarnate Lord Śrī Puruṣottama. (28–29)
For the sake of preserving my word, I too have manifested Viṣṇu himself as a mental son named Dṛḍhadhruva,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus as his weapons. (3.7.30)
As soon as he was born, Viṣṇu, resplendent with the sovereignty of youth and other attributes,
was established in the immovable and supreme station at the end of heaven.
He is indeed the foundation for the worlds, as well as for the planets and the luminaries.
The circles of the constellations, the stars, and the sages revolved because of the stability of the Pole Star, which was made firm by the name Dhruva.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Caladeva was sent by me to the Imperishable One.
The immovable and imperishable abode has been protected by me according to my word.
(34) I am likewise the immovable Anādi-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the son; I am myself the Supreme Brahman known as Anādi-Ārṣa-Nārāyaṇa. (35)
"My son, Viṣṇu himself, named Dṛḍhadhruva,
was likewise rendered immovable by me until the end of the kalpa through the power of my word.
Thus indeed, O Lakṣmī, did my manifestation occur upon the earth in ancient times."
And the kingdom shall be for your son in the world of Sutala, above even heaven.
Then, O daughter of the sages, remember your own [wife] Ārṣapadmā. O Ārṣanārāyaṇī! The manifestation of my Lord has been described. ||37-38||

He performed extensive penance for the duration of a Manvantara dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Then the blessed Lord Brahmā was pleased and granted him a boon:
"O Indra among kings, do not perform further penance; choose whatever boon you desire."
Thus addressed by Brahmā, he said: "My life span is only two years;

"So be it," the Creator replied, and he bestowed this boon upon Dhruva.

When the ninth year arrived, that two-year lifespan was divided in two.

when the tenth year of the restraint of breath had arrived,
it was then the fourteenth kalpa of the Creator’s day.
O beloved, during that first Manvantara,
a period of two Brahma-years passed there by means of days and nights;
he too, remembering his past lives, began his ascetic penance once again.
Indeed, for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, he was restrained by the gods;
by the sages from Satyaloka, and by the ancestors from Janaloka and the other realms.
He was forbidden from heaven by the deities and from the surface of the earth by human beings.
Honored by the Dānavas at that time, he went to Atala for the sake of performing penance;

he indeed performed fierce penance, propitiating Rudra during the sacrifice.
He offered his head, together with the eyes, into the fire in the sacrificial pit;
at that moment, Rudra appeared there in person, blazing with divine splendor.
"Tell me, what pleases you here? Choose, and I shall give you everything."
Then Thurānanda said, "O Lord, grant me invincibility.
Hara replied, "Except for Kṛṣṇa, the eternal Supreme Brahman, your invincibility has been granted; let your head be joined [to your body]."
Thus addressed, Dhruvānanda, the son of Dhruva, was exceedingly delighted;
he then brought to an end both his ascetic penance and his own sacrifice.
Then the king also, accompanied by the Dānavas, set out to take [him] back.
Accompanied by Daityas and Asuras, he established the earth and the heavens as truth.
Wherever there was a supreme station consecrated for sovereignty—whether belonging to kings, gods, or inhabitants of other worlds—he occupied it. (55–56)
Having conquered all those powerful beings, he who was fierce in battle brought the dānavas under his own control; having made his dependents submissive,
he consecrated various daityas and asuras as kings in their respective positions.
On the surface of the earth, in all its regions, there were kings, Daityas, and Dānavas;

They were devoid of righteous action and were possessed of fallen conduct. (58–59)
Lacking virtue, acting according to their own whims, and filled with violence and wickedness, they became consumers of the people's wealth while being devoid of sacrifice.
They were empty of merit from sacred fords, gifts, and worship; they followed wrong paths and were bereft of the Veda.
Out of fear of him, even the gods, the ancestors, and the great seers all became distressed;
likewise, all human beings were tormented by the Rākṣasas.
Even Surānanda, accompanied by the Asuras, was present throughout all the worlds.
He indeed travels by means of a celestial chariot and proclaims in every way:
"Let people worship, honor, and propitiate me, the lord of men;
and regarding me as the Supreme Lord in person, let them offer their gifts."
Let them worship me indeed at sacrifices and also in the temples of the deities;
let people always worship me in the place of Gaṇeśa,
let them pay tribute to me, and let them proclaim my virtues.
"Let them behold my image and offer me ritual services;
let them take my name in the morning, for I am Viṣṇu and no other.
Let them cry out: 'Thurānanda! Thurānanda! Thurānanda! (66)
In *thura* there will arise great bliss and the bliss of Brahman.
(67) I am *thura*, known as Brahman; in *thura* illusion does not exist.
Having attained and cultivated *thura*, suffering shall forever be destroyed. (68)
Having obtained me, the Lord of Mathurā, may you always be happy.
I am the king of the yogis, as well as of the ancestors, the celestial dwellers, human beings, sages, daityas, and likewise of the rākṣasas. (69)
"I am the king of the Vasus, of the treasures, and of the guardians of the quarters;
I am the king of the oceans, of the forests, and of the Gandharvas. Thus [he spoke] in the tenth region, known as Prāṇarodha, of Ajāta.
In that fourteenth kalpa, during the first Manvantara, O King,
there was a powerful king who was worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas.
Then the subjects, gods, ancestors, sages, and women became devoted to him.
O Goddess, the truthful and virtuous ones have propitiated me;
remaining hidden in their own homes and concentrated within their own hearts, human beings and others have offered praise to me, Śrī Hari, for the sake of protection. (73–74)
O Lord Hari, ocean of mercy, friend of the distressed, Janārdana! O crusher of unrighteousness, end-maker of the Daityas, Supreme Lord!
Protect, protect me, O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, beginningless Nārāyaṇa, Master!
“You are the Supreme Brahman, the inner self; protect us who are oppressed by the Dānavas.
Thus did all embodied beings offer their prayers in many ways.
Then, having reflected upon that deed of Thurānanda, I— ||97||
Even until the end of the granting of the boon, there shall be a reunion with you on the surface of the earth, in the world of humans, in the western region of Meru,
in the district named Bhāmantaka, at the abode of the wise twice-born.
Then, upon being seen in the presence of Viśokā, who was without a husband,
I appeared in the form of a youth, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
the Lord bearing the wheel, thunderbolt, spear, trident, staff, and noose.

I am that eight-armed Hari, the Supreme Brahman Nārāyaṇa; resplendent with the upward radiance of ten million Cupids, skilled in battle, a knower of all weapons and mantras, and devoted to the state of Brahman. || 8.1 ||
Then, O Lakṣmī, commanded by me, you went quickly (8.2).

you were then at the king's palace, fit for a svayaṃvara;
and the king convened an assembly on earth known as a svayaṃvara.

When the day had been determined, the Daityas and Dānavas arrived there,
as did the kings, the lords of the earth, the rulers of Pātāla, and the lords of heaven;
the guardians of the fourteen worlds and the protectors of the quarters.
Desiring to behold the maiden Jyotsnā, they arrived there at that pavilion.
A gathering of hundreds of kings took place there in the royal palace.
Then, at an auspicious moment, Jyotsnā, adorned with finery, cast the garland upon her bridegroom.
Having been led away by her kinsmen, who were skilled in the finest weapons,
the maiden Jyotsnikā— truly so named— was one who drew all beings toward her;
she was accompanied by a highly capable attendant woman who knew the purity of her lineage.
Accompanied by her preceptor, the Brahmin, she entered the pavilion.
You, whose form is supermundane, cause the dullness of the assembly;
everyone there was enchanted upon beholding you, who dwell within the syllables.
"Never before seen nor heard of anywhere—may she be mine!
Thus did the hearts of the kings there become for a moment;
indeed, the minds of those whose union with perfect beauty was incomplete were utterly shattered.
Even the minds of those who were full [of pride] became objects of doubt;
O Lakṣmī! at that time, the assembly of hundreds of millions of kings appeared, in the very presence of your splendor, as if devoid of luster within a mere moment. (94–95)
Even the kings of heaven then became despondent in their hopes, thinking:
"She will certainly not choose us, for we are unworthy and devoid of beauty.
Thus, they were deprived of their desire; what then can be said of others?
Then, having gone to the gatehouse and bowed to the deity of the gatehouse,
you entered the pavilion by way of the divine path that shone with gold;
and there you saw the king and heard [his account] from the old woman.
Having failed to find him there, her heart unattached,
she wandered around the pavilion three times, looking everywhere;
not seeing me, she returned to the gateway still holding the bridegroom’s garland.
There I was a Brahmin who had not yet gained entrance; I was poor, wearing a yellow washed garment and a yellow tunic, with my head wrapped in a cloth, a sixteen-year-old youth. (3.7.100–101)
Endowed with beauty of form and equipped with all subtle weapons,
he arrived having concealed his subtle form for the sake of destroying the Daityas;
he bore a mark like the moon upon his forehead and held a rosary for recitation in his hand.
Wearing wooden sandals upon my feet, I became one who was extraordinary to the world.

(103) Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Wise Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Overcoming Thurānanda—the Son of Dhruvadeva and Grandson of Dāna—who was raised by [the gods] in order to ensure the immovability of Dhruva during the ninth year of the Creator [Brahmā] in the lineage of Caladeva within the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*; as well as the Self-choice Marriage (*svayaṃvara*) of Jyotsnākumārikā Lakṣmī. (7)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: O Lakṣmī, then, beholding your own ancient beloved, you placed the garland of choice upon my neck while the kings looked on. (1)
The entire assembly was struck with wonder and filled with great amazement;
the cry arose, "Oh, a brahmin has obtained the princess!
"The maiden has gone to a poor man, an unfortunate beggar."
The maiden, unequalled and peerless, has gone unto death.
Alas! Birth in the royal palace brought her fortune that yields the sorrow of poverty;
she who was like a wish-fulfilling creeper with the luster of gold has fallen into the hands of a hunter.
A beautiful golden lotus-pond has fallen into dry mud;
a garland consisting of land-lotuses has come upon the neck of a monkey;
lightning, accompanied by the waters of the sky, has fallen upon a parched mountain.
The divine Lakṣmī, worthy of a king, has now fallen upon a pauper.
(6) Kaumudī, having abandoned the moon, has resorted to a tiny star;
Prabhā, having forsaken the sun, has taken refuge in the empty sky. (7)
Having abandoned the virtuous man, learning has taken refuge with the mere caviler;
like the sky, having deserted Mahendra, it has sought shelter with Nairṛta.
Luster, like a delusion, has abandoned the beloved and resorted to the deluded.
Having abandoned truth, Satī went to the illusory Māyin by means of illusion.
Having left Śambhu, her matted locks leaped onto a clump of *vaṭa* trees.
Having deserted the foot of Viṣṇu, Gaṅgā has come to the salt ocean. (3.8.10)
Having abandoned the dharma of devotion, she has become immoral; having cast aside her husband, she has followed after another man. Like a lioness who, having forsaken a lion, has approached a boar.
The female elephant, having abandoned the male elephant, has taken refuge with a ball and a beast;
the female serpent, having abandoned the serpent Śeṣa, has gone to a crawling reptile;
and Kālī, having abandoned her crown, has gone to a tattered rag.
"Oh, the power of fortune! The Queen has resorted to the speech of a dog.
Never before has such a thing been seen anywhere, nor is it ever seen by people anywhere:
a divine garland of wish-fulfilling gems placed around the neck of a dog. (14)
People consider this to have been brought about by fate;
for, having observed the assembly, the maiden was overwhelmed by the splendor of that gathering and, rendered lusterless, performed this act. (15–16)
For that which has arisen is indeed undesirable, as it will surely not be accepted by the maiden;
or rather, the maiden does not know that this is the bridegroom’s garland.
Having observed it to be common property, she has offered it to a poor man.
"Either she will become the second bride for the monkeys, or perhaps this maiden is intended for the purpose of honoring Brahmins;
therefore, while there are virtuous kings, a daughter should not be given to a poor man. (18–19)
Or rather, if the king gives her to him, we shall take her away;
for even when a *svayaṃvara* has taken place, a maiden remains subject to war. Having fought [for her], we shall obtain this virtuous jewel; there is no doubt in this matter. (3.8.20)
Thus did the king and others speak there in many ways.
(21) And the girl’s father too fell into grief for a moment;
seeing that his daughter had gone to a poor man, he was seized with fever. (22)
Then, considering it some small measure of fortune for the sake of his son,
the king indeed desired to give [the girl] to the bridegroom according to the prescribed rites;
at that moment, however, the queen and the elderly preceptor restrained the king.
O King, do not be hasty in this matter within the pavilion.
For this situation has become improper, since the maiden is indeed bewildered;
or rather, she is distraught in mind and devoid of mental stability. || 24–25 ||
"Therefore, the garland must be given once again for the sake of the *svayaṃvara* itself.
Having heeded these words, the king said to them, "So be it.
Then the assembly of kings also considered that to be appropriate.
The maiden was questioned repeatedly regarding this matter by Janaka and the others;
yet, knowing the gestures of the Lord of Ramā, she said nothing at that time.
Then the king, having gone to the brahmin and having led the maiden far away, [spoke].
Having led her back, he returned to the pavilion and again gave her a supreme garland;
the maiden, having wandered everywhere in the pavilion, placed the garland upon his hand.
In this very manner she remained there, not offering it to anyone else at all.
She does not speak, nor does she look at anyone else, nor does she desire anything;
she seems to be contemplating the pretext for the destruction of the asuras.
Then, O Lakṣmī, he said to you as you arrived at the city gate: (3.8.30–31)
Thinking her to be Māmakī, I seized Samālā by force with my hand;
and as I was leading you away alone, taking hold of the garden wall,
the messengers, the host of servants, and the warriors approached me.
They indeed struck me and seized you once you were separated from me.
Then a great clamor arose and the assembly was thrown into agitation;
for the virtuous maiden, who ought to be won by strength, was being carried away by servants.
"Kill them! Fight them! And seize the maiden!"—with these words, the battlefront was indeed commenced in an instant.
While they were looking on, I quickly placed [the girl] upon my shoulder.
Having seized you, he fled; then there was a rain of arrows.
I then remembered my own celestial chariot, called Akṣara, which is exceedingly brilliant, shining on all sides with supreme great splendors.

O Lakṣmī, having stationed you in their midst for battle against the Dānavas, [the army] was resplendent with attendants, hosts of Muktas, and white elephants; it bore all kinds of weapons and was accompanied by divine Muktānikās. 38.
I alone remained armored, a Brahmin assuming the form of a Kṣatriya.
Taking up my own most excellent bow, which brings about the destruction of the world,
I indeed cut down all his arrows with my own feathered shafts.
He crushed the armor of the warriors, even those made of gold. Then all the kings, the foremost of the Daityas,
the Asuras, and the Dānavas, having surrounded me on all sides, struck at me.
"Then I must bring about their destruction. Thus he thought.
Some were slain there by his power, others were struck down by the *bhūśuṇḍī* weapon, and still others were felled by *toma-ra* missiles and moon-like arrows.
Others were broken by maces, and others pierced by swords;
some were killed with staffs, and others split apart by axes. Still others were shattered by the force of thunderbolts, and others pierced by spears.
Others were rendered lifeless there on the field of battle by spears;
others were slaughtered with swords, while some were mangled by iron balls.
Then, the bodies of the warriors were pulverized by mallets.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by me alone there, crores of asuras were deprived of their lives and sent either to heaven or to the abode of Yama; likewise,
some were even established in the imperishable station of Vaikuṇṭha and immortality.
Indeed, the powerful ones were brought to Goloka, which had been attacked.
Then the thousand-armed King Kapālahetuka came to Sutala to fight with me at that time. ||48-49||
All his arms were severed by my Sudarśana discus;
having bowed down and become my devotee, he departed from the battlefield.
At that time, I granted him only two hands, no more.
Having endured his assault upon his elevated shoulders, he returned home. Then King Śatamūrdhan, whose vehicle was a deer, fought with Vitala— who was accompanied by me— using crescent-headed arrows.
He too was indeed cut in the throat by me with arrows resembling the sun;
his headless trunk fell upon the earth, and he died.
Then the king of Atala, named Sāmarāyodhana, [was struck].
Sahasrapād approached me for the purpose of combat.
Then, indeed, his feet were severed by me with my discus;
his headless trunk fell down and he died.
Then the great king Bhuvana, the lord of nine regions,
known by the name Mahendrabhīṣaṇa, came toward me to fight.
He hurled many spears, intending indeed to cut through my throat.
With my trident, I split Dakṣa’s arm from his shoulder.
Then that hero, now possessing only one hand, took up an excellent sword and rushed at me;
thereupon, I struck off his head with my blade.
Then those Daityas who were appointed to positions of authority in heaven arrived through the path of the sky to fight me in the atmosphere.
I fought them with thousands of forms using various weapons.
They were torn apart by the Sudarśana discus and by many other weapons.
Thus, the brave Arbudas there were sent to the state of the departed by my hands and likewise by my weapons; indeed, they were liberated even from their bondage.
Thurānanda, the sovereign of all, was indeed captured alive by me in that battle and bound with nooses and reins, brought under my control.
But you, O Lakṣmī, being overcome by affection for your father, did not speak out then.
"Do not speak thus," I said, "for the king has been liberated by me.
Having sought refuge, the monarch bowed at my feet;
through my granting of fearlessness, he was established as a sovereign of unwavering devotion.
Then other armies of the Dānavas fled;
having abandoned the earth for the sky, and the sky for the earth, they retreated to places such as the palm of the hand.
Having thus cleared the surface of the earth—and even heaven—of all thorns, [he remained].
Then he desisted from the battle, saying, "I am in my father-in-law's house.
The king led me to his own abode in the midst of the wedding pavilion and,
according to the prescribed rites, then gave me his daughter Jyotsnāśrī and you as well.
The king indeed bestowed as a dowry countless gold and jewels,
celestial chariots and vehicles, elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth;
he gave male and female servants, cities, wish-fulfilling creepers, and pools of nectar.
Having taken golden chariots and human carriages for you,
and having performed the funeral rites for those who had died, I then returned with you to my own home, the dwelling of the wise twice-born.
Then, indeed, I made the kings and the Brahmins upon the earth;
the earth became dependent on the Brahmins, performing the rites for the gods and the ancestors.
The earth, heaven, and the world of men—each of those abodes became as it was before.
In the past, he likewise gave that to them again according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, at that time the world was liberated from the wicked by me,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
By Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa, the source of all incarnations,
I indeed became the beginningless Śrī Prājña Nārāyaṇa at that time;
and I remained in the Bhāmaṇḍala-khaṇḍa until the end of the kalpa.
Thurānanda, your father, was my devotee who realized the Self;
at the end of his life, being pure in devotion, he went to my imperishable abode.
Remember your own splendor like moonlight; everything beneficial is within my reach.
In this way, other innumerable incarnations of mine have also occurred from that time.
Now, O beloved, listen as I describe another manifestation of mine:
during the year of Brahmā known as Pratyāhāra, in the tenth decade.
Furthermore, in the ninth kalpa and also during the second Manu,
atheism arose everywhere in the world due to the power of past times; and by the influence of the Tiṣya age, my worship was destroyed.
Temples were destroyed and sacred shrines vanished;
idols went to ruin and holy fords were demolished.
At that time, the beastly bull [of ignorance] indeed pervaded among human beings.
At that time, people of little knowledge and short lifespans forgot me;
they lived as outcasts, dwelling in pits, naked, and subsisting on wild grain and crops.
They were of small stature, short-lived, and filled with atheism. (8.1–8.2)
The Vedas have reached dissolution for me; the ritual section has vanished. Even my worship, my chanting, and my recitation and so forth have gone to destruction.
It was as if something unreal had come into being; then I was entreated by Brahmā.
Out of compassion, for the purpose of establishing devotion to the Dharma, I became visible [to him]. In the house of King Vīraśarabha, I, the four-armed Lord, appeared,
endowed with great virtue and vows, accompanied by the bull of the virtuous.
At the time of my manifestation, the gods showered down flowers and other offerings,
and the celestial drums of the gods resounded then.
His queen, Saurabheyī, beheld me upon his bed.

She presented to the king that highly desired child, who was not born from a womb and was endowed with all divine qualities, saying, "Behold this boy near me. The king said, "O Queen, this child was conceived by me through my own resolve! (87-88)
"A son of yours who is not born from a womb exists; protect him.
Then, as soon as he was born, that son appeared there as a youth, endowed with all sciences and virtues, a treasure-house of all specialized knowledge. (89)
Perfectly accomplished in the attainments of yoga, he has reached the further shore of all languages;
he is filled with all artistic skills and is an awakener to the path of devotion.
He is endowed with the sacred thread and possesses the excellence of a celibate student.
Out of great joy, he taught the true doctrines to mankind: celibacy, non-violence, truthfulness, refraining from theft,
purity, contentment, and constant devotion to the Supreme Lord.
Vows, contentment, as well as forgiveness and detachment;
service to the elderly, service to the virtuous, and abiding in the bliss of the Supreme Self;
charity, compassion, fire-offerings, hospitality, and the worship of Hari. (93–94)
Austerity is the restraint of the impulses of the senses and the abandonment of delusion;
it is the vision of the Self in all things and affection for the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self.
Likewise, it consists of hearing, chanting, and remembering Kṛṣṇa, as well as offering obeisances.
He offered himself to Kṛṣṇa, the supreme relationship with Hari.
Thus he indeed taught the duties of liberation (mokṣadharma) at that time,
and he adopted the life of a paramahaṃsa until the end of his life.
And you, Lakṣmī, commanded by me, were born there as the mind-born daughter of the sage Śārdūla; from the moment of birth she was eloquent,
youthful, possessed of the form of Brahman, and endowed with all sovereign powers.

Devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), she was a virtuous woman who understood the duties of a faithful wife (*satīdharma*). Relying on the conduct of a virtuous woman, she was dedicated to my vows;
she was intent on daily worship, possessed of devotion, and likewise a bringer of liberation. (3.8.100)
She was indeed entrusted to me by her father and mother for the very purpose of initiation;
initiation was bestowed upon you by me, and you have always remained a celibate student (*brahmacāriṇī*). You became the most venerable among all virtuous women and a giver of instruction.
O beloved, at that time your scripture was indeed virtuous and rooted in dharma;
it consisted of the Śārdūlikā and the Śrī-saṃhitā, and it shall endure until the end of the kalpa.
And then, by us both, it was [established] for all the worlds upon the surface of the earth.
The duties of the lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and devotion to Hari were thus taught;
innumerable living beings were delivered and established in the Imperishable.
Remember this, O Lakṣmī, as your own glory, like that of Śārdūlikā!
Likewise, my own self is the beginningless Lord Śrī Vīranārāyaṇa Hari.
(1.05) In this way, my other incarnations were then innumerable;
I know them all, for by remembering them, liberation is granted. (1.06)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Offering of the Garland of Boons by Jyotsnāśrī to the Primordial Wise Nārāyaṇa upon His Neck; the Battle of the Kings; the Destruction of the Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras by Hari with the Sudarśana and other weapons; the Liberation of Thurānanda; the Entrustment of the Earth, Heaven, and other realms to humans and gods respectively; and the Manifestation of the Primordial Hero Nārāyaṇa in the eleventh year for the purpose of establishing the dharma of the perpetual ascetic," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*.

and despite having countless undertakings and thousands of followers, (4)
That Blessed One never forgets me at any time;
having risen in the Brahma-muhūrta at dawn,

Then, satiated by meditation, my utterances were accompanied by the playing of palm-clapping instruments:
