Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! (6–7)
While he was thus reciting, he then bathed in the waters of the river,
offered handfuls of water to his ancestors, performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and paid worship to me;
he then performed my worship with all materials before my golden image.
Invocation, the seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and likewise water for sipping;
tooth-cleansing wood, gargles for cleansing the mouth, purification with clay, and thereafter purification with water. (3.9.9–10)
Anointing the limbs with fragrant oils and massaging the body;
likewise, bathing and immersion with milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, sugar,
and the waters of sacred fords.
Even the cleaning of garments and the wearing of priceless clothes;
likewise, the gift of fragrant substances and the offering of beautiful articles;
as well as collyrium for the eyes and the excellent tilaka upon the forehead. (12–13)
A crescent moon on the head, oil for coloring the palms,
all kinds of ornaments, sandals, and flower garlands;
saffron, *abīr*, *gulāla*, and auspicious sandalwood paste.
Unbroken grains, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
various kinds of foods, betel leaf, water, sprouts and leaves of *tulasī*, and garlands of gold and diamonds. (15–16)
Having performed the nightly lamp-offering, prostrations like a staff, hymns of praise, circumambulation,
the offering of a priestly fee, salutations, and the seeking of forgiveness for transgressions,
he then offered a handful of flowers and completed the ritual of worship.
She bows down even to virtuous people, guests, and Brahmins;
having respectfully honored cows, chaste women, children, the destitute, the helpless, and mendicants as well when they have arrived, she always worships them. (18–19)
Having caused food and other necessities to be prepared, he gives them according to their needs.
Every year, upon the arrival of the new grain, he establishes a most magnificent perpetual charity (*sattra*).
He indeed performs this Vaiṣṇava rite, which gods and humans alike enjoy.
Thus he performed that auspicious sacrifice of new grain;
there, hundreds of thousands of virtuous people, including Brahmins and others, arrived.
During those seven days of the sacrifice, I was his constant devotee.
"O Śiva-sattva-śrī! Having come in an invisible form, I shall take this offering presented [to you], eat it, and then depart for my own abode.
Thus, when the sacrifice of the Brahmins, who were masters of many scriptures, had commenced—
And for those who had come from various regions and were engaged in different rituals,
when there was disagreement regarding the auxiliary elements in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and the rites of Rudra became deficient,
a deficiency in the sacrificial components arose, leading to the provocation of the Fire-god.
Suddenly, a circle of fire, scorching to the touch, leaped from the sacrificial pit and instantly adhered to the canopy above the pavilion;
it then quickly spread out, blazing with flames.
The pavilion was quickly set ablaze, and the fire spread on all sides;
with its flames flickering, it expanded and grew even more by the wind,
reaching everywhere among the sacrificial offerings, the dwellings, and the houses.
Then, in the garments, in the sacrificial halls, and even among the men,
the fierce fire— cruel in its action— increased with great intensity.
Kālī, Karālī, Vikarālī, Nīlā, and Lohitā [also increased].
The flames were tawny, white, and greenish-yellow, appearing variegated.
There, fifty thousand men were reduced to ashes by those flames, and from that a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose. (3.9.30–31)
Śoṇabhadra, my devotee and king among devotees, fell into great sorrow;
he performed all the funeral rites for those who had died there.
Then, he became the cause of many murders and sins for them.
This Vaiśya, the sacrificer, was afflicted by great sorrow;
for a long time indeed, he found neither peace nor sleep.
Desiring to rescue the deceased, he performed my propitiation.
Having renounced food and water, he observed the vow of fasting;
with his mind absorbed in me, he performed worship day and night.
O Blessed One, becoming my son yourself, O Lord, grant him deliverance.
O Janārdana, ward off the stain of destroying the sacrifice!
(36) Thus, as I have been petitioning you, a year has passed without food;
a year has passed without water for me, a yogi whose purpose is death. (37)
Then I granted him a boon: "I shall become your son, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Having spoken thus, the mind-born son appeared before her.
His wife, a virtuous woman named Bhadreśvarī who observed vows of moral conduct,
saw me as a beautiful boy, augmented by all splendors, bestowing all perfections, gentle, and adorned with every ornament. (3.9.40)
Then the proud lady accepted that divine [garland] endowed with celestial qualities;
at that moment, a rain of divine flowers fell from the sky.
Liberated, the gods and lords honored me with those flowers.
With shouts of victory, the sounds of musical instruments, and worship with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice,
my father celebrated my birth-festival more grandly than ever before;
abandoning his own fast, he fed millions of people.

Then, on that day, the father Śoṇabhadra bestowed gifts of the most excellent of all things upon the virtuous, his devotees, the destitute, the helpless, the best of the twice-born, as well as young girls and boys.
O Daughter of Śiva! At that time, there were indeed festivals for the birth of Kṛṣṇa in every house. Then you said to me, "O Lord, if I must take birth, then grant me your command. || 46 ||
Then, having been told by me, "So be it," you, the daughter of a Vaiśya,
the fair-faced daughter of the virtuous woman named Sarayūkā,
were born as the mind-born daughter of Sarambhadrā, known by the name Śrī.
Endowed with all auspicious marks and accompanied by Hari within the heart;
inside the heart, there is a sign like the light of a lamp, marked by a golden line.
Above that is the sign of Hari, four-armed and of beautiful form.
And seeing you there, golden-hued as you were, your mother spoke to your father, who was named Sāravatsa:
"Truly, this daughter of ours is Kamalā herself, endowed with every splendor. (3.9.50)
"Lord Hari dwells in her heart, His form adorned with golden lines;
therefore, she must be given to the Blessed Supreme Soul Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and to no one else. Thus the Vaiśya also affirmed that truth.
As soon as you were born, a young woman endowed with excellent qualities, your mother and father,
having heard that the son of the merchant Śoṇabhadra was the Supreme Lord,
then gave you to me, the husband of Śrī, by means of a formal resolve.
Then, for the sake of rescuing the deceased, I performed a sacrifice again.
At its commencement, O Padmaja, you were offered to me by my parents according to the prescribed rites,
and you were accepted by me in the sacrificial pavilion.
Then, according to the prescribed rite, I caused the sacrifice to be performed;
O auspicious lady, the sacrifice was carried out by me together with you.
Thereafter, the hosts of the departed were duly summoned according to the ritual injunctions.
By means of ancestral *śrāddha* rites, offerings of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), oblations (*havana*), and divine rituals,
all of these were delivered [to higher realms] through the enjoyment of the grace of the sacrificial offerings.
At that time, all fifty thousand of them became four-armed.
Then those ghosts, having turned back and become four-armed gods,
were the attendants seated upon excellent celestial chariots in that pavilion;
and they were all sent by me to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
They were then released, and from that time on, I was always engaged in the service of my parents. Anādi-Śrī-Bhadra-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Puruṣottama,
and many other incarnations of mine appeared during that kalpa.
"O beloved, I know them all completely as they were born through the power of destiny.
Remember that Sarobhadrā, who was dear to Śrībhadrā and to me.
Now, O daughter of Śiva, hear of another of my manifest intentions! || 62 ||
In the thirteenth year of the Creator, known as Pradhyāna,
during the fourth Manu of the third Kalpa, on the southern side of Meru,
in the region of Aghamarṣaṇa upon the earth, she was a celibate student (brahmacāriṇī). || 63–64 ||
By the power of yoga, that Yoginī, who was devoted to me and possessed great capability, became known by the name Tuṅgabhadrāsana;
she would spend half the day in my worship in a secluded place. (61)

At midday, having gathered fruits, roots, and other forest-grown produce from the wild trees, he offers it to me and eats; thereafter, he performs the ancestral rites (paitrya). In the evening, he constantly worships me, the Supreme Lord and Teacher of the World.

Having meditated at night, she indeed sleeps; in the morning, she likewise performs meditation. Whether in bathing, meditation, recitation, fire-offerings, libations, or worship—on land, in water, in the air, by day, or by night—the Yoginī remembers me alone.

By the power of long-standing practice, she became a treasury of all accomplishments. Just as you, Lakṣmī, are endowed with sovereignty, so too is Vāṇī perfected in self-knowledge, possessing the power of will and the attainment of all goals. (3.9.70)
With her body perfected, free from the touch of dualities, and superior in every respect,
that great virtuous woman was born capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise;
she could travel through the sky and even enter the bodies of others.
She possesses the power to obstruct the movement of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
This beautiful woman is ever devoted to Hari and is a chaste wife to her husband Kṛṣṇa;
she is the protector of her devotees and the eternal guardian of the poor and the helpless.
Devoted to serving the virtuous and dedicated to righteous deeds,
she remained thus in the great forest at all times, even during the night. There, in the darkness, she encountered Rākṣasas who had come out for the sake of food.
Indeed, he beheld predatory beings such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*—evil-doers who devour flocks of sleeping birds and beasts;
and even the beasts, though terrified in the darkness, remained awake. (75–76)
Falling under the power of the unseen, they are unable to run away;
and as they run, the *bali-rākṣasas* seize them by force.
And every night, that virtuous woman [seizes] the embodied beings as they cry out.
He reflected again and again for the sake of removing the suffering of others,
so that the perpetual great misery of embodied beings might indeed perish;
having thus deliberated at length, [he resolved upon] the destruction of the Rākṣasas.
She meditated upon Mahālakṣmī, the fierce one who removes suffering;
commanded by me, you became manifest before her—
a sixteen-armed maiden bearing every kind of weapon.
With a serene countenance, she then entreated you for her own daughter.
You, Mānasī, having then become her daughter, remained in that hermitage as the slayer of all rākṣasas and spirits and the protector of cattle and other animals.
By name, for the sake of her mission, she was the beautiful Sarvabhadrāśrī; a female ascetic (yatinī) under the sway of dharma, endowed with every capability,
a virtuous woman who brings about auspiciousness, a youthful yoginī, and one who is auspicious.

Then, while she was living in this manner, all the *rākṣasa*s abandoned that forest region and went to another forest. There, living beings were thus being harmed by the *rākṣasa*s and others. (84–85)
Helpless, they came having heard that you were their protector of embodied beings; and having approached you, they entreated you for the sake of protection.
Your mother gave you to them for the sake of protection, and from there you departed.
Out of fear of you, the rākṣasas fled from that forest.
Indeed, even in that forest, such violence occurred because of those rākṣasas; they sought to seize even the sacrificial animals intended for the All-Beneficent (Sarvabhadrikā).
Thus, because she was called "Sarvabhadrikā" (Auspicious in Every Way) from all sides, she became renowned throughout the worlds as a bringer of protection.
Her mother reflected: "There will certainly be no end to this."
"My daughter does not remain in my house; she dwells in the forest as a virtuous woman.
Even though I have no desire for the acquisition of wealth for the sake of destroying the Rākṣasas, I shall nevertheless act in such a way that my daughter may dwell in my home. (3.9.90–91)
The strength of the *rākṣasas* shall also perish by its very nature;
I shall act in every way so that it may not become night.
For at night, the strength of the *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, and *rākṣasas* increases.

Therefore, "May night not come," thus praying to you, she then took water in her hand; having reflected upon that water in her joined palms, she consecrated it with mantras and threw it into the sky again and again. (93–94)
May the motion of the luminaries and the planets, beginning with the sun, become fixed;
and may there be a cessation of motion such that day shall indeed prevail forever,
so that night does not arrive and the setting of the sun never occurs.
Thus, with drops of water sprinkled upon them, they ascended to heaven.
(96) The gods, who possess rays of all-encompassing power, acted as an obstruction;
at that time, the course of the sun was blocked, and the circle of the constellations was obstructed. (97)
Indeed, everything attained permanence; day existed forever. Sunset occurred, yet that which had gone to its setting never returned.
Consequently, the evening twilight vanished, and the day became exceedingly long.

Everyone awaited evening, wondering when it would arrive. The entire circle of gods and humans was agitated and distraught; therefore, they then offered praise to me, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, as the sun set. (3.9.100)
All the morning and midday rituals had indeed been completed;
the gods and other beings were hungry, as were the people who were deprived of their seasonal rites.
Everything was scorched by the continuous rays of the sun.
When the state of being consumed by fire has arisen, the luster of the moon cannot be obtained.
(102) Even with medicinal herbs in the forest, nectar is never attained;
the trees and other plants wither away when drenched by the heat of the summer season. (103)
In this way, a great loss occurred through the singular gain;
by that heat, humans and others then fell into madness.
Thereupon, the waters of the lakes became dried up and then vanished.
Thus they fled in every direction, and a fierce suffering ensued. The army of the Rākṣasas was destroyed, and they entered the netherworld (pātāla);
the bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and others likewise entered their caves.
For them there is no suffering at all, but rather a burning with heat;
O Supreme Lord, protect them from this unbearable misery that has come upon them. 107.
Protect, protect, O Ocean of Mercy! The three worlds have fallen into a state of paralysis.
The planets and stars have ceased their motion, and the measurement of the day has come to rest.
O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, as the world lies asleep, the night has also come to rest;
likewise, there is no rising of the moon, and the limit of the month has come to rest.
The seasons do not arise at all, and the multitudes of medicinal herbs do not bear fruit;
all coldness has vanished, and fire breaks out even in the forest.
Save me, save me, O ocean of compassion, O friend of the day, from this scorching heat!
"Thus, O beloved, embodied beings in the three worlds praised me at that time.

(111) Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prayer to the Supreme Lord when the Yoginī Tumagabhadrāsana obstructed the movement of the Sun and other celestial bodies during the thirteenth year of profound meditation, for the sake of the liberation of those who had been consumed by fire in the Śoṇabhadrā sacrifice during the twelfth year of Brahmā in the third period, the Dvāpara-santāna," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Then indeed, O Śivasatyeśri! O beloved Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇi!
I, having ascended a celestial chariot, arrived from the abode of Akṣara.
In the assembly of the deities, the gods, filled with anxiety, performed purificatory rites;
likewise, they all announced the obstruction of their path.
The resulting great suffering was a torment even for human beings.
I have proclaimed the reason for that in that assembly:
the strength of the *rākṣasas* in this world is always present at night, and the strength of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas* is likewise present at night. (3–4)
They indeed devoured the sleeping creatures in the forests at night. The local beings, for the sake of protection, petitioned the Yoginī who resides on the Tuṅgabhadra; she, in turn, invoked Lakṣmī.
Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa now exist as her two daughters.
(6) Thus indeed all embodied beings were protected from the Rākṣasas;
nevertheless, Rākṣasas still abound in all regions. (7)
But when Lakṣmī departs from them, the mother remains alone;
as a daughter she wanders through the worlds, and no happiness is found for a daughter.
Therefore, she reflected and decided that it must not remain night.

Tuṅgabhadrikā, a great and virtuous devotee of mine, a treasure-house of yogic power, has indeed stopped the wheel of the planets by her own strength. This is truly the supreme reason for the obstruction of its movement. (3.10.9–10)
"Therefore, let us go to that very place where the movement [of the breath] has been suppressed.
Having reflected thus, O Narayani, I, together with the gods,
arrived at the spot where your mother was seated upon the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā.
Having observed the celestial mansions with her yogic vision, that great virtuous woman mentally created another heaven within the forest for the sake of welcoming him,
complete with various gardens and wish-fulfilling trees that grant one's desires.
He gave rivers filled with water as friends to those who were thirsty for the nectar of water;
he gave excellent halls for bathing and other rites, and palaces worthy of the gods—
white like the moon and enriched by the splendor of golden pitchers.
There were sacrificial halls, kitchens, and most beautiful bedchambers;
recreation halls, training rooms, women’s quarters, and central pavilions;
as well as chests for garments with fine door-panels and caskets for ornaments. (15–16)
There were excellent treasuries of gems, diamonds, and gold;
well-provided channels of clarified butter, channels of curd, and channels of milk;
as well as kitchens for nectars, juices, and sweet foods.
She fashioned swings and mirrors, hollows within walls for objects of enjoyment,
dwellings for those seeking a comfortable residence, and beautiful houses;
likewise, she created lamps from streams of lightning.
Then she fashioned garlands of sandalwood, exquisite flowers, and diamonds, with ripples naturally arising from the breezes; meanwhile,
female attendants stood by, holding vessels for the honey-mixture and other offerings.
The Yoginī indeed created ten million maidens;
there were those who played musical instruments, as well as those who performed dances and songs.
Likewise, there were maidens resembling milk and gold who carried banners. (21–22)
There, the virtuous lady, by her resolve alone, created a throne for Tuṅgabhadrā;
she fashioned vessels for inexhaustible offerings, bowls of saffron and unbroken rice,
and young maidens to perform services such as massaging her feet.
By the power of her own sovereignty, she fashioned a new city called Svarga (Heaven), which was not inferior to heaven itself. Indeed,
for the sake of welcoming him, she quickly appeared before the city gate.
Beholding those manifestations, all the gods were struck with supreme wonder.
Indeed, we descended swiftly from the path of the sky into the forest.
At the top of the city gate, countless maidens came forward to offer a welcome.
They honored all the gods with offerings of garlands;
they celebrated them with shouts of victory accompanied by saffron, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, they led all the gods to their respective dwellings that had been prepared according to their needs.

They gave them the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), edible nectar, and the essence of immortality; they offered water for drinking, services, and massages to relieve their bodies. "We gods are all satisfied, having been gratified by the maidens for a moment. (29)
That became heaven, and yet another heaven; it was not deficient at all.
For a moment, the gods, being deluded, forgot their own enjoyments.
Then, at the end of that moment, that virtuous and chaste lady, seated upon the lofty Bhadrāsana— || 3.10.30–31 ||
Indeed, she had wished to know the reason for the arrival of the gods;
and that virtuous woman, having quickly come to the assembly hall and summoned the deities,
announced her own fortune in the presence of the gods.
"Aha! My entire lineage has been purified, and this forest has been purified (33).
This surface of the earth has been purified, and my hermitage has been purified, since you venerable ones have come together to my home. (34)
Today, indeed, another heaven has been created; I am blessed in every way, since there are heaps of ten million merits acquired in the past within my home.
There, the gods themselves arrive in person, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa.
"I have presented myself for the service and the command of the inhabitants of heaven.
I am indeed your slave; please give me your instructions.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself before the gods seated upon their golden thrones.
Having gazed again and again upon the sun, the moon, Venus, the planets, the best of the seven sages,
the lunar mansions, Mahendra, Bṛhaspati, and also Agastya,
he repeatedly paid homage to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Beholding me again there in my presence with eyes filled with tears,
she quickly approached and fell at my feet; being virtuous,
she said to me, Hari, the Supreme Person, "I am surrendered."
Then, O beloved, having been swiftly commanded by me there, Bṛhaspati informed your mother, Satī, who was present; listen:
"We are all devoted followers and gods who have taken refuge in Nārāyaṇa. ||41||
But for the offense of devotees, we flee to a great distance out of fear.
You are endowed with devotion; you are our object of worship, worthy of honor, and virtuous.
We bow down to these gods; be gracious, O Yoginī!
O beautiful lady, you have indeed obstructed the course of the sun and the moon for the purpose of destroying the power of the Rākṣasas and for the sake of ending the night;
however, this destruction of the world has now arrived through your heat.
Religious rites have been obstructed and even the seasons have gone to ruin.
Indeed, the entire world rejoices in dependence upon the movement of the planets;
therefore, O Goddess, we beg you before your presence for the cessation of their movement.
This is the divine Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person;
he has come here for the sake of alms, accompanied by tens of millions of gods.
We are your guests, and we have no other purpose whatsoever.
"O you of auspicious deeds, we choose this place before you; give us alms!
(48) Having heard this, O Nārāyaṇī Lakṣmī, your mother Satī then said to the gods and to me as well: "I too shall beg for a place of auspiciousness. (49)
The Supreme Lord, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama—
for whose sake I am a Yoginī and whom I worship as the supreme among men—
if even the gods were to offer him up, he is the eternal Supreme Lord.
I grant the Supreme Brahman, the Lord, to me, so that there may be no obstruction to my departure.
May there be supreme welfare for me, as well as welfare for you, and may there be welfare for all people; may everything become a source of auspiciousness.
Then the gods said: "The Supreme Person is independent;
He cannot be commanded by us, for the Lord Himself listens [to our plea].
Janārdana will act as He desires for the sake of the happiness of all."
O Śivaśaṃjikā, having heard these words of the gods, I then asked your mother: "What do you desire, O excellent Yoginī? She replied: "O Blessed One, this Lakṣmī here is my daughter and my servant."
She remains waiting for you; accept your own beloved.
This entire new heaven has been prepared as a dowry for your sake, and these tens of millions of maidens have been arranged for your benefit.
"O Puruṣottama, accept all [these women] according to the rites of marriage.
Having become my son-in-law, dwell here for eternal years. Thus she entreated him; thereafter, night became day, and everything was as she had wished.
"I am your devotee, O Lord, and you are renowned as one who is affectionate toward his devotees.
You act for the benefit of the gods, of the worlds, and of me as well.
You are capable of doing so; no effort is required on your part. (59)
"O Blessed One, accept everything; grant me your auspicious word.
Take water in your hand, and once it is taken, tell me here [the truth].
Then I shall indeed create an obstruction to the path of all the gods."
And Hari, smiling at her, spoke "Om" indeed;
he took the water in his hand, and the gods proclaimed victory. Then musical instruments were sounded, and the deities were delighted.
Then, showers of flowers fell from the goddesses in that assembly hall.
At that moment of the Abhijit muhūrta, all the maidens became radiant;
in an instant, they seated the daughter upon a lofty throne and adorned her with ornaments.
And he presented a decorated young woman while they were looking on;
"The bridegarland was placed upon my neck by you there.
Then, your hand was placed into my hand by my mother.
"You were seated upon my lion-throne, occupying half of it.
Then other maidens quickly arrived before me according to my command and offered the bridegroom’s garland to me, who had assumed ten million forms. (66–67)
Then, at that moment, the preceptor Bṛhaspati himself quickly recited Vedic mantras suitable for the auspicious conjunction (*lagna*) there by the neck;
and with a swift resolve, he had the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) prepared by a yogi.
And Viśvakarman, the creator, established the fire;
he caused the oblation to be performed and gave the maidens away.
"You are the principal one, and the other ten million maidens are my wives. (3.10.70)
All of them were obtained there by me, a yogi devoted to the Supreme Person;
those women who are here are the very ones bestowed upon you by your mother.
Those groups of your co-wives were formerly my own wives.
And those women who were married by me in Kāśī at the house of Śivasvāmin—there, those ten million women become young maidens.
Remember all this past history, O Lakṣmī! This divine narrative.
Then, having quickly performed the circumambulation of the fire, I sat down there upon my seat; at that time, the couple was made to prosper.
All the couples were then caused to flourish with auspicious blessings.
Then, there was an exchange of saffron, unbroken rice, flowers, and other offerings.
Thereafter, your mother provided various kinds of foods, diverse drinks, and all manner of enjoyable delicacies. (75–76)
Then all were satisfied, yet midday did not pass by;
that very moment was the one known by the name Abhijit.
O Lakṣmī, it continued there indeed even without the movement of the sun at that time.
Then, having been commanded and honored by her, all those gods numbered in the tens of millions asked for forgiveness for their offense; Satī,
having bowed down and presented them with gifts, then dismissed them to heaven.
I always dwelt together with you and other women in that city known as Puruṣottamapura, which was called heaven; at that time,
it had attained such renown that it endured until the end of the kalpa.
At that time, O beloved, the paths of the gods quickly manifested;
and then the hour following midday began to proceed slowly.
Thus am I, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, the source of all auspiciousness.
At that time, I was the Supreme Lord, the husband of the daughter of Tuṅgabhadrā.
There, I had one hundred beautiful sons for each of my wives,
and twenty very beautiful daughters for each.
They all possess a lifespan of an entire kalpa, and now they are all liberated within my imperishable abode; remember this, O Subhadrakā, and behold!
[I am] Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
O virtuous lady! For the sake of accomplishing the purpose of my devotees, I dwelt in their homes in that manner. My devotee’s house is my own home;
O beloved! wherever you are, there indeed is my residence forever.
Through your yoga, my own yoga also came to be for the others.
At that time, you became the remover of suffering and the bestower of happiness to them all;
you became renowned as the Lord Anādi-Śrī-Hari-Nārāyaṇa.
And you, by name Sarvabhadrāśrī, shall be the queen of the great king;
all the others at that time shall indeed become renowned as the beloveds of Śrī Hari.
And thus shall there be the manifestation of my supreme incarnation there.
And at that time, O beloved, my incarnations there became innumerable.
I know all of this as clearly as a jewel held in the palm of my hand.
Remember those divine forms and the wonders performed then.

that house and those two parents are the divine Śrī Nārāyaṇa and Nārāyaṇī.
Seeing the liberation of their sons, the parents attained great joy.
However, in worldly convention, a certain inferiority is observed;
for [it is said]: "While performing worship, the lawful wife, devoted to her vows, made a request desiring a son, thinking:
'May I have an only son who shall live long. (3.12.70–71)
Thus she always made her request with a handful of flowers as an act of devotion. And I said, "So be it; he shall be long-lived.
Your eleventh son shall be [the one], and I, Hari, shall be the twelfth."
Having spoken thus, I ceased; she, however, spoke to her own husband.
Then the couple became joyful, and after a year had passed, my elder brother Saṃkarṣaṇa was born there, O Janārdana.
Two years later, I became the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa there; a rain of flowers fell for the gods,
and my parents became joyful, gracious, and partakers of happiness.
Then, O Lakṣmī! You too have desired your own incarnation.
Having received my command, [take birth] as a mother observing the vow of a goddess, with a father who is a Brahmin devoted to dharma and observing the vow of a god. || 76-77 ||
I shall grant [myself] to one who is the purifier of all the Vedas, a knower of them, a perceiver of Brahman, devoted to the Supreme Brahman, always serving Hari,
worshipping me as Yajña-Nārāyaṇa, and seeing the Self in all.

To that yogi of former births, established in samādhi and pure in his excellent vows, you yourself, Lakṣmī, were born there, adorned with all your emblems. At that time, a rain of flowers and other things fell from the sky on every side. (3.12.80)
The celestial drums resounded and the gods worshipped you; indeed,
adorned with all the purificatory rites beginning with the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
you became fit for marriage, and then you performed my vow.
The auspicious vow of Kāntapradyumna is delightful, bestowing all prosperity.
In a dream, I appeared before your mother and father;
having granted them my own vision along with another bridegroom, I said, "Give me your daughter. (82–83)
Considering that your parents were awake and that the dream was true,
they summoned you and gave you to me according to the prescribed rites, with fire as witness.
At that time, you were named Jayā, the daughter of Devavrata.
I, the beginningless Śrīvara Nārāyaṇa, married her.
At that time, there was a great assembly of gods and great sages; then, a grand festival took place everywhere upon the earth and in the heavens. (85–86)
My brother Saṃkarṣaṇa married Sarojinī, the eldest daughter born there,
who was the daughter of Devavrata.
When that marriage had been completed, your two illustrious parents—
They gave as a dowry the finest and priceless jewels and diamonds;
elephants, horses, bulls, land, an excellent mansion, a garden, male and female servants, wealth, and gold. (88–89)
Many golden vessels, as well as ornaments and garments,
I took and went to my home, which was a place of happiness;
thus did Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, depart.

The Supreme Lord, the eternal one, who transcends the imperishable Supreme Brahman—then I remained there with you until the end of the kalpa. My brother Saṃkarṣaṇa also was there, endowed with the splendor known as Vijayā. (91–92)
He remained indeed upon the surface of the earth until the end of the kalpa as a protector of the Dharma.
Remember, Lakṣmī! Your birth and my birth also took place at that very time.
I alone know this, and no others, for they have been worn away by the decay of time.
Other such incarnations of mine, numbering in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions,
were born there in that year— auspicious, bestowing liberation and happiness. Thus, all of my manifestations at that time have indeed been told.
For it bestows liberation through mere remembrance, hearing, and reflection.
One who is childless obtains a son, and one who is destitute becomes wealthy.
For those who suffer, there shall be the destruction of suffering; and the student who recites it shall attain perfection.
The lineage shall become prosperous, and a wife finds her husband.
The reciter certainly obtains a kingdom, heaven, and abundance.
For those who practice devotion to me, no stain of *māyā* arises.
Nor indeed shall there be a fall, O Lakṣmī! There shall always be prosperity;
there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and one shall surely attain eternal happiness.
One shall also obtain the fruit of all sacrifices and the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
One shall obtain the fruit of serving the virtuous as well as the fruit of devotion to one's husband;
and by hearing this, one shall likewise acquire the fruit of all forms of worship, the fruits of all vows, and the fruit of all acts of charity.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Vara Nārāyaṇa with His Elder Brother, Following the Liberation of One Hundred and Ten Sons in the House of the Brāhmaṇa Dharmavrata during the Fifteenth Year of the Creator [Brahmā] in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age," in the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga. Chapter 12.

Chapter 14 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! Furthermore, it was during the sixteenth year of the creator Brahmā known as Prajñāta,
specifically in the eleventh Kalpa and under the ninth Manu,
that my manifestation occurred.
At that time, there was on earth the dharma of the yogi Brahmakumāra.
There was a son of Brahmā known as Brahmakumāra;
from his very childhood he had been a celibate student (brahmacārī) in Satyaloka in ancient times.
His lifelong disciples then resided in Satyaloka;
devoted to his instructions, they wandered through heaven and upon the earth.
And the disciple named Ārṣakumāra taught on the earth.

From humans [comes] the dharma of moral conduct, the lifelong practice of celibacy (brahmacarya). (5) Whether they be men or women who possess bodies, if those meritorious ones— or even sinners— abide in celibacy and remain steadfast in it, (6) [they attain the goal].
They indeed become liberated, freed from the snares of illusion.
For embodied beings, celibacy is the burning away of desire and the conquest of desire;
through virtuous conduct and vows, one must perform the supreme means that grants liberation.
A woman should remain chaste, and a man should remain free from transgression.
(8) Thus, one should always maintain this conduct and vow here throughout one’s life.
Celibacy is the very form of Brahman and the cause for attaining the Supreme Brahman. (9)

When the Supreme Brahman is attained, neither debt nor sin exists; there is no impurity at all in the virtuous woman, the virtuous man, or the lifelong celibate. Celibacy is the great initiation; celibacy is the supreme strength.
Celibacy is the path to liberation; celibacy is the supreme state.
(11) Even for those who perform sacrifices and give gifts, many births may still occur in this world;
however, through the vow of Brahman and liberation [therefrom], one shall attain release. (12)
For one who observes the vow of Brahman, liberation shall occur in a single birth alone;
for the Supreme Lord is always well-pleased with the one who maintains the vow of Brahman.
(13) Furthermore, the sacrificial fires, the deities, and others approach the student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*).
The progress of a celibate student toward liberation is unimpeded, even in other circumstances.
(14) A celibate student purifies even those who have committed great sins at that very moment.
Furthermore, the ancestors drink the water with which a celibate student has bathed. (15)
The celibate student is himself a god, and the female celibate student is a goddess;
indeed, those people who are devoted to celibacy are incarnations of portions of Hari.
Through association with celibate students, they truly become one with Brahman.
Beholding, touching, saluting, serving, and so forth;
the water from his feet, honoring him, welcoming him, providing food, and the like—even these, when performed for a *brahmacārī*, purify one instantly. (17–18)
In this world, there are many gurus who bestow knowledge yet strive in vain;
those gurus who are endowed with virtuous conduct are the true and supreme saviors.
Even a woman who possesses virtue and vows is directly to be understood as the goddess Nārāyaṇī, the chaste Satī. (19)
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, the man endowed with virtuous vows, is the one to be awakened directly.
(3.13.20) Thus, indeed, the final tradition of the celibate student was established upon the earth at that time by the Ṛṣi Kumāra. (21)
Indeed, millions of men and women were then devoted to the practice of celibacy;
they became lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) and lived separately.
Those virtuous women also lived separately in their own monasteries for women.
Those men dwell separately in the hermitages of men;
neither women nor men enter one another's hermitages.
Those of virtuous character do not touch one another, whether men or women. (23–24)

Listen, O Śivarājñiśrī! Indeed, even the gods and the ancestors come to behold those who are thus radiant with their virtuous conduct. Those virtuous women, possessing the character of Brahmā, shine like the moon.

Then they shine with splendors born of their virtue, like the sun. Thus, having seen those bodies composed of light, gods and men [beheld them] from afar, whether from the hermitage, or from the sky, or even from the forest.
Many who lack fortitude fall into delusion regarding virtuous women—
whether they be Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, gods, or men;
whether they be human beings, groups of kings, or even men possessed of strength.
Seeing groups of virtuous women— immersed in Brahman, possessing the character of Brahman,
dwelling as ascetics at various holy sites in forests, wildernesses, and on riverbanks—
the deluded [women] fell into a state of extreme infatuation and, in some places, indeed committed acts of violation.
Arrogant asuras and human piśācas, having broken their restraints, enter the hermitages;
they violate women of virtuous conduct or even carry them away from the hermitage.
Indeed, these demonic beings cause them to fall from their vows of sacred knowledge.
Kings, royal servants, thieves, and likewise warriors,
forcibly entering hermitages, cause chaste women to fall from their vows.
When this had indeed occurred in many ways, once upon a time, the asura Śukraka—
Then, having arrived with the Daityas on the bank of the Mandākinī,
he suddenly descended through the path of the sky into that well-guarded hermitage of celibate women among the assembly of Yoginīs.
And the women dwelling in the hermitage, devoted to celibacy, upon seeing those Daityas accompanied by Śukra, fled in fear;
overcome with terror, they ran hither and thither among the trees of the hermitage. (35–36)
There, the virtuous women, being assaulted and their vows violated, were filled with terror;
yet among them there was one virtuous woman named Sudarśinī,
who remained unbroken, untainted, devoted to celibacy, and radiant with spiritual power.
The Yoginī is perfected in speech, possesses a divine form, and is like a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā).
She is intent on wonder through her words and brings all things to ashes.
Radiant as the sun, well-nourished, she is a young woman who observes celibacy.
Seeing her beneath the tree— immersed in meditation, fixed in *brahmalagna*, and trembling with fear at the touch of fire, sun, and wind— Śukraka quickly approached to violate her.
As soon as he had forcibly touched her, the virtuous woman looked at him and cursed him:
"May this obstacle to my vow be reduced to ashes this very instant!
At that moment, even Śukra, the preceptor of the Daityas, was turned to ashes.
Then other female celibates reported the violation of her vow;
thereupon, the virtuous Sudarśanī became enraged and cursed them once more: "From this day forward, those who act with violence toward chaste women... [43]
"Whether on the surface of the earth, in heaven, or wherever else they dwell—
let them all this very day be reduced to ashes in an instant!
Having spoken thus, that Satī released the water held in her hand.
Meanwhile, all those who had been destroyers of the Brahma-vow were burned in whichever worlds they might have been; yet even so,
the virtuous Sudarśanī became filled with wrath.
There he reflected upon men for the sake of pacifying obstacles:
"May those inhabitants of the heavenly realms and other worlds who have come to this earth, and even those who merely desire to violate them, not assault these virtuous women. (47–48)
Let them always be women there and never men again;
and those who dwell upon the earth— whether they be men, kings, or others—
who by force violate virtuous and faithful wives, they too shall always remain on this earth as such.

"Let them always be women, and never men again! Let this human race on earth, which breaks its vows, cease to exist; let everyone indeed become women, and let there be no men at all. (3.13.50) "Let them all be women; let there be no men among them. (5.1)
"Whether they be children, the elderly, or young men,
let all people— indeed, even women— not be givers of harm out of fear of the vow of *satī*.
Having said this, Sudarśinī released the water held in her hand.
Indeed, by the power of Satī, this entire world of mortals quickly became female; all men turned into women, and not even a single group of human beings remained in male form. (53–54)

In every house, boys took the form of girls, the elderly became old women, and young men indeed became young women; this occurred in every city, in every district, and everywhere throughout the world. 55.
Even the women situated upon the ships then became like travelers abroad;
there was a great cry of "Alas! Alas! and that was a supreme marvel, occurring throughout the fourteen worlds, and especially upon the earth.
All the men indeed beheld their own secret marks—the manifestation of the limbs of their bodies consisting of the signs of women—and they experienced extreme shame; they did not show their faces. 58.
Beardless, yet possessing hair, with breasts and endowed with beauty,
all the men on earth then became like women in form;
and though they all remembered their past lives, they experienced supreme suffering at that time.
In other worlds, within their respective circles of kinsmen, the Daityas and others felt profound shame and became objects of ridicule;
even the gods likewise acted in such a way that they became creators of obstacles.
They even took on female forms among the gods and became objects of ridicule;
in the presence of their own wives, they were then subjected to contempt, and being violators of virtuous conduct, they even incurred cries of "Fie! upon themselves.
A great wonder arose among the men and women of the three worlds: indeed, no men remained on the surface of the earth who were objects of anger;
the entire surface of the earth became, in every respect, a kingdom of women.
At that time, the entire surface of the earth indeed consisted of women and children.
Then, the son of the Creator, Kāmadeva, as well as Nara—
who had been residing within the body of the virtuous woman— was born in female form.
Having abandoned his wife Rati and Prīti, he, assuming the form of a woman,
went swiftly to Satyaloka, seeing that even in heaven there was a similar state for the gods,
consisting of the calamity of becoming women, which existed even in Satya.

There, on the road, he indeed heard of the burning of Śukra and the cause of Sudarśanī’s wrath throughout all creations— that violation of chaste women which was the root of the destruction of men. (68–69)
In every place and throughout the entire world, this report spread:
that because of Sudarśinī’s great anger, men and women on earth had become like Kāmadeva. Then, indeed, Kāmadeva went to Brahmā while he was in his assembly.
He also reported everything exactly as it was to the sons of Brahmā.
Then, seeing that form of a woman which was yet bodiless, they all laughed, struck with wonder, saying, "Oh, how true is the power of Love!"
The power of celibacy is the most excellent, the strongest among all powers;
there is no other strength equal to or superior to celibacy.
All means of accomplishment and all forms of austerity [are likewise surpassed by it]. (73)
All vows indeed reside within celibacy (brahmacarya).
This celibacy is distinguished as the means for liberation, the supreme means for protection, and the most excellent means for attaining sovereignty. (74–75)
Then, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen:
subsequently, all those women on earth, even without their husbands—whether they were pregnant or young girls—all performed my worship while filled with grief. (76)
They were indeed resentful toward the children, and because of that, they became deeply distressed.
"The seeds of the lineage are destroyed; how will the flow of the family continue?
Thus all those women, as well as the men, became possessors of the memory of their past lives.
They propitiated me, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Person;
for such a curse, there is no other who can ward it off. Even the gods spoke likewise, [saying] that none could do so except for me, the Supreme Person.
Then Brahmā and Hara likewise spoke thus:
"Except for Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, the Illustrious Parameśvara, there is no other Lord who exists as the maker of the pacification of this curse. (3.13.80–81)
"The curse of the devoted, celibate Satī is inexorable;
only a supreme man, whose soul is fixed in the eternal dharma of perpetual celibacy, is capable of countering it.
Having thus resolved, the throngs of women throughout all the worlds—
And with devotion they worshipped me, Hari, the Supreme Person.
(83) On that earth there exists only a kingdom of women; the offspring are likewise all female.
Furthermore, whoever comes to that land indeed becomes a woman. (84)
They all indeed performed my worship with devotion for a hundred years on earth; it was solely the creation of women.
No other creation occurred, for that ancient one indeed persists.
At that time, out of fear of female existence, even some deities did not come to the earth for worship;
neither Gaṇeśa arrived, nor did the sages come. (86–87)
During worship and the observance of vows, the gods indeed do not come out of fear;
for this curse is exceedingly terrible, and even Viṣṇu is afraid of it. Furthermore, Brahmā does not come at all due to his dread of being transformed into a woman.
At that time, even the young son of Brahmā did not come to the earth.
Indeed, no gods came at all for the sake of averting Satī’s curse;
for those who do come are born on the surface of the earth as women.
Thus a great and unbearable obstruction arose, consisting of women;
for even those who arrived unawares became women.
Even the attendants of Viṣṇu, who came to take away the deceased women, [became so]. || 91 ||
And those messengers of Yama who had come to the earth became women.
Thus, having gone before Hari in the form of women, those attendants became a source of wonder; the curse was true and difficult to overcome. ||92-93||
The messengers of Yama, having become women and assuming a state of laughter,
have thus blocked the arrival of those who lead [souls] even in the next world.
Indeed, even after they have enjoyed themselves, the messengers likewise become women.
What need is there to mention others? Death does not come there out of fear of him.
At that time, death indeed does not occur even when one's lifespan has reached its end.
The earth became immortal, and the woman was like Vaikuṇṭha itself.
"Aha! Here indeed was the power of the strength of a celibate student;
otherwise, Nārāyaṇa himself would have become the agent [of her destruction].
At that time, Time itself did not come to the earth out of fear of becoming a woman."
Indeed, the male host does not come to the earth for fear of Satī’s curse.
Then both Śrī Hari and I, being propitiated by women,
did not wish to come to the earth at that time due to fear of [being born in] female form.
However, without reflecting upon it, the abode itself, thinking that the warding off of the curse must be performed by its own power,
arrived there having assumed the form of a woman.
Divine, possessing a divine form, and accompanied by divine attendants adorned with divine pearls— || 3.13.100 ||— [she appeared].
Having all assumed the forms of women, we arrived upon this earth. Laughing, we were all well-united with Lakṣmī and the others;
rejoicing together with one another, we were all with you.
They arrived at the beautiful surface of the earth where the virtuous Sudarśanī resided;
there were gods, sages, liberated souls, and others as well. Then all those women became filled with curiosity.
All the gods, having become women, arrived to witness [the event].
This festival of the female universe pervaded the three worlds in every way,
spreading everywhere from ear to ear.
In former times, women beheld women and men beheld men;
all of them, remembering their past lives, rejoiced and even laughed.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa also arrived from Goloka together with Rādhā.
She too became a friend of Rādhā; indeed, Rādhikā was her second.
Nārāyaṇa also arrived from Vaikuṇṭha together with Lakṣmī;
she too became Nārāyaṇī, a splendid friend of Lakṣmī.
Then Nara and Nārāyaṇa became Nārī and Nārāyaṇī on earth; they were beautiful women, ascetics at that time. Śaṅkara and Śāṅkarī were born there, and Satyā was seen there as well.

Likewise, all the other women who had gathered there out of curiosity became like that; for it was a great festival, and they looked at one another and touched one another according to the nature of women.

They laughed and rejoiced, for the world is indeed made by women; she [Sudarśanī] made Nārāyaṇa into Nārāyaṇī. Thus, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the sixteenth year of the Creator’s life, [it describes] how, due to the fault of Śukra and others who had attempted to violate her, the celibate student Sudarśanī—disciple of the Ṛṣi Kumāra—[acted].

Chapter 14.
[The Author: Chapter 15.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: "O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! Thus [is] the Supreme Lord, who is like unto himself."
Upon seeing him transformed into a woman, the women were filled with wonder;
then, beholding the two Nārāyaṇīs and the two Rādhās who were identical to one another,
worthy of service and even to be touched, the virtuous wives attended upon them.
All those women, who were celibate practitioners (*brahmacāriṇī*), there at the festival,
served Hari with all their being and through various modes of appropriate service.
All the women who had arrived from every direction were preceded by men.
An innumerable assembly gathered on the bank of the Mandākinī.
(4) In that assembly of women, I appeared there in the form of a woman.
I was then entreated by the women to release them from their female state. (5)
"We women, who were previously men and were worthy of being beheld, have been born here as women through a curse, though we were without fault, due to the wickedness of the Daityas and others,
and by the sins of corrupt kings who violated chaste women. (6)
"Though they were faultless men dwelling on earth, they have attained womanhood.
Because of their devotion to Sudarśanā, the punishment was exceeded;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, show mercy and grant us our male bodies as husbands. (7–8)
Even the women, whose desires were innate, made this request:
"O Blessed One, grant us husbands; make us young and youthful.
Create men here who dwell in the world of men, such as the men of old. (9)
Having heard that, Hari and I spoke in the assembly of women:
"I am devoted; I am dependent on others, and I do not transgress what has been said by my devotee.
We, the women, have gathered together here requesting a vision of the Lord. (3.14.10–11)
Having thus instructed [her], I rose from the assembly; and then, in that assembly, I spoke to Sudarśanī, who had been summoned there:
"O virtuous lady, devoted to Brahman and endowed with great sovereignty! (12)
It is proper to punish the wicked and to protect one's own vow;
however, it is indeed improper to punish innocent beings—whether they be children, the elderly, the young, or even those who are righteous. (13–14)
Therefore, I myself, the beginningless Supreme Person, beg you:
by my word, act so that your speech [is not fulfilled] while you are in the form of a woman.
O beautiful lady, prevent the curse for the sake of all the worlds.
"The entire world consists of women; it will not pass away without a man.
Having reflected upon the revocation of the curse, fulfill what has been requested by me, your devotee.
Hearing this, the beautiful goddess reflected and quickly spoke to me:

O Kṛṣṇa, because gods, Daityas, humans, and others constantly assault virtuous women even within hermitages, I have always made women [unapproachable] so that such a thing might not happen. This is the reason for my curse. (18)

"If you are indeed our protector and the destroyer of the wicked, then dwell upon this earth until the end of the kalpa; only then shall I withdraw my curse. Having spoken thus, that virtuous and beautiful woman then [fell] at my feet.
Falling prostrate like a staff, she performed worship with flowers and other offerings;
she placed a garland around the neck of the one who had assumed the form of a woman amidst the multitude of women.
"I am here for the protection of my devotees," he said to her, "Om, so be it."
Later, Satī, the beautiful one, placed water in her hand;
by means of that curse, the Supreme Lord was brought down to the earth. Blessed indeed is this world where the Best of Men has arrived.
And here Hari shall make his own abode until the end of the kalpa;
though associated with evil company, he shall provide protection for those who observe the vow of Brahman.
Thus, by this exchange, I have [received] my most terrible curse.
"I shall withdraw the world here into the presence of Śrī Hari, restoring it to its state of equality.
Having said this, she released the water from her hand onto the feet of Kṛṣṇa; at that moment, it fell upon the ground, in the assembly, and elsewhere in the world in various places.
Those women who had previously been men in Satyaloka, Svarga, Mānava, Pātāla, and other realms,
instantly became men at that time.
Then this triple world (trilokī) existed as it did before, consisting of couples.
Kṛṣṇa became Kṛṣṇa in his true form, Nārāyaṇa himself;
and Puruṣottama likewise assumed the form of Puruṣottama.
And in that very manner, everything was produced there just as before.
Nārāyaṇa himself spoke again at that assembly:
"He who has committed the violation of Satī must indeed be slain by me here with the Sudarśana discus.
Of this there is no doubt; at the end of his life, he shall become a woman."
Then the Daityas, the Dānavas, the kings, and millions of gods—
those wicked ones who had violated Satī— beheld the Sudarśana, which was fiery,
cutting, unbearable, and terrible.
Then they implored him for forgiveness, and they were banished at that time.
All of them, indeed, departed for a great distance into the depths of the forest, filled with sorrow.
Even so, those of evil intent who had been cut down by the discus [remained].
Those who were endowed with wicked intentions have been destroyed in the other world.
All those virtuous and truthful women, devoted to celibacy—
even those who suffered violation— have reached the presence of Hari.
Having come together, they drank the auspicious water from the feet of Hari;
purified by that which cleanses all sins, they indeed attained purity.
Having served the manifest Puruṣottama with the ninefold devotion, [they were liberated]. (36)
For those who have been placed in the sacred [state] have become liberated, seeking the meaning of the single syllable.
O Lakṣmī! I, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, dwelt together with you;
I am known as the beginningless Śrī, the Woman, and Nārāyaṇa, the Man. (37–38)
O Lakṣmī! Just as you are renowned by the name "Sudarśanī" because you are not born from a womb, are independent, and have resorted to manifest splendor;
so too are you, the Supreme Goddess, renowned as the illustrious Sudarśanīśrī.
"Born through union with Sudarśana, she is the nourisher of virtuous vows.
Thus was the manifestation of the glory of Śivasukti told to me in the past; remember all that, for this wondrous world is composed of woman.
Moreover, O Lakṣmī, there were indeed tens of millions of other incarnations of mine as well;
I know them all, O Lakṣmī, according to the specific purpose for which each was performed by me. Listen now to another manifestation of mine in a different year.
In the seventeenth Kalpa of Brahmā, known as Aprajñāta,
and during the tenth Manvantara,
the world was then exceedingly oppressed by a great multitude of Daityas.
In ancient times, there was a great Daitya named Timiṅgila, who moved through the waters and could assume any form at will;
he dwelt on the island of Śrīśīla, which was entirely surrounded by water, in the domain of Varuṇa.
Likewise, others of that same kind, even those capable of assuming any form at will,
as well as crocodiles numbering in the tens of thousands, were dwelling there.
Men and women emerged from the water and came outside.
They dwell in great islands and in houses adorned with the splendor of precious gems;
yet they go abroad into various lands as meat-eaters,
seizing men and animals to devour them in the midst of waters or on islands.
And they, in human form, go upon the earth to cities and other places;
they carry off women, as well as boys and girls.
Moving through the sky, those makaras also go even to the peaks of great mountains.
Indeed, those mines of man-eaters forcibly carry away ascetics dwelling in forests, on mountains, or in caves, as well as sages, brahmins, beasts,
and flocks of birds; having led them to the island, they devour them.
In the midst of the ocean waters,
they forcibly devoured the fish and other aquatic creatures, as well as the men within their ships;
in this manner, humans and others were eaten for a hundred years.
A great clamor arose throughout all the regions of the world—
in the mountains, in the caves, and among the ascetics everywhere.
Fear of the Makaras seized them, and all living beings trembled.
In the presence of the powerful, no one at all went to offer protection.
Then, even the kings became agitated with fear on all sides. At that time, there was a great emperor, the sovereign Dharmavāhana.
He went through the sky to the edge of the ocean to fight in battle against the Makaras;
however, he was struck down by a shower of illusions from the sky by those who assumed many forms.
And that King Dharmavāhana died in the ocean as well.

Then others in the world fall into fear due to the battle of the sea-monsters (makaras). The strength of the makaras increases following the destruction of the king; they forcibly seize the wealth and women of those dwelling on the shores of the ocean. (58–59)
Boys, girls, and even cattle, adorned with ornaments and rich in garments,
enjoy themselves without fear as they flourish on all sides.
Then, those who were the regional kings (khaṇḍarāja) were also gradually [subdued] by them.
They were also seized individually by the flesh-eating makaras;
and islands, as well as regions resembling islands, were brought under their control.
Assuming various illusory forms, they enjoyed these territories as they pleased.
At that time, great atrocities occurred in every region;
the weak people wept, and men and women were violated.
Children whose wives and husbands had likewise been devoured were also eaten.
At that time, many became lineage-less due to the calamities caused by the sea-monsters (mākaras).
Thus, at the end of those hundred years, those sea-monsters indeed attained growth;
they were born in numbers reaching ten million, appearing everywhere like Rākṣasas.

These creatures dwell even on the banks of water, and though they possess strength, at times when they are weak, they enter the water instantly. In battles, human kings do not obtain victory through them.
Employing illusions and mantras, assuming many forms, and being exceedingly cruel,
they conquered kings and divided their kingdoms into fragments under their control. Then, at that time, the subjects suffered from the extreme tyranny of the Mākarakāsuras.
They could not endure what had been done; we [then] brought about the total destruction.
At that time, sacrifices were destroyed everywhere by them through the path of the sky;
even festivals and the abodes of the gods were destroyed on all sides.
Even gardens filled with fruits and flowers are being destroyed;
crops rich in grain are likewise ruined on every side.
Whatever in the world consists of jewels, all of that is being carried away by them.
Thus, when this calamity arose, the Mānavas repeatedly entreated me— the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the Imperishable—
and they worshipped me within their hearts with all the emotions born of their hearts.
The wretched, the helpless, the weak, and others prayed for protection.
Then, in that imperishable place, I heard their propitiation for the sake of destroying the Makaras and for the purpose of protecting Dharma.
Then, for the sake of protecting human beings, I too, equipped with weapons, quickly descended from the sky toward the earth in a celestial chariot along with you,
and swiftly reached Dvāradvīpa. ||75||
Indeed, I rendered that celestial chariot invisible there in an instant.
I assumed the form of a forest-dweller, and you likewise took on the form of a forest-dweller;
having assumed the appearance of an ascetic, I wandered through the forest.
Then those Makaras, having come from the island, carried me along with you to their own island;
thereupon, I beheld that island, adorned with settlements, villages, and cities.
Then those makaras came toward me with great excitement to devour me;
at that very moment, I hurled the Sudarśana discus,
which indeed struck them down and likewise consumed them with its flames of fire.
In the mere space of a ghaṭikā, the ocean was made devoid of makaras;
the makaras, sea-monsters, reptiles, and large fish fled,
and having become aquatic creatures [of that kind], they entered the abode of makaras.
At that time, I lived with you on an island as an ascetic.
Indeed, the cities were then empty.
Then the Daitya Mākareśa [emerged] from the midst of the waters for the sake of battle.
Having become fully prepared for battle, he approached with his army;
indeed, those makaras were cut down by me with the Sudarśana alone.
Seeing his defeat, the Daitya became intent on saving his own life.
He suddenly fled into the ocean and entered its deep bottom;
then the Daitya, possessing a thousand arms, a thousand heads, and endowed with a thousand feet, returned once more for the sake of battle. (85–86)
Furthermore, my Sudarśana discus was dispatched by me;
his many arms were indeed severed at that time, and he entered the ocean once more.
Then, I too entered the ocean.
Having searched for those Makara-asuras stationed in every region,
I destroyed them on all sides with the Sudarśana discus,
wherever those Makara-dānavas were located upon the earth. (88–89)
Then, at that opportune moment, I struck them all with the edge of my discus.
Thereupon, the Daitya Mākara, endowed with ten thousand arms,
ten thousand faces, and ten thousand feet, approached.
"It is my thought that his destruction must certainly be carried out;
then the calamity of the Makaras will come to an end. Then I entered into a pact with that wicked-souled Makara. (91–92)
When he had three thousand hands and three faces,
the Lord of Makaras fled and went into the ocean. At that time, O Lakṣmī, I too became a water-man along with you.

With a hundred thousand hands, a hundred thousand faces, a hundred thousand shields, and a hundred thousand weapons, and equipped with a hundred thousand nets, I entered the abode of the Makara. Seeing me, he assumed a massive form and fled in fear.
From one ocean to another, and from there to yet another ocean between them—
seeing me thus traveling upon his back,
he became utterly agitated with fear and, intent on saving his life, entered the Ocean of Milk.
I dispatched the Sudarśana discus for his death.
Following closely behind him, it blazed up and consumed him on all sides.
The entire ocean was agitated and the earth trembled repeatedly. (97–98)
Then, realizing his own impending death, he stood face-to-face for the sake of battle.
I gave that great-souled one a fight that was the very essence of justice;
yet, in whatever manner I struck him down, he became renewed.
Even Māra himself arises through illusion, assuming millions of forms.
At the end of the month, that asura was killed by me after giving battle in the ocean with my Sudarśana discus; hundreds of thousands of necks were severed.
Then, indeed, the kettledrums of the celestial dwellers resounded in the sky;
a rain of flowers fell, and the ocean honored me.
All the attendants of the omnipresent Lords and the liberated souls arrived.
The gods and humans also worshipped me, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
They worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person, who had assumed the form of a man in the water,
possessing a hundred thousand faces, a hundred thousand hands, and endowed with a hundred thousand weapons.
I am indeed the abode of water, white in color, tender, and shining like the moon; I am worshipped by the goddesses and gods of the waters.
Liberated from suffering, embodied beings have worshipped me, the Supreme Lord.
O beloved! At that time, I am myself the Supreme Lord Śrī Puruṣottama, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, appearing in the form of a human being in the water,
known by the name Anādi Śrī Jala-Nārāyaṇa.
They indeed worshipped you as the beginningless Jala-Nārāyaṇī.
Then, having emerged from the water, I took up residence on the surface of the earth at Śrīśīlika,
in the city of the Makaras on the island.
Then many of my attendants arrived there at that time.
Śrīdvīpa became my island situated on the shore of the ocean,
serving as a place for the practice of austerities by ascetics seeking liberation during that kalpa.
O Lakṣmī, remember him in the seventeenth year of Brahmā!
Just as there was the first Śvetadvīpa, so too shall there be one named Śrīdvīpa;
indeed, it shall become Śrīśīladvīpa for the sake of my dwelling there.
Likewise, that was the island of Jala-dvīpa, and it was also the abode of Śveta-Nārāyaṇa.
At that time, the people and the scriptures recounted this in many ways;
remember all of that, O Lakṣmī, for it is more ancient than the ancient.
This divine station, consisting of the sound *cakatkāra*, was acquired by me in the past.
Through reading, hearing, or remembering it, one shall attain liberation.
Likewise, thousands of other incarnations of mine have also appeared.
I know them all indeed, for I possess direct knowledge.
Therefore, on this earth, my devotees have been made Vaiṣṇavas by me, by my yogic attendants, as well as by sages, seers, and holy men.
From that, all creatures were born; they belong to Viṣṇu and have taken refuge in me.
The path to liberation was set forth, and sacrifices, offerings, and other rites came into being.
The subjects became happy, and human beings were also free from fear.

Indeed, Vaiṣṇavas devoted to my worship are seen upon the earth. Men and women, as well as those traveling through the sky, come from all directions to behold me; thus Śrīdvīpa has become the bestower of liberation.

"Then, O beloved, I dwelt on that island of Śrī-Suśīlikā until the end of the kalpa; thereafter, I returned to my own imperishable abode. Thus ends the [section] concerning the beginning of the month of Makara in the seventeenth year of Brahmā, within the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, following the prayer for the protection of the inhabitants of the earth who had become women, by the beginningless Nārāyaṇa in his female and male forms.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Jala-Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Destroying the Daityas," etc.
Chapter 14. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 15.
[The Author: Chapter 16.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivajanyā! O Śrī! Then, during the year of Brahmā...
In the eighteenth [chapter], titled "The State of Dissolution," within the twelfth Kalpa,
during the eleventh Manvantara, indeed due to the power of the decline of the Yugas,
when the virtuous dharmas have perished and likewise the initiation of the virtuous has come to an end; (1–2)
When the path to liberation was obstructed and the rites for the gods and ancestors had fallen into disuse,
Hari himself appeared together with Revā in the excellent home of the elder Brāhmaṇa Vaṣaḍ to re-establish them once again.
There was a brahmin named Vaṣaṭkāra, devoted to his vows.
(4) A practitioner of austerities whose entire property had been seized by wicked atheists, this devotee of mine, being oppressed, abandoned his village and went to the forest. (5)
He always worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari,
with fruits, roots, leaves, flowers, as well as with meditative contemplations and mental offerings.
Every day at dawn, he indeed worships me with these very materials.
His wife was likewise a virtuous woman, devoted to the practice of japa.
She constantly worshipped you, the eternal Śrī Satī Lakṣmī, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, according to the prescribed rites, and indeed fed you with excellent fruit.
They respectfully offer water, flowers, and even leaves;
they both always perform kīrtana and bhajana for me.
At midday and likewise in the evening, they remain devoted to meditation upon me.
Those two, indeed, were always dwellers in the forest and were truly bodiless (videhin).
O beloved, he for whom worldly splendors and enjoyments do not exist anywhere for the sake of the body, and whose splendors are solely for the sake of Hari— he would be bodiless (videha).
Thus living, childless yet resting in happiness,
they reached a certain old age while dwelling among the trees in the forest.
As they lived in this manner, a desire for sons and daughters arose within them.
In the mind of Vaṣaṭkāra, the desire for a son arose;
and in the mind of Svadhāvatī, the desire for a daughter arose.
For a mother indeed desires a daughter who shall be her companion in all affairs. (13–14)
The father indeed questioned his son, who was a helper in all affairs;
both were intent on the duties of the household and possessed a longing for sons and daughters.
At the conclusion of the worship, they both requested of me their heart's desire.
O Lakṣmī! In this world, people indeed repeatedly give rise to three kinds of longing:
the longing for the world, the longing for wealth, and the longing for sons.
For those who are devotees of Nārāyaṇa, the longing for the world is completely stilled.
From this, devotees will certainly attain the supreme abode through devotion;
moreover, the desire for wealth among virtuous and contented people subsides,
since for the saints, the acquisition of water, food, and clothing is merely for the sake of sustenance.
The desire for sons subsides for those who possess sons as well as for the wise. (19) Creditors are born in the form of children for the sake of recovering their wealth;
when such children do not exist, there is indeed happiness. (20)
Indeed, there is suffering during the conception of offspring, as well as at their birth, protection, nourishment, marriage, and expenditure, and likewise during illness;
nevertheless, for those who come into contact with the words of the world, [this is so]. (21)
"He is destitute; he is sonless; he is without lineage; likewise, he is all alone.
For those who lack tolerance for such words, suffering arises from their desires, as they are overcome by illusion (māyā).
The devotee devoid of knowledge has value in the worldly realm;
but for my devotee who possesses knowledge, everything within me is burnt away.
Indeed, for one by whom all that is illusory has been burnt, what remains here in this world?
Through a son, through the work of the world, through sovereignty, or through worldly power—
this desire for a material son leads to bondage. Indeed, it is said that for the Brahmin Vaṣaṭkāra, this very desire resulted in a son.
"But may she come within my range and become my daughter;
and may this Lakṣmī, the daughter of Svadhāvatī, also become my girl.
Thus did their two auspicious resolves regarding me remain.
Those two divine resolutions were always free from the bonds of illusion.
Therefore, let those two auspicious ones remain; for that reason, I have performed meditation upon them.
They are to be established as my parents for the sake of establishing righteousness.
In order to fulfill those two forms of devotion and those two intentions,
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, together with you,
reflected upon that matter and went to that forest, where I became a wandering ascetic.
"I have become your guest, and you are my caravan-companion and a mendicant.
(31) Thus they went to the dwelling of those two devoted ones in the forest—a city [of hermits]—where there were two ascetics with matted hair, clad in rags and bark, and of austere appearance. (32)
Two brahmins named Nārāyaṇa, wearing garlands and following the dharma of holy men, arrived as mendicants at midday.
Then, with joyful hearts, they offered them a gracious welcome.

Then they both gave us water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), a seat, the honey-mixture (madhuparka), fruits and other items, as well as pure water and auspicious words. "Alms have been accepted by me," [he said], and then, "They have also been accepted by you. (34–35)
The two of them massaged their feet and offered them worship, saying:
"Blessed are we that today we have obtained the service of these two holy men.
Service to the virtuous destroys sin and bestows divine merit."
She is the giver of enjoyment and the giver of liberation, the fulfiller of all intentions.
(37) Her service is like the wish-fulfilling creeper, equal to the wish-granting tree in bestowing fruits, and like the thought-gem and the cow of plenty for the virtuous. (38)
That house where saintly persons, who are dear to Lord Hari, come to dwell,
is always a sacred pilgrimage site— whether it be a forest or a city.
Other holy places purify one only over time and according to their own power.
A holy place of pilgrimage quickly purifies those people who serve it.
Where there is the arrival of a saintly person, there the arrival of Lord Hari is certain;
where there is the arrival of Hari, there the arrival of the liberated souls is certain.
Where there is the arrival of liberation, there indeed is likewise the arrival of the scriptures of liberation;
where there is the arrival of liberation, there the arrival of devotion is also certain.
Where there is the arrival of devotion, there the arrival of dharma is also certain.
And where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is present together with the virtuous, there the attainment of knowledge and dispassion is certain,
as is the constant and eternal presence of Lakṣmī, Kamalā, Śrī, Siddhi, and Dhruvā. (43–44)
Where Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa is, there are the sacrifices and the vows;
all austerities and all the gods are also there.
Where Nārāyaṇa, together with the virtuous, partakes of fruits, water, and other offerings—
There indeed the gods and the ancestors enjoy the three worlds.
Today, our dwelling in the forest has truly become fruitful—far exceeding even our kingdom—and it brings us joy for the sake of the arrival of these two virtuous ones. (46–47)
Today our childlessness has dissolved through the service of the virtuous;
today our poverty has become a source of fruit for a great purpose.
Today our life has become meaningful—a truly noble existence.
Today our mental dispositions have been fulfilled and confirmed here; we both consider that even time itself shall attain sanctity today. Auspicious omens alone arise from your arrival. (49–50)
Through your teaching, our auspicious understandings and limbs are now throbbing with life.
May you two, who are worthy of worship, dwell here; we shall serve you with devotion.
By attending upon the virtuous, embodied beings cross over the ocean of worldly existence.

And here in this secluded forest, by your dwelling, our association with the virtuous will become beautiful and a source of joy every day. This leaf-hut is indeed at the foot of the Bakula tree. (52–53)
"A beautiful hut, which wards off cold and heat, has been offered by you both;
however, we shall construct another hut for ourselves that provides shelter.
Having spoken thus, the pair of brahmins fell at our feet.
Then I said to them: "May it always be well with you both;
may there be freedom from disease, prosperity, and eternal happiness.
We two are forest-dwellers here, not inhabitants of a single fixed place. (55–56)
Free from all attachments and dwelling in a secluded hut,
we remain here milking the cows whenever, by the will of fate, there occurs a gathering of devoted Brahmins such as yourselves. (57)
Nevertheless, in the house of some pure ascetics devoted to the Lord, a partiality toward us has arisen quite by chance;
with affection, our hospitality was accepted, and likewise our welcome was received. (58–59)
"Having received your command, we shall go to another forest; may there be peace for you.
Then, shedding tears, they both spoke with joy:
"That dwelling where there is association with the virtuous is a true home, not one made of leaves."
Where there is the company of the virtuous, that is the true dwelling, not merely a place upon the earth. (61) Life lived together with the virtuous is true life, not merely eating.
One should always serve the virtuous for the sake of happiness; no other auspicious duty need be performed. (62)
"We two, being of virtuous nature, shall go to the state of experiencing [the Absolute];
or rather, let us dwell here, for we shall surely obtain alms.
