At your arrival, the trees rejoice along with the forest birds.
Upon your arrival, the creepers blossom with beautiful flowers;
(64) upon your arrival, all the limbs of our bodies, enriched by the heart, experience unprecedented and blissful joys. (65)
"And so, you two shall remain right here as my servants.
When I had spoken thus to them, they both asked, "Why is such a persistent insistence being made by you two here? Tell us your true hearts' desire. (66)
There in the forest, those two always spoke thus while alone:
"We shall make our dwelling here, for you are already established in this place. Indeed, there would be a shared residence with you, for the company of the virtuous is difficult to find. (67–68)
For a householder who has a wife, dwelling alone in the forest is indeed fearful; therefore, he should remain there with a companion.
Or rather, the residence of two householders together within the forest is truly auspicious.
The residence of these three, as well as the additional ones, is indeed most excellent.
For women endowed with the virtues of faithful wives, there shall be assistance in the observance of dharma; for virtuous women are the refuge of happiness.
"Therefore, we choose to dwell here with you both, who are so devoted to righteous conduct. Indeed, without your presence, peace will not prevail.
Then I said, "So be it," and they both assented, saying "Om."
They quickly attained happiness and were filled with joy.
Having performed worship, we two remained comfortably in their dwelling;
in the evening, the time passed happily in conversation that awakened them to the true Dharma.
Having performed their twilight prayers during the night and having engaged in conversation concerning Hari, the four of them slept; and at the end of the night, both groups likewise slept.
Then, at the auspicious time of the Brāhma-muhūrta, they indeed awoke.
And to the Brahmin and his Brahmin wife, we two appeared in a dream;
we, Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa in person, have come here as ascetics.
Though I was born in the form of a son, you became a daughter in the dream.
That [vision] in the form of a child was indeed obtained by the two twice-born ones as a pair;
having received it, the two brahmins were greatly delighted, and then the dream ceased.
They both then awoke, having become invisible.
Then both of them were unable to see [the child] within their own hut.
Not seeing him, they experienced a great wonder and were filled with joy.
At that time, O Lakṣmī, we two saw Vāyudeva indeed situated within the womb.
Having summoned them, they both granted the command for conception and the vision of the embryo,
so that the woman might indeed become pregnant according to the prescribed manner;
and Vāyu likewise acted thus, dwelling constantly within the womb of the embryo.

Just as a pregnant woman displays her belly, so did she show her abdomen. At that time, when the appointed hour had arrived, we two remained within that support— that is, within the womb— in an invisible form, indeed as twins.
When Vāyu emerged from the opening of the womb, there appeared two twins bearing the conch,
discus, mace, and lotus;
both a girl and a boy were born before him like two fires.
At that time, although they were not born from a womb, they appeared as if they were indeed born from a womb.
A rain of flowers fell from the sky, released by the gods; drums resounded, and a great festival took place in the forest upon his birth.
The sages also gathered there for the purpose of seeing us;
then many kinds of auspicious events occurred there for the people and for us two. Having undergone all the purificatory rites, we were twins in every respect.
We both grew up there in that forest as celibate students (brahmacārins),
devoted to the dharma of the virtuous and endowed with the initiation of the virtuous, having performed our duties ourselves;
even though we were invested with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), we remained like two unborn beings right there.
Then we taught the dharmas of the virtuous who seek the stage of renunciation—both to those dwelling in the forest and to those dwelling in villages:
namely, the renunciation of Kāmadeva and the avoidance of the tongue’s relish for flavors. (90)
The abandonment of deluded views, the avoidance of affection and touch;
the renunciation of unstable sounds and the like, the avoidance of unnatural odors; non-attachment to possessions, and the complete relinquishing of passion and hatred. (9.1–9.2)
Taking only as much food and water as is necessary for sustenance, having no fixed abode, observing silence,
renouncing ritual actions, and surrendering the self entirely to Hari;
practicing austerity as dharma, self-restraint, and the constant abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās).
The abandonment of the notions of "mine" and "I," as well as the realization that the body is not distinct [from the Self];
the refraining from all forms of malice, forgiveness, endurance, and compassion; constant contemplation of the supreme self, and the worship of the Supreme Lord. (94–95)
Living in accordance with the state of Brahman, the abandonment of grief and delusion, contentment when what is unasked for is obtained, as well as straightforwardness;
wearing saffron-colored garments, and likewise using the hands as a bowl.
Just as there is no grasping for space, so may one dwell in the forest at ease.
(9.7) Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Śīlanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
Even the mere recitation of this and devotion toward the Supreme Self [bring liberation]. (9.8)
"In this way, indeed, the virtuous conduct of men and women—
which brings happiness to human beings— was taught by us both from the people at that time;
[it was taught] by the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self."
Then, by me and by you, the eternal dharmas of the virtuous were set in motion—
by the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Śīlanārāyaṇa,
accompanied by you, the beginningless Mistress Nārāyaṇī. (100–101)
Indeed, through me, your uterine brother who possesses a virtuous form, and through you, my uterine sister who are a virtuous and noble wife,
millions of human beings have been born as saintly ones abiding in good conduct.
And millions of virtuous women were born, devoted to moral conduct and vows.
Then sacrifices arose, as well as various religious observances, and also my worship, my adoration, and my temples. (103–104)
The restraint of moral conduct, as well as rites for the gods and ancestors,
service to sacred fords, and service to the virtuous— all these dharmas were set in motion by me at that time, through my beginningless and glorious practice of *śīla*, O Nārāyaṇa.
"I know everything, O Lakṣmī! Remember that very manifestation [of mine].
(106) Furthermore, many other incarnations of mine occurred there at that time, brought about by the necessity of specific tasks; I alone know them, and no one else. (107)
Thus have I described to you this manifestation for the sake of virtuous conduct;
through its recollection, hearing, and even reading, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Until the end of the kalpa, that was our dwelling place.
For the sake of the Dharma, accompanied by ten million virtuous ones in the form of holy men,
his branches of disciples and grand-disciples then flourished upon the earth.
Having then granted liberation to his mother and father, he departed to his own imperishable state.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Śīlanārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Establishing the Dharma of the Holy Ones in the Eighteenth Year of Brahmā," in the third section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 15] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 16.
[The Author: Chapter 17.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! After that, in the year of Brahmā...
In the thirteenth Manvantara, during the sixty-fourth Kalpa named Sākṣātkṛt,
Rudra, who dwells on Kailāsa, indeed went to the earth for the sake of visiting sacred fords (tīrthas). While wandering, he arrived at Viṣṇutīrtha on Mount Cāṭula.
On that very mountain, there was a delightful and excellent river named Śāradā,
a daughter of Brahmā; on its bank,
having drunk the auspicious water and sprinkled himself, he sat down and became absorbed in meditation for a moment.
He meditated upon Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of all, the Supreme Sovereign. (4) Just then, a boar of intoxicated speed arrived from the forest;
running with his head toward Śambhu, Hara, he struck him like an anthill. (5)
Having looked up and seen Hara clearly covered in ash,
Śaṅkara rose quickly from his meditation; but seeing Vārāha,
he suddenly became enraged, his brow knitting and his eyes turning red.
From her arose the great *tāmasa* asura Vyāghrānala, who resembled a mountain and was enveloped in garlands of blazing fire;
impelled by Śambhu, he destroyed the boar in a mere instant. (7–8)
Taking up a boar’s hide at the command of Hara, Vyāghrānala requested food from Hara for the sake of pacifying his digestive fire.
Śambhu, however, said: "The multitude of aquatic creatures dwelling within the ocean—"
"Indeed, food has been given by me; go to the edge of the water.
Vyāghrānala, an exceedingly powerful attendant capable of assuming any form at will, fearlessly approached the shore of the ocean for the sake of satisfying his hunger.
He devoured aquatic creatures— makaras, tortoises, and whales—
and as he consumed his food,
his digestive fire blazed forth and increased in its power to digest.
And likewise, his body grew like a mountain;
having become ten yojanas in width, he entered the ocean.
And day after day, he devoured many aquatic creatures.
At the end of a month, he became a hundred yojanas in extent;
at the end of a year, he became a thousand yojanas in length.
Having entered the great ocean, he drinks up the water with his breath.
Tens of millions of fish and other creatures enter his belly and are cooked there;
furthermore, all the water is consumed by fire.
Then, after time has passed, he expands to a width of ten thousand yojanas.
Vyāghrānala became [the fire] in the ocean, drinking it day and night;
he dries up the ocean for a thousand yojanas, making it waterless.
In this manner, all the oceans were indeed drunk by him one after another.
The entire great ocean, born from the waters of the earth, was gradually drunk up by him.
Indeed, without water, clouds do not arise from the ocean-circle; within the oceans there is fire, and from that fire, Vyāghra emerged. (3.16.20)
The cavities of the oceans became composed of fire, and the earth likewise became so;
it was parched and devoid of water, and the waters within its womb were consumed by the fire.
The entire surface of the earth became dry, and a cessation of rain occurred.
Most embodied beings died, but the yogis, having realized the three worlds, indeed dissolved them within meditative absorption (samādhi). The sages departed for heaven;
an untimely dissolution occurred upon the earth through the fire of the tigers.
In the absence of water, the tiger-like fire indeed devours the mud and other things from the depths;
and due to the loss of water everywhere, the earth has become parched.
The rivers, as if dead, have gone for refuge to Śrī Hari.
Protect, protect us, O compassionate Lord, from the tiger and the most fierce fire!
(25) The aquatic creatures devour the mud and the waters;
an untimely dissolution has occurred, and because of that, we are as if dead. (26)
This terrible [fire] is now occurring, extending for ten thousand yojanas;
increasing in its length, it will swallow the entire universe.
You must bring it to an end; we have come to you for refuge.
Indeed, when the alkaline liquid was drunk, all others were likewise drunk up in pieces;
there is no other besides you who can bring about the end of this asura.
Everything is protected by you at all times, as if it were your own offspring.
We are all indeed oceans, the sons of Rādhā, whose very nature is water.
Our father is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, the Blessed Lord and husband of Rādhikā, who is the very incarnation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (3.16.30)
"The Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the Gopīs, the Lord of Śrī, the Sovereign—O Puruṣottama, we are your sons; protect us! Thus was I entreated by the seven oceans at that time.
O Mahālakṣmī! Together with you, I became the object of the oceans' gaze, bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, svastika, banner, and trident.
Worshipped and saluted by them, I was honored with offerings of sweet water.

Then, I was born as the son of the ocean from the wife of Miṣṭoda, Puṣkariṇī; though I was but a newborn child, I immediately became a youth. At that time, O Śivasatyeshvari, you were the daughter of Puṇḍarīka.
And you became a sovereign of the earth, distinguished by all-encompassing sovereignty and beauty;
by name, Śrī Puṇḍarīkaśrī, the bringer of all auspiciousness.
Then I too remembered my vehicle that travels upon the waters.
Then, from the sweet water, there emerged a wondrous aquatic horse:
winged, possessing a trunk, and also having webbed feet; capable of assuming any form at will, and endowed with the power of stilling the flow of its breath through meditative concentration.
The horse is like the wind in strength, like the ocean in size, and like lightning in speed;
it is invincible, mountain-like in stature, and white in color. It can travel over land, through water, and through the sky, and possesses the powers of both the gross and the subtle.

He is a speaker of all languages, possesses a divine body, and is indivisible; he is accompanied by ten thousand women and is a treasure-trove of skill in battle. He is endowed with the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) and is adorned with jewels and pearls.
The luster of a lamp within water, yet possessing brilliant light even in darkness;
naturally endowed with firm armor and carrying quivers that produce weapons;
rich with filaments from which nectar flows, and adorned with a sword that severs death.
Nourished and richly endowed with copper-colored feathers on all his limbs, he bowed down to me.
With the sound of his joyful wings beating, with praises, the spreading of his wings,
and with high-pitched tremors of speed, he offered me a welcome.
I worshipped him in the form of a vehicle so that there might be no obstacle;
for the sake of victory, I placed my skillful hand upon his back.
Furthermore, he was made to drink nectar and likewise marked with a tilaka on his forehead.
O Lakṣmī! When he was urged for the sake of a journey and dispatched for the sake of battle, his sound of neighing indeed went to the abodes of the guardians of the quarters;
the entire sky trembled, so what must have been the state of the earth? || 46-47 ||
The mountains, the oceans, the water-deities, and the Mothers;
Varuṇa, the rivers, and the streams—all have assembled with me for the sake of battle.
Accompanied by their respective mounts, they have arrived as summoned by me.
O Lakṣmī! Having mounted a great white elephant born from the palm of Viṣṇu’s hand, the king of the gods arrived there;
as did he named Pauṇḍraka, who was black in color and born from the vital energy of Rudra. (3.16.49–50)
Then Dharmarāja arrived,
having mounted a buffalo that was dark-hued, born from the ear-wax of Brahmā, and named Jaladhī.
Varuṇa also arrived there, having mounted a porpoise.
Likewise, the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) stands mounted upon a beautiful, winged man shaped like a mountain and resembling the axle of a cart-wheel;
he is likewise mounted upon Gandharvas, lords of serpents, and white bulls. (52–53)
The Rudras arrived there for the purpose of destroying the fierce Asuras.
And the Moon came, mounted upon a chariot adorned with five hundred swans;
likewise, the Ādityas arrived, riding on chariots drawn by horses and camels.
The Vasus arrived mounted on elephants, and the Yakṣas with men as their vehicles;
the Kinnaras were mounted on serpents, and likewise the two Aśvins were mounted on horses;
and the powerful Maruts also arrived, seated upon antelopes.
The Gandharvas were mounted upon their musical instruments, and Agni was positioned on the back of a ram;
the oceans were mounted upon sea-monsters, and the gods traveled in chariots and celestial palaces;
Brahmā was mounted upon a swan, and Viṣṇu had Garuḍa as his vehicle.
The sages were seated upon their thrones, as were the ancestors who ride upon merit;
the Earth was borne by Śeṣa, and Śeṣa was borne by the Tortoise;
the Tortoises were borne by the clouds, and the clouds were borne by the winds. (58–59)
Mountains with wings, lightning borne upon clouds,
and rivers with their waves— armed and ready— they arrived together. Then, the celestial musicians of the gods sounded their instruments.
Then the roars of the gods, which bestow strength,
were heard; Vyāghrānala, hearing those cries reaching to the ends of the quarters,
became enraged and, unable to endure them, repeatedly slapped his arms with haste.
He also released loud bursts of laughter as he struck their thighs with his palms;
then, leaping upward and beholding the gods standing ready for battle,
he— deluded by pride— swiftly seized his heavy mace.
Filling the sky with his body, he approached me and the gods.
Reaching as high as the heavens, ten thousand *yojanas* in length, and as broad as the ocean, Vyāghrānala came for the sake of battle. (64–65)
He waged war against Indra and Dharmarāja; he waged war against Varuṇa and Dhanada.
Likewise, he also fought with Candra and the Rudras, as well as with the Ādityas.
Having fainted, the powerful one fought again and again;
the powerful one also fought with the yakṣas, the kiṃnaras, and the winds.
He fought repeatedly with Agni, with Brahmā, and with Viṣṇu.
Assuming a thousand forms, he fought most fiercely with the mountains and the lightning bolts, and he also fought with the gods;
rushing along the path of the sky, he dragged the entire circle of the planets.
Causing the stars to fall, he rushed forward and even fought;
at that time, the firmament appeared to tremble, and the winds, shaken, utterly abandoned their steadiness and strength. (3.16.70–71)
Then, by the trembling of the earth, they abandoned their positions;
even the courses of the stars became obstructed.
Even Vijaya’s confidence fell into doubt regarding both [outcomes]. (72)
And Pralaya rejoiced greatly upon seeing his own future prosperity.
All the weapons, having entered the body of the asura, emerged from his pores like travelers reaching the further shore of a path. (73–74)
At that time, not even the touch of weapons cut into his body or its fetal parts;
he remained such as he was and fought with extreme vigor.
Having made his very life-breaths the stakes and having set destruction as the wager, he then fought.
Or, having resolved upon his destruction, Vṛkāsana fought with a mace, a lance, a spear, a noose, and a sword;
with a scimitar, projectiles, mountains, stones, and the like. (76–77)

Then that asura Vṛkānala waged war in this manner, striking with a trident, a discus, a staff, and likewise with arrows; he also struck with his chest, his arms, and blows from elephants and other mounts.
And even the gods, though powerful, underwent great exhaustion.
Then, O Lakṣmī, having resolved that he was difficult to overcome,
I released at him the Sudarśana discus, which possesses a hundred thousand edges.
Fierce as the fire of universal dissolution and burning both heaven and the netherworld,
that great form increased in size and consumed him on all sides.
Then, indeed, millions of fragments fell from the body of the tiger-fire.
Even those tigers and fires that were severed and separated become, moreover, asuras equal to him in that battle;
for the discus, swiftly commanded by me, surely burns them as well. (82–83)
Then the entire atmosphere became like the sky of fire,
or indeed it was as if pervaded by the fire of universal dissolution, like the Brahmāstra weapon itself.
At that time, you, whose nature is Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), were commanded by me.

Assuming the form of a *mohinī* for the sake of inducing stupor in the asura, she arrived in the sky in his presence; the asura fell into a state of delusion. Abandoning his countless forms in the battle, he came to seize you. (85–86)
As soon as you embraced him, the entire fire of Vyāghrānala was indeed drawn inward by your own fire;
thus Vyāghrānala remained without radiance and without his fiery element.
Having become paralyzed, he was then split asunder by Sudarśana;
he fell into the great ocean in a hundred and even a thousand pieces.
Fragments of his body became the sword-blades upon the sea.
And they became lifeless in the midst of the water like mountains;
thus, O Lakṣmī, when the tiger-fire was extinguished by the roar of the clouds,
the oceans appeared in the sky and attained a state of moisture.
Then, from my body, due to that exertion, streams of water emerged;
as they increased, they filled the oceans.
From the sky there fell a rain consisting of flowers and unbroken grains of rice as offerings for victory.
The gods were filled with joy and worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī;
and I, in turn, honored the gods. O Lakṣmī! Having accomplished their task, the gods then departed for their own abodes, and you likewise attained a state of invisibility.
"Even my horse, your father's mount, has arrived at Miṣṭoda together with you.
Having escorted you to your home,
I too have come to Miṣṭoda after paying homage to the gods."
Then, on this earth, I became renowned by the name Anādi-Śrī-Vārdhi-Nārāyaṇa;
and Puṇḍarīka, your father, was my own. (96)

He gave his daughter according to the prescribed rites to my inner self, who is worthy, the Lord of lords, the Supreme Soul worshipped by the gods and others. Then, having married you— who possess the splendor of a white lotus— according to the sacred law, [he departed].
Having obtained the horse Uccaiḥśravas, I wandered through the three worlds and remained until the end of the kalpa for the sake of protecting dharma.
I am that beginningless Śrī Hari, the eternal Supreme Brahman.
I know all of this; my supreme manifestation is such that my incarnations have indeed arisen there in countless numbers.
[This occurs] from reciting, hearing, glorifying, or even remembering [this].
"All [these forms] bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and are devoted to wonders.
O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! O Daughter of Śiva! Remember this marvel!

(102). Thus ends the manifestation of the beginningless Śrī Vārdhinārāyaṇa for the purpose of destroying the demon Vyāghrānala, who was fierce, during the nineteenth year of the Creator in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
The sixteenth chapter, titled "Description," [Chapter 16].
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga),
Chapter 17.
[The Author: Chapter 18.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, and [hear] of my manifestation thereafter.
In the first kalpa, during the year known as Sṛṣṭimāna of the Creator,
when the first Manu had begun his reign, Brahmā abandoned his sleep and, at dawn, went to bathe in the celestial river while reflecting deeply. (1–2)
"Today, what kind of creation shall I bring forth that will beautify the three worlds?
I shall create one like myself, entirely devoid of the sense of duality.
Having thus resolved, he bathed, performed his twilight devotions, and went home.
Having performed his daily worship, he entered the chamber of creation.
He touched the engine of creation and inspected the womb-engine, [thinking]:
"May the entire four-faced creation be brought forth today."
As he was thus forming this resolution, all the great sages and twice-born ones became like him, each possessing four faces;
and likewise, all the gods also became auspicious beings with four faces.
Also humans, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Sādhyas;
what are males, animals, birds, and reptiles;
and embodied beings born from sweat, from eggs, and from wombs. (7–8)
And the aquatic creatures arise from the *kalala* stage; those born from mud, those produced from leaves,
those arising from grass, those emerging from fissures, and those originating from the netherworld (*pātāla*) and elsewhere—
all these, O Four-faced One, have indeed been born from the creative resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of Brahmā.
The Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and likewise the Āsuras;
the Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Bhūtas—all became four-faced.
By Brahmā, by the Pitṛs, by the gods, and by men who were preeminent among devotees.
In every context of discourse, I am described as four-faced;
indeed, the Vedas declare that all are four-faced.
All liberated souls are four-faced, and all lords are four-faced.
In this manner, the storytellers imagined [the situation] as if it were their own.
(13) Then, wherever the Brahmanical seers, the Sādhyas, the virtuous, and the celibate students gathered in the storytelling hall and debated on my account, (14)
Some say that the Blessed One remains with a thousand heads;
others say that the Blessed One remains with innumerable heads;
and still others then declare that he remains with faces on every side.
And others at that time said, "The Blessed Lord indeed exists as one-headed;
he is four-faced. Others spoke thus:
"As we are, so is he; as Hari is, so is the Unborn (Aja)."
"As Brahmā is, so are all the great sages and the gods;
as all human beings are, so is Hari.
Thus some spoke there, and such was the debate that took place.
For the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion on this matter, many disputes arose.
(19) Then, by the sages, the proud ones, and the gods, acting in concert upon the earth, an assembly was convened on the northern bank of the Suvarṇagaṅgā. (20)
There, the foremost of the twice-born, the bull-like sage Śrautarṣi, asked: "Of what nature is that Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman, who is thus worshipped as the Sovereign?
Then those followers of the Vedas, who uphold the authority of the Veda, replied:
"The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Others then spoke of that Hari, the Lord of the lords of gods, saying:
"He has hands and feet everywhere; he has eyes, heads, and faces on every side."
The Lord of Śrī, the soul of all, who possesses ears everywhere, abides there as the Supreme;
others call him Hari, the eternal Supreme Lord,
devoid of qualities, formless, actionless, and free from material form.
Then others spoke to him, who had four faces and appeared as they themselves did:
"Brahmā and Hari abide in the imperishable abode as one-headed, two-armed, two-footed, two-eyed, and two-eared. (25–26)
Then others said at that time: "Certainly not, certainly not so;
he is indeed the three-eyed Hari, the Supreme Lord, existing eternally.
When such deliberation arose, no final decision was reached there.
Then Brahmā spoke regarding the propitiation of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow:
"Of what nature indeed is Hari so that he may become the object of our worship?
We have been propitiating that Janārdana for a long time. (28–29)
Then the divine Blessed One will likewise become visible;
then all of them, having gathered together on the bank of the Golden River,
[shall perform] the primary form of sacrifice consisting of japa, augmented by great devotion.
"O beloved, let this be my sphere of activity," they said, and they began the propitiation of me.
They performed for me that propitiation for a thousand divine measures;
thereafter, they performed the oblation consisting of the concluding rite of completion.
They celebrated a truly grand festival consisting of congregational chanting (kīrtana),
as well as acts of charity and feasting, preceded by dancing and singing.
This was for the fulfillment of their spiritual aspirations and for the definitive realization of My form.
And in order to bestow the fruit of devotion, I then became perceptible to him.
First, a supreme light consisting of the ether of consciousness, composed of a mass of splendor, was seen there, dense on all sides. (34–35)
It is shoreless, invisible, impenetrable, and of a single form;
it overwhelms the splendor of infinite suns, moons, fires, and planets.
Then, there [within it], were innumerable beings, shining with countless distinct radiances.
Emerging from one spot, multitudes of rays, each equal to a parārdha in number,
were seen on all sides— below, above, and in every direction. And in that place, there was a pure, cool, and pleasant state visible beyond the horizon.
A heart-pleasing, irreproachable, and all-pervasive veil of splendor was seen as a circular fringe surrounding the root;
within its center appeared a mine of affection and love, enriched with gentle smiles.
Indeed, she was divine, surpassing the pride of form among countless beauties.
Her singular body possessed one face, two eyes, and two ears;
it had one head, two hands, and two feet, and was exceedingly radiant. (3.17.40–41)
She appeared beautiful, full of bliss, and enchanting;
her hair was curly, glossy, shimmering, and endowed with a radiant luster.
She wore a crown adorned with glittering golden stars.
Adorned with excellent golden earrings in the shape of makaras encrusted with jewels;
her auspicious face radiant with the luster of ten million moons and graced by a gentle smile; her full chest resplendent with rows of golden necklaces. 43–44.
Abounding in the splendor of arms like serpents, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem and necklaces,
marked with the Śrīvatsa sign, and beautifully adorned with armlets;
richly endowed with golden bracelets and graced by the conch, discus, and other emblems.
Clad in yellow garments, she is adorned with a mantle and bodice of yellow and red;
she is equipped with a golden girdle and beautified by golden anklets;
she is joined with a golden chain and resplendent with golden armlets.
Her fingertips were adorned with rings set with golden bands;
she shone with hands marked by the fish, trident, banner, bow, arrow, and swastika;
and she was auspicious, graced with a pair of lips resembling the ripe bimba fruit.
Her eyes were as restless as fish and as broad as lotus petals;
her nose resembled a sesame flower, and her cheeks possessed the luster of two moons.
With the power of her two eyebrows—worthy of drawing in ten million Cupids—she captivated all. (3.17.50)
Less than sixteen years of age, yet adorned with a line of beard;
with well-developed shoulders and hands as soft and delicate as land-lotuses (sthalapadma);
richly radiant with the hue of lac-dye, her thighs were as beautiful as the trunk of an elephant. (51)
Soft as a *śirīṣa* flower, radiant with moon-like nails,
adorned with the three folds of the abdomen and a deep navel, overflowing with all bliss, lotus-eyed, peaceful, and beautiful with wrists like lotus buds. (52–53)
Her knees were beautifully rounded and well-proportioned, and her shanks were straight and upright;
her hips, which were the abode of all desires, were exceedingly enchanting;
she was endowed with every fragrance, beauty, and sweetness.
Filled with universal affection, virtuous conduct, magnanimity, and friendship;
a treasury of the wonders of all sovereign qualities, virtues, and powers;
you are resplendent with Lakṣmī, enriched by the adornment of every ornament. (55–56)
Accompanied by many attendants, served by circles of liberated ones,
and saluted by female emancipated beings, my form was seen;
it was graced by Lakṣmī, who possessed a single head and was radiant with every kind of ornament.
She was fanned with a beautiful, divine fan held in the left hand,
and she was gazed upon by Śrī with lovely lotus garlands,
as well as with eyes that know the inner secrets of the eyes.
Beheld with wonder by all the gods and others, for she was indeed unprecedented—
the eternal form of the primordial Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then they all worshipped me, their Lord, having bowed down before me in that manner.
Seeing me alone with a single head, they reached a supreme conclusion;
the gods and others indeed offered praise and then performed the lustration rite (*nīrājana*).
And I instructed them directly concerning how I truly am.
O gods and others, may you here hear me in my true form:
I am eternally two-armed in the imperishable abode that is beyond the supreme;
I have one face, a divine form, and I assume manifold bodies by my own will.

I may have four arms, or a hundred arms, or a thousand hands; likewise, I may possess various kinds of faces, assuming such forms as are required for the accomplishment of my purpose. Indeed, diverse manifestations of my own nature come into being by my own will.
Having accomplished the appropriate task, I shall withdraw that body.
O Supreme Lord, having been propitiated by you for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion,
I am here before you in my true form and within your range of perception.
This is my true nature, which should be worshipped incessantly.
Indeed, that form of mine does not undergo dissolution even during the destruction of infinite creations, nor does it ever become invisible. (67–68)
"May you hold this in your hearts and worship it without interruption;
may you honor and praise this eternal and auspicious form of mine.
Then, I shall indeed become invisible to you who look upon me here. (69)
"Abandoning all dispute, worship me always in this manner.
When the gods, humans, and great sages had spoken thus, mental resolves arose within them to establish me upon the earth. (3.17.70–71)
They said to me, "O Supreme Lord, indeed for the sake of liberating embodied beings, please always establish your residence in the world of men;
for through service to you, the path of dharma and liberation shall belong to embodied beings. (72)
"O Śrī Puruṣottama, show mercy and do this!
(73) Then I reflected with compassion upon the welfare of embodied beings, thinking:
"May ultimate well-being arise for them through association with me. (74)
Through my yoga, they shall become my devotees in age after age;
they shall also be holy men who accomplish righteousness and liberation.
Through their yoga, the liberation of living beings shall come to pass.
Therefore, I shall remain upon the earth together with purifying human beings.
Having assumed a human form according to the various classes of men,
and likewise Lakṣmī, assuming a four-faced form, must certainly remain there as well.
Having thus resolved, O Lakṣmī, I then said "So be it" to the people and the sages; at that time,
all those wicked ones worshipped me with great affection using flowers, unbroken rice grains, and excellent sandalwood paste.
Then I beheld my four-faced parents upon the ground;
at that time, O Lakṣmī, you also became visible along with me.
Then all the gods and humans departed for their respective worlds.
Then I appointed the auspicious and righteous brahmin Kṛṣṇayaśas as his father, and I became his mind-born son; meanwhile,
the four-faced one was occupied with his wife Prabhāvatī.
I appeared right there as a son seated upon the lap of Prabhāvatī—
eight-armed, with the form of my father, four-faced, and exceedingly beautiful.
Then the divine drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Then shouts of victory arose from the sages, and there were blessings:
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Puruṣottama! Born with the sacred mantras, the youth Anādi-Caturmukha-Nārāyaṇa! (84)
I myself became so for the sake of fulfilling all desires.
Therefore, you were commanded by me to go to the house of the Brahmin Madhuvinda; there, as the truthful Mākṣikī, you were born as the mind-born daughter of his wife.
You yourself were born as Ramā, four-faced and eight-armed,
endowed with all auspicious marks and graced with every excellent virtue.
By the law of the age, you became a young woman immediately upon birth, though you are of mental origin.
"O Supreme Goddess, you were intended for me by your parents;
and according to the rites of marriage, I wedded you, the most excellent maiden, who possesses the splendor of all the Smaras of old. (88–89)
Then the creation, possessing four faces, having approached me, Hari,
and having approached you— who were equal to me— served us both with identical disposition.
O lady of auspicious countenance, I remained together with you until the end of the kalpa.
For the sake of accepting service from the creations of the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
O beloved, there have been innumerable incarnations of mine along with yours;
in various ages and kalpas, such [incarnations] have occurred.
They are the performers of all that is auspicious and the fulfillers of all intentions;
I know all this entirely, whereas others do not know it in its totality.
O Śivadevi-Śrī, remember your own birth as the four-faced one!
At that time, you indeed attained renown by the name Pramākṣikīramā.
In that kalpa, your form and my four-faced form existed alike here in temples and likewise in the heavens and other realms. (94–95)
Indeed, in every house upon the earth, there were such forms;
those people who had worshipped me departed for the divine abode,
having abandoned their four-faced corpses and assumed celestial bodies.
Having abandoned their eight arms and quickly becoming single-faced, they were led by my attendants to the imperishable abode, higher than the highest;
at that time, the names of their faces became the names of the directions. (97–98)
The faces of the Brahmins were indeed renowned as bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation, possessing the knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and devotion.
And those of the Kṣatriyas possessed conciliation, gifts, sowing dissension, and punishment.

For the Vaiśyas, however, there were well-known pleasures consisting of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation; and for all [the people], there were pleasures composed of truth, compassion, sacrifice, and austerity, which indeed bestowed their respective fruits.
"The satisfaction of the servants' resolve and their devotion to you shall also be directed toward you. Thus did the faces that grant fruits manifest themselves at that time.
O son of the illustrious Śivasvāmin! Such was my very manifestation.
Then, together with you, that abode of happiness was born and proclaimed.
(103) From reading, hearing, and remembering this, there occurs the destruction of sins, the attainment of desired supernatural powers, and the acquisition of liberation. (104)

"The fruits of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), as well as the fruits of all sacrifices, and indeed the fruits of all vows, are produced [here]; there is no doubt about this. (105) Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Four-faced Nārāyaṇa, who is like the Creator himself, accompanied by Pramā and Kṣīrā in the twentieth year of the *dvāpara* cycle," in the third section, the *dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*. (17)
← Chapter 17: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 18 [[Author: → Chapter 19
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to my supreme and virtuous narrative.
Indeed, in the twenty-first year of the Creator, which is a year of the Vedas— || 1 ||
In the eightieth kalpa, during the twelfth Manvantara of old,
there was a brahmin named Puṇyarāta who was devoted and dedicated to bhakti.
His wife, named Rādhanikā, was a devoted wife.
The husband and wife performed daily bathing, meditation, and worship of me;
they also engaged in devotional service and the sacrifice of recitation in groups,
and from time to time, they performed the vow of the unbroken name.
They performed my worship with one hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves,
and during the month of Kārtika, they indeed observed vows and their concluding rites for my sake. They prepared offerings of fresh and most delicious foods as *naivedya*.
In the month of Māgha, they likewise celebrated the Vāsantika festival;
in Vaiśākha, they performed the festival of the flower-swing and the religious observances,
and during Cāturmāsya, they carried out their restrictive vows with devotion.
Eagerly, they both constantly performed service to virtuous men and women.
From those two, they heard from the mouths of the virtuous during the course of their conversations:
"The gift of clothing is proclaimed to be superior even to the gift of food. (8)
The gift of wealth is proclaimed as the gift superior to the gift of clothing;
the gift of a cow is proclaimed as the gift superior to the gift of wealth;
and the gift of a daughter is proclaimed as the gift superior to the gift of a cow. (3.18.9–10)
The gift of a daughter is a supreme gift, and the gift of a son creates a noble lineage.
The gift of land is proclaimed to be a gift superior even to the gift of a son.
The gift of health is a gift superior even to the gift of land.
The gift of a livelihood along with a house is superior to the gift of health;
the gift of merit is considered superior to the gift of a livelihood along with a house;
and the gift of righteous action is considered supreme over the gift of merit. (1–3)
The gift of knowledge is always superior to the bestowal of righteous deeds;
the gift of devotion surpasses all gifts, including the gift of knowledge.
The gift of heaven, which bestows eternal bliss, is superior even to the gift of devotion. (14)
If that [gift] is accompanied by devotion, it is the most excellent and bestows fearlessness.
(15) All delightful gifts that grant the higher world, whatever they may be—even those equal to the gift of the entire universe—[are surpassed by this]. (16)
The gift of fearlessness to living beings is not equaled by even a sixteenth part of other gifts.
Fearlessness [is granted] from Time, from Illusion, and likewise from Karma;
from sin, from the messengers of Yama, from evil-hearted ones, and likewise from enemies. (17)
Liberation from bonds through the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) is the granting of fearlessness.
That liberation which consists of non-return is superior to that [fearlessness].
Among those, Sālokya is indeed excellent, and the state called Sārṣṭi is even more venerable than that. (18–19)
Then the state called Sārūpya is declared to be more excellent and endowed with bliss; the state called Sāmīpya is indeed even more supreme than that;
and the state called Sāyujya is the most excellent of all, for there is nothing higher than it.
There exists another [gift], consisting of the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), which is preeminent and supreme.
Therefore, the gift of fearlessness excels all other gifts; it is such as has never before been offered or performed by others in former times. (21–22)
"In this world, such a gift as that— consisting of the granting of fearlessness— must indeed be given.
Having heard this nectar-like discourse from the mouths of the virtuous,
Puṇyarāta and his wife then reflected upon it repeatedly.
In this world, those wealthy with riches give gifts such as wealth and the like.
But we must give that which has not been given by anyone before; we must indeed give exactly what has not been given by others. (24–25)
Then, having deliberated thus, the two performed acts of devotion and giving;
and as they gave knowledge and devotion, they themselves always practiced them as well.
Thus, when those months and even years had passed, then—

Devoted to breath-control (prāṇāyāma), dedicated to the practice of yoga, and capable of restraining the vital breaths, those two ascetics remained established in meditative absorption (samādhi). Then, intent upon Brahman and having renounced all bodily pleasures, they lived as practitioners of austerity. (27–28)
The two Videhas were liberated while living, free from attachment to Māyā, with their binding karmas exhausted and their desires burnt away;
they were yogis devoted solely to the dharma of granting fearlessness to others. (29)
Constantly reflecting on how the liberation of embodied beings might become absolute,
they concluded that giving alone must be performed therein;
for there is indeed no gift equal to the gift of fearlessness.
Indeed, the gift of fearlessness should be given to all living beings;
and here, through instruction, the gift of liberation may accrue for each and every one.
Through the giving of mantras, it may accrue for hundreds and thousands here in this world. (32)
Therefore, great effort must indeed be exerted by both of us who rely upon the means for the sake of the goal,
Lord Hari Himself;
one must properly apply oneself so that the Supreme Lord may be attained.

In this way, liberation would be possible even for humans dwelling on the earth who have a connection with Him, as well as for animals; thus the Supreme Lord is worthy of being sought. Whether in an age, or in ten ages, whether during the reign of Manu or when another Manu is established— ||| 34-35 ||
Śrī Hari is directly present here; He shall come and grant eternal liberation to all human beings.
Just as there is effort elsewhere, so indeed must great effort—not even the slightest—be exerted here with this very body.
Having thus resolved, both of them, filled with devotion, stood near my image and firmly undertook a vow:
"From this day forward, the auspicious sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) for Śrī Hari must be performed. (37–38)
Having made one's dwelling in the open air day and night, eating only once a day,
drinking water only once a day, and consuming only one kind of fruit—
one should indeed continue in this manner until Hari is met.
"Virtue and vows must always be protected, and one must indeed dwell in the forest.
Having thus undertaken these vows and observances, the couple began that supreme austerity from the very first day of the Yuga.
Capable of sustaining the body and likewise abandoning it at will,
and capable of obstructing time, the two became conquerors of death;
constantly worshipping me and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
They were dear to me as well, and entirely devoted to my service.
For their protection, I established Sudarśana there in that forest by my side, in an invisible form, to dispel all fears such as those of Time (Kāla). ||43-44||
Forest fires, excessive rain, violent storms, extreme cold, snowfall,
or obstacles such as cruel beasts are always warded off by my Discus,
which protects its devotees.
When four yugas had passed, filled with a lack of fortitude, I then went before them in the form of a brahmin. At midday, I said to them, "Give me alms. ||46-47||
Rising quickly, I offered water, fruit, and a seat to the brahmin, as well as water for his feet,
the honey-mixture (madhuparka), prostrations, and an apology; saying,
"May Nārāyaṇa be pleased," I indeed presented it all to him.
Having obtained [this boon], I said to those two devotees, "May it be well with you both at all times.
(49) Having replied "Om," they both said to me, "Grant us blessings so that the highest welfare may come to all embodied beings here. (50)
I have said that sinful souls are composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Their welfare may indeed be achieved through austerity (*tapas*), yoga, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but certainly not in a short time, only after they have been practiced for a long duration. (51)
The two of them said: "When indeed will Hari meet us here?
When, for the sake of liberating all human beings, will he manifest before us?
When will Kṛṣṇa appear for the sake of the liberation of all embodied beings? (52–53)
Having heard that, I said to you both: "Indeed, Hari has united with you both for the sake of liberating all humanity when half of the *manvantara* has passed.
Hari will manifest here in person through the power of your austerity and devotion."
"When a full Manvantara has passed, the Lord will appear here for the liberation of even the animals;
I shall speak according to my understanding.
Having heard these words of Sīma, both of them were greatly delighted. (55–56)
They fell at my feet and worshipped me again and again;
they bowed repeatedly and then licked the dust of my feet.
Realizing that this was Nārāyaṇa, they became filled with longing.
He said to me, "Grant me a vision of your own true form.
Then, being pleased, I granted him a divine vision of myself,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and filled with serenity.

They massaged his feet and performed various forms of worship for him, whose face possessed the luster of many millions of moons and who was adorned with ornaments. Then, having been told [to ask] for a boon, the two of them made their request.

O Lord, we both simultaneously desire the supreme liberation for human beings dwelling on earth, as well as for those connected to them— indeed, for all living beings. This is the best of boons, the most excellent, which grants fearlessness to all.
"O Lord, ocean of mercy, grant [us] this; O Keśava, be gracious!"—thus did those two, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, pray for the supreme boon.
I, however, spoke to you both here for the sake of bringing about your liberation.
"I have arrived quickly; indeed, let them come with me.
They both said, "O Lord, our liberation will surely come from you through yoga; there is no doubt.
And the liberation of living beings, that is, of human beings, is already known [to us]."
"Without us two, we shall not depart; do as you wish, O affectionate one!
Hari said: 'Even such a desire will indeed be fulfilled by time at some point.
Through your penance and devotion, it shall come to pass; I am going so that there may be well-being for you both.'"
Having spoken thus, O lotus-born one, I quickly vanished from sight.
Those two, their desires fulfilled and their joy increasing,
remained devoted to me while remembering my form as a brahmin.
Possessing ever-new enthusiasm until the end of forty yugas, they performed penance and devotion;
then I, the Blessed Lord Śrī himself, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, returned once more. (69)
He spoke to the two ascetics, who were devoted to him though their bodies were withered:
"Take all men dwelling upon the earth and go to my imperishable realm;
I have come here to bestow such a fruit of your penance."
"Accept the perfection of asceticism that grants liberation to human beings.
Then, having worshipped me and served me with supreme devotion, the two of them said,
"O Blessed One, here, in every house of human beings..."
Cows, horses, elephants, camels, goats, mules, and deer;
sheep, beasts of prey, lions, and wild oxen (gavaya) and the like; whatever animals there may be, and whatever birds such as parrots and others—[all these were born]. (73–74)
"May even those such as reptiles and others who are useful to human beings all attain liberation along with mankind; act accordingly.
We do not desire the liberation of humans while excluding them."
Having heard this, I said to them, "It will happen in a short while.
Then, having reached that time limit, they became filled with joy.
Having received my worship, I then quickly vanished from sight.
Then, likewise devoted to austerity and devotion,
they became affectionate toward me, subsisting thereafter on nothing but water and food.
Their austerity was then completed, and their devotion became perfect.
Covered with grass and known as earth, their bodies were produced through ascetic penance.
When the period of a *manvantara* had passed, those two came into being for my sake—for the benefit of embodied beings and for the liberation of those with animal bodies. (3.18.79–80)
For the sake of bestowing fearlessness and for the sake of granting me yoga, those two indeed renounced all happiness for the sake of living beings in every way;
devoted to austerity, they became like stone and clay. (8.1)

Then, accompanied by Lakṣmī and my attendants, and provided with all the requisites for worship and the like, I arrived there suddenly. Then the lords, the sages, the gods, and the seers as well— ||82-83||
Then all the holy fords (tīrthas) arrived at that spot as if to honor me;
and then, in the sky, the drums of the gods were sounded.
There was a fine rain of sandalwood and a rain of nectar (amṛta).
And from all sides, around and on every side, there arose the cries of "Victory! from the living beings.
At that time, countless celestial chariots belonging to the denizens of heaven arrived, and by my will, crores of those who were liberated also came together.
Tens of millions of celestial palaces, tens of millions of lords,
tens of millions of gods, and tens of millions of great sages—
by means of those celestial vehicles, the sky was completely pervaded in every way.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having descended from my celestial chariot onto the ground at the waters of the Brahma-lake,
I appeared upon the earth— specifically on the clay of a grove— due to the power of their penance.
As I cast it there with my joined palms, a great fire, composed of divine splendor and surpassing the brilliance of heaven, burst forth from the earth. Then,
from the midst of that radiance, the divine body of the twice-born one was born.
A most beautiful form bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus appeared;
his wife likewise was like one liberated from the syllable (Akṣara), possessing the very nature of Muktānikā and resembling Ramā. ||91-92||
Both were addressed by me regarding security, liberation, and happiness;
they replied out of compassion alone, "We have reached the further shore, having taken refuge in you.
They are fit for liberation along with their human followers and those embodied beings connected to them.

If [we] were conceived together with beasts, birds, and the like, then, O Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord, Higher than the highest, grant us liberation; the time for our mantra has passed because of your word. (94–95)
O Mādhava, Supreme Lord, grant this gift:
for countless celestial chariots have arrived here;
salutations to them, even as they are joined with you in their millions.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Lord, the self of all beings; let there be salutation to you!
O Sovereign of the Imperishable, O Inner Controller, O F fulfiller of the aims of devotees, grant liberation indeed to embodied beings and quickly fulfill my request.
"O Blessed One, forgive my offense; indeed, by me, through asceticism and devotion, you were restrained for a period of Manu's duration for the sake of the liberation of all.
O Keśava, offenses beyond even the highest number have been committed by me."
"O Mādhava, having endured [all things], lead all embodied beings to their respective abodes. Since you are independent, lead them to the abodes that are appropriate for each;
O Blessed One, I have no insistence here regarding heaven, truth, or the imperishable."
"O Supreme Lord, fulfill all that I have requested. O Master, my desire for the gift of fearlessness to countless beings has been fulfilled by You.

(3.102) Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, during the twenty-first year of Brahmā, when the Manvantara period had passed, [the Lord appeared] to fulfill the desire of the two brahmins, Rādhanika and Puṇyarāta, who were performing penance for the sake of the liberation of all living beings on earth.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Arrival of Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa, Together with All the Lords, Devas, and Others," [ends].
Chapter 18. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 19.
[Author: Chapter 20.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! Therefore, I am Puruṣottama.
Having observed the merit, devotion, and austerity of the two devotees, Manu and Kāla—
those two yogis who were my divine vessels for grace, who had become lords, and who had previously requested that their inner hearts be fulfilled— [I acted]. (1–2)
In the world of mortals, those who are men, women, and eunuchs;
children, the elderly, and the young; likewise the widowed and the householders;
the renunciants and the forest-dwellers—all of them indeed from every side.
Simultaneously, having fashioned divine bodies for them and established them within celestial chariots,
I dispatched some to Śvetadvīpa, some to the Ocean of Milk,
some to various heavens, and some to the Janaloka, Maharloka, and Tapoloka.
Some indeed they enveloped in Satyaloka, some in Vaikuṇṭha;
some in the worlds of Virāja, and some in the abode of Viṣṇu.
Some they placed in eternal Kailāsa, and some in the unmanifest state (Avyākṛtapada).
To some he granted the abode of nectar (Amṛta-dhāma), to others the supreme Vaikuṇṭha;
to some even Goloka, and to others the highest Imperishable (Akṣara); and to some various other abodes, whichever were appropriate for each.
I, the illustrious Puruṣottama, brought them all to that state.
Furthermore, those who were beasts, birds, deer and the like,
as well as reptiles and others whose life depended on the earth, [were likewise brought there].

All those inhabitants of villages and forests who looked toward Manu were instantly transformed into divine bodies with two arms; then, having placed all of them within celestial chariots, [he departed]. (3.19.10–11)

I dispatched the various classes of living beings to their appropriate abodes according to their devotion and desire: to heaven, to the people, to the great realm, to truth, to the solar, the lunar, the Varuṇan, the fiery, the ascetic, the ṛṣi, and even to the Vairāja station. (12)
Having burned away their worldly karmas, I liberated the living beings dwelling on earth. By my grace, according to their respective needs, I led them to the divine worlds.
O Lakṣmī! This mercy was shown by me in accordance with the devotion of those who follow me.
The world of mortals was for the most part sent to the worlds of the blessed;
the earth became empty, devoid of human forms, as well as of the forms of animals and others endowed with that yoga. (15)
The entire earth has become empty by the power of the asceticism of my two devotees.
Previously, living beings were liberated through the giving of fearlessness and gifts by a brahmin devotee of mine, who was a yogi and a treasury of merit. (16–17)
At that time, I, who am compassionate toward all creation, became renowned as Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and Śrī-Puruṣottama because of my other devotee, the Brahmin woman Rādhani. (18)
Being subservient to my devotee, I, the Lord, brought about his supreme welfare. Thereafter, I indeed became the Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose glory and compassion are beginningless.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Then [I favored] that devotee Puṇyarāta as well as Satī. (3.19.20)
Having transformed Rādhanikā and myself into divine bodies in the form of Viṣṇu,
I placed us both in my own celestial chariot and sent us to my own imperishable abode.
Then, Brahmā and the other gods, beholding the surface of the earth devoid of people, [departed].
They prayed most fervently for me to create humans once again,
and for the sake of creating animals and other beings, they requested that I remain until the end of the kalpa.
Consequently, I dwelt upon the earth in this world, possessing a divine form.
Together with you, Lakṣmī, who possess a divine form, I, the Supreme Person,
again performed the mental creation exactly as it was before—
of humans, animals, birds, and all embodied beings. (24)
And by the will of the Creator, I also dwelt until the end of the kalpa.
(25) Thus liberation was brought about, and again creation was performed.
Remember all this, O Queen of Śiva! Others do not know it at all. (26)
Indeed, my incarnations have occurred innumerable times for the sake of my purpose;
O beloved, I know them all throughout those years and kalpas.
And at that time, you, Amā, became compassionate along with me.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, my manifestation was indeed described at that time.
Now, listen as I tell you of another year:
during the two-hundredth kalpa known as the Rudra-year of Brahmā. (28–29)
There was a devoted Cāraṇa named Rakṣālaya,
and his wife was a Cāraṇī named Santayoginī. Having fallen from yoga, though formerly devoted, they both became capable of recollecting their past lives.
Worshipping me, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, with devotion,
and devoted to ritual bathing and service, they lived in the cow-pasture of Mahiṣī, which was thick with trees, intent on serving virtuous men and women.
In a hamlet near a small town, beautiful with grass and fodder,
bright as the open sky, on the bank of the Kāmakalpā river,
he constantly tended cattle, subsisting on curds, ghee, and other such products.
They wear woolen garments and constantly remember Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Without first offering to Me a plate filled with cakes and yogurt, they eat neither in the morning, nor at midday, nor likewise at night. (34–35)
Having gathered water, leaves, fruits, and flowers—beautiful, excellent, and pleasing—from the wild trees themselves, I offer them;
and thus the virtuous and guests come to my own hut. (36)
To them, he offers milk-rice, ghee, curd, and cakes. Satisfied, the virtuous ones perform the chanting of Hari’s names;
they go about day and night as they please, or even remain where they are.
Virtuous yoginīs, who are deities of truth, also arrive there;
even those who are celibate students come to that famous abode of wandering singers (cāraṇa).
Just as a temple is for the gods, so is that village (pallī) the very soul of the cow-pasture.
Because of the presence of Satī, the virtuous and saintly woman, that place became equal to a temple of the gods.
Where there is constant devotion to me, where there is perpetual worship of me, and where there is constant glorification of me—that is my temple. (3.19.40–41)
Thus, O Lotus-born One, although I am beyond the reach of the senses, I dwell eternally there— in the hearts of devotees, in their homes, in the sacred mandala,
and even at holy pilgrimage sites— for the sake of the welfare of my devotees.
Day after day I eat, I sleep, I dance, I drink, and I take delight;
I wander, I laugh, I go with others, and I enter [into them].
Whatever I speak, sing, find pleasure in, or worship, [I do for you]. (43–44)
I bathe, I purify myself, I perform rituals, I contemplate, and I even sing;
having gathered together with my devotees, I engage in various activities.
I experience all divine pastimes that grant liberation, and I rejoice as well.
Even while wandering in the form of a donkey among the cowherds and cowherdesses,
I always dwell within the dwellings of my devotees;
thus I lived in the abode of the Cāraṇas, amidst that circle of devotees.
In every way and at all times invisible, so that they did not know [my presence],
I dwelt in their hut in the cow-pen in the form of a physical body.
Then, on one occasion, there occurred a beautiful [festival] on the bank of the Kāmakalpā river.
Indeed, there was a gathering of the virtuous and a great festival consisting of a distribution of food.
To that festival, the *cāraṇas* and the holy men (*sādhus*) also went,
in order to feed the people at that sacrifice consisting of a distribution of food.
The giving of food, the giving of milk, the giving of clothing,
and the offering of ghee were performed according to one's ability for mendicants on the riverbank;
from that, this sacrificial session (satra) became renowned as the "Festival of Giving" (Dānotsava).
Thereupon, all the male *cāraṇas* had departed,
and the female *cāraṇī* remained alone in the house for the purpose of guarding it—
for the sake of tending the calves, as well as for the sake of household duties. (52–53)

Then the gods arrive from the path of the sky upon the earth at that great sacred site of charity; intent on great wonder, they become brahmins and mendicants, appearing in the forms of holy men. (54)
They accept some gift that yields fruits according to one's desires.
Indeed, in that case, the fruit arises equally for both the giver and the receiver.
Therefore, out of a desire for merit, the gods accept gifts.
Since the variety of rewards at this sacrificial feast of giving yields fruit on both sides,
then a celestial deity of meager merit, traveling in his aerial chariot,
emerged from the sky along the path of the heavens, looking toward the village by the river.
By that man of deluded vision, the chaste Cāraṇī was seen— beautiful, radiant,
with a well-nourished body, a young woman wearing a small cloth,
pervading the solitude with her splendor, and possessing limbs of exquisite beauty. (58–59)
Opening her voice in a sweet melody, her mind was absorbed in singing;
with her entire body wet from bathing, she sprinkled water upon her own form,
possessing the luster of a golden campaka flower like another embodiment of Rati.
Having observed her thus in that secluded place, that bewildered celestial being (vaimānika) desired the virtuous goddess; he descended to her side,
having become a handsome youth and an excellent singer (cāraṇa).
Adorned with all ornaments, well-nourished, and in the bloom of youth,
he shone there with exceeding splendor like the very embodiment of Kāma.
Laughing, he approached her presence, wishing to touch her as he pleased.
Seeing the new man accompanied by his lover,
that devoted woman quickly rose and went to her hut to maintain her virtuous conduct,
saying: "O Lord, do not look upon me, who am endowed with virtue, with a wicked eye."
I worship you; I bow down to you. Go forth, go, O powerful one!
For the violation of an unwilling woman yields a lowly fruit.
The gods are always to be honored and worshipped; they must certainly not be struck by me even for a slight offense.
O celestial chariot, you who have abandoned the sacrifice and happiness for a hope that ends in misery!
I offer this handful of milk to you as a mark of honor;
having duly respected my words, depart as you came. (67–68)
O virtuous one, the rod of Yama is irresistible against those devoted to their husbands, ascetics, cows, and likewise toward those practicing celibacy.
Whether he be a god, a sovereign, a Brahmin, or even a lord—
"One who goes astray on a wrong path deserves punishment; one who stands firm on the path is worthy of honor.
(3.19.70) Even though he was told this, he approached the hall to touch and violate that virtuous woman. Distressed, the chaste lady spoke to him: (3.19.71)
Having been a god and enjoyed divine pleasures, you have now fallen into delusion in this human body; O lustful one, be reduced to ashes!
Let no gods come from here on earth, traveling in their celestial chariots.
"Those who shall approach this spot on the earth will surely be reduced to ashes.
As soon as these words were spoken, he was instantly turned to ashes.
And those gods who were present upon the earth at that time during the sacrificial session for gifts (dānasatra) [were likewise affected].
O beloved, they too were instantly reduced to ashes by the mere curse;
then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on earth due to the curse of Āraṇī.
Having understood through their divine intellect the cause of their own destruction, the gods [acted].
They quickly fled through the sky to their own abodes, abandoning their gifts.
The arrival of the gods was obstructed; Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, as well as Indra, Candra, and the others, did not come to the earth out of fear.
The deities did not assemble; the gods of the sacred fords departed for heaven.
Filled with fear due to the curse of the devoted wife, they went to the celestial realm.
Then those men in the world who were sinful became pilgrims to the sacred fords.
Indeed, they wash away sins at sacred fords situated upon the earth;

yet those deities do not come to burn away the sins of those sacred fords during the Kumbha festival, on the occasion of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or even at the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), out of fear.
Then all the holy places (tīrthas), overwhelmed by the sins of the wicked,
became distressed and propitiated Acyuta.
Due to the curse of Satī, the gods did not come to the earth out of fear.
"O Lord, our destruction will surely come before long due to the accumulation of our sins;
therefore, please come and deliver us here on earth.
I myself shall then offer praises to the gods and to the Supreme Brahman. || 82-83 ||
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who has come to this earth;
having arrived at the home of Cāraṇī, I attained the state of a son upon her lap.
Honored by holy places and deities, I bear the marks of the conch, the discus, and other symbols.
At that time, you were the daughter of the Cāraṇa named Ratnadhana.
Having recognized you by your signs, he declared, "You are Ramā, the consort of Ratnanārāyaṇa.
Thus, by the power of destiny, you, the Śrī of Ratnanārāyaṇa, were bestowed upon me.
I am the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa, the primordial Śrītīrtha; I, the Supreme Sovereign, have been proclaimed as such by all the holy fords and celestial bards.
Therefore, together with you, as well as with my two parents, [I shall proceed].

Having visited all the sacred fords (tīrthas) again and again, I purified my sins and brought about the release from their curses. Indeed, at the command of my mother, I performed this on earth for the sake of the arrival of the gods. (88–89)
Then the gods arrived after the withdrawal of the curse;
thereafter, for the duration of a kalpa, I became Tīrthanārāyaṇa. Abiding in righteousness, I dwelt there, taking my parents along with me.
Having taken the food of his devotees, he then went to his own ancient abode.
Thus, O Kamalā, I have told you that manifestation which occurred in my land in the past for the sake of removing the curse of Cāraṇī. ||91-92||
I know all of that, whereas others, being forgetful, do not know it.
O beloved! Remember Ratnanārāyaṇī, who was born from the fire-drill (araṇī).
At that time, many other incarnations of mine were also born upon the earth.
O Queen Śivā! Together with you, I recognize all of them.
Then, I conducted an investigation among the divine classes of people to see if they were truly as virtuous as the Brahmins, those who are honored by the earth. (94–95)
Through reading this, hearing it, causing others to hear it, as well as remembering and reflecting upon it,
and even through my manifestation, a person shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, they shall become wealthy, righteous, possessed of sons, and endowed with all powers.

Even a woman shall become possessed of good fortune, happiness, sovereignty, and other such blessings. (97) Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Anādi-tīrtha Nārāyaṇa in the Arms of Cāraṇyā for the Purpose of Purifying the Tīrthas during the Twenty-second Year of Brahmā in the Dvāpara Age," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 19: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 20 [[Author:
→ Chapter 21
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Hereafter, hear of my manifestation as the Supreme Self, the controller of all lords of lords.
Long ago, in the twenty-third year of the eternal Creator,
during the fifty-second Kalpa and in the first Manvantara,
on the earth, on the bank of the celestial river, in the forest of Kālādana.
On the side of Mount Madhucchṛṅga, there indeed dwelt gods among mortals (kṣmāsura):
ascetics devoted to meditation, dedicated to sacrifices and rituals,
intent on the duties of Brahman, and absorbed in the supreme reality.
Established in the duties of householders, devoted primarily to ritual action and analytical discernment,
they did not regard manifold devotion as the means to liberation.
Indeed, they highly esteemed knowledge conjoined with dharma and discriminative wisdom.

Those who possess discrimination between the insentient and the sentient, and who are devoted to their own duty, cross over the bondage [of existence] through knowledge—even if they are rich in all enjoyments.
Furthermore, the Self is a non-doer and a non-enjoyer; it remains eternally pure within the bodies.
Free from the sense of "I" and "mine," devoid of attachment and aversion,
and liberated from pleasure and pain, one is indeed liberated— of this there is no doubt.
Free from the repository of latent impressions (vāsanā) and devoid of ritual action and effort.
One who is devoid of external perception is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
(9) One who is free from the state of passion (*rajas*), devoid of desire, anger, and the like, and free from futile exertion, is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt. (3.20.10)
Even though he is joined with wife, son, and home, and endowed with forest groves; even if possessed of buffaloes, cows, and bulls—if he is free from worldly attachment, he is indeed liberated.
Constantly engaged in worldly conduct yet devoted to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures—‖ 11 ‖
"Abiding within the bounds of discipline, one is indeed liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did those eminent bulls among the twice-born, performers of sacrificial rites, dwell upon the riverbank together with their virtuous wives, daughters, and sons.
Subsisting on fruits, roots, and leaves, as well as eating food ripened by the sun and even food ripened by the seasons, they lived without any worldly desires;
devoted to the conduct of Brahman, they wore garments of rags and bark.
Adorned with matted hair, ashes, and the like, and dwelling in leaf-huts and similar dwellings,
they observe celibacy and various vows as appropriate;
they perform sacrifices and festivals, even those celebrated by the wise.
Thus conducting themselves among the people on the earth and other realms,
they indeed established that knowledge together with its ritual action as the means to liberation.
They did not remember devotion nor did they take refuge in dharma.
Then, on one occasion, the husband Dharmadeva was entreated with devotion by his very emaciated wife for the sake of her nourishment:
"O beloved protector of the worlds, you are indeed a guardian of your wife's vows. (18–19)
In this Kalpa, the lords of the earth provide nourishment for you;
however, my place is not there, and therefore I shall indeed meet my death.
O Lord, you must never depart from me, leaving me behind.
Your prosperity and my loss—this is never appropriate.
Your beloved should be protected in such a way that I may also prosper;
however, if I am unpleasant to you or if I am no longer a woman, then she should indeed always be abandoned.
"By what means might my death be more beneficial than my life?
Having been told this, Dharmadeva indeed grieved for a moment;
then, fixing the nourishment of devotion in his heart, he reached a decision regarding that course of action.
He went to Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, the eternal Supreme Brahman. Having come to me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, in the supreme abode called Akṣara, he worshipped me.
The Bull (Dharma) prayed for the purpose of establishing the Goddess of Devotion upon the earth:
"O Supreme Brahman, Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Lord!
In this present age, the people on earth are devoted solely to dharma. (26)

Even those who are devoted to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) but lack devotion, though they possess discernment, recognize the distinction between the insentient and the sentient; indeed, they seek only liberation (kaivalya). O Lord, for them there is no worship of Nārāyaṇa whatsoever.
O Lord, there is not even the scent of an image of You, Hari, anywhere upon this earth;
therefore, [You have established] the worship, service, and other rites of Your iconic form (arcāsvarūpa) in order to promote devotion and nourish it. (29)
"O Mādhava, exert yourself to revive the various forms of devotion!
Having heard this prayer of Dharmadeva, which nourishes devotion, O Lakṣmī,
[he quickly summoned] Sadāśiva, who is ever-yoked in yoga.
He indeed impelled [them] upon the earth to go forth and likewise to break down both the doctrine of action alone and the doctrine of knowledge alone;
for without devotion, action is indeed fruitless, and knowledge does not bestow liberation.

Thus, for the sake of instruction, he dispatched Śaṅkara. He, having gone quickly to the earth and seeing the world-protectors and others engaged in ritual acts yet devoid of devotion, performed a marvel.
Becoming a radiant youth clad in the sky alone, with a body that bewilders even the wise,
Hara, nourished and joined by the Goddess, went to the village of the earth-lords (brahmins),
where all those diligent brahmins and others dwell. (35)
Their wives, their daughters, and the sons born of the twice-born—
all of these were indeed devoted to ritual action and intent upon the knowledge of duality;
yet they were devoid of devotion, lacking divine vision, and possessed only the conceit of the body.
Those who are devoted to lust and anger, devoid of the majesty of the Divine;
likewise, those devoid of the majesty of yogis, holy men, and such;
those lacking hospitality, and deprived of the state of Brahman.
Possessed of views regarding cyclic existence and endowed with hearts full of faults—such are those gods of the earth who dwell there together;
[and likewise] men and women living in villages or residing in leaf-huts and the like. (3.20.40)
There, Śaṅkara went about naked, imitating the gestures of a lover; he went from house to house, while girls, boys, young women,
and likewise other women, beheld that intoxicated embodied being.
Chasing after that intoxicated, handsome, well-nourished, and deluding one,
they spoke playful words, looked at the Lord with longing, laughed at him as he desired them, and threw dust and other things upon him. (42–43)
Some, however, struck them on the hips with sticks;
deluded, the wives of the Asuras followed them, deprived of their luster.
Out of greed for pleasure, they touched them and led them into secluded bowers.
Having seen and heard this, the brahmins,
who were devoted to the ritualistic portion of the Vedas and who bore the banner of false discrimination, rushed toward him to kill him;
having reached him, they struck him excessively with staffs and clubs.
Śaṅkara, though indeed skilled and experienced, did not at all understand the pain;
having received a powerful blow, he fell to the ground and died.
Having become a corpse there, he no longer drew breath at all.
Just as he remained absorbed in samādhi when he died, so did he remain then. Having abandoned the fallen body, those brāhmaṇas departed for their respective homes.
Then the goddess Satī, becoming enraged, cursed those Prātadakas.
For those twice-born ones who possess the banner of discrimination yet produce false knowledge,
who are devoid of the reality of the Self and falsely imagine themselves to be non-agents—
[they fail to realize] the non-agency, the non-experiencer-ship, and the eternal purity within the Self. (3.20.50)
Those who know only the grandiosity of words do not consider it even a mere fraction [of the truth].
They are merely ritualists, embodied by their physical forms, devoted to lust and anger, and likewise ignorant of the divine majesty of the true yogis. (51–52)
"Devoted to lustful acts, intent on your own interests, and full of suspicion;
merciless and like those who commit the murder of a Brahmin—may you meet death just as Hara did!
When Satī had spoken thus, [the gods] went to the forest near the village of Khaṭvaka.
Those classes of men, the gods upon earth, quickly met their death in due course.
Corpses appeared in every house, even within the dwellings of men;
a great cry of lamentation arose on all sides, even in the abodes of the Brahmins.
The Brahmins are indeed dying from the curse of the naked women;
what should be done, and where should one go for protection here today?
The women weep on all sides, and even the young girls weep.
