And men, having heard this, wept at every place;
they were devoid of self-nature, bereft of discriminative knowledge,
performers of mere verbal knowledge, and lacking the knowledge of [true] distinction.
At that time, throughout the entire world of men and in all regions upon the earth, those who were diligent in ritual action, yet possessed of defects such as anger and lust and filled with grief—
the lords of the earth— lost their luster and became as if lifeless.
Then, throughout the entire earth during the day,
there were cremation grounds consisting of tens of millions of billions of corpses;
in every house, a corpse was produced at every single moment.
Women considered this anger to be something extraordinary and most formidable,
while other people— those who were not Brahmins and so forth— regarded it as the destroyer of all.
Wherever there were Brahmins who were performers of rituals yet proponents of divergent doctrines, [there it prevailed].
Then all those who were devoid of devotion attained the state of corpses.
When such a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, the remaining men and women performed worship of the Supreme Lord, my own Self.
"You are the vital breath, you are life itself, and you are the protector, O Mādhava.
You are the refuge of women, O Lord; restore my husbands, these people, to life.
Having heard this praise and having understood the reason for my arrival, [he spoke].

O Lakṣmī! Puruṣottama, adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and other [emblems], resplendent in golden ornaments and garments, and shining with divine luster, came swiftly to the earth along with you. (66–67)
Wherever the corpses of Śivas and likewise the corpses of twice-born brahmins lay,
there I manifested my own form and comforted the women;
likewise, I granted supreme courage to the men who were not of the brahmin caste.
Those who are merely ritualistic, who perform actions for the sake of knowledge while devoid of discernment and right conduct;

those whose knowledge is dry and who lack devotion; and those who commit offenses against holy men—these, without even realizing they are offenders, immediately obtain the fruit of their actions. (3.20.69–70)
There is great sin in dry knowledge for one who knows but lacks right conduct;
that which is known and even proclaimed, yet is neither practiced nor retained—there is no other sin for embodied beings equal to that sin. (71)
These people, devoted to the ritualistic section of the Vedas and bearing the banner of discernment,
do not at all maintain freedom from passion and hatred.
By them, this ascetic, though devoid of worldly ties and possessed of discernment, has been killed.
The death of the virtuous man was announced by those devoid of devotion.
Then the people, the men, and the women questioned the Supreme Lord:
"How may this great calamity be dissolved? Please instruct us. (74)
O Lakṣmī! I then said to them:
"Go and worship that corpse which has been slain and installed;
perform the consecration of life (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and worship that image. (75–76)
Let them worship Him with the sixteen primary offerings and others, by presenting food offerings (naivedya), service, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and hymns of praise;
then this affliction of death will go to its destruction.
Having heard this, both women and men, devoid of discrimination regarding falsehood,
all brought together excellent materials: sandalwood, unbroken rice, garlands,
incense, lamps, fine food offerings, garments, ornaments, and sandals.
Having performed the invocation and other rites, and having worshipped with all manner of objects,
my ancestors— the women, men, and others— performed the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
They then performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), at which point Śambhu became endowed with consciousness.
Having done so, he opened his eyes and arose in a moment.
Then they offered him food offerings and gave him water to drink.
At that time, Hara became pleased and spoke to them for the sake of granting a boon.
Then everyone requested the restoration of life for the deceased.
Having worshipped this Goddess and received her auspicious blessings, Hara said:
"They shall be restored to life; it shall never be otherwise."
Then, O Lakṣmī, those women and men worshipped the Goddess;
they even entreated her for the restoration of life to the deceased.
And Śivā, being worshipped there together with Śaṅkara, spoke as follows. || 84–85 ||
"Likewise, let all worship this Lakṣmī together with the illustrious Nārāyaṇa; then, upon death, they shall attain life.
Having been addressed thus, the men and women worshipped me accompanied by you.
Then they all rose up, freed from the death resulting from their offense.
Having regained their lives, they cried out to me, "O Jīvan-Nārāyaṇa!
Thereupon, I too attained the renown as the primordial Jīvan-Nārāyaṇa.
Together with you, my form— which is essentially Nārāyaṇa through devotion—
people have always served with intense devotion, as revealed by me,
having abandoned dry intellectual analysis. ||89||

They indeed composed the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), which consists of the complete surrender [of all actions] to me. Then Śaṅkara instructed them all that every kind of ritual action should thereafter consist of devotion to me.
Knowledge endowed with righteousness and devotion is indeed my realization;
from that, the auspicious path granting liberation was set forth in that Kalpa.
The revitalization of devotion occurred, and the path of devotion was inaugurated.
My forms and those of Śambhu, together with their Śaktis, [were established] upon the earth.
Then, having been brought to life by them, they were installed and displayed as prescribed;
they were worshipped everywhere, and devotion indeed attained full growth.
Thus Śambhu, joined by Satī, having performed the supreme rite of auspiciousness (kautuka),
and having established on earth the worship of the image as well as the highest devotion,
I, the Lord Jīvanārāyaṇa, became invisible according to the prescribed manner.
Together with you, he dwelt upon the earth for a duration reaching until the end of the kalpa.
Thus, O Śivarājñīśrī, I have narrated the manifestation of the beginningless Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

For the nourishment of the Dharma endowed with devotion, for the cultivation of spiritual practice, and for the worship of my own form as well as the form of Śaṅkara, there was indeed no *liṅga* in that kalpa; rather, there was only the image (*mūrti*) of Hara. (98)
At that very moment my form appeared, but the Viṣṇu-śilā was not there.
Thus, I know all that occurred previously;
remember also my worship and the like at the time of my manifestation. (3.20.100)
"O Lakṣmī! By reading this, by hearing it, by remembering it, and even by reflecting upon it, the fruit of my worship shall surely be attained; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Jīvanārāyaṇa at the Request of His Devotee in the Twenty-third Year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the Dvāpara Age, and the Propagation of the Path of Devotion through Śaṅkara," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 20: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 21 [[Author:
→ Chapter 22
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! Hear now of another manifestation of mine:
in the twenty-fourth year of Brahmā, known as the Ārṣa [yuga]. || 1 ||
Just as it occurred formerly in the sixth Manu-period of the hundredth Kalpa,
at that time there were Brahmins learned in the Vedas, as well as ascetics,
deities, sages, and ancestors, born in the creation of Aja.
In that sacrifice consisting of the "Sacrifice of All" (Sarvamedha), held on the banks of the Mokṣadā river, deliberations arose among everyone who was devoted to me:
"What is the nature of this Hari? Is he to be served as one alone, or as a pair? || 3-4 ||
Whether devoid of attributes or possessed of attributes, whether indeed embodied or formless,
whether in the form of fire or in the nature of the sun, or even formless—
then there, Brahmā himself, existing as a couple, spoke.

Other great sages have declared that he alone is higher than the highest. The gods said: "He is possessed of attributes (saguṇa)," while the ascetics said: "He himself is without attributes (nirguṇa). Others sang: "He should be served according to what is appropriate, and he possesses form."
The ritualists say that this formless one is indeed to be served;
others say that Hari is directly the fire itself, while the supreme ones say he is the sun.
Thus they engage in such debate, asserting that the embodiment of Brahman is to be served.
The decision was not uniform; then Viṣṇu spoke:
"Whatever this Śambhu says to us, that alone shall be the decision.
Having heard the words of Hari, Śambhu addressed the members of the assembly: [3.21.10]
"Let them meditate for a moment; he himself will provide the decision.
Thus were the words of Śaṅkara spoken then at the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
And the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans became absorbed in meditation.
At that moment, a mountain composed of divine splendor emerged from the sky.
It pervaded the entire atmosphere, the heavens, the earth, and the quarters of space.
In its center was my beloved, the excellent celestial chariot named Akṣara.
O Lakṣmī! At that time, I was seen there together with you—Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, whose body is half-lotus. I appeared visibly before them, and thereafter became the object of their meditation.

In one half of her head resides the crest-lock (*śikhā*), while in the other half is the beautiful braided tress (*dhammilla*) consisting of her hair. On one half of her forehead is a fine sectarian mark (*tilaka*), and on the other half is a beautiful crescent moon.
In her right ear is an earring (*kuṇḍala*), and in her left is a female bee-like earring (*kuṇḍalika*).
On the right side there is stainless powder, while on the left eye there is collyrium;
likewise, on the right there is a mustache and a bare nose, while on the left it is accompanied by a nose-ring.
The right chest is elevated, and the left is endowed with a breast.
My two right hands are joined with the conch and the discus and adorned with beautiful bracelets;
my two left hands hold a lotus, a garland, a chain, and a fan.
On the right side is half of the Śrīvatsa mark, and on the left is half of my form.
On the right side of the abdomen there are three-and-a-half folds; on the left, it has the nature of a flat abdomen.
On the right is half a human *liṅga*, and on the left is half a vulva (*yoni*).
On the right there is indeed one testicle, while on the left there is a concealed gland.
His right foot is hairy while his left is hairless; it is brilliantly radiant.
His hoods are long like those of a man, yet short and excellent like those of a woman.
The right half of his body possesses the beauty of a dark complexion, while the left half is brilliant with gold.
The right half [of the body] is adorned with yellow garments and the like, and possesses a golden crown;
the left half is adorned with a bodice, a lower garment, and a golden tiara.
The right half is richly decorated with male ornaments, while the left is adorned with female ornaments. (22–23)
The right side was endowed with masculine strength, while the left was exceedingly soft and feminine;
thus, though being one alone, he likewise possessed a dual form.
Manifest before them stood the Lord Nārāyaṇa, whose body was half that of Lakṣmī.
And they envisioned me as being of such a dual-and-unitary form between them.
Men, gods, sages, and even the ancestors worshipped me;
Brahmā and the others entreated me, saying, "Dwell forever here upon this earth."
In this very same form, you exist for the sake of the world's welfare.
Therefore, on the bank of the river Mokṣadā, to the west of Mount Meru,
I have eternally dwelt upon the sacrificial ground, accessible to all.
The Supreme Lord, the beginningless and glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, who possesses half of Śrī, remains as the Master throughout the dissolution of the kalpa, instructing the worship of the image.
Likewise, He is present in every way within temples and in every single house. (28–29)
My form became of one kind: half that of Śrī and half that of Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, my worship, meditation, ritual service, and the wearing of attire—all were of that same nature;
indeed, my body was thus served by my devotees.
"O Lakṣmī! By my own will, I acted in that manner during that kalpa.
Indeed, I assumed whatever form I desired, even one superior to the Imperishable (Akṣara). Then the gods and others perceived me as such, beyond [the Akṣara]."
They worshiped and served [me], and they attained liberation.
Thus was my manifestation declared to you in that kalpa.
O Īśvarī, remember thus the oneness of the couple as your own manifestation!
"O Lakṣmī, I know all things, as well as my many incarnations.
Now I shall describe to you my future manifestation, which will take place in the twenty-fifth year of the current Dharma Kalpa. || 34-35 ||
In the first of the five-hundred aeons, long ago, the hosts of ancestors descended to the earth from their lineages and proclaimed the ritual feeding of the *śrāddha*.
People born of those various lineages, being possessed of knowledge, performed it accordingly.
With faith, they offered the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and other offerings intended for the assembly of ancestors.
All those ancestors, having emerged with half their bodies visible, joyfully received the funeral cakes with both hands outstretched. (37–38)
With serene faces and likewise with hands uplifted,
their bodies visible from the navel upward, they stood firm after receiving the morsels of food;
all of them remained thus steady, with the food held in their hands.
They remained without eating, observing silence, peaceful, and free from worldly desire.
(3.21.40) Then, they were observed not eating by the brahmins and others born of their lineage; and all the fathers were asked: "Why do you not eat what has been offered? (3.21.41)
They replied: "That which is pleasing to Hari is precisely that which is always forbidden to us, for we are indeed Vaiṣṇavas.
Then the descendants asked: "How, then, can it be pleasing?"
"Since Narayana is neither seen nor present here, your ancestors have said: 'Recite the Harisūkta here;
Hari will come and accept the rice-balls, the milk-rice, and other offerings. (43-44)
Then, at that moment, they worshipped me—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama— with the *Harisūkta*. O Lakṣmī, because of the devotion of the ancestors, I was there together with you.
There,
in the presence of his kinsmen, the Nābhi sat down with his ancestors and partook of water,
milk-rice, sweet food, fruit, leaves, and roots. (46–47)
And you, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, whose form is visible above my own navel,
have been adorned by me and have partaken of milk-rice (pāyasa) along with me.
Now, all your ancestors [have received] only water, food, and so forth.
"Delightful food has been given by me; having eaten, they are eager for happiness.

(49) Having eaten and being satisfied, they all departed from the world of the ancestors to their own abodes. While I was still preparing, [the food] on the ground was [consumed] by the Brahmins and others. (50)
Requested to dwell there eternally, those two who possessed no further physical bodies remained on earth forever,
appearing as half-visible, divine, beautiful beings of gentle form.
Accepting this as appropriate, they thought, "So be it," and remained always upon the earth.
Until the end of the kalpa, they always bore the form of half-bodies above the navel;
likewise, their forms in the house, the forest, and the temple,
as well as during meditation, worship, and festivals, remained with such half-embodied figures.
I became the celebrated Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, known as the beginningless Half-Father Nārāyaṇa. Remember, Lakṣmī! At that time, my form was half-female along with you.
Furthermore, at that time, there were also other incarnations of mine by the millions;
I know all of those who have passed away, while others truly do not know them.
These auspicious incarnations bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation through remembrance and salutation. (55–56)
The portion below the navel is illusory and bestows rebirth in hell;
the portion above the navel is purifying and has been shown by me to bestow liberation.
Then, through the form of his half-body facing upward, knowledge likewise arose.
Having understood this and having worshipped [me], people have gone to the imperishable abode.
Now I shall speak: in the twenty-sixth year of the Vedhas Kalpa, during the Aṇgava cycle, in the seventh Manvantara of the seven hundred [cycles], I am the Supreme Lord.
I appeared in the midst of the Plakṣa tree as the beginningless Plakṣa-Nārāyaṇa.
In that kalpa, there were indeed noble and wise beings who were devoted to the knowledge of the Self and dedicated solely to Nārāyaṇa.
Wearing matted hair and garments of bark, eating food such as alms obtained without asking,
content with whatever comes by chance, they bring about the welfare of the world;
they are endowed with the sacred thread and their bodies are marked with sectarian tilaka.
Adorned with necklaces, garlands, and other ornaments,

those who practiced meditation and worship once gathered together on the auspicious bank of the Viṣṇu-nadī in the Forest of Devotion for the sake of penance and for the sake of devotion to the Supreme Soul.
Well-united with one another, they held a discussion among themselves:
"O twice-born ones, is austerity the bestower of the highest good, or is devotion the bestower of the highest good?
Or if both are considered bestowers of the highest good, which indeed is the superior?"
When such a core question had arisen among those practitioners of auspicious yoga, some said that austerity is supreme, while others said it is not so.
Through austerity, evil is destroyed; merit is produced, which is auspicious.
Through that, there is the attainment of enjoyments, as well as heaven and death at the exhaustion [of merit].
Therefore, worldly prosperity and asceticism at the end do not yield such results;
hence, supreme devotion is the most excellent, for it is the eternal bestower of the highest good.
Others say: "That [devotion] accompanied by desire does not bestow ultimate welfare;
desireless devotion is superior and more excellent, for it indeed bestows the highest welfare.
But others say: "If devotion is desireless, that is, devoid of longing—"
"For that [practice] is fruitless and in vain, consisting merely of exertion.
Therefore, it should be performed with desire, so that it may yield its own desired and true fruit.
While the great sages were speaking thus, Vṛṣa then—
Dharmadeva, in the form of a brahmin, standing in the assembly, spoke this:
"He who is the inner self of all, who shines as the witness of all—that God shines here in this righteous *plakṣa* tree. (72)

"Having first performed worship for him, the burden of the questions should be placed here upon Pippala; and Kṛṣṇa, who resides within him, will provide the answer. Having thus formed this single resolution, the great seers then—
Having worshipped the Pippala tree there and addressed the Supreme Lord:
"O Lord, what is the ultimate supreme good— is it austerity or devotion?"—
they remained for a hundred years engaged in penance after having thus made their proclamation.
Nevertheless, even though they had obtained [the fruit] from the Plakṣa tree, those whose wealth is penance did not attain the ultimate goal.
Then the Lord, the Supreme Ruler, spoke to them with a voice from the sky:
"O ascetics, through penance alone, the supreme good that is final liberation shall not be attained."
"O twice-born ones, may you propitiate me, the Supreme Brahman, the witness of all. O brahmins, when I am satisfied by desireless devotion, I am forever pleased.
Through such devotion, you shall attain ultimate and final welfare."
Thus addressed, they replied: "How can there be devotion without Hari?
Without Hari manifest before us, how could there be devotion—that is, loving service?
O Mādhava, if we have been purified by austerity, we have become worthy recipients [of your grace]. (3.21.80)
O Abode of Mercy, come among us and remain forever;
for the sake of your devotees who are eternally dear to you, you have stayed in the sky.
Though invisible, O affectionate one, you favor the side of your devotees even through a voice from the heavens.
You carry out the teaching that bestows welfare, considering it for your own people.
Just as you do through your word, so too instruct us through your very form.
O Mādhava, gladden us, your own people, by appearing before our very eyes.
Thus addressed, I said to them: "Let them meditate with concentrated minds;
for when the fruit of their worship is attained, I shall indeed become visible to them.
Then, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, [they shall attain] their own supreme fortunes.
Thinking thus, those twice-born ones remained there for a hundred years,
worshipping the Lord of Gods, the Lord of Lords, the Lord of Lords of Lords.
Those holy men were free from desire, intent solely upon the hope of attaining Brahman.
Having the form of Brahman and having become one with Brahman, they took refuge in the shade of a Plakṣa tree;
they chanted my name, Nārāyaṇa, and worshipped me through the recitation of my names.
They honored me with offerings such as Tulasī and held me within the temple of their minds.

When a hundred years had passed, while I was practicing [meditation] in the presence of the virtuous, I appeared in person, taking refuge at the foot of a Plakṣa tree; accompanied by you, Lakṣmī, I was Śrīplakṣanārāyaṇa himself. (88–89)
Within the womb-like portion of the Plakṣa trunk, infused with divine splendor,
in the open space of the sky of consciousness, situated within the Plakṣa-Brahman,
the four-armed Narāyaṇa dwells upon the left lotus together with you.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
I have manifested by my own will alone for the fulfillment of the desires of the virtuous.
I am endowed with the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the svastika, the banner, and the trident.
Adorned with all divine ornaments, wearing a golden crown and earrings,
possessing the luster of a divine campaka flower, and likewise clad in divine garments;
pervaded by divine splendors, the Supreme Lord is the soul of the couple.
There, the fulfiller of virtuous desires, the bestower of all blessings, became manifest before their eyes. (94) Then, with divine vision, they beheld me within a tree;
there, in the midst of a celestial mansion in the sky, they saw that Supreme Person indistinguishable from the tree. (95)
They prostrated like a staff, offered praises to the Supreme Lord,
and then worshipped Him there with gathered offerings and services.
Out of love and devotion, they always served Me, having first protected the sacred circle.
Thus, O beloved, I have become the bestower of the highest good upon all the worlds;
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the eternal one, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) himself, appearing by my own will within the circle of the virtuous.
I am established as the primordial, glorious Plakṣa-Nārāyaṇa;
I know everything— remember me as the one who dwells in the Plakṣa tree,
your auspicious form, the eternal embodiment of Lakṣmī.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of other incarnations of mine have occurred.
Even the lords do not know them, much less the gods or human beings.
By reading, hearing, causing others to hear, and even by remembering this [account], [one attains liberation].

"From the service of her who dwells in the *plakṣa* tree, and from my own service as well, there shall be both worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*), and indeed, the highest liberation shall come to pass.
Whoever worships the glorious Narayana under the *pippala* tree, [they too shall attain this]. (102)

For him, there shall be no loss of prosperity, and the attainment of liberation will be certain. (10.3) Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless, Illustrious Ardha-Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa in the twenty-fourth year of the Creator [Brahmā], the Beginningless, Illustrious Ardha-Pitṛ Nārāyaṇa in the twenty-fifth year, and the Beginningless, Illustrious Plakṣa Nārāyaṇa in the twenty-sixth year," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. [Note]
3.21.45 The Hare Sūkta
— Chapter 21 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā / Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga)
— Chapter 22
[The Author: Chapter 23.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī-Śrī! Hear of another manifestation of mine.

In the twenty-seventh year of the Kalpa known as Avṛṣa, during the third Manvantara, in the fourth century [of that period], there appeared upon the earth certain Brahmins who were performers of sacrifices;
they performed many sacrificial rites. (1–2)
The Agnihotra, the Darśahoma, the Paurṇamāsa, the Prayāja offerings, the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice, the Pitṛyajña, and the Vaiśvadeva;
the Cāturmāsya, the Sākamedha, the Soma sacrifice, and the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi. (3)
Likewise, the Avabhṛtheṣṭi, the Atirātra, and the Vājapeya;
the Agniṣṭoma, the Sautrāmaṇī, and the Rājasūya;
the Aśvamedha, the Sarvamedha, the Puṃmedha, and many other Soma-sacrifices.
The Bṛhaspatisava, the Vaiśyasava, the Somasava,
as well as the Gosava, the Brāhmaṇasava, and the auspicious Audanasava;
the Pṛthisava, the Marutstoma, the Putreṣṭi, and others likewise.
Once they performed various sacrifices and commenced the Nṛmedhaka rite.
During that sacrifice, for five days, they duly offered one hundred and ninety-eight men to the deities, and thereafter—
The twice-born, deluded though they were knowers of reality, began to slaughter men for the sake of the omentum and for the purpose of offering oblations.
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, as to who those human-beasts were.
They were less than twelve years of age and wore the sacred thread (yajñopavīta).
Among those Brahmins and others who had been assembled for the sake of the sacrifice, some were devotees and some were non-devotees;
however, there was one among them who was a yogi, solely devoted to me.
Unattached to time, illusion, and the like, the man was indifferent toward the body and its possessions;
he was of a bright complexion, known as Sundara, tender, and his face bore an expression of joy.
Purified by the foremost Brahmins, he was consecrated and brought together [with them].
In the sacrificial hall of Viśasana, he was duly honored.
With his mind fixed on the thought, "O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa,
O Inner Self," he was constantly one who had offered himself and whose every action was for my sake.
Knowing that such a devotee of mine intended to slaughter [me],
I quickly arrived at the slaughter-house in Padma.
At that time, I was indeed invisible to the ritualists, but visible to my devotee.

Having rendered my devotee invisible, I remained clearly manifest in that very place. I assumed his form and observed silence for the sake of protecting the devotee, for the purpose of destroying his delusion, and indeed to bring an end to violence. (16–17)
For the sake of protecting the Dharma, for the cessation of false actions, for the purpose of bestowing awakening upon the Brahmins, for the engagement in truthfulness,
and for the destruction of the evil karma of those possessed by darkness, [he established it] in the seat of instruction.
"O Lakṣmī! At that time, I, your own protector, appeared before their very eyes.
(19) Then those twice-born ones, having received initiation for the sacrifice, chanted the mantras;
having sprinkled everything according to the proper rite, they took hold of me, the Supreme Person. (3.22.20)
The merciless and wicked ones bound his mouth with fillings of barley;
eager for the task, they crushed his testicles and cut them off.
While I was still alive, those evil men, possessed by delusion, acted according to a method rooted in error.
Then I, the destroyer of sinners,
carried out their execution. With my two testicles, which were like thunderbolts, I swiftly struck the skulls and the cranial apertures (*brahmarandhra*) of those ritualists.
Struck by those two [beings] who resembled diamond-jewels and were accompanied by fire, the twice-born ones blazed and perished,
their heads and skulls shattered.
Thousands of others arose, great and spherical in form.
Having the form of great rocks and resembling the fire of universal destruction,
they indeed began to burn the earth, the sky, and the stars;
being like mountains, they then shattered everything.
They destroyed the sacrifice on all sides as well as the sacrificial implements.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, signaling the dissolution of heaven.
On earth, the great prosperity of cities was consumed by fire.
The forest dwellings of the sages were consumed by the fire of the *vṛṣaṇas*.
The halls, villages, and residences were likewise burnt by those *vṛṣaṇa*-fires.
Then the Brahmins, remaining alive, offered prayers to the gods.
May the gods protect us, who are enveloped by the jaws of death;
we shall perform expiation for our transgressions and the like—protect us!
We shall never act thus again; we shall surely abandon this delusion.
"Protect us, protect us, O Mādhava, who has reached the further shore of the ocean of compassion!
Thus did they fall at the feet of Hari as they were dying. Then, commanded by me, the presiding deities of the sacrifice spoke to the twice-born:
Indeed, from the two testicles of Śālā, those villages emerged;
for they are the divine Śālagrāmas of Hari, possessing divine wonders.
For the sake of protecting his devotees, Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa himself [resides therein].
Hari, assuming the form of a bull-man, has appeared to instruct you.
Indeed, these Śālagrāmas are his two testicles;
O twice-born ones, they are the instructors of you all, having the forms of fire and the thunderbolt.
"You are indeed performers of what should not be done, deluded by violence, and followers of a wrong path.
To us gods, the sacrificial oblation is never meat;
rather, milk-rice (pāyasa) is most desired, so with that perform the sacrifices. (36)
Fruits and also sugar-candy, seeds and lotuses;
grains of millet and rice, as well as barley and *śāli* rice and leaves; sesame seeds, sweet food, honey, and excellent juices. (37–38)
"Fuel-wood is always dear to the gods, but never meat.
You twice-born ones have surely gone astray; do not commit violence here.
We are pure deities; do not join us with impurity."
Indeed, the fruit of that evil will be suffering for you;
O twice-born ones, by performing this sacrifice, you are bringing about the destruction of your own virility in heaven. (3.22.40–41)
Even for you, the destruction of heaven will arise through the fault of violence;
and we shall be devoid of purity here due to the fault of meat-eating at the sacrifice,
O twice-born ones, and we shall be subject to rites of expiation.
Indeed, being unable to enter their respective abodes in heaven without having performed the rite of atonement,
let them therefore commit no violence;
so that peace may prevail here for the Śālagrāma and the Great Fire.
Likewise, let us gods, sages, ancestors, and humans worship Viṣṇu, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, right here.
Hari himself will perform the pacification of the fire there.
And this god Nārāyaṇa himself, who is without testicles, is a man (nara).
He has been consecrated here by you for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
Let them all go for refuge to him, the Supreme Self.
"For he, having established protection and exercising forbearance, will indeed act as our protector.
Having been told this, O Lakṣmī, those gods, the lords,
the ancestors, humans, and brahmins then praised me, Hari, who am without testicles.
You are the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord, the primordial Śrī Puruṣottama.
You alone are the one without a second, the Lord of all lords and the Highest Lord. You alone are the cause even of the Imperishable and of those who are liberated within the Imperishable. (3.22.50)
You are the cause of the incarnations of those who possess power;
you are the cause of all powers, and you are the cause of all lords.
You are the cause of sacrifices, and you are the cause of sacred mantras.
You are the cause of the ordinances, the treasures, and all material substances.
You are the cause of all ritual sections and of the gods.
You are the agent, the impeller, and the knower; you alone are satisfaction itself.
The twice-born, the ritualists, and you yourself as the sacrificer—
you alone, O Blessed One, are all the materials and all the oblations.
Knowledge of the purpose, knowledge of the injunctions, and Vedic knowledge of the mantras— all are yours alone.
And who else besides you is capable of demonstrating the knowledge of ritual action?
O Lord Hari, having granted forgiveness, protect, protect this world that is being consumed here;
O ocean of mercy, forgive our transgressions.
"O Lord, please forgive us out of compassion for this slaughter of a man that we have committed, being ignorant of the true nature of mantras.
Wise people forgive the offenses of those who are ignorant."
You are the father, the mother, the protector, the wise Maheśvara;
you are the Lord, the creator of all, the teacher of all, and the bestower of happiness.
You are the one who reveals the truth as it is; O Puruṣottama, instruct us.
"Having come to you for refuge, protect us who have sought your shelter"—
thus entreated by them, O Lakṣmī, I, the Supreme Person,
then instructed them all in the meaning of the Vedas as spoken by me.
The state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) arises through compassion, the performance of what is beneficial, and non-violence;
it is produced through purity, devotion, freedom from attachment and aversion, as well as through lack of greed, lack of desire, absence of thirst for worldly things, and austerity. (61–62)
Through right conduct, righteousness, and contentment, one is born as a virtuous person;
through truthfulness, divine service, and dedication to the Lord, one attains the status of a Brahmin.
Through non-malice, the granting of fearlessness, and the bestowing of liberation, one is truly born [into that state].
That state of Brahminhood shines forth through knowledge and the Veda.
To commit an act of malice against those twice-born who have attained that state is not even righteousness;
for in this matter, malice is a great violence that obstructs both heaven and liberation.
The self, which causes suffering to others, likewise experiences such suffering;
while living under the dominion of [the senses], boundless suffering arises therein.
Thus, by inflicting suffering, dharma itself becomes adharma.
Moreover, O best of Brahmins, listen with great discernment:
even pure, delicious, and fragrant rice-pudding (*paramānna*), once it has entered the mouth, becomes leavings; and once it reaches the stomach, it turns into impurity. (67–68)

Its transformations—such as the fleshy mass and so forth—are of the nature of impurity. O Brahmins, reflect upon the ultimate truth: how can gods and others, who consist of pure *sattva* and partake of nectar-like food, consume such things? (69)
For where flies swarming with darkness (tāmasa) are agitated,
that food is indeed impure, foul-smelling, dark, and filthy.
O gods and twice-born ones, how could they ever desire such a meal?
Milk is fragrant, excellent, essentially flavorful, and enriched with ghee;
it is the pure food that those of the *sattva* nature desire.
As for honey, which is fragrant and sweet, that is what flies desire.
The deities desire various kinds of sweet juices;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, do not perform a sacrifice characterized by violence,
nor the binding, the slaughtering, and the dismembering of animals.
For the extraction of fat, the oblation, and so forth—all that is indeed of the nature of violence.
"Violence must never be committed" is the Vedic revelation;
likewise, "All should be offered to Hari" is my Vedic revelation.

"Leaves, flowers, fruit, water, clothing, a house, wealth, a son, a daughter, a wife, a husband, a cow, a field, prosperity, and even one's own self—these should be offered to Nārāyaṇa; such is the Vedic revelation. (76–77)

Having meditated upon [the victim] as being of the nature of Nārāyaṇa and having offered it to Nārāyaṇa, one should consume it as is appropriate; however, no killing is ordained. Indeed, after having consecrated it for those respective deities, it is to be offered exactly as it was assigned.
Having made everything pleasing, one should indeed yoke the bull of Viṣṇu;
having meditated thus, "All this belongs to Nārāyaṇa," and thereafter, it must be accepted in no other way—one should offer all that is one's own to Hari. (3.22.79–80)
In the Vaiśyasava sacrifice, a four-year-old female animal is likewise offered;
she is to be released for Hari, and she must never be consumed.
That goddess is to be worshipped—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
In the Gosava sacrifice as well, cows should likewise be offered to the Supreme Lord. Ten thousand cows, honored and worshipped, are considered the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
they should be released, worshipped, and given for the sake of obtaining milk.
In the Marutstoma sacrifice as well, seventeen five-year-old male animals,
as well as female animals that have not yet been touched by pregnancy and are three years old,
are to be offered to the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self.
May those virtuous men and women likewise become bestowers of the awakening to Brahman.
In the first, second, and third year,
as well as in the fourth and fifth year, there shall be countless men and women [who attain this].
"In the renunciant stage (tyāgāśrama), those belonging to the Acyuta-gotra are to be given;
they are to be made Vaiṣṇavas—such indeed is the Vedic revelation.
Even in the Aśvamedha sacrifice, that divine [offering] must certainly not be consumed."
Even a horse that has been offered to the god who is the path for the deities [should be given];
the fruit known as *kuṣmāṇḍa* should be offered to Agni, the one who enjoys the gods.
*Puroḍāśa* cakes and sacrificial porridges (*caru*) should also be presented as is appropriate.
Thus it is; let no doubt be entertained here by the Brahmins.
I am the speaker of the Vedas, and I alone am the very soul of sacrifice.
I abide within the mantra itself; let the twice-born know me in their hearts.
"Let them make this solemn vow: 'A living being must certainly not be killed.
Let them perform worship of my two testicles in the form of Śālagrāma stones;
by that, there will indeed be peace for the fire. (91–92)
Otherwise, there would be no extinguishing of the fire, and the world would be reduced to ashes.
Indeed, my two testicles, which were the source of virility, were cut off by me while in the workshop.
From those two, villages and settlements were produced, numbering more than millions and billions.
"For all those Śālagrāmas are my very form and consist of my essence.
They are all capable of reducing the universe to ashes; let the twice-born indeed worship them.
Having been addressed thus, all the gods of the earth worshipped them with many ritual offerings.
The Vaiṣṇavas worshipped them again and again with Sāman mantras and the Puṃsūkta hymns;
yet even then, those Śāla stones did not become pacified.
Then I said to the brāhmaṇas, "Listen with concentrated minds!"
"Without a suitable seat, those stones will not attain peace.
Let them pray for Śrī; Lakṣmī will provide what is appropriate.
Then, you were worshipped by the brahmins with the Lakṣmīsūkta and other hymns. (97–98)
Having been worshipped, saluted, and offered for the sake of peace,
you then became the nature of a seat in the form of a *pippala* leaf.
You were born as the essence of a divine throne, possessing a divine golden form.
Indeed, those rocks were named after the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), and they too remained steadfast.
Then the rocks attained peace and stability, becoming motionless;
they were free from all disturbances, and the fire was extinguished in every direction.
Then the Śālagrāmas were worshipped by all the gods, the ancestors, human beings, and sages with various offerings such as sandalwood and fragrant services;
thus they became divine Hari-s.
Those who consist of Hari, who are portions of Hari, and who always possess the form of Hari’s image;
who are composed of my own limbs, whose essence is myself, and who bestow liberation—those blessed ones, endowed with Śrī, became stone images. (103–104)
Then, when I held my two testicles in their proper place and they became firmly fixed for me, I was endowed with virility;
indeed, I attained a complete form, for devotees are protected by me.
Formerly, at the Naramedha sacrifice, having appeared in a manifest form,
I then became the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
and the beginningless Śrī Śālapuṃstva Nārāyaṇa.

O Lakṣmī! I became a gentle form of Śālagrāma upon a beautiful and auspicious pedestal for the duration of an eon; remember me as being in such a state, and likewise remember you in that same condition.
And I dwelt together with you as the embodied Lord of Śrī, a personified being.
O beloved, those other incarnations of mine occurred during that kalpa;
O beloved, I indeed know all my incarnations according to their respective purposes.
By reading or even hearing [this account], both worldly enjoyment and liberation arise.

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī-Puṃstva-Nārāyaṇa for the Protection of Devotees during the Human Sacrifice in the Twenty-Seventh Year called Avṛṣa of the Creator, along with the Knowledge of the Purpose of the Naramedha and Other Sacrifices," in the Third Section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 23 [Author:
Chapter 24 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this most purifying and divine narrative of mine concerning the manifestation [of the Lord] during the year of the Fire-born (Agni),
in the twenty-eighth kalpa of the first Manu, within the eight-hundredth cycle. || 1 ||
There was a king named Sūryavarcas, who had been enlightened by Brahmā;
he was devoted to the path of the Vedas, the sovereign lord of all the circles of stars, and seated in the assembly of the gods in a celestial chariot that travels through the sky. (2–3)
In the netherworlds as well as on Mount Meru and among the planets,
that observant youth, ever intent upon my worship and a servant of the Siddhas,
was diligent in his efforts for the sake of the devotion of all creatures, possessing the virtues of a holy man. (4)
Once, while in his own residence with the queen, he reflected:
"O beloved, this human body of mine was bestowed by the king;
O beloved, when will it truly function according to its literal meaning—that it 'protects men' (nṛ-pāti)? || 5-6 ||
The queen said: "This human body is for the sake of attaining liberation.
In granting liberation to men, the king acts for his own purpose;
otherwise, the word 'king' (nṛpa) would not be considered meaningful in the teaching. (7)
Having come into being again and again, human beings, driven by their karma, dissolve away.
Even when the task of protecting them has been performed, they go to destruction.
Indeed, the protection of the body is not true protection; lordship over the body is not protection.
Food, water, fire, and wind protect by their very nature;
there is no need for kings where protection is provided by nature itself.
In the Golden Age, there is indeed no theft, no deception, and no plundering.
Therefore, the age simply passes away there, for kings are not protected [by dharma].
Since the king is useless during the Kṛta Yuga when the dharma of truth prevails, the meaningfulness of kingship must be sought [in other ages] if it is to exist at all. (11–12)
"O Lord of Subjects! It appears clearly to my mind that you, O King, have made yourself meaningful by bestowing the gift of liberation; therefore, please do so.
Just as a king himself attains liberation through devotion, [so should he act]. || 13 ||
If even the subjects were to attain liberation through supreme devotion,
then the kingship would have been made meaningful by that knower of birth.
O King, you too should exercise such a kingship that it grants liberation.
Having heard these words of his queen, the king rejoiced within himself,
considering his wife— who was equal to the Vedas— to be a virtuous companion in the pursuit of liberation.
He then questioned his beloved again, she who was named Mudgāyanī.
"By what method can liberation be achieved for human beings? Instruct me.
(17) Then Mudgāyanī spoke to the perfected sages, the ascetics, and having summoned the virtuous men and women from other worlds as well. (18)

Having caused a temple to be built and having installed the image of the Supreme Goddess who bestows liberation, you should always perform great festivals. Let the subjects offer service, worship, sight, and likewise remembrance.
They will perform chanting, hearing, servitude, service, salutation, and praise;
they will perform worship, dancing, and the offering of their devotion; and they will offer food, clothing, vessels, and sandalwood paste. (3.23.20–21)
By offering articles of adornment, as well as fragrant substances,
the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), songs, and the recitation of mantras,
and by performing the surrender of the self (ātmapraṇidhāna), they shall go to the supreme state.
Sweeping and smearing [the ground], as well as the offering of lamps and the offering of banners;
(23) the offering of musical instruments and their playing, likewise the offering of fruits and flowers;
the offering of saffron, unbroken rice grains, and garlands, and the offering of incense. (24)
The offering of food (naivedya), likewise the offering of the waving of lights (nīrājana),
circumambulation, praise, prostration, as well as the gesture of joined palms (añjali);
the gestures (hāva) and expressions (bhāva) of Hari, as well as the observation and meditation [upon Him].
People will engage in discussion, deliberation, and even decision-making regarding wealth, gold, silver, copper, or a staff;
as well as divine ornaments, gems, jewels, and diamonds. (26–27)
Mañjarīs, flower garlands, clusters, and most beautiful garments;
likewise, a crown, bracelets, a wreath, a chain, a girdle,
as well as rings and weapons such as the conch, the discus, and so forth.
A fine garment, a comfortable bed, sandals, and an excellent vehicle; a mount, a celestial chariot, wealth in cattle, and flavorful juices;
most delicious sugar-candies and the like, honey, clarified butter, and spices such as long pepper.
Men will indeed offer water-pots, beautiful jars, bowls, vessels for worship, wicks, and the various implements required for the festival;
having made these offerings to Hari, they shall go to the supreme abode.
Even those devoted to ritual action, having performed sacrificial sessions in the temple of Hari,

and even mendicants, having eaten the food of grace (prasāda), shall go to His abode. Even those who have committed offenses, having begged for forgiveness in the presence of Hari, [shall likewise attain that state].
Even the wicked, by confessing their evil deeds, shall go to the supreme goal;
the observer of vows, having fulfilled his vows, shall go to the highest state.
Women, too, by worshipping the god Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, [shall attain the same].
They shall go to that beloved Lord of All, the supreme state.
Whether they be young or old, wealthy or even destitute, by worshipping that Blessed One in every way, they shall go to the supreme state. (25, 365)
Therefore, O King, in order to open the path to liberation for living beings and to make your kingship truly meaningful, have a beautiful and excellent temple of Śrī Hari constructed,
provided with one thousand pots.

Establish there, according to the prescribed rites, the golden Lord Hari— the Blessed One, the Sovereign, the Divine— who possesses a thousand peaks, is beautiful, adorned with golden domes, touches the heavens, and abounds in splendor. (38–39)
The Supreme Lord, the creator of the universe, who possesses a beautiful and handsome form, who is awakened by the hosts of gods and celestial sages,
who is endowed with His own power, and who is served by His own attendants of sovereign power. (3.23.40)
And there, establish the Lord Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, who is joined with his own abode,
who is visible to all, worthy of service by all, the destroyer of all sins,
and the bestower of all peace. (41–42)
Having spoken thus to her husband, the queen then remained silent for a moment.
The king considered those words—which were wholesome, truthful, and conducive to liberation—to be most excellent.
He then performed a month-long sacrificial session of recitation accompanied by congregational chanting.
He summoned the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, the gods, and human beings. He caused them to perform the monthly worship known as Akhaṇḍa-nāma-bhajana, [chanting]:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, Supreme Person!"
"O Inner Self, O Lord Viṣṇu, O Supreme Ruler, salutations be unto you!"—
in this manner the king performed worship incessantly.
He indeed provided various foods that were as delicious as nectar.
He joyfully performed every kind of service for all the performers of the sacrifice.
O beloved! Gods and others constantly arrived from the various worlds and departed; there, worship took place perpetually and without interruption. || 47-48 ||
Thus, when the month of Śrāvaṇa had passed and on its final day, on the full moon,
the king posed a question in the midst of the assembly:
"May there be an unimpeded path to liberation for human beings here in this world."
"In whatever way the gods and others may grant me a glorious renown, so shall it be.
Then the Siddhas said, "In that case, have a temple built here.
The sages, the gods, and the humans likewise spoke thus.
"Through this temple, supreme nourishment for liberation will arise here.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, cause it to be built and establish therein the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord. (52)
Having uttered "Om" and completed the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) for the Lord who bestows all liberation and exists in the form of an image,
the king then had a golden [mountain] fashioned, endowed with a thousand peaks. ||53-54||
The first temple on earth, visible and reaching to the stars,
was completed with all its primary and secondary parts; thereafter,
he reflected upon the matter of the [divine] image, wondering from where and by what means it might come to be.
At night, the king, filled with despondency, reflected in his mind;
he remembered me, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī, the Puruṣottama.
O Padmaja! Knowing the remembrance of my devotee, I appeared together with you.
I went to where that king was, and I became visible to him. Then Sūryavarcas, seeing me within his range of vision before him,
bowed, offered me the madhuparka, and prostrated himself like a staff.
He offered me a seat, which was adorned with every ornament,
for the inner self who blazes with all splendor, who is endowed with all sovereignty,
and who causes a rain of grace toward all.
Filled with devotion, the king offered food, drink, worship, and his own self; indeed, he made the offering of all that he possessed.
There, in a beautiful temple that had been constructed, he entreated me.

O Blessed One, dwell here permanently; remain forever steadfast in this place, which is indeed fit for eternal residence and surrounded by great gardens. Dwell there together with Lakṣmī, accompanied by your attendants and all necessary requisites.
"For the sake of the liberation of the world, I have spoken thus: 'So be it.
Then he said, 'Go, O Indra among kings, to the great and excellent śiṃśapā tree standing in the midst of the hermitage of the sages at the edge of the forest.'"
To its side, situated on the left, is the most auspicious banyan tree (vaṭavṛkṣa).
Just as my dwelling is here in this temple, it is exactly the same there;
O King, those two trees in your kingdom are our very forms in personified shape.

By my own will alone, both Lakṣmī and I have fashioned these two eternal and divine forms of mine, which are ancient and many years old. Śrī and Narāyaṇa remain eternally nourished and worthy of worship by the gods.
"O King, come and worship and honor those two; they are our own selves.
Worshipped by the sages, we two always abide here in the form of trees. Now, indeed, we have manifested ourselves here in our true embodied forms. || 68–69 ||
"And we two shall remain here, O King, established by our own power according to the prescribed rite.
Having been addressed thus, the king went to the vicinity of a banyan tree in the great garden,
which was joined by a *śiṃśapā* tree and possessed divine, celestial flavors.
Beholding the white banyan tree, the king was struck with wonder.
Having prostrated before the sages according to the prescribed rites, the king himself performed worship for the two trees joined together, as directed by the assembly of great seers.
Having offered incense, lamps, water, food offerings, and a handful of flowers,
I then performed the three-fold circumambulation at that *śiṃśapā* tree.
Within its trunk resides Nārāyaṇa himself, the eternal Supreme Self.

The glorious Puruṣottama, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, appeared before me with a dark complexion and a divine form. I myself became that very trunk of the *śiṃśapā* tree; indeed, I am not distinct from the trunk. (74–75)

Then all my male attendants and indeed my female attendants appeared, endowed with bodies like mine and possessing my own nature; they were seen as branches upon me. O beloved! Then, O you who are within my range of vision, [they appeared] on the tree, the banyan, and the trunk.
Not distinct from the trunk, yet containing the trunk within, she is the very form of the cause of the banyan tree.
Your branches and your friends appeared as beautiful, beloved ones who were non-different from you—your yoginīs, whose essence is you. (77–78)
Thus, having beheld you and me, King Sūryavarcas was filled with joy;
quickly prostrating himself like a staff and consecrating us with Vedic mantras,
he indeed caused you and me to ascend the chariot with due honor.

Then, accompanied by a great festival, he brought [the image] onto the grounds of the palace in a golden chariot, beautifully adorned with a hundred jars, capable of being drawn by a hundred elephants,
and according to the prescribed rites within a pavilion.
Having established [the deity] according to the prescribed rites and performed the consecration through all the ritual acts,
he installed me, you, as well as your attendants and your consorts within the temple—
divine beings who had appeared before his very eyes.
I have indeed dwelt in my own abode together with you until the end of the kalpa.
For the sake of those who possess divine vision and are endowed with devotion, I exist in a divine form;
for the sake of those who possess physical eyes and are subject to māyā, I exist in the form of a physical image.

I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). As the beginningless Śrī Śiṃśapā Nārāyaṇa, I became dark-complexioned (Śyāmala) and attained the renown as the beginningless Śrī Śyāma Nārāyaṇa. (85)
"You have attained the fame of Vaṭaśrī; you are exceedingly beautiful by my side.
Indeed, you possess a fair, white-golden, divine body that is enchanting.
Therefore, humans, as well as gods and great sages, shall always [worship] you. (86–87)
O Lakṣmī! In that kalpa, both the Pitṛs and the Asuras attained liberation by serving me and you; they indeed became kings there as companions.
By that king, acting upon the instruction of the queen, [the city] was made a bestower of final release.
"Indeed, by surrendering me to you, the king has granted the gift of fearlessness to all.
I know this, O Lakṣmī! My form is dark, while your form, O Lakṣmī, is fair; remember that palace as well. (3.23.90)
Remember also that attendant, the king, and the queen-consort as your friend;
remember the countless millions, billions, and trillions who were born at that time and have since been liberated.
Even then, many other incarnations of mine were born in great numbers.
"O beloved, I indeed know these [devotees] according to their respective actions.
Thus, through my dark form, I accept the supreme devotion of my devotees:
hearing, chanting, serving the feet, and likewise bowing down. (92–93)
Worship, as well as friendship and self-surrender;
anointing, sweeping, massaging the feet, and feeding;
drinking water, offering garments and ornaments, and likewise decoration.
Worship, prostration, traveling together,
dancing, singing, sporting, playing in the garden, strolling, and laughing— all this I accepted, having become truly pleased with them. (95–96)
She led even me to my own abode, the supreme station known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Through my yoga, the entire earth became Vaiṣṇavī, and men and women became Vaiṣṇavas;
even beasts and birds attained liberation.
"Śyāmala, Śyāmala"— thus chanting, O beloved, the multitudes of living beings then approached me, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, at that kalpa. Even sinners, by praising Hari Śyāma, became righteous.
By reading, hearing, and remembering this, one shall attain liberation.
At the end, the king, along with his country, his lineage, his subjects, his dependents,
his servants, and his wives, indeed attained liberation.
Even cows, horses, and other such beings have attained supreme liberation.
Therefore, the construction of my temple and the installation of my image constitute the best gift of fearlessness for living beings on this earth.

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Primeval Śrī Śiṃśapā (Śyāma) Nārāyaṇa together with Vaṭaśrī in the Temple by means of King Sūryavarcas," in the twenty-eighth year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the lineage of the Dvāpara age, within the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 24 *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga),
Chapter 24.
[The Author: Chapter 25.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! during the year of Brahmā’s father.
In the twenty-ninth kalpa, consisting of ninety [cycles], during the seventh Manvantara, O Padmaja, hear how my manifestation occurred here in this world!
From the secret pores of Brahmā, an Asura of variegated form appeared. || 1-2 ||
He was born as one named Mayūra, possessing wings, tail-feathers, and a beak;
endowed with feet, able to assume any form at will, and resembling a mountain.
Soaring through the sky, he would draw toward himself the entire circle of the planets.
Moving upon the earth, he drags along village chiefs and mountains;
having entered into the water, he agitates the oceans,
makes the very earth tremble, and strikes terror into the gods.
He even carries off thousands of humans, nāgas, and serpents;
at times he becomes a god, possessing his own natural form with a splendor like that of Mahendra; and at other times he assumes a human form resembling that of a sovereign emperor.
In some places he was like a great seer, resplendent with a halo of brilliance;
indeed, he could assume any form at will, being both delusive and powerful.
Out of greed for the kingdom, he performed austerities for a thousand years.
Brahmā, being pleased, granted him a boon: "Death shall not come to you, except for Hari.
Having thus received these words, he was indeed satisfied and became entirely free from fear.
[He moved] through the world of truth (Satyaloka), among people, in heaven, in the human realm, and in the netherworlds (Atala) and so forth.
Assuming various forms, he goes, eats, and rejoices.
Sometimes, having gone to the abodes of the gods and partaken of the nectar of immortality, he departs;
or, having abducted a divine or human woman, he goes to another place.
Having taken a yakṣiṇī or a rākṣasī, or having taken wealth, he departs;
or having taken a dānavī, a virtuous woman, or a nāgī, he goes to another forest. Having taken cows, heifers, horses, and elephants, he likewise departs.
In a forest grove rich with trees on Mount Meru, extending for a hundred yojanas,
he established his own opulent residence, beautiful with excellent enjoyments.
Having repeatedly abducted men, women, goddesses, and even rākṣasīs, [he settled there].
Having performed all his own duties, he enjoys that which consists of worldly pleasures;
due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā, he does not meet death in battle, and because of his ability to go everywhere, he always attains victory. (15)
Thus, by his own power, he became like a sovereign on earth;
having gradually conquered other kings, he then became a lord of kings and declares, "My sovereignty extends everywhere over the realm of mortals. (16–17)
And he made this proclamation: "I alone am the universal monarch; having gone everywhere, being powerful, I conquer the entire circle of the earth.
Having established kings over the realms of the asuras, I rule the kingdom. (18)
Thus, in due course, Mayūraka became a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Then, desiring to violate Indrāṇī, he went to the heavenly world;
and having lifted her up, he flew through the air toward the earth.
Indra advanced toward him and struck him with his thunderbolt;
however, that bird caught the thunderbolt, which resembled fire, in its beak and swallowed it.
Then Indra was seized with terror upon beholding the power of the peacock.
He returned to his own abode and informed the guardians of the quarters.
All the guardians of the quarters, fully prepared for battle, assembled together:
Yama, Kubera, Īśāna, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, and Anila.
Anala, Arka, and Rudra all arrived upon the earth;
accompanied by their armies and with weapons ready, they roared in the sky. Having uttered war-cries as well as the thunderous roars of the celestial dwellers, [the battle commenced].
Mayūra quickly set forth with his forces for the sake of battle.
Accompanied by ten thousand generals and joined by the soldiers of Abja,
he indeed fought a terrible war against Mānava for a full year.
He indeed restored his own army, which had been slaughtered in many ways, to life;
through a demonic science (*āsuryā vidyayā*), he fought with the lords of the gods.
Extremely cruel *māyūrakas* belonging to the asuras were present on all sides.
Together with all the hosts of gods, they fought most fearlessly.
There was no end to the battle, nor did the peacock perish;
there was no cessation for the gods, and human beings became miserable.
The daughters of Manu, the daughters of the gods, the truthful daughters of the Nāgas,
and even the daughters of the Daityas— stricken with terror, they did not emerge at all from within the three worlds, throughout all the realms, among the subjects, or even among the kings.
At that time, anxiety and suffering were constantly present for him.
Then the gods became despondent, having undergone great exhaustion;
the sun became lusterless, and Mahendra’s mind was broken.
Varuṇa’s power was exhausted, and Yama fell into a state of confusion;
likewise, Nirṛti’s army was depleted in that battle.
Īśāna’s enthusiasm was destroyed, and Kubera’s strength failed.
Agni was deprived of his fiery heat, and Marut began to weep.
The other gods became despondent, while the kings fell under their control. Thus, when this time had arrived, suffering became excessive on all sides.
Abandoning the battle, the gods went to the abode of Brahmā;
they entreated him most fervently, declaring their own inferiority and restraining the power of the Asura for the sake of protection. (36)
Having heard them, Brahmā said: "I shall strive for your sake.
Let all of you remain here and worship Hari, the Supreme;
for by my boon, there is indeed no one other than Hari who can destroy him."
Thus addressed, the deities and others, filled with eagerness, worshipped me—
the beginningless Śrīśa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. O Lakṣmī, I, mounted upon an elephant, quickly descended from the imperishable realm (Akṣara) along with you.
Then he went to Satyaloka, to the assembly hall of Brahmā.
Thereupon, Brahmā and the other gods offered him a welcome and worship;
they recounted their own suffering and resolved upon the destruction of the Asuras.
Then, O Lotus-born One! I contemplated the destruction of the asuras and said to the gods, "Go to your own regions.
The gods departed quickly for their respective lands, and I went to the land of men.
Assuming a form, he came to the earth where the abode of the asura was indeed located.
Having assumed the form of a kṣatriya, equipped with a bow and an arrow,
I went to his city gate and caused him to perform the act of begging alms.
Then Mayūra himself, having been informed by his messengers,
came eagerly to his own gate for the sake of hospitality.
Having bowed to me, he said, "What indeed do you ask for in alms?"
"Give me alms in the form of battle here; I beg for nothing else," he said.
Thus entreated, he then took water in his hand and gave the alms;
having joined weapon with weapon and bow with bow, that [alms] was received by me as well.
Right there, at the front of the city gate in that excellent forest, a terrible and most fearsome battle took place with him alone for the duration of a month,
involving the gods, humans, and the ancestors who are devoted to virtuous conduct.
It caused the hair to stand on end even for the most heroic kings.
Then, the gods, perceiving that the battle was underway, came through the path of the sky and watched right there; they then proclaimed victory to me.
"I alone shall indeed fight with the peacock, and no one else.
At the end of the month, by my arrows, weapons, missiles, clubs, and other arms, his feathers will be torn away;
he will quickly become [mangled] and then lose all hope. || 5.1 ||
He joined the Mayūrakas, who had emerged victorious in their own battles, in the fray.
Those Arbudas and Mayūrakas, acting as his auxiliaries, surrounded me on all sides and fought with great speed. (52–53)
They assume illusory forms and likewise bear illusory weapons;
they wear illusory disguises and likewise engage in illusory battles.
They assume illusory bodies and present illusory armies.
All of them were slain there by me, one after another, with the Sudarśana discus.
Those peacocks were burnt and killed by the splendor of the Sudarśana;
the city of Māyūrakī was burnt, yet those who were devoted to me were well protected by me.
Śacī and the other beloved ones, as well as the Mānavīs and the Mānavas—
men, women, and deities— I protected them all right there.
All those Asuras who belonged to the lineage of Mayūra have been slain.
Indeed, they were all completely destroyed by Sudarśana. Then Māyūraka, seeing his own total destruction,
became blind and, seizing a great sword in his hand, leapt into the air.
Having assumed a body consisting mostly of stone, he fell upon my head with the edge of a sword to kill me; at that moment, I hurled the Sudarśana [discus] from below,
and it then consumed him in the sky.
Everything was indeed reduced to ashes and merged into the very sky.
Divine drums resounded, and a rain of flowers fell upon me;
there was a shower of sandalwood and unbroken grains of rice, as well as shouts of victory.
Then the women born of the Māyūra lineage wept in vain;
having summoned the gods, I descended there at that city,
in the great forest of Māyūraka, which was resplendent with every prosperity.
Even upon seeing prisons, I liberated the people from those places.
I quickly liberated the gods, as well as the goddesses; I liberated the deities headed by Śacī, and likewise the human women.
In that kingdom, all the deities and even the gods and men bathed me—
the Kṣatriya, the Supreme Self, Śrī Hari, the Puruṣottama—
with the waters of sacred fords and worshipped me according to the prescribed rites.
And full of eagerness, they established [him] together with Śrī.
At that time, many maidens and women born of the lineage of Mayūra,
being without a protector, joyfully chose me as their supreme lord.
Purified by me at the sacrifice and taken by me according to the prescribed rite,
they were all then offered as my wives by Brahmā and the other gods.
In this manner, the great asura named Mayūra was slain by me in the past.
"Indeed, his destruction could not have occurred without me, for he was created by no other;
his splendor, having issued forth, found rest in me alone.
That asura attained liberation, as did the others who were slain. (3.24.70–71)
All those who were slain by my Sudarśana have indeed attained liberation;
even the kings, having worshipped me as the Supreme Lord, were liberated.
They returned to their own lands, and the gods went to the third heaven.
The wives of the Nāgas, the daughters of Manu, and even goddesses who were previously without protectors—
all of them remained as my wives after marrying me at that time, O beloved. You, however, became Śrī, the name of the queen of all those royal ladies.
Born not from a womb, assuming the form of a Kṣatriya, and standing by my side—
you then took the feathers of a peacock and fashioned a broom for the purpose of sweeping the floor, and likewise by my attendants as well. (75)

All the Mārjanikās were made beautiful and splendid. Then, by means of my own celestial chariot, I traveled everywhere on the surface of the earth in every direction to wherever those Asuras were who had been turned into peacocks by me.
Having gone to each of those very places and having uprooted them by killing them, O beloved,
I bestowed all the kingdoms upon the Kṣatriyas according to their respective rights. In this way, my entire empire on the surface of the earth was established everywhere.
And at that time, the supreme Vaiṣṇava [weapon] was established by the Supreme Self,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the discus,
who protects in the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṣatra Nārāyaṇa.
"O beloved! Remember [this]: together with Anādiśrī and Rājarājñī, all the bulls among Kṣatriyas have been protected by me upon the circle of the earth;
all sacrifices have been performed, and the subjects as well have been protected. (3.24.80–81)
The deities were protected and the paths of Dharma were set in motion;
the traditions of sacrificial sessions were established and the ways of the Vedas were nourished.
Political principles were firmly established and the virtuous were protected at that time.
Excellent monasteries were established, and temples dedicated to the gods and others were constructed.
The holy places of pilgrimage (tīrthas) were indeed protected, and the mendicants were also protected.
Furthermore, all the narratives concerning Nārāyaṇa were recited constantly.
The virtuous women were protected and always guarded in righteousness;
devotion to me was also established by them throughout the entire earth.
Furthermore, at that time, the Vedic knowledge of the Self was proclaimed by me in that Kalpa.
O Lakṣmī! At that time in my assembly, there were ten thousand virtuous men;
ten thousand Brahmins, ten thousand virtuous women, ten thousand young students (baṭu), and ten thousand Vedic scholars.
Ten thousand guests, ten thousand mendicants,
ten thousand destitute ones, and ten thousand reciters;
ten thousand performers of sacrifices and ten thousand performers of long sacrificial sessions.
Ten thousand Yaminas, ten thousand Tāpasas;
ten thousand Vratins, ten thousand Paṇḍitas;
ten thousand male servants and ten thousand female servants. (3.24.90)
Knowing ten thousand yogas and possessing ten thousand modes of movement,
they always abide established in purity, devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
All of them, endowed with devotion to me, partake of food at my sacrificial feast.
Those who bore my image were devoted to the path of meditation;
they took up residence there and remained constantly dedicated to the offering of their own selves.
By me, sovereignty over the earth was established, encompassed by the seven oceans. (92–93)
Indeed, for the sake of the liberation of human beings and for the gods to attain happiness,
all those dwelling in the netherworlds (pātāla) and elsewhere, as well as those residing in heaven and other realms,
followed me and took refuge in me, the Lord of All.
Then I dwelt incessantly upon the surface of the earth for an entire kalpa.
At that time, the earth became free from distress and was equal to Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, there were wish-fulfilling trees, the celestial cows, and desire-granting creepers.
Through my yogic power, wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi) were present everywhere at that time;
there was always the Kṛta Yuga, and time became uniform.
There were also [beings] belonging to the mental, the tactile, and likewise the visual [spheres].
And so, at that time, there were indeed creations dwelling together.
O Queen of the King of Kings, remember all this regarding your status as the sovereign over kings!
I know all of that, but others of dull intellect do not know it. (98–99)
"Furthermore, other incarnations of mine have occurred at that time as was appropriate,
taking the forms of gods and humans to accomplish their respective tasks.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, I have described here to you my manifestation."
"By reading or even by hearing this, one obtains the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(101) Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Rājanārāyaṇa, together with the Queen Śrī, for the Purpose of Destroying the Asura Māyūraka in the Twenty-ninth Year of Brahmā during the Dvāpara Age," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (24)
