Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! My manifestation occurred after that, during the thirtieth year of Brahmā known as Deva-vatsara. || 1 ||
In the past, in the fourteenth Manvantara, during the thousandth Kalpa of that Yuga,
O Lakṣmī, I shall indeed tell you of your wonder along with me.
Listen to how your manifestation then occurred upon the surface of the earth.
When the funeral rites were completed, five devotees of us two arose in Surāṣṭra:
Devasakha, Kīrti, Ciklīta, Kardama, and Jātavedas. O brahmins, they were brothers, born of the same womb, and endowed with the quality of goodness (sāttvika).
The ascetics were disciplined in dharma, contented, and exponents of the Veda;
they were devoted to purity, austerity, contentment, self-study, and worship.
They abided in non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, virtuous conduct, and non-possessiveness.
They have practiced [self-restraint] and are devoted to the tranquility of the senses and their control;
they abide in forbearance, patience, gentleness, and what is most beneficial;
and they are ever established in yoga born of discernment, in knowledge, and in the excellence of sattva.
Established in meditation, fire-offerings, recitation, worship, and respectful service;
established in the knowledge of the Self as Brahman and in self-surrender;
they likewise always possess the eight supernatural powers and the nine treasures.
Their speech is like that of the wish-fulfilling tree, and they serve as wish-granting cows in their ministrations.
(9) They sleep in the open air, wear the directions as their garments, and subsist on fruits;
they drink water and nectar, possess the radiance of lamps, and abide in meditative absorption. (3.25.10)
They were self-controlled, with their inner selves supported by the abode of Brahman;
endowed with devotion, they associated with the virtuous and were intent on honoring chaste women.
All of them honored guests, were free from worldly desire, and were disincarnate (liberated).
They are unobstructed in nature and move without impediment;
they are devoid of the touch and other qualities of the elements, and are free from bodily defects and the like.
Their divine bodies are like adamant, and they are devoted solely to divine bliss. (12–13)
They possess the power to enjoy all things obtained by mere thought and travel by means of yoga;
they have mastered speech, are destroyers of suffering, and are compassionate toward those who seek refuge.
Like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, Arka, Candra, and other gods, [they appear in various forms].
They were renowned on earth, as well as in the worlds of Bhuvaḥ, Svar, Mahar,
Jana, Tapas, and Satya, and likewise on Mount Meru and in all the nether regions (pātālas).
All of them possessed sovereign power like other lords.
Like gods, they remove suffering; like yogis, they reveal the Self; like merchant chiefs, they bestow wealth; like husbands, they grant sons;
like protectors, they are masters; and likewise, like Viṣṇu, they are givers. (17)
In their knowledge they were all like the assemblies of Brahmā; in their fulfillment they were like the wish-fulfilling trees of the kalpa.
Their bodies were radiant with celibacy, and likewise, they possessed the splendor of the earth in their steadfastness.
These thousands of holy men were like those who have attained liberation, their desires being entirely fulfilled.
Having indeed recognized such well-known [beings], suffering people come day and night for the sake of destroying their own afflictions;
[they come to those who are] sick, as well as those who enjoy pleasures, the wretched, and those sharing in poverty. (3.25.20)
Misers, those suffering from enemies, the destitute, those without sons,
those lacking food, clothing, or palaces, those full of desires, the hungry, those seeking liberation, and those on the verge of death— these always come for refuge. (21–22)

Devoted to bestowing blessings, they indeed destroy the afflictions of those [who approach them]. As givers of all things—of happinesses and of wealth and prosperity—men and women go forth with their desires fulfilled. (23)
They are joyful, their desires fulfilled, their hopes realized, and their minds content. To those seeking wealth, they indeed grant riches born of spiritual perfection;
to those seeking sons, they grant offspring and whatever else is desired.
They bestow husbands, wives, home, kingdom, fields, elephants, and likewise cows; they grant health, the expansion of one's lineage, and prosperity.
To those who seek refuge, they bring about freedom from the three types of suffering and other afflictions.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, all those who possessed miraculous powers became like Īśvara on this earth; they were my devotees in every respect. Then once, in their abode, there was one endowed with fortune who was devoted to his desires. (27–28)
An Asura named Prasaviṣṇu, possessed of great strength, approached;
assuming the form of a Brahmin, he was an ascetic driven by lustful desire, thinking, "May she who is the wife of Nārāyaṇa become my wife. (29)
Filled with desire for Lakṣmī, he came before the devotees.
Then the asura begged for his desired alms from even those five:
"O givers, grant me Lakṣmī, the wife of Nārāyaṇa. (3.25.30–31)
Upon hearing of that unworthy alms-offering, the devotees then thought it was so;
however, in order to avoid the stigma of being considered non-givers, they said "Om.
[Thinking: "Either Hari or Lakṣmī will surely take this away by force."
Having reflected thus, the lords of givers remembered my beloved Śrī.
And she, commanded by me—who act in accordance with the desires of my devotees—quickly arrived from the Imperishable Abode (Akṣara) before the five [gods]. 33–34.
The maiden was beautiful, twelve years of age,
enriched with the splendor of all ornaments, her body like a golden campaka flower.
Then, beholding you, so lovely and enchanting in form, the asura—
He considered the accomplishment of his own purpose and rejoiced in his heart, being equal to them.
Then those companions of the gods and others, having seen her, worshipped the sovereign Goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is capable of all things, even after making their request for forgiveness.

O beloved! Having presented water for the purpose of a gift to the Asura, they then took it in their hands and gave it to the Asura. Then the procreative Asura, assuming the form of a brahmin, approached you.
He went to his own home; there, you observed a supreme vow. Indeed, that which is called lifelong celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be strictly maintained.
An Asura must never be touched by one who is an ascetic and whose conduct is unimpaired.
Then, having reached that house, he desires to touch you; however,
seeing you surrounded by garlands of flames possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction,
his mind becomes terrified, and he retreats just as he came.
Then, after deliberating for many days on another cause for the sake of accomplishing your touch, he returned once more to those five devotees,
as well as to Rati personified, for the sake of obtaining abundant food.
"May they grant me Kāma personified in form and arrows, along with Vasanta," they thought; and as they had so resolved, those five devotees remembered them there,
and Kāma and the others, being thus invoked, quickly appeared before them.
Then, even though they were being given away as gifts to the great Asura, he took them at that time;
the Asura, having taken Kāma and the others, went toward his own abode and commanded them to enter the body of Kamalā.
"By those [means] by which that Lakṣmī has been tormented, she will come to me of her own accord"—
thinking thus, that Asura also waited expectantly.
Then Kāma discharged his arrows, beginning with the Unmādana.
Spring, truly enchanting on all sides with its flowers,
was in full bloom there with splendor, and it even brought others to a state of blossoming.
Then Rati herself, personified along with Lakṣmī, gradually [arrived].
As she was about to enter, Lakṣmī approached her accompanied by her laughter;
having recognized that wicked woman, the wife of Kāma, who was evil-minded, the Supreme Goddess immediately fell into a state of wrath. (3.25.50)
She herself produced the fire of universal destruction from her two eyes;
she beheld Rati, Kāma, Vasanta, and his arrows,
as well as the Asura, and reduced them all to ashes in a mere moment.
O Queen of the Gods! As soon as she had performed [the act] characterized by her lifelong vow, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among both the gods and humans.
This was due to the destruction of Rati, the destruction of Kāma, and the destruction of Vasanta and the others.
In the absence of the proper seasons, the groves, forests, gardens, and other such places became devoid of flowers;
they were stripped of new sprouts and, at that time, became bereft of beauty.
Indeed, even though beauty still existed, the world became as if it possessed no beauty at all.
The joys of both women and men have gone to dissolution;
all pleasures have met their end through the destruction of the prolific one.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Rati and the others have been consumed by you with the fire of your eyes.
Indeed, by your vow, the entire world has become established in its ultimate state.
Both gods, humans, and great sages—all embodied beings—having reflected together on what this is and how it came to be, have become united [in their resolve]. (57–58)
They went to Satya and Vaidhasa and said, "Alas, this is a calamity!
There is no pleasure, there is no desire, and indeed, there is no spring anywhere.
What is this, and how has it come to pass? Please ward off this intense affliction."
Thus addressed, Brahmā then reflected for a moment and said:
"Those who were formerly the five gods and the five Indras— beyond that,
these five devotees indeed worship the Supreme Lord in this kalpa."
The Deva-sakha and all the others are givers who fulfill the needs of supplicants;
those five lords are capable of bestowing every kind of prosperity.
And the prolific great asura offered Lakṣmī to them.
A powerful, wicked being, full of great defects, was born from the impurity of my *liṅga*.
Then those brahmins summoned Lakṣmī and gave her to him;
taking her, the asura went toward his own home. (63–64)
Lakṣmī also observed a vow, maintaining the lifelong celibacy of a student.
The Asura, driven by the force of passion, approached Lakṣmī to touch her;
but seeing her possessing the brilliance of the fire born at the time of universal dissolution, the great Asura was struck with terror.
Having returned, he likewise begged from the brahmins Rati,
Kāma, Vasanta, and the Bāṇas; O twice-born ones, those [brahmins] gave him all of them in embodied form, and taking them, the asura went to his home.
He indeed incited them all to make Lakṣmī fickle;
Lakṣmī, enraged, produced the fire of universal dissolution from her two eyes and reduced them all to ashes,
as did the world itself.
Devoid of Rati, it is rendered useless by the arrows of desire and the spring season;
it has become joyless, and this alone is the cause. Indeed, that which was spoken there is the only means; there is no other way to prevent this.
Through the wrath of Lakṣmī, Kāma, Rati, Asuraka,
Prasava, Bāṇa, and Vasanta have always been dead.
If Lakṣmī, being propitiated, were to bring them all back to life again—
Even if one has completed the lifelong vow (naiṣṭhika-vrata) before the presence of Hari,
if one should support all living beings by the command of the Supreme Lord,
then this defect of impotence will depart from the three worlds.
Thinking, "It shall not be otherwise," we strive toward Śrī Hari for that purpose.
We perform worship here; Hari himself, being well-pleased, will come here quickly and dispel our suffering.
Having been addressed thus, they performed my worship in Satyaloka.
And though I was remembered by you, Lakṣmī, who were distressed by our separation,
I arrived at Satyaloka and stood before Brahmā and the other gods.
And they indeed beheld me, the eternal one, in my divine form—
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, bearing the conch and the discus,
enriched by the splendor of all ornaments, with a gracious countenance and eyes.
They honored me, offered a welcome, and then praised me.
O beloved! Having heard their prayer for the sake of pacifying all suffering, I then spoke to them regarding myself as Hari, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 78-79 ||
"I am not able to undo what has been done by Lakṣmī in this matter;
therefore, let us go to that forest where the goddess Lakṣmī shines.
That virtuous woman remains in the vow of celibacy within the Prasaviṣṇu forest."
That great lady, the ascetic woman, abides in the dharma of lifelong celibacy (naiṣṭhika).
Then we all arrived at that place where your hermitage was;
upon seeing me, you were pleased and fell at my feet.
She offered a most heartfelt welcome to the deities and informed them of the sorrow caused by Rati and the others.
Praised repeatedly by all the gods and other beings, she was propitiated once again.
"You have said that this day has come to an end for all the gods and others.
Tomorrow morning, however, Kāma and the rest— the sons born from the body of Brahmā—
will indeed become capable embodied beings, such as Rati and the others."
The asura named Prasrava will also be born with a flowing nature;
however, at this time of twilight today, they have no need for him.
Let them, having undertaken the lifelong vow, worship the Supreme Lord.
I worship here Śrī Puruṣottama, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, together with my Lord who is seated upon his throne. May the Blessed One, my beloved, remain here forever. (87–88)
"I have indeed maintained this lifelong vow until the end of the dissolution.
Let all those who bestow blessings remain steadfast in that very vow.
Thus were the gods, humans, and sages addressed by you at that time.
All remained there in their lifelong vow until the end of another day.
O Lakṣmī! Then, by your wish, I dwelt upon the ground in the forest, addressed by you as the beginningless Śrī-Brahmacārin Nārāyaṇa.

"O beloved Lakṣmī! You have undertaken a vow together with him; you have always remained steadfast in austerity. You are a virtuous wife, possessed of dharma, the ultimate glory—'Naiṣṭhikī-Śrī' indeed!
Now, at that time, creation was obstructed on all sides by Manu."
Then, as the people gradually died off and grew old,
the time of universal dissolution arrived at the onset of night; everything was withdrawn by the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) in due order, as if it were an eternal process.
O Lakṣmī! Having completed your own vow, you went with me toward the hermitage of the Friend of the Gods (Indra);
from there, taking those five devotees who were destined for the bodies of future Indras, you led them to heaven. (95)
Having led her through Maharloka, Janaloka, and Satyaloka, and beyond that,
having presented her to Brahmā and then to Vaikuṇṭha along with me,
she departed for my own supreme abode, the Imperishable (Akṣara), and attained it.

Thus, O beloved, my manifestation and theirs have been described to you. Remember that form of the ascetic, O Mistress of the Imperishable, which is steadfast and eternal. In that year, there were also other manifestations of mine, and they too were innumerable.
I indeed know all those who were born [in that manner], but no other gods do; 99. Then, in another kalpa, Rati and the others were born as the offspring of Aja;
by his word, they indeed provided assistance to Aja while remaining embodied. 100.
From reading and hearing this definitive work, there shall arise the fruit [of liberation];
one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and likewise attain whatever one desires. (101)

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Brahmachārī Nārāyaṇa Together with His Eternal Śrī for the Purpose of Maintaining His Vow of Celibacy, Following the Reduction to Ashes of the Asuras Prāsra-vaṇa, Rati, Kāma, Vasanta, Bāṇa, and Others through the Devotion of Devasakha and Others," in the thirty-first year of the Creator [Brahmā] within the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 26 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 26.
[The Author: Chapter 27.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! Hereafter, I shall describe my manifestation.
O Creator, in the thirty-first year of the Manu-kalpa,
during the thirteenth cycle of six hundred [years] of that Manu in ancient times,
from the low-lying posterior region of Brahmā, the Asura Malimluca emerged. (1–2)
There was also one named Hallaka, a terrifying eater of corpses;
he performed a most dreadful and fierce penance for half a kalpa.
Then Brahmā was pleased, and he became a wanderer upon the earth.
The Asura, having become like clay and climbed upon the creepers and trees—
[where] there was only the existence of bone and earth— the Creator of the Universe went there,
sprinkled it with water, and cleared the trees from the side. (4–5)
From the portion of the root of the tree in the earth, he brought forth Hallaka;
he had a body like a creeping vine, was green in color, and extremely frail.
Bearded, the son of the Creator rose up from the network of roots.
Beholding the Creator who was restoring his own life, he did not bow down out of excessive devotion.
He even requested a supreme boon that effects the destruction of Time—
namely, either Time itself, or one in the form of Time, the destroyer of embodied beings.
"I shall likewise effect this withdrawal; grant me a boon, O Grandfather.
Brahmā said: "This boon [you seek] exceeds my power;
I am not able to grant it, for I am subject to Time (Kāla)."
Then Hallaka said: "O Grandfather, give me that one and no other;
I shall perform constant penance for his sake.
Indeed, no one except Hari is capable of slaying Kāla."
There is no specific manifestation born of creation in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, O Hallaka, listen to what I say if it pleases you.
Indeed, there are many forms of Time within the creations.
"You shall become the slayer of one of them alone at once.
"If this pleases you, then accept my boon," he said;
thus addressed, Hallaka, overcome by delusion, then accepted the boon. (1.3–14)
Abandoning that ascetic practice, he departed for a cave on Mount Meru;
by virtue of a boon from Brahmā, he remained forever filled with pride toward the gods, Daityas, Rākṣasas, Dānavas, Kinnaras, and others. (15)
He does not even count as gods of the *tamas* and *rajas* qualities, nor as *yakṣas*, *kiṃpuruṣas*, and the like,
nor as *gandharvas* or *cāraṇas*. He indeed treats them with contempt and fights against them at every turn.
He reveals even the futility of Brahmā’s granting of boons,
and he proclaims himself to be the very destroyer of Time (Kāla).
Having attained victory in heaven, he then proceeded to the netherworlds (pātālas).
Having achieved victory even there, he indeed went to the Lokāloka mountain;
having attained victory everywhere, he then went to the realm of Yama. Yama honored him, recognizing him as the destroyer of Time (Kāla).
Then, having learned that his own supreme master was victorious,
Hallaka went to the realm of Kailāsa to conquer Rudra, Śiva, and Hara. Indeed, the attendants dwelling on Kailāsa, such as Jaṅgama, Bhadra, and others, [approached him].
Then that Hallaka, out of rage, blocked [the way] from the gate-tower (gopura).
He fought with the gatekeepers, and having conquered those other Gaṇas,
he then [fought] the lords of the Gaṇas, Bhairava and the others, who stand at the head of all beings.
The cruel, wicked, and impure-minded one went to the abode of Śambhu—
specifically to Kailāsa— in order to bring it under his own control as well as Satī;
likewise, seeing the riches there, he desired to make the Gaṇas his servants.
He said to Śambhu: "O Śambhu, I am your servant;
otherwise, I shall bring about your destruction. Grant me Satī, and having given me the kingdom of Kailāsa, go to Mount Meru. || 25-26 ||
"Furthermore, at another time, I shall give [it] to you as you desire; I am satisfied with you.
Śambhu then reflected: "How great might be the strength of this one?
Shall I fight with this powerful being, who is joined with the boon of Brahmā?"
"I shall destroy this Asura in an instant with ten million boons.
Having reflected thus, Śaṅkara assumed a fierce form like Time itself (Kāla) and took up his trident,
which was made of fire and brings about the final dissolution.
Assuming the terrifying form of Sāṃkarṣaṇa, he quickly approached him for the sake of battle; meanwhile,
Hallaka also assumed a mountain-like form that was both fearsome and destructive.
He held in his hand an iron weapon, a blade marked with a crescent moon and spikes.
Just as the Destroyer of Time appears, so did Hallaka appear there. War-drums, struck by the Gaṇas on Kailāsa, resounded.
The gods, the lords of the deities, arrived there drawn by curiosity;
all the guardians of the quarters came as well to assist Śambhu. A battle between Hallaka and Hara ensued, causing the dissolution of the world.
The clouds were destroyed by the *phaṭāka* weapons, and the mountains were destroyed by the *hetis*.
The earth was shattered by the impact of falling [missiles], and the oceans were agitated by earthquakes.
By their force, the stars fell, and the quarters of the sky roared with thunderous sounds.
There, the hosts and the lords of the hosts were struck with terror at the prospect of death.
Some were broken at the waist, others at the region of the shoulders;
others were broken at the throat, and still others at the joints of the knees, and thus they met their end.
Grasping with one hand spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and others as terrifying as Kālabhairava, Hallaka places them in his mouth and devours them.
[He likewise devours] Śūrabhadra, Vīrabhadra, Jaṅgabhadra, and Subhadraka. (37–38)
Placing them simultaneously in his mouth with his left hand, he devoured them.
Such was that great Asura, the Death of Death himself.
Śaṅkara fell into doubt regarding victory because of the discharge from his trident.
The trident in Śambhu’s hand slipped again and again.
At that time, both the bull and the lion were likewise cut down by Hallaka’s discus and met their death. (3.26.40–41)
Satī, having fallen into doubt regarding the life of Śaṅkara,
quickly vanished from the body of Śambhu.
Realizing that Kailāsa was shattered and broken due to his following the deceased, Śambhu [departed].
Abandoning all hope for his life, he fled toward Hallaka.
Quickly approaching him, he hurled his trident, which was like the fire of universal destruction,
and struck it upon the head of Hallaka, right over his throat.
Having been violently severed from his hand,
that trident of Hara, which resembled fire, went to the throat of Hallaka;
having entered there, it became fixed and attained the state of being dissolved (rasabhāva).
What was wholesome for him became like nectar in the belly of Hallaka.
This most wonderful thing occurred: indeed, the "time-pain" (kālaśūla) was digested.
In this same way, other pains, tridents, and weapons [were likewise digested].
All of them, having attained the stature of the *hallaka* and entered into the state of *rasa*,
then became the painless Śaṅkara; likewise,
Śiva quickly remembered Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu, the unborn, arrived there.
He gave his own discus to that Hara, and Hara also released that discus at the throat of this Hallaka; for it became a savory juice (rasa).
Then he took up another discus, but that which was released attained the state of being juice (rasatā). (3.26.50)
In this manner, all the wheels had then moved away with the speed of the wind.
Just as Brahmā arrived there and beheld Śaṅkara,
he was struck by a swift-moving spear released from the moon.
Indeed, Śiva’s head was severed from his throat by Hallaka.
A great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for even the fierce Rudra had been slain.
All the gods, humans, and great sages were overcome with grief.
Moreover, all living beings became filled with grief;
even the power of Hallaka, along with his spear and crescent-moon weapon,
was entirely gone due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā.
He became powerless and was recognized as such by all the warriors.
Then, having understood exactly what Brahmā had said, the gods and the hosts set out to slay the Asura.
Then all those tridents and discuses that indeed existed melted away; having emerged,
they quickly returned toward Viṣṇu and toward Śaṅkara’s corpse respectively.
Viṣṇu released his discus at him;
meanwhile, that demon Hallaka cried out, "O Hari! O Viṣṇu! O Kṛṣṇa! Save me, who have come to you for refuge! and suddenly fell at the feet of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 58-59 ||
"The vow of Viṣṇu is that one who has come for refuge must not be slain;
therefore, O Viṣṇu, O Viṣṇu, your discus did not strike that speaker.
Furthermore, due to the granting of a boon by Brahmā, he was protected by that very circumstance."
And Hari bound with nooses that devotee of Brahmā, a son of his back, an ascetic and yogi who had offended Śaṅkara, even as he cried out, "O Hari!
O Viṣṇu! O Nārāyaṇa, protect me! (61–62).
To him who was thus shouting and remembering me with his mind and heart— him, the slayer of Hara— the sin of killing a god, which is as foul as wine,
took the form of a cruel goddess, Harā, holding a hundred wheels in her hands. She coiled around him.
Capable of devouring the life-breaths, with distorted and hideous faces, Hallaka beheld that fierce and leaping demoness who was a source of misery;
he cried out many times there on the field of battle in the presence of the gods. (64–65)
Struck by the gods and beaten by tens of millions of Gaṇas, nearly dead as he lay dying, he sought refuge with Hari, the protector.
"O Mādhava, grant protection to me, who am in the form of a devotee and have come for shelter. (66)
Indeed, the supreme state of great sovereignty belonging to Śaṅkara was taken from his enemy;
and by the granting of a boon from Brahmā, as well as from Mahākāla,
this single form of Śaṅkara was destroyed by me without any gain for myself.
"Having been killed, I am born again, incited by pride through illusion.
O Lord, all my ascetic merit has been cast away into tamasic action.
Therefore, O Viṣṇu, out of compassion grant me happiness; have mercy!"
"O Keśava, this sin of killing a god is burning me; ward it off!
Having said this, she wept bitterly and even reached the point of death.
Viṣṇu then spoke: "The time of Manu has likewise come to its full completion as a night. (3.26.70–71)
"O Hallaka, eat the sin committed by killing a god in the Raurava hell for fifteen manvantaras, at the end of time, during the interval between days;
having experienced as much suffering as there is, you shall remain defiled, performing the deeds of a mleccha."
"You shall become a devotee of me, Brahmā, as the lord of the Mlecchas;
you shall be the great preceptor of innumerable Asura worlds.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu, along with the messengers of Yama, [dispatched] Hallaka.
He sent that wicked Sahatya to the abode of Yama.
Then the gods, sages, ancestors, humans, twice-born brahmins, attendants,
hosts, devotees, goddesses, and virtuous women—
The yoginīs, the Mothers, and even the planets and other celestial bodies—
all these devotees assembled on Kailāsa and were summoned by Hari.
Then Viṣṇu [sent] them and her [the goddess] for the sake of Śambhu’s restoration to life.
He spoke [to them] to perform the worship of me, the Lord who manifests in all forms,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the True Master. Then, eager for Him, they worshipped You, the indweller of all.
"Having heard of your worship, I—Śrīpati, Puruṣottama, who eternally abide in the imperishable abode—have come here immediately along with you.
I am visible to those with sight upon Kailāsa, possessing a divine and beautiful form. (3.26.80)
Seeing me, they all became free from grief and then made their request;
thereupon, for the sake of restoring Śambhu to life, I entered his body—
both into the headless trunk and into the head— by means of yoga.
Having bestowed the power of life-force (*prāṇa-śakti*), I restored him to life and joined his limbs together.
Then, I worshipped the head of Śambhu upon the trunk by means of millions of gods, as well as by the ancestors, humans, and great sages. (82–83)
Śūrabhadra and the others who were chewed up and died at that time,
as well as all those who died, O Lakṣmī, and those hosts who were slain—
all of them, when remembered by me, became endowed with life, born from my mind.
Having arrived before Śambhu, those newly created beings stood there;
even the bull and others who had died were restored to life by me there.
Indeed, all the crores of Gaṇas as well as the crores of gods [were present]. (81, 86)
Having meditated upon them all, I then restored them to health and brought them back to life.
Furthermore, a festival for the restoration of Śaṅkara’s life was celebrated on Kailāsa.
Then Satī emerged from the very form of Śambhu and became perceptible once more.
Then the Great Goddess became directly manifest and well-pleased.
She requested me to remain forever upon the surface of the earth on Kailāsa together with you, Lakṣmī; and Śambhu likewise made this very request.
Both the gods and human beings entreated me, the Supreme Person,
to remain in the sacred field of Kailāsa for the welfare of all embodied beings.
Therefore, O Śivarājīśrī, I have always dwelt there together with you.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is Śrī Puruṣottama.
At that time, O beloved, you became Śivanārāyaṇī there as the Lord of Śivā, known by the name Anādi Śrī Śivanārāyaṇa. (91–92)

Then all the gods, humans, and ancestors departed for their respective worlds, as did the sages; I, however, remained on Kailāsa until the end of the kalpa, O Queen of Śiva! I alone know this, and no one else.
Remember also that divine manifestation of mine, O Kamalā! O beloved!
(94) On Mount Bhadra, cool, delightful, and vast—extending for ten thousand yojanas—I always dwelt there upon the region of Kailāsa. (95)
At that time, the entire earth became Vaiṣṇavī, created by me;
and all the gods were indeed Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to me with supreme devotion.
O Lakṣmī, the fruit of my devotion shines forth even in those who are characterized by passion (rājasa) or darkness (tāmasa).
Whether among the Asuras or the Suras, when the time arrives, it sprouts forth.
Therefore, devotion is the most excellent of all, bestowing the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
indeed, endowed with righteousness, it is established by me at the proper time, in the age, and on the day. (97–98)
Whether at the end of an aeon or at its commencement, I shall always establish that which is beneficial;
through the recitation and hearing of this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
One shall possess prosperity, wealth, and sons, and become a treasure-house of bliss.
Endowed with great sovereignty and possessing a form identical to that of the Supreme Lord,
he shall be the destroyer of all obstacles and the partaker of all immortality;
he shall have an eternal dwelling and attain union with Brahman.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Śiva-Nārāyaṇa for the Purpose of Reviving Śambhu’s Severed Head during His Conquest Expedition, Following the Granting of a Boon by Brahmā to the Asura Hallaka," in the thirty-first year of the Creator [Brahmā] within the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇāśrī! To this supreme nectar of a narrative.
Just as my manifestation occurred for you, so it was for the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) in the thirty-second [cycle].
In the fifty-sixth aeon (kalpa) of the Kalpadru year, during the eighth Manvantara, once there was a Yakṣa named Suvarṇamālika belonging to Kubera. || 1–2 ||
He went to sport in heaven, and from there he went to the city of Viṣṇu.
Then, having beheld Satyaloka as well as the abodes of the guardians of the quarters,
he went to the city of Saṃyamanī to see the residence of Yama.
At that moment, the end of his life arrived and he indeed passed away.
Yama, the King of Death, performed the final rites for the Yakṣa.
Having learned of the Yakṣa’s death in the abode of Yama, Kubera [acted accordingly].
Thinking then, "I have been slain by the messengers of Yama," he blazed with rage and went in person to the realm of Yama accompanied by his army. There,
he indeed fought with Yama in many ways.

Having conquered Yama, he led Svarṇamāla back toward his own home. (7) Then King Yama quickly summoned Nirṛti along with his army of Rākṣasas; and Nirṛti likewise [summoned] those stationed on the ground. (8)
He summoned to his side those Rākṣasas dwelling in Pātāla and other regions who were skilled in combat, numbering in the millions, billions,
and trillions; and then they set out from there to conquer Kubera and his kingdom.
War drums resounded in the sky in the vicinity of Alakā.
Having learned of this, Kubera set forth with ten million yakṣas;
then a sudden battle occurred there, causing universal destruction.
Millions of Yakṣas were slain by the messengers of Yama, and likewise by the Rākṣasas;
even Kubera was then struck by Yama at the throat and split in two.
The entire kingdom of Kubera was indeed brought under the control of Yama.
Likewise, by Nirṛti, the Rākṣasas were brought under control in the kingdom.
Then certain other Yakṣas, being terrified, went to Indra—the lord of the eastern quarter—as well as to Varuṇa and Vāyu, and reported that matter to them. (13–14)
They all went quickly toward the city of Kubera;
having seen Dharmarāja in such a state, as well as Nirṛti,
Īśāna took the side of his own disciple, Kubera.
Indeed, for the sake of avenging their enmity, they waged a terrible war.
Mahendra, as well as Agni, Vāyu, and Varuṇa—taking the side of Kubera—they fought against Yama. (16–17)
Then Sūrya supported the side of his own son Yama;
likewise Svarbhānu, Śanaiścara,
and other Rākṣasas also joined the faction of Yama and waged a most fierce battle.
Furthermore, crores of hosts of gods and yakṣas were slain there;
yet those of Yama’s side, who were practiced in the art of war, achieved victory once more.
The rākṣasas belonging to Yama’s faction obtained triumph in the battle.
Cruel and performers of cruel deeds, with hands scarred by iron and the like, experts in clods of earth, fire, weapons, machines, and missiles,
these pitiless Yamas excessively slaughtered Vāyu, Indra, and Varuṇa. (21)
Īśāna and Anala as well were broken; their armies were destroyed. (22) A great cry of "Alas! arose everywhere on earth at that time.
The gods, terrified, went to the truth, while others likewise fled into mountain caves. (23)
Then, on earth and in heaven, as well as everywhere throughout the regions of the world-protectors and the dwellers of the netherworld, that power increased.
O Lakṣmī! At that time, the atmosphere indeed trembled in every direction.
In the disputes of the world-protectors (*dikpāla*), millions of servants were slain and killed.
Yama became the king of Alakā on all sides, and Kubera’s very existence was indeed expelled from every direction. (25–26)
All the Nirṛtis, Rākṣasas, Yamas, Ārka, Śani, Rāhu,
and others likewise became strengthened by their own powers.
Acting as if independent within the three worlds, they, being full of hostility, began to strike down one another.
They drove out the unyielding gods and others from their own abodes.
Thus, a state of disorder arose even among themselves in the heavenly world;
the power of the guardians of the quarters was destroyed in the presence of Yama’s rod of punishment.
Under Indra’s command, the others—the Sun, the Moon, and so forth—no longer abide;
even the gods who depend upon them have indeed departed for the highest heaven.
Then, O Kamalā, having observed this, Īśāna, Indra, Agni, and Vāyu [acted].

Varuṇa and the other gods went to the palace of Mahendra. (3.1) There, being at a loss as to what should be done, they held a consultation; those lords also called Brahmā to mind and called Viṣṇu to mind. (3.2)
Those supreme lords then remembered the remainder [of their task] and restored it;
they heard of the destruction of Kubera and the defeat of others,
and for a moment they felt grief for the King of Dharma’s victory.
"In that abode of the King of Dharma, no injustice shall ever occur.
Having understood every cause for the death of the Yakṣa, and having considered both what was just and what was unjust, he [resolved] upon the battle against Kubera. (34–35)
Shaking their heads, they did not believe in victory again;
for where there is injustice, victory can never occur.
Since Kubera was the one who committed the injustice, this death is certain—of this there is no doubt.
Yama is the leader of the fourteen worlds and of all embodied beings;
he leads them away at the end of their lifespan—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
[He leads away] Indra, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Īśāna, Agni, and those other lords. (37–38)
Yama, the Lord of Death, surely leads [the deceased] away; what need is there to mention anyone else?
Therefore, the god Vijaya has indeed been won here by the god Yama.
We must, however, consider our defeat in this undertaking.
If Kubera, having become the guardian of the quarter, should act unjustly,
then suffering would indeed increase again for all those on his side.
Therefore, in this matter, neither Viṣṇu, nor Śeṣa, nor even Brahmā [should interfere].
O gods, even the cleverness of others will surely lead to defeat;
therefore, you must not go to that place where Yama himself resides,
and especially not to Alakā, O gods, for it leads to total destruction.
But the Great Lord of the gods, the supreme deities,
and the lords is Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama,
the Sovereign of Akṣara, the Lord of Śrī, Śrī Hari, the Supreme Lord. 43–44.
In this debate, he will indeed provide the final decision; you must reflect upon this.
Let them perform a great sacrificial session (*mahāsattra*) consisting of progeny in the house of Indra.
O gods, the Lord himself will come to the abode of the Supreme Master.
Thus addressed, Hara and the other gods then performed a sacrificial recitation (*japasattra*) in the abode of Indra;
all those lords of the gods chanted from every side:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Supreme Lord, higher than the highest! || 46–47 ||
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme Lord, protect us!
Thus they performed constant kīrtana for a full year.
At the end of Indra's year, Śrī Hari and I arrived.
The Lord who possesses the conch, the discus, and other emblems is the domain of all the gods.
O beloved! Then, together with you, Lakṣmī—who is enriched by every ornament—the gods, beholding me, moved very swiftly, intent on their purpose.
Rising up, they bowed in many ways and performed worship for me;
they offered *madhuparka* and then provided hospitable honors.
They gave me a great seat, and there I sat down together with you.
And those guardians of the wealth reported the entire account:
the destruction of the Yakṣas, the defeat of their own people,
the victory of Yama, and likewise his sovereignty in heaven.
O Lotus-born One, I heard that there was no fixed order among the gods;
then, having meditated for a moment, I spoke thus to the guardians of the quarters:
"You must indeed go with me to where Yama resides."
"For in the city of Kubera, all happiness shall prevail.
By means of conciliation, I shall bring an end to every dispute that brings misery.
Having spoken thus, I [set out] together with you and all the hosts of gods.
I went to the realm of Alakā in the presence of Yama and Nairṛta.
O Lakṣmī! Having heard of me, he quickly approached with a terrified mind; even though he was seized by fear, he came on foot into my presence. I, however, did not think anything of it.
He washed my feet and drank the nectar-like water from them.
He offered a welcome and a seat, and had musical instruments played.
While all the gods looked on, he spoke to me like a servant.
"I have committed an offense, O Kṛṣṇa! Kubera was slain by me.
This city has been brought under my control; forgive me, O Puruṣottama!
Punishment is inevitable, O Keśava, for those who tread the path of injustice."
"If I were such [a person], then let punishment be imposed upon me as well.
Having said this, he sought refuge and fell at my feet.
Indeed, for one who is free from injustice, punishment is not at all appropriate.
"O Yama, that this Kubera has been killed here is not fitting;
the Lord of the Yakṣas must be restored to life, as must his attendants,
and those led by the gods who were slain in battle."
The city of Kubera must indeed be given back to him.
O Dharma, you must proceed toward the city of Yama, the King of Death;
always protect Saṃyamanī and do not act with greed for another's property.
Thus addressed by me, Dharmarāja indeed begged for forgiveness;
having relinquished his northern quarter, he then departed.
O Lakṣmī! Thereupon, I performed the invocation of Kubera once again.
Then my son Mānasa was born as the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), a supreme devotee of Viṣṇu; furthermore, the Yakṣas were born. All the other gods who had died were likewise born as my mind-born sons.
The gods and others who were my sons indeed worshipped me with great joy.
Furthermore, I bestowed the region of Mānasa upon Kubera.
Then, being requested by him for the sake of a permanent residence, I agreed.
I indeed resided in the city of Svarṇavatī, possessing a golden complexion.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara and the others, they indeed departed for their own abodes;
Yama went to his southern realm, and the others went to their respective dwellings.
Upon the new birth of Kubera, a great festival was celebrated by me in the Golden City; he was worshipped and thus brought to prosperity. You, the golden Lakṣmī, shone there forever alongside me.
Together with the beginningless Śrī-Svarṇanārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign Lady, dwelt in Svarṇavatī until the end of the kalpa.
[She was] the beginningless Śrī-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
The controller of all the world-protectors and guardians of the quarters,
the manifest bestower of protection upon all, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Sovereign— O Lakṣmī of golden hue, remember me and then you shall manifest yourself before me.

[He assumed] the form of Rājarājeśvarī, overflowing with all bliss. (76) Then the Sun and other gods, as well as the followers of Yama, having asked for my forgiveness, thereafter worshipped Svarṇanārāyaṇa. (77)
To the golden-hued Puruṣa, with a beard of gold, the subduer of Yama;
the controller of the guardians of the quarters, the discipliner of adversaries;
the bringer of peace to afflictions, and likewise the bestower of prosperity. (78)
Indeed, the gods and others worship me— the eternal Supreme Lord, the burner of heaps of sins, the remover of calamities,
the Supreme Brahman beyond the imperishable, the true Lord served by the liberated. (3.27.79–80)

By reading, hearing, or even remembering this, one shall partake in liberation and also partake in enjoyment; there is no doubt regarding the attainment of golden splendor. (8.1) Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī-Svarṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Kānakī-Śrī, for the Purpose of Reviving Kubera Who Was Killed by Yama in the Thirty-second Year of Brahmā during the Dvāpara Cycle," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, consort of Nārāyaṇa! Hereafter I shall describe my manifestation in the thirty-third year of Brahmā, formerly known as Sasya.
In the thirty-first kalpa and likewise in the eleventh manvantara,
there arose the mountain Aruṇācala on the Śveta-khaṇḍa to the east of Meru.
This mountain is exactly one yojana in height and ten yojanas in extent.
The fire always dwells within it, its caverns rich with the essence of flame.
(3) There are no humans on its flanks, nor even wild forests;
the rivers indeed have hot currents, and the ground resembles glowing embers. (4)
In the year one hundred and eight years, two years, and eight years [hence],
Mount Jvālārūṇa shall become entirely composed of flames.
Fires shall break out in the lands and even in the rivers.
O beloved, by his majesty even those in distant lands are scorched.
Men, beasts, and even birds that travel through the sky, overcome by the heat of that fever, indeed fall into a swoon and meet their end. (6–7)
By sprinkling fire upon crops and forests,
there occurs a parching that destroys the fruits, flowers, and other produce even of those situated at a distance.
In whatever direction the currents of the winds blow, in that direction the fires [spread].
Regions extending for a hundred yojanas were scorched;
indeed, living beings who died from the sprinkling of fire remained in a state of dissolution.
Then, at one time, a great storm arose in the sky.

And the mountain Jvālāruṇa also became the form of fire. Driven by the wind, they carried floods of fire-flames and heat with great speed toward the east, traveling at a velocity of a hundred yojanas.
By the side of Meru, there were hundreds of thousands of embodied beings dwelling;
their bodies were consumed by the heat of the long-flowing [river], and they perished— elephants, cattle, horses, and the like by the tens of millions, and cities by the thousands.
There was a city there called Svāminagara, one yojana in length,
inhabited mostly by my devotees and holy people.
There were also auspicious monasteries for male and female ascetics and for renunciants.

There were many hermitages for those observing the vow of celibacy and for virtuous women who were the consorts of Dharma; likewise, there were great abodes for Vaiṣṇavas, yogins, and those devoted to ritual action who performed the sacrifice of silent recitation.
There, temples dedicated to me were established for the sake of the gods by those who sought refuge;

there, indeed, were devotees free from the body (videhins) who, through austerity, were intent on me alone and had renounced all enjoyments for my sake. They were focused solely on the goal of attaining me.
Having me alone as their object of focus and being intent on my propitiation, they are devoted to the dharma of serving the circles of my devotees;
offering all their own wealth and possessions, they have me as their very self. (18–19)
In this city, everyone is devoted to the worship of the goal, while those established in the means of attainment are few. Thus, due to the heat of the blazing fire,
the devotees who were devoid of the practice of yoga have perished on all sides.
The virtuous ones, knowers of yoga, truthful, and manifested in the state of Brahman,
remembered me— Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, beyond the Imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, the Puruṣottama— wherever they were. (21–22)
The Rudras and Maruts, joined together with single-minded devotion, praised him:
"Protect, protect us, O Supreme Brahman, O Inner Self, O Puruṣottama!
O Lord of All, come hither; protect our lives from this blazing fire! (23)
Thus entreated by those who were single-minded and possessed of intense devotion,
I quickly became visible in every house and among every person, together with you, Lakṣmī, for the sake of rescuing the living beings. ||24-25||
I cast a drop of nectar from my own Brahma-lake directly into the mountain of blazing fire. By way of the path of the sky, I moved swiftly;
the fire was dissolved, and the flames attained coolness. (26)
Then that heat, having transformed into coolness, brought relief from burning.
And when that nectar-like coolness touched whatever embodied beings—whether stationary or moving—who had died due to the wind, they were restored to life. || 27–28 ||
Having attained new life, the living beings became joyful;
even that mountain, Aruṇācala, through contact with the nectar of the Brahma-lake,
became a cool mountain of nectar and in an instant was transformed.
Thus the mountain remained cool as nectar until the end of the kalpa,
frequented by all devotees, yogis, ascetics, those of brahminical character,
holy men, virtuous women, saintly wives, and likewise renunciants.
I was gazed upon by Vaiṣṇavas and men as well; there, I was constantly requested to remain as a protector among the devotees. Honored and saluted, I indeed dwelt together with you.
In that very city of Svāminagara, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the beginningless Lord Nārāyaṇa,
is present together with you, the Mistress Lakṣmī. Thus, O Śrī Svāminī, my own manifestation has been described to you.
O Lakṣmī, my mistress!
Remember the protector of the city of the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, together with you, the beginningless Mistress Śrī, who are his protectress. (35)
Indeed, through both reciting and hearing [this], protection from calamities shall arise.
Now, in another thirty-fourth year called Pāśa,
long ago in the 367th Kalpa of the Creator (Brahmā).
And in the twelfth Manvantara, on this earth, there was in the city of Kauśeyaka a pair of the twice-born caste who were purifying and possessed of devotion and fortune.
The wife of the twice-born was a virtuous woman named Nirvāṇikā, who was childless.
Seeking happiness, she spoke to her own husband, a twice-born man named Kṣmācolaka:
"Poverty persists constantly; the hearth remains fixed in its fast-like state, and our teeth, free from disease, perform a vow of total fasting. (3.28.40)
The smoke does not enter the house, as if it had departed on a journey;
the fire, overcome with shame, does not even show itself.
The living beings, such as ants and other insects, have gone from the house to the sacred bathing place.
Even for the closing of a door, there is no purpose [in this case].
The door remains perpetually open, like the auspicious gateway to heaven;
the hall stands adorned with garlands, solitary and free from passion.
O Brahmin, liberation has arrived at your home, even though it is footless!
Though I am of the nature of *māyā*, I am now free from the snare. In your house, which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), I have taken refuge in the state beyond qualities (*nairguṇya*).
O twice-born one, even while living, your existence remains without support!
I, who once had a support, have now become supportless and free from possessions.
Oh, how great is the power of fortune: that which possesses qualities becomes as if devoid of them!
Having come into being again and again, they dissolve when the vision of nirvāṇa is attained.
Crows, pigeons, sparrows, dogs, deer, and mice—
cats and the like do not enter our house, nor does our boat ever sink anywhere.
Who, possessing any latent tendencies (*vāsana*), would dwell in that place where all prosperity has been cast out?
There is no mortar or pestle, no broom, and no bedstead;
by day it is illuminated by the light of the sun, and at night by the moon, planets, and so forth. (48–49)
"O Brahmin! Our home shines like heaven, equal to the abode of Brahmā.
And our matted hair, natural to us, gleams like the matted locks of a yoginī.

Even though the prosperity of the household exists, the prosperity of good fortune is not present.

Therefore, O twice-born one, this house of yours shines as a place that must certainly be resorted to by yogis;
it is not a home fit for householders, being devoid of prosperity and lacking in merit.
Therefore, O Lord, I constantly reflect upon how prosperity might come to my home; thus,
through the practice of vows and yoga, I must perform the worship of Lakṣmī so that my house may become a vessel of wealth.
Thus requested, her own master said to him, "So be it.

she slept upon the bare ground, devoted to celibacy, and remained without a seat.

Having arrived, he performs the worship of Lakṣmī daily with one hundred and eight lotus flowers, as well as with incense, lamps, and other offerings;

thus, having shown compassion toward me— who possess one hundred and eighteen names— come to my home, O Sovereign of Vaibhava.

"O Lakṣmī, O beautiful Śrī, come to the house of my devotee!

"I shall not remain here in your house without Nārāyaṇa.

Having spoken thus, she vanished into her body.
O beautiful maiden, you were born as a daughter of exquisite form;
by you I was propitiated, and thereupon I, the Supreme Lord, appeared from the tree named Savana as a youth of divine appearance.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, who bears the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and possesses radiant splendor;
he whose name is the beginningless Śrī Sāvanadrū Narāyaṇa. (84–85)
She begged for alms, and her mother then gave you to me;
indeed, according to the rites of marriage, you were given to me as one beautiful with every auspicious fortune.
Thereafter, Nirvāṇikā protected both you and me at all times.
O beloved! By the command of Kṣmācola, she remained in her own home serving him;
thereafter, I dwelt upon the earth for an entire kalpa, endowed with the glory of liberation and establishing dharma on the face of the earth.
From that, the house of Nirvāṇika was properly furnished;
for indeed, at the wedding, many jewels, vessels of the gods, cows, and celestial wish-fulfilling creepers were offered by the lords of the gods. (89)
At that time, there were celestial chariots, palaces, and ornaments;
various garments, beds with coverlets,
as well as golden thrones, couches, swings, hammocks, and the like.
Wealth consisting of gems, rubies, pearls, and auspicious ornaments;
necklaces, fields, groves, and likewise great gardens;
as well as elephants, horses, bulls, and hundreds of male and female servants.
Thus, by virtue of your arrival, that house became prosperous and exceedingly magnificent (93).
With its golden pitchers, it was like the palace of Indra upon the royal mountain peak.
Indeed, it was on your account that my manifestation occurred at that time (94).
O Lakṣmī, remember all the manifestation of my former happiness and prosperity;
there were also countless other partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*) and so forth of mine.
O Śrī, I, Nārāyaṇa, know them all, but no other people do.
The house in which I dwell becomes like a celestial abode;
it becomes a sacred dwelling frequented by liberated souls, lords, and others, and it always remains a most purifying field for the virtuous. (96–97)
Even the forms of sacrifices and incarnations exist within me;
all abodes likewise dwell within my own dwelling.
Thus, by virtue of my residence, both worldly enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of one's hand.

By reading or even hearing it there, as well as by remembering it, all perfections arise for people; of this there is no doubt. Whatever supreme merit arises from all the various vows, [it is attained here]. (3.28.100)

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa with His Consort Śrī for the Protection of the Subjects Residing in Svāminagara, Who Were Being Consumed by the Flames of the Aruṇācala Fire during the Thirty-third Year of the Creator [Brahmā] in the Dvāpara Age; and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Sāvana Nārāyaṇa together with Lakṣmī, the Nirvāṇika Brāhmaṇa Woman, during the Thirty-fourth Year, as she Worshipped Him with One Hundred and Eighteen Names. *** **Chapter 29** Śrī Bhagavān said: O Vidhi (Brahmā), at that time, the subjects residing in Svāminagara were being consumed by the flames of the fire from Aruṇācala. Then, the beginningless Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa, accompanied by His Consort Śrī, manifested Himself there for their protection. At that very moment, O Brahmā, the beginningless Śrī Sāvana Nārāyaṇa also manifested Himself there along with Lakṣmī, who was a Nirvāṇika Brāhmaṇa woman and had worshipped Him with one hundred and eighteen names. O Brahmā, the subjects residing in Svāminagara were then saved from the fire of Aruṇācala by the grace of the Supreme Lord. Thereafter, they all attained liberation. O Brahmā, the beginningless Śrī Sāvana Nārāyaṇa, having manifested Himself there, established a great city named Sāvana on the banks of the river Sāvana. He then performed a great festival for the installation of His own image. O Brahmā, the beginningless Śrī Sāvana Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by His Consort Lakṣmī, resided there for many years. At that time, the people of that city worshipped Him with devotion through various offerings such as flowers, incense, lamps, food, and water. Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, in the kalpa named Yakṣa, during the thirty-fifth year and the eighty-eighth yuga-cycle of the Creator.

O beloved, hear now how my manifestation occurred during the third Manvantara. At that time, there was a royal sage named Aṃśumat, a performer of vows, who was the lord of subjects in Nālaveya, in a region near Mount Meru.
He was the ruler of the entire land of Nalava.
Other thousands of kings also became his tributaries.
He was a donor, a meditator, one who observed vows, a devotee, a servant of the virtuous, a listener to sacred texts, and a performer of sacrifices.

O Lakṣmī, King Aṃśukra was devoted to me, offering oblations, full of faith, and a worshipper; he performed the excellent rites of a great Vaiṣṇava. Just as he was, so too were his wives initiated into the service of Hari.
There were a hundred Vaiṣṇava women, devoted solely to Hari;
they were givers, meditators, observers of vows, devotees, and servers of the virtuous.
They were also listeners of sacred texts, performers of sacrifices, and those who had offered everything to Hari.
All those who offer themselves, who are full of trust, and who worship me; those devoted to their husbands and yet showing every respect toward me;
those whose minds are fixed on my image and who possess the pure, divine vision of me—(8) [these are the ones who attain me].
While their husband Hari was present, they always served him with equal devotion and respect.
(9) There were three hundred sons and two hundred daughters of the king; even while he was present, they were devoted to serving Hari as if he were their father and mother. (3.29.10)
With their minds, material objects, and bodies, they served the family of the Blessed One.
All were of divine nature, bodiless, and the foremost among the perfected ones (siddhas).
In their kingdom, there were never any policies that caused the calamity of suffering.
There was no drought, no excessive rain, no war, and no earthquake. There was never anywhere any overwhelming cold nor any affliction from heat.
No diseases occurred in the kingdom, nor did people suffer untimely deaths.

The subjects were always delighted by food, clothing, and other such things; they adorned themselves and celebrated great festivals. They were ever-mutually affectionate and full of love for one another, assisting each other and constantly engaged in the worship of the Divine Mother. (14)

Having surrendered their magical powers (*khādinī*) to me, and having surrendered everything to me, O possessors of enjoyment (*bhoginī*), the men and women in their kingdom were then joyful and well-nourished, free from hatred, violence, and the like; there were no thieves nor any misers in their realm. (15–16)

The earth bestowed all flavors, and the seasons granted fruits and flowers; even the creepers and shrubs, down to the smallest herbs, bore fruit and blossoms without fail. Among men there was no untruth, nor was there any deceit among the subjects.
There was no craving for the enjoyment of wealth; contentment prevailed.
(18) Gods, great seers, holy men, perfected beings, virtuous women, ascetics, and those of Brahmanic character ate from his [offerings] by the thousands, day and night. (19)
In the kingdoms of that monarch, food-donations were established;
hundreds of thousands of students seeking knowledge and young women seeking learning partake of them.
Indeed, in every hamlet, every village, every town, and every city of his, [these provisions are made].
At the feast of food, guests partake of excellent nourishment.
Every morning, in every village, the worship of the gods— the source of all prosperity—
and of the king himself is carried out with wealth and other offerings.
Having performed the congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana) of Hari for a period of one ghaṭikā,
the groups of guests, the destitute, and others eat during his assembly.
In the evening, people worship me, and at night they also perform saṃkīrtana.
During the day, people will be intent on their own duties and devoted to their own interests;
such will be his subjects, dedicated to disregarding their bodies, performing austerities, full of devotion, and devoted to serving the virtuous. (24–25)
For the Blessed One is indeed the embodiment of the virtuous, ever-conscious here upon this earth;
he shines as ten million forms, the one who brings about the welfare of all creatures.
Truly, the Blessed One is the virtuous one; truly, he is the savior.
The Lord himself is the virtuous one, the giver of the good state, and the embodiment of goodness.
(27) That human form which is seen as being even like us is indeed divine;
his actions are divine, for he is the Blessed One himself, the bestower of liberation. (28)
Beholding, touching, massaging the feet, serving, eating, and various forms of service— all these lead to the liberation of the virtuous.
Whatever service is rendered to the saints, whether once or many times, [brings about that same result].
She destroys all sins and bestows the liberation of Brahman.
Those sons who are initiated, divine, and indeed of the lineage of Hari, who abandon birth and worldly prosperity— they alone are the very form of Hari.
In performing that action, celibacy, vows, charity, and sacrificial fees;
austerity, righteousness, discernment, and devotion—all are established [in him].
The hands of the virtuous man are the hands of Hari; his feet are the feet of Hari.

The mouth of the virtuous is the mouth of Kṛṣṇa; the skin of the virtuous is the skin of Śrī Hari. (33) The two eyes of the virtuous are the two eyes of Śrī Hari; the tongue of the virtuous is the tongue of Hari. The head of the virtuous is the head of Hari; the nose of the virtuous is the nose of Hari. (34)
The ears of the virtuous are the ears of Śrī Hari; the teeth of the virtuous are the teeth of Hari.
The throat of the virtuous is the throat of Hari; the chest of Hari is the chest of the virtuous.
The belly of the virtuous is the belly of Hari; the waist of Śrī Hari is the waist of the virtuous.
The vision of the virtuous is the vision of Hari; indeed, the touch of the virtuous is the touch of Hari.
That which is the serenity of the virtuous is the very serenity of Hari.
The happiness of the virtuous arises from service [to Him]; that happiness of mine is the happiness of Hari alone.
Whatever joy, delight, bliss, and festivals are esteemed by the virtuous—all those are indeed the bliss of Śrī Hari alone; they are certainly not separate from me.
Everything that brings satisfaction to the virtuous is truly my own satisfaction.
The senses of the virtuous are indeed my own senses;
the intellect of the virtuous is my intellect. I am always the virtuous ones on earth; I am the virtuous ones in the world, assuming many forms. (3.29.40)

"Those who possess the quality of non-possessiveness are, to me, embodiments of Brahman. Whatever constitutes the virtue, wealth, and pleasure of the virtuous, all of that is always considered by me to be my own. Thus spoke the king and the queens, whose inner hearts were stainless, to Kamalā.
The princes, the princesses, the subjects, the servants, and all others—
all these became devoted to me through their association with the virtuous;
for in that house, the supernatural powers were like wish-fulfilling creepers and the vessels of the Kalpa tree.
Even wish-fulfilling gems and cows of plenty dwell there constantly;
and hundreds of thousands of virtuous men and women,
who have offered their devotion, dwell in my hermitage, free from desire and devoted solely to me.
Then, observing their devotion offered through self-surrender,
out of compassion I resided for that period among the assembly of virtuous saintly women.
During my month known as Mādhava, the king performed a kīrtana.
The monthly sacrifice consists of thirty uninterrupted days.
O Hare, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, Keśava, Mādhava;
O Supreme Brahman, Lord, Śrīśa, Puruṣottama, Satpati!
Salutations to the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the Inner Soul, whose nature is that of the saintly, the Soul of all.
Salutations to the Lord of Śrī, whose nature is that of the virtuous wife, the Eternal Soul.
Salutations to the wielder of the discus, who is attainable through devotion and accomplished through service.
You are independent and the Lord of the imperishables, dwelling among the millions of liberated souls;
therefore, come here in person in your divine form, just as you appear to us.
Thus did the king, the subjects, and the virtuous perform their worship.
Together with them, I proclaim [His name], I dance, and I laugh;
I eat, I stand, I walk, I sit, and I speak.
I drink and I smell, I taste and I sleep;
I rejoice and I delight, I sport and I bow down.
Clad in the garb of a holy man, I serve among the virtuous at their sacrificial festivals.
But they do not recognize me, Mādhava, in my hidden form;
some in the assembly know me only as some ordinary saint.
At that time, you were a virtuous and chaste young woman, devoted to moral conduct.
Clad in saffron robes, she was visibly manifest yet possessed of hidden virtues.
Concealed in form and concealed in her emblems, devoted to the service of virtuous women, she moved about there within the circle of those holy women with impartial conduct. (55–56)
Even those virtuous ones do not recognize you, Lakṣmī, though you are within their range;
for my Māyā likewise exists as independent and of the nature of concealment.
[She manifests] the sacrifice of food, the sacrifice of ritual, and likewise the sacrifice of chanting.
At the end of the month of Mādhava, when the full moon had indeed arisen,
on that evening during the great festival, the virtuous, the truthful, the king, and the subjects recounted the narrative that reveals my majesty. (28–59)
Then they performed my worship at night with excellent materials before the image;

thereafter they performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and then they offered handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali). Then they presented food offerings accompanied by musical instruments and dancing.
Accompanied by rhythmic measures and tempos, with melodious voices, hand-claps,
and the jingling sounds of small bells, they performed the kīrtana while keeping watch throughout the night.
At that time, drawn by the kīrtana, I appeared before them as a dancer.
"You are a dancing girl and indeed a young woman, while I am a boy of sixteen years;
you are fourteen years of age, beautifully dressed and adorned with ornaments.
You wear a crown of peacock feathers and are radiant with divine earrings."
Adorned with every costume suitable for dancing, gracious, and skilled in dramatic performance—
(64)— I too, assuming such a form and accompanied by all the necessary attendants, entered the midst of the stage in the assembly hall from an unobserved place. (65)
"Indeed, I was not recognized by anyone, nor how could these two have been known?
Seeing us filled with awe, the king and the members of the assembly were startled. At that time, our great splendor indeed radiated throughout the hall."
Joy, delight, and happiness indeed spread throughout the assembly.
At that time, there was great bliss consisting of sweet, desired, and cherished things for the people through the union of us two, accompanied by dancing, singing, and rhythmic clapping. (67–68)
Then all of them, completely absorbed and extended solely by their conviction,
with the speed of mere vision yet their minds drawn by hearing,
gazed without blinking at me, at you— the divine Śrī, the Lord of Śrī.

The worlds beheld you—me—who possess the radiance of infinite millions of suns and the splendor of countless moons, who are compassionate and filled with mercy; for the cause was chanting my name, loving devotion, and the service of the virtuous. (3.29.70–71)
Indeed, the divine nature is always the cause for our vision among the virtuous.
Then other devotees danced, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa,
immersed in supreme bliss, and transcending the perception of the body.
There, for all embodied beings, the auspicious vision of us both became divine for a moment, just as it is in the imperishable abode. Immediately thereafter,
I caused that splendor to vanish.
Their mental dispositions were drawn back and their senses regained their composure.
Then they beheld us two standing before them, equal to themselves.
They immediately desisted from dancing, singing, and even chanting.
Overwhelmed by great wonder, the people prostrated themselves before you and me like staffs.
Kings and others offered us their principal seats— golden lion-thrones—
and with great reverence, they honored us both as we sat upon those thrones.
With sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, fragrant garlands, and jewel-necklaces; with golden girdles and the like for the king and others;
with crowns and other ornaments, incense, food offerings, and meals. (78)
With sweet drinks and betel leaves, with the waving of lights (nīrājana),
with hymns of praise, and with repeated prostrations like a staff; likewise, with shouts of "Victory!", with cries of joy, and with the proclamations of the cane-bearers.
Then they all greatly propitiated both you and me;
having realized that we were indeed the Supreme Lord, they praised us with supreme affection.
The virtuous ones said:
Wherever our birth may have occurred, we have subsequently attained refuge in you, O Blessed One, through the power of our merit; we are your sons.
Indeed, those whose father is Acyuta (the Imperishable) themselves become imperishable.
And we have attained the state of non-falling; this is Your compassion, O Śrī Hari.
Out of mercy, You have come to these divine and excellent sons; having beheld these vessels of affection, that other compassion has become manifest. 83–84.
Therefore, one should always dwell among the virtuous just as one dwells in the body;
O Kṛṣṇa, dwell in the midst of the virtuous, for this is the ultimate grace. Just as one resides in the divine abode, so too is one’s dwelling within the circles of the virtuous.
May she, who is always in the form of the virtuous, grant supreme grace.
The virtuous women said: "O Mother Lakṣmī, O Great Mother, we have come to you for refuge."
"O Mother, we are your daughters, virtuous Brahmin women seeking liberation.
For mothers, affection for their children is born of nature and is exceedingly great;
honoring that, O Mother, you indeed grant us your vision. (87–88)
Today, fortune endowed with strength prevails for those who were weak;
having attained divinity through yoga, we shall indeed reach liberation.
Your compassion is likewise incomparable, in that you have shown such regard for virtuous women.

Even in that regard, there is great compassion if you would grant me residence. Having accepted my prayer, O Sovereign of the Imperishable, by the command of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, let him do as he pleases here.
The queen said:
"I am blessed, as are my daughters, my sons, the kingdom, the king, and the subjects;
O Lakṣmī, I am blessed that here I have the sight of you. (92)
Dwell here forever; everything shall be yours.
I am always your servant; stay, O Lakṣmī, and show me your grace.
In this cycle of existence, this alone is the true gain attained: union with a virtuous woman.
"Direct vision of you is itself that which cannot be obtained by any other means.
The King said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, my family, kingdom, wealth, lineage—everything is for your sake."
Everything performed and offered by me is of your very nature and for your sake alone.
(95) Through this meeting with the virtuous, this direct vision of you has been attained here;
today everything that was to be attained has been reached, including the ultimate fruit. (96)
"O Supreme Lord, having shown mercy, dwell forever in my home.
Having spoken thus, the king prostrated himself at his feet and fell down.
"So be it," he said to him, and dwelt within that circle of virtuous men.
O beloved! Then, together with you, the beginningless Śrī Sādhu Nārāyaṇa, I dwelt upon this earth as the virtuous Nārāyaṇī until the end of the kalpa.
Remember me, you, and everything else, as well as all my other incarnations.
"Through reading, hearing, or even remembering [this], one shall attain liberation.
Out of compassion, I have indeed revealed my manifestation to you, which bestows salvation.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Sādhu Nārāyaṇa along with the virtuous Nārāyaṇī Lakṣmī through the Devotion of King Aṃśukramatha in the Twenty-fifth Year of Brahmā," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
