Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then, being constantly served by the king, I, Hari, indeed granted to that monarch the fruit of serving the virtuous: Śvetadvīpa.
Having enjoyed happiness together with his family, he then went to heaven;
having enjoyed pleasures there as one whose nature is that of the Vairāja deity,
and having experienced further joys, he went once more to Satyaloka.
Then, having reached Vaikuṇṭha and enjoyed happiness there, he returned to heaven once more by my will alone for the purpose of promoting devotion. Thereafter,
he shall become the lord of more than ten million worlds.
Having led those countless worlds that have taken refuge in him, along with his devotees endowed with bhakti, he— who is the very form of Nārāyaṇa— will go to my imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma).
Indeed, this devotee of mine has become exactly like my own self.
There will be no others like them as informants in this world:
sons, daughters, queens, kings, subjects, and followers;
indeed, all kingdoms shall possess every kind of wealth for my sake.
The Vaiṣṇavas, facing all directions, remained there having fulfilled their purpose.
Now I shall tell you something else; listen, O Mādhavī, to the manifestation [of the Lord].
Then, in the thirty-sixth year of the Brahmā known as Rākṣasa, it occurred once again.

O beloved, listen as I declare how my manifestation occurred during the ninety-sixth kalpa and in the seventh Manu-period, for I am the very incarnation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (3.30.10)
In the fifteenth Kṛta Yuga, a yogi named Haripratha became a potter on the auspicious bank of the Viṣṇupadī river on this earth.
From his childhood, through the practice of yoga, he became a king among my devotees.
His mother, Śreṇīmatī, also gave him excellent instruction:
[12] "On her lap, while nursing at the breast, on a swing, in a loincloth, on a small stool, during yoga, and even when children are stumbling. [13]
"Speak, my son, the name of Hari: 'Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa!
Speak, my son, the name of Śrī: 'Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī!
(14) Thus does the mother instruct her own son for the sake of liberation.
For the sake of the highest good, for the destruction of evil, and as a cause for making this birth meaningful—
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama,
O Supreme Brahman beyond the imperishable, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Lord! (15–16)
In this way, her mother herself always performs my glorification in all her undertakings, for she is indeed devoted and possessed of virtuous qualities.
And the potter Viraṇa by name is also ever devoted to me.
Even while being a servant of the virtuous, he remembers me in every undertaking.
He constantly worships Hari, remembers Janārdana, and performs the act of offering everything to me; thereafter, he eats as is appropriate.
Every evening she constantly recites my *mālā-mantra* with her mind fixed on me;
she also always performs auspicious service for the virtuous and the devoted.
Likewise, she attends to household duties, the needs of mendicants, and service to the village.
Whenever he performs any task, O Śrī Narāyaṇa, he recites [the name] there as well.
The potter always keeps a rosary in his hand and a rosary around his neck;
chanting the name of Hari, he makes every moment meaningful at all times.
Listen, Lakṣmī: for one who is truly devoted, devotion is not difficult to attain at all;
it is always easily accessible in all undertakings for one who has surrendered the self.
Viraṇa, rising early in the morning, would utter the name "Nārāyaṇa."
Taking a jar, he goes to the river; he bathes and cries out to me, Hari.
Having filled it with water, he goes home; at the foot of a Pippala tree, he remembers me and there pours that water as well. (24–25)
Having bowed to the sun and having prostrated before me, who am fashioned from clay,
he cries out as he eats the flatbread offered to me this morning.
Likewise, the potter’s wife eats, and his son also eats.
Then, chanting the praises of Hari, the three go to fetch the clay;
when they bring the clay suitable for the back of the donkey, the three who chant the praises of Hari return toward home. (27–28)
Even for a female donkey or a male donkey, they sprinkle grass and the like, as well as water and the like,
with the waters of Hari’s grace;
they moisten them with water and clay, and at that time, they chant the praises of Hari.
They knead even the clay and yet they glorify me;
they fix the discus upon a pivot and whirl it about while remembering me;
they place the ritual ball (piṇḍa) upon the discus and remember me, Janārdana.
They fashion pots, bowls, and vessels while remembering me;
having separated them with thread, they also lower them down.
Remembering me, they mark the vessels with the tools for marking.
They prepare and cook [food] in a fire-heated pan, and they remember me;
they sell their vessels and the cooked food, and they remember me;
with the wealth obtained, they purchase rice, vegetables, and other provisions from the market.
They prepare foods, remember me, and call out to me;
having filled a vessel and offered it to me, they eat what has been presented to me.
Thus, being devoted to me, they carry out the maintenance of their household.
In the evening, they listen to the discourse from the mouths of the virtuous in my abode.
At night, they indeed remember what was heard and reflect upon it for the sake of liberation.
There is no liberation without food, and no devotion without merit.
Without merit there is no service, and without compassion there is no service;
without servitude there is no compassion, and indeed without faith there is no servitude.
Without knowledge there is no faith, and without hearing there is no knowledge. (38)
Scriptural learning does not exist without the company of the virtuous, nor does the company of the virtuous exist without the virtuous themselves.
The virtuous do not exist without spiritual disposition (*bhāva*), nor does spiritual disposition exist without contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) known as contemplation does not exist without what was previously acquired. (3.30.39–40)
That which was acquired previously is enjoyed right here in the form of its fruit;
that which is acquired today will be enjoyed elsewhere, in the state of the highest good (śreyas).
All forms of welfare are to be accomplished, yet the supreme welfare is Nārāyaṇa himself.
Liberation from that [bondage] exists at his feet and is to be attained through the thread of love.
The embodiment of Hari known as the "saintly" is the conscious vessel of love;
those seeking their own welfare should propitiate the saints with services. (42–43)
Food, water, and clothing—these three are the means for sustenance;
a home, a wife, and a cow—these three are considered the supports.
Industry, a son, and health—these three are the instruments of fortitude.
The treasury, the fortress, and kinsmen—these are the three means for achieving power.
Friendship, honor, and fame—these are the three means for maintaining stability.
Knowledge, conduct, and self-mastery—these are the three means for achieving freedom from craving.
Contentment, dispassion, and sovereignty are the threefold means for achieving tranquility;
virtue, forbearance, and endurance are the threefold means for achieving happiness;
and the virtuous, Hari, and good character are the threefold means for achieving liberation.
Suffering, solitude, and humiliation—these three are the means for achieving dispassion (vairāgya).
Action, craving, and latent impressions—these three are the causes of worldly existence (saṃsāra).
Malice, slander, and atheism—these three are the means for attaining hell.
Negligence, delusion, and worldly striving—these three are the invitations of death.
Freedom from action, self-surrender, and devotion—these three are the means for liberation.
Therefore, one should strive here incessantly solely for the sake of liberation.
Having completely renounced all other things here for the sake of the causes of Nirvāṇa,
beings and people in this world, as well as their actions and daily pleasures, are destroyed just as jars are shattered into pieces. 51–52.
By the force of time, the wealth of the body and its worldly possessions perish.

Who is the woman? Who is the man? What is the son, or the daughter? In this world, all relationships are merely artificial. Just as names and designations arise from clay, so too do these [relationships] exist.
Likewise, the names and designations of the six sheaths (ṣāṭkauśika) and so forth are artificial.
Having attained this artificial body and having known the means to liberation, if liberation were to be achieved, then human birth would indeed not be in vain. //54-55//
Everywhere there are sense objects, hunger, thirst, and pleasure;
all this worldly existence is but a momentary bondage for the living being.
And ever anew, a fresh bondage is constantly being produced.
There is no end to these bondages; in every new year, new jars are made.
The makers of the jars meet their death, yet another takes their place.
The stream of jars and the makers of jars does not cease.
Living beings fallen into the stream of worldly existence are bound by the noose of "I" and "mine";
even when the pot is destroyed, they remain bound in fragments by the noose of delusion.
In this world, the destruction of all things inevitably occurs through time.
"Those who behold [Him] strive for the sake of liberation, for they are not dead.
Again and again they will die unless they serve the Eternal One.
Therefore, Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu is Śrīmat Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (3.30.60–61)
Śrī Hari, the inner self of the supreme Brahman, is to be served at all times on this earth.
Let them worship the Supreme Soul and chant the name of Hari;
let them meditate upon Hari-Kṛṣṇa and attain the Supreme Lord.
Thus, every night,
Viraṇa and the others reflected upon their own welfare for the sake of the ultimate truth, and they always worshipped me.
In this way, after a short time had passed, those three potters—
They became entirely devoted to serving the virtuous and took refuge in the virtuous;
through my service to the virtuous, that house became a temple.
The virtuous always perform recitations of My stories and other such acts there.
Haripratha himself, the son of the potter Viraṇa,
received the excellent initiation from Ānandabrahmaguru.
Having become a virtuous man, he constantly worships me, his Lord, day and night.
His perfection of speech was accomplished such that whatever he spoke came to pass.
Then once, while my worship was being performed there in the assembly of the virtuous,
Manu himself descended from the sky into that gathering of the Tānamiśras.
The seventh, named Varṇiśālā, indeed departed by means of a celestial chariot.
The virtuous men, such as the potters and others, along with the virtuous women, went to the bank of the Viṣṇupadī for the purpose of bathing and other rites, accompanied by kīrtana. (3.30.70)
Some were bathing, while others were chanting the praises of the Supreme Lord; meanwhile,
that very mantra, having wandered far through the air at the landing-place,
descended by chance upon the bank of the Viṣṇupadī.
In the form of a king, accompanied by his servants, he went to the descent into the water (72),
where those virtuous ones and others were immersed in worship for the sake of bathing,
standing while worshipping me and chanting the glories of Hari (73).
There, the arrogant Manu, the master of the ashram, said to his servants:
"Drive all these people here—both men and women—far away from the riverbank and keep them confined. (74)
"Until I have gone and performed my bath in the river water,
let the servants seize me by the hands and cast me far away!
Having spoken thus, those groups of servants rushed forward from all sides.
They indeed drove them far away and even restrained them;
for even the saintly, though impelled by the bliss of Brahman, turned back.
Then Haripratha, the devotee of the saints, said to the messengers: "How can this be?"
"An obstruction or a prevention is being arranged by you during the ritual bathing.
The messengers replied: "What is the purpose of this investigation?
Go far away; let everyone depart, for there shall be no possession here. (78–79)
Speaking thus, the messengers seized his very arm and cast Haripratha and the others far away.
Then Haripratha said: "Let the king indeed meet his death at your hands."
When this was said, O lotus-born one, at that very moment the man died while still alive; bereft of life,
he quickly became a corpse and fell to the ground with his hands and feet outstretched, crying out with violent intensity.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, for an improper act had been committed.
The messengers went quickly to his side and attended to him with fanning, massaging his feet, and offering him water to drink; yet even so, he—
Then Manu departed for the abode of Dharma, having cast off his very life-breaths.
At that time, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among all the guardians of the creatures, among all the world-protectors, and among the gods who dwell in truth.
Indeed, Śuka died among the great sages, beginning with Mahendra;
then Brahmā, Śiva, and all the others came to the place where he had died.
At that time, they all performed worship of Hari for the sake of restoring him to life.
O daughter of Padma, O Narayani, I, the eternal Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, have arrived there together with you;
I am the glorious Puruṣottama, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. (87–88)
When they requested the means for their livelihood, I then enlightened them;
yet, I am not able to turn back what has been done for my devotee.
My devotee must be propitiated, for he will surely bring about his own welfare.
Then the gods bowed to Bhakta and made this very request:
they repeatedly asked for life and forgiveness.
At that time, Haripraśasta likewise honored the virtuous ones.
Having recognized me as the Supreme Self, and having bowed to and worshipped me upon the corpse, he sprinkled water; at that very moment, Manu became endowed with life.
He rose up, and he praised and fully worshipped me, Hari.
Having bowed to the holy ones and obtained their forgiveness, he returned once more to his own abode.
And at the request of the virtuous, O Lakṣmī, I dwelt forever in the house of Haripratha— a home of the righteous— along with you.
Then, by the name of the beginningless Śrī Bhaktanārāyaṇa, you yourself became the Lord; at that time, you attained the renown as Śrī Kumbhikāśrī.
I know all of this, as well as the dissolution of the mind and the living state.
Remember all [those places], such as the banks of the Viṣṇupadī, and the virtuous people;
for a full cycle of four yugas I dwelt together with the holy ones.
Furthermore, other traditions also arose from me at that time.
Other incarnations have appeared for the sake of protecting the world;
by reading or hearing this [account], both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall indeed be attained.

Thus ends the [section on] the beginningless Śrī Bhaktanārāyaṇa, for the purpose of reviving Varṇiśālamanu—who had died due to the curse of Hariprabhakti in the thirty-sixth year of Brahmā during the Dvāpara cycle—in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
The thirtieth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of [the Lord] Accompanied by Kuṃbhikāśrī," etc.,
[ends]. Chapter 30 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age),
Chapter 31.
[The Author: Chapter 32.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another narrative concerning the glory of my manifestation.
Formerly, in the thirty-seventh year known as Aṇḍaja of the Creator,
during the ninety-ninth kalpa and in the sixth Manvantara,
there was a great ascetic named Ṛṣi Ajahārita who had appeared.
Though dwelling alone in the forest, he who is a knower of the Vedas and a practitioner of righteous dharma teaches the Brahmins and others, honors those who arrive,
worships other guests, and provides them with shelter.

He dwelt in a leaf-hut within a grove of trees in that hermitage. For the sake of his livelihood, he would always take water and nourish those trees, which were rich in fruits, tubers, shoots, leaves, and roots. (4–5)

He offers welcome and other courtesies to the gods and to virtuous guests who have arrived, with offerings of ripe and sweet fruits, roots, and the like. Then the king, the lord of Vidrava, accompanied by his army, [approached].
Setting out on his journey, he arrived at a hermitage by way of the path.
At midday he found rest, yet he did not know that sage;
for he had considered him to be merely some forest-dweller capable of providing shelter in the hermitage.
The king did not honor that virtuous brahmin of noble character;
on the contrary, he released camels, elephants, bulls, and horses upon his trees, pillars, and other objects,
and they indeed began to devour them.
"They broke them down from the roots; they destroyed them," so it is said. (3.31.10) Having seen the trees in flower and bearing fruit, the sage said to the king:
"O King, do not bring about the destruction of my trees from their very roots. (11)
"Drive the cattle far away to the side, to the forest filled with trees.
The king said: "The entire forest belongs to me; it also belongs to the king.
My cattle, overcome by hunger, will surely devour the trees."
Because you, a forest-dweller, have come from so far away to this place, the sage Garviṣṭha quickly conceived a punishment for the king;
taking water in his hand, he cursed him: "Become a horse! (13–14).
Instantly, the king there became an exceedingly beautiful horse;
the entire army fell into distress and entreated that sage.
For the sake of the king’s liberation, the queen also entreated him repeatedly.
Then the sage said to her: "O Uttara, this horse is your husband.
When the time comes for the Aśvamedha sacrifice to be completed by your son, King Nara shall bathe in the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) through union with Nārāyaṇa."
"There will be no doubt; now, indeed, let him go home.
Having spoken thus to her husband, she took the horse and went to her own home.
Having gone home with her army, she propitiated the Supreme Lord.
The son of Queen Yaśovara, named Dharmadhara,
commenced a sacrifice for the sake of his father’s liberation, whose name was Varmadhara.
Having been initiated, he gathered the various materials required for the sacrifice.
On pure ground, at the four corners of the sacrificial pavilion for the horse sacrifice (*vājimedha*),
while the sacrificial rites were being performed by the preceptor who was conducting a divine session (*devasattra*),
[he acted] for the attainment of everything, for victory over all, and for the severing of all curses.
While the clarified butter was being offered into the fire for the pacification of all evils,
the gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— along with the Sādhyas and other deities entitled to their respective shares, arrived in person. (22–23)
The priest of the gods, the venerable Brahmin, worshipped that horse,
which was black in its forepart and white in its hindquarters,
marked on its forehead with a *puṇḍra* shaped like a cart, and possessed of auspicious form.
Having repeatedly drunk the juice of the Soma plant during the month of Āśvayuja since his birth,
and having been nourished while still an infant after being fed the Soma juice,
the king then performed the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice on the full moon day of Caitra and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice on the full moon day of Vaiśākha.
Thereafter, he performed a sacrifice dedicated to Prajāpati;
likewise, he performed the New Moon (Amāvāsya) sacrifice and had his hair shaved.
Wearing new garments, observing silence, and having duly performed the Agnihotra rites, [he remained].
On the following day, having gone to the pavilion and performed eleven oblations,
and having fed the *brahmaudana* to the officiating priests and properly honored them,
the sacrificer [approaches] the sacrificial horse and the four-eyed dog.
Having led them both to the water of the pond and other reservoirs, he, together with the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), performed the ritual sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*).
Then the Adhvaryu priest sprinkled the dog,
and the king himself released the horse upon the earth for the purpose of its wandering.
Then, accompanied by four hundred brave archers who served as his guards,
the king performed daily the fire-offerings known as *viṣṇukramaṇa* both evening and morning, while two lute-players sang the *pragātha* hymns.
Having summoned both Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, he indeed caused them to sing his glory; he listened to the *pāriplava* recitations and awaited the arrival of the horse.
Along the tracks of the horse's hooves, he had the appropriate *homa* offerings performed.
The king himself performed the oblation while recollecting the horse’s primary parts— the teeth, the jaws, the thighs, the feet, and the penis—
as well as its walking, running, neighing, and whinnying. (34–35)
Remembering the horse’s bedding, its scent, and its rolling on the ground— its various qualities— and having deified it, the king offered oblations to them.
Then, having achieved victory, he brought back the purifying horse.
Having honored him, the king established him in his position and caused the Soma-pressing ceremony to be performed.
On the second day of the three pressings,
the king appointed the Udgātṛ priest together with mares to occupy the place of the horse.
The horse neighed, and that *udgītha* was produced;
then he caused twenty-one sacrificial posts to be fashioned from the earth,
well-positioned in the middle and at the northern and southern corners.
He bound that horse to the sacrificial post made of *rājjudāla* wood situated to the east;
on its two sides were two posts made of *devadāru* wood, and on those two sides were three posts each, fashioned from the *bilva* tree. (3.31.40–41)
On either side of that [central post], there were three each made of *khadira* wood;

on the sides of those [latter] posts, there were three each made of *pālāśa* wood. He worshipped them all equally. Having bound the horse with a cord, he [prepared] thirteen other sacrificial animals.
The king bound [the victims] with rope-ties upon the girths;
and on the forehead of the horse, he bound the victim for Agni, while in the fifth part he bound the victim for Pūṣan.
Above these, the king bound the victim for Indra and Pūṣan.
The king bound two goats with black necks, dedicated to the Ājñeyas, upon his arms;
two with white backs, dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ, upon his thighs; and two belonging to Bṛhaspati, upon his sides.
Furthermore, he bound beneath him one with a white-colored belly, dedicated to Dhātṛ.
Then the king tied a white goat to the tail;
he likewise tied a black goat dedicated to Sūrya on his right side,
and he tied a black goat dedicated to Yama on his left side in the same manner.
He bound three hundred and forty-nine domestic animals;
he also bound three hundred and sixty wild animals. Those called domestic include goats and the like; those called wild include beasts of prey and the like.
He performed the ritual preparation (*upākaraṇa*) for them as well as the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*).
Having paid homage to all the animals and designated them for the sake of the deities, the king removed those divine and worshipful animals and released them. (3.31.49–50)

Having placed a well-prepared *kuṣmāṇḍa* under the name of "horse" upon a blanket smeared with ghee, he performed the ritual slaughter (*saṃjñapana*), with its head toward the east and its feet toward the north.
Thereafter, the queens and wives uttered reproaches using vulgar words.
He offered six oblations of the entrails of the sacrificial animal to Prajāpati;
he performed the Viṣṇukrama steps and other Kuṣmāṇḍa rites; having immolated the victim at the designated places, he caused all the remaining oblations to be performed.
Having offered three oblations of clarified butter and other substances,
and having thereafter performed the rites concluding with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, the king desisted. On the third day, the day of the *soma* pressing, he performed the rituals pertaining to the *soma*.
Having offered eleven animals dedicated to Prajāpati in the form of Kuṣmāṇḍas,
and having performed the ritual acts, he indeed proceeded with the avabhṛtha bath;
[he placed them] upon the head of a man who had tawny eyes and white leprosy.
Having offered three oblations, he gave a hundred gold pieces;
and having performed the Traidhātavīya sacrifice for an entire year,
the king worshipped the horse, offering the specific fruits of each season.
The most righteous king regarded the horse as if it were a god.
At the end of each year, he observed virtuous ascetics,
as well as chaste and faithful women, Brahmins, and young students of learning.
The king indeed fed female students and female mendicants;
until the end of the year, he gave gifts with devotion at the conclusion of his daily fire-sacrifices.
He waited, wondering when his father, who had the form of a horse, would regain his human state.
While reflecting on the thought, "I shall go," the king fell asleep at night.
At the end of a year, during the suspension of his sacrifice, he beheld Acyuta in the night, possessing a divine form and adorned with a crown.
Adorned with all ornaments, endowed with every splendor,
and complete with all sovereign powers and the like, he was sixteen years of age minus a few months,
shining with you, Lakṣmī, who were fourteen years old.
Then, with a serene face and the splendor of her good fortune, while still in the midst of sleep, she praised Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person:
"You are the sacrifice; you are the horse, and you alone are the Aśvamedha."
You are the king, you are the protector of the kingdom, and you are indeed the sovereign of kings;
you are the world, you are the lord of the world, you are the god, and you are the lord of the gods.
You are Viṣṇu, you are Brahmā himself, and you are Vairāja Maheśvara.
You are the Infinite, you are the Lord of Pradhāna, Vāsudeva, Janārdana;
you are the Lord of the Abode, Mahākāla, the Lord of Māyā, and the Supreme Sovereign;
you are the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the King of all. (67–68)
You alone are the creator, the sustainer, the controller, the protector, the destroyer, and the one dwelling within;
O Blessed One, you are everything, for everything is offered unto you.
You alone, O Lord, are indeed the refuge for my father, who has become a horse.
"O Nārāyaṇa, O Keśava, quickly destroy that which was caused by the curse!
Thus the king praised me; then I said to him:
"O King, you have excluded me from the great horse sacrifice."
Indeed, other deities have been worshipped without my remembrance;
even the horse-sacrifice has not been offered to me, being devoid of dedication to me.
O lord of men, today I do not exist as one who fulfills your desires.
Therefore, perform the horse sacrifice once more and worship me again.
Then, in all matters and in every undertaking, that man Janaka will undoubtedly regain his human state once more. (73–74)
"O Śrī Narāyaṇī, having said, 'My vision shall be renewed and everything will become suitable,' I attained invisibility before your eyes.
O King Dharmadhara, you immediately abandoned your sleep."
Having arisen, he then truly considered his dream to be as it had appeared;
and having fashioned a golden image of me exactly as you saw it,
he performed the horse sacrifice once more, worshipping me according to the prescribed rites.
Furthermore, at the concluding bath (avabhṛtha), I, possessing a divine form, arrived once more; then, O Lakṣmī, having bathed together with you in the purifying water,
I, indeed Nārāyaṇa myself, cast [the horse] into the father.
But that king, named Varmadhara, having shaken off his sinful former form,
immediately regained his royal appearance. With tears in his eyes and remembering his past lives, he praised me with many faltering words.
The queen named Yaśovarā performed a hospitable reception for you, O Śrī;
her priest, Devasatrī, worshipped me, the Supreme Lord. He then entreated me once more with the sixteen types of offerings and other articles. 8.1.
"O Blessed One, because he did not take [the food], he has come here.
O Blessed One, remain here always as the sister of this king for the sake of his release from the curse.
"So be it," said the divine ascetic, whose wealth is penance, when thus addressed by me. (82–83)
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama),
became established under the name Anādi Śrī Medha Nārāyaṇa,
together with you, Medhāvatī Lakṣmī, in the region of Vidrava.

Thereafter, many horse-sacrifices (aśvamedhas) were indeed performed upon the earth. The lords of men, according to their capacity, repeatedly performed various sacrifices after worshipping the divine horse, even without engaging in battle. || 85-86 ||
While I was present on earth, honored during the horse sacrifice,
some kings, out of fear of me, did not tether the released horse. All the kings came to know that the performer of the horse sacrifice was Nārāyaṇa.
The Supreme Lord dwells visibly within the party, the home, and the sacrifice.
(88) One must by no means create an obstacle to his sacrifice through war;
it is certain that no one shall achieve victory by means of battle. (89)

Thus, in that kalpa, the sacrifices were indeed free from violence; those who partook of the offerings to the gods and animals were devoted to pleasing me. And the Brahmin Ajahārita was dedicated to the dharma of the virtuous.
Having heard this, he quickly came to me, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama.
After meeting with the king at Rājagṛha,
that devotee of mine, appearing in the form of a holy man, shone while engaged in my service.
Commanded by me, he bestowed upon the subjects the Manus for their welfare; he instructed them and caused those who take refuge in me to perform [their duties].
Though he was an armor-bearer, through detachment he received the true initiation.
Indeed, he taught me the direct worship (pratyakṣopāsanā) for the sake of the worlds.
The virtuous [king], who was devoted to the dharma of the good, constantly attended upon me;
and Queen Yaśovarā also, having obtained initiation from me, remained a virtuous woman.
Endowed with splendor and eternally devoted to the dharma of virtuous women,
she bestowed upon the other women the auspicious Vaiṣṇava initiation;
she caused them to perform worship and indeed caused them to practice the Vaiṣṇava rites.
"O virtuous one, abiding in the nature of Brahman, you who maintain the spring of Brahman-discipline! O Nārāyaṇī, I shall remain with you until the end of the kalpa.
Remember, O Śrī of Nārāyaṇa, your own all-encompassing wisdom, Medhāvatī! || 97-98 ||
In this way, other incarnations of mine have arisen from that [source] many times over.
I, however, know them all to be devoted solely to the work of Dharma.
By reading, hearing, remembering, and even retaining this [account], [one attains these fruits].
Having attained the fruit of the horse sacrifice and having shaken off all sins in every way,
if he possesses desires, he shall enjoy many heavens for a long time; thereafter, through my constant devotion, which is ever dear to me, he shall go to the supreme abode of Brahman.
But for a disinterested devotee, devotion to me arises swiftly;
fully satisfied with all forms of happiness, he goes to my supreme abode.
He likewise attains the fruit of all sacred pilgrimage sites and the fruit arising from all religious vows.
"And one shall also obtain the fruit of all forms of service by merely hearing [this] birth.

(103) Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Medha-Nārāyaṇa together with the Goddess Medhāvatī at the Horse Sacrifice performed by the son of King Varmadhara—who had been turned into a horse by the curse of Brahmā in the thirty-seventh year of the Dvāpara cycle for the sake of his liberation"—in the Third Section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (31)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! After that, my manifestation occurred during the thirty-eighth year of Brahmā, in the sixth Kalpa and the eighth Manvantara.
Born from the essence of Brahman’s dharma, the Asura Ariṣṭa, the devourer of fire, grew as soon as he was born; he was hungry and possessed of extreme splendor.
All other splendors dissolved entirely into his body.
From birth, he consumes all fires and eats nothing else;
he does not swallow water or earth, but consumes only fire.
Wherever there are fires, wherever there are flames, there he is.
Having gone again and again, he forcibly seized the fire and, having held it, ate it entirely;
he devoured Mahāgni, the mind-born son of Brahmā, as well as his three sons:
Pāvaka, Pavamāna, and Śuci.
Likewise, he devoured the son of Pāvaka along with the Rakṣas;
he also devoured the son of Pavamāna, Kavyavāhana.
Having seized Havyavāha, the son of Śuci, the Asura likewise devoured him.
She devoured Agni’s fourth son, Brahmaudana;
she also devoured Brahmaudana’s son, Bharata;
and likewise, she devoured Bharata’s son, Vaiśvānara.
Then he devoured Agni’s fifth son, Atharvan.
Furthermore, that great asura devoured the four sons of Atharvan—Amṛta, Dadhyañc, Aṅgiras, and Nirmatha. (3.32.10)
He likewise consumed the son of Nirmathya, Gārhapatya;
he likewise consumed Śaṃsya and Śuka, the two sons of Gārhapatya.
He [consumed] the sons of Śaṃsya: Āvasathya, Sabhya, and Āhavanīyaka.
The great Asura named Alāda devoured the Mahāriṣṭas;
likewise, that great Asura devoured the other sons of Śaṃsi who were born from rivers, as well as the sons known as the Dhiṣṇis.
Ṛtu, Pravāhaṇa, Agnīdhra, Samrāj, Kṛśānuka, Pāriṣada, Pratalka, and likewise Nabhasa and Vasu;
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and likewise Gṛhapati.

And he consumed the Hotṛ’s portion, as well as Śāntapracetas; likewise, he consumed the Viśvadeva portion and the Avakṣumat portion for the Acchāvāka priest. He also consumed the Uśīra portion for the Kavi Potṛ priest, and the Āvāri portion as well. (15–16)
He also devoured Bhāri, Naiṣṭhīya, and Vyaratni;
likewise, he consumed Mārjālīya, Avatphūrja, Abja, and Jāṭhara.
Furthermore, he devoured Manyumān, the son of Jāṭhara.
The great Asura devoured Savartaka,
Manyumajja, and Vāḍava; he also devoured Kṣāma, who was born from Vāḍava along with Rakṣas, as well as Kravyāda, the son of Kṣāma and the offspring of Rakṣas.
He devoured the son of Śuci, Āraṇeya, and another as well;
and he devoured the son of Āraṇeya, Āyu, the son of Āyu, Mahimānaka,
the son of Mahimāna, and Savana.
The great asura devoured the Soma arising from the libations, the various wonders born of the Maruts, those born of the Maruts,
as well as the Sun; he also consumed the sons of the Sun, namely Vājasṛg and Anīkavat.
The great asura devoured Yaṣṭikṛta, Rakṣohan, Surabhi, Vasu, Annāda, and Rukmarāja; likewise,
he devoured other [beings] dwelling in the cremation grounds.

Thus, O illustrious Nārāyaṇī! the world indeed became devoid of fire; it arose as if like snow—devoid of burning and devoid of cooking. Seeing everything facing death, the Earth was indeed filled with grief. (54–55)
She went there to the abode of Truth and sought refuge with Brahmā;
for the sake of protection from the fire, she praised him with supreme devotion. She repeatedly offered prayers to ensure she would not perish by the fire.
Then Brahmā remembered me, Puruṣottama—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, Hari, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the Imperishable (Akṣara), and the inner controller of all. (27–28)
O Lakṣmī! Having heard your prayer, I became manifest before Brahmā.
Then, O Lotus-born one, Brahmā worshipped me along with you.
He worshipped you as well, and she [the Earth] then requested protection. (29)
Then, by my command, for the sake of destroying the Asura,
you became the daughter of the Earth, the virtuous maiden Pārthivīśrī.
Taking you with her, she of pure intent quickly departed for the mortal world.
Assuming the very form of fire, I became composed of flames.
Seeing me, the asura Analāda rushed toward Mount Meru;
he came there for the purpose of devouring me, and I fled toward the earth.
Where you, together with the Earth, await my arrival—
in that very cave of the Sun-like Mountain— there I shall come;
and while you and the Earth look on, there the great Asura [will appear].

I entered within that Great Lord Agni, who was ablaze with great flames and was consuming me; having done so, I indeed burnt that great Asura. Having reduced him to ashes, I restored the fires to life once again.
Then all the fires, together with the living beings, became auspicious and conscious;
they became as they were before, and they praised and worshiped me, the beginningless Śrī Vahni-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 36-37 ||
Commanded by me, those fires quickly proceeded to their respective places,
engaged in their own functions, endowed with power and fully equipped.
Then indeed the worlds, the people, and the subjects became possessed of fire.
The state of being stone passed away for them, and they indeed became alive once more.
Then, all the gods and others, having learned of my manifestation there, arrived for the purpose of worship; thereafter, a rain from the sky occurred.
There arose the sound of "Victory! amidst sandalwood and flowers;
a great festival was celebrated there for me by all the gods and others.
You were offered to me by the Earth, and the earthly goddess Śrī was wedded to me.
O Nārāyaṇī, I shall remain with you until the end of the kalpa.
O Lakṣmī, I have told you of my manifestation which bestows happiness; remember it!
At that time, many other incarnations of mine occurred during that year.
I indeed know all these [mantras], and no one else knows them;
by reciting or even hearing them, enjoyment and liberation arise.
There shall be no calamity from fire, nor shall diseases ever occur.
The reciter shall indeed obtain here the eternal bliss of Brahman.
(45) Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, after that, I shall describe to you in brief another auspicious manifestation of mine, which bestows great merit. (46)
In the thirty-ninth year of the Creator, during the Nāga-kalpa, in the sixth Manvantara, there was formerly a great Asura named Ilodara.
He was Rasāda, a fierce devourer of the essence of all principles (tattvas).

The son of Rāhu, an asura by his deeds, was a consumer of the earth and the heavens. Having come to the earth, he performed most rigorous penance for a thousand years on Mount Meru; Śaṅkara himself was pleased with him.
He came into his presence and said, "Choose a boon.
Thereupon, the asura requested that he be allowed to consume all essences.
Having said, "So be it," Hara quickly vanished.
That Asura constantly enjoys the earthly juices situated in the waters as he pleases, and he attains nourishment from all sides. Then,
being satisfied, for more than a thousand years he performs supreme austerity.
He performed [this] with Brahmā in mind, solely for the purpose of making himself invulnerable.
Seeing him withered of limb and subsisting only on air, Brahmā approached;
having sprinkled him with water and restored him to life, he then spoke.
"Choose a boon as you desire; I am pleased with you, O great Asura.
He too, opening his eyes, spoke: "Grant me supreme invincibility;
I shall not be conquerable by those dwelling in the fourteen worlds. (54–55)
The great asura received the words of Brahmā, "So be it.
Then Brahmā, having vanished from sight, departed;
and the great asura, free from fear, enjoyed divine and human pleasures many times over.
Then he thought: "May death not come to me.
Thereupon, he reflected that he must again perform austerities on Mount Meru for a thousand years;
having deliberated thus, he indeed performed penance directed toward Viṣṇu.
At the end of a thousand years, Viṣṇu, impelled by the gods, arrived before him and said:
"What is desired by you? Choose it! I am indeed Viṣṇu here;
I have come for the purpose of granting a boon—do not delay."
The Asura said: "If it be so that death shall not indeed befall me, then I choose from you, Viṣṇu, this boon desired by me. Viṣṇu replied: "O Asura, for one who has birth, death is certain."
The death of your father, who is known as Rāhu, is indeed certain;
likewise, the death of his father Kaśyapa, and even of his father, is certainly fixed.
There is no one who is exempt from death except for the Illustrious Puruṣottama.
The self is eternal, the enjoyer of karma, and dwells within the cage of the body.
When it has departed from the body, one speaks figuratively of it as "dead. The body consists of six sheaths, and these sheaths arise from the elements and so forth.
The transformations of the elements arise constantly;
since transformations are always impermanent, the body is indeed impermanent.
That which is impermanent cannot possess permanence; choose another, stable alternative.
"O Asura! I grant you sovereignty, heaven, the netherworld (pātāla), and even long life;
I give you wealth such as gold and silver, the earth itself, and the status of Sūrya, Candra, Mahendra, and Kubera. (66–67)

"Choose another supreme state, which I shall grant you; do not delay. Upon hearing this, he said: "O All-eater, let there be no death for me here from the three gods or from those born of their creation; grant this to me."
"So be it," Hari said, and he quickly vanished from sight.
Then that Asura, having abandoned his ascetic penance and being devoid of fear of death,
began to enjoy the pleasures of gods, Daityas, and humans by force.

Having forcibly seized all the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva as well, he, strengthened by the power of his boon, enjoys them. Once, having conquered the gods, he even went to Kailāsa.
He said to Śaṅkara, "Give me battle, or else give me Kailāsa.
Śambhu replied, "This half of Kailāsa shall belong to you in every respect;
take it. Then, having obtained that half, he rejoiced.
Then he went to Satyaloka and said to Brahmā:
"O Brahmā, give me either your entire position or even a battle.
Brahmā replied: "Take this half of my supreme office (pārameṣṭhya-pada)."

Having obtained it, he too became pleased and went to Viṣṇu, who was like an ocean of milk. He spoke to him angrily: "O Viṣṇu, give me the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), or else give me battle; do whatever pleases you."
Viṣṇu said to him, "I have always granted you half of the Milk Ocean as your portion.
Having received it, the Asura was pleased and went to Meru, his own abode.
Then that great Asura sought after the goddesses Śivā, Śrī, and Brāhmī.
While they were thus entreating him, the gods resolved upon his destruction;
they quickly displayed curiosity toward the asura,
and Hara himself assumed the forms of those three female ghouls.
He sent him forth, and then Ilodara, of deluded intellect, rejoiced.
The *piśācinīs* undertook a vow consisting of consuming all flavors.
This vow, known as "the consumption of all flavors," was to last for exactly one month.
"Then, once the vow is completed, we shall be at his service.
Hearing that they were ready and knowing it to be so, the asura rejoiced, for he was capable of amassing all kinds of flavors. (81–82)
He quickly brought all kinds of terrestrial juices and even those of the water, whether processed by cooking or not;
he gave them to those three groups and also to the female piśācas.
He fed them in many ways and caused them all to drink [the water].
Indeed, the earth was devoid of flavor, and the water was devoid of flavor; even those elements which are flavorful became tasteless. (84–85)
Food devoid of flavor, even ghee considered nectar,

and all offerings to the gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya), including meat and the like, were rendered tasteless by him. Consequently, everything that had arisen became unfit for eating and unfit for drinking.
All living beings—gods, asuras, sages, and humans—were overcome by afflictions.
Even when the food offering was dedicated to the Supreme Lord, it became devoid of flavor; consequently, all those beings ate their food with harsh throats. (87–88)
Then they all, being deeply distressed, gathered together and propitiated me;
for the sake of destroying the belly of Ilā, they praised me in many ways.
And having heard them, I, the Supreme Brahman, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama—
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Supreme Lord—O Lakṣmī, Hari himself came from the imperishable abode along with you; he appeared visibly before millions of gods. (3.32.90–91)
Honored, entreated, and informed regarding the destruction of the asuras,
I went to the region of Mount Meru where the asura rejoices.
There, having assumed the form of liquid, I remained established as a lake.
Sweet, cool, fragrant, bestowing bliss, granting happiness, and auspicious;
radiant, white like nectar, intoxicating, and soft;
in the form of a flowing stream yet incomplete, I became a lake in his presence. (93–94)
Upon seeing that lake of supreme nectar, the three Piśācinīs spoke of it;
he too arrived there quickly.
He drank the nectar and, full of joy, made them drink it as well.

There was no satiety in drinking, nor did any belching arise; indeed, he drank again and again. Having cast aside all fear, he drank excessively, even unto his throat. "I am the essence," he thought, yet it did not remain in his stomach; rather, that [essence] increased within him.
Having drunk and drunk all that inexhaustible essence, he became Mahodara;
as great as his accomplishment of power was, so great did he become.
Even after reaching the pinnacle of pride, he drank the essence again and again.
Having indeed abandoned his abdomen and his power consisting of concentration,
[the embryo] was split from the region of the navel in the middle up to the heart;
the pelvis was also split, and I emerged in the form of vital essence (rasa).
It fell outside his very belly and he died;
yet I, Anādi-Śrī-rasa-Nārāyaṇa, remained there together with you,
along with Anādi-Śrī-rasa-Lakṣmī.
The Piśācinīs, being pleased, worshipped me as Hari and departed for Kailāsa; the gods and others arrived there,
showered flowers, and praised me, whose essence is rasa.
The lords always requested Śrī Puruṣottama, the primordial Nārāyaṇa of the essence of prosperity, for the purpose of making his permanent residence there.
"I shall always dwell upon this earth for the sake of increasing its nourishment and growth."
At that time, I became manifest in embodied form for the duration of a single Manvantara.
Thereafter, O beloved, having become the essence of nectar (rasa), I remained so until the end of the Kalpa.
Remember, Lakṣmī, that manifestation of mine as the essence of nectar! (105–106)
Then all the gods went to their own abodes in the heavens and other realms.
At that time, thousands of other incarnations of mine also came into being.
I, the Supreme Brahman, became Rasanārāyaṇa, the Incarnate One.
"From reading and hearing this, even the attainment of enjoyment and liberation shall occur.

(108) Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Vahninārāyaṇa together with the Earthly Śrī for the purpose of destroying the great Asura Anālāda in the thirty-eighth year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the Dvāpara lineage in the third book of the *Śrī Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, and likewise the manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Rasanārāyaṇa together with Śrī Rasalakṣmī for the purpose of destroying the great Asura Ilodara-Rasāda in the thirty-ninth year. (32)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Thereafter, I shall tell you of my manifestation:
in the fortieth year of the Creator, during the eighth Kalpa. (1)
And when the tenth Manu is present, throughout the world during the final Dvāpara age,
when the power of Dharma has been weakened by the force of time among sinful embodied beings,
and when the strength of Adharma has pervaded, increasing the power of the Asuras.
The subjects were indeed oppressed, and sacrifices were obstructed on all sides.
Generosity, compassion, self-restraint, and the like had entirely vanished;
non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing were no longer seen upon the earth.
Purity, austerity, and religious vows have indeed perished among living beings;
neither beneficence nor good conduct is seen at all.
Everyone oppresses the weak, and the powerful enjoy their possessions.
They forcibly seize all of your prosperity in every way.
(6) Tens of millions of Daityas, Dānavas, and Asuras are seen everywhere on earth, having gone to their destruction during pilgrimages. (7)
The boundaries of conduct for men and women have indeed been destroyed by the Rākṣasas; all social classes have become independent and devoid of righteousness and justice.
All forms of worship due to the gods have completely vanished in every way.
The protection of children, the helpless, and guests has come to an end;
atheism has arisen in all undertakings and in all religious duties; there is contempt for the elderly and the oppression of the righteous. (3.33.9–10)
In this world, all manner of things were done by the Asuras— who ate what should not be eaten, drank what should not be drunk, and committed actions that were improper and loathsome.
All the kings belonged to the lineage of the Daityas, and the teachers likewise belonged to the lineage of the Daityas.
When even the preceptors were born on earth from the lineage of the Daityas,
then all that pertains to the gods, the ancestors, and heaven quickly went to ruin.
At that time, the gods, the sages, and men whose minds were set upon dharma [acted].

Indeed, the glorious Supreme Lord himself— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama— was propitiated by me. At that time, I became his very self as a son in the home of Jñānaviṣṇu.
The Lord Cakranārāyaṇa was accompanied by Sudarśana.
My mother was Vedinī, and I manifested from her womb.
At that time, by my command, you became the auspicious princess.
Then Sudhākṣiṇī was born from the womb of Queen Śobhālikā, the wife of King Sārvabhauma Brahmacitradhara.
Your father, the emperor, himself arranged the svayaṃvara for you, O Sudhākṣi.
Then, at that great festival, all the kings who were leaders among the asuras,
as well as the emperors residing in their own realms and those from other realms, even the powerful celestial beings traveling in their aerial chariots, arrived there out of hope for you.
"I am indeed a Vaiśya, the son of Jñānaviṣṇu, endowed with the discus and possessed of beauty, sovereignty, and virtue; I went there to the svayaṃvara.
O Supreme Goddess, having beheld me, you abandoned all of them."
In the midst of the assembly, he placed a most beautiful garland around my neck.
(21) Then those groups of kṣatriyas rose up in anger for the sake of battle;
by me, with the Sudarśana [discus] alone, ten thousand kings were struck down. (22)
There is no counting those who were common; all the Daityas have been slain by me, and the Dānavas have been struck down, as well as all the Asuras brought to their end.
Only your father was spared, for he became devoted to me.
Being childless, he gave his own kingdom to Sudakṣiṇā.
(24) Thereafter, I ruled the entire kingdom for a thousand years; I established the duties toward the gods and ancestors among the subjects in the world. (25)
Furthermore, the boundaries for gifts and sacrifices have been established by me, the beginningless Śrī Cakranārāyaṇa, the conqueror of all.
O Śrī, consort of Nārāyaṇa! Remember that sovereignty was indeed yours at that time.
Indeed, I know all that; no others know it at all.
By reading and by hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.
My other incarnations, numbering in the hundreds, are for the purpose of protecting the Dharma.
At that time, many beings were born—gods, humans, and perfected siddhas—who protected the Dharma and bestowed liberation; remember them, O Lotus-born One!
Furthermore, in the forty-first year of Brahmā’s life, [the following occurred].
In the seventh Manvantara, during the fifty-third Kalpa known as Adhvara,
and specifically in the sixty-seventh Kali age, my manifestation indeed took place;
listen to that, O Śrī, for it is truly from the Supreme Brahman itself.
When the power of the Kali age has completely pervaded, when people consist of barbarians,
when the entire world is uniform and devoid of the system of castes and stages of life,
and when the body is only a span in height with its dwelling place being a hole in the earth; (32)

In this world where one subsists on roots and grass, devoid of rites for the gods and ancestors; where the family line is everywhere severed and there remains only the pursuit of one's own self-interest;
in this world of arbitrary pairs, bereft of the light of my [divine] presence. (33–34)
When afflictions were predominant, happiness was meager, and the refuge [of the world] had been abandoned,
Hari himself appeared on earth for the sake of establishing the true dharma of those who possess truth,
having entered into the state of being the son of a devotee. (35)
At that time, you were the four-armed Lord himself, the Brāhmaṇa named Drāvaṇa;
established in the splendor of Brahman within my body, you remained forever present. You became Śrī, known as Vijayā, invisible in form, together with me.
For the sake of destroying the Asuras, Garuḍa was summoned by me;
as well as a divine chariot and elephants with four tusks and white luster.
All weapons were present: maces, swords, arrows, and scimitars.
Bearing bows, spears, thunderbolts, discuses, javelins, lances, and barbed missiles,
and carrying various weapons and arms, I shall mount with you, Vijayā,
the victorious chariot that bears the soaring Garuda upon its banner.
Mounted on elephants and traveling through the sky, he fought against tens of millions of asuras.
Previously, the kings, the mlecchas, the powerful lords of the daityas, the lords of the dānavas, the lords of the asuras, and then the mleccha subjects and others were destroyed. 41.
And those who had come for refuge were protected by me there in the battle;
having made those brahmins drink water and prostrate at my feet,
they were all led out from within the fire of my manifestation.
And ten million twice-born ones, whose bodies were unpurified, have been purified;
in all of them, my Dharmas born of truth have been established.
Indeed, by the power of my existence, beings have become truly characterized by goodness (sāttvika). 44.
All men and women who were born were exceedingly virtuous (sāttvika);
by my power, they were all devoted to truth and righteousness.
The elements—air, fire, water, earth, ether, and the rest—attained a state of purity (sattva).
At that time, the trees, creepers, grasses, and other plants became filled with sap.
Indeed, the Brahmins were established as kings, and fame was also set in motion.
Faith, the duty of giving, and marriages were also instituted. (47)
I have also made the virtuous men and women, as well as the holy ones, perfected and auspicious. Tiṣya has been destroyed and Satya has been established by me.
All the gods have been protected and the ṛṣis have been re-established.
Temples were caused to be built and fire-offering halls were established;
at that time, I dwelt upon the earth during the ages of Satya and Tretā.
O Lakṣmī, remember my ancient miracle from those days!
The beginningless Śrī Satyanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Śrī Vijayā;
the Supreme Brahman himself, the establisher of truth and the one who descends as an incarnation;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (51–52)
In this way, thousands of other incarnations of mine have also appeared here and there;
I alone know them all, and no one else.
By reading or hearing this, one shall become established in the true dharma.
There shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and one shall possess whatever fruits are desired. (54) Now, I shall tell you of another divine manifestation of mine:
in the forty-second year of Brahmā, during the age named Hiraṇya. (55)
In the ninety-eighth kalpa, at the beginning of the first Manu,
there were mountains on earth that divided the twelve regions; these included those with wings,
independent ones, and other island-mountains.
The conscious beings, powerful and embodied, engaged in debate for the sake of a dwelling place:
"I shall dwell in the vicinity of Meru, not far away," and "I shall do likewise"—thus was their mutual contention. (57–58)
Those who were powerful there remained by force as they desired; others, having gone toward Manu, dwelt in their preferred places.
Summoned by Manu to report their respective hardships, they were instructed by him.
Nevertheless, those mighty ones did not heed the word of Manu.
Then he gave the command to Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt,
to instruct Parvata to grant [the mountain] and to punish the other mountains otherwise.
Indra, having arrived at the region of Mount Meru near the peak of Meru,
summoned the mountains in their embodied forms and spoke for their benefit:
"You were created by Brahmā for the sake of providing stability to the earth."
For the purpose of dividing the territory and for the sake of securing treasure-troves;

for the task of protecting the subjects and for the purpose of constructing regional fortifications—those who were appointed to whatever task, in whatever place, remained there in every respect. (63–64)
"Let them dwell [here], for otherwise my word would not be beneficial;
otherwise, having forcibly shattered your wings, I shall strike you all down to the ground with my thunderbolt in every way. (65)
Having thus heard Indra’s words full of pride,
those formidable mountains immediately leapt into the sky;
all of them were powerful, exceedingly arrogant, and at that time capable of assuming any form at will.
Equal to the planets, they indeed fell upon Mahendra;
Indra, being crushed there, became as if dead.
Even the thunderbolt of the wielder of the thunderbolt was destroyed and turned to dust.
Then Indrabala was slain and crushed by the long mountains;
the gods and others fled in all directions.
The mountains, even those moving through the sky, engaged in battle with the gods.
Deprived of its weight and losing its level balance, the earth indeed became sloped toward the sides in order to sink into the great depths of the waters.
Then, portents occurred everywhere, even among the planets.
Even the winds were rendered unstable by the mountains;
indeed, the entire sky, along with its celestial spheres, trembled as if at the time of universal dissolution.
The stability and protection of the earth depended entirely upon the stability of the mountains.
"Then, upon the stability of the earth, there will indeed be stability for Meru and for Dhruva;
and this being so, there will be stability and happiness for the heavenly worlds.
Having reflected thus, Brahmā, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and the other deities [acted] suddenly.

Great and humble in disposition, and endowed with consoling wisdom, they then attempted to instruct those mountains in many ways regarding their duty to dwell in their assigned places; nevertheless, these mountains did not heed them. (74–75)
Hiraṇyaka, Kānaka, Rājata, Rātnaka, Māṇeya, Vaiṣṇava, Haimeya, and Digīśaka;
Bhairava, Mahendra, and likewise Udayanaparvata.
Āruṇa, Mahābha, Lokāloka, and Meruka—
these and other most formidable gods did not then consider Nārāyaṇa for the sake of pacifying the great suffering of the mountains. (77–78)
They quickly remembered the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Hari; and I, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
arrived there instantly as the Supreme Brahman himself.

The Sudarśana discus was held [by me], and the mace was placed upon the earth. Wherever the earth rose up, I then adjusted it accordingly; thus it became level and was protected from the weight of the weapon.

Then, O Lakṣmī, having summoned the mountains by means of a boon, they were established by me; for they have been made my dwelling places. Those mountains which shall remain upon the earth in the regions designated by me—
"In each of those places, I myself, Śrī Puruṣottama, shall remain.
Then those mountains quickly took refuge in my word;
Meru was placed in the center, and Lokāloka was established all around it.
In the four corners, four rivers flowing to the ocean were created:
Hiraṇyaka in the southeast, Kāñcana in the southwest,
Rājata in the northwest, and Ratnaka in the northeast.
In the east, the two [deities] Māṇeya and Vaiṣṇava extend toward the north;
in the south, the lord of the quarters Haimeya hangs toward the east and west;
and in the west, Mairava and Mahendraka extend toward the north and south.
In the north, Mahābha and Cāyatu were established; and Udayana, endowed with all splendors, was placed in the eastern ocean.
In this manner, other mountains were also situated at various intervals.
Then they made this request: "Indeed, let there be no destruction of our wings.
I replied, "Let them remain firm along with your wings;
if you shall possess the power of motion in the sky, then indeed this [shall be so]. (3.33.90)
Mahendra will have his wings clipped by Vajradhara;
thereafter, they shall attain stability and dwell happily in their respective abodes.
Then all the gods and others, having worshipped me, departed.
Assuming many forms, I, the Lord who provides protection, established my own realms and a dwelling upon the mountains together with you. Indeed, until the end of the kalpa, I dwelt with you, Hiraṇyā.
Anādiśrī, Hiraṇyaśrī, and Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person—
bound by my word, I dwelt upon the mountains, awakening the gods,
as well as humans, the ancestors, and the great sages who travel through the sky. (94)
Then the earth became firm and the mountains became happy;
by my dwelling, the subjects likewise became fearless and contented.
[I meditated upon] the beginningless, glorious, golden Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord.
"O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, remember! And likewise, remember Hiraṇyā.
In this way, there were other incarnations among gods, humans, and living beings;
they appeared according to the requirements of their tasks, and I know them all."
From reciting and even from hearing [this], auspicious enjoyment and liberation shall arise.
For one who remembers me, my residence is always present in their home;
and wherever my devotees, endowed with devotion, dwell, there I am also present.
I dwell indeed, without a doubt, upon the mountain and in the forest,
as well as in the house, the palace, the great abode, and even in the water—
for the sake of protecting my devotee, and likewise for the sake of his nourishment.

Moreover, for the sake of the creation and protection of the worlds of the gods, I dwell there, having made that place my abode, even though I am non-human (amānava). Wherever I reside, right there is my imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma). || 101–102 ||
All those who are liberated come to that very place, and there they attain [the goal].
Those possessed of illusion do not see it; only those with divine vision see it.
Siddhas, liberated ones, holy men, the virtuous, and stainless renunciants [perceive it].

"O beloved! They behold virtuous, truthful, and devoted ones as my very self. Thus [ends the section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the third section concerning the lineage of the Dvāpara age, in the fortieth year from the Creator's perspective, regarding the destruction of the Daityas; and in the forty-first year, regarding the establishment of the dharma of the Satya Yuga by the beginningless Śrī Satya-Nārāyaṇa accompanied by Vijayā-Śrī; and in the forty-second year...
Chapter Thirty-Three: The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Hiraṇyanārāyaṇa, together with Hiraṇyāśrī, for the sake of the stability of the mountains; thus ends the thirty-third chapter.
