Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! My manifestation and that of others—listen to this.
Formerly, in the forty-third year of the Brahmā-kalpa,
during the thirteenth Manvantara, in the seventh century augmented by sixty-two [years],
there was a lifelong devotee of Viṣṇu named Nirañjana. (1–2)
The brahmin lived among the trees, subsisting on roots, leaves, and fruits;
he was eternally devoted to truth and righteousness, intent upon the chanting of my mantra, Hari;
he was dedicated to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and fully absorbed in the perfected posture (siddhāsana).
Furthermore, he is devoted to sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra) and intent upon concentration (dhāraṇā) and meditative absorption (dhyāna).
With body, mind, speech, and soul, he is dedicated to Viṣṇu;
he is self-controlled, a knower of Brahman, and free from attachment, aversion, and the like.
Radiant like pure crystal, with an inner purity as stainless as the sky;
filled with the affection born of association with the virtuous and devoted to the service of the good;
possessing the vision of Brahman, exerting himself for Brahman, he is a treasury of perfection like Brahman itself. (6)
Just as Brahmā, just as Viṣṇu, and just as Śambhu, so indeed am I.
By the power of his worship, he became an ocean of all sovereign powers;
he assumed manifold forms and possessed the ability to enter the bodies of others.
Possessing unimpeded movement through the worlds of the lords of gods and others, accomplished in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), my devotee was entirely devoted to me.
Once, while standing at the foot of a tree, he reflected as follows: [9]
"Today I shall ask Viṣṇu, who resides within my heart,
about the divine vision of Nārāyaṇa— what is it like?
Having reflected thus, he bathed at dawn and sat down for worship.
Having installed the four-armed Viṣṇu, he worshipped him with all ritual offerings.
Then, entering into meditative absorption, he invoked Viṣṇu, who stood before him.
Filled with humility, he questioned Viṣṇu, who possessed a divine form.
"What indeed is the divine vision of Nārāyaṇa like? [He asked].
Viṣṇu said: "I am indeed Nārāyaṇa; behold me!
Four-armed, the abode of Śrī, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus."
Nirañjana said to him, "You are another Nārāyaṇa;
there is no higher Nārāyaṇa. Show me here that which is supreme.
Having heard this, Viṣṇu then became possessed of a thousand arms.
"Behold Nārāyaṇa, who is stainless and superior even to me; he is like a thousand Viṣṇus in splendor, age, and virtues. Indeed, Viṣṇus such as myself are produced from him day after day. (16–17)
Year after year, thousands [of beings] dissolve again and again.
Having heard, seen, worshipped, and bowed down, Nirañjana said:
"Even though this Lord possesses a thousand eyes and a thousand arms,"
There is also Paranārāyaṇa, yet there is another who is even beyond him.
Nārāyaṇa indeed becomes [manifest] for one to whom my vision is dear;
having perceived and understood the desire of his devotee, Viṣṇu then appears as something even beyond that.
He quickly transformed his form into that of Mahāviṣṇu,
which was served by Mahālakṣmī and resembled ten million Vairājas;
[endowed] with splendor, youth, sovereignty, virtues, and the majesty of divine manifestations.
He revealed that form and said to his devotee, "Behold me!
I have ten million times ten thousand arms and ten million times ten thousand lotus-eyes.
This is my supreme form, the cause of ten million emperors."
Having heard, known, seen, bowed down to, and worshipped [him], the stainless one said to Viṣṇu: "This is not even the supreme form of the Lord;
there exists yet another, which is the cause of this very form."
"Show me that form which is indeed supreme and even higher than this.
Having heard the devotee's state of mind and knowing it, Viṣṇu then manifested a form even greater than that.
Equal to ten million Great Viṣṇus, yet superior to ten million sovereigns,
he is preeminent in beauty, charm, sweetness, splendor, and other qualities.
He possesses ten million times ten thousand eyes and arms, and ten million times ten thousand lotus feet.
And he said, "Behold that which is even more than ten million times ten millionfold greater than that.
Then Nirañjana, having beheld him, bowed down, worshipped with devotion, prostrated like a staff,
and offered a handful of flowers, spoke as follows.
O true guru, out of compassion for me, I have beheld this form of yours:
the possessor of all sovereignty and the controller of all lords;
the creator of the worlds of the lords and the ruler over them. (3.34.30)
I am satisfied, O Supreme Lord, having beheld this supreme form of Yours;
yet I am not entirely satisfied, for my mind runs forward to see Your even higher, most divine form.
Having heard and seen his state of devotion, Viṣṇu, whose form is the infinite earth,
quickly transformed himself from one with two eyes into one with ten million eyes;
then [he manifested] feet with ten billion eyes, and thereafter qualities equal to ten million lotuses.
It produces ten million [manifestations] and performs the drawing-in of ten million;
it has Vāsudeva as its essence, is divine, and is served by ten million Pradyumnas.
It is endowed with the great sovereignty of ten million splendors and is accompanied by Aniruddha and the others. (34–35)

Beholding the Lord Vāsudeva, his mind was indeed exceedingly thrilled; he instantly became the king of devotees and joyfully prostrated before Him like a staff. Afterwards, he praised Viṣṇu within his heart, and He spoke to him again.
Show that the mind finds no satisfaction here, but something greater than that;
as long as there is a quartet, so long it cannot be the supreme form.
He alone is the non-dual Supreme Lord, higher than the highest. (37–38)

Having heard this and understood his state of devotion, Viṣṇu then again revealed his own beautiful form as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. The devotee, having bowed to him and worshipped him, prostrated himself like a staff.
Viṣṇu told him that this was not his true form;
then he revealed his own nature as Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa.
Having bowed down, worshipped, and offered praise, the devotee spoke again in that manner.
Beyond even this is the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of lords,
the inner controller of all, the glorious Supreme Lord, the Puruṣottama,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign.
The Lord who is the sovereign of the syllables, served by millions of liberated beings and others—
O Viṣṇu, if you have compassion for me, I truly wish to see him, the stainless one, who is both the source of incarnations and the one who descends. 43–44.
Viṣṇu said to me, "I have no authority there;
indeed, no one is capable of assuming the form of that Incarnate One.
Whether they be incarnations or lords, whether endowed with attributes or devoid of them," || 45 ||

The portions (aṃśas), the manifestations (vibhūtis), the partial incarnations (kalās), and the great lords (maheśvaras)—whether they be called vibhavas or vyūhas—are never able to sustain those forms;
only the Incarnate Lord himself is truly capable of sustaining them. (46–47)
Therefore, I am not capable of showing Him to you. O stainless one! If you desire to behold Him, worship that Supreme Lord who dwells within me.
To the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (49) He who is your Self is indeed my Self, abiding within my heart;
in the imperishable, supreme abode, that very Self is eternally situated. (3.34.50)
The Supreme Brahman himself, being pleased by your meditation,
service, intense worship, and excessive affectionate devotion,
will come here of his own accord, impelled by compassion, within the range of your vision.
Worship that Lord of Śrī, the Lord of all, the one Supreme Lord; worship Him,
the Lord of all liberated souls, the Lord of all powers,
the Lord of Ramā, who carries Māṇikī— then you shall behold Keśava.
"Having two arms, enriched with all splendors, and the inner controller of all"—
having spoken thus, Viṣṇu suddenly vanished thereafter.
Nirañjana then performed meditation upon me, who manifest in all incarnations.
He performed *dhāraṇā* and likewise performed *dhyāna*;
then he attained *samādhi* upon me, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
Through that *samādhi*, he merged into the imperishable, supreme abode.
And he beheld my supreme and transcendent form together with you—divine, characterized by liberation, and distinct from all incarnations;
that which is one alone, without a second, the most exalted, and the Supreme Self. (57)
There, Nirañjana beheld all incarnations and all abodes;
he beheld all the lords, those worlds, and all the complete creations, as well as the primordial form itself. (58–59)
The devotee requested me to go with him to his own world, saying,
"Become accessible to living beings for the sake of their ultimate liberation.
Though I am subject to my devotees, I then said to him, "So be it."
O Lakṣmī! At that time, Śrī Puruṣottama himself arrived upon the earth together with you, Śrī, and my devotee. Fulfilling the desires of my devotees, I became a human being in the world of mortals.
Indeed, my manifestation took place in the house of Nirañjana. At that time, O beloved, you were born as the daughter of a brahmin ascetic living nearby, who was named Niṣkiñcana.
And in time, having realized that I was an incarnation—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
the Supreme Brahman beyond the Imperishable (Akṣara), the eternal Supreme Lord— he offered himself to me. (64–65)
And thereafter, O beloved, I became known as the beginningless Śrī Nairañjaninārāyaṇa, together with you, who possess the glory of absolute detachment (naiṣkiñcanī-śrī).
For a Manvantara, I dwelt there, liberating the human beings who sought refuge in me.
Remember me, O Lakṣmī! Remember that beautiful manifestation of yours! (67) Other incarnations of mine also occurred during that very kalpa, my beloved!
I know them all, O Nārāyaṇī, but others do not know them. (68)
At that time, indeed, countless living beings were sent by me to liberation;
and by you as well, countless beings and virtuous women have been liberated.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and even retaining this [teaching], [they attain the same].
There shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and he shall possess bliss according to his desire.
(3.34.70) Your mother, named Agrahā, is my mother Āśutoṣiṇī;
having obtained her daughter Śrī as her son, she has attained the Supreme Lord, Hari, the Master. (3.34.71)
Those two [wives] always attained the fulfillment of their births as they were liberated from their husbands;
however, those two who became the teachers [of yoga] became the mothers of the worlds—
renowned, bestowers of liberation, worthy of all worship, and the supreme abode.
O beloved, those two lineages were then always worthy of worship.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, listen to my manifestation:
it occurred in the forty-fourth year of the Creator’s cycle, during the Kapālaka [age]. ||73-74||
In the ninety-ninth kalpa above the nine hundred, during the Manu period of Advaya,
there was a virtuous woman named Puṇyavatī who was devoted to me and faithful to her husband.
She was the wife of the Brahmin Devapuṣpa.
Devoted to moral conduct, devoted to the Dharma, and intent upon the worship of the gods; likewise devoted to service to her husband and intent upon truth and righteousness;
she was a performer of pilgrimages, a performer of vows, and intent upon the yoga of meditation. (76–77)
The Brahmin was also righteous and devoted to the service of the virtuous.
Yet, the couple remained childless and were overcome by old age;
no son was born to them, nor did a daughter ever come into being.
Distressed by her longing for a son, Satī lamented her ill fortune again and again.
Once, she cursed the Creator, the ordainer of destiny:
"Become dull-witted and childless; become just as we two are! (3.34.80)
Then, in the world of truth (Satyaloka), the rod of creation suddenly fell from the hand of the Creator,
just as a potter’s staff falls from his hand;
the wheel of worldly existence (saṃsāracakra) fell from its pivot onto the ground at its side.
The jar-like vessel of the universe was shattered and blown apart by the force [of his movement].
The thread was cast far away, as were the various implements.
Brahmā, however, fell into a state of stupor and became unconscious like a corpse. (82–83)
Due to the friction, the potter’s workshop began to tremble;
other vessels that had been made were shattered by the wheel.
Then, a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from all around the potter’s workshop.
"Brahmā is the creator and he has died"—for one who is unconscious is as good as dead.
We do not know what the cause is; thus spoke those who perform the ritual duties.
Then Sāvitrī and the others arrived and wept upon seeing him unconscious. (85–86)
The perfected ones, the great seers, and the lords of creatures also refreshed themselves there;
the sons of Brahmā, who carry out his tasks, arrived at the hall.
All the guardians of the quarters arrived, as did other Brahmās as well.
Seeing him thus rendered inert by the curse and deprived of his creative power,
they all gathered there and lamented in many ways.
Then, those who were the sons of Brahmā and likewise those who were the daughters of Brahmā—
Overwhelmed even by the curse of Brahmā regarding their childlessness,
they quickly became afflicted with disease and fell into a swoon,
just as those two were deprived of sons, so too were they deprived of daughters.
Likewise, Brahmā was also deprived of his daughter and others,
and Sāvitrī likewise was ordained by fate to be deprived of her sons, daughters,
and so forth; he beheld his own sons and daughters as dull-witted and diseased.
Since the curse was terrifying, they suddenly fled from there lest they die;
the curse of Satī had been unleashed for the purpose of leaving only two remaining.
Then Viṣṇu, Śambhu, Virāṭ, and Narāyaṇa were remembered by all.
All arrived in an instant for the purpose of restraining the curse.
Having gathered together and sought out the cause, they went quickly toward Satī, the meritorious one on earth, and indeed began to console her. (94–95)
Having worshipped all the Blessed Ones, she spoke what was in her heart:
"O lords of the gods, how has my fortune been made so that I am deprived of both sons and daughters? I shall not revoke the curse that has been bestowed."
"Go home as you have come; otherwise, you shall be cursed.
Having understood and heard these words of the devoted woman, they were all then overcome with fear and remembered Śrīpati, Puruṣottama.
Remembered by them, O lotus-born one, I, the Blessed Lord Hari— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa— arrived there along with you.
Upon seeing the Lord, Puṇyavatī became bowed down with modesty.
Having beheld her chosen deity, the Supreme Lord, she went for refuge to me.
Together with my husband and you, she quickly fell at my feet.
Consoled by me, she then requested that very pair.

"Then, through the ascent of my good fortune, there shall be the cessation of the Creator’s curse for my son, for me, for your son’s wife, and for you as well. "So be it," I said, and she spoke to the Creator.
"Let there be insentience for both of us, and let there be no equality between us either;
let there be the state of having offspring, indeed the state of having many sons and daughters.
As soon as this was said, that potter’s workshop immediately became fully conscious. 104.
Brahmā and the conscious progeny of Brahmā were born desiring to live, impelled by the words of Satī.
I, the Supreme Lord, was born as her son right there.
The beginningless Śrī Puṇyanārāyaṇa is Śrī Puruṣottama. And you, O auspicious one, became my daughter through your devotion;
you were born as the offspring of the twice-born Agnihotra.
By him you were bestowed upon me; according to the prescribed rites, you were wedded to me. At that time, O Lakṣmī, you became known as Kalyāṇīśrī.
Remember all of my births, which bring about every form of prosperity.
Through reciting, hearing, and even remembering [this], one obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(3.34.109) Furthermore, O beloved, thousands of other incarnations of mine have likewise appeared at that time, bestowing both enjoyment and liberation, and acting as protectors of the world. (3.34.110)

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Nairañjanī-Nārāyaṇa together with the Niṣkiñcanī-Śrī for the sake of His devotees in the forty-third year of the Creator during the Dvāpara cycle in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Puṇya-Nārāyaṇa together with the Kalyāṇikā-Śrī for the purpose of removing Brahmā’s affliction by Puṇyavatī in the forty-fourth year. || 34 ||

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, thereafter my manifestation occurred in the ocean of Apsaras,
in the forty-fifth year of the Kalpa of Brahmā, during the thousandth cycle.
And in the second Manvantara,
O Lotus-born One, listen to how I, the bestower of liberation, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, was drawn by the devotional sentiments of all the Apsarases and indeed appeared upon the earth.
In heaven, in the assembly hall of Mahendra, among tens of millions of gods,
and likewise elsewhere, praise indeed arises for me everywhere—
regarding my form, qualities, nature, sovereignty, happiness, and splendor.
In touch, sound, and movement; in conduct, satisfaction, taste, and strength;
in bliss, companionship, yoga, laughter, and jesting;
in sleep, service, delusion, gesture, emotion, and attraction. (5)
In the modes, in delight, in pleasure, in festival, in eating, and in stability;
in sitting, in riding, in traveling, in the home, in drinking, and in dancing;
in love-making, in fragrance, in vigor, in prowess, and in action. (6–7)
"In passion, in action, in clarity, and in enjoyment,
there is no other equal to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Upon hearing this praise, millions of celestial nymphs in heaven [were filled with wonder].
They conceived a longing for union with me, for my portion, for dalliance, and for pleasure.
(9) Abandoning all enjoyments and eager for the attainment of me, those women, like men, performed many vows. (3.35.10)
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
become our husband, by which we may indeed be satisfied in every way.
Having thus resolved, they all performed my worship.
Then, by means of a voice from the sky, I also informed them:
"May all of you become auspicious human maidens through your own portions—
daughters of kings, daughters of brahmins, and daughters of devotees in every way."
"From this day forward, take birth upon the earth as you desire,
in the region to the west of Meru, in the realm known as Hemaratha. There,
I shall indeed meet you as a human being, a preeminent warrior."
"The Supreme Brahman, Hari himself, is the preeminent leader of the Varcīṣṇu lineage.
Having been addressed thus, those Apsarases took birth in every way;
O Lakṣmī, I was born together with you in the region named Hemaratha.
Then, in the radiant royal palace of King Bṛhadindra, within the illustrious lineage of the Kṣatriyas, I appeared swiftly from the queen Prabhāvatī,
resplendent with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, Kaustubha gem, and other divine marks.
"My parents are devoted to me; therefore, my fortune and destiny are blessed. (1.8) The celestial drums resounded, and the great sages also offered auspicious prayers.
They performed remembrance and worship, and the lords of the gods increased [their blessings]. (1.9)
A rain of flowers fell from the path of the sky, foreboding auspiciousness.
The king, his subjects, the gods, and the great sages celebrated the festival.
Then you [were born] to Queen Rukmacampā, the consort of King Gavendra.
Then, you were manifested in my womb as Sarvasaubhāgyasundarī,
with a body possessing the luster of refined gold and endowed with all auspicious marks;
and when the time suitable for marriage had arrived, you were offered to me.
This beautiful woman was given to me by your father and likewise by your mother;
there, that most lovely lady was wedded to me according to the prescribed rites during the marriage festival of that sovereign king. (23)
By command [of the Lord], royal lineages, as well as other merchant lineages,
brahmin lineages, kṣatriya lineages, and vaiśya lineages, all arrived.
And those celestial nymphs who had seen me in a dream at night—
Our marriage took place with Hari, the Supreme Soul.
On the night of your wedding, they saw me as their husband and Lord.
Then, for my sake, they indeed made a decision regarding the *svayaṃvara*.
"We ourselves shall choose our husbands by the offering of the bridegarland.
Then the Supreme Self, endowed with great sovereignty,
granted those maidens— who were for his sake— a vision of their parents.
In a dream, during that festival, they both gave me their own daughter;
then, having awakened, the parents naturally gave each of their respective daughters to me, the Supreme Soul.
Having obtained me as their beloved according to their desires, millions of apsarases attained supreme bliss and unsurpassed happiness. At that time,
I became a universal monarch for the duration of one manvantara.
By name he was Samrāṭ Bṛhadbrahmanārāyaṇanṛpeśvara.
At that time, my sons were in the tens of millions, billions, and hundreds of millions, and likewise my daughters;
they were as numerous and were established within the royal lineages.

My grandsons and granddaughters’ sons, consisting of the Brahmin, Kshatriya, and Vaishya castes, as well as those born of the common people and kings upon the earth, were thus produced. Then, at the end of the Manvantara, having liberated those wives, thereafter—
O Nārāyaṇī! I too went to the forest together with you;
in the forest, I became invisible along with you.
Thus, my worship was established throughout the worlds.

O lotus-born Śivarājñī, remember always, until the end of the kalpa, your own manifestation and mine as well, together with you, Rukmavatī, and the beginningless, glorious, great Brahman Nārāyaṇa. //36-37//
In this manner, many other incarnations also occurred during that kalpa.
By reading or even hearing [this account], there shall be enjoyment of worldly pleasures and supreme liberation.
It shall yield the fruit of all sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as the fruit of all religious observances (vratas).
Whatever fruit may arise from giving, and whatever fruit may arise from sacred learning— may there be the destruction of all sins and the attainment of all bliss;
may one partake in all joy, and likewise may there be the attainment of Me.
Now I shall declare another manifestation of mine; listen to that.
In the forty-sixth year of the Creator, during the Brahma-sarasa Kalpa, in the sixth cycle of nine hundred years, in the first Manvantara, long ago in the Kṛta Yuga.
Created by Brahmā, those wise great sages, the Brahmins,
dwelt upon the surface of the earth in this land of action (karmabhūmi), though they were not inhabitants of the [higher] realms.
They all perceived everything directly and were devoted solely to all the dharmas.
The knowledge of Brahman became their natural impeller.
Then, when the Tretā Yuga arrived, it underwent a partial decline;
at that time, the great sages engaged in dialectical disputations with one another.
Stricken by ignorance, they became forgetful over time.
Thereupon, they propitiated me— the glorious Lord, the Supreme Person,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Supreme Controller.
I appeared among them as the bestower of knowledge.
I taught them the supreme and the lower Vedic sciences,
as well as the knowledge of the Vedas, the knowledge of the Self, and those consisting of ritual duties.
At that time, he taught other sciences to the great sages—
sciences that destroy fallacious reasoning, which are auspicious for those possessing devotion and the awakening of worship,
and which grant liberation, heaven, and beneficial results.
I was the preceptor of the great seers and the bestower of Vedic knowledge.
Being the son of the sage Brahmasvara, I remained established in a position of honor;
having become a brahmin, I indeed taught while being served by the hosts of great seers.
From this time until the end of the Dvāpara age, I shall remain together with you, Suvidyā—the daughter of the Ṛṣi dwelling within my heart, known by the name Suvidyā, the embodiment of Śrī.
I am the beginningless Śrī Guru Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama. (51)
Remember yourself, O beloved, as the presiding deity of all vidyās at that time.
In this way, many other incarnations also occurred then;
I know them all—remember them, O Supreme Goddess! (52–53)
"From reciting and hearing this, darkness shall dissolve from its very root;
the light of Brahman shall arise, and one shall attain the vision of the Self.
Thus, O Kamalā, my manifestation has been described to you."
Now I shall relate another account concerning the Supreme Brahman alone:
in the forty-seventh year of the Svardhunī [era],
during the eighteenth kalpa, and in the eighth Manvantara, which consists of one million three hundred thousand years.
King Bṛhaddharmā, the lord of men, was devoted to me;
he commenced the magnificent Rājasūya sacrifice in his renowned capital, Ojasvatī, in person. (57)
He caused the *iṣṭis*, animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*), and Soma sacrifices to be performed.
He had one hundred and twenty-nine distinguished *iṣṭis* performed;
he had six Soma sacrifices and seven *darvīhomas* performed.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna,
he commenced that sacrifice, and for one year there,
the king performed the Cāturmāsya rites according to the prescribed injunctions.
And he also caused the sacrifice for Vaiśvānara and Parjanya to be performed.
Then followed the sacrifices for Agni, Soma, Savitṛ,
Sarasvatī, Pūṣan, the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, and Dyāvāpṛthivī (Heaven and Earth).
In that parvan known as the Vaiśvadeva, the king himself performed these eight sacrifices; there, he offered the deities their shares in due order,
presenting to Agni a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) prepared on eight potsherds.
He offered a *caru* to Soma and a cake on twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapālaka*) to Savitṛ;
likewise, he presented a *caru* to Sarasvatī and a flour-cake (*piṣṭacarū*) to Pūṣan,
as well as a cake on seven potsherds to Marut.
He gave the *puroḍāśa* cake to the Viśvedevas and gave the *āmikṣā* curd-mixture to Dyāvāpṛthivī; he offered the auspicious one-pot-sherd cake to them.
Then, there, he gave the *puroḍāśa* cake to Madhu and Mādhava.
The king himself gratified Śukra, who is pure, with oblations of clarified butter. Having thus performed the Vaiśvadeva festival, the king then duly performed the second festival, the Varuṇapraghāsa.
There he caused the nine sacrifices to be performed— the Āgneya, Saumya, Sāvitra, Sārasvata, Pauṣṇaka,
Aindrāgna, Māruta, Vāruṇa, and Kāya—
as well as the Agni-stoma.
Likewise, he duly propitiated Savitṛ, Sarasvatī, and Pūṣan;
and also Indra, Agni, the Maruts, Varuṇa, and Ka, each in their proper order with the respective materials, oblations, and other offerings, O King. (3.35.70–71)
Having offered oblations with the mantras "nabham," "nabhasyam," "iṣam," and "ūrjam," he also satisfied the deities;
he performed the avabhṛtha bath and observed the prescribed vows as well.
Thereafter, he also caused the third festival, the Sākamedha, to be performed.
He also caused the Anīkavatī and other sacrifices, as well as the Mahāhavis offerings,
to be performed; he likewise had the Pitṛyajña and the Tryambaka oblations performed,
and he even commissioned the sacrifice known as the Ṛṣabha for his amusement.
He gratified Saha, Sahasya, Tapasa, and Tapasya;
and then, according to the prescribed rite, he performed the great Pitṛyajña sacrifice.
He also gratified the Pitṛmantas, the Barhiṣadas, and the Agniṣvāttas.
He offered rice-balls according to the prescribed rite and presented oblations to Tryambaka;
he performed a fire-sacrifice for Rudra and conducted a ritual for Aditi as the presiding deity. Afterwards, he performed the Śunāsīrīya festival with sacrificial porridge (caru).
The king caused the Āgneya and other sacrifices to be performed according to the rules;
likewise, he caused the Aindrāgna, Vaiśvadevaka,
Śunāsīrīyaka, Vāyavya, and Saura sacrifices to be performed as well.
He performed those various rites and also gratified the respective deities.
Furthermore, he offered a cake on a single potsherd (ekakapāla) according to the specific name of each month;
thus, he completed all the sacrifices pertaining to the full moon within the course of a year.
Then the king also caused the six Soma sacrifices, beginning with the Pavitra,
to be performed in due order, each accompanied by the gift of a thousand cows as a sacrificial fee;
he gave away [the wealth] and likewise had the eight sacrifices, beginning with the Anumati, performed.
He offered a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati;
likewise, the king also offered a pap (caru) to Āditya,
and he gave a cake on eleven potsherds to Agnāvaiṣṇava.
The king gave her an offering for Agni and Soma consisting of eleven potsherds,
then an offering for Indra consisting of eleven potsherds, and subsequently an offering for Agni;
he also gave her an eight-potsherd offering for Indra and curd.
He offered a cake on twelve potsherds to Indra and Agni, a sacrificial porridge (caru) to the Viśvedevas,
a porridge of śyāmāka grain to Soma, and a porridge to Sarasvatī;
he also offered a cake on eight potsherds to Agni and a porridge of gāvīdhuka grain to Rudra.
He offered curd for Indra and a sacrificial pap made of barley for Varuṇa;
thereafter, the king caused oblations of *apāmārga* to be performed.
He gave a cake on twelve potsherds to Dhātṛ.
The king offered a sacrificial pap (caru) to Anumati and a pap to Rākā;
he also gave a pap to Sinīvālī and a pap to Kuhū, as well as sacrificial fees.
He then gave two bulls and other offerings for the subsequent sacrifices.
The king offered a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu;
likewise, he offered a similar sacrificial cake dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu;
and the monarch also offered a cake on three potsherds dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Then he offered a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma;
likewise, he offered a similar cake dedicated to Indra and Soma.
He also offered a sacrificial porridge (caru) dedicated to Soma, and he offered a sacrificial porridge dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan.
The king likewise offered a *caru* oblation to Indra and Pūṣan, and another to Pūṣan alone; then he performed the auspicious Vaiśvānara sacrifice with twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*),
and subsequently offered a *caru* to Varuṇa.
He offered a sacrificial pap (caru) for Bṛhaspati, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra,
and then a sacrificial pap for Āditya; furthermore,
he offered a sacrificial pap for Nirṛti and a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni.
He offered a sacrificial cake on ten potsherds dedicated to Varuṇa;
likewise, he offered a sacrificial cake on seven potsherds dedicated to the Maruts;
and he offered a sacrificial cake on twelve potsherds dedicated to Savitṛ.
Likewise, he offered a cake on two potsherds (puroḍāśa) dedicated to the Aśvins;
then the king offered an oblation (caru) to Pūṣan and also an oblation to Rudra.
Thereafter, the king had twelve sacrifices performed by the brahmins.
He performed the Dīkṣaṇīyā sacrifice for Mitra and Bṛhaspati;
thereafter, he offered eight oblations in the Agniṣomīya rite,
just as he gave the eight-pot-sherd cake (puroḍāśa) to Agni.
Then the king himself offered a *śyāmāka* oblation to Soma;
he gave a cake on twelve potsherds to Savitṛ,
and thereafter the king offered a *gāvīdhuka* oblation to Rudra.
He also gave an offering of wild rice (*naivāraka*) to Bṛhaspati;
he gave a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds to Indra;
and he gave an offering of cooked rice to Mitra and an offering of barley to Varuṇa.
Having thus given [the kingdom] and performed all the sacrificial rites, the king stood by.
Brahmā, touching the hand of the king, announced him to the subjects:
"This king is yours. The subjects accepted the king.
They performed the consecration with waters, and the king performed the *ṣaḍhoma* sacrifice,
which was complete with all necessary materials and substances, bringing delight to the deities. (105) After the *pārtha-homa*, the two kings ascended the chariot.
Having performed the oblations for releasing the chariot and remaining seated,
the king listened to sacred stories from the Brahmins and gave them gold;
thereafter, he performed the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the Māhendra sacrifice.
Having performed the Avabhṛtha sacrifice, he prepared ten oblations;
then he offered a cake on eight potsherds for Agni,
and thereafter the king also offered a sacrificial pap for Sarasvatī.
He offered a cake on twelve potsherds dedicated to Savitṛ;
likewise, he offered an oblation of cooked rice to Pūṣan and an oblation of cooked rice to Bṛhaspati;
and thereafter, the king offered a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra.
He offered a cake on ten potsherds to Varuṇa, a sacrificial porridge (caru) to Soma,
a cake on eight potsherds to Tvaṣṭṛ, and a cake on three potsherds to Viṣṇu;
he likewise presented the *puroḍāśa* offerings and performed the *saṃsṛp* sacrifices.
In the pavilion, the king himself bestowed excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās):
two golden mirrors adorned with jewels for the Adhvaryu priest;
a golden garland for the Udgātṛ; and a circular one for the Hotṛ. || 1.12–1.13 ||
The king gave a horse adorned with ornaments to the Prastotṛ and the Pratihartṛ;
to the Brahman priest he gave ten cows pregnant with calves;
and then the monarch gave a barren cow to the Maitrāvaruṇa.
Then the king gave a bull to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin;
he then gave two clean, beautiful garments to the Neṣṭṛ and Potṛ;
and he then gave a cart filled with barley to the Acchāvāka.
The king likewise gave a bull to the *agnīdh* priest according to the prescribed rule;
having performed the *daśapeya* sacrifice,
he then undertook a vow known as the shaving of the hair, lasting for the duration of one year.
Then he performed the Soma sacrifice consisting of the Atirātra rite;
he also caused the Vyūṣṭi-dvirātra and the Kṣatradhṛti to be performed. Thereafter, the king likewise performed the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice according to the prescribed rules.

The king performed the oblation consisting of the milk-offerings (payograhātmaka) dedicated to Indra, the Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra-Vāyu, and indeed offered the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Thus he made offerings and bestowed many gifts as well.
He desired to give away his kingdom and to undertake the auspicious and virtuous initiation (dīkṣā). He announced his intention to the brahmins, and from his chosen deity,
he indeed offered the entire earth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in that gift to the brahmins.
For my sake, he and his wife undertook the vow of fasting.
Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
came in person, initiated me, and caused me to become a perfected saint (sādhu).
He then offered the fruit of the Rājasūya and other sacrifices to Hari.
Knowing that firm resolve and even the request of the brāhmaṇas, O Lotus-born One, I indeed went with you for the purpose of fulfilling the desire of the devotee. || 1.24–25 ||
He suddenly appeared, resembling ten million suns;
they offered him a welcome and performed worship for him,
and thereafter I bestowed upon the king the auspicious Great Initiation (mahādīkṣā), which is conducive to spiritual practice and grants liberation.
Having observed her, the brahmin great sages bestowed the initiation upon the queen;
those [sages], numbering one hundred thousand, received the great initiation from me alone.
And I, in the form of an ācārya, instructed them in the duties of the virtuous.
O beloved, all those beings born were Vaiṣṇavas destined for liberation; then you were born as the great preceptress of the virtuous women (Satīs).
Thereafter, I became the beginningless Śrī Mahācārya Nārāyaṇa.
Accompanied by the beginningless Śrī Mahācāryāṇī and Śrī herself, Hari himself,
being entreated by the virtuous, wandered upon the surface of the earth for the duration of a Manvantara in a divine form, devoted solely to the dharma of liberation.
"Remember both you and me, O Lakṣmī, for we are the very forms of the Great Teacher!
In this way, there were thousands of other incarnations of mine as well.
There was a king named Rājasūyāyana who had indeed been initiated for the Rājasūya sacrifice."
And at that time, the queen became the auspicious glory of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
O beloved, from reading or hearing this, there shall be enjoyment and liberation;
heaven and final emancipation shall come to pass, and passion shall turn into dispassion.
Ignorance shall dissolve, and all bonds shall go to destruction;
one shall become possessed of a divine form and become worthy of being served by those who possess merit in this world. (135)

Thus, in the illustrious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, in the forty-fifth year of the Creator (*Vedhas*), for the sake of fulfilling the desires of the celestial nymphs (*apsarases*) who had become human, there appeared the beginningless Śrī Bṛhad-Brahma-Nārāyaṇa together with Rukmavatī-Śrī; and in the forty-sixth year, for the sake of bestowing the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) and other sciences upon the great seers (*maharṣis*), there appeared the beginningless Śrī Guru-Nārāyaṇa together with Suvidyā-Śrī; and in the forty-seventh year, [there appeared] the devotee of Hari.

Chapter Thirty-Five: A Description of the Manifestation of the Anadi Śrī Mahācārya Nārāyaṇa and His Consort, the Śrīmat Ācāryāṇī, when they were requested for the purpose of the Great Initiation (*mahādīkṣā*) following the gift of all possessions (*sarvasvadāna*) by King Bṛhaddharman at his Rājasūya sacrifice. [Chapter 35 of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age]
Chapter 36 [Author:
Chapter 37 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! After that, my manifestation occurred during the Kalpa known as Vedhas, in the year named Arcirmārga,
specifically in the fifth Manvantara, at eight hundred and sixty-seven [years].

Born from the womb of Rudra was indeed the Rākṣasa Vidyutsrava. He performed severe penance for the purpose of pleasing Śambhu and to obtain a splendor that surpassed the brilliance of the sun, the moon, and fire.
When five hundred years had passed, Śaṅkara himself was pleased with supreme affection and urged him to choose a boon.
He, in turn, chose as his boon the supreme splendor of the sun, the moon, and fire.
"May I possess splendor at will, indeed, and may it be truly indestructible even by gods and others.
"So be it," Hara replied; having received this boon, he was filled with great joy.
Abandoning his asceticism and becoming radiant, he went to heaven and returned.
The Apsarases were bewildered, and even the goddesses fell into a state of infatuation;
seeing him, those fickle women pursued him, though they were restrained by the gods.
Indeed, this was a new affliction that arose for the gods in the heavenly world.
The Daitya, assuming the form of a Rākṣasa yet radiant like a god,
adorned with divine ornaments, traveled from heaven to heaven.
He deluded the goddesses and even incited quarrels among them.
Becoming more radiant than the sun, handsome, possessed of great splendor, and bearing a magnificent luster,
he approaches the sun and eclipses the maker of light.
He approaches the moon and the fire and eclipses them with his own brilliance.
He approaches the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni) and likewise approaches the planets;
he approaches the jewel-holders in Pātāla and the like, and surpasses them.
Furthermore, in the great waters at the bottom of the ocean, [he approaches] the jewels and the aquatic creatures.
Having indeed eclipsed the luminaries,
that Daitya, who could assume any form at will, realizing his own great power,
desired to become king and went to the city of Kubera.
He fought intensely with Kubera and brought that city under his own control.
Then he went to Vahni in battle, conquered him, and placed him under his sway.
He also went to conquer Candra, and he too became subject to his power.
Desiring to conquer the Sun, he set out toward the Sun for battle;
the great asura Vidyut-srava fought for four months,
yet he did not suffer defeat nor did he experience even the slightest exhaustion.
Manifesting flashes of lightning, he burns the worlds;
with splendors exceeding even the sun, he consumes these three realms.
Then a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose, and the sun, distressed, lamented.
He remembered the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Lord, the Eternal One— me,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣottama. Accompanied by Śrī, I, the Lord who provides protection from the sun, arrived there.
The Supreme Lord is indeed golden, possessing all splendor and all weapons;
together with you, O Lakṣmī, who are named Īśānī and endowed with all powers, he has received the appropriate worship performed by the Sun and other hospitable rites. (3.36.20–21)
Indeed, with my Sudarśana discus, I struck down that asura; Vidyuṣṭrasva met his destruction and fell into the ocean. Furthermore, I extinguished the fires released by him throughout the worlds.
Then, praised by tens of millions of celestial rishis, gandharvas, grahas, and humans,
I indeed wandered among all beings.
In the sun, I am Hari, golden-hued and with golden hair.
In the moon, I am one with a silver body and curly hair, myself Hari;
in fire, O Lord, I become one with a blazing body and radiant hair and beard.
Upon the earth, however, when entreated by men together with you, [I appear].

At that time, I became the beginningless Śrī Mahāvidyunnārāyaṇa. Endowed with the splendor of lightning, I dwelt here in this world of men for the duration of a Manvantara, indeed for the liberation of human beings.
Remember, Lakṣmī! Both you and I have indeed manifested in this way;
likewise, many other incarnations of mine have appeared upon the earth.
By reading and hearing this, there shall be the destruction of suffering in this world.
"And here there shall be worldly enjoyment, and at the end, my liberation in the eternal state.
(29) Now, O beautiful one, I tell you something else; listen to my manifestation: in the year of the Creator known as *Abdhi-mathana* (Ocean-churning), increased by nine [months]. (3.36.30)

O Lakṣmī! Then, in the third Manvantara, during the one hundred and fifty-second Kalpa, I was born in this world together with you as the son of the Daitya Rasātala, who subsisted on the essence of flavors (rasa).
In ancient times, the powerful Daitya became a consumer of honey.
He then performed intense penance on the mountain named Sundara;
having propitiated Śaṅkara through his austerities, he indeed chose a boon from Śaṅkara.
May I possess abundant power to consume savory juices and to consume honey;
and as I consume them, may there be digestion accordingly, so that indigestion shall never indeed occur within me. (34)
"May I have no loss of appetite, and may there be great nourishment and strength for me.
Having heard this, Śaṅkara said: "Without destroying the medicinal herbs and trees, eat juices and honey; otherwise, what else but death awaits you?"
Having thus granted the boon, Hara indeed became invisible; meanwhile,
the Asura Madhubhakṣa entered into the trees and other plants on Mount Sundara and,
by means of his illusory power, sucked all the honey from within them.
He sucked the honey from all the leaves, flowers, and other parts on every side.
Consequently, no fruits were produced at all, even the leaves withered, and from that point forward, no new sprouts grew.
Then he consumes the sap of the roots, the sap of the trunks, and the sap of the stumps; thereafter, he enjoys all the saps of the stems and the branches.
He also sucks the saps of the secondary branches and the saps of the leaves.
He indeed drinks all the juices of flowers and the juices of fruits;
from trees, from creepers, from shrubs, from the roots of grass,
from bulbous roots, and from stalks, he enjoys every kind of juice.
Through his illusory power (*māyā*), Śatarūpa assumes hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, billions, and trillions of forms; appearing again and again, he devours excessively.
In whatever manner he enjoys these flavors, they all digest them completely.
He becomes nourished, strong, and highly capable in eating;
by means of his illusory power (māyā), he possesses a vast body upon mountains and in forests, in wildernesses and great gardens, and even among the trees of palatial mansions. ||44-45||
In the gardens, among all the crops and plants,
as well as in the sprouts— whether raw or ripe, in every way—
he always consumes their honeyed juices and causes the dry trees to flourish.
For the wildernesses, fields, and forests indeed become parched;
likewise, by means of people, livestock, birds, creatures, and living beings, neither juices nor even honey-flavors are obtained at all. (47–48)
Afflicted by hunger, everyone died untimely deaths;
a famine destructive to life arose even without drought.
And among the worlds of men, it descended from the nether regions.
The great asura sucked the moisture from the earth,
the plants, creepers, and trees; he suddenly rendered all earthly sovereigns, as well as the vines, grasses, and other vegetation, sapless and withered in form.
The foods of men and the foods of the gods,
all of which have their essence in flavor, have been utterly destroyed.
All kinds of honey have been drunk by that Rākṣasa.
Having grown strong, he became all-pervasive like the wind.
By virtue of a boon, he became pervasive among the plants through his great power;
and by means of his illusory energy (*māyā*), that Daitya became a devourer of all living beings.
Since the clouds were rendered useless, and likewise the cultivation was rendered useless, the earth’s capacity to bestow essence was then made futile;
and the entire potency for essence within the seeds was also rendered useless. (55)
And for the sake of the subjects, the world was indeed afflicted by hunger by that Asura.
Consequently, the people propitiated both Hari and me—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
Having heard their prayer and perceiving the oppression by the asuras,
as well as the loss of vitality in the medicinal herbs, he came toward the earth himself,
bearing weapons such as the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the Śārṅga bow.
I, that very Hari of divine form, then fought with him;
Madhubhakṣa was slain by me with the Sudarśana discus.
Having made you, Mādhavī Lakṣmī, I established you within trees.
O Lakṣmī! At that time, you became the essence of sweetness in the form of nectar among all species of trees, the exalted glory of the Mādhavī vine.
And I am the beginningless, glorious Madhu-Nārāyaṇa, even among living beings.
I dwelt with you for the duration of a Manvantara in that realm.
Because of your entry there, the trees then became full of sap;
indeed, throughout all the worlds, the trees everywhere began to yield honey.
The rivers flowed with honey, and the cows yielded milk sweet as honey;
at that time, the medicinal herbs were filled with honey and perfumed by the spring.
Then all trees became sprouted and laden with fruit, yielding the sweetness of honey.
Then, O Lakṣmī, I, Mādhava, whose essence is rasa,
dwelt together with you upon trees and other places as the Supreme Lord;
and there the people worshipped us both, Mādhavī and Mādhava.
"Remember me in the form of Mādhavī and me as the essence of Madhura-sā.
O beloved, at that time the other gods and great sages also worshipped me with supreme devotion— the Supreme Lord who grants life."
O Nārāyaṇī! Thus has my own manifestation been described to you.
It was for the sake of protecting the worlds, the subjects, and all embodied beings.
Now, however, I shall speak further concerning the manifestations of both you and myself.
In the fifty-first year of the Creator, named Nārada;
in the eighth Manvantara, during the four hundred and eighty-eighth Kalpa; and when the Tiṣya star was at seventy [degrees] upon the earth, the Daityas and Dānavas likewise [arose].
The Asuras became entirely nihilists and destroyers of dharma. Human laws were lost, and great cruelty prevailed.
All men and women became meat-eaters and took on the characteristics of barbarians (mlecchas).
Evil-minded, performers of evil deeds, and devoted solely to wickedness;
snatchers of all, devourers of all, and consumers of all—those men follow the wrong path and indeed devour animals, flocks of birds, and living creatures. (73)
What need is there to mention that humans were devouring even other humans?
O Lakṣmī, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose on earth for all other living beings;
indeed, the wild animals were being devoured by men.
Just as birds, even when eaten, do not meet again,
so too did the forests and wilds become devoid of beasts and birds due to their destruction.
Consequently, those humans were indeed left destitute of both beasts and birds.
They began to devour domestic animals and birds.
All the buffaloes, ewes, and rams were devoured; horses, camels, donkeys, and even bulls were likewise eaten. (77–78)
Elephants, gavayas, deer, and even monkeys;
bears, lions, beasts of prey, dogs, boars, and so forth—all were devoured by the cruel rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas. (79)
All such humans have devoured the cows and their calves. When cows are being devoured on earth by meat-eaters, then I come for the sake of protection, even though I am not impelled [by anyone].
All the gods reside within cows;
by virtue of propitiating them, I am the destroyer of the gods' suffering and the lord who provides protection for the cows.
O beloved, together with you on this earth, I am also the protector of dharma.
Then Hari himself, the wielder of all weapons, arrived swiftly—
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Supreme Lord— who had indeed assumed the form of a cowherd for the purpose of protecting the cows.
I am the creator of all protection, the guardian of Dharma, the Lord of Śrī, and the Master;
I, the destroyer of the defects of the Kali age, quickly became visible there.
Standing upon the chariot called Akṣara, I slew the cow that was being killed on the earth.

Having gone quickly through the path of the sky to that place, I indeed struck him—the killer of the cow and the slayer—as well as his other assailants. I struck them right there, one after another; because of that, those who were marching at the front became enraged.
Having gathered together, they came to strike me down at every place—
crores of Dānavas, Daityas, and Asuras, mostly Mlecchas.
Having traversed the entire earth, I slew them in battle.
Hundreds of billions of predatory beings were slain, and the virtuous subjects were liberated.
Through the power of my wind, the disciplined ones became endowed with goodness (*sattva*).
Thus, protection was afforded to the cows, protection to the brahmins, and likewise protection to the righteous.
The protection of the Dharma has been accomplished by me, and the gods have been gratified;
those who follow the true Dharma have been established, while barbarian kings have been struck down.
Non-violence has been established, and my own worship has been performed.
Furthermore, everything was re-established for the purpose of worshipping the gods.
Again, the duty of service and the duty of compassion were established by me.
Thus, the beginningless Śrī Nātha Nārāyaṇa became firmly established upon the earth.
But you, O Lakṣmī, became the protector of the ownerless cows, bearing the name Nātha,
and at that time you were known by the name Śrī Ghenumatī.
Having remained on earth for half a Yuga, I am indeed Puruṣottama.
He went with you to the imperishable abode; remember that birth of mine.
Indeed, for the sake of instructing the worlds of the Tiṣya age, such incarnations as partial manifestations, entries, portions, and powers occur again and again. (95–96)
Indeed, there is no counting them, for they arise according to the necessity of a task;
having accomplished that task, O Śiva-Śambhu, they dissolve back into me alone.
In kalpa after kalpa, I manifest by my own will or under the influence of my devotees.
Out of compassion, I, the Lord who acts for the welfare of all, have indeed descended upon the earth.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the incarnate Parabrahman, and the very Self of the glorious Supreme Lord.
"From reading and hearing this, there shall be both enjoyment and liberation;
indeed, the attainment of all desired fruits shall occur here in every way.

(3.36.100) Thus ends [the section concerning] the primordial Śrī Mahāvidyunnārāyaṇa for the purpose of destroying the Rākṣasa Vidyutsrāva—the conqueror of the sun, moon, and other celestial bodies—during the forty-eighth year of Brahmā in the third period, the Dvāpara-santāna, within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

The thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Manifestations," etc., concerning the manifestation of the beginningless Śrīmadhunārāyaṇa together with Mādhavī-Śrī in the forty-ninth year for the purpose of destroying the Daityas such as Madhubhakṣa; and the manifestation of the beginningless Śrīnāthanārāyaṇa together with Dhenumatī-Śrī in the fiftieth year during the Kali age (Tiṣya) for the purpose of destroying the Daityas who were killers of cows and destroyers of dharma.

Chapter 38 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:

Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! My manifestation as an incarnation occurred during the fifty-first year of the Creator’s life, in the first *kalpa*, in the first fire, during the Kṛta Yuga. || 1 || In the first *kalpa*, in the first fire, during the Kṛta Yuga of the Creator.
The gods and others celebrated a festival for half of his lifespan and a festival for his golden splendor.
(2) There, in Satyaloka, an assembly of the celestial dwellers took place; those who dwell at the base, those who dwell in heaven, and those who dwell in the world of penance were present. (3)
Those dwelling on Meru, those residing on Mānasa, those inhabiting the Lokāloka mountain,
and others dwelling in the realm of Vairāja, all arrived at Satyaloka. Siddhas, Sādhyas, those of Brahmanic conduct, and celibate students also came there.
The great seers, the seers, and the ancestors assembled.
The world-protectors, the guardians of the gods, and the lords of the world assembled;
as did the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Manus, and the two sons of the Aśvins.
Indra, the planets, the stars, and the constellations arrived;
the yakṣas, the cāraṇas, the followers of Yama, and the gandharvas also arrived.
The kiṃpuruṣas, kinnaras, serpents, nāgas, and rākṣasas likewise came.
Those residing on Kailāsa and those dwelling in the Ocean of Milk also arrived.
(8) Men, rivers, streams, trees, and creepers arrived;
sacred fords, seasons, times, and the fortnights and so forth also arrived. (9)
The ages and the years, as well as the elements and principles, arrived;
the lineages of dharma, virtuous and chaste women, and likewise the yoginīs, arrived;
and even egg-born creatures who remember their past lives arrived.
The Sutas, the Māgadhas, and the learned bards also went forth.
The Vedas, the Rudras, the kings, and the aquatic creatures assembled there; the oceans, both natural and artificial, and the mountains and other lands also arrived.
The Apsarases of the Brahma-lake, male servants, and female servants arrived;
various mounts, weapons, and missiles arrived.
The musical notes, the scriptures, the sciences, and the daughters of the sciences arrived.
Countries and regions arrived in embodied form, as did those born of sweat.
Those born of the mind, those born of the body, those produced by touch, and those produced by sight came forth.
Both the insentient and the sentient, assuming forms at will, assembled together.
The hosts beginning with Kāma and those beginning with Vasanta, along with their attendants, departed;
the devotees, the liberated souls, the lords, and the goddesses also arrived.
Indeed, there was a gathering of all of them, overflowing with immeasurable bliss.

In the morning, they performed the consecration of Brahmā there. Then those gods of the earth, gods of heaven, gods of truth, and forest deities purified the goat, adorned with ornaments, according to the prescribed rites.
All the kinsmen and the gods worshipped the Supreme Lord;
they offered blessings and presented auspicious gifts.
They also offered the auspicious [offerings] of the gods, beginning with Bṛhaspati, who were their proclaimers.
In the assembly hall, there were recitations of the Vedas and various expositions;
then dancing and singing occurred in many ways, as well as diverse musical performances and banquets. (3.37.20–21)
At that time, even the most excellent gifts of reward were bestowed.
Then, having partaken of the drinking of nectar and the eating of food such as ambrosia,
they all celebrated the great festival of devotion to me.
My worship is of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Victory to You, O Supreme Brahman, beyond the Imperishable, Supreme Lord, Puruṣottama! O Brahmā, Īśa, Lord of All, Śrī Hari, Supreme Controller! 23–24.
"Victory to You, O Sustainer of the Incarnations! Victory to You, the Manifestor of the Divine Arrays!
Victory, O Lord of Lords, Lord of Gods! Victory, O Sovereign Inner Controller!
Thus did all embodied beings, accompanied by musical instruments, offer their worship.
Then indeed, all those beginning with Brahmā, being composed in meditation, praised me:
"Come, O Blessed One, O Sustainer, O Creator of all creation! O Supreme Lord, having shown us mercy, purify our homes today. (26–27)
O Lord of incarnations, Lord of abodes, Lord of liberation, O Sovereign!
O Lord of the attributeless, O Lord of the qualified! Purify our homes this very day.
You are life, you are supreme existence, you are the sacred seat, and you are sovereign splendor.
You are illumination and consciousness; you are will and you are effort.
You are action, you are application, you are the fruit, and you are the giver of the fruit.
You are the enjoyer, you are the object of enjoyment, and you are the presiding deity of the experience.
"You are the self, you are the supreme self, you are everything, and all actions reside in you.
You are in all things, O Great King; purify our homes today!
Thus requested then, O Lakṣmī, Hari himself [appeared] together with you.
Having reflected thus, I suddenly arrived in Satyaloka.
Indeed, at the moment of the devotees' worship, the Great Lord appeared within the assembly hall—endowed with all splendor, possessing a divine form. (32–33)
I shone resplendent upon a beautiful golden throne offered by all the gods and others.
Then Brahmā bowed to me, and Viṣṇu and Śambhu also bowed;
the gods and others likewise worshipped me and prostrated themselves like a staff.
Sāvitrī and the other virtuous women honored you in that manner.
We two then offered blessings to Brahmā, who was strengthened by us and sprinkled with water.
Then Brahmā and the others indeed gave us auspicious food consisting of a sacred offering (naivedya).
They offered betel leaves and other refreshments, as well as water which they regarded as nectar; they massaged his feet and, full of longing, made this prayer:
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Supreme Lord, you who have purified us by your grace!"
By good fortune, O Lord, you have been seen by us, the Sovereign of all.
Through your grace, this entire universe has attained sanctity;
today this assembly, this day, and even we ourselves have become purified.
Just as you have shown favor by granting a vision in the realm of truth (Satyaloka),
so too, having shown favor, grant a vision to all the worlds.
Dwell in Satya, in Tapa, among the people, in Mahar, and upon the surface of the earth.
"O Śīśa! Dwell in that which is not the unreal; have mercy upon the Supreme Brahman!
(41) Thus entreated by you, O Lotus-born One, I then, together with all of them, gave my promise there, saying: "So be it. (42)

I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the Supreme Brahman myself, dwelling in Satyaloka, Janaloka, Tapoloka, and on the surface of the earth. Likewise, I have set my mind upon going to Maharloka and Svargaloka.
At the conclusion of Brahmā’s festival, having received their leave, human beings, as well as the gods,
lords of the gods, the ancestors, and the great seers, led me—
the omnipresent Lord who assumes various forms— to their respective worlds.

At that time, I dwelt upon the surface of the earth and in various other places by his grace for the duration of one manvantara, serving the beginningless Lord Nārāyaṇa, the all-pervading Śrī Puruṣottama, together with the omnipresent Śrī.
Remember, Lakṣmī! My manifestation as well was that of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara).
Furthermore, at the end of fifty years, during the festival of the golden mountain, He went to Śvetadvīpa together with you. 47–48.
And at the conclusion of fifty years, during the festival of Svarṇaka,
O Supreme Goddess, you also went to Kailāsa together with Śambhu.
Brahmā is the eldest, Viṣṇu is the middle, and Śambhu is the youngest.
Those three brothers were born from Vairāja on a single day.
Then, on the first day of the fifty-first year,
I indeed attended their great festivals there.
O Lakṣmī! Through my yoga, in the fourteen worlds, there were mental progeny—
namely the Pārśanī, the Dārśanī, and likewise the Saṅginī—
and all of them became Nārāyaṇīs, taking refuge in me.
In all the Manvantaras, they were likewise born as Vaiṣṇavīs;
and by my yoga, all those virtuous subjects who were devoted to me then became Nārāyaṇīs, remaining so until the end of the Kalpa.
"O Śrī, my incarnations are indeed innumerable, and those incarnations are truly countless. Remember them along with yourself; I know them exactly as they are.
Thus have I described to you that most excellent manifestation.
Now I shall tell you something else regarding the year of Soma of the Creator:
in the fifty-second *ṣaṣṭikalpa*, during the fourth *manvantara*, Brahmā once addressed his sons, the sages, and the deities in his assembly hall. (56–57)
The Pitṛs also instructed them regarding the ritual sections that bestow happiness:
"Perform meditation in the morning, and then indeed perform your bath;
perform worship of the gods, especially those who are portions of Brahmā. (58)
Perform the Vaiśvadeva offering and present the food offering (naivedya) as well. Perform the sacrifices such as hospitality for guests and other worldly duties.
Perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), obeisance, devotion, hearing [the scriptures], chanting [the Lord's names], and so forth.
Take rest, sleep, purification, and food;
perform rites for the gods and ancestors, meritorious acts, giving, and service.
Practice service to the virtuous, keep the company of the good, and perform righteous deeds and hospitable hospitality.
Support your wives, sons, daughters, husband, kinsmen, and relatives;
support your livestock, cattle, birds, and all living beings.
Perform acts of service for others, and likewise provide houses and gardens.
Nourish the fields and the various crops that sustain those who depend upon them. Acquire virtue, wealth, and pleasure as is appropriate,
and may you attain happiness and heaven again and again, day after day.
"O sons, maintain the flow of creation without interruption.
At the end of the kalpa, you shall indeed go to Satyaloka;
then, at the beginning of the next kalpa, O great seers and gods, you shall be born once again."
The Pitṛs and the World-Guardians, whose purpose is the maintenance of creation—
those sons of Brahmā who were perfected yogins, possessing the character and vows of Brahman— hearing this, questioned the Grandfather. (66–67)
"O Grandfather, for those who have no interest in that [knowledge], there remains their karma;
whether it be as previously stated or otherwise, explain it to them by distinguishing it separately.
Having heard this, the Creator said to them: "In this world, karma is of two kinds."
The fruit of these two is indeed twofold: that which is active (*pravṛtta*) and that which is withdrawn (*nivṛtta*).
All that is active has been described; it arises from wife, son, wealth, and so forth, and is joined with passion, hatred, and the like, and produced by desire, anger, and the rest. (3.37.70)
And where there is no renunciation of that connection born of greed for home, which is joined with the delusion of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the desire for worldly life—
[namely] the dualities of pleasure and pain, as well as birth and death.

There is indeed no escape from whirlpools, nor is there an end to saṃsāra where one returns again, accompanied by old age and death; where there is the attainment of desires for sense objects, consisting of the thirst for enjoyment. (72–73)
Well-endowed with cold, heat, and the like; joined with sorrow, agitation, and so forth; overcome by festivals and non-festivals;
and extended through the expansion of the lineage—all this which has proceeded is declared by me to have its cause in creation.
The seven ṛṣis of old, as well as the ten great ṛṣis,
the Prajāpatis, and the Manus, having performed their duties for the maintenance of the world, indeed resorted to cremation grounds characterized by rebirth. (75–76)
That which is joined with passion and hatred, filled with grief, agitation, suffering, and the like,
where the pair of impure actions resides— that house is a cremation ground.
It is there that the threefold affliction arises, as well as the emergence of merit and demerit.
The connection with the three types of seeking— that house is indeed a cremation ground (78).
Where beings die and become ghosts, where they are born in suffering,
and where they are cast forth from dwelling in the womb— that house is indeed a cremation ground (79).
Wherever union is desired between two impure bodies,
that cremation ground is indeed the birthplace for the dead, serving only for their further death. The entire cycle of worldly existence is a cremation ground, for it is the source of all activity.
Then, that action which is distinct [from worldly activity] is cessation, and it bestows liberation.
(81) Where there is no taking of a wife, there is no latent impression of desire; where there is neither passion nor hatred, neither lust nor anger, and no greed for a home. (82)
Where there is neither delusion nor desire, and where dualities do not exist—that state is the hall of Brahman, the bestower of the knowledge of Brahman;
it is where celibacy (brahmacarya) exists and where, indeed, there is the offering unto Brahman (brahmārpaṇa). //83//
It is the abode of freedom from desire for sense objects and likewise the abode of freedom from thirst for enjoyment;
it is self-contentment, delight in the Self, and absorption in the Supreme Brahman.
Indeed, there is no sorrow, agitation, or even the touch of heat and cold there.
Where there is always a festival of Brahman, as well as belonging to the lineage of Acyuta;
where for the virtuous, association with the good is itself the state of being intent on offering everything to Brahman;
indeed, that action which consists of love and devotion toward Hari is what has ceased [from worldly motives].
Indeed, having fully practiced that which bestows liberation upon all,
the virtuous— namely renunciants, perfected ones, ascetics of sublimated vital energy,
those whose character is Brahman, those devoted to Brahman, the truthful, and likewise saintly women— [attain the goal]. || 87-88 ||

Those of old, relying on the path of renunciation, attained the eternal heavens; yet those [who followed] later attained a supreme heaven that is unassailable, free from suffering and the like, and not subject to decline, a bliss from which there is no return. (89)
Those ancient followers of the Śrīmad Bhāgavata indeed attained that heaven by worshiping the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign Nārāyaṇa,
the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is the Supreme Brahman beyond the imperishable.
Having worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the source of all incarnations,
the Lord of Śrī and the Lord of the liberated, they attained His abode. [92] They performed service to Him, worship of Him, beholding of Him, and rendered unto Him the duty of a servant.
Having offered their worship to Him, their friendship with Him, and the surrender of their very selves to Him (93),
and having surrendered everything they possessed to that yoga,
they attained the abode— the imperishable, supreme realm, the eternal station of ultimate liberation (94).
Having desisted from worldly activity, they attained that mass of eternal bliss;
through union with the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), they reached the highest abode.
You are virtuous ones, perfected beings, devoted to the dharma of Brahman.
"Having accomplished the karma of renunciation, let them proceed to the supreme, imperishable state.
Having been addressed thus, those ascetics were indeed satisfied with their renunciation;
having performed total surrender and devotion, they attained the state of having fulfilled their purpose.

Then Brahmā spoke again to both the sages and the ascetics: "Whether it be the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) or the path of renunciation (*nivṛtta*), whether it be the offering to Brahman (*brahmārpaṇa*) or its cessation,
and whether it be action pertaining to the body or that which arises from the body— indeed, both kinds of action have been performed."
If it is indeed offered directly to the Supreme Lord, the Lord of all, then through union with Hari, that [offering] becomes withdrawn and bestows liberation;
just as everything is reduced to ashes by the extreme intensity of fire. (3.37.100)
"By the direct application of *suyoga* to Hari, everything likewise becomes reduced to ashes.
Upon hearing this, the sages, who were devoted to ritual action, were exceedingly delighted;
all of them, joyful and satisfied, withdrew from their previous state and questioned him further.
Having bowed to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and remembered Śrī Puruṣottama, [they asked:
"O Hari, how indeed may there be direct union with You here in this world?
Show us that method by which we may perform service consisting of total self-surrender."

"Even after performing active duties within the sphere of sensory experience, by offering them to Hari, we shall attain the supreme, imperishable abode from which there is ascent to ever-higher realms.
Brahmā said: "Then, O Lakṣmī, he spoke these words quickly to them all."
Let them perform a sacrificial session (*satra*) right here, consisting precisely of propitiation.
By that, Hari will be quickly drawn [to them], becoming subject to their devotion;
he will appear before their eyes and will accept your service.
Having heard this, all the gods and others, both groups together,
performed the sacrificial session of chanting the names with concentrated minds in Satyaloka.
Having heard that devoted glorification by those ascetics, I indeed [acted].

And, O Lakṣmī, he came together with you from the land of Cākṣara. Within the midst of his assembly, they beheld me, the Supreme Lord; they bowed to me, worshipped me, and made a request for my eternal residence there.
"Among the ṛṣis in Satyaloka, likewise among the Siddhas;
among the Pitṛs in Janaloka, and likewise among humans on earth—let it be so!
Thus I have spoken, remaining forever with you."
The beginningless and glorious Mokṣanārāyaṇa is the illustrious Puruṣottama;
you are the illustrious Puruṣottamī, known by the name Muktiśrī. You two dwell in all the worlds, assuming manifold forms.
Then, having completed the sacrificial session, they went to their own homes;

those engaged in worldly activity attained activity, and even those withdrawn from it attained withdrawal. By offering everything to Me, they reached the state beyond the three qualities (nirguṇya) and entered My abode.
Other great sages and meritorious souls were born in that place.
Thus, together with you, I have manifested myself here as the bestower of liberation;
remember that for the duration of a Manvantara, I myself was present on this earth.
In this way, thousands of other incarnations of mine have also occurred;
indeed, I know all those hundreds of thousands, but others do not.
By reading and hearing this, one shall certainly obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And [he attains] divine prosperity and happiness, both of this world and the next.

Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa together with Vibhvī Śrī in the Golden Festival during the fifty-first year of the Creator in the Dvāpara Age, and the Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Mokṣa-Nārāyaṇa together with Mukti Śrī in the fifty-second year," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the third section concerning the lineage of Dvāpara.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, Lakṣmī! Then, in the year of Gāyatrī, during the first Vārāha-kalpa and in my first Manvantara, O Ajā; 1.
The manifestation of the beginningless Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa—
who exists even now— takes place here in this realm known as Akṣara, together with you, Śivarājñī-Śrī.
On the bank of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, near Kuṅkumavāpikā,
in the house of Mahālakṣmī Kambharā which was filled with all desired objects,
[he was born] from his father known as Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa in Surāṣṭra.
For the sake of fulfilling the desires of hundreds of billions of celestial maidens,
for the purpose of protecting the Dharma, and because I have come here out of compassion—
drawn by the fierce austerities of my parents— I, who dwell in the imperishable realm, [have arrived].

My manifestation has occurred here; you have been made my own by me here, O Nārāyaṇī, my beloved, along with crores, billions, and hundreds of millions of maidens. Nevertheless, I shall manifest again and again in kalpa after kalpa.
O Lotus-born One, together with you alone in the field inhabited by Lomaśa, there have been many of my incarnations: as a fish, a boar, and a tortoise;
as Kapila, a lion, and a horse; and as a swan, Vāmana, and Nārada.
Vāsudeva, Haridatta, Ātreya, Parśudhara, and Ṛṣabha; Pṛthuyajña, Kumāra, and others, as well as Vyāsa, Rāma, Adhirāja, Dhanvantari, Buddha, Kṛṣṇa, Kalki, and Mohani. (3.38.9–10)
Harikṛṣṇa, Naranārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇanarāyaṇa,
and others shall appear by the thousands on earth and in heaven according to the requirements of their tasks.
In age after age there are my incarnations, and in age after age there are also the Vyāsas.
They will become establishers of the Dharma and awakeners of the Dharma. There will be a sage named Śikhāyukta, a descendant of Śveta and Kṛṣṇāyana;
he will be Śvetavyāsa, the narrator of the stories and the compiler of the Saṃhitā.
"Today my incarnation is to be accomplished: the Lord Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, who is worthy of homage in the world of Brahmā, shall become the teacher of Dharma.
Likewise, other Vyāsas as well, who are portions of myself, shall be the awakeners of Dharma. (14)
Satya, Bhārgava, Savitṛ, Vasiṣṭha, Aruṇi, and Sṛñjaya;
Ṛtañjaya, Bharadvāja, Tṛṇabindu, and Dvaipāyana; Prabhū, Vallabha, Saureya, Devānīka, and Ṛtaṃbhara. (15–16)
Those who possess the great fire of the Vāreyaka Mahāvidyā,
who have mastered the Dhārīṇaka, Sukaukṣeya, Vārṣadhāra, and Vanavrata [mantras],
shall become my own portions (aṃśas) and will bring about the manifestation of the Vidyās.
It cannot be calculated by anyone else due to the vastness of time.
Indeed, thousands of millions of Sva-bhuvas have passed away;
again and again, there will be thousands of millions of them.
By implication, all those protectors of creation who consume time are innumerable;
likewise, the Nārāyaṇas who do not consume [limited] time are the Śrīs, whose nature is my own.
So too are the eternally liberated ones and the millions of those who are being liberated.
All those who eat at improper times are residents of the various abodes.
O Lakṣmī, all this that was asked has been told exactly as it is;
I myself, the Incarnation, have been revealed and described by me.
"O Lakṣmī, may you always obtain your own happiness from me, who am ever-incarnate! Furthermore, O Narāyaṇī, ask whatever else you most desire.
Śrī Śivarājñī Śrī said:
I am satisfied, having recognized the previous forms from the mouth of my beloved.
Salutations to you, the Lord of my life, who possesses manifold forms and wields the Śārṅga bow.
O Raudrī, O Lord of beautiful women, O Śrī, O Dyunārāyaṇa, salutations to you!
Salutations to you, the Nārāyaṇa who is Meru, joined with the Mairavī-dhṛti.
Salutations to you, the Nārāyaṇa who is Viṣṇu, joined with the Saurī-śātanī. Salutations to you, the Nārāyaṇa who is the Lord of Devas, joined with the Cāndrī-kaumudī. 25–26.
O Lord of the glory of the Bhūyasī river, O Three-stepper, salutations to You!
O Brahman Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the Vaiṣṇavī river, let there be salutations to You!
O Lord of the glory of Devavīthī, O Ādityanārāyaṇa, salutations to You!
O Lord of Infinite Glory, O Garuḍa-vehicled One, O Nārāyaṇa, salutations to You!
O Lord of the Ṛṣi-lotus, O Ṛṣi-Nārāyaṇa, salutations to You!
O Lord of the Splendor of Moonlight, O Wise Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutation to You!
Obeisance to you, Śārdūlika-Śrīśa Vīra-Nārāyaṇa; obeisance to you, Sarobhadra-Śrīśa Bhadra-Nārāyaṇa;
obeisance be to you, Sarbhadra-Śrīśa Hari-Nārāyaṇa.
