"I have reached the end of this other bliss; again, salutations to you, my beloved!

Now, O one whose essence is that [bliss], I desire to hear other deeds of yours—those concerning devotees whose souls are absorbed in you—which lead to liberation and to the welfare of dharma. (3.38.280)
This *Sahasranāma* hymn, titled *Yugalaśrīkāntastotra*, enriched with one hundred and twelve names, is supreme and bestows the four aims of human life;
it grants good fortune, increases the lineage, bestows prosperity, and confers all forms of wealth. (28.1)
It bestows sovereignty, bestows heaven, bestows all objects of enjoyment, and is the supreme bestower of one's own desires.
It grants spiritual perfections, merit, and meditative absorption; it is purifying, it destroys sin, it overcomes death, it dispels obstacles, and it eliminates suffering. (282–283)
It bestows divine nature, leads to the ground of supreme liberation, and is auspicious;
it grants what is difficult to obtain, as well as constant health and prosperity—to those who read it, listen to it, and likewise remember the meaning of all its names. (284)

O Hari, this [stotra], which fulfills all the desires of all men and women, has emerged directly from my own mouth; it is born of Lakṣmī and bestows prosperity. I am Lakṣmī in the form of the hymn, and you, my husband, are the recipient of the hymn.
"May there be equality between us and those who praise us. O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to You, the Inner Self!
Obeisance again and again to all Your wives; obeisance, obeisance, obeisance! (287)
Tell me of other deeds that indeed inspire affection for you—
auspicious acts that manifest your state as Puruṣottama—
and of those incarnations such as Nara and Nārāyaṇa that exist upon this earth. (288–289)
O Ocean of Mercy, tell me how those who have descended [as incarnations] bring about awakening, if it is for the benefit of the world;
for without knowledge of the incarnations, there can be no supreme worship. (3.38.290)
"Therefore, O Lord, my beloved, please tell it to me, your beloved one.

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa together with Queen Śrī Śivarājñī in the fifty-third year of the Creator [Brahmā] during the Dvāpara lineage, and the Description of the Thousand-and-Twelve-Name Hymn for the Couple," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 38: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Dvāpara Yuga Lineage)*
Chapter 39 [Author:
Chapter 40 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate the story of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
which is rich with the realization of Puruṣottama and which brings about direct, intuitive knowledge of Me.
Once, in Viśālā, great sages [assembled] for the purpose of seeing [Him].
They went to me, who am Nara-Nārāyaṇa in my own form.
There, Śrī Śaṅkara also arrived accompanied by Satī; Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sanandana likewise came.
The most excellent great sages beginning with Aṅgiras, who were self-luminous,
as well as other ancient twice-born ones such as Lomaśa and others devoted to their wives,
desiring to perform a sacrificial session of austerity, beheld the pure son of Dharma.
Having duly worshipped Nārāyaṇa, Nara, myself, and the auspicious female ascetic,
and having praised them with Vedic hymns,
all those foremost knowers of yoga, filled with devotion, prostrated themselves like a staff.
With joyful hearts, they spoke to Nārāyaṇa, the supreme teacher:
"We have taken refuge in you alone, the Puruṣottama;
[we seek] Nārāyaṇa himself, manifest, the ancient Supreme Lord. (7)
Yoga is the highest austerity, and knowledge is the supreme austerity.
That austerity which is performed while worshipping you is the best austerity, for it grants liberation.
Tell us that, O Hari: from what does this world proceed?

"Who is the Self? What indeed is liberation? What is this saṃsāra that has been created? What is that supreme Brahman? You ought to tell us all this. Having asked thus, the sages beheld that Nārāyaṇa.
Having cast off his ascetic garb, he appeared as the eternal Supreme Brahman—
resplendent with splendors, attended by a circle of liberated souls,
established in the abode of the imperishable Brahman, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and embraced by Śrī.
O Lakṣmī! Having seen me— the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person—
laughing together with you and endowed with all my divine weapons,
Śambhu and all the others were momentarily struck with bewilderment.
Immersed in supreme bliss, they attained the state of the glorious Supreme Lord.
Then, having concealed my divine nature from them,
Nārāyaṇa became an ascetic, just as he had been beneath the banyan tree.
Then, Narayana spoke there to all the sages who were established in their own states:
"That form of mine, which is invisible and designated as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), shines forth here within me as the revealed Narayana. (16)
That which even the gods do not perceive, despite their efforts, in the absence of compassion;
having obtained that vision through compassion, the greatest sages become one with Brahman and,
as exponents of Brahman who have entered into Brahman, they do not return to the cycle of worldly existence.
Today I shall declare that knowledge of the knowers of Brahman who possess devotion:
this Self of embodied beings is translucent, pure, subtle, and eternal.
Within it dwells the glorious Lord Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, the innermost of all.

He exists in the form of the vital breath; He is the Inner Controller, the supreme person. Indeed, from this abode of the Imperishable, all things come into being. By means of His own Māyā, He creates various bodies for the purpose of emanation.
For living beings such as the *jīva* and others, bound by karma, transmigrate again and again;
but those liberated and unbound by karma proceed to that supreme state.
Just as a connection between light and darkness is not possible, [so it is with the bound and the liberated].
Likewise, a relationship between saṃsāra and Hari is not tenable.
(23) Just as shadow and sunlight are distinct, so are saṃsāra and the Lord of Śārṅga;
thus the self of embodied beings is distinct from the form of saṃsāra. (24)
The notion that "I am the doer, happy, miserable, thin,
or fat" is projected by people onto the Self due to the agency of the ego (ahaṃkāra).
Therefore, transmigratory existence, which is bound by karma, has its root indeed in ignorance.
Through the lack of discrimination regarding the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), this person incurs the bondage of karma.
(26) The seers, the devotees, and the people who are supreme worshippers behold the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, the Supreme Controller, within their own pure self. (27)
Having understood nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), time (kāla), and likewise one's own self (ātman),
he who is united with Hari indeed partakes in eternal bliss.
If, however, one does not realize one's own self as the imperishable Brahman, [then...]
The cognition of a self in that which is not-self bestows suffering and saṃsāra.
All defects, such as passion and hatred, are based upon ignorance;
for they cause embodied beings to perform meritorious and non-meritorious actions. (3.39.29–30)
It is solely by virtue of that [Brahman] that the arising of all bodies occurs for everyone.
Therefore, the virtuous should indeed contemplate their own self as Brahman;
those of sound intellect should pervade their own innate identity with the Supreme Lord, realizing its oneness.
Just as space does not become soiled through contact with the earth, so the Self is not tainted by the states arising from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Just as the sun shines everywhere by its own radiance, [so does the Self]. || 3.2–3.3 ||
Likewise, the self, consisting of knowledge, shines forth when joined with that [knowledge].
Therefore, being of the nature of knowledge, it is of the nature of consciousness and free from worldly existence.
Just as a crystal appears colored to people due to the proximity of a dye, so too does this [self appear].
And thus it is observed that this [Self] possesses the excellent quality of being in proximity to all beings.
(35) I am that Self—imperishable, pure, and eternal; I am the Supreme Lord, who is to be worshipped, meditated upon, and heard of by me incessantly. (36)
Thus, when Mādhava shines everywhere within his knowledge,
then Hari is attained by that faithful devotee.
Indeed, when the Supreme Brahman, the soul of all, shines within himself, [he attains Him].
Then he beholds Him, who is of the nature of direct perception, within his very own self.
When he perceives that Supreme Lord in all beings, then, for that devotee, the Supreme Brahman unfolds everywhere. (38–39)

When, established in the Self, one perceives nothing else at all, then, united with the Supreme, one beholds the Parameśvara. When the desires of the heart indeed dissolve and no longer exist— 3.39.40. 3.39.41.
Then, having become immortal, he beholds the Supreme Lord.
When he beholds Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa abiding in all things, then, having attained union with Him, he becomes fit for His own nature.
When one beholds the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Person, the Sovereign,
who has transcended all that is merely illusory, there is for him no state beyond Brahman.
When [one beholds Him] who is the sole remedy for birth, old age, suffering, and disease—
When one’s own knowledge becomes the realization of Brahman, then that person is Śiva.
Just as all rivers and streams flow into the vast ocean,
so too do devotees enter the imperishable Brahman through their meditative practices.
As long as those deluded by ignorance do not acquire true knowledge,
they— drawn away by the darkness of nescience— do not attain the supreme state.
Therefore, one should cultivate self-knowledge and the yoga of Nārāyaṇa.
Through both [of these], Śrī Hari, as the Supreme Self (paramātman), reveals Himself to him. Furthermore, through union with Hari, all His sovereign powers (aiśvarya) become manifest—
either in this very body or at the end of the body, by virtue of Hari’s own grace.
One shall attain that divine sovereignty which is esteemed by all;
he who bestows that sovereignty is the Supreme Lord of all.
He is the Self of all beings, abiding in all, present everywhere, and facing in every direction.
He possesses all forms, all tastes, and all fragrances; he is undecaying and immortal.
(3.39.50) That eternal Śrī has hands and feet everywhere; He is the inner controller.
Though without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper, dwelling within the heart. (51)
Though without eyes, he is the seer; though without ears, he also hears.
He knows all this very thing, yet no one knows him.
Those of pure intent call him the Supreme Lord, the Great Master.
The sages perceive the cause, which is unsurpassed sovereignty;
having understood it, they attain union with that [cause] once they have entered therein.
Those who have transcended its māyā—which exists in the form of bondage—[attain this state]. || 53–54 ||
They attain the supreme abode, Nirvana, together with Hari;
by his grace, they do not undergo rebirth again.
This knowledge must indeed be imparted to sons, disciples, and yogis.
O best among the knowers of Brahman! [This] indeed grants liberation and bestows supreme peace.
Listen further to what else arose from the Supreme Lord:
the Puruṣa known as Kāla, and likewise Prakṛti, which is Pauruṣī (the feminine principle). ||56-57||

From those two [the male and female principles] arises Pradhāna; from those two arises the Golden One (Hiraṇmaya) who is unborn (Ajā), and from those two arises the Golden Female (Hiraṇmayī). From those two arise Virāj and Vairājikā.
From those two arise the three deities, and from them the world consisting of men and women.
Thus, all this world is composed of Brahman because it belongs to Hari;
for Hari is the Self of all beings, the knower, the Self, and the Supreme Lord.
O twice-born ones, listen further: in ancient times, indeed, the desire of Hari arose.
That Māyā, though possessing a divine form, is endowed with the karma of living beings; she is characterized by the nature of the qualities (guṇas) and their corresponding actions:
when associated with the action of *sattva*, she is *sāttvikī*; when associated with the action of *rajas*, she is *rājasī*;
and when joined with the action of *tamas*, she is *tāmasī*, having the form of action.
That [nature] is described by people according to the specific form of the karma of living beings,
just as light is said to be red when it passes through a red glass;
in reality, however, she is pure in form, but she is entered into by living beings.
That illusion (māyā), which yields fruits according to one's karma, is of three kinds:
the root (mūlā), the pure (śuddhā), and the uneven (viṣamā); it follows the course of karma.
Thereafter, it indeed causes the principle of the Great (mahattattva), known as the intellect (buddhi), to manifest.
From the principle of Mahat arises the intellect (buddhi), which consists of self-identification (abhimāna);
from that arises the group of sixteen, comprising the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, and the mind.
And from the subtle elements arise the gross elements, which possess the qualities (guṇa).
From the gross elements, indeed, that world is born;
though it is insentient in nature, being pervaded by sentient beings, it performs actions.
The wandering [of beings] in accordance with their karma is transmigratory existence, which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
That [desire] as well, being subject to time and arising from a lack of discernment, proceeds by obtaining the assistance of the mind;
therefore, a wise person should destroy latent impressions (vāsanā) only after having restrained the mind. (68–69)
Having become one whose form transcends time and illusion, one should worship Mādhava.
There is nothing superior to Him; by worshipping Him, one is liberated. This [liberation] is not attained through various austerities, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice.
For he can indeed be known by men, except through unsurpassed devotion.
He dwells within all beings everywhere;
by knowing him, the witness of all, one is released from every bond.
Within Him all this exists, yet He is the supreme ender of all;
the scriptures proclaim Him alone as the one true Supreme Lord.
Brāhmaṇas worship Him with various sacrifices and millions of sacrificial sessions.
Yogis meditate upon Him; stainless saints worship Him.
He is the embodiment of all deities; the righteous revere Him.
To them, He grants that abode, the state of supreme bliss.
"Men and women as well, established in their duties, devoted and free from sin, worship Him with devotion; they attain the supreme goal.
Having thus understood that Lord Hari to be the Supreme Ruler, the sages [proceeded].
"Having meditated upon the Inner Controller of all, may they proceed to the supreme state.
Having spoken thus to the lords of sages, Śivarāja, the Lord of Badarī,
again revealed the Lord within the body of the ascetic.
Abounding in the splendor of ten million Cupids, endowed with glory, and higher than the highest;
possessed of manifold sovereign powers, shining as the king of kings;
having the nature of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, he is most beautiful.
It is beloved by all, endowed with the honey-like sweetness of every divine loveliness;
it is the supreme state of the Lord, served by infinite liberated souls and by those who have been liberated;
and it is likewise honored and praised by the manifestations and emanations of the Lord.
The sages, having beheld the form of Hari— which is of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, divine, served by the Lord of All and others,
filled with all splendors, the Lord of Abodes, the glorious Puruṣottama—
were satisfied and filled with happiness. (82)
Having obtained the fruit of their ascetic penance, the delighted ones praised him again:
"83. You are the Lord; you are the Supreme Brahman; you are Kṛṣṇa; you are Nārāyaṇa.
You are Nārāyaṇa, the supreme light, the possessor of the imperishable abode. 84."
You possess a golden form, you are Viṣṇu, and you are the all-pervading one;
you consist of all the gods, you are the ascetic, and you are the Supreme Lord.
Having seen you and having attained you, O Puruṣottama, we have accomplished our purpose.
Today we have reached the further shore of illusion; your compassion bestows boundless liberation.
By your will we have arrived here, and our heart’s desire is fulfilled.
Nothing else remains to be done or accomplished beyond this vision of you.
"May Your supreme, supramundane form always shine before us! We desire only this; grant us this boon, for it is our boon!
O Śivārājñīśrī! Having praised [Her] in this way, they remained in silence.
Then that divine form of the Supreme Brahman vanished there.
I indeed immediately became an ascetic, identical in essence to Nārāyaṇa;
and while I was situated beneath the Badarī tree, they worshipped me in that manner.
Having received my command, they departed for their own abodes while honoring me.
You should know that form of mine to be of the nature of Nārāyaṇa,
appearing as an ascetic for the sake of protecting the world and always for the preservation of dharma.
Know me as the inner controller (antaryāmin), whose very self is Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and who is designated as Puruṣottama— your husband.
Having fully grasped this knowledge, Śaṅkara and the others [spread it] thereafter upon the earth.
The sages have taught liberation and bestowed it everywhere upon embodied beings who practice my worship, through the very essence of Brahman.
This [work] grants liberation by means of reading, hearing, and even remembering it.
"O Lakṣmī! It bestows all bliss; there is nothing higher than this to be known.

(95) Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction to Mankind by the Great Sages who had Attained Satisfaction through the Vision of Nara and Nārāyaṇa as the Supreme Brahman-form, after Arriving at Badarī for the Purpose of Austerity," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 40 [Author:
Chapter 41 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"Tell us the duties and practices of those who are beloved by the Supreme Person,
so that the faults of household life may not arise here.
You abide as the Supreme Brahman, and we are your wives belonging to the realm of Brahmā."

Divinity exists in its entirety wherever not even a trace of fault is found. Nevertheless, for embodied beings who follow the duties of the household, including men and women, there may still be the attainment of dharma; therefore, please tell us the duties of the household.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! Listen, all you who are dear to me! I shall describe the duties of householders, which remove faults and bestow auspicious benefits. (4)
The home is to be known as the imperishable abode (dhāman), and the husband is Śrī Puruṣottama.
The five sons are to be understood as the five deities, and ritual action is my worship.
Those women who abide in the state of householdership proceed in this manner.
For those women whose state of being consists of total surrender to me, that is the Vaiṣṇava dharma.
(6) A woman should always meditate on Hari as her husband and upon me, the Supreme Person, as her lord;
she should always meditate on Lakṣmī as Śrī, the virtuous and supreme woman. (7)
One should meditate on the attendants (*pārṣada*) among one's sons, on Śrī, Ramā, and others among one's daughters,
on Garuḍa and others among the vehicles, and indeed on the liberated souls among one's kinsmen and so forth.
In this manner, one should meditate upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*), within one's own body.
One should offer everything to Him who dwells within one's own heart.
(9) Thus indeed has this yoga of action been described for you; when joined with the realization of actionlessness and endowed with devotion to Me, it bestows liberation. (3.40.10)
Among all forms of the yoga of action, this yoga is distinguished as superior:
the yoga consisting of service to Hari through deed, mind, and speech.
Thus, Hari alone is to be constantly propitiated by means of the chanting of His names and other such practices.
One should perform circumambulation and worship my image;
one should eat food offered from my temple and fix the mind upon my feet.
One should dance and converse loudly before Hari.

One should practice singing with beautiful melodies accompanied by the clapping of hands and other instruments; one should constantly listen to sacred narratives and wear the remains of the offerings (nirmālya) upon the head.
I am the Lord who grants liberation, always to be worshipped and saluted.
Therefore, worship and behold me, Śrī Hari— the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī, the infallible— in every moment. O beloveds, always remain devoted to your husband, Hari.
Constantly worship me, Hari, through the yoga of action;
offer sacrifice to me, Hari, the consort of Lakṣmī, with baths, meals, and services.
Rising before me in the morning, perform the massage of my limbs while I am still asleep.
"O beloveds of Brahmā, perform the massaging of my feet constantly. Delight me, your husband and lord, with service as you desire.
Then, for the sake of purifying your own bodies and so forth, depart indeed from here with hope."

Remembering me, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa, bathe in the waters of my feet; and while reciting my name, perform the libation with water. Remembering the gods and the ancestors, offer oblations with joined palms.
Pay homage to the elders, to the Brahmins, to the virtuous, and to the cows.
Always bow down to the trees of the gods, to the sacred fords, and to the deities.
Having bathed, offer appropriate gifts to worthy recipients.
Bestow upon them whatever is required— wealth, food, clothing, ornaments, and so forth—
and having arranged for their audiences with the gods, they shall then return home. And let them perform my auspicious service consisting of the preliminary rites of bathing and the like.
Perform the rites properly indeed, bathing me with warm water;
having massaged me as is fitting with oil, fragrant unguents, and other ointments— me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Clothe them with garments of gold, silver, star-patterned silk, and the like;
adorn them with ornaments and embellish them with excellent unguents,
as well as fragrant flower garlands, sandalwood paste, and other such scents.

"You should worship me with incense, lamps, and the like, as well as with the grooming of my hair and other services; you should feed me with meals of milk and sweet rice-pudding, and you should always offer me water and betel-leaf with love. (27–28)
Sweep the courtyards of the houses and gather up the beds;
likewise, bring water and perform the milking of the cows.
Prepare curds, yogurt, and other such items, and also honor the elders.
"Perform the cooking and other preparations, and feed the deities.
Feed the sages, guests, brahmins, and holy men as well.
Offer mouthfuls of food to the cows and perform the oblations and other rites for the sacred fires."
Feed excellent food to the destitute, the wretched, the young, and others;
perform acts of service for others, and bow to the Sun at all times.
Feed those who have arrived as guests, and offer them a welcome and other such courtesies.
Always adorn your bodies with ornaments and the like.
You are all my beloveds, identical with me, and dedicated to my purpose; may you, burdened with the weight of such contemplation, attain my grace. (33–34)
May they eat their most desired sweets, and may they remain joyful;
may they honor the commands of their elders and the wise counsel of their seniors.
May they protect the traditions of their family, as well as the customs of their kin and other duties.
Let them adopt local customs, yet primarily my dharmas as superior;
let them always ensure the purity of garments and other items through washing with earth and such substances;
and let the Lakṣmīs always follow the most excellent [forms].
May they always study discourse, knowledge, the arts, and various forms of skill; likewise,
may they always master prosperity, the arts such as cooking,
and the service of mothers, sisters, and mothers-in-law.
May they increase their affection for their co-wives day by day;
may they protect those worthy of honor and honor them with meals; and may they also show respect to mendicants by providing all manner of gifts. (38–39)
Let them honor virtuous men and women, and especially the Vaiṣṇavas;
let them enjoy pleasures with favor, offered up to me as well.
Let them chant the Sandhyā, the Goddess Gāyatrī, while fixing their minds upon me.
Let them perform their recitations (japa) in my name, remembering me as the Supreme Lord.
Let them carry out their household duties with clarity and auspiciously; let them properly protect all kinds of household goods. 41–42.
Let them cause dance, song, fine attire, and the like to be performed for my sake;
let them serve cows and other animals, as well as calves and the like, through their meditations.
Let them also offer libations to Śuka, Menā, Haṃsa, Citra, Garuḍa, and the others.
May they protect the elephants, horses, bulls, and so forth, as well as the queens;
may they effect the purification of food and the like, and the cleansing of spices, oils, and other ingredients;
may they guard against ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) and the like, and transform the various preparations.
May they perform the purification of their homes, may the members of the family provide for them,
may they increase their glory and fame, and may they be endowed with forbearance.
May they also be possessed of the virtues of compassion, patience, mercy, and service.
May those who are dear to you always be characterized by altruism;
likewise, may they be free from desire, dividing their resources for their own benefit while remaining devoted to the welfare of others and dedicated to the ultimate truth. 47–48.
May they always possess faith in the performance of rites prescribed by the gods;
may they be devoted to the service of the world, intent on the service of their disciples, dedicated to the service of their subjects, and devoted to the offering of blessings and the like. 49.
May they always have pure intentions that bring about the excellence of others; rejoicing in the prosperity of others, may they cultivate the thought of offering their own prosperity to them;
and may they possess the virtue of non-possessiveness, being dedicated to me.
Free from injustice, immersed in righteousness, endowed with virtuous conduct and vows,
devoid of greed for thirst, and liberated from passion and hatred;
they are united with the lineage of Dharma and have abandoned the succession of unrighteousness.
May the wives of Brahmā possess the very nature of Nārāyaṇī;
may they be possessed of illusory power (*māyā*) toward their own kinsmen and relatives, and may they always be full of affection for their own family members. (53–54)

May the goddesses who practice the dharma of the untouchable become like daughters-in-law; may those who practice the dharma of the touchable adopt the conduct of mothers. And may these goddesses always remain humble before their elders.
May they remain on low seats with their hands joined in *añjali*, speaking sweetly with heads and minds bowed;
and may they see that their own household duties remain unfinished even as they stand before me. (56–57)
Let the beloved wives within the home act without pride and cast aside stubbornness;
let them produce mutual joy that provides assistance.
Furthermore, let these co-wives render help to one another.
Let them serve one another with the arranging of hair and other such services. (59) Let them, permeated by pure intention, perform mutual service when there is illness.
And for the sake of cleaning vessels and the like, let them always maintain female servants. (60)
Let them provide for the protection of the female servants by means of food, clothing, and wages,
as is appropriate, through such considerations as honor and gifts.
Let them observe the period of menstrual impurity and maintain physical purity.
Indeed, let them avoid those things born of faults such as anger that bestow suffering;
let them renounce in every way greed and other vices that destroy happiness.
Let them not kill even tiny insects or sweat-born creatures, nor even those born from eggs.
Let them not kill any living beings born from a womb, even the most minute ones, anywhere.
Having strained water and milk, let them drink these purified liquids.
Let them not consume things that cause disease, nor those that produce dullness and lethargy.
May they never engage in intoxicants, meat, sexual intercourse, or theft— those things which cause the mind to wander and are filled with foul odors and the like;
nor indeed may they practice untruth, falsehood, or deceit.
Let my dear ones never speak words of reproach for the sake of some other's loss;
let them never speak what is unpleasant, painful, or cruel. And let them never indeed show their own face with an expression of anger.
Let them never act impulsively or without reflection;
let them not enter an improper place or another's palace;
let them abandon all doubt and act with firm resolve. (68–69)
May they not perform fruitless actions, nor engage in vain speech or futile deeds; may they not indulge in idle sleep, nor likewise in aimless wandering.
May they never, under any circumstances, cause obstacles for others that serve no purpose.
Let them not practice the conduct of beasts, and let them cast folly far away.
Let them embrace inquiry and discernment, and receive instruction with ease.
Let them abide in accordance with the will of the most excellent, the venerable, and the virtuous.
By constant practice, they should restrain the mind in every way;
they should abandon on all sides those desires that bring suffering, and fulfill through righteous means those desires for women that grant happiness. (73)
Let them never place their trust in objects that are not to be trusted;
let them never be naked with their bodies uncovered,
nor ever be devoid of the ornaments of good fortune.
Let them not indulge excessively in pleasures that cause disease and suffering, even if they are dear;
let them not practice the neglect of their vows, nor ever abandon their gains.
Let them cast far away both unfitness for action and negligence, as well as women.
Let them practice gentleness, skillfulness, and enthusiasm;
let them cultivate mutual affection and abandon stubbornness.
Let them renounce futile obstinacy, which is both destructive and a source of suffering.
Thinking, "This is yours, not mine," or "This is mine,
not yours," let them never do anything harmful toward their own kin or others.
Let them all regard the female servants of Nārāyaṇa as they would themselves.
Whatever belongs to me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
let all of that be seen by you as your own respective property;
for it shall be yours alone, not belonging to another.
Let them never show partiality toward any of their enjoyments;
let them well protect their divine prosperity and wealth, making it ever new and fresh.
Let them spend appropriately, according to their desire, in a manner that bestows happiness.
And on the occasion of their own birthdays and other such times, let them give gifts abundantly.
Let them always maintain their devotion to their husbands, strengthened by the vows of wives.
Let them perform offerings to the gods and the ritual offerings of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites.
Let virtuous women never look upon naked men;
let them pacify disputes and quarrels arising from others.
Let them never place trust in water, fire, or a flood.
Let them not place their trust in animals or those who are like them;
let them not dwell with deceivers, rogues, or women; and let them avoid association with atheists or women who are hostile.
Let them not, through a lapse in moral conduct, commit suicide or cause division;
nor let them inflict beating, cutting, or even the destruction of limbs.
Let all these young women, who are like mothers, promote the welfare of everyone.
May they act for their own welfare and likewise always for the welfare of their husbands.
May they not allow impurity to arise in their vessels, their garments, or their bodies.
May they consume medicinal herbs that are wholesome and grant benefit. (3.40.90)
May they proceed appropriately through assemblies accompanied by their circles;
may they also strive for positions of preeminence within female assemblies.
May they be enriched with foremost virtues among women and others.
Let them not indulge in childish behaviors or those various games;
let them engage in wholesome play, but let them not take up gambling.
Let them also avoid excessive sleep and overeating, which cause disease.
May they enjoy all kinds of objects of enjoyment for the sake of satisfaction— all things obtained through righteous means and pertaining to the five sense-objects—
as well as auspicious vehicles, mounts, palanquins, and celestial chariots.
Ascending to the forest regions, let them gaze upon the sky;
let them indeed enjoy all flavors that satisfy the tongue, offered by me; and let them experience with longing all sensations of touch directed toward me.
May all actions be entrusted to me, Mādhava; may they accept from me whatever is deficient and indeed everything that is required.
Though always dependent upon me, may they remain eternally independent.
May they never, in any way, be outward-looking;
may they be tolerant of the scent of others, dear to me, endowed with modesty, happy, and always auspicious. (98–99)
May they become visible to Brahmā and visible to the divine, liberated from the limits of [samsaric] existence;
may they perceive the seasonal purity within earth, water, fire, air, and the rest.
May their beloved wives practice such auspicious and virtuous conduct.
[These mantras] bestow a [favorable] state of existence when accompanied by ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), gifts, and devotion;
they grant wealth and grain, as well as sons, daughters, and progeny;
they bestow longevity and fame, and even increase one's good fortune.
May these oceans of joy become for me the bestowers of splendor, the bestowers of cheerfulness, and the bestowers of bliss, bringing about clarity of mind;
may they be endowed with all happiness and possessed of the fulfillment of every desire. (103)

May my virtuous wives, who are as dear to me as my own life-breaths, always be victorious! (104) And whatever other women shall exist in the world according to what has been described, they are considered by me to be like delightful mines of merit and the goddess Devikā herself. (105)
Heaven shall be in their very homes, and liberation in their very hands;
they shall possess eternal good fortune—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends [the section] in the third book, the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

Chapter 41 [Author:
Chapter 42 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
A man and a woman should both, with a concentrated mind, preserve their sacred thread (upavīta).
A wife should always perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) and bow to her elders,
as well as to the teacher, her father, and her elder brother.
A king, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a maternal grandfather and a paternal grandfather;
(2) a man of the highest caste, a paternal uncle, a maternal grandmother and a mother;
a paternal sister, an elder female teacher, a mother-in-law, and likewise a paternal grandmother; (3)
The daughter-in-law should bow down to her senior nurse, her co-wife, and her sister.
She should follow their will through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Upon seeing them, she should attend to them, rise from her seat, and offer them respectful salutations.
One should not sit together with these [types of women], nor should one argue with them for one's own sake.
(5) Even for the sake of one’s life, one must never insult one’s elders out of hatred;
for even a wife who is exalted in status falls into ruin if she harbors hatred toward her elders. (6)
The husband, the brother, the teacher of knowledge, the mother, and the father—
these five are especially worthy of worship as the foremost gurus.
One should serve them with every effort, even at the cost of one's own life.
One should always act for the welfare of them, as well as of one's mother-in-law and father-in-law.
(8) Having urinated, one should rinse the mouth three times; likewise after eating.
After voiding excrement, one should perform a bath for the sake of comfort. (9)

Upon touching hair, a hidden part of the body, or the nose, one must perform a ritual washing; likewise upon touching the ears, the navel, and so forth, one should touch the feet. One should not [wash] in fire, in a cremation ground, on wood, on a grassy plot, or on cow dung.
One should not discharge feces, urine, and so forth in water, in a temple, in an anthill, or in a pit inhabited by living creatures (11). Nor should one do so on the royal highway,
nor in chaff and the like, nor in a field, nor in a hole, nor at a sacred ford, nor in a garden, nor in a city reservoir (12).

A virtuous wife should always be absorbed in diligent effort and devoted to righteous conduct; she should never place her feet upon the lap of her elders. Likewise, wherever there is censure of the teacher or even the disparagement of his wife, [she should avoid it].
In such a situation, one should cover one's ears as if from elsewhere;
likewise, one should go about and perform service endowed with right contemplation.
One should always employ speech that is sweet and beneficial. (14–15)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic,
or even spiritual knowledge, the women of the household should not bear malice toward the one from whom they receive it.
And the wives of their teachers who are of the same caste should be honored like their own mothers.
The elderly women should be served by the young wives with ointments, baths, and the like, as well as by massaging their limbs, dressing their hair, and other such services.
The wife of the guru must be saluted; thereafter, one should study the Vedas.
Established in Brahman and composed in mind, she should daily study and practice the Sāvitrī, the name of Śrī Hari, and the Vedāntas refined by self-discipline.
Having first uttered the syllable Om, she should thereafter recite the Vyāhṛtis.
Then she should recite our name, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (3.41.20) The young bride should never appear with worn or dirty clothes.
She should cultivate friendship with her female companions and act for her own spiritual welfare. (21)
She should live in the house practicing conformity in age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage, as well as in place, speech, and intellect.
She should serve only that which is excellent and practiced by the elders and elderly women.
She should not serve [him] with that [which leads to his ruin]; by doing so, she is never at fault.
She should be a follower of the three aims of life (trivarga) and should be distinguished by her discernment.
Such a woman is always called a true housewife, the upholder of heaven and other realms of truth.
One should diligently protect the body, for it is the abode of Dharma;
indeed, without the body, I, Nārāyaṇa, am not within the range of attainment.
One should not harm any living beings, nor should one ever perform any act harmful to others.
One should not be a stealer of the property of the gods; indeed, the wealth of a deity is like poison.
One should not commit an offense against the gods, nor likewise against one's guru.
One should not commit an offense against one's master, nor should one act with malice toward one's mother-in-law.
Indeed, through falsehood, the pursuit of excessive enjoyments, causing pain to others,
and by means of curses and diseases, one's long life comes to destruction.
A bride should never dwell anywhere with those who are utterly foolish or sinful.

Since sin is transmitted through living together, social contact, and the like, a daughter-in-law should never engage in groundless enmity, nor should she utter words that pierce the vitals of others. She should never enter into conflict with many people at once. (3.41.29–30)
One should not prevent what is being given to the gods, teachers, or Brahmins;
one should not praise oneself, and one should also avoid censure.
One should not speak of the sins of sinners, nor should one attribute false faults to others.
One should never eat from the same vessel as one's master.
One should not cause pain to anyone; rather, one should instruct one's daughter and one's disciple.
One should not despise oneself and should always avoid dejection.
One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one ever utter insults, nor likewise speak vulgar words.
One should never sleep in an empty house, in a secluded place, or on another person's seat.
One should not cut down a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), nor should one ever deceive one's elders.
One should not enter a temple by passing to the left of the sanctuary.
Furthermore, a bride should not form an association with those afflicted by disease.
One should not revile yogis, those who have attained perfection, those observing vows, or ascetics;
nor should one revile the gods, the abodes of the gods, virtuous women, chaste wives, or female gurus.
At night, one should avoid and not eat curd mixed with sesame seeds.
One should not eat curd-milk with milk; one should avoid that which is infested with worms.
For the sake of prosperity, one should indeed give wealth to a worthy recipient.
One should always give water, food, and so forth, and on certain occasions, such as during vows, one should give [special gifts].
One should give what is auspicious for the sake of offspring, victory, and sovereignty;
indeed, one should give to those who discourse on Brahman out of great devotion to me, Hari.
A worthy recipient honored with a gift certainly delivers [the donor] in every way.
It should be given with devotion, bringing joy to both the donor and the worthy recipient.
One should give land endowed with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice;
likewise, one should give knowledge, as well as gold, silver, and gems.
One should give diamonds, jeweled ornaments, and the like, as well as garments and woolen blankets;
one should offer food, vegetables, vessels, honey, and clarified butter;
and one should give sesame seeds, saying: "May the Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, my Master and Protector, be pleased with me."

Having spoken thus, one should honor the male ascetics and virtuous men, as well as the female ascetics and virtuous women, and present them with fruits, roots, drinks, vegetables, and likewise medicinal herbs. One should give an umbrella and sandals, and whatever else may be desired, one should offer it.
One should perform the gift of one's daughter to a virtuous man who is rich in beauty, endowed with excellent qualities,
of noble birth, prosperous,
full of wealth, and firm; his own daughter, adorned with all ornaments, should be given away.
The sale of a daughter must never be performed by those seeking their own welfare, for it destroys prosperity.
(47) By giving land, cows, gold, wealth, clothing, grain, and a dowry to the son-in-law, everything becomes inexhaustible. (48)

A girl given away without a dowry enters into a state of servitude. She must never be given to one who eats excessively, one who lives far away, one who is full of calamities, one who is exceedingly wicked, one of low birth, or one who is a fool. (49)

A daughter should certainly not be given in marriage to one who is excessively old, extremely wretched, diseased, a destroyer of all things, or even one who is overly angry and dissatisfied. The giver of a daughter attains heaven and a husband who is the Supreme Lord.

The giver of a daughter shall obtain a wife of excellent complexion in the next world. The five slaughter-houses of householders— the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom— are destroyed by the five great sacrifices.
One should bestow gifts upon living beings and likewise offer them to the ancestors;
one should give to aquatic creatures, and likewise to cows, trees, and birds;
one should also present offerings to the deities and to guests according to one's wealth.
In this way, through giving, faults are indeed destroyed; there is no doubt in this matter.
Giving, purity, and likewise a pure recipient, certainly save one.
Fire is always pure in every respect, and women are always pure.
The virtuous, the extremely pure, and the gods—these three are considered worthy [of offerings].
A woman who drinks liquor, one who is diseased, or one who is hateful should never be made a bride.
There should never be any conflict between a wife and her husband or others.

Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish. She who does not go to another man, whether her husband is dead or alive, attains fame in this world and rejoices in her own home as a virtuous wife (satī). ||58||
Wives must carry out the word of their husbands; in this there is no fault.

Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, she should perform what is commanded by her husband, brothers, father, kinsmen, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or brother-in-law, without hesitation. (3.41.59–60)
Women should be honored by their kinsmen with ornaments, clothing, and food;
they should keep the household utensils in order, be skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure.
They should always perform prostrations at the feet of their mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Having attained fame in this world, she should go to heaven for the benefit of her husband.
A woman whose husband is away on a journey should abandon play, bodily adornment, attendance at social gatherings, witnessing festivals, laughter, and visiting the houses of others. (62–63)
She should not remain apart from her husband by day, at twilight, or at night.
She should honor her beloved according to the prescribed rules, delight him, and likewise bring him joy.
She should have no relish for food prepared by others, except when invited by those whose company is blameless.
A woman should indeed avoid restlessness of speech, hands, and feet;
she should practice a conduct that is appropriate, straightforward, and free from deceit.
She should also avoid hypocrisy, heretical sects, and the behavior of a "heron" (one who feigns virtue for gain).
One should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it.
One should avoid forbidden actions and shun the smoke from a funeral pyre.
Likewise, one should revere the Guru, the scriptures, the preceptor, the king, women, and the husband.
She should not step over her mother-in-law, nor should she avoid her shadow.
She should avoid the beds and such belonging to others, and she should avoid the property of others.
Having become one who relishes flavors, she should not take refuge with another man.
She should never be without oil, nor should she ever be a secret agent.
Indeed, the purification of vessels made of gold, silver, or lotus, as well as of conch shells, ropes, leather, bowls, and seats, must be performed with water. (3.41.70)
By heating, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are purified; by sprinkling, grains;

by planing, wooden sacrificial vessels, horns, and the like; by scrubbing, other sacrificial implements; and by means of alkaline substances, sour liquids, water, and cleansing agents, vessels made of tin, lead, and copper. (71–72)
Iron and bronze vessels are purified by ashes and water; the ground is purified by sweeping and other such means.
That which has been smeared with impurities is cleansed by earth and water through the removal of odor and stain.
One should not eat food while sitting on one's lap, nor should one ever sleep naked.
One should not cut one's nails or hair with the teeth, nor should one awaken a sleeping person.
One should not enter through a side door, nor cross a river by swimming with one's arms.
One should never stand upon charcoal, ashes, hair, or similar refuse.
She should be skilled in lighting the mechanical stove, the hearth, the lamp, and so forth;
she should always be vigilant when fetching water on the path;
and she should remain as if in meditation on the banks of wells, rivers, ponds, and the like.
She should be skilled even in placing her feet during activities such as plowing and so forth, and with regard to grass and the like.
She should be skilled even in gathering dried cow dung, wood, and other materials;
she should be skilled even on ground that is dilapidated, infested with insects, or located in a corner. (77–78)
On the road or even while traveling in a vehicle, a wife should follow her own husband;
she should remain vigilant behind him so that no confusion with another may arise.
She should be skillful in protecting children, grandchildren, and other young ones.
She should be skilled in discerning what is wholesome and unwholesome regarding food and other matters.
A virtuous woman should properly discipline her sons and refine them with auspicious virtues.
She should instruct them in pleasant duties and always maintain a sense of faith in the hereafter.
A young woman should always bathe with water, excluding the head;
however, she should always perform an oil bath for the head.
She should likewise perform an auspicious scrubbing bath and the "bath of knowledge."

She should always perform the bath of meditating upon Brahman and the purification. With her mind established in peace, the bride should daily recite the rosary of Hari’s names, consisting of a maximum of one thousand, a middle number of one hundred, or a minimum of ten.
One should constantly worship the ancestors; they are traditionally remembered as being threefold:
here on earth, they are the manifest human beings; likewise, there are the gods who have gone to heaven;
and others are the *preta*s who have attained birth—these three are considered the ancestors.
Mother, father, teacher, mother-in-law, and husband are present before one's eyes;
the moon, the sun, and fire are indeed deities stationed in the sky; and those deceased ancestors who have passed away and entered another birth exist in the state of *preta*. (86–87)
These third [ancestors] are to be awakened; the householder should bow to them:
Candra is the father, Ravi is the grandfather, and Agni is the great-grandfather.
They are, respectively, the Somapas, the Barhiṣads, and the Agniṣvāttas.
One should feed those worthy of sacrifice, the drinkers of clarified butter, the wise, and the virtuous.
(89) The ancestors beginning with the mother and father are lunar; the twice-born and others are auspiciously solar;
guests are of the nature of fire; and the virtuous are one's own ancestors when they come within the range of one's sight. (3.41.90)
She should always feed those [guests] according to her ability and according to her wealth.
Desiring prosperity, abundance, and good fortune, she should tend to cows and other such animals.
She should offer salutations to the deities and likewise bow daily to the elders.
The wife should bow to the guru and recite my mantra joined with her own name.
During the time of recitation, she should not speak; she should remember Acyuta, the Lord of Śrī.
Meritorious is the worship of Hari; she should worship Hari constantly. (5.2–5.3)
The bride should offer herself to the glorious Supreme Soul;
she should daily worship Lord Hari during the twilight hours, her husband who bestows all peace.
She should also give food to the deity, for that indeed constitutes the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña).
One should offer [the food] to an image, or into water, or upon the ground, even during the Vaiśvadeva rite.
One should offer the remainder to cows, to outcastes (śvapacas), to dogs, and to all beings;
that which is given to the wretched, the fallen, and birds is called the Bhūtayajña.
One performing the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*) should feed virtuous Brahmins, chaste women, and children;
he should always feed his guest until they are satisfied, treating them as if they were his own father.
He should honor arriving guests and virtuous travelers according to his ability.
And one should give alms to a virtuous mendicant who observes the vow of celibacy;
and a wife, free from greed, should also give to those who seek her help.
This human sacrifice is said to be a means for accomplishing great blessings.
One should always give food to me, who am Śrīmat Paramātman;
and one should offer it to the knower of Brahman—that indeed is considered the Brahma-yajña.
In every instance during the act of eating, a virtuous woman should wash her hands.
One should indeed offer [the food] preceded by purification; by that, the deities are satisfied.
For the purpose of eating, one should sit down after having washed both feet and hands;
then, having performed the *āpośāna* rite, one should offer [the food] to the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
One should eat food preceded by praise and offer it as an oblation into one's own self. One should not eat before a solar eclipse, nor until after the evening of a lunar eclipse.
During the time of an eclipse one should not eat; rather, having bathed, one should eat after offering [the food] in dedication.
She whose eating is for her own sake, whose sexual pleasure is for the sake of enjoyment,
and whose arts are for the sake of livelihood— her life ends in emptiness.
She should not sleep facing south, nor should she sleep facing west.
Neither in the open air, nor naked, nor on another seat, shall the virtuous bride ever fail to remember me, Śrī Hari, daily in all her undertakings.
Day and night, she should indeed remember me, the Supreme Person, the bestower of liberation.
A wife should serve her husband as she desires, without any reserve.
(107) By observing these duties and the conduct of the virtuous, remaining established in happiness, she shall always rejoice in the home and become possessed of an abundance of bliss. (108)
By reading or hearing this, one obtains the fruit of practicing the Dharma;
by preserving it, there shall be the destruction of sin and the attainment of the path to liberation.
A virtuous wife shall obtain the fruit of visiting sacred fords, giving gifts, and observing vows.
She shall likewise obtain virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as sons and daughters.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Duties and Right Conduct of a Young Wife," in the *Vadhūgītā* within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*). Chapter 41.
Chapter 42 [Author:
Chapter 43 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the glory of Śivarājñī-Śrī; Hari [has described it]. Beyond that, O auspicious one, I shall tell you of various customs.
Fresh, flavorful foods should always be given to the seeker.
For it is the sacrifice of the first-fruits that bestows long life here.
(2) All human beings—both women and men—when there is new grain, should worship the Supreme Lord with fire using pure food. (3)
One should worship the Supreme Lord with curd that possesses a sweet, sour, and sweet taste, as well as with milk endowed with a sweet essence.
One should worship Mādhava with milk-rice, preparations cooked with milk, and milk.

One should worship the Supreme Self with ghee, with food cooked in ghee, and with auspicious foods smeared with ghee; (5) with auspicious fresh butter mixed with sugar, and with offerings filled in milk-pots. (6)
O Lakṣmī! Worship me, Hari, with offerings of *pūrikās*, *polikās*, and hidden *puṭaka* snacks, by which I am satisfied;
as well as with sugar, candied sugar and the like, honey, jaggery, and saffron.
One should worship me in every way with the six flavors and cool drinks;
one should worship with mango fruits, sweet fruits, grapes, plantains,
ambrosia, and the ripened fruits of coconuts and the like.
With cool fruits, *rāyaṇa* trees, *jambū* trees, and likewise *panasa* trees, as well as with fresh *cirbhaṭa* and *karkaṭī* gourds, let my bride indeed worship me.
These two— honor and dishonor— are always to be understood as poison and nectar.
Encountering the overwhelming touch of that [fire], the group of young women perishes.
Therefore, the womenfolk should conduct themselves with a spirit of servitude.
They should walk along a path purified by their sight; they should perform actions purified by their mind.
A daughter-in-law should perform service purified by her master and dwell in a home purified by righteousness.
She should always obey her master’s command and never act in violation of that command.
For the duty of wives is obedience; therefore, she should desire the highest success through it.
The bride should avoid deceit, hypocrisy, guile, and backbiting.
(14) With every effort, the bride should avoid excessive laughter, arrogance, playful coquetry, and acting according to her own whims in the presence of her elders. (15)
One should not speak words that are contrary to the teacher's speech, nor should one speak what is improper; for the group of wives should never recall anything unpleasant.
One should not touch a woman in her menses, a woman who has recently given birth, or one who is carrying filth.
On the fourth lunar day, the bride will certainly not be capable of fulfilling the duties of pleasure;
she will give birth to offspring who are short-lived and destitute of vows, learning, wealth, and other such qualities. Therefore, she must indeed be under the influence of a powerful planet. (17–18)
One should associate with virtuous women, for she becomes the accomplisher of all goals;
one should abandon association with unvirtuous women, which brings no benefit either in this world or the next.
One should also avoid the company of the base and maintain harmony with one's own kin.
One should avoid association with those devoted to serving enemies and with evil company.
For one who forms alliances with the excellent, engages in noble discourse with the wise, and cultivates friendship with those free from greed, does not come to ruin. (3.42.20–21)
A man should never engage in association with others that is laughable or inappropriate for men and women, nor should he ever dwell in another’s house.
Even if she is a stranger, if she acts for one’s welfare, she is a kinswoman; if she does not, she is otherwise.
A disease born of the body is harmful; forest herbs are beneficial.
She alone is a kinswoman who is kind; he alone is a father who provides nourishment.
He is a friend in whom there is trust; that is one's country where one lives.
He is a servant who serves according to the prescribed rule; that is a seed which sprouts.
She is a wife who is devoted to her husband; he is a son who brings about happiness.
She truly lives whose virtues [endure]; she truly lives whose righteousness [endures].
For the life of one devoid of virtuous qualities is fruitless.
(26) She is a true wife who is skillful in the home, devoted as her own life, sweet-spoken, beneficial, loyal, compliant, and the increaser of all good fortune. (27)
He whose wife is devoid of affection, whose eyes lack love, who is deceitful, fond of quarreling, talkative, attached to others, shameless, and arrogant;
she is a wretched woman lacking service— she is old age, not mere old age.
She whose wife is of equal conduct, appreciative of virtues, and devoted; who shares her husband's fortune, is easily satisfied, affectionate, and acts for his benefit;
who is dedicated to her husband's dharma and inseparable from him—she is truly beloved, not merely a woman who is loved.
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant intent only on his own interests,
and where there is a serpent— in such a place, residence indeed brings death.
A husband who does not recognize virtue, an angry co-wife, and one who points out faults [are likewise causes of ruin].
Wherever one dwells amidst all manner of doubt, there can be no peace.
(32) May you abandon association with the wicked and cultivate the company of the virtuous;
may you perform meritorious deeds incessantly and remember me, Hari, as your husband. (33)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; one should protect one's wife by means of wealth and other resources.
One should always protect one's husband, one's son, and one's virtuous wife by means of wealth and other resources.
One may abandon a single individual for the sake of the family, but for the sake of dharma, one should abandon the family.
One should abandon even the Dharma for the sake of Hari; for the sake of liberation, one should renounce everything.
It is better to dwell in a forest region than ever in a wicked house. A household is a life of misconduct and affliction—both are manifest hells. (35–36)
The wise woman moves with one foot while standing on the other;
she should not abandon her former dwelling until she has examined another place.
She should abandon a residence where the tenfold conduct is wicked, and she should leave a home that is fraught with calamity.
One should abandon a miserly master, a deceitful person, and a wicked man. (38) Those who are friends only while one holds a position of power are not truly so;
indeed, friends become meaningful only when one is devoid of wealth and status. (39)
A wife is a friend who provides protection in times of calamity and a source of comfort when resources are exhausted; she is a companion during famines and other hardships for the fortunate man.
[She abandons] a tree whose fruit is spent, a dried-up lake, and a husband who is destitute.
Shadows, fish, and lawful wives never abandon them;
however, birds, cranes, and courtesans indeed do abandon them.
One should understand that such people act out of self-interest, and one should not place trust in them.
One should win over a greedy woman by the gift of wealth, an excellent woman with joined palms,
a foolish woman by following her whims, a wise woman with truthfulness,
a virtuous woman by service, and a young bride with sweet speech.
Virtuous women and even the deities are pleased by pure intentions;
an unchaste woman is pleased by food, drink, and the like, while a deceitful one is pleased by deceit.
Whatever a woman’s disposition may be, the bride should enter into her with that very same nature.
Rivers, clawed animals, horned creatures, those with weapons in hand,
the royal court, and beggars are by no means to be trusted in every respect.
[They cause] loss of wealth, agitation, and likewise misconduct within the home.
A bride must never reveal her husband’s insults or his deceptions.
Abandoning one’s master and associating with the lowly are both destroyers of a bride’s character.
Being arrogant, being a transgressor, and being addicted to vice—these three are the destroyers of one’s gains.
Where there is no honor, no joy, no learning, no peace, and no affection; where there is no love for the husband in the wife—that house is indeed a dwelling of fire.
Wealth should be acquired free from fear, and friendship should likewise be free from fear.
Likewise, joy free from fear is heaven itself; it is without dread. A woman should always be charitable and never stingy, patient, virtuous, and a seeker of merit for the sake of happiness.
Naked, emaciated, a mendicant, wretched, and devoted to begging—such is the state of one who does not give; therefore, a daughter-in-law should be a giver.
If that which has been accumulated, requested, or obtained is not employed for a worthy purpose, [it is of no avail].
That wealth will indeed be seized by thieves, kings, and the earth;
the property of a miser goes to the king and to thieves of the land.
For a woman, the punishment is a separate bed, while for a husband, the punishment is non-service.
Wicked people, servants, drums, and likewise animals,
as well as a wicked woman and a man addicted to vices, become mild when struck.
Rivers, women, and great deep-flowing streams are all equally impetuous in their nature.
If those who follow their own whims cause family after family to fall, [what can be done]?
There is no satiety in desire, nor in sons, nor in wealth, nor even in pleasure or life itself; having conquered these, one should devote oneself to Hari.
One should accomplish the eternal through future means such as the worship of the gods;
however, that which is corporeal must be abandoned once it is known to be impermanent.
For she who abandons certain liberation and pursues the uncertain [worldly state]—
One should pursue that which is permanent, for the impermanent will not go along with the self. (59) An oblation may be accepted even from a family of outcasts; a well-spoken word even from a child;
gold may be taken from an impure place; and likewise, liberation is to be sought from a virtuous person. (3.42.60)
Servants, ornaments, and even women should be employed only in their proper places.
A virtuous woman, a noble horse, a hero, and a person devoted to truth—these do not tolerate a blow or falsehood without regard for themselves. (61)
Even when deprived of wealth, a virtuous woman does not serve a base person.
One should never again reconcile with a friend who has once proven treacherous;
by such a reconciliation, death may come, especially in the case of a wife.
The offspring of an enemy is like a vessel of poison; it is never a vessel of trust.
When adverse times arrive, it brings about calamity.
When fate is favorable, everything else becomes meaningless.

If fate is not favorable, everything done is rendered useless. A woman who casts aside shame in the acquisition of wealth, in expenditure, in the acquisition of knowledge, in eating, in sexual pleasure, and in accomplishing her own purposes, shall obtain happiness.
Shame, protection, water, the king, the teacher, the temple, and one's own people—
where these do not exist, staying there is indeed a source of suffering.
A virtuous person, an astrologer, a man of knowledge, and an elder— these should meet with one another.
One should not dwell where there is neither oil, nor food, nor a physician.
A virtuous daughter-in-law should properly support her own kinsmen with food, clothing, and other necessities,
and she should constantly worship Viṣṇu, who bestows longevity, fame, and strength.
In an instant wealth perishes; wealth and such are not under one's own control.
Realizing that time is but a moment, O virtuous woman, serve me and surely achieve liberation.
For both the tigress of old age and the enemy of disease approach with irresistible force.
Knowing that life is like a broken jar, one should strive for liberation.
She who looks upon another man as her father, upon another’s wealth as straw, and upon all beings as herself—she indeed is a virtuous woman (satī). (71–72)
Friends belong to the woman who possesses wealth; relatives belong to the woman who possesses wealth.
The woman who possesses wealth shall be highly honored; indeed, the woman who possesses wealth is wise.
One devoid of the scriptures is always blind; therefore, one should be possessed of the scriptures.
A woman who possesses the eye of the scriptures prospers in the happiness of sovereignty.
By her, the Lord was satisfied; by her, servants were rendered grateful; and by her, the group of women in the household and the rest conquered the earth. (74–75)
A wife should never give way to mental anguish even in the face of great calamity;

possessing equal wisdom and rich in discernment, she should remain equanimous toward both pleasure and pain. She should not regard the house of another as such, for her husband’s home is her own home.
Whatever belongs to her husband is entirely her own; this should be understood with discernment.
She should restrain her gaze from fickleness and restrain herself from false speech.
She should ward off the mind from deceit and restrain herself from the cycle of worldly existence.
She should never utter the sound "huṃ" nor knit her brows when facing her own kinsmen.
Upon seeing a group of women, she should please them and bow down to the young wives.
Diligence, discernment, fortitude, capability, and excellent character—

And enthusiasm—these six qualities in a woman always grant success and happiness. (3.42.80) Gentleness, a disposition of service, humility, forbearance, compassion, cheerfulness, and affection—these seven in a wife bestow happiness. (3.42.81)
Endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, devoted to truth and righteousness, beautiful and serene— she indeed shall be the superintendent of women.
Knowing strength and weakness as well as the intellect [of others], she indeed shall be the commander of the army.
Rama should be a female doorkeeper who understands gestures, facial expressions, and inner dispositions.
She should be intelligent, eloquent, devoted to truth, and one who has conquered her senses;
she should be skilled in many scriptures and serve as an instructor. (83–84)

A woman who is intelligent, capable of discerning the minds of others, truthful in speech, of noble birth, and endowed with the power of her lord—she is considered a messenger (*dūtī*). She who knows all the rules and possesses an abundance of logical reasoning power [is likewise qualified]. (85)
She should be knowledgeable regarding place, time, and other such factors, and she must indeed be a supervisor of religious duties (dharmādhyakṣā).

Skilled in the traditions of her mother and maternal grandmother, having exerted herself in the preparation of cooking, pure, well-acquainted with the process of purification, and possessing a refined palate, she shall be the cook. (86–87)
One who has practiced Āyurveda, who acts for the benefit of all,
and who possesses the wisdom of the system of diagnosis, shall indeed be an excellent physician.
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas), and who is devoted to meditation, fire-offerings, and recitation, [is likewise qualified].
The preceptor should be one who utters blessings for welfare, as well as an instructor;

she should know proper conduct and the rules of discipline, and understand place, time, and other such factors. Indeed, the preceptor should be skillful and clever as both a scribe and a reciter. (3.42.90)
A woman who is double-tongued, a giver of affliction, as well as agitating,
deceitful, cruel, and harsh— she is considered one who causes harm.
A wicked woman must be avoided, even if she is adorned with learning.
Likewise, a wicked wife should be abandoned in legal proceedings.
One who has equal wealth, equal capability, knows one's secrets, is industrious, brave, and endowed with influence— such a woman should be employed in the affairs of state.
Free from laziness, contented, bringing happiness, and providing wise counsel;
equanimous in pleasure and pain, and steadfast—such servants are rare everywhere.
Yet those devoid of patience and truth, cruel, deceitful, and slanderous [are common]. (94)
A woman who is hypocritical, greedy, and one who plunders food should be abandoned.

One should employ in the home, the kingdom, or in an auspicious place a beloved wife who is endowed with virtues; however, one who lacks virtue should be employed on the path of liberation or in service.

A beautiful woman should always sit in the company of virtuous women; she should not sit with unchaste women, nor should she form a friendship with them. She should likewise associate with wise women who are devoted to the vow of truth.
Even while remaining in confinement, she must never associate with wicked women. The bridegroom’s people should carry out their tasks until they are fully completed;
if they abandon them before completion, it results in loss for themselves.
A virtuous wife should gather the honey from her husband like bees from a hive;
she should never let a day pass in vain, always serving him with devotion and the like.
She should abandon passion that is devoid of moral conduct, but cultivate affection that is accompanied by virtue.
Knowledge produces diligence; she who possesses it shall conquer the three worlds.
A house is not truly called a home by its master alone, but only because of the mistress;
therefore, the home must always be protected by the mistress as if she were a tutelary deity.
"This must be done by women— by brides and by virtuous wives— who,
considering everything as their own duty, should serve and especially cultivate [their husbands].

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Demonstration of Right Conduct and Other Matters," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
