Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to that which the Supreme Lord has spoken;
[he spoke of] the excellence of Śiva’s queen, O Śrī, and thereafter of virtuous conduct.
Good character is the ornament of virtuous women; a husband is the ornament of wives;
modesty is the ornament of all; and Lord Hari is the ornament of ornaments.
(2) She who is not Lakṣmī herself, nor even one equal to Lakṣmī— [she is not truly adorned].
She whose fortune is fixed upon Hari is indeed known as Nārāyaṇī.
Lakṣmī herself becomes the mother of her, and Janārdana is her father.
She whose fortune is not fixed upon Hari is to be pitied, for she is bereft of Hari.
Indeed, the embodied being experiences in due order everything that was previously performed;
for the bed of the womb was created by Brahmā for the ripening of karmas—
according to which age, at which time, in what manner, and from what cause [a particular action] was fashioned.
That comes to pass exactly as impelled by destiny, and never otherwise.
Indeed, gifts given, knowledge acquired, and desires fulfilled in the past—
all of that surely returns in due time for the enjoyment of embodied beings here.
In this body acquired through karma, there are indeed numerous diseases;
moreover, the disease of the womb-cavity always resides within women.
Therefore, having reflected with an intellect pregnant with the scriptures, the beautiful woman—
One should make oneself free from disease out of a state of sickness.
(9) She whose self is always purified by truth and purity is pure; she attains heaven, and thereafter the station of the Supreme Lord. (3.43.10)
With a heart captivated by worldly existence and joined with the feverish emaciation of craving,
one is not purified even by thousands of ritual baths at sacred fords.
There is no joy in honor and no distress in dishonor.

Where patience and virtue always reside, she is considered a virtuous wife, a true companion to her husband. (12) Just as a river becomes a downward-flowing torrent by the accumulation of millions of grains of sand, so too does a woman become a downward-flowing torrent by the accumulation of millions of karmic deeds. (13)
A collection of water-consciousnesses forms the riverbank; a collection of ethical-consciousnesses forms the woman who has crossed to the other shore (14).
[This applies] to women of divided households who are attached to distant lands.

Devotion is the supreme action that directs me, Kṛṣṇa, [toward the devotee]. (15) She who has sincerely uttered even once the name "Hari" with true feeling has attained the imperishable abode of eternal bliss. (16)

If one desires eternal love for me, Mādhava, the Lord of Śrī, one should maintain devotion toward me; this is considered my supreme means of realization. Trust in all beings and a disposition of goodness born of one's own nature—these are my views.
A virtuous wife who always performs service in secret is indeed esteemed by Hari.
Even if she is beautiful, the Lord abandons a woman who is dirty, has stained teeth, eats excessively, is harsh, or sleeps at twilight. 18–19.

Even a lord abandons a consort who writes on the ground, cuts grass with her teeth, has unclean teeth, wears soiled garments, has coarse hair, or sleeps naked— even if she is endowed with fortune (Śrī).
This is likewise true for a couple, two women, two animals, or two swift machines.
One must never pass between two people who are angry and fighting.
(21) A verse heard by six ears is leaked; one heard by four ears is maintained;
but a secret heard by only two ears never comes to light. (22)
Indeed, people impute faults to a person endowed with forbearance;
they perceive it as incapacity, a lack of strength, worthlessness like a withered flower, and insignificance.
For such a person is considered ungrateful, ignoble, long-suffering in resentment, and lacking in integrity. (23)
For there are four kinds of *cāṇḍālīs*, and beyond those, a fifth by birth.
She who is tranquil in her youth is always a peaceful wife;
however, when the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) have declined, all women become tranquil. (24–25)
For where there is a renunciant who has undertaken asceticism for the sake of visiting holy sites, truthfulness accompanies him on his journey, while deceit remains at home;
and where poverty and quarrels abide in the house like kinsmen. (26)
Violence is the nature of his wife, and his home is a hollow of Yama.
There is no contentment with a wicked master, nor is there contentment with a bad wife;
there is no fearlessness with a bad friend—one should act only after such considerations.
The food of others, the property of others, the beds of others, the wives of others, the men of others, and the palaces of others—these indeed cause the destruction of prosperity.
The base are truly attached to affliction; those with attachment for alliances are mediocre.
Those who possess pride and passion are the best, while those whose luster is broken become fit for destruction.
Those who possess passion for wealth are the lowest; those who follow both pride and wealth are middling;
and those who abide in pride alone are the best wives for embodied beings.
Separation, humiliation, debt, service to the wicked,
poverty, and quarrel— these six are burners even without fire.
Life, wealth, youth, and likewise the mind are all unstable.
Therefore, even sons, wives, and husbands should worship Hari steadfastly.
Time, consisting of days and nights, carries away the multitude of embodied beings; knowing Hari to be the Death of Death, one should take refuge in Me, the Supreme Person.
What is the life of that woman of pleasure in this world, who is not compassionate toward her own kin, her teacher, her servant, her husband, or the destitute—
she who passes even a single moment in her home devoid of virtue, devotion, and other such qualities? (35)
For that house should be understood as a bellows, providing a dwelling for the inhabitants of the breath.

Women fall away from it through indulgence, negligence, and misplaced trust, as well as through pride and the pursuit of their own interests; therefore, one should always keep them at a distance. (36–37)

One should indeed fear as long as the danger has not yet arrived; but when a terrible danger has actually presented itself, one must stand firm like one who is fearless. That compassion which one does not extend toward the wretched, the servant, the teacher, or the woman—
If she has no protector, whether it be a friend or a husband, let her life be like that of a crow.
(3.39) Those dependent on others are as if dead; those who are self-dependent are seekers of life.
Those who perform service for others are truly alive, even though they have died. (3.43.40)
For in whatever measure women here become disciplined by the scriptures,
in that same measure they shall be wise and even exponents of Brahman.
And in whatever measure they direct their own minds toward what is auspicious, [so shall it be].
In that way, women indeed become worthy objects of honor and very dear;
yet she who destroys one's interests behind one's back while speaking sweetly to one's face must be avoided with great effort, like the indravāruṇī creeper.
Even a virtuous woman perishes through association with a wicked woman;
therefore, a wife must diligently avoid the company of a wicked woman.
Indeed, wherever there is serenity of mind, there truly are auspicious blessings.
Wherever there is favor toward women, there indeed is the abode of prosperity.
(45) She is a true woman who does not give way to pride; she is a wife who is dear to her husband;
she is happy who is free from craving; and she is a daughter-in-law who increases the lineage. (46)
One should not excessively investigate the origins of the virtuous, of rivers, of faithful women, of brides, or of medicinal herbs.
The glory of a kingdom ends with the exhaustion of merit; the character of a woman ends with sexual union.
The family's reputation ends with the character of its women; indeed, the end of the family is the women themselves.
(48) There is no excellent residence in a place without a leader, nor even in one with many leaders.
There is no excellent residence in a place led by women, nor even in one led by children. (49)
In childhood she is dependent on her father; in youth, she is dependent on her husband;
in old age, she is dependent on her sons; likewise, in the life-stage of renunciation, she is dependent on truth.
In times of calamity, she is dependent on modesty; but in prosperity, she is dependent on destiny.
A wife who is submissive to her husband’s generosity brings happiness.

Having carefully avoided a woman who is barren, whose children have died, who is a mother only in name, who speaks unpleasantly, or who bears no sons, one should marry another for the sake of obtaining male offspring. (51–52)

For a woman who lacks wealth, even if she is fearless, she remains dependent on her lover; indeed, it is praised when a woman who is full of wealth is dependent on her lover even though she is fearless. For one distressed by wealth, there is neither dharma nor fear for the sake of a lover. (53)
A wife who is consumed by anxiety finds no happiness; one should avoid such things for her.
(54) How can there be happiness for a servant, a poor woman, or an unchaste woman?
How can there be happiness for one burdened by debt, one afflicted by disease, or a barren woman? (55)
For Padmā while remaining in her place, Varuṇa and Bhāskara are her friends; for her when she has fallen from that place, they are the ones who cause her affliction and emaciation.
Even women and even children, when established in their proper place, are well-honored.
Hair, teeth, nails, and kings are not honored when they have fallen from their proper place.
(57) Sleep is pleasant for one free from debt; likewise, sleep is pleasant for one who is fearless.
Sleep is pleasant for one free from disease; likewise, sleep is pleasant for one who has renounced worldly life. (58)
The sleep of one who is unattached to men, yet united with the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and who is free from craving— whether she be his own wife or another's— is blissful;
just as a lotus attains full expansion through contact with water.
Likewise, through a powerful husband, a wife may attain a high position. Here, the value of conduct is known by one's lineage, the value of speech by one's country,
the value of affection by one's eyes, and the value of food by its appearance.
There is indeed no price for rain upon the ocean, nor for food for one who is already satiated;
there is no value for a gift given to one who is already wealthy, and likewise none for merit bestowed upon a base person.
It is said that even in the heart of one who has gone far away, a dwelling place remains through affection.
Dwelling far away due to enmity toward one who is nearby is declared [to be a sign].
Miserliness, a dejected voice, emaciation of the limbs, and intense poverty—these, along with meanness and fear, are the marks of those seeking alms. (64)
For even the great Lord Viṣṇu became a dwarf when he was a petitioner;
therefore, what other seeker would not incur insignificance?
Knowledge is always to be acquired as wealth, for it is the true bestower of goodness.
Learning is the endearer of respect, the bestower of honor, and the destroyer of suffering.
Learning is the supreme deity and the treasure-trove of divine knowledge.
Learning should be understood as equal to a bride, for it accomplishes the prosperity of the household. (66–67)
All external possessions are indeed permeated by the fear of destruction;
however, the wealth of the self exists as knowledge, free from the fear of destruction. A wife who possesses the knowledge of the Self is undoubtedly a sacred pilgrimage site.
The sons and daughters of the holy sites (*tīrtha*) are purifiers and partakers of liberation. (69) Even for a man who possesses the yoga of the holy sites, liberation may occur through his wife;
likewise, the members of his household are enjoyers of the purifying objects of the holy sites. (70)
Purified by the merit of having a wife who is a sacred ford, they go to the state of liberation—
those whose wife is a great saintly woman, devoted to virtuous vows,
constantly intent on righteous conduct, and dedicated to her husband. (7.1)
Possessing limbs of great merit, having excellent sons, worthy of auspiciousness, and speaking the truth;
pure, acting for the pleasure [of her husband], devoted to pleasing vows, serving her husband;
knowledgeable, virtuous, listening to sacred stories, and practicing much austerity. (72–73)
By virtue of her nature, the auspicious wife is eternally a partner in meritorious deeds;
she follows the path of her husband and is devoted to sacrifices for her husband as a deity.
Furthermore, that beloved woman who, through her true devotion, never distances herself from her husband— 74.
Just as her shadow, so too she is devoted to the dharma of undivided vows;
she who always abides in the vow of devotion to her husband (*pātivratya*), which grants liberation to women,
is a meritorious wife, and he whose wife is such is indeed a husband composed of Brahman.
She who, being the devoted wife of her husband, always regards his left foot as the imperishable abode and his right foot as the nature of the Supreme Brahman—
that beautiful woman, having bathed in the water from his feet, becomes one with Brahman.
She is indeed considered equal to all sacred fords and the abode of all sacred fords.
Whatever merit arises from performing sacrifices, a much greater merit than that arises through devotion to her husband. (78–79)
There is no dharma for a woman apart from service to her husband;
therefore, accompanied by her beloved, she always bestows happiness.
Meritorious, most meritorious, and virtuous, she is distinguished throughout the three worlds.
She should never be abandoned, neither in this world nor in the next.
By him who has cast off a wife who is well-conducted and a follower of dharma,
even the tenfold dharma itself would be abandoned in this very life.
Whenever her husband goes to another village,
the virtuous wife indeed sleeps upon the ground and does not even apply cosmetics;
she does not consume ghee, oil, milk, or drink, nor does she eat curd or sweets.
The virtuous woman indeed does not consume betel, honey, or sweet foods;
she wears her hair in a single braid and dons a single bodice and garment.
Unable to endure separation, she awaits his arrival.
A union with a husband arises for women through the connection of merit;
indeed, for women, the husband is always their sacred pilgrimage site, and he is likewise [the sacred site] for the wife.
They should constantly invoke one another mutually through speech, body, and actions.
One should always worship with the mind and with a spirit of truth toward one another.
Indeed, both the right limb and the left limb are always two sacred fords (tīrtha);
they constantly enable a family of one hundred members to cross over [to liberation]. || 87-88 ||
Great happiness, the good fortune of having sons, and even the good fortune of wealth—
as well as beauty, splendor, renown, and fame— come to a husband through the favor of his wife.
For women, youth and beauty are considered the husband’s own prosperity.
When her husband is satisfied, all the worlds are auspicious for a woman.
Even if she is beautiful and endowed with riches, how can there be happiness, beauty, fame, renown, sons, and so forth for one who is deprived of her husband? (3.43.90–91)
A sinful woman, deprived of her husband, experiences misfortune and great suffering.
When the husband is satisfied, the gods, sages, humans, and deities are pleased;
even the ancestors become gratified, bestowing happiness upon both worlds.
The husband is the protector, the lord, the guru, and the deity along with all other deities.
For women, the husband is the sacred ford and the merit; he is the weight of their good fortune.
He is their adornment, their beauty, their complexion, and even their fragrance. (93–94)
The husband is heaven, the husband is dharma, and the husband is indeed good fortune;
the husband is the lineage, the husband is beauty—for the woman, her very existence depends upon the husband.
Without dharma, without a wife, and without a virtuous master, there is no auspiciousness.
Even the home acts like a forest and indeed like a cremation ground [where these are absent];
but where there is a chaste wife and likewise a husband devoted to his wife, where there is prosperity, affection, and true devotion to Brahman—[that is a true home]. (96–97)
Where there is constant worship of the gods, where there is honor for women,
where there is the protection of maidens, and where there is service to mothers;
where children rejoice and where women find delight.
Wherever a woman’s heart truly blossoms and rejoices, there lie the heavens of the lords, as well as wealth and the state of the world of Brahmā.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī! May women become devoted to virtue and dear to Brahmā. (3.43.100)
They are always devoted to me, truthful, and dedicated to virtuous conduct;
they are eternally intent upon the true Dharma and devoted to the worship of the gods. They are entirely devoted to their husbands and likewise devoted to the vow of serving Lord Hari.
"May all my beloved brides, who are eternally devoted to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, accept this treasure of bliss; for through your happiness,
all my own eternal happiness is secured."
"The duties of a bride are as sharp as the edge of a sword, yet they remain dear when performed for the sake of her beloved.
By guarding these well, you shall become one with my very self.

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct and Duties of a Bride," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this auspicious narrative of a former birth.
Long ago, the great sage Vedāyana related it to his own wife.
I shall proclaim the most excellent and unsurpassed devotion to one’s husband;
listen, O beautiful lady, to how this is practiced through speech, thought, and deed.
Listen with joy to the duties of a bride that bring about her welfare during the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
She performs service for her husband every day with her own devotion.
(3) A devoted wife does not abandon him even when he is angry or destitute;
she does not take note of his faults and remains satisfied even when struck. (4)
She who serves her beloved husband— whether he be afflicted with leprosy or even a mere beggar— always standing before him in all his duties,
goes indeed to the auspicious world of her husband through the grace of her lord. (5)
Even if her husband has fallen [from his caste], is diseased, humpbacked, maimed, or afflicted by illness;
or if he is impotent, devoid of dharma, a sinner, or beset by calamities—a wife who desires her own welfare must never abandon him. (6–7)
If she should abandon her beloved husband and go elsewhere for the sake of some purpose, devoid of affection,
she will incur her husband’s curse and attain the state of a wanton woman.
If, after her husband has departed, she indulges in amorous passion and lewdness, [she likewise incurs his curse].

But she who, having abandoned her own husband, always dwells in her father’s house, shall fall from one birth to another through the force of passion. That woman, devoid of ritual and devoid of dharma, is worthy of punishment. (3.44.10)

She who, having abandoned the life of a housewife, wanders elsewhere in another's dwelling, is not complete; for she who regards her husband as a deity is indeed unfortunate. And she who, having abandoned her husband, stays in great gardens and such places [is likewise ill-fated].

Adorned with ornaments and attire fit for amorous passion, that merciless and sinful woman is called a *puṃścalī* (unchaste woman) by whom her own husband has been abandoned. A wife who sleeps separately [from her husband] is declared a *puṃścalī*, devoid of dharma.

Deprived of sight and lacking the eye of Dharma, she was abandoned by her husband. For in every situation, the husband alone is the protector of his wife who upholds the Dharma. A maiden who remains long in her father’s house goes to ruin.
A beloved wife who remains in her husband’s house attains long life.
Devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, and chaste, she embodies all sacred fords;
she is the goddess who is eternal and composed of all righteousness. (15–16)
Furthermore, if one bestows upon any woman whatsoever— even one who has gone to an evil rebirth— the merit arising from a single day of devotion to her husband,
there shall be liberation for that *piśācinī* (female spirit), and likewise, there shall be the pacification of her sins.
The body inevitably perishes; therefore, one should cultivate the virtue of devotion to one's husband.
Piṅgalā and Śṛṅgalī are the two worms at the roots of the ears;
Capala and Pippala are these two at the tips of the nostrils.
Bhṛṅgalīs and jaṅgalīs reside within her eyes;
likewise, ever-new worms exist throughout all her limbs.
By them, the body of this woman devoted to the duty of her husband is being devoured.
Therefore, a husband must be won over by a wife through reflection; for such is the duty consisting of devotion to her husband.
Indeed, the incomparable power and majesty of virtuous women who regard their husbands as deities cannot be endured even by the Creator, nor by the sun, nor by fire.
Worthy of honor and true, their virtue is ever revered;
likewise, patience, tranquility, celibacy, compassion, self-restraint, friendliness, wisdom, contentment, sovereignty, straightforwardness, and purity. (23)
The supernatural powers (siddhis) are indeed like wish-fulfilling creepers that dwell within the body.
The gurus and the parents, as well as Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī, Hara together with Satī, and the Creator of the Universe along with Sāvitrī [reside there]. 24–25.
The gods, led by Agni, come to the home of a *satī*—
that woman who stands upon the path to liberation, who is the mistress of the household,
who abides in wisdom and magnanimity, and who is devoted to the dharma among virtuous women. (26)
The deities always reside even among virtuous householders.
Mādhava dwells in the home of even a devotee’s family; wherever there are capable saints and saintly women, there I dwell as well. (27–28)
Indeed, my home is a house of satīs, filled with ten thousand who are dear to Brahmā;
I always move about within that dwelling, which is adorned by the virtues of wifely devotion and the like.
Even all the lords and masters come there for the sake of a vision.
O Nārāyaṇī, that house where I dwell is the home of a devoted wife.
O Beloved, for women, beauty, good fortune, amorous charm, happiness, and even prosperity— indeed, all these together— constitute their entire essence and shine forever.

A beloved wife who is empty-handed should never indeed be abandoned by her husband; the one who effects such abandonment incurs fault and becomes a destroyer of the dharma of virtuous women. He who departs after abandoning a modest, pure, and meritorious bride [incurs this same fate].
All the merit he has performed becomes useless because of his lamentation for his daughter-in-law.

He who departs, abandoning a virtuous and meritorious wife who is devoted to righteous conduct— she being chaste, endowed with excellent qualities, and like a young calf— does not obtain the fruit of dharma.
A wife who is virtuous, devoted to all proper conduct, intent on accumulating merit, steadfast in her vows, dedicated to service, wise, and pleasant;
a wife who possesses the quality of knowledge and is auspiciously devoted—[he whose wife is such as this... (35)
And the great Satī always dwells in that house with the gods. Parents desire such a son and daughter-in-law in every way;
the meritorious Satī, endowed with truthfulness, resides in the home as their daughter-in-law.
There, sacrifices, gods, and merit-bestowing sacred fords,
as well as wish-fulfilling cows and wish-granting creepers, dwell forever.
Therein reside all meritorious sacred sites, rivers, and streams.
There, fortunes dwell and riches also abide.
(39) At the sacred ford of the wife, yogis of every virtuous character reside;
through the union with the wife, the husband’s feet take on the very form of a sacred ford. (40)
By the residence of a virtuous wife, the household life becomes truly auspicious and divinely blessed;
it indeed consists of all sacrifices and bestows the fruits of all vows.
For a householder, the home is meritorious, and the wife is meritorious when she is devoted to her husband.
Everywhere, all eternal dharmas prevail:
the practices of giving, festivals of great joy, and so forth.
A forest devoid of a wife is infested with tigers and filled with suffering. (42–43)
There is no sacred ford equal to a wife, the supreme means for accomplishing dharma;
whether in the forest, the village, or the wilderness, the sacred ford of a faithful wife indeed bestows liberation. There is no merit equal to a wife, and there is no happiness equal to a wife.
There is no knowledge equal to a wife for the sake of crossing over [saṃsāra] and for one’s welfare.
(41) If one abandons a virtuous wife who is devoted to dharma and sets his mind elsewhere, what fruit indeed can there be for him who has forsaken the duties of the household? (46)
When an auspicious *śrāddha* or gift is performed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) without one's wife, everything becomes fruitless; therefore, one should not abandon one's spouse.
Just as the satisfaction of the ancestors is produced by the offering of nectar (*amṛta*), [so too is the efficacy of rites dependent on the presence of the wife].
Satisfaction is likewise produced by the funeral ball (piṇḍa) offered by one’s wife.
Indeed, the wife is the mistress of the dharma of the householder;
without her, a śrāddha offering becomes merely lukewarm.
When the wife herself cooks food with her own hands that is like nectar,
the ancestors eat that very food with delighted minds;
by that alone they attain satisfaction and become fully contented.
Therefore, without a wife, the dharma of men is not accomplished.
(5.1) A wife who is virtuous and faithful always certainly establishes dharma.
Sacrifices do not reach fulfillment in a home devoid of a housewife. (5.2)
The sons of Dharma—Puṇya, Jñāna, and the others—are powerful and have truth and righteousness as their gateway;
they are indeed the companions of Dharma who protect Satī in every way.
Satī remains devoted to her protection, dedicated to self-restraint and tranquility.
Neither Time nor Yama himself would indeed be able to conquer her;
for when any person should look upon a virtuous wife in the absence of her husband,
he too shall surely be reduced to ashes by the fire of the virtuous wife's eyes.
Wherever the highly fortunate Satī, the bride who is all-auspicious,
resides, the gods, satisfied by her truthfulness, grant even boons;
and even the divine fires follow her as she departs.
The household deities follow her, and the forest goddesses follow her as well.
As she goes to bathe in the water, the water-deities follow her;
and as she goes on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, the sacred fords themselves follow her.
When Satī was going to the temple of the gods, the goddesses of the gods approached her;
when Satī was going to the garden, the goddesses of the fields approached her;
and when Satī was going to the sacrificial ground, the goddesses of the sacrifice approached her. (59)
When Satī departs on a journey, the Earth follows after Satī.
When Satī bathes, the ancestral goddesses who seek water attend upon her;
they drink that water from Satī’s body as it is squeezed out by her garment.

The wife who always rejoices in her own home through devotion to her husband finds no such happiness even in heaven; the bliss of a virtuous wife is attainable only through spiritual perfection (siddhi).
Indeed, the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest serve the devoted wife.
Desires that are true reach fulfillment, even when they are fashioned in whatever way.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Hara, Indra, Sūrya, Candra, Yama, and Guru bow to Satī and worship Satī, the virtuous woman. (63–64)
All the gods desire their own wives to be virtuous in every way;
even the kings who protect the quarters of the world stand in awe of the power of a woman’s virtue.
She in whom truth and religious observance reside is considered in every respect to be a *satī*.
Where there is devotion to her husband, she is *satī*; she is a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
She who possesses devotion to Brahman is a *satī* and a *brāhmī* devoted wife.
And she who is exclusively devoted to me is a *satī* belonging to Śrī Puruṣottama.
I, the Lord Śrī Puruṣottama, am attainable through abundant merit; my attainment occurs here from the treasury of virtuous conduct accumulated over a hundred births.
By the mere resolve of a chaste woman, diseases depart far away.
Obstacles indeed depart far away, and even Gaṇeśa is truly afraid;
Yama, the King of Death, feels fear, and Kāla goes far off.
And the Mothers become gracious in that house where a devoted wife resides.
Having attained peace, Caṇḍī and the other goddesses protect the house of the virtuous woman;
indeed, the spirits that afflict children do not come within the boundary of the house of the virtuous woman. Nor do plagues, diseases, or even those spells that cause delusion and confusion [enter].
Having encountered fear such as exorcism and the like, even those who are otherwise virtuous avoid the home of a chaste woman.
Though Hanumān was of a Brahminical nature and the commander-in-chief was possessed of good character, they—
those persons known as celibates— bow from afar to the chaste woman.
Even lightning, rain, and oceans undergo terrifying portents;
even the virtuous abandon their own persistence at the word of a faithful wife.
Even the lords themselves [yield] in the presence of a devoted daughter-in-law.
Having met with defeat in some instance, they honor the command of Satī;
through the wrath of Satī, serpents and other creatures become reduced to ashes along with their venom, mountains and the like dissolve away, and even the oceans dry up. (75–76)
The planets, being chastised, become motionless and abandon their course;

the mental deities, such as desire and the rest, go to dissolution through the power of a virtuous woman. The latent impression of worldly existence is utterly consumed by the true blessing of a virtuous woman.
Through the will of a virtuous woman, even the dissolution of Mahāmāyā occurs;
through the anger of a virtuous woman, drought arises; through the delight of a virtuous woman, rain falls;
and through the curse of a virtuous woman, even the lineages and the worlds themselves perish. (78–79)
By the will of Satī, the entire world is born anew;
wherever Satī, the bride, resides, there I myself am present as the Lord,
together with Virāja, the abode, and likewise accompanied by the liberated souls and others.
In Virāja, Śrīpati Puruṣottama is joined by his attendants; in Virāja, he is endowed with dharma;
and in Virāja, he is possessed of devotion. Endowed with all prosperity, I am manifest in the house of Satī.
She is indeed Satī, the virtuous one, devoted to Brahman, and a devotee of Nārāyaṇa; she is considered a chaste wife, a follower of the Sāttvata path, and a great Bhāgavatī.
I, known as Saccidānanda, dwell in the home of Satī.
And by the will of Satī, I shall manifest within her lineage.
I am always pleased in the home of Śrī Satī; I am the Lord Himself, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is ever affectionate toward His devotees.
In that state, I am most perfectly complete; no deficiency exists there, nor does any lack arise, nor even any doubt.
Indeed, for such a person, birth is fruitful, and the home is likewise fruitful.
The expansion of one’s lineage is fruitful when Hari and a virtuous wife reside in one’s home.
For such a person, dharma is fruitful, their ritual actions are always fruitful, and all their efforts are fruitful when Hari and a virtuous wife reside in their home. (87–88)
There is constant bliss, as well as welfare and every form of physical well-being,
wherever there are virtuous women, Hari, Dharma, ascetics, holy men, and gods;
for from such a place, both worldly and otherworldly perfection arises.
Wherever that virtuous woman stayed for even a moment, there Hari himself was present. In a previous birth, he performed supreme and incomparable merit,
by which he obtained a faithful wife and Lord Hari, the Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama).
The principal gods and the virtuous come constantly to behold Satī;
this lake, Aśvapaṭṭasara, is my own abode named after Śiva.
Therefore, indeed, supreme merit accrues to this region.
O Lakṣmī, where there are millions and billions of my wives who are true, they have been beheld by you; they are equal to you and are of my own essence.
And I am Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the most perfect one.
In the divine land of Surāṣṭra, at the sovereign city of Saṃrāja,
in my own sacred field known as Kuṅkuma, which is imperishable and divine— there I,
the Lord of the Abode of Creation, have been brought under control by your devotion.
"O Lakṣmī, I dwell before you, under my own control in your palace.
Oh! All these beloveds of Brahmā receive the nectar of Hari;
by his grace, they drink the mass of bliss that is my own nectar. || 96-97 ||

May you, who are dear to Brahman, whose form is the Supreme Brahman, and who are identical with me, be devoted to my dharma; for women are indeed the bestowers of auspiciousness. Blessed is this Kuṅkumavāpī, and blessed indeed is this Vyāghravana forest.
Blessed is the horse-pasture, and blessed is the land of Surāṣṭra;
blessed is the country, as well as its people, its trees, and its creepers.
Blessed are the clumps of grass, the plants, and the trees; blessed are the cattle, the men, and the women. (3.44.100)
Blessed indeed is this time, and blessed too are these beings,
for whom union with the glorious Hari occurs here moment by moment;
wherein Dharma, rich in family life, exists eternally and happily.
Wherever there is liberation, as well as devotion and love, they indeed exist eternally.
Thinking thus, those men and women who consider themselves blessed and remember the dharma of virtuous wives shall also go to my abode.
From reciting, hearing, and reading this dharma of virtuous women,
as well as from its preservation, liberation and spiritual perfection shall certainly be attained.
Lineage, prosperity, fame, honor, health, and influence [shall also be gained].
"Through such reflection, his state of sovereignty becomes abundant.

(1.05) Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Power of Satī’s Truth," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Chapter 44] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*)
Chapter 45 [Author:
Chapter 46 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O God of gods, ocean of mercy, Supreme Person, Mādhava!
You are devoid of qualities; how can devotion to you, which is itself beyond qualities, be practiced?
I wish to hear this for the benefit of all people and for the sake of all women.
Whatever duty has been performed by all of us who are dear to Brahmā, as well as by other women and men, I desire to hear that correctly; tell me that. (2–3)
All these sisters of mine, numbering in the hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions, desire to hear this; they have sent me here, O Beloved.
I ask about the path of devotion (bhaktiyoga) that is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa); please tell it to us here.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Indeed, actions accompanied by the qualities (guṇas) are possessed of fruit;
those very same actions, when their fruits are surrendered unto Me, are truly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
O beloved, action joined with the desire for fruit becomes a cause of bondage;
action joined with the desire for no fruit becomes a giver of liberation.
Having performed actions characterized by *sattva*, people who are *sāttvika* go to heaven.
In the world of men, those characterized by passion (rājasa), having performed passionate deeds, [attain their corresponding state].
Those characterized by darkness (tāmasa) go to worlds of impurity, people who are absorbed in darkness.
But having attained Me, who am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), they indeed go to My imperishable state.
O beloved, those people who dwell in the forest practicing the five-fire penance, who are free from blemish,

and who partake of the fruits [of their austerities], go to the world of the Seven Sages. Likewise, those who reside in the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and carry the staff and other [emblems] do so as well.
Those who have conquered their senses, mind, and qualities go to the world of truth (satyaloka).
Endowed with the eightfold yoga, self-controlled, with vital energy drawn upward,
and cleansed of all taints, they go to Maharloka and Janaloka.
Sacrificial priests and those who perform sacrifices go for long to the abode of Indra;
donors go to the world of Soma, which rains down nectar. Those who observe vows, possessing great splendor, likewise go to the world of the Sun.
By virtue of their merit, the followers of external paths go to the radiant world of Agni;
likewise, those devoted to truth go to the supreme world of Varuṇa;
and those endowed with devotion to Viṣṇu go to Vaikuṇṭha, from which there is no return to rebirth.
Those endowed with devotion to Śambhu go eternally to the upward-moving Kailāsa;
those who sacrifice for their ancestors, desiring the happiness and sovereignty of sons,
proceed by the southern path of Aryaman to the world of the Pitṛs.
Those who perform meritorious deeds and are devoted to the dharma of mindfulness go to heaven.
Those rich in the worship of the five deities go to the celestial realm.
Those who perform sacrifices to Prajāpati go to the world of the Prajāpatis, such as Dakṣa and others.
Those who perform sacrifices to the spirits (bhūtayajña) go to various kinds of spirits;
those who worship the principles beginning with the earth (bhū-tattva) indeed proceed to the enclosures (āvaraṇas).
Likewise, those who sacrifice to the Yakṣas of Kubera go to the worlds of the Yakṣas.
And those who perform sacrifices go to the stations of the lords;
ascetics go to Badarī, while the virtuous go to Śvetadvīpa. But those of the Brahma-vow, being disciplined in their conduct, go to the worlds of the Vairājas.
Virtuous women, possessing the splendor of the sun, go to the worlds of the *satīs*;
likewise, those women devoted to dharma go to the worlds of Lakṣmī and the worlds of Śrī.
Chaste wives devoted to their husbands go to the worlds of Hari and to the worlds of their husbands.
Those who practice celibacy attain the worlds of those who practice celibacy;
courtesans go to the worlds of the *gaṇas* of those who know their duties;
devotees of Īśa reach the worlds of Īśa; and devotees of Prāṇa reach the realm of the Maruts.
The Asuras go to the worlds of Nirṛti, while sinners go to the worlds of Yama;
those who practice self-restraint and perform austerities go to the worlds of the Ṛṣis, such as Janaloka and others.
Those who delight in Vedic knowledge and are free from passion go to Satyaloka.
The renouncers go to Vaikuṇṭha, situated above the ocean;
those who sacrifice for the sake of power go to the worlds of perfected beings with beautiful women;
those who give wealth go to the worlds of the Vasus; and those who smear themselves with ashes go to the abode of Rudra.
Those who practice the penance of the five fires go to the solar orb;
those possessed by desire go to the world of the Moon, as do those devoted to the giving of cooling gifts. Those who perform cruel deeds go instead to the abodes of the Rākṣasas.
Even those possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā) go to the womb of a Piśāca.
Those who perform acts such as the offering of lamps proceed to the circle of fire.
Bestowers of prosperity indeed go to heaven, which is like a celestial mansion full of exquisite delights.
Those who give orchards and fields attain the status of a sovereign on earth;
likewise, those possessed of learning attain the station of Sarasvatī.
Those who cause the destruction of dharma go to the terrible realm of the Dānavas.
The Daityas become indeed unrighteous and filled with agitation;
and the Nāgas, being angry and performers of cruel deeds, become serpents and go to births among aquatic creatures that cause the depletion of water.
All worlds are considered to end in truth and are subject to return;
for actions accompanied by their causal motives, the path consists of coming and going.
Joy and delight endure only so long as merit remains.
When merit is exhausted, one indeed returns to the lower worlds in the course of time.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, whatever action has been performed should be offered to the Supreme Lord;
through the renunciation of the fruits of action, that which is devoid of qualities arises within me.
O beloved, having become disinterested devotees endowed with knowledge and detachment,
and filled with loving devotion, dear to Kṛṣṇa and the people who are devotees of Hari,
worship my fearless feet, which are served by the *haṃsas*.
O beloved, always resort to Me, where death is not powerful.
O Lakṣmī, the yoga of devotion is twofold: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa).
The saguṇa is indeed manifold, while the nirguṇa is considered to be of one kind. 37–38.
The disposition of women is indeed always characterized by qualities;
from the threefold group of qualities, they arise as devotees beautiful in their threefold divisions.
[They manifest] violence, hypocrisy, envy, deceit, and self-interest.
Having taken hold of an object of thought, she who becomes possessed by emotion out of anger is considered *tāmasī*.
O Queen Śivā! She who, with great effort, worships me while aiming for fame, sovereignty, and sense-objects is proclaimed as *rājasī*. (3.45.40–41)
She who, thinking "this must be done," performs service free from attachment for the sake of liberation, is known as a *sāttvika* servant.
But the one who serves me while suffering, seeking self-interest, possessing discrimination, and being wise, [is of a different nature].
Women indeed serve me for the sake of merit;
my devotees, full of affection, always serve me with happiness;
and others also serve and remember me, whether through virtues or faults.
The virtuous perform the path of devotion (bhaktiyoga) toward Me which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
and those virtuous women who are free from passion worship the excellent Hari.
[They worship] Him who is the most perfect, the cause of all causes.
In the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī, there is a beautiful, uninterrupted, and unbroken flow of love that is causeless;
that is divine, quality-less devotion, which has as its fruit my own gracious favor. || 46-47 ||

That affection which is for the sake of destroying suffering, neither for one’s own sake nor purposeless—by that, the grace of Hari is obtained; she who possesses it is considered *nirguṇā*. Just as devotion is *nirguṇā*, so too is the maidservant *nirguṇā*.

That stream of natural love which flows toward Śrī Puruṣottama has taken the form of love for me; it is devoid of [worldly] qualities (nirguṇā). Its fruit is the nature of bliss, and its fruit is also eternal satisfaction. (3.45.49–50)
Full blossoming is its fruit; enthusiasm is its fruit; and joy is its fruit.
Oh, oh! Its state is like nectar, most desirable and confident;
it bestows the essence of ambrosia—this is considered the fruit of the *nirguṇa* [soul].
Just as, immediately after her marriage,
a stream of longing for union with her own beloved flows forth from a young bride, so too do fresh bliss, joy, blossoming, and serenity arise. || 52-53 ||
Just as oiliness, satiety, contentment,
and bliss appear to a bride as entirely sweet and excellent,
so too does everything appear to a noble woman full of devotion toward me.
This very Vidyā is the mother of the Vedas; she is devoid of qualities (nirguṇā) and has my own nature as her form.
She is never born anywhere at all apart from me.
This is that eternal Vidyā of the Bhāgavatas, belonging to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
This very state of clarity is obtainable through my dwelling within;
it is indeed not obtainable by any other means, for it is devoid of attributes and cannot exist without that which is devoid of attributes.
Just as a servant has no affection for a king nor any grace from a king without [the king's own presence].
Likewise, without my grace, this yoga does not arise at all.
O Lotus-born One, hear from me the characteristics of my devotees who are beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa)!
[They attain] the Imperishable, as well as Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the White Realm (Śvetabhūtala). ||58-59||
The abode of milk, Badrikā, or the station of the Supreme Lord (Pārameṣṭhya);
the Unmanifest (Avyākṛta) and the Immortal (Amṛta), as well as the world of Lakṣmī and Prakuṇṭhaka;
the Vairāja realm and the various stations of the Īśvaras.
The throne of Śakra, universal sovereignty, and even lordship over the [six] tastes;
the status of a world-protector, the state of Yama, the supernatural power of yoga, and the supreme Vaiśravaṇa-hood;
likewise, wonders, the perfections (siddhis), and even great powers of lordship.
O Lakṣmī, those devotees who serve at my feet do not desire even the supreme state of *sālokya* being offered by me;
filled with the bliss of my service, they never accept it. (62–63)
Out of pride in their love, they do not even desire proximity, for it is indeed a wound;
even separation, which obstructs union, is a great obstacle to touch.
Yet, at times, the very love that exists when one is near attains a state of distance.

Therefore, my presence is never found in those who consider themselves equal to me. Furthermore, even when I bestow the mental realization of my own nature, my devotees do not accept it because of their pride in their own equality [with me]. (65–66)
Impartiality toward my servants is an obstacle, and indifference is likewise an obstacle;
therefore, those eager for my service do not accept a state of equality with me.
Furthermore, my own people do not desire unity [with me] when it is being offered.
Indeed, in a state of liquefaction or dissolution, there would surely be oneness.

That being the case, how could there be happiness arising from the relationship of master and servant? Surely the pleasure obtainable by a maidservant could not possibly come from a beloved husband, such as Hari. || 68-69 ||
If, however, there were formlessness, unity would indeed be possible for the devotee.
This being so, how could the bliss born of yoga exist within one form after another?
Therefore, the bliss of service would not be obtained, nor would one desire unity.

Free from attachment, peaceful, and endowed with equal vision, women who follow after their beloved’s happiness become free from the *guṇas*. Freedom from attachment is the great bliss; those who are free from attachment take refuge in Hari.
Those with desires attain great happiness, but those free from desire do not.
Indeed, the yoga of devotion without desire becomes the ultimate state.
Those who are indifferent to worldly things always worship me in various ways as their beloved.
Indeed, they practice devotion through mindfulness, by chanting [His names], and by hearing [of Him];
through service, worship, and prostration; through servitude and friendship; and even through self-surrender and love. (74–75)
Rare are those women who possess devotion for me and are imbued with the contemplation of my true nature;
who show honor toward great beings and likewise extend compassion;
and who practice loving-kindness toward the wretched as well as toward their equals.
They are honey-bees at my lotus-feet, longing for union with me;
they do not forget me, their lord of life, just as women whose husbands are away from home do not forget their absent spouses.
At the mere thought of me, their hair stands on end and perspiration breaks forth. (77–78)
With tears of joy falling and their complexions changed by the intensity of their love,
they constantly chant the names of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
day and night, being attached to Me, they are indeed the most excellent of devotees.
With their minds fixed on me, their hearts centered on me, and offering all their limbs unto me alone;
with me as the sole enjoyer of their bliss, they are the most exalted of great devotees (mahābhāgavatas).
[They perceive me] in earth, water, fire, air, space, and in the stars. (3.45.80–81)
In the woods and forests, among moving beings, seeing me, the Supreme Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, they are filled with great joy; gazing upon me,
those loving women weep and speak.
In some places they rejoice, run about, laugh, and search;
they sing, call out fiercely, dance, and take delight; they sport, chatter, and behold me within the trees. (83–84)
In some instances, these women, who are my own form and whose essence is me, remain silent;
they have accomplished their duty, achieved their purpose, and are overflowing with all-encompassing bliss.
Merely by the sight of them, others likewise attain the fulfillment of their aims.
For those brides are divine, possessing divine rites and divine forms. Indeed, for those eternal ones, neither Time nor Yama has power;
neither the Earth nor Mahārudra is ever capable of inflicting punishment upon them. (86–87)
In whose left hands are the mace Kaumodakī and in the right the Sudarśana;
in front is the Śārṅga bow and behind the conch Pāñcajanya;
and likewise in front is the great sword Nandaka, adorned with a hundred moons.
Arrows are positioned all around, and a parasol is situated above;
at the feet and on both sides are the peaks of sovereignty.
All the supernatural powers (siddhis), my beloved ones, protect me within this form.
Above, the great lotus umbrella provides beautiful shade;
Garuḍa also becomes the remover of fatigue with the winds from his wings.
Wherever the Satīs go, there the Lord Hari is present.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and I wander about.
I sanctify the regions of the earth with the dust of my glorious lotus feet;
for wherever the Satīs remain for even a moment, there indeed are sacred pilgrimage sites.

Even a sinner who dies there attains the supreme goal; and upon seeing her from afar, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, neither mental agonies nor physical ailments prevail. Likewise, ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like, as well as seizing demons, obstacles, and rākṣasas [are dispelled].
The Asuras, partaking of faults, flee from me out of fear.
Rivers, streams, mountains, walls, moats, pits, abysses, oceans, and likewise fires [all become my weapons]. (95–96)
I grant the path only to those virtuous women who are indeed indifferent [to worldly things].
For those virtuous women who are established in knowledge, detached,
whose very selves are absorbed in Me— there is no obstacle whatsoever for them anywhere.
Purified by ascetic penance through a hundred births and endowed with a mass of merit,
she attains their company— a state difficult for those who have lost their merit to reach—
when a woman possessing the marks of Brahman is born as a devotee in my lineage. (98–99)
That family is to be known as stainless, and even if lowly, it shall ascend upward.
O Lakṣmī, she who is endowed with devotion toward me is possessed of all sovereign powers.
She delivers her ancestors born of ten generations, herself, and those belonging to her husband’s side.
She rescues even as many members of her mother’s lineage;
she is considered endowed with such power that she is capable of uplifting the entire cosmic egg and casting those bound by sin out of the hells.
Those who possess bodies, as well as relatives—whether male or female—and those such as servants, friends, and laborers;
even birds, animals, and living creatures such as mosquitoes and the like. (103)
Ants, moths, insects, flies, and the like—
whatever male or female creatures dwell in my house— they shall surely attain liberation, without doubt, even without sacrifices, pilgrimages, or bulls.
Through association with virtuous women, even they go to the abode of Hari.
Indeed, even in an impure place, my devotees purify the worlds.
She who fixes her mind upon me with any disposition whatsoever [attains the same].
Through my repeated practice, she too attains my very form in whatever way that may be.
Having become one with me through affection, desire, fear, anger, unity, friendship, and delusion, that virtuous woman goes to my abode. (107–108)
Out of affection, parents and common folk; out of desire, those dear to Brahmā;
out of fear, the Daityas and Dānavas; out of anger, warriors on the field of battle;
out of unity, countless members of a family; and out of friendship, the stainless sages. (109)
Out of delusion, many millions of noble women became absorbed in meditation upon me;
with their minds fixed on the power of my form and qualities,
they indeed attained me, the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, one should direct the mind toward Me with whatever disposition possible;
by means of constant remembrance of Me, one attains My state of being.
(11.2) Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Nirguṇa Bhakti-yoga," within the *Vadhū-gītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
