Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this specific application of devotion;
neither fame, nor sacrifice, nor dharma, nor austerity restrains me. (1)
Neither yoga nor even solitude, neither vows nor restraints (yamas), nor sacred fords, nor Vedic hymns, nor public works, nor observances (niyamas);
neither charity, nor sacrificial fees, nor any desired rite ever [bear fruit] without devotion. (2)
Whatever is attained through fame and other such means, all that is indeed attained [by this].
But by even a small amount of devotion, O Lakṣmī, the state of devotion—which is higher than that—is reached.
This state of devotion cannot be attained by those who are incapable and who rely on these [other] pedestals.
My devotion is indeed the purifier that removes all worldly sins;
it is the deliverer from the ocean of existence and the destroyer of karmic bonds.
It is the bestower of honors, the giver of spiritual perfections, and the grantor of the state of Hari.
Vasantapañcamī bestows delight upon devoted followers;
she is a wish-fulfilling creeper for the affectionate and a thought-gem for those possessed of desire.
She is a flash of lightning for the blind devotees and a lamp for those who follow the scriptures.
The Dīpāvalī festival is the preeminent celebration for those of virtuous deeds;
this Vijayā-daśamī is auspicious for those who are victorious and self-controlled.
It is a boat for those desiring to reach the further shore, and a celestial chariot for those seeking the heavens.

She is the warming power for those submerged in cold, the giver of life to those afflicted by hunger, and the restorer of life to those consumed by poison. She is the bringer of the highest good to those seeking it, the ladder to the imperishable abode, and the mother of those who receive initiation. (3.46.10)
My devotion is beyond the gunas, my staff-bearer is always the giver of yoga;
she bestows the abode of Brahman, grants the bliss of Brahman, and is never-receding.
She is Śrī, Pārvatī, Kamalajā, Tulasī, and Padmā.
Padmāvatī, Bhṛgusutā, and Padminī;
Rādhā, Ramā, Virajā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Ramā, Badarī, Padmaratī, and Lakṣmī. (12)
Revā, Rati, Lalitā, Jayā, Haṃsī, Bhakti, Mādhavasutā, and then Māṇikī;
Nārāyaṇī, Suguṇā, and Mañjulā.
By reciting [His name], women here cross the ocean of existence.
Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable, Puruṣottama, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Supreme Lord, and the Lord of Lords.
The Master, the Lord, the Sovereign of the supreme abode, the Supreme Ruler dwelling within all—here He has assumed a human form as Kṛṣṇa;
dark-hued yet white, the Lord of all devotees, He dwells within the heart. 14.
Though he transcends even Brahmā, he dwells among the assembly of his own devotees;
by chanting my auspicious name "Brahmapriyeśa," those men who possess devotion to me reach the further shore. 15.

Through association with the virtuous, the sprout of devotion surely becomes well-leafed; and when watered by association with the virtuous, it grows with extreme rapidity. Therefore, one should indeed cultivate association with the virtuous through body, mind, and speech.
One should always perform service through action, attendance, and total self-surrender.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now declare the method of service, by which a householder may cross over [saṃsāra].
Through such service, one may attain me, Hari, the Lord of Śrī, who is the Supreme Brahman.
By taking refuge in a virtuous Guru who is solely devoted to meditation upon the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, a human woman becomes a perfected being (siddhā).
By taking refuge in a virtuous female Guru, a human woman becomes a saintly woman (sādhvī).
Indeed, human beings, having found a guru, cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
My guru, the most excellent of teachers, shall be initiated by me;
he, or she, shall be an authorized servant of mine.
One should indeed teach the ritual of service for me, my Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should cause a beautiful temple for me to be constructed facing north,
enriched with a thousand pitchers or even more than a single pitcher.
There, a lofty elephant-throne with its pedestal, adorned with a water-pot (kumbha), should be fashioned.

It is known as the Imperishable (akṣara), consisting of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), made of gold, beautified by many steps, and decorated with gems, jewels, and other ornaments. (23–24)
Covered with precious gems, it was resplendent with a cloth on its back; its upper garment was a protective covering, and it was adorned with cotton mattresses and the like.
It was provided with soft side-cushions and other such items, and was beautified with gold.
It was furnished with luxurious cushions and shaded by canopies and the like;
it was enriched by the beauty of variegated sacrificial pits and featured the Sarvatobhadra mandala, resplendent with beautiful arches, latticed windows, and water-fountains. (26–27)
It was illuminated by the light from the vast latticed windows of its four-winged halls,
and the courtyard was beautifully adorned with a magnificent assembly pavilion.
It was lovely, graced by *tulasī* plants and resplendent with two elephants.
Adorned at the front with auspicious lions, tigers, Garuḍas, and others, the Sudarśana discus, bearing its name, should be placed above the archway at the entrance;
my names should be inscribed upon the arches on all sides. (3.46.30)
A conch, a lotus, a mace, and the Śārṅga bow should be painted on the walls;
arrows, quivers, and scabbards are prescribed on both sides in every respect.
On the rear part of the temple, there should be the hundred-moon design and the Nandaka sword.
A plow and a pestle, beautiful in nature, should also be depicted.
On the back of the elephant-throne, on my side, let the queen Pata-yosita be painted;
and then the beloveds of Brahmā, the gopīs, the cows, and the maidservants. (32–33)
There were liberated souls, virtuous women, truthful and stainless holy men,
and incarnations in the form of cowherds on the steps and at the door-panels;
there were wish-fulfilling trees at the threshold and creepers upon the pillars.
On the walls [should be depicted] the Gomatī, the Gaṅgā, the Svarṇarekhā, and the Aśvapaṭṭaka;
the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Bhadrā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; as well as paintings of the Rāsa-dance, the festival of birth, the horse sacrifice, and other such rites. (35–36)
The paintings of the ten incarnations, the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
and sacred pilgrimage sites should be fashioned with colors in the middle of the hall;
[the deity] having the form of a youth, with conch, discus, mace, and lotus in his hands.

Having caused my own image, measuring sixty-five and a quarter finger-breadths and possessing the luster of the color of a white campaka flower, to be fashioned, one should install it in the temple by the rite of consecration through the hand of the Guru and worship it. (38–39)
With supreme devotion, the devotee should worship the Supreme Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Brahmapriyā. Both the female devotee and the male devotee should always, day and night, remain intent upon Me.
One should make one’s tongue the taste of my grace, the nose the scent of my lotus leaves;
one should make the skin the touch of me, and likewise the ears the hearing of me;
one should apply the eyes to the sight of me, and likewise the hands, feet, and other limbs.
She should offer herself in the practice of my service and thus remain devoted to service;
indeed, they call that devotee, who is filled with the weight of love, the most excellent of Bhāgavatas.
Even ten thousand horse-sacrifices and ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices [are not equal to her].
They can never equal even a fraction of my service.
(44) The demonstration of worship to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa and service unto Him indeed bestows fruit; there is no doubt in this matter. (45)
Ten million sins are destroyed by serving one’s guru and preceptor.
At the end of the body, those who possess the luster of white campaka flowers, being liberated in my divine state,
come leading an elephant to take them to my imperishable abode.
They lead her away, placing her upon a celestial chariot, a garuḍa, or even an elephant.
Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, the virtuous woman should remember my name;
then, having bowed to me, her guru, she should perform the rinsing of her mouth.
Having quickly sat upon a seat and mastered one's breath,
one should then place both hands in the lap and meditate upon me, the beloved of my devotees—
bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and intent on bestowing blessings. (49)
One should meditate upon Acyuta, seated in the svastika posture, profoundly peaceful, accompanied by Brahmapriyā, attended by noble women,
beautiful in every limb, delightful, and adorned with all ornaments. (3.46.50–51)
Having thus meditated upon me as a youth of white form, encircled by a halo of splendor, one should then depart elsewhere for the sake of purifying the body;
for otherwise, all ritual actions performed during a state of impurity become fruitless.
O Dear One, one should perform the purification of the body with water and so forth, as well as through bathing and other such rites.
Devotion does not flourish at all for one who is devoid of the purification of the inner being (sattva).
For one who is devoid of the purification of the mouth, the recitation of mantras is useless.
Longevity, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, and wealth—as well as sacred knowledge, wisdom, and retentive memory—the supreme purification bestows these.
One should bow to the sun; one should bow to the elders; and likewise, the elders should bow to virtuous women.
One should bow to and serve virtuous women, as well as virtuous people;
one should lead devotees of Hari and [visit] temples and other such places;
one should utter the sacred names and likewise remember them.
Sāketa, Madhupurī, Māyā, Kāśī, Avantī, Kāñcī, Suvarṇanagarī, Purī, Puruṣottamī,
and Kuṅkumavāpikā— these grant liberation; one should likewise bow down to them.
Śālagrāma is in the Gaṇḍakī river; Śambhala is in the abode of Hari.
Nandigrāma is situated in Kosala; likewise, one should remember Akṣaragrāma, Daṇḍaka, the Saindhava forest, the region of Jambū, and Puṣkara. (3.46.59–60)
One should likewise remember the forest of Utpalāvarta, Naimiṣa, Kurujāṅgala, Arbuda, Hemavanta, and Vyāghrāraṇya.
One should apply a tilaka mark on the forehead, adorned with red saffron.
O virtuous lady, one should likewise apply a crescent-shaped mark made with saffron in the center of the forehead.
Then, having gone toward the temple, one should ring the bell and perform kīrtana and bhajana while remembering the Supreme Lord.
She should bow to the Lord while uttering cries of victory and clapping her hands;
she should also light a lamp scented with fragrant ghee.
"Arise, arise, O Blessed One! O Lord, abandon your yogic sleep!"
Saying, "I have come for service," one should thus cause Hari to rise.
One should perform the massaging of His feet and attend to the service of His limbs.
Having offered a tooth-stick, one should bathe Him with scented waters.
One should offer me the essence of fragrance and other such items, and then offer garments;
one should worship me with sandalwood paste and the like, and perform the auspicious *ārtikya* rite.
One should cause the lamp, lit before my face, to be circumambulated nine times.
Having whirled the five-fold wick, water, and cloth, one should utter "Victory! (jaya).
Having offered various cooked foods and milk mixed with sugar, and having performed the act of adornment with devotion through garments, ornaments, and auspicious rites.
One should perform the offering of light with lamps, necklaces, and other such items, as well as with erotic adornments;
one should present sweetmeats, *laḍḍu*s, fresh butter, curd, and milk.
Then, having offered these five types of enjoyments, one should bow and offer betel leaf and water.
Then, eager for worldly affairs, she should attend to her own duties;
at midday, she should offer various delicious foods of great enjoyment.
Having prepared everything necessary for royal luxury, she should arrange my bed.
The virtuous woman should always eat food accompanied by *prasāda* and *tulasī*.
When four *ghaṭikās* remain of the day,
she should awaken me with the sound of musical instruments and devotion, and offer the enjoyment of fruits.
Then he should perform service for me and carry out his own daily rites and so forth.
Then he should perform the waving of lights (ārati) and offer milk and other substances.
At twilight, having again performed the waving of lights and offered my desired enjoyments, [he should proceed].

She should prepare a delightful bed and perform service to the King; by making a total offering of herself, the virtuous woman shall attain supreme bliss. Thus, that chaste lady, devoted to Kṛṣṇa, keeps her mind fixed on his service.

Devoted solely to the service of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, she delivers a hundred generations of her lineage and goes to my imperishable abode. Likewise, the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī and Rādhāṣṭamī festivals should be observed by me. (77–78)
The Lakṣmī-navamī should be observed with vows, festivals, and worship;
likewise the Rāmāditya-navamī and the Vāmana-dvādaśī.
There should also be a festival of food-heaps (annakūṭa), as well as the Ananta-caturdaśī.
The fourteenth day is for Nṛsiṃha, as well as my own birthdays; the seventh day of the bright fortnight in Kārtika, known as Ramā-saptamī, should be observed as a vow,
and the meritorious full moon of Caitra should be celebrated with festivities.
On a sacrificial ground endowed with five colors,
one should cause a beautiful and auspicious mandala called Sarvatobhadra to be made, consisting of seven kinds of grain,
possessing thirty-two petals, and radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
O virtuous one, one should place me upon a golden lion-throne in the pericarp (karṇikā),
along with Ramā, Rādhā, Śrī, Bhū, Virajā, Māṇikī, Rati,
Padmāvatī, Lakṣmī, Amṛtā, and Maṅgalā.
One should install Durgā, Sarasvatī, Haṃsī, Mañjulā, Sadguṇā, Jayā, Campā,
Kastūrikā, Haimī, Śāntā, Muktā, and Devikā in the midst of those virtuous women,
and myself, who am dear to my devotees.
One should also establish the other companions of Rādhā, as well as my attendants;
[and one should place] the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the Śārṅga bow, the arrows, and the sword Nandaka;
the club, the plow, the staff, the Kaustubha gem, and likewise the svastika.
One should establish the forest garland (vanamālā), the Śrīvatsa mark, the yellow garment (pītāmbara), and the staff-bearer; also Garuḍa, and the palm-tree that adorns the chariot;
as well as Sumati, Dāruka, Kumuda, and Kumudākṣaka.
Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Bala;
likewise Prabala, Vallabha, Śuka, and Bhāgavata;
Svaprakāśa, Hemanta, and Bhagavant—the lords of the directions.
One should likewise install Viśvaksena, the Imperishable (Akṣara), Śiva, Viṣṇu, Vināyaka,
the planets, the gods, the Mothers, the circle beginning with Brahmapriyā,
Vītihotra, and all the incarnations.
Then, the virtuous woman should worship you with devotion through the rites of invocation and so forth:
invocation, the seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering, fragrant scents, the five nectars, a bath with water, ornaments, garments, and sandalwood paste. (91–92)
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), incense and lamps, fragrance, a sacred thread, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), delightful liquids, saffron, excellent water, water for sipping (ācamana),
food offerings (naivedya), betel leaf, and likewise a priestly fee (dakṣiṇā). || 93 ||
One should perform circumambulation, offer prayers, prostrate like a staff, and ask for forgiveness.
Then one should present the waving of lights (*nīrājana*), prostrations, and a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
After that, [one should worship] all the presiding deities, the goddesses, the attendants (*pārṣada*), and so forth.
A devoted woman, firm in her vow of chastity, should worship with supreme devotion while sounding bells,
cymbals, bronze lutes, flutes, and other instruments,
and performing hymns and dances accompanied by hand-clapping, mṛdaṅga drums, and the like.
Those devotees who, overwhelmed with love, should dance before Śrī Hari;
and those intent on recounting and narrating the sacred stories, uttering cries of "Victory!"—
they all should perform the dance and then the circumambulation.

And those who are truthful and devoted to me should have a bed prepared for me; for such a wife, a woman whose primary concern is service, I always dwell upon her lap and likewise within her heart. (99)
She too, having established her station in the celestial realm (nāka), indeed proceeds to my abode. Whoever— be they anyone at all— shall perform worship to me within the three worlds,
they shall go to my imperishable abode, which bestows the four goals of human existence.
May he worship me with devotion, remember me, or serve me; may he feed me, delight me, adorn me, and gladden me.
Having become my companion, may he lay me down upon his bed.
One should massage me, carry me, place me on one's lap, and even make me dance;
one should practice all forms of devotion consisting of love, and cause others to do so as well.
She indeed shall be dear to me, ever accompanying me, and she will become beloved by Brahman.
Whether he be a human or one liberated through Brahman, whoever truly knows the Self is indeed a divine attendant, eternal and equal to Me; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Yoga of Śrī Puruṣottama," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 46: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age), Chapter 47 [[Author:
→ Chapter 48
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to my supreme and transcendent yoga, directed toward Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the Universe, who bestows the fruits of all desires. (1)
She who would place her love in me, Kṛṣṇa, shall attain the supreme state;
O Lakṣmī, even a Cāṇḍālī woman intent on meditation upon me becomes a deity. A courtesan established in yoga with me transcends the qualities (guṇas) and follows a divine course.
Endowed with knowledge of the inner self and devoted to the worship of Hari,
one attains the imperishable abode from which there is no return—
(3) that from which this universe was born and by which consciousness is experienced. (4)
In whom all things dissolve, and by whom they are pervaded so that they live;
who, though devoid of qualities, appears as if possessed of qualities—He is the Supreme, the Infinite, who, ever abiding within, is the destroyer of the fear of saṃsāra. (5) He who am I, He is that.
By worshipping Me, the Lord of the beloved, one is completely liberated from the cycle of worldly existence.
Through action the embodied soul obtains a body, and through desire it is bound;
by uniting that desire with Me, one shall attain the state which has Me as its supreme goal.
Deprived of me, she becomes possessed by desire and overcome by anger;
greed indeed enters her and brings about the destruction of her virtue.
It produces confusion of mind and leads the person toward sin.

Thus, O beloved, the body would be the root of evil without me. Therefore, having attained union with me, one should go beyond the qualities that are defects; having withdrawn all perception, one rests in the abode of the Imperishable.
Knowing Him to be the giver of liberation, let the woman devoted to truth serve Him;
He is worshipped with various sacrifices by those who know the meaning of the Vedas and understand ritual action,
by those observing vows, by ascetics, by practitioners of yoga, and by those for whom knowledge is the sacrifice.
He alone bestows the fruits of action and grants liberation to those whose actions are free from desire.
(1.2) The sages know that Blessed One who, assuming the forms of deities and ancestors during the offerings of *havya* and *kavya*, partakes of my oblations; He is the giver of liberation. (1.3)
Whether meditated upon, saluted, or worshipped with devotion, I grant the eternal abode; one should worship that very Hari, me.
I alone am the Supreme Lord, the support of all beings.
I am Hari, the imperishable, liberated from old age and death, the bestower of liberation.
O Nārāyaṇī, even embodied beings who fully worship my lotus feet quickly attain immortality; know me to be Puruṣottama. 15–16.

Blissful, undecaying Brahman, the supreme eternal light, higher than the highest—that am I; that is the supreme state of Viṣṇu. It is non-dual, devoid of qualities, eternal, without a second, and incomparable.
This is the most perfect means for liberation, consisting entirely of knowledge.
O Lakṣmī, that Yoginī who worships me in such a manner with total devotion reaches my supreme state. (18–19)
Free from qualities, devoid of attachment, adorned with virtues such as tranquility,
and liberated from latent impressions, that beloved Brāhmī attains the imperishable state.
Indeed, my forms of incarnation appear as pairs.
All of them support me, Hari, the bestower of the eternal abode.
(2.1) Having meditated upon Him—who is the undivided whole of all this, both that which moves and that which does not move—the virtuous woman is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence. (2.2)
Having conquered their vital breaths and conquered their food, they are solely devoted to my service;
in their hearts they behold me as the Beloved, the bestower of all bliss and happiness.
Though devoid of qualities, I become the substratum of qualities for the sake of the service performed by the virtuous woman.
I accept [this prayer], assuming a form for the grace of all the worlds.
(24) The overseer of all actions, dwelling in the hearts of embodied beings, incomparable and the support of all—let him indeed go to me for refuge. (25)
Know me to be that Hari, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the flawless one, by whose will the principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas were produced through his creative act;
and by whose command Aniruddha creates the world in its various forms.
Pradyumna remains as the protector, and Saṃkarṣaṇa draws [all things] away.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa are His portions, devoted to His activities. One should know Me to be that sustainer of all portions; from that, one attains liberation.
That knowledge which is rooted in devotion is indeed the knowledge that bestows liberation.
Devotion consists of the performance of action and the service characterized by affection; it is the most auspicious and supreme.
[It encompasses] gifts, various sacrifices, vows, pilgrimages, worship, and so forth.
May there be devotion toward me, Hari, for that [devotion] which was practiced by those of old.
Even a mere fragment of devotion shines as the eternal, supreme dharma.
Endowed with supreme faith, one becomes a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata) unto me.
When the defects are dissolved, the intellect always becomes serene.
Those defects, such as attachment and the rest, have been cast into me by the wise;
since they transform into virtues within me, only virtues arise.
And the intellect endowed with those qualities is supreme, serene, and confident.
It is a stream consisting of knowledge, and through it, I am attained.
That intellect, being of the nature of knowledge, indeed bestows liberation and grants my abode.
Having performed *kriyāyoga* toward Me, one should acquire purity of mind;
then, through the yoga of service, one should constantly serve Me as My maidservant.
[The elements] arise from the earth, water, fire, sun, the Brahman, the heart, and various minerals.
Virtuous women, cows, yogis, the intellect, and so forth—these are my forms (mūrtayaḥ).
Deities, shrines, sacred fords, and so forth—these are my manifestations (vibhūtayaḥ).
Among these, I alone am to be worshipped, just as Janārdana is worshipped in his consort.
She who, endowed with devotion, worships me— the omnipresent one— with action, mind, speech, and devotion, shall become one with Brahman (brāhmī).
Just as a wife, when united with her husband, possesses his human nature and even his divine nature.
Divinity is certainly not attained by observing faults such as desire and anger.
However, if a wife were to always maintain divinity toward her husband with her mind,
serving him with the vision of Nārāyaṇa, that service would grant liberation.
If divine vision is directed toward the form of a woman or an image,
that [vision] shall indeed grant liberation, just as the mind [directed] toward a Śiva-liṅga.
Likewise, virtuous men and virtuous women are my forms and my images.
Having established a pure and divine vision toward them, one should perform service.
These images composed of the five elements are indeed sentient and are truly mine;
for by pleasing them, I myself become well-pleased.
Therein, the offering of action is performed; I accept that which consists of service.
And I bestow upon the female servant the supreme, imperishable state, the abode.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, celibacy, and non-possessiveness—these are the [virtues].
Freedom from envy, compassion, tranquility, and service—these are the virtuous qualities.
(45) Having entrusted all things to me, one should practice my yoga.
The Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama is the self of all moving and non-moving beings. (46)
Realizing this, the beloved wife should make Śrī Hari her own husband and worship Him;
for this yoga is of the nature of the goal to be attained, supreme, and directly identical with Me.
It is the very essence of attaining Me, and the wise know it thus.
Having abandoned faults and indeed making my virtues her own form within Hari,
the virtuous woman should worship me, the beloved Lord of all, with complete devotion.
For the sake of liberation, the beloved wife, dedicated to the yoga of action, should worship me constantly.
She is devoted both to the welfare of the world and to her own welfare;
that virtuous woman, performing divine rites, indeed worships me— Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe, Hari, the inner controller of all.
One praises me in the morning with hymns and the like, and sings to the Lord with recitations;

furthermore, through fasting and other observances, by listening to and reflecting upon the sacred stories, and by worship with flowers and other offerings—that indeed is considered divine action. (51–52)
For those who thus possess the practice of devotion, faults are destroyed at their very root;
even desire, anger, and the like surely attain a divine state.
Furthermore, the intellect becomes divine, bestowing liberation and filled with knowledge.
Except for me, the one Nārāyaṇa, everything is impermanent.
(54) Indeed, all things are impermanent, while the Lord Hari alone is eternal;
therefore, one should take refuge in that one eternal being by means of impermanent instruments. (55)
One should always remain detached from enjoyments both here and hereafter;
for one who is not detached never turns back from saṃsāra at all.
Endowed with qualities such as tranquility (śama) and the rest, one should practice that which brings about the awakening to liberation.
She should be devoted to meditation on Hari and possess a purified intellect. (57) She should contemplate me everywhere as Śrīpati, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Pervading the entire universe consisting of the perishable and the imperishable, I, Kṛṣṇa, abide [therein]. (58)
Knowing this, one who has taken refuge in devotion should worship me everywhere.
By its very nature, the Self is twofold: the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (apara).
I, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama, am the supreme Self and the supreme [reality].
Many of my incarnations, such as Rādhā, Kṛṣṇa, and others, are recognized.
The auspicious splendor of my form is called the imperishable Self (ātman).
There are many liberated souls, and they are all considered secondary (aparā) to me.
The lords, the powers, the gods, the goddesses, humans and others— all these,
as well as all other living beings, become possessors of bodies within this world.
Thus is the conscious awareness of both the individual soul (jīvātman) and the supreme soul (paramātman).
Having performed [these rites], the virtuous woman should always worship the supreme Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

He is the one, the pure, the one beyond the imperishable (akṣara), the Supreme Self, and the Lord of individual souls; the Lord of Māyā, Time, and the Imperishable, as well as the Master of incarnations and the Sovereign.
Hari is the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of those dear to Brahman,
the Lord of the chaste, the Lord of devotees, the Lord of his devotees, and the Lord of his beloved.
He is the Lord of Brāhmī, the Lord of all, the Lord of himself, and the Supreme Lord.
And one should contemplate that He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
(66) That which is the one, non-dual, supreme, eternal Brahman, knowable through the Vedāntas—that very Imperishable One, having known Me as such, one shall attain. (67)
I alone am supreme bliss, devoid of qualities, higher than the highest;
I am Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, filled with divine attributes.
To the wise, I appear as the Supreme Self, shining eternally within the heart.
Having ascended the eight steps, she attains my supreme state.
(6.9) Purity of food is the first; purity of body is the second;
purity of the senses is the third; and internal purity is the fourth. (3.47.70)
"The fifth is indeed the purification of the self, the sixth is the concentration on the Supreme Self;
the seventh is the practice of meditation, and the eighth is absorption therein.
Having thus established this group of eight, the virtuous woman should take refuge in me in brief. (7.1)
For by eating my grace, that indeed is the purity of food;
and being joined with my initiation, that is considered the purity of the body.
Indeed, the third purity is that the senses are employed for my sake.
The instruments [of action] are for my sake, and purification occurs in the interval; indeed, that is considered purification.
Self-surrender to me, Kṛṣṇa, consists in possessing divine and excellent qualities.
For in this context, the excellence of *sattva* itself is considered to be self-purification.

A virtuous woman should always contemplate her own self as being of the nature of Brahman—eternal, liberated, the great liberation, and the primordial Lakṣmī. Indeed, that is declared to be the purity of the self, free from Māyā and its products. (75–76)
Having made his own throne, he should cause me, the Supreme Lord, to be mounted upon it;
he should bear me, establish me, and practice my yoga.
I dwell within the consciousness in the form of that which is fit for my support.

That very state is my abode; it is considered the supreme sustenance of the Self. (78) It is the one-pointed concentration upon me as the object of cognition, and it is the one-pointed flow of all bliss. (79)
That which is the one-pointedness of the flood of all light;
that which is the one-pointedness of the flood of all consciousness; and that which is the one-pointedness of the flow of wisdom as far as it extends.
That very state in which the uninterrupted flow [of consciousness] is fixed upon Me is called the seventh meditative state (*dhyāna-vṛtti*), the excellent "staircase" (*sopānikā*).
This occurs when the dissolution of the self into the cycle of mental states has reached its highest point within Śrī Hari.
The offering of the attracted consciousness is non-dual yoga;
that is the supreme *samādhi*, which yields eternal bliss.
Wherein the manifestation of the nature of the Supreme Lord is found, [that is it].
Indeed, there exists no appearance of one's own [separate self]; that is the eighth state, the supreme abiding.
When the form consisting of the bliss of Brahman, which is one's own true nature and the very form of the Supreme Lord, shines forth, one attains all desires together with Me.
Happiness, contentment, satisfaction, fulfillment, bliss, celebration, delight, serenity, joy, great joy, and the coloring of consciousness;
wave, expansion, enjoyment, goodness, and supreme sovereignty. (86)
Full blossoming, horripilation, affection, love, cessation [of worldly activity],
attraction, rest, the great deep sleep, and also the fourth state (turya), innate bliss— thus it is known by many names. (87–88)
The fruit is described by those who know it, and that very state is the eighth stage.
Having attained it, there is no returning again—indeed, no, indeed no.
Thus, O Nārāyaṇī, has the eightfold yoga been explained by me.
May she indeed marry me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

His throat is in her throat; Hari’s chest is upon her chest. [Likewise] his arms, hands, forearms, fingers, and nails are there. (74–75)
Her arms, hands, forearms, fingers, and nails are Hari’s;
her sides are Hari’s sides, and her belly is indeed Hari’s belly.
Her navel is Hari’s navel, and her hips are Hari’s hips.

her private parts were in Hari’s private parts, and her thighs in Hari’s thighs;
his knees were in her knees, and her shanks in Hari’s shanks. (77–78)
In the feet and the hoods of Hari, there are also the feet and the hoods;
in the bones of Śrī Hari, there are bones, and in the skin, there is also skin.
In the hairs of Śrī Hari, there are hairs, and in the mind, there is the mind.

Indeed, through taking refuge in the company of the virtuous and by serving the Guru, that [impurity] is purified; becoming stainless, it shines and even transcends. Released from the bonds of Māyā, Kāla, and Kriyā, it attains liberation for me.

Then the swans flew up and rolled in the dust at Cyavana’s feet;

Once consecrated by Cyavana, they indeed became white;

O grandfather, who indeed were those swans that were previously black in color?
"Afterwards, how did they become white, and where did they go thereafter? (15) Having heard that, Kuñjala spoke to his son Samujjvala:

These were indeed all the sixty-eight sacred fords (tīrthas).

Betrayal of friends, breach of trust, causing division among the gods, cutting off one's livelihood, destroying the range of pasture, setting fire [to property],

Guru-tīrtha is the supreme and most excellent pacifier of sins;

Then Kuñjala asked his third son:

Beside her stood a single beautiful woman, lovely-faced and resplendent;

Both of them, being delighted, descended from their celestial chariot onto the ground.
Just as they had finished bathing on the bank, they both died;
those two divine corpses lay separately on the bank.
I beheld two women and two men;

O dear one, two other women also arrived separately from the sky; while eating, those two laughed, saying, "Even though we were joined with us, nothing was offered. (48–49)

I witnessed all this anew.
"Tell me, dear father, what is this? Why is there the eating of one's own flesh?
(51) Having heard those words of his son, Kuñjala said to his son:

One who has performed meritorious deeds rejoices here and in the next world through food and other such things;
the gift that was given follows him wherever he goes.

Whatever kind of seed a farmer sows in the field,

Whatever kind of action is performed, such a fruit is obtained.

Indeed, five things born of karma are created for this embodied being within the womb.

divinity or humanity, the state of a beast, or that of a bird;

It remains attached like a shadow; it yields enjoyment as its fruit.

"Therefore, whatever food is given is enjoyed by the gods in heaven.

There, virtuous women and virtuous men who have attained the yoga of devotion go.

If the fruit of giving is indeed enjoyment, and at the end of that enjoyment there is a fall,

(1.29) By reading and hearing this, and by performing the means of attainment, a person shall go to the world of Brahmā and achieve the four goals of human existence. (3.51.13)

in order to delude Vihuṇḍa and to destroy him through a stratagem.
Seeing that Vaiṣṇavī illusion, Vihuṇḍaka indeed became deluded.
He said to her, "O lady of beautiful hips, O sinless one, grant me union.
Māyā said, "If you desire to enjoy me, then..."
Worship Śaṅkara with seven crores of divine flowers,
fragrant, rare even to the gods, and produced from the Kāmoda tree.
Offer a garland fashioned from those flowers around my neck.
"Then, O sinless one, I shall become your most beloved wife.
Having been addressed thus, the asura searched for that tree;
failing to find that woman, he went back and questioned the tree again.
The woman said: "Indeed, no such tree exists anywhere.
There is a maiden named Kāmodā who resides in the pool of the Gaṅgā.
That virtuous woman, known as Kāmodā, indeed laughs whenever [the tree does]. (79)

Indeed, from her smile, beautiful flowers arise—fragrant with passion, yellow, and truly splendid. Whoever worships Śaṅkara even with a single one of those flowers, [attains great merit]. (3.52.80–81)
Śaṅkara fulfills his great desire;
however, from her weeping, red flowers indeed arise,
and one should never touch them.
Since contact with flowers produced from weeping would result in misfortune, go to the pool of the Gaṅgā and cause that woman to laugh;
for many flowers will surely arise from her laughter. (83–84)
"Take those that fall into the current of the Gaṅgā. Thus addressed, the Dānava looked into the current of the Gaṅgā and saw the flowers arising from the tears shed by Kāmboja.
He took them with simplicity and worshipped Śaṅkara.
That [offering] produced an undesirable result for him, and Śaṅkara indeed became enraged.
He uttered the sound "Hum," and by that, the Dānava truly died.
Thus was the work of the gods accomplished by the powerful Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu, having assumed the form of a woman, then vanished from sight.
And the deities became exceedingly joyful due to the destruction of Huṇḍa.
Then, in ancient times, four maidens were born from the churning of the ocean:
Alakṣmī, Vāruṇī, Kāmodā, and Lakṣmī as the fourth.
Thereupon, the Ocean gave Alakṣmī to Uddālaka.
The goddess Vāruṇī was indeed offered by the Ocean to Varuṇa;
and Kāmodā, who will become Tulasī, was given to Viṣṇu.
Lakṣmī, who dwells with Viṣṇu in Vaikuṇṭha, was also given to Viṣṇu.
That Kāmodā, the daughter of the ocean, having indeed heard from Nārada again and again that Viṣṇu’s birth would once more occur in the human realm,
was unable to endure even the prospect of separation from Viṣṇu. (92–93)
Having gone alone to the root of the Gaṅgā, she wept indeed many times;
from that very weeping, those red flowers were produced.
The death of the Daitya arose as the fruit resulting from her worship of them.
Listen to the cause of Kāmodā’s laughter; I shall indeed tell it to you.
When she takes the form of Tulasī, she will become useful by offering her own leaves during the worship of Viṣṇu. (95–96)
The Lord of the World will indeed always sport with her.
Remembering this, the maiden Kāmodā laughs here and there.
It should be understood that Mañjarī is born from laughter within the manifestation of Tulasī.

One should offer even a single leaf or a cluster of blossoms of *tulasī* to Viṣṇu, as well as to Brahmā and Śaṅkara; thus one shall partake in the desired fruit. In this manner, the auspicious fruit arising from worship with flowers is to be understood. (98–99)
O Kapiñjala, likewise the woman Kāmodā was shown to you, accompanied by weeping and laughter, as the producer of flowers;
and even Vihuṇḍa, the stealer of merit, was shown to you by me.
Thus, by means of the pilgrimage to the Guru who is Viṣṇu’s very form, the Tulasī plant is always to be worshipped as the bestower of desire;
its merit is also worshipped, and the entire circle of deities is always worshipped with flowers, O son. (101–102)

The great Gurutīrtha is proclaimed to always bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation. Through the power of Śambhutīrtha, Vihuṇḍa met his destruction and went to Kailāsa itself by means of royal yoga.
"Indeed, one who has gone to heaven [is surpassed]; therefore, the *guru-tīrtha* is preeminent.
Having spoken thus to his own sons, Kuñjala ceased.
Then, O Lakṣmī, having heard this, Cyavana questioned the bird.
"Who are you that abide here, O divine-knower of birds?
The bird replied: 'Formerly, I was indeed the son of a Vidyādhara of Kaśyapa’s lineage, known by the name Dharmaśarman.'"
I was once a fool, but at one time a perfected great sage (siddhāyana) and a holy man arrived at my house. He was served by me, and he bestowed auspicious knowledge upon me. (107–108)
That sage Siddhāyana indeed bestowed a blessing upon me:
"Becoming free from attachment and desire, and taking refuge in a solitary place, you shall become a knower who illuminates all things and a seer of all. (109)
"And even while remaining in a single place, you shall know all that is born within the three worlds.
(3.52.11) "Thus, by the grace of my preceptor, I know everything born within the three worlds.
I know you, Cyavana, to be the supreme true guru who bestows liberation. (11)

I shall tell you the cause of my state as a parrot; listen. "Sin arises from association, and merit likewise arises from association. (1.12) Having purchased a young parrot, I became forever infatuated with it.
"He says this to me: 'O father, come here and sit down;
go and bathe, O illustrious one, and worship the gods.
Through the diversion of his words, my duty has been forgotten."
Then, having gone to the garden for vegetables and other provisions, I was killed by a cat while I was still in the house; however, upon my return, I saw the bird [I had killed].
Following that, out of extreme grief, I died with the thought of becoming a parrot.
At death, I became a parrot;
having entered the birth of a parrot, I became one who remembers my past lives here through the power of Siddhāyana.
Indeed, there is no sacred site equal to the Guru for the sake of knowledge and liberation in every respect.
External impurity is destroyed by water from the land, but internal impurity is not;
however, through the Guru-tīrtha, the impurity created in previous births is destroyed.
For the sake of crossing over saṃsāra alone, the moving tīrtha is supreme.
"Then, O Guru Cyavana, I wish to cross over; please ferry me across.
Having spoken thus, the king of birds, accompanied by his son and joined by his wife, came before the feet of the high-souled Cyavana.
The venerable Cyavana gave the mantra of the Name to Śuka and caused him to drink water consecrated with the name of Kṛṣṇa.
Those birds, having bowed to their guru and remembered me, Nārāyaṇa—
Having cast off their bodies, they became my attendants and went to Vaikuṇṭha. (1.22) Having obtained that divine true guru as a sacred ford, they attained liberation;
for the sacred ford of the guru is indeed the most excellent of all sacred fords. (1.23)
Whether a man or a woman, she is the giver of liberation, venerable, and the very embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites.
Whether she is a wife or even unmarried, she who is truly devoted is indeed the bestower of liberation. By taking refuge in her, one shall surely attain eternal emancipation.
The virtuous Goddess, the destroyer of sins, should be served by daughters-in-law.
She is Brāhmī, beloved of Brahmā, and beloved of Hari; she is the devoted wife.
The virtuous man, the true person, and the true Guru are likewise beloved of Hari. (125–126)
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and should always be cultivated by people;
through its recitation and hearing, O Lakṣmī, liberation shall certainly be attained.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Story of Nahuṣa, the Story of the Kuñjala Parrot, the Story of Kāmodā, the Story of Cyavana, and Others," within the *Guru-tīrtha* section of the *Vadhū-gītā*, in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 52: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā / Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 53 [[Author: → Chapter 54
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! By performing that which purifies the self, young brides attained complete purity and departed for the supreme state. (1)
One should indeed know the Guru as the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) in the form of Brahman;
one should know the Guru’s wife as Lakṣmī in her true form and serve her as a daughter-in-law.
Both of these—respect and disrespect—should be understood as poison and nectar, respectively.

In that state, disrespect is nectar, while respect is indeed like poison. (3) One should show honor to the guru, but never to one's own self. That bride who remains eternally free from pride is then a bestower of honor. (4)
She shall always receive honor and become worthy of respect among women;
through service, even a lion and even a planet come under her control.
Indeed, the practice of serving elders brings subjection for the sake of a bride.

Everything is accomplished through service by a daughter, a daughter-in-law, a handmaid, a slave, or even a servant; likewise by one who has taken refuge, a guest, or a female attendant. Whether she be a queen, a preceptor, a teacher, a goddess, a cow, or even a demoness—(6–7).
Through service, Prosperity becomes submissive and the virtuous Ramā is won.
Service to the guru is a great weapon that provides assistance in bringing others under one's control.
Therefore, indeed, by means of the bride of good conduct, the mother-in-law—Service—is to be served without pride.

Service to her husband, service to the gods, obedience to her mother-in-law’s commands, service to the household, and service to her children—these are indeed the five vows of a daughter-in-law. Absence of anger, service to elders, purity, and attendance upon the aged. (3.53.10)
For the sake of her husband, all the possessions of the wife are considered to be under his restraint.
The wife’s household duties consist of sacrifice, hospitality toward guests, and the worship of the gods;
as well as devotion to pleasing her husband, the performance of the twilight prayers, and pleasing her mother-in-law. (11)
Bathing, service to her husband, and self-restraint are the means for accomplishing dharma and worldly prosperity.
Devoted to virtuous conduct, peaceful, and a protector of her own duty,
she conquers all worlds and proceeds to the realm of Brahmā.
One should perform all acts of rising to greet, prostration, and salutation toward elders who possess the instructions of the guru and follow the traditional sequence;
doing so by means of a full prostration with eight limbs or five limbs, or by bowing at their feet. (14)
By performing three circumambulations to the right, one should salute the venerable woman who is firm in her vow of chastity.
(15) All elder women are to be saluted, and an aged woman should be saluted again and again.
One should not disobey their command if one desires one's own spiritual success. (16)
One should avoid with every effort the forest-caves of wicked yoga, the practice of inferior mantras, and afflictions such as poison and planetary seizures.
A virtuous woman should also avoid deceit, stinginess regarding wealth, and slander.

One should avoid excessive laughter, excessive pride, playful gestures devoid of modesty, and wandering about according to one's own whims in the presence of the guru. Furthermore, one should not speak anything that is contrary to his words, nor anything that is improper. (18–19)
One should never recall what is undesirable, nor should one ever recall a quarrel;
one should not utter abuse, nor should one practice dejection. One should not kick any vessels containing liquids or cooking pots with one's feet.
One should neither touch nor remove eating vessels or garments.
Likewise, sacrificial vessels, vessels for ritual substances, vessels fit for purificatory rites, and whatever household articles there may be—[one should not touch or remove them]. (21–22)
The broom, the hearth, the fire, and whatever fruits and vegetables there may be;
all drinking vessels and the liquids for personal adornment;
books and the like, *darbha* grass, flower-offering bowls, and collyrium.
Weapons, ornaments, garments, and articles of decoration;
whatever foods there may be—whether chewed, eaten, licked, or sucked;
vessels for seasoned meats and the like; and wooden seats and such—[all these were provided]. (24–25)

A bride should never touch [the ground] with her foot, nor should she ever move it away. She should never commit an offense against the gods, an offense against her elders, or even an offense against her mother-in-law and others;
she should never commit an offense against the village or against the virtuous.
One should perform all [ritual acts] with water that has been drawn up, is free from warm froth, and has been purified by the "cloth-eye" (a cloth used as a filter);
one should avoid turbid water, as well as water that is corrupted by smell, color, or taste, or that has remained in an impure place. (27–28)
One should avoid water that is contaminated by mud or stones, such as seawater or pond water, as well as water covered with moss or otherwise defiled by other defects.
[This applies to] the vessel used for fetching water, whether it be a jar, a pot, or one with a spout.

Having cast [the water] away, one should never wash the face or the feet with that same water. Having drawn up more water from above, one should likewise not perform the act of rinsing while still impure.
A drinking vessel touched to the mouth should not be submerged in a water container.
One should certainly not touch food items and the like without having washed one's hands;
nor should one perform tasks such as serving food with unwashed hands.
One who wears unclean clothing should never perform the work of cooking.
The bride should always effect the purification of liquids by means of fire;
she should always effect the purification of items such as grass and wood by inspection and by sprinkling with water. (33–34)
One should indeed purify even the pestle and mortar with water;
[one should purify] horns, bones, and wood by scrubbing them with cloth or the like.
As for solid objects, their purification is indeed declared to be by sprinkling.
But when a portion of unhusked grain or rice is defiled,
one should remove only that much and sprinkle it with water mixed with *kuśa* grass.
For vegetables, roots, fruits, and the like, purification is indeed achieved by washing.
One should purify smooth surfaces by wiping them, while rough surfaces are cleansed with water and the like;
likewise, the purification of a house is achieved by sweeping or scraping,
or sometimes by smearing it with plaster, sprinkling it with water, or by means of air.
One should perform the purification of the earth by means of dwelling upon it.
Water situated on the ground is pure, stainless, and possesses a wholesome fragrance.
A calf is pure at its watering-place, during milking, and also at birth.
When fruit falls, a bird is pure; during sexual intercourse, the face of a wife is pure;
merchandise spread out is pure when cleansed by wind and sunlight.
(4.1) All that comes from a mine is pure, as is the mouth of a dog in a hunter’s house.
Shadows, droplets, Brahmins, virtuous people, and flies—O twice-born ones—are pure.
Dust, the earth, wind, and fire are pure to the touch, as are children;
likewise, [the body is pure] during sexual intercourse and after the discharge of impurities, but not upon touching those who are defiled.
Purity through bathing is declared for touching those who have reached their menses and the like;
a physician, a butcher, and a servant are considered always pure.
[44] So too are the domestic animals, children, birds, and the courtyard of the house.
The four railing trees, the door-panel, and the parasol;
the swing, the board, the ball and so forth, the cart, the broom, as well as the grinding stone, the tablet, the stairs, and the peg. 45–46.
A chain, a tethering rope for cattle, water-cords, and tubes;
a pot, a cooking vessel, a staff, a ladle for giving, and a puppet;
a pen, a book, a lamp, an image, and likewise a fan. 47.
An ornament, a vessel, a chest for clothes, and vessels for ghee, oil, and so forth;
a window, a turret, a granary, and likewise a king;
a virtuous person, an ascetic, a celibate student, a teacher, pure things, and a cow—these are always [auspicious]. (48–49)
Indeed, by their very nature, both wind and heat are purifying;
likewise, those initiated, storytellers, and those devoted to ritual action are always purifying.
Grain in a threshing floor is always pure, and so too are men in an assembly.
In times of festival, women are considered pure, and maidens are always considered pure.
This applies to lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), kings, queens, the wives of preceptors, female members of the council, those who perform dance and song, and female slaves. (51–52)
The purity of *sairandhrīs*, courtesans,
and women skilled in dance and instrumental music must always be understood;
in the Satya Yuga, women were always pure and free from menstrual flow.

In other ages, women are purified at the end of every month by their menstrual flow; however, in all times, women are purified by bathing and by religious observances. A woman in her courses must not, with great care, touch another woman who is in her courses. (24–55)
Having bathed on the fourth day, one should indeed worship the Lord as the husband;
however, by worshipping at night on the fourth day, one gives birth to a son of short lifespan,
devoid of learning and poverty-stricken, who brings no satisfaction to his father.
On the fifth day, by engaging in union, she gives birth to a daughter; on the sixth, a son.
On the seventh day, by engaging in union, she gives birth to a daughter; on the eighth, she gives birth to a son.
On the ninth day, by engaging in union, she gives birth to a daughter; on the tenth, a wise son.
On the eleventh day [one obtains] a daughter; on the twelfth, an auspicious son devoted to dharma;
on the thirteenth, a dull-witted girl; on the fourteenth, an excellent son;
on the fifteenth, a virtuous girl; and on the sixteenth, one who has reached the further shore of knowledge.

Then, having become pure, she should indeed serve her husband. But during her menstrual period, she always gives birth to a low-caste *caṇḍāla* who is defiled; yet through the power of the husband’s sacred sites (*tīrtha*), the offspring of the woman becomes pure.
As is the sacrificial ground, so will the offspring be;
if the field is corrupt, corrupt offspring are born.
As is the purity of the mind, so will the offspring be.
Whatever the purification of reality may be, that indeed is the ultimate purification.
Purification itself exists as the very form of purity within a pure vessel;
in an impure vessel, purification indeed abandons its state of being pure.
Indeed, in an unworthy vessel, even refined qualities lose their refinement;
even gods, within a mortal body, lose their divinity.
In the house of a base man, even a virtuous woman’s chastity surely dissolves.
In the house of the Asuras, the divinity of the Goddess is surely destroyed. In the house of a Kaulika, the queenship of the Queen does not endure at all.
In another’s house, a daughter-in-law cannot preserve her wifely devotion.

Chastity does not abide at all in the house of a courtesan, nor does devotion exist in one who is atheistic; and atheism never resides in one who is devoted. Therefore, one should be dear to her husband.
A woman who is devoted to her husband becomes beloved of Brahmā; she becomes beloved of Hari.
A woman who is a friend of the virtuous always becomes beloved of Nārāyaṇa.
She becomes beloved of the holy for the sake of liberation, but never beloved of the unholy. (3.53.70)
She should always be fond of dharma and not fond of adharma and the like;
that virtuous woman should be fond of religious observances and not fond of improper conduct.
That goddess should be beloved by the gods and not beloved by the asuras.
She should always be fond of virtue, and not fond of vice;
she should always be fond of purity, and not take delight in impurity;
she should be fond of austerity and self-controlled, and not fond of what is not austerity.
She should always be beloved by Hari, but never beloved by the one who takes away (Hārin).
She should always be beloved by Brahman, and indeed never beloved by delusion (Bhrama).
She should always be beloved by Kṛṣṇa, and likewise she should be beloved by the Self (Ātman).
She should always be fond of liberation and never fond of worldly enjoyment;
she should always be fond of the All-pervading Lord and never fond of the trivial;
she should always be fond of the embodied soul and never fond of the physical body. (75–76)
She should always be dear to another, and not dear to anyone else;
she should be beloved by the Supreme Person and never beloved by anyone other than Him.
The Supreme Person is Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shall become her beloved;
Nārāyaṇa himself shall be her husband, and she shall always be his beloved.
Indeed, she shall be beloved by him through his very self alone, and never by means of his body or other such things. (78–79)
This very state, O Lakṣmī, is the abode of Brahman, which manifests the beloved of Brahman;
this alone is the purity of Brahman, and having attained it, one rejoices in Me.
That [purity], which causes increase, should be brought forth by the bride while she is in the state of a bride.
She bestows the yoga of Hari and grants liberation.
Indeed, this body is impure, as are the senses;
the objects of the senses are also impure, being products of *māyā* consisting of nothing but delusion. (81–82)
The mental modifications arising from that should likewise be understood as impure;
the enjoyments and their fruits are also indeed impure.
The latent impressions are likewise impure, as are thirst and desires of that same nature. (83)
Indeed, active functions and their effects are truly impure;
likewise, the qualities (guṇas) are eternally impure and lead to hell.
All this is entirely impure; what purity can be found therein?
The one pure Self is itself endowed with the Supreme Self;
through acts of self-surrender, one should desire the divine purity residing in the Supreme Self.
Just as brass, through contact with gold, becomes similar to gold.
Just as silver [is purified] by the price of gold, so too is the body of bile (pitta).
Through union with Hari, a person becomes golden and made of light (hiraṇmaya).
All the sense organs [are purified] with the juices of indravāruṇī.
O Lotus-born One, those honeyed offerings mixed with Hari indeed become divine and eternal;
through union with Kṛṣṇa, one realizes one's own eternal true nature.
Immersion in eternal bliss is attained through the beloved Kṛṣṇa.
O Lakṣmī, in ancient times there were indeed thirteen sons of Māyā created by Brahmā:
the five Ākūtis, the five Citayas, and also Mana. || 3.53.90–91 ||
Then Ego (ahaṃkāra) and Intellect (buddhi), impelled by the desire for progeny, were told:
"All of you, whose bodies are invisible, indeed create progeny.
But they did not welcome those words of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).

Having abandoned their own duty and disregarded the command [of the Creator], seeing indeed the defects in ritual acts, they grew weary of such works and desisted from creation. Having forsaken wealth, virtue, and pleasure, they truly became inactive.
Desiring birthlessness, they remained inactive and steadfast.
But Brahmā, having become enraged upon learning of their intention, said to them:
"Indeed, you were appointed by me for the creation of progeny."
"In the past, I told you, 'Procreate and perform sacrifices.
Yet, disregarding my words, you did not welcome progeny.
Therefore, I always curse you: 'May you be devoted solely to ritual action! (96–97)
Thus cursed by Brahmā, they became devoted to ritual action;
those thirteen always engaged in their own vast occupations day and night, never ceasing at any time. (98)
Those very gods known as the Jayas, who were all of diverse activities, are to be understood as the Tuṣitas, the Satyas, and the Sāntis;
they are also the Haris, the Vaikuṇṭhas, the Sādhyas, and the Ādityas. (3.53.100)
O Lakṣmī, one should always offer them to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
for by that, O Ādityās, they become bestowers of liberation upon me.
Indeed, a virtuous woman should cause the offering of all rites to the gods to be made to the Guru.
The dedication of both their functions and their activities must be performed toward me, your guru; by that, they all become divine, bestowing the abode of Brahman. This secret has been told to you.

Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Guru’s Secrets and Right Conduct," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the Creator (*Brahmā*), in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 54 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 54]
[The Author: Chapter 55.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the most supreme power of the Guru.
The supreme, most brilliant destroyer of great and even greater sins [resided there].
In the great sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, in the region devoted to the service of the Lord, a family of the Khaśa caste indeed lived in my city. (1–2)
There was indeed a Khaśa named Viṣṇudāsa who was devoted to righteousness;
he never ate food, wore clothes, or consumed fruits, water, or anything else at any time without first offering it to Viṣṇu and without having offered it to his guru.
There, Viṣṇudāsa’s guru was indeed one devoted to liberation;
he was a virtuous man named Ṛṣidharma, the bestower of liberation and the arouser of devotion.
He bathed daily at the three periods of the day and performed worship to the deities at the three times of the day.
His transformation is one of established stability, free from the three qualities and the afflictions;
he always subsists on unasked-for food, leaves, and the like, and remains naked.
Dwelling on a riverbank or beneath a tree, he stays in a solitary place.
He constantly worships me, Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He is indeed capable of enduring the pairs of opposites, free from attachment and aversion,
devoid of worldly effort and excessive desire, aged, and free from all defects.
He who is accomplished in speech and yet remains silent always triumphs over me;
when those afflicted come to him for refuge in order to destroy their suffering,
he dispels it through blessings, the giving of water, and the giving of dust.

To those seeking refuge, his very sufferings became a source of protection; he was adorned by his service to others. (3.54.10) People offer fruits, garments, sweet foods, and wealth before him, and having honored him, they depart. (3.54.11)
This virtuous man neither touches nor even looks upon the objects;
yet other mendicants, or even animals, carry them away.
He remains free from delusion and free from the sense of "mine," conducting himself without deceit.
The Khaśa serves such a guru who follows the dharma of the sages.
Rāmaṇī, the wife of the Khaśa, also serves him with tasks such as sweeping, by offering leaves, flowers, and the like, and by massaging his feet. (13–14)
Khaśa had a daughter, the auspicious Līlāvatī by name;
she was twelve years old and always engaged in service to the holy man.
For the sake of the deity, she performed tasks such as watering the flowering vines.

Endowed with faith and devotion, she was attentive to the hospitality and other needs of her devotees. (16) Under the influence of ignorance, that girl saw a female mouse with her young emerge from a hole to water the trees. (17)
Out of childishness, that girl took those offspring and,
having gone far away, cast off the children who were separated from their mother.
Filled with fear of mice, she remained within a heap of grass.
Taking up the small children, she then cursed the girl:
"Just as my children have fallen into misery, being separated from me, so may you, separated from your father, mother, and others, become miserable. (3.54.20)
Indeed, this terrible curse upon the mouse came to fruition within a few days; for that very night, the fruit of its ripening was experienced by the girl.
As the girl was returning home after attending upon her preceptor in the evening, [she encountered the mouse].
On the road, a certain young Mleccha encountered her and seized the maiden. Wailing piteously, the powerful man quickly led her into the forest;
from one forest to another, he traveled through the night until he had reached a distant land.

That maiden, a daughter-in-law (khaśī), was made a slave by a barbarian in his own home; she was indeed made to drink liquor and fed meat. Likewise, that sinner committed sexual misconduct with her and repeatedly caused her to commit acts of violence and other such sins.
Indeed, all manner of barbarian rites were performed by him with that maiden.
For she was a barbarian woman and a weakling, and being ignorant of the forest path, she did not know it at all; she only constantly grieved for the return home.
Then once, in the city, there occurred a wedding festival of the Mlecchas. At that time, singers and courtesans arrived at the festival;
among them was this beautiful Khaśa woman, whom the courtesans observed.
As a female slave, she offered betel during dances and other performances.
For, having been employed by a Mleccha, she engaged in the service of courtesans.
A courtesan questioned her: "O daughter, where are your mother and father? (28–29)
Having heard this, Khaśī related her entire account;
then, perceiving his intention to depart for the purpose of abducting her,
she inspired confidence in him and subsequently established a secret signal.

Then, after some time, in accordance with their agreement, the courtesan brought the girl out from the house of the Mleccha and led her to her own home. Thereupon, the girl became the auspicious maidservant of the courtesan.
Engaged in sexual intercourse and other such acts, she became devoid of dharma;
under the influence of the courtesan, she committed great sins and even more heinous crimes.
Then, after some time, that courtesan indeed fell seriously ill.

Afflicted by a disease of her abdominal organs, she consumed even medicines, yet that courtesan did not attain health at all; indeed, she lamented, "How might this fistula-like disease of mine be removed? (34–35)

The maidservant’s mother-in-law then said, "I have a great master who is capable of destroying disease; go there indeed, for he possesses the perfection of speech. Upon hearing this, the courtesan learned the auspicious news regarding her master.
Suddenly, she became ready, equipped with wealth and garments.
Other female servants and courtesans, taking along their belongings and even male attendants, departed for the forest where the courtesan shone. (37–38)
The saint arrived there on the riverbank with great devotion;
Līlāvatī, full of joy, became exceedingly serene within her heart. She bowed to the saint with deep feeling, as if she had encountered her own father.
Having bowed down to the Guru as a god, he reported his own circumstances.
He also reported the account of the courtesan regarding the means for the destruction of her disease.
Then the holy man spoke concerning the fruit of that karma.
Whatever was done by someone in the past, that very same thing is experienced by them.
O Līlāvatī! By you, the young ones were separated from the mouse.
At that time, during the season for giving water to the trees, [the mouse]— || 42 ||—by the mouse.
And you, having been cursed by the separation from your parents, have consequently fallen into suffering.
This courtesan suffers a wretched disease due to her sexual misconduct;
however, this is indeed the fruit of the service you previously rendered to me.
He brought about my acquisition [of her] again under this very pretext;
this Gaṇikā became devoted to the service of guests.
Through the power of your devotion, she has attained union with me.
Good company leads one toward virtue, while bad company leads one toward wickedness.
(46) A wicked deed causes suffering, whereas a virtuous action brings happiness.
O daughter, association with the righteous arises through merit and not otherwise. (47)
I shall indeed wipe away all your sins born of being a barbarian, O daughter;
I shall also wipe away the sins of the courtesan.
Dwell here in my presence, having constructed a leaf-hut.
And they performed a vow right there for the sake of purifying the body.
Having been thus addressed, they all, having constructed an auspicious leaf-hut on the ground beneath the tree, took up residence in its vicinity.
The sage, whose nature was that of a seer, gave them the vow of eating only once a day;
during that vow, he had them consume the five products of the cow for three days.
Then, O Lakṣmī, the best of sages gave them auspicious mantras.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Lord. (52) "For fear of time, māyā, sinful karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous hearts, [I take refuge in] the one who possesses the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and svastika. (53)
"May Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times.
I am eternally a devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, belonging to the realm of Brahmā.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (54)
He whispered these mantras into his ear and likewise placed water in his hand.
Having said, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," that sage Dharma poured the water upon the ground.
O Lakṣmī! At that moment, a great wonder occurred there; listen to it.
From the bodies of Līlāvatī and those courtesans, black-colored crows emerged on all sides. (57)
Then the owls emerged from there, and then the mosquitoes as well;
and then the piśācas, who were misshapen and of cruel form—mutilated, emaciated, hungry, weak, one-eyed, and lame. (58–59)

Then those afflicted with leprosy, the dull-witted, the blind, the foul-smelling, and those covered in filth— emaciated and with limbs distorted in every way— went forth. Seeing the sage, they all wept, naked and without refuge.
Līlāvatī, the courtesan, and the others experienced great wonder.
Having bowed to the sage, their preceptor, they asked, "O Preceptor, who are these?
The Preceptor replied, "O daughters, you indeed possess all manner of sins."
By the bestowing of this mantra, I have expelled from their bodies these crows, which are indeed the sins born of association with outcastes (śvapacas);
and these owls are the sins incurred in the state of being a courtesan.
Those very sins of yours that were mosquitoes— the evils of drinking liquor—
and those sinful piśācas who fed upon your flesh,
have all indeed departed from your bodies. (64–65)
All those [sins] wept as they beheld these women;
even the sins, O Lakṣmī, then made a plea, O Sage:
"We are all indeed supportless and exceedingly distressed. (66)
"O Sage, provide liberation here by all means through the gift of water.
Having heard this, the sage washed his own right foot and indeed cast it into them with his joined palms; and drops were taken up by them.
Then all the drops became yellow and the sins were indeed satisfied.
In this manner, the sage again cast another handful of water.
Thereupon, they assumed divine forms, just like the gods.
Then he cast a third handful of offerings over the deity.
Instantly, all the attendants of the Three-Eyed Lord became bearers of tridents;
even the sinful ones became holy beings by the thousands.
All of them, auspicious and possessing divine forms though appearing in human shapes,
took the sage’s command and, having bowed to Himālaya, departed.
Then they all went to Meru and indeed became holy beings.
All the renowned hosts of gods [arose] solely through the majesty of the virtuous one.
(73) Then, free from sin and the like, the courtesans became like deities with divine forms; he gave them water for their feet. (74)
Having drunk the water from the feet of the sage, the courtesan became free from disease;
others too, having drunk that water, had their worldly attachments destroyed.
Then all of them became like yoginīs and virtuous women.
The diseases quickly departed, bowed down, and went to Kailāsa.
Indeed, all those courtesans received initiation from the virtuous women;
at that time, the vessels there likewise received initiation from the holy men.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord of Akṣara, O All-pervading One! Thus did they perform their worship in that hermitage, reciting the Saṃhitā.
Having regained their daughter Līlāvatī, her parents became filled with happiness;
indeed, through the power of their guru, they became devotees of Kamalā.
There, those two Khaśas received the initiation of a saint from that true guru.
News of the nature of this destruction of sins spread in every direction;
then, men came in great agitation for the sake of destroying their own sins.
O Sage, both men and women received the Śrī Vaiṣṇava initiation from the Ṛṣi.
Having made those arrangements, she dispatched her liberated ones to the Imperishable One;
she also dispatched her male and female disciples to the Imperishable One.
By the mere will of the Sage, celestial chariots [arrived] from the sky of consciousness.
Accompanied by their attendants and indeed joined with the forms of Viṣṇu, they arrived; having ascended those very forms, they went to the supreme abode.
By the power of their preceptor, the courtesans and others became residents of Vaikuṇṭha.
Līlāvatī, as well as her five friends and thousands of others,
were present in my abode, Vaikuṇṭha, in the presence of Śrī Hari.
That very Līlāvatī is now this daughter of the King of Kāśī.
"Your sister, a beloved wife of a Brahmin, resides here;
she is a courtesan named Suśīlā and is your friend here, O daughter of the ocean.
Thus spoke Śiva’s queen, Śrī, by means of her yoga, [to him who was] beyond the guṇas.

The dharma of the sages is devoid of qualities; by union with that, men and women are born indeed devoid of qualities, liberated, without a doubt. Those men or women who worship Me out of desire, anger, fear, greed, or pride— [they too attain the same]. (88–89)
I uplift those who are my devotees, the virtuous, and my gurus.
Even those who are sinful and of evil conduct become purified through their connection with the guru;
they are born as residents of my abode—how much more so, then, those who observe vows for me?
Those who have surrendered their entire being to the Guru, who serve the Guru as their very deity, and who have attained full confidence in the Guru, go to the supreme abode.
The Guru is God; the Guru is Kṛṣṇa; for the Guru is indeed the purifying initiation.
She for whom Hari is considered the guru, the vow, the gift, and the supreme goal,
crosses even the ocean of worldly existence through the power of the sacred ford that is her guru;
she indeed attains the eternal, imperishable abode of supreme bliss.
This divine abode of mine is supreme among all realms and dear to me;
it bestows complete satisfaction and fulfills every desire.
There, nothing is lacking, and one enjoys pleasures together with me.
Whether they be brides, widows, or even those without husbands or without refuge,
having reached this supreme Guru-tīrtha, they are liberated from the ocean of worldly existence.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even speaking of this [work], [one attains the same].
For those with desires, there arises enjoyment, liberation, a divine state, and the attainment of the celestial abode; for those free from desire, there is the attainment of heaven;
for those who desire Me, there is the attainment of Me, the Supreme Person armed with the Śārṅga bow. (97–98)

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Līlāvatī’s Attainment of the Status of Brahmapriyā and Others through the Yoga of the Great Sage Ṛṣidharma at Guru-tīrtha, and the Dissolution of the Sins of Suśīlā and the Rest," in the *Vadhūgītā* within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 54. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 55 [Author:
Chapter 56 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:

Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to another most purifying narrative, which consists of sacred teachers and holy places, which delivers all beings and removes all sins. In the city of Upaleṣṭā in Saurāṣṭra, there was a virtuous woman who was the daughter of a dog-eater (śvapacī).
A devotee of Hari named Rakṣā, the beautiful wife of Sumara, lived with her family in the city of Malāpahāriṇī. Because she removed impurities, she indeed remained pure during the day. (2–3)
Then, having bathed at midday and purified her own hands,
she went to her own home, which had been constructed amidst the trees.
Having prepared her own *roṭaka* cake, she fed it to her husband Hari.
Having given [the food] to the dog, she then eats; her virtue is contentment and protection.
(5) Remaining in the house, she constantly reflects upon her own condition:
"How is it that even here among humans, I have indeed become a dog-eater's wife? (6)
Poverty persists at all times, as does servitude;
there is constant removal of filth and perpetual impurity.
There is humiliation in every household and a state of untouchability at all times.
Even though I possess a human nature, my life is that of a beast.
(8) Food is not seen at all, nor is anything flavorful obtained; the garments are coarse, and no adornment is found. (9)
The house is indeed beautiful, yet there is no wealth to enjoy;
there is neither honor nor fame—fie upon this life born of sin!
There are neither vehicles nor mounts, and there are not even vessels of metal.
There are no ornaments, nor is there even sweet food;
there is neither wealth nor coinage, and there is no beautiful couch.
Indeed, there is never any hope for gold, even in a dream. (11–12)
"Thus, I possess all manner of deformity as well as impurity;
yet there is one auspicious quality found in me, born of a *śvapaca* woman:
because of my untouchability, there has never been contact with another man. (13)
Devotion to my husband is always innate and more venerable than anything else.
Even members of my own caste live far away, in distant cities; there is no possibility of union with those men, nor even the touch of them for me. (14–15)

Thus I possess this vow, virtue, and merit that always bestow heaven; I am free from pride, detached, and likewise free from affliction. Moreover, there is a river by my side, so that I may bathe daily.
She always maintained her persistence like a forest-dweller, even while living in the forest as if at home:
"There is no fear of thieves for us, nor is there any fear of kings; devoted to my service, I sleep happily with my husband. (17–18)
By the power of my fortune, I occasionally obtain the sight of holy men as they travel along the path; yet, I always behold the sun.
Until midday, my task consists solely of removing impurities, and nothing else.
My cessation occurs for half the day and during the night,
specifically for the purpose of worshipping the names of the Supreme Lord.
I have the time for this, and such gains are likewise available to me.
When a great festival— whether divine or human— is underway in a village,
one obtains a purifying favor that pertains to both gods and men.
Even in that case, there is fulfillment for my human birth.
