Even for a dog-cooker, my character and devotion to my husband are indeed supreme.
(23) But for other women among men—whether in the midst of people or in the village—the sight of living together with children and other wives is seen to be destructive of virtue. (24)
Where men and women dwell together in close proximity,
there indeed righteousness is destroyed by the power of place and time;
likewise, so is the touch of another man by married women.
Even exclusive devotion to such women brings about hell for me, who am the Dharma.
For those women of such a kind who cause the intermixture of castes, there is indeed no hell today; for them, therefore, there is hell [only] from that [point forward]. (26–27)
That which is brought about by unrighteousness here may indeed manifest in another birth;
however, for me, who am in the form of a *śvapacī*, hell is visible right here.
But by the power of righteousness alone, there shall certainly be no hell after death.

Therefore, the state of being a woman who understands is the most excellent and supreme among all destinies. (29) Indeed, lack of prosperity leads to dispassion, while prosperity leads to bondage. Detachment from the world leads to the higher realm, while gentleness of character leads to bondage. (3.55.30)
Free from bondage, I wander like a virtuous woman; I roam from street to street like a chaste wife devoted to her husband.
My state is fearless, rich in happiness, and free from disease.
I cleanse the pits of impurity and I also attain detachment. (32) Indeed, all people in the world cleanse their own filth day after day;
everyone, having risen in the morning, washes away their own impurity. (33)
Indeed, women who have children wash their infants even when they are placed in the middle of the house,
amidst the clothes, or upon the bed;
for those like me remove all the impurities of a child.
There is no distinction for me in the purification of their impurities.
Indeed, all outcasts alike are engaged in the removal of the impurities from their own bodies.
Therefore, my preeminence alone remains unassailable even among outcasts. (35–36)
The king is constantly a partaker of suffering, and the queen is even more miserable than he;
she is perpetually confined by guards within a palace that resembles a prison.
And the wives of merchants go forth covered by veils of cloth.
Even the merchants do not go outside without soldiers out of fear.
Thus, submerged in suffering, they experience hell directly;
what difference is there indeed between them and the dog-cookers (śvapacas) here?
Moreover, this she-demon of craving cuts their hearts to pieces;
diseases, the manifest messengers of Yama, wither both their wealth and their bodies.
Wealthy people become dependent on servants, even upon the servants of their servants.
Dependence on others and hope for another are two hells situated within the home;
independence and freedom from hope are two heavens situated in one's own hand.
Blessed am I, though a dog-eater’s wife, pure and free from such faults.
A doe, though joined with heaven throughout her life, goes to heaven at the end as well;
she obtains food even in the forest consisting only of fruits and leaves.
A lioness, however, obtains food even in the great forest consisting of flesh.

The merchant’s wife receives food that is delicious yet fraught with disease; the outcaste woman receives food that is dry yet provides strength. "Blessed am I! I am an outcaste woman, endowed with great happiness. (44–45)
In the final stage of their lives, kings, queens,
and others indeed become renunciants or forest-dwellers for the sake of attaining liberation.
In the forest, I see them all, entirely free from attachment to worldly enjoyments.
I am more blessed than all ascetics like myself from the very moment of my birth;
I am forever a female renunciant, always one for whom her husband is a deity, always endowed with virtuous conduct, and even as a dog-eater’s daughter, I am auspicious.
"Aha! I have no bondage; I have no rejection of the Dharma.
Here I perform service to the village, which is appropriate for my birth and brings about welfare.
The holy ones, possessing the knowledge of Brahman, [remove] the sinful stains of the wicked."
By providing instruction, they cause the heart to cast out its impurities and stains of karma through knowledge. By offering service to the body, I shall cause [the soul] to emerge from the pit.
Since the removal of impurity must be performed equally for both,
I shall indeed become a female renunciant, just like one who has renounced action.
There are auspicious gurus in this world who effect the destruction of impurity.
By destroying the impurity of ignorance, they illuminate wisdom.
Having become my own great self, I cast off even the impurity of sorrow;
having myself become my own great self, I move about as stainless.
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune! I am a dog-eater among men, yet by the grace of Hari I am always happy compared to others.
Indeed, there is no one among the many who can take away my fruit.
There is no destruction of the Dharma for me, even though it arises from association with many.
Without the forest, dwelling in the forest brings me happiness;
and even apart from the life of renunciation, inner peace always abides within me.

I am blessed; I am a vessel of merit and a supreme vessel of happiness, for I enjoy every pleasure bestowed by my own husband. In whosever home there may be suffering or dejection for either man or woman—
That state where there is constant cause for suspicion is indeed the Raurava hell.
But that house where there is love and goodwill between man and woman,
and likewise an absence of mutual suspicion— that is truly the celestial realm of Indra.
Such a heaven as that exists right here in the house of this outcaste woman;
these trees are my garden, and this river is mine.
Your virtue, O noble lady, stands supreme over all and bestows liberation upon me.

"I am blessed, even though I am a dog-cooker, for I possess all forms of good fortune. While I was thus situated, as he was passing by the side path, I indeed beheld that holy man, the yogi absorbed in Brahman. (62–63)
By the name of the great accomplished master (mahāsiddha), the Lord Caitanyaśīla, protection swiftly went toward the saint; standing upon the path, it became present before him.
With palms joined and face bowed, she prostrated from afar to the holy man.
The virtuous one said: "Always be peaceful and possessed of liberation.
Having thus become a divine goddess, always be dear to Brahman. Be a devotee of Hari, O virtuous woman, and be one who serves the holy. (65–66)
Having spoken thus, Caitanyaśīla went a great distance to the foot of a tree on the bank of the Bhadrāvatī river and sat down for a moment.
Then, having gone into the river water, he bathed and performed worship to Hari.
Having offered fruit, water, and sugar-candy to Hari, the sage gave the remains as a gift to the outcaste woman who had arrived there. She too, having received that gift, presented it to her husband.
Then, considering his own fortune to be supreme, he ate the remainder. Thereafter, the virtuous man took up residence for the night beneath a tree.
Coldness began to afflict him, and seeing this, that outcaste woman gave it to him.
The virtuous man kindled wood for the purpose of lighting the fire;
he also rotated his rosary and performed worship, chanting:
"O Hare, Kṛṣṇa! O Hare, Viṣṇu! O Hare, Nārāyaṇa, Lord! (71–72)
The saintly one performed the kīrtana of the holy Name with the sounding of cymbals, [singing]: "O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama!
Then the outcaste woman, having come along with her husband to the vicinity of the tree—
Having sat at a distance, she performed that kind of worship. At the conclusion of the worship, filled with humility, she questioned that holy man:
"From where have you come, O holy one, and where is your permanent residence?"
"Where are you going? Do you perhaps have some auspicious business?
The saint replied, "I am coming from the abode of Lord Hari, which is very far away.
My residence is with Śrī Hari; I am going toward Śrī Hari."
"Everything is well in every way through the grace of the Guru-tīrtha.
Rakṣā said: "O virtuous one, what indeed is this Guru-tīrtha, by which all may be well? O Sage, please tell me out of compassion. (77–78)
The virtuous one said: "Viṣṇu is the Guru; Brahmā is the Guru; Hara is the Guru.
Hari the Lord is the Guru; the virtuous one is the Guru; the mother, husband, and father are the Guru.
The Guru is the bestower of knowledge, the remover of sin, and the Great One. (79)
The Guru is the bestower of liberation, and one’s own self is the supreme Guru.
The inner self, the venerable Hari, the Supreme Lord, is the Guru of the Guru.
By taking refuge in Him, there is the destruction of sins and even eternal liberation. (3.55.80–81)
Even one of evil conduct— a dog-cooker, a dog-eater, or even one who consumes liquor and meat, engages in sexual misconduct, and drinks wine— even such a person,
though a great sinner or an extreme offender, becomes purified by taking refuge in the Guru.
Neither vows, nor sacred fords, nor any supreme atonement [can liberate one];
he upon whom the grace of the guru has descended is instantly released from bondage.
One should receive from the guru the mantra and the supreme purifying name of Hari.
Having drunk from the lotus feet of the Guru, having meditated upon the form of the Guru of Gurus,
having served the Guru as a god, and having propitiated him at that very moment,
one who offers up everything as one's own possession shall immediately attain liberation.
The saint is a boat, the guru is a boat, Hari is a boat, and the husband of a virtuous wife is a boat.
Knowledge is a boat, supreme devotion is a boat, and taking refuge is a boat.
Pāpā asked that saint, "Grant me refuge. (86–87)
"Give me the mantra for a dog-eater; [give it] to my master, the dog-eater.
Caitanyaśīla first caused that auspicious water of Śrī Hari to be drunk by her, having poured his own foot-water into it.
Having made her pure and sanctified, he then gave her the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ.
"The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord, my Master, and my Husband. (3.55.90)
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama!"—
with these mantras the saint gave to the outcaste woman and to the outcaste man.
He caused a vessel to be made, and thereafter, for half the night,
both the husband and wife massaged the feet of the holy man.
Through that service to the saint, his status as a Cāṇḍāla then vanished.
Until morning, they had been massaging His feet;
then in the morning, Lord Hari arrived, resplendent in a divine celestial chariot,
accompanied by His foremost attendants and graced by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others.
Hari said to Sādhu, Rakṣā, and Sumaraṇa,
"My followers, you three are my devotees who have attained a divine state;
purified by your service to the Guru and the holy places, ascend this celestial chariot."
Having been addressed thus, those three bowed and, casting off their bodies upon the surface of the earth,
became divine male attendants (*pārṣada*), and likewise the female attendant (*pārṣadānī*) became divine.
Then, having become four-armed, they stood within that celestial chariot (*vimāna*).

They went with Hari to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme liberation. Thus, O Lakṣmī, this Guru-tīrtha is indeed instantly purifying even for women who are impure, including those women who are equal to outcaste dog-cookers.
It is the supreme bestower of liberation; therefore, one should serve the Guru.
By reading and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall be attained in this very life.

Thus ends the [section] on the sacredness of the Guru in the *Vadhūgītā* within the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Herein is described how, through the power of the Guru Caitanya Śīla, the wife of Sumara, who was a dog-eater (*śvapacī*), was protected along with her husband by the Guru.
The fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Attainment of Liberation," etc., [ends].
Chapter 55. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga*), Chapter 56.
[The Author: Chapter 57.
Śrī Nārāyaṇīśrī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, the Guru-tīrtha is the highest of the high.
"Tell me, indeed, what is the cause by which I have attained this state of supreme excellence?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"The purification of the earth is by wind alone, while the purification of the body is by water."
Purity of mind comes through dispassion, and purity of the self through discernment. (2) Discernment is the knowledge of reality, and that indeed cannot exist without a guru.
Because you swiftly bestow illumination, you are considered the supreme guru. (3)
Just as a lamp becomes the illuminator for people even among hundreds of thousands in the darkness,
so too is the teacher a lamp.
Indeed, a boat is the means of crossing for many creatures even though they exist in the ocean.
In the ocean of the world, although embodied beings exist in great number, the Guru alone is the savior.
(5) Just as there is no end to the stars in the sky, yet the moon is their illuminator; so too, there is no end to human beings, yet the true Guru is the giver of light. (6)

The night is never dispelled by other planets, nor is darkness ever removed by other people without a true guru. Water, sacred fords, earth, worship, sacrifice, vows, and shrines— [are all ineffective without him]. (7)
Indeed, it is said that in ancient times the holy places (tīrthas) originated solely through the true guru.
The holy place of the physical form is known as the image, while the holy place of knowledge is the book;
both of these have arisen from the true guru alone, and not otherwise.
All the gods possess the power of the guru; likewise, all mantras possess the power of the guru.
Yoga also possesses the power of the guru, yet the guru-tīrtha is even greater than that. Through my yoga, the state of being a guru increases and becomes manifest.
And even a sense of wonder arises from association with me.
Association with me, affection for me, devotion to me, and service to me—
by whomsoever this is performed for me alone, their status as a guru becomes eternal.
Since I am the eternal Guru, the Lord possessed of beginningless knowledge,
through my yoga, the eternality of the Guruhood of my devotee arises from that.
Just as by association with a precious object, a worthless thing becomes precious.
A cow accompanied by her suckling calf shall always be of great value;
a human being who is a mine of knowledge is born as one of great value;
and even one who possesses a pure and profound disposition is reckoned as being of great value.
Indeed, copper becomes highly valuable through association with gold;
in this world, a maiden who has chosen a husband is highly esteemed and well-honored.
Likewise, all servants, when joined with a king, truly become as precious as royalty.
O beloved, even a vessel filled with ordinary objects becomes as precious as a gem;
in the same way, one who is devoted, endowed with devotion, especially united with me, and possessed of a state of purity, becomes exceedingly valuable. (17–18)
A contented servant indeed performs the work of the subjects immediately;
moreover, filled with haste, he causes it to be done immediately through the king's door.
But a puppet-king certainly does not perform the work of the subjects.
Nor does a mechanical doll perform its task with such haste;
yet my servants, devoted to me and protectors of those who seek refuge,
carry out the duties of those seeking refuge even with sudden urgency.
"Indeed, on this earth, saintly persons are my very embodiments of consciousness;
likewise, the servants who carry out the king's business are his very embodiments of consciousness.
Having spoken thus, he laughed and accepted service and other offerings.
Having given gifts, they indeed perform the desired rites for embodied beings.
Since the gurus are the support for those living beings who have come for refuge,
I have indeed granted this station to the gurus, and likewise my authority therein.
Like me, they are worthy of worship; for in this world, they are indeed Nārāyaṇas.
Just as I am, so too are they, for they are the promoters of devotion to me.
Therefore, they are the most excellent gurus, and the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha) consists of the guru.
They quickly effect the cleansing of sins through the gift of water;
they quickly effect the destruction of ignorance through the imparting of mantras;
and by means of their blessings, they burnish even great prosperity such as heaven and the like.
By their grace, they swiftly send one even to the state of liberation;
at times, they effortlessly cause me to appear here quickly.
Through my divine form, my manifestation occurs within the heart by virtue of their compassion.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, those virtuous ones are always my supreme gurus.
Through devotion toward me, they indeed become my most excellent supreme lords.
I shall now describe that devotion by which they are truly the most excellent.

Service to the spiritual master, the gods, the ṛṣis, and the perfected ones (siddhas), association with the saintly, and devotion to virtuous activities—this is considered by Me to be another form of devotion. Furthermore, service to those who are My own portions, the spiritual masters, is also another form of devotion unto Me. (31)
Devotion alone is constantly considered by me to be the bestower of liberation.
Having attained the divine essence of Brahman and having drunk that which is filled with bliss,
the devotees, whose enjoyment is centered on Brahman, become eternally satisfied.
And they become flooded with the essence of Brahman, taking on the form of the Imperishable.
Just as fire entering fire, so does the self enter the Supreme Self.
One should always mutter the name "Hare Hare," which bestows the very form of Brahman.
I am Brahman, the supreme light, devoid of the principle of māyā.
I am Brahman, the supreme light; I possess knowledge for the sake of liberation.
The Blessed Lord, the Supreme Person, is attainable through devotion enriched by knowledge.
I, the Supreme Lord, am indeed attainable through meditation, worship, recitations, authentic hymns of praise, observance of vows, service, and loving devotion.
I am the root of great spiritual welfare and the source of a continuous stream of merit.
The fruit of life is sweet: the remembrance of Hari’s inevitable destiny.
Service accompanied by affection should be understood as devotion, which is the primary means of accomplishment.
Those devotees are intent upon my service with undivided thoughts.
Shedding tears out of great joy, their hair standing on end,
my Vaiṣṇavas are always devoted to the activities of Kṛṣṇa and ever affectionate toward one another;
they hear the imperishable Supreme Brahman and chant the Bhāgavata.
The best of Vaiṣṇavas should indeed glorify [the Lord] with devotion, preceded by prostration.
He who possesses affection for my devotees, who rejoices in the worship of my devotees,
and who is delighted by hearing the stories of my devotees— he is considered the most excellent of devotees.
He who has surrendered his heart with devotion to Kṛṣṇa with his whole being,
having taken refuge in the true guru, is indeed a great devotee (mahābhāgavata).
He himself worships Me, Viṣṇu, and likewise lives depending upon Him.
Even if he is a barbarian, if he is endowed with manifold devotion, he is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
That devotee is truly the best of sages; he attains the supreme goal.
To him gifts should be given, from him they should be accepted, and he is to be worshiped just like Hari.
Even a Cāṇḍāla who is a devotee of the Blessed One purifies by his own will;
but one who is my devotee is not a Cāṇḍāla—he is a divine attendant of mine. Show compassion to the one who has sought refuge and who entreats, "I am yours."
One should grant fearlessness to all beings; this is the vow of Hari.
One who knows the Vedas and Vedāntas is superior to thousands of mantra-reciters and sacrificers;
one who is a devotee of Viṣṇu is distinguished above all those who possess knowledge of the Vedāntas.
The single-minded ones, possessing divine bodies, go to the supreme state.
Viṣṇu is equal through his single-mindedness; Viṣṇu is devoted to his devotees. Those virtuous single-minded devotees are considered superior to ten million brahmins.
For you are indeed most dear to me, even among all those who are dear.
These virtuous ones, great devotees of the Lord, are considered always superior to ten million saintly persons and superior to hundreds of millions of brahmins. (3.56.50–51)
Brahmins are the teachers of the worlds;
among Brahmins who perform Vedic sacrifices, the virtuous are considered the teachers of all Brāhmaṇas.
Those Brahmins who were immersed in household life have indeed resorted to cremation grounds.
Those virtuous ones, absorbed in Brahman, have attained the supreme abode—
those whose devotion is always unswerving even in times of adversity,
and who possess that superior love for Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu which is eternal and never-failing.
Remembering Viṣṇu, my devotee does not remain far from my heart;
even one of firm devotion who is bound by ropes and snares binds me to himself.
He who carries devotion for Viṣṇu has accomplished everything.
He alone is truly virtuous by whom I, the Beloved, have been realized.
Even those who perform the principal sacrifices and have mastered the Vedas do not attain that supreme state which the best of sages attain.
Whosoever in this world is a Vaiṣṇava, even if they follow false conduct or belong to no stage of life (anāśramin),
purifies all the worlds just as I, the Blessed One myself, do. Likewise, those who are cruel, evil-minded, and devoted to sinful conduct—
Those who are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa go to my supreme abode.
(59) Firm devotion to Nārāyaṇa that is always unswerving—that alone bestows eternal happiness; what is heaven compared to its presence? (3.56.60)
Even after wandering repeatedly and on all sides within the great ocean called saṃsāra,
if one should somehow obtain Kṛṣṇa and hold him by his own hand,
yet does not hear the divine qualities of Śrī Hari, the Supreme Soul, [then that is a tragedy]. (6.1)

He should always be understood as deaf in this world, or rather, as one who constantly hears evil, he whose hair does not stand on end when the name of Viṣṇu is proclaimed. Even if he is a king and handsome, he should indeed be known as a corpse—a mere rotting carcass. (62–63)
For men, women, and even those with neuter bodies who possess devotion and whose minds are fixed upon me, liberation is certain to occur.
I am indeed the Lord, the King of Death, who addresses the Yamas holding nooses in their hands.
May they lead the sinful non-Vaiṣṇavas here to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Even one of wicked conduct, if he worships me while remaining fixed in me, is indeed a saint;
liberated, he is a teacher superior to ten million Brahmins.
Indeed, all the great bhāgavata-dharmas dwell within him;
likewise, O lotus-born one, every kind of peace dwells there.
And as for his dharma, artha, and kāma—what account can be made of them?
Liberation is his eternal servant, and liberation rests in his hand.
(68) Whether it be illusion or its products, the worlds, sovereign powers, or supernatural attainments—even when being experienced, these do not at all obstruct my yogin. (69)
What is the use of sacrifices, what use of vows, gifts, or other means of merit,
for one in whom love for Hari has arisen and by whom the Lord is worshipped through that?
[3.56.70] Not with other ointments, lamps, and the like, nor with sandalwood, perfumes, or ornaments.
O Kamalā, I am not so pleased by the offering of love as I am by [this devotion].
Indeed, there are two fruits of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra that are like nectar:
supreme devotion to me, Kṛṣṇa, and association with my devotees.
With devotion toward me, the Lord who bestows liberation, one should live by means of leaves, flowers, fruits, water, wealth, food, and ornaments.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance with joy.
"May some devotee in our family deliver us, even those among the hungry ghosts (pretas).
Those who have come to me for refuge, though they may be devoid of meditation and knowledge, shall transcend death and go to my supreme state. (74–75)

The person who bows to the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama, the cause of liberation, who is without beginning or end, becomes worthy of homage by all the world. [He bows] to that Viṣṇu, the treasury of bliss, the Lord Hari who dwells within.
One should always bow with devotion, with a mind joined to the body,
to that beloved Supreme Lord, the witness of all, who dwells within all beings and perceives their good and evil. (77–78)
Even a salutation offered with ease to the wielder of the discus (Cakrapāṇi) becomes the destroyer of the ropes of the snares of worldly existence.
[This applies] toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who possesses the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Even a prostration performed with devotion purifies even a dog-cooker (śvapāka).
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should perform the salutation with joy;
by a single prostration alone, one goes to my supreme state.
O Lakṣmī! By my salutation, there is indeed eternal liberation for me.
I, Kṛṣṇa, truly deliver the one who bows down from the ocean of worldly existence, whether he be sitting, lying down, standing, or wherever he may be.
The wise person should always recite the mantra "Namo Nārāyaṇāya.
(83) "The name 'Nārāyaṇa' is worthy of my tongue;
nevertheless, contentious people look upon my house as belonging to Yama. (84)
Vyāsa and others, as well as Śaṅkara and others, while praising the Supreme Lord,
turn back from their mental exertion, for there is no end to my qualities.
Even one who is helpless might repeatedly utter the name "Nārāyaṇa."
He has girded his loins for the journey toward liberation.
Even in a dream, the chanting or hearing of the name of Śrī Hari leads to liberation; how much more so here, while awake! (86–87)
By uttering "Obeisance to Kānta, to Kṛṣṇa; obeisance to Śrī Hari;
and obeisance to the Master," one shall attain the path of liberation.
Indeed, by the chanting of the names of Hari, there occurs the destruction of all sins.

O Lakṣmī, for those traveling the long road leading to the abode of Śrī Hari, the chanting of the names of Śrī Hari is the provision for the journey in every respect. Even women who are very modest, though remaining within the house, [should perform it]. (3.56.90)
By chanting "Kṛṣṇakānta, O Hari," people become liberated and go to the divine abode.
He on whose tongue-tip the two syllables "Ha-ri" reside will cross the ocean of saṃsāra and attain my own state.
Though she may be pervaded by a thousand misdeeds and devoid of righteous action,
if she desires purity and liberation found in taking refuge in my feet, she shall attain me by becoming devoted to my name, even while remaining concealed. (92–93)

O beloved, the propitiation of Śrī Hari, who is dear to the entire world, is the essence within this worthless saṃsāra; it consists entirely of flowers, water, and fruit offered by women with heartfelt devotion. 94.

By him, the gods have been worshipped by me, and the circle of liberated ones has been honored. Neither mother, nor father, nor even kinsman performs that which I perform when I, the Lord, am satisfied and worshipped through service.
O Lakṣmī, I am indeed propitiated by a woman who observes the conduct prescribed for her caste and stage of life;
that is the path that pleases me.
[I am also pleased] by wealth, sovereignty, greatness, progeny, and even by faith.
I am indeed to be propitiated by all who are endowed with loving devotion (premabhakti).
Without devotion, without affection, without love, and without meditative realization, I do not attain satisfaction; I am possessed by a hunger for such feeling.
Those of the past and even those of the more distant past have gone to my supreme imperishable state;
those of the most ancient times went through devotion, and so too may women go there as well.
Thus, [worship] me always as the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, whose form is Kṛṣṇa.
The virtuous protect their master and their inner self within their hearts.
(1.01) By my yoga, those very ones are the saintly, the truthful, and the virtuous;
the virtuous women belonging to the circle of gurus are considered by me to be the most excellent of all. (1.02)
Those who are of my nature, whose very form is mine, and who are not inferior to me— those Nārāyaṇas,
all virtuous men with truthful wives, are indeed my incarnations.
And all those virtuous women who are incarnate are truly my own incarnations.
Therefore, from my yoga, the gurus are the bestowers of mantra and also the bestowers of liberation.
Thus, O Śrī Nārāyaṇa, the preeminence of the guru indeed exists eternally;
I am the guru and the guru is I—there is not even the slightest difference here.

Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Reason for the Teacher’s Supreme Excellence and His Nature as Śrī Hari," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 57 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 57]
[The Author: Chapter 58.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī-Śrī, to this essence of all the Vedas.
The Supreme Lord is indeed to be worshipped as that which is to be accomplished by all means of attainment.
(1) The Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, is to be propitiated and realized through gifts, pilgrimages, austerities, sacrifices, and acts of service to others. (2)
Sixty thousand holy places and six thousand holy places indeed reside at the feet of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
All expiations, austerities, and vows likewise abide there.
For all of them together, the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa is supreme.
(4) For those people and likewise for women who desire the burning away of their sins, the remembrance of me, Śrī Hari, is the supreme atonement. (5)
Even meditation for a single moment upon Śrī Hari, the Supreme Self, surely bestows heaven; constant meditation, however, grants liberation.
Those who are devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa remain so throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
Those whose conduct is such, they are liberated, without a doubt. Whether rising, falling, walking, speaking, or entering [a place],
as well as eating or drinking— he who remembers me, Kṛṣṇa, is indeed liberated.
In every instance, one’s conduct in one’s respective duty should be performed with Acyuta as the refuge;
for by that, all such action becomes free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa) and bestows liberation.
Meditation is declared to be the supreme dharma, austerity the supreme [duty], and the vow the supreme.
Purity is supreme meditation on Hari; therefore, one should become absorbed in that meditation. There is no object of meditation higher than Viṣṇu, nor anything more to be sung or attained than He.
Therefore, one should perform meditation upon Viṣṇu, Hari, and contemplate Him within the heart.

Even that which is difficult to attain, supreme, and beyond the range of the mind— Hari, when meditated upon here with a gracious mind, indeed grants it. Even through negligence, meditation on Kṛṣṇa, remembrance, and obeisance [yield great fruit].
Once performed, it bestows the eternal state of the Supreme Brahman.
(13) There is indeed nothing equal to meditation for purifying sin;
the remembrance of Hari is the burner of the seed of future bodies. (14)
The perfected accomplishment of meditation indeed bestows concentration (*samādhi*).
Having attained concentration upon Hari, one attains liberation right here.
When Viṣṇu is established within one's own mind, the sins of the devotees are truly [destroyed].
The self is consumed from its very root, and one who has been liberated becomes Brahman.
Just as gold indeed becomes pure through contact with fire,
so too the soul of the devotee, through union with Hari, becomes the abode of Brahman.
Whatever sin dissolves through thousands of baths in the Gaṅgā and ten million baths at Puṣkara,
that very sin perishes when Hari is remembered.
Indeed, whatever sin is dissolved by thousands of breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma), [that too perishes when Hari is remembered].

By meditating on Hari for even a single moment, the meditator’s sin is destroyed. Time, Māyā, Antaka, the servants of Yama, and even Death themselves do not exist for him who possesses Puruṣottama as his refuge. (3.57.20)
That lunar day, that day and night, that astrological conjunction, and that moon;
that omen and that ascendant—all these are indeed auspicious when Hari is remembered therein.
That [otherwise] would be loss, that disease, that very injury, and that poverty.
In whatever moment Kṛṣṇa Hari is remembered in the home, and not Keśava;
in whose house Hari resides, for him there is always the Satya Yuga. In whose house Hari is not present, for him other ages prevail in that house.
In whose heart there is no Kṛṣṇa, nor Hari in his thoughts;
in whose house there is no image, and whose mind is a cremation ground;
Govinda indeed shines forth as the imperishable abode on all sides of this world.
For one whose mind is fixed upon Vāsudeva during the acts of drinking, eating, and performing duties,
that eternal and firm imperishable abode is surely attained.
Even one who performs the duties of a householder and is immersed in worldly affairs cuts through the illusion of human existence by dedicating those very actions to Keśava.
Obstacles depart far away, and even Time abandons its crest-lock.
Death does not behold one in whose heart Śrī Hari resides.
One should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, that Kṛṣṇa, in all actions.
His is the gain, his is the victory, in whose heart Janārdana dwells. (28–29)

Even for swarms of insects and birds who possess the grace of Śrī Hari, there is attainment of the world of Brahmā; how much more so for those who serve Hari? The shade of the Nārāyaṇa tree is neither too cold nor does it cause distress.
It pacifies the southern gate and should be resorted to by those seeking happiness.
Whether walking, standing, or performing other actions according to one's will,
he who does not forget Hari is indeed considered a perfected yogi.
Hari should always be meditated upon by a virtuous woman in the form of her guru, her husband, or the sun;
he is youthful, adorned with ornaments and fine garments, possessing ten million desires, and exceedingly beautiful.
Indeed, there is nothing equal to meditation for purifying the soul or destroying sin.
Even an outcaste (śvapaca) becomes pure by eating the food of an outcaste,
provided he possesses devotion to Viṣṇu and Viṣṇu abides within his own self;
such a person delivers tens of millions of those who have come to him for refuge from the cycle of worldly existence.
That is true knowledge wherein the Lord of Lakṣmī resides; that is the true story wherein Mādhava appears.
That is the true action which is for the sake of Keśava; that is the true service which is for the Lord of Śrī.
That is the true tongue which praises Hari; that is the true mind which meditates upon the Master.
Those two hands which are devoted to the service of Hari are likewise for the virtuous.
Bowing to Kṛṣṇa is the fruit of the head; mindfulness is the fruit of the intellect;
worship of Hari is the fruit of the hands; and devotion to Hari is the fruit of the mind. (37–38)
The fruit of speech is the hymn of praise to Hari; the fruit of the eyes is the sight of Hari;
the fruit of the skin is the touch of Viṣṇu; the fruit of the body is service to Him. The fruit of prosperity is the offering of everything; the fruit of life, however, is liberation.
Even a heap of sin as vast as the Lokāloka mountain perishes through the mere remembrance of Śrī Hari; by that remembrance alone, a person becomes a virtuous soul.
Whatever action one performs—whether good or bad, auspicious or inauspicious—[it is all transformed]. 3.57.40–41.
Whether it be voluntary or involuntary, for one’s own sake or for the sake of others—
having entrusted everything to Nārāyaṇa, the agent is not tainted by it.
The king is the refuge of the kingdom, and parents are the refuge of the child.
Indeed, Dharma is the refuge for all mortals, and Hari is the refuge for all.
Those who always bow to, remember, and worship me—the Lord—they alone are, in my view, the very embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites; they are non-different from me and bestow liberation.

O Lotus-born One, I consider even a Śūdra who is a devotee of the Blessed Lord, or a Niṣāda, or a dog-cooker (outcaste), or even a courtesan or an executioner, to be superior [to one who merely knows the Vedas].
Just as deer and other animals flee upon seeing a mountain ablaze with fire, [so do the ignorant flee from such devotees].
Seeing people illuminated by me, those whose nature is evil flee.
For whatever the extent of one’s faith, so great indeed is their success.
Herein, a special grace shall become the bestower of boundless fruit.
There is no end to His graciousness, nor is there any limit to its fruit;
in that regard, there is indeed no restriction whatsoever concerning Hari.
When the Lord, the Sovereign, is pleased, He is satisfied with even a mere drop of water.
The Lord gives the ocean of nectar; indeed, who is the Lord of the Lord?
(49) By giving a kiss to the King, a female companion obtains half his throne;
likewise, by giving it to Hari, one obtains my imperishable abode. (50)
Thus, O Nārāyaṇī-Śrī, you are the sovereign lady among all brides; you have been offered together with them. He is I myself, and she is you, Hari himself.
If anyone, by the grace of Harikṛṣṇa, worships even thus—
One does not cross over *saṃsāra*, which is difficult even for the gods to traverse.
One should always meditate upon and worship Viṣṇu, who resides within one's own self—the Lord Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa; by that, one shall be liberated from bondage.
By constantly meditating upon Viṣṇu— the creator of all bodies, the delight of all knowledge and the mind, the omnipresent true Guru— one is liberated.
He is beyond all abodes yet established in all abodes, the cause of all incarnations.
Meditating upon me as the very form of the Avatāra, one is swiftly liberated.
Meditating upon me as Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, and Narāyaṇa—the essence of Vāsudeva and the rest—one is swiftly liberated. (55–56)
Meditating upon me— the abundance that is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Puruṣa, the Supreme Person, the Lord of all lords, the Beloved— one is completely liberated.
[One meditates upon] the golden Mahāviṣṇu, and also Viṣṇu as Vairāja.

Meditating upon me as the nature of the inner self, one is instantly liberated. (58) Having meditated upon me—who am meditated upon by the liberated ones and their consorts, by the lords and their consorts, and by the incarnations and the gods—one is liberated. (59)
Any embodied being who desires liberation from the bonds of *saṃsāra* is fully liberated by praising, meditating upon, and worshipping me, Hari.
O Lakṣmī! Constant strength is to be obtained from me, who manifest in all incarnations.
I have taken refuge in the Lord of the Imperishable; what can death do to me?
(61) I have taken refuge in the Supreme Lord, who holds the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus, and who dwells within; what can death do to me? (62)
I have taken refuge in Him who is marked with the Śrīvatsa and endowed with the fish, trident, banner, bow, svastika, discus, and arrow; what can death do to me?
[I seek] Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the beloved husband, the son of Kambharāśrī.
I have taken refuge in the son of Gopāla; what can death do to me?
(64) I have fully taken refuge in the husband of the beloved of Brahmā, the husband of the beloved of Hari, the husband of Satī, and the Lord of Śrī; what can death do to me? (65)
I have taken refuge in the Lord of Rādhā, Ramā, Padmā, and Padmāvatī;
in the Lord of Māṇikī. What can death do to me?
[I take refuge in] the destroyer of Kamalā’s sorrow, the Lord of Lakṣmī, and the Lord of Nārāyaṇī.
I have taken refuge in Śivajeśa; what can death do to me?
(67) I have taken refuge in Divyādevīpati, Kīrāpati, Kāmodakāpati, and Suśīleśa; what can death do to me? (68)
I have taken refuge in Līlāvatī’s lord Khaśīnātha, the husband of the courtesan Huṇḍikā, the master of Haṃsikā; what can death do to me?
[I have taken refuge in] Aśokasundarī’s lord, the husband of Vikalendumatī.
I have taken refuge in the Lord of the Bhillas; what can death do to me?

(3.57.70) I have taken refuge in Hari, my beloved husband—who is the protector, wisdom, tranquility, and faith, and who is the Lord who has liberated his own consort—what can death do to me? (3.57.71)
I have taken refuge in Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, Rāmakṛṣṇa, Nārasiṃha, Janārdana, and Rājarāja; what can death do to me?
[I take refuge in] Vārāha, Vāmana, Viṣṇu, Mādhava, and Keśava as my Lord.
I have taken refuge in the Beloved of Kāntā; what can death do to me?
(73) I have taken refuge in Kapila, Hari, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, Śiva, and the Lord of the Imperishable; what can death do to me? (74)
I have taken refuge in the eternal, supreme Lord, the black-hued one with infinite heads, the source of Brahman; what can death do to me?
Standing by His side, I eternally drink the nectar of love for Hari.
I have taken refuge at the feet of Hari; what can death do to me?
(76) I drink the sweet, fragrant juice produced from Hari’s betel; having taken refuge in Him, what can death do to me? (77)
I constantly savor the grace known as the nectar of immortality;
having attained the essence of the lips [of the Lord], what can death do to me?
Having reached the bed of Śrī Hari, I carry within me great bliss.
I have taken refuge in that which dwells within; what can death do to me?
I have attained imperishable strength and reached eternal bliss.
I have taken refuge in the one Self; what can death do to me? (3.57.80)
Having attained identity with that bliss, enjoying the secret joy,
and having entered into that very state, what can death do to me? Even Mahākāla, the father of Death, by whom I was created and under whose control I am, [is subject to this].
"I have fully surrendered to that Lord; what can death do to me?
Thinking thus, my beloved, who has attained intoxication through Śrī Hari, serves me fearlessly and enjoys all my happiness. (82–83)
She is blessed, she has achieved her purpose, and she abides in all happiness;
her life is fruitful—she who praises the Supreme Person.
Oṃ, salutations to the one who dwells in the imperishable; salutations to you, who are served by the liberated.

Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of lords; salutations to You, the Lord of incarnations. (85) Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the liberated; salutations to the Lord of the virtuous. Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the Imperishable; salutations to the Lord of the hosts of the liberated. (86)
Salutations to you, O Supreme Bliss; salutations to you, O Supreme Imperishable.
Salutations to you, O Eternal Omniscient One; salutations to you, O Giver of Knowledge and Liberation.
Salutations to you who dwell in the Self; salutations to you, O Puruṣottama.
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the inner self of all.
(88) Salutations to you, son of Kambharā; salutations to you, born of Gopālā.
Salutations to you, Lord of Śrī; and salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (89)
Salutations to you who dwell in the Kuṅkumavāpī lake, who recline upon the ocean, who are the sovereign lord of Brahmapriyā, and who are beloved by Haripriyā.
Victory to you, the witness of the true universe; victory to you, the bestower of all human goals!
Victory to you, who are known through Vedānta; victory, O beloved, captivator of the mind!
Victory, O subtle consciousness-bliss; victory, O stainless one of the heart!
Victory, O Lord; victory, O All; victory, O peaceful and eternal One!
You are my guru, O Hari; you are my beloved, you are my master, and you are my sovereign lord.
You are my dharma, knowledge, and the rest; you are Viṣṇu, the bestower of liberation upon me.
You are the Lord, you are the deliverer, you are the protector, and you are the destroyer.
You are Śrī, you are Puṣṭi, you are Lakṣmī, you are Prabhā, and you are Māṇikī.
You are the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), you are the Supreme Lord, you are the sacrifice, and you are the consumer of oblations (hutāśana).
This entire universe is your form; you are the Supreme Brahman, you are the Sovereign.
The inhabitants of heaven worship your form as an incarnation;
O Puruṣottama, O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive whatever has been done or left undone by me during this worship, adoration, drinking, and eating. (96)
I am unable to perform worship correctly at all times; please forgive me.

Whatever recitations, fire-offerings, and so forth have been performed, O Puruṣottama, which were indeed difficult to accomplish—considering them as complete despite their deficiencies, accept me as your own, O Lord. (97–98)
"O Lord, day and night, at the twilights, and in all states of being,
may my devotion to you be unwavering, and may my abiding place be at the pair of your feet.
O Nārāyaṇī, worship me, the Lord, with devotion through this hymn.
If you desire me, O Ānanda, worship with devotion the Teacher of the World.
One who recites this hymn in the morning while remembering Puruṣottama shall attain heaven, liberation, prosperity, and all desired objects. (3.57.10–101)
One desiring a son obtains sons; one who is bound is released from bondage.
A woman seeking a daughter obtains a daughter, and a daughter obtains a virtuous husband.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and the destitute obtains wealth.
One who remembers past lives, the wise, and one seeking knowledge should acquire wisdom.
Even a lowly person may become preeminent, and even an evil man may become the best of the virtuous;
even a rogue may become truthful in speech—he who praises Puruṣottama.
Even those who are excluded from all religious duties are considered virtuous if every action of theirs proceeds with Hari as its sole objective.
No impurity exists for her who possesses devotion to the Supreme Lord.
Mind, speech, body, and all my possessions—I have cast these here into Hari.
(106) By constantly worshipping Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the bestower of happiness, a man, a woman, or even a eunuch attains their heart's desire in this world. (107)

Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Hymn of Total Surrender (*sarvārpaṇa-stotra*) and Other Devotions to Śrī Hari, the Object of Meditation," within the *Vadhū-gītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 58 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 58]
[The Author: Chapter 59.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Contemplating, "I am Brahman, the supreme light, indeed Viṣṇu."
O Nārāyaṇī, here indeed a human being becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
The power of worship, when accumulated during one's life, truly bestows joy;
and one who is endowed with ten thousand acts of worship attains liberation—of this there is no doubt.
He whose mind is attached to Viṣṇu perceives only Viṣṇu;
he who meditates on Viṣṇu and gives up his life-breaths goes to that supreme abode.
And by means of worship, women too, having reduced their sins to ashes—
Immersed in Hari, the beloved of Brahman attains the supreme goal.
(4) For just as fire is seen through churning, so indeed is Hari seen through contemplation.
Liberation is seen right before one's eyes; it is held that liberation resides in this very state. (5)
The Veda proclaims that Person who is of the nature of consciousness and beyond darkness;
for the sake of liberation from this sense of "I," there is no other path to freedom.
When all one's own states are offered unto the Supreme Lord...
Then, even while living, one attains immortality, abiding in the Imperishable (akṣara).
"I am Brahman, the supreme light, entirely beyond the reach of Māyā"—
by realizing the Supreme Self in this way, one should take refuge [in It] and become a partaker of liberation.

Recollection, worship, and prostration performed with devotion each bestow a fruit greater than that of a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha). Long ago, there was a Brahmin named Kauśika who was entirely devoted to me.
Constantly devoted to singing in chorus and accompanied by the clapping of hands,
he repeatedly remained engaged in eating, sitting, lying down, business, and recreation, perpetually singing my own life story.
Having reached the temple in the presence of the Supreme Lord,

he sang there of Hari, accompanied by rhythm, color, and tempo; it was distinguished by the application of melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*) and notes (*svara*), and differentiated by the variations of the musical intervals (*śruti*).
There, seeing him singing, the Brahmin named Padma gave him food for the sake of alms; and Kauśika remained singing,
while Padma remained listening and constantly gave him alms.
Then, Kauśika indeed had many disciples;
all of them, accompanied by the Kauśikas, sang in the temple of Viṣṇu. In that very place, there was a devoted Vaiśya named Mālava.
Accompanied by her wife, she constantly offered a garland of lamps to Hari.
Having smeared the entire area of Hari’s sacred precinct with cow dung, she remained there with great joy together with her husband, listening to excellent singing. (16–17)
Thus, that devoted wife, a performer of worship, honors Mādhava;
and other Brahmins skilled in singing have arrived from Kuśasthalī, numbering fifty, for the purpose of singing in the temple of Hari. (18)

They too, being experts in the true principles of the science of song, nourish the excellence of Kauśika’s singing; for they remain there listening. Thus, those who know the truth of singing have assembled together in the palace. (3.58.20)
His singing there was indeed renowned; having heard of that fame of Kauśika, the master of song, King Kaliṅga then arrived,
paid his respects, and thereafter spoke.
"Let all those skilled in song indeed come to my palace.
Let Kauśika also come to my great residence;
let Kauśika and the others perform my song in my abode."
"Let all my subjects listen to my excellent songs;
I shall give them excellent rewards and wages as well—gold, diamonds, and silver, fivefold more than usual. (24)
Having heard that, Kauśika spoke slowly to King Kaliṅga:
"O Great King, neither my tongue, nor my speech, nor even my mind praises anything other than Hari; nor has it ever praised another, nor will it ever speak of one."
And others, including the disciples of Kauśika, all spoke likewise;
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Hari, Sārasvata, Citra, Citramālya, and Śiśu— all of them spoke in the same manner.

We, the exclusive devotees of Hari, neither sing of nor shall we ever sing of any person or deity other than the Blessed Lord. Furthermore, those who were formerly Śrāvakas have likewise become Vaiṣṇavas. (28–29)
There they addressed the king, O King: "For we are indeed Vaiṣṇavas;
our body, senses, mind, intellect, ego, and self-attributes are dedicated to Viṣṇu. We are devoted to Viṣṇu and to none other, even as those who serve a Vaiṣṇava. (3.58.30)
They do not associate with one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, even out of delusion.
O King of kings, they indeed listen to the life stories of Viṣṇu and His devotees; these ears never attend to anything else.
We hear only of the fame of Hari’s singing and no other praise;
we speak with others only in mere social intercourse, as it were, with you.
O Vaiṣṇava, we do not touch any water, land, insentient object, or conscious being that belongs to another.
We do not speak of anyone other than a Vaiṣṇava, nor do we look upon one who is not a Vaiṣṇava.
We never accept water, food, or anything else from one who is not a Vaiṣṇava; if such things should happen to be obtained, we consume them only when they have been offered by a Vaiṣṇava.
Hearing that, the king became enraged and said, "These people are insulters of me; they must indeed be made to sing by force.
Let these experts proclaim my servants and my fame!"
Having heard this command, those Vaiṣṇavas of firm vows did not sing at all;
then the king commanded his own servants,
and by the king's order, the servants began to sing of his own glory.
Then those Vaiṣṇavas and others, wishing to preserve their reputation before the king,
quickly covered their ears with their fingers and other limbs.
Thereupon the king, becoming greatly enraged, banished them from his own country.
The singers abandoned him and departed toward the northern direction.
Singing the name of Śrī Hari, hearing of the Supreme Lord, and causing other men to hear of Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, they went forth. (3.58.40–41)
They went to the Himalayas for the sake of coolness, and then they met their end.
Viṣṇu, having arrived, said: "Come after me!
For you are my devotees who have sacrificed your lives for my sake. (42)
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Viṣṇu led them to the supreme heaven. Honored by the gods and others, and saluted by the ancestors,
those twice-born ones went swiftly to the world of Brahmā in a mere moment.
Then, seeing Kauśika and the others, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
went forth to meet them and honored them with a welcome as was appropriate.
Thereafter, the blessed Viṣṇu indeed took up those who had sought refuge in him.
The supreme Lord Vāsudeva went swiftly to the world of Viṣṇu.
There in Vaikuṇṭha, Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Sovereign,
was attended by liberated ones, Siddhas, devotees of Viṣṇu, and his personal attendants (pārṣadas).
[He was surrounded] on all sides by those equal to Nārāyaṇa, divine, auspicious, and possessing four arms; endowed with the marks of Viṣṇu, radiant and stainless—
such as Sanaka and others, Nārada and others, and celestial women.

Hari shines while being served within a divine, auspicious, and spotless jeweled palace, five thousand yojanas in extent, which is enclosed by a thousand gates and furnished with a splendid elephant-throne seat. (3.58.49–50)
Then the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama,
Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, beholding Kauśika and the others,
became single-formed while seated upon his divine elephant-throne.
"O Kauśika," he said with great affection, "you are most welcome.
Indeed, there was then a shout of victory from the devotees, sounding like a roar from the abode [of Viṣṇu].
The Blessed One said, "Let my devotees dwell in Vaikuṇṭha."
"Let those devoted to hearing my glory, skilled in the true meaning of song,
and singers of the exposition of the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* (Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā),
dwell near me as my devotees who worship no other deity. (54)
In my abode here, let my eternal attendants be present:
Kauśika, Mālava, and also Mālavī, Padmanetraka, as well as all other singers who serve me by singing. (55–56)
"Let them sing and dwell with me forever;
let Kauśika provide my singing accompanied by instrumental music.
Let this Mālava, together with his wife, prepare a garland of lamps."

"May this Padmākṣa become my Lord of Wealth and the bestower of food. Indeed, all those honored by the world attained his presence. Then, while Viṣṇu was speaking thus, they arrived there in an instant.
The goddess Lakṣmī, who knows the true nature of the qualities of the lute, is expert in the science of instrumental music; she smiles gently and softly, is charming with her sweet syllables,
adorned with ornaments, and sings while embraced by Viṣṇu.
She was surrounded on all sides by thousands of crores of her own female attendants.
There, the great virtuous Sarasvatī, being remembered by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
arrived together with musical instruments, adorned with every kind of ornament.
Rādhā, Ramā, Kamalā, Māṇikī, Śrī, Satī, Padmāvatī, Haṃsī, Mañjulī, and Sadguṇā—
these goddesses, as well as Gaṅgā and Durgā with their respective retinues, arrived there. (63)
Sāvitrī, Virajā, and the Apsarases are remembered as Nārāyaṇī;
at that time, Urvaśī and the others were experts in song, dance, and graceful play.
Menakā, Sahajanyā, Parṇinī, and Puñjikasthalī [were also there]. (64–65)
Kṛtasthalī, Ghṛtācī, Viśvācī, Pūrvacittikā, Anumlocā, Pramlocā, Manuvaṃtī, Sukeśikā,
Arūpā, Subhagā, Bhāsī, Haṃsā, Sūtā, and Sarovatī. (66)
Kāmalī, Abhayā, Haṃsapādī, Sumukhī, Dayā,
Anapāyā, Aruṇā, Varāmbarā, Vimanuṣyikā,
Asiparṇā, Miśrakeśī, Śucikā, Alambuṣā, and Ramā. (67–68)
Mārīcī, Adrikā, Vidyutparṇā, Tilottamā,
Jayā, Kṣemā, Rambhā, Lakṣmaṇā, Asitā, Manobhavā,
Ambikā, Subāhvī, Supriyā, Puṇḍarīkā, Surasā, and Prabhā.
Ajagandhā, Sudatī, Subhujā, Śāntikā, Himā, Muktā,
Devī, Haimī, Puṣpā, Campā, and Sāvitrī also arrived;
indeed, the Gandharvas remembered by Nārāyaṇa came as well.
Nārada and Parvata, Viśvāvasu and Vareṇyaka;
Vasuruci and Suruci, Varutha and Dāruṇa; Haṃsa, Jyotiṣṭama, Madhyācāra, and likewise Tumburu.
Subāhu, Hahā, Hūhū, Parjanya, and Kali;
likewise Śāliśiras, Citraratha, Bhīma, and Prayuta;
Arkaparṇa, Parṇavān, Sūryavarcas, and Dhṛtarāṣṭraka.
Gomān, Suparṇa, Varuṇa, Ugrasena, and Bhīmaka—
these and others arrived there accompanied by musical instruments and other offerings. Furthermore, the Gandharva Tumburu was commanded by me to be present there.
O Lakṣmī! Beholding you as the singer, he thought, "This is not me, nor anyone other than me.
Seated there according to his disposition, filled with various modulations (*mūrchanās*), he joyfully sang with melodious words and struck the lute (*vipañcī*).
Having been propitiated by his excellent singing,
the Supreme Lord gave divine jewels, ornaments, and garments— indeed,
priceless things— to Tumburu; and Tumburu was then filled with joy.
Praised by Hari, Tumburu stood there at the forefront;
many other Gandharvas also sang according to their strength,
according to their knowledge, and according to their practice, accompanied by musical instruments and vocal tones.
They too indeed received excellent rewards there;
yet even so, that reward was not equal to that of Tumburu.
Then all the Apsarases began to sing, employing the most excellent musical instruments.
Then the goddess Lakṣmī sang, and thereafter Sarasvatī sang as well;
they both thought, "We have received the most excellent reward.
Urvaśī then sang beautifully, a song that causes delight to all.
Others also sang according to their ability, accompanied by dance.
At that time, the Lord Śrī Hari and I became pleased;
I gave them diamonds, gems, garments, ornaments, and beautiful garlands.
Then all of them, both male and female, were satisfied, and Nārada sang;
he also gave him an excellent reward.
However, because it was slightly inferior to that of Tumburu, Nārada was not fully pleased.
Even while singing, he was not fully satisfied because he experienced distress;
he fell into deep thought there, his inner self agitated by grief:
"When shall I have performed a song that is the most excellent among all the most excellent? (86–87)
"I shall indeed obtain from Hari an excellent reward, the most superior one attained by Tumburu; shame on me, a fool and one devoid of sense!
Thinking thus, the brahmin sage devoted himself to austerity.
Nārada, remembering Śrī Hari for a thousand divine years, then mastered every art of singing even from Tumburu;
having learned everything from Tumburu, he sang it unto Nārāyaṇa. (3.58.90)
During the time of many manvantaras, the Supreme Person, the god Hari Nārāyaṇa, being pleased, bestowed all auspicious things upon him;
he also made his reward equal to that of Tumburu.
Thus, the illustrious handmaid of the Blessed One, the bride of Nārāyaṇa—
just as Lakṣmī indeed made a total surrender for the sake of Hari,
and just as Tumburu did, and also Nārada— (acted likewise). || 92–93 ||
Just as the brahmin Kauśika, and the twice-born Padmākṣaka;
just as Mālavī the wife and Mālava the husband;
and just as other brahmin singers have made their offering to Hari. (94)
In that same way, one should offer everything to Janārdana, the Supreme Lord.
(95) The functions, activities, and actions of the senses must be performed solely for My sake; by that, I am always pleased. (96)
Beholding, listening, touching, singing, dancing, laughing, and so forth— all these should indeed be performed with devotion for my sake.
Food, water, and clothing should be given to my devotees.

A house, a bed, a seat, a vehicle, a mount, a garden, or land—these should be given according to one's capacity; they bring me satisfaction. That gift indeed yields the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (98–99)

"O Lakṣmī, by hearing [this], by reflecting upon it, and even by causing others to hear it, one shall indeed obtain a fruit equal to that of Nārada; there is no doubt in this. A woman who is a wife obtains a fruit equal to Lakṣmī, and one equal to Sarasvatī."
People would undoubtedly regard them as equal to singers.

(101) Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Supremacy of the Vaiṣṇavas by Means of the Example of Singers such as Kauśika," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 58.

Chapter 60 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Beloved, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Lord!
By what yoga did Nārada indeed obtain the science of song?
And at what time did he attain equality with Tumburu?
"O Śrī Narāyaṇa, tell me this story of the previous kalpa.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Śrī Queen of Śiva, to that auspicious story in detail."
From that time forth, Nārada departed from Vaikuṇṭha;
sighing deeply and dejected as he recalled the honor shown to Tumburu,
he performed austerities for a thousand years and thereby became a mass of ascetic power.
Then he heard an incorporeal voice in the sky:
"O Nārada, for what purpose do you perform this difficult penance?
Go and look at the owl, if your mind is truly intent on singing. (5)
"On the Mānasottara mountain, there is one known as Gānabandhu.
Go quickly and behold him; you shall become a master of song.
Having been addressed thus, Nārada went swiftly to Gānabandhu.
Assuming any form at will, possessing a voice like that of Kāma, and surpassing even the gods,
he taught singing to the birds and indeed to all embodied beings;
likewise, the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, and hosts of Apsarases [were his pupils].
Then they sat down all around Gānabandhu;
having mastered the science of song and being instructed by that bird, they sang there in succession with sweet-toned voices. (3.59.9–10)
Beholding the sage Nārada, Gānabandhu said:
"Salutations to you, O tiger among sages! Welcome to you; this is my salutation.
For what purpose have you come here, O Blessed One—is it out of compassion or by chance?"
"Tell me what merit I may gain by granting you an audience; tell me, what may I do for you?
(12) Nārada then said to him: "Listen, O owl, to my most wonderful account exactly as it happened in the past; I shall relate it to you. (13)
In a past kalpa, during that bygone age, I went into the presence of Hari,
eager to perform a song there. Viṣṇu, accompanied by Lakṣmī, summoned Tumburu.
Having brushed me aside, he joyfully listened to that supreme song.
Because of that, I became afflicted with great sorrow and went away to perform penance regarding the majesty of the yoga of singing associated with the greatness of Viṣṇu.
Having reflected thus, I indeed performed severe austerities thereafter.
At the end of a thousand divine years, I heard a celestial voice directed toward you, saying:
"Go to Gānabandhu, if such is your mind."
"If he is engaged in singing, then look at the owl without delay.
Thus urged, I have come here into your presence;
therefore, regarding me as your disciple, instruct and protect me.
Having heard this, the learned Gānabandhu spoke to Nārada concerning this auspicious and most wonderful narrative centered on devotion to Viṣṇu:
"In a former kalpa, there was a king renowned as Bhuvaneśa."
By means of thousands of horse-sacrifices and tens of thousands of Vājapeya sacrifices;
by ten million times a hundred million cows, and by millions of gold lotuses;
and by half-parārdhas of garments, chariots, elephants, maidens, and horses.
Having bestowed gifts upon the virtuous Brahmins, he protected the earth;
he also caused his own fame to be sung day and night by singers,
and those who did not sing it, he would seize and imprison in a prison.
"He who does not sing for me shall be put to death"—this is my decree.
Let women and men constantly perform songs for me; let the assemblies of Sūtas and Māgadhas sing repeatedly for me. (24–25)
Having thus given his command, that king indeed protected his own kingdom. In the empire of that monarch, there was a brahmin known as Harimiśra, a devotee of Viṣṇu who sang the praises of Hari. (26)
Having reached the riverbank, he worshipped the auspicious image of Śrī Hari;
having offered food and water, he sang with great affection, accompanied by rhythmic beats,
vocal modulations, and melodic timing.
Then the spy, who carried out the king's commands, arrived; he ordered the brahmin to sing the praises of the king's glory. But that Vaiṣṇava brahmin did not accept his words.
Then the spy, having seized that Brahmin, led him into the presence of the king and reported him; the king rebuked the twice-born man and banished him from the kingdom,
having confiscated all his wealth and possessions.
The brahmin went into the depths of the forest and worshipped the glorious Supreme Lord.
The king, however, met his end through the exhaustion of his lifespan.
Having departed for that world, he fell indeed into the Kumbhīpāka hell.

Afflicted by hunger and thirst, and goaded by insults, he experienced manifold sufferings; thereafter, he ascended to heaven. However, there in the celestial chariot, whatever food and nectar-like water he obtained—
Only that which is seen arises and dissolves at the moment of perception;
likewise, neither drink nor food arises for the king or the deity.
Distressed by this, he grieved even here for me, though I had already gone to heaven.
Hunger and thirst arose; whatever food or drink was touched dissolved away.
As he was reflecting, "What sin have I committed that this fruit is now being experienced by me?", a voice from the sky indeed emerged: (36–37).
O King, out of delusion born of ignorance, you have committed a great sin:
you have inflicted a severe punishment upon a brahmin named Harimiśra, who was devoted to Kṛṣṇa and a singer,
even though he was not singing for you.
"His wealth was seized by you and he was exiled from his kingdom.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, he is indeed performing austerities in the forest.
O King, this devotee of Hari has been made deeply miserable by you. (3.59.40)
O King, by that sin, your food and drink will dissolve;
all your acts of charity, sacrifice, and the like will become fruitless.
[Yet you remain] accompanied by song and instrumental music, singing praises centered upon Hari.
"Since you have caused Harimitra, who was devoted to you, to suffer,
your heavenly realm is lost. Go to a mountain cave and dwell there for as long as a manvantara, subsisting on dust."
"Then, after some time, you shall become an insect named Kardamī;
only after experiencing the fruit of your sins will you attain human birth.
Thus, that king indeed fell from heaven into a hollow.
One born in mud came to a muddy place of water and earth.
There, I too had gone as an owl for the sake of inquiry;
questioned by me, he related the account of his previous deeds.
He declared that the fruit of betraying a devotee of the Blessed One is being devoured by mire;
thereafter, I emerged from his cave.
Then, traveling through the path of the sky, I beheld a celestial chariot accompanied by attendants.
Where the Brahmin Harimitraka dwells, accompanied by song;
being praised by gods and attendants in a celestial chariot,
that illustrious one went to the world of Viṣṇu— he too was seen by me.
The merit of singing the praises of Hari leads to a virtuous destination toward Vaikuṇṭha;
by the power of His sovereignty, my mind has turned toward that.
Consequently, I have sat down with the Kinnaras to study the science of song.

Then, through the practice of singing for sixty thousand years, my tongue attained clarity; thereafter, I began to learn singing. Even after that, for a long time, I practiced singing repeatedly. (51–52)
Ten *manvantaras* passed while I was engaged in the practice of singing.
Formerly, I was the master of song for the Gandharvas and their women, as well as for all the Kinnaras, singers, and human women. (53)
Likewise, O Nārada, in a previous kalpa I was the teacher of the Apsarases.
At that time, the assemblies of singers approached me as their teacher—
those very ones who are now present here before you.

But those disciples of mine, along with their pupils and grand-pupils, exist as practitioners of thousands of branches, forming lineages, sub-lineages, and successive descendants. O Nārada, this science of singing cannot indeed be mastered through ascetic penance alone.
"Therefore, endowed with sacred learning, you shall obtain mastery over song from me.
Having been addressed thus, O Lakṣmī, Nārada prostrated before me and, after paying his respects,
learned the art of singing there from Ulūka according to the sequence of instruction.
In conversation, in the company of women, in song, in gambling, in eating, in legal affairs, in the acquisition of wealth, and in income and expenditure for one’s own sake—
the person who casts aside shame attains victory; one possessed of shame certainly does not.
One should never sing with a hand clenched or hidden by the covering of garments; nor with the tossing of hands, nor with the mouth wide open,
nor by the protrusion of the tongue.
One should never sing with arms raised nor with the gaze directed upward; likewise,
it is not recommended [to sing] while looking at one's own limbs or while looking at another,
nor during a collision or when rising from a position on the hip.
Diminution, anger, trembling, and furthermore, distraction of memory—
these, O high-minded one, are not auspicious forms in the practice of singing.
It is not possible, O Sage, to coordinate the rhythmic beat (*tāla*) with only one hand.
One who is afflicted by hunger, afflicted by fear, or likewise afflicted by thirst, should not perform the yoga of singing; nor should it ever be done in darkness.
These and other such [conditions] that lead to negligence and laziness [are to be avoided].
Indeed, these should not be performed on stage by a wise singer.
Having thus received this instruction according to the prescribed rule, the sage Nārada practiced that divine song for a thousand years.

Then, endowed with all perfections, he was accomplished in singing, instrumental percussion, and so forth; he was proficient in the lute and other instruments, and was a knower of the distinctions of all musical notes.
[68] There were thirty-six thousand, six hundred, and ten thousand [beings].
Through the application of the distinctions among the musical notes, the best of sages understood them.
Thereupon, the hosts of Gandharvas and likewise the Kinnaras, joined together with the sages, became filled with joy. (3.59.70)
Having attained unsurpassed song, the sage said to Gānabandhu:
"Having approached you, I have indeed become an expert in song.
O Guru, O Teacher! What may I do for you in honor of your worship? (71)
Then Gānabandhu said: "Indeed, at the end of a day of Brahmā, fourteen Manus perish;
likewise, grant me this boon that I may live, for you must give me my desired sacrificial fee. (72–73)
"O Nārada, let this indeed be my sacrificial fee here: let there be such a state of long life for me, and let there be such supreme auspiciousness as I have desired in my mind.
Then Nārada said to him, "Let it be so, and even more than that."
"In another kalpa, you yourself shall become Garuḍa.
"May it be well with you, O highly wise one; may you be auspicious as the vehicle of the Blessed One.
I shall depart; salutations to you," having said this, the illustrious Nārada departed.
O Lakṣmī, in Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Nārāyaṇa where I dwell,
he performed many beautiful songs as a singer before me.
Having heard that, I spoke to him, who was indeed unskilled in singing.
"O Nārada, even today you are not superior to Tumburu in songs.
Indeed, only when you have attained Gānabandhu and become a knower of the true meaning of song will Mādhava be truly pleased with you. (78–79)
"When I am to descend upon the earth among the beings to be born as humans,
you shall then approach me and act exactly as is required.
At that time, I will make you one who is perfected in song and established in the great vow."
And likewise, together with Tumburu, who is endowed with supreme excellence,
you must train yourself according to the rules for as long as is appropriate within the wombs of gods and gandharvas. May it be well with you, O Surāṣṭraka!
Having heard the words of Nārāyaṇa and having bowed to Hari, Nārada took his lute upon his shoulder and wandered through all the worlds—
the realms of Varuṇa, Yama, Agni, Indra, and Kubera as well.
Having reached the assembly hall in the northwest and likewise in the northeast, Nārada,
skilled in playing the lute, sang praises of Hari perfectly while being honored here and there by hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases. (84–85)
Having reached the world of Brahmā, he spent a night lasting for a kalpa;
then, at dawn, once again in this kalpa, in the abode of the Unborn (Brahmā) within the world of Brahmā,
the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, who were experts in song and instrumental music, [performed].
There were two divine singers of Brahmā, eternally devoted to singing.
Having approached them there while they were singing of Lord Hari, and having received their reward, he bowed down to the Grandfather (Brahmā). ||87-88||
He wandered at his pleasure and went to the house of Tumburu;
taking up a lute, he sang while staying there and thus learned [the art].
Indeed, the seven notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, which are considered the musical scales (svarakalpa) residing there, were mastered by him.
Nārada indeed learned all those [sciences] from Tumburu.
Nārada also learned the seven notes from the Apsarases;
however, at the time of singing, when joined with the lute, the Apsarases [excelled]. (3.59.90–91)
The strings did not attain their proper tuning as they ought to have;
therefore, at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, in the hermitage of Lomaśa,
I, Śrī Narāyaṇa, then performed the singing again until it was perfected.
O Lotus-born one, I spoke to you, my beloved of eternally divine form;
and I spoke to Sarasvatī: "Instruct Nārada indeed in the union of the lute and song.
Thereafter, she replied, "So be it. ||93-94||
Laughing, Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī instructed him;
thereafter, he indeed performed singing in the presence of those dear to Brahmā.
Even as he was singing, he was told: "O sage, you truly do not know the musical notes."
Then, having obtained the celestial women, the lute-strings, and Nārada,
I summoned him and learned the unsurpassed art of singing.
Thereupon, O best of sages, I attained a level of excellence that surpassed even Tumburu.
Then, having approached and prostrated before me repeatedly, he danced.
I said to Nārada there, "You are omniscient; come into my presence.
With the yoga of knowledge, Nārada sang.
Being pleased, I granted him my eternal presence here in this imperishable field at Kuṅkumavāpī; that sage Nārada remains there,
having received the supreme reward bestowed by me in my gracious state.
By me alone was the preeminence also bestowed upon Tumburu;
then, in the course of time, Nārada shall sing [these songs] in the house of Kṛṣṇa.
O wives of Brahmā, this sequence of songs by the sage has thus been recounted to you here.

By this sequence, he shall gradually attain my same world (*sālokya*). Devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa through action, mind, and speech, one who sings of or hears me attains me; that indeed is considered the supreme song.
"Even this owl is Garuḍa, residing in the Aśvasaras lake;
he is my illustrious friend in song, my attendant, and my singer.

Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narration of Nārada’s Acquisition of Vocal Instruction from Garuḍa," within the *Vadhūgītā* section of the exemplary account of the preeminent devotee, in the third section (the Dvāpara Cycle) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 60 [[Author:
