The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Those who are called Vaiṣṇavas are those solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
they are the Bhāgavatas and Sāttvatas who have surrendered their entire being and soul.
"O Lord, tell me what are the characteristics of those [men] and of them [the women].
O Blessed One, O All-pervading Hari, what do You do with them?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:

Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my purifying discourse on love, which embodies the nature of my devotee and maintains a state of identity with Me. (3) Wherever My devotee resides, there I am always present.
I alone am always their supreme deity.
(4) While Hari is being constantly glorified, horripilation arises repeatedly;
trembling, perspiration, and likewise drops of water are seen in their eyes. (5)

Upon seeing men or women who are devoted to me, he whose heart quickly becomes filled with love for them is indeed a Vaiṣṇava. A virtuous woman should not wear clothing belonging to another, nor should she be dependent on anyone else.
Seeing a Vaiṣṇava or a Sāttvata standing before her,
she stands facing him with love and performs prostrations and other marks of respect, just as she would toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa or me.
Upon seeing a male devotee or a female devotee, a devotee or a devotee should quickly bow down.
He who is my very self is my devotee, and that beautiful woman is my devotee;
he attains victory throughout the three worlds, in all abodes and creations.
Casting aside the wicked, he worships me without shame.
He who gives everything for my sake is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, and she [who does so] is a Vaiṣṇavī.
(3.60.10) Even when hearing harsh words spoken at some point by one who is devoid of devotion, he attains joy therein and certainly does not give way to anger. (3.60.11)
One should accept [her] with patience, preceded by a prostration, and indeed recognize her as a virtue;
for she is a Vaiṣṇava woman endowed with divine vision.
Indeed, she who bears all things—such as perfumes and flowers—upon her head [is a Vaiṣṇava].
Thinking thus, "Everything belongs to Hari," she is indeed Vaiṣṇavī;
day and night she performs only auspicious deeds in my field, and filled with affection, she serves me and my true devotees. (13–14)
One who constantly worships my image with all types of offerings—
through action, mind, and speech— is considered by me to be the most excellent devotee.
Whether in sickness, hardship, calamity, obstacle, or distress, [one should worship].
May he who performs day and night service to me, to my service, to the company of the virtuous and to the saintly,
to the temple, to the perfected ones, to the wives of devotees,
and also to the service of the gurus— [may he attain the fruit of his labor]. (16–17)
Likewise, for those dear to Brahmā, there is the auspicious service of the sacred field,
consisting of the offering of food, clothing, and water, as well as the washing of clothes,
the application of ointments, cleansing, refinement, and sweeping.
She performed the washing of vessels, the tending of cows and buffaloes,
the service of guests who arrive unexpectedly, the service of providing food and drink,
and the service of massaging the feet and rubbing the limbs.

And [he should perform] service consisting of the offering of herbs and so forth, as well as the fetching of wood— according to one's capacity, according to what is appropriate, and in accordance with one's caste and stage of life—
as well as the most excellent service of a servant, the duties of a slave, and the conduct of a male or female servant.
Whosoever and whatsoever woman should offer honor, she should likewise offer service;

for whomsoever and whatsoever woman, Nārāyaṇa is the supreme goal and indeed their all-in-all; and for whomsoever and whatsoever woman, He is the ultimate refuge of the virtuous and indeed their all-in-all. (22–23)

Those two who, for the sake of dharma and liberation, surrendered even their entire possessions— they were indeed great devotees of Nārāyaṇa. He who performs all acts of feeding and worship according to his ability [is likewise a devotee].
He who is constantly devoted to Viṣṇu is indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. Whatever food a devotee intent on Nārāyaṇa eats, he eats from the very mouth of Hari; Hari himself is truly satisfied.
The man or woman who worships devotees of Viṣṇu with devotion, indeed like Viṣṇu himself,
attains proximity to Viṣṇu and eternal liberation.
A devotee of Viṣṇu is superior to thousands of other devotees.

A devotee of Hari excels over thousands of devotees of Viṣṇu. (28) A devotee of Hari is of the nature of Brahman and shall go to the abode of the Supreme Lord; for he is indeed a sovereign devotee of me, whose very form is that of the incarnations. (29)
Right here, O Lakṣmī, I indeed provide constant protection for one who is living and liberated; listen now to this supreme story of a devotee.
There was a queen named Citāmbārā, the sovereign consort of King Jiṣṇu.
In the land of Godāla in Saurāṣṭra, there was one devoted to me;
indeed, Jiṣṇuśakti, through his devotion, attained my abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara),
while his queen ruled the kingdom.
Devoted, intent on Brahman, equal to a goddess, and endowed with purity,
she rises in the morning and [worships] me, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme among men,
the Supreme Lord, the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of Śrī, and the Highest Person.
He constantly worshipped [him] through the actions of speech, mind, and body:
providing food, performing worship, offering water, presenting flower garlands, grinding perfumes and other substances, and preparing incense materials. (34–35)
She herself performed the smearing of the ground and likewise the cooking of the sacrificial offerings,
possessing the very essence of devotion and curiosity. Śubhā Cidambarā constantly uttered the words "Nārāyaṇa."
She repeatedly uttered, "O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
For ten thousand years, being devoted to Him with her inner self,
she constantly worshipped me, Kṛṣṇa, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
He constantly gratified other devotees of Viṣṇu, auspicious great bhāgavatas,
with gifts, honors, worship, wealth, and jewels. Then, on one occasion, after her worship was finished, that queen fell asleep.
And on the twelfth day, at the end of the night, Puruṣottama became manifest before her.
"O Lakṣmī, it was I myself who had become endowed with all splendor," [he said]. He fully accepted the worship performed by her in her dream.
I have given you these marks:
a garland of *tulasī* upon your neck, a beautiful saffron tilaka like the moon upon your forehead, collyrium for your eyes, and likewise earrings for your ears. (42)
On his neck was a lotus garland, and on his arms were the marks of weapons;
likewise, there were lines of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, as well as a sectarian mark (tilaka).
O Lakṣmī, I then became invisible at that very moment.
She suddenly became wide awake and beheld her body marked with signs;
overcome by great wonder and filled with joy, she became a great devotee of the Lord and likewise a great follower of the Sātvata path. 45.
She who had dedicated her entire being for my sake, she whose royal splendor was for my sake,
and she who offered her whole self for my sake— therefore that virtuous woman, the embodiment of supreme detachment, devoted solely to the Supreme Lord, attended upon me. (46–47)
Constantly devoted to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*) and dedicated to the company of the virtuous,
she always conducts herself like a chaste woman, having abandoned attachment to sense objects.
Indeed, she remains as one who offers herself, acting like a servant or a handmaid.
Then, after some time, he approached me to test me.
Having made his own Garuḍa inconceivable like Airāvata, Śakra himself arrived at the queen’s palace. (3.60.49–50)
"I am Indra; may it be well with you. What boon shall I grant you?
As the sovereign of all heaven, I have come to you to bestow heaven itself.
Accept either the preeminent Nāka or the supreme station of Mahendra."
"Let both heaven and earth be your slaves forever.
Accept the kingdom, O blessed lady, and cast away widowhood. Accept this supreme, auspicious fortune that shall endure for a Manvantara. (52–53)
Do not waste this divine body, so delicate and worthy of enjoyment;
having obtained what has come by chance, be happy, O beautiful woman.
For without a lover, the world is always harsh and burning for women.
"Therefore, O lady of meritorious deeds, accept me, who am so dear and beloved.
Having heard this, Citambara said: "I bow to the one whose senses are disciplined;
let there be salutation to the deity. O goddess, do not perceive any fault in me."
This human body is always inhabited by a divine, radiant spirit;
yet the human womb is a formidable destroyer of the status of Indra.
O best of gods, do not set your mind upon a human being, who is a gateway to the destruction of merit.
Do not be consumed by my curse; show me forgiveness.
O Lord of the Gods, having received this worship and my salutation, depart.
Kings are indeed gods who have attained purity, for they are born of their own nature as possessors of women.
That women desire [you] there is no cause for wonder; however, that does not please me.
I do not rule the earth by deceiving you.
You shall not take what was given by you; go, O Indra, to your own abode.
"Nārāyaṇa is my Lord; indeed, I worship that Beloved. Go, O Indra! Do not cause the destruction of my intellect.
I am a servant of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (61-62)
Upon hearing this, Lord Indra, having cast off his form as Indra,
himself assumed the form of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, the mace,
and the lotus; I, the Lord Hari, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Śrī, sat upon Garuḍa.
Having come face-to-face with her, she praised me and bowed down to me:
"Be gracious, O Lord of the lords of the gods, Lord of the lords of lords!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama! (64–65)
You are the beginningless Lord, the Protector, the Master, the Beloved, and the Consort of Śrī;
the immeasurable, all-pervading Viṣṇu, Govinda, the lotus-eyed one;
the Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, the Lord of the beloved of Hari, the Supreme Sovereign.
I have taken refuge in you, O Govinda, O Lord of Godāvarī, O Beloved Master!
Without you, I do not desire even sovereignty, heaven, or supreme happiness.
There is no other resort for me but you; you alone are my refuge. (67–68)
You are the Indra of truth, you are the Indra of the great elements, and you are the Indra of the self, O Supreme Lord.
Indeed, I worship You as the true Indra of all my senses.
I bow to You, the Lord of life; I bow to You who dwells within.
I bow to the one who rests upon the bed of bliss, the great yogi established in the fourth state (turya).
Having heard that hymn of praise, I said to her: "What is it that you desire in your heart?
I shall grant all of that to you; speak, for you are my supreme devotee."
"I am always fond of devotion; whatever you desire, I shall grant that. Having heard this, Citāmbarā said: "My mind and heart are eternally devoted to the beloved Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
May you, my Lord, who are beloved by your consort, abide within my heart. Just as you, O Hari, remain as the sovereign Lord who knows the inner self of all,
so too do I become, O Kṛṣṇa, one whose being is predominantly your inner self.
Out of compassion for you, I shall protect the earth as long as it endures;
having performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, I shall satisfy the deities.
I shall protect the Vaiṣṇavas, and may you dwell in my house.
"You are my beloved; remain always as my protector.
Or else, taking me to your own abode, make me another Lakṣmī.
O Gopāla, O Protector of Ramā, wander at your pleasure toward the realm of consciousness."
O Lakṣmī, as soon as I heard what Cidambara had said, my mace—
endowed with the splendor to annihilate all things—
was handed over to him; it is the protector of the kingdom, the destroyer of enemies, and the one that stays by his side.
At the time of battle, thousands upon thousands of maces, which by their very nature destroy curses, diseases, and enemies, arise;
having given that [weapon] to me, the Compassionate One returned to his own abode. (3.60.80)
She too, being greatly delighted, protected the kingdom of Godala;
she established all the social orders (varṇas) upon the path of dharma in their respective duties.
In every house, she caused devotion to the illustrious Pauruṣottama to be practiced.
Hari was present in every house, and in every house there was the chanting of the Vedas;
in every city there was the proclamation of Hari’s name and the sound of sacrificial rites.
The king’s daughter caused Vaiṣṇava sacrifices to be performed.
In the city of Cidambaram and in Śāstrya, the earth became a provider of nourishment;
the subjects were free from disease, possessed of grass for their cattle, and lived without affliction.
Devoid of famine and other calamities, auspicious and great festivals abounded.
There was no untimely death; neither disease nor mental anguish existed.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that queen indeed ruled a Vaiṣṇava kingdom, and she protected the virtuous in their dwellings throughout every region. (886–887)
The virtuous were honored by her with water, garments, food, and meals;
truthful and chaste women were protected and constantly served by her.
Cows were protected by that virtuous woman, and likewise, the helpless were nurtured.
Every morning and evening, my worship was performed regularly.
Circles of devotees were also established, accompanied by women devotees, chanting:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! (88–89)
"O Hare, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā!"—
in this manner she caused my glorification to be performed everywhere.
Likewise, she had beautiful feasts of food provided.
Water-stations were established and the shade of trees was provided;
likewise, dharma-halls were built and cow-sheds were constructed.
Schools were established, as well as schools for the knowledge of Brahman.
She also established irrigation works and canals;
furthermore, she constructed my temple here in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, which, like the peak of the sky, shines with the presence of the chaste woman Cidambārā. 93.
For every morning, that queen, having bathed and worshipped me,
would always come to the assembly hall of those possessing knowledge of Brahman.
There, Godalāyana would constantly engage in discourse on Brahman.
One performs the recitation of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*;
thereafter, the chanting (*kīrtana*) takes place, and following that, the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
Then, an auspicious association with saintly men and virtuous women occurs.
Service to those who are devoted to the sacred conduct of Brahmanas indeed becomes pleasing to the heart.
For in her kingdom, all five sacrifices are performed constantly.
Thinking thus, she carries out the governance of the kingdom for me. (97–98)
Divine, equal to the divine Rāmā, the sky of consciousness, beloved of Hari—
having obtained Hari as her husband, lord, and master, she took recourse to a state of dispassion.
May they worship that Blessed One, the Lord of life, the Supreme Lord.
"May they go to the eternal abode and attain supreme joy!"—
thus did that virtuous woman, possessing a divine body, cause all her subjects to hear this constant instruction, which yields the fruit of eternal merit.
"I always provide protection for such devotees;
I grant them my presence and likewise service at my feet.

(102) Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Marks of a Great Bhāgavata Devotee, the Testing of Queen Citrāṅgadā, and Her Devotion," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section (*Dvāparasantāna*) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 60: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā / Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 61 [[Author:
Chapter 62 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to how the protection of your devotee was likewise accomplished by the mace;
I shall relate that great and wonderful deed to you.
Once, a rākṣasa named Bhadraka, who made his dwelling in the ocean,
heard of and learned of the kingdom of Godala and the five provinces belonging to a woman.
Desiring to make his own wife, Cidambarā, [the queen], that rākṣasa—
Assuming a form at will, he enchanted hundreds of kṣatriyas.
(3) Having become a youth, exceedingly charming, well-nourished, and resplendent with beauty, he applied the Vaiṣṇava tilaka, while the Rākṣasas prepared the offerings for the virtuous. (4)
Accompanied by prepared Brahmins and adorned with the attire of a traveler,
he, endowed with royal splendor, arrived at the city named Godalā.
Indeed, in a circular hall provided with seats, he dwelt in the form of a community.
Having learned the queen's situation, the Vaiṣṇava, having become a Rākṣasa,
went to the king’s palace and beheld the beautiful queen. Recognizing him, the queen honored the nobleman with a welcome and other courtesies.
Then, deluded by passion, he begged the queen for the kingdom;
the queen immediately forbade him from going outside the realm,
and the Rākṣasa likewise quickly issued an urgent command.
Having bowed and led his own people away, he then departed for the ocean.
(9) But having arrived alone at another time, he approached the queen at night;
lifting her up as she lay there, he carried her upon his shoulder into the sky. (3.61.10)
The Rākṣasa departed swiftly when the queen awoke;
then that virtuous woman saw the demon in the sky carrying her away. She remembered the Kaumodakī mace, and the mace immediately appeared before her.
Having arrived there, she was indeed commanded by the queen for the sake of protection.
Then, in order to slay the Rākṣasa, that terrifying mace flew up into the sky and fell upon the shoulder of the demon.
Striking again and again upon the various limbs of Bhadraka— on his head, back, arms, thighs, and feet—
that [demon] struck the Rākṣasa, who, being thus beaten, fell to the earth.
He indeed fell unconscious near the garden of his seat;
then, remembering me, the Supreme Lord,
the Goddess departed for her own abode, leaving the Rākṣasa alive along with his mace.
The Rākṣasa departed for his own abode situated in the midst of the ocean.
Upon hearing that the Queen was protected, the subjects then became immersed in joy;
eager with blessings, they celebrated the Queen.
Having performed worship of Hari, the queen then performed the worship of the mace (gadā).
Thus, the queen was protected from the Rākṣasa by the mace at that time.
Yet the Rākṣasa returned once more at another time, accompanied by his army.
Prepared to seize that queen and reclaim his own kingdom,
he surrounded the city with many divisions of his army and let out a roar;
traversing the path of the sky, he sounded the war drums.
The queen praised me, Kṛṣṇa, and worshipped the mace with sandalwood paste (21).
With foods, necklaces, perfumes, and other offerings, she then requested protection.
Rising from its place, the mace instantly ascended into the sky (22).
In an instant, she became endowed with the brilliance of ten million suns and fires;
vomiting forth crests of fire and roaring again and again,
she shone, bringing victory and making heaven and earth resound.
She went swiftly toward Bhadraka’s auspicious army;
that mace killed Bhadraka with a fool’s death,
and thereafter the Goddess of the Mace slaughtered the army like a fool.
The army of the Rākṣasas was broken and the Rākṣasa himself fainted;
he fell upon the earth just as his mace became silent.
Having protected his life, the Rākṣasa then fled.
The remaining army fled, and there was a cry of victory for the woman.
That Śāntā mace returned to its place and became motionless.
The queen worshipped it according to the prescribed rites and likewise offered food offerings and other gifts.
Then, after some time had passed, many sea-born rākṣasas gathered together and held a consultation for the sake of regaining their kingdom and queen.
Some were experts in missiles and weapons, while others were masters of illusions and mantras.
Furthermore, thousands of *rākṣasa*s and *rākṣasī*s— possessors of the power of invisibility, masters of many forms, and endowed with supernatural attainments (*siddhi*)—
arrived at the city of Godāvarī, equipped with all the implements for war.
Desiring victory, the Rākṣasas roared through the path of the sky;
they raised shouts of battle and repeatedly sounded their kettledrums (dundubhi).
They blew conch shells and played various war-instruments.
Then they let out shouts of "kilakila" and the like, as well as slapping their arms and other such sounds.
Hearing these terrifying roars of the Rākṣasas, the subjects trembled,
and the royal armies also shook violently upon the earth.
The chief queens went before the king and informed him of the formidable calamity—
the Rākṣasas' intent for battle.
The queen rose quickly, bathed, and worshipped her mace.
He honored her with incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, and lustration rites (nīrājana).
Then the divine Gadā, the mistress of battle, having assumed a heavy female form and being fully equipped with all missiles and weapons, spoke.
I am the power of the Bhagavatī, appointed by the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of your protection. Today, this offender has approached me three times.

"O Great Queen, having given him various battles that shall indeed result in the destruction of his life, I shall [slay] him; salutations to you, may it be well with you and auspiciousness be yours. Having spoken thus, the mace Raṇeśvarī, endowed with all power, [then stood ready] in battle. (3.61.40)
From his own body, he brought forth well-nourished warriors who were invincible in battle;

he joined all of them with the lords of the quarters (lokapālas), who possess the power of movement through the sky. Having formed these armies equipped with missiles and weapons, they [stood] in the atmosphere.
Flying up, the demonic armies indeed launched their assault;
the Rākṣasas and throngs of Rākṣasīs, exceedingly fierce, fell [upon them] with weapons, maces, staffs, javelins, and iron balls. ||42-43||
With bundles of grass, stones, earth-clods, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, *śaktis*, trees,
iron arrows, reed-arrows, shafts, swords, *bhallas*, and iron balls; then, having seen the exceedingly swift arraying of the Rākṣasas for battle—
The lords of the *gadās*, intoxicated by the fury of battle, rushed through the sky.
Impelled by the goddess Gadādevī, those heroes struck down the *rākṣasas* with weapons, missiles, cannonballs, maces, lances, and other arms. (45–46)
They struck one another with various weapons;
those fierce ones killed [their foes] and divided the Rākṣasas into two parts—
from the neck, from the shoulders, from the waist, and likewise from the hands.
With their thighs they shattered and destroyed the Asuras;
indeed, those lords of maces crushed the fierce Rākṣasas, striking them down from the sky to the earth, depriving them of their lives. 48–49.
Seizing the Asuras by the neck with both hands, they sucked them dry;
perceiving fire, the lords set the Rākṣasas ablaze.
A great crushing occurred as the Rākṣasas fell to the ground.
Then that Bhadraka performed a magic spell that brings the Rākṣasas back to life. He revived the Rākṣasas, who were experts in all weapons and missiles;
rising up again and again, they repeatedly struck down the soldiers led by Gada.
Indeed, [he created] illusory elephants, camels, crocodiles, tigers, bears, lions, fish, śarabhas, leopards,
great serpents, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, mountains, lightning-bolts, and soldiers.
Having conjured up clouds of stone through their illusory power, they struck down the lords of the gods.
They brought forth a rain of wind and likewise created a rain of dust;
they produced a rain of fire and also a rain of stones.
They brought down a great rain of locusts and a shower of scorpions;
they produced a rain of serpents, lizards, and monitor lizards.
They also brought down a rain of poison and likewise a rain of blood.
They caused affliction for living beings with streams of hot water.
Then they brought down a rain of mud, a rain of elephants, a rain of trees, and a rain of lions. (57–58)
There, the Rākṣasas discharged a shower of fires and a shower of Rākṣasas;
they also unleashed a terrifying shower of weapons capable of piercing the body.
Thus did those Rākṣasas wage a battle that was destructive in form:
Brahmajit, Kratujit, Devāntaka, Narāntaka,
Kumbhagarta, Śaṅkuratha, Ayomukha, and Śatāhvaya.
Indrajit, Ekacakra, Prāpaṇa, Puruṇḍaka, Cūrṇanābha, Asiloman, Kumbhāmāna, Mahodaka, Śvalabha,
Tālaketu, Savyasivi, and Supuñjika.
Kālanābha, Yajñaha, Śrāddhāda, Vajraha, Vidyutputra, Rasana, Vapāśa, and Raktakarṇaka;
they had round eyes, were tawny, possessed eight tusks, and had large bellies. (63–64)
With thick heads and short shanks, with copper-colored faces and hair standing erect,
with sunken eyes, long tongues and lips, and with drooping eyebrows and thick noses—
these hosts of Rākṣasas were struck down there by maces.
The female Rākṣasīs— Vikacā, Brahmadhānā, Ālambikā, and the others—
were slain on the battlefields by maces arising from my own mace.
Those armies of maces [attacked] me, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the Lord.
Remembering again and again, they fell indeed upon the heads of the rākṣasas;
at that time, the heads and chests of the demons were crushed to pieces. "We shall slay all the rākṣasas forever, so that they may go to the abode of Yama!"
"We swear by Saṃkarṣaṇa that we shall not rise again!
Having spoken thus, the female lords of battle then struck with their maces,
and the hosts of Rākṣasas met with ultimate destruction.
Then, by means of her illusory power (*māyā*), all the rains dissolved into the sky;
the entire earth became covered with the corpses of the hosts of *rākṣasa* bodies.
Bhadra then rushed forward to seize the mace of the Goddess of Battle.
As that hundred of maces fell upon him from all sides,
Bhadraka was struck down by the Destroyer of the Deluded (Mūḍhamāra) on every side;
he caused a flow of blood and likewise made him vomit blood.
With his head shattered and his chest broken, Bhadraka fell to the ground crying out in distress;
having met his death, the other Rākṣasas who remained abandoned the battle and fled by the hundreds.
The maces fell upon their backs and struck them down because they had offered the gift of life.
Deprived of their breath, they fell with their hands and knees outstretched; opening their mouths wide as far as their navels, they met the law of Time.

Not even a single one remained; the entire army of the foremost Rākṣasas, numbering a hundred thousand, was brought to destruction by the mace. Then the queen remembered her husband, Nārāyaṇa—indeed, me.
O Lakṣmī, for the sake of purification and for the livelihood of all creatures on the fields of battle,
I then quickly offered that nectar of my foot-water into the unfathomable vessel consisting of the sky of consciousness. (78–79)
For the sake of reviving the subjects, she performed a consecration (prokṣaṇa) upon the earth by way of the sky, resolving: "May these subjects of mine, though dead, come to life.
Thus, whatever subjects were present there in battle at that time [were revived].
They were forcibly brought to their death in the midst of the land;
yet they all regained life once more, like those awakened from sleep,
while the bodies of the Rākṣasas were then consumed by fire from the maces.
O Lotus-born one, they were indeed reduced to ashes there by my will alone.
Having thus waged a supreme battle and slain the Rākṣasas,
the mistresses of the battlefield arrived before me at the palace of the queen.
Strengthened by blessings and impelled to grant boons, those maidens chose me, the Supreme Lord, as their husband;
and Cidambarā too, along with the Raṇeśvarīs, was filled with joy. ||84-85||
Then she, together with them, worshipped me with an excellent garland;
indeed, a thousand goddesses of war chose me as their boon.
Likewise, the goddesses of the mace chose a beautiful gift of boons from me.
When Dhruva said, "May it be so," that they might become attendants in my abode, I accepted them all as my attendants; they went to my imperishable realm.
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, the mistresses of battle and other beloveds [went] to my supreme, imperishable realm.
And those Muktānikās indeed abide in the supreme abode.
Cidambarā is also my devotee;
[I have given] everything to the gentle attendant Gadeśvara, the yogi who is devoted to me. (89)
Having given away the kingdom, he went to my abode, which is imperishable and higher than the highest.
The great king Gadeśvara, devoted to celibacy and adhering to the Vaiṣṇava dharma, ruled the kingdom for one hundred thousand years.
Having caused devotion toward me to arise, having made the subjects truly Vaiṣṇava,
and having satisfied the deities and the ancestors by performing sacrifices, offerings, and other rites,
he ascended my celestial chariot and went to my imperishable abode.
His heir was Yogeśvara, the king of devotees,
who was Sādhudharmā and Sādhuvarmā; he, a worshiper of virtuous men and women,
caused my devotion to be practiced and went to my imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described the greatness of my devotee;
indeed, I provide protection for my devotee in whatever manner is necessary. Wherever there is a female devotee and a male devotee of mine, there I dwell, within their very sight.
Or else, remaining in a place that is not my domain,

I shall indeed protect those who have taken refuge in me by means of my power, my weapons, my attendants, and my majesty— whether they be men, women, or even eunuchs, provided they are solely devoted to me.
One whose self is absorbed in me and whose actions are dedicated to me is perfectly protected by my inner self—by me who dwell at his side, in his heart, nearby, or before him;
behind him, above, below on the ground, in the middle, and even within his very limbs. (98)
By my dwelling here, the protection of my devotee is ensured in every way.
(99) For if those daughters-in-law are my devotees, being as they are dependent on others, they shall indeed be protected at all times by me while remaining together with them. (3.61.100)
"For I am the protector of the protectorless; I always provide protection.
Through the recitation and hearing of this [hymn], there is enjoyment, liberation, and protection.

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection of Queen Citrāmbāra from the Hosts of Demons such as Bhadraka by the Lord’s Mace," in the *Vadhūgītā* within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; know me indeed as Nārāyaṇa, who is the self of all, and who is Nārāyaṇa associated with all activities.
One should constantly recite the name of Nārāyaṇa and bow to me, Puruṣottama.
During sleep one should think of Nārāyaṇa; while traveling or going about, one should think of me as Nārāyaṇa.
While standing, one should think of me as Nārāyaṇa; and while eating, one should think of me as Nārāyaṇa.
In both the opening and closing of the eyes, one should indeed remember me, Nārāyaṇa.
(3) Even while awake, one should bow to and likewise remember me, Nārāyaṇa;
and whatever is to be eaten, drunk, or licked, [one should offer it] with the words, "Salutation to Nārāyaṇa. (4)
She who, having caused others to drink [the water], herself consumes it, goes to the supreme goal;
she also leads other noble-born women to the auspicious state. This is for the woman who is richly endowed with the remembrance and recitation of my name.
"You are Lakṣmī, my very own form, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
You dwell in his house, his field, his abode, and in his body.
O daughter of Indra, you are reciting the sixteen-syllable mantra for me. (6–7)
Jayantī, who had been born mute, attained omniscience and Sarasvatī;
she acquired supreme scholarship and became equal to Bṛhaspati.
"Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; salutations."
In this way, skill indeed arises in the mind of one who performs the recitation.
(9) For her who performs the recitation thus: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," good fortune shall become firmly established. (3.62.10)
"Out of fear of Time, Illusion, evil karma, enemies, Yama, and treacherous friends,
[I am] one who possesses the trident, fish, banner, bow, discus, and the svastika.
To her who was thus chanting, I, Nārāyaṇa, became her protector.
"Having become [this], I give unto me my own abode, the imperishable and eternal bliss.
(1.2) I am the eternal devotee of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (1.3)
Muttering thus, I indeed assume the form of Lakṣmī:
"Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman, is my eternal Lord;
may He be my father, kinsman, well-wisher, friend, protector, and guardian. (14)
"Thus reciting, 'I indeed perform that which is dear to Brahmā;
may Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa be my refuge at all times,' I destroy the accumulation of sins for her who recites in this manner. (15–16)

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, the Supreme Brahman who transcends the Imperishable (Akṣara), who assumes the essential forms of all incarnations— He is the Lord, the inner controller within us at all times, the cause of all. (17)
He is the inner self of all, the Lord of all, untainted, and indeed the bestower of liberation.
May He, the purifier who grants both worldly enjoyment and release when served, protect [you] forever.
To her who thus recites this prayer, I grant the state of Kamalā.
All the beloveds of Brahmā, such as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others,
are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman and are half-bodies of the Supreme Brahman.
They are the entire essence of the goal of the Supreme Brahman, divine, and the bestowers of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

"Even the actions associated with them are always devoid of qualities and grant liberation. Reciting thus, I indeed bring about the liberation of those who worship Bālakṛṣṇa and his beloveds, whoever they may be and in whatever manner they do so.
"Sa sa sā sā" is her very nature—divine, eternally bestowing liberation.
As she recites this mantra, a divine form arises.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Thus, while reciting this, I cause her to be absorbed within my own form.
(24) For her who recites the mantra "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my refuge," I indeed accomplish the four aims of human life. (25)
"I am the beloved devotee of Kṛṣṇa; Śrī Hari is my refuge. "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the ocean of all knowledge, Śrī Svāmī is my refuge. 26. "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved master, Śrī Hari is my refuge."
"Because I chant these mantras, she dwells eternally within me.
O Lakṣmī, these mantras have been revealed by me as my own forms;
they are equal to me, identical in nature to me, and like me, they accomplish all tasks and purposes."
"Śrī Kṛṣṇa is my beloved, my lord, and my refuge"—this is the mantra.
Bestowing all goals, it consists of twelve syllables; I shall describe its greatness to you.
Sarasvatī, the daughter of Brahmā, was born as Subālikā.
Complete in all branches of knowledge and endowed with the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
the maiden Śāradā, the daughter of Brahmā, was then born;
Sarasvatī spoke only the most excellent speech in Sanskrit.
Even though she had been initiated, Śāradā was not able [to speak];
she became mute, for her tongue did not move at all despite her efforts. The Creator became despondent, and Sāvitrī grew weary.
Then the maiden Śāradā grieved deeply in her mind;
she went to the side of Sarasvatī, displaying her own tongue.
Sarasvatī, having reflected upon it like the twelve-syllable mantra, [spoke].
Having consecrated the purifying water with mantras, he placed it upon his tongue.
(33) Repeating "Śrī Kṛṣṇavallabhācārya is my refuge," he consecrated the water again and again and placed it upon his tongue repeatedly. (34)
Then, by the power of the mantra, the goddess Śāradā’s speech came forth upon her tongue;
she sang all the vowels, consonants, and sentences, as well as the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
and everything pertaining to the past and the future.
Thus the divine speech, the virtuous Śāradā, became manifest;
Viśvasṛj, Sāvitrī, and Sarasvatī were also pleased.
O Lakṣmī, this indeed has been told: the majesty of the twelve-syllable mantra.
For those who read or even hear it, the supreme state is indeed certain.
Even those of sinful conduct, if intent upon these twelve syllables,
attain my auspicious and supreme abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).

"By chanting the single-syllable mantra *Oṃ*, one attains the supreme goal. By chanting the two-syllable mantra *Kṛṣṇa*, one goes to Goloka. By chanting the three-syllable mantra *Śrīkṛṣṇa*, one reaches the highest Goloka. (3.62.39–40)
Chanting the mantra "Vāsudeva" or "Rādhākṛṣṇa," one goes to the four-syllabled abode created by you;
chanting the five-syllabled "Oṃ Nārāyaṇa," one reaches the white-syllabled state.
Chanting "Namo Nārāyaṇāya," one attains the imperishable state of Brahman.
Chanting "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," one goes to the imperishable state.
Uttering "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Śrī-rom," one reaches Vikuṇṭha.
"Anādi-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇa" is the imperishable word;
"Anādi-śrī-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇa" is the divine imperishable word.
"Oṃ Māṇikī-śrī-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇa" is the supreme imperishable word. (44)
"Reciting [this], one attains my state; O Lakṣmī, grant me the most excellent of abodes.
(45) "The devotee who recites 'Oṃ Sukhadā-Lakṣmī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa' attains my state; so too does a female devotee engaged in this recitation. (46)
Reciting with enthusiasm this supreme mantra—“Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my beloved Lord, is my refuge”—one enters into my inner being.
[The mantras are: “Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇāya Namaḥ” and “Oṃ Nārāyaṇāya Namaḥ.”
"Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva; Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāviṣṇu.
(48) "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu," and "Oṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Hiraṇyagarbha," and likewise, "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. (49)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Rāmāditya; Oṃ, obeisance to Nṛsiṃha;
Oṃ, obeisance to Kapila; and Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Hari.
Oṃ, obeisance to Dattātreya; and Oṃ, obeisance to Ṛṣabha. [3.62.50]
"Oṃ, salutations to Vāmana; Oṃ, salutations to Paraśurāma.
Oṃ, salutations to Yajña; Oṃ, salutations to Sanatkumāra.
Oṃ, salutations to Vyāsa; and likewise, Oṃ, salutations to Buddha. || 52 ||
"Oṃ, salutation to Nara-Nārāyaṇa; oṃ, salutation to Brahmā;
oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Brahman; oṃ, salutation to the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin).
Oṃ, salutation to Mādhava; and oṃ, salutation to Govinda. (53)
Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava; Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīpati. Oṃ, obeisance to the Master; Oṃ, obeisance to the one beyond the imperishable.
Oṃ, obeisance to Puruṣottama; Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Self. 54–55.
We know Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is beyond the mind and other [limitations]; we meditate upon Him, the son of Gopāla Kṛṣṇa;
may that son of Kambharāśrī inspire us. (56)

O Lakṣmī, these mantras always bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation; they all grant their respective abodes, destroy sins and afflictions, provide all the aims of human life, and likewise fulfill every desire. (57)
A thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million recitations are considered effective;
they bestow their fruits according to one's faith, according to the number, and according to one's fervor.
"Oṃ, salutation to Śrī," "Oṃ, salutation to Lakṣmī," "Oṃ, salutation to Ramā."
"Oṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī; Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇī.
(59) "Oṃ, salutation to Brāhmī; likewise, Oṃ, salutation to Puruṣottamī.
"Oṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī; Oṃ, salutation to Kamalā; Oṃ, salutation to Māyā. (60)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudevī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā. Also:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Mādhavī; Oṃ, obeisance to Parameśvarī.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śivā; Oṃ, obeisance to Antaryāmiṇī. (61)
"Oṃ, salutation to Mahāvaiṣṇavī; Oṃ, likewise salutation to Padmā. Oṃ, salutation to Kambharā-Lakṣmī; Oṃ, likewise salutation to Prajñā.
Oṃ, salutation to Rādhā; and Oṃ, salutation to Brahmapriyā. (62–63)
"Oṃ, salutation to Hariṇī; likewise, Oṃ, salutation to Haripriyā.
Oṃ, salutation to Hiraṇyamayī; Oṃ, salutation to Kārṣṇavāllabhī.
Oṃ, salutation to Pārvatī; and also, Oṃ, salutation to Māṇikyā. (64)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Lakṣmī, the giver of happiness; Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī, the queen of Śiva.
Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇī-Śrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Dhāminī.
Oṃ, may we know Lakṣmī, the giver of happiness; may we meditate upon Nārāyaṇī-Śrī. (65)
May that Śivarājñī-Śrī inspire us.
We know Kṛṣṇa; we meditate upon Vallabha;
may his wisdom inspire us.
"Oṃ, we know the Teacher; we meditate upon the Guru;
may Pārvatī impel us.
(67) These mantras, O Lakṣmī, always bestow the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
They bestow the goals of human life and fulfill every desire for happiness.
When recited a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a hundred thousand, or even ten million times by those endowed with faith while remembering me and you, they grant eternal desires. (68–69)
"Thou art I, I am thou, O Lakṣmī; he is I, I am he"—whoever mutters this while remembering me, to him and to her I give my very self.
I grant him my seat, my abode, and my own soul.
For the sake of my devotees, I withhold everything from myself and do not offer it as an oblation.
Worship me, Lakṣmī; worship me, Rādhā; worship me, Kṛṣṇa, your beloved husband.
Worship me, O Beloved, at the beginning, at the end, in public, and in secret.
Worship Him in the body, worship Him in the home, and likewise worship Him within as the Beloved of life.
Worship Him in the hidden, worship Him in the sleeping state—the source of eternal bliss and absolute happiness.
Devotion (*bhajana*) is supreme love and delightful service.
One should serve me, the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, through the perfection of material resources, gardens, and so forth, as well as by the actions of speech, mind, and body. Indeed,
men and women should serve me while I am present and manifest before their eyes.
I am of divine form, having attained the supreme imperishable abode; that very same one has today become here in Saurāṣṭra the son of Kambharā,
the Supreme Lord, the delight of Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa.
O Lakṣmī, throughout the Manvantaras, I shall indeed remain right here in every way.
Just as I am the purifying Guru, so too am I Lomaśa;
and just as I truly dwell within minerals, stones, images, and the like.

And thus, O Lotus-born One, I shall indeed dwell together with you among those Vaiṣṇava teachers who are themselves the Supreme Lord; for I shall reside with you among those men and women who are worthy and have been consecrated in the position of a guru.
Therefore, indeed, the gurus in this world are my own divine forms;
for by seeing them, touching them, and serving them, they are the ones who deliver one across [saṃsāra].
Without me, the earth never becomes empty anywhere. (3.62.80)
I exist and abide through the forms of the current, the parts, and the immersion;
all conscious forms in the three worlds consist of the Guru.
In the Imperishable, I am eternally liberated and the Lord of those who are liberated.
In Goloka, I am the husband of the gopīs and the gopas;
likewise, in Vaikuṇṭha, I am the lord of the male and female attendants (pārṣadas).
Furthermore, I exist in the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and likewise in the immortal state.
In Śrīpura I am Wisdom itself; on Kailāsa I am Śaṅkara; in Satyaloka I am Brahmā and the Guru; likewise, in the world of the ancestors I am Aryaman;
in the world of the gods I am Bṛhaspati; and among humans I am the virtuous man.
Among the Daityas I am Uśanas, and among the Brahmins I am Vasiṣṭha;
among women I am the virtuous one, and among men I am the illustrious king;
among serpents I am Śeṣa, and among cattle I am the bull.
Among aquatic creatures I am the tortoise, and among the cruel I am the śarabha.
Among creepers I am the wish-fulfilling vine (kalpalatā), and among trees I am the celestial wish-granting tree (kalpapādapa).
Among those seeking knowledge I am the teacher, and among wives I am the mother of her husband.
Thus, O beloved, the Guru alone is everywhere my very essence;
I always abide there within that Guru, the most excellent of all sacred places (tīrtha).
He who, knowing me as the Guru within his own range of perception, worships me incessantly—
Indeed, no other search remains for me than that of him.
Abiding in my guru, I, possessing a divine form, await those who serve me; in whatever manner they approach me, I likewise honor them each in that same way. (3.62.90)
I fulfill all desires for those endowed with the state of faith;
I always make fruitful those who are bound by the moisture of love and affection.
I am the kinsman and the remover of bondage; I abide in every way within the Guru.
The bonds consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); latent impressions arise from mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
Mental modifications are attained through yoga, and conjunction arises from objects of enjoyment.
Furthermore, the non-attainment of objects of enjoyment and so forth is indeed an aid in separation.
By that [means], there is the dissolution of the mental modifications (vṛtti), and from that, the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā).
Through this, there arises a state of steadfastness; therefore, one should always strive in such a manner.
Indeed, the yoga of the Guru is the steadfast application that constantly brings about true realization.

Association with the virtuous brings one to the state of liberation and bestows great bliss; it is a divine purifier and a treasure-trove of the Guru. O Lakṣmī, in this way I am always attained through the devotion of love. (95–96)
I liberate all who are bound; I am the beloved Guru who is free from attachment.
I deliver men, women, and eunuchs from great sins, as well as beasts, flocks of birds, aquatic creatures, and even forest-dwellers.
I rescue trees, creepers, gods, ancestors, and even sages.
As the Blessed One, I am the protector of those who have come for refuge;
for my purpose is indeed to bestow happiness and to deliver embodied beings from suffering.
"I perform that very same [act] at the beginning of every creation, and likewise during all creations;
even at the end of a creation, I provide protection in the same manner.
Thus, O beloved, everything you asked has been told."
O Beloved, this knowledge consisting of the *Vadhūgīta* grants liberation to all women.
By its recitation and hearing, nothing remains to be known.
It truly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as the grace of identity with the Divine. 101–102.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Various Divine Mantras and the Power of the Guru," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 63 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 63.
[The Author: Chapter 64.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, O ocean of mercy, who indeed are the Vaiṣṇava servants?
Who are the devotees, what are they like, and what is their majesty?
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Those who perform service to the body [of the Lord] are indeed considered my servants.
The best are those who practice the secret [teachings], free from doubt and possessing divine vision.
(2) I wander among people in human form;
when people see me, they serve me as an ordinary worldly being, without any suspicion. (3)
They consider [the Lord] to be filled with the nature of desire and anger like their own selves;
they do not indeed recognize the Lord who fulfills the intentions of His devotees.
All my auspicious deeds born of the body—
Even when merely remembered or seen, they grant liberation; of this there is no doubt. (5) Indeed, the wicked who harbor doubts therein do not serve me;
perceiving me as non-divine, they consequently utter my censure. (6)
Because of that sin, they go to hell and even among the animals;
O Lakṣmī, the state of being an asura never ceases for them.
For servitude, O Lakṣmī, is indeed difficult, great, and consists of the total surrender of everything.
Whether a man or a woman, one should offer the physical body;
|| 8 || and one should offer everything without hesitation, for that servitude is the most excellent of all.
One should not allow reasoning, deliberation, or doubt to intervene during the performance of the rite. || 9 ||
"One should not place Dharma, modesty, or legal conduct between me and Nārāyaṇa.
Dharma was created by Nārāyaṇa; modesty rests upon Nārāyaṇa;
legal conduct belongs to Nārāyaṇa; these alone grant liberation, and no others. (3.63.10)
Considering all my actions to be rooted in dharma, one should reflect upon them:
desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and jesting, as well as the vulgar and the improper—all these are indeed entirely divine for me. (11–12)
I have no desire that is truly hellish, nor do I possess anger that is destructive;
I have no greed that bears sin, nor delusion that is deceptive. I have no pride that acts as a bond, nor jesting that is devoid of virtue.
There is nothing vulgar or trivial for me, nor is there anything impossible for me;
indeed, everything performed by me becomes divine and bestows liberation.
Therefore, this service (dāsya) is difficult for all people here to perform.
Those men and women who always desire to perform service for me must always remain free from apprehension; likewise,
my wives also must remain free from apprehension.
One should contemplate that even Lakṣmī and Rādhā are equal to the Beloved;
therefore, one should practice the supreme, unconditioned service (dāsya).
When all service is filled with love, it becomes beautiful and increases exceedingly.
Without the sense of separation, servitude increases eternally;
indeed, supreme servitude, free from doubt, becomes the bestower of great bliss.
[This occurs] toward the Supreme Lord, the husband Kṛṣṇa, the Master, the Supreme Self.
How could there be doubt or hostility toward one who possesses discernment?
Whatever Kṛṣṇa performs himself, all that indeed bestows liberation;
whatever Kṛṣṇa performs himself is indeed dharma, for it is merit-creating.
Therefore, O beloved, virtuous women should indeed perform service that bestows identity;
for when identity is attained, listen, those things which cause division are the veils.
Indeed, the state of difference within the state of oneness is considered a veil.
The second manifestation is the thought: "I am one and Hari is another.
This is an obscuration that creates obstacles and causes harm to [the state of] servitude (dāsya). It manifests as:
"I am a woman, a man, Kṛṣṇa, or indeed this other person. (23–24)
The manifestation of "I" and "another" is the third covering;
and whatever fear arises in one who stands by the side of Hari toward another,
that too is the fourth covering, which indeed causes injury to [the realization of] servitude.
This is indeed not the occasion, for that is the fifth enclosure;
nor is there any mind here for me, for that is the sixth enclosure. The seventh enclosure is the desire for wealth, and that too exists.
Arrogance (māna) is the great obstacle; it is indeed declared to be the eighth.
The ninth is the accomplishment of one's own ends, which obstructs the work of service. And the tenth is lack of divinity, which always obstructs the practice of service.
O Lotus-born one, in servitude there is the power to employ [the servant] according to one's will;
if that is absent, then servitude is not truly considered superior.
Ownership, servitude, being yours, being intent upon you, and being of the nature of you—these are the stages.
A group of five things strung together by a female servant is beautiful only because of that very servitude.
O Lakṣmī, just as all your service is indeed beautiful,
so too does the service performed by men or women shine with splendor.
Everything performed with devotion and full of love shines for me;
he who is free from all veils shines and rejoices in me.
Those who are constantly engaged in spiritual practices and devoted to my service [shine likewise].
The Vaiṣṇavas, marked with the conch, the discus, and other signs, indeed rejoice in me. Furthermore,
those devoted to the service of the virtuous, likewise those devoted to the service of chaste women,
and those devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu— the Vaiṣṇavas rejoice in me.
The Vaiṣṇavas—servants of Hari, dear to Hari, and those who act for the sake of Hari—always abound in devotion to me and rejoice in me.
They are intent on great enthusiasm and partake of the great offering of food (mahā-naivedya). ||35||
Those Vaiṣṇavas who speak with all-encompassing devotion truly rejoice in me. Because he abides in Viṣṇu, he is my Vaiṣṇava;
because he abides in me, Nārāyaṇa, he is my Nārāyaṇīyaka.
He is indeed the supreme devotee of all, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa;
he is a devotee of Brahmā and belongs to Brahmā, likewise a devotee of the Imperishable and belongs to the Imperishable.
He is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa and belongs to Kṛṣṇa; the Vaiṣṇavas truly rejoice in me.
The Nārāyaṇīyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and likewise the Akṣaras are my followers.
Those devotees who assume the form of Brahman are proclaimed as Brāhmaṇas;
from whose presence the Brāhmaṇas, who have mastered the Vedas, were born.
In ancient times, those virtuous ones beginning with Sanaka were the Brahmin gurus;
they were the virtuous practitioners of Brahman-yoga who served as gurus for the Brahmins and others.
Indeed, those virtuous ones beginning with Sanaka were created by Brahmā in the beginning.
Brahmaśīla, the ascetics, Skanda, and likewise Hanumān—
these are always the preceptors who are perfected through the process of re-creation.
Indeed, for Śūdras and householders, the twice-born are their preceptors.
Among the twice-born and others, householders who are brahmins are gurus;
for brahmins, however, virtuous men (sādhus) are gurus, since they bestow liberation.
Sādhus are the most excellent of all, being worshipped by gods, sages, and ancestors.
The virtuous are superior to the gods, and likewise most excellent even compared to the great seers (maharṣis).
The virtuous are superior to the ancestors and always most excellent among the Brahmins.
There exists no such excellence in the three worlds as that which is found in the virtuous.
From among virtuous women, the excellent ones are the ascetics who perceive Brahman;
from among cows, the excellent ones are the virtuous who are eternally devoted to Brahman.
And from among the goddess Earth, the most excellent are the virtuous who are endowed with forgiveness.
The virtuous are superior to idols through their bestowal of knowledge and their liberation [of others];
indeed, the virtuous are saviors superior even to temples of the gods.
And the virtuous who serve the Lord of Śrī are superior to women devoted to their husbands.
The virtuous who are dear to Hari are superior to the Brahmins learned in the six limbs of the Vedas;
from the Vedas, the words of the saintly are superior because they lead to union with Kṛṣṇa.
From the Vedas, the saintly are superior, for the Vedas themselves rely upon the saintly.
The virtuous are superior to sacred fords, because they swiftly destroy sin.
(51) The virtuous are superior to religious vows, for they bestow infinite merit according to one's desire.
The virtuous are superior to fire, for they purify the defilement of illusion. (52)
Even the Brahman-sages indeed worship the feet of the virtuous.
I am the Supreme Lord, Acyuta, the Lord who is the very form of Kṛṣṇa;
we worship the saintly devotees, the virtuous ones who purify all with their own being.
They are truly virtuous, for they are merchants enriched with excellent qualities; indeed, they are rich in virtue.
They are truly virtuous, for they are universal monarchs through their sovereignty over Brahman.
They are truly virtuous, for they are supreme teachers and scholars, treasuries of knowledge.
These very ones are true teachers, bestowers of liberation, and likewise givers of mantras;
they are the virtuous ones, knowers of the Vedas and sciences, the most excellent of Brahmins.
It is my view that only those Brahmins who are devoted to the six duties are truly virtuous.
O Lakṣmī, I am indeed always the Self of the virtuous; I am the Self of the virtuous at all times.

(57) Those endowed with truth, purity, and forbearance, free from attachment and aversion, possessing the knowledge of Brahman and the wisdom of discrimination—such Vaiṣṇavas are the supreme saints. (58)
They were devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice and constantly honored guests;
they were devoted to their fathers and mothers, supreme Vaiṣṇavas, and virtuous;
endowed with compassion, righteousness, and other virtues, they were likewise dedicated to merit.
The supreme Vaiṣṇava saints are those adorned with the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth;
(60) those who wear a garland of tulasī around their necks and hold Hari in their mouths, singing songs of Kṛṣṇa, are the supreme Vaiṣṇava saints. (61)
Constantly devoted to the *saṃhitās* and likewise to sacrifices,
respectful toward all dharmas, they are the supreme Vaiṣṇava saints;
they liberate people from every sin and never revile them.
The supreme saintly Vaiṣṇavas truly bring happiness to all embodied beings.
Those who worship me—Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, and Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—in my very form, are indeed the supreme saintly Vaiṣṇavas. (63–64)
The supreme, virtuous Vaiṣṇavas worship the Śālagrāma, they worship the Incarnate One, and they worship me, the beginningless Śrī Hari.
"This is Gopāla," "This is Kṛṣṇa," "This is Rāmāditya," "This is Acyuta."
In this way, the supreme and virtuous Vaiṣṇavas worship me—
just as my form is in Kuṅkumavāpī, as it is in Siddhapattana,
as it is in Gokula, and likewise even in the Himālaya.
And just as my form was assumed by me on the bank of the Narmadā,
so too do the supreme, virtuous Vaiṣṇavas worship that very form—
four-armed, two-eyed, and holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus.

My golden image, clad in yellow garments, holding a flute, adorned with a forest garland and other ornaments, endowed with a beautiful crown, illuminated by the Kaustubha gem, and accompanied by Rādhā, Ramā, and others. (3.63.70)
Having installed [the image] made of silver, copper, bronze, or likewise of jewels, with the mantras of the Āgamas and especially with Vedic verses,
they should worship it according to the rules with the mantras of the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Through loving devotion, the Vaiṣṇavas are indeed the supreme holy ones (sādhus) in their hearts.
Those Vaiṣṇavas are truly holy men, identical with Me, and embodiments of merit;
as is Viṣṇu, so are they all—there is not even the slightest difference between them.
Having understood this, O King Śrī, one should always honor the virtuous.
"I am Viṣṇu; I am the virtuous one; and I am the chaste wife devoted to her husband.
I am the mother, I am the father, I am the husband, the virtuous woman, and the yoginī. (74)
I am the virtuous Nārāyaṇa, and I am the mistress Nārāyaṇī.
I become Rudra and Rudrī, Aja and Ajī, and a god and a goddess.
I dwell eternally within all beings, and I manifest forth from them.
To one desiring a husband, I am worshipful as the husband himself;
to one desiring liberation, I am worshipful as Śrī Puruṣottama.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Keśava, how, when, and by what objects are you to be worshipped?
O Blessed One, tell me the ritual procedure for one who desires her husband.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
On the auspicious morning of the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra,
one should go to a grove and gather divine *damanaka* blossoms.
By the command of the Guru, the worship of the *damanaka* must indeed be performed.
And Kāmadeva stands at Damana, joined with Rati.
"O Kāmadeva, salutations to you; you are eternally the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
I seek Hari, who is Desire; show mercy toward me."
He should be brought toward the house to the sound of singing and instrumental music;
and having first performed the consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should place Hari, Kāma, Rati, and the *damanaka* tree within the *sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala.
Having covered [the image] with a white cloth, O beloved, one should worship the maiden.
*Klīṃ*, obeisance to Kāmadeva; *hrīṃ*, repeated obeisance to Rati.
At the onset of night, I worship Kandarpa with *hrīṃ* in the eastern direction. (83–84)
With auspicious perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, lamps, and food offerings, and with the waving of lights and other rites, I worship my divine husband, the Lord.
Homage to Madana in the east; homage to Manmatha in the southeast.
Salutation to Kandarpa in the south; salutation to Anaṅga in the southwest.
Salutation to Mohana in the west; salutation to Smara in the northwest.
Salutation to Īśvara in the north; salutation to Puṣpabāṇa in the northeast.
Then, having paid homage in all directions, the maiden should worship me with this mantra:
"Oṃ, let us know the person who is Kandarpa; let us meditate upon the god Kāmadeva; may Anaṅga inspire us. (88)
Thus, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations in the presence [of the deity]:
"Homage be to you, the Lord of Desire; homage to you, whose arrows are flowers. Homage to Manmatha, the giver of bliss; homage to you, the bringer of delight. (89)
Salutations to you, the gift of love; salutations to you, the seed of all things. (3.63.90) Salutations to you, the beloved, who possesses a beautiful form, the dwelling place of all.
Salutations to you, whose form is that of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the god Anaṅga. (91)
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, granter of desired wishes!
O Lord, beloved of Kāmeśvarī, fulfill the desires within my heart.
Having thus offered praise, Mañjarī said, "Water should be poured upon my feet."
A great festival should be celebrated with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
One should keep a vigil and, having bathed in the morning, worship Hari.
One should also honor the preceptor with wealth, clothing, ornaments, and food.

One should indeed offer it to the guru during a gift-giving ceremony and then eat together with the Vaiṣṇavas. By the worship of this Mañjarī for me, she has effectively bestowed all gifts— gifts of land, gifts of cows, and abundant great gifts.
The fruit of giving a thousand cows is obtained by worshipping with *damanaka* flowers.
She who, in the spring, worships me—the most excellent beloved—with *mallikā* blossoms and supreme devotion, will certainly obtain a beloved husband. (96–97)
Madhuka and Damanaka are exceedingly dear to Hari;
when I am worshipped with these two, I swiftly grant a husband to a woman.
To a maiden who is the very embodiment of Rati, Puruṣottama becomes well-pleased.
I shall give you a husband worthy of you—a beautiful and auspicious treasure-house of splendor;
one equal to the god of love, delightful, of the same age as yourself, and my own self;
gentle in character, free from disease, endowed with prosperity, and a mine of virtues. (3.63.99–100)
"I give you an excellent husband, a vessel of joy and a vessel of love.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described this vow which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is my worship here in this world and the highest form of devotion.
The form of the spiritual preceptor (*guru*) is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), and likewise, the forms of virtuous men and women are supreme.
O beloved, the forms of male and female servants, Vaiṣṇavas, and so forth, as well as unobstructed service, are said to lead to the attainment of Me.
"By reading this, by hearing it, by remembering it, and likewise by performing it,
a devotee— whether male or female— necessarily attains the fruit as described.

Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Unobstructed Service, the Excellence of Male and Female Disciples, and the Vow of Damanaka," within the *Vadhū-gītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
