Chapter 64 [[Author: → Chapter 65.
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord, Eternal One!
On which lunar day (tithi) are you to be worshipped, and in what form? Please reveal this to me. (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: On the first lunar day (pratipad), I alone am to be worshipped there as the Giver of Wealth;
indeed, I myself become Dhanada in the form of the image of Kubera.
O Lakṣmī, you indeed have a second [form]: you are the worshipful Puruṣottamī;
you are the bestower of all prosperity, my very self, Narāyaṇī.
O beloved, the third lunar day is declared to be auspicious for the goddess Pārvatī.
In that regard, Pārvatī is indeed to be worshipped, for she is considered the bestower of good fortune (saubhāgya).
On the fourth lunar day, Gaṇeśa is to be worshipped, for he is the remover of obstacles;
he is the very form of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa and the bestower of gains and other blessings.
The fifth lunar day of the moon is proclaimed [as mine]; indeed, I am the Moon who is to be worshipped. I become the giver of cattle, gardens, and groves, as well as the provider of nectar and food.
On the sixth lunar day of Kārttika, one should then worship Kārttika.
I become the bestower of victory and the remover of planetary afflictions, manifesting as Kārtika.
On the seventh lunar day, O beloved, the Sun is to be understood as the one to be awakened;
at that time, Sūryanārāyaṇa—who am I—bestows manifold splendor.
The eighth day is to be known as that of Durgā; Durgā, the bestower of auspiciousness, is to be worshipped.
She is the remover of all hardships and my eternal Śakti.
And the ninth day belongs to the Mothers; indeed, the auspicious Mothers are to be worshipped.
For they indeed become protectors and bringers of security to those of their lineage. The tenth [tithi] is to be known as belonging to Yama; at that time, Yama is auspiciously worshipped.
I myself manifest as Yama, the destroyer of the suffering of sins and hell.

On the eleventh day, Śrī Kamalā is to be worshipped there in every way; she bestows the abode of all auspicious things upon the one who honors her. O beloved, on the twelfth day, I am Mādhava; when I am worshipped then, I grant my grace.
I give honey of every kind, the most excellent, filled with essence.
On the thirteenth day, I am always to be worshipped there as Kāma;
I grant all desires in their entirety, for I am the fulfiller of every wish.
The fourteenth day belongs to Hara; for I am indeed identical with Mahādeva.
Śaṅkara is to be worshipped, the bestower of prosperity and the granter of sovereignty.
(15) The fifteenth day belongs to Vedhas; Vedhas is to be worshipped and the bestower of auspiciousness.
He bestows the increase of one's lineage and, like a father, grants all forms of spiritual welfare.
(16) The lunar day known as Acyutī and Puruṣottama is preeminent;
I alone am to be worshipped there as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (17)
I am the ancient Supreme Lord, the bestower of all desired things. Indeed, the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is the sacred occasion for the worship of the deities;
from the invocation until the dismissal, it is certainly fixed.
Worship is always considered to be enriched by the beauty of every kind of service (upacāra).
[These include] bathing, garments, ornaments, garlands of mantras, moist sandalwood paste, incense, lamps, excellent food offerings, water, betel, and pleasing [the deity]. (3.64.20)
Salutation, patience, and a sacrificial fee—these are indeed essential for worship.
The complete worship should consist of one hundred and eight items.
O Lakṣmī, it bestows all prosperity as well as all spiritual accomplishments.

It shall be the granter of all desires and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (22) Thus, a devotee should perform this great propitiatory worship for me; by performing it, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the doer of what is dear, becomes pleased. (23)
A garland of lamps should be offered in my palace and temple;
one should present four kinds of food offerings, most delicious in nature.
Having worshipped me according to the rite of garments and ornaments, one should honor the Guru.
May this worship of yours, though performed without the proper rites of mantra and devotion, be complete.
(25) I am blessed, I have fulfilled my purpose, and I am a fortunate woman dwelling upon this earth, since the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation, has accepted me as his own. (26)
Today, indeed, I have become divine, liberated from all latent impressions (vāsanās), and equal to Rādhā;
I have attained greatness on earth through the power of my guru.
Salutations to you, O Guru, whose nature is Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self.
You are the divine form of the consecration and other rites; you are indeed the Guru, Kṛṣṇa, the savior.
You are Hari, my Guru, the bestower of all bliss and the giver of liberation.
You are the destroyer of all bonds and the eradicator of the heat of sin.
"You are the giver of Brahman and absolute liberation to me, the bestower of the supreme imperishable abode, and the very nature of the Supreme Self; salutations to You, the Supreme Self!
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, and my life has become fruitful."
Blessed are those two parents of mine, my own birth and its cause,
by whom the Lord, the Beloved, was won through me from time immemorial.
O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that I may never again be separated from you.
Charity, austerity, vows, devotion, and service were performed by me in the past,
by which I have indeed obtained Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved, today upon this earth.
Through the power of much merit, I have obtained Hari as my Guru.
Viṣṇu is ever present within the guru, in every way, among his own devotees.
One should contemplate this greatness: "Hari dwells in the guru.
Thus, when the guru is seen, saluted, bathed, and likewise honored, [the Lord is honored]. (34–35)

She who, though possessed of faults, is constantly endowed with a spirit of devotion, bestows upon the one who serves the guru merit equal to ten million sacrifices. She who worships the form of the Guru becomes inseparable from Acyuta in his abode.
The form of Gurvī destroys the great sin of mortal slaughter and the most heinous crimes.
When remembered, glorified, meditated upon, worshipped, and saluted, that image of the goddess Gurvī bestows the imperishable abode. (37–38)
Having obtained and served a female preceptor who is virtuous, venerable, chaste, divine,
devoted to her husband, dedicated to Hari, and a yoginī, one is liberated.
Just as does deer flee in fear upon seeing a lioness, so it is here.
Indeed, all illusions consisting of evil vanish through the attainment of the Guru.
(3.64.40) That female disciple who bows to the Guru’s wife—who is pure and virtuous—with devotion or even without devotion, is meritorious and destined for liberation. (3.64.41)
There is no fear of Vaivasvata (Yama) for her at birth or death,
who, being virtuous, performs service and worship of the preceptor’s wife with perfumes,
water for the feet, offerings, food, lamps, incense, and ointments.
One should delight the goddess Gaurī with songs, instrumental music, and hymns of praise.
That virtuous woman who worships me, being devoted to supreme bhakti,
shall rejoice in my abode for tens of millions of billions of kalpas.
She who has offered salutations to the divine Guru even with her inner being—
that goddess is a recipient of my grace in the world of mortals;
she stands firm through the pride born of the power of my devotion and is solely intent upon the virtuous.
The virtuous woman who is devoted to the service of her guru rejoices in my abode.
O Lakṣmī, I always dwell within the one who is like an image of the guru and the god;
indeed, the fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu with thousands of millions of lotuses [is attained thereby]. 46–47.
A virtuous woman obtains that fruit which comes from the worship of the Guru-deva.
Those people in the mortal world who have not performed the worship of the Guru-deva are as if already dead; though they are born again and again, they remain subject to their past karma.
In the presence of the guru-deva, everything attains purity.
(49) By partaking of the guru’s prasāda, the fruit of ten million sacrifices is obtained.
By drinking the water from the guru’s feet, ten million murders are destroyed. (50)
Residing in Kāśī for eight yugas is equaled by serving one's guru for a single day;
therefore, with the desire for liberation, one must indeed perform the worship of the guru.
For Śrīpati, whose very nature is that of the Guru-deva, resides therein.
There indeed dwell the gods, the *surās*, the virtuous women, and the lords.
Whatever fruit may arise from all the millions of recitations of the *surās*, that same fruit arises from the recitation of the names of Śrī Hari and the Guru. (52–53)
Having offered oblations into the mouth of the Guru-deva even once,
the ancestors attain eternal satisfaction imbued with nectar by means of that funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Those people who drink the water purified by the feet of the Guru [attain the same].
What need is there for consuming thousands of the five products of the cow?
When an occasion for expiation has arisen, what is the use of gifts, what use of fasts,
or even what use of Cāndrāyaṇa penances, once one has drunk the water from the feet of the Guru?
Whoever gives ghee, milk, and sugar here to the preceptor has, by that act,
offered all desired foods and performed hundreds of sacrifices.
Even while dwelling at home, for him there is a bath in sacred waters day after day.
Initiation into all sacrifices belongs to him by whom the Guru has been satisfied.
In heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, Gurus exist as saviors;
there is nothing else in the three worlds that is a supreme purifier equal to the God-Guru.
In this auspicious human world,
life is truly fruitful for one by whom the attainment of a guru has been achieved, or by whom service to the guru has been performed—
offering leaves, flowers, fruits, water, clothing, wealth, and food. (3.64.60)
By offering [the fruits of one's actions] to the guru and the deity, one becomes equal to Mount Meru.

Even a woman who is devoid of ritual prescriptions and bereft of rites, mantras, and so forth, if she worships with devotion while being devoted to her guru, shall obtain the fruit declared in the scriptures. (61–62)

I always dwell there, within the body, and eternally within the Guru of Gurus. For that person who, having placed the Guru upon his shoulder as a vehicle, carries him along the road, the path to my abode is forever unobstructed for him.
Wherever the Guru-deva resides, there Hari is ever present.
Therein lie the sacred fords (tīrthas), great gifts (mahādānas), Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Prayāga, and likewise the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
There is also the Bālakṛṣṇa lake and likewise the Viṣaturyasa lake;
there too is the Nārāyaṇī and the river Irāvatikā. Menakāṅgā is also right there, and the Brahmaputrā is there as well.
Wherever the Guru resides, all sacred fords (tīrthas) are indeed present there.
Whatever sin arises among people, such as the killing of a Brahmin or any other, the service of the Guru, who is a god, quickly consumes it all. (67–68)
Where there is a union of both the form of the Guru and the form of Hari, that place should be understood as Dvāravatī; there, devotion to Acyuta bestows liberation.
In the worship of the Guru, there are no mantras, no chanting, and no meditative visualization.
It requires neither wealth nor diamonds and the like, nor gifts, nor anything else;
neither praise nor even supplication, but only love.
Even when one has committed an improper act, eaten what is forbidden to eat, or drunk what is forbidden to drink— [it still endures]. (3.64.70–71)
Whatever sin exists shall indeed perish when the venerable Guru and Hari are satisfied;
for the virtuous female disciple who daily performs the worship of the Guru’s consort and serves her by massaging her feet and so forth. (72)
Thereafter, for infinite time, she shall never indeed experience widowhood.
Having attained the good fortune of Kṛṣṇa, she becomes the lotus-like Ramā.
Taking refuge in the shadow of her guru, she should always bestow gifts.
A person here who fears Yama should not leave the side of the guru;
the messengers of Yama never come into the presence of the guru.
Service rendered to the guru is service to Hari, and service to the husband is service to [the Lord].
The life of that woman whose home always possesses these three things is truly fruitful:

(1) the complete restraint of her activities directed elsewhere; (2) the pleasing of her guru and her deity; and (3) the performance of service and worship with devotion by that virtuous woman. (76–77)

When a disciple offers water, flowers, or other articles to the Guru with faith according to their suitability, she obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice for every single flower offered, provided she is directly devoted to the Guru, who is Hari himself. (78)
Freed from the miseries of birth, old age, and disease, she is considered to have attained liberation.
Whatever fruit is obtained here by the gift of ten thousand cows, that same fruit one surely attains by offering a lotus garland to the Guru. (3.64.80)
Even that which is rare and difficult to attain within the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile—
that very thing, O Lakṣmī, when prayed for, service to the guru indeed bestows:
sovereignty, progeny, knowledge, kingdom, and the abundance of happiness.
The grace of the guru is indeed bestowed; for that grace is considered attainable through service.
(82) Sins as vast as Mount Meru and Mandara go to complete dissolution through service to the guru, for the guru is truly Hari manifest. (83)
Having daily uttered "Namo Nārāyaṇāya" as well as "Namaḥ Śrīgurave," she should bow to the God, the Guru, Hari, the Lord, and the Master.
She shall go to the Supreme Self, the abode dwelling in the Imperishable.
She who repeatedly chants the name of the Guru and the name of Hari— the giver of eternal bliss and established in the state free from all ailment—
goes to the supreme abode and does not undergo rebirth. (85–86)
And those hundreds and thousands born in her family also go to the supreme abode by whom the Guru has been satisfied.
At all great festivals, the virtuous woman should worship the Guru.
In the home of the worshipper, there shall always be great festivals. On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, a virtuous woman who possesses meditative realization should worship her guru;
that chaste lady obtains the fruit thereof: eternal good fortune. (88–89)
One should bathe [the image] with warm water, anoint it with fragrant substances,
massage it with scented oils, and wipe it clean with pure materials.
One should then perform the consecration and clothe it in garments.
She should adorn him with ornaments and worship him with unbroken grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings.
The virtuous woman should worship the Guru with flowers, sandalwood paste, and garlands;
she should also provide him with ornaments and cause incense, lamps, and so forth to be offered.
Then one should offer the fruits of one's desire, such as food and drink, to the venerable Guru;
furthermore, one should present an excellent sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one’s means.
One should also drink the nectar of his feet and perform the service of massaging them.
The female disciple, being virtuous, should always perform services such as massaging the limbs for the Guru’s wife;
having placed the Guru and the Guru’s wife in a carriage, she should likewise lead them to the garden, the great park, or the house, and, filled with devotion, she should please them. (94–95)
O Śrī Narāyaṇī! A virtuous daughter-in-law, or any other woman, should thus propitiate me, the supreme Guru, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, she should propitiate her own husband as Kṛṣṇa with heartfelt devotion.
Likewise, O Lotus-born One, all those virtuous women who please their own guru through service are indeed of the nature of Brahman and destined for liberation;
they are divine, possessing a divine form, and are supreme bestowers of divinity. (97–98)
Whichever women come into union with him,
they shall likewise become divine and proceed to the supreme state.
I am Hari, eternally divine, and my Śakti is also eternally divine.
And you are Śrī, as well as Rādhā, Ramā, Prajñā, and Māṇikī;
Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Virajā, Padmāvatī, and Mādhavī—
these and others are my divine powers (śaktis), for they are indeed the beloveds of Brahman.
The beloveds of Hari are not separate from me; they are always non-different from me.
All powers (śaktis), who are ever dear to the Guru, reside within the Guru, who is the supreme teacher.
Indeed, I dwell together with those powers among the women.
I dwell among my noble kinsmen and I reside with my husband.
Assuming the role of various gurus, I fulfill the desires of their hearts.
Thus, O Śrī Śivarājñī, serve me, Mādhava.
"From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, or even from bowing to it—and even from grasping its meaning with devotion—liberation shall surely occur; of this there is no doubt.

(105) Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of Hari in His Various Forms on All Lunar Days and the Constant Worship of Him in the Form of the Guru," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 65 [[Author: → Chapter 66
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī, to the majesty of the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who appears in the form of the Guru. (1)
I shall indeed proclaim my own majesty to you exactly as it is; yet, constrained by compassion for women, I am never satiated with speaking.
A virtuous woman who desires liberation and good fortune should worship [it] constantly.
One should devoutly bathe me with water, honey, milk, and ghee;
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with waters, and with waters scented with sandalwood;
with fragrant sandalwood, saffron, and gulāla.
One should smear me with *abīra*, as well as with saffron (*kāśmīra*), with water infused with *kesara* flowers,
and with liquid mixed with camphor and *uśīra*.
One should worship me with beautiful flowers accompanied by perfumes and incense.
O virtuous lady, you should indeed offer guggulu resin smeared with cow’s ghee in my presence.
And, O beautiful one, you should offer a lamp with ghee day and night;
as for the food offering, you should present milk, drinks, and the like, as well as rice cooked in milk.
Thus one should worship me, bowing down and prostrating repeatedly; one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇakānta" one hundred and eight times,
and offer oblations of sesame, rice, barley, and other grains smeared with clarified butter.

In that very way, one should worship my feet with lotuses for the sake of complete liberation and satisfaction under my name; one should worship my knees with bilva leaves as "Bhaktivardhinī," and [worship] me with [other offerings] as "Vilāsinī. (3.65.10)
One should worship my hips with royal campaka flowers;
the virtuous woman should worship my chest with land-lotuses and excellent lotuses;
and the beautiful woman should worship my head with jasmine and vṛndā flowers.
One should worship my entire body with sandalwood paste.
Abandoning the notion that it is a mere physical body, one should worship it with the realization that it is Hari.
One should perform every kind of service to me while remaining endowed with celibacy.
Wives must perform my worship at the command of their husbands; widows must perform my worship at my own command for the sake of increasing the happiness of liberation;
and maidens must perform my worship for the sake of the fulfillment of all desires.
For the sake of attaining all prosperity, men should perform worship.
O beloved, such worship as this grants me liberation and bestows prosperity;
indeed, this worship is the destroyer of the sin of selling women.
O Lakṣmī, I have described to you worship and devotion; now hear of that which is most excellent.
That devotion in which the mind is absorbed in Me is considered by Me to be the supreme devotion.
It is the inability to endure separation from Me for one who is immersed in a flood of love.
Devotion whose mental state takes on the form of my own nature is the most supreme.
Devotion through the self is the highest; that through the mind is middling; and devotion through the body is the lowest—thus devotion is threefold, bestowing liberation. (18–19)
For the liberated, devotion is directed toward the Self; for yogis, it is likewise mental;
and for the ignorant, it is born of the body. All three types of devotion are considered to bestow liberation. Through devotion to the Self, happiness is supreme; through the mind, it is middling.
Indeed, with the body, happiness is very slight; happiness is divided into three types.
Through the self in the form of Brahman, my bliss is eternal;
through the mind in its divine state, the bliss has yoga as its limit.
Bliss derived from the body through ritual action depends upon the moment of physical existence and so forth;
devotion directed toward one's own personal bliss is considered by me to be *tāmasī*.
That devotion to Acyuta which contains within it both types of bliss is *rājasī*.
Devotion that is intent on Hari’s bliss is sattvic and free from self-interest.
(24) If devotion to the guru and devotion to Hari are performed with a sense of identity [with Him], O Lakṣmī, it yields fruit quickly; for the guru is indeed directly Hari himself. (25)

The deities always grant peace to a devoted woman; Śambhu and the others provide her security, and the virtuous bestow blessings upon her. The sages, intent on pronouncing benedictions, grant her merit.
Even the planets become auspicious, and the piśācas become auspicious;
the rākṣasas become auspicious, and even the sages are pleased. Prosperity remains ever steady and auspicious in his home.
Indeed, all the flavors reside within her palace like honeys;
sweet nectars and ambrosias, along with devotion, abide in her home. All elixirs of immortality and great festivals likewise dwell there.
All varieties of heavens reside within the home of the devotee.
The devoted woman is always considered by me to be Rādhā and Lakṣmī;
she is considered by me to be Śāradā, Kamalā, Kāntā, Śrī, and Padmā.
Whosoever, endowed with noble birth, serves me with undivided devotion—she alone is my beloved devotee; she shall become Mukta-nikā in liberation.
By the mere sight of her, even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified.
That house is considered the most excellent, the very embodiment of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
where such a devoted and auspicious woman, Nārāyaṇī, resides.
She is indeed the form of Kamalā herself, a devotee who removes all sins.
Indeed, she bestows the fruit of liberation, just as Gaṅgā, Ramā, and Yamī do;
wherever such a devotee resides— whether in a place or in a temple—
in that family or on that very earth, everything indeed grants liberation.
What is the use of saying more in this matter? She is indeed Ramā, the beloved of Ramā.
Those virtuous women who, regarding my devotee as Ramā herself, shall bow down to her—even a woman who has slain a Brahmin is purified merely by the sight of them. (36–37)
O Lotus-born One, even Brahmā does not know the merit of that woman who serves her in the capacity of a maidservant; yet,
a Vaiṣṇavī woman should indeed worship her devotee who is marked with the conch and the discus.
By her, indeed, the entire world—both the stationary and the moving—has been honored.
That very day is blessed; blessed too is her mother and her family.
Likewise, blessed is the father of that virtuous woman by whom a devotee was thus worshipped.
All these virtuous women are most blessed, being solely devoted to me;
by the mere sight of them, even great sin is dissolved.
Indeed, all secondary sins and miscellaneous transgressions are likewise destroyed.
Indeed, all [impurities] perish at the mere sight of Vaiṣṇava women. Like purifying fires, women who are devotees of Viṣṇu always destroy sin—whether it be fresh or dry, subtle or gross. (42–43)
Indeed, whatever sin is committed through negligence, whether done knowingly or unknowingly,
as well as sin born of association— O Lakṣmī, it perishes very quickly from the sight of virtuous women and likewise from the service of the righteous.

The sinless go to heaven, while the most sinful attain purity. My devotee is always auspicious; she is skilled in liberating one from the bonds of worldly karma and is the purifier among all purifiers. 45–46.
That devotee of mine who remembers me day and night every single day should be understood as being my very form; she is Hariṇī, without a doubt.
[She beholds] me, shining white as camphor, with eyes as long as lotus petals.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, lotus, fish-banner, and bow;
wearing yellow garments, shining brilliantly with the Kaustubha gem;
having the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, well-nourished, and adorned with a forest garland and other ornaments. 48–49.
Hari, whose face and cheeks were adorned with golden earrings,
who was endowed with bracelets, armlets, anklets, a crown, and a girdle—
the gracious-faced Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the all-pervading Master.
Resplendent with the white Śrīvatsa mark situated on his left thigh;
(51) this most excellent of men measures fifty-six and a quarter finger-breadths in height;
he has four arms, a face as bright as the moon, and is adorned with eyebrows like bowstrings. (52)
That virtuous woman who meditates upon me, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, is indeed a Vaiṣṇava devotee; she is the embodiment of Śrī and possesses my own nature.
By even the sight of her, or by devotion to her, or by partaking of her food—
By worshipping the lotus [of her feet], she indeed becomes a female friend who attains liberation.
Just as one afflicted by thirst longs for water, so too does she remember me; just as one overcome by cold longs for fire, so too does she remember me. (54–55)
Just as a wife devoted to her husband remembers him, so too does she remember me;
just as one who is afraid remembers her protector, so too does she remember me;
just as a greedy person remembers wealth, so too does she remember me.
Just as one desiring a son longs for a son, even so does she remember me; (57) just as one who has been exiled longs for home, even so does she remember me;
and just as a female cātaka bird longs for the cloud, even so does she remember me. (58)
Just as one who knows Brahman remembers Brahman, so too does she remember me;
and just as ancestors remember the funeral cake, as gods remember the oblation at the sacrifice, as sages remember the mantras, and as men remember their wealth. (59)
Just as swans long for Lake Mānasa, even so she remembers me. As a passionate woman longs for her lover, or as a devotee serves the very one who honors them,
or as a mother longs for her child— even so does that virtuous woman remember me.
Just as the devoted worship Kṛṣṇa, just as Vaiṣṇavas practice devotion,
and just as animals seek grass, even so she remembers me. The virtuous seek dharma, the holy seek forgiveness, and the merchant seeks his due reward.
Just as a living being cherishes its own life, so too does she remember me;
and just as bees cling to a flower or a fly to the sun, so too does she remember me, her beloved, just as a lover remembers his beloved. (63–64)
Just as one situated at night longs for light, as those afflicted by fatigue long for rest,
and as those who are awake long for sleep, even so does she remember me.
Just as the diligent seek accomplishment and elephants seek the forest lands.
Just as a lion remembers the dense forest, so too does she remember me.
Just as fire arises in a sun-crystal upon encountering a ray of the sun,
so too shall a virtuous woman become full of love for Hari through association with the truly saintly.
Just as the moonstone drips nectar through contact with the rays of the moon,
so indeed does devotion to Hari arise for you through union with the Vaiṣṇava.
And just as the night-lily blossoms upon encountering the moonlight, [so does the heart of the devotee expand].
Having attained such a devoted and noble woman, the lotus of the heart blossoms.
Just as an insect becomes a bee by remembering a bee, so too does a virtuous woman, by the remembrance of Yoga, become equal to me upon remembering me.
And the brides, through their very desire for me, attained the supreme form of Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, by remembering me, each gopī became Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa himself. One gopī acted as my laughter, and another acted as my affection.
One virtuous woman acts as if she were longing for me, while another acts as if she were my mistress;
yet another behaves with love, and a beautiful woman acts as if she were Kṛṣṇa himself.
In this way, through the yoga of devotion, she finds me by her side in an instant.
Even though I am always present in their proximity, I remain far away for those who lack devotion.
Only through the yoga of devotion can the Supreme Lord be perceived by devotees.
Even though the gods and others obtained the nectar of immortality, they are indeed still subject to suffering.
Having obtained devotion alone as the nectar of immortality, all suffering perishes.
Having reached Vaikuṇṭha through devotion, one rejoices in the presence of Viṣṇu.
Abandoning everything else, one should take refuge in my devotion.
Whatever is performed without devotion, even after having attained a human body, is indeed in vain;
for without devotion to Viṣṇu, there can be no crossing of the ocean of worldly existence.
My devotion alone extinguishes the forest fire of suffering that has consumed me.
Even in another birth, my devotion indeed establishes itself within me;
having become my servant, Lakṣmī is then born from that.
Indeed, even a mere atom of devotion grants me my own abode.
Devotion is heard of by hundreds, it is understood even by thousands, and it is practiced by hundreds of thousands; among them, some devotee may become like Ramā herself.
In this world, there are many who grant wisdom, yet only a rare few truly practice devotion.
And even there, having attained that very nature within a multitude of millions, he is non-dual.
Devotion is mocked by [worldly] worship; likewise, devotion is made an object of ridicule by [mechanical] recitations.
Yet, through devotion, devotion is praised, and by me, devotion is embraced.
Just as branches, leaves, and fruits arise from a tree that has been watered at its root,
so too does Hari, when watered with devotion, become the source of the fruit of the devotee’s bliss.
Indeed, according to the nature of one's conduct, such is the devotion one performs.
O Lakṣmī, the fruit is indeed obtained in the future simply from my worship.
Just as a water-carrier girl gives her heart to the jar when it is drawn up onto the bank, so too, if she gives her heart to me, she is liberated. 84–85.
Just as the sky situated in the world is not defiled by the elements,
so too the devotee situated in the world is not defiled by actions.
Day and night my devotees subsist upon my bliss.
Even while remaining here, they abide in the divine abode; indeed, they are considered liberated.
(87) The fruit of sacrifices such as the Sarvamedha is heaven, which is like a vessel that may fall [back down];
however, the fruit of the sacrifice of devotion to me is free from returning again. (88)
By my grace, the infinity of this devotion of mine has been seen;
even as a stone situated in the midst of water is not smeared by the water,
so too the devotee, though standing within Māyā, is not smeared by Māyā.
By my power, coolness exists within my devotee even without water.
(3.65.90) A frog dwells in water, yet it does not perceive the fragrance of the lotus; but the bee, though its dwelling is in the forest, truly perceives the fragrance of the lotus. (3.65.91)
I dwell within the heart; outward activity does not know me.
One endowed with love and devotion knows me as established in the heart, even if standing far away.
Some dwell on the banks of the Gaṅgā; others dwell on Mount Arbuda.
Likewise, a person who knows my majesty and is endowed with devotion enjoys the fruit [of that knowledge].
(93) A donkey carries a load of sandalwood but does not perceive its fragrance;
similarly, one who remains outside [the Self] does not know Me who am within, nor does he attain My bliss. (94)
Deer, perceiving the scent of musk, smell its delicious fragrance; yet they do not know it resides in their own navels. Likewise, those whose faces are turned outward do not recognize Me.
Instruction is useless for fools who are devoid of knowledge.
Likewise, even joy is meaningless for those devoid of devotion to Me.
Just as milk drunk by a snake becomes poison, so too is the devotion of the deceitful;
and just as a blind man does not see a lamp, so indeed the one whose face is turned outward does not see Me. (96–97)
Just as skin covers the body,
as the body covers the sense organs, and as the sense organs cover the latent impressions (vāsanā),
so too is the individual soul (jīvātman) covered by those impressions; and because it is covered by that, I am indeed completely enveloped.
Smaller than the smallest, dwelling within, I abide as the Self; yet the Self does not go to me.
Just as ghee exists in milk and oil in sesame seeds, so am I present in such a manner.
Know me to be everywhere; those whose desires are directed outwardly do not know me at all. (3.65.100)
Just as gems strung upon a single thread are held by me in that manner,
so too all created beings and individual selves are strung together in every way, yet they do not know Me.
Just as fire residing within wood and other materials becomes visible from without through friction.
Likewise, though I abide within the Self, I appear [within] the visible world through the churning of devotion. Just as other lamps arise from a lamp when required,
so too do all-knowing ones, who attain liberation through devotion, spring forth from the Guru.
Just as light shines everywhere upon the rising of the sun, so too does the master himself shine forth when good fortune arises.
Or, just as the wind is all-pervading and carries all fragrances, [so is the master]. (104)
The Guru is Hari, all-pervading and the bringer of the fruits of both ritual action and devotion.
(105) Just as water is rich with whatever flavor it possesses, so too will such a flavor appear in the mouth;
just as the Self is full of love, so too is the essence of bliss within oneself. (106)
The earth is endowed with many flavors and consists of various kinds of crops;
likewise, the Self is enriched by manifold pleasures and possessed of the diverse bliss of Brahman.
Indeed, this Self, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is the devotee who possesses supreme joy.
United with my bliss, he becomes one who possesses great bliss.
O Lakṣmī, she who truly knows my bliss and my devotion within her heart is a devotee equal to Kamalā; she proceeds toward my abode. (108–109)
I dwell everywhere, yet people do not know me;
they do not know me because of ignorance, nor do they find me because of a lack of devotion. (3.65.11) If they were indeed to perform all actions with Viṣṇu as their presiding deity...
By those very same qualities-less yogas, they attain that which stands before them.
Thus has been spoken by me, O Lakṣmī, regarding my wondrous proximity:
having reflected upon it, having attained it, and having realized it, one shall worship me and reach me.

Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Excellence and Greatness of Devotion as Spoken by the Blessed Lord," within the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. [Chapter 66] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*— Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*), Chapter 66.
[The Author: Chapter 67.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī! I am indeed one, yet I am also manifold.
Indeed, through the differentiation of name-and-form, through the differentiation of the ages (yugas),
likewise through the differentiation of devotees, and through the differentiation of effects, I manifest myself.
And I am eternally established within every living being, determined for each individual soul.
For my will is Mahāmāyā; she is indeed the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti).
Rādhā and Lakṣmī are my two powers, for they are identical with me. Even the primary matter (pradhāna) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) was fashioned by me in that very manner.
Therein indeed dwell infinite conscious souls (jīvas).
From Pradhāna arise the elements that serve as the causes for bodies;
from those [elements], bodies are produced, which are truly the abodes of the souls and the rest. || 4–5 ||
O Lotus-born one, I am Viṣṇu, consisting of the *māyā* of *sattva*; O Lotus-born one, I am Brahmā, the lotus-born, consisting of the *māyā* of *rajas*;
and I am Śambhu, born from the forehead, consisting of the *māyā* of *tamas*.
In all those places indeed, I, the Supreme Lord, dwell.
Therefore, I am omnipresent within the entire sphere of creation of the three gods;
yet, due to ignorance, worldly people do not know me, who am hidden and seated in the cave of the heart.
"By means of that knowledge indeed do the virtuous and best of ascetics perceive;
for that knowledge is the realization of Brahman, wherein I am the supreme refuge.
This alone is the culmination of the Vedas, O beloved, wherein I am described."
The supreme, all-pervading, and eternal Brahman is attained by the self;
Brahman is contemplated by the mind and likewise seen with the eye;
Brahman is embraced by the body, and Hari is reached through grace.
Hari is worshipped by one whose self is disciplined and whose mind is pure.
The eternal Supreme Brahman is to be grasped by the mind, which is indeed a kinsman;
likewise, the veil of Māyā is to be abandoned by that very kinsman, the mind.
By means of the mind as a kinsman, living beings are uplifted by the yogi of Brahman;
by means of the mind as an enemy, living beings are cast down by those seeking sense objects.
Having meditated upon me, the Lord of Śrī and the Supreme Sovereign, with a divine mind... (13–14)
Indeed, even while performing divine actions, one is not tainted;
just as a lotus leaf situated in water is not smeared by the waters,
so too my yogi, though his mind has entered into *māyā*, is certainly not tainted.
When one knows the essence of Brahman, then everything else tastes like salt;
when one knows the essence of devotion, then everything else acts like poison;
when one knows the essence of service, then even sovereignty appears as filth.
When one tastes the essence of divine love, everything else appears loathsome;
when one knows my true value, everything else truly seems like refuse.
When one knows the food of bliss, liberation and the like no longer appeal to them.
When one truly knows nothing else but that which abides within the flow of my bliss,
then the mind, by virtue of that flow, attains a state of melting.
Through this melting devotion, having reached me, it attains the yoga of identity with me.
Through union with the Guru and through union with the scriptures, divine knowledge is attained;
through repeated practice, higher realization (vijñāna) is attained, and from that, the object of knowledge is reached.
I am that which is to be known—the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, Puruṣottama.
When that is attained, it arises as empty and illusory.
Purity of objective phenomena is the foremost stage; purity of mind follows thereafter;
and purity of the self is the highest stage; through these, Hari is attained.
Indeed, there are many kinds of women who embrace in various ways;
as is the state of being and the relationship, so is the result, such as the action and so forth.
One’s own beloved is embraced according to one's state of being, and the result is likewise.
Hari is embraced by living beings according to their disposition, and according to that disposition is the fruit obtained.

By whatever intellect one attains Me, by that very same intellect is the fruit acquired. Indeed, in accordance with the way one approaches Me through the intellect, in that same manner do I grant the fruit.
The supreme fruit, which is the bliss of the Self, must always be attained through service.
Indeed, when one is rendered gracious, the Great Bliss is bestowed by Me.
This grace is brought about by being favorable and by avoiding all that is unfavorable.
Through devotion characterized by service free from doubt, clarity of mind arises.
(28) That [clarity] is not obtainable through purchase, nor through notions of moments and the like;
it is not attained as something immediate, nor is it gained through self-interested conduct. (29)

She is not attained through pride, nor through cleverness, nor through skill; she is not attained through one's own desired mental state, but rather through total surrender. She is attained only by obeying all commands and through a sense of humility.
Through service, through servitude, and by being His own, He is attained.
(3.1) Thinking "I am His," and considering Him as mine, and likewise considering Her to be such a virtuous one, I maintain a state of joy; from that, I indeed attain Him. (3.2)
By that means through which I am to be attained, one must become a messenger;
just as when one wears one's own sandals, the earth becomes free of thorns, so too,
when one’s own state of servitude is achieved, Māyā ceases its insistence and bestows divinity.

When one’s own servant has achieved success, there is indeed for him the illusion of being devoid of lordship. When one’s own wretchedness has been achieved, his existence becomes entirely void of reality through that illusion.
When everything is offered to oneself and attained, the illusion shall pass into hopelessness.
If the intellect were of the nature of Brahman, the effect of *māyā* would dissolve;
however, that intellect which consists of *māyā* is the giver of birth to the world.
A poisonous creeper, even when sprinkled with milk, does not relinquish its poisonous nature.
If the intellect possesses demonic qualities, it does not abandon its demonic nature. (37) Even if a neem tree drinks the juice of sugar, it remains exceedingly bitter;
likewise, one of demonic disposition never pleases me. (38)
For such people who do not know the world, the multitude of scriptures is useless;
they do not abandon their own nature, nor do they even seek the company of the virtuous. Devotion does not please them, nor is there any natural affection.

For one who lacks the desire for liberation and delights in atheism, the hope for eternal bliss always becomes like a flower in the sky. Having cut down the mango tree, how could one expect to obtain its fruit and flowers? (3.66.40–41)
How can happiness be attained by abandoning devotion and service?
For if one seeks the pleasure of the senses, the birth of an embodied being is indeed in vain.
It is like cutting up pieces of camphor to protect mere blades of grass.
His effort toward those things devoid of flavor, beauty, and so forth is indeed in vain.
Having disparaged the service of the virtuous, he practices the service of the wicked;
being devoid of meritorious deeds, his effort is entirely in vain. (43–44)
In a golden vessel, the food of Saramā is cooked by a low-caste man;
yet in a human body, one is cooked through sin in the tortures of Yama.
A sickly birth is a useless birth, and a mind afflicted by illusion is a useless mind.
Labor is in vain for one who possesses no home or treasury; death is in vain without Hari.
Speech is in vain for the great fool, and medicine is in vain for the unrestrained.
Without Hari, a journey is in vain, O fool; indeed, birth itself is in vain.
He who abandons Hari, the Lord of all, and serves a monkey, is his equal—
merely nourishing his own body and devoid of liberation.
Without devotion, what indeed is the fruit even of extensive learning and sacred scriptures?
One should therefore resort to that which bestows peace, for by [this body] there is no peace for the self at all.
O Lakṣmī, what is the use of that body which indulges in sandalwood and the like, yet provides neither service to Hari, nor service to the virtuous, nor liberation? (3.66.50)
Even a dog-eater (śvapaca), if endowed with devotion, makes his birth meaningful; even a Brahmin’s body, if devoid of devotion, makes his birth a cause for hell.
It is like fastening a jewel bracelet upon one who looks into a useless mirror.
Having attained the company of the virtuous, other means are rendered useless (52).
Those who have taken firm refuge do not accept the sovereignty offered by the gods and others;
those with firm devotion do not accept even the sovereignty offered by Hari himself (53).
For one who eats without desire, victory resides at every step;
indeed, even Nārāyaṇa himself is unable to entice him.
By desire the embodied soul is bound, but by craving it is destroyed.
Indeed, even the Lord is not capable of giving [these gifts] to one who stands above both;
for He is unable to strip away the fortitude of one who is eternally satisfied and tranquil.
There is no one in the three worlds who can cause fear in a devotee who is fearless.

In order to delight such a devoted follower of my own, Narayana becomes manifest as the visible form by which he may be meditated upon. Having meditated upon me as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, people [attain their goal].

Indeed, those with form, possessing divine bodies, have reached Me, the eternal Abode. Innumerable embodied beings, my devotees, have attained My supreme Imperishable state by performing worship, devotion, divine service, and likewise the duty of a servant. //58-59//

Even by making me their slave, and even by practicing devotion to their husbands, women have not attained my imperishable state. Devotion does not exist toward the Void; devotion exists toward that which possesses form.
In me, the supreme Lord, the Master, the Consort of Śrī, who am the very form of the support—
having indeed established loving devotion toward me as their own Lord and Husband,
the women of former times attained me, even though they had resorted to the state of being mistresses.
How much more so my own wives, who have sought refuge by surrendering all their possessions?
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, I am the Lord, the embodied Master, the Sovereign, and the Consort;
having become the bestower of happiness and the giver of eternal bliss, I lead them away as well.
In the view of some, affection is greater through seeing; in the view of others, it is greater through touching.
For some, affection lies in dalliance; for others, even in sleeping together.
For some, it is in the enjoyment of desire; for others, in the act of dancing (rāsa). (64–65)
Some find delight in eating, some in the play of bathing;
some in kissing and the like, while others find it in great festivals;
some in companionship, and some in never being separated from you. (66)

In some, affection for me is perceived in their own beds; in others, in acts of jesting; and in still others, in secret intimacy. Having fulfilled the desires of those [women], I bow to my own imperishable abode.
Having indeed made that virtuous Muktānikā my wife,
I, possessing a beautiful form, shall lead her to my own abode of eternal bliss.
For the delight of service is obtained from groups of beautiful women when [the deity] has a physical form.
Devotees attain the full flavor of service within me, my abode. Indeed,
by my very grace, the bride who is the handmaid of liberation— her body bristling with horripilation and her eyes filled with tears of joy— shall come to be.
The maidservant sings of me with her speech, remembers me even with her mind,
and delights me through her actions by offering the gift of her hips and so forth;
she serves me through worship, recitation, adoration, attendance, and the massaging of my feet.
And through the states of mind consisting of the offering of secrets, one attains eternal happiness.
(73) In Me who possess form, the devotee serves Me with the sense of being My body;
through all the senses, she attains great bliss like a worldly friend. (74)
Having become a bride, she serves her chosen lover, me, her husband and lord.
Indeed, through the gateway of desire, I fulfill all the desires of women.
O beloved, I have no desire, nor even passion; I have no pleasure in sensual desire.
For me, whose desires are fulfilled, what need is there for desire through passion? (76) Since my form is completely filled with all bliss, I have no incompleteness;
nor am I subject to the senses—what need is there for desire? (77)
In the past, I, as a performer of ritual action, cultivated desire for the sake of attaining pleasure;
yet desire is indeed composed of illusion (*māyā*), and likewise, delight is composed of illusion.
Therefore, I have no need for that, nor any purpose in what is illusory.
But people—men and women under the sway of the body—project their own desires and mental states upon me, who am the perfect and eternal;
thus, imbued with those various desires, they grasp at those very same objects through those respective states of mind. (3.66.80)
Even through the gateway of desire, I grant them union and lead them to my own abode;
I cause even beautiful women who possess longing to attain the state of liberation.
Such is my compassion to be understood, for such indeed is the nature of worldly existence.
For my devotees who are devoted to the senses are well-known upon this earth;
likewise, devotees devoted to sense objects dwell in various places.
But those who are spiritual and have realized the nature of Brahman are indeed rare scholars found only here and there.
Therefore, having reached those who approach me in whatever manner they do, I, being of that same nature,
bestow upon them the yoga of liberation and lead them to my imperishable abode.
Generally, I become possessed of desire in order to bring about the spiritual perfection of women.
How can there be the deliverance of those who are so deeply attached to sensual desire?
Therefore, moved by compassion, I shall always serve them like a lover;
having fashioned them with divine forms, I lead them to the supreme liberation.
A bride, a maiden, young women, or even elderly women devoted to their husbands;
a eunuch, a widow, a woman whose husband is living, or a celibate student;
a female ascetic, a yoginī, a virtuous woman, a faithful wife, a noble lady, or one who is dispassionate—[all these may perform the rites]. (87)
She may be a female renunciant (sannyāsinī), one who has lost her mind (vicittā), an ascetic woman (tāpasī), or a forest-dweller (vānaprasthinī).
She may be a woman of renunciation (tyāginī), established in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, or she may even be a courtesan (gaṇikā).
She may be an unchaste woman (puṃścalī), a wanton woman (svairiṇī), a passionate woman (kāminī), or one who is free from desire (kāmavarjitā). (88–89)
Whether she be a widow, a eunuch, devoid of passion, in her menses, or past her period;

whether she be a fair-complexioned woman, a Rohiṇī, a maiden, or one who is like a corpse; whether she be consecrated or unconsecrated, pure or impure, or even avoided—[she may be accepted]. (3.66.90)
Whether she has been abandoned, or is possessed of mantras, or initiated, or even despised;

whether she has been exiled, or is a woman who carries off forest-dwellers, or a dog-eater’s daughter, or a sister; whether she is a young woman, or devoid of passion, or devoted to infidelity—(91–92).
Whether she be shaven-headed or long-haired, unfortunate or fortunate, humpbacked or short-statured, possessed of her senses or devoid of them,
indifferent, or whatever her condition may be— even if she be a woman who has recently given birth or one who is like a beast— [she must be honored].
Whether she follows the ways of a cow or the ways of a deer, or whatever else she may be;
whether she is clad in ash-colored garments, or red, or discolored, or dressed in green;
whether she is a goddess, a female demon, or a female rakshasa; ||94-95||
A female *dānava*, a female *nāga*, a naked woman, a female bird, or a female *jantu*; or a female tree-spirit, one lacking limbs, a female *śarabha*, or even a *siṃhikā*;
or a female beast of prey, a many-legged creature, a female *pṛṣṭhapadī*, or a *piśācī*.
Whether she be of the Ṛṣis, of Brahmā, or of the Pitṛs; whether she be the mother, or the guardian of the field (97);
or a female bird, a Kinnarī, a Gandharvī, or a dancer;
or even a courtesan engaged in sexual union, or one who possesses a thousand lingas (98).
Whether she be a goddess, a human woman, a *bhūti*, a *preta*, or a *ḍākinī*;
whether she be lowly, a doer of evil, or whoever she may be who has approached me—having accepted her with such a disposition and having purified her, even if she were a queen. (99)

Having purified her who was impure, I lead her to my own imperishable abode. For that purpose, I become Hari in human form as a man, in order to uplift hosts of women by the thousands of millions. (3.66.100–101)
O Lakṣmī, the secret has been told to you here: the bull [of dharma] possesses the quality of desire.
For when one attains Me, desire becomes righteous and brings about liberation.
Furthermore, union with women through the womb is the cause of supreme affection.
Having done so, I lead all these women to the supreme, imperishable state.
And having heard or recited this secret, which bestows divinity, rich in liberation, and dedicated to Nārāyaṇa, they shall go to my abode.
But those women or men who fall into doubt regarding this matter shall lose the merit previously performed and, being guilty, go to a lower state. Indeed,
doubts arise for those unworthy ones who merely repeat the words of the world.
No doubts arise in my disciples who possess divine knowledge.
Indeed, the secret of the *Vadhūgītā* which resides in my heart—that which bestows liberation upon the bride—is here explained to you without reserve. (106–107)
The bride-price, the attraction from my abode, and even their fondness—nothing more than this remains to be understood regarding women in this world.
For those who are possessed by the state of desire, I am the giver of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
One should worship Hari, placing one’s own duty (nijadharma) foremost.
For the duty of a woman consists of pleasure, with the duty of desire placed before it;
yet in my yoga, there is celibacy (brahmacarya)—that is the supreme vow for a woman.

Death in one’s own dharma is better, for the dharma of Hari indeed bestows liberation. Through the yoga of Hari, there shall certainly be deliverance within one’s own dharma; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Secrets of the Devotion of the Bride," in the *Vadhūgītā* of the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 68 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; I shall declare to you that which is dear to the heart.
I am indeed the common Great Lord of all living beings. (1)
"Only by propitiating me have all these beings been created here as possessors of sovereignty;
therefore, I grant them the sovereignty they seek.
According to the fruit of their actions, that which is to be given must be bestowed—this is my eternal law."
The fruit of favor is empty; this is the distinction in my house.
(3) For favor toward a servant consists of a reward;
however, favor toward one who performs his duty with diligence is innate. (4)

Whether among women or men, in whatever creation, or wherever it may be—whether among the women of Pārvatī, Sāmudrī, or Dvīpinī, or among others; whether among Hārītī, or even among the immortals, or among Gaurī or Paryā—I [act]. (5)
In a woman who belongs to the Rāśīya, Brāhmī, Raudrī, or Vaninī [classes],
or likewise in one of the Mānasī, Īśānī, Daridrā, Antyajā, Pūrvajā, or Madhyajā [classes]. (6–7)
Whether she be a Dhīvarī, a Śabarī, or a Yavanī, or likewise a Piśaṅgī, a Prācīnakāyā, or even an Abriktā;
whether she be white, black, or variegated—regardless of the woman [with whom one engages]. || 8 ||
Likewise, whether it be toward such a man, or toward a devotee of the gods, or similarly toward a sage, or toward the Lord,
or toward one who is liberated— wherever my favor resides, there indeed shall there be an incalculable abundance of all jewels. (3.67.10)
There shall be an incalculable number of all sovereignties and spiritual accomplishments;
there shall be an incalculable number of all prosperities and miraculous powers.
There shall be an incalculable number of blisses, joys, and delights.
Likewise, there shall be an infinity of festivals and of joyful diversions;
there shall be an infinity of fortunes and of auspicious things to be enjoyed;
and there shall be an infinity of all desires and satisfactions. (12–13)
Wherever I am pleased and bestow a reward,
there is my imperishable state, even if it be in the highest heaven.
Tell me, Lakṣmī, how could there be any deficiency from that?
Everything becomes divine for me; everything is the most excellent for me.
My devotee’s house is my own house, and I am that very devotee. Thus, this family dwells within my heart as my very own.
For me and for my devotee, there is not even the slightest difference.
What is illusion, what is time, or who is the Lord within my abode?
For that place where I dwell is indeed the supreme, imperishable realm.
That eternal supreme state is indeed in the form of an earthen hut;
where I am not present, even a palatial mansion is like hell,
and this ground where I do not dwell is like a cremation ground.
That Rākṣasī by whom I was never served, she too is merely a *ramaṇī*.
That Bhūtī who did not embrace me, O Lakṣmī, is but a *piśācinī*.
He by whom I was never saluted nor was Mādhava embraced—[he is nothing]. (3.67.20)
And there exists here a real rākṣasa who devours those at birth;
by taking refuge in me, even piśācas become supreme deities.
Even piśācinīs, having reached me, are born as the wives of Brahmā.
The defects (*doṣas*) are indeed *piśācas*, and those possessing them become *piśācinīs*.
The qualities (*guṇas*) are indeed pearls; those possessing them become pearl-women (*muktānyaḥ*).
Those who possess the knowledge "I am Brahman" truly become wives of Brahman (*brahmapatnyaḥ*).
All those who have taken refuge in the Supreme Brahman indeed become wives of Hari.
How could anyone perform the painful austerity of penance while abandoning Hari, who am I?
Without the Supreme Lord, no one at all can attain perfection.
Indeed, infinite bodies and the attributes of the body were created by Brahmā;

likewise, the attributes of Brahman, the attributes of the body, the attributes of the mind, and internal attributes, as well as the attributes of the worlds that bestow all happiness, were created by him. (25–26)
My dharmas are indeed eternal; even Brahmā has been created by me.
Relying upon my supreme, eternal dharmas, he attains me.
For my very graciousness is the dharma that bestows divinity upon me.
Having properly honored the duties of a Brahmin, one should practice my own duties.
For me, whose wife is the purpose of dharma, there is no other duty to be performed;
this is my own dharma, which is pure and free from the qualities of nature (nirguṇa). || 28–29 ||
One should indeed abide by pure dharma and always give what is pure;
even a very small amount of purity given to me results in infinity. Furthermore, whatever pure act is performed here for my sake, even if done merely as a play, [it bears infinite fruit].

Even that which is performed by means of the senses and so forth is attained as pure (śukla) within the abode [of the Self]. Merit is pure; for me, it is my duty. For one who possesses that [merit], no sin arises.
There is no suffering, nor indeed illusion, nor birth; how then could there be death?
Therefore, those who have taken refuge in me should always remain in a state of fullness and eternal bliss.
Those who, not taking refuge in me, carry the burden of bound action here again and again,
are indeed burdened by the weight born of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Just as a monkey goes from tree to tree,
so indeed is the living being led by its karma through the various wombs in the forest of saṃsāra,
like a ball thrown for play by children on a playground.
In this way, by means of his actions (karma), he is cast into a field within the realm of illusion;
bound like a horse, he is not independent, whether to move about or even to depart.
Bound by karma, he is not free among gods, sages, ancestors, or humans. (36)
Humans are the best upon the earth, yet they are devoid of wings;
birds fly through the sky, yet they are devoid of the means of hands;
and the gods possess divine forms, yet they are devoid of the grossness of the earth and such.
Women, though rich in beauty and virtue, were made subject;
the elderly were created as venerable, yet deprived of authority.
The young possess authority, yet they are devoid of long experience.
For the elephant, though powerful, remains devoid of means;
the lion, indeed, is a powerful king, yet he is a beast, the lowest of the tamasic;
the deer, however, is pure, even though it is made a wild animal. (3.67.40–41)
Even Brahmins who are treasuries of knowledge may be afflicted by the pain of poverty;
crows are clever in interpreting omens, yet they are born from a foul womb.
Pearls are the most excellent of gems, yet they are made difficult to obtain.
There are many pungent grasses, while sweet ones are indeed difficult to find.
O beloved, base men are easy to find, whereas virtuous men are rare;
truthful women are difficult to find, while unchaste women are easy to find.
Leaves are many, but fruits are indeed difficult to find.
Enjoyers are easy to find, but those free from passion are rare. (45) Insects exist everywhere, O beloved, but those who bear hoods are hard to find!
Death is easy to attain, O Lakṣmī, but immortality is very difficult to find. (46) Strife is easy to attain, O Lakṣmī, but reconciliation is very difficult to find.
Self-interest is everywhere easy to attain, but the interest of others is always difficult to find. (47)
O Lakṣmī! Enjoyment is easily obtained, but liberation is always difficult to attain.
O Lakṣmī! Men are easily found, but the Supreme Man (Puruṣottama) is difficult to find.
A man is easily found, but the Supreme Man is difficult to find.
Women are found everywhere, but a Nārāyaṇī is difficult to find. (49) Effort is always attainable, but service is difficult to obtain, O beloved!
The body is easily obtained in many ways, but the Self, indeed, is difficult to attain, O beloved! (50)
A house is easily obtained and accessible, but the imperishable abode is difficult to attain;
O Lakṣmī, an ordinary womb is easy to enter, but the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha) is indeed difficult to reach.
O Lakṣmī, caves are easily found, but the Peak of Brahmā (Brahmaśṛṅga) is truly difficult to find.
O Lakṣmī, latent impressions are easy to find, but Vāsudeva is indeed difficult to find.
(52) O Lakṣmī, husbands are easy to find, but the eternal husband is difficult to find; masters are easy to find in this world, but a supreme master is indeed difficult to find. (53)
O Lakṣmī! Indeed, everything is easily obtained; I, Kṛṣṇa, am always difficult to attain.
Māyā is indeed easy to obtain in the world, but I, the Lord of Māyā, am difficult to attain.
O Lakṣmī! By a capable Master, the womb of karma is cast away.
The entire world is bound by karma; I, Kṛṣṇa, truly deliver it.
Water is easily found everywhere, but the footstep of Viṣṇu is difficult to find. Indeed, among all things that are difficult to attain, the footstep of Viṣṇu is the most difficult to reach.
I shall make that which is difficult to attain easily accessible for those possessed of devotion in every way.
By acting thus, all the actions of my servants indeed grant liberation.
Tell me, Lakṣmī! What cause for grace or reward is there in this?
Having obtained this supreme merit, one shall go to my state of bliss.
Indeed, renunciation unto me is difficult to attain; everything else is indeed easy.
Indeed, entrustment unto me is difficult to attain; everything else is always easy.
Dedication to another is easy, but dedication to me is indeed difficult;
effort for another's sake is easy, but effort for my sake is difficult.
Indeed, being for the sake of another is easy, while being for my sake is difficult.
The state of being a widow is easily attained, but the state of being my consort is difficult for me to find.

(61) Everything illusory is easy to obtain, O beloved, but that which belongs to me is difficult to attain; for she who has taken refuge in the Kṛta age understands this, while she who is without such refuge has no such knowledge. (62)
Śrī Nārāyaṇī knows with how much effort I am obtained;
Satī Haimī knows how Śaṅkara is indeed obtained;
and Māṇikyāśvī knows how Dhārmī is indeed obtained.
Rādhā, Kṛṣṇā, and Kamalā know the difficulty;
Gāyatrī does not know it at all, nor does the daughter of the ocean (Lakṣmī). Padmāvatī knows it: how is the Supreme Lord to be attained? 64–65.
One who has obtained the grace of a forest-dweller does not know the toil of asceticism;
only disciplined yogis and virtuous women know that toil. Yoginīs and female ascetics who wither their bodies also understand it.
"O Lakṣmī! Do you know of the asceticism performed on Hanumat Mountain?
It was through great exertion that you obtained me, the Supreme Person.
O beloved, I am to be attained only in exchange for one's own death, and not otherwise."
He whose entire external and internal life is for my sake,
and who renounces everything for my sake through exertion— he indeed attains me.
He for whom all his possessions are for my sake, and whose very action is directed toward me— [he attains me].
She whose renunciation is for my sake attains me through her exertion.
Pure in conduct, having attained her body, a yoginī and a daughter of yogis,
she who has surrendered all her possessions for my sake— she, like the daughter of Bhṛgu, attains me.
In yoga, she knows me as the yogi, and she even remembers me in meditation.
Having surrendered her entire being for my sake, she indeed attains me, just like Padmā.
Even with very little effort, that auspicious woman becomes distressed by separation from me for my sake.
For that Mādhavī indeed attains me, who consists of consciousness and bliss.
All sacrifices performed for the sake of desires grant all happiness only when offered to me;
those devoted women established in me obtain eternal happiness.

O beautiful woman, she whose mind is not divided by desires for anything other than me attains sovereignty over all syllables and words, the bliss residing in the Lord of All, and the joy of all incarnations and the like. (75)
She indeed makes me—who was difficult to attain—easily accessible as her beloved.
Time and Yama both abandon a woman who is devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa;
even if she commits a thousand offenses, she becomes free from fault.
I am the protector dwelling within the heart, yet I stand swiftly outside;
though difficult to attain, I become easy to reach, like the dwelling of a cowherd.
Though difficult to attain, I indeed become easy to reach, just as Vāmana did.
Though I am very far away, I become as if standing near, like the elephant’s purpose;
though I am invisible, I become as if visible, reaching the pinnacle of delight for Prahlāda; though I am unapproachable, I become as if approachable, like a husband or a Lord.
O Lakṣmī! Through the offering of my affection, I give and I bestow everything;
I make all things, even those difficult to obtain, easy to attain for the sake of my servant.
Everything is done for your sake, and likewise, everything is done for the sake of my devotee.

Your auspicious Gāyatrīs, beloved by Him, bestow the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha).
Then [he taught] the two excellent Gāyatrīs of Ramā and Pārvatī;
then the triad of mantras whose presiding deity is the beloved Lord Kṛṣṇa.
O Lakṣmī, [this is] the accomplisher of all aims, the most excellent among all mantras.
Now listen also to the auspicious Gāyatrīs that bestow liberation:
"We know the Supreme Lord; we meditate upon the Best of Men."
May He who descends for our sake inspire us.
(39) We know Gopīśvara; we meditate upon Śrī Rādheśa.
May Kṛṣṇa inspire us. (3.69.40)
"Let us know Nārāyaṇa; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva. May that Viṣṇu inspire us.
"We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ."
May he who impels our intellects [grant us wisdom]. (42) We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva.
May that Rudra impel us. (43)
"Let us know the one born from the lotus; let us meditate upon the one whose mouth is the Veda.
May that Creator inspire us.
"Let us know the Great Viṣṇu; let us meditate upon Hiraṇyagarbha."
May that Infinite One inspire us.
(45) Listen, O Rame, to these seven Gāyatrīs, which are of my own nature and yet abide within your form; they are auspicious and bestow all human goals. (46)
"May we know her who is dear to Brahmā; may we meditate upon her who is dear to Hari. May that Brāhmī inspire us. (47) "May we know her who is Nārāyaṇī; may we meditate upon her who is Vāsudevī."
May the Vaiṣṇavī inspire us.
(48) We know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon the consort of Viṣṇu.
May that Lakṣmī inspire us. (49)
We know her who is golden-hued; we meditate upon Śrī, the tawny one. May Lakṣmī inspire us. (3.69.50) We know Mahāmāyā; we meditate upon Pārvatī, the Truth.
May Gaurī inspire us.
(51) We know the Great Sāvitrī; we meditate upon the Vedic Gāyatrī.
May Vāṇī inspire us. (52)
"May we know the Goddess Lakṣmī who bestows happiness; may we meditate upon the glory of Śivarājñī.
May that Kārṣṇī inspire us.
"May we know Nārāyaṇī; may we meditate upon Māṇikyā."
May she, Rādhā, inspire us.
(54) We know Nārāyaṇī; we meditate upon the goddess Ramā.
May Lakṣmī inspire us. (55)
"Let us know Nārāyaṇī; let us meditate upon Padmāvatī.
May she, the all-pervading one, inspire us.
"Let us know Nārāyaṇī; let us meditate upon the goddess Ramā."
May she, the sovereign, inspire us.
(97) We know the Goddess of Dharma; we meditate upon the Goddess of Devotion.
May Hari inspire us. (58)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these twelve Gāyatrīs are your names;
they are auspicious, bestowing the four aims of human life known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
In this way, all the mantras amount to one hundred and fifteen.
The fifteen hundred deities of power (śaktidevatā) are of my own nature.
Here, the secret has been told to you, which is devoted to the Supreme Lord.
Having recited even a single mantra among them, whether a man or a woman, [one attains the goal]. 3.69.60–61.
One may go from heaven to a higher heaven, from abode to a most supreme abode,
from festival to one rich with festivals, and from bliss to that which is filled with bliss.
There is no deity superior to Puruṣottama who bestows liberation.
Therefore, service should be rendered to me, who am known as Puruṣottama.
My mantras should always be recited day and night according to one's capacity.
My initiation should be received, and my marks should always be worn.
I am the Reality, Nārāyaṇa, and likewise Vāsudeva;
I am the Supreme Self, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Light, and the Supreme Lord.
I am Viṣṇu, higher than the highest, Kṛṣṇa indeed, the Puruṣottama.
I am Janārdana, the eternal Self, the inner Self, and the Witness;
likewise, I am Hṛṣīkeśa, the Sacrifice, and the Lord who is the Master of Līlā.
I am the Lord who is the head of all, the eye of all, and the feet of all.
I am the soul of the universe, the Lord of Śrī, the Sun, and also Rāmaṇa;
I alone am the Lord of all, the omniscient one, and the Master of the world.
I abide within all branches of knowledge, and I am also the wielder of all weapons.
I am the teacher of all and the object of worship for all, the glorious Supreme Person (Śrī Puruṣottama).
My well-known insignia are indeed the auspicious Sudarśana discus, as well as the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), the forehead mark (tilaka), and likewise the conch and other symbols. (3.69.70)
O beloved, I, the Supreme Person, am to be worshipped with food and honored by one who possesses the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth; indeed,
having borne these marks, one should perform the duties of a Brahmin.
The one who bears [the mark] on his two arms, the sustainer, goes to the supreme state which is beyond me.
Having marked himself and recited the mantra, he is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence.
A virtuous woman should feed a devotee endowed with the Sudarśana [mark] at the ancestral rites (śrāddha) and other ceremonies.
The ancestors indeed become eternally satisfied by eating the food of a Vaiṣṇava.
One should give cows, land, gold, and other gifts to one whose arms are marked with the discus.
Those marked with the discus are liberated from sin and go to my supreme abode.
On the auspicious and purifying Vaiṣṇava body marked with the discus and other signs, all holy fords, sacrifices, and millions of liberated souls reside.
For the sake of mantra-perfection and worship, the discus should especially be worn. (75–76)
For the sake of attaining the state of being a Vaiṣṇava, especially for the attainment of knowledge,
and for the sake of attaining the status of my servant, one should especially wear the discus.
One should always mark the lines of the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus upon the arms.
One should always perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the fish, trident, banner, bow, arrow, svastika, and staff,
either as lines or made of sandalwood paste or heated metal.
Richly adorned with these lines of the sacred wheel, they shall cross the ocean of sins.
The foot, the rim, and the Sudarśana discus of Hari are sacred.
Indeed, those whose bodies have been heated by it proceed to my abode.
O Brahmā, purify us with that pure [discus] which has been heated by fire.
O Agni, with that purifier of yours which is radiant, purify us.
(81) With that purifier by which the gods always purify themselves, may the Pāvamānī verses purify me with their thousandfold stream. (82)
That purifier belonging to Prajāpati is golden, with a hundred supports and a thousand rays;
by means of it, we who know Brahman purify the purified Brahman.
It is the wheel with its rim, eternally revolving for the Great Soul, the Imperishable.
In that body marked by the discus, he attained a state of supreme exaltation.
(84) Thus, my own words and even the Vedas declare:
"Those marks, such as the conch and the discus—the weapons—should be worn according to the prescribed rule. (85)
Likewise, they are supported by wives, children, servants, and other domestic animals;
by trees, creepers, and the like; and by houses, gardens, and so forth.
Furthermore, weapons such as lines and other implements are supported by vehicles, mounts, chests, and the like.
My form is within you, and likewise my signs are on the outside.
Devotion through yoga directed toward no other, preceded by the offering of all things and so forth, must both be performed and maintained by you; for my Vaiṣṇava devotees are indeed my servants.
One should apply the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) on the forehead together with the dot (bindu) of Lakṣmī.
O Lakṣmī, I indeed dwell within the vertical mark along with you;
for a body marked with the vertical line is truly my divine temple.
One who bears the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and has bathed is considered to have bathed in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Initiated into all sacrifices and honored in all worlds,
he ascends an excellent celestial chariot (*vimāna*) and goes to my supreme abode.
Upon seeing a devotee wearing the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark, one is liberated from sins;
or by saluting him with devotion, one obtains the fruit of all possible gifts.
Indeed, when he is fed at a *śrāddha* ceremony, the ancestors attain satisfaction for ten million kalpas.
The ancestors of such a person shall obtain the fruit of performing a *śrāddha* at Gayā.
For the yogi who bears the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) upon his forehead, merit equal to sacrifice, charity, ascetic practice, recitation, and fire-offerings arises in infinite measure. (93–94)
The single-minded, highly fortunate, virtuous, and celibate practitioners should indeed apply my mark (puṇḍra) with an interval, in the shape of my foot.
My foot-shaped mark is my temple, complete with its moon.
I abide in the center of the forehead, and Hari abides there with you and Śrī.

People should always apply the *puṇḍra* mark for the sake of attaining the same world as Kṛṣṇa, using either earth from a sacred site (*tīrtha*), sandalwood paste, saffron, or liquid [fragrance]. (96–97)
Or they may indeed fashion the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* with water and other substances, together with the *candraka*.
Having applied these marks upon their limbs, they shall attain union (*sāyujya*) with me.
One should meditate on me, Hari, as Nārāyaṇa on the forehead, and likewise on the belly.
One should meditate on Śrī upon the chest, and Śrī Puruṣottama upon the throat;
likewise, Nara and Kṛṣṇa upon the two arms, and the Lord of Māṇikī upon the neck;
Śrī Bhūpati upon the two sides, and me, Janārdana, upon the back. (3.69.99–100)
And on the two hands, one should remember me as the Lord of Ramā, Padmā, and Āvatī.
Thus, my devotee should always wear twelve marks (puṇḍras).
Such a woman is a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavatī), and such a man is a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavataḥ).
One who is adorned with the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and the beautiful moon is undoubtedly my own form; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have indeed described to you the mantras together with the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, along with the moon-marks, and all of them accompanied by garlands of *tulasī*.
Empowered by mindfulness of me, men become like Nārāyaṇas and women become like Nārāyaṇīs, bestowing gifts upon me.
What more need be said? They truly become my beloveds.
"From reading and hearing this, the path to liberation shall become certain.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of the Great Mantras, the Gāyatrī and Others, the Moon-Adorned Urdhva-puṇḍra, and Other [Practices]," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
