Chapter 71 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, you should cause the mantras of the true Guru to be grasped.
Even one who has studied the thousand branches of the Vedas and is initiated into all sacrifices,
or even an ascetic and the best of Brahmins, shall not be a Guru if he is not a Vaiṣṇava.
He who is a great devotee of the Lord and intent upon meditation, who is a lover of the path of devotion, is indeed a Vaiṣṇava and a wise guru.
He is the teacher, the true preceptor, the saintly one who tears asunder the bonds of worldly existence. (2–3)
Therefore, being pure, one should indeed receive the mantras accompanied by the syllable *oṃ*.
In all cases, one should employ the Lord *praṇava* at the beginning of the mantras.
I am the syllable *oṃ*, the Supreme Brahman; the *praṇava* is the leader of mantras.
First, the single syllable "Oṃ," followed by my name in the dative case;
then, one should complete it with the two-syllable name "namaḥ.
Thus the Guru should say: "Oṃ śrīkṛṣṇanandajāya namaḥ. (5–6)
The fourfold mantra is excellent, and the tenfold mantra is supreme.
Seven, twelve, and two *gāyatrīs* are also my highest [mantras].
Likewise, thirteen mantras and three others are always most excellent to me.
The thirty-three descent-mantras (avatāra-mantra) are likewise considered by me to be excellent.
All thirty-three Śrī-mantras are regarded by me as supreme;
whether one, or all together, or even many, they may be used according to one's preference.
Indeed, the mantras should be received by the disciple, or the guru may bestow them after due examination.
I am Hari himself, the deity of one hundred and fifteen mantras.
My own mantras are thirty-three, and others describe my very form.
Indeed, because of the identity between form and the formed, all [mantras] are appropriate within me in every respect.
(11) Whatever devotee hears from the guru the mantra of a particular deity’s essential nature—[the mantras are] the one hundred and fifteen branches of the tree of the Supreme Brahman. (12)
Having worshipped those various forms with their respective mantras and having propitiated them as my own manifestations, they shall indeed come to me, Hari.
O Lotus-born One, all those belonging to the tradition of the Supreme Brahman are my very limbs.
All this has arisen from me; nothing at all exceeds me.
(14) The lords are woven within me, who am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
likewise, the incarnations, the liberated ones, and the individual souls are woven within Hari, who is myself. (15)
"These powers, which bring about descent, reside within me;
all of them, in the form of mantras, are strung upon me, the Lord Hari.
Having realized this, [he recited] one hundred and fifteen mantras.
The learned one, having discerned [the disciple], should indeed bestow [the knowledge] upon a qualified scholar.
He shall be the sovereign emperor of teachers (*ācāryasamrāṭ*), the preceptor who imparts all mantras.
He is proclaimed as the "Sovereign Emperor of Teachers of the Tradition of the Supreme Brahman" (*parabrahmasampradāyācāryasamrāṭ*).
Those who bestow deficient mantras become indeed deficient preceptors.
However, the Lord, who is self-luminous, is established by me as the Guru—
the sovereign emperor of the lineage of the Supreme Brahman, the bestower of the Manu-mantra.
He who teaches all the mantras becomes my very own form.
O beloved, you and Lakṣmī, as well as the venerable [Guru], are indeed established by me as the Empress of the lineage of the Supreme Brahman and as the bestower of mantras. 3.70.20–21.
You are the instructor of all mantras, for you are indeed identical with my own nature.
Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, listen to this other matter: whatever name exists within a mantra, that person is its mantra-deity and likewise its preceptor; he always exists as a portion of me.
By my command, that mantra, as well as the Ācāryāṇī, should be awakened.
In this manner, one should employ the mantras and receive them from the mouth of the Guru;
thus this mantra becomes "seeded" (sabīja), radiant with the splendor of the Guru’s vital energy.
When the power of the deity is stronger than that of the Guru, the mantra bestows liberation.
When the power of the disciple is greater, the mantra indeed grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In all mantras, the seed-syllable is none other than I, Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved.
The eternal, inseparable power, Śrī Lakṣmī, resides within Manu.
O Śrī, the syllable *Oṃ* is my name; the letter *A* am I, the Supreme Lord;
the letter *U* is you, Śrī, yourself; and the letter *M* is my devotee alone. (26–27)
The letter *A* is I, the Supreme Self; the letter *U* is considered to be the Lord (*Īśvara*);
and the letter *M* is the multitude of individual souls (*jīva*). Thus, their essence is *Oṃ*, which is my own nature. Furthermore, the letter *A* is Aniruddha, and the letter *U* is Pradyumna.
The letter *ma* is Saṃkarṣaṇa; thus, "Om," I am Śrī Hari in three ways.
(29) The letter *a* is Viṣṇu himself, and the letter *u* is likewise Śaṅkara.
The letter *m* is the creator of the universe; indeed, I am the Supreme Lord in three ways. (3.70.30)
The letter *A* is my imperishable Brahman; the letter *U* is my infinite liberations; and the letter *M* is my incarnations. Thus, I am the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*) in three ways.
The letter *A* is my creation as Brahmā; the letter *U* is my creation as Īśvara.
The letter *ma* is the creation of living beings; thus, I am the Supreme Lord in three ways.
(32) The letter *a* is I, the Supreme Brahman; *u* is my beloved, the Goddess of Brahman.

"I am the master and you are the mistress; all others are likewise servants.
Such is my heart’s intent, for within the meaning of the *praṇava* lies this servitude.
My devotees—both male and female—are always my servants, dependent upon me."
The body, senses, mind, ego-sense, and the qualities of my devotee are under my control.
For they are dedicated to Me, divine, dependent on Me, and sustained by Me.
Therefore, for one established in My state, their conduct is subject to My will. (35–36)
By my very will alone, that man possesses his *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion);
by my power alone, O Lakṣmī, there is nothing unattainable for him.
With the burden entrusted to me, the Lord of Śrī, he should perform only my work.
For I am the Supreme Self, the Master; the devotee, however, is indeed my servant.
A servant must always be employed according to one's will.
Likewise, a female servant, a maidservant, and a handmaid who has taken refuge in me must be employed [by me].
I am indeed his very self, and he is mine; he is not anyone else.
Therefore, by taking refuge in me, he is eternally liberated from the bonds of the body and other such limitations.
For even while performing actions, those actions are truly performed by me alone.
And by those [powers], my devotee, freed from bondage, receives no stain.
My divine Māyā certainly delights the devotee;
that divine power gladdens him and even unites him with liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the majesty of my mind has been declared to you.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Akṣara;
I am known as Puruṣottama, the Supreme Controller who descends in incarnations.

I am indeed the Supreme Lord, the eternal Supreme Self; I am the Full Brahman, the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed One, the cause of all. My incarnations include Kṛṣṇa and others, as well as Vāsudeva and the rest. 44–45.
Brahmā and the others, as well as the lords such as Īśvara, and the powers such as Rādhā and Lakṣmī, are my portions (aṃśas).
Viṣṇu, Rudra, Brahmā, and the gods are portions, sub-portions, and further sub-portions.
Human beings and the like are their portions, as are animals and plants.
There are indeed creations of mine that have arisen from infinitesimal portions of my parts.
Among them, "nārā" refers to the collection of my own selves;
I make that my "ayana" (abode), and therefore I am Nārāyaṇa.
Among the principles born from Nara, I am Vāsudeva;
within the world of moving and non-moving beings, I am Nārāyaṇa.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
Since He has arisen from me, I am indeed that Supreme Lord.
Whatever has been and whatever is yet to be—all proceeds from the Supreme Lord;
I am He, the Sovereign of immortality, the illustrious Puruṣottama.
I am that Śrī Puruṣottama, from whom Vāsudeva shines forth, as well as Hiraṇyagarbha and Savitṛ;
and whose highly refined speech is the supreme Vāṇī, beginning with the Vedas.
I am that Śrī Puruṣottama from whose throat indeed the sound [of the Vedas] issues forth.
I am that Supreme Self who exists as the wielder of Māyā, worshipped through Māyā; yet, though the Lord of Māyā, I am devoid of Māyā—such am I, Śrī Puruṣottama. (53–54)
I am Śrī Puruṣottama, whose foot is indeed the world of manifestation and whose three-quarters are the imperishable abode; I am the Lord of the Earth, the Playful One, and the Lord of Śrī.
I am Yajñanārāyaṇa, and I am Sarvanārāyaṇa as well.
I am that Śrī Puruṣottama, who has assumed the form of the divided Nārāyaṇa.
I am that Śrī Puruṣottama, whose forms are all human beings—beginning with the Brahmins—as well as the gods, the moon, the sun, fire, heaven, and lightning. (56–57)
Men and women should respectfully perform service for one such as I;
having received the mantra, they should practice that secret which indeed bestows liberation.
I have hands and feet everywhere, and likewise, I am possessed of eyes everywhere.
Indeed, all the worlds and all abodes exist within you alone.
Thus am I, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), possessing a divine and auspicious form together with you, my sovereign consort. (3.70.60)
The great-bodied Hari, the eternal Lord who is to be honored by men, took delight with you; for he ever rejoices together with Lakṣmī and Śrī.
I am indeed the son of the Mother of the World, eternally youthful.
I abide in the supreme state, possessing the beauty of ten million Kandarpas.
My [abode] is the supreme sky, the station of liberation, resorted to by liberated women, imperishable, and filled with eternal bliss, happiness, and the like. (62–63)
Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the unmanifest (avyākṛta), and the immortal realm—
these abodes have indeed been created by me for the sake of enjoyment.
Likewise, there are those made of gold, such as Vairāja and others, which are likewise composed of māyā.
The levels of Sādāśiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Prādhānika;
all the enclosures (āvaraṇas) beginning with Satya and extending down to Manu and the others;
and the regions ending with Pātāla—all these are filled with the fortune of divine play and sport.
All the worlds were created by me for the purpose of my playful pastimes and the like;
my eternal abiding is in the enjoyment [of these] within my abodes in the form of incarnations.
But, O Lakṣmī, I withdraw that play, for it consists of Māyā.
The imperishable abode that pervades three-quarters is indeed my supreme and eternal realm.
That three-quartered manifestation is eternal; therein are all my abodes, such as Goloka and others, which are indeed eternally supreme.
One foot of this [Bhūmi] consists of the worlds known as Aisvara, Jaiva, and so forth, which are designated as impermanent;
for all of them are essentially playful, created by Me for the sake of sport.
My other foot is in the eternal, immutable Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the unmanifest, and the immortal.
I remain as the infallible, eternal, divine Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person, eternally endowed with youth— the Infinite One, the Lord,
who is both Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa. (71–72)
O Lakṣmī, Vāsudeva is always endowed with your forms,
joined by Muktānikā, Brahmapriyā, Haripriyā,
and the gopīs Rādhā and Virajā— my own powers in Goloka.
In Vikuṇṭha, the Lord is served by Lakṣmī, Hariṇī, Kamalā, and others; in Avyākṛta, the Master is served by the female attendants Ramā and Śrī;
and in the abode of nectar (Amṛtadhāman), He is served by the lotus-like women of Vāsudeva.
Served by liberated cowherds, attendants, and companions,
I indeed dwell in various forms as the essence of my incarnations,
in eternal enjoyment with Īśvarī, Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Rādhā.
O Lakṣmī, may I always find you together with Ramā, Vāsudevī, Kamalā, Bhūmi, and the divine [Śrī]; for you are eternal,
the Mother of the World, my inseparable Śrī.
She is all-pervading and eternally omnipresent, the sovereign of all worlds forever;
she is endowed with hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
She is the Supreme Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, Nārāyaṇī, the Golden One.
The entire world, both stationary and moving, is situated within your body.
The preservation and dissolution of the world occur through your opening and closing [of your eyes].
You are the primordial Great Brahmanī, the Great Lakṣmī, the Supreme Sovereign of all.
You, whose nature is both manifest and unmanifest, abide pervading the entire universe.
You are the sovereign power (vibhūti) in the supreme abode, Rādhā dwelling in Goloka;
you are Lakṣmī residing in Vaikuṇṭha, and Ramā dwelling in the unmanifest.
Padmā, the abode of nectar, and my imperishable sovereign power (vibhūti)—
in the worlds of the lords and within the cosmic eggs of living beings, you indeed become the embodiment of playful sovereignty, assuming the nature of the various planes of existence. 83–84.
The realms and abodes of the lords, millions of palaces,
opulent gardens, fields, and divine lands—
all these manifold riches are but my play, for they simply exist as "they are. (85)
You are the principles of obscuration (āvaraṇas), as well as those belonging to Sādāśiva;
you are the Vaiṣṇava principles and those pertaining to Māyā;
and you are the principles of Hiraṇyagarbha, such as Vairāja and the rest.
Those [worlds] beginning with Satya, which are the abodes of the gods, as well as those belonging to humans;
likewise, those principles within the netherworlds (pātāla) that are the grounds of enjoyment;
and those which consist of water, earth, fire, and air.
All those, O Lakṣmī, are indeed your playful manifestations (līlārūpa).
You, whose nature consists of form, taste, smell, and touch, are the embodiment of sound;
having attained the state of being Lakṣmī, you are named after wealth, property, and so forth.
Thus, you are the very nature of the world; O Śrī, you have taken refuge in Himālaya as the glory of the universe.
Indeed, O Lotus-born One, all that is to be known is your form.
O Lakṣmī, every female form is your form; it is your very body.
Beauty, virtuous conduct, brilliance, good fortune,
gentleness, happiness, loveliness, fragrance, and the power of attraction through taste and other qualities—
O Kamalā, such a form of yours as this is present in all women. (92–93)
Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Śrī, Ākṣarī, Muktānikā, Ramā,
Brahmapriyā, Kamalā, Haripriyā, Māṇikī, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Parāvidyā, Ramā, Śrī, and Nārāyaṇī. ॥94॥
Vidyā, Sarasvatī, Mātā, Vaiṣṇavī, Padminī, Satī;
Padmā, Padmajā, Abdhiputrī, Rambhā, Rādhikā;
Bhūḥ, Līlā, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, Hariṇī, and Mādhavīśvarī. (95–96)
Gaurī, Kārṣṇī, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī, Svāhā, Svadhā, Rati,
Sampat, Smṛddhi, Vāsudevī, Virajā,
Hiraṇmayī, Bhārgavī, Śivarājñī, Śrī, Rāmā, and Śrīkāntavallabhā.
Whoever indeed recites these names of yours every morning attains great prosperity,
fortune, and imperishable glory—
[the goddess] golden-hued, tawny, adorned with garlands of gold and silver. (98–99)
He obtains the golden moonlight, the Fortune who is my very own form—
she whose nature consists of supreme fragrance, beauty, and other qualities, and who increases nourishment.
Your giver is the glorious Lord, Puruṣottama himself.
The Lord is the supreme Nārāyaṇa, an ocean of affection and compassion;
he is of virtuous character, auspicious, one whose desires are fulfilled, and possessed of all powers.
He bestows the bliss of heaven and liberation, and is the refuge for all embodied beings.
Thus, O Goddess of gods, I, along with you, grant myself to my servant and your devotee; I bestow upon you both the realization of our mutual identity as the Self.
Śrīman Nārāyaṇa is the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, the Supreme Person.

I am that very Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning; I am the supreme goal. (1.04) I am the refuge, the abode, the dwelling, the kinsman, the father, the husband, the friend, the mother, the brother, the protector, the guardian, and the Lord of the worlds. (1.05)
The Lord of Śrī possesses auspicious qualities and bestows the fruits of all desires;
I am devoid of material qualities, attributeless, yet possessed of a divine form.
Endowed with divine, innumerable qualities, sovereignty, beauty, and charm, [He is the Supreme].
I dwell in the immortal, eternal, divine, infinite, imperishable, and supreme state;
in the world of Brahmā, which is endowed with the bliss of Brahman-joy, consisting of supreme luster, pure, and free from dissolution and the like. (107–108)
In that which is incalculable, undecaying, eternal, and devoid of waking, dreaming, and other states; free from common attributes and limitations, and lacking beginning or end;
auspicious, possessing a splendor more exalted than all else, and an ocean of bliss. (109)
That which is the imperishable, to be known through the Vedas, in which the gods and the Sādhyas are seated;
upon it all the gods are seated, and they know that in which they abide.
That supreme imperishable, the wise always behold.
Where the many-horned, tireless cows dwell on all sides,
those Sādhya-yogīs indeed know the majesty of the celestial realm (Nāka).
May we always abide there, O youthful Śrī Narāyaṇas.
Where my sisters, the youthful maidens beginning with you, who are my beloveds reside—
having attained that supreme abode of the Imperishable (akṣara), which is mine,
those who know the mantra proceed to this divine state of liberation.

Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attainment of Knowledge of the Hidden Meaning of the Great Mantra," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 71 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 71]
[The Author: Chapter 72.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the detailed expansion of the manifestation of the three-quarters (tripāda-vibhūti).
Indeed, there are innumerable abodes composed of pure being (śuddhasattva).
They are eternally rich with the bliss of Brahman-joy;
they are all changeless and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.
Indeed, these [lotuses] are divine, made of gold, pure, and radiant;
they are truly served by those devoted to the lotus feet of the Incarnation, as well as by eternally liberated beings of divine form, both men and women. (3)
And those dwellings, filled with perfumed women, forests, gardens, lakes, and cities,
are to be enjoyed by those who serve the imperishable Brahman;
indeed, they become palaces where the bliss of the joy of one's own Self resides.
Indeed, those supreme states of liberation known as *nirvāṇa* and *kaivalya*,
which consist solely of the enjoyment of the singular essence of service and devotion to the feet of Śrī Śaṅkara,
belong to my worshippers who are eternally liberated and most divine. (6)
And their eternal female attendants dwell within these very [abodes].
(7) Indeed, those who know the mantras go to those supreme abodes, which bestow the bliss of Brahman and grant me my yoga. (8)
Abiding in various places, I possess the nature of incarnations;
yet as the source of incarnation, I truly exist in the imperishable, supreme abode.
That which is Mahāmāyā, the primordial nature (prakṛti), praises me again and again.
Salutations to you who dwell in the imperishable; salutations to you, the Supreme Lord.
Salutations to you, the source of incarnations and the one who takes incarnations.
O Lord, I am your power of illusion (māyā), and the worlds of illusion are yours as well.
The abodes of the lords are indeed your own, as are these various planes of existence;
all the principles (tattvas) are truly your effects.
You are indeed the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa), the cause of all causes.
O Lord of Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, and Ramā; O Lord of Māṇikī and Muktikā!
(13) O Beloved of Prajñā and Padmāvatī; salutations to You, O Lord who bestows happiness!
O Lord of Lakṣmī and Padmā; salutations indeed to You, Nārāyaṇa! (14)
Salutation to the one whose nature is that of the Lord of all, the self of all the gods;
salutation to Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, who possesses infinite forms. Salutation to You, the infallible, the beloved, the Supreme Lord.
Salutations to you, the omniscient and all-encompassing son of Gopāla.
(16) Salutations to you, the soul of all creation; salutations to you, the supreme self. Salutations to you, the Brahman and the light; salutations to you of pure radiance. (17)
Salutation to the progenitor, the father, the cause of creation, preservation, and dissolution;
salutation to Nārāyaṇa, who dwells within the inner self of all beings.
Salutation to you, O possessor of infinite divine qualities, the bestower of the goals of human life!
And salutations to the one whose form is the cosmic array, who possesses the nature of the five states.
Be gracious, O Blessed Viṣṇu, for the welfare of all the worlds;
for these selves are indeed devoid of knowledge, formless, and without senses.
They exist without any activity and without any support;
you ought indeed to grant them worlds and bodies within me,
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and manifest your playful manifestation (līlāvibhūti) as it was before.
Behold the entire world, both conscious and unconscious, stationary and moving, as illusory and dissolved within me; awaken it!
O Supreme Lord, create once again along with me, Prakṛti. (22–23)
"O Lord, having contemplated merit and demerit, as well as pleasure and pain, within me,
you ought indeed to preside over me and perform your divine play with Śrī.
Thus was I requested by Māyā in the past, O Lakṣmī.
For within that very Māyā, he indeed proceeded to create the universe.
Released from his abode by his own will, the Puruṣa united with her;
therefore he is called Prakṛti-puruṣa, as well as Pradhāna-puruṣa. || 25-26 ||
The primary principle (pradhāna) is indeed the Great Principle (mahat-tattva); thus it is the Sovereign Intellect (buddhi).
From that Pradhāna and Puruṣa, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is born.
This very [ego] is called Hiraṇyagarbha and Mahāviṣṇu.
From that, the mind arises, as do the subtle elements and the sense organs.
This group of sixteen is the Puruṣa named Vairāja. From Vairāja were born the Lords Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
Brahmā became the earth and water, Viṣṇu the fire, and Rudra the most exalted light.
From him, breath became the wind, and the heart was born as the sky and space.
From these [elements] arose the sages, the ancestors, the gods, the elemental beings, and human beings.
Asuras, Dānavas, Daityas, Nāgas, and Sarpas were created;
all animals and living beings were born according to their respective kinds.
All are joined to appropriate wombs in accordance with their past actions.
For they always abide in their own nature, yet they manifest by the will of Hari.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, contemplate my sport as consisting of Māyā.
You yourself are that great divine Māyā, having resorted to union with me.
You are my very own nature, my will, and my power, possessing every form.
You are my half-body, the Brahmi, Narayani, Maheshvari, Mahalakshmi, Vasudevi, Vaishnavi, Kamala, and Rama. (34-35)
You are Rādhā, Lakṣmī, the beloved, the consort, and Śrī; you are the eternal bestower of happiness and the one who ordains the birth and other states of all living beings existing within creation.
Without my power, there is no manifestation of creation anywhere.
Therefore, O Supreme Goddess, you are the life-force of the entire world;
I am the life-breath whose form is that of life. You are the Supreme Sovereign, and I am your husband, the Supreme Lord.
I am the Supreme Master, the Highest Ruler, filled with all excellent qualities. (37–38)
I am indeed Śrī Kṛṣṇa for the sake of fulfilling the desires of Rādhā; I am indeed Nārāyaṇa for the sake of fulfilling the desires of Lakṣmī;
I am indeed Vāsudeva, the perfect one who assumes three forms.
From him indeed arises the form of Pradyumna, endowed with all sovereign powers.
He is the Lord of the abundant ones, of the lords, and of the lords of lords;
he is the mine of mastery, the ruler even of Time, and he indeed effects the divine creation.
Having attained the state of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin) and being permeated by Mahākāla,
he possesses my powerful sovereignty; assuming the form of Mahākāla,
he wields my potent will and sovereignty which is the cause of Time.
The son of Mahākāla is indeed known as Kāla.
Having attained absorption within him, Aniruddha, the creator of the world,
was formerly granted by me the knowledge consisting of the eternal Vedas.
Indeed, portions of Aniruddha arise as Brahmās.
From Vāsudeva, moreover, another was born, Pradyumna, endowed with my power, splendor, and sovereignty, performing the work of protection. (45)
He protects the creation of Īśa and sets in motion its maintenance.
Then, as the portion of that [Īśa] in the form of Viṣṇu, he repeatedly protects the entire world.
From Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa is born, who effects destruction.

When those born from my portions— Rudra and the others— become possessed of the power of knowledge, missiles, weapons, and the like, they perform acts of destruction and bring about the dissolution of creation.
O Lakṣmī, it is indeed always thus that these beings are my own portions.
And by my will, their portions shall also become their wives.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-Lion, and Vāmana;
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki—these are the ten.
O Lakṣmī, my incarnations arise within all creations;
these performers of my work are the necessary manifestations.
I become an incarnation by my own will, accompanied by you.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama—by devotion to Him, they indeed go to my abode, the imperishable state (akṣara-pada). By devotion to His incarnate forms, they indeed go to Goloka and other realms. || 52-53 ||
Having gone among them, those who have not been liberated do not return to me, equal to me;
for all are equal to me in happiness, just as you are happy.
By my will, they are born for the sake of the welfare of the world.
For those liberated by Me, there is no birth on this earth bound by karma.
Indeed, service to Me is liberation itself, and nothing else;
for servitude to Me is truly bondage that is eternally blissful and eternally imperishable.
Furthermore, those who abide in my abode shall go to that abode by their own will—
those beloved of Brahmā, the great liberated ones, the servants of Hari, who are free from all affliction. Others as well, though bound by the fetters of karma, indeed attain my mantra.
If they abandon worldly happiness—which is like consuming food mixed with poison—and resort to me alone through the chanting of my names and worship, they shall attain me;
indeed, with unswerving devotion, they should worship me, the abode of compassion. (58–59)
The Supreme Self, a treasure-house of affection for His devotees, protects them;
He leads them to the Vaiṣṇava abode, which possesses the radiance of a thousand suns.
Having placed her upon a celestial chariot (vimāna), the Blessed Lord Śrī Hari Himself [protects her].
Indeed, for those who have been initiated into my mantra and are devoted solely to me,
the supreme recitation of my mantra here— of Śrīpati, of Śrī Hari—
is a divine medicine consisting entirely of nectar, the highest of all medicines.
This supreme, divine elixir pacifies all agitation and the like, removes the noose of *māyā*, and is auspicious in curing the disease of *māyā*;
for while this great medicine, the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, exists here upon the earth.
Human beings do not accept it; that is considered a great loss.
Those fools who do not drink the elixir of Hari’s name remain within the delusion of Māyā, their past accumulated sins still present. (64–65)
Through the ritual service of worshiping Hari, through meditation, and through my attendance upon him,
as well as through truthful speech and generosity, the purification of my body and self has arisen.
Consequently, he dwells within my heart and likewise within my very self without interruption.
Having made the temple the heart of my devotees, I lead them to my own abode. O Lakṣmī, may all you who are dear to Brahmā, as well as others who are dear to Hari,
such as Līlā and the rest, listen to me and enjoy me as their beloved husband.
May they proceed upon the excellent path through all my dedicated states of being—
through service, through knowledge and realization, as well as through meditations and austerities;
through vows, sacrifices, and gifts, and even through the pleasures of sandalwood and the like.
May they worship me, their beloved husband, with gestures of love, emotional expressions, and playful charms.
And may they see me everywhere— at all times in both dry and moist things, in stationary and moving beings, upon the earth, in the clouds, and in all embodied forms.
In their own duties and even in the homes of others,
let them offer various gifts directed toward me,
the Supreme Person; and let them constantly chant my name as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Worship me and remember my mantra, which is full of meaning.
Drink indeed the Vaiṣṇava nectar; drink the nectar of the mantra, and drink the nectar of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Let them drink the nectar of the command, the essence of love, and the essence of service;
let all the beloveds drink the essence of liberation and the essence of the Beloved.
Let them also drink the essence of devotion, the essence of yoga, and the essence of the Self.
May they drink the essence of Brahman, the essence of service, and the essence of what is dear;
may they drink the essence of affection, the essence of wine, and indeed all essences.
May they always worship their beloved and meditate upon Madhusūdana.
"Let them sing of me, Mahākṛṣṇa, and let them constantly chant the name of Śrī Hari.
Let those who are devoted to me perform austerities for my pleasure and remain absorbed in meditation upon me.
Thus, whoever on earth shall practice devotion for my sake," ||| 78 ||

O Lakṣmī, by my power, all those humans and others who recite the hymn of praise for my worship shall indeed become free from mental anguish; they will surely become supreme devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas), of this there is no doubt. (3.71.79–80)
They shall be free from sorrow, meritorious, and free from disease;
endowed with all sovereign powers and devoid of all ailments such as illness.
They shall be immortal and ageless, possessing abundant wealth and grain.
And by my supreme grace, adorned with sons, grandsons, and so forth, he shall always abide in the section of my temple devoted to devotees, as well as in my heart and mind;
he is ever-true to his vows and the bestower of all jewels. (82–83)
At the doorways of the houses of devotees who are engaged in the practice of mantra,
there shall always be wish-fulfilling trees that grant the fruits of all desires;
likewise, there shall be cows that yield every wish and cintāmaṇi jewels.
Kalpa-creeper trees and wish-fulfilling vessels remain in the kitchen;
by my grace, O Lakṣmī, they become like immortals, endowed with every fortune and radiant with merit and auspiciousness. (85–86)
Devoted to charity, wisdom, and meditation, and filled with bliss— wherever my Vaiṣṇava devotees reside, intent upon my vows, there shall be neither famine, nor disease, nor untimely death. (87)
O Lakṣmī, those who drink my essence (majjapā) with their minds devoted to me are of the middle class.
Their homes are divine, meritorious, and even bestowers of liberation;
indeed, they become sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) resembling my imperishable form.
In my houses there are maces, discs, banners, and bows;
there are my emblems—the trident, the fish, the arrow, and the svastika.
And upon all the surfaces of the walls, there are my images.
At all house doors and in all sacred places,
there are divine paintings of my playful exploits in every way.
They are accompanied by images of Tulasī, Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, and Māṇikī.
Wherever I am depicted within the house, surrounded by Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Padmā, Sukhadā,
and Śrī— there the Vaiṣṇava disposition prevails on all sides and many auspicious signs are seen.
Those mansions in which auspicious women devoted to Viṣṇu are depicted in frescoes on the walls,
where sacred fords are present, and where there are images of water-sports and the circle of Rādhā’s play— those are my homes. (94–95)
In my devotee’s house, images of the marriage of Brahmā and Pṛthivī are painted;
that house possesses a divine form for me and is a sacred ford for liberation.
It is endowed with the form of cows and adorned with the study of knowledge.
The painting of mine situated in the celestial chariot, featuring the splendor of my sacrificial initiation;
the painting of Kuṅkumavāpikā together with Aśvapaṭṭasara; and the painting graced by the hermitage of Lomaśa and joined by the illustrious Kambharā. 97–98.
The painting of Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, worshipped by all the gods and others,
as well as my auspicious images that provide protection to devotees—
O Lakṣmī, all these grant liberation; my house is a sacred site (*tīrtha*) joined with my own form.

"O Lotus-born One, my fifty-three forms, including yourself, are incarnated; all of them grant liberation to those in whose homes they reside. For the lineages and sub-lineages of such families, liberation is certain to arise."

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of Divinity and Other Attributes within the Single-Legged Līlā-Vibhūti Created at the Request of Māyā," in the section on the Tripāda-Vibhūti within the Dvāpara-Santāna of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 72 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga),
Chapter 72.
[The Author: Chapter 73.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to my worship which bestows liberation.
O Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, Hara, Rāma, Mukunda, Madhusūdana!
O Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puruṣottama, Keśava!
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, O Lord, Consort of Lakṣmī! 1–2.
O Padmanābha, O dweller in the syllable, O one who delights in the Self, O ocean of compassion! O Vāsudeva, O Lord of liberation, O Śrīdhara, O omnipresent Lord of Śrī!
O Lord of Rādhā and Ramā, O Victorious One, O Lord of Prajñā and Padmāvatī!
O Bestower of Fortune, Lord of Fortune, Dweller in Fortune, Maker of Liberation, Lord of Māṇikī;
O Son of Kambharā, Beloved of Brahmapriyā, Janārdana;
O Child Gopāla, Lord of the Universe, Giver of Happiness, Lord of Śrī, Sovereign! 4–5.
"O Lord of Life, O Beloved of the Goddess of Beauty, O Supreme Lord, O Mādhava!"—
uttering these names of mine on earth,
women indeed go to my abode, as do men, even those who are aged.
Children, the elderly, and youths are devoted to my name;
even those engaged in household duties bow down to me, Hari.
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, or indeed during meditation and the pursuit of knowledge, they remember me as their Lord.
Playing, they offer salutations and go to my imperishable abode;
wherever they utter Kṛṣṇa’s name very sweetly day and night,
there the divine nature of Kṛṣṇa is perceived on the surface of the earth.

The equality of Viṣṇu’s world with my own abode and the similarity between them—there is always prosperity for that house; no doubt should be entertained here. I see no difference between that [divine] place and the house of a devotee, which is an imperishable dwelling. (3.72.10–11)
They constantly utter my name in my imperishable abode; likewise, wherever they chant my name upon the earth, that is my home.
That divine abode should be understood as the imperishable; there is no distinction between them.
The state of both worlds is equal in its entirety.
There, there is no fear of old age or disease, for the people are free from death;
and there, my name is sung and my mantra is recited. (13–14)
What more need I say? By my grace, divine illusion [prevails];
for the devotee, cows and buffaloes likewise become divine and auspicious.
Their gardens are divine, and their home is always a divine and auspicious abode.
His household utensils and even his foods are divine.
The courtyard of his house is always divine, as are his sons, grandsons, and others.
For the devotee, the vessels and the wealth are indeed always divine. (16–18)
May divine trees, creepers, and celestial coverings such as *khaṣṭu* and the like, as well as caskets, garments, ornaments, and other divine objects, always belong to me, your devotee.
May even the dust, the particles, and the waters from the house of my devotee [be mine]. || 18 ||
Even the divine grains where I am the Supreme Lord—
indeed, even the birds and animals that consume the food in those houses,
as well as the divine guests, are purified by my grace.

"All those sacred fords (tīrthas) are in every way to be enjoyed by my devotees; indeed, all kinds of objects fit for enjoyment become purifiers even for sinners. O Lakṣmī, such is the purifying power that exists through my dwelling.
Free from qualities, bestowing merit, and granting liberation, such is the house and dwelling of my devotee.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the narrative of Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa;
it is purifying in this world and grants liberation to the world for my devotee. (22–23)
Yayāti, the lord of the earth and a devotee of the Blessed One, performed a hundred horse sacrifices as well as a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices; that king, a Vaiṣṇava,
gave gifts of many forms with great faith.
He gave hundreds of thousands of cows, as well as hundreds of millions;
he performed ten million fire-sacrifices (koṭihoma) and bestowed gifts such as land.
Indeed, he lived for eighty thousand years.
Yayāti indeed lamented: "This body is bound by karma;
it will end as ashes, or as excrement, or as earth.
By means of this [body] sin is accumulated, and from that results the fruit of hell."
By this, merit is earned, as well as heaven and sovereignty again and again.
(28) By this, devotion is earned, through which liberation becomes certain.
Therefore, while remaining in this kingdom, that alone should be accomplished here by the man of discrimination. (29)
Having reflected thus, the king began the worship of the names of Hari:
"O Hare, Kṛṣṇa! O Hare, Viṣṇu! O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Lord!
O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Dāmodara, Acyuta! (3.72.30)
Thus honoring his own messengers, he gave them these auspicious words:
"Let my messengers go to my kingdom, the entire realm as far as the ocean's edge; let them instruct the subjects and cause them to perform worship of Hari. (3.1–3.2)
May they behold the Supreme Self, may they chant the glorification of His names;
may they worship Hari constantly and serve the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, I shall not take taxes at all from my devoted subjects.
"May the subjects always chant the nectar of Hari’s very name. (34) Thus instructed by the messenger, the subjects likewise performed worship;
they meditated upon Hari-Kṛṣṇa and sang the praises of Janārdana. (35)
They constantly chanted, performed austerities, and offered sacrifices to me; they were absorbed in meditation on me, resolved upon me, and devoted to my worship.
At that time, the entire circle of the earth indeed became Vaiṣṇava.
By my majesty, the humans born there were free from mental afflictions;
they were devoid of sorrow, meritorious, and exempt from all diseases.
They possessed every form of sovereignty and were endowed with wealth and grain. (37–38)
May there be noble lineages of sons, grandsons, and descendants, free from disease and calamities; may wish-fulfilling trees stand at the doors of their homes, granting the fruits of all desires;
and may there indeed be cows that yield every wish and wish-granting gems.
Unforeseen prosperities, such as the increase of the kingdom and other riches, came to pass.
The subjects became endowed with every form of good fortune, devoted to knowledge and meditation, highly virtuous, and dedicated to devotion and worship. (3.72.40–41)
There shall be no famine, nor disease, nor untimely death for men;
all human beings shall be Vaiṣṇavas, devoted to meditation upon me. They shall be absorbed in my remembrance, intent on service to my devotees, and dedicated to the chanting of my names.
Everywhere— whether in houses, trees, or even among animals— there was indeed a Vaiṣṇava disposition.
In every house there were radiant temples of mine,
and upon the walls of those houses were paintings of me together with you.
My songs are sung by women who are my devotees;
children, the elderly, and youths all worship me.
Even women engaged in household chores worship me, the Supreme Lord.
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, while drinking, standing, or eating;
during play, at festivals, or in the midst of desire, they worshiped me, Lord Hari.
They uttered the name of Śrī Hari and honored that which bestows liberation.
Thus the surface of the earth became equal to Vaikuṇṭha in every respect.
O Lakṣmī, all were devoted to bhakti and intent upon my love.
Having been instructed by Yayāti, they indeed became Vaiṣṇavas on this earth.
And by my grace, they became empty of old age and death.
Those Vaiṣṇavas who live long lives do not go to my world;
rather, those who travel by celestial chariot go to my abode, the realm of Viṣṇu. (3.72.50)
Even those men and women whose bodies have endured a hundred thousand years,
by my grace, all appear as if they were only twenty-five years of age;

I am more than fully satisfied by the worship of these [three], which is superior to all else.
They shall honor me in those [places], and for them there is no defeat.
Even upon seeing a virtuous woman or a celibate student who has arrived, one should bow, offer an oblation, and then eat; for that meal is indeed nectar.
Having performed the auspicious twilight devotions, one should then bow to the auspicious Sun.
He who has bathed in all sacred fords is liberated from all sins.
One should always protect the god of dharma, who possesses an auspicious form, within one's own home.
O king of devotees, having attained the company of the virtuous and the Dharma itself, you should protect it;
for that alone is considered by Me to be Dharma by which the virtuous and Myself are pleased.
Indeed, that which causes distress to the virtuous is considered by Me to be Adharma.
Of what use to me indeed is that by which my devotees are not satisfied?
(22) That alone is my true wealth by which the virtuous are satisfied;
for rising early every day, the holy ones must always be touched by me. (23)
Cows, clarified butter, curd, mustard seeds, and likewise *sādhikās*—
these should be touched by one who has risen in the morning for the destruction of their sins.
Even those who have killed women, those who have killed cows, the ungrateful, those who have slain a Brahmin, and those who have violated the teacher’s bed [are purified].
They are purified by contact with the virtuous and by serving me, O virtuous one.
(25) The righteous, cows, fires, virtuous women, and twice-born brahmins must not be touched with the feet.
If they are touched with the foot, all the merit of the toucher is destroyed. (26)
One should provide them with the finest food for their meal,
and sweet food that is auspicious and grants eternal satisfaction.
One should always offer hospitality and provide lamps in the homes of the virtuous.
One should indeed worship and serve him with mindfulness; for he is the most excellent of bulls (vṛṣabha).
(28) Even after performing hundreds of sacrifices, that sacrificial offering goes to destruction; but those virtuous qualities by which he has been fully pleased never perish. (29)
Even one who might sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices,
or who might hang head-downward or perform a continuous sacrificial session—
[if] his heart is not pure, he has not served me, the saintly ones. (3.74.30)
If service has not been rendered to me, he indeed goes to the hell of illusion (māyā-niraya). Service to the virtuous and purity of heart are indeed the givers of liberation;
by performing even a little with a pure mind, one is fully released.
One who possesses faith should always carry out the instructions of their gurus;
they should practice service to the virtuous, for by that one becomes radiant.
He who might give a tawny cow day after day for twelve years—
If a person were to constantly perform sacrifices with the *sattra* rite month after month,
or were to give away a hundred thousand cows at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara,
the fruit obtained by one whose virtuous friends are pleased would be even greater than that. (34–35)
Whatever holy places exist, whether consisting of water or land, frequented by Siddhas, gods, and others, and served by the great seers—
for all of them, an ablution with the water from the feet of the virtuous is prescribed.

Even a small amount of cool water given and food offered to a virtuous person—this is declared to be a river for the donor called "the Water of Merit. Therein, the water becomes inexhaustible, cool, and indeed like nectar. (37–38)
In that world, food as well as nectar reaches those who have departed to the next life;
furthermore, whatever else is given there also reaches them in the other world.
For in this world, humans are generally left-overs and full of many flaws.
Piśācas enter those who have abandoned virtuous conduct and proper behavior.
Piśācas do not enter those men who are devoted to the service of the virtuous, who take refuge in what is auspicious, who are devoted, and who perform meritorious deeds.
Wherever virtuous people eat what has been offered to the deities,
the Sādhyas, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, and the two Aśvins—
along with the Maruts and Vasus— partake of that food, being present therein.
He is indeed the abode of grace for the sages, the gods, the ancestors, and likewise for Hari;
he is the abode of grace for the liberated ones and the lords as well—[he] who serves and gladdens virtuous men and women. (43–44)
Even after committing an evil deed, one who has gone for refuge to me, the Holy One, is liberated from millions of sins; purified, he becomes a purifier.
A virtuous person whose self is conquered through service to me purifies even the sinful.
One should always cultivate association with me and avoid association with the sinful.
O Lakṣmī, one should offer a gift with the vision of Brahman, likewise offer it with the vision of a saint, and offer it with the vision of Hari; such a gift shall become eternal.
The gift of food, the gift of water, and the gift of knowledge are supremely auspicious;
the gift of fearlessness, the gift of the Veda, and the gift of liberation are even higher than that.
The gift of one's own self should always be given; there is nothing else on earth equal to it.

The virtuous Hari, as Dattātreya, having bestowed the attributeless Brahman upon his disciples, departed for the abode equal to the Imperishable along with his own followers. And likewise the virtuous Hari, as Kapila, having given [the knowledge] born of discrimination... [3.74.50]
Having imparted knowledge and liberation to his disciples,
Ṛṣabha likewise instructed them in the eternal Brahman;
then Hari also departed for his own supreme abode, the source of all happiness.
In this way, other virtuous kings as well, devoted to the practice of giving,
attained the eternal and imperishable state through the bestowal of the gift of the Veda;
and those kings, firm in their vows, beheld the nature of Brahman.

Having given even that which was not to be given to a Brahmin, Śibi Auśīnara became an inhabitant of heaven, as did he who surrendered his own life and beloved son for the sake of one most devoted to Brahman;
having offered these, he departed from here to the great celestial realm.
Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, having offered up his own body to the one most devoted to Brahman,
attained incomparable fame and reached the state of liberation.
And Rantideva, the son of Saṃkṛti, [offered it] to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.

Having offered the *arghya* and performed worship, Devavr̥dha went to the auspicious state of liberation after giving an excellent golden umbrella with a hundred ribs to the one most established in Brahman at the great sacrifice. ||57||
Ambarīṣa, that auspicious and most eminent devotee, having given his entire kingdom for the sake of the Lord,
went to the world of Brahmā through his devotion.
And Vṛṣādarbhi, having given away all his possessions, went to my own abode.
Having given his kingdom to Hari, Nimi went to my abode;
indeed, by giving his daughter to Agastya, the King of Vidarbha attained liberation.
Having given the earth to the brahmins, Paraśurāma dwelt at a sacred pilgrimage site.
Vāmana, too, having given the earth to the Brahmins and subsequently having granted heaven to the gods,
Hari went to his own abode.
Rāmāditya also, having given the earth to the Brahmins, went to the imperishable realm.
Having given his daughter to the descendant of Aṅgiras, Marutta also went to the imperishable realm.
Having given his wife to Vasiṣṭha, Mitrasaha went to heaven.
The royal sage Sahasracitti, having given up his life-breaths, went to heaven.
Śatadyumna, having given the earth to Maudgalya, went to heaven;
Sumanyu, having given the earth to Śāṇḍilya, went to my abode;
and Dyutimat, having given the earth to Ṛcīka, went to the Imperishable.
Madirāśva, having given his daughter to Hiraṇya, went to the imperishable realm;
Lomapāda, having given Śāntā to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, went to heaven;
Bhagīratha, having given his daughter Haṃsī to Kautsa, went to heaven.
On this earth, there will be other kings who are practitioners of charity;
by bestowing gifts upon the virtuous, they shall go to the supreme state.
O Lakṣmī, those lords of subjects, having given all their female companions to me, [shall attain that same goal]. (67–68)
Those who are devoted to Nārāyaṇa have gone to my abode and shall go there;
those who are servants of my saints, who are endowed with dharma,
possessed of devotion and pure intent, and established in me through identity.

Men and women shall go to my supreme, imperishable abode. Whether it be little or much, that which is always given to the virtuous out of righteousness, for the sake of wealth, out of fear, out of desire, or out of compassion, indeed conduces to liberation.
For the sake of Dharma, for the sake of the heavenly realm, for the sake of happiness and fame, a gift should be given;
furthermore, that fruit shall be obtained from this very act.
Thus, one who seeks wealth should give to a virtuous person, for it yields infinite and excellent results.
In times of calamity, when fear has arisen, or when the loss of one's possessions is imminent,
one should give away all one's wealth to a virtuous person who desires no reward.
For the sake of what is dear, one should give with full devotion to a holy being who possesses a virtuous form.
One should give with compassion to the distressed and the poor;
likewise, one should give what is most auspicious to a virtuous brahmin who is my devotee.
Indeed, for the sake of Hari’s pleasure, that gift which bestows liberation should be given.
"This must indeed be done by me; having reflected thus, one should offer it.
This which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) should be given to the virtuous one and also to Nārāyaṇa, my very self.
One should give this to Nārāyaṇa with the thought: 'This belongs to Nārāyaṇa; it is not mine,' for it is devoid of qualities."
That indeed bestows infinite fruit and grants great bliss;
I shall grant that fruit in my own abode, and I grant it even here upon the earth.
To the giver, I grant an immeasurable ocean of bliss in the supreme, imperishable state.

"O Lakṣmī, for me, who serves the virtuous in this way, there exists the supreme, eternal, and enduring state, filled with sovereignty and other such powers. Having made even a small thing very great, I bestow it upon the abode of the Imperishable. (3.74.80)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Supreme Lord, show me by Your grace what kind of fruit You grant for even a very small gift; have mercy upon me. (8.1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: "Behold, Lakṣmī, this devotee, a brāhmaṇa, approaching my presence;
by means of a very small gift, I shall indeed grant him that which is infinite."
When this was said, a brahmin named Paraśucandraka, who was miserly and destitute,
arrived there in a piteous state, bringing with him all the wealth of his household;
indeed, he was bereft of wife and sons, and was constantly chanting the name of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Carrying on his shoulder a small basket equipped with a pot, a pitcher, and a sacrificial ladle;
having tied a worn-out cloth around his waist and holding a staff in his hand;
[carrying] one prastha measure of rice as well as a winnowing fan and a cloak. || 84–85 ||
Wearing a helmet upon his head, endowed with only this much wealth—
O Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Puruṣottama, Mādhava—
he then stood before you, reciting the names of all created things while placing them at your feet.
"O Kṛṣṇa, refuge of all, protect me; grant me liberation at your feet.
Thus he entreated him, and [Kṛṣṇa] gave him roasted rice grains.
Having offered them, he prostrated himself there like a staff and rolled on the ground with his head bowed.
Closing his eyes for a moment, he slept upon the ground before me.
"I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, compassionate toward my devotees. What shall I do for this devotee? I am the protector of those who have come for refuge. (89)
"Speak, Lakṣmī! This man is dead and is giving up his life-breaths in my presence.
Having said this, I placed a few grains of rice in my mouth and indeed ate them, saying:
"Behold the fruit of this; I give him the imperishable abode."
Just then, a celestial chariot accompanied by attendants arrived there;
that brahmin, endowed with a divine body and filled with compassion, ascended it.
The opulent chariot traveled through the path of the sky to the imperishable abode.

"Behold, Lakṣmī, for his sake I have constructed a magnificent palace in my abode, endowed with every prosperity and provided with all kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks and the like. Behold with divine vision everything; I have bestowed upon him the fruit of all my wealth. (93-94)
Indeed, a celestial chariot that moves at will has been offered by me for his sake;
likewise, the infinite nectar of Brahma, rice, and fruit have been offered.
Furthermore, all kinds of drinks as well as golden garments have been presented.
Indeed, these were offered for the sake of enjoyment by one devoted to those who have sought refuge.
Then, beholding this, the gracious Śrī Lakṣmī rejoiced within;
and by the will of Kṛṣṇa, the body of the brahmin sank into the lake.
Having himself become endowed with the power of movement, he indeed attained dissolution there;
and Lakṣmī, having spoken this great marvel to all,
all those [goddesses], beginning with Brahmapriyā, gazed upon him.

Behold with divine vision the majesty of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa for me. Thus, such is my majesty; it yields a great fruit for everyone. Likewise, there is the highest fruit for those who read and for those who listen as well. (3.74.100)

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Pleasing Hari and the Attainment of Infinite Fruit from a Small Gift by the Miserly Brāhmaṇa Paraśucandraka," within the narrative of the greatness of the devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 75. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 75.
[The Author: Chapter 76.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Kṛṣṇa, having seen this great wonder, I have indeed become completely satisfied.
"Furthermore, tell me of your majesty and reveal it to me.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: "Behold, O Lakṣmī, this great wonder: fire has been produced from my mouth."
When this was said, a fire arose and spread throughout the surrounding forest.
Enveloped in garlands of flames, it instantly consumed the tiger-forest,
along with its trees, grass, creepers, vines, crops, and all else.
Having thus completely consumed the forest along with its multitudes of flocks of birds, its beasts of prey,
and its reptiles, the fire of great flames then approached Hari in person before him like a disciple.
And he indeed vanished from the sight of Hari at his feet.
(5) Then, seeing the entire forest completely consumed by fire, I, Hari, restored it to its natural state with my gentle glances. (6)
In that very same way, O Lakṣmī, behold that forest once again, with its creepers and trees in full bloom,
resounding with flocks of birds, and filled with beasts of prey and reptiles—
just as it was before, established in its original state.
Having seen this wonder, Lakṣmī questioned her beloved Nārāyaṇa:
"O Kṛṣṇa, who is this fire, and how does it abide within you at all times?
Having heard this, Nārāyaṇa said: "Listen; this is indeed my own splendor."
Indeed, that which consists of Saṃkarṣaṇa exists in many forms within the [divine] body;
likewise, it also consists of Rudra and consists of Śaṃkara as well. That very essence, like the nature of Mahākāla, is the performer of the universal dissolution.
And all forms of sovereignty exist within me at all times.
Whenever the dissolutions of the worlds occur,
then this very sovereignty of mine proceeds through the subsequent creations.
I indeed withdraw that entire [universe] by that very same means;
and again, by my power, I create it just as it was fashioned by imagination. I possess the sovereign power of creation, such that the forest which was created is [withdrawn and] created once more.
"O ladies, you have been created by me from a portion of my own self, possessing the form of Brahman.
Indeed, this entire world has likewise been created by me from a portion of my self, as I am pervaded by my own conduct and through my service to the virtuous. (14–15)

"Fire, though its very nature is time, does not burn me who am engaged in chanting [the Lord's names]. Behold this Lomaśa; having abandoned his hermitage and likewise the hermitages of the sages, fire has pervaded them all, yet it does not consume those dwellings. (16)
Thus, I am unable to bring about anything undesirable for those who are devoted to me.
For those men who worship me, time does not exist;
for them, there is no illusion, nor is there any agitation.
For them, the three-fold torments do not exist, nor does suffering find a place;
I consume all their hardships, of this there is no doubt.
(19) I alone am the Death of Death; I give life to those who have taken refuge in me.
"I indeed ordain the time for the eternal enjoyments of my devotees.
Never withdraw them, and never let them encounter old age;
in this way, I always remain for the protection of my devotees. (3.75.20–21)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this power and my dignity have been shown to you;
likewise, the great majesty of my devotion has been demonstrated, O one of great strength.
Non-violence, truthful speech, and compassion for all living beings—
Vows, charity, and tranquility—these qualities indeed depend upon devotion.
Even fasting certainly becomes meaningful through devotion;
and celibacy likewise becomes meaningful toward me only through devotion.
The Vedic vow, the fire-ritual, the fulfillment of the teacher’s service,

and the private recitation of scripture— these are the duties that, when their purpose is understood, produce devotion. Furthermore, the vow of hospitality toward guests and eating only what is offered with favor to me [are likewise required].
After the attendants have eaten, the couple should eat together with equanimity (26). The householders should offer food to the gods;
they should also constantly serve the virtuous. Thus, those who practice devotion achieve their purpose (27).
Protection, charity, diligence, sacrifice,
as well as sustenance, service to one's father, and service to one's master— these are the goals for those who practice devotion.
Furthermore, the protection of cattle and other livestock, the performance of the *agnihotra* fire-sacrifice, and walking upon the path of truth [are likewise required].
Renunciation, self-restraint, and hospitality—these are the goals attained by those who practice devotion.
(29) Service, virtuous conduct, humility, and the state of being a servant;
as well as the condition of a female slave and that of a male slave—these are the goals attained by those who practice devotion. (30)
The virtuous, who are indeed the essence of the world and preceded by Sanatkumāra,
were created of old by the Creator in this world for the sake of the world's welfare.
O Lakṣmī, those virtuous ones have been fashioned by me as well, endowed with devotion.
And in this world, there are many deities on earth capable of delivering all people who make known my greatness.
[These are] the knowledge of Brahman, devotion, my stories, meditation, and festivals. (32-33)
The giving of mantras—this group of six duties is always for the virtuous;
likewise, protecting those who have sought refuge, liberation, and the destruction of sin.
Giving devotion and the conduct of Brahman—these five duties are to be performed by the virtuous.

Learnedness, adherence to the scriptures, self-study, recitation, sacred learning, and right conduct—this sixfold set indeed occurs naturally among the virtuous. Furthermore, tranquility, withdrawal from worldly affairs, affection for the good, and honoring them likewise [belong to them]. (35–36)
Constant remembrance of Hari is the state of Brahman for the virtuous; it is the great dharma of the good.
It consists of being free from pride, anger, and other such passions, possessing affectionate speech, and having the mind turned inward.
Furthermore, it includes delighting in guests and eating only what remains as a favor.

Forgiveness, contentment, and satisfaction are the virtues of the virtuous, born of their very nature. Service to the elders, to cows, to guests, and to Hari; and the renunciation of delicious things—this dharma leads to liberation.
The liberation from the bonds of hope, non-attachment, contemplation of the inner self,
freedom from the fetters of affection, and the dedication of the self to the Self—
[these belong to] the virtuous one who wanders as a mendicant through actions viewed with the perspective of liberation. (3.75.40)
For one who is liberated wanders everywhere, yet remains ever steadfast in Me.
This is the dharma of those who know liberation for one who practices devotion;
there is nothing higher than devotion, which sustains the dharma of eternal bliss.
Free from suffering, supreme bliss, ageless, immortal, and imperishable— the state of liberation belongs to the virtuous one who practices devotion, and it exists simultaneously with him.
Such persons attain equality with the gods and illuminate the three worlds.
Devoted to devotion, compassion, and righteousness, their sins burnt away by austerity, these holy ones bear the discus;
they are meritorious and auspicious, wandering through my worlds.
Bearing garlands and the discus, they destroy the sins of the wicked upon the earth. (44–45)

Those who practice devotion wear a necklace upon their necks, hold a garland in their hands, bear my name in their hearts, wear the sectarian mark on their foreheads, and maintain virtuous conduct throughout their bodies;
they possess forgiveness in their minds, cherish affection in their inner being, and are characterized by love.
They are intent on liberation through their intellect, always possessing the nature of Brahman within the self alone;
they possess affection for those who have sought refuge in them, and are steadfast in their wisdom regarding discernment.
They take delight in my stories and maintain equanimity toward all living beings.
They are unattached to objects of enjoyment, yet they maintain their lives with what is necessary, like those on a journey;
having attained identity with Me, they are as pure as the expanse of Brahman.
They are devoted to the path of worship and always foster association with the virtuous.
The virtuous, adorned by goodness, are those who have taken refuge [in the Lord], offered themselves [to Him], and are fully satisfied.
O Lakṣmī, by taking shelter of them—the very abode of the Lord—liberation is achieved;
once one has met those who reside in that supreme station, no further duty remains to be performed. (3.75.50–51)
The dharma of a seer is the dharma of the virtuous: constant delight in truth and moral conduct;
one should be neither arrogant nor conceited, neither displeased nor astonished.
One should be devoted to the worship of ancestors and deities, always regarding the night as day.
One who considers himself asleep while awake, one who considers himself lowly before the most venerable,
one who considers darkness to be light, one who considers poison to be the finest nectar,
one who considers laughter at great prosperity, and one who considers himself miserable in the presence of pride— [these are the marks of a fool]. (53–54)
Regarding prosperity as calamity, regarding life as death, regarding the association with Hari as dharma, and regarding delight in Him within the heart;
regarding those who possess devotion as happiness, and regarding the forest and such places as the true people. (55)
One who considers himself wise in the lineage of Acyuta indeed delivers the virtuous person.
O Lakṣmī, the saint is considered the deliverer, and the virtuous woman is considered the savior.
For me, there is no price for renunciation; indeed, in my house, the price is devotion.
I always honor the feet of virtuous ones who possess devotion;
I also show respect to devoted women.
Indeed, there will be true devotion toward me only when there is renunciation of everything else.
Delight in tranquility is found in me; even the playfulness of sport is truly in me.

(59) Those who are masters of their senses are my saints, and likewise those women are my saintly ones, who are completely immersed in the flood of the mass of bliss brought by devotion to me. (3.75.60)
In various regions where I dwell, by rivers and waterfalls,
in the thickets of streams, on mountains, and in forests— indeed,
wherever the abodes of my devotees are located— my saintly yogis reside.
Furthermore, those devoted to the practice of yoga likewise sleep and sit upon the open sky;
they constantly subsist by clinging to trees, always have wild forest fare as their attendants,
are clothed in rags and bark, and are entirely intent on devotion to me.

Established in goodness and having renounced everything, those who have been initiated into me, Mādhava, dwell happily and without obstacle together with the hosts of virtuous gods. Such are they— of righteous conduct, of virtuous character, and taking refuge in me.
Men and women are indeed dear to me; for them, there are eternal worlds. Even those who have remained in sin, having cast off that sin, perform virtuous deeds;
through merit and devotion, they too indeed attain the state of the righteous.
Established in the dharma most conducive to Brahman, one attains the state of a Brahmin;
whoever, through my yoga, reaches the state of becoming Brahman.
This supreme spiritual path is practiced by the virtuous who desire Brahman.
I am the forest and Nārāyaṇa; for the virtuous, their dwelling is in Me, who am eternal.
(68) The forest is the guru, and the guru is to be understood as such; the dwelling of the virtuous is always in the guru.
My oblation is the food offering, and I, Śrī Nārāyaṇa, am the sacrifice. (69)
I am the four-monthly sacrifice of the virtuous, and I am always the vows of the virtuous.
Indeed, those who possess such conduct are the righteous ones, adorned by righteousness;
liberated from all sins, those righteous ones move within me.
The peaceful ones, ever devoted to the path of truth, attain the supreme goal.
O Lakṣmī, the perfected sages who take refuge at my feet go to the most meritorious world of Brahmā, which possesses divine prosperity and is eternal.
The virtuous, who are themselves fearless and grant the gift of fearlessness here,
are constantly intent on devotion and spiritual attainment; they are adorned by their goodness,
compassionate toward all beings, and devoted to the vow of sincerity toward all beings.
And the virtuous, adorned by goodness, have become the very self of all beings.
(74) Whether it be bathing in all the Vedas or beholding all beings—those for whom there is equality toward all selves are the virtuous, adorned by goodness. (75)
Uprightness is indeed the dharma of the virtuous, for crookedness is unrighteousness. In this world, the deities dwell within the range of those endowed with uprightness.
Free from deceit, devoted in soul, and having taken refuge in the path of the righteous out of love—
The Buddha, for whom right conduct is supreme, is fit for the state of Brahman.
Listen, Lakṣmī: even if one performs virtuous deeds while abandoning me, their fruit will be merely of this world and perishable, for without devotion [to me], it cannot endure. (77–78)
By means of the vows of fasting, they go to the supreme world of the Gandharvas; indeed, one who sleeps in water like a frog goes to the world of the Nāgas;
and one who subsists on young grass, leaves, and the like, proceeds to Amarāvatī.
One who subsists on *śaivāla* (aquatic moss) and leaves attains the world of Varuṇa. One who consumes only fruits, roots, and air goes to the world of the Yakṣas.
A king devoted to the austerity of fire-bathing becomes a restrainer of life-force (*prāṇa*). (3.75.80–81)
The king who delights in fasting rejoices in heaven in the celestial realm;
by drowning his body in the ocean of water, he attains the world of Varuṇa.
By piercing his feet with a stone until he dies, he becomes a Guhyaka.
Having slain [the enemy] and cast off the body in the fire, he is born in the world of Fire.
Having gone to that world by way of the hero's path, he obtains the state of a powerful being;
he rejoices with the gods and others in a celestial chariot that moves at will.
Having received the initiation of a yogin, he goes to the world of Rudra;
having given gifts of wealth, he reaches the abode of Kubera;
and having given gifts of gold, he goes to the world of the Sun.
Having given gifts of food, he goes to the world of the Moon;
having given gifts of clothing, he goes to the worlds of the Planets;
and having given gifts of maidens in marriage, he attains the world of the Apsarases.
By giving gifts of vehicles here, one goes to the celestial mansion;
by giving gifts of food here, he goes to the world of the ancestors;
and by giving gifts of the Veda here, he goes to the world of truth.
By bestowing sovereignty and other such boons, he indeed goes to the abodes of the lords;
by giving everything with devotion, he goes to my world.
If he remembers me there, he remains; otherwise, he goes to the realm of light.
Through devotion to me, this very state of Vairāja becomes my own state.
If one remembers all those gifts and offers them with devotion to me, who am there as the inner self, I lead that person to the eternal Brahman.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, my majesty is accessible only through the sphere of mental cultivation (bhāvanā).
I am the devourer of mental cultivation, yet I am bound by the threads of mental cultivation;
and by means of the wing of mental cultivation, I manifest in your presence.
The virtuous ones, rich in contemplation, are therefore embodiments of my own self;
they follow my conduct, they are my very bodies, and they are always the saviors of sinners.
In the application of all purposes, there is not even an atom’s worth of difference between them and me.
I am indeed they, and they are I; thus has my heart's secret been told to you.
All of you are devoted to me, women beloved by Brahman.
You are always virtuous here, auspicious saviors who grant liberation.
Indeed, your dwelling here is that very same imperishable abode;
your presence is eternal association with the virtuous.
And service to you is always the supreme service to the Self.
The sight and other [perceptions] of you all are always auspicious and grant liberation.
All your activities, through my yoga, are designated as Brahman.
Indeed, your bodies possess the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 98–99 ||
I, Śrī Puruṣottama, am the very everything of you;
therefore, you are in every way Śrī Puruṣottamīs.
There is not even the slightest difference between me and you, both here and in the hereafter.
"You are I and I am you; everything has been made mine by you.
Thinking thus, when another woman becomes endowed with devotion to Me, then she will indeed attain equality with you.
From reciting this, from hearing it, and even from hearing of this knowledge, the arising of the state of a virtuous wife occurs, and one attains the status of a beloved of Brahman.
Through devotion, one becomes equal to Rādhā and Ramā; of this there is no doubt.
"Through devotion, one shall attain equality with those liberated by Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Manifestation and Disappearance of Fire, the Splendor of the Holy, the Attainment of Various Fruits, and My Own Attainment through Association with the Holy," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 75.
Chapter 76 [Author:
Chapter 77 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to my majesty which is even greater than that:
I dwell among children who are free from sin and without protectors.
The hearts of children are pure, devoid of the crookedness of *māyā*.
In this [Self], which is free from latent impressions and the like, I dwell like a virtuous man.
(2) All children are my forms, pure and like mirrors;
therefore, children are states of Brahman, just as people are states of yoga. (3)
My forms in the stage of childhood and those up to eight years of age—
these were all indeed saintly beings like Sanaka and the others of old. They were saints in their religious duties, but in their youth, they followed the duties of householders.
But virtuous celibates (brahmacārins) are devoid of youthfulness [in the sense of passion].
(5) Virtue consists in abiding by moral conduct; being a householder arises from the connection with desire.
Indeed, virtue arises even for one who possesses desire, provided there is mastery over that desire. (6)
Even for one who has no desire for sexual union, that very desire constitutes the state of householdership (*gārhasthya*).
Neither union with a woman nor union with a man would be the cause of being a householder. Sexual union is the practice of *gārhasthya*, and dependence upon it constitutes its excellence.
And that [state] occurs in both woman and man through the cultivation of desirelessness.
Indeed, one who is free from desire becomes truly desirous and possesses all desires;
he alone is to be known as Brahman, endowed with the true nature of a Brāhmaṇa and goodness.
O Śrī, being most devoted to Brahman is difficult to attain, and likewise, goodness is difficult to attain.
Yet, through my grace, both devotion to Brahman and goodness come to be.
Through my grace, the auspicious state of being a virtuous wife arises, which bestows liberation.
And she was a restorer of the lineage and a virtuous wife, just as you are.
Likewise, the virtuous women were devoted to truth and dharma; the holy men were intent upon Brahman, content with whatever came by chance, and free from forceful display.

Those who enjoy wealth obtained through righteous means, who offer it to the Supreme Lord, who are free from persistence in worldly desires, whose hearts are pure, who are virtuous, and who are adorned by goodness—
O Śrī, through their qualities, actions, and austerities, such a man becomes Nārāyaṇa. (1.3)
Having completely cast off impurity, even a lowly person becomes most exalted.
Just as in another birth a Śūdra, through actions accumulated by dharma and by the power of merit, is born as a Brāhmaṇa in a subsequent life.
Likewise, even within a single lifetime, one may become a Brāhmaṇa through Vedic practices;
conversely, even a learned Brāhmaṇa may descend to the state of a Śūdra.
The power of merit and demerit arising from attachment to auspicious and inauspicious actions is indeed great.
Indeed, the Brahmin possesses an abundance of *sattva* and thus turns toward the *dharmas*.
One who has an abundance of *rajas* becomes a Kṣatriya, while one with an abundance of *tamas* is a Śūdra.
Touched by both *sattva* and *rajas*, one becomes a splendid Vaiśya. (17–18)
Touched by both rajas and tamas, a Vaiśya becomes ignoble;
but one who abounds in a preponderance of tamas alone becomes a killer or an outcaste (śvapaca). One who abounds in a preponderance of sattva alone becomes a virtuous Brahmin or a faithful wife.
"One who is abundant in the yoga of Brahman indeed becomes liberated on this earth.
(3.76.20) Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this excellence that brings auspiciousness been described;
and here, even Nārāyaṇa himself becomes intent upon my yoga. (21)

Through union with that [state], others likewise become Nārāyaṇas. Thus, by my power and through the attainment of sovereignty and other qualities, there arises a succession of Nārāyaṇas through my yoga. (22)
All men are Nārāyaṇas, and likewise all women are Nārāyaṇīs;
through my worship they are born from me alone, the Supreme Self.
The gods, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Viṣṇus are likewise born [from me].
Through worship of Me, O Rāma, they become Brahmās and likewise Īśvaras;
through worship of Me, they also become the consorts of the Īśvaras.
Those free from passion are liberated from their actions and the bonds of karma.
And those by whom they are performed with full dedication are indeed born as Nārāyaṇas.
For all those actions consist essentially of my worship;
indeed, apart from worship of me, there is no such thing as the ritual of offering (bali).

Worship performed by those with desires shall fulfill their longings; for those free from desire, I—being ever-attained—shall surely grant them prosperity. Indeed, the devotee worships me through action, mind, and speech.
When one acts with goodness, one does not fall into bondage at all.

(29) Those who are disciplined in conduct and yoga, who have desisted from the destruction of life-sustenance, who are equal toward the hateful and the dear, and who are self-controlled, are liberated from the bonds of karma. (30)

Those who possess compassion for all beings, who are trusted by all embodied beings, and who have practiced the conduct of devotion— such people go to the divine abode. They are devoid of self-interest, they assist in the affairs of others, and they are free from expectation.
Content with the dharma they have attained, those people go to the celestial abodes.
Among groups of women, they look upon them as mothers, sisters, or daughters;
among groups of men, they look upon them as fathers, mothers, or good sons. (32–33)
Those people who are enriched by service to the virtuous as described, who are devoted to me,
