who are free from theft, and whose lives are sustained by good fortune, go to my abode. Likewise, those who delight in their own rightful enjoyments and who attend to the time for dharma are also destined for that realm.
Those who do not crave vulgar pleasures, who possess the brilliance of heart and vision,
who follow the path of Indra, who have mastered their senses and are established in the Self,
and who have made their dwelling in devotion to me— such people go to my abode. (35–36)
The path created by the absence of passion consists of charity, righteousness, and austerity;

it is enriched by ethical conduct, purity, and compassion, and is accompanied by devotion, service, and self-surrender. It is characterized by freedom from expectations and clarity of mind, and it increases the fruit of association with the virtuous. (37)
Abounding in the excellence of a stainless intellect, they should always be served by the wise.
Whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even through the medium of jest and laughter, those who are free from falsehood proceed upon the true path, devoid of all passions. (38–39)
Those people who do not speak untruth for the sake of livelihood, for the sake of dharma, or out of personal whim— truly they proceed along the excellent path free from defilement.
[They utter] sweet speech, free from harm and devoid of even a trace of sin.
Those who speak with heartfelt affection go upon the true path free from defilement.

(41) The virtuous who delight in freedom from backbiting, who promote non-divisiveness among friends, who are free from malice, and who possess truth and friendliness, go upon the true path free from defilement. (42)
Free from deceit, gentle in speech, and devoid of anger and malice, they are free from the desire to tear others' hearts; such people proceed upon the true path that is free from defilement.
Endowed with gentleness, speaking beneficial words, possessing the quality of truth, and taking refuge in Hari—
O Lakṣmī, those virtuous men and women who proceed upon the true path free from defilements go to that state.
Even in a solitary place, they do not desire even the slightest wealth, whether it be left behind for them or encountered by chance; those who act thus go upon the true path free from defilements.
Whether in a village or even in a house, they never desire anything belonging to another;
those who have no enemies proceed upon the true path free from all taints.
They are learned in the scriptures, full of devotion, and protectors of truth and compassion.
Always content and free from passion, they proceed upon the true path that is free from defilement;

(47) delighting in a mind of loving-kindness, facing with faith, affection, and a desire to help, and possessing knowledge of the ripening of karmic fruits, they proceed upon the true path that is free from defilement. (48)
Those who are reasonable in their grasping, whose nature is heavenward, who are devoted to exertion,
established in the self, and intent on Me— they proceed along the stainless path of the righteous.
They are of great wisdom, devoted to Brahman, and characterized by both theoretical knowledge and realized insight.
Those who are devoted to the science of logic proceed upon the true path free from passion (akaṣāya). Those who are possessed of a dread of sin, intent on the means of attaining the highest good,
and desirous of discharging their debts, they too proceed upon the true path free from passion.
But those who belong to the white class, who are free from self-harm,
who cause no terror to living beings, and who bestow the gift of fearlessness;
who possess an affection for themselves [and others] like that of a father, and who are as auspicious and well-disposed as gods— (52)
Those who follow the conduct of the gods, possessing gentle dispositions, proceed upon the stainless path of the righteous.
(53) Those of good character, performers of noble deeds, and those who refrain from harming living beings, become long-lived in this world and proceed upon the stainless path of the righteous. (54)
He is a giver to the virtuous and a respectful host; he bestows food, edibles, meals, and drinks upon the poor, the afflicted, the wretched, and others, and is a provider of garments and such.
He dwells in the practice of devotion and is a bestower of the gift of knowledge.
And by protecting those who have come for refuge, one proceeds along the stainless path of the righteous.
One should construct shelters, assembly halls, wells, lotus ponds, and water-stations;
as well as seats, beds, vehicles, houses, jewels, wealth, and a [generous] mind. (56–57)
All kinds of grain, cattle, fields, and maidens— whosoever, with a joyful mind, bestows these as gifts upon a worthy recipient;
indeed, one who offers all his possessions goes along the stainless path of the righteous.
He is a worshiper of the gods, the twice-born, the virtuous, and likewise of faithful women;
he is one who offers salutations, is humble, does what is pleasing to all, and is pure.
He seeks the welfare of all, possesses a pleasant countenance, and is devoted to performing respectful hospitality according to the merit of each person. (3.76.60)
Beholding the true path and honoring the guru, he proceeds along the stainless way of the virtuous;
esteemed by all beings and saluted by all the worlds, he is born of a noble lineage and possesses a noble ancestry. (61)
Possessing a vision of loving-kindness, he is like a father to all beings and is trusted by every creature.
(62) Devoted to me and of great merit, he proceeds upon the true path free from all impurities.
O Lakṣmī, one such as this always prospers in unimpeded happiness. (63)
This is the supreme path of the virtuous, wherein no affliction is found;
it is followed by those who serve with devotion the righteous, the knowers of the Vedas, the perfected ones, and likewise those endowed with faith,
while always avoiding that which is inauspicious.
For them, there is a path rich in eternal happiness that leads to the state of Brahman.
O Lakṣmī, through their gatherings, indeed auspicious things arise—welfare of every kind and countless heavenly realms. (65–66)
Indeed, those who abide in the dharma of the virtuous proceed correctly in this matter;
for the sake of the welfare of men, I have proclaimed this to you here.
Furthermore, one whose self is established in discernment knows his own true benefit within.
One cannot accomplish the supreme goal without taking refuge in a true guru.
O beloved, human beings always desire to attain merit,
yet these deluded ones do not perform the causes of merit even while possessing great wealth.
From association with the virtuous, from my own company, and from the company of the righteous, supreme auspiciousness arises;
indeed, the highest welfare surely comes to pass, and they know it to be so.
Nevertheless, those who follow the path of logic are afflicted by the torments of sin.
Constantly seized by the gaping maw of the great evil of arrogance,
they do not serve the virtuous nor do they worship me;
being attached to sense objects, they fall into the hells and other lower realms.

Those who are evil and corrupt, the nihilists, those devoid of charity, those empty of true disposition, the defilers, those lacking the spirit of devotion, and those bereft of the divine state— these do not cross the enchanting river of illusion.
Always possessed of a wicked disposition and constantly clinging to the view of a self in the body, they delight in base actions and are devoted solely to their own interests.
Satisfied with the belly and the senses, their vision is fixed upon external pleasures. (74–75)
Those who take delight solely in the non-self go only to hell;
whereas servants who delight in the self alone, who delight in the virtuous Dharma,
and who carry out the king’s commands, go upon the stainless path.
O Lakṣmī, whether they be men or women belonging to any of the castes or stages of life,
those who possess the auspiciousness of the blessings of the elders go indeed to heaven.
This applies to daughters-in-law, unmarried girls, young maidens, or even mistresses accompanied by their sons.
Whether they are childless or elderly, they go forth as recipients of blessings;
whether they be eminent kings or servants living in poverty,
(79) they are always those who serve the aged, regardless of their status or lack thereof.
Those who are upright and whose essence is humility undoubtedly go to heaven. Those servants in this world who partake in fame are partakers of heaven;
by virtue of my grace, they shall go to the higher state. (3.76.80–81)
Those who possess virtuous character, follow righteous conduct, are patient, and likewise serve [the Lord],
who grant happiness through their service, go to My abode upon departing for heaven.
Those in whose mouths is the name of Hari, and in whose hearts is Śrī Hari Himself—
Furthermore, those who follow my path—even if they are merely obedient to the words of their elders—go to my abode.

Those who give away cows, sons, or daughters, or who bestow gardens, fields, and palaces, as well as those who give their hips, thighs, or even a single limb, go to my abode when they depart for heaven. (83–84)
I gave a cow to a Brahmin, a daughter to a youth, and a son to a virtuous man;
a garden to a deity, a field to me, and a mansion to a householder-yogi.
I gave my hips and strength to one who was afraid, and my thigh as a refuge to one in distress. (85)
People go to heaven after giving even a small amount of wealth to the poor.
Then, having attained devotion to me and offering everything to me,
those very ones who are virtuous go to my lotus-abode.
Those who give their hair, lips, cheeks, and teeth; those who give their chest, back, and hands;
and those who give their neck, calves, and feet, go to heaven and to my own abode.
Having given away their hair, they take refuge in renunciation, [attaining] Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu.
My devotees go from heaven to the immortal state.
Having received the two lips and the mantra of instruction, those who have taken refuge at the feet of the teacher and are devoted to me go from heaven to the imperishable abode. (3.76.89–90)
O Śrī! Having offered their cheeks—the states of love and affection, heartfelt and preceded by devotion—to me, my devotees then go from here to the imperishable state.
Having also placed their chest—trust itself—upon me and having given that to me, [they depart].
Trusting [in this], one indeed goes to heaven, and from there to my imperishable state.
Having offered their back as assistance, they attain the auspicious realm that grants the next world;
first to heaven, and thereafter, through devotion, they go to my supreme abode.
Having performed service and servitude, and having offered everything to me as a surrender, he goes to heaven; thereafter, through devotion, he proceeds to my abode.
[He may offer] his neck, his entire possessions, or even the gift of his life.
Having granted me the gift of life, he goes from there to heaven and then to the imperishable state (akṣara).
Indeed, having given me both his calves, his prosperity, and his lineage, he goes to heaven;
then, having surrendered everything, he proceeds to my abode.
He who gives his feet, wealth, and a livelihood to a great soul,
having gone to heaven through devotion to me, proceeds to the imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, having understood these gifts, both woman and man [should practice them].
These [gifts] should be given according to the truth, well-concealed, and with a desire for liberation.
Indeed, the gift of a woman (yoṣādāna) should always be bestowed with great devotion.
A woman is declared to be Māyā; she is Uṣā, the dawn at the beginning of night.
For that [bond] which binds living beings must be given to the Supreme Self;
being himself free from *māyā*, he attains the supreme state.
The gift of a maiden, which bestows happiness, should be bestowed upon the youth.

Having given his own self—the maiden of craving, the hope for pleasure—to the Supreme Soul, the Youth who wields the Śārṅga bow and is devoid of Māra, one shall proceed to the abode. Furthermore, the gift of a cow should be bestowed; the cow is auspicious knowledge of Śrī Hari. (101–102)
"Having given, both the giver and the receiver go to the imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, having thus understood my majesty, those who here in this land of action perform [deeds] move about for the sake of liberation.
Those who take refuge in my state become enjoyers of eternal bliss.
Thus has this majesty of mine, born of yoga, been described to you here;
by reading or even hearing it further, one attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Attaining Brahminhood and Sainthood, the Means for Going to the Divine Abode, the Means for the Untainted Path, Divine Gifts and Other Virtues, and the Yoga of Hari," in the third section, the Dvāpara Continuum, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 76. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Dvāpara Yuga Continuum).
Chapter 77 [Author:
Chapter 78 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Mādhava, you ought indeed to explain all the duties of virtuous women;
for all those virtuous women born from your body are, in truth, beyond *māyā*.
How indeed should they conduct themselves constantly in this world?
For they are the wives of Kṛṣṇa, renounced, and indeed practitioners of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
All of them are beloved by Hari, for these women have Kṛṣṇa as their lord;
they are the consorts of Brahmā, highly blessed Mahābhāgavatas, and truly Sāttvatas.
"In every way, by what path should they exist as those who offer themselves to Him?
How can their devotion to their husband (pātivratya) persist without a wedded husband?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! For women who have been consecrated by renunciation, the initiation is indeed the marriage itself, joined with me. "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā."
With this mantra, that virtuous woman was wedded in the presence of the fire.
Having performed the oblation and been initiated, she then worshipped me together with my own form; having presented herself, she entered the sacrificial pavilion.
That virtuous woman accepted my saffron robes;
by the command of my guru, from the very moment of her initiation, she became my beloved.
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa alone is her husband, and I am Nārāyaṇa.
She remains indeed married, always devoted to me with wifely fidelity.
That virtuous and purifying wife of mine must be protected by her.
For they would travel along my path, and they would dwell upon my path. (3.77.10)
They should live with divine devotion on the path of liberation, the true path;
they should practice service to the virtuous, for the virtuous are my very forms. They should live with a desireless disposition and likewise offer their service.
"In every way, they should offer themselves to my forms.
O virtuous women, these duties of yours as wives were established by the sages at the time of marriage;
you shall practice the shared dharma and other obligations with your husbands, remaining under their guardianship."
Therefore, just as a devoted wife who possesses constancy is obedient to her husband,
so too is my virtuous wife, who possesses renunciation, obedient to me.
Having taken fire as witness, as well as the preceptor and my parents, [I have made this pledge].
Both Gaṇeśa and I, as well as that virtuous wife—both of us are indeed equal.
That bull [Dharma] equally upholds the supreme duty of devotion to one's wife;
likewise, the devotion of a husband to his wife is equal for both me and Hari.

In the presence of the sacred fire and other witnesses, she becomes a partner in dharma for her husband; in the presence of the sacred fire and other witnesses, he becomes a partner in dharma for his wife.
With her mind fully surrendered, she should always remember her beloved as one who practices dharma together with her.
Of excellent character, pleasant in speech, virtuous in conduct, and delightful to behold;
with undistracted mind, fair-faced, and a companion in the practice of dharma for her husband—may she be devoted to the true dharma and may she be a partaker of the true dharma. (18–19)
The virtuous woman should constantly gaze upon her husband, the god of gods;
she should perform service and attendance, endowed with divine conduct.
Indeed, being free from other thoughts, undistracted, pure in disposition, and bestowing happiness, she should remain so.
She should gaze constantly at her husband’s face as if it were the face of her own son.
Rich in self-restraint, the woman who walks the path of dharma should bow to her husband,
having understood the duties of husband and wife and the religious obligations they share together.
Realizing this, she should be devoted to dharma and share the same vows as her husband;
indeed, with a mind full of tranquility, she should serve her husband, who is a god among gods.
Even when instructed, she should always maintain a most gracious countenance toward her husband.
Though she is beaten and spoken to harshly, she remains ever submissive;
that virtuous woman shall not touch another man, nor look at him with desire,
nor even engage in jesting or other such behavior with another.
For her, there is nothing dear except her husband; even his leftovers are dear to her.
Everything joined with her husband is dear, and that is indeed a great grace.
Her husband’s command is the command of the Lord himself; her husband is the illustrious Supreme Lord.
She who is devoted to her husband shall indeed be a practitioner of dharma.
She who attends upon her beloved husband— whether he be poor, diseased, wretched, suffering, exhausted, or frail— shall be a partaker of dharma.
A woman who has sons is blessed, while a mother of daughters alone is fruitless;
she who is dear to her husband and whose very life is her husband shall be a partaker of dharma. She who performs service, servitude, and even menial labor [for him]... [29]... [is likewise blessed].
Performing service and attendance, she becomes a partaker of dharma.
(3.77.30) Humble, gentle in conduct, affectionate toward her husband, and firm in resolve—she who has dedicated her entire being to her husband shall be a partaker of dharma. (3.1)
She who has no longing for sensual pleasures, nor for wealth, nor for powers, nor for comforts, but only for her beloved— he calls her a virtuous wife, a partaker of Dharma.
Rising early and devoted to the service of the household in the morning— (32) — [she is a virtuous wife].
She who is always devoted to purity through sweeping, smearing, and other such acts;
she who is likewise intent on the fire-ritual and intent on the service of the gods;
and she who is devoted to her duties—she shall be a partaker of dharma. (33–34)
She who satisfies the deities, guests, dependents, her husband, and the elderly by providing water and other necessities according to their needs,
and who eats only the remaining food after having fed all of them— (35) — [she is a devoted wife].
With her family contented and well-nourished, she shall be a partaker of dharma.
(36) Always bowing and serving the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, and constantly devoted to her own mother and father, she shall be a partaker of dharma. (37)

She who supports the virtuous, the poor, and the helpless with food and other necessities according to her ability fulfills her duty toward her husband and shall partake in the merit of righteousness.
She who, like one devoted to Brahman, regards her husband as her deity, never seeks another man anywhere.
Moreover, one whose eyes are bound does not perceive even that which stands before her at a distance of four cubits.
Such a person is rare in this world unless Lakṣmī resides in her heart,
or unless a virtuous wife dwells in the heart of Śambhu, having attained a state of invisibility.
She who observes the difficult vow commanded by her husband,
being devoted to her husband’s mind and intent on his welfare, shall be a partaker of dharma.
This is merit, this is heaven, this is austerity, and this is that very vow.
For her whose husband is indeed Nārāyaṇa himself, he is the supreme deity.
Indeed, for women, the husband is the god; the husband is the teacher, the husband is the refuge;
the husband is the kinsman, the husband is fortune, the husband is life, and the husband is the ultimate goal. (42–43)
Reconciliation with her husband is heaven; his displeasure is hell.
Whether it be an improper act, an unrighteous deed, or even one that threatens her life, she should do exactly as her husband commands. Such devotion to her husband is the highest virtue.
Whether it be poverty, disease, misfortune, enmity, or being consumed by a curse;
or even the mental instability of her husband—she should perform all these things in accordance with his disposition.
Considering all of this as her own good fortune, she should indeed serve her husband.

Thus, the total surrender of all one's possessions that proceeds toward the husband, when considering the duties for times of distress, is the practice of a devoted wife. And I am always the husband of that virtuous woman, just as I am married in the world.
"Let that virtuous woman remain here solely for my sake, being devoted to me;
let her be purified by bathing for my sake, endowed with stainlessness for my sake, having prepared her attire for my sake, and possessing beauty for my sake. (48-49)
She who has renounced all conditioned things for my sake is indeed a virtuous wife devoted to her husband;

for my sake she wears red garments, and for my sake she wears saffron robes; seeking only me, she is adorned with the marks of the *puṇḍra* and the *candra*, and for my sake she is anointed with fragrant unguents.
For my sake she wears flower garlands; for my sake she wears wreaths.
For my sake that virtuous and devoted wife adorns her neck, hands, and feet.
For my sake she takes her food; for my sake she partakes of drink.
She who has adorned herself for my sake, she who has prepared her enjoyments and vehicles for my sake,
she who has fashioned ornaments for my sake— that virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, is mine.
She has dressed her hair for my sake, and she has put on her bodice for my sake.
She who has fashioned a bodice for my sake, she who wears a waist-cloth for my sake;
she whose hands and feet are for my sake, she whose head is made for my sake;
she whose trunk is made for my sake, and she who moves within me for my sake. (14–15)
That virtuous woman, my devoted wife, exists for my sake as a subordinate quality; she showers the rain of bliss for my sake; she is immersed in my name and virtues;
she eternally abides in the state of sattva for my sake, and she eternally abides in the state of rajas for my sake.
She who is intent on obstructing what is for my sake, she who guards the affection directed toward me,
she whose heart is always fixed on me, and she who acts according to my desires—
she who conducts herself in this manner is truly my virtuous wife, devoted to the vow of Hari.
Even while performing meritorious deeds, practicing the Dharma, or engaging in auspicious actions— or whatever else— a virtuous woman, endowed with good character and fortune,
should be intent on me, resting in me, regarding her life as mine, and united with me. (59)
May that virtuous woman, devoted to Hari, exist as my very own form—
she who practices the dharma of renunciation for my sake, who is characterized by truthfulness for my sake,
who has slept for my sake, and who remains awake for my sake. (3.77.60–61)
She is occupied for my sake and has withdrawn from all else for my sake;
thus she finds contentment for my sake and observes the vow of non-violence for my sake.
She performs sacrifices and renunciations for my sake, and her ritual offerings and good deeds are for my sake.
For my sake they remain in celibacy, and for my sake they practice non-possession;
for my sake they observe purity and right conduct, and for my sake they are established in austerity;
for my sake they are devoted to sacred study, and for my sake they are intent on worship.
The functioning of the senses is for my sake; the mind is always for my sake;
the thought "I am" is for my sake, as is the determination regarding me;
the effort of living beings is for my sake, and they take refuge in the contemplation of me. (65)
The attainment of sovereignty for my sake, remaining established in meditation for my sake;
abiding on the pure path for my sake, honoring guests for my sake;
performing the work of cooking for my sake, and having food as one's domain for my sake. (66–67)
Rich in houses and halls for my sake, singing songs and hymns for my sake;
established in dance and emotion for my sake, and listening to stories for my sake;
possessing great enthusiasm for my sake, and wandering to sacred pilgrimage sites for my sake. (68)
She has undertaken her journey for my sake; she has created a flower garden for my sake.
She has engaged in various activities for my sake; she has performed buying and selling for my sake.
She is rich in the effort of agriculture for my sake; she protects the kingdom for my sake.
She whose service is for my sake, who possesses devotion as my servant,
who has entered into servitude for my sake, and for whose every arrangement I am the sole purpose;
she whose going and coming are for my sake, and who is endowed with reflection directed toward me.
Thus, that virtuous woman, devoted to Hari, has come to exist for my sake.
For my sake she observes the Kārtika vow; for my sake she is an ascetic in Pauṣa;
for my sake she is rich in merit during Caitra; and for my sake she remains steadfast in Śrāvaṇa.
She offered lamps for my sake; she partook of meals in rows for my sake.
She attained the status of a disciple for my sake, and she assumed the role of a teacher for my sake.
Even as a servant, she was accompanied by all her disciples for my sake.
That virtuous woman has attained the status of a Guru and has become my own form.
She is a chaste wife whose conduct is ever-virtuous; she is mine, devoted to Hari.
Such as she is, O Lakṣmī, my wife is one whose dharma is renunciation and who is faithful to her husband.
Likewise, there were the friends of Rādhā, the friends of Lakṣmī, and also the friends of Śrī; the friends of Māṇikī, the auspicious friends of Satī,
and also the friends of Sāvitrī, as well as the friends of Sītā.
Those who are devoted friends (bhaktisakhīs), all those who are considered Nārāyaṇīs,
as well as the Vāsudevīs, the Kārṣṇīs, the beloveds of Brahmā,
the Vaiṣṇavīs, the Bhagavatīs, the Brāhmīs, and those who are liberated (muktānīs). //78-79//
Those who possess supreme sovereignty, as well as the women of the East, and all those who are goddesses— may they indeed be virtuous wives devoted to their husbands for me.
Whatever belongs to them, and whatever is their entire possession, may all that be for the sake of my beloved.
Thus, the state of being a virtuous man and a virtuous woman is mutual; I am the Supreme Lord.
Without me they are not virtuous women, and without them I do not exist.
Established in mutual union, they bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon human beings. (81-82)
We are the bestowers of enjoyment and liberation upon the gods, the lords, the perfected ones, the exponents of Brahman, and indeed upon all embodied beings.
O Lakṣmī, understand the majesty of your friends and of yourself as well.
Listen also to this greatness of mine and of my liberated ones:
I am the true Lord, the manifest Supreme Brahman, the Sovereign of the Highest;
you are the virtuous Consciousness, the foremost among chaste women, the beloved of Brahman and the beloved of Hari. (84–85)
Through union with that, we two possess constant bliss and great bliss;
indeed, the enjoyer of that is eternally blissful and truly liberated.
I am the virtuous one, and Ramā is the virtuous Lakṣmī, ever-truly faithful.
Śrī (fortune), Sampat (prosperity), Māṇikī (jewel-like woman), and Saubhāgya (good fortune)—these five are the supreme deities. (87) The virtuous man bestows and brings about every kind of happiness.
The virtuous woman bestows and brings about every kind of happiness. (88)
Being virtuous, one abides in truth; prosperity leads to supreme auspiciousness.
From that, one surely protects [oneself], and eternal happiness indeed proceeds.
This great state, consisting of the Supreme Brahman, is always truly equal to liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, you are forever virtuous, my true Brahmic consort;
filled with every bliss, you rejoice with me, your Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self. (3.77.90–91)
This body—whether man or woman—is not the Self; nor is the Self either man or woman.
So too are the sages who delight in the Self, the virtuous men, and the virtuous women.
Established in Brahman and the Self, they are absorbed in Me through My yoga, possessing My nature and taking refuge in Me. 92.
Men and women are the residual parts; among them, I am Nārāyaṇa. She who takes refuge in man is a woman (nārī), and the self (ātman) is dependent upon me.
Thus, all selves and women are so by virtue of their nature as dependents.
"I am the refuge, the man, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the Master.
Having thus understood this truth here, a virtuous woman, endowed with good fortune,
recognizing me as her own beloved, should always practice devotion to her husband.
That virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, was beloved by the world and beloved by Kṛṣṇa.
(96) In this world, a young man becomes beloved through his union with the body of a young woman;
but I am always beloved—in the womb, in childhood, and in youth. (97)
In old age and in death, even when one has passed away to another world;
in saṃsāra, in the heavenly realms and so forth, and even in liberation—O beloved, I alone exist as the eternal Self of all beings, indeed by my very essence. (98)
I am always the controller within myself, situated inside;
likewise, there too, I am eternally indeed the beloved, and the state of being beloved resides in me.
Through my yoga, the state of being beloved exists truly within the self alone.
Thus, as the eternal and beloved one, I manifest within all; indeed,
through my radiance, all— whether liberated souls,
lords, gods, humans and the like, animals, and even trees— become truly radiant.

Both the insentient and the sentient, as well as Māyā and its products—those who possess luster through my own luster are my consorts by their very nature. Thus, everything consists of the beloved; indeed, widowhood exists nowhere at all.
Therefore, virtuous women, endowed with good fortune, should worship me as their beloved.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this secret of virtuous women has been declared by me;
it is the thought of the souls of all, profound and filled with the essence of reality.
Therefore, a man should never give way to pride, thinking "I am [the self].
Rather, one should worship the Lord and Master, making the thought "The Self is He.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Lord. (105–106)
O virtuous ones, having understood this secret, those who are thus disposed toward their offspring will reflect upon it and practice accordingly; they shall attain the supreme goal,
as well as worldly enjoyment, liberation, happiness, and even bliss.
"My yoga is eternal, as is the supreme state of Nirvana.

Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge of the Supreme Limit of Chastity and Other Virtues of Satī and the Faithful Women," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 78 [Author:
Chapter 79 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! You shall hear the most excellent narrative of a virtuous woman.
In the city of Jālakapura in Saurāṣṭra, there was a gopī named Sucandrikā.
Her husband, a cowherd, also worshipped Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.

He was always devoted and intent on bathing, following the cow-pastures. Gopāla, dressed as a cowherd, always served me, Bālakṛṣṇa, in the forest with forest-grown fruits and other offerings. || 2-3 ||
"He worships me with milk-porridges, boiled milk, milk, curds, ghee, and so forth, as well as with fresh butter,
flowers, and water. And he, indeed,
having abandoned his own body due to fever during the rainy season,"

When half of his lifespan had passed away, my devotee Gopāla, who possessed the marks of pregnancy and was full of longing for me, abandoned his wife— the cowherd girl— and, out of compassion for me, ascended an excellent celestial chariot and went to heaven. || 5–6 ||
Accompanied by Apsarases and cows, he shines resplendent;
all provided with every requisite, including various kinds of food and drink.
And on the surface of the earth, his wife is devoted to me and carries a child in her womb.

Though she was pregnant, she desired to die following her own beloved husband. (8) The devoted wife, unable to endure the suffering without her husband, went toward the funeral pyre of her lord, even as she was being restrained by the people. (9)
"O Gopī, by destroying the fetus, you have incurred great sin;
yet for your husband, heaven has become a celestial chariot. Protect the fetus, and within a year you shall become a mother of sons. (3.78.10)
Upon the death of her husband, the merit indeed belongs to the wife who dies on his back. This applies to one who is not pregnant; however, for one who is pregnant, it is a source of defilement.
Therefore, do not kill yourself; dwell happily in Govraja.

Even though she was thus being dissuaded, she fell into the funeral pyre along with her husband; at that very moment, this husband of hers was seen traveling through the path of the sky in a celestial chariot, saying: "Do not do this, O Gopī! Do not act in this way!"
He restrained [the fire] and lifted up his beloved with his own hand.
Having comforted her while she was still unburnt and having instantly extinguished the flames,
he took her onto a celestial chariot and gave instructions for the protection of the fetus.
"Having protected your son and then married him off, come thereafter to my heaven; do not make a funeral procession. Thus addressed, she became tranquil and happy, devoted to her husband's word.
Having fallen from her celestial chariot onto the earth, she was delivered by him, freed from all sorrow.
Having bowed to the funeral pyre and having bowed to her husband, Gopikā indeed went home, saying, "O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, you have truly favored me. || 17-18 ||
The cowherd woman Gopikā indeed maintained her devotion to Dharma, her vows, and her virtuous conduct;
and that cowherd woman Sucandrikā gave birth to a son with a beautiful face.
That boy grew up, became a youth, and was married.
Then she related her former existence to Gopīputra.
Her son also rejoiced at all that had transpired regarding his own father.
Then [she said], "I must now go to heaven to my father."
Having spoken thus, she smeared the ground with cow dung and sat down;
then, after meditating for a moment, she abandoned that body.
At that moment, her husband’s celestial chariot appeared, accompanied by the goddess of the gods.
The excellent apsarases,
increasing her splendor with cries of victory, caused that beautiful moonlight to ascend from the sky as it arrived;
meanwhile, the cowherd’s son, accompanied by his bride, beheld her in the heavens.
Then he mentally perceived his father as a divine form and his mother as the vital breath;
in a mere moment, the celestial chariot ascended to the heights of the sky.
Seated upon that chariot, Mañjughoṣā, the most excellent of apsarases, [beheld] Gopikā.
And she asked Sucandrikā, right in the presence of her husband:
"O auspicious one, by what vow and by what conduct was this cowherd woman purified of her sins and brought to the world of the gods? (26–27)
Wearing garments as bright as fire, beautiful with golden campaka flowers, and blazing with splendors,
how has this divine woman come here of her own accord?
O cowherd girl, she could not have arrived through meager penance, nor by means of charity or religious observances.
"How did they reach the heavenly world? Tell me how they came together.
Having heard this, the cowherd girl Sucandrikā spoke to Mañjughoṣā:
"Tell me how heaven is indeed attained; tell me the cause for that."
Then Mañjughoṣā spoke: "Listen, O Gopī, to the reason:
she who wears saffron robes and is devoted to the path of renunciation—whether she be shaven-headed, or have matted hair, or likewise wear bark garments."
A female ascetic who is supremely devoted to charity, highly meritorious,
and who gives everything to a guest who is a virtuous and great-souled person—
she, being chaste and dedicated to devotion to her husband, shall go to heaven. (22–23)
The husband is a god; the husband is Kṛṣṇa; the husband alone is the supreme bull.
The husband’s command is the highest Veda; the husband’s satisfaction is the virtue of a woman.
The virtuous wife who conducts herself in this manner attains the imperishable heaven.
Having heard this, the cowherd woman then said: "Listen, O rider of the celestial chariot!
I am not one clad in saffron robes, nor am I devoted to renunciation. I am neither shaven-headed nor do I wear matted locks, nor do I wear garments of bark. (25–26)

I am not a female ascetic wearing woolen garments and the like, nor am I one who dwells in the forest merely for the sake of giving milk; rather, I am a cowherd girl appointed by the cowherds, performing service to the virtuous, yet I do not even know how to honor a guest. (37)

I was devoted to the service of my husband, by which I attained the status of a goddess. I never spoke harsh words to my husband, and I remained intent upon the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord, and the saints. (38–39)
I am a servant of my husband’s cows and remain devoted to my mother-in-law and father-in-law.
I do not engage in backbiting, nor do I harbor deceit even in my mind. I do not stand in improper places, nor do I utter vulgar speech.
Whether it be untrue, or laughter, or even that which is harmful and born of evil;
whether it be secret or not secret—I shall certainly never do such a thing.
For the sake of the cows, my husband has gone out, having returned home. (41–42)
I always serve as his follower by providing water, food, a seat, and other necessities.
Whatever food is not to his liking, whatever edible is not to his taste,
and whatever is to be chewed, licked, or drunk— I avoid all of that.
For the sake of the household, I always perform every duty;
for the sake of my husband, I perform all kinds of auspicious rites,
such as applying collyrium, yellow pigment, bathing, and anointing with garlands and unguents.
I do not take pleasure in my husband’s adornment when he has gone out, nor do I ever wake my husband while he sleeps soundly. Indeed,
filled with happiness, I attend even to his internal needs.
I do not cause distress to my husband; therefore, my mind is content.
I always keep secrets well-guarded and remain obedient to his commands.
Having thus fulfilled my duties toward my husband, I shall follow him to death upon his funeral pyre.
Though she had settled there, was forbidden [to stay], uprooted,
and cast down upon the earth, she returned to heaven after ensuring that her son, together with his bride, was established there.
Thus indeed have I come to this heaven because of Mañjughoṣa.
"My husband has been found by me here, and my son exists upon this earth.
Such various kinds of gopīs indeed exist on the surface of the earth;
and those gopīs of Kṛṣṇa have appeared even in the intervals between kalpas.
"Having worshipped Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa as my husband,
and having thus worshipped my husband as the Lord, I have come here.
Upon hearing this, Mañjughoṣā was delighted and praised her.
Other celestial nymphs also praised that devoted wife.
Having dwelt there for a long time and enjoyed manifold pleasures,
the virtuous Sucandrikā went to Satyaloka together with her husband.
And there Sāvitrī asked: "The gods indeed go from heaven to the mortal world to experience what remains; how is it that you are here?
O virtuous lady, you have arrived at the truth; tell me the reason for that."
And Sucandrikā, with a joyful heart, said to Sāvitrī:
"In heaven, I have seen every supreme happiness consisting of enjoyments; however, that indeed lacks restraint and is devoid of virtuous vows. (56-57)
The gods indeed possess no virtue, nor do the wives of the gods;
even among the celestial nymphs (apsarases) in heaven, sexual intercourse is found to exist to the highest degree.
And among the gods as well, the conduct of the goddesses is for the most part of that same nature.
O Sāvitrī, there is indeed a certain custom there; what can I say?
The gods and goddesses, assuming forms at will, sport as they please, being truly devoid of all restraint. (3.78.60)
Such devotion to a husband is not found among the goddesses, nor is the vow of a wife found among the celestial beings;
such remnants of those who have enjoyed [their fruits] return to the abode of mortals.
Furthermore, even among the principal gods, the vow of a wife does not exist.
What need is there to speak of the minor deities? They die and return to the mortal world.
Among them, Saṃjñā, Rohiṇī, Paulomī, and the wives of the sages—these and others of few number are indeed devoted to their husbands.
In heaven, within my husband’s celestial chariot, I have always observed the vow of devotion to my husband in every way, just as I did on earth;
I have performed the worship of Hari daily, and I have also protected the bull.

"O Sāvitrī! By virtue of my past merits and also through the grace of Śrī Hari, I have become one who cannot be touched by any other man. It is solely by His power that I, together with my husband, have come to Satyaloka; there is no other cause. (65–66)
"Having dwelt here, I shall depart out of compassion for you, my lord, to Vaikuṇṭha, which is above the waters, by virtue of my vow to Lord Hari.
Thus spoke the virtuous woman; indeed, they both dwelt there for a long time.
Then both of them went to Vaikuṇṭha, to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu.
Having gone there, the great virtuous woman bowed to Lakṣmī, the beloved of Hari;
the cowherd bowed to Viṣṇu, and they both honored them with joy.
Questioned by Lakṣmī, "O virtuous one, how did you come from Satyaloka?
Sucandrikā said to Śrī, "I have come because of devotion to my beloved. This beloved of mine is indeed Gopāla, who is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord. (3.78.70)
I always worship my beloved, who is eternally the most beloved of the beloved.
Having attained the dharma of a virtuous wife and being devoted to my husband,
I have reached Vaikuṇṭha through the power of the dharma of my beloved.
Then, having dwelt there for a long time together with her husband,
that gopī, adorned by the gopa, departed for Goloka itself.
This gopī did not bow to Rādhikā, nor did the gopa bow to Kṛṣṇa.
The two of them dwelt there in that world, even among the hosts of cowherd girls and cowherds.
Rādhā said to Sucandrikā: "How did she come here?
Tell me the reason, O cowherd girl! By what merit has she arrived?"
Sucandrikā said to Rādhā: "By service to the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, by service to the Beloved, and by service even to the Beloved of the Beloved;
through the dharma of wifely devotion and through the dharma of Kṛṣṇa, [one reaches] the house of the Cow. (76)
I have come here, O Rādhikā, joined to the duty of a virtuous wife.
Devotion to one's husband is the supreme dharma, the highest of all dharmas;
the dharma of Kṛṣṇa is the supreme dharma, the highest of the highest dharmas for a virtuous wife.
By me my beloved, the best of cowherds, has been constantly worshiped;
and Kṛṣṇa, the protector even of the cowherds, has always been fully honored.
By that merit, O Rādhikā, I have come here to this world.
"And after dwelling there for a long time, I shall indeed go to the imperishable abode.
By the command of Kṛṣṇa, that virtuous woman, having dwelt for a long time with her beloved and having maintained her devotion to her husband,
then departed for the imperishable realm.
Taking refuge in the Supreme beyond the supreme, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
she bathed in the lake of Brahman and became a great female liberated soul (mahāmuktānikā).
At that time, her husband also became liberated, endowed with the nature of Brahman.
Then all the effects of Māyā indeed dissolved into the two;
at that time, the principles (tattvas) became of one nature within the two.
Then the entire principle of the Self (ātmatattva), embodied, beautiful, and supreme, [arose]. || 83–84 ||
Then, they were manifested in the form of the Supreme Person; having attained the states of male and female, they reached a divine condition.
There, they attained identity of form (sārūpya), residence in the same realm (sālokya), and equality of power (sārṣṭitā) with Śrī Hari.
They came into the presence there and bowed to Puruṣottama;
they dwelt in the imperishable abode, chanting the names of Puruṣottama:
"Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Parameśvara. (86–87)
"O Supreme Brahman, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, O Puruṣottama!"—
by thus [chanting], O Lakṣmī, those two then became liberated in my imperishable realm.
Previously, on the surface of the earth, they had received my mantras from Lomaśa.

By the power of that [vision], my devotion toward them both increased over a long time. (89) The excellent vow of devotion to her husband, the vow of devotion to Hari, and the vow of devotion to her husband likewise increased ever further for the cowherd’s wife and for the cowherd as well. (3.78.90)
Indeed, through service to the virtuous, through their character in every respect,
and through devotion in all the worlds, they have obtained me as their husband.
Māṇikyā is my beloved in my abode, as are Jayā and Lalitā.
They asked that cowherd girl, "How have you come to be here?
Sucandrikā said to Māṇikyā, "O Śrī Parameśvarī, O auspicious one,
[I am here] through service to my husband and by following the virtuous conduct of a faithful wife."
Through her beginningless devotion to the conjugal fidelity of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, she has arrived here;
"This husband of mine is a great liberated soul (mahāmukta) who emerged from immersion in the Brahma-lake.
And I too have become his very own beloved of Brahmā in every respect. (94)
The virtuous Muktānikā was born, for the Māṇikī is indeed liberated in form.
Supreme liberation is obtainable through grace; of this there is no doubt whatsoever.
For service to the virtuous is association with the good, and through such service, one gains a treasure-trove of merit.
Through masses of merit, discrimination between one's own self and the Supreme Self arises.
From discrimination, an engagement toward the welfare of the self is born;
from those two [merit and discrimination], the destruction of sin and purity occur, and devotion (bhakti) emerges.
And through devotion, there arises the remembrance of His names, abodes, and so forth, filled with affection.
(98) By the offering of such affection, various desired accomplishments come to pass.
The Supreme Self is indeed the beloved, the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, Hari. (99)
"Thus has this perfected Lord Kṛṣṇa, my most beloved, been attained;
in this way have I obtained Hari as my consort here in the abode of Akṣara.
Having spoken thus, the delighted Māṇikī praised Sucandrikā.
Having obtained the virtuous Śīlavatī as her friend, she became filled with joy.
Sucandrikā, ever liberated, lived there like another goddess Śrī.
O Lakṣmī, she is a devotee of me, the beloved of Hari, in that imperishable abode. || 101-102 ||
"Thus has the supreme greatness of a virtuous wife been shown to you here;
for my devoted and virtuous mistress has indeed brought about my liberation.

(103) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, concerning how the cowherd woman named Sucandrikā—along with her husband—through her wifely devotion (*pātivratya*) and her devotion to the Lord of Lakṣmī (*hari-pātivratya-bhakti*), attained the celestial realms of Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Imperishable Abode (*akṣara-dhāma*).
The seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wondrous Wonder of the Departure," etc., [ends].
Chapter 78. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age), Chapter 79.
[The Author: Chapter 80.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Kṛṣṇa, if a virtuous woman devoted to her husband remains within the state of household life, [what is her fate]?
"O beloved who bestows happiness, tell me: by doing what does one attain supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"By a virtuous woman, having entered the state of a householder, [worshipping] Śrī Kṛṣṇa Puruṣottama..."
He should indeed be constantly propitiated, for he bestows prosperity.
Sages, ancestors, gods, humans, virtuous twice-born, elders, guests, and noble women are especially worthy of worship. (2–3)
One should worship the gods with sacrifice and offerings, humans with constant hospitality,
the seers and ancestors with funeral cakes and *śrāddha* rites, and having offered oblations into the fire, one should perform worship.
One may also perform a *śrāddha* with milk, roots, and fruits, and feed the virtuous.
She should also honor the twice-born with wealth, food, clothing, and other gifts.
(5) She should feed the guests; she should feed virtuous women and faithful wives.
She should also feed the officiating priest, the accomplished student, the holy man, the teacher, and the father-in-law. (6)
She should honor her master and husband with sweet offerings of madhuparka;
she should scatter food on the ground for dogs, outcastes, and birds.
She should give [offerings] here to Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by the words "Svāhā."
One should give bundles of grass to the cows and sugar and other sweets to the children;
one should give water to the trees and chickpeas and the like to the fish; one should give grain-particles to the flocks of birds and the remains of food (prasāda) to those who stay nearby.
One should give gifts in this manner according to one's capacity, listen to the sacred narratives,
and likewise perform the spinning of the rosary and the beholding of the deity.
One should also offer water and perform bathing, meditation, worship, and so forth.
One should perform the chanting of the Name, as well as worship and remembrance.
One should practice purification of the body, purification of one's conduct, and purification of the mind.
One should serve the virtuous and serve the chaste women according to one's ability and as is appropriate.
One should offer gifts of flowers, incense, and lamps according to the prescribed rite.
The lunar rays, medicinal herbs, and various species of flowers are always endowed with nectar; they remove both poison and the fierce heat born of affliction. (13)
Indeed, these flowers bestow nectar, delight to the mind, and immediate satisfaction;
they remove the poison [of worldly afflictions] from embodied beings by their fragrance. Truly, these "well-minded" (sumanas) flowers gladden the heart and bring about prosperity.
The gods and others are pleased by flowers, and being pleased, they bestow nourishment as well.
Contemplate that flowers with desirable fragrances belong to the gods. Indeed, white flowers from thornless plants are beloved by the gods.
Water-born lotuses and garlands are for Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and serpents; flowers with pungent thorns and red in color are for those seeking malevolent magic (abhicāra);
and black flowers with sharp thorns are for the Bhūtas.

O beloved, flowers from impure grounds, though they may delight the minds and eyes of men and are indeed dear to them, must be avoided in every way. The gods are satisfied by their fragrance, while the yakṣas and rākṣasas are pleased by the sight of them.
Through the enjoyment of these three alone, humans [attain their ends];
however, fragrances from flowers and sandalwood immediately gratify the gods.
And being gratified, they [the gods] sustain these mortals with perfections and riches.
Incense in the form of resin is indeed considered excellent, namely guggulu;
the gods are pleased by this incense, which bestows prosperity upon the householder's life.
Aguru is likewise the most excellent for yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhogins.
The artificial incenses of the Daityas and those made from sallakī resin are of that same kind.
Through the offering of incense made from turmeric, the bhūtas become satisfied and depart.
Incenses such as those made from sarjarasa are indeed favored by human beings.
The gift of a lamp always produces beloved increase of splendor; having overcome blinding darkness, the darkness of delusion, and even the southern course [of the sun],
a lamp offered with devotion grants the northern path.
A lamp is the giver of upward movement and the medicine for the destruction of darkness. (26) Indeed, by the gift of lamps, the gods became powerful and illuminators;
they were born radiant in the heavenly world. Therefore, one should offer a lamp. (27)
By giving light, one becomes possessed of vision and endowed with the radiance of intelligence;
by stealing a lamp, one becomes blind, destined for darkness, and deprived of luster.
Likewise, [one who steals] sacrificial oblations, medicinal herbs, juices, or resins [incurs similar retribution]. 28.
Those who give lamps indeed become as radiant as the full moon.
For as many years as there are twinklings of an eye during which the lamp burns, for that long shall the giver of the lamp possess keen vision, beauty, and power. (3.79.30)
Therefore, lamps should be offered by a virtuous woman devoted to her household duties;
furthermore, she should practice austerity in every way during the latter part of her life,
so that by means of that austerity, Brahmā may attain the state of the imperishable abode.

Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the unsurpassed dharma of virtuous women (sādhvī), by practicing which one may attain liberation; this is a narrative from a former kalpa. In a former kalpa, there was a Manu named Haripratha.
His wife was Brahmaprathā, a virtuous woman endowed with sacred initiation;
she was the daughter of the great sage Kaṇḍāyana and was devoted to the Supreme Brahman.
She was born as a mind-born daughter (mānasī) in the house of Kaṇḍāyana.

Full of wisdom, full of austerity, and free from mental fluctuations, she was a young woman living in the forest; remaining in her father’s house, she took the vow of a virtuous woman and, established in celibacy, became an ascetic even within the home. (35–36)
With her body uninjured and untouched by any man,
that virtuous woman, radiant as the moon, was indeed in the forest sacred to Viṣṇu on the bank of a river;
having gone with her father to bathe, she had finished her bath and was wearing wet clothes.
Though she was a mature young woman, established in virtuous conduct and endowed with the quality of generosity,
she was seen by Manu Haripratha as he traveled through the sky—
Brāhmī, radiant with the luster of Brahmanic austerity, beautiful and auspicious. (38–39)
The goddess was divine, worthy of her station, and a virtuous bringer of splendor to the home; her body was pervaded by radiance, and her beauty surpassed even that of the sun.
She was endowed with all prosperity and was the abode of the Fortune of Sovereignty.
Among all women who were like Nārāyaṇī, she was preeminent in beauty and other qualities.
Upon merely seeing her and reflecting on this by the riverbank, the king quickly descended from his celestial chariot and joyfully paid homage to that ṛṣi.
He honored him like a father and gave his own introduction;
and having heard it, the sage Kāṇḍāyana then rejoiced at Manu.
Seeing the king, the son of Brahmā, he worshiped him in return.
The maiden also arrived quickly and performed the hospitable reception for Manu.
Having inquired after each other's welfare, they indeed praised the sight of one another.
Manu, having bowed to the Brahmin, remained silent for a moment.
The sage said quickly, "O Manu! What may I do for you? Manu replied, "O Guru, whatever desire dwells within my heart—if you are capable in this matter, you ought to fulfill it."
Having thoroughly understood Manu’s mind through meditation, the sage questioned his virtuous daughter, who was inclined toward renunciation, for the sake of making a gift:
"Tell me, daughter, Manu desires you; what shall I do? (47–48)
The daughter said: "The dharma is equal for me, so that the father's command may be fulfilled.
Good conduct always pleases me, since I have entered the path of the virtuous woman's dharma.
Nevertheless, a maiden remains under the authority of her father; she must act according to her father's word. (49)
"Having obeyed the word of their father, daughters indeed become dependent upon their husbands;
they become truthful, virtuous wives, and devoted to their husbands.
Act as you wish in this matter; I am pleased with your obedience."
Kāṇḍāyana became pleased and gave his daughter to Manu;
through that connection with Manu, he became honored throughout the three worlds.
Having married Brahmaprathā, Manu led her to his own abode.
For the sake of the expansion of the Veda, she granted him the oversight of the kingdom in the three worlds.
Like Manu, that wife of Manu ruled the excellent kingdom;
devoted to the consecration of the household, she always served the virtuous.
Though she was served by virtuous women, she accepted their words of blessing;
during the time of Manu, that chaste lady performed all kinds of sacrifices,
as well as various excellent and meritorious gifts and vows.
She performed all acts of hospitality beautifully.
She attended upon virtuous men and virtuous women, as well as great seers; she served female renunciants and ascetics, and she attended upon those who practice austerities.
When the time for Manu’s term of office was complete,
that virtuous woman traveled with Manu by celestial chariot to my imperishable abode of Hari.
There, she was honored by me and by millions of liberated souls, and questioned by me.
"By what merit have you come here as a syllable? Tell me, O beautiful one.
She replied: "I am a great devotee of the Sātvatas and a servant of the virtuous.
O Blessed One, O Beloved, O Lord of the Beloved, I worship and I bow down to You. (3.79.60)
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, you are omniscient; nevertheless, I am your obedient servant. Just as I am commanded by my beloved husband, the Supreme Lord, so shall I report everything to you; listen to me. (61)
I gave a gift of one hundred thousand gold coins to a twice-born man;
I bestowed gifts of jewels and offered ten billion silver pieces.
I observed the vow of Brahmā, yet because of its fruit, I did not come here.
I performed fifteen-night sacrifices, ten-night and one-night rituals, and a hundred Jyotiṣṭomas; yet even here, I did not attain the fruit thereof.
Having practiced most severe penance for a hundred years on the banks of the Gaṅgā—
I gave away a hundred thousand horses, yet I did not attain the fruit thereof.
I gave ten ayutas of horses and twenty ayutas of milk-yielding cows,
as well as a city of women in charity, yet I did not attain the fruit thereof.
Likewise, I gave away a thousand maidens adorned with golden crescents,
as well as sixty thousand women embellished with every kind of ornament;
and during the Gosava sacrifices, I gave ten arbudas of cows together with their calves.
I did not go there because of the fruit of possessing vessels made of gold, bronze, and other such materials.
(68) In the Āptoryāma sacrifices, one regularly gives ten cows to a twice-born;
I gave a hundred thousand cows multiplied by ten, yet I did not go because of the fruit of that. (69)
I gave ten thousand beautiful horses born in Bāhlīka, adorned with golden garlands and young sprouts; yet I did not go [to heaven] as a result of that merit.
Likewise, I gave eighteen crores of gold coins every single day.
Nor indeed did I ever fail to attend each individual sacrifice for the sake of its fruit.
O Supreme Lord, I gave ten and five crores of green horses with black ears, adorned with golden garlands.
I gave fifteen thousand other elephants— tall, large-bodied, with long tusks and golden ornaments—
and ten million well-adorned chariots with golden frames.

In that sacrifice, I gave away horses yoked to chariots and adorned with golden ornaments. Furthermore, in ten Vājapeya sacrifices, I bestowed the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed by the Vedas, along with all their constituent parts and other requirements.
I indeed gave away great male servants with necklaces around their necks, female servants, and sacrificial fees during ten Rājasūya sacrifices; yet I did not go [to heaven] by the fruit thereof.
And I remained concealed by the waters of the Brahmaputrā river along with the sacrificial fees and other offerings.
Indeed, through gifts of gold and gifts of jewels, I obtained that fruit here from the Nagas;
I gave a hundred million villages to the Brahmins throughout the seven continents,
and I worshipped the gods with sacrifices performed at the throw of a yoke-pin, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of Sadyaska offerings.
I performed thirteen *dvādaśāha* sacrifices during the Pauṇḍarīka rite;
nevertheless, because of those *japā* flowers, I have not come here.
During that sacrifice, I gave eight thousand *kakudmin* cows to the twice-born.
I gave white bulls and white cows adorned with gold;
I gave heaps of gold and jewels, trees laden with pearls, and orchards of grain and crops; likewise, I gave gifts of sugar-candy.
I performed sacrifices lasting eleven days and repeatedly those lasting twelve days,
along with horse-sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), as well as sixteen Ādityāyaṇas.
[There was] a forest a hundred yojanas long, filled with mountains.
I gave necklaces of a single gold coin, fresh ornaments, and great gardens;
yet, despite those merits and the daily and occasional vows I performed, I did not come here. (83–84)
I performed thirty Agni sacrifices, as well as eight Soma sacrifices;
likewise, seven Sarvamedhas and ten Naramedhas,
one hundred and eight Viśvajits, and Aśvamedhas.
Nor did I come here, O Blessed One, by virtue of their merits;
[I came] to the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Brahmā, and likewise to the Irāvatī, to the great river Menakāṅgā, and also to the Bālakṛṣṇa lake. ||86-87||
Furthermore, at Śvetavārddhi, Śītavārddhi, and likewise at Nārāyaṇī,
I performed penance, devoted to the service of the virtuous.
In each of those places, I indeed served the holy men who are adorned by Kṛṣṇa.
And virtuous women were served and gratified with all manner of gifts;
they were fed, honored, gazed upon, touched, and their bodies were massaged; their feet were rubbed, they were bowed to, and they were attended upon. (3.79.89–90)
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa! Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama!
Thus do the saintly men and virtuous women sing this kīrtana in succession.

The virtuous have been pleased with me, and the virtuous women have always been pleased with me. The Brahmins, the sages, and the devoted guests, as well as the Sāttvatas, the goddesses, and the Yoginīs, have all been fully satisfied.
My father was indeed fully gratified by their compliance with his words; having received their great blessings, I attained merit and,
at that very moment, became perfected, virtuous, purifying, and divine.
Possessing a divine body born from the sacrifices of Hari, she is a companion dear to Brahmā.
Together with her beloved husband, she has reached the further shore of Māyā.
I was told by holy men and women: "Go to the imperishable abode of Hari. (95–96)

I am she who has attained this world through service for the sake of obtaining His satisfaction— the Supreme Soul, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Immutable Abode. (97)
"O Kṛṣṇa, take my hand; dwell with me here forever.
Make me your own peerless maidservant, along with Māṇikyā and her companions.
Having been addressed thus, O Lakṣmī, I then made you my companions.
There is indeed no higher duty than service to the virtuous;
it bestows prosperity, liberation, heaven, and likewise peace.
Thus has been described to you here the practice that follows upon giving.
"From both reciting and hearing [this], there shall likewise be enjoyment and liberation.

(101) Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of a Virtuous Woman, such as Worship and Charity; the Residence of the Virtuous Woman Sādhvī—the Wife of Brahmaprathā, the First Consort of Hari—in Heaven; and the Fruit of Serving Saints and Holy Women, including the Departure for the Abode of Akṣara," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
