Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Service to saintly persons and saintly women bestows the supreme fruit; it grants a full lifespan eternally. (1)
Dharma is characterized by conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by their behavior. Whatever is the actual way of life of the good people—that is the definition of conduct.
Even if one has not seen him, by his reputation alone, one may recognize a virtuous person who practices the true Dharma.
Even those living far away remember the subjects who perform acts of devotion.
(3) One who desires his own prosperity should indeed protect the dharma of the virtuous;
for the bull among the virtuous destroys the sin even of one whose body is sinful. (4)
Through the practice of right conduct, a full lifespan is attained:

ten thousand years in the Kṛta age, ten thousand years in the Tretā age, one thousand years in the Dvāpara age, and even a hundred years in the Tiṣya (Kali) age; thus a full lifespan is always produced.
From good conduct, prosperity is always present; in the home of one who practices good conduct, the Goddess Śrī dwells permanently.
Fame arises for the practitioner of good conduct both in this world and in the next.
It is my view that good conduct is the cause of the favor of the virtuous and of long life.
Everything else is indeed subject to sublation, but the word of the virtuous is never sublated.
Those endowed with devotion to me, possessed of good character and vows, tranquil in form, intent on the work of my worship, and the ornaments of the righteous— these are the true saints.
They rescue even the dead and purify those who are living.
(9) For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world;
for living beings tremble before him, and fear is the destroyer of life. (3.80.10)
Those who are revilers of the virtuous, cruel, transgressors of the commands of their gurus and the scriptures, unrighteous, and of evil conduct—they become short-lived.
Those who are arrogant, who have broken the bounds of propriety, who are violent, and who are addicted to sensual objects—[they too are short-lived]. (11)

Those who are devoid of devotion become short-lived and shameless. (1.2) Indeed, even a person who lacks all auspicious marks, if they possess noble conduct and are endowed with faith and devotion, is a virtuous one who lives for a full span of years. (1.3)
Free from envy, truthful in speech, and devoid of anger, deceit, and the like; straightforward and non-violent, such a person lives for a full hundred years.
One who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites their nails, and is covered in filth [does not live long].
One whose mind is unsteady does not attain a supreme lifespan here;
nor indeed does one who is unfaithful or profligate live for long.
For there exists nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as these.
Just as there is no atonement here for a man who consorts with another’s wife,
so too one who betrays his guru, betrays his father, or betrays a holy man does not live;
nor does one who betrays women, betrays his mother, or betrays the gods live.
One who harbors passion for women, one who attempts to cross a river, and one who practices with weapons do not live long.
Indeed, a drinker of liquor, an eater of meat, one whose mouth shoots word-arrows, and one who pierces the vital organs are beset by extreme disease and do not live for long. (18–19)
One consumed by a curse, one who acts with reckless violence, and one who does not live for long;
one who practices malevolent magic, a murderer, and one who neglects the worship of those worthy of worship;
one who slays those who have sought refuge, and one who kills those under his own control—in every way, these are to be avoided. (3.80.20)
A betrayer of trust and a slayer of children does not live for long at all.
One who binds with a noose, one who pierces with a spear, one who destroys the testicles, one who binds the female organ, and those who destroy the fetus,
one who destroys the fertile season, one who destroys living beings, and a stealer of honey— these do not live.
One who follows the profession of a hunter, a wheel-maker, or a butcher does not live long.
One afflicted by poison, one with a spirit-possession, one suffering from wind-disorders (vāyu), consumption, urinary disorders (prameha),
phlegm-disorders, asthma, blood-disorders, or weak digestion, as well as one who causes distress to others, does not survive.
One who seizes by force, one who sets fire [to a dwelling], and one who travels through the sky do not live [long].
He who is a constant traveler, a deceiver, a consumer of intoxicants, and one addicted to opium does not live for long at all. (24–25)
He who rises early to salute his mother, father, teacher, preceptor, the virtuous, the chaste wife, the husband, the deity, and the elderly,
and who always eats what is wholesome, shall live for a long time. (26)
One who eats ghee and consumes clarified butter attains a long life.
(27) Indeed, one who eats while facing the east finds great longevity.
One who eats food mixed with wholesome ghee shall certainly become long-lived. (28)
One who eats with wet feet certainly lives a full lifespan.
One who is still impure from eating must never touch the four luminaries:
fire, a cow, a Brahmin, or a virtuous person; thus, his life will not be harmed.
For the vital breaths of a young man indeed ascend when an elder approaches;
he recovers them by rising to meet him and by saluting him.
One who is impure from eating should not touch the head, for all the vital breaths are dependent upon it.
One should not bathe one’s head too frequently; thus one’s lifespan will not be impaired. One should not eat food mixed with sesame seeds; thus one’s lifespan will not be impaired.
However, if one studies on a day when study is forbidden, one’s lifespan is diminished.
Those who urinate facing the sun, facing fire, facing a cow, or facing a woman,
as well as those who urinate on a path, become short-lived.
There is no doubt that reviling one's teachers consumes the lifespan of human beings.
One who desires to live long should not cause distress to a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, or a serpent; one should not revile a virtuous man, a chaste woman, a cow, a deity, or the sacred law (dharma).
One should not seek conversation with those who have fallen from their status and should avoid looking upon them.
One should certainly not associate with them; thus one attains a long life.
(36) One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day, nor with a maiden, nor with a harlot, nor should one approach a woman who has not bathed; thus one attains a long life. (37)
The elderly, the virtuous, virtuous women, the gods, and the supreme gurus are worthy of worship;
they should be invited to dwell in one's home, for that brings both merit and long life.
To show disrespect toward great-souled beings always causes the depletion of one’s lifespan.
The most secret matters of great-souled ones must never be spoken.
One should praise virtuous and holy men; thus one attains a long life.
One should never sleep during the twilight hours; by reciting prayers for a long time, one lives long.
One should have the work of shaving performed while facing either the east or the north;
one should not utter slander, for in this way one attains a long life.
Envy is detrimental to longevity, as is the disparagement of those worthy of honor.
Sleeping during the day shortens one's lifespan, as does such behavior as adultery.
(42) Right conduct generates prosperity; right conduct increases fame.
Indeed, through right conduct life is prolonged, and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (46)
Dharma originates from right conduct, and from Dharma, life is increased. The benedictions of the virtuous truly bestow long life.
Mārkaṇḍeya’s possession of long life resulted from the words of the Seven Sages.
Indeed, that is the supreme illustration from the words of the Creator as well:
Nāciketa likewise met death due to his father’s anger;
and those monkeys who were slain in battle were restored to life by Rāmacandra.
O Rame, the body is twofold: the material body and the form of fame.
The material body depends upon longevity, while fame is bound to one's conduct.
Through blessings, the auspicious longevity of the material body increases here in this world.
Through right conduct and service, auspicious fame increases.
Through virtuous deeds, a mass of merit grows along with fame.
And through devotion, both arise and increase eternally.
If someone virtuous or a virtuous female practitioner of Brahman-yoga should arise in a family,
that family will certainly attain fame and secure renown in the world.
For indeed, in a meritorious family, men are known for their noble conduct.
Indeed, in a wicked family, many kinds of evil people are born.
In whatever family sinful men are born, all manner of misfortunes arise;
they surely produce infamy and even destroy one's reputation.
A single son who is learned and devoted brings forth fame;
he alone, being of virtuous conduct, delivers his kinsmen in this world.
If a daughter or a daughter-in-law should likewise be virtuous and of good conduct, [the same result follows].
Having purified his entire lineage, he certainly delivers it.
(54) In whose heart the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa resides, by him the worlds are delivered; or she [the Goddess] certainly delivers them. (55)
His lineage shall be long-lived, his fame shall endure for a long time, and liberation is certain for him; from her, auspicious offspring are born.
In this matter, the teacher (upādhyāya) is said to be ten times superior to the preceptors (ācāryas).
In every respect, a father is ten times more excellent than a teacher;
a mother is always more venerable than ten fathers.
A virtuous, chaste, and devoted wife is as great as ten mothers.
Endowed with virtue, devoted to the holy life, and indeed fond of Brahman,
she is my own form— ever chaste, Vaiṣṇavī,
and Nārāyaṇī; she is Kārṣṇī, Mādhavī, Lakṣmī, and indeed the power (Śakti) of the Supreme Person.
I am always of virtuous form in all creations;
indeed, the virtuous are my very own form, and the virtuous women are my powers.
O beloved, they all bestow my abode and are all purifiers.
In all creations, there is nothing more purifying than the virtuous;
there is no merit or austerity equal to service rendered to the virtuous in every respect.
Those wealthy with riches serve embodied beings worthy of worship solely through their wealth.
The poor who are rich in service to the virtuous attain the eternal Brahman.
The wealthy indeed go to heaven, while the poor go to the divine abode;
for though lacking wealth, they serve the holy ones with their very bodies and with devotion.
They perform fasts that bestow the fruit of ten million sacrifices;
therefore, the sacrifice of service is superior to a sacrifice consisting of material wealth.
A sacred ford (tīrtha) should always be joyfully resorted to by oneself as a means of liberation.
The gross sacred site (*tīrtha*) consists of earth, water, and so forth; the subtle is the service of the virtuous.
The divine sacred site is the purification of the mind; one should practice the service of those sacred sites.
One who is purified at the sacred site of the mind is liberated at the sacred site of the Self (*ātman*).

One should bathe in the mental sacred ford— a deep, stainless, pure lake whose waters are truth— relying upon eternal goodness. O Lakṣmī, listen as I proclaim this purity of the sacred ford, which bestows liberation.
That by which goodness arises and by which illusion is destroyed—
namely, non-appropriation, lack of desire, straightforwardness, truthfulness, as well as non-violence, gentleness, tranquility, compassion, self-restraint, and inner peace. (3.80.70)
Freedom from possessiveness, freedom from egoism, freedom from the pairs of opposites, and purity— these are the qualities by which virtuous people become sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
A knower of Brahman is a great ford, a savior that destroys all sin.
Delighting in all forms of renunciation, possessing devotion and knowledge, and viewing all things with equanimity;
free from the impurities of passion, peaceful, virtuous, and the ornaments of the sacred ford—therein, having bathed in the supreme purity of the mind, one is liberated. (72–73)
One whose body is merely moistened with water is not truly called "bathed.
He who has bathed with self-control is the one who is pure both externally and internally.
Those who are always free from the sense of "mine" do not grieve for what is past, even when it was directly perceived.
For those in whom no longing arises, their purity is indeed like that of a sacred ford.
Absence of possessions for the body, clarity of the mind,
and the purity of knowledge regarding the self— these are the three true sacred fords.
Purity of conduct pertains to the body, purity of vows pertains to the mind, and purity of the sacred ford pertains to the self; these three indeed bring about liberation.
The supreme purity arises from knowledge, consisting of the water of the realization of Brahman.
He who bathes there in the mental lake attains liberation; of this there is no doubt.
A person who has established purity through the realization of reality, who is constantly endowed with devotion, and who is perfected by the virtues of service, is always a true sacred ford (tīrtha).
By the glorification of the holy place, by bathing there, and by the libations offered to the ancestors, all sins are consumed; thereafter, one goes to the imperishable state.
This occurs through the acceptance of the virtuous and by capturing the mind of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

By being bathed in the river of devotion, they cross over the darkness of material nature. (8.1) Indeed, the virtuous are the best of holy places, and goodness itself is the most excellent of holy places. He who bathes in both shall quickly attain perfection. (8.2)
Good conduct is the highest dharma, and it is indeed the supreme sacred ford.
By carrying out the dharma of the virtuous together with them, an individual attains the supreme goal.
Dharma alone is the companion for human beings in the world beyond.
If that [state] is attained here through the service of the virtuous, it then becomes divine;
it bestows liberation, bestows the [divine] abode, and is the supreme giver of eternal bliss.
There is no dharma equal to the Dharma of Liberation (mokṣadharma) that is more exalted within all creations.

The Dharma consisting of all sacred fords is the Dharma of liberation found among the virtuous. By him who has protected, served, and propitiated the virtuous, every Dharma has been performed and the Supreme Self has been propitiated. (86)
For one who has become the self of all beings, who perceives all beings [as himself],

and who is intent on serving the virtuous, the supreme state of liberation shall come to be. Just as, indeed, all other footprints are contained within the footprint of an elephant, so too is everything contained within that state.
In that same way, all virtues enter into the service of the virtuous;
for those who serve the virtuous, the world of Brahmā is ordained.
[This was achieved] by Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa, Gaya, and Citraketu.
By Āyu, Anaraṇya, and King Dilīpa; by Śibi, Mucukunda, Māndhātṛ, and Bharata;
likewise by Janaka, Rukmāṅgada, and King Alarka. || 3.80.90–91 ||
By Pṛthu, by Sāgara, by the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, and by these kings, the virtuous have always been served;
the virtuous and the truthful have been honored, and thus I, the Supreme Self, have been worshipped.
Having bathed in the sacred ford of the Self and being strengthened by the auspicious blessings of the holy ones, they became devoted to the dharma of the virtuous and attained the supreme goal.
[This occurs] as long as the pacification of the activities of all the sense organs has not yet arisen. (93–94)
As long as there is the cessation of activity, so long does saṃsāra continue, creating the flow of existence and death;
for when activity ceases, there is goodness, and in goodness, supreme liberation.
Indeed, all the messengers of Nārāyaṇa here are virtuous ones.
Having caused monuments of fame to be built, they lead [beings] to the imperishable abode.
(96) These virtuous women are indeed the saving powers of Nārāyaṇa;
having caused service to Hari to be performed, they lead [beings] to the imperishable abode. (97)
All those who are beloved of Brahmā, virtuous, devoted to their husbands,
followers of the Bhāgavatas, and adherents of the Sātvata path, have been born by my will through divine play in various lands for the sake of the welfare of those regions. (98)

It was solely for the purpose of instilling devotion toward me among the people that those virtuous women were born as my wives. May you all, being steadfast in your husband Śrī Kṛṣṇa, protect the duties of virtuous wives. (3.80.99–100)

those sinful cravings, and the innumerable sins— [all these must be abandoned]. (74)
All those deeds performed by the courtesans, whatever they may have been—
by the touch of my feet, by the touch of my linga,
and even by bearing my dust, they have indeed departed from their bodies.
And having beheld the sanctity of your bodies, those sins—
which were indeed unable to remain— have fled away in all directions, taking the form of moths.
(77) All those sins have thus become like moths.
Having become all things, they have gone to Lake Mānasa in the Himalayas;
there a lake shall truly come into being, and their liberation will be through dissolution.
By my yoga, indeed, the sins of all have been cast out.
"Then, all of you together, receive this supreme mantra.
Having said this, he gave the mantra to the courtesans—the mantra of mine:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā."
Having received the mantra of the Gaṇikā goddesses, they quickly became four-armed;
having become the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavī goddesses with divine bodies and great beauty,
the Nārāyaṇīs went by means of celestial chariots to my imperishable abode.
"Thousands of those courtesans then became beloved of Hari;
they remain in my imperishable abode, devoted to my service.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even through association with the virtuous, even unchaste women [attain this state]. (83)
One who is rich in dharma becomes instantly purified and becomes a servant of the divine.
Therefore, service to the virtuous is the purifier of even the most heinous sins;
by whatever disposition they may be served, they purify one.
Then other courtesans, having heard this, approached that sage;
for their purification, he then taught them the science of love (kāmaśāstra). Having caused them to hear it, having instructed them, and having bestowed his own service upon them, he then [departed].
The great sage Vātsyāyana also brought about their liberation.
And Śaṅkara himself, having become manifest in bodily form, became the object of his perception and said:
"O Sage, you are blessed, for you have effected the liberation of courtesans."

O virtuous one, you are of a noble nature; having fulfilled your desire as you well-considered it, you remain entirely unstained by passion, O author of the Kāmaśāstra. Just as I am both the burner of passion and its healer, so too are you.
Just as Kṛṣṇa is the conqueror of desire even while delighting [others],
so too you shall be the conqueror of desire even while describing it.
O virtuous one, become a bestower of liberation upon women by destroying their sin.
"The scripture shall become renowned in the world by your very name.
Having spoken thus, Lord Śaṅkara, your father, vanished;
and that virtuous one wandered upon the surface of the earth in Kāśī.
Vātsyāyana, who liberates all classes of living beings, is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
By reading, hearing, remembering, and even serving this [work], great sins are destroyed and the attainment of liberation becomes certain. (93–94)

Thus has been told, O Lakṣmī, this secret concerning the service of the virtuous— a divine narrative that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants a divine state of being. (95) Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the third book, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*, concerning how even wanton women, lustful women, unchaste women, and courtesans attained liberation after the destruction of their sins through their meeting with the virtuous Vātsyāyana in Kāśī, and so forth.
The eighty-second chapter, titled "Description," [Chapter 82] from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age;
Chapter 83.
[Author: Chapter 84.
Śrī Nārāyaṇīśrī said: For what reason indeed is the virtuous one called Nārāyaṇa?
Although there may be many reasons for that among those of firm resolve,
nevertheless, please speak of that reason which is either simple, or the most excellent and unsurpassed, or even difficult to comprehend. (1–2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the various causes of greatness:
forbearance, good character, dispassion, tranquility, and non-possessiveness. (3)
Freedom from thirst, being devoid of attachment to flavors, and abiding in the Self; lack of greed, freedom from hatred and the like, and universal friendliness;
the duty of performing the means for self-realization, and the total surrender of everything unto Me. (4)

Affectionlessness, freedom from bondage, emptiness, and the avoidance of service for the sake of illusion; (5) the acquisition of only what is necessary for the maintenance of the body, senses, and so forth; the expectation of the world of liberation, and likewise the abandonment of "mine" and "I. (6)
The cessation of the onset of new impulses and stability within the self, and not elsewhere,
as well as the purity of mind and good character, are indeed the causes for saintliness.
For one who possesses altruism, there is the revelation of the path to liberation.
He who possesses the supreme vow and moral conduct for the sake of Nārāyaṇa;
he who possesses fierce austerity free from the bondage of Māyā; and he whose every mental activity is always within my sphere of perception—[to him I grant my grace]. (8–9)
O Lakṣmī, these four alone are the primary causes of saintliness;
for neither saffron robes, nor external marks,
nor initiation, nor dress are the supreme means to saintliness.
Those who obstruct my own liberation, those who desire liberation through illusion and the like,

ascetics who are experts in the Supreme Brahman and the best among holy men, as well as virtuous women devoted to the dharma of faithful wives and intent on moral conduct— [may they all be destroyed]. 1–2.
Virtuous women who are devoid of passion, full of devotion, and adorned by their own virtue—
this freedom from attachment to bodily enjoyments is the first step on the ladder of the virtuous. Freedom from passion for the sense organs is the second step.
Subjugation of the internal organ is the third step;
the offering of the self to Kṛṣṇa is the fourth step;
and the abiding of my form within one's knowledge is the fifth step. (14–15)
The effort toward the fruit of liberation is indeed the sixth step;
the constant abiding in the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*) is the final step.
One who has ascended these seven steps is truly a virtuous person, the most excellent of the good.
Moreover, those virtuous women who possess such conduct are considered by me to be the most excellent of the virtuous. Indeed, these virtuous women whom I have described belong to the highest rank;
now listen as I show you those who belong to the middle rank. (17–18)
Those who are attached to the body, senses, and so forth, and who desire the pleasure produced by them, are different;
however, those who offer everything to Kṛṣṇa and surrender their very selves to me—though Māyā possesses secondary power, they find their supreme refuge in my power. (19)
Such are the middling ones, O beloved, who are virtuous men and virtuous women.
Now, hear from me, Lakṣmī, about those even lower than them, who act for my sake:
they are entirely possessed by passion and are attached to the body, the senses, and so forth. (3.83.20–21)
Even those who have received initiation and take refuge in me, being intent on their own self-interest,
merely display me before others while remaining dwellers of the renunciant order;
yet they do not perceive even a tiny fraction of the scent of true renunciation.
Nevertheless, even when encountering hardship, those whose minds are base remain as if established on the path of renunciation;
though they bear the yellow banner and are ensnared by the net, they are all indeed called "virtuous" in name alone. (23–24)

Just as an elephant made of wood, or a tiger made of leather, so too is a "sage" who is merely clothed; these three possess useless powers. To the ignorant they cause fear, but to the wise they are like mere stones. (25)
These three betrayers of trust do not grant the desires of those who depend upon them.
They destroy determined objectives, oppose one’s advancement, and like glass ornaments, they bring about ruin through association. (26–27)
Austerity, sacred learning, and power—these are the characteristics of a virtuous person.
Forgiveness, devotion, and detachment are indeed the causes of virtue.
When such a virtuous person is satisfied, the gods and other celestial beings are truly satisfied.

For just as a farmer reaps fruit from a fertile field, so indeed does the giver enjoy the fruit after having offered it to a virtuous person. What is given to one who is not virtuous becomes fruitless; there is no doubt about this.
The one who is not virtuous destroys the food, and the one being eaten destroys him;
but the virtuous man protects that food, and he preserves the food for the future.
That preservation, when bestowed upon a worthy recipient, ensures its benefit even in the next world. (31)
For the virtuous master, by eating food, nourishes even his donor.
Therefore, one should bestow food upon a worthy recipient through meritorious action;
for the merit gained by the giver is exactly the same as that of the receiver.
If both recipients should indeed be virtuous and stainless vessels—
wherever there are holy men endowed with learning and good conduct—
the meritorious fruit of a gift produced there is truly manifold, even a thousandfold.

Those who are pure in their spiritual practice (*brahma*), constantly pure in their ethical conduct (*śīla*), and virtuous; those who are devoted to austerity and are full of devotion—they are indeed most worthy of worship.
The path established by those holy ones is truly divine; of this there is no doubt. (35–36)
Those who have traveled by that [path] are not deluded even in the realm of Māyā, the domain of Īśvara;
for the virtuous, whose vehicle is Brahman, reach the further shore.
It is difficult to follow, difficult to assail, difficult to attain, and difficult to transcend.
Through a true blessing, everything is attained; there is no doubt in this.
Even a drinker of liquor, a killer of an embryo, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—by means of a holy man, all is crossed over and one is liberated from every sin.
For the virtuous who possess knowledge are worthy of worship by all, possessing the wealth that is truly venerable;
those who practice austerity, delight in giving, and are full of devotion are indeed saviors. They lead one to this world of Brahmā and to the unsurpassed state of liberation.
Worldly people who have performed meritorious deeds attain the service of the virtuous.
When honored, these virtuous ones honor them in return; when respected, they likewise show respect.
Indeed, by kindling the fires that consume the sins of the wicked, the virtuous deliver them across [the ocean of suffering].
Where there is such mutual goodness—that the master is pleased with his servants and the servants are pleased with their master—there lie millions of blessings.
Just as impurity is removed from the body by water, or darkness by the light of fire; ||| 43 ||
Likewise, through service to a virtuous person, one likewise dispels all evil.
Such a person brings well-being to all and purifies embodied beings;
devoted to these practices, the virtuous person is the bringer of welfare in the three worlds.
O Lakṣmī, for the liberation of living beings, I have composed this Sāman.
The virtuous sing this Sāman here to awaken people;
they instruct them in the mantras and the like, and they glorify me repeatedly.
They describe my stories and my many deeds;
they describe my virtues and my activities in every way.
Thus, indeed, those virtuous ones recite [my praises] with conciliatory words and songs.
The learned constantly praise me through the portals of the scriptures;
the poets compose verses about me, and those who accomplish their goals offer hymns of praise.
Thus, indeed, do human beings purify me in many ways through the Sāman chants.
Having obtained [the mantra] from the mouth of the Guru through conciliation (sāman), one should worship me with the gift (dāna).
Giving with a total state of being is what is meant by "offering" (nivedita);
the offering of oneself is the true gift, and by that one should always win me.
The virtuous acquire [merit] through the practice of giving and they also bestow it:
the gift of knowledge, the gift of mantra, the gift of the name of Hari, as well as the gift of grace, the offering of garlands and the like, and the imparting of instruction. ||52||
The gift of gain, the gift of happiness, and the gift of liberation are supreme among the supreme.
(53) That gift which bestows fearlessness is a gift of austerity and a locus of auspiciousness.
The virtuous, who are the ornaments of the righteous, perform such gifts of merit. (54)
The gift of compassion, as well as the bestowing of delightful blessings, the granting of one's sight, and the gift of service bring auspiciousness.
Indeed, by means of these various ways, the virtuous bestow excellent qualities. (55)
They indeed acquire both me and Hari, and they bestow them upon their devotees as well.
Having performed the initiation and the gift of themselves, they deliver others;
having performed the auspicious gift of devotion, they deliver people from worldly existence.
Finally, by providing shelter, offering the nectar of their feet, giving words of counsel, and even acting as witnesses, they deliver others.
They also grant the gift of their minds, the gift of affection, and the bestowing of purity and other virtues.
By bestowing instruction in the practice of noble conduct and granting the gift of mindfulness, they enable others to cross over;

by making gifts of necklaces and gifts of insignia, they too enable others to cross over; and by making gifts of images and gifts of worthy recipients, they too enable others to cross over. (3.83.59–60)
Now they apply the distinction where neither gift nor conciliation is effective:
"This body is joined with impurity, defiled, and momentary;
the self, however, is pure, a devotee of Hari, fit for liberation, and eternal. (6.1)
In this way, the virtuous indeed apply discernment and discrimination.
Then they administer punishment as an expiation for the unrighteous;
the holy ones restrain those who have strayed from the path by means of their noble vows.
By means of expiatory rites consisting of actions such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
by great sacrifices and festivals involving the expenditure of wealth and joyful celebrations;
and by food-donations such as communal meals, as well as worship, giving, and offerings.
They engage them in purifying efforts that lead to the highest good;
they also compel them to perform duties such as religious acts,
or else the virtuous restrain them by means of severe punishment.
"Just as sins may be destroyed and liberation itself attained,
so indeed do the virtuous apply corrective discipline for one's own benefit.
However, they sometimes administer a severe punishment even to those who are most arrogant."
For the sake of their purification and for the sake of their liberation,
the virtuous urge them toward divine and auspicious punishment, such as the recitation of prayers (*japa*) and so forth;
by means of which, having attained freedom from stain, they go to the supreme state.
Whether he be sinful or meritorious, or a mixture of both,
whether he be devoted or undevoted, an atheist or even a theist— whosoever that embodied being may be, they lead him to take refuge before [the Lord].
Having refined them through various means, they purify them again and again;
having constantly gladdened them and made them pure and eternal, the virtuous then lead them to their own equal, imperishable abode. (71–72)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the quality of being intent on helping others is ever-present in the virtuous;
indeed, it cannot be obtained through any recompense, and by means of it embodied beings are purified.
Just as I am, so too are your gurus, the saviors of the world.
The virtuous, from their nails to the crown of their heads, are my pure forms.
Just as a piece of sugar-candy is sweet and of excellent flavor in every part,
and there is no portion of it that is not so, even so are you, the holy ones, to me.
Or just as a lump of butter is entirely composed of fat,
such that there is no part of it that is not so, even so are those holy ones to me.
Or just as a pearl is pure, or a crystal is transparent, [so too are they].
Just as the Kaustubha gem [is dear to me], so are those virtuous ones to me.
Or as Gaurī is to Kāmadhenu, or as milk is to waterless [desert land], or as pure gold is—so are those virtuous ones to me. (77–78)
Just as the wish-fulfilling gem is supreme, as is the celestial wish-granting tree,
and as the wish-granting creeper is most excellent, so too are those holy ones to me.
Just as my heart is supreme, and as my form is the highest, [so are they].
Just as the Imperishable is the supreme abode, so are my virtuous ones to me.
(3.83.80) Just as Viṣṇu is eternally pure, just as good conduct is the highest vow, and just as peace is the greatest wealth, so are my virtuous ones to me. (3.83.81)
As a field rich with grain, as a cow ready to calve,
as a sacrifice concluded with its sacrificial fee— so are the virtuous ones to me.
As trees laden with fruit and as creepers abundant with flowers.
Just as one who performs wonders, so are those holy men of mine;
just as the earth consists of jewels, and just as Māyā consists of the qualities (guṇas), and just as the Self is enriched with the three states (avasthās), so are those holy men of mine. (83–84)
Just as I am possessed of all powers, and just as Lakṣmī is indeed all prosperity;
just as everything has Kṛṣṇa as its soul, so too are my saints yours.
Just as the Sudarśana discus is [mine], and just as the staff belongs to Yama; [so are they].
Just as Viṣṇu possesses clarity, so do those virtuous ones toward me.
(86) Just as is the devotion shown to Śambhu, just as is the service rendered to Satī, and just as is the affection felt for Kāma, so do those virtuous ones feel toward me. (87)
Just as forgiveness is the ultimate goal of the virtuous, just as speech directed toward a devotee,
and just as service rendered to a saintly woman, so too are you considered by the holy ones to be such [a person].
Just as a vow is fulfilled through one's wife, and just as satisfaction belongs to one free from craving.
Just as the waters of the Gaṅgā are purifying, so too are those virtuous ones to me.
(89) Just as a lineage passes through a son, just as a gift bestowed upon a daughter, and just as worship directed toward Gaṇeśa, so too are those virtuous ones to me. (3.83.90)
"Just as I am truly virtuous and you shine as a virtuous woman, and just as our union is indeed [fitting], so too are the virtuous yours and mine.
What more need I say? No further praise can be found here. (9.1)
"O Blessed Ones, you are my virtuous [refuge]; I am devoted to the righteous in every way.
He who, without offering to the virtuous, eats merely to fill his own belly, is born in a desolate land as a wretched Brahmarākṣasa."
He who rejoices at home without performing worship appropriate for the virtuous,
out of self-conceit, becomes a Brahmarākṣasa at the end of his body;
even though endowed with wealth and power, he does not serve holy people.
He who reviles and despises others shall become a Brahmarākṣasa.
He who, bound by pride in his own virtues, looks down upon those who are wise and virtuous, and who despises the poor, shall become a Brahmarākṣasa. (95–96)
He who treats even invincible and virtuous men with contempt and imputes false faults to them shall become a *brahmarākṣasa*. He who,
acting as a lord, subjects virtuous men who have no enemies to suffering [shall likewise become one].
Even one who was accomplished, if he dies afterwards, is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*.
Even a learned man, by insulting and showing contempt for the virtuous and peaceful, and even if he is being degraded by those of evil conduct, becomes a *brahmarākṣasa*. (98–99)
But he who is a friend in appearance yet a foe,

a slayer by his very breath, ignoble and a hater of the noble, is born as a *brahmarākṣasa*. And he who, while existing among the wicked, mimics the conduct of the virtuous, [is likewise reborn as such].

One who praises those with wicked dispositions is born as a Brahmarākṣasa. (101) But he who, though devoid of great virtues, desires everything great, and who insults the virtuous—upon attaining that [state], he is born as a Brahmarākṣasa. (102)

He who treats with contempt by force an ascetic, one endowed with forgiveness, a preceptor, a man of realized knowledge, or a lord, is born as a Brahmarākṣasa. Likewise, he who, upon seeing holy men wandering in the forest, does not rise up before them [is also born as such].
He who does not act for his own welfare is indeed a Rākṣasa while living.
Even a Rākṣasa, having bowed down, serves the virtuous devotees of Hari;
he propitiates them with his services and receives their blessings.
O Lakṣmī, he who accepts the virtues that grant happiness from a virtuous person becomes indeed a true saint in this world, one whose conduct is righteous.
Neither birth, nor effort, nor outward appearance brings about saintliness. (106)
The service of the company of the virtuous and other such means are the causes for the attainment of saintliness.
O Lakṣmī, those very [saints] are the saviors; by seeing them, by touching them, by serving them, and by attending upon them, embodied beings cross over the cycle of existence.

Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Various Causes and Conditions for Righteousness, as well as the Results of Praising and Not Praising the Righteous," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 84: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 84.
[The Author: Chapter 85.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O ocean of mercy, O bond of living beings, O Lord of my own life-breaths, O All-pervading One!

When a body of a man or woman—a field for karma—has been obtained that brings about auspicious results, yet one is entirely destitute, seeking welfare, poor, and lacking in fortune, such that even the company of holy men is not found there at all; [in that state... (1–2)
In that regard, what liberation can one obtain by performing the prescribed rite?
How does one who desires his own spiritual welfare attain that welfare?
(3) Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! You ask about what is most excellent and auspicious.
This human birth is the supreme field for action;
having obtained this, one should by all means perform service to one's mother, who is the sacred pilgrimage site of the home.
In whatever way one's own mother may become pleased, in that very way,
having served her, one should indeed obtain her blessings which bestow great merit,
destroy poverty, and grant auspicious prosperity.
The fortune of even one devoid of luck increases through service to his mother;

for the mother is Nārāyaṇī and Brāhmī, and she brings about welfare through her blessing. (7) Thus, auspicious service should be rendered to the father, who is the very embodiment of sacred pilgrimage sites.
Indeed, by receiving their blessing, one obtains well-being and merit.
(8) One's fortune shall become vast and prosperous, filled with excellence. Then, through such service and the dawning of good fortune, there arises a virtuous mind. (9)
One should then acquire knowledge by contemplating the meaning of the scriptures;
after knowledge comes discernment, and thereafter one should meditate upon me, Hari.
One should always meditate and practice auspicious devotion unto me alone.
Wherein the mind may attain purity and steadiness in many ways, one should perform the chanting of the Name: "Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama. (11–12)
Thus, indeed, while performing and causing others to perform kīrtana and supreme worship,
one should establish friends and cause fellow devotees to flourish.
Subsequently, one should establish a circle for association with the saintly and worship Me.

One should always perform my *kīrtana*, and in the evening, one should form a circle (*maṇḍala*) in a single place. Those who are devotees of Hari within that circle should then be understood as saintly persons (*sādhu*s), through the gain of hearing the scriptures or by the words of the elders. (14–15)
Having obtained virtuous qualities and friends, one should then increase the company of the righteous;
by doing so, one should indeed expand one's own circle.
Truly, through the power of great merit arising from the circle of the company of the righteous—

The desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) is the highest; from that, through devotion of pure disposition, one should worship Me and accomplish one's own spiritual welfare—he is the king of devotees. Thus, O Lakṣmī, he should always increase his own innate strength along with its seed.
That which nourishes association with the virtuous leads to both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
indeed, there is no easier means of practice equal to the chanting of the Name.
For one who has not attained the company of the saintly, the chanting of the Name is supreme.
One’s own virtuous tongue should be awakened; one should practice union with it.
One’s own virtuous intellect should be awakened; through it, one should contemplate Mādhava.
One’s own virtuous mind should be awakened; by means of it, one should always contemplate Me.
Thinking, "The Lord is virtuous," one should serve Keśava;
having thus attained such an association, one should worship me, the eternal.
Teachers and gurus are the performers of millions of auspicious deeds.
Thus, by their own power alone, they themselves crossed the ocean of existence;
and by the grace of Śrī Hari, they caused others to cross as well.
For Hari assists his own striving devotee here, even when that devotee is without any other aid.
Having descended there himself and dwelt even within the heart,
or having dwelt in the midst of the circle of devotees, he bestows the highest good.
O beloved, no one who performs kīrtana ever encounters anything inauspicious.
He alone is truly virtuous there who is born through chanting [my names].

O Lakṣmī, even a dog-eater in whose house I am being glorified is like a saint; for he is a virtuous-minded person, affectionately devoted to the saintly, and is indeed like a saint, even if he dwells far away.

Even a leather-worker who is rich in virtue, devoted to me, affectionate toward the virtuous, and a true saint who glorifies me while performing his own duties; even a barbarian, if he is endowed with virtue and devoted to me— [is likewise dear]. (28)
One who is affectionate toward the virtuous, who speaks of me as truly virtuous, and who is non-violent;
even a hunter who kills is indeed virtuous if he abandons killing, being affectionate toward the virtuous, speaking of me as truly virtuous, and being non-violent. (2.84.29–30)
Whether he be a banner-bearer or a wheel-bearer, a virtuous man devoted to the love of the saintly,
observant of moral conduct and vows, non-violent, and chanting my praises day and night;
or whether she be a courtesan or a woman of loose conduct— provided they are both devoted to the love of the saintly.
The virtuous, established in their vows, praise me while being free from desire.
(32) Even a fisherman who eats fish may be one who observes the vow of non-violence;
such a virtuous person, devoted to love for the good, praises me as the Supreme Lord. (33)
If the Jallādas, Hārakas, and Stenas— who are devoted to affection for the virtuous—
and the Sādhus, who possess moral conduct and vows yet are devoid of action, cry out to me;
or if the Bhujiṣyas and Vṛndalas are likewise Sādhus devoted to moral conduct.
They praise me, Hari, the Supreme Person, with virtuous affection.
(35) Merchants, actors, dancers, and bards—virtuous men who possess good character and vows, who are affectionately devoted to the saintly, and who praise me, Hari. (36)
They assume many forms, engage in jesting, carry corpses, and act as virtuous ascetics;
they observe vows and disciplines, are affectionate toward holy men, and glorify me, Hari.
From all sides, some have prostitutes for their mistresses, others eat iguanas, and some feed on snakes.
The virtuous, observers of vows, and those affectionately devoted to the good cry out to me:
"O fish-catchers and meat-eaters, abandon your cruel way of life!
The virtuous, observers of vows, and those affectionately devoted to the good cry out to me! (38–39)

"Those who set fires, those who administer poison, those who wield spears, and even those who cast nooses—[all these] cry out against me. For the virtuous are indeed gentle and affectionate toward the good. Even if one who lives by the sword, a physician, or one who dismembers corpses [should act thus]," [2.84.40]
Indeed, the virtuous, who are kind and affectionate toward the good, cry out to me; even the bharṛbhaṭṭhīkaras, who destroy the forests and wildernesses,
being devoted to virtue and kind toward the good, truly cry out to me.
Mad, insane, deceitful, and self-interested indeed are the wicked;
those who are affectionate toward the virtuous, devoted to moral conduct, and possessed of good qualities cry out to me.
Even the asuras, rākṣasas, daityas, dānavas, and sinners [cry out].
Even when they cry out to me, the virtuous ones who are affectionate toward the good and possessed of moral conduct are truly saintly.
For even the spirits, ghosts, and piśācas who cry out to me are indeed saintly;
they are devoted to moral conduct, firm in their vows of goodness, and likewise affectionate toward me.
The honey-gatherers, the fish-catchers, and the bird-killers are indeed virtuous;
they are of good character, affectionate toward the good, and free from worldly action—they are the ones who cry out to me.
Those who carry beasts of burden, those who keep birds in cages, and those who are betrayers of trust [are not so].
Indeed, virtuous men of good character and sincere affection cry out to me: "O virtuous ones!
You who follow the ways of beasts, you who even sell your own wives and blood—yet you, O virtuous ones, are truly of good character and sincere affection! (47–48)
Indeed, those who possess mechanical engines, discuses, and weapons are virtuous;
for they cry out for me, being of virtuous character, affectionate toward the good, and endowed with the quality of goodness (*sattva*).
Kings, commanders of royal troops, and lords of justice are indeed virtuous.
Indeed, those of virtuous character, who are kind and sattvic, cry out to me:
"Those who castrate, those who feed on fangs, and those who cut off the linga—these are indeed of virtuous character, kind, and sattvic! (2.84.50–51)
Even those who are inactive, those who perform improper deeds, and even the cruel—those of virtuous character, who are kind toward the good, are indeed saints.
They cry out to me; for saints are affectionately disposed toward the virtuous.
They destroy malice, subsist on minerals, and are devoid of [worldly] purity.
Crying out to me, those virtuous ones are indeed truly kind and good.
Those for whom the pentad is perfected are always considered virtuous:
freedom from desire, lack of greed, absence of pride, and lack of attachment to taste. (53–54)
Being free from affection toward all things, possessing those five modes of conduct, being devoid of the latent impressions of desire, and being accordingly free from longing—
this is freedom from craving; it is the absence of greed regarding desires that exceed one's necessities.
Absence of pride is being entirely free from conceit and devoid of arrogance.
Indeed, obtaining food for the sake of sustaining life while remaining without relish for its taste—that is remembered as [the practice of] non-tasting.
Thus, the virtuous person devoted to ethical conduct is one who is dedicated to the path of devotion.
For he is a great devotee who crosses over [samsara] and causes others to cross;
or those for whom there is the other pentad: the desire for liberation, hearing the sacred narratives, association with a devoted saint, and the practice of service and devotion. (58)
And the offering of oneself—these are considered the five duties of the virtuous.
Or else, for those others, there is another set of five: morning bathing and worship, and the daily, constant offering of food to Hari at midday. (2.84.60)
Likewise, a twentieth part of one's earnings should be offered to Hari;
there should be the daily turning of the rosary and, at the conclusion, the offering of oneself.
These are the practices for the virtuous, whether in the home, in the forest, or in solitude.
Indeed, they become the saviors of living beings even in the midst of society.
He who abandons wicked qualities and acquires virtuous ones becomes a saintly person here; and if he constantly worships Hari, he attains liberation.
Illusion is evil; indeed, living beings possessed of illusion are wicked.
Having cast off the evil quality of illusion and attained virtuous qualities, may they be devoted to me.
In this world, the virtuous who take refuge in the power of Dharma are the ornaments of the righteous.
But those living beings who are wandering in saṃsāra are all burdened with evil qualities;
later, having attained the excellent qualities of the virtuous, they become holy men.
Devoid of the impurity of māyā, those saints become stainless.
He who does not regard with even his heart the jewels, woolen blankets, garments, and riches being offered as objects of enjoyment;
and for whom the functioning of the sense of being an enjoyer and the enjoyed no longer recurs repeatedly— [he is liberated].
He should be known as an ascetic of virtuous conduct who scorches away all faults.
By that high-souled one, the pleasures of the tongue and the genitals have been conquered; thus, everything has been conquered.
He who is deaf is beyond hearing, and he who is devoid of sight is beyond what can be seen.
Touched by the untouchable, he was deprived of skin; smelling the unspeakable, he was bereft of the sense of smell.
Deprived of speech, he lacked a tongue; tasting the inedible, his sense of taste failed.
Grasping the ungraspable, he was empty-handed; approaching the unapproachable, he was destitute of feet.
He who is devoid of the organ of excretion toward that which should not be abandoned, devoid of desire for that which is unseemly,
and devoid of the sexual organ toward that which should not be embraced— he is in every way devoted to Me.
This virtuous one is indeed bodiless, yet he grants liberation even to others.
For him whose eating is like that of a deer, whose reclining is like that of a python,
whose sleep is like water, and whose mental constructions are like flowers in the sky;
for whom the body is like a shadow and the multitude of objects is like a dream.
For whom prosperity is like ashes and festivals are like a cremation ground;
for whom existence and non-existence are equal—he is a saint, he is the most excellent of the good.
For whom everything resides in Me and he is equal to Me—that person alone is a saint. (74–75)
Just as water situated in the sky falls as rain through the force of lightning,
so too does a devotee shower with affection due to the association of a holy person.
Just as clouds dissolve in the sky by the force of the wind, [so do worldly attachments vanish].
In the same way, O virtuous one, millions of sins dissolve through association with a saintly person.
Just as a dream instantly dissolves for one who is awake, so too do the impurities dissolve in an instant through the company of a saint; of this I am certain. (77–78)
Just as the destruction of darkness indeed arises through the rays of the sun,
so too, O virtuous one, sins are dissolved by the wonders of the holy.
Just as millions of sorrows are dissolved by the birth of a son.
In the same way that millions of sorrows dissolve through association with the virtuous;
just as festive joys arise during the occasion of a wedding,
so too do the celebrations of the bliss of liberation arise through association with the virtuous.

Just as happiness arises for a child upon seeing its mother, so too does happiness arise for a devotee upon seeing a holy person. Just as young boys and girls rejoice at obtaining sweet food, [so do they rejoice in the sight of the saint]. (82)
Indeed, millions of devotees rejoice upon obtaining a virtuous person,
just as peacocks utter their cries upon the arrival of the rainy season.
Likewise, people proclaim the glories of Hari upon encountering a virtuous person.
Just as the loss of an only son brings about a state of bodilessness for aged parents,
so too does separation from virtuous devotees bring about a state of bodilessness for them.
Just as a barren woman becomes intoxicated with joy upon obtaining a son, [so do they rejoice in their union].
Likewise, when a gain occurs in the house of a saintly person, those who have taken refuge in me become intoxicated with joy;
just as the mind blossoms through the scent of sandalwood and other such fragrances,
so too does the heart of a devotee blossom through Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the saintly, and the dharma.
Just as all joys indeed arise from the attainment of what was desired, so too do all joys truly arise upon the arrival of a holy person.
Just as an actor on stage brings great delight to the audience, [so does the virtuous one]. (88)

Likewise, the servant of a saint greatly pleases the saints. (89) Just as a virtuous wife always serves her beloved husband with happiness, so too does the devotee joyfully and happily serve the saintly Hari. (2.84.90)
Just as a hunter’s affection for his son and others is always directed toward their nourishment,
so too is the devotee’s affection for the virtuous and others always directed toward their liberation.
Just as a cow, having reached her calf, gives milk in a flowing stream.
Having encountered the virtuous, the devotee indeed offers them his entire being.
Just as trees, having drunk water, put forth new sprouts in full bloom,
so too do devotees, having approached the holy ones, produce the fresh sprouts of abundant offerings.

Just as rivers, intoxicated by the swelling of their floods, rush to reach the ocean, so too do devotees, intoxicated by the growth of their devotion, seek to attain the Lord. And just as a barber rejoices upon obtaining service from a king.
Likewise, the devotee, having obtained the service of the virtuous, always rejoices. Just as a youth, upon obtaining a young woman,
attains an identity with her, so too the devotee, having obtained Hari and the virtuous, attains an identity with them.
Just as servants abide by the path of humility through the king’s command,
so do devotees abide on the path of righteousness through the command of the Saint.
Just as a lamp, possessing its own radiance, shines forth when joined with the night.
Likewise, the devotee who is absorbed in the yoga of the saint shines with the splendor of Hari.
(98) Just as a ripe fruit falls from the tree in due course of time, so too the matured devotee surely casts off that which is illusory. (99)
Just as a virtuous wife follows her noble husband,
so too does the queen of devotion follow the saintly man;
and through dwelling with Nārāyaṇa, one becomes like Nārāyaṇa himself.

Likewise, by dwelling in goodness, the individual indeed becomes good, just as a human being becomes devoted by dwelling in devotion. O Lakṣmī, by dwelling in goodness, a human being becomes good. (10.1–102)

Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Means to Liberation Even for One Devoid of Association with the Holy, the Attainment of the Holy, the Attainment of Holiness, and the Description of its Various Kinds," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 84.
Chapter 85 [Author:
Chapter 86 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! You [should hear] the eternal dharma of the virtuous;
that by which the worlds are sustained is the dharma of the good, which is Hari himself.
(1) The playful exploits of Hari must always be remembered by me.
The virtuous dharma, Kṛṣṇa, should always be protected within one's own heart.
(2) It yields the fruit of great fame as well as the fruit of all gifts;
it is the fruit of cows, the fruit of pilgrimage sites, and likewise the fruit of religious observances. (3)
That person who possesses the virtuous dharma attains this fruit;
for the virtuous one, the work of liberation always proceeds through taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, the destruction of bondage is proclaimed as the task of the virtuous alone.
Those who speak of them, those who practice devotion toward them, and those whose minds are pure—
for such virtuous people who associate with the virtuous, the worlds are clearly won.
They are liberated from evil and are not defiled by sin.
The embodied being who associates with the virtuous always attains righteousness,
and from that, through a drop of the grace of the virtuous Hari, he attains liberation.
But humans, O Lakṣmī, are always like children, deluded by Māyā.
Those who revile the virtuous, who are my very form, go to many hells.
(8) And those cruel men in the world, devoid of compassion and murderous, considering the virtuous to be useless and like a burden, abandon them. (9)
Indeed, because they have accumulated no merit, there shall be no destination for them anywhere;
being cruel revilers of the unrighteous, they follow their own tamasic ways and,
deluded, they harm living beings who have entered the wombs of animals.

Even if insects, ants, snakes, scorpions, beasts, and birds should go for refuge to the virtuous for the destruction of their sins— if they indeed serve the virtuous with both body and mind— (they shall attain liberation). 11–12.
Then they are liberated from sins, provided they do not commit violence again;
by serving the virtuous, merit arises that is exceedingly powerful.
Through that merit, auspicious intentions arise, and gradually, auspicious actions as well.
The abandonment of improper actions, proficiency in the company of the virtuous,
remorse for one's own deeds, supreme atonement through austerity,
fasting and the like, devotion, sacrifice, giving, and self-surrender. (14–15)
The worship of deities and others, the recitation of mantras, meditation, and virtuous praise;
pilgrimage to sacred sites and the attainment of knowledge—these are the fruits for the righteous.
From that, the path to heaven follows, and subsequently, the path to liberation may arise.
All this quickly arises as most excellent for the virtuous through yoga. (17) All the virtuous are indeed Nārāyaṇas; they destroy sin and bestow liberation.
In them I always abide, the eternal Person, Hari. (18)
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, marked with the Śrīvatsa, Hṛṣīkeśa, who is worshipped by the Lord of All and others;
he is omniscient, united with all, omnipresent, and facing in every direction. (19)
The Supreme Self, dwelling in the heart, all-pervading and eternal;
the leader of all creations and even of the abodes that house light—Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed one, whose womb is Śrī, who dwells together with Śrī. (3.85.20–21)
Bearing the marks of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and other emblems, he was endowed with self-restraint, virtuous conduct, and tranquility;
and by his prowess, supreme heroism, and vision;
by his enthusiasm, stature, fortitude, and the perfection of his uprightness. (22)
Endowed with compassion, affection, and devotion toward his own people, he possesses all-encompassing wisdom and perception; he is devoted to the Brahmanas and is a worthy refuge.
He is the remover of fear for those afflicted by fear, and he is ever intent on protecting the distressed.
He is learned, replete with all meanings, and the bestower of boons upon those who seek them;
he is the Supreme Lord, the Lord of Ramā, the Lord of Me, and the husband of Brahman’s beloved.
All the deities dwell happily within my body.
Thus, I am the Supreme Lord himself, the husband of Śrī, Bhū, Līlā, and Ramā.

Indeed, whoever desires to see me—the one who descends through various incarnations—must behold my holy devotees, who are the embodiments of righteousness and adorned with the virtues of the saintly. (26–27)
When these are seen, I am seen; there is no distinction between them and me here.
Know, O my beloved, that all virtuous beings are Nārāyaṇas.
I am that very Śrī Puṇḍarīkākṣa with whom you have pleased me.
The host of gods is pleased with him, and all his goals shall come into his hands.
And whatever man in the world of mortals shall take refuge in me,
for him there shall be fame, victory, and even heaven.
He shall be a teacher of the dharmas, worthy of worship, and a partaker of the Dharma.
He alone should be considered virtuous and always honored by people.
Indeed, he alone would be supreme in Dharma, in whom I am held in high esteem.
Thus, for the sake of the welfare of all creatures, I indeed sent forth millions of perfected beings (sādhukoṭīs)—
all those beginning with Brahmāyana and Saccidānanda, including Sanatkumāra and others who were ancient and even more ancient than the ancients.
Thus, I am the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, whose nature is that of the Holy One;
I am the Blessed One, the sustainer, creator, and destroyer of all forms.
I am praised, and I praise Him; I am honored, and I honor Him as well.
When he has been honored, I honor him; when he has been worshipped, I worship him.
When he has been seen, I see him constantly; when I have taken refuge in him, I take refuge in him.
Thus, O beloved, for me who performs meditation, I am his meditator at all times.
"Such is my constant vow: only such saintly persons are mine.
This vow of mine is practiced by the virtuous; it is not shared here by others.
Therefore, the virtuous are my very form—the saviors of embodied beings in this world."
Indeed, the virtuous should be served through action, mind, and speech.
(38) Upon seeing the virtuous, it is as if I myself have been seen;
for all the gods truly dwell eternally within the body of the virtuous. (39)
I dwell in the virtuous as Sureśvara, as well as Viṣṇu, and as myself;
I am Sarvārāma, Surāma, Raṃmeśa, and Parameśvara.
I reside together with you in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Accompanied by the beloveds of Brahmā and served by the beloveds of Hari;
wherever Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Rati, Ramā, Bhukti, Mukti, Śrī, and Līlā reside, there I myself am present.
O beloved, fame and other virtues always abide in the virtuous; therefore, I always dwell within them, for the virtuous are my very form.
Furthermore, he who understands in every way the power of the assembly of the virtuous—
But he, having taken refuge in me and attained me, goes to my state.
And all his desires, exactly as they are wished for, come to pass.
O Lakṣmī, those who indeed cry out [my name] here with concentrated minds—‖44–45‖
The desires of those devotees who engage in *kīrtana* are fully realized.
These devotees of *kīrtana* are worthy of my worship, and I too bow down before them.
Together with Mukta, Satī, Sādhvī, Brahmapriyā, and Haripriyā.
I bow to those who pay homage to Śānta and Aśvapaṭṭabhūmi.
(47) I bow to those who pay homage to Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Śrī, Māṇikyā, the bliss-bestowing Śrī, Ramā, Padmāvatī, and Kṛṣṇā. (48)
I always bow down to those who pay homage to my incarnations, my manifestations, my devotees, and even my attendants— to my forms, to them I always prostrate.
[49] [I also bow to] Varuṇa, Bhāskara, Vāyu, Vahni, Candra, and Balāhaka.
I bow to those who pay homage to Śiva, Viṣṇu, the Unborn, and the gods. I bow to those who pay homage to Durgā, Sarasvatī, Bhūmi, Śāradā, Virajā, as well as Maṅgalā and Amṛtā. (3.85.50–51)
I bow to Bṛhaspati, Nārada, Sanatkumāra, and the infallible Acyuta;
and to those who pay homage to Nara and Nārāyaṇa. I bow to the great seers whose wealth is austerity, and to the virtuous people whose wealth is devotion.
I bow to those learned ones who possess the wealth of knowledge and who pay homage [to their teachers].
(53) I bow again and again to those virtuous ones who, being dear to the Lord, perform their divine duties without eating, and who are contented and patient. (54)
I bow to those who, with their senses conquered and well-composed, perform sacrifices and rituals;
and I bow to those who worship in the morning and in the evening—those dear to my heart.
I bow to Dharma, to devotion, to my parents, to cows, and to my teacher.
O beloved, I perpetually bow down to those virtuous ones who are indeed self-controlled and tranquil, who dwell in the forest subsisting on roots and fruits,
who possess no accumulations, who nourish their dependents, who provide refuge for guests, and who eat only the remnants of offerings.
I always bow to those virtuous ones who speak the truth and observe the vow of celibacy;
who possess hearts full of compassion toward all living beings and are endowed with discernment;
and who are devoted to the study and meditation of the sacred scriptures. I bow to those noble people.

I bow down to those virtuous people who are diligent in devotion to me through the grace of their guru, who are firm in their vows, desirous of hearing [the truth], and free from malice; who are of excellent conduct and noble wisdom, devoted, most established in Brahman, and bestowers of Brahman. (59–60)
I always bow to those virtuous ones who are the bearers of my grace— those devoted to the life of begging for alms, humble, taking refuge in the teacher’s family,
free from cruelty, whose wealth is the Imperishable (Acyuta), devoid of possessiveness, and whose latent impressions have vanished.
I bow to those virtuous people who are speakers of Brahman and followers of Īśa;
(62) I bow to those virtuous people who are devoted to non-violence, firm in their vow of truth, self-controlled, free from craving, and who live like pigeons, accepting only what is offered. (63)
Established in the four goals of life, peaceful, and practitioners of desireless yoga, who are engaged in the conduct of the virtuous—I bow to them; in them I always delight.
(64) O Brahmins, whose bodies are the Brahman, devoted to devotion, and highly meritorious!
I always bow to those who subsist on nectar, who are devoted to their vows, and who have taken refuge in them;

I perpetually bow to the virtuous ones who are not born from a womb, who are born from fire, who are born from Brahman, who arise eternally, and who belong to the lineage of Acyuta and the lineage of Śrī.
And those who desire to go to the imperishable Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the immortal station, or the unmanifest state of Īśvara;
or likewise those wishing to reach the abode of Viṣṇu or the virtuous stages of life (āśramas).
O Lotus-born One, I indeed pay homage to all those virtuous ones—
those who are the eldest in the world, the eldest in their lineage, the destroyers of darkness, the suns of the world,
the bestowers of the abode of Kṛṣṇa, the holy ones, and those who have reached the further shore of existence.
I bow to the virtuous and true people who are worthy of worship, who nourish and sustain well-being, and who protect one from time, illusion, and other such evils.
In this world and the next, these saintly devotees of Hari are indeed the bestowers of happiness.
I always bow to and ever delight in those who are eternally hospitable to all guests. Those who follow and find joy in such devoted, virtuous, and Brahman-yogis cross over all difficulties. (71-72)
Those who are devoted to peace toward them, who praise them, and who serve them—
those devotees free from envy cross over all difficulties.
Paying homage to all virtuous beings, to the gods, and to the auspicious elders, they proceed.
One who possesses faith and devotion overcomes even difficult obstacles.
(74) Indeed, ascetics, the virtuous, and those who have observed celibacy from youth—having their souls empowered by devotion—deliver even sinful people. (75)
Those people who dwell with devotion toward their mother, father, and elders,
and who are always the recipients of blessings, cross over all difficulties.
O Lakṣmī, they conduct themselves just as you do and just as the virtuous conduct themselves.
They abide as beloveds of Brahmā, and they abide as beloveds of Hari.
Just as the men and women residing at Kuṅkumavāpī abide, all are liberated and dwellers of Brahman; such virtuous ones are indeed my opinion. || 77–78 ||
In the fourteen worlds,
there are no ṛṣis, nor indeed pitṛs, munis, gods, or humans,
nor any other brāhmaṇas, who are as purifying as these, for they are my very own forms.
This field of Kukumavāpī is my imperishable abode.
Residing there are all the liberated ones and my other liberated Śaktis;
all are women beloved of Brahman, and all the men here are likewise liberated. (3.85.80–81)
Trees, birds, those born from a womb, and other living beings as well—
whether born of sweat or otherwise— all who dwell within the field of the Imperishable (akṣarakṣetra) are indeed divine and liberated; they are all worthy of worship.
All those virtuous ones indeed grant liberation merely by their presence. (83) All the limbs of the wish-fulfilling tree are truly purifying;
likewise, the inhabitants of the Imperishable Realm are indeed purifying to me. (84)
Those virtuous ones are indeed worthy of refuge, for they protect those who have come for shelter.
Just as I am, so too are they filled with compassion and bestowers of liberation;
having given even their very all, they protect those who have sought refuge.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the account of the virtuous Vṛṣāyana.
Indeed, the virtuous Vṛṣāyana, having received initiation and dwelling in the forest,
worships me, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, free from dualities and without possessions.
O King, like Videha himself, he was indeed like the sun in his splendor;
through compassion, he was a grantor of fearlessness to living beings, established in their highest welfare.
He shone while dwelling beneath a nimba tree in a forest of tigers.
Once, while being pursued by a hawk, a terrified sparrow sought refuge with the yogi named Vṛṣāyana. Seeing her without support, having come to his lap out of fear, [he took her in]. (3.85.90)
Having comforted her, he said, "O sparrow, let there be no fear for you here in my presence.
Having spoken thus, he took the sparrow in the palm of his hand and placed her upon his seat;
meanwhile, he protected her from the hawk, who then spoke to him:
"O sage, O virtuous one, let this little sparrow be given to me as my food.
Obtained with great effort, do not abandon her; let her be my meal.
For the flesh of her alone would be sufficient to satisfy me today. (92–93)
"O virtuous one, hunger afflicts me; let food be given to me quickly.
For this woman, whom I have followed, has taken the form of my very prey.
"A virtuous man should not remain here as a mediator between two parties of such different ages."
"Since you remain in a state of indifference here, what gain do you have from hatred and attachment?
A virtuous person should be even-minded; partiality is not dharma for you.
O holy man, I am very hungry; otherwise, my death will occur. (95–96)
"O compassionate one, give me this sparrow that I have struck down.
If you do not protect the sparrow, the sin of killing me will fall upon you;
but if you grant me my life, the sin of destroying the sparrow shall be yours."
"And in this matter, he should maintain an attitude of indifference toward worldly existence.
Having heard this, Vṛṣāyana reflected for a moment and, after considering the granting of safety to both parties, spoke to him thus: [98–99]
"Speak, O hawk, for your own sake, so that your hunger may indeed be appeased; I shall do exactly as you say, but I will not release the sparrow.
She has come to me for refuge for the sake of her life, and I am her protector."
"She does not release my limbs; behold her, for she seeks protection!
Even there, a woman is present—one must never kill her.
Furthermore, she is pregnant; you must not kill her, O twice-born one. (10.1–10.2)
"I shall give you fruit and roots as desired food obtained through alms;
indeed, I will bring sweet food for your sake—please eat that.
The hawk replied, "I have no need for fruit or roots, nor for alms."

"But that which has been ordained by Your Majesty as my food, consisting of sparrows—meat is the food of the hawk species; this is the ancient custom. O virtuous one, if you have such affection for the sparrow, let it be like partiality for a wing. (104–105)
"Therefore, give me today your own flesh, measured by the weight of a sparrow;
let it be weighed on a scale for me, sufficient and not more than that.
Hearing this, Vṛṣāyana became pleased and quickly said to him:
"O bird, this is a great favor you have bestowed upon me.
(107) Then, having fashioned two leaf-cups and prepared a scale as was appropriate, he cut off his own flesh again and again and weighed it against [the hawk's] requirement. (108)
The son of Bāhu gave his own flesh, equal in weight to a sparrow, to the hawk;
having obtained it, the hawk ate it, drank water, and departed for the forest.
The sparrow was saved, became joyful, and was rendered entirely fearless.
Having bowed to the sage, she then slowly departed from his side into the forest.
Having obtained the excellent medicinal herb *sandhinī-pūraṇī*, she returned;
she placed the juice of the leaf in the hand of the virtuous one, and his arm was restored.
Thereafter, she too became free from disease as before;
that excellent bird lived forever by the side of the holy man in service to him,
bringing fruits and leaves solely for the purpose of offering them to the sage.
Then, in due time, she performed [her duties] and gave birth to five eggs.
By the fruit of their service, all those children became knowers of the elements and so forth;
they all became perceivers of the three times and possessed the nature of Śveta.
Indeed, those were made by the great sage known as Dīpotsavīghoṭaka;
they were birds capable of knowing omens, and they were honored by those who understand destiny.
Then, in the course of time, that sparrow reached death in her old age.
By means of a celestial chariot she went to heaven, born as an auspicious and excellent Apsaras;
thereafter, known by the name Alambuṣā, she became a servant of Indra.
Indeed, through the fruit of serving the holy man, she attained liberation in the world of Brahmā.
Thus, the virtuous, having given away their entire possessions for the sake of helping others,
protect embodied beings and send them toward liberation.
They are the guardians of devotees who are devoted and seek refuge.
Those who know that he is both virtuous and compassionate grant him happiness.
Furthermore, in this world, a person of good conduct practices virtue;
what could not be attained by one who showers such self-sacrifice for my sake? (3.85.120)

For the Blessed Lord, who moves as a bull, resides at Aśvasarovara; by taking refuge in him, many go to my imperishable abode. Behold, Lakṣmī, how he stands on the water's edge, absorbed in meditation for my sake.
"In this way, the virtuous ones in the world become bestowers of the highest good.

(122) Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Primary Duty of the Virtuous, Nārāyaṇa, and How the Virtuous Attain Their State through Him; the Prostration to Nārāyaṇa by the Virtuous; and how the Sparrow was protected by the Virtuous Vṛṣāyana by giving the flesh of a sparrow-load to the hawk," in the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*.
