The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"By doing what here do kings, others intoxicated by wealth, and people arrogant with power attain supreme happiness?"
Śrī Puruṣottama said: One who desires happiness should always perform service to those most established in Brahman;
one should also honor the virtuous, the devotees of Nārāyaṇa, and the elderly. (2)
One should honor the virtuous people of the city and the countryside who are deeply learned with devotion, gifts, service, and prostrations.
One should serve the virtuous just as one serves oneself or one's own children.
One should especially honor those among them who are most worthy of worship.
(4) The virtuous are to be honored, saluted, and revered like the gods on earth;
when they are pleased, there are always abundant riches such as sovereignty and great happiness. (5)
One should constantly perform service and celebrate the fame of the virtuous who are devoted to meditation on Kṛṣṇa, who practice devotion to Brahman, and who possess knowledge of dharma;
as well as that of the gods, the ancestors, the Gandharvas, and the Brāhmaṇas. (6)
Since they are worshipped by the Vasus, the Ādityas, and the Rudras,
they can turn a non-deity into a deity and a deity into a non-deity.
Whomever they wish to favor shall become a god, and whoever is rejected by them shall perish.
Those who commit slander shall perish; there is no doubt about this.
Therefore, one should indeed honor the virtuous, who are the lords over both happiness and suffering.
These are to be fed and honored with whatever excellent things are desired by those seeking merit.

They should be protected by kings like fathers through salutations, offerings, and other such acts. (3.86.10) Furthermore, the pacification of calamities and obstacles is brought about by the virtuous;
for the virtuous, who possess spiritual luster, are indeed sacrifices personified. (3.86.11)
A king should always maintain in his home one who is most devoted to Brahman, endowed with devotion, and possessed of the virtues of righteousness and character— a holy man who bestows liberation.
For the lords accept the sacrificial offering presented in the mouths of the virtuous.
The ancestors and the deities, as well as the liberated yogis, are satisfied.
The seers, the Vasus, the Siddhas, the Manus, the Suns, the Śivas, the Suras, the Viṣṇus, the Brahmās, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts [are likewise satisfied]. (13–14)
The Vālakhilyas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and the best of men—
these auspicious beings enter into food as incarnations of the Truthful One and enjoy it.
Wherever our devotees of the Blessed One are present, whether at a festival or a great celebration, [there they gather].
Those prosperities and those pleasures are proclaimed to end at the cremation ground.
Those festivals in which virtuous people of auspicious appearance are present are meritorious, auspicious, and grant upward progress. (16–17)
Without a saint, even a great kingdom is like a cremation ground that nourishes the realm of Yama;
yet even a forest inhabited by a saint is divine, bestowing Goloka and liberation.
Wherever a holy man dwells, sports, or remains—whether standing or moving—that very spot is sacred.
The messengers of Yama behold [him], yet they do not approach that place.
Upon merely seeing a virtuous person, obstacles vanish far away;
diseases, illusions, and the onsets of time flee far away, terrified.
By whatever sacrificial offering the virtuous are repeatedly gratified here,
and those who follow after the virtuous— their merit is infinite.
They do not perish after death, nor do they suffer defeat.
Those people who accept the virtuous words received from the mouths of the wise do not suffer defeat, even if they are sinners.
Whatever is seen, heard, or recited in this world— 22–23.
All that arose from the words of blessing of the glorious and meritorious ones.
Formerly, the Earth indeed questioned the Lord Śvetavārāha:
"By what means are the sinful deeds of householders destroyed at their very root?"
Then Vārāha, having meditated, spoke these most excellent words:
"The sins of those who serve the virtuous dissolve entirely.
One should always serve the virtuous, the pure ones who sustain the world. (25–26)
From these, prosperity, fame, abundance, and wisdom are born;
through them, devotion arises and the purifying intellect is attained.
A devotee of Hari is indeed a great sacrificer and a true saint—of this there is no doubt.
O King, one should constantly serve the virtuous for the sake of all prosperity.
(28) Beyond the Brahmins there are others who are gurus as instructors;
beyond those gurus who are instructors, the teachers (upādhyāyas) are considered superior. (29)
Superior to them are always the teachers; superior to the teachers are those endowed with virtuous conduct; superior to the celibate students are those devoted to the glorious Supreme Soul;
and superior to the devotees are those who are eternally self-surrendered.
Saintly persons who have surrendered their very selves are superior to me; they are my own forms.
They are higher than others, higher than those higher still, and even higher than the highest;
they are more supreme even than I. I am but a servant of such saintly beings.
The man whom the virtuous praise shall become like Mādhava;
he who reviles the virtuous shall soon be overcome.
Just as salt thrown into the great ocean dissolves completely, [so does the fault of the reviler vanish].
In the same way, indeed, sins cast upon a virtuous person become dissolved.
He whom the virtuous praise flourishes here,
born with fame, prosperity, abundance, nourishment, fortune, a wife, and sons.

The virtuous indeed understand the path to heaven as well as that to liberation; they likewise know the course of hell and the destiny of karmic actions. Furthermore, virtuous people discern the course of fortune as well.
They know [the past] and the future as well through births and deeds.
(37) The powerful splendors of all the classes of Kṣatriyas are pacified within Brāhmaṇas, and specifically within virtuous Brāhmaṇas. (38)
For those who serve the virtuous, all passion (rajas) is destroyed;
they may desire fame, prosperity, and even the highest of high worlds.
A king, a merchant-leader, or anyone else should likewise abide by the approval of the righteous.
He who is born wonderful by his very birth and is most devoted to Brahman,
he is the son of Acyuta, a virtuous man to be saluted by all beings.
In every way, the saintly are friends who provide nothing but the highest good.
Worshipped by those who have taken refuge in them, they contemplate the highest welfare of their devotees through recollections associated with Kṛṣṇa and through auspicious words and the like.
Prosperity, growth, splendor, and powerful majesty [attend them]. 42.
Indeed, all kinds of fortunes arise through the virtuous resolve of the righteous.
There are various types of holy men who are difficult to approach and who seek the welfare of others;
some possess the nature of Nārāyaṇa, while others possess the nature of moral discipline.
Some have the essence of vows, some the essence of austerity, and others likewise the essence of meditation;
some have the essence of dispassion, some the essence of knowledge and so forth, while others possess the power of devotion.
There are also those whose essence is righteousness, as well as those for whom equanimity and other such qualities are paramount.
One who seeks liberation should serve all kinds of people, yet grasp only their essence.
Some possess the nature of lions, others the nature of deer; some have the nature of serpents, and others the nature of monkeys.
There are beings of the nature of fire, others of the nature of water, beings of the nature of earth, and beings of the nature of air; they are of such various kinds.
Indeed, some possess the nature of lions and are unable to endure anything, while others, like deer, are capable of enduring everything.
Those who are full of hatred are like serpents; those who steal are like monkeys. Those who destroy evil have the nature of fire; those who grant peace possess the nature of water.
Those who are patient are equal to the earth; and those who appreciate virtues are like the wind.
A wise person should rely upon those who are like lions, serpents, and monkeys as much as necessary; for the sake of liberation, he should rely upon all others.
For the virtuous are great-souled ones, the very deities even of the gods.
One should constantly worship the virtuous through service and attendance as a servant.
(52) Once, Queen Mālatī, a chaste woman, having paid homage to King Citraketu—who was honored by the three worlds—questioned her husband. (53)
"O King, by what conduct do you preside over the three worlds?
Tell me, by what vow indeed was such preeminence attained?
Citraketu replied to her: "The vow of service to the virtuous is mine."
Not a single day of mine ever passes in vain without the service of the virtuous.
Indeed, the virtuous are before me; the virtuous are behind me here;
the virtuous are at my sides; and the virtuous are in my assembly.

On journeys, in my meals, and at festivals and the like, those who are virtuous and possess the nature of Brahman indeed act as my attendants. Service to them is my vow; by that very great vow, I am bound. (57)
I preside over the three worlds and I practice devotion to Hari.
O wife, hear from me other auspicious qualities by which one possesses honor in the world as well as invincibility. (58–59)
I do not find fault with the virtuous anywhere; I honor them according to their comfort.
I do not disregard those most devoted to Brahman, nor do I ever commit an offense against them. Having honored them, I inquire after their welfare and constantly perform service for them.
Having offered salutations with my staff, I grasp their feet and [drink] their water.
Whatever command they issue, I carry it out and satisfy them.
I always listen to the masters who delight in the nectar of the stories of the virtuous.
This is indeed the supreme, divine, and immortal eye that transcends all;
it is the word that proceeds from the mouth of one most devoted to Brahman, as does the scripture and the command.
Those most devoted to Brahman, possessing the strength of intellect, always attain perfection through austerity and devotion.
Those who possess the power of the self and are endowed with my own powers can indeed deliver others.
Residing in Brahma-abodes as ascetics of equanimous vision, they are established in Nirvana upon this earth; they are the bestowers of the highest good and the givers of happiness.
The earth indeed swallows him who does not serve one most devoted to Brahman.
Arrogance destroys the prosperity of even a wealthy man of little intelligence.
Therefore, having abandoned arrogance and likewise the intoxication of royal power—
I indeed constantly and joyfully perform the massaging of the feet of the virtuous.
And having heard of me, Citraketu, their devotee, the saintly ones come from every region of the earth,
from the heavenly realms, from the netherworld (pātāla), and even from the ocean.
Indeed, the purifiers such as Nārada and others come from Satyaloka.
Fortunate is my good fortune, for this king is the husband of ten million women;
he is renowned as a saintly devotee, and toward him even the saints themselves turn their regard.
What house is more fortunate than mine, where virtuous people abound and where noble women serve the virtuous?
(3.86.70) What king is more blessed than I, who eats only the remains of offerings (*vighasa*)?
Whatever anyone asks of me, I grant it to them at that very moment. (3.86.71)
I constantly gratify the virtuous, the Brahmins, and the yogis;
just as a kingdom is for the sake of one's own senses, my mind considers it to be greatly for the sake of the virtuous.
My kingdom exists, O beloved, for the sake of those most devoted to Brahman and for the sake of liberation.
Without oppressing the circle of kings, I shall bestow all that pertains to this world.
Just as the virtuous are worthy of my worship, so too are the Brāhmaṇas, the officiating priests, the family chaplains, the teachers, the disciples, and my kinsmen and relatives. (73–74)
Women, boys, and girls who are helpless and without support;
those who have come for refuge, guests, and likewise mendicants;
and those without a protector—whether forest-dwellers or householders—are worthy of my worship. (75)
Those people of Hari who are learned in the scriptures and perform virtuous deeds are always worthy of honor.
Those who act otherwise are indeed to be punished according to the principles of the scriptures.
Devotion, righteous conduct, and knowledge consisting of self-discrimination [are the means]. (76–77)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, straightforwardness, self-control, mastery over the senses,
freedom from anger, absence of arrogance, lack of malice, modesty, forgiveness, restraint, endurance,
the destruction of latent impressions, the destruction of craving, and purity. (78)

O beloved, he in whom these qualities are seen, and who indeed never performs improper acts, shall be a worthy recipient in this world and always deserves honor. Whether it be something unprecedented or previously owned, whether belonging to another or even one's own— [it should be given]. (3.86.80)
Whether he be distinguished by special qualities, or whether he has just arrived,
whoever is most devoted to Brahman and established in the highest good is a worthy recipient who deserves honor.
In this world, there are many people burdened with pride.

Filled with envy and hatred, and unable to tolerate others, such men cannot endure the fame, happiness, or prosperity of others; they burn with jealousy and consequently revile those who are virtuous. (82–83)
Considering the Vedic words of the virtuous to be invalid even though they are esteemed by the world,
they transgress the bridges of dharma;
and those who fancy themselves wise create disorder for themselves.
Proclaiming doctrines of causality, they commit acts of malice toward the virtuous.
(85) Likewise, these wicked men are revilers who speak in opposition to the scriptures;
they are fools, harsh in speech, and devoted to sin. (86)
Having approached those who are equal to themselves and well-satisfied, the wicked indeed worship dogs.
O Mālatī! Such hypocrites are dog-men in the three worlds;
they do not perform any good at all, but destroy their own and others.
They invite their own destruction and must be punished in every way by kings.
Just as a dog is intent on both barking and biting,
so indeed do they burn with the intent to destroy the moral order of the world.
Therefore, O Queen! Having observed the assembly of people, the law, what is beneficial for oneself, one's own welfare, the heart, the place, and the time, a person should carry out their commands.
By conducting oneself thus constantly, one prospers for eternal years.
Whether they be kings, wealthy men, or powerful people in this world,
if they conduct themselves in that same manner, they will never be overcome.
Having become devotees of Hari and freed from debt, they attain liberation in the end.
Thus Citraketu spoke to Mālatī, and she,
having attained the supreme power of Hari, served the virtuous day and night;
she worshipped the Supreme Self through service, adoration, and chanting.
She indeed performed her entire range of duties for the sake of the virtuous.
By the king’s command, she constantly attended upon holy men with food,
gifts, service, and the offering of water, clothing, and fruit.
And she, her heart filled with devotion, beheld me, the Supreme Lord,
in my divine form during the worship— four-armed and seated upon a celestial chariot.
Having obtained the king’s permission, she also requested liberation.
Quickly casting off her mortal body, she ascended a celestial chariot.
Having become divine, four-armed, and fair-faced like Lakṣmī’s companion,
Mālatī now dwells in the abode as Narāyaṇī, the beloved of Brahmā.
Thus, through association with the virtuous, the king indeed became virtuous;
and through association with her virtuous husband, she attained the path to liberation.
Having attained the state of liberation, Mālatī became a companion of Ramā.
O Lakṣmī, beloved of Brahmā, association with the virtuous is fruitful as long as it lasts.
Whether one is poor or wealthy, possessed of qualities or devoid of them,
by taking refuge in the virtuous, one indeed becomes Nārāyaṇa.
Through the force of devotion, a portion of My own self is born as one possessing supreme fame;
he is the savior of all worlds, the sustainer of all who follow dharma,
the attainer of even the Imperishable, and the protector in His own presence.
"From reading or hearing this, even one may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of the Power of the Righteous, Illustrated by the Example of Citraketu’s Attainment of Liberation despite the Supreme Welfare of Kings Arrogant with Wealth, Pride, and Strength," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 88 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Those Brahmins who are the sons of Brahmā are my very body;
for they are purifiers in every way throughout the world, being the highest of all castes.
They are, however, always ensnared by the nooses of desire, anger, great delusion, and greed.
The householders who possess wives are enveloped by hope, craving, and the like.

(2) Or rather, those who are without support, free from passion, virtuous, and devoid of desire, anger, and so forth, being liberated from craving, hope, and the like—they are the best among your followers. (3)
Free from the snares of greed and other such bonds, all these excellent stages of life are auspicious;
they follow the dharma of non-possession, are faultless, and are devoted to the path of liberation.
O Lord, tell me: between these two [groups], which possesses the superiority?
"Both these bodies of yours exist; is there a difference between the two, or not? (5) Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, to that which is beneficial, true, wholesome, and perceptible to the eye."
Indeed, those free from desire are far superior to those who possess desire. Ascetics are always most excellent and dearer than those accompanied by women;
for when one is joined with a woman, desire, anger, and great delusion truly arise.
My bodies that delight in passion are excellent, yet they are not the most excellent;
the virtuous, who are entirely free from illusion, are the most excellent for me.
Householders, however, being full of illusion, are indeed eternally destined for hell.
The denizens of hell constantly frequent cremation grounds and hells.
(9) Indeed, the ascetics who are empty of illusion are eternally practitioners of Mādhava;
the yogis of Hari serve those who dwell in the eternal abode of Vaikuṇṭha. (3.87.10)
The householder stage is always lower than the stage of renunciation;
among the social orders, the Brāhmaṇas are superior, yet not so in every respect when women are present.
Indeed, among all social orders and stages of life, my saintly devotees are the most excellent to Me.
Celibacy is always supreme, and goodness is likewise supreme. (1) The forest-dweller’s stage of life is slightly superior, yet not like that of the virtuous.
Those who delight in sensual pleasure bear their pride in vain, like those bound for hell. (1.3)
There is no place anywhere as great or as excellent as renunciation (saṃnyāsa). Illusion (māyā) and the actions born of illusion are by their very nature base;
however, virtuous practitioners established in vows free from illusion are superior to all. (14)
Even lords, when established in their households, honor virtuous people.
Indeed, twice-born brahmins, kings, and even gods worship the righteous.
Yet, those who live by the profession of service are always superior to those who practice agriculture.
The protectors [should provide] for the farmers, and the ascetics for the protectors;
the ascetics are Brahmins, and from them come the virtuous who are free from worldly attachments.
The virtuous are indeed devoted to the Brahman, devoted to the Self, and devoted to liberation.
Free from defects and with their vital energy directed upward, the virtuous are indeed of Brahmanic nature.
Among the social classes, the Brāhmaṇa is the best; among Brāhmaṇas, however, are the virtuous.
Among the twice-born, they are worthy of worship, for they are the purifiers of the purifiers. (18–19)
My tamasic bodies are the rākṣasas, daityas, and dānavas;
my rajasic bodies are the kṣatriyas and others who seek their own self-interest;
and my sattvic bodies are the learned twice-born brahmins.
The virtuous ones, who are free from qualities and possess divine bodies, grant me liberation.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous are far superior; they are not merely twice-born brahmins.
For all the splendors of the kṣatriyas are indeed contained within the splendor of the brahmin.
Indeed, all the splendors of the Brahmins merge into the splendor of the virtuous;
all the splendors of the virtuous dissolve into me, Mādhava.
On this earth, the virtuous who are like me are the saviors of the Brahmins.
Though they are normally inflammers of sin, they bestow liberation upon yogis who practice with women.
(24) The splendor of austerity, religious observances, truthfulness, wonder, virtuous conduct, and merit—all these flow away from an embodied being through union with a woman. (25)
All these qualities increase for the virtuous who are disciplined in their conduct; indeed,
the good arise as Nārāyaṇas,
and among them, the Brāhmaṇas are always the most excellent and the very best.

In ancient times, Brahmā became angry with the virtuous Sanatkumāra and indeed weighed the excellence of goodness against that of being a twice-born Brahmin. Goodness attained the state of being most excellent even in the presence of the status of a twice-born.
Thereafter, he again placed within the middle of the single balance the states of being a Brahmin,
a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a student (brahmacārin), a householder, and a forest-dweller;
then the Unborn One placed another state as well.
For all embodied beings who perceive goodness solely in truth,
goodness has attained dignity in every respect even over the seven [worlds].
Therefore, in creation as well as in liberations, goodness is the most excellent.
Brahmins are indeed the best recipients, but the virtuous are the very best;
among them, the householders who are great devotees of the Lord are the most excellent, and among those, the virtuous are superior.
Those who possess renunciation and are ever devoted to Nārāyaṇa are the most excellent of all.
Those who merely carry burdens are not indeed the best; rather, those who know the fragrance are the most excellent.
(33) In the same way, those who merely carry wood are not the best; the virtuous alone are the best. O Lakṣmī! I am a householder, and I honor righteous people. (34)
Those who are liberated and abide in the world of Brahmā— all of them are my virtuous ones.
I mutter the name of and worship those Nārāyaṇas,
the Brahmin among Brahmins, the Brāhmaṇas of Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇas who are yogis of Brahman.

I constantly honor those who possess virtue and those who are even more virtuous, those who are ascetics and those who are higher ascetics; those who are free from craving for flavors, who are seekers of the truth, who do not indulge in the pleasures of the senses, and who are endowed with the fragrance of vigilance.
"O Lakṣmī, this householder's life does not please me, for it is indeed defiled. Yet, out of a desire to favor you devoted wives, I became a householder.
Indeed, in whatever way people surrender unto Me, in that very same way do I reward them. (38)
My vow has always been this: I am indeed the fulfiller of the desires of my devotees.
By granting the objects of desire to those who long for them, by destroying the suffering of the afflicted, and by bestowing wealth upon those who seek it, I fulfill their heart’s wishes.
O beloved, having become devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) for the sake of the wise, I bring about their liberation.
The virtuous (sādhus) are indeed my incarnations; I dwell within them eternally. I dwell in all virtuous beings, but especially so in those who are most excellent.
But elsewhere, it is according to one's duty, according to one's pleasure, and according to the fruit [of one's actions].
Therefore, virtuous people who are disciplined in their character are always most excellent.
Now, on one occasion, Viṣṇu himself, accompanied by Lakṣmī, went to the forest.
He performed various kinds of austerities for many thousands of years.
Lakṣmī remained intent on serving him, yet the ascetic did not touch her.
Then, with a humble disposition, Lakṣmī questioned the Supreme Lord.
"Why do you not touch me, O Viṣṇu? Tell me the reason for this.
Viṣṇu replied: "This is the most excellent vow, wherein there is no contact with women;
it is the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), a supreme austerity that bestows the perfection of spiritual power."
Contact with women is the highest excellence; excellence is the strength of ascetic powers.
Through excellence, the unassailable perfection of ascetic powers arises.
Even Nārāyaṇa himself, though he is the very embodiment of prosperity, fell into doubt regarding Lakṣmī.
"How can the Lord, though free from fault, speak like an ordinary living being?
(48) Then Viṣṇu, having attained the perfection of his penance, indeed went to Vaikuṇṭha itself for the purpose of dispelling Śrī’s doubt. (49)
There the god Nārāyaṇa shines together with Lakṣmī;
he too constantly honors the virtuous, saintly yogis.
Having thus shown this to Lakṣmī, he then departed for the supreme realm.
Having thus demonstrated that Kṛṣṇa, together with Rādhikā, eternally worships the saintly devotees in Goloka, the abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
Viṣṇu then departed for the supreme and most excellent abode known as Akṣara.
There, the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Brahmapriyā,
honored the liberated saints and revealed His splendor to them.
Thereupon, Lakṣmī’s doubt was indeed dispelled from its very root.
Then Viṣṇu, having internally visualized Lakṣmī within his own form,
revealed that eternal form of Lakṣmī to her;
for she who is Śīla is indeed Lakṣmī herself, whose very nature is celibacy (brahmacarya).
A woman acts according to her will, yet in reality she is the very embodiment of virtue;
she is non-different from the Goddess herself. O Lakṣmī, you are my beloved!
You exist as the form of virtue and as the form of a chaste wife, dear to me.
The virtue of Brahman is exceedingly dear to me; nothing else is so.
You, being of that nature, are eternally dear to me, and nothing else is dearer than you.
Furthermore, all those virtuous ones who possess your very nature are most beloved to me.
The virtuous are my heart, and Lakṣmī is likewise my heart;
the Kaustubha gem is in my heart, and the Śrīvatsa mark is also in my heart.
Indeed, the Śrīvatsas—the virtuous—dwell within my heart.
Just as Śrīpati is, so am I; and just as Satpati is, so too am I. I am always the Lord of Love, and I am always the Lord of Virtue.
I am always the Lord of the Holy, and I am always the Lord of Lakṣmī.
O Lakṣmī, the mark of [true] fortune, which consists of love and is called virtuous conduct, resides within me.
Wherever that exists, it is indeed proclaimed as "Lakṣmī.
You possess that; you are my will, and the virtuous are my very forms.
Virtue is my eternal quality; therefore, I am one whose nature is that of a saintly being.
Consequently, among all created beings, those who are most excellent are the few Brāhmaṇas therein who are free from the taint of women.
Neither the gods, nor the lords (Īśvaras), nor even the ṛṣis and attendants who have attained union with women are in any way equal to the virtuous (sādhus).
O Lakṣmī, compared to them, the sādhus are the most excellent, higher than the highest.
Austerity joined with ethical conduct is supreme; such austerity is found among the virtuous.
Therefore, O Rame, the virtuous are indeed superior and should always be honored by you.
Now, let there be no doubt in you as to how the virtuous are indeed superior.
In the sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ, honor the holy men who have assembled there;
welcome your guests and those devoted to renunciation with respectful offerings.
Through their words of blessing, the highest well-being is attained.
Indeed, the merit arising from their devotion shall be eternal.
The fruit of serving them is equal to the bliss of ten million Golokas;
and from that, all the beloveds of Brahmā and the beloveds of Hari are born. (3.87.70)

Let them practice service to the virtuous and please holy people; [let them serve] gurus who are free from passion, bestowers of liberation, and crossers to the further shore of illusion. Durgā, Caṇḍī, and Mahākātyāyanī, having slain the great asuras...
Then the Supreme Goddess questioned Śambhu regarding Mahiṣa and the others:
"O Śambhu, you yourself declare that non-violence is the supreme dharma;
yet I have committed an extremely terrible act of violence which causes destruction. (72–73)
For many have been struck down and many Kāśyapas have been torn asunder—
those Dānavas, Asuras, and Daityas who encountered him in battle.
Their sin, as well as the weeping and other lamentations of those women, [shall be destroyed].

And as for the sin born of widowhood, and the wailing of a young, helpless child—how indeed am I to avoid this, and by what means of purification? Tell me: by what action, or by what vow, or by what expiation? || 75–76 ||
Having heard this, Śambhu then said: "You are the manifest Pārameśvarī, the divine Brāhmī, the Great Power (Mahāśakti) in whom no sin exists.
You are eternally pure by nature; you are Lakṣmī, you are Ramā, and you are Rati."
You are Māyā, you are Mahālakṣmī; no sin exists in you at all.
I am Rudra, the agent of dissolution, and you are Rudrāṇī, the destroyer;
you are Mahākālī, the Great Power, the purifier, and the devourer of the worlds.
You are indeed always of my own nature; I am Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
You are Nārāyaṇī, the sustainer of the world, Śivā, composed of merit, and auspicious.
You are Satī, the virtuous one, the embodiment of fire, pure, and the consort of the Supreme Person.

Nevertheless, O Maheśvarī, for the sake of the peace of your mind and for the purpose of sustaining the world, I shall show you that reality; practice it accordingly. Indeed, these three—a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), a vow (*vrata*), and austerity (*tapas*)—are capable of washing away sins.
And among those [powers], the service of the virtuous is the most powerful and supreme fortress;
the sight of the virtuous is meritorious, as is their touch, their propitiation, saluting them, serving them as a slave, and massaging their feet and so forth. (83)
It brings about clarity of mind and instantly destroys all sin.
Therefore, go to Viśālā, where the virtuous Hari himself resides—the son of Dharma, the Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa, who shines there. (84–85)
He is always observant of vows, an ascetic, a celibate student, and my guru.
Through service to him, the destruction of great sins and other evils will occur.
O virtuous lady, there are also other divine sages there who are great devotees of the Lord.
They abide there, endowed with devotion, bestowing liberation through their very sight.
Purifying and of the nature of Brahman, the virtuous ones such as Nārada and Sanatkumāra constantly come there. (87–88)
"By the sight and service of the virtuous ones, such as Lomaśa and others, and by residing at Badarikāśrama, there shall be the destruction of all impurities.
Having been addressed thus, Satī said to Śambhu: "I shall go at your command."
"If it pleases you, O Śambhu, you should indeed come, O Lord," [he said].
Thinking, "So be it," Hara went together with the Goddess and his attendants to Badarī by way of the sky; he did not bow to his guru, Nārāyaṇa.
Then Satī, having reported all that to Nārāyaṇa, performed service consisting entirely of attendance upon the virtuous,
as well as upon the seat of Nārāyaṇa and the vicinity of Badarī.
Every morning, Durgā performed the sweeping of the ground and the offering of water;
she also offered leaves, flowers, and garlands, as well as meditation, visualization, recitation, and so forth, in their proper sequence. (93–94)
Śambhu also performed service for the great sages and offered a warm welcome and other courtesies to the virtuous as required.
In this manner, he indeed remained for a full month with the noble guru, Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Being pleased, the Blessed Lord Hari performed service for her.
He said to her, "Speak, O Durgā! What do you require?
Durgā replied, "O Ocean of Mercy! I am indeed your daughter, Vaiṣṇavī."
I have received from Śambhu a purifying initiation that is eternally sanctifying;
nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world and bringing about the destruction of the Daityas, I have become one who fears the great sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin. (98)
By the command of Hara, we have come to you for refuge to be cleansed.
O Lord, through service to the holy Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Hari, may all my sins be destroyed, for such is the desire dwelling in my heart. (3.87.100)
Having heard this, Śrī Hari Nārāyaṇa said: "O Śivā!
There is not even a trace of sin in you; you are Brāhmī and Pārameśvarī.
You exist as Śiva-śakti, the destroyer of great sins. (101)
Nevertheless, for the sake of worldly gain, you perform such a vow.
Indeed, all your sins consisting of the slaughter of Daityas have been pacified; by the mere sight of me, a virtuous man, you are truly purified.
"O virtuous lady, because you have served the sages, those powers which were lost have now returned to you.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa then gave her water;
Satī drank that nectar-like water from his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) by his grace.

Then Śivā and Śiva, together with their own attendants, having worshipped the Lord Hari and received his command, departed for Kailāsa. Thus, O Lakṣmī, has the supreme majesty of Śambhu toward the virtuous been described.
The fruit of service has been shown to be the destroyer of sin, bestowing both heaven and liberation, as well as worldly enjoyment and ultimate release.
Furthermore, the supreme service of the virtuous also bestows wealth and prosperity. (107)

O Rama! Service to the virtuous bestows progeny and delivers one from the cycle of rebirth; it destroys the suffering of poverty, dispels the darkness of ignorance, and leads to the attainment of Narayana. It grants happiness and bestows a divine abode. (10.8–109)
"From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, or even from reciting it, there shall be worldly enjoyment and heaven, and there shall also be liberation belonging to the Supreme Lord.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Viṣṇu as an Example of the Householder Brāhmaṇas and Durgā as an Example of Service to the Holy," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 87.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord of Śrī, O Supreme Person, you are one whose form is virtuous;
knowing this, I rejoice exceedingly, especially from your own mouth. (1)
The virtuous are the saviors in the world, and the virtuous women are likewise the deliverers;
detached from worldly ties, established on the path of renunciation, they are the constant bestowers of liberation for living beings.
Indeed, we always worship them out of even a slight portion of their compassion.
Beloved by Brahmā, we are always delighted by the blessings of the virtuous.
We exist through various and most extraordinary yogic unions with you;
there is no end to our merits, for you, Hari, are our beloved. (3–4)
Now, I wish to know here regarding that vow known as *sahadharma*, which is considered by the couple to be always in effect from the time of the taking of hands onwards:
what is the nature of this *dharma*—is it momentary or eternal? (5)
Whether it be Vedic, imagined, sensory, or even demonic—how does this [state] exist for the couple either here or in the hereafter?
For, due to the difference in their respective karmas, the death of the husband and wife does not occur simultaneously. (6–7)
Furthermore, there is no such thing as going together with a single entity; how then could there be a "concomitant" (sahadharma)?
Is this concomitance voluntary, or fixed, or even forced?
Tell me in its entirety: what is it like, and what is its fruit?
"By hearing which, the attainment of all dharmas shall occur here.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall proclaim the eternal, co-existent dharma."
In the presence of the marriage fire as witness, the bridegroom takes the hand of the bride;
she, exceedingly joyful, gives her own hand into the hand of the bridegroom.
This is their *sahadharma* (dharma performed together), which lasts indeed for as long as life endures.
Whether by their own will in the union of two, or likewise by the desire of the parents,
or by the desire of the relatives, or even by force in some cases;
or from a previous forced union of two, there is the shared religious duty (*sahadharmaka*).
O Lakṣmī, the duty of giving belongs either to the daughter or likewise to the son;
in this way, the shared religious duty of husband and wife proceeds.
There is a unity between the two through their minds, their bodies, and likewise through their actions.
There was a unity of virtues, a unity of wealth, and a unity of home for both;
there was a unity of utensils and a unity of all objects of enjoyment.
There was also unity in matters of food, recreation, and in jests, counsel, and secret consultations.
Oneness through vows, gifts, and pilgrimages; oneness with the two hearts as well as with the senses (16).
Oneness through waking and sleeping; oneness through assistance and service;
oneness with the vital breaths, with my ego, and with the bonds of affection (17).
There is unity with internal states and with external dualities such as fruits and the like;
likewise, there is unity with merits and so forth, as well as with income, expenditure, and preservation;
and with vehicles, mounts, ornaments, decorations, jewelry, gold, garments, and the rest.
Likewise, there is identity with abundance, prosperity, fields, gardens, kingdoms, marketplaces, and so forth;

identity with young children, sons, and offspring; identity with pain, pleasure, and the like; and identity with their respective specific qualities, such as the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded. (3.88.20)
Through joys, delights, great festivals, and the like,
as well as through all meritorious deeds, that which constitutes the very oneness of the husband and wife—
this is declared to be *sahadharma* (the shared dharma), preceded by *pātivratya* (devotion to the husband). ||21||
If it is maintained in its entirety and accompanied by devotion to one’s wife,
then, through the power of dharma, the husband and wife shall indeed travel together toward heaven at the same time, according to their desire. || 22–23 ||
O Lakṣmī! To whatever extent there is destruction within the Dharma, to that same extent death and the destination after death for the two [husband and wife] occur at different times;
indeed, they become separate in another womb, just as they are in heaven.
Likewise, in another world, there would be a different destiny for those who follow opposing dharmas. If there were no loss of shared dharma, it would be eternal forever.
Both have gone from here to heaven; therefore, truth is supreme.
He attains both Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, my supreme imperishable abode;
as a couple sharing the same dharma, they both attain liberation together.
If dharma is practiced here with mutual devotion, it is indeed considered *sahadharma*.
Then the separation of the husband and wife will surely occur; of this there is no doubt.
(28) Therefore, that dharma is momentary and not of an eternal nature.
This Vedic dharma of cohabitation [is subject to change] according to place and time. (29)
And there is no imagined [reality], O Lakṣmī, since imagination is dependent;
if dependence arises from the disparity of place, time, and so forth, then co-existence with dharma is secondary and occurs only in certain calamities. (3.88.30)
There is no loss incurred therein by this much; one is purified through expiation (prāyaścitta).
Even though it is merely sensory and not ultimate, there exists a dharma for the sake of the self which, in this world, is dependent upon the body. (3.1–3.2)
In the next world, one who is established in the Self and situated in liberation is free from desire;

indeed, if there is a desire for the state of husband and wife, that is proclaimed as being based on choice (*caicchika*). However, that state of husband and wife which is obtained by force is proclaimed as being *āsura* (demonic).
The state of matrimony is attained by anyone through whatever path; that which follows is the eternal fulfillment of shared duty (sahadharma). When properly observed, it remains perfect;
when neglected, it becomes impaired and is the very cause of separation.
For as long as he is protected, so long indeed does he bestow fruit.
If the youngest is protected, he becomes the giver of the fruit of the youngest;
the middle one gives the middle fruit, and the eldest gives the most excellent and true fruit.
At the beginning of creation, pairs were indeed fashioned by Brahmā.
Having produced these pairs, they thereafter proceed together according to their shared dharma;
upon death, they go either to the supreme world of liberation or to heaven.
By the power of devotion to her husband alone, and by the strength of her wife’s vow,
there arose weakness in her companion in dharma due to the frailty of time;
and in that state of shared weakness, there was weakness regarding the world beyond.
Thus, when decline has arisen, men and women follow divergent paths;
having entered different wombs, they experience the uneven fruits of their own actions.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this secret of the common dharma been told.
Divine beings protect their offspring; others do not, being intent solely on their own self-interest.
For their paths are divided, and they wander in the ocean of worldly existence, unconnected to one another and sharing no common lot.
Those who do not know each other's duties and who repeatedly dwell in cremation grounds are never separated from Lakṣmī, who is equal to Rādhā;
those who are equal to Sītā and Padmā in fame are never separated [from their virtues]. (43–44)
Those equal to the splendor of a ruby are never separated;
those equal to the cotton of Paulomī (Śacī) are separated here and there;
and those equal to servants are separated, yet they are also joined here and there.
It is not at all fitting for it to be like another's, yet once it has departed, it does not return.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this wheel revolves here in the world, which is difficult to overcome;
indeed, the Wheel of Dharma is the protector of yoga, as powerful as it is.
That very weak enemy does not protect the union at all;
therefore, there is separation for all—of couples, of men, and of women.
O Lakṣmī, unrighteousness and the burden of debt are the causes of separation.
Some, having married quickly, are indeed separated and pass away;
some are separated by time, some in middle age, and others at the end.
Those who carry debts are separated according to how their debt remains established. (3.88.50)
In that matter of union and separation, I delight in my own cause alone;
therefore, one should practice virtue after observing it, never abandoning the shared dharma.
Having abandoned the shared dharma and having cast aside the scripture and the word of the guru—
Those who, abandoning the bull of worldly conduct, proceed by a wrong path,
go to a terrible hell filled with suffering and poverty.
Those householders who merely fill their own bellies do not perform the rites for the gods or the ancestors.
Those who do not honor guests go to a most terrible hell—
those devoid of charity, devoid of purity, and bereft of auspicious conduct;
those possessed by the Kali spirit, fallen from the dust of virtue, and those who live by the livelihood of dogs.
Those who are beset by weeping, affliction, and quarreling indeed go to a downward state.
O Blessed One, those who are devoid of the Name,
who eat the leftovers of others, who are evil-minded, and who lack the mantra, go to a terrible hell.
Those who are devoid of ritual action, devoid of ancestral rites, devoid of devotion, and devoid of the Lord;
those who are devoid of great festivals and the like, go to a most terrible hell.
So too do those who are fallen, the dull-witted, the insane, those afflicted with leprosy, and those with vitiligo.
Eunuchs, those afflicted by consumption, and evildoers indeed go to a downward state.
(58) Physicians, temple-priests who live off idols, those who prescribe vows in vain, those who revile the sick, and those devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state. (59)
Singers, dancers, acrobats, and likewise musicians;
storytellers and warriors who are devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state.
Those fallen from dharma, fallen from their vows, and fallen from their family and kin [follow the same path].
Those who are entangled with others, devoid of devotion, go to the lowest state.
Those who neglect the fire-sacrifice, those who omit the ancestral rites, those who indulge in adultery, atheists,
teachers [who lack integrity], and those devoid of devotion— these indeed go to a downward path.
Those who sell the Vedas, as well as those who sell women,

those who sell their husbands, and those devoid of devotion, indeed go to a downward state. Likewise, those who consider all attachments as their own and those who perform the purification of corpses [go there].
Thieves, those who live off their daughters, and sinners indeed go to a downward state.
Those who live off their daughters-in-law, those who live off their maternal kinsmen, those who live by unknown means, debtors, snatchers, and those devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state.

Those who sell living beings, those who subsist by trafficking in women and other such goods, those who have no master but their own desires, those who do not recite the sacred prayers (*japa*), and sinful people indeed go to a downward state. So too do those devoid of vows, those who cause suffering to their own wives, and those who are like beasts.
Those who perform improper actions, being sinful, indeed go to a downward state.
Those who harbor mutual ill-will, those who deceive one another,
the crooked, the deceitful, and those devoid of devotion, indeed go to a downward state.
Those who do not recite the Sāvitrī, those devoted to false trade and the like, liars, those whose speech is false,
those whose actions are untrue, and the sinful— these indeed go to a downward state.
They are impoverished, dependent on the fortune of others, violent, full of deceit, and wicked.
Those who are stained by blemish, those who inflict blemish upon others, and the sinful indeed go to a downward state.
Gamblers, those without a livelihood, those who eat all kinds of food, those who are wanton, those engaged in cruel deeds, and those devoid of devotion indeed go to a downward state. (3.88.70–71)
Those who take false oaths, those who eat meat, those who drink liquor, and those who do not observe Vedic vows or conduct— these sinners indeed go to a downward state,
unless they repeatedly refrain from such acts for the sake of their guru, fear, or other such purposes.
Those whose speech, actions, and minds are rooted in falsehood are indeed destined for hell.
Those people who destroy the property of others, those who seize the wives of others, and those wicked ones who speak slander are indeed destined for hell. (73–74)
Those who deceive those who provide water-stalls, rest-houses, assembly halls, dwellings, shade, and alms-halls;
those who deceive the helpless, women, children, the elderly, and the frightened; and those who deceive holy men, virtuous women, and female ascetics—these go to hell. (75)
Those who destroy livelihoods, homes, friends, wives, trust, and the Dharma;
those who violate boundaries, justice, virtuous deeds, charity, and sacrifice; those who are ungrateful and corruptors—such people go to hell. (76–77)
Those who follow heretical paths, those who lack discernment, people who sell poison,

those who perform malevolent magic, those who set fires, and those who administer poison— these sinners go to hell. So too do those who frustrate hopes, those who break their promises, those who destroy devotion, and those who ruin the efforts of others.
Those who cause division, those who destroy prosperity, and those who go to hell;
those who employ weapons and thorns [against others], those who slaughter cows, virgins, and women, and those who kill young creatures and so forth—such people go to hell. (79–80)
Those who obstruct paths with stakes, stones, and thorns;
those who abandon their servants, their food, and their wives; and those who extirpate testicles, pierce noses, or knock out teeth—all such people go to hell. (81)
Those who cause suffering to animals, those who slaughter them, and those who go to hell;
likewise, kings who do not protect their subjects, lords of wealth who are devoid of charity, and fools who abandon those who have sought refuge—such men are considered destined for hell. (82–83)
Those leading people who, without giving to their dependents and the distressed, consume [resources] for themselves;
those sinful men who rule unrighteously, are considered destined for hell.
They are devoid of worship, devoid of the gods, devoid of devotion, and lacking in service.
Those devoid of affection, who act with deceit and are sinful, indeed go to a downward state. There is no commonality in dharma for them or for those women who follow unrighteousness;
for the life of such unrighteous sinners is indeed like that of a beast.
In this world, they have no happiness, no righteousness, and no religious observances;
they possess neither charity, merit, nor compassion. Being equal to beasts, how could they be happy?
Even in the next world, they indeed become miserable ghosts (pretas).
Those who have not obtained water, food, or sustenance, who do not look after their families,
who wander alone among the nets of others, go to the abode of hell;
they do not know the common duty (*sahadharma*), being consumed by thirst and the objects of the senses.
Those who are dominated by darkness (*tāmasa*) do not recognize the suffering of others for the sake of their own happiness;
like serpents that carry poison, they go to the abode of hell.
They neither know how to protect women nor do they know how to protect cows.
They do not desire the happiness of slaves or slave-girls, yet they go to a downward state.
Those who seize wealth, those who violate vows, those who steal righteousness, and corrupters—who turn truth into falsehood—these sinners indeed go to a downward state. (91–92)
Those who are never satisfied with righteous conduct, yet persist in unrighteousness;
who do not perceive the welfare of others and are devoid of devotion, indeed go downward.
Those householders who live like paramours or like courtesans [are likewise lost].
And those who act like enemies toward their own kin—all such people indeed go downward.
Those who behave like murderers, thieves, rogues, gamblers, as well as like Time and Death—they indeed go downward. (94–95)
Where there is mental distress between two people in the home over matters of dharma, that is hell manifest before one's eyes; it is likewise so in the next world.
Therein lie lack of affection, enmity, contempt, and humiliation.
Defeat and extreme censure are indeed manifest hells;
great disease, poverty, and confinement in prison, as well as the lack of food, ornaments, and so forth, are indeed manifest hells. (97–98)
Childlessness, as well as having many enemies,
a life of excessive toil, and indeed hell itself—
these belong to him whose wife is a female demon of anxiety, equal to a male demon.
And the demon named poverty has Raurava as its abode.
Therefore, having reflected, a wise person should practice his duties together with righteousness;
casting aside all failings, being skillful, he shall become happy.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Shared Dharma and the Demonstration that One Who Does Not Share Dharma Goes to Hell," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
