[The Author: Chapter 90.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Indeed, the hells themselves are truly causes of anxiety and grief.
"O Lord Hari, tell me here what those things are that cause anxiety and grief.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Nārāyaṇī, O Śrī; indeed, [I shall describe] those things which cause anxiety and grief."
They cause loss of vitality, emaciation, and other diseases that wither the body.
Indeed, those things which are directly hells consisting of nothing but suffering—all of these indeed come to pass for one who was highly esteemed when that esteem is lost. (2–3)
Without friends, without a wife, and apart from one's family,
that state of being in a foreign land is indeed the realm of hell.
Even by the service of virtuous people, the satisfaction of the members of one's household [is not attained].
Reproach and humiliation—this is the hell that is present here.
(5) The endurance of humiliation inflicted by people superior in wealth and power, and even by one's own kinsmen—this is the hell that is present here. (6)
When one's own virtues are superior, others who lack such virtues will be highly honored;
yet even in their very presence, hell becomes one's domain.
That hunger which exists between the means of livelihood and begging arises from shame and fear.
He who is constantly consumed by passion is here within the sphere of that [hell]. (8) Even in a dispute over matters of excellence, he may be defeated by one who is inferior;
this perpetual defeat is hell, and he is here within its sphere. (9)
He whose friends are always afflicted people will experience suffering and fear; hell shall be his domain.
Even a person esteemed for wisdom, when treated with contempt by fools, [suffers].
The assault by those of evil conduct—that is the hell within this realm.
And the host of enemies with the faces of friends, intent on deception on all sides—by that very deception, too, is hell within this realm. (11–12)
Even one who is skilled in secrets and understands the course of all matters is not honored by those who know [the truth], and for him, hell is his destination in this world.
Furthermore, when many wicked people are present at one's side, one's own virtues [are obscured].
The wicked act with base qualities, and hell is their sphere of experience here (14).
Even those devoid of wealth, intelligence, or scriptural knowledge, upon seeing great men, are consumed by the fire of hope for greatness; indeed, hell is their sphere of experience here (15).
Relatives do not rejoice in one who has achieved his purpose, attained success, and gained renown for his scholarship; for him, hell is the destination here.
A neighbor—strong, wealthy, and young—takes another's wife.
One's own disagreeable state becomes one's domain here [in this world], and hell likewise becomes one's domain.
(17) Indeed, even for a statement that is true in its factual value, if it is not accepted among those who know the truth, hell becomes one's domain here. (18)
Dwelling constantly among fools, residing among those who revile others,
and even living among people possessed of envy and malice— this is indeed hell in this world.
Furthermore, when a master binds someone to a task and subsequently [withholds] wealth and other such things...
Since he constantly seeks after wealth, his destination here is indeed hell.
It is impossible to reveal the intention hidden within;
due to dullness, fear, and laxity, hell becomes one's sphere of experience in this world. (3.89.20–21)
If one who lacks virtues desires to conquer a virtuous person out of envy,
and cannot endure seeing his merits, hell is his destination.
He who is ignorant, timid, and of little purpose yet desires great fame— [is destined for that same fate].
He who constantly burns with anxiety has hell as his domain.
For the miserable man whose long-cherished desire is never attained, or who finds what was obtained snatched away by others, hell is his domain. (23–24)
Cursed by his mother, by women, by brahmins, and by the virtuous,
he who has fallen into this wretched state through his own fault becomes a denizen of hell in this world.
He who, upon seeing virtuous people who have attained liberation, utters insults toward them—
He who commits evil, for him hell is considered his own abode here.
Even upon seeing the suffering of others, he who is unable to remove it certainly grieves over wealth; hell is the domain of such a person. (26–27)
Sons who do not obey their commands, a wife who disregards her husband’s words,
and disciples of contrary conduct— for him, there is indeed hell even in this world.
Having consumed food given by the wicked, he lives without his own home.
He by whom the forest is scorched has hell as his domain.
He whose sin increases and whose merit perishes, and he who is considered a vessel of reproach—hell is his domain. (3.89.30)
He who has become a prey to his enemies, who is separated from his friends,
and whose life ends unexpectedly— hell is his destination.
The same applies to one who is intent on meditating upon wicked enemies and one who desires that which cannot be attained.
For one who dwells on what belongs to others, hell is his domain.
(32) For the wealthy man possessing a kingdom, childlessness, illness, infamy, and mental derangement—these indeed are the hells within this very world. (33)
For a virtuous man and a virtuous woman, the desire for worldly enjoyment is hell in this world;
reviling teachers and elders is hell in this world;
and a sluggish digestive fire and chronic diseases are always hell in this world. (34)

In youth, being without a wife, being deprived of a beloved, widowhood, and the state of being husbandless—these are the hells experienced here in this world. Furthermore, while having sons, being a servant, and maintaining one's own livelihood dependent on others [are also such states]. (35–36)
Dependence on others in old age—these are indeed hells in this world.
Long life for one without sensory faculties, and poverty for one who is strong;
having many children while living in poverty—these are truly hells in this world.
Dwelling without a fixed abode, living in the houses of others,
subsisting on the fortune of others, and always adopting the lifestyle of a mendicant— O Rame, these are the hells manifest here in this world for the householder! (38–39)
A wife’s lack of affection for her husband, sons wandering onto wrong paths,
and even the pregnancy of daughters— these are the hells manifest here in this world.
Furthermore, the imposition of shackles due to the fault of the circle of chief ministers [is a hell].
The imprisonment of the queen, the prince, and likewise the preceptor of the land;
the confinement of the king, the brahmin, and his wife; and the detention of the courtiers and the learned—these are the hells manifest here in this very world. (41–42)
Obtaining food that is incomplete and the acquisition of wealth that is incomplete;
food that is tasteless, dry, or leftover—this indeed is hell in this world.
Furthermore, when an elder exists, the destruction of one's offspring is also hell in this world.
The entry into the realm of hungry ghosts and so forth is the manifest torment of Yama;
the suffering of royal punishment and the like is the manifest torment of Yama;
and even the calamities and miseries are the manifest torments of Yama. (44–45)
Rivalry with co-wives, constant beating, and dependence on others;
an animal-like existence—all these are the manifest torments of Yama. Being overtaken by famine and being struck down by fire, poison, nooses, and the like— 46–47ab.
Falling headlong into water-filled pits are the manifest torments of Yama;
so too are the blows from pikes, weapons, and missiles, and confinement in caves and the like.
The pain of the womb and the agony of childbirth are the manifest torments of Yama. (47–48)
Indeed, the unbearable enjoyment of sensual pleasures is like the consumption of unwholesome food;
the afflictions of the three-humored fever and the like are the manifest torments of Yama.
There are constant fermentations and moist excretions within the body; the physical form is always a vessel of feces.
The constant flow of phlegm, mucus, and other secretions is hell right here before one's eyes.
(3.89.50) A perpetual lack of peace in the mind, as well as exile from one’s country and untimely death when alone—these are hell right here before one's eyes. (3.89.51)
Being solely a daughter, being devoid of sons,
being a eunuch, and being impotent— these are hell manifest in this very world. Furthermore,
there is the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste), the carrying of filth, and the affliction by moisture and the like.
And because it is like a dwelling place of foul odors, hell is indeed manifest here [in this world].
There is constant agitation in the mind, and the forest fire of the flames of craving;
for one who has neither peace nor happiness, hell is indeed manifest here. (53–54)
Childhood, extreme old age, and likewise addiction to sexual intercourse—these are not purified by earth and water; indeed, they are hells manifest here on earth.
Wine, meat, sexual pleasure, and lust—these are hells manifest here on earth.
For times of adversity are indeed hells, while times of prosperity are always nectars.
O Lotus-born One! Affection is heaven, whereas hatred is hell in this world.
Knowledge is heaven, and discrimination is the celestial realm; the cow is dharma, and she is one's own kingdom.
Contentment is eternal heaven, while liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
Having understood all this, the wise man should renounce that which is to be renounced;
the discerning one, whose intent is on the highest good, should acquire that which is to be acquired through contentment.
The virtuous person is heaven; Hari is heaven; devotion is indeed eternal heaven.
The abiding state in Brahman is the supreme heaven; the attainment of Brahman is the highest heaven.
Fearlessness is the great heaven, which one enjoys forever even while living, O Ramā! (3.89.60)
Listen: there was a certain servant, diligent in his labors and devoted to his daily duties;
indeed, he worked in the fields for the sake of receiving a regular wage.
By name he was Viśrāmagupta, and he was the one who nurtured the crops and other plants in the field.
Every day he goes out at dawn and performs labor in the field.
Having obtained his ethical earnings and food from the farmer in the evening, he returns to his own home, which is devoid of gates or walls. (62–63)
Likewise, [the hut] was adorned with beds made of leaves and stalks,
beautified by two or three earthen vessels, and graced by a movable hearth;
and having placed a frying pan upon three unrefined stones, it was heated with fire.
Having cooked and eaten *roṭaka* with salt water,
or constantly with black pepper or radish,
or having eaten it with a bulbous root, he then drank the water brought there. (65–66)
Having washed his earthen vessel while chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa,
he sleeps upon the ground, covered with a single worn-out rag;
fearless, free from anxiety, well-nourished, healthy, and full of strength.
Neither cold nor even the heat of the sun smeared with poison afflicts him.
The lifelong student (brahmacārī) always sleeps free from all anxiety;
because he possesses nothing, he has no fear of theft.
For a humble servant, there is no fear of enemies;
indeed, even though he is unwilling, sleep comes to him who is tranquil as early as morning.
That sleep becomes profound and is entirely free from the anxieties of dreams.
Then, he is suddenly awakened by the sounds of the morning watchmen.
Having quickly prepared his *roṭaka* (a type of bread) and taking it with him, he departs for the field; exhausted by toil, he eats there at the proper time.

While he was living thus in happiness, a most excellent merchant named Somacandra, whose mind was devoted to helping others, lived nearby; indeed, considering him to be one who was suffering, [he took pity on him]. (73)

Overcome by compassion, he summoned the farmer’s servant and gave him two hundred silver coins as a gift; the man also accepted his assistance. Then, anxiety arose regarding how to protect [the money] in his own home. (74–75)
He concealed it in a corner so that no one else would know;
having dug a hole in the dust at the spot where he had spat, he cast it therein.
Having buried it, he would then go out daily for the sake of his business alone.
Even when gone to the field, he remembers the wealth well-protected at home;
having returned from there at midday, he looks upon it and departs. Returning in the evening, he inspects the ground, eats, and sleeps as usual. (77–78)
At night he indeed slept, yet he would wake quickly at the slightest sound;
and as a vigilant guardian, he remained constantly anxious for the sake of protecting what could be stolen by thieves. Thus, his pleasant sleep gradually diminished day by day.
Indigestion occurred, as did a loss of digestive power;
there was also instability of the mind, which was entirely attached to material things.
Furthermore, a gradual lack of engagement with one's duties, whether in action or in the field of work, came about little by little. (3.89.80–81)
Day after day, the work of one whose mind is distracted becomes deficient.
Then, indeed, he was questioned by his master, the high-souled farmer:
"How do you conduct yourself? You are bewildered, agitated, and possessed by a spirit."
"You do not perform even the full work of cultivation in any way whatsoever.
Thus addressed, that servant, after reflecting for a moment with the farmer regarding his wages, daily food, and the meager rations provided according to his labor, [spoke]. (83-84)
He said, "The reason for this is that two hundred silver coins remain here;
they were indeed offered by the merchant and belong to me alone in this leaf-hut.
Yet, though I am constantly thinking of them, I have become utterly bewildered."
Material wealth is indeed hell itself, since from it comes the destruction of sleep;
from it comes the destruction of nourishment, the destruction of peace, and the destruction of spiritual action.
Wealth is manifest fear, and death is established in wealth.
Time shines in wealth, and decay shines in wealth;
wealth is a hell visible to the eye that increases the threads of craving.
For possession is indeed a hell, while renunciation is considered the supreme heaven.
Peace is internal heaven; renunciation is external immortality.
(89) Having obtained wealth, I have either destroyed my heaven or cast it away.
Therefore, by abandoning it, I shall become happy once again as before. (3.89.90)
Having spoken thus, he led the farmer away along with the plowman and showed him that very hell of sin in a corner—
a place of suffering, a source of misery, a destroyer of peace, consisting of two hundred [tortures]. (91)
Having extracted all of that from the pit, he gave it back to the merchant once more.
"O merchant, wealth is a manifest hell; it does not please me at all.
You, however, take this very hell in the form of wealth, which brings about the destruction of happiness. (92–93)
Having spoken thus and having bestowed [the teaching], he slept peacefully as he had come.
Indeed, free from thirst and without possessions, he became happy once more;
rich in all his duties fulfilled, he was just as he had been before.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, in this world, hells are indeed givers of suffering.
For all those possessions are givers of suffering; they are truly hells in this world.
But for the virtuous man, heaven always exists, and he dwells there together with happiness.
Likewise, Nārāyaṇa and I dwell within the minds of the virtuous;
gladdened by my bliss and rejoicing in their own bliss,
they deliver other people and send them to the imperishable state.
They kindle evils and strike down the hells;
they instruct in the principles and even grant discernment.
Having caused me to practice devotion and having established divine contemplations, [they lead me]. (98–99)
Having fashioned images in the form of Nārāyaṇa, they lead their true devotees to the imperishable state;
indeed, they are always bestowers of heaven.
Therefore, virtuous people who are adorned by goodness should be constantly served.
One becomes a partaker of liberation through reading, hearing, or even remembering [this].

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Manifest Hells, the Demonstration that Wealth and Other Such Things are Manifest Hells by Means of the Example of the Farmer and the Servant, and the Definition of Manifest Heaven," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 89. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 90 [Author:
Chapter 91 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī!

Those who possess a constant inclination toward charity and righteousness, who are ever devoted to the gods and pure in intention, and who are dedicated to austerity and truth—these pure ones go to the eternal, stainless heaven. (1)
Those who are pure through service to their gurus, who are beautifully adorned by learning and virtuous conduct,
and who have no desire for the stain of accepting gifts, go to the stainless heaven.
[They do so] out of self-interest, for the sake of fame, out of fear, from disease, from hardship, or from the affliction of poverty.

Through knowledge, through freedom from greed, through their refuge [in the Lord], through affection, through the bond of relationship, and through living together, those who possess devotion go to the stainless heaven.
They are rich in forgiveness, fortitude, and endurance, and are always diligent in virtuous deeds.
Those who are perfected in conduct such as worship go to the stainless heaven.
(5) Those who abstain from intoxicants, meat, sexual intercourse, and the like, who avoid theft, and who enjoy the grace of the gods, go to the stainless heaven. (6)
Those who construct dharma-halls, those who perform the restoration of regions and similar works,
and those who maintain groves, gardens, and hermitages, go to the stainless heaven. Those who found villages and cities and provide for the protection of the subjects [attain the same].
All those who provide assistance in times of distress go to the stainless heaven;
likewise, those who give ornaments and garments, as well as those who provide food and drink, and all those who serve their families, go to the stainless heaven. (8–9)
Those who have desisted from violence, malice, and the like; who always endure calamities;
who grant refuge to all; and likewise those who provide shelter and offer beds and seats for those in need—all these go to the stainless heaven. (3.90.10)
Those who give vehicles and carriages go to the healthy heaven;
likewise, those who give villages, fields, and so forth, as well as houses, cows, and bulls, and those who bestow worthy recipients and their requisites, go to the healthy heaven. (11–12)
Those who serve their elders, their teacher, the gods, their beloved, their mother, their father, Hari, and their virtuous wife, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are affectionate and act for the welfare of their family members as is appropriate [attain the same]. (13)
Those who accomplish the welfare of others, being wise, go to the stainless heaven.
(1.4) Those rich in dharma, strengthened by Mādhava, having conquered thirst and subdued their desires, the steadfast ones intent on propitiation, go to the stainless heaven. (1.5)
Those who are compassionate toward offenders, affectionate, endowed with gentleness, free from anger even when punishment is due, and learned in the scriptures, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who are hospitable, providers of refuge, givers of thousands, and truly virtuous—[go to that same state]. (16)
Those who provide protection in many ways go to the stainless heaven.
Givers of gold, silver, and gems, as well as givers of garments and pearls, go to the stainless heaven. (17–18)
Likewise, those who bestow wealth and articles during great festivals,
as well as those who give dowries and other such gifts, go to the healthy heaven.
So too do those who provide articles for marriages and those who offer items required for initiation rites.
Those who give away male and female servants also go to the stainless heaven.
Those who establish water-stations, groves, assembly halls, wells, and lakes, and those who construct long ponds and perpetual alms-houses, go to the stainless heaven. (3.90.20–21)
Givers of fields, dwellings, and palaces, as well as of caves, rivers, and reservoirs, go to the healthy heaven. Likewise,
those who give grains, pulses, and other cereals [attain the same].
And those who give juices go to the healthy heaven;
likewise, those who give sweet foods, fruits, bulbs, leafy vegetables, and potherbs go to the healthy heaven. (23–24)
O Lakṣmī, those who remove sufferings, who destroy burning heat,
and who eliminate calamities, go to the stainless heaven—
even if they are born into any family whatsoever, provided they possess a nature of affection. (25)
Possessing extensive lineages and endowed with sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons;
compassionate, virtuous in character, and established in shame and moral restraint; sincere of heart and tranquil—such people go to the stainless heaven. (26–27)
Those people who do not perform what is undesirable for others, who are untouched by censure or hatred, who are rich in contentment and service to their gurus, go to the stainless heaven;
they accept blessings and are devoted to meritorious deeds. (28)
Those who provide assistance in meritorious deeds go to the stainless heaven.

(29) Those who are free from greed during a consecration ceremony, devoid of attachment to their own dignity, humble, and possessed of a disposition like that of servants, go to the stainless heaven. (3.90.30)
Indifferent toward wealth and filled with great contentment,
those whose entire possession is non-attachment go to the stainless heaven;
even while in the midst of possessions, they always keep their hands and faces free from the burden of grasping.

Those who are free from plucking [hair], eating forbidden food, and so forth, go to the healthy heaven. Likewise, those who are free from killing all living beings, those who have avoided self-destruction, and those who are free from the killing of Brahmins and the like, go to the healthy heaven. (32–33)
Householders who always abide by the Dharma, perform righteous deeds,
are devoted to faith and charity, and are pure, go to the stainless heaven. Likewise, those who constantly observe moral vows and those who follow the forest-dweller’s vow [attain the same].
Those who possess the vows and conduct of renunciation go to the stainless heaven.
Even those who have committed offenses against what has been done, those who have violated trust, and those who have harmed what is desired—such meritorious ones go to the stainless heaven. (35–36)
Those who perform service for the world, those who provide assistance toward liberation,
and those who bring about beneficial aid, go to the stainless heaven.
Those who provide service to the scriptures and those who perform service during the Kali age [attain the same].

Those who provide assistance for the sake of exertion go to the stainless heaven. Those who possess new initiatives, who remove obstacles from the land, and who bring about the happiness of the subjects go to the stainless heaven. (38–39)
Those who are always free from malice, who observe the vow of non-violence, who take refuge in the divine, and who are self-contented, go to the stainless heaven.
But those people here who, though called "killers," do not actually kill, [attain the same state]. (3.90.40)
They do not form associations with them; they go to the stainless heaven.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Those men who, even without having caused killing, are considered killers—
"I desire to know each and every one of them; show them to me here, O Hari.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe such human beings as well."
Indeed, even without having committed violence, people may become violent; they [should be known as such].
One who causes suffering like that of being killed is proclaimed a killer (*ghātaka*);
likewise, one who yields a fruit like that of being killed is also proclaimed a killer.
He who, having personally summoned a mendicant for the sake of alms at a time other than that of a guest,
says "there is nothing" when the time has come, should be known as a "murderer of a mendicant.
Furthermore, a king who considers one established in justice to be deserving of punishment [should be punished].
Because he takes away their livelihood, he is a "slayer of livelihoods" (vṛttihāraka).
He who creates an obstacle for thirsty cows or for others becomes, in this world, a "water-thief," a "cow-slayer," and even a "slayer of life. (46–47)
He who destroys the scriptures, the rules, the discipline, and the instruction, being ignorant, corrupts them; he is a destroyer of logic and a destroyer of the authors of the scriptures.
[And] his own young daughter, at the proper time, to a suitable husband...
He who does not give his daughter away becomes a destroyer of dharma in this world.
And he who causes piercing pain and grief to virtuous men, to the twice-born, to those worthy of worship, and to others who are entitled to gifts, is considered a destroyer of those worthy of honor.
He becomes the plunderer of all possessions, the slayer of life, and the destroyer of everything for the lame, the blind, the foolish, women, and those who are helpless.
Likewise, he does so in villages, forests, groves, hermitages, sacred fields, houses, and the like. (51)
One who gives fire is considered a slayer of all, a slayer of the village, and a slayer of a Brahmin.

So too are one who administers poison, one who hands over weapons, one who besieges, one who crushes, one who sets snares, one who shows the path of fear, and one who provides unwholesome medicine. (52–53)
One who performs malevolent magic, one who falsely brings disgrace, one who destroys reputation, one who seizes a kingdom, and one who steals mechanical arts and such;
one who cuts off a thumb, one who destroys the seasonal rites, one who destroys dharma, and likewise one who destroys sacrifices.
One who destroys the sacred thread, one who destroys the study [of scripture], one who destroys worship, and one who destroys devotion;
||55|| one who destroys the fetus, one who destroys the eyes, one who strikes the hands, and likewise one who destroys the *liṅga*;
one who destroys the seed, one who destroys the testicles, one who steals the livelihood or cattle, and one who destroys what is desired. ||56||
One who reviles his gurus is a slayer of all;

he is declared a destroyer of liberation and a destroyer of the self. An atheist is considered a slayer of Brahman. One who destroys virtue is said to be a destroyer of dharma; a doer of evil is considered a destroyer of heaven.
One who defiles a chaste woman is called a slayer of women and a destroyer of dharma as well.
Because they have abandoned their fear of Brahmā, of Śrī Hari, and of Me, the Supreme Soul, all such people become killers of Brahmins. 58–59.
Indeed, they shall dwell in the hells and the realm of Yama for eternal years;
likewise, they shall experience the state of hungry ghosts, residence in the womb, births as animals, and so forth.
Wherever they may be, those hell-beings shall remain situated in hell.
They are always experiencers of suffering, utterly devoid of even a trace of happiness. (61) Indeed, this world is not theirs, nor heaven, much less the imperishable state.
However, having attained devotion to Me, they eventually cross over by My grace. (62)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"But how indeed can compassion arise for those who commit sins, and especially for those who are killers, cruel, and destroyers of the world? (63)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Hear how compassion arises within me;
I shall explain to you here clearly the sequence by which liberation is attained. (64)
Indeed, curses from those who strike with fierce force become effective;
through the breaths of their curses, living beings suffer a swift loss of merit.
And an endless succession of experiences of suffering quickly awaits them.

The home, the gates, the sons, the daughters, the family, the cattle, and the wealth—all these perish before long; unbearable poverty arises, as do terrifying diseases, and even total destruction occurs. (66–67)
The acquisition of food, water, and clothing—all such gains vanish.
Like servants, those miserly ones wander about as mendicants;
they are subject to reproach, inauspicious, deprived of their status, and banished from there.
In this world, they wander about like dogs, oppressed by suffering and poverty.
Having experienced these miseries for a long time, devoid of fortitude and lacking endurance, they have become submissive under the blows of pain. (3.90.69–70)
Somewhere they grieve intensely for their fortune, fate, and likewise for Hari;
they seek refuge in the heart in Him who wards off suffering, thinking:
"May this unbearable misery of mine dissolve, and may it never occur again. (7.1)
O Nārāyaṇa! Alas! Destroy my unbearable suffering.
I have fallen to You for refuge; ward off this unbearable [suffering].
I shall perform charity, merit-making, pilgrimage, and auspicious virtuous deeds.
"I shall perform japa, service to the virtuous, or honor for Hari;
I shall observe vows, penance, and even perform atonement for my teacher"—such auspicious resolutions indeed arise even in one who is helpless. (74)
Through royal punishments, worldly punishments, divine punishments, and multitudes of calamities;
through the punishments of suffering, the punishments of Yama, and through great and most extreme hardships,
auspicious wisdom arises, and thereafter one goes to Hari with the heart.
Regarding righteousness, merit, vows, devotion, recitation, charity, and auspicious acts— thus,
through such auspicious association and the performance of virtuous deeds,
even a small amount of merit is indeed attained, and there is a slight, gradual destruction of sin.
And through gradual meritorious deeds, excellent yogic conjunctions arise.
Service to the virtuous, service to sacred fords, helping others, uprightness, devotion, fear of sin and violence, and likewise the remembrance of Me [are the means]. (78–79)
In this way, after a long time, he comes to take refuge in me through his senses;
the saintly devotees cause him to perform the chanting of my names, devotion, the offering of the mantra, the wearing of the garland, and association with the virtuous.
Thus, when the mind has arisen merit and is pure, the desire for liberation (mumukṣutā) arises;
the desire for enjoyment (bubhukṣatā) dissolves, and having attained [the state], he becomes a disciple. He is indeed a Vaiṣṇava who seeks Hari through a guru.
Through the service of sacred narratives and the company of the virtuous, one increases in devotion incessantly.
Just as one ascends the steps of worship,
so too does my powerful and blissful adoration increase.
In this way, one whose sins are burnt becomes a treasure-house of merit.
From that, he attains service to Me; from that, the offering of his very self;
from that, My compassion arises for him, and he becomes a sanctifier of the assembly.
He becomes a virtuous devotee, or he is born auspiciously as a liberated soul;
indeed, he even becomes Maheśvara, worthy of the supreme abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, a man becomes Nārāyaṇa—that is His grace.
In that regard, one should understand the cause to be my command, which bestows liberation.
Even those who are sinful or most sinful certainly cross over, though after a long time;
however, they must endure unbearable sufferings of torment that are like the weight of their own sins.
In this world, punishments sometimes serve as deterrents;
likewise, those who are afflicted and greatly distressed generally resort to me.
And similarly, those seeking wealth cross over [the ocean of existence] without a doubt.

If saintly people (*sādhu*), who are saviors, quickly meet [one] out of the power of their compassion (3.90.90), then even sinners cross over by giving them their mind and life-force. Having always worshipped the saintly and bowed down to the elders in the morning... (91)
By offering [these] to the gurus and the brahmins, they cross over tens of millions of sins;
one should offer all kinds of objects and satisfy the most excellent of holy men.
My devotees possess virtuous conduct, are free from desire, and are devoid of attachment to pleasant tastes.
What is given to those holy men who are oceans of merit yields great fruit.

(93) What is given to those ascetics who are free from desire, anger, and the like; who endure all things; who have conquered their senses; and who are beneficial and friendly, yields great fruit. (94)
To those who are free from passion, who have reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment, who are devoted to truth and virtuous vows,
and who delight in the path to liberation— to them, what is given yields great fruit;
they whose disciples await [their teaching] like farmers awaiting a timely rain.
What is given to them shall be multiplied a thousandfold in this world.

(96) To those Brahmins who are endowed with virtuous conduct and character, who are emaciated, who live by the pursuit of sacrifice, and who are righteous mendicants—what is given to them yields great fruit. (97)
If the twice-born are devoted to him, dwell in his house, depend on his strength, and rely upon him,
and if they are purifiers and seekers of aid, then what is given to them yields great fruit.
For one in whose house there exist almshouses for students and virtuous men, [the merit is immense].
Whatever person they may be, even for one who eats [at their home], a gift given at their sacrificial session yields great fruit.
(99) For those virtuous ones who are destitute, having been robbed of all their possessions, and who are devoted solely to devotion—whatever is given to them yields great fruit. (100)
For those who abide in the study of the scriptures (*pārāyaṇa*), who abide in sacrifice, and who abide in great festivals— to them,
even that which is given merely for the sake of fulfillment yields great fruit.
(101) In times of calamity, they have meager strength, meager wealth, and meager vows.
Nevertheless, that which is given to those who possess virtuous conduct yields great fruit.

(102) Those who are generous, free from attachment, devoid of hypocrisy and pride, and who are the ornaments of the virtuous—those are the true saints; to them, what is given yields great fruit. (103)
To those reciters who possess the entirety of Brahman, who subsist on alms, who are ascetics,
who are virtuous and free from the scent of falsehood— gifts given to them yield great fruit.
They are devoid of offenses against children and are themselves free from faults.
That which is given to those who are free from offenses against Brahman yields great fruit.

(105) Furthermore, that which is given to those who are objects of the compassion of the virtuous, as well as devotees of Hari, and vessels of the satisfaction of noble wives, yields great fruit. (106)
Having thus given this supreme gift— consisting of food, water, clothing, and suitable articles— to the virtuous, O Kamalā, one may then cross over;
for the virtuous are indeed the boat, while the wicked are truly the stones.
The virtuous boat indeed crosses over [the ocean] itself and carries those who have taken refuge in it across as well.
(108) By reading and hearing this, there is the destruction of sins and obstacles;
having obtained the fruit of serving the virtuous, one shall attain eternal heaven. (109)

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of Those Going to Heaven, the Deliverance by Compassion of Even Killers Who Have Not Killed, and Deliverance through Service to the Holy," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 91: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 91.
[Author: Chapter 92 → 3.91 Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
If no yoga arises for those who are killers, tell me, O Supreme One: how can their liberation occur? (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:

"If saintly persons (sādhus), who are the best of all, do not meet on this earth, then one should go to the most excellent holy places (tīrthas) or to the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) of a sacrifice. (2)
When the Sun is in Aquarius (Kumbha), one should set out; by bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha), one is liberated.
There is the Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha, and also the Gomatī-tīrtha. || 3 ||
The Svarṇarekhā is a great tīrtha, as is Nārāyaṇahrada itself;
the confluence of the Hiraṇyā at Somanātha is a most excellent tīrtha. (4)
The confluence of the Narmadā and the ocean, Oṃkāreśvara, Śrīśaila, Sahyādri, and likewise the excellent Pampā lake. (5)
The Setu (Rāmasetu), which is the prosperity of the Southern Ocean; Kanyākumārikā;
likewise the Godāvarī, Candrabhāgā, Kāverī, and Sarayū. 6.
The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Brahmaputrā, Sindhu, and Sarasvatī;
the Candravīnā, Śālavīnā, and likewise the river Mānapīṅgā. (7)
Menakāṅgī, Śikṣāṅgī, Aṅgaśikṣāṅgikā, as well as Hoyāṅghrī, Amurā, Vīṇā, and Yānākṣikā; ||8||
Also Bālakṛṣṇasara and the lake called Dvikalā; likewise Ovī, Terimā, Dvinā, Volgā, and Nīparā. (9)
The Nārāyaṇī is the river of all long life; Viṣatūrya is the lake.
Kaṅgū is the river, Nāyajīrā is the river, and Citta is the Tūṅgā lake. (3.91.10)
The Āmajā river, as well as the Miśūrī and Mīnakaṃjhukī;
the Sulūvana lake, the Vinipega, and the Supāraya lake. ||11||
The Erāsara, the Kāruliṅgī, and other auspicious rivers—indeed, in whichever rivers I have bathed together with the sages. ||12||
O Ramā! I delight in lakes, in excavated ponds, in oceans, and upon the earth, by bathing according to the prescribed rites at each respective sacred ford (tīrtha). ||13||
The sins of killing perish if one does not commit them again;
one who has bathed in the nectar-like waters from my image becomes pure at that very moment. (14)
Even by consuming food granted through my grace, as well as by serving me and the like, or by constructing temples and other edifices, a killer is purified immediately. (15)
The builder of temples and the like, as well as the installer of my image;
one who gives his life for the sake of the virtuous, and one who sacrifices his life for the sake of dharma. (16)
One is indeed purified from even the great sin known as "murder," along with its very root, at Puṣkara, Mānasa, and also Himālaya, the lord of mountains. (17)
One should, indeed, unweariedly resort to Badarikāśrama-tīrtha and all other purifying sites, as well as Mātṛtīrtha and Pitṛtīrtha. 18.

One should diligently resort to the holy ford of the guru, the holy ford of the chaste wife, the holy ford of the beloved, the holy ford of knowledge, and thereafter the supreme holy ford of the Self. (19)
Therefore, devotion is the supreme holy ford; I am the highest of the high.
One who constantly serves me is liberated from all sins. (3.91.20)
One should bestow a gift of gold upon the one who has committed the killing; one should likewise perform the gift of an elephant, the gift of a kingdom, or the gift of a village. 21.
One should likewise perform the gift of a livelihood for one's lineage and the gift of a daughter;
one should give the gift of a cow and the gift of land, which destroy the sin of killing. (22)

One should bestow oneself as one would one's own property, and one's servant according to how he follows; one should entrust him as one would a slave, as one would a disciple, or as one would a commodity for sale. //23//
By that as well, O Lotus-born One, the destruction of the sin of killing occurs;
one should especially give everything that would cause satisfaction. (24)
One should give a house, ornaments, wealth of garments, and cattle in their entirety;
by that, the destruction of the sin of killing indeed occurs. ||25||
Prabhāsa, the Naimiṣa forest, Mount Gandhamādana, the Blue Mountain (Nīlādri), Kailāsa, and the sacred field of Puruṣottama. 26.
Śuklatīrtha, Bhṛgutuṅga, Dharmāraṇya, Daṇḍaka, Vyāghrāraṇya, Vipāśā, Karatoyā, and Gaṇḍakī. ||27||
Karmanāśā, Devadāruvana, Kālañjara, as well as Brahmasaras, Rāmahṛda, Citrakūṭa, and Vindhya; ||28||
By performing such pilgrimages as these, one's sin is destroyed.
The Himavat mountain is renowned and meritorious, being the abode of Siddha-Nārāyaṇa. (29)
In that regard, if a living being goes there after having fully worshipped the deities and sages, being pure and perfected, he shall go to heaven, to the eternal world of Brahmā. (3.91.30)
Having conquered desire, anger, greed, delusion, and pride, and having worshipped his mother and father and bowed to his teacher and Gaṇeśa, he should enter the sacred bathing place. ||31||
The destruction of his sin shall come about through visiting sacred fords;
however, by merely remembering inaccessible sacred fords, one may cast off evil. (32)
Brahman is pure, Brahman is meritorious, and Brahman is the unsurpassed heaven;
the virtuous are said to be Brahman, for Brahman is eternally purifying. (33)
The virtuous, who are always purifiers, should indeed make him their refuge;
for the virtuous gods performed sacrifice unto me, Hari, through sacrifice. (34)
Through sacrifice, ritual action, constant worship, and service—these duties consisting of service are the first and the most excellent. (35)
Through those religious acts, they attained greatness;
indeed, those virtuous ones reached the celestial realm, the abode endowed with eternal bliss. || 36 ||
Where the Sādhyas, eternally liberated gods who serve [him], dwell; and where indeed the ancient ones, even more ancient than the ancient, also reside. (37)
By making them their support, liberation itself is attained; of this there is no doubt.
O Lakṣmī, this is the secret of the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī. (38)
Through knowledge of Brahman, devotion, my stories, meditation, festivals, and the imparting of my mantra—by these means they deliver their own dependents. (39)
Protection for those who have come for refuge, liberation, the destruction of evil, the attainment of devotion, and the virtue of Brahman—all these arise from association with the virtuous. (3.91.40)
O Lakṣmī! Whoever should hear this doctrine of mine, the glorious Supreme Self, shall attain my abode by worshipping me and the virtuous who belong to me. 41.
I, the peaceful Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who bears the name Śrī Kṛṣṇa, dwell here from time immemorial all around the Viśvapaṭṭasaras lake. 42.
In this imperishable realm dwell these sages, Lomaśa and others, as well as other virtuous ones;
these sages abide there, self-luminous. (43)
O Lakṣmī! That region is purifying; its water destroys sin.
[It is attained] through austerity, celibacy, sacrifice, renunciation, and service. 44.
One would not attain that state by serving the Aśvapaṭṭa [temple] which one attains when the limbs of embodied beings are touched by the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭa lake. (45)
By a mere fragment of my grace, let there be for them all liberation that is imperishable.
By the waters of Aśvapaṭṭasara, let all the karmic deeds of embodied beings be purified;
having abandoned this earth, they shall go to the supreme state.
All sins of killing perish at Aśvasarovara. ||47||
As long as a human's bone remains here in this lake, for that many thousands of years one enjoys heaven and is liberated. (48)
Thousands of *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts are not equal to the water of the *aśvapaṭṭa*; indeed, the water of the *aśvasaras* is the most excellent. (49)
The Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha, the Aśvapaṭṭa Sarovara, and the hermitage of Lomaśa—these are of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss. (3.91.50)
Just as grass cast into a fire is consumed, so too the sins of one who has bathed in this lake perish; such a person shall become a partaker of liberation in this very world. 51.
For all beings here whose minds are afflicted by suffering and who are seeking a refuge, the lake Āśvasara is the superior resort. (52)
And for those who are of improper conduct and those who take refuge in unrighteousness, I have resorted to Āśvasarovara, which bestows liberation upon them. (53)
It is remembered that the lake of horses (*aśvasaras*) indeed delivers those lowest of men, sinful persons overwhelmed by powerful sins, as they fall into hell;
[those who are] inauspicious, non-beneficent, and turned black by their impurities.
Having bathed in the waters of Aśvapaṭṭa, they indeed become auspicious and pure white. ||55||
The person who bears upon their head the dust of Kuṅkumavāpikā becomes like the sun in this world and attains the eternal Brahman. 56.
Whosoever is touched by the breeze from the Aśvapaṭṭasaraḥ field, their manifold sins are instantly destroyed from the very root. (57)
Furthermore, by the mere sight of this imperishable field, it protects and purifies a human being who is facing destruction through calamities and misfortunes. 58.
But for a sinful person seized by the evils of speech, mind, and action, Kuṅkumavāpikā, when remembered, certainly and swiftly delivers them. (59)
It delivers seven generations of ancestors before him and seven generations after him from the ocean of existence.
Thus, it is heard, drunk, seen, touched, and likewise immersed in. (3.91.60)
By seeing, touching, drinking, or even by the mere mention of the name "Aśvapaṭṭā," she purifies hundreds and thousands of men who lack merit. (61)
And he who, as his vital breaths are departing, should remember Lomaśī Bhūmikā and suddenly bow even with his heart, shall attain the supreme goal. (62)
For one who desires liberation here and has bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, there is no fear of Time, nor of sins, nor likewise of Yama. (63)
Listen, Lakṣmī! The status of being twice-born, the status of being a Brahmin, and even goodness—these arise perfectly through virtues, and virtues arise from frequenting sacred fords. (64)

The sacred ford (tīrtha) is indeed both stationary and moving, yet it is established within the self. Through my yoga, the stationary is my [manifestation], and the moving are my holy practitioners (sādhus). //65//
I am established within the self as the inner soul; indeed, these three sacred fords (tīrthas) are the deliverers.
Virtues come to embodied beings through merit, and defects through sin.
Merit arises from the performance of good deeds; listen indeed to what those deeds are.
My worship, my meditation, and my supreme glorification. ||67||
My entire collection of duties consists of my constant service to Him, and my service to the virtuous through offerings such as flowers and garlands. (68)
By offering water and food, by massaging the feet and so forth, by presenting food offerings, rich perfumes, garments, saffron, and excellent fruits; 69.
The night vigil, prostrations, circumambulations, hymns of praise, and requests for forgiveness;
as well as sacrifices, offerings, and oblations, and the service of guests. (3.91.70)
Service to the destitute, the weak, and others; the honoring of faithful and virtuous women;
showing honor, welcoming, and so forth to the earth, cows, and Brahmins; and service to such beings. //71//
Service to devotees, the elderly, one's parents, and one's guru;
the recitation of mantras with a rosary; and the performance of acts that benefit the world. (72)
Such works as these should be undertaken: the construction of wells and ponds, the building of gardens and halls, and the planting of trees for rest. (73)
Constructing water-stations, shelters, and the like; protecting fields and other such assets;
constantly honoring the elderly; and protecting those who have sought refuge. (74)

Rituals for the gods and ancestors, virtuous deeds, honoring one's own chosen deity, as well as the guidance of teachers through the gift of knowledge and the like, and likewise the gift of devotion; ||| 75 ||
One should indeed perform such auspicious acts of hospitality;
by that, virtuous qualities such as moral conduct and vows truly come into being. (76)
Through these qualities, both goodness and the state of being most devoted to Brahman arise;
for such a person, enjoyment and liberation are in the palm of his hand, and no duty remains to be performed. //77//
Formerly, a certain son of a twice-born man named Kṛśāṅga yoked a buffalo capable of bearing a heavy load to a cart according to his own desire. (78)
He struck him with a staff indeed fitted with a sharp spike;
blood, having been pierced by it, flowed out from his hip. (79)
Seeing that, the queen-mother, filled with grief and longing for her son, spoke to her lamenting son: "Do not grieve, my son! [This is] a sinful woman! (3.91.80)
"This man is not a twice-born; he is a Cāṇḍāla, your driver.
There is no cruelty in a twice-born; a twice-born should always be friendly. (81)
Indeed, the twice-born should be endowed with goodness, compassionate, and likewise a protector;
he should be non-violent, possessed of devotion, pure, and regard all beings as equal to himself. (8)
When punishment falls upon the innocent, a Caṇḍāla, a hunter, or even a cruel, merciless, and arrogant executioner proceeds [to act]. (83)
"This wicked man, devoid of compassion, follows the nature of his own kind.
Having heard these harsh words from the queen, Kṛśāṅgaka—
Having bowed, he asked the queen: "Tell me, if you know me;
my mother is a Brahmin woman—by whom could she have been defiled? (85)
"O Queen! Tell me quickly, how am I a Cāṇḍāla?
The Queen replied: 'Your birth was from a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra. (86)
Then, while your father was away in the field, you slept at night upon the bed; meanwhile, the low-born follower slept in the field where the father had gone. (87)
Then, while the laborer was alone in his own courtyard with his wife, they arrived in the darkness, unseen; at that time, his mother came there as well. (88)
Having slept together on a bed and fallen into a state of passion, you then conceived a child by fate; therefore, you became a *vṛṣala*. (89)
"I know that you are a young girl standing nearby, bound in this field; born from a low-caste man to a Brahmin woman, you are indeed a Cāṇḍāla. (3.91.90)
"Indeed, those evil qualities, which cause destruction and death, have persisted from conception.
Having heard this, Kṛśāṅgaka then quickly bowed to his mother. (91)
Then, having bowed to the queen and asked the buffalo for forgiveness, he remained engaged in ascetic penance for the sake of destroying his sinful birth. (92)
There, on that ground in that sacred field, he performed most severe austerities for a hundred years;
he scorched even the gods, and Mahendra approached him.
"O emaciated one! Why do you suffer, having abandoned agriculture which bestows happiness?
I shall grant you a boon; tell me what it is, for I shall grant you even that which is unattainable. (94)
The emaciated Cāṇḍāla said: "I am a Cāṇḍāla, yet I perform penance out of a desire for the status of a Brāhmaṇa. Grant me the status of a Brāhmaṇa and ward off the defect of my ancestors. (95)
Mahendra said to him: "O, this state of being a Brahmin is difficult for you to attain!
Due to the fault of your father, you are not fit to become pure in seed; on the contrary, you will perish. Therefore, strive diligently to cease from that. (96)
Purity may indeed be attained, yet the state of being a Cāṇḍāla does not perish.
Having spoken thus, Indra departed; but he remained there with emaciated limbs, firm in his resolve, engaged in asceticism for the sake of either death or victory. 98.
He stood on one foot for another hundred years;
then Indra approached again and said, "Cease your exertion!
This status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain, and you will perish through such rashness."
For it is not possible to remove the state of being a *vṛṣala* that resides in the very act of impregnation. (3.91.100)
This being the case, you will not quickly succeed in your efforts at austerity. For everyone born in the animal realm must first attain human birth [before such success is possible]. (101)
Through some connection with merit, one is born as a Cāṇḍāla in the past;
thereafter, at the end of a thousand periods, one repeatedly attains the status of a Śūdra. Then, after another interval of time, having repeatedly become a Vaiśya, and after that— 102. 103.
And thereafter, by the connection with merit, he is born as a Kṣatriya. ||103||
In time, he is born as a Brahmin who is a mere kinsman of Brahmins;
after that, in another period of time, he becomes a learned Śrotriya; and thereafter, by observing the duties of a Brahmin and practicing forbearance, he attains the state of a virtuous man. (104)
And therein, joy and sorrow, as well as desire and hatred, [arise] for one whose body is emaciated. (105)
Excessive pride and harsh speech enter him, and by these he is cast down;
therefore, his status as one born of a *vṛṣala* shall never be far removed. (106)
Having spoken thus, Indra departed; then Kṛśāṅga became firm and stood on one foot for another thousand years. (107)
Devoted to the holy life (brahmacarya), pure, and chanting the eternal Veda (brahman), he was present when Mahendra arrived and said, "Choose a boon, O Dhruva. (108)
Kṛśāṅga said: "My supreme moral conduct has lasted for a thousand years.
Because of that, O Mahendra, let the status of a Brahmin be granted to me, and nothing else. (109)
Indra said: "Choose a supreme boon, but do not choose the state of a Brahmin;
for one born from the seed of a Cāṇḍāla, this exertion of yours is in vain. (3.91.110)
Having spoken thus, Indra departed, and thereafter Kṛśāṅga reached Aśvapaṭṭasara and remained there for a thousand years. (111)
Subsisting on mere air, he became emaciated like a withered tree;
he fell upon the earth to die, and at that moment Indra approached.
Devoted to compassion through the granting of boons, Indra caught him as he fell.
He said, "O emaciated one! Choose a boon here; I shall grant it to you. ||113||
The emaciated-limbed one chose a boon: "Grant me the status of a Brahmin forever.
Indra said: "That is indeed not difficult for you; it is easily obtained somewhere. (114)
It is not attained at all through austerities performed for ten million years;
rather, the ancestors, the gods, and others are fully satisfied by [offerings made] to the Brahmins. ||115||
The earthly deity, the Brāhmaṇa, remains; your status as a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain.
Choose another boon—either the state of being worthy of worship or preeminence. (116)
The emaciated one said: "O Indra! You do not appear to be capable at all.
Why do you pierce me, who am already filled with suffering? How can you kill one who is already dead? (117)
The status of the twice-born is attained by the three castes through their qualities and actions;
furthermore, the status of the twice-born and the status of a Brahmin are identical in terms of qualities and actions. (118)
A twice-born man is such by virtue of the sacred thread and by his discernment; however, it is proclaimed that true Brahminhood exists there through union with Brahman alone. (119)
Through steadfastness in Brahman comes the state of being most devoted to Brahman, and through that, goodness in liberation;
thus, by the union of these qualities, everything is accomplished. (3.91.120)
Through the ripening of fire, the earth becomes filled with the most excellent of many jewels; through the ripening of merit, bodies take on the forms of Brahmins and holy men. (121)

In this world, one is a beast by virtue of one's qualities, a yakṣa by virtue of one's qualities, and even a rākṣasa by virtue of one's qualities; a brahmin becomes a kṣatriya or other caste by virtue of his qualities, and a virtuous man becomes the king of the liberated by virtue of his qualities. (122)
A man and even Nārāyaṇa himself are born according to their actions and qualities;
you are to be pitied, for you do not recognize that Brahminhood is the supreme wealth. (123)
Even having obtained it, you do not recognize it; O Kṣatriya, you are but a human being.
You are not worthy to grant a boon; go, Śakra, to your own abode! 124.
Having established myself in the virtues of a Brahmin, why should I not deserve the status of a Brahmin?
Through my asceticism, the defects of my mother and the defects of my father have been destroyed. (125)
"I am a Brāhmaṇa, there is no doubt; go, O Śakra, to your own abode!
When he was addressed thus, O Lakṣmī, Mahendra indeed granted him an auspicious boon:
"O you of emaciated limbs! You have been purified and cleansed by your austerities."
O Kṛśānu, you who are of the nature of fire, become the essence of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.
May you be worthy of worship by all, always honored by the Brahmins, the best of gods, the most excellent of the twice-born, and most devoted to Brahman even throughout other kalpas. 128.

Through your virtues, the status of a Brahmin was earned here; furthermore, through those same virtues, the state of being most devoted to Brahman was always attained, and indeed the nature of fire itself was reached. (129)
Having thus granted the boon, Śakra departed for heaven;
meanwhile, Kṛśāṅga became Kṛśānu at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
O Rama! Here resides the Kṛśānu-tīrtha, which bestows the state of being most devoted to Brahman;
indeed, here one attains saintliness, purity, and stainlessness. (131)

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Purification of Butchers through Contact with Holy Places; Mobile Holy Places such as Virtuous People; and How, in the Past, at Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, Kṛśāṅga—the son of a twice-born man born of a Śūdra woman—attained the state of a Brahmin and the nature of fire through his penances and a boon from Indra, despite being a Cāṇḍāla," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. 91.

Chapter 092 [[Author: → Chapter 093
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; by my word alone, even one born of another caste shall attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and so it shall come to pass in the world.
Divodāsa, the king of Vārāṇasī, was a great devotee.
Once defeated in battle by the Haihayas, he went to Prayāgaka.
There he bowed down before the sage Bharadvāja, the son of Bṛhaspati.
Then the sage informed Pratāpa of his suffering.
Through the Putreṣṭi sacrifice, a son was born to Divodāsa from his wife;
that son was Pratardana, who, having grown into a youth, went to the city of Vārāṇasī.
He fought with the Haihayas, but the Haihayas were defeated;
intent on flight, they went for refuge to Bhṛgu’s hermitage.
Pratardana followed behind them and, having bowed to Bhṛgu, spoke.
"Give me the enemy kings, the Haihayas such as Vitahavya and others;
by their slaughter I shall be freed from my debt to my father—show me your grace!
Bhrigu, overcome with compassion, replied: "There are indeed no Kṣatriyas here."
Pratardana replied: "O Bhṛgu, I have indeed accomplished my purpose;
even kings have been deprived of their own status by me through my prowess.
Having bowed to Bhṛgu, Pratardana [addressed] the twice-born king Vitahavya.

For the sake of saving the life of the Brahmin, at the word of Bhṛgu, he then abandoned his own capital, Vārāṇasī, and departed. By the mere word of Bhṛgu, the Haihaya Vītahavya likewise [departed]. (3.92.10)
Out of fear, he completely renounced his status as a Kṣatriya and attained the state of a Brahmanical seer (brahmarṣi).
His son was Gṛtsamada, who became a Vedic sage among the Brahmanical rishis.
His son was Dvija, and Sutejas was the son of Dvija; Vihavis was indeed the son of Sutejas.
From him came Vitatya; from him, Satya; from him, Śrava, O twice-born one.
From him came the seer [Ṛṣi]; his son was Prakāśa; his son was Vācika.
His son was the brahmin Pramiti, and his son was Ruru, the excellent sage.
His son was Śunaka, and his son was Śaunaka, the best of Brahmins.
Thus, by the word of that virtuous great seer, the state of being a Brahmin arose;
likewise, it arises through devotion to Brahman and also through initiation.
Through initiation (*dīkṣā*), those born of the three castes become the most excellent Brāhmaṇas.
All virtuous Vaiṣṇavas are Brāhmaṇas born of the lineage of Acyuta. Thus, the state of being a Brāhmaṇa arises through these qualities, through speech, and through initiation.

Even if he has resided in a Brahmin’s house since childhood and been refined there, he becomes a Brahmin only when he is taken onto the lap by a twice-born man. That infant, who was nourished with milk, food, water, and the like, [is truly born]. (17)

One attains the status of that [caste]; a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Brāhmaṇa through austerity, miraculous powers, and blessings—indeed, O twice-born ones, even those who are not Brāhmaṇas by birth become Brāhmaṇas, distinguished by their virtuous deeds and the like. (18–19)
Listen, Lakṣmī, and hear another thing as well: the capable one indeed explains it.
Even though Nandin was a human being, he was made into Śaṅkara’s own attendant (gaṇa).
But Ramā, born from the ocean, was made by Hari into his own Nārāyaṇī.
By Viśvāmitra, O King, Triśaṅku was made into a god.
By Kṛṣṇa, Śiva and others were made into female cowherds in Goloka;
and month after month, Sudyumna became a man and likewise a woman.
Śambhu as Ardhanārīśvara and Viṣṇu as Mohinī likewise [manifested].
In every creation, the seed of man produces both daughter and son;
the sons of the gods and the sons of men—indeed, all progeny—are born of Kaśyapa.
In this way, even from a seed, a non-retrogressive state arises that obstructs rebirth. (24) Furthermore, all those born from moisture are indeed of diverse species;
and from the insentient, insentient beings are likewise produced as diverse species. (25)
Therefore, birth is not fixed; it depends upon qualities and actions.
Excellence is the highest of all states and must be attained through auspicious deeds.
Listen, Lakṣmī: Nahuṣa became a serpent while retaining that very same body.
Due to the curse of Agastya, as he was carrying that king,
he suddenly became a Rākṣasa with only half a foot because of the curse of Vasiṣṭha;
for twelve years he roamed within the depths of the forest.
And Ahalyā became stone due to her husband’s curse;
then, in another moment, she became Vṛndā, that Tulasī tree.
Hari took the form of the Śālagrāma stone, and Kālī likewise became Gaurī.
Śanaiścara attained the state of a serpent, and Indra became a cat;
Hari assumed the forms of a fish and others, and Vahni took on the form of gold.
Likewise, King Bhaṅgāsvana, having bathed in a lake in the forest... [3.92.30–31]
Even the father of a hundred sons attained womanhood according to the facts;
then she became the wife of a sage in the forest, giving birth to a hundred sons once again.
Śrī Nārāyaṇīśrī said:
"How did King Bhaṅgāsvana become a man and likewise a woman?
O beloved Hari, I wish to hear that story; tell it to me.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Formerly, there was a righteous and pure royal sage named Bhaṅgāsvana who,
being childless, performed the auspicious Putreṣṭi sacrifice.
Because Indra’s preeminence was challenged, Indra blazed with wrath.
He desired to create an obstacle, yet he could find no opening whatsoever;
then, at the conclusion of the sacrifice, the king went to the forest for the sake of hunting. Indra, having found a supreme opportunity, arrived and entered the monarch.
He led that king, Aśvattha, who was lost in delusion, far away into the forest.
And there, the thirsty king beheld an excellent lake;
he caused his horse to drink the water and tethered it to a tree.
Having drunk water himself, he afterwards performed his bath in the lake.
By the mere act of immersion, he quickly attained womanhood. Seeing himself transformed into a woman, he became truly ashamed. (38–39)
He reflected, "What kind of face shall I show in my city?
I have a hundred sons; what indeed shall I say to them?
Thus the king, distressed, mounted his horse with great difficulty.
Abandoning all shame, he departed for the city on horseback.
Then his sons, wives, servants, citizens, and countryfolk, seeing this, were filled with wonder and amazement, thinking, "What indeed is this? || 42 ||
He said: "I had gone to a lake within the forest for the sake of hunting;
having bathed there, I suddenly attained womanhood.
Therefore, I shall hand over my kingdom to my sons and then depart for the forest."
Having said, "I am departing," and having given away his kingdom, he went to the forest.
That wife of the sage indeed became female in form for Svarvaha;
from her, the queen of Svarvaha, one hundred sons were then born.
Taking them with her, she went toward her own kingdom and her former sons, and said:
"O sons, you were male, while these others are female;
O dear children, let us enjoy the kingdom together in the spirit of brotherhood."
Heeding the words of their father and mother, they enjoyed the kingdom together.
Then Indra arrived there and sowed dissension among the kinsmen, saying:
"Sons of a father are fit for the kingdom; sons of a woman are never so. || 47-48 ||
"O Brahmins, you have wives and sons; indeed, you do not deserve the status of kings.
Therefore, he spoke of those born later, saying, 'You are indeed the superior ones.
The Kṣatriyas are the earlier-born; they are considered to be your servants."
"Let them not rule your kingdom, for the brahmins are indeed worthy of sovereignty.
Having thus incited mutual enmity, they were destroyed by war.
Hearing this, her mother, an ascetic woman, wept, overwhelmed with grief.
Indra, having approached her, said to her, "By what sorrow do you weep?
She, assuming the form of a brahmin, replied to him: "O best of brahmins, my two hundred sons have perished in battle; I grieve for them and I weep. (52)
Indra said: "O Queen, in the past you performed a sacrifice for the attainment of sons, having disregarded me;
thus you have caused me grief.
O Queen, the enmity has now been requited by me, so do not weep."
Having heard this, the queen fell at his feet and said, "Forgive me.
Indra granted her a boon, asking, "Which of your sons shall live?
She replied, "May my sons born of women live."
Indra said, "Tell me here, why did those born earlier not live?
She replied, "A woman's affection for her offspring is indeed greater than that of a man;
therefore, let all my sons born later live."
Indra said, "Indeed, let all these two hundred sons of yours live.
Out of compassion, I shall restore them to life; let them rule the kingdom together.
Having been addressed thus by the speaker of truth, all those excellent sons were restored to life.
Then Indra spoke again to the woman for the purpose of granting a boon:
"Choose a boon—either manhood or womanhood, whichever you desire.
The woman replied: "May I always possess womanhood; let there never be manhood for me."
Indra asked, "How can there be such a fixation on the distinctions of womanhood?
She replied, "A woman always has greater pleasure in union with a man;
moreover, as one in the form of a woman, I am satisfied by the tenfold pleasures of desire. (61)
"So be it," said Indra, and having granted the boon, he departed for heaven.
That virtuous woman, assuming a female form, enjoyed her lovely celestial vehicle even while intoxicated by the sound of *bhaṅgā*.
Out of her feminine nature, she questioned her lover about the characteristics of women, and the lover spoke to her.
For women are the root of faults; they are fickle-minded and destructive.
Pañcacūḍā, the foremost of the Apsarases, spoke thus to Nārada when he questioned her:
"O Nārada! The nature of women is fickle and dependent upon men."
Even a weak woman desires a lover who is eager for dalliance.
Noble-born women, beautiful women, and women who have protectors do not abide by the bounds of propriety; this fault lies with the female sex.
Women always desire womanhood, which brings about dependence upon men;
indeed, the sovereignty of the household is dependent on women, and the man himself is dependent on the woman.
Without effort, women always enjoy all manner of objects of pleasure.
They are honored and deserve respect, yet they harbor delusion and pride;
(68) free from anxiety regarding livelihood, effort, and so forth, they always desire the state of being enjoyed.
They desire womanhood and good fortune; this constancy is ever the nature of a woman. (69)
Having obtained those who are compliant, prosperous, handsome, and under their own control,
they abandon their own kin and enjoy others instead.
Indeed, this great fault of women exists, for it lies beyond the scope of [ordinary] understanding.
For those women who desire a man, repeatedly grant him what he wishes,
and perform service for his pleasure, devour that shameless man as long as he, a traveler on the wrong path, does not depart.
There is no fear for the family, nor is there any restraint for others;
yet, if they fear the king’s punishment, they do not then engage in sexual intercourse.
There is no man whatsoever who is inaccessible to them, nor do they have regard for age.
They do not enjoy [the pleasures] of form and so forth with firm resolve, thinking "this is a man.
Even though they are protected by all kinds of gifts that fulfill every desire,
they still consort with hunchbacks, the blind, the dull-witted, and dwarfs.
The fault of desire is great for them; women act perversely toward one another.
They are fickle by nature, difficult to satisfy, and hard for their own husbands to restrain—even when he is a giver of their desires and a doer of what is pleasing to their minds. (76)
For women are unrestrained; they do not take account of a husband who protects them.
Indeed, for these women, the primary human goal that accomplishes their desired ends is the very favor of sexual pleasure.
Dharma, wealth, and liberation are considered by women only in accordance with that [pleasure], specifically during their youth.

Rashness, deceit, folly, greed, secrecy, obstinacy, falsehood, impurity, and cruelty—these are the faults found in women. Dependence, sense of ownership, service, endurance, and being the giver of life [are their virtues]. (79)
Gentleness, affection, and submissiveness— these indeed are the virtues found in a woman.
In sorrow there is sorrow, in joy there is joy, a unity of heart,
a single-mindedness in wealth, self-surrender, and servitude— these are generally the qualities found in women.
Virtuous conduct, observance of vows, faith, worship of Hari, hospitality,
and fame for her own kin— these are indeed the most excellent qualities in a woman.
Generosity, preeminence in the household, and never hearing disparagement of her husband [are likewise required].

Forbearance and the capacity for protection—these qualities indeed exist in a woman. Likewise, the performance of household duties, a mind intent on acquiring wealth, and even a fear of expenditure—these qualities indeed exist in a woman. (83–84)
Indeed, the qualities present in a woman are: sexual pleasure, the enjoyment of taste, the alleviation of physical ailments, and the pacification of an agitated mind;
as well as the capacity to expand the lineage, the protection of children, and the preservation of the household. (85)
Indeed, women possess virtues such as the habit of helping others.
They laugh when he laughs and weep when he weeps;
they satisfy him with pleasant words whenever he is distressed, employing their artful charms.
The fickleness of female monkeys, the secrecy of female cats, the quarreling of female ruddy geese, and the conduct of female mice;
the gathering of ants and the searching of vultures.
The manifestation of the rising sun is indeed the swelling of bliss;
likewise, grief is that of one whose only son has died, and folly is that of a camel. Softness belongs to a thief, and sharpness indeed to a razor. (3.92.90)
These qualities indeed exist especially in women.
In former creations, however, women here were virtuous and truthful.
Those daughters of Prajāpati were equal to the gods; they indeed went to heaven.

Then, for the sake of deluding human beings, Brahmā created unrighteous women who delude the entire world; they were devoid of virtuous action and devoted to lust and anger. [He also created] beds, seats, ornaments, food, drink, and ignoble conduct. (92–93)
The Lord of Creatures bestowed upon women a harsh disposition and a fierce passion;
by those qualities, women can never be restrained in any way.
Nevertheless, O Lakṣmī, they are born through austerities, vows, and fasts.
Through service to the virtuous and other such means, women become purified and sanctifiers of the world.
Devoted to their husbands as Kṛṣṇa, these chaste women attain perfection through yoga;
having burned away their defects like a forest fire, they are indeed born as liberated souls.
Those twice-born women who are born in any family whatsoever and have taken refuge in a Brahmin are indeed twice-born;
those virtuous women who possess the initiation of a *sādhvī* are truly virtuous and are twice-born.
Those Brahmins who possess the initiation of Yoga are indeed *yoginīs* and are gods.
Endowed with Sāṃkhya and Yoga, those wives of Brahmā were liberated;
having attained the status of Hari’s consorts, those Brāhmaṇī women became beloved of Hari.
Having attained renunciation, they became givers of renunciation, and are always considered beloved of Brahman.
The cowherd’s daughter, having obtained Brahmā, became Gāyatrī;
she is the venerable, worshipful Brāhmaṇī, the consort of Brahmā, and the mother of the worlds.
The auspicious daughter of a dog-cooker, having obtained Vasiṣṭha, became a Brāhmaṇī.

And the daughter of the Ṛṣis, named Arundhatī, became a venerable woman devoted to her husband. As for the maidens of many castes who, having obtained Kṛṣṇa, became Gopikās, they were born as the dark-complexioned wives of Kṛṣṇa; through yoga, these women attain purity.
Rākṣasīs, having approached a god, become goddesses in every respect;
indeed, Paulomī became a deity by approaching Mahendra.
And Devayānī, though she was a goddess, [became a mortal] by approaching a human Kṣatriya.
Having become the wife of Yayāti, that Mānavī gave birth [to sons].
Some daughters of Dakṣa became celestial goddesses in heaven;
they were the wives of Dharma, the deities, the wives of Brahmins, and the consorts of sages.
The wives of Manu were Mānavīs, Kāśyapīs, and many other types;
they were born from him, for there is no fixed caste-status for women anywhere.
What is the use of saying more on this? My own wives are in the tens of millions.
Born from all the worlds—whether from the heavens, the earth, the nether regions, or from embodied beings—and arisen from every caste, they became of the Brahmin caste through my yoga.
Wearing the sacred thread, these beloveds of Brahmā were like goddesses Ramā. (107–108)
There, in this very field of syllables (akṣarakṣetra), there exist with me certain Brāhmaṇī women who are worthy of worship by all; they are divine, bearers of my own form,
and are all supreme goddesses, the sovereign mistresses of Puruṣottama.
She is the purifier of all creations, as beloved as the divine Śrī, Bhū, and Gaṅgā.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, through my yoga, may you become Nārāyaṇī; and by the power of the gods, may she indeed become Devayoginī through her union with a virtuous man.
From separation she is Viprāṇī; from union with Brahman she is Brāhmaṇī and Brahmayoginī.
From the yoga of liberation she is Muktānī; she is Siddhi and Siddhaprayogiṇī.
From the yoga of the Gaṇas she is Gaṇikā; and from the yoga of the Yogins she is Yoginī.
Through union with Īśa they become Īśvarīs, and through union with Manu they become Mānavīs;
likewise, women are born as Satīs through constant union with Satya.
In all these cases, I am the supreme one—the Lord of Śrī, the Puruṣottama. (113–114)

Through my yoga, the state of being Pauruṣottamī—the supreme among the supreme—is to be attained; by worshipping me alone, the state of being a virtuous wife is attained through service to the saintly. Since liberation itself is achieved thereby, that home is eternal for all time.
Having abandoned the impermanent, one should indeed take refuge in the eternal.
By reading and hearing this, the state of Brahman arises here;
there shall be both enjoyment and liberation, and one attains the nature of Nārāyaṇa.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of Many Examples Concerning the Transformation of Various Castes and the Attainment of Brāhmaṇahood through the Conjunction of Virtuous Vows, Conduct, Initiation, Boons, and Planetary Alignments, Including the Example of King Bhaṅgāsvana’s Transformation into a Woman," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
