[The Author: Chapter 94.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which is difficult to attain in this world but easily obtained through vows.
Through austerities, through blessings, through service, and through self-surrender—
before the power of the yoga of Brahman, all other powers whatsoever bow down in every way, just as all things sink before the power of celibacy, O Lotus-born One.
I shall relate a story concerning a former birth that illustrates the preservation of moral conduct (*śīla*).
A wife was protected in her virtue by a disciple who was a practitioner of yoga (*yogin*).
There was a brahmin named Devaśarman, a great sage (*maharṣi*), in the land of Surāṣṭra.
His wife, named Ruci, was equal to Rādhikā in beauty;
she was equal to Lakṣmī in virtues, possessed divine youth, and was the most excellent of goddesses.
Because of her beauty, even the gods, the Siddhas, and human beings were infatuated. (4–5)

They were born in great numbers, and Mahendra fell into a state of delusion; in a brief moment, he resolved to take her for himself. Devaśarman, too, who knew the nature of women, [acted] according to his strength.

He kept her in his own abode and did not grant her to anyone at any time. Indra came repeatedly to the vicinity of the hermitage seeking her; yet, despite his efforts to obtain her, he did not find her for even a moment.
Indeed, fearing the curse of the Brahmins, he does not come within the range of sight;
remaining concealed, he moves about in many different forms.
Through the power of his asceticism, Devaśarman knows that Indra is searching for him.
While he was living as a lover, wandering at the edge of the forest,
O Lakṣmī, once that ṛṣi, desiring to perform his own vow,
summoned his beloved disciple Vipula, a practitioner of Brahman-yoga. (3.93.10–11)
He is capable of protection, established in dharma, and steadfast in his word; my livelihood is maintained by him at Aśvapaṭṭasara while I abide in my vow.
Accompanied by this vow, I shall go to the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
"After performing the Cāturmāsya vow, I shall indeed return from there.
Mahendra desires to enjoy my beautiful wife Ruci;
you must protect her constantly so that there may be no violation of her virtue."
"O Indraka, remain vigilant so that your devotion to your husband may not perish;
for Indra comes here constantly, assuming many forms.
At times he wears a crown and holds a thunderbolt, and at other times he carries a bow or a staff."
In a mere moment, he appeared as a Cāṇḍāla, or a fire-worshipping Brahmin with matted locks observing vows;
sometimes he was clad in bark garments, sometimes stout, and sometimes thin like a guest; sometimes he was an ascetic of fair complexion, and sometimes a dark-skinned forest-dweller.
Whether a child, an old man, or one who is insane; whether a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a servant;
or even a parrot, a crow, a swan, a deer, or a tiger;
or a king, a god, or a Daitya, he indeed becomes even a mouse. (18)
For that yoga proceeds exactly according to how it may be pleasing.
Even a fly or a mosquito becomes a flowering creeper;
such is Mahendra seen with the eye of yoga. (3.93.20)
"You are capable; therefore, protect her vigilantly against him.
Be on guard against Indra so that he does not violate Ruci.
Having heard these words of his preceptor, Vipula became lost in thought.

"Indra is illusory, powerful, invincible, and assumes many forms. How can he be restrained by me? Having established a hermitage, how shall I protect it?"—having reflected thus in many ways, Kāyā considered "entering his body" to be the best course of action. (22–23)
"Since this cannot be protected by others through human effort alone,
I myself, remaining within her body, shall protect her by the power of yoga.
Having thus resolved, Vipula entered into meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He dwelt with composed mind within the body of the guru’s wife;
unattached, he became like a drop of water resting upon a lotus leaf.
Having fashioned his own subtle body throughout the entire body of the guru’s wife... [25–26]
Having dissolved his pervasive body into the ground through yoga,
he entered the heavy body of the preceptor on all sides by means of his gross form;
having thus pervaded it, Vipula dwelt there, while she did not perceive him.
He protected his mother for the full duration of the four-month period;
remaining motionless, he dwelt there constantly like a shadow, having entered the hermitage in his youthful, divine form as Indra. (28–29)
Becoming most alluring and adorned with every kind of ornament, he beheld before him Ruci—
the lotus-petal-eyed maiden whose splendor was equal to the moonlight—
and seeing that tender young woman, he was cast into delusion.
Bewildered by the sight of his genitals through the hem of his exceedingly fine and subtle garment,
and struck with amazement at his extraordinary beauty, she desired to ask, "Who are you? and even wished to rise to greet him, yet she was held fast by the vast [Viṣṇu].
Restrained by meditative absorption, she was unable to rise at all.
Indra, laughing, said to that young woman who had surrendered her mind:
"Mahendra, the lord of the gods, has come here for your sake. (32)
"Grant me your pleasure; come quickly to my celestial chariot.
But she was unable to rise or say anything at all.
Vipula, having understood everything regarding the conduct of the two there, [acted accordingly]. (34-35)
He bound all her senses with the bonds of yoga.
Then, seeing her motionless and free from any emotional change, Indra was indeed ashamed;
yet Vipula spoke to her once more, saying, "Come, come! (36).
Abiding within the body, he replied: "O sir, what is the purpose of your coming?
Then Purandara, having reflected, being devoid of a mind for an answer, gazed with divine vision upon the sage Vipula who was situated within the body.
Seeing that practitioner of terrible austerities, Purandara became terrified of the curse;
he trembled and stood motionless, like one rendered senseless, for a moment.
Then Vipula quickly emerged from his body and spoke to Indra.
"O evil-minded one, O wicked-souled one, O you of sinful intellect, O lowest of gods!
You have come here with the intent to cause a human Brahmin woman to fall from her dharma; therefore, you deserve punishment. However, I release you—go indeed! (3.93.40–41)
"Has Gautama marked you with his *bhaga* sign—have you forgotten that?
I know you to be of wicked conduct; therefore, I protect her from you.
Depart quickly, lest my guru consume you with the fire of his wrath."
Never again, indeed, do you issue such an invitation to destruction.
(43) Even for an immortal, death may indeed come unexpectedly through the power of asceticism;
neither a god nor a brahmin stands before a virtuous man. (44)
I am a virtuous man, devoted to the nature of Brahman, a yogi taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
here I perform service to my guru and always protect his wife.
I shall indeed remain a celibate student (brahmacārī), yet I am capable of subduing you.
Thus addressed, "Go!", the lord of the gods, filled with terror, departed for heaven.
In this way, that Vipula constantly protected his mother.
Then, one day at twilight, the Rākṣasa Loma-marṣaṇa appeared.
Vipula arrived there intending to abduct that virtuous woman;
lifting her quickly and placing the heavy burden upon his shoulder, he departed through the sky.
Seeing this, Vipula suddenly leapt up into the path of the heavens.
Then he seized the Rākṣasa Loma-marṣaṇa by the throat;
having formed a noose, he throttled his life-breaths and protected his guru.
The terrifying Rākṣasa, deprived of life, fell upon the earth. (3.93.50)
Lifting his heavy mother into the sky, he slowly descended to the earth;
though he was immense, he prostrated before his mother and indeed protected her.
Then, on one occasion, the great asura Kapardaka, situated upon the ocean—
Wandering along the path of the sky, he saw Ruci in his own hermitage,
sporting at the foot of a tree and watering it; overcome by delusion, he suddenly descended from the heavens and approached her.
He forcibly seized Ruci and then ascended into the sky;
Vipula, with great speed, pursued him from behind along the path of the heavens.
Suddenly, he forcefully seized that wicked Kapardaka once again.
He struck him repeatedly on the head with his fist;
he pierced the *brahmarandhra* of that Kapardaka in mid-air and then crushed his skull at the base of the neck. 55–56.
Having quickly carried his own heavy corpse through the sky, he departed;
then Vipula returned to the leaf-hut and became calm.
In this manner, he protected that goddess again and again during the Cāturmāsya period.
Once, for the sake of testing him, that guru became a beautiful woman;
the second [guru], however, having become Ruci, in a secluded place shrouded in darkness,
grasped his penis at the tip of the ear with a desire for sexual union.
Vipula, endowed with perfect virtue, having perceived the transformation of Ruci,
became a stone statue himself by means of his yogic power.
Nevertheless, Ruci embraced that stone statue.
Then Vipula quickly produced from the effigy a fire that was both burning and terrifying; it consumed her,
and the eager Guru, Ruci by nature, abandoned Vipula.
Thus, seeing his excellent disciple so attentive in guarding his moral conduct, the sovereign guru was pleased and then vanished from sight.
Vipula did not know this; he simply continued to protect Ruci at all times.
When the four-month vow with the guru had thus concluded, he reported everything to the guru upon his rising from the vow:
how the obstacles had arisen and how they had been removed. (64–65)
The king of gurus was well-pleased upon hearing the account of Śīla’s protection;
delighted, he said: "I am pleased with you, my disciple, because you have protected your virtue, even by entering and remaining within the body of a woman according to the method of yoga. (66)
You have repeatedly protected me from wicked gods and *rākṣasas*.
Furthermore, you do not even touch Ruci, though she is full of longing for you;
therefore, I am pleased with you. Be forever liberated and happy.

O best of disciples, had I seen you acting wickedly, I would have cursed you; however, you are steadfast in righteousness. You have achieved victory in every way, and you truly abide as a virtuous man.

And from serving those such as you, liberation will certainly come. (3.93.70) In this world, virtuous people like you, free from delusion, are rare. You have yourself encountered them, yet you, whose nature is like a stone, have abandoned your desire for them. (71)
If a man’s own kinsmen or women should prove to be seductive,
yet he remains virtuous, then the woman shall abide in righteousness.
Association with the virtuous brings about virtue and protects one’s character.

Association with the wicked destroys both chastity and goodness. (73) The company of the wicked is the destroyer of dharma and the giver of suffering. Association with the unrighteous kills the virtuous and elevates the non-virtuous. (74)
When one's livelihood comes from unrighteousness, and when the intellect and mind engage in sinful actions,
the self is then struck by defilement.
Therefore, one should cultivate association with the virtuous and seek the company of holy men who bestow righteousness.
Association with the virtuous is an eternal treasury; association with the virtuous is the supreme hoard.
(76) Through reading, hearing, remembering, and practicing this [work], as well as through righteousness, devotion, and virtuous conduct, men shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (77)

Having spoken thus, O Lotus-born One, Devaśarman ceased; and Vipula, free from desire, continued to serve his teacher and his teacher’s wife. Thus ends the account of the victory of the yogi named Vipula and the defeat of Indra, occurring within the preservation of Ruci’s virtue through the power of Brahmanic yoga, which is superior to all other powers, in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

The ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Lomamarṣaṇa and the Rākṣasa Kapardaka, the Guru’s Propitiousness and Blessing, and the Reverence for Sainthood," etc., from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section Three: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age.
Chapter 94.
[The Author: Chapter 95.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! You are always the refuge of the great.
Greatness and auspiciousness arise, as does the protection of dharma.
Indeed, through association with the virtuous, all forms of excellence come into being.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient account that is a source of well-being.
This land of Ājanābha extends for ten thousand *yojanas*,
reaching as far as the Sahya mountain to the west and the region known as Mātrāgaskara;
its central portion is Siṃhāraṇya, a most excellent sacred site (*tīrtha*).
In ancient times, there was a place called Gokarṇa, rich with the dwellings of great sages.
Indeed, that western region of the earth was excavated by the sons of Sagara;
the southern part of the earth, extending for eight thousand yojanas, was likewise excavated.

Of this region, two thousand [yojanas] remain as its remnant. Since long ago, at the holy site of Gokarṇa, which lies beyond the Earth-Devourer (Pṛthvīkhāta), the ocean water has reached [the land], and the earth has been submerged by the salty waters. (6)
The holy site known as Gokarṇa and the holy site called Śārabha,
as well as the entire Siṃhāraṇya forest, then became submerged in water; indeed,
the ground at Gokarṇa became half a yojana in extent.
The sacred field known as Gokarṇa belongs to the sage who is an incarnation of Hara. There, innumerable holy fords (tīrthas) and temples of the sages exist;
there dwell hosts of perfected beings (siddhas) and sages of rigid vows.
They have attained the supreme Nirvāṇa, which is free from rebirth.
O Lakṣmī, in that field Śaṅkara always dwells with affection along with hosts of spirits, the Goddess, and all the gods. (3.94.10–11)
Certain sages, desiring spiritual perfection, resided there;
by its power, they attained that perfection in no time at all.
Seeing the hermitage and the ground submerged in the waters of the ocean—

Those virtuous ones, repositories of ascetic power, as well as the subjects, ascended Sahya Mountain, situated on its eastern side, for the purpose of making it their dwelling. Having deliberated among themselves while residing there, those virtuous ones [acted accordingly]. (13–14)

They set out to go to Rāma, who was performing austerities on Mount Mahendra and other peaks— the supreme means for deliverance and one who relies upon the virtuous. Likewise, those dwelling on the Malaya mountains and those residing on the Nīla mountain also departed.
The inhabitants of the country also set out to go toward Rāma.
Śuṣka, Sumitra, Dharmā, and other sages of rigid vows went toward Mount Mahendra, desiring to behold Rāma. (16–17)
Having traversed many countries, forests, valleys, and rivers,
they reached the best of mountains and beheld the region of Rāma.
It was rich with all creatures in a state of perfect peace and adorned with trees of every season.
Having entered the hermitage, they beheld the Lord who wields the axe (Paraśurāma).
They saw the Master seated comfortably upon a deer-skin, surrounded by his disciples;
observing him in profound silence, they paid homage to Hari and honored him with offerings of water for the feet and other ritual gifts.
Having offered hospitality to the sages, Rāma addressed them with a smile:
"Welcome to you, O highly fortunate ones! I am purified by your auspicious arrival.
May the sages grant me the service they deem worthy; indeed, I shall perform it."

Having heard this, the great sages said: "The region known as Gokarṇa on the earth was cast into the waters of the ocean by those born of the sea while they were digging. Once the waters of the ocean were cleared away, that sacred field became the purifier of all."
We desire to obtain [this], so please show us your compassion.
You are an incarnation of Viṣṇu, a virtuous man who is the source of strength for the righteous.
Jamadagni, the stainless son of Ṛcika, the son of Bhṛgu, [is here].
You are his priest and upholder of dharma; you are capable and a great lord.
Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by you.
We have come to entreat you, who bestows all desired objects.
Therefore, O Blessed One, by your own power, having cast aside the waters of the ocean,
you ought to grant us— all the best of sages— the field known as Gokarṇa, which is submerged in the water within the Siṃha forest.
Having heard this, O ascetics, Rāma then spoke what was appropriate:
"The duty of the virtuous must be performed; there should be no hesitation in this matter.
However, having renounced my weapons, I have come here to practice penance. (28–29)
"Without weapons, that [task] is impossible; what should be done? Please instruct me.
Having heard those words spoken by Rāma, the sages, Śuṣka and the others, said:
"The taking up of weapons is indeed for the sake of protecting the virtuous."
It surely nourishes one's vow, promise, duty, or truth.
It does not cause one to deviate from truth, nor from duty, nor from one's vow;
therefore, O virtuous one, you should accept this weapon for the sake of our welfare.
"Your austerity here shall indeed become great,
and by that, your practice of dharma shall become truly vast.
Having been addressed thus, the virtuous one, holding his axe, reflected upon the protection of the righteous.
Armed with his weapons, he went forth together with the supreme Bhāgavata dharma;
abandoning asceticism and adopting the asceticism of protecting the virtuous, he traveled through the sky and subsequently arrived at the Sahya mountain and the Malaya mountain.
He called out to Varuṇa with a voice as deep as a thundercloud:
"I have come together with the hosts of sages, desiring to behold you.
Therefore, O son of Pracetas, assume your true form and grant me an audience. (36)
When he did not come even though summoned again and again,
the enraged Hari desired to turn the ocean into a waterless sea;
having sipped water for purification, he took up his bow, strung it, and made the twang of the bowstring.
He fixed and discharged that most terrible arrow of Bhārgava, which had a golden shaft, was consecrated by the fire-god, and was accompanied by its mantra.
Thereupon, the earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
All the worlds and the oceans reached a state of supreme agitation.
The quarters of the sky became enveloped by masses of clouds emitting a burning glow,
and the waters, ignited by the fire of the weapon, then went to their destruction.

Even though he was full of pride, the god Varuṇa was reduced to ashes by the fire of the arrow; the ocean quickly went to dryness. At that moment, Brahmā and the others arrived there and offered praise to the Lord.
"Enough, enough, O Hari! Accept peace, O Supreme Lord.
There is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for you, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Self.
Varuṇa has been reduced to ashes, and the water is being destroyed."
The entire world, deprived of water, will go to destruction in an instant.
Be gracious, O ocean of compassion; restrain this fierce weapon.
And restore Varuṇa, the god who is the source of water, O Lord.
Salutations to you who possess the form of Rudra; salutations to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Salutations to you whose nature is Mahākāla and whose form is Death;
salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, who performs the destruction of all and possesses the form of a holy man.
"Salutations again and again to the ender of the kṣatriyas and for the welfare of the gods;
salutations to you, Śrī Hari, Rāma, who brings benefit to the virtuous. Having been thus praised, Hari beheld the gods standing before him there.
Having attained peace, he restrained the fire-weapon (*vahnyastra*) for the sake of desisting.
Having withdrawn the weapon, Rāma stood still; Varuṇa had reached the state of destruction.
For the sake of his very restoration to life, the Aśvins, the gods, and others [intervened]. (3.94.50)
Arriving swiftly at the command of Brahmā, they sprinkled the heap of ashes belonging to Varuṇa with medicinal juices and mantras. Having received life from those ashes, Varuṇa rose up there.
With palms joined in reverence and trembling with fear, he fell at Rāma’s feet.
He said: "O Rāma, protect me by your grace, for I have come to you for refuge;
do not take this offense into account, but grant me your favor."
To Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, who was speaking thus, Rāma said: "Formerly, while digging for the earth in the water,
the sons of Sagara caused the holy site of Gokarṇa, frequented by sages, to fall below."
"Grant that auspicious field as before for their dwelling.
Let no water ever come there within two hundred yojanas, nor ever at the holy sites of Gokarṇa and Śūrpāraka. (55-56)
Having heard this at Bhavatīrtha, Satītīrtha, and likewise at Śārabhatīrtha, Varuṇa accepted it by saying "Om," and after performing worship,
he gave up his earthly life and departed together with the gods.
The sages were filled with wonder upon beholding Rāma’s prowess.
Having reached their appointed place, the seers were delighted and exceedingly joyful;
feeling they had accomplished their purpose, they honored Rāma with blessings.
Commanded by them, Rāma went toward Mount Mahendra.
In the sacred field (kṣetra) emerging from its waters, the great sages and their subjects dwelt;
those islands within the water exist there in the form of holy fords (tīrtha).
"Indeed, the sages who are practitioners of yoga travel by way of the sky.
Thus, O lotus-born one, through the virtuous yoga and the yoga of Rāma,
your father bestowed the earth and life itself upon Varuṇa.
Hari bestowed right there the attainment of the holy place once again;
for a virtuous person indeed grants everything—enjoyment, liberation, and exaltation.
Truly, virtuous people are devoted to the service of others and are never turning back.
Listen also to another story concerning virtuous people that brings about welfare.
There was a most excellent king named Ikṣvāku, the son of the Sun;
and in his lineage, in Ayodhyā, there was a king named Kuvalāśva.
A righteous and great hero, a performer of sacrifices and a protector of the virtuous,
[he lived] near the Himalayas, close to the hermitage of Uttaṅka. There, a fierce Rākṣasa named Dhundhu, the son of Madhu, dwelt.
Indeed, Uttaṅka himself appointed Kuvalāśva for the purpose of destroying him.
Kuvalāśva, eager to destroy Dhundhu,
became ready and quickly set forth with twenty-one thousand sons.
Then the Lord Viṣṇu entered him with his own splendor,
at the command of Uttaṅka and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
And the gods showered him from all sides with divine flowers.
And Dhundhu was indeed beneath the surface of the earth, within the sands.
Having gone there with his sons to that spot on the ground, the king caused a vast excavation to be made, and Dhundhu was discovered at the bottom.
Indeed, through Dhundhu’s mouth, he released a terrifying fire;
by that fire, all the sons of Kuvalāśva were completely consumed.
Only three remained there, standing at a distance, still endowed with life.
Kuvalāśva extinguished the fire with a water-missile (jalāstra).
Then, having swiftly slain Dhundhu with a Śiva-weapon (śaivāstra),
the king showed Uttaṅka that Rākṣasa who had been dead.
Uttaṅka also became pleased and granted a boon to the king:
inexhaustible wealth, invincibility against enemies,
constant delight in righteousness, and likewise an eternal residence in heaven.

And by the grace of Uttaṅka, the deities then arrived, bringing celestial chariots for the sons and for those Rākṣasas who had been slain there, granting them imperishable worlds; and those twenty-one sons also arrived. (76–77)
Having assumed divine bodies and being seated in celestial chariots, thousands [of them] went to heaven while all the Jayanas and others looked on.
Thus, by the power of the sage, the king attained victory.
Through the power of that virtuous man, his sons attained imperishable heaven.
Then, in this manner, Kuvalāśva had a son named Dṛḍhāśva who lived for a long time;
in his lineage was born King Satyavrata, who was possessed of great strength.
And that one of great strength went to the marriage pavilion of the King of Vidarbha; indeed, at the time of the taking of the hand, he fought a battle out of desire,
force, delusion, exultation, and power.
And by the power of destiny, he forcibly carried off his wife from the pavilion.
Having shown contempt for the gods and the brahmins, that wicked man committed a sin;
consequently, he was abandoned by his father, who was named Trayyāruṇa, because of his unrighteousness.
And he was told by the outcaste dog-cookers (śvapākas) that he must dwell outside;
so, having gone outside, he lived near the dwelling of the dog-cookers.
Then, for twelve years, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, did not send rain.
Then Viśvāmitra performed severe austerities in that region.
And Viśvāmitra’s wife, accompanied by many sons,
sold her middle son for the sake of maintaining the family.
Having understood that, Satyavrata indeed liberated his son,
giving him many foods produced from the power of truth.
In this manner, Satyavrata then provided for her maintenance.

For the sake of pleasing Viśvāmitra and also out of compassion, he who was the son of Viśvāmitra was indeed liberated; for Gālava became a great ṛṣi, heroic and endowed with devotion to his vows. (88–89)
By virtue of his vow, devotion, compassion, and promise,
Satyavrata indeed supported Viśvāmitra’s wife and the others;
meanwhile, Vasiṣṭha became the ruler of the kingdom of King Trayyāruṇi.
In Ayodhyā, O Satyavrata, he appeared entirely dejected.
For this reason, Vasiṣṭha did not harbor even the slightest suspicion regarding Satyavrata; for the power of destiny was indeed at work there.
Then Satyavrata, out of anger, went to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha;
like a child, he then seized all the food and other provisions and fed them all to the sons of Viśvāmitra.
Then Vasiṣṭha said to him: "You are indeed always possessed of three sins:
the abduction of a maiden and a woman, cohabitation with a Cāṇḍāla, and the taking of food and other offerings from me; therefore, you are considered Triśaṅku."
Viśvāmitra, having desisted from his ascetic penance, realized this and became pleased; he granted a boon, saying, "Be as happy as a god.
Then Triśaṅku, though virtuous and devoted to truth, made his choice.
Having enjoyed an unimpeded kingdom in heaven while still in his physical body in Vraja,
he consecrated Triśaṅku as king upon the death of Trayyāruṇa.
Having ruled the kingdom, he departed for heaven in that very body.
While the deities and Vasiṣṭha looked on, Viśvāmitra, the descendant of Kuśika, caused the king to ascend to heaven in his physical body;
this occurrence of the impossible became like a marvel.
By the grace of Viśvāmitra, Triśaṅku shines in heaven.
This great majesty belongs to that virtuous and ascetic sage;
therefore, indeed, the righteous should be served, for they are the deliverers of sinners.
His wife Satyaratā gave birth to Haricandraka. His son was Rohita, who was a vessel for the compassion of Viśvāmitra;
he was delivered from many hardships by the wise Viśvāmitra.
In this world, women, sons, and kings have achieved eternal fame.
O Lakṣmī, I have thus described to you how various kinds of auspiciousness, as well as even liberation, arise from always taking refuge in the virtuous.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Prowess of the Virtuous," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. It describes how the inhabitants of Siṃhāraṇya regained access to the Gokarṇa Tīrtha which had been submerged in the ocean through the refuge of Paraśurāma; how Kuvalāśva attained the status of Dhundhumāra by the grace of Uttaṅka; and how Triśaṅku, known as Satyavrata, ascended to heaven in his own body through the grace of Viśvāmitra.

→ Chapter 096
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O Beloved, what should be constantly chanted by beautiful women for their own liberation?
Who is to be worshipped, and who is to be saluted? Tell me this, you who are compassionate toward women. (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"The name 'Śrīkānta' (Beloved of Śrī), which bestows happiness, should always be chanted by women.
Because of that supreme name of mine, I indeed grant liberation. (2)
"O Lord Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O my husband!"— thus should widows repeat my name again and again for their own liberation. (3) By young maidens, my name "Rādhāvara" should always be chanted.
The mantra "Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa" should always be chanted by elderly women.
(4) The supreme recitation is "Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa," which should be performed by all women for the attainment of all perfections. (5)

"I am worthy of worship and salutation; I am the beloved wife and husband of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. O Supreme Lord, I am also present within my husband even when he is in the form of a golden image or other such representations. (6) Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
At all times— whether during a vow, a great festival, at home, in a temple, during the worship of a deity, at a *śrāddha* ceremony,
or likewise upon departure; whether setting out, entering [a new home], at a wedding, or during any auspicious rite— [one should perform this].
When beginning a house, in agricultural work, in enterprise, or when desiring victory;

likewise, during prosperity, well-being, or in states of dejection and misfortune—what should be recited for auspicious or inauspicious matters and so forth, in order to obtain one's desired fruits and the like? (8–9)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: It bestows gain everywhere, grants peace and nourishment, destroys fear, provides protection, eliminates enemies and obstacles, and is approved by the virtuous. (3.95.10)
I shall now proclaim the Brahma-śara mantra, which destroys all sins;
by chanting it anywhere, an embodied being is liberated from all evils.
Through it, one becomes long-lived, and supreme prosperity approaches them.
That verbal composition was fashioned together with the circles of liberated souls for my satisfaction in that abode which is equal to the imperishable Brahman;
it was when, O Lotus-born One, I entered into creation along with you.
Salutations to the illustrious Supreme Lord, salutations to the Sovereign of the Imperishable;
salutations to the Lord of the Liberated, salutations to the one who delights in the beloved of Brahmā.
Salutations, salutations to the Lord of the beloved of Hari and others, salutations to the Incarnate One.
Salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
(15) Salutations to the Lord of Lords, the husband of Īśvarīṇī;
salutations to the sovereign of the Vyūhas, the husband of Vaiṣṇavī. (16)

Salutations to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī; salutations to You, the Lord of Śrī Lakṣmī. Salutations to the Inner Controller, the treasure-house of the Vedas; salutations, salutations to You. Salutations to the Thousand-headed One, and salutations to You whose names are infinite.
Salutations to Viṣṇu, to Śambhu, to Aja, and to you who possess three forms.
(18) Salutations also to the Ādityas, and salutations, salutations to the Vasus;
salutations to the two Aśvins, and salutations, salutations to all the gods. (19)
Salutations indeed to the sacrificial deities and to Time and Death;
salutations again and again to the Viśvedevas and to the ancestors. Salutations repeatedly to the Siddhas, the sages, and the virtuous.
Salutations again and again to all the lords of the Gaṇas and to all the attendants.
Salutations again and again to the virtuous women, the chaste ones, and the goddesses;
salutations again and again to the mothers, the fathers, and the elders.
Salutations again and again to the Brahmins, to the venerable classes, and to the sacred pilgrimage sites;
salutations again and again to Kambharā, the Great Lakṣmī, who is ever-contented. Salutations again and again to Māṇikyā, to Prabhāvatī, and to Prajñā.
Salutations again and again to Lakṣmī, Śrī, Rādhikā, and Kamalā.
Salutations to the glorious Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa, the Great Viṣṇu.
Salutations again and again to the seven Ṛṣis, to the descendants of Manu, and to the Brāhmaṇas.
Salutations again and again to the wondrous sages, the true gurus;
salutations again and again to Dharma, to Bhakti, to Kṛṣṇa, and to Hari.
Salutations again and again to Nara, his elder brother, and to those born of the Bull.
Salutations to all the guardians of the directions and to the protectors of the worlds.
(27) Repeated salutations to the gurus who bestow liberation and grant peace;
repeated salutations to those who protect, purify, and sanctify. (28)
Salutations again and again to the purifying principles and to the sovereign powers;
salutations again and again to all the sciences of Brahman that grant liberation.
Salutations repeatedly to the noble ones, who are like great wish-fulfilling cows.
Salutations again and again to the ascetics who possess virtuous conduct, to those practitioners of yoga.
Salutations to You, the Self of all, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to Him whose nature is self-luminous, the treasury of mantras.
One should glorify these [incarnations], who are of the nature of Brahman and increase one's fame;
likewise, one should glorify the liberated lords and the gods.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the Supreme Brahman, as revealed by all the scriptures.
One should indeed proclaim my praise, which is auspicious for all beings and purifying;
it pacifies diseases, bestows success, and likewise provides nourishment.
One should always recite my praise at the end of the day in the evening, and throughout the night and day without ceasing.
These deities bestow the accomplishment of all undertakings upon men;
when praised, they protect, shower down desired objects, and nourish them.
All these leaders are also witnesses of one's actions.
When these have been recited, they become pleased and dispel the inauspiciousness of men.
Thus, having risen at the time of the *kalpa*, one should repeatedly perform prostrations;
for such a person there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor any obstruction on the path. (36–37)
Inauspiciousness shall not befall him; indeed, auspiciousness shall attend him at every step.
He shall not experience bad dreams; he shall be endowed with well-being at every moment. All his sins shall perish, and great merits shall arise.

Diseases and ailments perish; one should perform rites for well-being within the family. The arrow of Brahmā shall provide protection for oneself, one’s sons, wives, household members, wealth, and medicinal herbs.
In battle, enemies perish and victory belongs to the reciter;
it should be recited at rites for the gods and ancestors, so that the ancestors and deities are satisfied.
Impurity shall be driven far away, and purity shall prevail forever.

Through the recitation of the Brahmaśara mantra during travel or for auspicious undertakings, supreme success in one's desired goals will be attained; of this there is no doubt. He shall have no fear of kings, nor any fear of wild beasts.
He has no fear of enemies, nor of *piśācas*, serpents, or *rākṣasas*;
he has no fear of fire, water, wind, or space, nor of earthquakes or malevolent planets.
Wherever the hymn of Brahmāśara exists, there suffering dissolves away.
There the fool does not die, nor is he born with his hopes frustrated.
Wealth is his treasure-trove, and his cows have many calves.
Such is this *Brahmaśara* hymn, which protects like an arrow. (45–46)
To you, O Lakṣmī, has been declared the truth, the eternal Brahman;
it is the heart of all beings, my hearing is the eternal Vāk.
By chanting [this], they go to heaven, to the gods, and likewise to the great Viṣṇus and the lords.

By chanting [my names], they go to the worlds; by chanting [the names of] my incarnations, they go to my abode. (48) But by chanting me—the beginningless Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa—they go to my imperishable state; by chanting Lakṣmī, they obtain prosperity. (49)
By chanting the names of Rādhā as well as the Aśvins, one attains a most excellent form;
by remembering Dharma, one attains a bull (the state of righteousness); by remembering Brahman, one attains imperishable happiness;
and by remembering the virtuous, one always attains supreme merit and freedom from obstacles.
The *Brahmaśara-stotra* should be recited for the sake of accomplishing all tasks and purposes.
Holy men (*sādhu*) should be worshipped for the pacification of all sins;
indeed, the slighting of holy men can even bring down the gods themselves.
Having fully propitiated virtuous people, one never comes to harm;
the holy ones are to be honored, saluted, and served like the Supreme Lord.
One should always behave toward virtuous people as if they were one's own inferiors.
The compassionate saints sustain all these worlds;
endowed with devotion, they protect those who have come for refuge. Indeed, through their union with the Blessed One, the great saints are the bridges of dharma. (54–55)

They renounce the wealth of women, are disciplined in the restraint of speech, and are worthy of being beheld by all beings; they are endowed with virtuous conduct, firm in their vows, liberators of the worlds, and likewise protectors of the scriptures. (56)
The scribes and the spectators, too, were devoted to the exertion of dharma.
(57) For them, austerity and devotion were their wealth, and Śrī Hari was their great strength;
they were the refuge of all dharmas—saintly beings who possessed divine vision. (58)
Those who desire liberation abide in devotion and in dharma, as well as in the bridges of dharma;
relying upon them, all subjects and embodied beings live.
The virtuous are the steps to Brahman, the paths for those traveling toward liberation.
The eternal givers of sacrificial merit and food,
who deliver both ancestors and gods, and who consume the first portions of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings,
protect the three worlds through their blessings from the fear of illusion.
They are suns for all the worlds, as well as eyes for those who possess sight;
they have the wealth of hearing all narratives, they are skillful, and they are bestowers of liberation.
They know the destinies of all sentient beings and contemplate the course of the inner self.

Those who understand the beginning, the end, and the intermediate stages are the ones who go to the supreme goal. (63) Those who possess knowledge of the higher and the lower, who are adorned by the awakening to the Self and other virtues, are liberated, free from evil, and have taken refuge in the abode where sin has been shaken off. (64)
Free from dualities, devoid of bonds, without spokes [in their wheels], and without possessions;
they are worthy of honor and are honored by the virtuous, the great-souled, and the true Vaiṣṇavas.
They regard mud, a smear of dirt, sandalwood paste, food, a blade of grass, and a sweet flavor all as equal.
Clad in linen, antelope skins, or fine silk, they remain devoted to fasting;
they wither their limbs through austerities, sacred knowledge, and vows.
They shall render that which is godless into something possessed of gods and endowed with wealth.
For by the power of their asceticism, the virtuous can indeed create other worlds;
they are the Brahmins among Brahmins, the deities even among deities.
The virtuous, adorned by the scriptures, are the authorities among all authorities.
Among those for whom the old and the young, the poor and the wealthy—
whether woman or man alike— deserve equal honor,
it is only through the distinction of austerity and knowledge that one deserves superior honor.
Whether ignorant or a knower of Brahman, a virtuous person is a great and supreme vessel.
A learned and virtuous person, being the Supreme Brahman, is a purifying and most excellent vessel.
Both the ignorant and the learned, if truly virtuous, are indeed a great divinity.
For even in a cremation ground, the radiant fire is not defiled;
likewise, in the wheel of worldly existence, the virtuous person is never defiled.
Just as the fire that licks the oblation shines most brightly during a sacrifice, so does the virtuous person shine forth.
Even when thousands of Brahmins are feasting at a great sacrifice, it would be in vain if there were no virtuous person present, because the virtuous one is Nārāyaṇa.
The virtuous ones are worthy of worship by the Moon, the Sun, and others; they are the lords of the lords.
Indeed, through the worship of the virtuous, longevity, fame, glory,
strength, devotion, liberation, and divinity always increase day and night.
Those who worship the virtuous indeed become lords of the worlds and the non-worlds.

In matters of dharma, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; in fame, prosperity, and the pacification of disease; and in the worship of deities and ancestors—the stainless holy ones (sādhus) are to be propitiated.
For those holy ones are indeed Mādhavas (Vishnus) in this world and in the next.
May they, being well-satisfied like the Lord of Śrī, deliver the entire world.
(78) In the house of Kaśyapa, there was a virtuous Vaiṣṇava ascetic and mendicant named Praṇada-Brahman, who was the mind-born son of the Creator. (79)
Wearing matted hair, emaciated by his vows and observances, he possessed the siddhis such as great sovereignty;
he was deeply absorbed in the recitation of mantras with garlands and was generally devoted to silence.
Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, always attended upon him in the morning.
Through such acts as massaging his feet and by offering him food, drink, and other necessities, this virtuous man worships Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and me;
devoted to me, he is constantly engaged in meditation. (81–82)
He wanders at will through the divine worlds, among the *nāgas*, and among humans;
then he returns again to the abode of the high-souled Kaśyapa.
Once, while chanting the *Brahman*, he said to Kaśyapa, "O Lord, feed me."
Kaśyapa fed him milk-porridge and cakes.
Then the sage Praṇada spoke to his attendant, the seer Kaśyapa:
"Anoint my limbs repeatedly with this milk-porridge. (84–85)
Kaśyapa performed everything, including the anointing with milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
He bathed the great sage Praṇadbrahma with milk-rice.
Then, having risen, [he honored him] with the remnants of the milk-rice.
He also anointed the face and the head of Kaśyapa.
Then, seeing the young woman Aditi standing nearby,
he took her by the hand and anointed her with the milk-rice porridge.
Then that lord of sages, chanting the sacred *brahman*, discharged her [the semen] upon his face, chest, waist, thighs, back,
and hips. Thereafter, he spoke again to Aditi, whose body was saturated with the milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Placing me upon his shoulder, he went outside in the presence of everyone.
Aditi likewise placed him on her shoulder and then went outside;
meanwhile, the sage struck that girl, who was in the bloom of youth, with creepers.
She too, placing virtuous people upon her shoulders, wandered everywhere;
while all the world looked on, she returned toward her own home.
That sage, with [the people] seated upon his shoulders, came home by way of the royal road.
Neither Kaśyapa nor Aditi experienced even the slightest bit of sorrow.
However, as soon as the king of sages arrived at their home, he quickly fell to the ground from his shoulder; at that moment, Kaśyapa, Aditi, and the other women likewise [fell]. (93–94)
They performed services [for him], saying, "Be gracious, O Blessed One!
Then that king of sages, composed and having looked upon Kaśyapa in such a state, spoke to Aditi with a satisfied soul: "You shall become the mother of the gods."
"Since you have conquered anger, you shall therefore be Kaśyapa here;
you will undoubtedly become the father of all creatures.
And in your lineage, there will indeed be crores and billions of virtuous ones such as myself."
All shall be upholders of their lineage, devoted to the meditation on Brahman;
likewise, they shall be joined with wives and possess wealth such as houses.
Indeed, all kinds of offspring shall belong to you alone.
Your merit and fame shall be eternal; of this there is no doubt.
O Kaśyapa, the manifestations of you and of Hari shall indeed occur again and again for the sake of uplifting the worlds. (3.95.100)
Neither old age, nor disease, nor even Aditi shall overcome you;
you shall become the foremost among all women, O Aditi.
Let this very disposition toward the virtuous always remain yours.
Having spoken thus, he ceased; having bathed, he indeed became pure.
He said, "O Aditi, those auspicious deities who consume the nectar shall always be the recipients of the milk-rice and the fruit for your sons."
By the turn of fate, some other women will at some point become recipients of your grace; as for you, Kaśyapa, be happy.
Indeed, all the houses of Kaśyapa shall be endowed with every prosperity.
"Let it be so," the Sage said, and it became exactly thus.
O Lakṣmī, in this way the words of blessing from the sage Praṇada and from the saintly Sādhu, as well as the services rendered by Kaśyapa free from doubt, have indeed borne fruit. || 105-106 ||

O virtuous one, service to a saintly person yields the fruit of Aditi and even gives birth to Hari; indeed, Aditi is born again and again as the mother of the gods, but no other woman is so born repeatedly.
O Lakṣmī, the fruit of service to a saintly person bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It bestows all prosperity and fulfills all desires.
(108) Holy beings are constantly worshipped by all—by deities and others, as well as by humans, the lords of the world, the guardians of the directions, Īśvara, and so forth. (109)
On one side is the service of all beings, and on the other is the service of the virtuous;
before the fruit of serving the virtuous, all other things do not merit even a sixteenth part.
By reading and hearing this, one shall obtain the fruit of serving the virtuous.
One shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and become a partaker of eternal bliss.

Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Kaśyapa and Aditi Attaining the Status of Parents of the Devas through the Blessing and Service of the Saint Praṇadbrahma," within the section on the Greatness of Holy Persons to be Worshipped and Saluted, in the Third Book, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 096 [[Author: → Chapter 097

Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: "O beloved, regarding the statements that 'the virtuous, Hari, you, Dharma, the virtuous woman, liberation, and spiritual practice are [the means],' what indeed are the authoritative proofs for such claims? (1)
For that which is not proclaimed by valid means of knowledge is not firmly settled in the heart.
Therefore, what do you consider to be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for making those [scriptures] authoritative?
Tell me, O Lord of the World, you who are the treasure-trove of all sciences and so forth.
"Wherein there may be no doubt for me, indeed for the benefit of the worlds.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī, [I shall explain] the supreme authority indeed."

That which is repeatedly observed by oneself as a direct object, and which is indeed determined directly by the senses through familiarity— that is perception (pratyakṣa). Furthermore, those who are virtuous, observant of vows, devoted, and likewise free from latent desires— || 4-5 ||

Even while sleeping on the bed, those of virtuous character should be examined through their cohabitation and devotion; likewise, those of latent tendencies should be examined through the giving of enjoyments. Indeed, the virtuous should be examined directly and never otherwise.

Those great saints who possess such character are Nārāyaṇas themselves in this world; they are those for whom there is no transformation whatsoever in their embrace or in their effort, and who indeed never experience weariness in their manifold and constant practice of devotion. (7–8)
In dancing, singing, service, and so forth, shame does not restrain them;
they should be understood as truly devoted, auspicious, and saintly.
Various kinds of enjoyments should be given to such a saint, even if they have already been prepared for others.

One should not eat [if the mind is impure], for the mind may become dejected; thus, there is a direct determination of goodness. Indeed, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the tongue (*rasanā*), and the signs (*liṅga*)—such as the objects of examination—are present there, yet it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that serves as the beneficial means of determination.
Speech that merely follows the crowd should never be uttered;
for there is no inference free from defects without the presence of a true logical reason (*saddhetu*). An inference based on a fallacious reason cannot be determinative.
O Kṛṣṇa, grant me the direct vision of Your marks within myself;
let there be the perception of the marks and so forth upon my hands, feet, and body.
Indeed, direct perception is proclaimed here as the proof of one's being the Blessed Lord.
The authoritative standard for these marks is indeed the scripture transmitted through tradition,
which consists of the words of reliable authorities and is likewise rooted in the Veda.
The Vedas are also the authority regarding the form [of the deity] and whatever weapons it bears.

Having seen it written by those possessing divine vision who were present at my side, whoever has the mark of that weapon on their hand or foot—he alone is the Blessed One; he may assume the form of a human being or other such forms. (16–17)

"Just as I am marked upon my hand with the fish, the trident, and other signs, so too am I the Lord of Ramā, possessing a manifest divine form and the splendor of ten million lotuses. I exist as one endowed with the sixteen marks, both upon my feet and throughout my body. (18)
I possess innumerable marks; I am manifestly endowed with the discus, mace, and other [emblems].
(3.96.19) Thus is the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, to be understood through these means of knowledge.
Dharma is honored by men for the sake of worldly conduct and happiness. (3.96.20)
He indeed resolved that this must be followed as the proper path:
charity, service to others, marriage, protection of others, purity, acquisition through righteous means, worship, and likewise industrious effort. (21)
Thus, these and other paths, according to place and time,
are determined to be Dharma itself for the sake of happiness and the absence of obstacles.
The word of the authoritative one and the action of the authoritative one shine forth as the very form of Dharma.
A virtuous and noble woman is always to be awakened by her husband through excellent conduct such as devotion to him;
through living together, she is constantly awakened by her companion.
Indeed, the truths and sovereign powers [of women] are recorded in the scriptures.
Those women in whom such wonders are seen are virtuous wives.
Liberation consists in the emptiness of the self; here, it is understood through the cessation of afflictions and the like.
Therein, there shall be perpetual peace, innate happiness, and likewise eternity.
Thus, the acquisition of the worlds of bliss that bestow eternal joy—
belonging to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as well as to me and myself,
and serving as the abodes for the realms beginning with Akṣara— is [described]. 27.
O Lakṣmī, liberation must always be ascertained, at least slightly, both through the method of the scriptures and through direct perception. It is held that it is indeed attained through devotion;
or else, when delusion is destroyed by the path of knowledge, there is the state consisting of realized wisdom.
That which is to be known as the nature of liberation has the scripture as its authority;
O Beloved, there exists no other means of knowledge equal to this wonder.
In that wonder lies the salutation, for therein everything is dissolved.
Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony;
as well as presumptive testimony, apprehension, probability, tradition, gesture, silence, intuition, dreaming, portents, and mental cognition. (3.1–3.2)
Indeed, even the fourteen means of knowledge dissolve into the Great Wonder (camatkāra).
Therefore, the very nature of accomplishment (siddhi) is indeed the most powerful authority (pramāṇa).
Even direct perception, though already established, is further transformed by accomplishment.
What then can be said of other means of knowledge, O Lotus-born One?
Serve virtuous people, Lakṣmī, honoring them with respect; for among the virtuous, there is enjoyment as well as liberation, and in every way, the supreme goal is found among the virtuous.
Hari, dharma, devotion, and liberation prevail among the virtuous; goodness, chastity, and everything else prevail among the virtuous.
Knowledge, service, my devotion, and likewise every kind of charity [prevail there].
For these dharmas are the highest of all and are endowed with contentment. In them there is happiness, in them there is delight, and in them the supreme bliss is considered to reside.
In them is liberation, and the union with Hari occurs only among the virtuous, O beloved! (37–38)
Those who are pervaded by passion and ignorance, who are nihilists, revilers of the virtuous,
and envious of the righteous and their dharma, fall into hell. But those who serve the virtuous, practice the dharma of the virtuous, and attend upon the holy man— [they attain the highest state].
Being devoted to truth and uprightness, they become saintly and go to my abode.
Through service and worship of me, devotion to dharma becomes their refuge;
for those virtuous ones, being full of devotion, attain my realm.
Householders who possess only a measure of merit go to the heavenly world—
those virtuous lay followers (upāsakas) who are endowed with good character and refined conduct.
Having given food to five [others], the virtuous eat what remains.
Those who perform circumambulation around a cow, a deity, the sun, a virtuous person, a chaste woman, a teacher, an ascetic, a brahmin, an elder, and a righteous person;
and those who do so for guests, servants, family members, and women— [43–44]
Those who protect those who have sought refuge with them,
those who are devoted to the service of their guru, and those who serve the elderly;
those who always maintain a solitary disposition, dwell at sacred fords, and are dear to Hari.
They are wise, contented, and always filled with happiness;
they follow the words of the elders and are devoted to the study of the Vedas.
Yet, even though they have withdrawn from the objects of the senses, they do not exist without Śrī Puruṣottama. (46–47)
For all those who are afflicted by disease and who long for longevity and the like, the virtuous,
who are adorned by goodness, are free from the use of the address "thou.
Just as salt, when immersed in water, dissolves away.

Likewise, every sin offered to the virtuous perishes instantly. A wise person should not conceal a sin; if concealed, it increases. Having committed one, it should be confessed to the holy ones, for they indeed bring it to rest. (3.96.50)
One should practice dharma endowed with devotion; one should not be a hypocrite who uses dharma as a banner.
For those who trade in dharma fall back again even after having enjoyed heaven.
One should worship the gods without ostentation and serve the virtuous without deceit.
One should follow the gurus with devotion and practice generosity for the sake of liberation.
One should acquire good fortune through devotion, service, austerity, and vows;
thereafter, one may find good luck even without effort and without exertion.
When it is not the time for gain, one does not obtain it even when effort is exerted;
but when it is the time for gain, a virtuous person, by serving appropriately, shall attain that supreme state.
For what is done at the right time remains unattracted, yet comes of its own accord and stays.
Service accompanied by blessings shall never be fruitless.
(55) If, after studying the treatises on ethics, one does not become endowed with ethical conduct, then that study is in vain and leads to rebirths in hell. (56)
Having attained a human birth, one must perform worship of me;
if that is not done here, whatever else is performed is fruitless.
Even if one is endowed with knowledge, if one does not apply that knowledge for the sake of the Self, it is likewise in vain.
For one who is not tranquil and has created craving, knowledge is indeed fruitless.
(58) If a learned man, having abandoned tranquility and forsaken his own liberation, conducts himself according to worldly views, his life is fruitless. (59)
Those of passionate nature (rājasa) and others do this which has been done, will do it, and are doing it;
if those of virtuous nature (sāttvika) were likewise to follow such paths, their livelihood would be fruitless.
[Yet] that which is honored indeed demonstrates service to others for the sake of the world.
Having taught those who are equal to themselves, he indeed causes them to recite [the scriptures] immediately for the sake of his own fame.
(61) The wicked, having attained physical renown, do not follow the path of devotion;
they alone are the destroyers of dharma, perceiving only the external and not the internal. (62)
If a person attains peace by relying upon knowledge, that is his most excellent fruit; nothing greater than that has been accomplished.
A wise man should not, for the sake of his livelihood, depend on one who is devoid of knowledge.
A wise man should not praise wealthy fools out of a desire for petty gain.
(64) Petty desires do not belong to the wise, nor does wisdom belong to one of base mind.
A wise man is eternally contented; he is virtuous and possesses the joy of Brahman. (65)
There is equality between the virtuous and the wise in contentment, in self-realization, in truthful speech, in devotion, in being most established in Brahman, and in the Supreme Lord. Furthermore,
if one desires to undertake actions but does not find assistance, [one should remain equanimous].

One should undertake fierce austerity; for what has not been sown does not sprout. (67) What was given is obtained later, and service bestows prosperity. Through non-malice one gains long life, and through devotion to the virtuous, the supreme state. (68)
One should give abundantly to the virtuous, constantly serve the good, and act for the welfare of all embodied beings; having attained victory, one should go to the Imperishable.
One should never beg from those who enjoy their wealth, nor should one dwell among the poor.
One should certainly not practice friendship with the wicked; one should serve the virtuous for the sake of liberation.
One should enjoy the happiness established within the self and always be an heir of Hari.
One should become a son submissive to the good and desire liberation in the supreme, imperishable Brahman.
One should pay homage to virtuous and chaste women and worship me, Lord Hari;
being devoted to me alone, one should indeed offer everything belonging to oneself unto me.
Whatever is not offered perishes, and whatever is acquired through labor becomes fruitless.
Having offered that very [gift] and performed it accordingly, one shall obtain eternal liberation.
The giving of dharma, peace, joy,
and celebration must be performed for the attainment of bliss and even immortality.
One should perform service as a gift in every way, even with one’s own prosperity; and one should give away one’s house and family for the sake of attaining that [higher state].
One should place one’s trust only in what is a virtuous deed, and never in what is not a virtuous deed.
One should breathe with confidence in the Dharma-Buddha and then proceed swiftly. (76) Dharma, when practiced quickly, will turn the mind toward devotion.
By practicing devotion, one attains me, the Supreme Lord, as a son. (77)
In this very way, the righteous indeed cause the self to attain the Self. The Supreme Self is truly the goal to be acquired, for dharma is the bestower of victory.
[This applies] to all bodies composed of the five elements, which possess an identical nature.
Where one's own eternal dharma is firm, there Hari is certainly present.
(79) For all embodied beings who possess equal dispositions and follow the path of dharma, devotion and service to the true guru, to the father, and to Hari grant liberation. (3.96.80)
Service to the lineage of the virtuous is indeed said to be the supreme good;
likewise, by serving them, one becomes free from sin and attains happiness. Indeed, the auspicious service of the virtuous is the destroyer of all impurities.
Whether sin has arisen through the body, the sense organs, or likewise through the internal faculties—
whether done knowingly or unknowingly— all of that is dissolved by service to the virtuous;
it perishes for one who recites [mantras] at night or during the twilight hours.
Service to the virtuous and the recitation of mantras bring well-being to the yogi;
indeed, birth as an animal, hell, and the mixed castes are destroyed.
Through service to the righteous, there is neither fear nor sudden death.

I am the universal Guru, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. O Lakṣmī, I am the life-force of all, the inner self, the Lord of souls, and the Supreme Sovereign; likewise, my millions of incarnations are always to be remembered. (85–86)
Mahāviṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and also the Creator of the Universe; Viṣṇu, Śiva, Satī, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Sūrya, and Candramas—
these are to be remembered, as well as Nara and Nārāyaṇa and their attendants.
Yama together with Dhūmorṇā, the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa) together with Gaurī;
the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) with Ṛddhi, as well as the bull Surabhi and the host of Maruts;
the Vālakhilya sages and the great seers such as Nārada and others. (88–89)
Urvaśī, the daughter of Śrī Hari, should always be remembered at dawn.
Also [to be remembered are] the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, along with the Aśvins and the Pitṛs;
as well as Dharma, Śruta, Tapas, Dīkṣā, Bhakti, and Bṛhaspati.
Also Aśvapaṭṭasara, Prabhāsa, and likewise Gomatī;
Gaṅgā, Revā, Gaṇḍakī, Yamī, Sarayū, Gautamī, Nārāyaṇī, Indratoyā, Brahmaputrī, and Hiraṇvatī.
Puṣkara, Bālakṛṣṇa, and the lake Sarasvatī;
likewise Meru, Himālaya, Vindhya, Uraḥ, and Raivata;
as well as Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, and Gandhamādana. (93)
The oceans and the principles (tattvas) as well should always be remembered.
May all the divine deities, whether named or unnamed, protect me;
may all the virtuous men and women protect me at all times.
May Kambharāśrī protect me always; may Gopālakṛṣṇaka protect me.
May the goddess Pārvatī protect me, and may Prajñā Rādhikā protect me.
May those dear to Brahmā protect me always, and may those dear to Hari protect me.
May the Blessed One and Śuka and Vallabha protect me.
May the Brahmin seer devoted to his wife, the self-luminous Lord,
and the aged preceptor Lomaśa— all of them— protect me always.
May the Goddess Kuṅkumavāpikā, the sacred field known as Akṣara,
Sādhu, Lālāyana, and the others— those supreme lords— protect me.
By thus chanting this, one is liberated from all sins.

By praising and rejoicing [in this], one is liberated from all fear. (3.96.100) For the virtuous who have taken refuge in me and whose minds are absorbed in the Self as described in the *Saṃhitā*, by remembering my divine sports (*līlās*), they indeed attain my supreme, imperishable state. (101)
"By remembering the divine wonders of the virtuous women who have taken refuge in Me—the wives of Brahmā—they attain the supreme state.

(102) Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Authority of Evidence Concerning Śrī Hari, Holy Men, Dharma, and Virtuous Women; the Means to Liberation, Devotion, and Other Matters; and the Demonstration that the Company of the Holy is a Powerful Authority, while Divine Wonder is the Most Powerful Authority," in the Third Section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:

What ought to be done by a human being who is engaged in the activities of the world? What dharma, being truly virtuous, should one contemplate for the sake of sustaining the body and navigating the affairs of the world? (1)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Having abandoned malice, having renounced theft, and likewise having given up sexual misconduct, one should abandon sins with the body and perform all that is most excellent. (2)
Having abandoned these four through speech— village gossip, harshness, slander, and falsehood— one should always utter the truth.
One should have no desire for the property of others and maintain friendliness toward all living beings.
One should always maintain in one's mind faith in the existence of the fruits of action and so forth.
One should not give rise to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), abandon craving, and renounce possessions.
Having avoided that which causes fear, one should take refuge in a virtuous person through one's own self.
Having surrendered all one's possessions, one should practice the ninefold devotion;
having attained Me through love and meditation, one shall go to the supreme state.
Thus, one should always practice that which is most excellent, auspicious, beneficial, and of true fruit.

One should never perform that which is impure or contrary to righteousness. (7) One should practice service to one’s mother, service to one’s father, service to one’s husband, as well as service to women, service to the teacher, service to cows, and service to the elderly. (8)
One should practice service to the gods, service to the virtuous, and service to chaste women;
one should always practice hospitality, altruism, and similar deeds.
One should perform my worship and practice service to the poor.
One should practice service to the world, service to the nation, and service to the subjects.
One should practice service to sacred fords (*tīrtha*), service to Brahman, and service to liberation.
Listen, Lakṣmī, how in ancient times, having served a sacred ford and a circle of virtuous men...
The great sage known as Ālambāyana attained liberation at the great holy site of Gokarṇa in the Siṃha forest;
that king of sages himself dwelt there for a hundred thousand years, happy through the service of the virtuous.
When he reached the age of ten years,
that boy born in the land of Saurāṣṭra bowed to his own mother, Keśariṇī, and said:
"O Mother, if there should arise in me a desire for constant association with the virtuous..."
Indeed, saṃsāra is impermanent, and human birth is difficult to attain;
devotion to Hari is difficult to find, and the company of the virtuous is likewise rare.
(15) So too are home, gardens, wife, kinsmen, and even wealth.
Cows and servants are easily obtained, yet they are causes of bondage. (16) Saintly persons, devotion, and refuge in Nārāyaṇa are difficult to find;
liberation too is difficult to attain, O Mother. A wise man should strive for these. (17)
"Such is my understanding; instruct me as to how I may act accordingly.
The mother said to her son: "O son, you are indeed blessed, for you are like a deity.
O son, from your very childhood, your intentions have been filled with discernment."
Blessed am I, and blessed too is your mother, O son, and blessed as well is your father!
For you, their son, desire to perform service and devotion to the Blessed One;
your mind, worthy of praise, seeks to attain liberation through the virtuous.
"O son, having today heard this supreme teaching of the Supreme Lord from you,
who possess great merit and desire liberation, my discernment has been awakened.
Your auspicious intentions regarding devotion to Hari shall indeed be fulfilled."
And, O son, may you always be free from obstacles in your service to the virtuous.
Since you have abandoned childhood play and the like, cast aside the conceits of youth,
and disregarded passion and other such impulses, your mind is set upon liberation.
"I am pleased, my son; you are the deliverer of your family members.
Human birth is for the sake of liberation; other births lead to the ocean of worldly existence. Abandoning those which grant the ocean of existence, make this human life fruitful."
Having informed the people and received their permission for crossing over,
go to the abode of the virtuous path so that you may attain the state from which there is no return—
there where those steadfast sages are heard to dwell, who have reached the further shore of Brahman.
"O you who are beyond qualities, who possess the qualities of Brahman, and who bestow liberation—go there indeed!
Remember me, do not remember me as a mother anywhere; [remember] neither father, nor kinsmen, nor home, nor various bonds, nor place of birth, nor friends. (27)
Do not remember sense objects, my son; do not apply your meditation to worldly things.
Never fall into the current of flavors or tastes. O my son, may you never have attachment to sense objects anywhere.

And may your path to liberation, my son, proceed to its end without obstacle. Always dedicate this human body to the service of the virtuous, my son; by doing so, you shall attain the auspicious supreme good.
"May you attain Nārāyaṇa before long and dwell in His abode.
Having taken leave of your father, Brahmātāra, go and perform what is auspicious.
Having spoken thus, she, with a heart full of joy, smelled the head of her son.
The mother caused him to eat and gave him firm resolve;
she sent her son toward his father for the purpose of entering the stage of renunciation (tyāgāśrama).
The son went to his father, who was sitting comfortably, and bowed down to him.
He reported everything to the yogi Brahmatāra.
Then the brahmin Brahmatāra spoke to his auspicious-souled son:
"Oh, I am truly blessed, for such a son as you dwells constantly in my home!"
Devoted to the Lord, with a mind intent on the company of holy and virtuous men,
free from worldly enjoyment and devoid of desire for pleasures, he is auspicious from his very childhood;
indeed, by virtue of past merit, such a son is born who is both devoted and observant of vows.
"O son, you are virtuous, detached, steadfast, and possessed of higher conduct. Always worship Hari and serve holy people.
Having gone to the sacred site of Gokarṇa, establish yourself in liberation. || 37-38 ||
Make this human body fruitful and endowed with the highest fruit;
I am truly possessed of a son through a son such as you, a great yogi.
When the merit accumulated over a hundred births arises, then [this state] occurs.
Inquiry indeed [arises] on the path to liberation and also on the path of serving the virtuous.
But one must sever the firm bondage consisting of service toward family members and kinsmen;
having done so, some person becomes a hero, immersed in the battle for liberation.
Whether among insects, moths, gods, demons, humans, birds, reptiles, animals, perfected beings (siddhas), or seers (ṛṣis), enjoyments are indeed equal.
They are merely moisture born of water; they are material and consist of food for the body.
The senses are the same, and the vital breaths born of wind are equal;
likewise, the days pass equally for all embodied beings.
Yet those who are deprived of divine grace do not strive for liberation, being intent only on sleep.
Those very objects of human pursuit that exist here in this world as hellish states are likewise created for the next world;

liberation is the true aim of man and the goal of the self, whereas other aims concern only the body and do not lead to emancipation. He who, having crossed over the three groups [of qualities], enters indeed into the fourth, the northern one— || 45 ||
He alone is the God here, he is the Lord, and he is also the King of the Liberated.
He alone has accomplished all that was to be done; he is indeed the virtuous one.
He alone is Nārāyaṇa, and he alone is the Savior and the Guru.
The mental resolve for sensual desires is difficult to conquer; women, wealth, and the like are difficult to comprehend;
one's own mind is difficult to master, and likewise, latent tendencies (vāsanā) are hard to overcome.
Even craving is difficult to subdue, yet it has been conquered by you, O self-controlled one.
He by whom the penis is conquered here, and by whom the tongue is restrained;
he by whom the king of the mind is conquered—by that self-conquered one, everything is conquered.
O son, quickly attain victory in this essence-less world composed of illusion.
Attain victory even over the supreme, eternal Brahman.
May there be prosperity for you, may there be auspiciousness for you, may there be joy for you, and may there be great celebration.
May you be immersed in eternal bliss and liberated in the abode of Hari.
"Standing in the midst of the circle of yogis, I shall behold you in the imperishable abode;
for, O son, you are accompanied by your wife, having the very form of Nārāyaṇa.
Having been addressed thus, the son, who had applied the *tilaka* and was full of affection, [prepared himself].
Having bowed to the lotus feet of his parents, drunk their water, and performed auspicious rites,
and likewise having bowed to his hundred brothers, he went to the holy ford of Gokarṇa,
chanting: "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!"
"Hare! O Lord of Rādhā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, Hare! Hare! O Master!
Reciting thus, he then proceeded from Jālikā to the excellent holy site of Somanātha, keeping time with the clapping of his hands. ||55-56||
Then he went to Bhavanātha, Śarabha, and Satītīrtha;
thereafter, he went to the Gokarṇa tīrtha and worshipped Viṣṇu with devotion.
Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, known as Divyakarṇa, he departed from there.
From there he went to the great sacred ford of Svargalakṣmī, then to the great river Brāhmī;
thence he proceeded to Gokarṇaśambhu and then to the dwellings of the sages.
Thereafter, he made his residence in a grove of coconut trees.
He performed the propitiation of Hari and served the virtuous; he performed the chanting of my names, O Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. Thus, constantly remembering me, he indeed engaged in my worship.
He maintained his bodily existence by obtaining alms-food from the virtuous.
For nine thousand years he subsisted on alms-food;
thereafter, for a thousand years, he lived on roots and tubers.
Then, for five thousand years, he subsisted on withered leaves;
thereafter, he remained absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), subsisting on air alone.
Meditating upon the Self within the self, he united himself with the Supreme Self.
When a full hundred thousand years had passed,
a celestial chariot belonging to Viṣṇu arrived from the sky, accompanied by his divinely beautiful attendants.
Seeing that [chariot], this noble king Ālambāyana [prepared to depart].
Quickly casting off his physical body, he then became possessed of a divine form;
four-armed and marked with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and other signs.
That sage, an eminent attendant of Viṣṇu, bowed to the hosts of sages.
He departed for the abode of Hari-Kṛṣṇa, causing the people to marvel as he spoke. Then, during his departure, the sages praised that lord of munis:
"O great devotee, lead us to the supreme abode of Vaikuṇṭha. (67–68)
And he said: "O all you sages, be ready quickly!
Having gone to Vaikuṇṭha itself and having consulted with Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, I shall return by means of celestial chariots to lead you along."
Having been told "Om" by the sages, he went quickly to the abode of Hari.
Honored by the attendants and brought down from his celestial chariot,
he entered that most excellent palace within the supreme divine mansion in Vaikuṇṭha.
Not seeing Śrī Hari in the palace, he quickly went outside;
he searched for that palace where Śrī Narāyaṇa resides.
Having gone there and prostrating like a staff, he indeed performed worship within his heart.
"Victory to Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa! he cried out again and again.
He shed tears from his eyes and for a moment his voice became choked with emotion.
He fell at the feet of Viṣṇu and then drank the nectar of those feet.
Questioned with a welcome by Hari, he spoke what was in his heart:
"O Lord, by your grace I have joyfully attained your eternal feet.
And as for those sages, whose wealth is their austerity, who dwell at Gokarṇa—" || 75 ||
"At the time of departure, they said to me, 'Come with us to your abode.
But I replied to them: 'Go ahead; I shall certainly come after you. Having received the command of Hari, let everyone be prepared in every way.'"
Thus addressed, they awaited the arrival of Vaikuṇṭha, [saying]:
"If you have the command, I shall go and bring him into your presence.
Then Nārāyaṇa said: "O devotee, you have acted appropriately."
Now hear from me something further, the most excellent of the excellent.
Without devotion to me, there can be no dwelling for me in Vaikuṇṭha.
At Gokarṇa dwell the sages, whose wealth is austerity and who are lovers of penance. (3.97.80)
Those who possess control over the mind and likewise control over the senses, who always delight in the Self alone and are devoted solely to knowledge;
and many others who are intent on their vows and are free from passion. (81)
Even those intent on yogic practices and engaged in dry austerities,
if they are devoid of devotion to me and lack my worship,
how could they be worthy of the meaning of the scriptures or of my abode? || 82-83 ||
Vaikuṇṭha is not for those who are devoid of devotion, even if they constantly perform austerities;
nor is Vaikuṇṭha for ritualists who do not know how to worship Me. Love and devotion are always the cause for coming to My abode.
Indeed, for my devotee, service rendered unto Me and the self-surrender of oneself to Me;
meditation upon Me, worship of Me, and constant glorification of Me;
and the dedication of austerities, vows, and gifts unto Me—[these constitute true devotion]. || 85-86 ||
The dedication of all actions, as well as the reception of initiation from me,
and likewise the reception of my divine mantra, are the causes;
for even the propitiation of me leads to the arrival at Vaikuṇṭha.
Those yogins who are unripened practice for a long time:
some for ten lakhs [of years], some likewise for one lakh, and others are long-lived for many thousands of yugas. (88–89)
"Give this mantra of mine, which bestows liberation, to them;
having bestowed initiation, conduct the Nāmasatra, the great sacrifice:
'The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my refuge and my Lord.'"
Having bestowed this mantra, then grant the grace-bestowing initiation (dīkṣā).
[Place] a tulasī necklace upon the neck, as well as a rosary for recitation, a sectarian mark (tilaka), a crescent moon (candraka), and likewise the branding with the discus and other emblems.
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Puruṣottama!
O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O All-pervading Lord, O Master!
Thus, constantly cause the virtuous to perform this chanting.
Let those who have been initiated remain there day and night for the great sacrifice;
their worship shall be complete and their devotion shall become perfect.
I shall [carry] them constantly upon my own resplendent celestial chariot.
"I shall indeed lead you to Vaikuṇṭha; go and carry out the sacrificial session.
Thus addressed, Ālambāyana, the king of devotees and a personal attendant (pārṣada), bowed and departed for his celestial abode in a divine body and a celestial chariot.
Then Gokarṇa was instantly illuminated by his splendor.
