The sages, filled with agitation, fled from that attendant;
but having bowed to those who were ready, he delivered the words spoken by Viṣṇu.
"Let those well-initiated ones perform here the sacrificial session of chanting the Name.
The auspicious sages likewise performed it for the sake of attaining Vaikuṇṭha;
and by the power of their austerity, they realized that devotion is the supreme excellence.
Having become devotees and been initiated, and having received their rosaries,
hundreds of thousands of sages as well as other people of the world performed kīrtana with musical instruments day and night for the sake of liberation. (3.97.1–2)
Having heard that glorification, they gathered there and performed worship;
from that time on, that holy place became famous by the name Vaikuṇṭha-satra.
At the end of the month, for those who had become mature through devotion, Hari [appeared].
The Lord arrived in his own celestial chariot accompanied by Lakṣmī and Śrī.
That Supreme Controller led a thousand saintly persons to Vaikuṇṭha;
likewise, at the end of each month and also at the end of every three months, he brought some others.
At the end of four, five, or more months, Hari led hundreds of thousands of people away;
having become fully ripened, those sages depart for his abode.
Those virtuous ones residing at Gokarṇa have all departed completely at the end of the year.
That supreme abode, Vaikuṇṭha, was indeed filled with great wonders.
Having commenced the Nāmasattra sacrifice, the gods and others, as well as human beings,
then proceeded from the holy site of Gokarṇa to the Supreme Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the supreme majesty of devotion has been described;
for by associating with the virtuous, the Blessed One caused the chanting to be performed,
purified the ascetics, and led them to His own most excellent abode.
At the end of the year, having completed this sattra of names, this very saint,
possessing a divine body and traveling in a celestial chariot, went to the abode of Hari. Thereupon,
crores of saints came to be present there in Siṃhāraṇya.
That great Gokarṇa became a sacred abode equal to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the service of the virtuous indeed bears fruit for the good after a long time;
even association with the virtuous bears fruit for those born as humans, albeit after a long duration.
Therefore, the virtuous should cultivate association with the truly good, for it shall be fruitful.
O Lakṣmī, through reading, hearing, and remembering this, even the attainment of liberation occurs; indeed, the yoga of association with the good bestows eternal emancipation.

Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of how Liberation is Attained through the Company of the Virtuous even by those Engaged in Worldly Exertion, and likewise by Ascetics—Specifically, the Attainment of Liberation at Gokarṇa by Hundreds of Thousands of Men through the Association of the Holy Ālambāyana," in the Third Section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 98: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Continued] Chapter 98.
[Author: Chapter 99.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: Tell me how one who has fallen into great calamity may be swiftly delivered.
"O Kṛṣṇakānta, show it to me thus indeed for the welfare of the world.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"I always bow to the virtuous, whose wealth is the Supreme Brahman."

I bow to those pure and virtuous ones—whether children, youths, or elders—who bear the burden of devotion to Hari; for them, heaven and even liberation rest within the palm of their hand, as does [the fulfillment of] every word they speak. (2–3)
They were experts in the sciences of Brahman, humble, with minds under control;
they spoke of Brahman, were learned in the Vedas, observant of vows, and adorned by their virtuous conduct.
(4) In assemblies, they were speakers of Brahman, being of the nature of the imperishable Brahman.
I bow to those virtuous people who are auspicious in form and beautiful;

(5) and to those who are worthy of being served even by them, who stand at the forefront in the assembly of Brahmā, and who are perfected in wisdom and meditation—to them I aspire with deep longing. (6)
When they serve those who are worthy, there is great happiness both in this world and after death;
they are auspicious ones who bring about deliverance and the destruction of all calamities.
Well-prepared foods and cool waters [are also provided].
O Rame! Beautiful garments should always be given to them.
Blessed is he who, being meritorious, obtains birth in a virtuous family, and who, in a future time, becomes the liberator of ten million embodied beings.
"O Lakṣmī, there is no one on the surface of the earth dearer to me than you.
All beloved women are dear to me, but saintly persons are most dear to me.
O Kamalā, even my parents here are not as dear to me as they are. (3.98.10)
Just as the virtuous, peaceful, and most excellent of dear ones are always [to me], so too,
even when one has fallen into great calamity, the virtuous here bring about auspiciousness;
they are to be honored and worshipped as deities even by the gods.
The worlds call me "Sāttvata," and I am pleased by that;
those who practice devotion call me the virtuous Lord through their union with the good (sādhu).
Just as the dharma of women consists in taking refuge in a husband, so it is for me.
Good conduct for all is considered the refuge of the virtuous and the path of dharma.
(14) Furthermore, among Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas, the virtuous are regarded as gurus;
indeed, the virtuous are to be worshipped like gods and served like Krishna. (15)
Those virtuous and stainless ones should be served by Brahmins like fire.
Through the service of the virtuous, that Brahminhood which purifies all remains established.
Just as a woman, in the absence of her husband, takes her brother-in-law as her husband.
Likewise, in the absence of a virtuous ruler, the subjects create a leader as a representative.
One should always serve the virtuous—those who are upright, truthful in character, devoted to the welfare of all living beings, and friends to every creature. (17–18)

Just as a king should protect his own kinsmen, so too should he protect virtuous people; he should look after those in the hermitage, considering what means of livelihood they possess. Furthermore, one who possesses wealth should protect those most devoted to Brahman and the Veda in every way.
A wealthy man should obtain the blessings of virtuous people who have been satisfied by his alms-giving.
Having made a promise, one must not fail to give; for that very act leads to a great hell.
Indeed, the sin of one who destroys hope is the destroyer of all merit.
The offering made, the gift given, and the austerity performed—all these are frustrated by one who destroys hope.
Indeed, the fulfillment of hope produces the merit of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
The satisfaction of hope yields the fruit of a thousand sacrifices to Viṣṇu.
Therefore, having granted this hope, one should fulfill it to the best of one's ability.
(23) Once, in a cremation ground, a dog-cooker and a vulture met;
then the dog-cooker quietly asked the vulture as he was devouring a corpse. (24)
"What sin have you committed that you eat such putrid food—
this loathsome corpse, so foul-smelling, moist, and decayed?
The vulture replied, "In the past, I was a wealthy man possessed by greed."
Even after having given his word, he did not give at all, or he gave only an incomplete portion.
Because of that sin, he was born here as a vulture dwelling in the cremation ground.
Therefore, being hungry, I devour such an extremely wicked creature as this.

"Tell me now, how did this birth as a dog-eater (śvāpaca) come about for you? (27) The dog-eater replied: "O virtuous one! Although I was formerly a Brāhmaṇa endowed with wealth and grain, I was a reviler of the holy and possessed a heart devoid of compassion. (28)
Seeing virtuous people, I revile them, I treat them with contempt, and I mock them.
Nowhere do I give alms; on the contrary, I even forbid others from giving.
By that sin, my entire possession—house, wife, children, and so forth—[is lost].
"Lost through the fury of fire, burnt; I am burnt!"—thinking thus, he went to the world of Yama.
There, by the servants of Yama, his eyes and tongue were extracted and cast into the blinding darkness for many years. (3.98.30–31)
Then I became a female hunter with a snare;
after that, I became a snake, then an owl, and then a lizard.
Then I was born as a caṇḍāla indeed because of my reviling of the virtuous.
Therefore, those who are dear to Hari should never be treated with contempt anywhere.
Their begging should not be forbidden, nor should their giving ever be obstructed.
One must not take away anything belonging to them; rather, one should give to them for their satisfaction.

One should avoid dispute with those who are most devoted to Brahman, with virtuous men, and likewise with virtuous women; one should give what has been promised. One must never engage in their censure, nor ever listen to it.
One should certainly not harbor pride regarding one's status as a Brahmin in the presence of the virtuous. Those Brahmins who are householders frequent women and cemeteries;
they follow a path lower than that of the holy ones, for it is the holy ones who are to be honored by Brahmins. (36–37)
Those who are drenched and stuck in urine indeed go to hell;
those virtuous ones, disciplined in ethical conduct (*śīla*), are capable of rescuing them.
A thief cannot save a thief; he who is not a thief can save him.
One who is full of desire cannot deliver one from desire; one free from desire can deliver another from passion.
One must not seize the property of the virtuous, and one should always be patient toward them.
Furthermore, children, the wretched, and those who are powerless must never be held in contempt.
One should not constantly place expectations upon the virtuous for the sake of achieving one's own self-interest;
nor should one employ the virtuous like servants merely for the sake of obtaining food,
or likewise for the sake of obtaining water, or for the sake of acquiring gems such as the *khaṣṭva*, *gaja*, or *induka*.
In the house, one should provide for the saint a seat, lodging, and shelter;
one should not subject him to labor, for by doing so, merit is destroyed.
Householders should never reside in the dwelling of a saint. (42–43)
One should go for the sake of the company of the virtuous, never for the sake of the afflictions;
one may always go to the hermitage for the sake of sleep or for the evacuation of excrement and urine,
but one must never go merely to accomplish one's own bodily needs.
Even during a time of peace, agitation and restlessness toward virtuous people [are faults];
likewise, one should never engage in improper conduct.
One should never sit upon a high seat in the presence of virtuous people.
One should never engage in dispute through speech, wealth, action, knowledge for the sake of one's own livelihood, force, or greed;
nor should one engage in debate with wicked men, even if they are well-born. (47)
One should not harbor expectations for wealth from them, nor should the virtuous be brought under one's control.
Indeed, one should never engage in the physical inspection of the virtuous;
those who are by nature subject to passion and hatred should not be employed toward the virtuous.

In a virtuous hermitage, one should not engage in talk of villages, talk of afflictions, false talk, or talk of sensual enjoyments; nor should one utter anything that causes humiliation. One should not display pride, nor should one exercise power or assert one's status among the virtuous.
The virtuous should certainly not be humiliated, for by doing so their merit perishes.
Thinking, "I know who this saintly person knows," one becomes arrogant;
indeed, arrogance should never be practiced anywhere, as it is the cause of one's downfall.

Upon seeing a virtuous person, one should bow; failing to bow destroys merit. One should not direct toward the virtuous the impurities of one's own nature—such as desires and other faults, the faults inherent in women, or those belonging to one's own self. (53)
One should indeed go to a virtuous hermitage for the sake of attaining excellence alone.

(54) For in this world there are many people who are masters of wickedness, acting merely for the sake of satisfying their own sensual desires and for the sake of satisfying their sense of touch. (55)
They go to the grounds where groups of women gather solely for the sake of visual gratification;
they likewise attend festivals, sacred sites, and places where there is a thronging of women,
as well as crowded gatherings, and [they indulge] in playful conversations and the like.
They seize upon the faults of virtuous women right there.
Because of that sin, they are born blind from birth, afflicted with leprosy, or as eunuchs; likewise, they become long-suffering from disease, impoverished, and wretched.
Women also become afflicted with diseases, manifesting such symptoms;
they are deprived of children and the like, and destitute of wealth, grain, and other possessions.
Therefore, one should not accept the faults of virtuous women or even of the righteous.
One should indeed grasp only those qualities that grant happiness, merit, and auspiciousness.
Just as people, having set aside the thin thorns, the leaf-sheaths, the bark, and the bristles from the sugarcane stalk, take only its juice. (3.98.60–61)
Just as people, having discarded the leaves and other parts of vegetables that have been cooked along with burnt cumin seeds,
eat only the vegetable itself;
and just as they indeed discard the seeds, skins, and so forth contained within fruits.
Indeed, embodied beings consume only the essence of the embryo and suck its juices;
just as one takes the fruit of a tree having abandoned its defects, and just as one takes the flower of a creeper having abandoned its defects. (63–64)
Likewise, having abandoned those qualities found in the wicked which are to be shunned, one should acquire their virtues.
For one who conducts oneself in this manner, there is the attainment of merit at every step:
an increase in lifespan, knowledge, and fame, as well as the abundance of wealth, grain, and prosperity.
Inexhaustibility shall arise for those who possess the virtues of the virtuous.
Indeed, when the virtuous are pleased and rejoice in their servant,
that person’s home becomes truly enriched with all kinds of jewels.
One who finds satisfaction in the virtuous should nourish their sons, grandsons, cattle, kinsmen, and family members, as well as the village and the country.
By giving to virtuous people, one certainly attains the unsurpassed heaven.
And liberation can be attained through the supreme practice of serving the virtuous. (69) By what is given to the righteous, the deities and the ancestors also live;
the liberated ones are satisfied, and indeed the Blessed Lord partakes [of offerings] among the virtuous. (3.98.70)
Therefore, gifts should be given to the virtuous by one who possesses discernment;
for the virtuous person of pure consciousness is indeed a most divine sacred ford.
The virtuous are the uplifters of the lowly; they are my very own forms.
They provide protection for the helpless and remove the suffering of those who suffer;
they are the washers away of sins for the wicked and the destroyers of the faults of offenders.
Indeed, the virtuous are the granters of refuge to those who have been insulted. (72–73)
Listen, I shall tell you an ancient tale: a twice-born man was rescued by holy men.
On the Himalayas there was a delightful hermitage frequented by seers;
it was known as Ṛṣidhāma-āśrama, graced by perfected seers and brahmins.
It was inhabited by those observing vows, ascetics, those bound by restrictive rules, and the initiated;
likewise by self-perfected ones, virtuous mendicants, and the yogi Dīrghatapas, the best of the twice-born. (75–76)
Then a certain Śabara, living in the forest, arrived there and beheld those auspicious hosts of sages, who were like gods and devoted to asceticism.
He resolved to perform penance and questioned the long-lived ascetic.
"O Blessed One, you ought to speak the Dharma to me and grant me ordination.
I am a Śūdra and I wish to perform service for you; be gracious to me.
Then Dīrghatapas said: "Since you exist as a Śūdra... (78–79)
"It is not possible to ordain you, for you have abandoned your duty;
therefore, remain here in this very manner and perform service, if it pleases you.
By such service, O forest-dweller, you shall attain the highest worlds."
Thus addressed, that Śabara was also delighted near the hermitage;
having prepared his own spot beneath a tree, he indeed dwelt there.
He provided food such as fruits and flowers, and performed service for the sage.
Once, by his own nature, he caught a wild hare;
having killed it, he ate it in the vicinity of the sage’s hermitage.
Then those sages abandoned that Śūdra, who was a perpetrator of violence.
"And may Śepu become a Rākṣasa and suffer misery in the midst of the forest.
(84) Having quickly become a deformed Rākṣasa, he roamed the forest;
then, filled with the extreme suffering of hunger and thirst, he went to the bank of the Gaṅgā. (85)
There, he beheld a holy man named Nārāyaṇa-muni, the best of Vaiṣṇavas, who was immersed in austerity and devoted to worship.
To devour the holy man quickly, the Rākṣasa rushed to the bank.
Having seen that rākṣasa, the virtuous one gazed at him with his vision;
he then sprinkled water upon the head and body of the rākṣasa, saying:
"Become pure, become righteous-souled, and be freed from suffering. (87–88)
"O sinner, you shall be freed from the curse right here in the presence of me,
the ascetic. Having been addressed thus, the Śabara quickly cast off his demonic nature by touching water and became a divine human being.

Then the world-purifying [Śaunaka], who was himself a purifier, served the virtuous Uddhāraka, the sage Nārāyaṇa, with supreme affection. Even though he was a Śūdra, through his association with that holy man, he thereafter became devoted.
Having received the command of the holy man, he departed for the depths of the forest.
There he constantly worshipped Nārāyaṇa and performed severe austerities.
At the end of his life, that Śabara attained a supreme kingdom.

Indeed, he became King Vīravikrama of Ujjayinī. Having enjoyed worldly pleasures and likewise performed supreme devotion to Hari, he went to the imperishable abode and became liberated through the company of the virtuous. || 93-94 ||
That family, having served the holy man (sādhu), attained the supreme state.
Therefore, O vulture, the virtuous who are adorned by goodness should always be served.
Come here; there is a holy man nearby named Kṛṣṇa.
"Relying on him, we two shall indeed become purifiers who have shaken off all sin.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, Kṛṣṇa and you both went toward him; you bowed, praised him, and made your request. (96–97)
Then the virtuous one caused them to be liberated and made them drink water; the purifier quickly granted them grace, fed them,
and swiftly caused their sins to be consumed by fire through the proclamation of his glories.
He also quickly gave them both the name Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having cast off their physical bodies through the power of that virtuous man, they departed, freed from sin; they went to heaven and became gods.
Having enjoyed heaven as the fruit of grace through their reliance on that virtuous person,
the two of them eventually went to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Supreme Soul.
Thus, Lakṣmī, even a mere fraction of association with the virtuous is indeed [of great consequence].
It purifies indeed and swiftly bestows a heap of merits;
it grants a kingdom, heaven, and even liberation. Association with the virtuous yogis of Kṛṣṇa bestows supreme bliss. (102–103)

Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How Even for One in Distress, Association with the Holy Brings Welfare— The Liberation from Heaven and Beyond of the Vulture, the Outcaste, and the Hunter," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 98.
Chapter 99 [Author:
Chapter 100 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"It is true, O Blessed One, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Lord of the Universe! Wherever Your saints reside, there the accomplishments of the goals of human life are found.
And those virtuous, stainless people who are most dear to my husband—"
I always carry their dust upon my head with my crown.
For your sake, I bear their commands— whether they be beneficial, auspicious, or even inauspicious—
with total fearlessness and at all times.
The speech of the virtuous is purified by truth, however it may be;
indeed, the speech of the virtuous is the supreme Veda wherein you are established. And the vow of silence always resides in the virtuous, though their articulate speech is never concealed.
The virtuous speak only of the supreme reality, not of the worldly.
(5) One should say that "the mouth exists," yet this is not the natural disposition of the wise;
for the subtle course of truth is indeed difficult to understand for those of unrefined self. (6)
The wise should never speak in accordance with the inclinations of the deluded; since fault may be transferred through speech, silence is better for the virtuous.
Such people are born and exist in this world.

If even the teacher and the instructor should speak according to their own personal opinions, then that king of teachers is the best; otherwise, he is proclaimed as ignorant. Such disciples indeed become shrouded in most terrible darkness.
A teacher who does not oppose his own doctrine is indeed a teacher, and not otherwise;
therefore, they indeed become denizens of hell both here and in the next world.
Thus, whatever doctrine is held by female disciples or by male disciples here—

If that doctrine is indeed contradictory and subverts the scriptures, dharma, and so forth, then it should not be accepted by the teacher; rather, such disciples should be abandoned. For generally, many in the world possess the conceit of false scholarship.
Disciples who consider themselves wise become subordinates who control their gurus;
while treading upon the wrong path, they surely fall lower and lower.
One must never speak unwholesome words that lead to great sin.

In that regard, the virtuous should not say anything whatsoever in the presence of anyone. O Kṛṣṇa, sages perform the excellent initiation of self-restraint through silence; out of fear of ill-spoken words, they do not speak in vain or falsely.
Righteous, endowed with virtues, and possessed of truth and devotion,
the sages lead others to the supreme state through teachings of truth;
indeed, by the gift of the Veda, they shatter the evil deeds of their listeners.
Those who grant the grace of the Supreme Lord cause one to reach the ocean of bliss.
(17) One who is unworthy should seek refuge, yet must be examined in every way;
instruction should not be given hastily without first ascertaining their standing. (18)
By teaching one who is an unfit vessel, that sin transfers to the teacher.
Therefore, the gift of knowledge must indeed be bestowed by one devoted to truth after careful deliberation.
For teaching one who is false and an unfit vessel destroys oneself.
Such understanding should be imparted by which one may protect the truth,
and by which the eternal Lord Nārāyaṇa is propitiated.
Such people, whose character is truth, take refuge in Satyanārāyaṇa.
The virtuous gurus who are devoted to the eternal Truth are my [gurus].
O Blessed One, I dwell wherever my stainless gurus reside;
there, those fortunate knowers of Brahman are honored by you together with me.
Confident, skilled in devotion, and intent upon the service of Śrī Hari;
devoted to the gods, grateful, and masters of their senses—these sattvic, divine, and virtuous persons, who are dedicated to the goals of human life, are where I dwell. (23–24)
Wherever my beloved Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, dwells with you, there I shall reside by giving away all my possessions.
I do not dwell in one who is devoid of the goals of human life, nor in an atheist, nor in an ungrateful person.
I do not dwell at all in one who causes confusion of the Dharma or who has breached the boundaries of conduct;
nor do I dwell in any way whatsoever with the cruel, the slanderer, the wicked, the thief, the one who is envious of their gurus, the hater of the virtuous, or the arrogant. (26–27)
I do not abide in one who has little splendor, who is devoid of being, who is bereft of strength, who is afflicted, who is angry, who is unstable, or who is lacking in steadfastness;
nor in one who does not seek [the goal], who is by nature obstructed, or who is easily satisfied with little. (28)
I do not dwell forever with one who is extravagant in spending or addicted to vice.
(29) I dwell in great celebration with one who is rich in dharma, learned in dharma, self-controlled, a servant of the elders, devoted to forbearance, and fulfilled in his duties. (3.99.30)
I dwell among women who possess the nature of truth, who are self-controlled, and who are not overbearing; I dwell among those rich in uprightness, who serve the virtuous.
I also dwell among those who worship their bodies, the twice-born, their gurus, and their masters.
I always avoid a woman who is impure, fickle, indolent in her own duties,
antagonistic, hostile toward her husband, allied with the enemy’s side,
shameless, and intolerant. (32–33)
I abandon her who is full of evil and service to the wicked, who is angry and devoid of fortitude, who is deceitful, the root of quarrels, and excessively prone to sleep;
yet I embrace those women who are devoted to truth, divine, and bestowers of virtue and good fortune.
I dwell among women devoted to their husbands, those of virtuous character, and those who are adorned; I dwell in vehicles well-yoked with draft animals, among devoted young maidens,
in sacrifices well-performed, and in temples.
I dwell in flowers, in the bodies of grain, in elephants, and in stables; in cow-pens, in the feet of the virtuous, and in lotuses;
in regions endowed with rivers, and among ascetics, perfected ones, and yogis.

O Mādhava, I always dwell upon a bull, within a herd of cattle, among kings, and likewise among virtuous people; on a high seat, in one who consumes sacrificial offerings, in a worshipper of gods, cows, and Brahmins, and in a palace resplendent with hospitality.
In the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, in the saintly man who is Your follower, in the virtuous woman, and also among the devotees, I dwell eternally in my full splendor.
O Keśava, wherever I dwell, they become gracious and invisible in nature.
By your command, I shall increase [the world] through dharma, fame, wealth, and desire.
O Blessed One, I shall tell you my secret here in every respect:
wherever virtuous people are served, there I always dwell.

The virtuous are the forms of the Blessed One and the embodiments of my Lord. For the sake of attaining service to them and for the sake of obtaining your grace, I dwell eternally within the servant and the female servant of the virtuous. (43)
Where Gopāla-Kṛṣṇa is, where the virtuous Śrī-Kambharā is,
where she dwells contented, and where Śrī-Harivallabha is—
there indeed I dwell eternally, wherever the worship of you and Hari takes place.
Those people who worship Hari with the spirit of offering their all,
being devoid of any sense of self-interest— I never abandon them at any time.
Where there are always noble food-distributions and noble hermitages, [there I remain].
I dwell wherever the virtuous perform auspicious service that bestows prosperity.
Wherever a sincere intellect exists among one's servants,
and wherever the mind is free from fault, there I dwell in every way.
I dwell in every way in the house of that person for whom the virtuous are considered superior to home, wife, children, sons, and wealth;
and where the virtuous are indeed held in higher esteem than the husband, the father-in-law, and other elders.

I dwell in every way in the homes of those women who honor [the virtuous]. Where there is the chanting of the righteous, where there is the sight of the righteous, and where there is always affection for the virtuous—there I dwell in every way. (3.99.50–51)
Wherever the Blessed One, the Blessed Ones, Hari, and the saints,
as well as the master and his servants dwell, there I always reside.
But where my master does not abide, nor do his saintly devotees, [there I do not stay].
Having risen like the sun through the power of my merit, I am now going to my setting.
That house in which a day passes without the chanting of your name,
that house I utterly abandon, being afflicted by a swoon.
That house where the food of virtuous men is not found, I consider a dark abyss and abandon it like a cremation ground;
that place where the footstep of a holy person is not seen even in a year.
I truly abandon that house, devoid of merit, like a cremation ground (56),
where no festival of Kṛṣṇa takes place even within the course of a year; I utterly forsake that home which is bereft of your festivals (57).
Where there are no devotees of yours, and where they do not dwell anywhere,
there my residence is not pleasing at all—
be it in a palace, a mansion, a house, or a temple. 58.
I do not dwell there where my husband Nārāyaṇa is not present.
(59) Even in a golden mansion, a golden treasury, or upon a royal throne, I do not dwell at all if there is no morning offering to Nārāyaṇa. (3.99.60)
Where there is no ghee lamp before the worship of Hari,
where there is no incense and no *ārārtika* offering, there I do not dwell at all.
Where there is no food offering for Viṣṇu and no water [for the ritual], [there I do not dwell].
Wherever the devotees of Viṣṇu do not eat, there I do not dwell.

(62) Where there is no great festival for the eighth day (Aṣṭamī), the Jayantī, or the thirteenth day (Trayodaśī) in the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, there indeed I do not dwell at all. (63)
O Lord, where the verses of incarnation are not heard,
nor is there worship or an image, I do not dwell there at all.
Nor is there the marks of the conch, the discus, and so forth, nor even the tulasī tree.
I do not dwell at all where ignorance is not found.
(65) Where there is neither the story nor the image of the incarnations of Lakṣmī, nor even those of the incarnations of Nārāyaṇa, there I do not dwell. (66)
Where there is no honoring of the virtuous, no service to the elders, and no respect for cows, there I do not dwell at all.
Where there is no performance of *śrāddha* for the gods, the ancestors, or for the living, [there I do not dwell].
I do not dwell at all where there is no gift of merit (puṇya).
I do not dwell at all in that house where children are not protected with food and other necessities, nor where women are tormented. (68–69)

I do not dwell at all where there is a breach of social order within the household, where there is oppression of those who have sought refuge, or where there is the confinement of animals. Nor do I dwell where there is an image of Nārāyaṇa at the city gate.
Even there, it does not exist, nor do I dwell there for long.
But where Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, and the one garlanded with elephant-lotuses shine—
in the upper chambers and other parts of that house— I reside.
Where there is no Gaṇeśa and the Śrīmātṛs have not been installed,
and where the Bindus do not exist, I never dwell for long in such a place.
Where there is discord between man and woman, or regarding sons and the like—
I do not dwell where there is indifference between servants and masters;
nor do I dwell where a master resides who is a mere predator, devoid of dharma, and a hater of Nārāyaṇa—such a place is like a thief's den. ||74-75||
I do not dwell at all in that garden where divine trees are found, nor where there are sacrificial creepers and trees;
nor do I dwell in that field which, though beautiful with crops, is devoid of the wandering of the virtuous. (76)
In that regard, I do not exist at all as one who transgresses among the grains [of rice].
(77) Where virtuous people bathe—in a lake, a river, a stream, a small pond, or even a well—I do not dwell in that water or its flavor. (78)
I do not dwell in that assembly of people, nor likewise in an assembly of gods,
nor in an assembly of the learned where there is no virtuous person. Nor do I dwell in an assembly of kings, nor likewise in an assembly of subjects.

There is no one with a devoted soul at a sacred ford; therefore, I shall depart from here. I shall depart even from that assembly which is devoid of virtuous men, from that work which is not offered to Hari, and from that acquisition which is devoid of charity.
Wherever Indra, victory, and prosperity reside— in the sacrificial post, the pillar, or the house—
and wherever the Lord of Śrī himself dwells, there I dwell, O Keśava.
Where there is no lamp at night and no offering by day, [there I dwell].
I shall depart from that place where there is no arrival of those who are to be treated with affection.
I shall also depart from that place where poverty flourishes in matters such as religious duties and ritual offerings,
and where gifts are given only to the aged.
Where Sītā and the bulls are not worshipped at the time of plowing,
where the earth is not honored— there I do not dwell at all.
Where there is no mark of vermilion or sandalwood paste upon the forehead, [I do not dwell there].

The ornament of good fortune does not exist there; therefore, I depart from that place. O Keśava, I dwell where there is the granting of fearlessness, the pointing out of the path to liberation, and the songs and life-stories of devotees. (86–87)
I always dwell with joy in the speech, the heart, and the feet of the virtuous— those whose nature is ethical discipline and who are free from possessiveness.
And I dwell in the water, leaves, flowers, and grains remaining after the worship of Hari.
I dwell in clarity, in food, in the sky, and in all material objects. I reside, indeed,
unweariedly in the initiated, in the devotee of pure nature, in the virtuous wife of a Brahmin,
and in the woman who cooks for the sake of Hari.
Since you are indeed Nārāyaṇa, ever devoted to your wife,
you never accept what is offered by another without my hand being in between.
Therefore, by command, I dwell swiftly within the one who makes the offering.
Whether one is a petitioner of my own form or any kind of servant,
or whether she is any kind of female attendant, she is undoubtedly Lakṣmī herself.
Indeed, those virtuous ones who offer themselves in every way are truly your servants.
O Lord, I too always practice dwelling among them;
so too do the devotees of Hari, whether they be women or men, as well as gods, ancestors, great sages, and human beings. (94)
The Nāgas, Daityas, Rākṣasas, and Dānavas were performers of devotion;
as were the Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, Maruts, Ādityas, Rudras, and the most excellent Vasus, along with the Siddhas, Kinnaras, Sūtas, Māgadhas, and Bandins. (95–96)
Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases who are mistresses;
Yoginīs, Mātṛs, Śaktis, and likewise Sādhikās;
Gaṇikās, Gaṇas, maidens, and likewise young boys.
Yakṣas, world-protectors, guardians of the quarters, and millions of tīrthakas;
animals, whether luminous or dark, or quadrupeds;
insects, birds, and whatever else exists, sentient or insentient—(98–99).
"These [beings] have been raised up here and there solely for the sake of your devotion.
Having gone there quickly, I shall purify them.
Then, O Nārāyaṇa, you shall receive from my hand that which is given by me."
Such devotion to one's own wife is not found elsewhere;
likewise, such fidelity to her husband is not found in Lakṣmī nor anywhere else.
Truly, the virtuous are always endowed with truthfulness and fidelity to their husbands. (101–102)
As is Lakṣmī, so are the virtuous; the virtuous are the objects of Your grace and are dear to You.
Therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, You are called the beloved of Lakṣmī and the Lord of the virtuous.
Consequently, I [dwell] forever within the bodies of the virtuous, who are my co-wives.
I dwell with them as if inseparable, yet the other does not perceive this.
(104) Salutations to that Blessed One, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the virtuous, to Lakṣmī, and also to those enriched by Lakṣmī. (105)

Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Eternal Residence of Lakṣmī among Righteous People, the Places of Lakṣmī’s Abode, and Her Non-Residence among Sinners and Others," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 99. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* – Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 100 [Author:
Chapter 101 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:

O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, Kṛṣṇa is the supreme wealth of the saintly, the very life of the liberated, and the highest deity of the gods. By Your grace alone, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, You have appeared here upon this earth. (1)
"Or have you come for some other reason? Is there indeed any other cause?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"O beloved of Śivarājñī, compassion is always the primary cause here."
My will alone is the cause of my coming into this creation in every respect.
Nevertheless, I shall manifest another fixed cause for whenever I arrive within another creative cycle (kalpa). (3–4)
"At first, having obtained some pretext from the great sage Bhṛgu in certain places, I come repeatedly; and also by the desire of my devotees.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O Lord, for what reason was Bhṛgu born, and for what purpose do you repeatedly assume manifestation here in human form? Please tell me.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the cause of what occurred in the past:
due to the curse of Bhṛgu resulting from the slaying of Bhṛgu’s wife, Viṣṇu’s manifestation occurs in the human world in every way on many occasions. (7)

When the age-dharma has revolved and the bull [of dharma] has become slack, the imperishable Viṣṇu is born to establish the order of dharma— [he who is] Śārṅgin, possessing divine sovereignty, and whose birth is fixed for the sake of the work of the gods. (8–9)
In ancient times, the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu was the sovereign ruler over the kingdom of the three worlds for ten crores of years,
as well as seventy-two lakhs of years.
Likewise, O Emperor, he remained free from disease for eighty thousand years.
After that, King Prahlāda ruled the earth for ten yugas;
then King Bali likewise reigned for ten koṭis of years.
For thirty-six million years,
these three Indras were renowned as the lords of the Daityas; at that time,
this entire kingdom throughout the three worlds was established under the Daityas.
In the meantime, there occurred twelve fierce battles that brought about the destruction of both gods and asuras; in these, Viṣṇu, being entreated by the gods,
repeatedly joined them and annihilated the Daityas with his divine discus.
O beloved, hear from me about all those battles in the Vārāha-kalpa.
First was the Nārasiṃha [incarnation], in which Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain;
second was the Vārāha, in which Hiraṇyākṣa was killed.
Prahlāda was also defeated as the third [enemy] during the churning for nectar;
Virocana was the fourth, who was indeed slain in the Tārakāmaya war.
That Tārakā was the wife of Bṛhaspati, who had been carried off by Candra.
On account of that, a hair-raising battle took place;
at that time, there was a great battle in which Bali was bound by Vāmana.
Indeed, in the sixth [kalpa], Āḍībaka and Jambha were slain by Śakra-Viṣṇu.
In the seventh [incarnation], the Daityas, Tripura and others, were destroyed by Śambhu. In the eighth, Andhaka was slain along with all the Daityas and Dānavas.
In the ninth, Vipracitti and others were killed by the hundreds of thousands by Indra.
In the tenth [manvantara], the asura Vṛtra was slain by the wielder of the thunderbolt;
in the eleventh, however, all the Daityas were destroyed by Raji;
and in the twelfth, Ṣaṇḍa, Marka, and the others were struck down by the gods.

These twelve battles indeed took place between the gods and the asuras. And in all of them, Viṣṇu was the ally of the inhabitants of heaven. In turn, the sovereignty over the three worlds came to be held by Indra, the subduer of Pāka.
Then the gods indeed approached their respective shares of the sacrifice at the ritual;
Yajña-Nārāyaṇa also then became an ally of the gods.
When the gods had thus departed from the sacrifice, the Dānavas spoke to Śukra.
"O foremost of the Daityas and Asuras, having become powerless and overcome by terror, we are unable to remain upon the earth; let us enter the netherworld (rasātala).
Thus addressed, the preceptor of the Asuras, being dejected, spoke these words of consolation.
"Do not fear; by my own splendor I shall sustain for you, O Asuras, rain, herbs, foods, juices, nectars, and comforts.
Having sustained them through my own power, I shall bestow them for your sake."
"I shall go to Mahādeva for the sake of the mantra and for victory.
Having returned here later, I will bestow my grace upon you once more.
For now, you must indeed perform austerities in the forest, clothed in bark garments."
If the gods do not slay me until my return, then,
having obtained these formidable great mantras from Maheśvara,
I shall return; thereafter we shall fight and surely conquer them.
The Dānavas remained in the hermitage of their father Bhṛgu and awaited him.
Having instructed the Asuras and sought refuge with Mahādeva, Kāvya (Śukra) received a warm welcome, paid his respects, and having bowed down, spoke to Śaṅkara.
"O Śambhu, I desire those mantras which do not exist even in Bṛhaspati—mantras that bring about the defeat of the gods and bestow fearlessness upon the asuras.
Having heard this, Maheśvara said: "I shall proclaim the *caravrata*."
"For a full thousand years, remaining a celibate student (brahmacārī) with your head hanging downwards, you shall drink the smoke from a pit; then you will obtain the mantras.
Thus addressed by her, Śukra indeed became an ascetic who subsisted on smoke.
Constantly hanging from a branch of a banyan tree on Kailāsa with his head downward,
at that time, out of indignation toward that opening, the gods,
led by Bṛhaspati and seizing their weapons, swiftly rushed against the Daityas. (37)
Then the Dānavas, thinking, "We shall not be able to conquer the gods," bowed down to Śukra’s mother, Khyāti herself. Terrified, they then sought refuge with her for protection from fear.
The wife of Bhṛgu performed a protective rite; however, the gods, filled with wrath, slaughtered the Asuras on all sides. Then Khyāti became enraged.
By the power of her devotion to her husband, the chaste woman paralyzed Indra and continued her worship.
Indra was instantly paralyzed, brought under control, and rendered motionless;
seeing him thus, the gods fled in the ten directions.
Then Viṣṇu said to Śakra: "Quickly deposit yourself within me."
"Having caused you to enter, I shall protect you; do not fear, O best of gods.
Viṣṇu, having caused Indra to enter his own form, indeed protected him.
Seeing that he was protected by Viṣṇu, the enraged Khyāti spoke these words:
"I shall burn Viṣṇu and Mahendra in a mere moment.
(44) Hearing this, Indra said to Hari: "O Supreme Lord, act quickly!
Strike her with the Sudarśana before that virtuous woman burns us. (45)
Viṣṇu, in great haste, released his discus for the sake of her life;
it severed Khyāti’s head, and having fallen, she died.
Hearing of the slaughter of his own sister, Bhṛgu quickly became enraged.
"You shall be a destroyer of women among humans again and again;
having taken birth, experience intense sufferings repeatedly. Suffer sorrows caused by women in this world over and over. (47–48)

Thus, by the power of Bhṛgu, Viṣṇu Acyuta was born here among men for the sake of the welfare of the world’s affairs when Dharma had perished. Then Bhṛgu, taking up his head, quickly joined it to his body.
"If the entire Dharma has been practiced by me, or even if it is known to me;
and if I am devoted to my vow toward my wife, and you are intent upon your vow toward your husband—by that truth, live! Live in the presence of Viṣṇu!"
Having spoken thus, Bhṛgu sprinkled her with water and restored her to life;
at that very moment, Khyāti, having awakened from sleep, quickly understood what had occurred.
Viṣṇu, through his yogic power, then neutralized Indra’s paralysis.
Bhṛgu then became pacified and praised the Supreme Lord.
He repeatedly begged for forgiveness, and Viṣṇu offered him auspicious food and other gifts. However, Mādhava did not accept them at all, and spoke thus to Bhṛgu. (53–54)
"When your daughter becomes my future wife, O Bhārgava,
then I shall come and take my meal with her.
Having spoken thus, Viṣṇu then departed, leaving behind the Daityas and the others.

Indra, established in well-being, went to heaven, and the gods departed for their own abodes. (56) The Daityas and others, also restored to health, remained near Bhṛgu’s hermitage in the field; they performed austerities and awaited the arrival of Śukra. (57)
Śukra, too, by the command of Śaṅkara, performed severe penance beneath a banyan tree with his head downward in the presence of Hara and Pārvatī.
When a full thousand years had passed, Śaṅkara himself—
Having approached in a divine form and become invisible nearby at the banyan tree, Śakra, while hanging from the banyan tree, praised that Śambhu:
"Salutations to the blue-throated one, to the one with matted hair, to Śambhu. (3.100.60)
Salutations to you, the giver of gifts, the possessor of excellent vigor, to Rudra, to the ruddy one;
to the Lord of the Mountains, the sun-eyed one, and to him who sports with Takṣaka;
salutations to the wielder of the Pināka bow, to the white one, to the terrible, and to the fierce one.
Salutations to you, Mahādeva, Śarva, and Mṛgavyādha. Salutations to Sthāṇu, Bahurūpa, the three-eyed one, and Death.
Let there be salutation to Tryambaka, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva.
Salutations to you, the meditative, the all-pervading, the Sadyojāta Īśa;
salutations to Vāmadeva, the wearer of animal skins, the sovereign lord.
Salutations to you, the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, the Lord of creatures (Paśupati).
Salutation to you, the Lord of beings, to Pūṣan, and to the slayer of obstacles;
salutation to you who are the form of the sun, to Nyagrodha, and to Kāla.
Salutation to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Rudra, to Vahni, and to the Yogi.
Salutations to you, the signless one who possesses the eightfold form beginning with earth;
salutations again and again to you, the Lord of Pārvatī and the Lord of Rays (the Sun).
Salutations to the Great Lord and to you who hold the hand-drum as your musical instrument.
Salutations again and again to you who dwell on Kailāsa and are praised by the gods.
Salutations to the lord of the Gaṇas, whose name is Mahāvaiṣṇava;
and salutations again and again to the father of Śukra, who is most established in Brahman.
Having spoken thus, Śukra ceased; Śaṅkara said to him:
"O best of Brahmins, do not perform penance; your resolve is fraught with danger.
Nevertheless, at the end of a year, I shall fulfill it for you, O virtuous one."
"O Śukra, for the sake of [your] vows and observances, I shall grant you mantras as you desire.
Having spoken thus, the god Śaṅkara vanished right there.
Then Indra dispatched his own daughter, Jayantī.
"O daughter, it has been told that Śakra is indeed performing a severe penance for the sake of sleeplessness throughout the three worlds; therefore, go to him quickly.
Serve this Śukra immediately with beds, service, and other such attentions."
With various services agreeable to his mind, she remained unwearied;
having heard [the news], that beautiful maiden Jayantī went toward him.
Being virtuous, she carried out the words spoken by her father regarding Śukra.
Śukra said to her: "O fair-hipped one, remain with me for ten years in an invisible form, and grant me union.
Thus commanded by Śukra, she remained with him for ten years.
Having become an ascetic woman endowed with semen, she was always possessed of subtle yoga.
Then, after ten years, Bṛhaspati assumed his own body in the form of Śukra and instructed the asuras at that time.
Then, after ten years had passed, Śukra approached the Daityas and said:
"I am Śukra, O lords of the Daityas; understand my words.
The Daityas replied: "You are not our master, Śukra; you are certainly not the truth."
"For ten years our master has been this very Śukra, who is indeed truthful. Thus insulted by the asuras, Śukra cursed them:
"O Daityas, though you were informed that he was the truthful Śukra, you did not welcome him."
"Therefore, with your vigor utterly destroyed, you shall meet with defeat.
Having been thus cursed, and having understood the curse, those gods fought with the Dānavas and others,
and slew many Asuras.
Overcome by the curse of Kāvya and deprived of their store of semen,
those Asuras, being slain, entered the netherworld (rasātala).
Victory was achieved for the gods, with Viṣṇu as their ally.
This, O Lakṣmī, has been told to you: the cause of Viṣṇu’s births.
Taking Bhṛgu as the occasion, Viṣṇu is born again and again.
From Dharma, Nārāyaṇa was born, and Hari appeared during the Cākṣuṣa Manvantara.
In the Vaivasvata [Manvantara], Pṛthu, Viṣṇu, and Vāmana were the sons of Aditi;
he also became Dattātreya and likewise Paraśurāma.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu always becomes Rāmāditya and Vyāsa.
Vāsudeva, Viṣṇu, and Kalki shall also be Viṣṇu; likewise,
other incarnations of Viṣṇu appear as human beings for the sake of destroying the Daityas and for the purpose of protecting Dharma.
In some places for the sake of women, in some for the protection of the gods,
in some for the sake of dharma, and in some indeed out of compassion— O Lakṣmī, all these are my incarnations and manifestations. (3.100.90)
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Out of my own will and by way of grace, I come for the benefit of the virtuous.
As a human sage, I protect the saintly, the brāhmaṇas, dharma, and the cows.
The virtuous are my incarnations, and likewise my weapons;
my sovereignties are my incarnations, and likewise my powers.
Indeed, the liberated are my incarnations, and likewise my devotees.
The gods as well are my incarnations, appearing in every way for the protection of Dharma; by my command, they are born and dissolve within the worlds of creation.
Whatever divine forms I possess, all of them are indeed mine.

The incarnations are always the foremost recipients of service and are affectionate toward their devotees. (95) Those gods and asuras, as well as Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, men, and women, who have obtained the connection with my incarnations— (96)
Animals, beasts of burden, elephants, and horses,
as well as camels, bulls, and others, have attained union with me;
having entered into my auspicious yoga, they have gone, and are going, to the supreme state.
Thus, such compassion dwells within me, and my very nature is likewise. For one who has fully attained union with Me, equality with Me arises.
Through association with the virtuous, one becomes virtuous; and through association with the divine, one becomes a deity.
Through my yoga, one such as I indeed becomes a sovereign devotee;
by the yoga of Nārāyaṇa, a man may become Nārāyaṇa himself,
and a woman may become Nārāyaṇī, just like Muktānikā and Ramā.
"Just as Padmāvatī was born, so too were the two Nārāyaṇīs, my dear.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"O Lord Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, my husband!"

"O Kṛṣṇa, fulfill my inquiry; for when the two daughters of Nārāyaṇa, Ramā and Abjakā, were born, how and by what cause did the union between you and Padmāvatī and Ramā come about? Tell me this clearly."
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; you are indeed omniscient like me.
Nevertheless, having assumed a human state, you wish to inquire about this.
I shall relate the ancient account of how the union of these two—
the descendants of Kakutstha and Sūrya— came to pass within the Kārava lineage.
Long ago, when the thousand-rayed Sun was born...
It was a region of high and low elevations, containing the fire that consumes the cosmic egg;
it possessed unbearable radiance and was exceedingly fierce, for from it the cavities blazed forth.
Having recognized the sun to be full of splendor, it was fashioned and offered by Viśvakarman.
That maiden named Saṃjñā also blazed with the brilliance of the sun;
having abandoned her own husband and made her shadow her wife,
she took up residence in that [shadow] as her own station and departed from her own home.
With a distressed heart, she concealed her own [nature] and went to the abode of Viśvakarman.

(3.100.109) Nevertheless, though instructed by her father to go to the house of the Sun, that virtuous woman did not go; instead, having become a mare, she roamed in the Himālaya mountains. (3.100.110)
Then the Sun arrived at the Himalaya mountain to seek her out;
having become a horse, he began to pursue her, but she did not yield to his desire.
Then the Sun offered his face, and she released [her seed] into his nostrils.
The two delicate sons of Aśvinī were born from her two nostrils.
Then she went together with Sūrya toward the solar orb;
however, she blazed intensely from the splendors of Sūrya, just as she had previously.
Then the father spoke to his father, Sūrya, for the sake of dulling [his] brilliance;
Viśvakarman then ground down the Lord of Day with a whetstone.
Thus thoroughly whetted, Sūrya became exceedingly beautiful and exceedingly enchanting.
Born from the splendor of Sahya, Saṃjñā became firmly established within him.
Then, beholding that beautiful, pleasant, delightful, and divine form which bestows enjoyment, the young woman, having become the quarter of the sky (Diśā), desired him as a noble maiden.
With gestures such as amorous glances, emotional expressions, and playful charms, she sought to entice him; she was desirous of sport, exceedingly lovely, standing by his side, and in her menses.
Seeing her there, the Sun said to the Goddess of the Quarter: "Why have you come here?"
The goddess of the quarter said to him, "O my beloved, grant me the desire that gives complete satisfaction. (1.18) The Sun replied, "My enjoyment must not be in vain; therefore, consider this.
If you have a desired pregnancy, then accept union with me. (1.19)

Then the goddess Diśā herself, though she reflected, "I do not desire pregnancy," being utterly deluded, desired enjoyment from the Lord of the Day. The Sun said, "O dear goddess, I shall grant you enjoyment accompanied by its fruit."
"Perhaps you will be born as a maiden in human form;
then, through union with a noble human woman, my yoga shall bear fruit for you.
When the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama..."

Wandering upon the earth in human form as the fulfiller of desires, the Lord Kṛṣṇa— the cowherd boy and son of Kaṃbhārā— will appear. At that time, the fruitfulness of your birth will be realized in every respect.
Having spoken thus, the Sun ceased; the maiden of the quarter vanished from sight.
(1.24) Then Sūrya, being pleased, spoke with joined palms to his own father-in-law:
"Choose a boon that is dear and agreeable to your mind; I shall grant it here. (1.25)
Then Viśvakarmā said: "O Lord, if you are pleased, even though he is indeed my son-in-law appearing in the form of a son, I nevertheless request a beautiful boon out of a desire for a son:
O Bhāskara, become my son."
Sūrya replied, "So be it," and spoke further regarding that supreme goal:
"When Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa shall appear on earth as a cowherd boy, the blissful son of Satyā and Kambharā."
Therefore, if I truly desire birth for the sake of attaining that yoga—
whether today, at the end of a Yuga, or even after ten thousand Yugas—
I shall become an excellent human being for the sake of attaining the yoga of Śrī Hari.

At that time, O Viśvakarman, you must manifest upon the surface of the earth in the human realm for the sake of establishing my fatherhood. Having obtained you as his father, he shall become your son, born from a womb of artisans.
"I shall become your good son and fulfill your heart's desire.
Having reached this agreement, when Hari himself became the cowherd boy Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa on earth from time immemorial, [he fulfilled his promise].
Having reached that abode of the Lord of the Kabharas, Viśvakarman stayed there for a moment.
In the house of the potter Maṅkaṇaka, the sovereign architect Bāluja was himself born as Viśvakarman, known as Jaṭilāpati.
Having designated Bāluja, the supreme incarnation of Viśvakarman and a master artisan, as his father, Sūrya then became his son.
Nāka, the sovereign of artisans, the best among all craftsmen, and a lord of great yogis, [was born]. (135)
Kakub became the wife of this Pūrṇarūpa.
She was a virtuous human woman born from a portion of the quarter (Digaṃśā),
the auspicious daughter of Ambāmātā and Manojit, the best of artisans.
That portion of the directions, wedded on earth by the portion of the Sun and conquered by the Moon, gave birth to five daughters for the couple; among them, Abjikā was the eldest.
She who was the very embodiment of a portion of the directions was the first-born daughter of Ambā.
Padmāvatī was equal to a chaste woman, the beloved wife of Kṛṣṇakānta.
Sūryaprabhā herself was born from the Sun and was deeply infatuated with Hari;
that daughter of the Sun, being human, desired to make Hari her husband.
The daughter of Sūryamānava was indeed born beautiful;
she was the second [daughter], Ramā, born from the daughter of Nākajit through a portion of the Sun.
That excellent Ramā, the daughter of the Sun, was born of Ambādevī.
The beloved of Hari is endowed with the beauty and virtues of a lotus-lady (padminī).
Indeed, those two daughters of Brahmā from ancient times, named Ramā and Padmāvatī, [attained this] through the vow of the thirteenth day of the month of Puruṣottama. || 142–143 ||
Upon reaching the supreme abode, the imperishable, they were again born on earth by the will of Śrī Hari as the daughter of the Sun, in order to perform service to the Blessed Lord;
thus Ramā was born, and likewise Padmāvatī was born as the daughter of the Quarters.
When Hari was born as a human, both of these were bestowed upon the earth in the form of his wives.
These two, Bharga and Hemanta, who reside in my abode as my attendants, I have brought here along with me for the sake of service; they are brothers.
Wherever their wife was born, there in that house these two were born;
for the Lord Bharga became the season Hemanta, known as Hema.
Devoted to the Supreme Brahman, those two served me, Hari.
That son was indeed born as Bhagavān in the midst of the assembly of Bhagavats.
Then Hemanta was born as his younger brother, most excellent like gold.
After him were born three daughters: Mālatī, Haṃsī, and Sadguṇā.
Those three friends of Vaikuṇṭha became the sons of Ambikā.
Thus, the entire family, endowed with devotion and taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
became an excellent embodiment of divinity for the sake of devotion.
"He came to this earth solely for the purpose of serving Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
(151) Thus, O my beloved, I have related to you here this ancient account concerning Padmāvatī and Ātmā, who are always my two dear ones. (152)
Just as Lakṣmī, Jayā, Rādhā, Māṇikyā, Lalitā, and Priyā are dear to you,
so too is Padmāvatī, Ramā, here my beloved.
This is the *Brahmapriyāṣṭaka*, the most excellent among millions of crores of women.
"By reading or hearing this, one shall likewise obtain worldly enjoyment as well as liberation.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Incarnations of the Lord in the Creation [of the World], the Arrival [of the Lord], the Cause of Bhṛgu’s Curse, the Twelve Battles with the Daityas, and the Previous History of the Family of Padmāvatī and Ramā," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age. Chapter 100.
Chapter 101 [Author:
Chapter 102 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me that which is beneficial: how can the liberation of that deceased person be achieved who had no association with the virtuous in this world?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñīśrī: after the deceased,
virtuous people should be fed at the *śrāddha* ceremony and honored with excellent gifts—
clothing, ornaments, jewels, silver, gold, wealth, and vehicles.
The virtuous and the Brahmins who know the Veda should be gratified.
(3) Gifts of cows should be bestowed, for cows are indeed eternal deliverers;
by the gift of a cow, the deceased who has arisen shall attain the eternal worlds. (4)
A cow acquired by righteous means, when given away, immediately delivers one's entire lineage.
Listen to this which Bṛhaspati spoke to Māndhātṛ in ancient times:
"Having worshipped a virtuous brahmin, and likewise having worshipped one's guru and a cow..."
One should give a cow to a worthy recipient of noble soul under the name of the deceased. "The cow is my mother and my father; it is pure; therein heaven is established.
Having remained in the cow-pen at evening, the observer of the vow should be devoted to the service of the cows and other such duties.
Rising early in the morning, one should perform the gift of a cow while recollecting the *Paretaka* hymn;
O Kamalā, the deceased goes swiftly to heaven—of this there is no doubt.
One should dwell for a single night with cows, sharing their companionship and observing the same vows.

One who is united with the state of the single Self is liberated from impurity. (9) At the sight of the morning sun, milch-cows accompanied by their calves should be given away—youthful, beautiful, containing nectar within, and yielding abundant growth. (3.101.10)
May these cows drive me forward toward the journey to heaven;
may they protect me like a mother and bestow their blessings upon me.
[May they be present] for the destruction of disease, for supreme liberation, for heaven, for prosperity, for happiness, and for wealth. (11)
May the cows, being gracious, grant the arising of all blessings;
O meritorious ones who are the refuge of all gods, bestow upon us the highest state.
Being united in spirit and mind, may they grant the fruit of self-surrender.
I offer water for honor (*arghya*), clothing, a golden-winged bird (*suparṇa*), wealth, and as many portions of cooked rice as there are [deities].
I give a well-pleased, upward-faced cow, together with her calf, dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Having recited "The giver of a cow," one should give; thus he shall obtain the supreme fruit.
One who possesses a cow, is virtuous, a worshiper, a giver of respectful offerings, and a servant;
one who is devoted to the virtuous, devoted to his ancestors, devoted to his teachers, and a worshiper of the gods;
one who is truthful in character and an ascetic—such persons shall never be miserable anywhere. (15–16)

One who practices ritual bathing, one delighted by sacred stories, one intent on the worship of Brahman, and one enriched by service to cows— these four are Vaiṣṇavas who have attained union with the Divine Abode.
One who observes the vow of the cow, one who gifts cows, one who eats what comes from the cow, and one who lives for the sake of cows.
One should know that the Vaiṣṇava is supreme; he for whom the cow is the mother and Viṣṇu is the deity.

One who observes vows to the gods, vows pertaining to the Vedas, vows regarding cows, and vows of the virtuous and the good, as well as vows such as the Gomedha sacrifice, attains foremost abodes of radiant splendor.

The giver of a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu) here enjoys all desires and great festivals bestowed by her— offerings to gods and ancestors, and both earthly and celestial pleasures. He should drink barley mixed with cow's milk and sleep on the ground in a cow-pen.
One who possesses virtuous conduct should give a milch cow; he shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices.
For the sake of the initiation of a virtuous person, one should give a son of auspicious deeds.
By that merit performed by him as well, the deceased embodied beings are uplifted.
One should give a virtuous maiden who possesses detachment,
a young woman endowed with knowledge and intent on uplifting the world,
one who is devoted to moral conduct and free from attachment to the duties of a householder. ||23||
Likewise, the king should grant to his preceptor a beautiful and auspicious female attendant of noble conduct; he should give a female slave to a Brahmin,
and he should give a son of a Brahmin to another Brahmin, and he should give land to a virtuous ruler.
To a twice-born man who is indeed equal to a guru and a treasure-trove of knowledge and the company of the virtuous— one of such character and nature— one should give a gift;
for the gift of a Brahmin youth is considered equal to the gift of a cow.
The Brahmin shall always be a deliverer in this world and the next.
He should indeed give gold and much wealth to the father of the Brahmin boy;
having thus purchased the son of the Brahmin, he should bestow gifts upon the twice-born.
For the purpose of completing sacrificial rites, for the sake of a school,
or for the sake of attaining the dignity of royalty, one who is childless may accept [a son].
[He may also accept] the gift of a son, the gift of a daughter, the gift of a cow, or the gift of gold.
The gift of one's self, the gift of liberation, and the gift of liberation— these are indeed considered the gifts of liberation.
By going to a cow that is affectionate, endowed with vitality, young, and adorned,
and giving her as a daughter in charity, one is joined with all merits.
By giving such a cow, one does not escape the worlds of suffering and poverty.
A cow that is toothless, covered in wrinkles, whose milk has dried up, whose fertile season has passed,
who is aged, diseased, irritable, or wicked— such a cow should never be given away.
Among all [cows], the Kapilā is the most excellent; she should be given away especially.
The gods and the Sun indeed bring rain when they are gratified by sacrifice.
Sacrificial rites are accomplished through the products of the cow—milk and clarified butter.
In ancient times, Prajāpati himself attained satisfaction with clarified butter;
thereafter, he created the cows residing in Goloka, who are the mothers of the world,
golden-hued, tawny, and flowing with torrents of milk.
These cows flow with milk that is like nectar, providing sustenance for all living beings.
Then that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) gave them to the sages and to the gods;
he also gave them to human beings for the purpose of performing sacrifices and other rites involving milk.
And he gave them away to the Brahmins for the successful accomplishment of the divine rites.
Indeed, the gift of Kapila cows is considered the most excellent of all;
they are givers of milk, givers of merit, givers of life, and givers of liberation from the state of the departed spirits.
By giving cows, one becomes a bestower of all desires both in this world and the next.
A man who gives cows obtains sacrificial offerings for gods and ancestors, libations, peace, vehicles, as well as clothing, and the satisfaction of the elderly, children, and others.
Cows possess a fragrant scent as well as the aroma of guggulu resin;
cows are the foundation of the worlds, and cows are a great means of securing well-being.
Neither the wind, nor fire, nor gold, nor the ocean is ever defiled.
Neither milk, nor nectar, nor sunlight, nor the virtuous man, nor even the Lord [is as precious] as the cow.
(42) Cows are wealth that is eternally obtainable; cows are everlasting nourishment.
Cows are the supreme root of fortune; they are indeed the very root of all prosperity. (43)
For food is the supreme stall for cows, and they are the supreme oblation for the gods;
indeed, what is given to cows is eternal, for they abide in the *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* calls.
Cows are the fruit of sacrifice, and sacrifices are established in cows.
From cows, essences increase; calves are nourished by milk-rice.
Those who give a cow as a gift—whether their sins be many or few, or even very slight—they indeed cross over them and attain liberation.
Those who bestow a tawny cow along with her calf, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel,
adorned with ornaments, and covered with cloth, conquer both worlds. In ancient times, Kṛṣṇa gave a bull to Śaṅkara.
Indeed, the gift of a bull has been established as the most excellent on earth.
Those who bestow a young, tall, white bull with many horns and well-adorned become endowed with sovereign power.
Having remembered the cows and remembering the virtuous Hari, one should always sleep at night;
having risen, one should likewise remember them and pay homage, and thus one shall obtain prosperity.
Upon perceiving an inauspicious dream, one should repeatedly recite the name of the cow.
One should cook with cow-dung and perform purification with cow-manure.
One should offer oblations with cow-ghee and have benedictions recited with ghee.
One should give ghee and consume ghee; thus one attains the nourishment of cows.
May cows always be before me, and may they always be at my back and at my sides. I give this cow, composed of all jewels, for the attainment of auspiciousness.
May cows with golden horns and yielding milk attend upon me.
May the fragrant cows, the daughters of Surabhi, always look upon me.
(54) Cows are truth, deities, virtuous women, Lakṣmīs, and devoted wives;
they are the holy ones, the liberated, the lords, the teachers, the righteous, and the brave. (55)
Devotion, merit, virtue, service, what has been given, what has been practiced as austerity, and acts of kindness—these protect one in great dangers, whether in times of equality or adversity.
Listen, Lakṣmī: even animals, such as cows, have come to this earth.
In ancient times, they all performed austerities, thinking, "May we attain preeminence.
[They thought: "We shall be the most excellent even among all sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās);
we shall destroy all sins, yet we shall not be stained by defects. (57–58)
"O Lotus-born one, may all people indeed be purified by our cows and other such means;
likewise, may all embodied beings be purified by our dung and urine.
Furthermore, O daughter of Padma, may the givers of cows go to Goloka."
Brahmā granted excellent boons to the female ascetics and the cows:
"May you become thus, O yoginīs; deliver the worlds, and may you be pure in every way and bestowers of liberation."
"May Lakṣmī dwell in cow dung; I grant those boons to you.
Having thus granted the boons, Brahmā then departed for Satyaloka, and they [the cows] were thereafter to be saluted in the morning, worshipped in every way, auspicious, and bestowers of nourishment.
They became performers of the world's welfare and saviors from worldly existence.
(63) By giving away a tawny, milch cow that has a calf of the same age, adorned with ornaments and garments and gentle in nature, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. (64)
By giving such a red cow, one is glorified in the world of the Sun;
by giving such a brindled cow, one is glorified in the world of the Moon;
and by giving such a white cow, one is glorified in the world of Śakra.
By giving such a black cow, one is glorified in the world of Fire; by giving such a smoke-colored cow, one is glorified in the world of Dharma;
and by giving such a white cow, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
By giving a cow with the color of a speech-maker (a parrot), one is glorified in the world of Vāyu;
by giving one that is golden-colored with reddish-brown eyes, one attains the state of Kubera;
and by giving a yellow one of similar description, one is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
By giving such a brindled cow, one is born as a Viśvadeva;
by giving such a Gaurī cow, one shall attain the world of the Vasus;
and by giving a cow with the color of a white woolen blanket, one becomes a Sādhya deity.
By giving a cow with a broad back, one attains the world of Maruts;
by giving such a cow enriched with jewels, one obtains the state of a Gandharva.
[One who gives] a draft-ox or a great bull adorned with all kinds of gems—
Having given a young bull to the world, one is glorified in the realm of Prajāpati. The giver of a cow goes to the supreme heaven, Goloka,
by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot or a vehicle drawn by bulls through the sky.
In heaven, a thousand celestial damsels constantly serve that giver of cows and awaken him each morning with auspicious hymns;
he rejoices for as many years as there are hairs on the cow’s body.
And thereafter, he becomes a king of the earth who possesses cows.
(75) May cows that yield ghee and milk, whose bodies are ghee, from whom ghee originates, who are rivers of ghee, and who possess whirlpools of ghee, always remain in my home. (76)
May cows dwell eternally in my heart, in my navel, and likewise in my self;
may cows dwell everywhere in my body and within my mind.
Ghee from them abides in my body, senses, and vital breaths.
May cows be before me, and may milch-cows be behind me;
may cows be on all sides of me, for I dwell in the midst of cows.
For one who contemplates in this way, millions of sins are destroyed.
Where there are golden palaces and an inexhaustible influx of gold;
where the goddesses are skilled in the Gandharva arts, and where nectar and prosperity abound; and where there are streams of curd, streams of ghee, and streams of milk.
Wherever those who give cows go, there flow streams of fresh butter.
One who gives a thousand cows shall become a lord of the gods in heaven;
one who performs the gift of a hundred thousand cows shall become an emperor of the three worlds, O Rame.
One who performs the gift of ten million cows attains Vaikuṇṭha and partakes in liberation;
one who gives a hundred million cows attains Goloka and partakes in liberation.
Furthermore, one who gives a lotus-like cow indeed proceeds to the imperishable abode.
By means of ten gifts of cows, a preta is released from the bondage of its form.
Recalling his mother and father, and recalling his wife and grandfathers, the giver of a cow certainly delivers eleven generations of his lineage. (84–85)
By remembering a cow and by the gift of sesame seeds or even the gift of water, one indeed dispels the torments of the deceased in the world of Yama.
"The cows are my mothers who gave me milk; they are indeed the garments of the gods."
"One should constantly recite: 'May cows attend upon me.
Since the gift of a cow is supremely meritorious and its fruit is eternal, nothing remains for the giver of a cow to do for the sake of attaining heaven. (87–88)
Indeed, those cows intended for a gift rescue that person;
they sustain their calves and nourish them with the nectar of milk.
Cows truly exist in the world of men, in heaven, and in the realm of truth.
Indeed, in Aiśvara, Vaikuṇṭha, and Goloka, there dwell cows with many horns and horses. Cows constitute the sacrificial nature of sacrifice; they are the deity even for those who dwell in heaven.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are the supreme merit and ultimate refuge.
In brief, cows are the sacrificial session itself, as they desire to bestow their very hooves;
furthermore, at the end of the tenth month, the Creator bestowed upon them their horns.
From them were born horns, each according to its own specific nature.
These cows protect a great and divine splendor;
they are virtuous, meritorious beings who partake in merit and are devoted to the service of cows, like gods themselves.
There, the trees possess sweet juices and are laden with fruits that exude honey;
their flowers are fragrant as honey, and the ground is likewise composed of jewels.
There, the regions of golden earth are both comforting and grant every desire.
Where the reservoirs of water shine with every kind of lotus;
where filaments, rich in fragrance, are carried by the wind;
where there are stalks bearing fruit of the six tastes, as well as vegetables and honey.
There, the creepers are covered in pearls, laden with fruit, and bestowing nectar;
the mountains are made of gold and possess an eternally fresh splendor. Women of ever-new forms serve there, adorned with millions of pearl ornaments.
All desires become flavorful, and all enjoyments come to pass.
Where the Chandana forests are, there the givers of cows rejoice;
they are enriched by all their intentions fulfilled, free from sorrow, and increased in fortune. (3.101.99–100)

The givers of cows travel in various celestial chariots and through great gardens; they rejoice and sport in every way. They enjoy themselves with women and are likewise honored by the inhabitants of heaven.
They enjoy joy, delight, bliss, and pleasures every day.

(102) Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Greatness of Cows and Other Matters," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning how the gift of a cow was the cause for the liberation of a saintly person who had died as a ghost lacking yoga.
