Chapter 102 [Author:
Chapter 103 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
The descendants of the deceased— the wife, the son, the relatives, and the kinsmen— should perform the vow known as *gavārādhanasaṃjña* for the sake of liberation.
They should likewise dwell in a cow-pen and attend to the cows.
Even the bringing of fodder for the cow, as well as providing her with water to drink;
likewise, providing a place for the cow to lie down, as well as waking her up in the morning;
the cleaning of the cow-pen and so forth, and the warding off of gadflies and other such insects. (2–3)
He should provide grass and fodder, as well as food consisting of cow-products, and offer them due honor; he should protect them in every way, always keep them in the cow-pen,
and never harbor malice toward the cows even in his mind, but always bestow happiness upon them.
One should worship [the deity] with the thought that it is Ramā and honor it with prostrations.
(5) For three days one should drink warm urine, for three days one should drink warm milk, for three days one should drink warm ghee, and for three days one should subsist on air alone. (6)
One should carry clarified butter on one's head and offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter;
likewise, one should give clarified butter as a gift, eat clarified butter, and have benedictions recited with clarified butter.
By eating barley that has been the leavings of a cow, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Then the gods, having been forcibly fed their own respective foods by the Daityas and Dānavas,
performed for the sake of purification alone a month-long vow known as the propitiation of the cow (gavārādhanasaṃjña). || 8–9 ||
Then the gods became pure again, perfected in their own duties;
therefore, cows are sacred, purifying, and likewise bestowers of merit. By giving that auspicious gift of a cow, one becomes purified and attains heaven.

Even while dwelling in the midst of fire, in the midst of cows, or in the midst of the virtuous; even while dwelling in the midst of Brahmins, in the midst of chaste women, or in the midst of the Vedas;
and while dwelling in the midst of sacrifice or in the midst of sacred fords, one is purified from sin. (11–12)
Cows, when satisfied, bestow sons, wealth, a husband, and a beloved wife.
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñīśrī! Formerly, you were by your very nature Śrī.
Having fashioned a beautiful form, you came to dwell in the midst of cows.
And the cows, endowed with wonder, beheld the perfection of her form.
They asked you: "Who are you, O maiden? From where have you come, you who are so beautiful in form?
And how did you arrive here, O gentle one? Tell us, if indeed you think it right. (14–15)
Then, having been propitiated, you bowed down to the cows and said:
"I am the beloved of Viṣṇu; may it be well with you. I am Śrī, the dear consort of Hari. Protected by me, the gods and others rejoice for eternal years. (16)
The sun, the moon, Mahendra, the Vasus, and millions of gods;
fire and water—when entered by me, these indeed become prosperous and manifest.
But those cows which I do not enter perish in every way.

For that house wherein dharma, artha, and kāma are enjoyed by me shall be rich in joy, delight, and tranquility, and filled with great bliss. And I also desire to dwell among you; therefore, be united with me.
"Indeed, a firm desire has arisen in me to dwell forever among the class of women.
Having heard this, the cows said to you, "You are indeed fickle; we do not wish for you who go everywhere. May it be well with you; please go elsewhere. (3.102.20–21)
Having heard [of me], you have requested [my presence]; why then do you not rejoice in me?
After performing great and fierce austerities, human beings serve me;
so too do yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, lords, serpents, and gods.
"How can you accept me? For I am truly difficult to obtain.
Having heard this, the cows said: "You are entirely fickle-minded;
what is the use of saying more? Therefore, we reject you."
Having heard this, you said, "I shall abandon my fickleness;
for your sake, O cows, grant me a place to dwell.
Then the cows replied, "Dwell securely in our dung and urine."
"O Lakṣmī, you are present in the word *om*, in the urine of cows, and in their dung.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, cow-urine and cow-dung are indeed your home;
where you dwell, there I too shall dwell—of this there is no doubt. (26–27)

Knowing its greatness in this way, those people who bestow land upon it are indeed eaters of the remnants of the oblation; they are performers of long sacrificial sessions and officiants of the sacrifice.
Without curd and clarified butter, no sacrifice whatsoever can proceed here.
Therefore, the very nature of sacrifice is established as being rooted in the cow.
(29) The sons of the cow constantly practice the application of agriculture in this world; they produce grains, and by means of them, sacrifices are carried out. (3.102.30)
Afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other sufferings, they carry various burdens;
here on earth, they support holy men both upon their backs and within carts.
When given as a gift, they lead the deceased indeed to Goloka.
Therefore, the abode of cows is above heaven, beyond truth, and likewise beyond Īśvara.
Goloka is indeed the place of cows, my own temple as Kṛṣṇa;
the giver of cows goes to Goloka, the abode of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Listen to another thing, O Mahālakṣmī, which indeed took place in a former age of the gods:
Aditi performed penance, [praying], "May Viṣṇu become my son.
Then, seeing her performing penance on one foot, the daughter of Dakṣa—
Surabhi also performed austerities together with her.
Then Brahmā himself went there and granted a boon to Aditi:
"Viṣṇu, the Lord Hari, shall become your son, performing the work of the gods."
Then the Creator of the Universe granted a boon to Surabhī:
"O daughter of Dakṣa! O ascetic! You shall indeed attain immortality;
you shall attain the status of a sovereign goddess and the state of being a cowherd woman, along with all those born of your lineage. (37)

You shall attain the state of being the liberator of those who are already liberated, and likewise, you shall become the bestower of liberation. You will dwell above, as the most worshipful one in the three worlds; and by the grace of the Lord of Cows (Gopati), you shall go to those Goloka realms where cows are given.
They shall attain those dwelling places where the cows reside—
where the many-horned cattle and their descendants likewise go—
that supreme abode, the station of the far-striding Kṛṣṇa.
By virtue of the merit from offering oblations and other such acts,
those daughters of yours who serve the gods shall dwell in their abodes;
and all the enjoyments you have mentally envisioned shall be attained by you in happiness.
For those who give cows, there are supreme worlds endowed with all desires,
wherein neither death, nor old age, nor fire prevails;
and neither poverty nor anything inauspicious exists anywhere, even as much as a cow’s hoofprint.
There, there are divine forests and divine palaces;
there are also most excellent celestial chariots that travel at will.
There are also streams of ghee, streams of curd, and streams of milk.
There are lotus ponds filled with nectar, as well as pools moist with fresh butter;
heaps of ambrosia exist there, tasting like sugar and honey.
There, young cowherd girls adorned with divine ornaments dwell.

O Saurabhi! Those who give cows shall go to your supreme abode through celibacy, austerity, service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, gifts, meritorious deeds, self-restraint, truthfulness, and the visiting of sacred fords. (47–48)
Through devotion to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, and especially through devotion to Rādhā,
it is possible to attain Goloka, which is adorned by Kṛṣṇa.
A devotee of the cows obtains everything auspicious that he desires according to his wish.
Devoted women obtain everything they desire that is most excellent.
One seeking a son obtains a son; likewise, one seeking a daughter obtains a daughter.
One seeking wealth obtains wealth; one seeking dharma shall attain dharma.
One seeking liberation shall attain liberation; one seeking prosperity, prosperity;
one seeking knowledge, shall obtain knowledge; and one seeking happiness, attains happiness.
Likewise, one seeking flavor obtains flavor, and one seeking firmness obtains firmness.
One seeking a husband obtains an excellent husband; one desiring a wife obtains a beautiful and auspicious woman.
One desiring a daughter obtains a daughter, and one desiring heaven attains heaven.
Furthermore, a giver of cows obtains a great kingdom, even a royal one.
The station of Indra, the station of Sūrya, the station of Candra, the station of Kubera;
likewise the station of Yama, the righteous station, the station of Vahni, and also that of Īśa;
Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, and also the station of Vairāja.
One shall attain the supreme Goloka and obtain the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma).
The giver of a cow attains health and gains fame and renown;
indeed, the donor of a cow obtains elephants, horses, and cows.
The giver of a cow indeed obtains forms, jewels, garments, rubies, and a treasure of gold; this is recorded as the fruit of the time of the gift of a cow.
Untimely death shall perish, and the state of being a preta shall go far away.
"May all sins be utterly destroyed for the giver of a cow and for the one who remembers her.
Thus indeed did Brahmā grant boons to the cow.
O Lakṣmī! Nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to attain in this world for one devoted to cows. (3.102.60)
O Dhenude! O Rama! The supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others, all the riches of universal sovereignty, and whatever wonders there may be—all these arise [from you].
Likewise, the merit of the Vedas, the merit of sacrifices, the merit of giving a daughter in marriage, and sacrificial fees [all derive from you].
The merit of the earth and the merit of gold are produced by the gift of a cow.
Gold, in the form of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), should be given as equal to the gift of a cow;
for when a physical cow is unavailable, a golden cow should indeed be given. (62–63)
Gold should always be given for the sake of land and cattle; O Lotus-born One, gold, a cow, and earth—
these three gifts bring liberation from the state of a ghost, of this there is no doubt.
By giving cows, land, and wealth, even a sinner is purified.
The goat, fire, the ram, the sun, and the horse were born in ancient times;
indeed, gifts of these very things lead to the liberation of the deceased.
Elephants, deer, serpents, and buffaloes are indeed asuras;
for the sake of liberation from the asura womb, the gift of elephants and other such beings is supreme.
Fowls and boars are proclaimed to be rākṣasas.
For the sake of liberation from the womb of a *rākṣasa*, each respective gift is praised.
(68) Cows, milk, *soma*, and land indeed arose as the *iḍā*;
for the sake of the liberation of the deceased and others, the gift of cows and land is praised. (69)
For Agni is indeed the deity, and gold is praised as having him as its deity;
therefore, the gift of gold is declared to be supreme, a divine gift that bestows auspiciousness.
In the absence of fire, however, one should place gold in the locations where the fire would normally reside.
One offers oblations into a clump of *kuśa* grass when fire is not present;
likewise, one may offer into gold placed there, or into the hand of a Brahmin, the hand of a virtuous person, a clump of *darbha* grass, the ear of a goat, water, wood, or gold. (71–72)

When the oblation has been offered, the Lord of Śrī bestows delightful supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); moreover, the practitioner regularly grants gold according to his capacity. He attains residence in the same world (*sālokya*) as Brahmā, Vāyu, Agni, and Soma.
The household life is auspiciously threefold, consisting of mother, father, and son.
The gift of cows, gold, and land is the supreme triad.
Faith, affection, and respect are the three ways of pleasing a guest.
Likewise, land, cattle, and gold indeed bestow [benefits] in the next world;
a residence, wealth, and a livelihood—these three are the means for achieving happiness.
Thus, cows, land, and gold are indeed the providers of happiness when given as gifts.
Knowledge, peace, and cessation—these three are the causes of bliss.
Indeed, the cow, the earth, and gold are the bestowers of great bliss.
Devotion, Hari, and liberation—these three are eternally interconnected.
The virtuous man, moral conduct, and patience—these three are likewise interconnected;
similarly, gifts of gold, cows, and land are eternally linked.
They bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and likewise effect the deliverance of the deceased.
These three bestow heaven, destroy heaps of sins, and grant merit:
the sacrifice of cows, the gift of cows, and the ancestral sacrifice of libations (tarpaṇa).
Having performed the sacrifice for the virtuous by providing food and giving a golden sacrificial fee, [one attains these rewards]. 3.102.80–81.
Having performed the Nārāyaṇabali and having caused the libation (tarpaṇa) for the one with the blue tail and others to be made,
one should release the deceased by giving a gift to the person who was requested.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the auspicious liberation of the deceased has been described.
Even the thorough study of the treatises on liberation shall bring about release;
likewise, the chanting of my names and uninterrupted devotion to me,
as well as the water from the hands of the virtuous, grant liberation from the state of being a ghost.
The final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), the purifying rite, the ritual bath, and the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*) performed at an auspicious moment;
likewise, the sight of holy men, their touch, and following their instructions;
and the resorting to the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*)—these grant liberation even from the state of existence as a ghost (*preta*).
Wherever one may go, one is liberated by the worship of Hari.

Whether one is a Yakṣa, a Rākṣasa, a Bhūta, a Preta, or a Piśāca; whether a serpent, or even one with the body of an animal, or belonging to Yama, or possessing the body of the Wind-god—[by worshipping Hari, such beings are liberated]. 86–87.
Whether it be a ḍākinī, a śākinī, a bhūtī, a piśācinī, a vetālinī, or a vetāla— wherever they may have gone—
or whether it be the sight of holy men or the grace of Śrī Hari. (88)
He obtains water as well, and is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
For the virtuous are indeed saviors in the world, destroyers of sins, removers of impurities, and bestowers of divine liberation.
"O Rame! The virtuous are always superior to cows, gold, fire, and the gods.
Indeed, association with the virtuous is my own yoga, which bestows all the goals of human life.
Once, there was a Puṣkasa named Bhāruṇḍa, who was a drinker of liquor.
A meat-eater, devoid of virtue, and a thief died in the depths of the forest (92).
Led by the messengers of Yama to the city of Yama, he was cast into the hells.
But his wife performed a gift of a cow at a sacred ford and offered gold (93).
At that very moment, all the sins of the preta were cast far away;
the preta swiftly went to heaven, while his sins went to Surabhi.
That Surabhi spoke to Brahmā in order to destroy those sins.
“O Father, tell me, where must I go so that the sins of the Puṣkasa, which have attached themselves to me because of his gift, may be destroyed?
Having heard this, Brahmā said to that cow: ‘Go to Sanatkumāra. (95–96)
"That saint will quickly destroy your sins; his virtuous conduct and vows are such that they will swiftly eliminate your evils.
Having heard this, Surabhya went to that saint and requested him accordingly.
For the very purpose of destroying his sins, the saint gave him the water from his feet.
That cow Surabhi quickly drank [the water], and her sins were instantly destroyed.
Then Surabhi, being purified by the virtuous, approached Brahmā;
bowing to her teacher, the venerable Creator, she spoke these verses with great satisfaction. (98–99)
"Blessed indeed are the virtuous in this world—those of good character, free from passion, devoid of deceit, and possessing divine forms—by taking refuge in whom evil is destroyed.
[They are like] sacred fords, wish-fulfilling cows, chaste women, and ascetics. (3.102.100)
Whatever sins belong to the Brahmins perish in the presence of the virtuous.
Whatever sins belong to the ancestors, the gods, the great seers, women, and all embodied beings, they perish in the presence of the virtuous. (101–102)
Indeed, the sins of kings, rākṣasas, yakṣas, bhūtas, and inhabitants of Yama’s realm—
even those destined for evil rebirths— are surely destroyed when they encounter the virtuous.
This is likewise true for those possessed by lust, anger, greed, and delusion.
Whatever sins belong to those who commit violence perish in the presence of the virtuous.
(104) Indeed, the sins of those who commit murder, those who slaughter animals, the cruel, those who obstruct life, and those who betray trust, surely perish in the presence of the virtuous. (105)

The sins of courtesans, unchaste women, those who bear banners, those who bear wheels, as well as those who bear weapons and physicians, perish when they encounter the virtuous. [Likewise,] the sins of those who betray those who have sought refuge, those who kill children, arsonists, and those who administer poison [perish]. 106.
"The sins of those who administer poison and those who destroy forests perish when they encounter the virtuous.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, the cow Surabhī, firm in her vows, departed for the cow-pen.
By reading or hearing this, tens of millions of sins shall be destroyed.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow Named *Gavārādhana*, the Abode of Lakṣmī in Cow Dung and Cow Urine, the Various Fruits of Giving Cows, the Means of Delivering the Dead, the Refuge for the Virtuous, and the Savior of All," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 103: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 103 begins]
[The Author: Chapter 104.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: At what time does the fruit of giving gold, cows, and land [accrue] through donation?
"O Keśava, explain to me what kind of gift one should bestow.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"O Daughter of the Lotus, having given gifts on the first day of the bright fortnight,"
Fortunate and beloved wives shall obtain [husbands] who provide Śrāddha feasts.
Likewise, by giving on the second lunar day, one obtains daughters and sons;
likewise, by giving on the third lunar day, one obtains excellent horses. (2–3)
By giving on the fourth day, one then obtains cattle and wealth;
by giving likewise on the fifth day, one obtains sons endowed with excellent qualities;
and by giving likewise on the sixth day, one obtains immediate fame and strength.
By giving in this manner on the seventh [lunar day], one obtains a field and a garden.
By giving in this manner on the eighth, one obtains excellent wealth.
By giving in this manner on the ninth, one obtains elephants, camels, horses, and the like.
By giving likewise on the tenth day, one becomes endowed with a wish-fulfilling cow (kāmadhenu);
by giving likewise on the eleventh day, one becomes possessed of a treasury of silver;
and by giving likewise on the twelfth day, one becomes possessed of gold, jewels, and the like.
Likewise, by giving on the thirteenth day, one becomes a king of the world;
by giving on the fourteenth day, one shall attain universal sovereignty;
and by giving on the full moon day, one becomes a person of wondrous power.
Likewise, by giving on the new moon day (Amāvāsyā), one shall attain all desires;
and likewise, by giving on the Jayantī day, one shall attain supreme liberation. I shall now describe specifically the fruit of giving according to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
By making a gift under Kṛttikā, one shall indeed be free from distress.
By making a gift under Rohiṇī, a person shall possess offspring.
By giving under Mṛgaśiras, a man shall become radiant with splendor.
By making a gift under Ārdrā, one shall always be victorious;
by making a gift under Punarvasu, one shall become wealthy and prosperous.
By giving gifts under Puṣya, however, one shall be nourished in every respect.
By making a gift under Āśleṣā, one obtains wise sons;
by making a gift under Maghā, one attains preeminence among one's progeny;
and by giving under Pūrvā-phālgunī, one becomes endowed with excellent fortune. (14–15)
From a gift given under Uttarāphālgunī, a person shall have many offspring;
one who performs a gift under Hasta shall obtain the fruits of his undertakings.
By giving under Citrā, however, one shall obtain handsome sons.
Under Svāti, one who gives gifts shall become a merchant possessing jewels.
Under Viśākhā, a giver shall have an excellent son or many sons.
Under Anurādhā, a giver shall become a preeminent universal monarch (cakravartin). (17–18)
One who gives during Jyeṣṭhā indeed attains sovereignty in this world;
one who performs acts of giving during Mūla shall obtain supreme health;
and by giving during Pūrvāṣāḍhā, a person shall possess glory.
By giving a gift under Uttarāṣāḍhā, one shall always be free from sorrow.
By making a gift under Abhijit, a physician shall attain success.
And the giver of a gift under Śravaṇa shall obtain the supreme goal.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā, one may become a donor, a teacher, a preceptor, or a king;
by the gift under Śatabhiṣā, one attains mastery over the elements (dhātusiddhi).
The fruit of giving under Pūrvabhādrapadā is goats, sheep, and the like.
Under Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, one will possess cattle, horses, and elephants;
under Revatī, by making a gift, one will possess gold, silver, and the like;
and a person who makes a gift under Aśvinī will possess buffaloes, horses, and so forth. (23–24)
One who gives a gift under the asterism Bharaṇī will undoubtedly become long-lived;
indeed, a giver of cattle, land, and gold shall obtain all fruits.
One who knows the dharma of giving should never examine the worthiness of the recipient for a gift.
One should never examine [the suitability of] those invited for rites for the gods, for the ancestors, or for virtuous purposes.

[Such persons are]: the learned, the devoted, those most established in Brahman, the purifiers of all, those intent on right conduct, those who have received gifts of land from Brahmins, and the twice-born singers of the Sāmaveda. (26–27)
Those who serve their parents, as well as those who serve the gods;
those devoted to celibacy, pure ascetics who purify all;
those whose conduct is rooted in truth, dharma, vows, and virtue; and those who frequent sacred pilgrimage sites. (28)
Those who have performed the great consecration and those who have performed the purificatory bath;
those who recite the complete scriptures, ascetics devoted to chanting, those intent on the path of liberation, narrators of sacred stories, and teachers of dharma. (3.103.30)
Those who bestow the guru’s mantra, who show reverence to the elders, and who serve the cows; those who are virtuous,
rich in service to the holy, worthy recipients, and purifiers of all—
(31) they are foremost in the writings on Dharma and leaders in the writings on liberation.
Those who have knowledge as their refuge, whose character is wisdom, and who are truly tranquil, are purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
As long as these look upon the assembly, they purify it at that very moment—those devoted to meditation and wisdom, devoted to devotion, and likewise devoted to austerity. (32–33)
The virtuous who are endowed with disinterested action are purifiers of the assembly;
when fed, honored, and bowed to, these holy ones grant liberation to the departed spirits.
Devoted ascetics and saints are the sanctifiers of the entire universe.
The restraint of these senses is considered the highest austerity (tapas).
Furthermore, the restraint of the mind, the constant meditation upon Śrī Hari,
and the perfection of renunciation— that indeed is the supreme austerity.

Fasting, celibacy, silence, forgiveness, supreme austerity, endurance, contentment, generosity, forbearance, and the highest penance; as well as truthfulness of speech and eating only the remains of offerings—these constitute the highest austerity. (37)
Even the eating of nectar alone is said to be the supreme austerity.
One should indeed always eat but one meal, as if constantly fasting; one should remain a celibate student, observing the vow of having only one wife.
He who engages with women only during their fertile season shall indeed be a virtuous man; he who is free from attachment to women in general is liberated on this earth, without a doubt.
Free from the snare of gold and women, he is the two-armed Supreme Lord.
Such a woman endowed with righteousness is considered to be Nārāyaṇī in person.
She is a virtuous wife, a worthy recipient of gifts, and likewise a most excellent vessel of purity.
A widow is also a worthy recipient of gifts, as is a woman who is without a protector.

A maiden is a worthy recipient of gifts, and an elderly woman is also a vessel for charity; even one who is destitute is a fit recipient if she is endowed with the strength of devotion. Indeed, a donor who possesses such devotion always becomes purified.
Having divided [the food] and then eaten it, he indeed becomes an eater of nectar (amṛtabhojin).
Having offered it to the gods and then consumed it, he indeed becomes an eater of remnants (vighasāśin).
For in the house of such a person, even supernatural powers (ṛddhi) remain invisible.
Having attained that supreme embodied form,
the deities, ancestors, Siddhas, yogins, ascetics, as well as the virtuous,
lords, and sovereign goddesses rejoice and cause him to rejoice in the abode of the donor.
Apsarases and Gandharvas, gods and goddesses, and the virtuous;
those who are truthful and fortunate, as well as the wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu)—these indeed become his sons, grandsons, daughters, daughters-in-law, and cattle. (47–48)
Thus, for the donor, the entire household indeed becomes a temple of the gods;
the livestock become divine animals, and even the crops become deities.
All gold, silver, and so forth are forms of Lakṣmī and possess excellent divinity.
All fortunes, beauty, ornaments, and even the deity itself—
thus the divine family of the giver shall become celestial.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, gold, cows, and auspicious earth should be given.
If one has the capacity to digest it, one should accept [the gift], and not otherwise;
for from accepting [a gift] when one lacks such capacity, there is indeed the destruction of merit.
Long ago, King Vṛṣādarbhi was filled with eagerness regarding the Seven Sages.
He displayed the jewels to give them away, but the sages did not accept them at that time.
Vṛṣādarbhi himself said: "You are capable of receiving gifts;
a gift saves one. Choose this supreme wealth!"
I shall offer gold, silver, pearls, and diamonds;
gems, white elephants, horses, and white bulls;
as well as cows that have calved once, wish-fulfilling cows, villages, and fields. (55)

"Kingship, queens, groups of male servants, female and male slaves, great assemblies, palaces, rivers, mountains, and forests everywhere—I shall give these all. Let the Brahmins take them from me today, and let the virtuous sages accept my gifts. (56–57)
"I have nothing that cannot be given away, for I am striving for liberation;
by giving to worthy recipients, I shall obtain here the eternal fruit.
Thus did he speak, as he stood ready to bestow his gift.
The sages, composed, steadfast, tranquil, and contented, said:
"O King, the acceptance of gifts from kings is like honey in taste but like poison; once obtained, the acceptance of royal gifts may consume one like a forest fire. (3.103.60)
Therefore, one who desires happiness both in this world and after death must never accept what is unfit to be accepted.
Indeed, by accepting royal wealth, one attains the most sinful destination.
Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth—
All that is not enough for even one person; therefore, the wise man should dwell in tranquility.
(62) As the deer grows, its body increases;
likewise, the desire of both man and woman always increases. (63)
There is no substance in this world that could completely satisfy the world;
a person whose thirst is like that of the ocean is never satiated.
When desire is pursued by one who longs for it, that very desire continues to consume him.
If one is full of desire, it increases; if one is possessed by thirst, it pierces excessively. (65) Indeed, restraint in receiving gifts sustains austerity firmly;
but in the possession of property, all austerity is surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (66)
In this world, the accumulation of austerity alone is superior to the accumulation of material wealth.
Therefore, O King, let that wealth be yours; do not sprinkle poison upon a brahmin.
We great seers, being peaceful, do not desire the forest-fire of royal wealth at all.
"May it be well with you, O Great King! We shall return to heaven once more.
Having spoken thus, all the sages departed without accepting any gifts.
Thereupon, Vṛṣādarbhi correctly understood the terrible nature of accepting such gifts.
Indeed, a gift bestowed upon an unworthy recipient is most certainly unwholesome.
Therefore, the twice-born are indeed the worthy recipients of gifts, for they are the locus of merit.
Even those who are virtuous, if they are devotees of the Lord, to them especially should one give.
Even Brahmins who are devotees of Hari—to them, gifts should especially be given.
(71) To those who do not harbor greed at all and are entirely free from self-interest, who are worshippers of Śrī Hari—to them, gifts should especially be given. (72)
A person who possesses a sacred vessel (pātrajana) should always avoid greed in every way;
considering it an offering to Hari, he should accept [gifts], and never otherwise.
O Lakṣmī, thereafter Vṛṣādarbhi [performed this] at Prayāga during the Kumbha conjunction.
Having gone there, the noble-minded one gave gifts to the virtuous.
Then, a celestial chariot arrived from Vaikuṇṭha at the bank of the Yamunā,
at the confluence of the Gaṅgā, adorned by the attendants of Viṣṇu.
The attendants took the king and went to the abode of Vikuṇṭha. O Rama!
Thus, through the service of virtuous people, liberation certainly occurs; there is no doubt. Therefore, one should cultivate such worthy company.
And one should give it to him with devotion, thinking, "May this be an offering to Hari.
Then one should also give the gift of an umbrella and the gift of sandals,
as well as the gift of an ear-cleaner and a bodice, and the presentation of a helmet.
By that [act], one becomes a lord of an umbrella and likewise a dweller in celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
One should give the gift of a lion-throne; from that, one becomes a sovereign of a kingdom.
One should give the gift of a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) and likewise offer the gift of a staff (*vetra*).
One should perform the gift of a banner and likewise practice the gift of a chariot;
one should perform the gift of a treasury and the gift of a collection of grain;
as well as the gift of a field of sugarcane and the gift of a field of crops.
One should also diligently perform the gift of a lake, the donation of a vegetable garden, and the giving of parks, flower gardens, and the like; likewise,
one should indeed make gifts of shawls, ornaments, and bodices.
One should provide gifts of a bed and a couch for the liberation of the deceased.
One should give gifts of vessels, water-pots, jars, and cooking pots; one should give gifts of decorative articles for the liberation of the deceased. (83–84)
The gift of a water-jar, a jar of milk, and a jar of curd;
the offering of a water-cistern, a jar of ghee, a mortar, and so forth;
the gift of a pestle and the presentation of a broom. (85)
The giving of fans and the like, the offering of a lamp-stand,
the gift of a bedstead, the gift of a vessel-stand,
the donation of a hearth and a grinding stone, and the presentation of a ladle and a wooden mortar. (86–87)
One should cause the gift of tongs, the gift of *kāṅgakeśī*, the gift of a mirror,
and the gifts of a girdle and a rope to be made for the liberation of the deceased.
[88] Likewise, the gift of water, the gift of cooked food, and the offering of fruit.
One should offer milk-porridge and the like, as well as gifts of sweet foods;
various offerings of wheat, rice, and sesame seeds; and the presentation of juices, honey, and salts for the liberation of the deceased. (3.103.89–90)
One should perform the giving of great woolen blankets, the bestowing of fine garments,
and the offering of grand ornaments for the liberation of the deceased.
One should diligently perform acts of charity on auspicious days such as the Ekādaśī.

One should perform the gift of vows, the gift of austerity, the gift of devotion, the offering of sacred narratives, the gift of recitation, and the gift of dharma for the liberation of the deceased. One should also perform the gift of the vehicle of Vāyu and the gift of the vehicle of Agni. (92–93)
The gift of a water-carrier, the gift of a vehicle for the earth, the gift of a human vehicle, and the gift of a mechanical vehicle;
the gift of a palace, the gift of a temple, and the gift of a mansion. (94)
One should perform the gift of a village and the gift of armor for the liberation of the deceased.
Listen, Lakṣmī: formerly, while dwelling in his own hermitage, the sage Jamadagni discharged arrows while playing with his bow. (95–96)
Having brought those arrows, his wife Reṇukā gave them to him again and again;
meanwhile, at midday, the fierce heat of the sun became intense.
Her feet being scorched, the wife slowly approached her husband.
The sage said, "O beloved, why does it take so long to fetch the arrows?
His wife replied, "My feet are indeed being scorched by the heat of the sun. Upon hearing this immediately, the sage released his arrows toward the sun.
Terrified of the sun, he approached the sage in the guise of a brahmin and said: "O Ṛṣi, spare me! I implore you for grace; forgive me!
The sage replied: "May the path to my wife be easy for you to traverse."
"O Sun, act in such a way that he may indeed be freed from his distress.
Having heard this, the Sun immediately gave him an umbrella and sandals,
as well as a small vehicle that travels at will, along with ornaments and garments.
The Sun also gave him an inexhaustible vessel, a canopy providing shade for an entire kalpa,
a necklace that removes all heat, and likewise nectar that bestows satisfaction;
he also gave other implements and comforts.
Having bowed, the Sun departed for heaven, and Reṇukā became a source of happiness.
Her tender feet were healed by the sage, who attained a state of serenity.
Thus, indeed, the practice of giving umbrellas and other such gifts originated from the Sun.
By the offering of various gifts for those living beings who possess the bodies of the deceased, the suffering of the departed is surely pacified; through merit, their liberation shall come to pass.
By reading or hearing this, the fruit of all possible gifts shall be obtained.
"O Lakṣmī! All the fruit of giving returns once again to the giver.

(107) Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Departed through Various Gifts, the Excellence of the Recipient of Gifts as a Holy Person, and the Examples of Vṛṣādarbhi and Sūrya," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 104 [Author:
Chapter 105 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Supreme Lord, tell me the essence of the dharma of the householder’s life:
by doing what does a householder with sons and wife attain prosperity?
What must necessarily be performed, and by doing what is one’s duty fulfilled?
By which the convergence of all duties that must be performed arises.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
The virtuous, the ancestors, the gods, the gurus, and the great sages—
The virtuous are to be honored, devoted, worshipped, and sacrificed to constantly according to one's wealth.
(3) Indeed, the virtuous are to be gratified with food, flowers, prostrations, and so forth;
the virtuous are to be propitiated through service and through following their will. (4)
Indeed, the ancestors are to be gratified with offerings of water, food, milk, roots, fruits, leaves,
and prepared foods accompanied by excellent flavors.
One should cause the offering to the gods to be made and perform the worship of the gods.
One should perform sacrifices constantly and always satisfy the gods.
One should serve one's gurus and always carry out their commands.
One should offer everything to the gurus and dedicate it to one’s mother and father.
One should offer what is desired to the elders and serve them with joy for their delight;
likewise, one should bow to and offer gifts to the sages and the twice-born.
One should also recite the Sāma Veda and cause the gift of knowledge to be bestowed.
One should give food, water, and so forth to virtuous and chaste women;
one should provide shelter and clothing, and satisfy those who are destitute.
One should always worship devotees and cultivate association with the righteous.
One should cultivate the path to liberation and always accumulate merit;
one should act in such a way that embodied beings who come to one's home may indeed be happy. Having provided them shelter and rendered assistance, one should satisfy them.
This Hari-Nārāyaṇa has indeed arrived as a guest who has come to the home.
Nārāyaṇa resides there; may this Janārdana be pleased. Thus one should offer a welcome, and everything shall become an offering to Brahman.
The householder should give to the mendicants and likewise give to the cows;
he should give to the dogs and also offer to the crows.
He should give to the aquatic creatures and also present [food] to the destitute.
One should offer the *bali* at night to the night-roaming spirits (*niśācara*) and elemental beings (*bhūta*).
One should also give to living creatures such as nagas and snakes, and even to insects,
flour, grain-particles, cooked food, fodder, and leaves, as appropriate.
One should always announce: "This is in my house for the teacher, the father, the virtuous friend, the trusted relative, and the guest.
The householder should always be one who eats only what remains after [the gods and guests have been served], like a disciple of the Beloved of Kamalā.
Standing in the place of her husband, the wife is the mistress of the house and the protector of the home. Always acting as a guardian of dharma, she should cultivate all virtuous qualities.
O auspicious lady, you must always practice generosity and attend to the honoring of others.
By receiving blessings and other such honors, a woman becomes Nārāyaṇī, and a man becomes Nārāyaṇa; the earthly world shall attain the state of Goloka.
This is declared to be the nectar of the home, by performing which one becomes prosperous.
Having heard this essence of the Dharma, whoever acts accordingly shall attain heaven.
(21) Listen further in brief, and contemplate that which resides in the heart:
"I am the Lord, Nārāyaṇa himself, ever present within the home. (22)
You are Śrī herself in the form of a woman, always present as the wife in every householder’s home;
my attendants indeed exist in the home in the form of sons and daughters.
My guests are great souls, saintly persons who have arrived from afar.
Thus, indeed, with divine vision, the family lived within the home;
they served one another in the spirit of offering everything to Kṛṣṇa. Through devotion, there remained nothing that was not to be offered to Him.
Those very same sense objects, those very same senses, and those very same enjoyments—
when conceived within Me, Kṛṣṇa, O beloved, they become free from the gunas and grant liberation.
This auspicious essence of dharma has been told, which yields the nectar-fruit of the household life.
It bestows supernatural powers, merit, freedom from bondage, liberation, and bliss.
(27) Such a reality is known through the merit of a thousand births;
however, it is difficult for the unworthy, the sensualist, and the defiled to grasp. (28)
O beloved, the virtuous should be gratified in every way by means of the body, senses, mind, intellect, and consciousness; abiding in that, I myself become satisfied.
[They are also gratified] by houses, gardens, fields, horses, elephants, cows, buffaloes, and wealth.
The virtuous should be gratified with offerings of water, clothing, food, and service. Perform various sacrifices with abundant food and gold as the sacrificial fee.
Serve the virtuous and the virtuous women, and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Delight those dear to the Brahmins and serve the elders;
honor those who depend on you with auspicious hospitality according to their merit.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in former times, there was indeed a thief named Naraśāya.
Always living by theft, accompanied by his wife and son,
he dwelt constantly in the forest of lions; indeed, at night he would go to their dwellings,
forcibly breaking into the mansions of the wealthy and carrying off their riches.
Taking food, clothing, and other necessities, he would go back again into the forest;
thus he constantly sustained himself by theft in that forest.
Then, a virtuous Vaiṣṇava named Śrīcakrabhāsa was traveling along the path.
He met that king of men, the thief, near the edge of the lake.
Recognizing that the holy man was blameless, fearless, and auspicious,
the thief approached him, bowed, and then sat before him for a moment.
The holy man, having drunk the water, gave him water born of his grace.
The thief, honoring his good fortune, quickly drank that nectar-like water.
Merely by drinking it, his heart turned toward the auspicious refuge.
His mind became purified and his body attained discernment.
Regarding him as holy, peaceful, and a bestower of happiness, he asked him:
"O virtuous one, how may there truly be the destruction of sin? Show me the true path."
Having heard this, Śrī Cakrabhāsa said to him: "Indeed, worldly theft is [forbidden];
rather, abandon that and perform the theft of the virtues of the virtuous and of Hari.
With a pure heart, always practice the service of the holy man and of Hari."
Having heard this, that protector of men questioned the holy man again and again:
"O sage, tell me, in what manner should I perform service?
The holy man replied: 'In the forest, serve with forest-grown offerings presented to me.'"
Subsist on a diet of fruits and roots, abandon theft,
worship the form of Hari here, and perform his devotion constantly. In this way, through the service of Hari, all sins shall perish.
Thus addressed, that thief spoke kindly near the lake:
"O virtuous one, my dwelling is here; come to my house.
I shall serve you, and through you, I shall worship Hari."
Sins will perish, and wives and sons shall become pure.
Having heard this, Śrī Cakrabhāsa, chanting the name of Hari Nārāyaṇa, wearing bark garments and matted hair, joyfully held a rosary in his hand. (47)
The old man went to the thief’s hut, which was occupied by his wife, sons, and others.
When a seat was offered, he sat down, worshipping Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
The thief’s wife, sons, daughters, and the rest, perceiving the old man to be their father’s guru, [honored him].
At that very moment, they placed a water vessel, excellent fruits, and ripe mangoes near the holy man, and then said, "Please eat.
Delighted with joy, they repeatedly performed the service of massaging his feet.
The virtuous man ate the fruits and drank the cool water.
While eating, he gave [portions] to them again and again at intervals;
and the women, sons, and others, considering what was given to be a supreme favor, [were satisfied]. (51–52)
They ate the most delicious foods; even the thief then ate, having remembered me, Nārāyaṇa, and offered it to Viṣṇu.
The virtuous man ate and gave to them; and they, having eaten, were freed from sin.
They were quickly purified by service and by touch;
their hearts were transformed in the presence of that virtuous man.
They all said, "O Blessed One, please grant us that which will surely bring about our welfare."
"Act accordingly; while dwelling here in the forest, stay in our hut as a guest.
"So be it," the saint replied, and remaining there in peace for a long time, he instructed me in the constant worship of Nārāyaṇa.
Meeting at night, they perform worship and chant with melodic intonation:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O All-pervading Lord of Lakṣmī! (57-58)
Having thus recited this to me, they always sleep; then,
rising in the morning, they perform worship together with virtuous people,
go to the lake, bathe, and pay homage to the Sun.
Having bowed to Sādhu and the Mālikā, and having recited the mantra five times,
they go toward the forest to gather fruits and return to their own hut.
At midday, they roast fruits, roots, and other provisions with fire.
Having given [the offering] to that guru and having presented it to Hari,
they feed him and then eat themselves; thereafter,
they perform worship in the evening and partake of the nectar of the sacred narrative.
Sons serve the virtuous man, and a woman serves him day and night.
Even a thief constantly serves the virtuous one who is the very self of Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever deeds characterized by theft were previously committed by his wife, sons, and others— 63–64.
He reported everything to him, including all the wealth he had gathered;
the saintly man took it all and went to the Gokarṇa-tīrtha.
There, saying "This is offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa," he cast it into the midst of the water.
Then that entire wealth became the maiden Śrī Lakṣmī;
having become a virtuous woman, she said to the saint: "I have been offered by you to Kṛṣṇa. I have indeed become purified; my impurity has vanished. (66–67)
"Moreover, having purified both the thieves and those who were formerly wealthy, I shall lead them to the feet of Kṛṣṇa; this indeed is my duty.
Having spoken thus, Lakṣmī took that virtuous man and went to that forest.
Where those who were thieves became astonished, they too questioned her upon seeing the virtuous woman. The virtuous one said to them:
"Lakṣmī herself has arrived to lead [him] to the abode of Nārāyaṇa. (3.104.70)
"Be ready quickly and go to the abode of Nārāyaṇa!
Having heard this, they were filled with joy; having become ready and bowed to that Guru, they ascended the celestial chariot, which was richly adorned with divine splendor, as it arrived.

By the command of the saintly one, those attendants went along with their followers to Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of the Lord, O Lakṣmī, because of their association with the saintly one. Then that maiden, who was the very embodiment of Śrī, went ahead together with the saintly one.
She went to the palaces of those wealthy men; and upon seeing her, even those wealthy men, filled with agitation, honored the Queen of the Gods with welcomes and other marks of respect.
Having learned the account from the beginning, they all honored the holy woman.
Wealth that has fallen into the hands of a thief, when entrusted to the hand of a virtuous person,
attains divinity in Śrī Kṛṣṇa and becomes a cause for auspiciousness. Having understood this, they too, by the command of the saintly one, became ready.
For the sake of liberation, even then, a great, radiant celestial chariot arrived from the sky,
accompanied by his attendants and others;
Lakṣmī, taking all the guardians of wealth with her, boarded the chariot.

Having stayed with him, having led him away, and having bowed to that virtuous one who shines as the Śrīcakra, he departed for Goloka, the abode of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord Hari who is higher than the highest. Thus, O Lakṣmī, formerly by you [the fate] of the families of the best of thieves was determined. (78–79)
Through the practice of yoga, that virtuous one, having united with Hari, performed a meritorious deed;
and the illustrious Cakrabhāsa departed for the realm of Lomaśa.
For the sake of visiting sacred sites, he sat in meditative absorption for the duration of an age after age.
He beheld the path to liberation, showing how people depart from here:
having pierced through Svarga, Maharloka, Jana, Tapa, and Satyaloka,
they go above the waters to Vaikuṇṭha, there into the presence of Hari.
They obtain rest, happiness, and great honor through a warm welcome and other honors;
then, by the command of Hari, they go to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha,
or they proceed to Goloka, the imperishable abode, or the highest realm.
Possessing divine bodies and divine qualities, wise and of solid form,
they enter the celestial chariot called Praṇava, which is richly adorned with rays; having entered it,
they proceed to the world of Brahmā, becoming indeed of the nature of Brahmā and free from the flow of rebirth.
Having attained the bliss of Brahman, they have gone to immortality;
in the world of Brahman, they enjoy the imperishable Brahman, the priest of all, the Lord of liberation,
the sovereign who is the nectar of bliss.
Without sovereignty, they become equal to the Supreme Self (87).
They are similar in form, power, victory, lordship, and capability.
Such is this eternal sacrificial session of Brahman (brahmasatra) known as the Nectar (amṛta) (88).
They have gone to that state from which there is no return, for the sake of immortality;
devoted to Brahman and disciplined, they abide in the supreme goal.
Free from passion, having mastered their vital breaths, devoid of delusion, and speakers of truth.
Peaceful, devoted to the welfare of living beings, compassionate, and masters of their senses;
unattached, pure, and devoted—they are said to attain union with Brahman.
Those heroes who, free from desire, have burnt away their sins through ascetic penances.
For them there are worlds that do not decline, auspicious and of immeasurable bliss.
This is my divine, supreme station of Brahmā, radiant in the sky.
Having gone there, the immortals do not grieve, for they dwell together with Brahmā.
Because for them there is supreme vigor, supreme longevity, and supreme austerity;
supreme power, supreme righteousness, supreme knowledge, and supreme fortitude;
as well as the supreme Brahman, supreme wisdom, and supreme sovereignty. (93–94)
Therefore, there exists no being higher than Brahman;
for this Supreme One abides in the Highest, and thus he is supreme among all things.
Having become the Supreme Brahman, he perceives [reality] and not otherwise.

Thus, by being established in knowledge, one perceives everything as Brahman. (96) O Lakṣmī, for those liberated from the perishable field, there exists an eternal abiding in the imperishable abode, which yields eternal bliss. (97)
O Lakṣmī, the constant association with the virtuous bestows the world of Brahmā;
it removes all sins and likewise purifies prosperity.
It also effects the purification of the self and the purification of liberation.
It brings about the purification of knowledge and likewise the purification of worship;
it bestows the purity of liberation, is auspicious, and purifies omniscience.
It is the purifier of self-surrender and the purifier of service. (3.104.100)
It is the purifier of defects and likewise the purifier of illusion;
it is the purifier of discernment and the purifier of bonds.
Indeed, having studied this sacrificial session of nectar, the sacrificial session of Brahman, [one attains liberation].
"He becomes one whose nature is Brahman both in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt.

(102) Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation through the Divine Lakṣmī by Means of the Holy Cakrabhāsa for the Thief Naraśāya, as well as the Liberation of Former Wealthy Men and the Knowledge of the Brahma-Sacrifice," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-Santāna*, concerning the essence of the duties of householders (*gārhasthya-dharma-sāra*).

Chapter 105 [Author:
Chapter 106 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Mādhava, tell me the root of both phenomena and actions,
by depending upon which a human being attains full nourishment in virtue.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī! You are the eternal root of dharma,
shining within me as Lakṣmī does in Nārāyaṇa and Rādhikā does in Śrī Kṛṣṇa—
within me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
As Lakṣmī resides in Viṣṇu, as Kambharā resides in Gopāla,
as Durgā resides in Hari born of Sāvitrī, and as Siddhi resides in Vināyaka—
so too does a wedded wife abide [in her husband]. For she is indeed the root of dharma for embodied beings.
The married wife is the root of the ancestors, the gods, guests, one’s own kin, the household, the lineage, and the branches of the family.
Having adorned the daughter, one should give her away with water first to a worthy groom on an auspicious occasion.
A young woman of beautiful form, whose very body is the dwelling place of the bodiless god of love;
and whatever maiden is desired by a man, and whatever man is desired by her— for them, their marriage should indeed be performed with joy, for it brings about mutual welfare.
This is indeed the rule for virtuous Brahmins and those of a sattvic nature:
one who desires happiness should never, under any circumstances, seize the property of another by purchasing it at an exorbitant price or by forceful means. (8)
Indeed, everything struck by the sighs of a woman is consumed by fire.
(9) One who desires his own welfare should marry a wife who has manifested the characteristics of womanhood;
one who possesses full youth and vigor should marry a woman whose youth has blossomed and who is well-nourished. (3.105.10)
One should never cause one's own wife to be violated unless she is in her menses;
however, if she is lustful, she may be touched out of affection by nature.
If she herself approaches her husband for sexual union, there is no fault at all.
One should not marry without the consent of one's wife, lest one become fickle toward women.
A lustful man who acts according to his own whims destroys the dharma based on the household. Even if it is performed by force, an act done out of affection is considered to be like a bull (vṛṣa).
Listen, Lakṣmī: In Mahārāṣṭra there was a Kṣatriya named Jāṅgalāmukha.
He chose as his bride a beautiful girl of twelve years, who had not yet reached the state of youth and whose heart was devoted to dharma. (14)
Endowed with right discernment after her menses, she approached her husband;
desiring the fulfillment of her lawful desire, she did not act otherwise, for she was devoted to the vow of a virtuous wife.
Having first performed her religious duties, she remained ever intent upon the service of her husband.
Her husband, full of desire, sought to touch her by force for the sake of satisfying his passion; she said to him, "O beloved, dharma obstructs me.
O husband, I am not fit for this without dharma during my season. (17)
"I shall indulge in physical contact here; abandon the pursuit of sensual desire.
Though addressed thus, the lustful man, disregarding his duty as a husband, forcibly seized his wife; the virtuous woman then heaved a sigh.
From her breath, fire manifested in embodied form at that very moment;
it set ablaze the husband, the mansion, the wealth, and the household utensils.
When her husband was lost, the devoted Satī lamented in many ways.
Then Dharma himself, manifest with four arms, remembered her;
he came and said to the blameless girl, "Do not grieve.
O child, I am pleased for the sake of protecting righteousness; I am Dharma."
"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—but do not swerve from dharma, O beautiful lady!
Dharma, when protected, protects; when destroyed, it destroys as well.
Therefore, I have caused its destruction, and consequently, his destruction has occurred. (23)
"Indeed, you have been protected by him, and therefore you live free from harm.
O girl, the fire did not burn you here in my house by its power.
Choose a boon as you desire; I shall grant it to you today, do not delay."
Having heard this, the young woman named Kundadharmā then chose as her husband one who would provide for his family,
restore life to her home,
and be a master of all household requisites, endowed with righteousness and knowledge. (26)
Dharmadeva said, "So be it," and her husband was quickly restored to life.
Together with his family and all the household utensils,
and endowed with both dharma and knowledge, he rejoiced with profound devotion.
He praised the supreme duty of a wife regarding the observance of the fertile period (*ṛtu*).
Then Dharma departed after receiving worship, followed by the sacrifice of the *jāṅgala* meat.
She always observed the duties of a wife exactly as they had been prescribed.
Satī Satyavatī regained even her husband who had been consumed by fire. (3.105.30) Thus, this is the eternal boundary established by the desire of the wife;
protecting it, one generates merit, whereas otherwise it is considered a sin. (3.1)
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another rule regarding young maidens:
a maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years;
then, when the fourth year has arrived, she may seek a husband for herself.
Her offspring does not diminish, nor does her pleasure diminish.

If she behaves otherwise than this, she would be subject to public censure. Therefore, one should marry a woman who has the characteristics of a menstruating woman, and one should not guard her [in such a manner].
A man should follow this woman who is not a sapinda of his mother and who is not of the same gotra as his father; for this is the rule.
Indeed, people repeatedly request [this] even before the grasping of the hand.
The most excellent boon should be granted to him, setting aside all others. One should certainly not give it to one who is undesirable, nor to one who is inferior, nor to one who is diseased;
one should not give it to an enemy, nor to one who is loathsome, nor to one of cruel deeds.
One should certainly not give [a daughter] to one who is unrighteous, nor likewise to one who is harmful.
Indeed, a wife must never be purchased, nor should she ever be sold.
She should be given away where she is desired, adorned and free of any price.
When her husband has died, a woman may indeed give herself to whomever she desires.
If she has been abandoned by her married husband, he must give another wife to him;
and if he has been abandoned by his wife, he may marry another wife.
Even when his wife has died, he may marry another wife;
or the brother-in-law may enter [the bed of] the widow, or the brother-in-law’s wife may go to him.
If there is mutual consent between the two, this is the eternal law.
One may find a virtuous woman born of Manu who is not born of a father nor born of a mother;
having circumambulated the god Agni, a father, or a cow in every way, or else having offered a garland to one another in the presence of the elders. (42–43)
Having joined their hands or even having bowed to one another,
one should perform the marriage ceremony in the presence of the preceptor, either in the pavilion or in the temple,
without causing offense to the people, the family members, or the king.
The taking in marriage of two [persons] without causing distress to the subjects is auspicious;
that which is the public union of the two, free from conflict, is beautiful.
Here, the witness is the hearts of both; that too is the ancient dharma. (45–46)
Born in secret like a fetus, they are censured and deprived of their paternal rights;
like the lineage of slave-girls, they do not attain the status of the righteous.
Even sons born through the *niyoga* rite are regarded as belonging to the father.
The Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are the perpetuators of the lineage, and that too is the ancient Dharma.
Furthermore, the conduct of the virtuous is the weightiest characteristic of Dharma.
Commanded by her father, having chosen him for herself, she has entered into union with her husband.
She was born with virtuous conduct and is indeed considered married;
for the relationship between husband and wife is auspicious until death. This eternal dharma is common to all forms of pleasure.
The mere connection for the purpose of sexual union between a man and a woman is not religiously sanctioned.
Even in the matter of inheritance, it is indeed the son who is reckoned as the heir to the lineage;
only if there is no son does the daughter become the rightful heir to the inheritance. (51–52)
A son and a daughter are to be understood as equal heirs with respect to the division of inheritance.
Even for one who has many sons and likewise many daughters,
both the sons and the daughters shall be the authorized heirs in the division of that inheritance.
They should be given in equal shares; this is the eternal law (dharma).
Those who, having performed the marriage, send away [the daughters] without giving them their inheritance share—even while they themselves enjoy the daughter's portion—truly fall into hell.
Having sold a son or a daughter for the sake of their livelihood, those who consume that wealth are in fact consuming the flesh of those very children.
Furthermore, no other human being should be sold, much less one's own offspring.
No one shall forcibly sell a submissive maiden;
rather, with a sense of righteousness, he should bestow her upon the son-in-law together with her dowry.
Whatever may be the dowry belonging to the mother, that indeed is the portion of the maiden.
The daughter's son alone shall take the inheritance of a father who has no son;
according to the law, there is no distinction between a son and a daughter's son.
[This applies even] when there are fathers, brothers, fathers-in-law, or brothers-in-law.
Those who desire abundant auspiciousness should honor and adorn women;
women dwelling in the home should always be honored and cherished. Where charming women are satisfied, there prosperity dwells.
The *siddhis* rain down and grant all desires;
yet where women are held in contempt, there all ritual actions are fruitless.
Lineages devoid of prosperity neither shine nor flourish.
The dharma that has women as its cause is always supreme, bestowing the celestial realms and the world of truth.
The procreation of offspring, the protection of those born, the pursuit of pleasure, and the maintenance of the worldly course—all these are established upon women. (63–64)
There is indeed no sacrifice such as that, nor a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), nor a fast;
there is no other dharma equal to the affection of a couple that bestows both celestial glory and liberation.
The father protects [her] in childhood, and the husband protects her in youth.
Sons protect their aged mother; such is the ancient way women are guarded.
These women are indeed named Śrī (Prosperity); they should be honored by one who desires land.
A woman who is protected and favored shines forth as Śrī herself.
Now, O Lakṣmī, it is also agreed that a share of the inheritance should be given to a woman;
her wealth always consists of a portion equal to that of a son or a daughter.
And she is entitled to enjoy that wealth given by her husband according to her own desire.
For women, the inheritance from their husband is considered to have enjoyment as its fruit.
When one man has many wives, the Brāhmaṇī wife is in every way the most excellent.
[She should attend to] the husband’s bathing, his adornment, his cleansing of the teeth, and his application of collyrium. (3.105.70)
A Brāhmaṇī woman should perform the offering to the gods, the offering to the ancestors, the worship of the deities, and the preparation of food.
She should provide her husband with food, drink, garlands, garments, and ornaments; for she is indeed most venerable to him. (71)

Alternatively, O Brahmins, whether she be a Kṣatriya or any other woman, he should serve her in such a way that she remains favorable— through lack of hardship, through joy, through affection, and through compliant conduct. (72–73)
Having fully accepted her husband’s command, she must never act otherwise.
The purity of the womb should be recognized by those who possess innate excellence of character and form.
Indeed, offspring is the reflection of either the father or the mother.
An offspring of that same nature should be known as born of a pure lineage.
In those cases where there is a separation [of lineages], that is considered impurity of the womb. Through the mixing of the seed, deformity will manifest in the child. (75–76)
In the presence of undesirable objects, a confusion arises in the heart;
that [confusion] transfers to the seed, and its state emerges in the womb.
Therefore, the bestowal of the womb should take place in an invisible, secret, and obstacle-free location.

When sounds are stilled, when the world is stilled, when the speech of beasts and other creatures is stilled, and when all principles (tattvas) are perfectly stilled—this [rite] should be performed, and not otherwise.
She will be born of a pure lineage; of this there is no doubt. (78–79)
The refutation of the nature of other sounds, touches, forms, and tastes proceeds from the sowing of the seed and even from the sight of the image.
Therefore, at that time, it is held that the husband’s face alone is visible; nothing else is visible. (3.105.80)
One should possess a serene heart, and not harbor anger or resentment;
one should not be stained by impurity, but be suffused with fragrance. One should maintain a tranquil mind and abide in the quality of goodness (sattva).
The giver and the nurse must cultivate [this thought] with one-pointed mind in every way;
that lineage alone shall be pure, and nothing else should be remembered at that time.
Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, higher than the highest.
Indeed, at the time of the sowing of seed, the husband and wife alone are to be remembered, and no one else;
for the dispositions and inherent natures proceed according to the qualities of that which is remembered.
Therefore, the husband is the supreme deity, the God of gods, Janārdana.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate an auspicious ancient tale:
when Pulastya, the son of Brahmā, gave his seasonal gift,
then Pulastya’s wife Prīti remembered a Rākṣasa.
From that [Nirṛti], Rāvaṇa was born, and from him the Rakṣasa-dharma arose.
When he (Rāvaṇa) remembered Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, during his period of distress,
a son named Vibhīṣaṇa was born, permeated by that same disposition and devoted to Him.
In the past, Pārvatī and Śaṅkara remembered their son, the commander-in-chief, who was endowed with strength, the destroyer of the Daityas, and the bestower of victory.
By that [act of remembrance], Skanda became the leader of the Gaṇas for the purpose of destroying obstacles.

Vairāja, having recollected the three qualities (guṇas), indeed brought forth the triad known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; their birth was according to his recollection. [This applies] to cooked rice, fruit, a gift, a seed, and even a word of blessing.
Whatever kind of remembrance arises, such indeed is the offspring that is born.
Whatever the nature of one's contemplation and devotion may be, the fruit is permeated by that very state of being.
[This applies] toward the wish-fulfilling tree, the form of Hari, the guru, the husband, the wife, and the virtuous man.
As is one's disposition toward medicine, mantras, and asceticism, so is the fruit [obtained].
(93) In learning, exertion, battle, agriculture, the management of servants, the attainment of worldly prosperity, and in speed, the fruit is exactly according to the effort applied. (94)
As grace is bestowed upon a virtuous king, Hari, one's parents, a guild-leader, a master, a god, or a father when they are well-pleased, so too is the fruit [obtained].
[Likewise, it is obtained] from an enemy, a restrainer, a serpent, a Brahmin, an armed man, or an ascetic. 95.
In quarreling, obstructing, and destroying, the fruit is exactly as the anger was.
In devotion, yoga, prayer, service, divine rites, sacred scripture, enjoyment, and long-term undertakings, the fruit is exactly as the tranquility was. (96–97)
In matters of duty, in battle, in giving, in speech, in removing obstacles, in theft, in liberation, and regarding place and time— the fruit is exactly according to the swiftness [of action].
In poetry, in logic, in instruction, in a command, and at the final moment [the same applies].
In dissolution, in times of adversity, at the commencement, and according to what has been studied, there is the fruit.

Indeed, in a field, in heaven, in a woman, in a disciple, in a son, in an undertaking, and in the acquisition [of wealth], as well as in a mantra, in a scripture, and in composition—just as the seed is, so is the fruit. (3.105.100)
In fame, in devotion, in virtue, in lineage, in happiness, in toil, in food, in the treasury,
in guests, in the home, and in heaven— just as one has a wife, so one reaps the fruit. Therefore, O Lakṣmī, a wife who is ever devoted to her husband [is the source of such results].
For indeed, in every respect, it is the root of all phenomena.
(102) The four aims of human life, their means, and the instruments of accomplishment—all activities proceed and reach fulfillment through one's own wife. (103)
A wife is indeed the field for all dharmas, the garden for the attainment of sons, the wish-fulfilling creeper of happiness, and the root-herb of existence.
She is the stable for the horses of the mind and the refuge for the birds of the vital breaths.
She is the boat for those wandering in saṃsāra and likewise the vehicle for those destined for heaven.
In sacrifice, lineage, happiness, suffering, merit, great festivals, at home, in duty, and in wealth, she is renowned as the true half of one's own self. (105–106)
"O Lakṣmī, through recitation, hearing, and likewise by taking refuge in Dharma, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall accrue in every way to both the woman and the man.

(107) Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Root of All Religious Acts and Duties as Being the Married Wife; the Marvelous Account of Saradharmā, the Wife of Kundadharma, the Kṣatriya Jāṅghala; and the Qualifications for Giving a Daughter in Marriage, the Qualifications of a Bridegroom, the Right to Inherit Property, the Purity of Seed, and so forth," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
