→ Chapter 107
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Just as a wife is so regarded, a son is considered by his father to be the very refuge of dharma.
The father exists in the form of the son, and the father’s dharma is established in the son. (1)
Whether he is born in secret or openly, a son is proclaimed to be his father's own.
Nobility, a virtuous character, gentleness, perseverance, devotion,
and discernment— these qualities reveal a son to be excellent.
Lack of nobility, improper conduct, cruelty, and an inactive nature;
lack of devotion and lack of discernment—these indeed manifest impurity.
One inherits the character of the father, or that of the mother, or both. (3–4)
One born from a pure womb indeed does not incur the state of social confusion;
yet even one who is senior in age, if deficient in character, does not deserve honor.
Even a Śūdra, if rich in virtue and of good conduct, is honored by people.
In this context, one should proclaim oneself alone by means of one's conduct, behavior, and deeds.
(6) One's own legitimate son is said to be one's very self; he is the father himself. However, a son begotten through the rite of *niyoga* on one's own wife is the second [kind of son]. (7)
The third is one born in secret from his own wife without formal authorization;
the fourth is one born of a wife who was already pregnant at the time of her marriage.
The fifth is one given by someone at birth and subsequently raised [by the adoptive father].
The sixth is also one who was taken as a son of adoption during youth;
the seventh is one who arrived in the form of a disciple; the eighth is said to be one who was purchased; and the ninth son is one born of an unmarried woman. (3.106.10)

The tenth is said to be the son born of the mind (mānasa), who was abandoned on the road immediately after birth and taken up; he is known as the adopted son (kṛtrima). The eleventh is to be understood as such, and the daughter's son (dauhitra) is remembered as the twelfth.
Likewise, the daughters born of the lineage should also be understood as being of twelve kinds.
Indeed, their sacramental rites (saṃskāras) occur according to the status of the self [the father] and the status of the owner [the husband].
For the son of an unmarried woman (kānīnaka), born of an unwed mother, attains the caste of his mother.

The offspring of courtesans are indeed to be understood as having the same caste as their mothers; likewise, the offspring of slave-girls who are without husbands are to be understood as having the same caste as their mothers, or alternatively,
the same caste as their masters.
For those children who are to be obtained through the initiation of mendicancy belong to the lineage of Acyuta.
All virtuous women and virtuous men become members of the lineage of Acyuta;
indeed, the sons and daughters of Nārāyaṇa are the classes of renunciants.

"O Lotus-born one, such is indeed the established order in this world on the surface of the earth; however, in other worlds, it proceeds according to one's will, and this same [order] also functions there.
O Lakṣmī, wives are generally found to be of four kinds."
The wife is said to be the one who has been married; the female slave is she who has come along with [the husband].
She who stays in the house for some time as a student (upakurvāṇikā) and has entered into secret yoga is celebrated as the protected woman (rakṣitā). || 18–19 ||
O Lotus-born one! Listen: the husbands of women also exist in four ways.
The husband who has been married is called the primary husband; he alone is the most excellent. The second is proclaimed to be the secondary lover, such as a brother-in-law (devara) and others.
The third is the *niyogamāpta*, who is the *upakurvāṇaka* (the student);
for he is one who has entered into a secret union and is thus proclaimed as "protected.
Their offspring, according to the circumstances, belongs either to the woman or to the man.
In this dispute, the offspring alone belongs to him whomsoever one might desire;
for due to differences of place, differences of time, and differences of custom, there are various opinions.
How can it not be considered that a daughter given away is of the nature of a gift?
That [object] is conceptualized as having the form of an object of enjoyment; therefore, the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) is indeed the cause.
Whatever the nature of the impression in a given case, such is the subsequent worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*);
whether it be after having enjoyed [the object] and then abandoned it out of anger, or likewise out of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Even through renunciation and discernment, she is indeed abandoned, for she is like a mother.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī! the flow of great illusion (mahāmāyā) consists of melodic modulations (mūrchanā);
it constantly leads embodied beings into various modulations. 26.
In whatever manner a current exists at a particular time, place, and age,
dharma fashioned according to that method shall be the giver of happiness and peace.
The ways of the gods are one thing, and those of the yogis are another.
The various customs of human beings, as well as those of animals and other creatures,
are indeed dharma provided they do not lead to harm;
a path that brings about harm is never considered to be the essence of dharma.

There is no dharma that brings suffering; dharma is in every way the bestower of happiness. Wealth is pursued when attended by dharma, while it becomes a source of misfortune when joined with adharma.
Pleasure is desirable when accompanied by dharma and wealth; devoid of these, it is not a human goal.
He who has reached the further shore of dharma, artha, and kāma attains the Imperishable;
whereas the unrighteous man, seeking worldly gain and attached to sense-objects, undergoes the torments of Yama.
Even the regulation of family life and other such matters is ultimately directed toward the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).
A style of expression devoid of the goals of human life is bestial, not human.
(33) Indeed, the scripture, which is the law of instruction, applies to humans and the like; it certainly does not apply to those of animal birth, for they are indeed destitute of knowledge. (34)
Force, habit, and delusion are the bonds of animals;
upon these depend the beasts, the aquatic creatures, and those born as insects.
Thus, for those who remain in this state, there is no end to existence.
By chance, through association with the virtuous, one may sometimes reach the further shore of existence.
For the self cannot be slain; therefore, one should practice deliverance.
One should cultivate the sight of the saintly through affection, and their company through service.
A person should serve a saintly being who has initiated the practice of dwelling in Brahman—
one who, having destroyed pride, grief, anger, joy, and latent desires,
is a vessel of confidence for all beings, pure, and whose deity is Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (38)
Established in the supreme state of Brahman, tranquil, and pleasing to behold for all;
having brought all worldly undertakings to an end, steadfast in meditation, with senses under control;
proficient in the knowledge of Brahman, possessing equal vision toward all, and supremely compassionate. (3.106.40)
One should likewise seek refuge in and pray to such virtuous people:
"O Teacher of the World, wash away the sin committed through ignorance!
O Teacher of the World, show me the staircase to the path of liberation!"
"O Teacher of the World, having burnt away the knot of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), purify your own people.
O Teacher of the World, manifesting supreme devotion, grant us liberation!
One should indeed offer such a prayer, so that [the Lord] may bestow his grace accordingly. (42–43)
And I must say before the virtuous again and again, "I am yours.
Whatever command you may give, I shall perform it all, however difficult it may be.
Whether it be a kingdom, wealth, cattle, or my own home— [I am yours].
"Tell me of sacrifice, charity, a son, or a garden; I shall give you everything.
Thus one should request the virtuous man and satisfy him with offerings.
One should offer everything without hesitation; indeed, such a person shall become a partaker of liberation.
Illusion is said to be doubt; there is no doubt regarding Brahman.

If there is doubt concerning the company of the virtuous, their service, their speech, or their actions—when will there be liberation? When will there be purity? And how can service be performed here?
When, indeed, will there be here the firm abiding in one’s own pure nature?
Therefore, having become free from doubt, one should serve an excellent holy person—one capable of washing away sins, the giver of liberation, and whose conduct is divine. (48–49)

One should always serve my form— contented, a treasury of knowledge, the support of Brahman, without external dependence, without any prop, yet my own support. Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you of the supreme fruit of serving the virtuous.
Because of him, there was the liberation of masters, cattle, birds, kinsmen, and friends.
(51) In the land of Karṇāṭaka, there was a devoted ascetic sage named Śambhalavāra, who by birth was born of the Sūta caste. (52)
He indeed took up residence alone on the bank of a river;
though young, he remained without a woman, having no desire for the enjoyment of love.
Having performed supreme and excellent penance, he enjoyed pleasures in accordance with righteousness.
"Then I shall go to heaven, the eternal and supreme state.
Having reflected thus, he departed from his home to undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords.
He arrived at a beautiful, elevated, and auspicious spot on the bank of the Godāvarī.
Then, having observed a favorable terrain for performing austerities on Mount Ucchraya, he established his own residence in the village named Satrāśaya;
honored by the people with food and other offerings, he set his mind upon [his practice]. (56)
Then, after that, the ascetic sat amidst five fires for six months;
thereafter, he stood on one foot for the duration of a year.
Worshipping Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, he performed supreme penance.
At the end of the year, having bound his own feet to a branch of a banyan tree with a creeper, he hung there for a full year with his head downward.
Having performed penance in this manner, at the end of that year, [he placed] his head upon the ground.
Standing on his tiptoes, he performed severe austerities.
At the end of a year, with his hands raised and his body reduced to the size of a thumb,
he performed severe austerities, gazing at the sun without blinking.
After that, he remained within the waters of a river for six months;
then, in the fifth year, Viṣṇu,
assuming the form of a fish marked with the discus, arrived and devoured the skin of that sage.
He ate the flesh, yet the sage did not tremble.
Then Viṣṇu, by means of the fish’s voice, said to him: "You dwell here in the water;
who are you? How do you remain here? Tell me, what is your purpose here? (63–64)
Having heard that, the merchant of Śambhalapura spoke to Matsya of auspicious intent:
"I shall perform austerities for the sake of happiness, since happiness is the fruit of dharma.
[For] kingdom, home, wealth, wives, sons, daughters, and cows—"
Through austerity, male and female servants as well as vehicles are always obtained.
Through the practice of the householder’s life, virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation are attained.
Having become a householder, I shall perform austerity and proceed to the supreme state.
Thus addressed, the fish replied: "Do you still have a latent desire for worldly enjoyments?
Perform penance and enjoy the fruit thereof in the supreme state of liberation.
Indeed, enjoyments are impermanent, they bring suffering, and are of the nature of bondage. (68)
"Abandoning those, go to the eternal abode of Nārāyaṇa.
Having heard this, Śambhalavāra then spoke again to the fish:
"Just as you, O Fish, are wise even while remaining amidst sense-objects..."
Even having known this, one does not turn back from enjoying sense objects;
rather, having enjoyed various objects and attained complete satisfaction,
one should bring about the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and then proceed to the supreme state.
Thus, this path is easy to follow; any other is fraught with doubt.
There is no progress for one who possesses passion; therefore, one should pacify that passion.
Consequently, having propitiated Viṣṇu and gratified Mādhava through austerity, I—
"Having enjoyed these pleasures and having ruled over them, I shall go to that state through devotion.
Hearing this, the Fish then said: "Behold my sovereign form!
I am pleased with your austerity; I am Nārāyaṇa, and I have come here."
"Choose whatever you desire; I shall grant it to you entirely and for all time.
(75) The sage chose wealth, a kingdom, women, sons, cattle, daughters, elephants, horses, bulls, cows, and the four aims of human existence. (76)
"So be it," Hari said, and having granted the boon, he vanished.
Then Śambhalavāra also emerged from the water,
reciting the garland of names of Nārāyaṇa, indeed of Hari.

And he dwelt on the delightful bank of the river, on its elevated portion. (78) Then a village named Satrāśaya, inhabited by ten thousand people, was completely surrounded on all sides by the floods of the river during the rainy season. (79)
The king also became submerged in the water and met his death;
many other people as well— men, women, and subjects—
five thousand in number, went to their destruction by the flood of water.
Then others went to another region for the purpose of dwelling there.
A thousand men lived there, sustained by fortitude;
they were all devotees, ascetics, and solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
Then Śambhalavāra also became a supreme and auspicious vessel of honor; for he was an ascetic residing there among the inhabitants of that village,
and thus he ruled the kingdom of the village, being honored by the subjects.
Thus the king became honored there by a thousand men;
the subjects of the village gave him twenty-one maidens,
as well as cows, livestock, male servants, female servants, and the local people.
From that, goats, sheep, horses, and bulls all became his;
thus, through his austerity, he obtained a kingdom, enjoyments, women, sons, and so forth, as well as devotion to Nārāyaṇa and the service of the virtuous. (86)
Through devotion to him, the subjects, who were upholders of dharma, flourished once again.
The citizens became ten thousand in number and more;
all of them were indeed made Vaiṣṇavas by this sage.
He performed the chanting of the names and the worship of Śrī Hari as was appropriate, and he also had a temple constructed. Thousands of saintly persons (sādhus) resided constantly in his house.
And he caused ninefold devotion to be practiced constantly in his excellent palace. (3.106.90) Then, when some time had passed, the discerning king spoke to his subjects:
"By fate, my hundred and five sons and likewise my wives remain here. (91)
I have twenty-one daughters and two hundred more;
I possess thousands of cows, as well as bulls and horses;
I also have parrots, mainas, elephants, and dogs.
In this world, you subjects have become masters while you yourselves were once slaves;
thus, dharma has been fulfilled, as well as artha and kāma, and now liberation is in sight.
Therefore, I desire to immediately bestow my kingdom upon my son.
"Then I shall go to the supreme, imperishable state of Nārāyaṇa, which belongs to the Eldest.
"So be it for our progeny," they said, and they spoke another auspicious word:
"We all shall go together to that highest state."
Having established each of his sons in their respective duties according to their authority,
and having deliberated thus, that king attained union in meditative absorption;
entrusting everything to his son, he fixed his resolve upon liberation.
Then all the queens and all the subjects, having joined their senses and vital breaths to Śrī Hari at that place, remained absorbed in their own selves;
they were worshipping Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, their beloved Master and Lord. || 97–98 ||
Then Viṣṇu indeed arrived there with his attendants in celestial chariots,
illuminating all directions and making the quarters of the sky resound with their thundering.
He said to that devotee Śambhala, "Come onto the chariot."
Having bowed to and worshipped that Blessed One, the Lord of Śambhalavāra said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, please lead away all those subjects who are eager and ready to come here for the sake of liberation."
Cows, horses, bulls, goats, sheep, cattle, parrots, and so forth— likewise, whatever others there may be here, purified by your grace;
my sons and daughters, the queens, and the members of my household.
"Lead whoever are ready here to your own abode.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, fulfill this desire of mine; show me your grace.
Hari said, "So be it; out of devotion for you, I shall do so."
Your sons are of different castes, born of women of different classes:
some are Brāhmaṇas, others Kṣatriyas, others Vaiśyas, and others Śūdras. These sons and followers are the offspring of queens of various castes.

"Let the male servants, the male attendants, the female servants, and whoever else follows the path of devotion, ascend my celestial chariot; I shall lead them to my own abode. Having been addressed thus, all those who were seekers of liberation ascended. (106–107)
Then, by the grace of Śrī Hari, all those nine thousand animals and birds ascended that celestial chariot;
having assumed divine bodies, they became four-armed beings and mounted that vimāna.
Then all the women, including Kamalā, became four-armed Śarvas. All the subjects, radiant with divine splendor, ascended the celestial chariot,
each leaving behind one son as the seed of their lineage, according to their respective status.
All the subjects, as well as the king together with his royal family,
all went by means of a celestial chariot to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme abode.
Thus indeed was the virtuous Śambhalavāra, even while remaining at home.
The ascetic, too, having enjoyed the pleasures of the earth and having worshipped Keśava,
went to the supreme abode through devotion, taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa;
he was the husband of wives of different castes and was accompanied by his sons and others.
Thus, through association with the virtuous, the family shall rejoice in every way!
It attains the supreme abode; indeed, there is no distinction between the worthy and the unworthy.
By reading and hearing this, one becomes detached from worldly enjoyments.
Having attained worldly enjoyment through devotion, one shall attain liberation from Hari by force.
Through virtuous conduct, one may go to liberation; such conduct leads thousands to liberation, just as that Śambhalavāra, along with his subjects, attained liberation by it.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Sons, Various Wives, and Various Lords in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Lineage; Liberation through the Yoga of the Holy; and the Liberation of a Descendant of the Sūta caste, Śambhalavāra, a devotee of the Holy, who—after attaining a kingdom, sons, cattle, birds, and other blessings through devotion and austerity—was liberated along with his progeny," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 107: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Dvāpara Yuga Lineage).
Chapter 107.
[The Author: Chapter 108.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the wonder of the virtuous yogi Śrīcihna.
I shall now describe to you, O inhabitants of Saurāṣṭra, [this practice] which bestows both prosperity and liberation.
There was a virtuous man, my devotee, residing in the city of Kīśādana;
he was perfected in the yoga of the Śrīcihna-yogin, possessed of divine deeds, and established in meditative absorption (samādhi).
He worshipped me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa; I exist sometimes in an invisible form and sometimes in a visible one. At times I dwell in water, in a forest, in a tree, or on a mountain.
In rain, in heat, sometimes on the shore of the ocean, at Lake Aśvasaras;
sometimes in fire, in wind, and sometimes entering into a deep cave—even though he is so capable, he worships me incessantly. (4–5)
"O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Parameśvara,
O Lord of Akṣara, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Śrī Puruṣottama!"—
thus he constantly chants my name and worships me again and again.
He constantly wears a garland with the name Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
he performs my bathing, meditation, and worship perpetually.
Indeed, within his mental heart, he always beholds me in embodied form.
Thousands and hundreds of thousands of men worship him;
whatever they imagine regarding him, who is like the wish-fulfilling tree,
all that bears fruit for them by the mere act of imagining it in his presence.
There was no need for blessings, nor any need for service.
Once, such a saint, wearing only a loincloth, arrived by chance before King Devānīka. (3.107.10–11)
The King of Saurāṣṭra, having recognized him as a saint, bowed to and honored him;
having offered a welcome and a seat, he then presented the *madhuparka*.
Having received the water that was nectar for his feet, the king, together with his family, drank it.
The queen Sahajāśrī was the wife of King Kalyāṇadevānīka.
He gave him sweet food, fruit, water, and ghee;
the sage accepted it with devotion, drank the water, and was satisfied.
The king, having honored the sage in many ways, spoke to him again:
"O Blessed One, we are at your disposal; tell us, what shall we do?
Whether it be the kingdom, or wealth, or cattle, or a beautiful woman."
“Tell me what you desire—a vehicle, a daughter, a son, or a palace—I shall give it all to you.
This house, this kingdom, and this seat of dharma are yours; O King, you are the ruler, govern the earth, for I am now subject to you. (16–17)
Having heard him, the yogi Śrīcihna said to that royal devotee, the brahmin:
"O King, I do not desire sovereignty; O King, I desire neither wealth nor a beautiful woman.
I do not desire cattle, drink, a daughter, a palace, or even a son, O King."
"But I have taken a vow, and I must fulfill it;
therefore, I shall serve you two without hesitation.
Hearing this, the king was delighted and said to that sage, "So be it."
He led him into the interior of the house and showed him what was beautiful to behold:
"This is the bedchamber of the Blessed One; please stay here as you wish.
Let this palace and these enjoyments—the fruits of your own prosperity—be used."
"Perform your vow perfectly; accept everything for the sake of fulfillment. What food, what water, or what else do you require?
I shall strive to bring you joy; what may I provide?"

Having heard that the food was excellent and as it had been prepared, the sage said, "Serve me milk-rice and other delicacies. The king brought these forth. After eating and drinking water, the Lord of Sages, whose speech bore the marks of prosperity, spoke.
"I wish to sleep upon my bed; I am not to be awakened by any means whatsoever.
My feet must be massaged for me, and you must remain awake throughout the night.
Having spoken thus, he fell asleep for seventy-one days.
Then the two queens and the king, intent on service, remained without food; thereafter the virtuous one, established in his vow, arose and said:
"At this moment, an oil massage is pleasing to me."
The queen and the king performed an anointing with oil rich in fragrance (28).
They caused him to bathe, adorned him likewise,
and also fed the virtuous man sweet foods (29).
All kinds of sweet dishes, *laḍḍukas* of every variety,
special preparations of minced meat (*veśavāra*), *polikās*, *pūrikās*, and so forth;
various types of savory foods and diverse kinds of vegetables.
Liquids of all kinds, roasted grains, and likewise parched kernels;
alkaline substances, sour condiments, sweet powders, and various fruits; delightful fermented gruels, and all manner of foods fit for a king. ||31-32||
There they both fed him, and the great seer ate with pleasure.
He said to the auspicious king and queen, "Carry me to the forest.
Placing him upon his shoulder in a palanquin, the king and queen were filled with joy.
Having placed that sage upon a magnificent litter adorned with gold, silver, and other precious materials,
his two servants— whose minds were serene and who remained free from agitation— carried him through the city, to the edge of the city, and likewise into the forest. (34–35)
The serene yogi, marked with the signs of Śrī, descended from the palanquin.
Having released those two excellent boons, he said to them, "Speak, I shall grant them.
And they, pierced in their feet as well as their shoulders, were delicate.
The King of Yogis touched them with his two hands, which were like nectar;
both became perfectly formed and free from fatigue, like two divine deities. They appeared in a new form and likewise possessed fresh youth. (37–38)
The sage said to them: "You two may go to your own city, Kīśādana;
I shall dwell here in the forest and observe my vow.
Whatever you both desire, all that shall indeed come to pass."
When this was said, the king and queen spoke to that lord of sages:
"O lord of sages, if any offenses have occurred during our service,
all of these must be forgiven by you, whose great soul is an ocean of compassion."
"O Sage, we always desire your affection and grace.
Śrīcihnayogī replied while they were beholding his divine form:
"I am pleased; I am Hari; I am he whose heart is marked by Śrī."
"May my name be Śrīvatsavakṣas; may I become the Lord of Lakṣmī.
Having assumed a virtuous form, I have come here to your house by the power of compassion.
My incarnation is always for the sake of the welfare of my devotees. (43–44)
Therefore, I move about as a virtuous one, indeed Janārdana with a divine body.
O Devānīka! I am pleased and I delight in Sahajāśrī.
Choose excellent boons that you desire; I grant the fruit of service.
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, Devānīka then bowed to him;
having worshipped the Supreme Self and considering it his own good fortune,
he then spoke to me, the Blessed One, with words full of affection.
O Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, through your arrival, everything has been attained by me; together with my wife, I have crossed over much by means of complete service.
O Hari Kṛṣṇa, since you are pleased, my lineage has been protected and delivered.
"This is my favor there, as well as the fruit of my life's service;
this is the fruit of this kingdom and also the fruit of my devotion.
Moreover, you appear pleased; dispel my doubt. (3.107.50)
"What is his vow, what is it like, and for what reason has all this been performed?
Having heard this, Śrīcihnayogī spoke to Devānīka:
"Listen, O devotee, to everything that I have determined for myself."
"I shall be born in your lineage as the Lord who is dear to his devotees (Bhaktavallabha).
Having come here for the sake of purifying you and your queen,
I shall indeed descend into that purifying lineage of devotees."
My form in the guise of a saintly being indeed purifies human beings;
having first purified you, the seed, by means of that saintly form,
thereafter [I shall manifest] Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is truly Śrī-Kṛṣṇa himself.
"I am the glorious Gopālabāla, Hari, the son of Śrī Kambharā.
I have come here in every way for the sole purpose of bestowing the fruit of service and making you perform that service. (55–56)
Indeed, you have performed for me the service of a woman as described:
massaging my feet, bathing me, providing food, and carrying my palanquin.
Since all this was accomplished for me by you, your descendants shall indeed remain here.
Likewise, in the hereafter, all shall be endowed with happiness.
You too, at the end of time, shall go to Goloka;
together with your wife, you shall attain the great bliss of my own abode.
The Brahminhood of you, a Brahmin devoted to his wife, endures;
under your control, the sovereignty of royal fortune is once again Brahminhood.
By my dwelling here, your Brahminhood shall certainly be eternal.
The state of being most devoted to Brahman, the status of a great seer, asceticism, and saintliness;
liberation, divinity, and also the dark complexion, the bestowing of liberation;
the state of being worshipful by all, and likewise the ocean of all jewels. (61–62)
A mine of all good fortune, as well as abundance of all sovereignty,
and a constant refuge for the prosperity of Śrī Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Bhūti—
all this shall come to pass in my family through my dwelling. (63)
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One gave me a golden necklace, as well as a garland of jewels, and bestowed the supreme mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine namaḥ. (64–65)
Having thus given the inexhaustible vessel and having given the Sudarśana discus,
I vanished from sight; Devānīka went home [to see] the golden-colored,
magnificent palaces and the golden rampart.
Having seen his own abode surrounded by pleasure gardens and filled with celestial nymphs,
likewise adorned with a divine chariot,
and possessing hosts of divine male and female servants marked with the conch, the discus, and other signs; ||67-68||
On all sides were wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu), Gaurīs, Lakṣmīs, and maidens;
subjects equal to those of Vaikuṇṭha, and elephants with eight tusks;
white horses with black ears, and white swans as birds.
The celestial host rejoiced in chariots that traveled through the sky with the splendor of the multitude of suns and moons,
and in the attendants who were forms of Viṣṇu. [They also rejoiced in] the sacrificial pits, the pavilions, the great ṛṣis, and the assembly of virtuous men.
The king of devotees beheld hundreds of thousands of saintly persons and all the gods;
he also saw the river of gold flowing alongside.
O Lakṣmī, by the grace of Śrī Hari, the host of gods likewise became present.
Like Mahendra, the king was a self-ruling sovereign; like Ramā, the queen was his consort.
Through my grace and yoga, an imperishable abode was born.
That city, Kīśādana, became Śrīśāyana.
The host of gods went toward that great wonder and toward me, the Lord;
remembering my form as a holy being, they worshipped me with supreme love.
Then, after some time had passed, I, who am affectionate toward my devotees, was born.
The Lord Śrī Puruṣottama is the master of millions of billions of lotus-wives.
Thus, through repeated association with a saintly person and likewise with Hari, the entire family of a servant indeed becomes the family of Hari. (76–77)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"You are the beloved, you are the lord of all, the Supreme Lord, Hari himself.
For you, the illustrious Hari, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, there is no lineage, for you are beyond all lineages. (78)
"Nevertheless, in the world of human beings, lineage-based tradition proceeds;
therefore, O Kṛṣṇa, I desire to have that explained.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī: in ancient times, before creation, I was Nārāyaṇa.
From my limbs arose Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the gods, and the rest.
And at the beginning of that creation, there was Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.
From Mukhapiṇḍa was born a Brāhmaṇa named Śrīpatnīvrata.
His wife was known as Pativratā, and they formed a couple whose lifespan was equal to that of Parameṣṭhin, and who were indeed of the nature of the form of Vṛṣa.
O Lakṣmī, understand from me this first one, known as Pūrvapitāmaha.
The son of Patnīvrata was indeed Brahmavrata, born of his mind;
and his wife, Śīlavratā, was likewise born of his mind.
Both of them possessed a lifespan equal to that of Parameṣṭhin and were born from ten million cosmic manifestations (vyūha).
They both became Vāsudeva and Vāsudevī.
Even their disciples numbered in the hundreds of thousands, [all] yogins who were self-luminous.
And they were gazed upon from every direction in Saurāṣṭra.
There was a Brahmin, a lord of the earth, the son of Brahmavrata,
named Kalyāṇadevānīka, the master of Kīśādāna.
And he became a couple with his wife, named Sahajāśrī.
They both possessed a lifespan equal to half the duration of Brahmā’s life.
He was Bhūmānārāyaṇa, who was joined by the earthly Śrī.

Indeed, by my command, these two have manifested here within this universe. By me, existing in the form of Śrīcihnayogī, a blessing was bestowed upon them for the sake of their manifestation in my lineage. (89)
Then the son of Kalyāṇadevānīka was also Mānasa;
he was the soul of the crest-jewel of Kṛṣṇa, honored by the king of Ānarta, named Picudevānīka, and possessed the very form of Nārāyaṇa. (3.107.90–91)
There was a son of Miṣṭādevī here by Mukuta-kalyā;
these two had a lifespan equal to the first half of Brahmā's age.
Mahāviṣṇu himself, the Lord, was the son of Picu and Devānīka.
The illustrious one named Gopālakṛṣṇa indeed had a lifespan of ten kalpas.
He was accompanied by the goddess Mahālakṣmī, known as Kaṃbharāśrī;
they both arrived for the sake of King Khaṭvāṅgada and to grant him a boon.
Considering these two to be my parents, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa became my mental son, Śrī Puruṣottama;
I am the Lord and Master of millions of billions of consorts and devotees.

O Śrī, Queen of Śiva! I am the Lord of syllables, the illustrious Lord who descends as an incarnation, higher than the highest; I am Kṛṣṇa Mādhava, your beloved. I am his father, his father’s father, and likewise his father’s father. (96–97)
His father, his grandfather, and their fathers—these ancestors are all Nārāyaṇas, portions of Nārāyaṇa, and identical in nature to me.
Likewise, all the mothers are Nārāyaṇīs; they are indeed of my own essence.
O Lakṣmī, what is the use of saying more? You know this in every way:
having become the soul of all, I manifest that divine play.
From hearing or reciting [this account] of the lineage, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained. (3.107.100)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Examination of the Service of the Devotee Kalyāṇadevānīka and the Instruction on the Lineage of Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

The water-shed, the drink, the tawny one, the yellow-eyed, the singer, Gaya,
the dancer, the actor, the master of illusion, the counselor, the lute-player, the one who has conquered his senses,
the wish-fulfilling gem, the one of great heroism, the great passion, and the foremost Person.
The virtuous person, the woman-folk, the imperishable one, and the group consisting of daughters-in-law;
the infant at the breast, the Sādhya deity, the son of Dharma, and the son of Vṛṣa;
the upholder of truth, the marvel, the utterance of Svāhā, and the diligent performer of rites.
The nightly lamp-offering, the consecration, the crown, the necklace, and the beloved sindūraka;
vermilion, saffron, dūrvā grass, rice, barley, sesame,
the betel leaf, the sugarcane stalk, and the bilva fruit— these increase devotion.
He is the very essence of the betel nut, fragrant, the abode of supreme well-being;
he is composed of glory, his attire is fashioned by Śrī, he is the limb of Śrī, and the bestower of the bliss of Śrī.
He is the tilaka of Śrī, his vast form is created by Śrī, he reclines upon Śrī, and he is the refuge of the stories of Śrī. (86–87)
He is the service of Śrī, the assembly of Śrī, the food of Śrī, and possessed of the meditative absorption of Śrī;
he is marked by Lakṣmī, the source of Mahālakṣmī, and the creator of prosperity;
he has Lakṣmī at his side, the womb of Mahālakṣmī, and the earth (Dharā) as his lower lip.
He is the knower of Brahman, the one for whom Brahman is supreme, the reciter of Brahman, free from debt, and a jewel (89).
He is the guest, the full moon, the path of the gods, and he who moves through the sky;
he is the teacher of the world, the Lord of Victory, the beloved of Lalitā, and the solitary one (3.108.90).
Praise, recitation, stability, steadfastness, existence, prosperity, the possessor of power,
joy— the fivefold witness, the essence, affection, the one with perfect attainment;
the one clad in saffron robes, the radiant soul, the ascetic of the five fires, the mountain.
Nāga, Nirāśa, Naptṛ, Kāmaphala, Kumāraka;
Svastika, Pratibhārūpa, Pratijñātmā, Pramāpaka;
Sahaja, Svabhāva, Śaṅku, Kuśa, Śālaśila, and Śiva. (92–93)
The Caitya, the Garta, the Huṃkāra, the Jaghana, the Vīthi, the Ajvara; the Udgītha, the Upaniṣad, the Purāṇapuruṣa, and the Śanī;
the Satpara, the Sannivāsa, the Śrīdruma, and the Asuranāśaka.
The key, the self, the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), the lake of Brahmā (*brahmahrada*), and the great pole (*mahādhruva*);

the circumference, the ray, the hair, the five-crested one (*pañcaśikha*), and the supreme seat (*parāsana*); the *pravargya* rite, the great means (*mahopāya*), the distinguished one, the coral-colored one (*vidruma*), and the subduer (*vaśa*). ||95–96||
Modaka, taṇḍula, apāmārga, devādhidaivata,
devānīkatilaka, mahāśvapaṭṭasārasa, jāmātṛ, dharmavṛddha, saṃkalpa, and madhuparkaka. (97)
Sarvatobhadrarūpa, Pīṭha, Vedī, Bali,
Jala, Sthaṇḍila, Maṇikṣetreśa, Pādmakṣetramaheśvara, Lomaśānandada, and Patnīvratavaṃśaprabhākara. (98–99)
The protector of Indradyumna’s site, the Lord of the Narasiṃha forest,
the dweller in the tiger-forest, the bestower of desired boons upon Rukmāṅgada;
the radiant light of Prabhāsa and the nourisher of the sacred field of Soma.
The lord of the night-lotus of the Sāman, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati);
Vāsanta, Kiśora, Mahendra, Śampada, and Sahas;
Maṅgaleśa, Manaseśa, Reveśa, and Virajāpati. (101–102)
Ratīśa, Gomatīśa, the incomparable Kāmadugheśvara,
Ekādaśīpati, Svarṇarekhākānta, and indeed Amūrtaka; Nandinīśa, Doleśa, Puṣpa, and Kalāvatīpati.
Badarīśa, Pampeśa, Darpahā, Bāndhava, Dhava;
Bhaktavatsala, Unnetā, Mānakṛt, Lokadhṛk, Dhara;
Dhanya, Caturbhuja, Durga, Tantukṛt, Sukṛta, Kṛtī. (104–105)
Sundara, Aśvamedha, Parjanya, Amṛtāpati, Sulabha, Adurlabha, Aśvattha, Rakṣohā, Daityanāśana,
Saptāśva, Saptajihva, Prāgvaṃśa, and Prabhātaka.
He is the hermitage and self-restraint; he has the sun and moon as his eyes and possesses three eyes.
He has the sky as his navel, the earth as his feet, the wind as his breath, and the quarters as his ears; he dwells in heaven.
He has another as his mouth, the ocean as his bladder, and the entire universe as his body; he is the essence, yet he is beyond all objects of desire.
He is dark as a rain cloud, beneficial, truthful, the abode of Brahman, and possessed of His own inherent glory;
He is eternal, conscious, the inner controller, and endowed with specific knowledge.
He is both the effect and the cause, the instigator, possessed of fortitude, and the one who bestows the fruits of action.
He is the one who inspires confidence, who is accessible through sacred revelation, the author of the Vedic sentences, the reckoned, and the imperishable.
He is the bestower of well-being, the maker of well-being, the embodiment of well-being, and the most praiseworthy.
He is the foundation of creation, the lofty one, the sphere of light, the blissful, the ether, and the sky-goer.
The middle state, the middle abode, the twilight portion consisting of Abhijit;
it is immortal, auspicious, a gain, a bringer of security, and the leader of success.
Dhanvantari, Nala, Nāla, Pravāha, and Dadhimaṇḍapa.
He is the son, heaven, the blessing, the self, and indeed the dissolution worshipped by the Vaiṣṇavas;
he is the fresh butter, liberation, the lamp of the heart, and the giver of the supreme goal;
he is the remover of fear from time, illusion, evil deeds, and the messengers of Yama.
The door, the doorkeeper, the moon-chamber, the consumer of ghee, and the peerless one;
the one with many offspring, the childless, the wakeful, the progenitor, and the innermost self;
the knot, the knotted, the citizen, the boundary, and the one devoid of boundaries.
He is unassailable, unlimited, immutable, and subject to no transformation.
(1.16) He is the delimiting factor, sovereignty, the definition, the defined, and the Lord.
He is the end, the sole food, and the most ancient Being. (1.17)
The flute-player, the cluster of Kadamba trees, the wedge, the assembly, the caravan, and the respectful one;
the noble one, the dual-natured, the merchant-leader, the three-era one, and the pair-natured;
the husband of women, the lord of himself, attainment, identity, creation, and action.
Reality, selfhood, intention, and the arising of activity; the state of being, emergence, and the rain-cloud; the vision of the form of Suṣumṇā;
giving, self-restraint, compassion, destiny, Diti, the ladle, and milking.
He is the speaker, the reciter, the scribe, the teacher, and the one possessed of creative intuition (*ūha*).
He is beyond the reach of speech and mind; he is merit itself, worthy of being chanted by those of holy learning.
His very life is a gentle smile, his conduct follows the path of the righteous, and battle is his wager.
The son of Ātman, the one who comes through scripture, Naigameya, and indeed the Unobstructed;
the Innumerable, the One-in-Number, the Fearless, and the Destroyer of Fear; the Sacrifice, the one from whom oblations arise, the one who bestows existence, and the Remover of Saṃsāra. (122–123)
He is one whose vigor is upward-turned, who does not stumble, and who destroys obstacles; he is the best among men, the destroyer of bad dreams, the bestower of peace, and the creator of joy.
He is the attractor, the vessel of the imperishable, the ultimate end, and the legitimate son.
The utterance, the worldly discourse, the manifestation, and the single-syllabled sound;

the bestower of enjoyment, the bestower of liberation, the cleanser of sins, the giver of merit, the renowned; the self of fame, the universal army, the direction, the savior, the resonance, and the lord. (125–126)
The Sphoṭa, the boat, the fruit, the flower, the flour, and that which consists of both being and non-being;
the Brahma-sūtra, the bracelet, the true cause, and the possessor of all weapons;
the root, the root-and-its-consequence, the first of all roots, and that which abides at the end of everything. (127)

The Ālaya is the foundation, the belly of all, and the body of all. (1.28) He who is both the positive concomitance and the negative concomitance, eternally joined with the city of names; he who is the perfected one, whose nature is blossoming, the true being of the universe—Oṃ, salutation! (1.29)

Thus, O Lakṣmī, this thousand names of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, known as the *Puruṣottama Sāma*, has been uttered by me; it is purifying, meritorious, and the destroyer of all afflictions. (3.108.1) 30.
Indeed, the sins of the listener, the speaker, and the reciter perish.
(1.31) There shall be no affliction here or in the hereafter; obstacles shall be swiftly destroyed.
A learned Brahmin shall become a knower of Brahman, and a Kṣatriya shall become victorious. (1.32)

A wealthy man shall become a merchant or a member of the Vaiśya caste, and a Śūdra shall become happy; a student shall be wondrous, and a householder shall be endowed with wives and riches. A forest-dweller shall be possessed of the prosperity of the forest, and a holy man shall be tranquil.
One who delights in dharma shall find dharma; one who desires wealth shall become wealthy.
One who desires pleasure shall attain the fulfillment of pleasure; one who seeks liberation attains liberation.
One who seeks a kingdom shall obtain a kingdom, and one who seeks subjects shall obtain subjects. (134–135)
One desiring a son shall indeed obtain a son; one desiring a wife shall obtain a new bride;
one desiring a daughter shall obtain a daughter; and one seeking a husband shall obtain a husband.
One desiring knowledge shall attain knowledge, and one desiring wealth shall attain wealth.
One who desires a livelihood shall obtain a livelihood; one who desires enjoyments shall possess enjoyments;

one who desires what is wished for shall attain that which is wished for; and one who desires a home shall obtain a home—provided that he recites this daily with devotion in the morning, his inner self being purified. (1.37–1.38)
One attains preeminence, fame, renown, prosperity, and the highest good;
no fear whatsoever arises for such a person, and their splendor and prowess increase. By reciting this, one becomes free from disease, well-nourished, strong, and endowed with virtue.
By reciting this, one is born handsome, delightful, and desirable.
The bonds of the speaker are severed, and fear perishes entirely.
Calamities are destroyed, and even enemies perish.
For one who offers praise, even difficult passages indeed become easy to traverse;
he who takes refuge in Puruṣottama and possesses devotion to Puruṣottama—his soul being free from the collyrium of *māyā*—attains Puruṣottama. (142)
For my devotee there is no inauspiciousness, nor is there fear of saṃsāra.
(143) Evil conduct, birth, death, disease, old age, infirmity, futility, and oppression never arise for my devotee. (144)
From the recitation of this, there shall arise the bliss of the Self, peace, excellent prosperity,
wealth, fortune, fame, magnanimity, preeminence, nourishment, and sovereignty.
Liberated lords, ancestors, perfected ones, gods, and great seers [attain these].
By the mere recitation of this hymn, they attained supreme perfection.
By hearing it, one becomes long-lived; by reciting it, one becomes free from sin.
The speaker who is endowed with faith and devotion rejoices both in this world and after death.

I, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, have spoken this Lakṣmī-stotra to you; it is devoted to me, and by its recitation one becomes devoted to me. Even by the recitation of a single verse, the recitation of the entire work is considered accomplished.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall recite to you a verse full of wonder: "I bow to the one who ordains the three worlds; I worship the one who possesses billions upon billions of powers. (149)
I meditate upon Him who directs the inner self, and I offer my entire being to Him who knows the Self.
Salutations to the one whose nature is infinite; salutations to the one who possesses innumerable forms.
Salutations to the one in the form of the divine couple; salutations to the glorious Supreme Soul.
Salutations to the Lord, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
salutations to the one born as Gopāla from Śrī Kambharā-Lakṣmī. 151–152.
Salutations to the Lord of the helpless, salutations to the one compassionate toward his beloved.
Salutations to You, the protector of Dharma; salutations to You, Bālakṛṣṇa. Salutations to You, the husband of Śivarājñī, and to the Lord of Nārāyaṇī.
Salutations to you, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā and Padmāvatī.
Salutations to you, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved Lord of Brahmā. Salutations to you, the Lord of Teachers, the omniscient Master of all instructors. 154–155.
This hymn, when recited and offered unto you for the attainment of its fruit, grants all things; O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, protect me! Salutations, salutations!
By reciting this one thousand times, one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
Great calamities perish and great happiness becomes certain (157).
Through its recitation, his knowledge of all principles increases;
and by a mere drop of Kṛṣṇa’s compassion, he shall attain a state equal to omniscience (158).
The king is preeminent on earth, preeminent in heaven, preeminent as a giver of wealth,
preeminent in learning, and preeminent in worthiness.

O Lakṣmī, by the mere grace of a fraction of my compassion, the person who becomes a good reciter of this hymn shall possess the fulfillment of all desires through a single daily recitation; therefore, dwell in that person’s home. (3.108.160)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Thousand-Name Hymn of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Known as the Śrī Puruṣottama Sāman, which Destroys All Obstacles and Grants All Desires," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 109: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 109.
[The Author: Chapter 110.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Blessed One, this supreme hymn of yours, which brings one to the further shore of worldly existence, has been obtained.
It is the supreme destroyer of obstacles, the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(1) O Lord, those devoted to ritual action, by reciting this hymn, either enjoy the fruits of their performed deeds and subsequently attain liberation, or they attain liberation even without enjoying those fruits. (2)
If they indeed depart after having enjoyed [the fruits], where do they go and what kind of fruit do they enjoy?
Or, as a result of what action do they depart after having enjoyed such fruit? (3) If they indeed depart after having enjoyed those worlds belonging to those who perform virtuous deeds—
"Tell me, what is that state wherein delusion never arises again?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! I shall describe the fruits of the virtuous."
Furthermore, once these [fruits] are known, they do not lead one toward further delusion.
(5) Indeed, austerity is always the foremost among all actions;
for through austerity, heaven—supreme and filled with glory—is attained. (6)
Through the power of austerity, long life, excellent enjoyments, prosperity, beauty, health, learning, and supreme discernment are obtained;
as well as sovereignty, great wealth, good fortune, and the expansion of one's lineage. (7)
Through austerity, the state of the most excellent deity is attained; through austerity, it is reached.
(8) Having enjoyed all this fruit of long-term austerity, the ascetic thereafter enjoys the fruit of his hymn of praise in the eternal world of Brahmā. (9)

The vow of silence is declared to be austerity; for him by whom it is observed, mastery over speech arises, and likewise the power of issuing commands is born. He becomes the instructor of many, known as a Guru and even an Ācārya.
One shall become a royal preceptor and likewise a commander-in-chief;
one shall also become a teacher of the Dharma and likewise a helmsman.
Having enjoyed the fruit of this hymn in this world and in the heavenly realm, || 11–12 ||
To enjoy the fruit [of his merit], he indeed proceeds to the supreme, imperishable abode of Hari.
The giver of the gift shall become a lord of gods in heaven and a wealthy man on earth.
Having enjoyed these pleasures, he shall become a king and obtain the fruit of the hymn of praise.
Indeed, one who partakes in all happiness shines in the supreme state known as the Imperishable (akṣara).
Celibacy (brahmacarya) is the most excellent vow; it is austerity that excludes worldly pleasure.
Such a person shall become long-lived in this world, powerful, robust, firm, and youthful.
He shall become invincible, incapable of being defeated, and a lord equal to Brahmā.
Having enjoyed the fruit for many years, he thereafter attains the fruit of the hymn.
He surely goes to the world of Brahmā and rejoices with those who know Brahman.
Non-violence is also declared to be the highest austerity, known as a *niyama*. One who does not harm living beings attains happiness alone, free from suffering;
having enjoyed supreme bliss there, he shall thereafter obtain the fruit of the hymn of praise.
He goes to the supreme, imperishable abode and rejoices with those who discourse on Brahman. Initiation endowed with righteousness and joined with austerity is considered the highest austerity.
One who is initiated and possessed of devotion shall attain the station of the Supreme Lord.
He shall obtain the station of Bṛhaspati and even the station of the Great Teacher (Mahācārya). Born into a venerable family, into the family of the virtuous, or in the house of Acyuta,
he who has been initiated there obtains enjoyments, and after that, [liberation].
One enjoys the fruit of praise as happiness in my supreme, imperishable abode.
Even subsisting on fruits and roots is declared to be the highest austerity;
having attained the fruit of that, one reaches sovereignty and finds the most excellent heaven.
Those who subsist on leaves and those who subsist on milk go to the heaven that bestows prosperity.
Then, having enjoyed the fruit of the hymn, they proceed with imperishable joy.
By the gift of gold, one attains sovereignty and even the status of a universal emperor (cakravartin).
Wherever one may obtain [this] in the world, from that he goes to the Imperishable;
there he enjoys the fruit of the hymn, which is a treasure-trove of eternal bliss.
Service and attendance upon the Guru are declared to be the supreme austerity.
Through service, knowledge is obtained, as well as favor and auspicious blessings.
Whatever is desired—be it merit, the highest heaven, or anything else—it is indeed attained.
[This applies] toward one's mother and father, the elderly, the husband, the wife, and one's kinsmen. (26–27)
Serving cows, the virtuous, the gods, guests, those living abroad, the sick, the helpless, and the wretched is auspicious.
Indeed, austerity is declared to be supreme; its fruit is the highest happiness.
Whatever is most desired in the world, one obtains all that through service.
Having attained omniscience through service, one is honored in the heavenly world.
Having enjoyed the fruit in heaven and in the realm of truth, they proclaim the fruit of the hymn of praise.
One shall become a server of those who possess the bliss of eternal, perfect joy;
in the supreme imperishable abode, one shall forever be a great liberated soul.
Furthermore, whoever performs a *śrāddha* ceremony here and offers the highest gifts to the ancestors [shall likewise attain this].
By offering *kavya* and *havya* to the twice-born, as well as food, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and so forth,
one enjoys the fruit of heaven for a long time and then proceeds to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).
Having enjoyed the fruit there for a long time, one thereafter obtains the fruit of the hymn of praise (*stotra*).
Leaving Satyaloka behind, he proceeds to the imperishable world (Akṣaraloka).
Furthermore, there shall be an abundance of progeny for the performer of the Śrāddha;
that family becomes devoted to Viṣṇu by worshipping the Supreme Lord.

O Rama! Even those who, having offered the food offering (naivedya) and constantly worshipped with devotion, attain the imperishable abode through the power of this hymn; thus, O Rama, the progeny of the one who gives the ancestral offerings (śrāddha) indeed flourish throughout their lineage.
They go to the imperishable abode, and the speaker of the hymn rejoices;
his descendants and those living with him always rejoice in the imperishable.
By serving cows, one goes to heaven, and beyond that is Truth.
By the merit of this hymn, one goes to the supreme Goloka and the imperishable realm.
Women who bathe at the three junctions of the day obtain excellent boons; through this hymn, they attain the state of being Brahmins, the status of goddesses, and the imperishable realm. (38–39)
One who subsists on air and performs austerities shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice and reach heaven;
through this hymn, he then attains the supreme, unsurpassed, imperishable state.
One who bathes daily becomes wise, intelligent, and radiant.
One devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) goes to heaven; by means of the hymn, one attains the Imperishable (akṣara).
One who is rich in sleeping upon the bare ground indeed obtains palaces fit for kings in heaven; by means of the hymn, one goes to the Imperishable.
Adorned with garments of rags and bark, he attains ornaments and fine clothes;
thereafter, he obtains beautiful beds and seats. By means of this hymn of praise, he goes to my imperishable abode and finds supreme joy.
One who has performed the fire-bath (agnisnāta) goes to the world of the Sun, and from there, further on, to the world of Fire;
then, by the power of hymns of praise, one goes to the imperishable state.
Through the restraint of the tastes (rasas), one attains good fortune and the highest heaven.
One who eats without attachment goes to heaven and is born with long life in the celestial realm;
thereafter, indeed, through hymn of praise, one attains the imperishable abode, the source of happiness.
One who dwells in water becomes a king and shall become the lord of the ocean.
And having become Varuṇa through the power of praise, he then proceeds from that imperishable abode;
one who observes the vow of truth surely goes to heaven by means of praise and the imperishable.
Merely by the gift of water, one becomes an eater of nectar in heaven.
Even the giver of food goes indeed to the supreme heaven, rich in enjoyments;
having enjoyed desires and pleasures as a lord, he goes by means of this hymn to the imperishable state.
The giver of consolation to all beings goes to the auspicious and true state.
Through service to the gods, one goes to the world of the Siddhas created by Brahmā;
and through hymns of praise, one then goes to the imperishable state, my supreme abode.
A giver of lamps becomes possessed of divine vision and attains perfect success.
Having remained for a long time in the world of truth (satyaloka), one goes to the imperishable (akṣara) through hymns of praise;
and the giver of mirrors and other such gifts attains the excellent state of Vairāja.
Through the gift of perfumes, garlands, and so forth, one attains the rajasic state of the Gandharvas.

One who has five locks of hair and abstains from the act of shaving shall possess the expansion of his lineage. By performing the rite of giving away a daughter in marriage, he attains the celestial realm, the excellent station of Vairāja, the divine state, and a thousand male and female servants.
Through ornaments, great enjoyments, and divine, most excellent palaces;
through sacrifices, fasting, and other such rites, one likewise attains heaven and the station of the ancestors.
Furthermore, by the gift of fruits, flowers, and the like, one becomes the lord of gardens and similar places.
The giver of a sesame-cow indeed goes to the world of the Vasus;
the giver of land goes to the unmanifest abode, the source of happiness;
and by the gift of a draft-ox, one goes to the world of the Vasus, the refuge of bliss.
By the gift of an umbrella, a person attains lordship on Kailāsa;
by the gift of sandals, one comes to possess vehicles and celestial chariots.
By the gift of fragrance, one becomes as fragrant as a million lords.
The giver of a tree with flowers and fruit shall go to the state of immortality.
The giver of juice shall go to the abode of nectar, becoming like ten million lords.
By the gift of garlands, incense, and ointments, one attains the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
The king of devotees who indeed performs the rite of giving a bed goes to Goloka;
having enjoyed great blisses here and there, he attains the imperishable abode through this hymn,
O Lakṣmī, by my power— the most excellent of all supreme realms.
The donor of a pond indeed goes to the abode of immortality.
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures there, he attains the imperishable state through this hymn;
for the dedication of a lake is the giver of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
By means of a pond, the splendors of a region reach full bloom;
creatures dwelling in the fourteen worlds take refuge in that reservoir of water.
Likewise, it yields the fruit of the *agnihotra* sacrifice as well as the fruit of gifting a cow.
The giver of a lake obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice as well as the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice,
and even the fruit of the horse sacrifice (vājimedha).
Cows, virtuous people, excellent birds, and all living beings [rejoice].
Animals, trees, water-dwellers, and even other living beings drink from it;
they roam upon its banks, bathe therein, and cleanse themselves.
Thus, the fruit for the donor of such a pond shall indeed be infinite.
Among all gifts, water is indeed the most excellent, the supreme bestower of peace.
The giver of water becomes an enjoyer of nectar in the abode of the Lord;
and by staying on the bank of the Virajā, he goes to Goloka for a long time.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures, he then attains the Imperishable through hymn; indeed, my devoted worshiper goes to that supreme, imperishable state as the fruit of his hymn.
Furthermore, the giver of trees [attains] the auspicious, divine Vṛndāvana.
One who gives a thicket,
one who gives a creeper, one who gives a vine, one who gives a bamboo, and one who gives grass goes to that very place where Goloka resides.
Having enjoyed the auspicious world of the gods, he then proceeds to the world of the ancestors.
Trees indeed worship the hosts of gods with flowers, the ancestors with fruits, guests with shade, and living beings with sap and leaves;
these species of trees provide excellent shelter to all embodied beings.
Just as one protects a son, trees rescue their planter in the next world.
One who plants trees performs the sacrifice of action; he is truthful and has conquered his senses.
He dwells in heaven, in truth, in the Vairāja realm, in the immortal, and in the unmanifest abode.
Even in Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka, they are honored with great joy;
yet even they, O Lakṣmī, attain the supreme imperishable state solely through this hymn of praise.
Having granted fearlessness to all beings, they find fearlessness in the supreme, imperishable Reality.
One certainly attains [this] even through praise and shall become a partaker of eternal bliss.
Even amidst the calamities of people, supreme virtue is to show favor;
one who removes suffering and casts away misfortune goes to heaven, the abode of happiness.
Whatever one desires, if it is given to a thirsty person who asks for it,
and if that gift is quickly utilized by the recipient, the giver attains satisfaction.
Indeed, that gift alone reaches the giver here as something most excellent.
The gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and the supreme gift of land;
the gift of a palace, the gift of a maiden, and the bestowing of knowledge; the giving of food and water, and the giving of ornaments and garments. (3.109.80–81)
The gift of household utensils is the gift of adornment;
the gift of vehicles and mounts, and especially the gift of fearlessness;
the gift of trust, the gift of wealth, and the gift of a son. (82)
The gift of bulls, elephants, and horses is supreme;

the gift of umbrellas, seats, and so forth, as well as the gift of a staff, is considered excellent. Likewise, the gift of a lion-throne and the gift of an elephant-throne [are highly esteemed]. (83–84)
The gift of knowledge, the gift of devotion, and the gift that bestows the goals of human life—these are the gifts that fulfill desires; they are pure and most excellent.
O Lotus-born One, when these are given to the virtuous who are like deities, [they yield great fruit]. 85.
Indeed, they always liberate the donor from evil;
they endow him with masses of merit and lead him to the highest heaven.
They lead him to Satyaloka and to the worlds of the Vairājas.
They lead them indeed to the worlds of Viṣṇu and the worlds of Sadāśiva;
they cause them to reach the worlds of Māyā, the worlds of Īśa, and Goloka.
They also cause them to reach the worlds of Lakṣmī, the worlds of the Liberated (Mukta), and the worlds of Śrī.
They cause [the devotees] to attain the specific abodes of the immortal, which are beyond description;
they lead them to the great worlds of the attendants (*pārṣada*) and to the worlds of women;
and they lead the giver to the worlds of virtuous wives and to the worlds of faithful women.
They lead [the deceased] to the worlds of fire, the worlds of dharma, and the worlds of the moon.
Whatever is most desired in the world, and whatever is cherished and dear,
that should be given to a worthy recipient (supātra), for that indeed yields inexhaustible fruit.
One who does what is pleasing always obtains what is pleasing; one who bestows what is pleasing shall become beloved.
He becomes dear to all living beings both in this world and in the next.
Even an enemy, if he is wretched and has come seeking refuge— ||| 92-93 ||

He who bestows favor upon one in distress is indeed considered Nārāyaṇa. To one who is emaciated, whose learning has been mastered, whose livelihood is exhausted, and who is perishing, he who gives and destroys suffering is indeed considered Nārāyaṇa. (94)

One should satisfy with every possible means those virtuous people devoted to good deeds who have wives, children, and families, even if they do not ask; for such people harbor no longing for worldly enjoyments, nor even for the heavens. (95–96)
Those who are eternally contented, free from desire, and have made their dwelling in a hermitage—
such persons devoted to Brahman should be honored with all prosperity and given [gifts] with respect.
If they should accept what is offered, purified by faith.
That gift becomes the bestower of ten million merits and the bestower of liberation.
Indeed, righteous people, the devoted, the learned, those who observe vows, ascetics, those endowed with virtue and yoga, the self-controlled, and holy men are worthy recipients. 98–99.
A gift given to them is a great sacrifice; it is a constant offering to Brahman.
It is superior to all other sacrifices and always bestows freedom from debt.
They do not become angry when they receive nothing, nor do they covet even a blade of grass.
They are satisfied and happy upon seeing [him], and they rejoice and increase [his merit].
They constantly remember me, Nārāyaṇa, always through hymns of praise—
those virtuous ones, the Brahmins, the upholders of Brahman, and the stainless officiating priests.
Likewise, the family priests, the teachers, such virtuous women, mothers who bring about the welfare of their sons, and those who are most worthy of honor—
these should always be honored with wealth and other gifts, and saluted according to their respective rank.
These should always be bestowed with supernatural powers, for they are considered to be goddesses.
Just as in this world the eternal duty of women is to rely upon a master,
so too the duty of these deities consists of giving and relies upon their master.
One should repeatedly give auspicious things first to virtuous people who know the Veda;
after that, one should give to the helpless, and after that, to mendicants;
then one should give to Brahmins, and after that, to women.
Then one should give to the Brahmins, and after that to others;
then one should give to the servants and so forth. Thus the giver rejoices.
Having enjoyed the fruit of his giving in the worlds, he subsequently attains Brahman.
By means of the hymn known as the *Puruṣottamasāma*, one attains the imperishable state,
the fruit of all gifts, happiness, joy, bliss, and festivity;
established in union with Brahman, one attains an eternal form.

"By reading or hearing this, one shall attain union with Brahman. (3.109.11) Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Giver Enjoys the Fruit of Chanting the Puruṣottama-Sāman— Consisting of Eternal Bliss Residing in the Imperishable Abode— Following the Enjoyment of the Fruits of Giving," in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
