Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Lakṣmī, knowledge, good conduct, noble birth, initiation, and a virtuous refuge—wherever these are found together, that person is the most excellent recipient for gifts. (1)
That which is given to one who asks is declared to be for one's own spiritual welfare;
however, a gift given to one who does not ask is a donation that divests the giver of their own ownership.
Indeed, one most devoted to Brahman is the worthy recipient of a gift, while a virtuous person is the ornament of such a worthy recipient.
When a virtuous and wise person, having obtained wealth, uses it to please the deities and his teachers, he acts rightly.
O Lakṣmī, begging is in every way a cause of degradation and distress;
for one who begs becomes a thief in broad daylight, and thus he is indeed a doer of evil.
Begging is indeed death, and death is nothing but begging.
Since it bestows suffering, one should not give to a beggar.
Generosity is said to be life itself, provided that what is given is bestowed upon one who begs. (5)

Life itself is indeed a blessing, and the giver attains a blessing as well. (6) Likewise, the recipient becomes endowed with prosperity; thus, unrighteousness does not prevail. The giver is truly the superior one; therefore, giving is highly praised. (7)
When one asks for something, compassion is manifested by what is given; but when one does not ask, the fruit of heaven is manifested through the act of giving.
For those people who are endowed with sacred knowledge (*jñāna*), realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), austerity (*tapas*), and devotion (*bhakti*) are indeed worthy of honor.
Yogis and virtuous men are worthy of worship; everything should be given to them.
(9) That which is given to a learned guest who is of good character and in need produces inexhaustible fruit, leading to eternal heaven. (3.110.10)
Those whose disciples, sons, and wives await food and water—
by eating what is given to them, they please the three sacred fires (tretāgni).
Indeed, they consume what has been given to the virtuous and to those practicing celibacy (brahmacārin).
They gratify the fire of Brahman, for that is indeed the supreme pressing (savana).
But the midday pressing is always the offering to mendicants;
and the offering to the gods and the ancestors is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
That third extraction (savana) is the threefold sacrifice that bestows heaven;
for it is indeed a divine sacrifice given to me, Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, this [sacrifice], consisting of the surrender of the self, must be performed by one who possesses true knowledge.
Non-malice toward all beings, sharing with followers, service, contentment, self-control, and renunciation— these are sacrifices characterized by *sattva*.
Purified by faith and accompanied by sacrificial fees, these very acts constitute the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
The virtuous do not accept [offerings] from people who have committed evil deeds;
therefore, in a sacrifice consisting of material wealth, that which destroys sin should be given.
If the virtuous accept it from this sinner, then indeed it becomes purifying.
The power to wash away evil arises from the strength of the recipient.

One should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with whatever objects they most desire, [offering them] to those who are friendly, virtuous, knowers of the Vedas, and devoted to good conduct, vows, and austerity. (18–19)

One should satisfy devoted people who possess offspring by means of various gifts, delicious foods, sacrificial fees, and so forth; for indeed, O Ka, one who possesses offspring becomes possessed of offspring. Indeed, as many virtuous duties as the saintly truly cause to flourish...
Those who bring about the welfare of living beings should be supported with many gifts:
cows, bulls, ornaments, garments, wealth, clarified butter, food, vehicles, umbrellas, clothing, and sandals. (21–22)
Vehicles drawn by horses, houses, and beds—
these should be given to virtuous and holy men, for they grant both heaven and liberation.
Indeed, the donor, freed from sins and purified, goes to heaven.
Whether in secret or openly, he should protect the virtuous through his conduct;
he will certainly partake in the fruits of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. He attains security and well-being, as well as the eternal and imperishable state.
One should never do that which the virtuous do not praise.
Indeed, one should give great enjoyments [to them], for this would dispel the fear of hunger for the good.
In whatever land children see delicious foods, [one should provide them there].
They merely look on and do not eat; such a land is of a sinful and impure nature.
In whatever land virtuous men, the helpless, women, and children suffer from hunger, that land will utterly go to ruin.
In whatever region women, cows, and even the subjects themselves are held by force while crying out, that region is on the verge of death.
Therefore, the gift known as the granting of fearlessness (abhayadāna) is considered the supreme gift.
The giver of fearlessness indeed goes to the imperishable state of fearlessness;
the chanter of the Puruṣottama-sāman goes to the imperishable state of fearlessness;
and the giver of the earth, O Lakṣmī, goes to the earth whose nature is imperishable.
Having been given here, the Earth assumes a divine form and rises up in the Imperishable;
she is immovable, inexhaustible, a milch-cow who fulfills divine desires and more,
yielding jewels, beautiful garments, nectar, rice, barley, and ambrosia.
The giver of land obtains all kinds of nectar in the imperishable realm.
The giver of land prospers in all worlds for eternal years; as long as there is life upon this earth, so long does the giver of land prosper.
Those who give land enjoy the highest land;
land is prosperity, the great fortune that makes the donor beloved.
As is the gift, so is the enjoyment; giving is considered the supreme glory.
Even if it is offered by one of evil conduct, a slayer of a Brahmin, or devoid of devotion—if it is accepted by holy men, the earth itself is purified;
for she considers herself blessed and fortunate, now having come into the hands of the virtuous. (36–37)
Just as a mother makes her own child pure, she makes the donor pure;
thus the name of the earth is "Dharmā," and "Priyadattā" (the one who gives with love) is meaningful. Having given land to a virtuous person, one obtains divine land in heaven.
He who seizes the land of a virtuous person indeed finds no land for himself.
(39) In this world, the land of a virtuous person is praised; it is considered to belong to Nārāyaṇa.
Even a sinner is purified by the gift of land measuring a *gocarma*. (40)
Whoever should perform the horse sacrifice, or should give land to a virtuous person—
the gift of land is praised as bestowing the fruit of eternal bliss—
[as well as] gold, silver, clothing, jewels, pearls, and wealth.
He who bestows the earth has given all this:
austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, service to the guru, worship of cows, and the honoring of holy deities; these all reside in the giver of land. ||42-43||
Intent upon the ultimate welfare of the giver, she bestows the highest good;
just as a mother nourishes her own son daily with milk,
so does the earth sustain the donor with all fragrances and flavors.
Death, Time, the staff of Yama, illusion, fire, fever, and indeed the enemy;
the noose, afflictions, obstacles, fear, and even misfortune; as well as sudden calamities and plagues—these do not approach the giver of land. (45–46)
The giver of land fully satisfies the ancestors, the gods, the great seers, the perfected ones, practitioners of yoga, virtuous women, chaste wives, and those devoted to Brahman.
[He gives] earth to one who is emaciated, destitute of livelihood, helpless, and suffering.
By giving land, which is the mother of livelihood, a person becomes a benefactor to all.
Just as a cow, out of maternal affection, gives her milk to her own calf and nourishes it,
so too does the earth exceedingly nourish the donor.
He who bestows food that contains grain, seeds, or even mere particles,
and provides an excellent dwelling, becomes a performer of the Brahma-gift;
he becomes like the waxing moon, which increases day by day during the bright fortnight.
In this way, he attains supreme prosperity in every kind of crop.
Then the Earth herself, in embodied form, said to the lords of the earth:
"By taking me, by giving me away, and by having given me back, you shall obtain me once more. (51–52)
The gift of land is an atonement that purifies ten generations on both sides;
he is truly of noble birth, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, and he is indeed a doer of merit—
he is a donor, he is a sacrificer, he is a virtuous one— who gives the earth.
Just as crops grow, so do the desires of a person on earth.
The earth is the mother, Lakṣmī is the father, and food is life itself;
beings flourish upon the earth and indeed reach their final end upon the earth.
The Ādityas, Varuṇas, Rudras, Brahmās, Viṣṇus, Analas, Vasus, Śaśins, and the gods became [true] deities after having given the earth as a gift.
(56) The gift of gold, the gift of cows, the gift of land, and the offering of a house—
By giving these to a virtuous person here, one is liberated from all sins.
A devoted wife who is half the body of her husband and strives for her husband’s ultimate welfare should perform the gift of land;
by that, the husband attains the imperishable state.
One who gives land strewn with jewels and endowed with all desirable qualities shall become a king of kings; such a meritorious person is glorified in heaven.
[He who gives] the earth, which is like a cow that milks all desires and rains down every wish—*Śloka 59*.
By giving a virtuous daughter who perpetuates the lineage, one is glorified in heaven.
Rivers flowing with honey and clarified butter, as well as those carrying milk and curds, provide satisfaction here; moreover, the giver of land [is honored] in the world beyond.
Having given away the earth conquered by the sword, one dispels the sin of war;
his worlds in heaven do not perish, for he truly rejoices there.
Desiring prosperity, one should give the land that is meritorious and endowed with the essence of wealth.
The earth, when given away, bestows oceans, rivers, mountains, and forests in every direction;
it also bestows ponds, wells, streams, and lakes, as well as all unguents and all flavors. (63–64)

By bestowing the earth, one grants the livelihood of all living beings— herbs endowed with potency, trees laden with flowers and fruit, forests, stones, mountains, minerals, and mines in every respect. (65)
He who gives land covered with sugarcane, and filled with barley, wheat, and rice;
land abounding in cattle, horses, and vehicles, containing hidden treasures and all means of subsistence—he attains great joys in imperishable worlds. (66–67)
For him, there shall be a land-sacrifice that destroys all impurities;
in this world and in the next divine realm, the giver is honored by the virtuous.
Even a hundred divine women, adorned with celestial garlands, [shall be his reward].
And all perfections attend one who gives land in the world of Brahmā:
the conch shell, the auspicious throne, the parasol, excellent horses, noble vehicles,
flowers of righteousness and merit, and likewise heaps of gold.
The lord of the earth obtains command that is ever unimpeded, shouts of victory, and riches;
he attains golden flowers, medicinal herbs, *kuśa* grass, gold, and meadows,
as well as ground yielding nectar and prosperity.
There is no gift equal to the earth; there is no teacher equal to a mother.
(72) There is no dharma equal to truth; there is no treasure equal to generosity.
There is no worthy recipient equal to the virtuous; there is no happiness equal to liberation. (73)
There is no hymn that bestows liberation like the *Puruṣottama-sāman*.
The giver of the gift and the reciter of the hymn go to my imperishable abode,
having enjoyed the supreme fruit of their giving in heaven, Satyaloka, and likewise in Īśvaraloka.
Then, by means of this praise, one goes from there to my imperishable abode in the divine world.
Just as the earth is praised, so too is food praised in the form of a gift;
the course of the world depends upon food, for life-breaths are established in food.
That food is the primordial Brahman, always providing life and satisfaction;
it is the source of food, the bestower of vigor and power, and indeed its sustainer.
Ascetics, mendicants, the virtuous, and householders alike are established upon food.
One who gives food to the hungry will certainly possess a treasure in the next world.
A householder should quickly honor a guest who has arrived with water and food.
The giver of food obtains the highest nectar both in heaven and here on earth.
Food given to an outcaste or even to a dog is not lost;
one who gives to a person never seen before shall obtain great merit.
[One should give] to the ancestors, the gods, the seers, the brahmins, the virtuous, and women who are without protectors.
He who gratifies guests with food gains infinite merit.
The gift of food is praised among all social classes, for it bestows merit.
One should not inquire about their lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or even their native land. (8.1–8.2)
If one should indeed give the most excellent food when requested by a mendicant,
the grains of that giver of food will always bear fruit;
for in this world and even in the next, they truly yield fruits as sweet as nectar.
The ancestors also wait, thinking, "May there be one among us in the family who gives food.
Holy Brahmins, the destitute, the disabled, and those who beg for food—having been honored and having received their merit as a divine gift—they turn back satisfied. (84–85)
One who constantly gives sweet food dwells in heaven, highly honored.
A giver of food is born possessed of cattle, sons, wealth, and enjoyments;
he is also endowed with vitality and beauty, and is worshipped by the gods.
The field is one afflicted by hunger, and it is the worthy recipient (pātra) into whom that seed is sown and grows.
It is directly perceptible, producing joy, and is the immortal fruit of merit.
Indeed, for both the enjoyer and the giver, it becomes the very sprout of life. (87–88)
The root of the elements, the root of desire, the root of the womb, and food itself are ever-present.
Birth, as well as dharma and artha, and the destruction of disease are considered to arise from food.
O Lotus-born One, earth, heaven, and the world of truth—all abide within food.
In the absence of food, the five elements in the body become disordered.
Strength, beauty, vigor, and so forth perish due to the cessation of food.
Indeed, festivals, marriages, and sacrifices are brought about by means of food.
Whatever is stationary or moving, all is established in food;
both the insentient and the sentient depend upon the principle of nourishment (puṣṭitattva).
Even machines require oil and water—what need then be said of the self?
The palaces of those who give food shine in heaven;
they appear as constellations, white as the moon, or else they possess the color of the rising sun and are adorned with networks of small bells. ||93-94||
They possess hundreds of stories and contain aquatic creatures within;
they shine with the luster of beryl and the sun, and are composed of silver and gold.
Within them as well, there are creepers and trees that yield the fruits of all desires.
In those [palaces], there are ponds, pathways, assembly halls, wells, and oblong lakes.
Even within the dwellings, there are celestial chariots that make a sound.
There are mountains consisting of various kinds of food, as well as garments and ornaments. (96–97)
There are rivers of milk, rivers of curd, and rivers of clarified butter here;
there are celestial palaces of divine beauty and splendid couches shining with gold.
In that mansion, enchanting and worthy goddesses are obtained.
For those who give food, prosperity always increases, raining down nectar.
Rivers of ambrosia flow forth, as do oceans of elixir.
Having thus enjoyed auspicious worlds according to their merit, they proceed thereafter. (3.110.99–100)
O Lakṣmī, by means of the Puruṣottama Sāman one indeed goes to my abode; one enjoys the imperishable, supreme realm and all desires together with me.
One should indeed gratify virtuous brāhmaṇas with ghee and milk-rice.
One should satisfy [the guests] with *kṛsara*, *polikā* cakes and the like, soups, and boiled rice;
with foods cooked in sesame oil, various edibles, molasses, auspicious milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
vegetables, fruits, radishes, tubers, leaves, and parched grain flour (*saktuka*).
One should satisfy the virtuous with black gram, sweet foods, and *laḍḍuka* sweets;
likewise, one should offer gold and silver as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
By reciting the *Sāman* hymns, even a single syllable leads one to enjoy the heavens and eventually attain liberation.
"O Lakṣmī, he enjoys eternal supreme bliss along with me.

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Giving to a Worthy Recipient, the Fruit of Gifting Land, the Fruit of Gifting Food, and the Fruit of the Puruṣottama Sāman," etc., in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
