Chapter 112 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Water is indeed eternal life.
The gift of water is proclaimed to be the gift of life, having the nature of nectar.
Having made the water cool, sweet, delicious, and fragrant— || 1 ||
One should cause the virtuous Brahmins and others who are afflicted by thirst to drink sugarcane juice (śārkara).
One should establish water-stations (prapās) and cause them to be built, and indeed cause excellent waters to be drunk.
One should have wells, step-wells (vāpīs), and tanks constructed, which grant satisfaction to the world.
The gift of water and the gift of juice attain their fruit in the next world.
Water given, which bestows perfect satisfaction, removes half of one's sin.
Water shines as the very embodiment of witness and as the essence of Varuṇa.
O wise ones, you should offer water—the most meritorious gift—to those who possess consciousness and Brahman.
(5) The cows, the Brahmins, the virtuous, the chaste women, and all other living beings who drink the water from one's dug well rescue their entire lineages. (6)
Just as water, so too should one give ghee for consumption;
by giving it to virtuous twice-born ones and guests, one becomes handsome and flavorful.
One obtains fruit, nourishment, fame, affection, and nectar in heaven.
One who gives clarified butter obtains strength, as well as cows and female buffaloes.
(8) One should give milk-rice as a gift, and especially one should give clarified butter;
in the house of the giver of clarified butter, Rākṣasas, Yamas, and other such beings do not dare to cause harm. (9)
One who gives water from a jar does not die of thirst;
indeed, for one who gives a cart, there shall be vehicles.
There are delightful celestial chariots and auspicious aerial palaces for those traveling to heaven.
Thorns are always destroyed for one who gives sandals.
Indeed, a cart yoked with draft animals is as good as given by him.
One should perform the gift of sesame seeds; sesame seeds are auspicious and fit to be eaten by the ancestors.
He who bestows sesame seeds performs all sacrifices—
those that grant prosperity, those that bestow beauty, and likewise those that destroy sin.
Where there is no ghee, no rice, no fruits, and no milk-rice (pāyasa), [there sacrifice is not performed].
In that regard, one should offer oblations with sesame seeds; thus the ancestors and the gods are satisfied.
For the giver of sesame, immortality and heaven are ever-present.
The giver of sesame is declared to be a giver of food and is also said to be a giver of fruit.
Thus, O Lakṣmī! the giver of land obtains a sixth part of the merit of a sacrifice.
He does not perish in times of distress, nor does he encounter difficulties.
[He gives] a beautifully adorned house-site that endures cold, wind, and heat.
He who gives [a shelter] rejoices in heaven and is not displaced even at the end of his merit.
Indeed, the giver of a dwelling goes to heaven and rejoices;
and the builder of a hall of righteousness rejoices in the world of heaven.
He whose palace contains a school, a hall for the virtuous, and a herd of cows— that donor shall attain his own Vaiṣṇava abode, the preeminent residence of Virāṭ.
A provider of shelter saves as many as a hundred lineages.
The giver of land attains constant prosperity; the giver of jewels, an expansion of his lineage. The giver of a garden obtains the essence of fruits; the giver of a sacred ford, supreme liberation.
The giver of a cow goes to Goloka, while the giver of a Brahmin reaches the imperishable Brahman.
The giver of a young bull attains the world of the earth; the giver of a maiden, the auspicious Śrīsthalī;
the giver of a female slave, the world of the Apsarases; the giver of a lamp, the presence of the Sun;
the giver of ghee, the world of the Moon; and the giver of milk, the abode of nectar.
The giver of jewels attains the neutral abode; the giver of a woman attains the supreme station of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇupada).
The giver of a house reaches Satyaloka, and the giver of prosperity reaches the realm of Prakṛti.
The giver of ornaments goes to the abode of Viṣṇu for eternal years.
A giver of a cow is declared to be a bestower of life, as is one who grants protection to a seeker of refuge. He who gives ten thousand cows attains the status of Indra.
A giver of sesame seeds attains the great abode of Svayambhū.
And the preceptor Lomaśa said: "The gift of life is considered supreme.
That by which the vital breaths are preserved is indeed regarded as the gift of life—whether by means of food, water, or sometimes by medicines and the like. (26–27)
By providing refuge, fearlessness, and shelter, one grants protection to living beings. O Kamala, those gifts are always considered gifts of life;
they should be bestowed as they yield the fruit of long life and grant the attainment of heaven.
The water that is offered here becomes the nectar (*amṛta*) of the gods;
for the *nāgas* it takes the form of *sudhā*, and for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) it consists of *svadhā*.
Even for calves and young children, the water becomes the nature of milk.
One who desires his own prosperity should always give the gift of water;
these gifts are auspicious, conducive to long life, and bring happiness.
They indeed grant all desires and bestow bliss after death.
Having given these gifts here and enjoyed pleasures in the third heaven,
and having dwelt there for many kalpas, one goes from this hymn of praise to the Imperishable;
indeed, the fruit of the Puruṣottama-sāman is the abode of the Imperishable.
A householder should bestow his own auspicious gifts upon the renunciant;
having surrendered everything to the holy man, he becomes one who offers himself to the imperishable state.
Having become liberated and free from end, the devotee who knows Brahman rejoices.
In the past, O Rāma, kings as well as Brahmins offered their own selves to the renunciant;

they indeed offered themselves to the teacher for the sake of the renunciant’s stage of life (tyāgāśrama). Having become a forest-dweller and then a renunciant (nyāsī), one shall go to the supreme state.
Indeed, by means of the Puruṣottama Sāman, one may attain the abode of the Imperishable.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the Brāhmaṇa Dīrghaśīla,
who lived in the village of Virāmaṇa on the bank of the river Śatruñjayā.
Even while other Brahmins were residing there, the Brahmin Dīrghaśīla remained steadfast in his long-standing virtue.
(38) Then Yama spoke to one of his own terrifying messengers: "Go and bring Virāmaṇa’s son, Dīrghaśīla. (39)

Do not bring another who is similar to him in name and lineage— such as one belonging to the Bhāradvāja clan, devoid of ritual bathing and worship, an atheist, a reviler of the scriptures, and a speaker of falsehoods. (3.111.40)
Dānaśīla was staying in Virāmaṇa, while Dīrghaśīla had gone away.
A messenger went and brought back Dānaśīla, who had been forbidden [to leave].
A great clamor arose in the village, for Dīrghaśīla had indeed died.
Relatives and friends arrived at the houses of both [the brothers].
Seeing that only one was alive, they returned in confusion.
Some said, "We have seen the terrifying messenger of Yama."
Having followed the long-standing path of virtuous conduct, I was traveling swiftly with the gait of one moving through the sky.
Even an atheist, upon hearing this, would have been struck with terror at his own approaching death;
yet, though the messenger had arrived so close, he forgot me entirely.
"Since I have indeed taken away the wealth of a believer, I shall therefore perform an act of charity.
He immediately gave him cows, sesame seeds, garments,
ornaments, a house, clarified butter, and excellent food, and he chanted [the mantra] again and again.
Even one who is joined with fear of death [attains this] through the Puruṣottama-sāman.
That merit, which destroys all sins, arises in many ways;
yet he repeatedly awaits the messenger of Yama as he approaches from every direction.
Then, having gone to the city of Saṃyaminī, the Brahmin Āstika was seen by Yama Dharma; bowing down, he was raised up and honored.
He was properly welcomed with the madhuparka offering and other rites, and likewise saluted.
He was fed with foods of ambrosia and then requested to grant him forgiveness.
Then King Dharma said to the messenger: "This man does not deserve punishment;
let him be honored and sent away, and let that other one be brought here."
When these words had been spoken, the believer (Āstika) said to the Son of Dharma:
"I am weary; I wish to dwell for all time in the remaining period [of my life].
O Yama, I do not desire to dwell in this body, which is so full of suffering. (52)
"Proclaim the Dharmas—may prosperity be yours—by following which happiness is attained.
Then the King of Dharma said: "Listen to the truth, O Brahmin:
the gift of land is equal to all gifts and bestows all happiness."
The gift of a house, augmented by all necessary implements and furnishings, O Brahmin, is considered supreme; it bestows happiness, merit, and heaven.
The gift of gardens and groves, as well as the gift of juices, is likewise held to be supreme.
One obtains all flavors as well as fruits, flowers, and food.
The gift of tanks and rivers is considered the best, providing satisfaction;
O Brahmin, the gift of a cow is regarded as supreme, bestowing both heaven and liberation.
The offering of a cow indeed delivers one from the Vaitaraṇī river, destroys the bonds of illusion,
rescues one from the ocean of existence, and washes away sins.
The offering of ornaments and other such gifts is considered supreme, for it bestows heaven.
The gift of fine garments and ornaments is considered the supreme bestower of prosperity.
The gift of a maiden is the most excellent, granting a husband and wife and bestowing heaven. Likewise, the gift of male and female servants, as well as the gift of wealth, is auspicious. (3.111.60)
Indeed, the gift of coin is the means for procuring all the enjoyments of household life;
likewise, the supreme gifts are those of sesame, ghee, and lamps,
as well as the giving of sugar, molasses, barley, and wheat.
The gift of an umbrella and sandals is considered to bestow the kingdom of heaven.
All those [other gifts] should be given, as well as the gift of fearlessness;
however, the gift of liberation is supreme and indeed excels all others.
O Brahmin, you have bestowed all these many things upon me in every way;
you are truly meritorious. Act rightly for the welfare of embodied beings.
Recite repeatedly the hymn known as the *Puruṣottama-sāma*.
It bestows liberation, grants eternal bliss, and gives the joy of emancipation;
it grants perpetual happiness, destroys sin, and bestows the imperishable state.
Even one who was previously a sinner becomes a reciter of the Puruṣottama Sāman.
"I do not inflict punishment here; he is indeed proclaimed as pure.
O Brahmin, even if he were a great sinner, a reciter of the scriptures would be exempt from my punishment.
Go in peace, O Brahmin; the King of Dharma must be forgiven."
Thus addressed by the messenger, Dīrghaśīla quickly bowed to Dharma and returned to his own body; he perished. His kinsmen became joyful, and the Brahmin indeed gave gifts.

Having recited at the end my beloved hymn called the Puruṣottama-sāman, which removes all obstacles, he went to the imperishable abode. The messenger of Yama returned to Yama after leading that atheist away.
Then the King of Dharma (Yama) informed Citragupta through his staff-bearer.
Having seen him, Citragupta said: "Indeed, his merit increases;
all the sins and evil deeds that were committed have been purified."
All [sins] are dissolved through the grace of the Supreme Person;
however, in this world, masses of merit always increase through various gifts and other such acts.
Therefore, he is certainly not to be punished, but rather is to be honored in every way.
Having heard this, the illustrious Dharmarāja also honored Dīrghaśīla,
who was a performer of meritorious deeds and a reciter of hymns.
Out of reverence, he offered him water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), and water for washing his feet.
He offered a welcome, honor, and food, including the *madhuparka* and other offerings; having entered into an agreement with him, he then dismissed him.
He then asked that King of Dharma, "How was my [sacrificial horse] lost after it had been found?"
"I am an atheist, a reviler, unrighteous, and a sinner;
yet even so, there is no punishment for me—this is a great wonder to me.
Tell me, O Dharmarāja, why indeed there is no punishment for me? (77-78)
Having heard this, Dharmarāja said to him: "That which has been done is always experienced.
There is a constant rule in the world: that which is blazing cannot be consumed.
Food, clothing, house, vehicle, bed, sin, and the bull [are likewise governed by this law]."

O twice-born one, those blazing fires are not consumed by your blazing sin. O brāhmaṇa, by the recitation of the hymn known as the *Puruṣottama-sāma*, the supreme merit of all gifts has been produced for you in every way. (3.111.80–81)
Enjoy the merit on earth after dwelling there for a long time;
thereafter, go to Svastataḥ, then to Satya, Vairāja, and beyond that to Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, go to the eternal Akṣara and enjoy great bliss.
For those who are devotees of Puruṣottama, no inauspiciousness exists at all.
Fear of time, of māyā, and of evil karma is entirely destroyed.
Furthermore, I have no power whatsoever over the devotees of Puruṣottama.
Then that former atheist Brahmin asked Yama:
"Having gone there, tell me what must be done by me;
I shall perform it according to my ability and cause it to be performed excellently."
Having heard this, Yamarāja also spoke to the brāhmaṇa regarding the bull of dharma:
"Listen, O brāhmaṇa, a temple for the Supreme Soul must be constructed;
there, Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with Śrī, should be installed. (86–87)
All kinds of services should be rendered to him whenever the opportunity arises;
virtuous people should be fed and served continuously with massages of the feet and so forth, as well as gifts of all necessary articles.

The virtuous are always to be honored; they are the givers of liberation and the saviors from worldly existence. (89) In the temple, one should offer lamps and provide flowing springs of water; likewise, one should offer fragrances and present the materials for worship. (3.111.90)
The gift of vehicles and carriages, the donation of gardens and groves,
the offering of banners, the offering of water-pots, the offering of alms-bowls,
the offering of beds, the offering of juices, and likewise the offering of perfumes. (91)
The offering of golden ornaments, as well as the offering of divine garments and the like;
the offering of leaves of the *śāka* tree, as well as the offering of betel and so forth;
the offering of fans and the like, and likewise the offering of blankets and the like. (92–93)
Likewise, the offering of substances for the continuous flow of worship,
the auspicious giving of musical instruments, the presentation of garments,
the gift of large vessels such as *mahāsthālīs*, and also the gift of water-pitchers (*gargarī*). ||94||
The gift of couches and the like, the offering of a great throne,
the donation of cows, horses, and elephants, as well as the presentation of bulls, and the giving of jewels, gems, and so forth— these should always be performed in the temple. (95–96)
Everything should indeed be given to the guru as an offering worthy of one's chosen deity;
likewise, the gift of male and female slaves, the gift of assembly halls and pavilions,
and the construction of wells, step-wells, tanks, and so forth, should be performed at the temple.
The gift of parasols and fly-whisks, as well as the offering of thrones and the like;
likewise, the offering of books, and similarly the offering of chests and such;
the offering of grains, and also the offering of wheat and rice. (98–99)
Such gifts, indeed including water and food,
should especially be given by a householder who is a devotee of the gods.
One should perform ritual bathing, the twilight prayers, recitation of mantras, devotion, and the chanting of hymns.
One should likewise study the knowledge of Brahman, which bestows liberation and consists of self-knowledge;
one should serve one's parents and also perform service to others.
One should be characterized by the conduct of Brahman and likewise be devoted to the practice of devotion.
One should be free from passion and always avoid hatred;
one should perform the worship of Viṣṇu and remain devoted to the scriptures of liberation.
One should constantly glorify Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord.
One should meditate upon that Hari, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Lakṣmī, the Lord of the Liberated.
The singer of the Puruṣottama-sāman should pay homage to the Supreme Lord of Śrī.
Having thus performed these virtuous deeds, which bestow merit and liberation.
"Having conquered illusion as well as time, and having conquered death, one shall go to the Imperishable.
Thus, O Brahmin, having gone there, always perform the worship of the gods;
always perform the worship of the ancestors and the honoring of the virtuous, treating them as yourself."
"Victory shall always be yours in heaven, in truth, and in the imperishable [Brahman].
(107) Thus addressed, O Lotus-born One, the brahmin went home and performed those [rites].
In the end, having enjoyed many heavens, he went to the imperishable abode. (108)
"O Ramā! Having heard, remembered, recited, or even performed the worship of the Deity, any living being who has become my refuge attains my imperishable state.

(3.109) Thus ends [the section on] Dīrghaśīla, the faithful devotee who gave water, land, and various other gifts, and who chanted the Puruṣottama-sāman; and also [the account of] Dīrghaśīla, though he was an atheist, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 111: The Description of the Instruction on the Gates of Yama and Liberation, etc.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age), Chapter 112.
[The Author: Chapter 113.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! A cow should always be given according to the prescribed rite.
The cow of knowledge is threefold and most excellent: the Earth-cow, Sarasvatī, and Brāhmī. The cow of learning should be given to a disciple; the Brāhmī knowledge to one seeking liberation;
the knowledge of arts to an artisan; and material knowledge to a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor.
Knowledge of one's own self should not be given even to a group of calculators, nor should the art of cooking be given to a noble woman;
likewise, knowledge of the scriptures should be given to a learned man, for that is equal to the gift of cattle or land. (3) The gift of a cow should be bestowed, for cows are always like mothers.
One who constantly desires prosperity should always circumambulate cows from left to right.
These divine and most auspicious beings must never be struck with the foot; rather, they are to be worshipped.
Those who drive cows and those who seize them are Rākṣasas destined for hell.
Thirsty and hungry cows might destroy people along with their kinsmen;
yet the dwellings of ancestors, palaces, and temples are purified by their dung—what could be more sacred than that? (6)
Whoever gives even a handful of grass or a handful of food to a cow for a year,
having first refrained from eating himself, performs that vow which fulfills all desires;
he attains the fruit of sons, fame, wealth, and prosperity as well.
His inauspiciousness perishes and no bad dream ever arises for him.
A cow should not be given to one who is wicked, nor to a greedy person, nor to an atheist (9),
nor to one who lacks compassion for a calf, nor to a cruel person, nor even to a killer.
It should never be given to one who lacks the service of fodder;
nor to one who is destitute of a household, nor to one who is devoid of grass and such provisions;
it should never be given to one who is bereft of devotion and righteousness.
A cow should be given to a virtuous person who has many children, to a mendicant seeking a deity, to one who possesses a field, and to one who performs service with grass.
O Rama! Service to cows, service to gurus, and service to ancestors are always [to be practiced].
They destroy heaps of sins and deliver those who offer them.
O Lakṣmī, association with the virtuous likewise delivers one for certain.
But in the absence of cows, one should give a cow made of clarified butter, which brings auspiciousness.
For him, these [streams] flow carrying ghee like affectionate mother-cows.
In the absence of ghee, one should give a milk-cow with enthusiasm and faith.
Having been rescued from distress by that cow, he rejoices in a river of milk.
If milk cannot be obtained, one should give a sesame-cow; one rejoices through the sesame seeds.
If sesame cannot be obtained, one should give a fruit-cow; one rejoices through the fruits.
If fruit cannot be obtained, one should give a grain-cow; one rejoices through the food-grains.

In the absence of food, one should give a "hidden cow" (gūḍhadhenu), for one rejoices through sweet things. In the absence of a hidden cow, one should give a "garment-cow" (ambaradhenu), for one rejoices through clothes.
In the absence of all these, one should give a "water-cow" (jaladhenu); one rejoices in the rivers.
Even a single tawny cow given away becomes for him a river of nectar. Even a single cow given to a virtuous person, when employed in the worship of the deity,
surely leads the donor to my imperishable and eternal abode.
To whatever worlds the giver of a cow goes, those are eternally joyful.
There, time does not prevail, nor does old age, nor fire.
Therein exists no inauspiciousness, nor disease, nor indeed any exhaustion.
Indeed, by the power of the merit of the cows, they approach whatever they desire;
there the cows arrive, moving at will and acting according to their wish.
Likewise, the ponds, lakes, and rivers consist of clarified butter and milk.
They go to houses, mountains, wildernesses, and forests;
they obtain what is pleasing, desirable, sweet, and endowed with flavor.
There, indeed, those who are all-enduring, patient, and givers of cows proceed.
Those who serve their gurus, those who are generous, and those who honor guests go [to the higher realms].
Indeed, even sinners who have stolen cows attain the world of merit.
Having purchased a cow with one's own inheritance, one should bestow it for the sake of spiritual welfare.
Having purchased [the image] with unrefined coins, one should offer it specifically for the sake of liberation.
Having won wealth in gambling, one should purchase [the image] with that and give it to attain the celestial realm.
One should also give a cow from an inheritance, or one obtained through a gift.
The fruit of one who observes the vow of truth and gives a cow is equal to that of giving a thousand cows.
(28) He who bows daily to a cow in the morning and likewise offers her mouthfuls of grass, and he who causes her to drink water, shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. (29)
He who, observing the cow-vow (govrata), abstains from food and gives the first portion of his meal to a cow,
obtains through that service the fruit of giving a thousand cows for a year.
Indeed, he who, eating but one meal a day, buys a cow and gives it to his guru, [attains the same merit].
One shall obtain as many fruits of the cow as there are hairs upon her.
But he who, having sold himself, purchases a cow and bestows it [upon a worthy recipient],
for that giver of a cow, imperishable worlds exist for every single hair.
He who protects a cow, a Brahmin, or a virtuous person in the forest obtains a fruit equal to that of the horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) and rejoices;
at the time of death, whatever desire he may have shall be fulfilled through divine power.
The protector who provides refuge attains all of that.
Gold is the supreme gift, and it should indeed be given along with a cow according to one's ability; it bestows prosperity and is always purifying. (34–35)
He who is poor, devoid of wealth, and without possessions may perform the vow;
indeed, by performing such vows, he shall attain the supreme state.
O Rame, the restraint of the senses is indeed the most excellent of all vows.

One who has conquered the senses and is devoted to Brahman rejoices in the world of Brahmā. Self-restraint bestows happiness; those who are self-controlled turn away from the multitude of sense objects, and having withdrawn the impulse of the mind, they, purified, enter into Brahman. (37–38)
Through valor, austerity, sacrifices, gifts, service,
devotion, tranquility, and knowledge, there exist eternal worlds:
the worlds of the ṛṣis, the worlds of the gods, the worlds of the perfected ones (siddhas), and the abodes of the cows.

Indeed, those devoted to moral conduct and vows go to the worlds of the Liberated and the Lords. Likewise, the teacher, the performer of fire-sacrifices, one intent on service to the guru, and the worshiper of chaste and virtuous women, goes to my imperishable abode. (3.112.40–41)
They were heroes in devotion, in duty, and in vows; in giving, in the act of study, in sacrifice, in battle, in service, and in the acquisition of wealth as well.
They were heroes in self-restraint, except for the pursuit of knowledge; they were heroes in the forest and even in the home through renunciation.
Some are heroes in self-restraint, discipline, tranquility, and straightforwardness;
others are heroes in service to their teacher, mother, father, and husband; and still others are heroes in mendicancy, hospitality toward guests, and asceticism. (43–44)
All go to the worlds of the lords, which bear the fruits of their respective actions;
but those devotees who are observant of the vow of truth go to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha.
He who remains a celibate student (brahmacārī) from birth until death in this world—
Indeed, for Nārāyaṇa, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unattainable.
Celibacy (brahmacarya) burns away defects when practiced, and it consumes all sins.
A celibate student (brahmacārī), strengthened by his powers, shall indeed reach the abode of Brahman.
He who serves his mother, father, guru, or the infallible teacher,
attains my abode, the imperishable and eternal state.
Nothing is born without a seed, nor is there fruit without a seed.
Whatever kind of seed one sows, one reaps a corresponding fruit.
(49) Indeed, the seed consists of human effort, characterized by service and virtue;
the field consists of the true guru, the mother, the father, the cow, and the Lord of the gods. (3.112.50)
Just as a farmer sows and reaps accordingly,
so too does one obtain happiness through virtuous action and suffering through sinful action;
everywhere, one reaps the results of what has been done, including heaven and the joys of heaven.
Beauty, fortune, great good fortune, and various kinds of jewels;
stars, the thirty-three gods, the Siddhas, Yakṣas, the moon, the sun, and the winds—
all these have attained divinity from the human state through the practice of dharma.
Wealth does not attend one who does not give, nor does it attend one who performs no action;
wealth does not attend one who lacks merit, but it attends the one who accomplishes purposeful ends.
He who, without making human effort, waits for fate alone—
O Kamalā! Success does not come to him, just as it does not to the wife of a eunuch, in either world.
For one whose service is valorous, whose strength consists of good character, and whose effort is directed toward destiny, success rests in the palm of his hand.
It is not fate alone that prospers, protects, and preserves;
when joined with one's own effort, fate flourishes well.
Indeed, a lamp devoid of oil is extinguished by itself.
Without merit and without effort, fortune subsides of its own accord.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī! one who desires prosperity must always exert effort in austerity, religious observance, merit, charity, acquisition, devotion, and service. (58–59)
One devoid of merit is never able to enjoy vast wealth, pleasures, women, and food; however,
abundant wealth comes to one who is inclined toward expenditure and charity.
O beloved, it sometimes comes about without effort through what was given in the past.
Whatever may be most dear, all that should be given in every way;
for this world, bound by its karma, enjoys only the fruit of giving.
Fortune is not obtained without being given; a beloved wife is not obtained without being given;
a cow is not obtained without being given; and the earth is not obtained without being given.
Intelligence is not obtained without being given; and prosperity is not attained without being given.
Service is not obtained without being performed; happiness is not obtained without being given.
(64) Life is not obtained without being performed; a kingdom is not obtained without being given.
Fortune and much sensual pleasure are not obtained without being given. (65)
Therefore, gifts should be given— ornaments, garments,
houses, foods, beloved objects, and whatever things are most cherished by oneself.
Having brought forth creations, I have produced the lords and deities of the incarnations.
By satisfying [the ancestors] with the gift of a daughter in marriage, one indeed obtains that fruit which is equal to ten billion women;
for although I am capable and Hari is the eternal refuge of merit,
from my left limb alone, tens of millions of billions are born.
I have no expectation for the fruit of my giving, for I am capable of protecting myself and others; nevertheless, this example has been displayed for the sake of protecting the world.
The entire universe is my body; men and women are its half-forms.
Men are half of me, Nārāyaṇa, and women are likewise my other half.
In this way, the maintenance of the world is sustained; through giving, the fruit is attained.
The virtuous, joined with austerity and discipline, are firm in their vows.
Having attained the fruit, they indeed become lords equal to Nārāyaṇa.
He by whom the three worlds were created in the past by me, the Lord of Śrī—
that very same I am now performing penance in the Ocean of Milk and delighting for a long time in Badarī.
Therefore, having assumed these forms, I shall manifest them; let [the sages] perform supreme austerity.
Having attained the earth as Vāmana, as Paraśurāma, and likewise as Pṛthu, Rāmāditya also indeed gave away the earth in ancient times.
Even though I am Yajñanārāyaṇa, the Blessed One taught the supreme gift to the subjects through sacrificial rites;
indeed, by me, Rādhā was given to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is my own self.
Likewise, Nārāyaṇī was given by me to the self of Nārāyaṇa;
formerly, the earth was given to Varāha, Śrī was given to Viṣṇu,
Lakṣmī was given to Mahāviṣṇu, and Sāvitrī was offered to Brahmā.
That primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the original form, was offered to Puruṣa in the beginning;
having thus performed this synthesis, the practice of giving was set in motion.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, all the joys are indeed the fruit of giving.

With whatever body one performs whatever gift, with that very same body one enjoys that very fruit. In whichever state one performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [in that very state one experiences its result]. (3.112.80)
In each respective state, the agent indeed experiences that fruit.
One should give sight, one should give the mind, and one should give speech that bears truth;
one should truly offer oneself and constantly serve the guru.
Thus, giving is declared to be supreme; one should give even one's own body as is appropriate.
Even by such a gift, one indeed crosses the ocean of karma.
Listen, for I shall now describe here the highest form of giving, which consists of knowledge.
That fruit known as the world of Brahmā which Brahmasatī attained in the past—
Brahmasatī was that young Brāhmaṇa woman who became a Yoginī by worshipping Śaṅkara at the auspicious Somanātha Tīrtha.
She is young, beautiful, endowed with virtuous conduct, and rich in ascetic merit.
On the banks of the Sarasvatī, she performs the three daily ablutions, japa, and other rites.
The pilgrims behold her as equal to the sun, yet they fall into delusion. (85–86)
She did not cast her gaze anywhere at all, in any way whatsoever.
Once, however, the Daitya Sthaṇḍilaghoṣaka beheld her and,
by sheer force, carried her through the sky to his own abode in the ocean.
He forcibly enjoyed that Brahmin woman as well.
She, though protectorless and despondent, knowing the body to be subject to detachment,
perceived both her grief and her lack of grief through her establishment in the Self.
Virtue and vows must always be protected; their violation is indeed sorrow itself.
If they are not protected during times of calamity, one should not grieve, thinking, "I am not this body.
Through discernment, he indeed considered the Self as distinct from the body.
Thinking that her body was destroyed, she who relied on the Supreme abandoned her grief.
Seeing her in such a state, the Daitya questioned her repeatedly:
"O beautiful woman, why do you not grieve, even though you have been violated? (91–92)
She replied: "This body of mine is indeed impure; it has been violated by you.
But I have not been violated, O Daitya! I am pure, consisting of consciousness.
Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Lord Brahmā, resides within you. (93)
The body presided over by that [consciousness] does not eat; the body is not sentient.
O Daitya, you exist as ignorant, but I do not exist as ignorant while situated in calamity.
The body is always to be pitied; how can I, being powerless, pity it? (94–95)
"The self is neither female nor male, nor is it of the nature of earth or stone;
such are the bodies and their designations—what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Upon hearing this, Sthaṇḍilaghoṣa attained the highest wonder.
Having attained knowledge, he then requested forgiveness for his actions.
Placing Somanātha upon his own shoulder, he brought him back;
through the yoga of knowledge, the Daitya also performed penance and devotion.
Having become purified through yoga and austerity, he attained the status of a Gaṇa of Hara over time and went to the supreme Kailāsa.
Brahmā’s wife Satī also lamented there: "Alas, I have fallen under the power of another!"
There, I became dependent upon the ocean, having then fallen into the hands of the Daityas.
Though my worldly sin has been consumed by the fire of knowledge,
an expiation must still be performed so that dharma is not lost.
She approached the peaceful yogi Kirīṭin, who was devoted to Hara, and asked him about the purity of conduct; then Kirīṭin spoke to her:
"O virtuous lady, you possess a beauty that would enchant even Śaṅkara himself!"
Therefore, obstacles will arise for you again and again during your youth.
For this reason, take refuge in a beloved person who knows Brahman and is dear to you,
so that your obstacles may be destroyed and your sin may be pacified.
"Through the purification of the body, as well as by marriage according to the prescribed rites,
your very penance shall be accomplished, and the menstrual flow itself will become a purifier.
Having been addressed thus, Jñānakośā became devoted to that very yogi.
She chose the Lord known as Kirīṭin as her husband and made him her preceptor.
In the presence of Śaṅkara, she received the initiation that adorns the life of a householder;
her forehead was marked with the *tilaka* by Pārvatī, who bestowed upon her the moonlight of good fortune.
By the auspicious blessing of Śambhu, she became a divine and capable Yoginī.
Thus, having offered her body, that excellent Yoginī, the consort of Gaṇapati,
endowed with divine power, remained eternal.
Once, Satī went to the world of Viṣṇu together with Śambhu. She, having taken the form of a maidservant, was brought there along with Brahmā’s Satī.
But upon seeing me, Nārāyaṇa, she was infatuated; and he too [was infatuated] with that beautiful woman.
When Satyā was revealed to me, she indeed became liberated;
eternal and in a divine form, she shines together with Ramā.
Then, by the very name Brāhmīsatī, she became my wife.
Furthermore, O passionate lady, Kirīṭinī also exists eternally on Kailāsa, rejoicing as a servant of Śambhu. Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this secret been told to you regarding the rite of offering.
If Nārāyaṇa is obtained, one should perform the gift of the body;
and the Lord who bestows Nārāyaṇa is the giver of liberation.
One should practice the gift of the body at all times for the sake of liberation.
The body that is enjoyed by others should rather be enjoyed by the Supreme Self.
O Lakṣmī, by offering it [to Him], the virtuous woman attains true prosperity.
By reading and hearing this, there shall be enjoyment, liberation, and the supreme goal.
This supreme secret was previously told to you;
thereafter, other beautiful women also offered themselves. Millions of virtuous and auspicious ladies indeed became [consorts] of Nārāyaṇa.
By means of my yoga, they crossed over saṃsāra and went to the abode of Brahman.
All those beloved of Brahman remain here before you;
among the beloved of Brahman are these yoginīs, liberated ones with divine forms.
O Narayani, this knowledge must not be given to those who are unworthy vessels;
nor should it ever be given to those who, upon hearing it, speak in disparagement.
However, this auspicious [knowledge] should indeed be given to those who have surrendered all their possessions for the sake of liberation.
"Having attained which divine state of Mine, those who have taken refuge in Me obtain [Me].

(121) Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of the Body by the Yoginī Satyā and Her Liberation, etc.," within the section on the description of the fruits of various vows, practices, and the gifting of cows and land in the third book, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 112.
Chapter 113 [Author: Chapter 114 → 3.113
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī! I shall indeed describe to you various types of austerities—both those that are purely [physical] as well as those joined with devotion. (1)
By that very same devotion through which heaven, merit, and stainless prosperity are attained,
my imperishable abode is reached.
Generosity is declared to be supreme, while austerity is always characterized by self-sacrifice.
One should give wealth, one should give a grove, and one should give a house as a beautiful refuge.
One should give a family and one should give even mere grains; such is the generosity established in magnanimity.
For the generous man, there shall be a world superior even to that of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Great magnanimity joined with devotion shall grant me my abode;
sleeping perpetually on the bare ground is considered the highest austerity.
Its great fruit in heaven is palaces resplendent with gold.
And delightful beds are produced that even bestow immortality.
Wearing rags and bark garments is proclaimed as the highest austerity;
its fruit shall be beautiful clothes and ornaments.
The yoga-mind is the highest austerity; its fruit is indeed celestial mansions, divine vehicles, supernatural powers, and residence in heaven.
Austerity consisting of exposure to fire is the highest austerity; its fruit is sovereignty and the celestial realm.
The renunciation of savory tastes is the best austerity;
its auspicious fruit is that a woman’s home shall be filled with good fortune and abundance.
Abstaining from meat is the highest vow; its fruit is the continuation of one's lineage through sons and progeny.
He who dwells with his head downward attains the supreme station of Indra;
he who dwells in water finds the world of the Moon as the fruit of his merit.
He who remains a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) indeed goes to the world of Brahmā.

One should offer water for the feet, a seat, food, water for sipping, and shelter to a guest; this five-limbed sacrifice is the highest austerity. Indeed, these acts performed with devotion grant me the imperishable state.
For the sake of the gods, for the sake of cows, and for the sake of one's guru, lying down as a hero (vīraśāyana) is a supreme austerity that bestows life, liberation, and heaven.
Silence is declared the highest vow, and non-malice is the supreme austerity.
Freedom from blame and freedom from cavil are considered the highest austerity (tapas).
By means of that, one becomes a commander in heaven with an uninterrupted course.
Fasting is the best austerity; its fruit is considered to be the enjoyment [of celestial pleasures]. (15–16)
Through self-restraint and virtuous conduct, one becomes long-lived and strong;
non-violence and austerity are supreme, bestowing sovereignty, health, and beauty.
Even subsisting on fruits and roots is considered an austerity that grants a kingdom.
One who eats the remnants of a meal (vighasāśī) shall attain heaven; one who gives *parṇa* leaves shall go to Hari.
Indeed, for one who sits fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśin*), there shall be supreme happiness everywhere.
One who gives vegetables becomes possessed of vegetables and is endowed with great gardens.
One who gives cows becomes possessed of cattle; one who eats grass becomes a partaker of nectar.
Bathing at the three periods of the day is most excellent, yielding the supreme fruit of austerity. Indeed, divine women belong to him who bathes at the three times of the day.
Subsisting on air as food is the highest austerity; its fruit shall be the fruit of sacrifice.
(21) The vow of truth is the highest austerity; heaven becomes endowed with jewels.
Initiation is the most excellent austerity; one’s lineage becomes most excellent. (22)
Subsisting on water is the best austerity; its fruit is always the consumption of nectar (*sudhā*).
The *agnihotra* sacrifice is the best austerity; its fruit shall be the world of fire (*agniloka*).
The recitation of mantras (*mantrajapa*) is the best austerity; its fruits are sovereignty, heaven, and liberation.
The vow of eating but once a day is considered the most excellent, yielding the supreme fruit of heaven.
O Lotus-born One, fasting as part of initiation is regarded as austerity that bestows heaven;
indeed, consecration is the highest austerity, for it brings about the status of a Guru.
The acquisition of knowledge is the highest austerity; he attains that which belongs to Bṛhaspati.
By practicing mental dharma, one enjoys the world of dharma.
The destruction of craving is the highest austerity; its happiness is like that of Vaikuṇṭha.
He who performs worship and constant austerity shall go to the abode of Goloka.
Brahmā is the father, the Earth is the mother, and the eternal Brahman is the guru;
by him who has satisfied these three, all austerity has been performed.
By him all dharmas have been performed, and the religious vows as well;
endowed with devotion, these indeed grant me the imperishable state. By that woman by whom all dharmas are performed, her husband is propitiated.
Dharma was performed by the husband by whom his wife was fully satisfied;
dharma was performed by the king by whom his subjects were fully satisfied;
and dharma was performed by the subjects by whom Nārāyaṇa was worshipped.
For one who is violent, the mantra is in vain; a sacrifice without a priestly fee is indeed in vain.
An oblation without a mantra is in vain, and a vow devoid of truth is false. Service is in vain without sincere devotion, and worship is in vain without Hari.
Without ethical conduct, dharma is in vain; without happiness, existence is in vain.
Without a virtuous person, giving is in vain; without devotion, birth is in vain.
Without prosperity, a home is in vain; without liberation, death is in vain. (33–34)
Knowledge is in vain without a worthy vessel; victory is in vain without battle;
everything is in vain without affection; and the acquisition of wealth is in vain without Kṛṣṇa.
Dwelling is in vain without a virtuous person; nourishment is false without one's mother.
Vision is in vain without the Lord; the ear is in vain without His story.
Even if it be beautiful, the skin is in vain without the touch of Śrī Hari. The tongue is in vain without tasting the nectar residing in the grace of Kṛṣṇa. (36–37)
Likewise, the utterance of Kṛṣṇa’s qualities in vain,
the sense of smell without the fragrance of Hari, and the intellect without remembrance [of Him]— all these are useless;
all the principles of the body are meaningless without Me.
Without me, strength is useless, fortitude is useless, and fame is useless.
Learning, eloquence, logical intellect, wisdom, and discernment—all are in vain without the propitiation of the Supreme Soul. (3.113.40)
Just as a woman, even if she be a young maiden, is fruitless when with a eunuch,
so indeed everything is fruitless when I, the eunuch, am rejected. And likewise, O Lakṣmī, without me— that which exists apart from my presence— is likewise [fruitless].
At the end of one's life, a prosperous kingdom, noble lineage, and honor become fruitless.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the ancient story of King Vaivarta, whose kingdom extended as far as the ocean due to his former ascetic penance. (42–43)
The entire dominion of the Single-Wheeled One was indeed prosperous;
messengers who traveled through the sky were the conscious agents within his kingdom,
and the governing scriptures were innate.
The suns always became excellent carriers of light, and the Śrāvakas became messengers of the sky throughout his kingdom.
Likewise, the messengers of the waters became downward-flowing currents within water-vehicles. 45–46.
Even celestial chariots belonging to other worlds came to him;
through the power of his merit, everything— whether human or divine—
seemed to have attained a state of identity with his kingdom.
Inanimate matter became always endowed with the nature of consciousness and engaged in the performance of action.
Memory became the god of love (Smara), and rain became nectar;
the crops were memories of Smara, and prosperity was the memory of Smara. (48–49)
His women were Smṛtis and Smaras, his male and female servants were Smṛtis and Smaras, and indeed,
all objects of enjoyment that presented themselves to him were Smṛtis and Smaras.
Such was the perfected one (siddha), the king named Vaivarta.
Once his queen, the virtuous Kālindharā by name, said to him:
"O King, as the Lord dwells upon the earth today, so are you peerless;
everything has been acquired by you on this earth through ascetic penance, just as it was by Viṣṇu."
Nevertheless, the essence remains within, shining like white milk;
for just as milk is [mere] milk once the butter has been extracted, so too is this [world].
Without Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, without the virtuous, and without the Bull [Dharma], [there is nothing].
Without sacrifice, without charity, without honoring guests,
and even without devotion to Hari, everything appears empty to me.
Therefore, worship Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa and serve his devotees.
"Having made self-liberation your bull [vehicle], you shall thus go to the supreme state.
Thus addressed, that lord of the earth did not at all believe the beloved's words;
he repeatedly rejected it all out of atheism.
Neither god nor mortal man, nor even Kṛṣṇa, is the bestower of anything upon anyone.
Everything is obtained through austerity; everything else is essentially false.
By austerity alone shall I go again to heaven, the highest of heavens.
"This second heaven, consisting of the stars, resides upon the earth;
I shall obtain it through asceticism alone, so do not worry, O beautiful lady!
Thus, deluded by the sun of pride, he paid no heed to his beloved.
The king spent a long time in a state of atheism.
Then, when his lifespan had reached its end and his accumulated merit was entirely exhausted,
he departed from his own body, driven forth by the noose of Time.
Indeed, no companions remained for him to protect him as time passed;
thousands of subjects, queens, principal ministers, sons,
and daughters stood there, gazing at him alone, weeping and overwhelmed with grief.

For this atheist, at that time, neither the gods nor the gurus, nor even the virtuous, came to lead the deceased to the next world. Neither dharma, nor merit, nor the goddesses, nor a good rebirth were present. ||63-64||
They did not come to take away the dead one, who had fallen from both his kingdom and his body;
for without merit, there was no passage for him to the other shore.
At that time, the subtle body, no longer presided over by the senses, was unable to proceed.
Neither mind, nor ego, nor intellect, nor breath were able to depart.
Having emerged from the body like an inert object, he remained at the top of the palace.
He awaited the merit that leads to the world of the departed—the merit consisting of righteous dharma.
For the nihilist, there is indeed neither heaven nor this world, much less the next;
for him, there is no path of the gods, nor even the path of smoke.
Having died in a state of delusion, he considered himself miserable, having found no way out.
"I have not given water or food; no sacrifice has been performed.
No service has been rendered anywhere, nor have the virtuous been worshipped.
Neither the worship of the gods, nor offerings of food, nor hymns of praise and the like have been performed by me. (3.113.70)
I have not protected the helpless, nor have I satisfied mendicants;
I have not honored guests, nor have I shown respect to virtuous and truthful women.
I have not given gifts of cows, gold, or land.
Endowed with all supernatural powers, I have acted without any ill-considered thought. Today, for me who am destitute of merit, there is no way out whatsoever;
indeed, neither vehicles nor celestial chariots attend upon me.

Those weapons which were formerly mine no longer remain in their transformed state; they do not present themselves as sentient beings as they once did. The supreme splendor of imperial sovereignty has vanished and is no longer seen at all.
That body, along with its gross constituents, has departed together with the yogin.
That which was made subtle by yoga does not at all come to his aid.
Indeed, everything that is done is obtained; my ascetic toil has gone to waste.
The gross has been considered non-existent; there remains only the subtle cause, which today exists as powerless. What is its use to me, and what is my course?
O Lord, the Fourth State (Turiya) has not been worshipped; what state awaits me now?

Nor do the messengers of Yama ever even come within the range of my vision, by which I might be urged to go to the city of the King of Dharma. There is no destination for the atheist; there is none at all for one who has not performed righteous deeds.
"Neither fortunate nor unfortunate, neither one nor yet another is my destination.
Alas! A body as a *preta* is what must become mine, yet even that does not exist.
It is entirely of the nature of wind, a mere entity consisting of a *bhūta* or *preta*, and nothing more. (3.113.80)
My eye is not whole here, nor my ears, nor my tongue;
neither my feet nor my hands remain, and I am indeed deprived of power.
Today I have become mere mind, stripped of all capability.
Just as is the state of the embryo while it remains in the womb, such is my movement;
my manifestation is free from conceptual construction and likewise devoid of mental cultivation.
Even in a dream, [the deity] is not capable of giving me a vision or even speaking to me.
"By which means may I tell my wife of the merit-bestowing journey?
Alas! Today there is no way for me, the sovereign lord of the earth; everything has been lost, for nothing was accomplished by that thief who deceived me. (84-85)
"My wife previously told me: 'Remember Nārāyaṇa Hari.
I remember that Lord today for the sake of uplifting the lowly; may He deliver me.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he held me within his unwavering concentration.
As he meditated upon me—the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama—so did inner light arise within him. Then, I spoke to him there: || 87-88 ||
Just as by an invisible form or by the voice from the sky,
you have not performed any merit, nor indeed any other;
therefore, your path to Yama has been blocked, and there is no path to Yama for you at all.
"Such a sin was never committed by you that there would be a journey to the realm of Yama.
Therefore, O Devarāta, go back once more to your wife's womb.
Your younger brother shall touch the queen, and you will become her son."
"By the touch of the hand, the birth of a son occurs according to the age;
such indeed it shall be. Therefore, O son, become the son of your younger brother.
Then, having performed worship in your own field preceded by gifts,"
Having performed sacrifices, honored the virtuous, and rendered supreme service to others;
having given gifts of cows, land, and unsurpassed gold,
and having observed sacred vows for a long time, he indeed became a rememberer of his past births.
"Having enjoyed pleasures and having worshipped me, you shall thereafter attain liberation.
Go now to the dream of your wife, as well as that of your younger brother and the fisherman's son;
having spoken thus, become so. (95) Thus spoke the son of the fisherman.
Having spoken thus, the voice from the womb then ceased in the sky.
Then, having become possessed of power, Vaivarta went at night into a dream and reported the truth to his younger brother and likewise to the queen.
Touched even by the hand of the fisherman, the queen,
who was in her fertile season and named Kālindharā, became pregnant.
And in due time, she gave birth to a son who indeed remembered his former births.
O Padmā! From his very childhood, he also practiced devotion to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu).
For the sake of his own liberation, he bestowed gifts of every kind, caused sacrifices to be performed, and had tanks constructed everywhere.
Everywhere he caused delightful food-distributions, water-stations, dharma-halls, and Vedic schools to be constructed on all sides;
he gave gifts of cattle, land, and gold, as well as gifts of maidens in marriage.
He constructed houses for the gods and temples for them;
O Lakṣmī, he built palaces for me there as well. Having caused dwellings for the virtuous to be made, he served them with his own person.
Having thus made the entire kingdom pure and full of devotion,
and having enjoyed various kinds of pleasant pleasures as its lord,
the royal sage named Saṃvarta cast off his own body.
And at the end, through devotion to me, he went to the supreme abode, the imperishable state.
Therefore, gifts should be given, the virtuous should be served,
the deities should be worshipped, and sacrifices should be performed according to one's wealth.

"By reading, hearing, remembering, or likewise performing [this], one attains worldly enjoyment, liberation, and a divine state; there is no doubt in this matter. (107) Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Various Austerities, how those same [austerities] grant liberation when joined with devotion, the rebirth of King Vaivarta as Devarāta in his own wife due to his atheism, and the subsequent attainment of liberation through theistic rites and devotion," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 113: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 114 [[Author: → Chapter 115

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! Through taking refuge in a saintly person, there is liberation; indeed, through taking refuge in a saintly person, there is protection, as well as life and auspiciousness. (1)
In the excellent forest of Saurāṣṭra, on the banks of the Ojasvatī in a region frequented by lions, there lived a cowherd named Romapada.
Devoid of righteousness, Romapada indeed behaved like a beast.
Even though he is a householder, he does not perform bathing, worship, or giving.
He maintains his livelihood with milk, curd, wild rice, and forest produce;
yet, having killed wild animals, he also partakes in eating meat.
Having gone far away at the onset of night, he would repeatedly bring back food and other goods belonging to others from fields and other locations, and thus he practiced theft;
in this way, Vṛṣaṅgama became the son of the path of unrighteousness.
Once born, that youth grew up and became a protector of the buffaloes. Once, while observing the vow of tending cattle, he went to the forest with his father;
there, a deer wandering in the forest was encountered by his father. (6–7)
In the vicinity of the forest, a black deer was struck down by his father’s dogs;
Vṛṣagamana also, joined by his father, quickly rushed toward the deer.
Indeed, as the deer was being torn apart by the dogs, it was dying.

Seeing him crying out in pain and striking his feet against the ground, he was overcome with compassion; he fell into a state of great terror, trembled violently, and indeed released that deer. (3.114.10)
Afflicted by natural compassion, he did not seize the deer there, thinking:
"I shall not eat meat, nor shall I ever kill anything;
such a sin consists precisely in the forcible taking away of life. || 11 ||

"What man would act so mercilessly for the sake of his belly?"— thinking thus, he was filled with compassion and abandoned the harming of living beings. Then Vṛṣaṅgama himself went somewhere during the month of Kārtika.
For the sake of the sacred ford at Somanātha, he bathed and beheld Śaṅkara;
he then confessed to Hara the sin committed by himself.
His sin was destroyed, and purity arose within his heart.
Then, virtuous men arrived there; he saw them and bowed before them.
He honored them, served them, and likewise cultivated their holy company.
Thus, he received the mantra: "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, You are my refuge."
A garland of *tulasī* has been obtained, and auspicious devotion has been attained;
one should never eat anything without first offering it to Śrī Hari.
Likewise, milk, curd, and ghee should be given to saintly men and virtuous women.
The virtuous should be served, and Janārdana should be worshipped.
(18) Having thus received these injunctions, she returned to her own home;
she continued to live in that very manner and remained devoted to Śrī Narāyaṇa. (19)
The virtuous come there once a year into the midst of the forest;
having received service, they indeed depart for another village or another forest.
Vṛṣaṅgama also [performs] the offering of food consisting of *roṭaka* cakes.
At that time, he indeed made gifts of milk and curds;
thus, the merit resulting from these gifts increased greatly for him.
Then, when his time had come, his father met his death.
The terrifying messengers of Yama, with weapons in hand, arrived;
terrified, he cried out in many ways, "Kill me!
again and again, [thinking], "May some of my kinsmen release me from these followers of Yama."
"They are tearing my veins and striking me with mallets.
O people, protect me indeed! O housewife, protect me!
O son, protect me, a wretch being beaten by the followers of Yama! (24–25)
To him who was thus crying out, the son said: "O father, remember the Lord Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa; He will provide protection.
Recite the mantra: 'Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my refuge.'"
O Lakṣmī, in this manner that son bestowed the mantra upon his father:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Svāmin, Śrīpati, Puruṣottama! (27–28)
Thus he proclaimed; meanwhile, the messengers were struck with fear.
They released their master and stood at a distance, whispering among themselves:
"This cowherd, who was our portion, has been delivered by his son."
When the messengers of Yama spoke thus— "He has been purified by the gift of mantras from Hari and by his devotional service"— at that moment,
a circle of saintly persons (*sādhus*) arrived there by chance. (3.114.30–31)
The son quickly offered a welcome reception,
and the virtuous ones, seeing that the time was right, bestowed upon him the water of grace.
Just then, his father Hari arrived, mounted upon an elephant, and drank [the water].
I am indeed Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa myself;
having extracted Romapāda from his body, I led him to the supreme abode.
Through the yoga of my son, I granted the sages the vision that occurs at the time of death.
The liberation of one's father and the fruit of giving arise from being endowed with true devotion.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, through the yoga of devotion, even for sinners, liberation may occur in an instant. Therefore, association with the virtuous should be cultivated.
Even Vṛṣaṅgama, at the end of his body, indeed followed me to my abode.
Listen now to another story, O Lakṣmī, concerning protection through association with the virtuous:
there was once a certain great thief named Nagrabhaṅga, who was exceedingly cruel. (36–37)
At night, a group of twenty thieves will plunder the houses of those who are known to possess great wealth; then, he considers their vulnerabilities.
When a favorable opportunity arises, he commits a terrible act of theft.

Having killed, beaten, and crushed people for their wealth—gold, silver, and jewels—he seizes it and rejoices. While he was living in this manner, once, by the force of circumstances on a certain day... [3.114.40]
At that time, on the royal highway, a goldsmith who fashioned golden ornaments for the king’s palace saw his long-time friend coming into his sight;
even though he was suffering from a broken nose, he met him on the road with great joy.
Then he inquired after his welfare and indeed asked about his exertion.
Thereupon, the goldsmith told him his entire personal history:
"Today, for a month, I have been engaged in the task of fashioning ornaments for the king."
I am going to the royal palace where ten million gold pieces reside,
as well as thousands of pearls and even tens of thousands of gems;
[I shall go] to that auspicious mansion by its side where the treasury is located.
"O goldsmiths, we shall indeed fashion ornaments for you.
Then Nagrabhaṅga said: "If my words please you, tell me a path through the interior that leads to a deserted place at night. (45-46)
"I shall steal gold and other valuables, and I will give you a share as well.
Thus addressed, the goldsmith indeed showed him that path,
as well as the location, the exit, and whatever secret doors there were.

He displayed his serviceable weapons and showed his firm missiles; likewise, he showed the secret exit used for carrying away [the enemy] while remaining concealed. Then, during the night, he entered that city with his own caravan, avoiding any destruction of the front.
Having stolen the palace, wealth, gold, silver, jewels, and excellent pearls, he fled well-concealed and unobserved by people.
Having given everything to his companions, he sent them away into the depths of the forest.
He quickly ordered his own men to cast that [body] into a pit in the earth.
But he, eager for the sake of dispelling his fatigue and for drinking at the *gañjā*,
slowly departed from Śrīnagara during the *brāhma-muhūrta*.
Where virtuous followers of Śiva lived, who were like ascetics amidst the fire of the *gañjā* tavern,
he went there and indeed begged for a drink of *tāmalagāñjika*.
He did not offer this with artificial devotion, but rather prostrated himself like a staff.
He sat down nearby and presented a coin as a gift.
Thinking that this follower was devoted just as the virtuous are,
and having received the coin for his worship, they gave him a tamālaka fruit.
He drank [water], slept, and at dawn, until sunrise, he remained awake;
thereafter, he stayed there until midday.
He indeed took his meal and so forth, and likewise dispelled his fatigue.
Having thrown all those caravan robbers and their wealth into a pit, they departed by way of the forest toward their own village, which was a *yojana* away;
meanwhile, it became evident that the theft of that wealth had occurred in the king’s palace. (57–58)
Having placed the foot-doctors at their head, the soldiers,
bearing weapons, set out from Śrīnagara at dawn to search for thieves,
accompanied by horsemen and the foot-doctors. (59)
Having gone to the forest, they seized those who were departing with their own shields;
they struck them excessively and brought them back.
Likewise, they imprisoned the king and confined those fierce men in a prison.
Then, by means of associating with the virtuous, Nagra-bhaṅga was protected;
even though he was a royal libertine, he was not detected by the king's soldiers.
Other thieves were cast into fetters, punished, and slain.
Having heard this supreme teaching, which is life itself when associated with the virtuous, he considered his own state to be truly free from affliction; and with joy, he entreated the holy men:
"The dharma of the virtuous must be observed by me, and the initiation of the virtuous must be received. (63–64)
I must serve the virtuous, and from this day forward I shall become a virtuous person.
I speak my sincere purpose before these holy men:
indeed, I have repeatedly committed many kinds of theft.
And how may I be freed from those faults, O sinless ones?
Holy men are always intent on protecting those who have come for refuge;
through association with them, I live, while others are indeed as if dead.
"Therefore, having attained dispassion, I shall worship the Supreme Lord;
I shall also constantly serve the virtuous, having myself become virtuous.
Thus were those virtuous ones, headed by Cidambarayana and others, entreated.

Having caused him to perform penance and having washed away his accumulation of sins, they purified him of the crushing weight of his transgressions and performed the Bhāgavata initiation. He too, being liberated from sin, was known by the name Bhāgavatāyana. (3.114.70)

He was always devoted and virtuous, worshipping me, the Supreme Lord. Having performed supreme service to the saintly, he came to the immortal realm of Kuṅkumavāpī for the sake of visiting holy places; on the bank of the lake, he attained liberation.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described here how protection is attained through association with the virtuous and how liberation is granted to him by the surrender of one's own self. Now, I shall relate another narrative concerning the past.
In former times, there was a great saint named Śukāyana, who was exceedingly righteous.
Day and night he constantly worshipped me, the Supreme Lord.
Possessing nothing as his entire wealth, clad in the directions for clothing, he was solely devoted to me.
He makes his dwelling at the foot of mango trees and takes his meal with fruits;
he sustains himself on wild leaves, petals, tubers, and flowers.
He always resides in the forest to the east of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He endures cold and heat, and he endures rain, hunger, and thirst.
Having bathed in the lake every morning, he performs circumambulation;
likewise at midday, he takes a single meal as alms.
Having performed my divine hymn of praise in the evening, he goes to sleep.
He always protects my image made of variegated cloth upon the trunk of a mango tree; having worshipped it, he meditates upon it in his heart every day.
The mango grove was exceedingly excellent and was always dear to him;
he, too, would repeatedly offer me only mango fruits.
While he was living in this manner, tending to the mango trees—

Once, by the turn of fate, a fire broke out in the forest. (81) Then the heaps of grass, the clusters of stalks, the masses of leaves, and likewise the medicinal herbs—all were set ablaze by the flame, and the trees as well were consumed by the fire. (82)
Then even the mango tree at its own place was set ablaze;
thereafter, the fire indeed blazed forth on all sides with great speed—
sharp, terrifying, and most dreadful, driven by the wind.
At that time, this virtuous man remained absorbed in meditation, not thinking of me, Hari.
However, I repeatedly awakened him with a voice from the sky:
"Go far away, leaving these trees; do not be consumed by fire here. (84-85)
And he said: "I shall not depart, abandoning my voices and my abodes—wherever I may find my own place, livelihood, home, shelter, happiness, and food; I will not forsake them. (86)
"These are all my kinsmen, as well as my fathers and children;
all these mothers and sisters—how indeed can I abandon them?
I am not ungrateful, nor do I act for my own selfish ends, nor am I a sinner. (87–88)
Where shall I go, having abandoned those by whose fruits I live well, in whose shade I dwell, and through whose juices I obtain nourishment?
These dull, lifeless things of a different species are not my true bondsmen.
"These are not my dependents, but rather those who have rendered service to me.
Such servants, ever intent on helping others, stand as my companions day and night, remaining as if they were my very own refuge. (3.114.90–91)
"How can I depart after burning these forest-dwellers who possess excellent virtues?
I shall be consumed right here; I will not go elsewhere.
I am a virtuous man and one who practices forbearance, and these trees are likewise forbearing. (92)
I do not depart from here, having abandoned those who are virtuous and adorned with goodness.
Let it be one way or another— whether there be ashes or life itself—
one must indeed exist together with a virtuous person who shares both one's yoga and one's nourishment.
Having spoken thus, he who was a treasure-house of fortitude neither moved nor rose;
as one meditating on Brahman, he sat down and remained exactly as he was.
Compassion and affection are always the great dharma of the virtuous.
"Relying upon this capable one, I shall indeed abandon this thicket today.
O Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī, Supreme Person!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, protect these trees! || 96-97 ||
Thus making this speech heard,
the virtuous one meditated upon me with a mind single-pointed in conviction through his devotion;
and then the fire indeed consumed the side of the yogi.
His feet, hands, matted locks, shoulders, body hair, and skin were covered everywhere with [ants];
nevertheless, even while serving me, he did not stir from that spot at all.
Then I spoke to that truthful saint, the protector of those who have come for refuge.

Knowing him to be my devotee, devoid of attachment to the body and other such things, established solely in the self, and endowed with the dharma of the virtuous, I said to him, "I am pleased with your dispassion; choose a boon. (1.1)

"Because of the abundance of the virtue of compassion and because devotion resides in my mind, choose a boon; I am capable of granting it, for I am Narayana himself. O wise one, I am he whom you meditate upon and for whose sake you have made this petition."
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama, was deeply gratified upon seeing your compassionate conduct. "Choose a boon, O virtuous one; I shall grant you everything you desire."
And Sādhu mentally chose the excellence of the tree and the forest—
its abundance of sap and its prosperity exactly as it had been before.
Having recognized his firm devotion to that virtuous one, which bestows supreme happiness, [he granted his wish].
Delighted, I sprinkled the excellent mango tree with the nectar-vision;
I sprinkled all the trees, the creepers, and the entire field and forest.
With showers of ambrosia, I sprinkled and brought the magnificent grove back to life.

Then, in that forest which had previously stood there, the fruits, leaves, branches, and flowers all became prosperous once again on every side. The fire was entirely extinguished, and not even its ashes remained there.
All the work performed by Agni dissolved away, and my own creative power emerged;
thus, near the lake, a divine grove of mango trees came into being.
It was a refuge for the virtuous followers of the Bhāgavata path who were endowed with devotion.
Just as that forest attained the fulfillment of all its purposes,
so too shall he who relies upon the virtuous obtain the auspicious perfection fashioned by the righteous.
This very virtuous one, whose path is the Bhāgavatas, shines in my abode.
"Indeed, by my grace and through devotion to Me, he attained liberation in due time.
By reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall likewise come to pass.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Cowherd Romapāda through His Refuge in a Holy Man; the Protection of the Thief named Nagrabhaṅga from Royal Fear by Meeting a Saintly Person; and the Rejuvenation of Mango Trees and Other Plants Burned by Fire through Living with a Holy Devotee of the Bhāgavata," in the Third Section on the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age within the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
