Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
"I have been born many times in this creation along with you—
Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇī, Śrī, Bhārgavī, Mādhavī, and Ramā."
Vṛndā, Tulasī, Śivarājñī, Śrī, Kamalā, Pramā, Padmā, Vidyāparā, and Padmāvatī— O Lord Śrī Hari, my forms exist here in this world by the hundreds and thousands.
A desire for knowledge has arisen within me: when and how did Mahālakṣmī come into being? And what was her name on this earth, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa?
Although I know that your mother is my own mother-in-law. (3–4)
Furthermore, I recognize that second [form] as Mahālakṣmī, who has the face of an elephant, who appeared in Surāṣṭra,
who was born in Camatkārapura from the Ocean of Milk,
and likewise as the Great Golden One (Mahāhiraṇmayī).
I recognize that third one; if there is another besides it residing on the earth,
and if she exists as the accomplisher of great deeds, then proclaim her to me— her,
by hearing whom I shall be filled with joy, and [tell me] what her power and wonder are.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the worshipful Mahālakṣmī who resides on the surface of the earth in the south, who is a source of wonder. (8)
In the city of Kāñcanī, that virtuous mother indeed shone resplendent.
Formerly, for the purpose of deluding Śambhu,
Kāmadeva arrived at Kailāsa for the sake of a divine mission, but he was reduced to ashes by Śaṅkara.
The group of painters took some ash and fashioned a doll; right there they infused it with life. That boy became conscious and exceedingly full of wrath.
He who was reciting the Śatarudrīya chanted it in the presence of Śaṅkara;
then Śambhu, appearing before him and being pleased, spoke to him regarding a boon.
He chose this boon: "May I possess the sovereignty of the three worlds, free from all thorns."
"May the missiles and weapons of my adversaries be rendered utterly useless in every way;
and may my own missiles, weapons, and mantras never be in vain.
Śambhu then said, "So be it," and likewise bestowed the kingdom upon him.
"May your kingdom be free of thorns for sixty thousand years. Then Brahmā himself, beholding him,
thought, "This one has indeed become Bhaṇḍāsphoṭa," and spoke thus by the name of Bhaṇḍāsura.
Then, scorched by the fire of Rudra’s forehead-wrath, he was reduced to ashes;
yet from those ashes, that son of Rudra was born again as a Dānava.
He grew up very quickly and summoned his preceptor, Śukra.
Then Maya again offered worship to those two;
he said to that artisan: "That ancient city which once belonged to the lords of the Daityas now lies in ruins; rebuild it anew."
Having heard that, Maya went and built that new city,
where the Daitya had formerly resided while ruling the three worlds. There he was consecrated by Śukra and by the mighty Daityas.
He shone with supreme opulence, splendors, strength, and other powers.
That very crown which Hiraṇyakaśipu had formerly worn—
indeed, that crown was alive, indestructible, and had been worn by Śukra.
Bhaṇḍa held two living fly-whisks, radiant with power.
He bore a parasol under whose shade millions of missiles could not prevail, for by its mere presence neither disease nor sufferings arise. (22–23)
Neither destruction, nor defeat, nor birth afflicts him.
The Sage granted him the bow named Vijaya, the enemy-slaying conch, ornaments, a radiant throne, and inexhaustible valor. (24)
Thus the king returned; he had eight [sons] of great strength who became his chief generals, honored by the army, and capable of traversing the three worlds:
Indraśatru, Amitraghna, Vidyunmālin, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Ugrakarma, Ugradhanvan, and Vijaya, who had mastered the Vedas—
all were indeed knowers of the Vedic scriptures and devoted to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa).
They were experts in warfare, skilled in the use of illusions, and full of prowess.
Then he cast forth the Daitya Viśukra from his right shoulder;
from his left shoulder he cast forth Viṣāṅga, who had a wicked crest.
And Bhaṇḍaka also cast forth his sister Dhūminī from his throat.
Then four women— Sumohinī, Kumudvatī, Citrāṅgī, and Sundarī— the daughters of Daityas, were presented to him.
There were also thousands of chariots, horses, elephants, and celestial vehicles.
They became conquerors of the worlds, following the doctrine of the preceptor Śukra. Bhaṇḍa, along with all the Daityas, became a devotee of Śaṅkara;
at that time, sacrifices to Rudra were being performed in every house on all sides.
The Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Tantras and the ritual formulas for receiving gifts,
proceeded even among the hosts of Daityas at their sacrifice.
At that time, during the sacrifices of the Daityas, those who consume the sacrificial offerings partook of them.
Accompanied by his two brothers of fierce valor and by his principal forces,
he conquered all the directions and then shone like the great Indra.
Elevated by his heroism and prowess, he shattered the cosmic egg.
Many times the gods and others, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the rest, were defeated by him at the forefront of battle; seeing his blazing splendor,
they all took to flight and dwelt forever in their respective abodes.
Some were in the depths of the netherworld, some in the waters of the ocean;
some in the far corners of the directions, and some in the groves of mountains.
Trembling violently, they wandered about, concealed in disguise.
Having regarded the Pitṛs, Siddhas, Sādhyas, gods, Nāgas, sacrifices, and the lords of the directions—
as well as Brahmā, Padmanābha, Rudra, and even the wielder of the thunderbolt—
as all no more than blades of grass, Bhaṇḍa indeed ruled over the worlds.
Thus, as Bhaṇḍa ruled the kingdom with the appearance of a victor,
sixty thousand years passed thereafter.
Then, observing that the gods were declining in strength, the Lord of Kamalā [Viṣṇu]—
In order to slay the fierce demon Bhaṇḍāsura and to protect the three worlds,
she suddenly manifested an illusion in her own form that was utterly deluding.
That supreme goddess became Lalitā in her own likeness.
My mother Kambharā is Mahālakṣmī herself;
her four arms are adorned with a noose, a goad, a bow, and arrows.
She is my supreme mother, the ultimate power (parā śakti), whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
To that Māyā, who is Mahāvaiṣṇavī and the destroyer of the hosts of Daityas, Hari said: "Slay the Daitya Bhaṇḍa.
Having received this command, she requested a group of Apsarases.
Hari gave her celestial nymphs, and she, along with Viśvācika and the others,
went to the Himālaya mountain where the demon Bhaṇḍaka resides.
There, that Mahālakṣmī remained at the foot of a campaka tree.
She made her dwelling in that lovely place while singing with a sweet voice.
Hearing her, a Daitya, afflicted by love, came there and entreated her.
She, too, [displayed] gestures, expressions, movements, and charming conversations.
Having done so, he indeed captivated the minds of the Daityas and Bhaṇḍaka.
Then Bhaṇḍa and the Daityas forgot Śrī Śaṅkara at evening, as well as the twilight prayers, hymns, worship, and the service of their elders. (3.115.49–50)
They abandoned all their auspicious sacrificial rites;
likewise, they ceased honoring Śukra, their own preceptor.
Having deluded them, this goddess obstructed the foremost of the Daityas.
Struck by this insult, Śukra then became repeatedly provoked to anger.
He said to the Daityas: "Truly, you are not fit for the prosperity of a kingdom.
Fall indeed from the sovereignty of others, and let your pride go to its destruction! (52–53)
Beholding the asuras, created through illusion, rendered motionless,
Indra and the other gods donned their armor and went to the Yamunā for the sake of penance.
They commenced an auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice that bestows strength.
The deities indeed performed the worship of Nārāyaṇī Mahālakṣmī.
Established in fierce austerity, devoted to recitation and meditation, Lakṣmī became single-minded and vigilant. (55–56)
After many years had passed, Śukra himself, the family priest, said to the Daityas:
"Indeed, for the sake of your destruction, the gods and others are performing sacrifices, meditation, and penance on the banks of the Yamunā. (57)
Indeed, by their mere birth, the gods and others shall slay you;
Hari will surely destroy all those on your side before long.
By him alone was created an illusion in the form of Mahālakṣmī.
"Seeing you bewildered there, Indra and the other gods will surely perform their penances;
go there quickly and create obstacles for them at once!
Hearing this, the Daityas, experts in warfare, joined by Bhaṇḍāsura, [set out].
Having reached the bank of the Yamunā, they created a great obstacle through a massive battle.
Seeing the Daityas who were obstructing her ascetic penance, Mahālakṣmī, who fulfills the purposes of her devotees,
constructed a brilliant and great rampart.
Seeing that firm city named Indraprastha, which was impenetrable by the Dānavas and Daityas, Bhaṇḍaka became despondent and returned to his own city.
O King, Śrutavarman, the friend of Bhaṇḍa, said to him: "Listen to these words."
Your kingdom, offered to Śiva, shall last for sixty thousand years.
Therefore, this time for the end of your reign has been ordained by Śiva;
since it is impossible to counteract, pass the time.
"Enjoyment should be pursued at the proper time, and withdrawal is supreme at the proper time.
Having heard this instruction, Bhaṇḍakāsura desisted.
The deities [resided] at Indraprastha in that vast and extensive forest.
Having prepared a sacrificial pit of suitable dimensions and established the fire,
and having made a firm vow and worshipped Mahālakṣmī,
they performed oblations all around for the sake of pleasing Hari’s Śrī.
"We shall become one with Brahman, or we shall enjoy the celestial realm"—
thinking thus, they performed the oblation; at that very moment,
a great wheel-shaped radiance appeared, and in its center was the supreme power of the Lord.
The Mother of the World, the Bestower of Life, Nārāyaṇī, the Supreme Sovereign; composed of the splendor of the divine manifestations (vyūha), the Delighter of Brahmā, the Beautiful Consort of Hari;
her radiant hands holding a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and a lotus garland. (3.115.70–71)
Seeing her, the gods were struck with wonder and, freed from their distress, bowed down.
They praised the auspicious Mahālakṣmī, the graceful mother of Viṣṇu:
"Victory to you, Lakṣmī, Mother of the World! Victory to you, Lakṣmī, higher than the highest! (72)
Victory to you, O abode of auspiciousness! Victory to you, whose essence is all the arts!
(73) Victory to you, O Brāhmī, O Mahālakṣmī, O you whose nature is Brahman, O Supreme Self!
Victory to you, O Nārāyaṇī, O Peaceful One! Victory to you, O Śrī Lalitā, O Rame! (74)
Victory, O Śrī Vijayā, Sovereign of Goddesses, O Śrīde, Bestower of Prosperity!
Salutations to the one with a thousand heads, with a thousand faces and eyes!
Salutations to her who is adorned with a thousand lotus-hands and lotus-feet!
O Lakṣmī, you are subtler than the subtlest and greater than the greatest.
(76) The netherworld (Atala) is considered your feet, Vitala your knees, Rasātala your hips, and the earth your belly. (77)
May your heart be the earth, may your face be heaven, and may truth be considered your head.
May the moon, sun, and fire be your eyes, the directions your ears, and the gods your arms.
May the winds be your breaths, and the Vedas be considered your speech. (78)
The creation of the worlds is your play; the Supreme Lord is your friend.
Eternal bliss is your food, and the heart of Hari is your dwelling.
Visible and invisible forms are your very nature, as are the worlds themselves. (3.115.80)
Your thick locks of hair are indeed the stars, and your flowers are the [celestial bodies];
Dharma and the other virtues are your arms, while Time and the other causal factors are your weapons.
Your fingers and toenails are the restraints (yamas) and the observances (niyamas).
Your two breasts are the utterances *svāhā* and *svadhā*, yielding the milk of all life.
Your breath is *prāṇāyāma*, and your tongue is Sarasvatī.
The hairs on your body are trees, and your garment is the dawn. (82–83)
In the beginning, Compassion, the lawful wife of Dharma, created all beings;
you are she who dwells in the heart, the pervasive Lakṣmī, the Enchantress, and likewise the Supreme One.
Now you are seen as Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, and the Bestower of Joy.

Salutations to that Mahālakṣmī; salutations again and again to her who has the face of a preeminent elephant. (85) Salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, the possessor of all powers, the sustainer of all;
she who created Virāj, and from him, the unborn Viṣṇu and Īśvara. (86)
Salutations again and again to that Lakṣmī, who is Rudra as well as the foremost of the gods;
salutations again and again to you, Hariṇī, who possesses the three qualities and yet is devoid of qualities.
Salutations again and again to you, the Mother of the Universe, whose nature consists of yantras and tantras.
Salutations again and again to Mahālakṣmī, the embodiment of the Guru, who possesses the splendor of speech. Salutations again and again to you, Kaṃbharā, the bearer of all knowledge.
Salutations again and again to her who manifests as Jayā, Lalitā, Pāñcālī, and Ramā.
"Obeisance to Padmāvatī, the consort of Rāma, who possesses excellent qualities and is the embodiment of the glory of the Command.
Obeisance! Thus praised, she became pleased and granted them excellent boons.
The gods said, "If you are satisfied, then destroy Bhaṇḍāsura."
"Grant long life and happiness to me who seeks your refuge.
Mahālakṣmī replied, "May they be joyful and fearless;
I, Lalitā, the great chaste lady, shall destroy the demon Bhaṇḍāsura. (91–92)
They will be my praisers, endowed with prosperity, fame, and virtue;
they will be possessed of learning and discipline, free from disease, and long-lived.
Rich in sons, friends, and wives, they will possess great abundance.
Having thus obtained the boon, the gods performed a sacrificial session (*satra*) until its completion.
Then that Lalitā Lakṣmī offered the garland of boons, raised by her own hand,
to the Supreme Self, who is the primordial form of Śrī Mahāviṣṇu.
While all the gods were watching right there, he placed it around his neck;
then the divine drums resounded and shouts of "Victory! arose.
There, songs of the Apsarases, the celestial women, broke forth.
The Apsarases danced and the best of the Gandharvas sang;
the sages offered hymns of praise, intent on pronouncing blessings;
the virtuous bowed down, and the attendants performed service.
Lakṣmī and the other goddesses performed the worship of the couple at Indraprastha;
they also gave them wedding gifts, ornaments, and wealth.
The gods and others likewise bestowed various kinds of jewels upon the husband and wife.
At the conclusion of the wedding, the gods and others prepared various foods there.
Then Brahmā spoke for the sake of the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura,
[addressing] Mahālakṣmī, known as Lalitā, and likewise Parabrahma-Hari.
Then, for the sake of protecting the Dharma and for the protection of the gods,
Mahālakṣmī, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, quickly summoned her divine weapons,
such as the discus and others, which possessed celestial forms.
They arrived in embodied form and stood before Hari.
Then Mahālakṣmī, the virtuous one whose eyes grant all desires,
accepted them by the command of Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who bestows all desires.
Seeing all the gods accompanied by Nārāyaṇa as her allies,
she set out, her victory increasing, to lead the Daityas to their destruction;
along with the armies of the Pārṣadas, the Gaṇas, and likewise the celestial dwellers.
Thousands of goddesses and Siddhas also set forth, equipped with their weapons; likewise, thousands of cows, horses, lions, tigers, birds, bulls,
śarabhas, swans, and garuḍas emerged.
Then thousands of celestial chariots (*vimānas*), vehicles, and chariots,
equipped with weapons and fashioned for the occasion, set forth from Indraprastha. Along with them went Mahālakṣmī’s great army, accompanied by Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Kamalā.
Accompanied by ten million goddesses, including Durgā, Satī, and Mahācaṇḍī,
that divine chariot— whose movement was unimpeded— proceeded through the sky;
it had been strengthened and protected by divine missiles, weapons, mantras, and other such means.
The sky, as far as the realm of Satyaloka, was filled with the roar of the army.
Hearing this, all the Nārāyaṇas and Īśvaras quickly arrived.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Armament of Lalitā and Mahālakṣmī Appearing at the Sacrifice of the Gods Arrived at Indraprastha for the Purpose of Destroying Bhaṇḍāsura, who was Born from the Ashes of Kāmadeva," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī; then the armies of the Mothers, who possess divine bodies, shone forth as they marched out. (1)
Mahākṣmī, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Śāradā,
Durgā, Gaṅgā, Yamī, Revā, Rādhā, Ramā, Padminī,
Kamalā, Śrī, Pāśavatī, Ramā, Māṇikī, and Mañjulā. (2)
Sukhadā, Kambharālakṣmī, Santuṣṭā, Vijayā, Jayā;
Suparṇā, Mādhavī, Haṃsī, Bhārgavī, Suguṇā, Satī;
Nārāyaṇī, Vāsudevī, Hariṇī, and Hiraṇmayī. (3–4)
Śārdūlavāhanā, Mattā, Gajānanā, Haṃsinī, Viśvā, Bhūti, Piṅgalākṣī, Kāmākṣī, Vallabhā,
Dayā, Kārṣṇī, Vṛndā, Vaiṣṇavī, Jyoṣṭrī, Kāmadughā, and Anaghā. (5)
Bhū, Dyau, Dhariṇī, Dhātrī, Bhāratī, Kariṇī, Kṛti;
Brāhmī, Raudrī, Revatī, Māheśvarī, Kumārikā;
Śākrī, Saurī, Nairṛtī, Saumyā, Śikhaṇḍinī, and Śivā. (6–7)
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Balā, Raktā, Sunandinī, Śakunī, Revatī, Kālī, Jayantī, and likewise Āditi;
Śyāmā, Vināyakī, Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Vinatā, and Svadhā.
Uṣā, Svāhā, Vaṣaṭkārā, Jyeṣṭhālakṣmī, and Muktikā;
Māyā, Rati, Maṅgalā, Amṛtā, and the sixty Mānasās; Śānti, Ekādaśī, Haimī, Urjaskā, and Puruṣottamī. (3.116.9–10)
All these were indeed Vaiṣṇavīs, with Mūrdhanī at their head, who destroyed the warriors; likewise, other Śāṅkarīs emerged in the battle,
as did Kātara, Niryayu, Śāṅkarī, Mālinī, Caṇḍī, Vāyavyā, Dūtikā, and Khagā.
Cāmuṇḍā, Śatānandā, Calacchikhā, Supicchilā,
Balā, Atibalā, Mātṛnandā, Nandā, Aparājitā, Mahākālī, Bhairavī, Karālī, and likewise Gaṇī. (1.2–1.3)
Mṛtyu, Mārī, Mahāmārī, Diti, Ghaṭodarī, Danu, Ulūkī, Karṇamoṭī, Vajrahastā,
Kapālikā, Piśācī, Rākṣasī, Kheṭā, Bhṛśuṇḍī, and likewise Lāṅgalī. (14)
Dhūmrā, Karālinī, Ekavīrā, Audumbarī, Kukkutī, Kekarī,
Pretayānā, Krauñcī, Śailamukhī, Sakhī, Kapardinī,
Kāmarūpā, Rocanā, and likewise Keśinī. (15–16)
Daṃṣṭrālolkāmukhī, Dhūmraśikhā, Kṣvelā, Prakampinī, Sarpakarṇī, Viśokā, Nikumbhā,
Bagalāmukhī, Mākarī, Kacchapī, Citrā, Koṇā, and Lāṅgalāvatī. (17)
Ayomukhī, Krodhanā, Aśanī, and likewise Hūṃkāriṇī;
Mahādevī, Rudrasaṭā, Kātyāyanī, and Karālinī; Gaurī, Sāṃkarṣiṇī, the goddess Prāleyī, and Bhūtaḍāmarī. (18–19)
Sṛṣṭigarbhā, Mahāmāyā, Khaṭīyārī, and Pāśinī—
these and other Rudrāṇīs, adorned with darkness, emerged for the battle.
Then all the Pārameṣṭhyas and the Brahmāṇīs also went forth.
The Transitions (saṃkrāntis), the Well-Accomplished Ones (susiddhās), the Accomplishments (siddhis), and those whose essence is Brahman;
Daṇḍanāthā, Mantranāthā, Dhūmorṇā, Mantranāyikā, Śyāmalā, Yantriṇī, Ghanaśyāmā, and Saṅgītayoginī. (21–22)
Tripurā, the mistress of the cakras, the sovereign empress, the universal ruler;
the Mistress of the Tradition of Great Knowledge, the Vedic one, and likewise the one who has reached the summit;
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī as well.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Caṇḍikā of red form;
Kṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, and likewise Vaśaṃkarī;
Unmādinī, Khecarā, Yaṣṭi, and likewise Mahāṅkuśā. (24–25)
And other powers of reality and so forth, dwelling within all seeds,

numbering in the millions, billions, and trillions, issued forth, intoxicated by the frenzy of battle. Likewise, there were goddesses who attract the vital breaths (*mātrā*) and those who attract the mind (*citta*).
There are also those that attract the self and likewise those that attract the body;
Anaṅgalekhā, Sarvajṛmbhaṇā, Mṛtyupradāyinī, Sarvavyādhiharā, and the secret yoginī named Rakṣā. (27–28)
Vaśinī, Jīvanī, Vahnivāsinī, Kulasundarī, Śoṣiṇī, Rati, Prīti, Kānti, Śānti,
Tuṣṭikā, Puṣṭi, Śraddhā, Bhū, Pramāthinī, and Nāgavīthikā.
Mātaṅgī, Siddhalakṣmī, Durgāmbā, and Potriṇī;
Yakṣiṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Lākinī, and Hākinī; Śākinī, Ḍākinī, Dhātunāthā, Vārtālikā, and Andhinī. (3.116.30–31)
These other Śaktis, born from the Arbudābja, emerged in the battle.
Then Indra, the Apsarases, the Sādhyas, and the Viśvedevas;
Viśvakarman, Maya, Agni, the Rudras, and likewise the Piśācas [also came forth].
The Rākṣasas, the Gandharvas, the Mitrās, and likewise the Kinnaras;
the Vidyādharas, and also Govinda, the Blessed Lord who is the husband of Kamalā;
Brahmā, the two sons of Aśvinī, the Gaṇakas, Dhanvantari, and Vāsuki.
The Nāgas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the family priests also went forth.
At that time, there were mṛdaṅgas, murajas, paṭahas, and various types of kulaṅgas;
selukas, jhallarīs, rāndyas, huḍukas, huḍḍukas, and gharas.
There were also ānaka drums, paṇavas, gomukhas, and ardhacandrikās;
likewise yavamadhyas, mardalas, ḍiṇḍimas, and jharjharas;
as well as varītās, uddhakas, tuhuṇḍas, and barbaras. (36–37)
During the exertion for battle, the sounds of *huṃ* and kettledrums resounded;
all the warriors, accompanied by chariots, horses, elephants, and so forth, were joined by every single weapon, missile, and ten million mantras. (38)
And they arrived at the abode of Bhaṇḍāsura in great celestial chariots of the Mahāyāna.
Seeing the sky pervaded by the army and filled with the roar of battle,
the asuras then trembled with agitation born from the *Lalitāgama*.
Then, for the asuras, misfortunes occurred at every step;
like walls breached out of season, the ramparts of the Daityas' city collapsed.
Great meteors fell, whirling down from the expanse of the sky.
Then earthquakes and tremors of the heart occurred again and again.
Furthermore, herons, vultures, cranes, and other birds perched upon the tops of the banners,
and a wheel appeared in the solar disc as a portent of destruction.
The left limbs of men and the right limbs of women began to throb;
there, banners were seen in the sky,
and the ornaments and garlands of the Daitya women fell off prematurely.
At that time, the mirrors, the armor, the banners, the excellence of the swords,
the jewels, and the garments all became soiled with dust.
Droplets of the water of blood fell upon the centers of the sacrificial altars.
Seeing the portents, the terrified Daityas spoke to Bhaṇḍaka.
Bhaṇḍa, overcome with anger, then summoned his two ministers and quickly held a consultation in the assembly hall regarding the undertaking of war.
Viśukra and Viṣaṅga were his ministers, bestowers of wisdom.
Likewise, the vassal lords and the lords of the Daityas arrived to receive his commands.
Then, while everyone was listening, Viśukra spoke: (48–49)
Surā and the others, having obtained their opportunity, created a woman who was proud of her strength;
and having prepared her, the gods arrived together with her. "They have come to conquer us! Alas, what a calamity ordained by Fate! [3.116.50]
If these women were to defeat us, it would be for our amusement;
yet today the female species rushes toward us for our victory.
Even though a woman may be an enemy, she must be slain by those who desire conquest.
"Having dragged her by the hair, that wicked woman must be brought here; she shall surely take on the status of your own servant.
Having spoken thus, he further incited Bhaṇḍa’s anger there.
Then Viṣaṅga spoke words endowed with wisdom that bring happiness:
"Everything should be done after due deliberation; discernment is the supreme recourse.
Any action performed without discernment leads to destruction. (54–55)

One who desires victory and success must understand the strengths and weaknesses of others through spies. Kings should not show contempt toward enemies— whether they be animals, women, or lowly persons— for power exists everywhere.
"Indeed, power alone is everywhere the cause of the glory of victory.
Let it be considered: who is she, what is her strength, and who are her allies?
Having heard this from Viṣaṅga, Bhaṇḍa spoke with great anger:
"O learned one, why do you entertain such doubt regarding this woman, having abandoned your discernment?
This charming lady was discovered by me through my spies to be devoid of strength. Having created a multitude of women through her illusory power (*māyā*), she has arrived here. (59)
"I have no fear of her; seize her and bring her to me!
Who can defeat Bhaṇḍa, whose greatness transcends the three worlds?
By my punishment, even the gods are not able to breathe."
They dwell indeed hidden in the netherworld, in the ocean, and in deep caverns;
yet these foolish women, conceiving vain and reckless impulses,
do not realize it and rush toward their own destruction, arrogant in their performance of improper acts.
Alternatively, if the gods come placing them at their head,
I am capable of crushing them all together, including Śambhu and the others—
Malaka, Kuraṇḍa, Karaṭaka, and Balāhaka.
Vikaṭa, Karkaṭaka, Humbaka, Halamalluca,
Karkaśa, Kukkura, Jṛmbhaṇa, Ghoṣaka,
Śirālaka, Kūpaka, Laḍuna, and Māraka. (65)
Viṣeṇa, Parūṣa, Draghaṇa, and likewise Kollaṭa;
Dāsera, Mūṣaka, Mahāṇḍa, and likewise Kubhāṇḍaka—
these were the Daityas who possessed the splendor of Hiraṇyākṣa and Hiraṇyakaśipu.
In their presence, even thousands of akṣauhiṇī armies would be reduced to ashes;
as for women, they are but objects of derision on the battlefield due to the play of their illusory charms.
Therefore, seize her by her mass of hair and bring her before me.
"Let all the others take whatever belongs to them as they find it.
Having thus addressed the commander of the army, the lord of three thousand [troops], he said: "O Kuṭilākṣa, arise and equip the forces on all sides! (3.116.70)
Bhaṇḍa went to the inner apartments of the great being Kuṭilākṣa;
then the Dānavas, having prepared their war cries,
equipped themselves with sharp-edged spears, mallets, bhindipālas, and slings.
With *druhaṇas*, *bhūśuṇḍīs*, axes, and even maces;
with clubs, *śataghnīs*, tridents, and arrows;
with half-moons, great discuses, bows, and those wielding the *śārṅga* bow.
With clubs, slings, thunderbolt-arrows, excellent stones, daggers,
snake-fangs, shafts, and likewise with fragments;
with nooses as weapons, maces, fire-balls, and swords.

Equipped with such weapons, those Daityas marched forth. Millions of Daityas, their hands bound with leather guards and clad in armor, set out—some mounted on horses, some on elephants, and others on donkeys. (75–76)
There were riders on camels, riders on wolves, and likewise riders on dogs;
riders on crows, riders on vultures, and those mounted on tigers and other beasts;
riders on lions, those standing upon *śarabhas*, and likewise riders on rhinoceroses.
Mounted on boars, mounted on beasts of prey, and riding upon spirits,
as well as traveling in chariots and celestial vehicles, they set out toward Lalitā.
[They went] toward the crooked leader of the army and the Dānava Durmada.
Accompanied by ten *akṣauhiṇīs*,
Kuṭilākṣa, Tālajaṅgha, Tālabhuja, and Tālakaṭi were dispatched toward Lalitā.
These men indeed guarded the city gates of Bhaṇḍapura.
Accompanied by forty akṣauhiṇīs, they stood there formidable.
Viśukra stationed one akṣauhiṇī around his own palace and dispatched the messenger Kapiśīrṣaka.
At the command of the Asura Bhaṇḍa, he went quickly and announced:
"O beautiful one, become the wife of the great king Bhaṇḍa!
Otherwise, death shall be yours; do as you wish, O passionate lady. (83)
Having heard this, Durgā, the beloved of Hara and friend of Mahālakṣmī, said:
"Kill Bhaṇḍa, you base one! Go quickly to Pātāla;
otherwise, your destruction here shall be brought about by a woman. (84–85)
The messenger related that matter exactly as it was; and Bhaṇḍa,
while Viśukra was listening,
spoke in great anger and immediately gave the order to those [demons] for battle.
Having caused all the generals and the Daityas, who were exultant in battle,
to raise a tumultuous shout of joy, thousands of warriors there,
intoxicated by the frenzy of war, fell upon Lalitā’s army from all sides.
"Kill! Slay! Tear asunder! they cried out;
brandishing their swords, they fell into the great ocean of women.
And then the goddesses, with uplifted staves, fought against the Dānavas.

The goddesses, with their unobstructed weapons, crushed the army of the Dānavas. The earth became crimson with the blood of the Dānavas being struck down by spears, and heaps of the heads of the Daityas fell.
Pierced here and there by spears and weapons, the Dānavas died;
meanwhile, showers of arrows fell in the battle.
The sky became entirely covered with arrows, becoming completely dense.
Durgā released fire and ignited a net of arrows.
The fire, augmented by the power of Hariṇī, set the Daityas ablaze.
Durmada died there, and Viśukra too was torn asunder.
All the guards of the ramparts were struck down by divine weapons;
and those forty guardians of the gate-towers who were there at that time—
those entire akṣauhiṇī divisions— were routed by the armies of Lakṣmī.

The very army that was intended for the protection of Bhaṇḍāsura’s palace, numbering ten akṣauhiṇīs, was destroyed by the goddesses. Bhaṇḍa’s city became like a void, resembling the abode of a ghost. ||96-97||
All the commanders of the army were destroyed because of Bhaṇḍa.
That which was not even conceivable in a dream, nor heard of before this,
and which the Daityas had not even suspected— that calamity then arrived.
Having reflected thus, he dispatched a hundred *akṣauhiṇīs*.
Day and night, a great battle raged, incited by the power of weapons and missiles;
it was joined by the asuras against the goddesses of fortune, those divine women.
A hundred akṣauhiṇīs fell in a single day;
the entire city was shattered and drenched in blood.
Then Bhaṇḍa mobilized an army of three hundred akṣauhiṇīs.
Then he dispatched the entire army of goddesses to destroy [the demons].
Seeing that army of sixty crores belonging to Goddess Lalitā,
they became enraged and, upon seeing it, rushed forward to rid the world of the Daityas.
Holding nooses, clubs, discs, and spears; bearing maces, sharp-edged spears, bows, and tridents—
they flocked there by the millions, as if they were drinking up the ocean of the Daityas.
Untouched by the weapons of others, those divine [missiles] pierced the asuras.
The two armies entered into each other’s midst;
indeed, the two oceans of troops attained a state of total confusion.
Those three hundred akṣauhiṇī divisions were indeed cut down by the goddesses;
by the grace of Mahālakṣmī, the women were not pierced at all.
No wounds occurred, nor did the weapons even touch them.
Victory then belonged to Mahālakṣmī, and Bhaṇḍa indeed grieved at that time.
"How might victory be mine? How might I remain alive?
Thus he thought again and again as he entered a cavity in the earth.
At that time, Bhaṇḍaka indeed remembered the Kaikasa Daityas—
those who had previously obtained a boon from the Sun and were capable of victory in a great battle.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Mahālakṣmī’s Armies Setting Out for the Destruction of Bhaṇḍa, the Counsel of Bhaṇḍāsura, the Annihilation of Bhaṇḍa’s Forces, and Bhaṇḍa’s Remembrance of the Kaikasas," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

→ Chapter 118
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: How did the Daityas named Kaikasas obtain their boon in former times, by virtue of which they achieved victory in the world, even in battle against Nārāyaṇī?
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you that nowhere else does victory ever choose anyone but Nārāyaṇī; in the end, victory belongs only to those who have taken refuge in Hari.
But for those who have properly kindled their fervor in the great battle,
O Lakṣmī, victory appears for a moment as both the bringer of destruction and the possessor of triumph. Formerly, the seven brothers born of Kaikasī [sought] the Sun.
Having set [him] as their goal, they performed austerities for a hundred years without water.
They then became almost withered when the Sun appeared; he spoke to the sons of Kaikasī: "By your austerity now—" (4–5)

"I am well-pleased; may it be well with you, O Dānavas; choose a boon," he said. Thus addressed, they chose this boon: "Whosoever shall be our enemy in combat—whether woman, man, human, god, or any other being created by Brahmā—" || 6 ||
O Sūrya, you must certainly remain so that their eyes are blinded; you should stand before them sideways so that, with your terrible splendors, you burn those who oppose us. (7–8)
Likewise, let every object within the range of their vision then become motionless;
let those enemies be deprived of the power of sight and fall into blindness.
Let their weapons become rigid and motionless so that they may be slain, and victory shall be ours.
Thus addressed by the sons of Kaikasā, Ravi said, "So be it.
He further declared: "When I behold unrighteousness, I shall go to my dissolution;
however, in a righteous battle, I shall undoubtedly be your ally."
Thus addressed by Śrī, those Kaikasas, who considered themselves victorious,
arrived for the sake of victory through the power of Sūrya as instructed by Bhaṇḍa. By the very power of the boon they had received, they moved about in battle, arrogant with pride.
Then, gazed upon by those [demons] whose eyes were entered by the sun,
the gods stood with fixed eyes; their enthusiasm became fruitless, and their powers, overcome by the affliction of blindness, remained silent.
The Daityas crushed the army of Śakti with unrighteous combatants;
the Lakṣmīs became despondent, paralyzed, blind, and devoid of activity.
Their vision failed them, for that battle was not born of dharma.

An enemy who has laid down his weapons, one who is defenseless, one who is drinking, one who is fleeing, one who has fallen, one who is bound, or one who has come for refuge— these must not be slain in battle. For unrighteousness indeed afflicts those who employ violence against such persons.
The Kaikasi-born ones struck the virtuous goddesses with arrows and other weapons;
their bodies were then touched by the floods of the Daityas’ missiles.
Crying out "Alas! Alas!", they then remembered Laliteśvarī.
Then Lalitāśrī quickly spoke to Sūrya regarding his unrighteousness:
"Behold this unrighteousness, O Sūrya, committed by the Daityas against warriors who were not fighting; how can you stand idly toward your enemies? (3.117.20)
The Sun himself emerged from the eye of the Daitya out of fear of the curse;
and the Śaktis, their blindness gone, then fought with great speed.
Uttering lion-like roars, they discharged formidable arrows.
The Daityas could not endure the arrows, which resembled black serpents;
being crushed here and there, they found no stability there.
And the Sāvitra weapon, dispatched by Sāvitrī, [fell] upon the crores of Daityas.
The seven Kākaseyas and likewise ten million soldiers were then slain by the force of his weapons; consequently, rivers of blood arose.
Only a few survivors, who were very dear to Bhaṇḍa, fled to him.
They indeed announced their own destruction, and Bhaṇḍa fell into despair.
The hosts of deities announced that Sāvitrī had attained victory;
then Bhaṇḍa also held a consultation with his remaining followers.
"Alas! The destruction of the Daitya clans has indeed occurred;
the powerful Fate has now begun to practice indifference toward them.
Merely at the mention of my name, the inhabitants of heaven flee. (27)
For us who are such as we are, this reversal has come here:
it makes the strong weak, the wealthy destitute, the long-lived short-lived, and the king a servant of the beggar. (28–29)
"Where is the strength of our arms, and where is this ill-behaved woman, by whom the highly arrogant army commanders have been struck down like mere maidservants? Indeed,
she must be captured alive and enjoyed by force."
"Then my liberation would be achieved; let them seize that Sujīvitā!
Or else, by you disguised in female attire, or by these Daitya women likewise, let Jīvayoginī be seized through a ruse as you gather together. (31–32)
Alternatively, let a most fierce and supreme battle indeed be waged first;
let our troops be drawn up at the front of those armies.
For with only a small force supporting her from behind, she will be easy for me to capture.
Therefore, assuming the guise of a woman, I shall go to that very place where she is.
Having forcibly seized her, devoured her, and then killed her,
and having destroyed all the others as well, I shall return to my own abode.
She alone is the most exalted root of all powers without exception;
by her destruction at the very root, the entire multitude of powers perishes.
Having drawn her forth and conquered her, I shall either enjoy her or lead her home.
Thus addressed by the mantra, this evil counselor Bhaṇḍa-dānava took his generals and his armies and went forth to the field of battle;
evening fell, and thick darkness set in. (37–38)
For the wicked asuras, the night alone provides strength;
indeed, their army, active during that time, stood at the front of the goddesses' army.
They fought with blows from weapons in the darkness that destroys life.
There, millions of Daityas were struck down and killed;
indeed, blows that both restored life and took it away occurred.
For Bhaṇḍa’s secret movements followed wherever the Queen of the Gods went. (3.117.40–41)
There they waged war, engaging in a great battle both behind and in front.
Then there were the Śaktis, headed by Kālī, who shine at night;
the Bhairavīs, the Bhairavas, the hosts of Rudras, the Rudrāṇīs, and the Īśikās.
The Bhūtyas struck down the Dānavas and Daityas, and the Dānavas in turn struck down the Bhūtyas.
That army of the Dānavas, consisting of ten Akṣauhiṇīs, was entirely destroyed during the night,
and Bhaṇḍa fled.
The night turned into dawn, and the quarters of the sky became clear;
Lalitā attained satisfaction with the victorious goddesses.
Then Bhaṇḍa, having consulted again with his own sons, [proceeded].
He dispatched his four sons, each with four arms and four faces, into the battle. Those thirty arrogant ones fought day and night.
An army of two hundred akṣauhiṇīs, most impetuous, marched forth.
The daughter of Mahālakṣmī, named Santoṣikā, was Śrībālā;
that maiden then became ready to fight in the battle,
accompanied by a hundred crores of female companions and bearing all types of weapons.
Endowed with eighteen arms, she rushed toward Bhaṇḍa’s army.
Then a battle commenced, characterized by exceedingly fierce valor;
Śrī Bālā assumed ten million forms, intoxicated by the fight.
The daughter of Lalitā displayed her prowess in battle;
by discharging weapon after counter-weapon, she struck down them all in an instant.
By the discharge of the Nārāyaṇa weapon, that illustrious young maiden [overcame them].
In a single day, she reduced an army of two hundred akṣauhiṇīs to ashes.
That young maiden simultaneously dispatched thirty horses and your sister-in-law’s sons—
the offspring of Bhaṇḍa— to the abode of Yama out of her satisfaction.
He suddenly dispatched [them], indeed piercing their heads;
and the Śaktis there repeatedly uttered cries of "Well done!
Then the other Daityas, with only a slight hope for life, fled away.
Having reached their own home, they expressed their grief to Bhaṇḍa.
Then, hearing that his sons were lost, Bhaṇḍa was overwhelmed by the fire of sorrow;
perceiving the destruction of his lineage, he lamented aloud.
"Alas! I am slain, I am ruined, and I am truly unfortunate today;
for even now, there exists a woman who will bring about the destruction of my lineage.
Having spoken thus, his consciousness lost as his vision faded, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Then, having risen and drawn his formidable sword, he declared:
"Right now, by cutting that Lakṣmī into pieces with this sword in battle, I shall attain eternal peace."
Thus brandishing his sword and uttering these words, he advanced into the fray:
"I shall suck dry all those [oceans]; I shall make them my own beloveds;
I shall cut down all the gods and shatter the abodes of the gods."
"Crush the armies!"—thus enraged, he advanced into battle.
Then all his brothers were appointed as generals, but they too were slain;
for three full days, the entire war raged for the sake of my destruction.
"Either there shall be destruction or victory; there can be no strength without one's own power.
I shall either recover that lovely wife or I shall bring about her end," he said repeatedly, brandishing his sword and shaking it.
Enraged like the fire of cosmic destruction, he stood at the head of the army of women.
Beholding him, Lalitā, whose beauty was exquisite, set out to fight with him;
her chariot, the king of all wheels, shone brightly as it advanced toward him.
He who is the great fear for the four Vedas, the Great Wheel, and the goals of human existence;
he who is resplendent with the banner of bliss and endowed with the nine stages (navabhūmi);
[he who is surrounded] by the goddesses residing in the nine stages, whose heavy bows are drawn.
Accompanied by divine and non-divine attendants numbering more than a parārdha,
[the chariot] was ten yojanas high and four yojanas wide;
the mounts of the other goddesses were likewise in numbers of a parārdha.
Assuming divine forms, they— namely lions, camels, men, beasts of prey,
wild animals, birds, horses, as well as elephants, bheruṇḍas, śarabhas, tigers, vātamṛgas, and so forth—
constantly roared for the sake of destroying Bhaṇḍa.
Divine drums resounded and showers of flowers fell;
auspicious omens appeared for Lakṣmī’s army at that time.
Then, battle commenced between both armies.
The hosts of Dānavas were incessantly slain by throngs of women;
at that time, the earth became filled with dancing headless trunks of Daityas, strewn with thousands of their heads adorned with hair, resembling coconut fruits. (72)
With villages whose elephants were sliced by wheels, with the intentions of asuras destroyed by spears,
filled with the faces of heroic Daityas, and muddy with the flow of blood— I beheld her, and even fear of death arose within me. (73–74)
On the fourth day, the destruction of the Daitya army occurred; thereafter,
a battle equal to that of Lalitāśrī took place against Bhaṇḍāsura,
involving the agitation of missiles and counter-missiles, as well as life-taking arrows.
Released by Mahālakṣmī, that single arrow became tenfold;
in the sky it became tenfold, in the army of the Daityas it became hundredfold,
and upon contact with the bodies of the Daityas, those arrows then reached the number of a hundred thousand.
She thoroughly pierced Bhaṇḍa’s vital organs with her arrows.
Bhaṇḍa then released a terrifying weapon called Andhatāmisra;
Mahālakṣmī dispelled it with the Mahābhāskara arrow.
Then, in the battle, the Daitya Bhaṇḍa discharged the Pākhaṇḍa weapon;
Lakṣmī discharged the Gāyatrī weapon and struck it down.
Then Bhaṇḍa released the Andha weapon, which obstructs all vision.
Then Mahālakṣmī released the great weapon, Cākṣuṣmata;
Bhaṇḍa then released the Aśakti weapon against the host of women.
In response, Lakṣmī released the fierce Mahāśakti weapon against it.
The demon Bhaṇḍa discharged the Antaka weapon, which causes the destruction of all;
Lakṣmī, however, discharged the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya weapon against it. Then Bhaṇḍa indeed released the Sarvādhītivināśa weapon.
I discharged the *dhāraṇā* weapon, which bestows fortune and intelligence upon my own [followers].
Then Bhaṇḍa discharged the *bhaya* (fear) weapon, and Kamalā the *abhaya* (fearlessness) weapon.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the *mahāmaya* (great illusion) weapon, and Lakṣmī the *nirāmaya* (freedom from illness) weapon.
Then Bhaṇḍa [discharged] the life-destroying weapon (*āyurnāśanāstra*), and Lakṣmī the yoga-weapon (*yogāstra*).
Then Bhaṇḍaka discharged the demonic weapon (*āsurāstra*), and Lakṣmī the Durgā-weapon (*durgāstraka*).
[This was done] against hundreds of thousands of demons and hundreds of thousands of Durgā-yoginīs.
The armies were in the sky and fought with great speed;
grasping tridents, discs, maces, spears, bows, swords, arrows, thunderbolts,
staffs, nooses, and balls, they struck one another.
They slaughtered them excessively, yet they did not touch the goddesses at all.
There, the Asuras were slain on all sides by the hosts of goddesses;
likewise, Durgā, having mounted her lion-vehicle, engaged in battle.
Nārāyaṇī Mahālakṣmī indeed attained victory.
Then Bhaṇḍa released the ocean-weapon (*arṇavāstra*) upon the host of women.
Thereupon, Mahālakṣmī released the drying weapon (*śoṣaṇāstra*) into the sky.
Then the enraged demon Bhaṇḍa let out a roar of defiance (huṃkāra).
Thereupon, thousands of demons were born; Durgā sent them to Yama.
Then Bhaṇḍa discharged the deer-weapon (hariṇyastra), and Lakṣmī unleashed the lion-weapon (siṃhāstra).
Bhaṇḍa discharged the Balya weapon, and Lakṣmī the Vāmana weapon;
Bhaṇḍaka discharged the Haihaya weapon, and Īśvarī the Paraśurāma weapon.
Then Bhaṇḍa discharged the Rāvaṇa weapon, and Lakṣmī discharged the Rāma weapon.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the Rāja-astra, while Lakṣmī discharged the Kṛṣṇa-astra.
Bhaṇḍa Daitya discharged the Brahmāṇḍa-astra, while Kamalā discharged the Vyūha-astra.
Bhaṇḍa Daitya discharged the Kalpa-astra, and Lakṣmī discharged the Kalki-astra.
Having all brought about the destruction of the asuras, those ten incarnations,
having offered salutations to Lalitā Śrī with their palms joined in reverence, stood there; then,
by the command of Mahālakṣmī, they departed for Vaikuṇṭha.
Bhaṇḍa discharged the weapon of delusion (moha), while Lakṣmī deployed the weapon of knowledge (jñāna).
With the Nārāyaṇa weapon, Lakṣmī reduced the Daityas to ashes;
with fire, she likewise reduced all the army commanders to ashes.
He reduced Bhaṇḍa to ashes by the fiery power of the weapon of the Supreme Brahman;
he turned the city to ashes until only its foundations remained.
Then Bhaṇḍa died, and the three worlds became filled with the sound of joyful celebration.
By reciting or hearing this, fear of the Daityas is destroyed. There is no doubt that fear of enemies and calamities perish;
moreover, they attain enjoyment, liberation, fortune, and supreme prosperity.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Destruction of the Armies of the Asura Bhaṇḍa by the Forces of Mahālakṣmī and the Subsequent Slaying of the Asura Bhaṇḍa," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 118: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 118]
[The Author: Chapter 119.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, Sovereign of the lords of sovereigns!
After the destruction of Bhaṇḍa, what happened at dawn on the fourth day?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
After the battle, Lalitā Ramā [removed] the fatigue of all the goddesses.
Mahālakṣmī dispelled [their distress] with glances like nectar and ambrosia.
Then Mahālakṣmī gave them most divine meals, along with honors consisting of gifts of respect, rewards, and other highly precious offerings. (2–3)
Then she bestowed all divine ornaments;
having placed within her own heart all those forms numbering in the millions, billions, and hundreds of millions,
the Great Ramā, overflowing with affection, embraced them all at once.
"O Brāhmaṇa, I shall give my daughter to each of you," he said;
"for I bestow upon all of them the eternal, imperishable abode.
They are the eternal beloveds of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (5–6)
"May you all be the queens of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
always possessing the right to his embrace," he said to them all; and he placed moonbeams upon their foreheads as a garland, giving it to them so that they might offer it around his own neck.
"Then, O beloved ones! all those millions, billions, and trillions of Brahmā’s daughters—those goddesses who are portions of myself—were placed by them all upon my neck as garlands;
they have all become my beloveds, who are now mine. (8–9)
O Lakṣmī, while you were indeed present, I then married those who are your beloveds in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā;
they are your co-wives and sisters, born from different lands for my sake.
For these women of mine—human, divine, ancestral, and others—are my wives who have attained many bodies.
Listen, Lakṣmī: at the fourth hour, at midday, the hosts of deities [assemble].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Mahendra, and Bṛhaspati;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and the Sādhyadevatās;
the Siddhas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Yakṣas, the Guardians of the Quarters, and the Protectors of the Worlds.
The Daityas, Dānavas, and Nāgas who were devotees of Viṣṇu,
as well as those on the side of the gods and those of the Asuras— whether characterized by tamas or rajas—
all heard of Śrī Vijaya’s victory and likewise beheld the happiness of the gods. (14–15)
Assembled there in the assembly hall, adorned by the entirety of womankind,
the Gandharvas together with the Apsaras praised the Great Ramā:
"Obeisance, obeisance to you, O Supreme Goddess, the foremost form among women, whose nature is half that of Hari!"
O Mother of the three-fold creation, who dwells in the abode of the Imperishable within the Great Imperishable, we bow down, we bow down to you!
(17) Salutations to you, the dwelling place of all incarnations and the like; salutations to you, the abode of tens of millions of all the Lords.
Salutations to you, the residence of all the Sovereign Goddesses; salutations to you, the supreme abode of the hosts of both liberated and unliberated women. (18)
Salutations to you, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa’s consort; salutations to you, the mother of Siddhas, Ṛṣis, and virtuous Pitṛs.
Salutations to you, who are well-served by the host of Sureśvarīs; salutations be to you, who possess the form of Śrīmānavī.
(19) Salutations to you, O Śrī-Kambharā, O Śrī-Lalitā, O Consort of the Lord, O Mother of Santoṣikā.
O Elephant-faced One, O Mother of corresponding form, salutations to you who possess the nature of a doe!
(3.118.20) O Sovereign of all, O Mistress of all Ramādhī, O Śrīmāṇikī, Pāśavatī, and Pramodā;
O you who are the source of the great ocean of Lakṣmī, O you who abide as the beloved of Brahmā, salutations to you constantly! (21)

O Yoginī, salutations to you! You who are the sovereign of desire, skilled in granting what is sought, the wish-fulfilling gem from whom the manifold world is born, the bestower of liberation, whose eyes are the sun and the moon, and whose smile is gentle.
Salutations, salutations to you, O Mother, slayer of the great asura Bhaṇḍa and destroyer of all the Daityas!
Homage to you, O Mistress of Mudrās, who take the form of the excellent Yantra and are the source of all sacred learning!
Homage to you, O Kṛṣṇā, the Supreme, stationed within the six excellent wheels, the destroyer of the six waves [of worldly existence] and the dispeller of fatigue!
Homage to you, O Mother, who are void of the six states of being, the locus of the eight qualities, the sovereign of all principal queens!
O beloved mistress of the lord of the lotus, O most pure one, O sovereign of the world, O dear one,
O elixir dwelling in all essences!
And let there be constant salutations to you of divine form!

(25) O Consort of the God of gods, O Mother of the world, O Progenitress, obeisance, obeisance to you—who are eternally served by the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*, who dwell upon the couch that is Gopālakṛṣṇa himself! (26)
O beloved of Brahmā, delight of Brahmā, glory of Hari, whose essence is Brahmā, Śrī Lalitā, salutations to you!

O stream of the nectar of Brahman, destroyer of rebirth, Sovereign of Brahmā, Śrī Lalitā, salutations to you! O auspicious refuge, bestower of welfare, known as the Imperishable, who has destroyed the host of enemies, Lalitā, salutations to you!
O Śrī Lalitā, supreme over all, omnipresent, bestower of all perfections— salutations to you! O Śrī Lalitā, fulfiller of the desires of all the immortals, granter of boons— salutations to you!
O you who abide in the *bindu*, whose form is the *bindu*, O Śrī with large breasts and a swaying necklace of lotuses;
O bestower of fruits, O trembling creeper, O one radiant as the sun, O lotus-faced one, O lovely one— salutations to you!
O Supreme Person, you who are the essence of the earth, O Śrī, Bhūpadmikā, and the very soul of Ajā and Kamalā;
O treasure-house of mercy, you who excel in the work of the gods, O Śrī-Vaiṣṇavī, you who manifest as all the glorious incarnations.
O mother of beautiful eyes like those of a young deer, O captivating one; salutations to you, O graceful and exceedingly beautiful one!
O glorious Mahālakṣmī, bestower of prosperity! (31)
O Mother,
who has transcended the cycle of rebirth, you have protected the entire world by slaying Bhaṇḍāsura and other demons in battle.
Manmatha was indeed reduced to ashes by Śrī Śambhu,
and even Bhaṇḍa, who arose from those ashes, was slain by you;
for even the ashes of Kāma have become beautifully ashed [by your power].
Freedom from desire and the state of being without water were demonstrated.
The gross body of Madana was burnt by Śambhu, but his subtle body was subsequently burnt by you.
Thus, beholding her husband devoid of both his bodies, Rati prayed for his life;
then again, there was the conceptualization of a causal body.
That which was composed of many latent impressions (vāsanā) became an invisible body for Rati; indeed, he gave her a vast, pervasive form belonging to Ramaṇa. ||35||
Rati, having beheld her own supreme beloved— who dwells within the hearts of all beings,
yet remains invisible— was filled with delight.
She embraced her husband with a heart full of serenity.
For although desire is formless, it performs the function of having a form when it is directed toward you. 36.
By your command, Skanda attained pervasiveness through union with the daughter of the mountain;
he became the conqueror of the gross Kama.
It should be understood that he becomes the very nature of Śambhu;
it should be understood that he becomes the very nature of Lakṣmī, the conqueror of subtle desire. (38)
"Kuvāsanā is the mother of Anaṅgaja, and Nārāyaṇa is indeed to be understood as one who has ascended upwards.
Thus, O Supreme Goddess, the Mistress of all, everything has been explained by you for our liberation.
Having thus praised and worshipped her, they sat down with joyful minds.
Everyone celebrated a festival on that occasion on the field of battle.
That kingdom, possessing charming prosperity, was given to the Lord of Rati;
and Kāma himself, assuming any form at will, became the king and ruled the realm.
He was born as the lord of nine hundred thousand [demons], Kāma, the master and lord of Rati;
he was full of affection, a devotee of Śrī Mahālakṣmī, and a follower of Nārāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, he has been captured by me today for the gratification of you all.
This devotee of mine is indeed divine; he truly exists as one liberated from the *guṇas*.
His very nature is that of one whose desires are fulfilled, and he bestows the bliss of the beloved of Brahman.
Although possessing *guṇas*, he has attained an infinite form throughout the three worlds.
O Lakṣmī, by your grace, the Lord of Rati remains all-pervading;
then the gods, the ancestors, the high-souled ones,
and the great sages all departed to their own worlds, while Mahālakṣmī remained ever-present.

He dwelt eternally in the city of Kāñcī, which is the very form of Mahāvaikuṇṭha. In his second form, he went to the abode of Mahāviṣṇu; indeed, in his third form, he exists as the illustrious Kaṃbharā.
In her fourth form as Gajānanā, she will manifest;
she who is known by the name Śrī Lalitā will experience [her glory] in Saurāṣṭra.
Indeed, there will be infinite incarnations thereafter.
They are unapproachable, indescribable, divine, and always bestowers of liberation.
The beginningless Great Power, the Brāhmī Śrī Puruṣottamī, is to be known as my mother Kambharā; she exists as Mahālakṣmī. (3.118.50)
Serve that mother-in-law, O Lakṣmī; she is the eternal bestower of liberation and the giver of mokṣa.
I serve her always and bow repeatedly to my mother.
For those devoted to the service of their mother, there shall never be an evil fate anywhere.
Service to one's mother brings about the destruction of great obstacles and demons.
Listen, Lakṣmī, and I shall likewise describe to you other auspicious temples of my mother Mahālakṣmī, who is Lalitā. (52–53)
Wherein she, divided into sixteen forms, makes her dwelling;
all these were fashioned by Maya and Viśvakarman upon Meru,
as well as on Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himācala.
On Mount Gandhamādana, on Nīlādri, on Meṣādri, on Śṛṅgaparvata,
and on Mahendra— these indeed are the auspicious terrestrial abodes.
These nine sacred sites (tīrthas) are truly bestowers of liberation.
Furthermore, there are other water-based [palaces] situated in the seven oceans:
indeed, the palaces are located in the salt ocean, the sugarcane juice ocean, the wine ocean, the clarified butter ocean,
the curd ocean, the milk ocean, and the sweet ocean.
Indeed, they are adorned with jewels, diamonds, and gems;
they are vast and lofty, and truly possessed of great gardens.
There are thousands of trees that always bear flowers and always bear fruit. (58–59)
Always rich in the beauty of fresh sprouts and perpetually filled with fragrance, these trees, embodying all seasons, serve as the cause of Lakṣmī’s adornment;
their sweet nectar is like nectar itself, and their flowers are her ornaments.
Those divine yellow garments are indeed like coral.
Such wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) stand before the mansions;
there are also wish-fulfilling ponds, wish-fulfilling halls, and groves of yellow sandalwood (haricandana).
There are groves of Mandāra trees, gardens of Pārijāta and other celestial blossoms,
and groves of Kadamba trees, all made of divine sugar.
Indeed, the dwellings of Mahālakṣmī are composed entirely of wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi).
O Lakṣmī! In ancient times, the great sage Mātaṅga was a devoted servant;
possessing the dharma of an ascetic, he performed the worship of Mahālakṣmī.
Mahālakṣmī, being pleased with him, granted him the fulfillment of his every resolve.
Overwhelmed with joy and overflowing with devotion, he praised Lakṣmī, the sovereign of his field of experience:
"O Mother, by the mere remembrance of you,
all my perfections (siddhis), beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as all other divine manifestations, have indeed come to be."
"There is indeed nothing in the three worlds that remains for me to attain;
however, act in such a way that I may behold you constantly.
Having been addressed thus in a dream by Mahālakṣmī, O wife of the elephant! (67–68)
She took a single cluster of *tāpiccha* blossoms from her ear-ornament and gave it to her;
thereupon, that wife Siddhimatī became pregnant.
That daughter was named Śyāmā because she was as dark-complexioned as Viṣṇu.
Indeed, from the womb of Siddhimatī, she was born as Janmavatī.
Thereafter, Śyāmā shone forth after having worshipped Mahālakṣmī;
she remained constantly by Mahālakṣmī’s side in her service as a companion.
Being served by her, she is considered Vaiṣṇavī, who is dark-complexioned (saśyāmā). There is also a second attendant, Ghanashyāmā, who likewise serves her.
And Meghaputrī indeed serves Mahālakṣmī from the sky.
Devoted to graceful worship, meditation, recitation, and praise, Madhuśrī and Mādhava attend upon the Supreme Goddess; Śukraśrī and Śuciśrī also attend upon the Supreme Goddess. (73–74)
The goddesses of the beauty of Nabhas and Nabhasya attend upon the Supreme Sovereign;
likewise, the goddesses of the beauty of Iṣa and Urja attend upon the Supreme Sovereign;
and the goddesses of the beauty of Saha and Sahasya attend upon the Supreme Sovereign.
The splendor of austerity and the splendor of ascetic practice attend upon the Supreme Goddess.
The powers of spring, who are Lakṣmīs themselves, serve the Supreme Goddess,
being devoted to the worship, meditation, recitation, and hymns of Lalitā.
Divine women endowed with devotion toward Lalitā reside there;
the birds there are most celestial, and the attendants are served by the Siddhas.
They constantly mutter the mantra of Lalitā and are ever devoted to the command of Lalitā.
Cāraṇas and Cāraṇīs, as well as millions of gods, are present;
they repeatedly sing songs composed in the style of Lalitādevī.
Multitudes of Gandharvas and Apsarases sing with the sounds of their lutes. (3.118.80)
Those of delicate form who possess devotion to Śrī Lakṣmī,
as well as yogins and yoginīs filled with devotion to Viṣṇu, serve Lalitā-Lakṣmī and meditate upon her, each according to their own capacity.
And the Kinnaras and Kimpuruṣas, together with their Kinnarīs and others, always recite that mantra for the sake of increasing their own good fortune;
dancing and singing, they serve Puruṣottamī.
Those supreme men who are devotees of Lalitāparameśvarī possess divine bodies and always serve their mother, Śrī Lakṣmī.
Those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) and are practitioners of the worship of Śrī Lakṣmī—
Having attained perfection, they dwell there as enjoyers of happiness.
Indeed, those who have muttered the Lalitā-mantra, who have been initiated into the Lalitā-śāstra, and who worship Lalitā, reside among them in those Śrī-nagaras. (85–86)
In that regard, those who possess knowledge, who are devoted, who are dedicated to Mahālakṣmī,
who are rich in devotion, and who are of the nature of Brahman— they enter the imperishable state. Jayā, Lalitā, and Jyeṣṭhā indeed lead them to the imperishable state.

They dwell in the presence of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. Residing in the world of the gods with their wives in the glorious Purottama, they live endowed with devotion, chanting the name of Śrī Lakṣmī.
The Siddhas, the divine rishis, and others who practice the mastery of breath (pavana),

as well as those liberated through the wind (māruta) and the divine, serve the Supreme Goddess. So too do the treasures (nidhis), the supernatural powers (ṛddhis), the prosperities (bhūtis), and the manifestations (vibhūtis).
Divine beings dwell right there and serve Puruṣottamī.
And indeed, many wish-fulfilling cows, proud of their milk-offerings, devoted to the pleasure of Lalitā, serve Laliteśvarī. || 91–92 ||
The Rudrāṇīs and likewise the Rudras, adorned with all ornaments,
as well as the attendants of Rudra, serve Laliteśvarī.
All of them are great-souled beings, possessing the supreme forms of Vaiṣṇavas.

Those proficient in the meditation on the Goddess Śrī, those who mutter the mantra of Śrī Lakṣmī, and the great devotees of Śrī Lakṣmī serve Puruṣottamī. The Śatarudras, endowed with devotion, and the divine Vaiṣṇavas serve her as well. (94–95)
Aryaman, the creator of the universe, accompanied by all the sages, serves her;
Marīci and the others serve Lalitāśrī, the supreme sovereign.
All the sciences (vidyās) and auxiliary sciences (upavidyās) serve her by the thousands.
All the *kalās* and the maidens serve me, the Supreme Sovereign.
Likewise, the eternal Lord Viṣṇu, the Lord of Śrī, serves her;
the Master exists in fourfold, tenfold, and twelvefold forms.
Mādhava, assuming various forms, constantly and perpetually serves her;
likewise, the deities of the ten incarnations serve that Supreme Goddess in the ruby pavilion,
bearing their conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
Nārāyaṇa, Keśava, Govinda, and likewise Mādhava serve the auspicious Mahālakṣmī, their beautiful and virtuous mother; and the personified scriptures also serve the supreme sovereign lady, Śrī.
The omniscient Mahādeva serves Satī with devotion;
all the planets, the hosts of zodiac signs, the lunar mansions, and even the stars,
as well as the fiery powers, worship the Supreme Goddess.
The Moon, together with the constellations, waits upon the Supreme Goddess.
(103) Through the recitations, meditations, hymns, and even hundreds of worship-rites dedicated to Lalitā, the Moon, joined by Aśvinī and the other lunar mansions, serves the Supreme Goddess. (104)
Others, graceful and lotus-eyed, adorned with various ornaments,
wait upon Mahālakṣmī— the goddess of charming beauty—
submissively. Agni, accompanied by his own wife, serves the Supreme Goddess.
Dhūmrārcis, Uṣṇā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī,
Visphulliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā—
these women, joined with fire, serve the supreme sovereign Mahālakṣmī. (1.06–1.07)
Accompanied by the twelve powers— Sūryā, Tapanī, Tāpī, Dhūmrā, Jvālā, Ruci, Kṣamā, Suṣumṇā, Bodhinī, Bhogā, Marīci, Dhāriṇī, and Viśvā— he serves her.
Candrakalā, Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣṇā, Rati, Dhṛti, Tuṣṭi,
Puṣṭi, Candrikā, Śrī, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Aṅgadā, Śaśā, Prīti, Pūrṇā, Amṛtā, and Pūrṇā serve the Supreme Goddess. (3.118.10)
Nourishment, prosperity, stability, intelligence, beauty, fortune, splendor,
fortitude, old age, and accomplishment— these digits of Brahmā serve the Goddess. Stability, protection, peace, the Sovereign, desire, and the multitude [of powers] likewise attend her.
Varadā, Hlādinī, Prīti, and Dīrghā are the portions (kalās) of Hari.
They always serve Śrī Lakṣmī, who is graceful, along with Viṣṇu.
Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Nidrā, Tandrā, Kṣut, Krodhinī, and Trapā— [are likewise his portions]. || 1.12–1.13 ||
Utkārī and Mṛtyu— these fierce *kalās*, accompanied by Hara,
serve the auspicious Mahālakṣmī, Lalitā, and the virtuous Kambharā.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Dīpikā.
Indirā, Rocikā, Muktā, Parā, Sūkṣmā,
Amṛtā, Kalā, Jñānā, Vyāptā, Vyomikā, Vyādhinī, and Cārikā— these sixteen attend upon that Great Lakṣmī, the Mother who is the Supreme Person.
Thus have the attendants of the Mother in Śrīpura been described to you.
By the mere hearing of their names, the destruction of sins occurs; for one possessed of devotion, liberation shall come to pass.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship for the Victory of Śrī Lalitā Mahālakṣmī, the Hymn to Mahālakṣmī, Rewards for the Victors, the Assumed Forms [of the Goddess], the Sixteen Temples of Mahālakṣmī, the Splendor therein, and Service to the Śaktis," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
