Chapter 120 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
In that same way, Śrī Lalitā Lakṣmī is always worshipped by the Śaktis;
she is eternally served by the Śaktis, the Śaktas, and others, and I rejoice in her presence on all sides. (1)
Those female servants and female disciples constantly perform worship;
all of them, though established in various distinct forms, are her own daughters.
Gāyatrī, Gaṇeśa, and likewise Mahāgaṇapati—
Sampadeśī, likewise Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Mahāramā, Śrīmahāśambhunāthā, and Parāmbikā worship her; as do Annapūrṇā, Pādukāśrī, Mahāpadmā, and Varāhiṇī. (3–4)
Tiraskaraṇī, Śrīpūrti, and Śrīpādā worship [her]; Raśmimālā and the lords of mantrins, as well as the lords of the staff (daṇḍanāthas), indeed worship her.
All of them worship Lalitā-Śrī in the palace of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Aṇimā and mahimā, as well as laghimā and garimā;
īśitā and vaśitā, mukti, and likewise prākāmya—desire, attainment, and the fulfillment of all wishes attend upon the Great Rāmā. (6–7)
The auspicious attainments of alchemy (rasasiddhi), the attainment of gold (mākṣasiddhi), and the attainment of strength (balasiddhi);
as well as the attainment of the sword (khaḍgasiddhi), the attainment of the feet (pādasiddhi), and the attainment of collyrium (añjanāsiddhi);
the attainment of speech (vāksiddhi), the attainment of the world (lokasiddhi), and the attainment of the body (dehasiddhi) attend upon him.
There are tens of millions of others as well, and various supernatural powers (siddhis) remain close at hand.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī likewise worship her. (3.119.10)
Kṣobhiṇī, Drāviṇī, Ākarṣiṇī, Saṃvaśinī,
as well as Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, and Bījikā;
and Trikhaṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī— these, being well-sealed, worship [him].
Tripurā is the Mistress, as well as Pālinī and Kṣobhaṇā;
likewise there is Kāmākarṣaṇikā, and another, Buddhyākarṣaṇikā;
similarly Rasākarṣaṇikā, and another, Gandhākarṣaṇikā. (12–13)
Likewise, there is the art of attracting the mind, as well as that of attracting fortitude;
also the art of attracting mindfulness, and the art of attracting names;
similarly, the art of attracting seeds, and indeed the art of attracting objects.
Amṛtāvarṣiṇī and likewise Śarīrākarṣiṇī—these are the divine yoginīs, auspicious and fulfillers of all desires. They are Pālikā, Drāvikā, and Mudrā, proud of their fresh youth. (15–16)
Deities of divine splendor, possessing exceedingly beautiful forms, worship Mahālakṣmī, the supreme goddess Lalitā;
so too do Kusumāmekhalā, Madanā, and Madanāturā. (17)
Rekhā, Veginī, Aṅkuśā, Mālinī, and Sundarī;
Hlādinī, Jṛmbhiṇī, Vaśaṃkarī, Rañjanakāriṇī, Unmādinī, Arthakarī, Sampatpūrā, and Mantriṇī. (18–19)
And the protectors of the tradition serve the Supreme Goddess— She who bestows perfection, She who grants prosperity, She who acts for the beloved's sake,
and the Auspicious One; likewise, She who grants desires, destroys suffering, removes death, and dispels obstacles.
She bestows good fortune, she is all-knowing, the Śaktinī who is the very form of knowledge;
she bestows sovereignty, she removes disease, she is the great stream, and she destroys sin;
she is blissful, she is a protector, she grants what is desired, and likewise she removes pride.
And Mālinī— all these serve Laliteśvarī.
Likewise Vaśinī, Kāminī, Īśā, Modinī, Vimalā, Vāgdhārā, Jayinī, Kaulinī, and Īśvarī.
All these Sarasvatīs worship the Supreme Goddess:
Siddhā, Khecarī, Kāmeśvarī, Bāṇeśvarī, as well as Vajrikā, Śataghnī, Bhūśuṇḍī, and Muśalī. (24–25)
Kṛpāṇikā, Paṭṭiśā, Mudgarī, and Bhindipālikā—
these goddesses of weaponry attend upon the Supreme Goddess.
Kāmeśī, Vajreśī, Bhagamālā, and Mitrikā [also attend her].
And Ṣoḍaśikā and Gocaryā serve the Supreme Goddess.
Bheruṇḍā, Vahnivāsā, Vajrīśā, Kulasundarī, Vijayā, Nīlapatākā, Jvālāmālā, and Sumaṅgalā [serve her as well]. (27–28)
For the prosperity of the worlds, he serves Lalitā, whose nature is consciousness;
likewise, the goddesses of the heart, the goddess of the head, and the goddess of the crest;
as well as the goddess of armor, the goddess of rain, and the goddess of weapons—these are her beautiful forms.
Those born of *bindu* and *nāda*, who carry out the command of Lalitā, serve her.
(3.119.30) Now, upon the couch consisting of the five Brahmans belonging to the venerable Goddess Lalitā, her four feet indeed become the forms of the [four] *vyūhas*. (3.119.31)
By the grace of Mahālakṣmī, they attained divinity,
becoming united with the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and Īśvara.
These are the feet in embodied form, the Puruṣas who bear weapons.

With eyes closed in auspicious meditation and bodies motionless in auspicious meditation, Mahālakṣmī—the sovereign of Brahmā and the mistress of Lalitā—reposes there. Indeed, the stairs of this couch have truly become personified. || 33–34 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, and space; smell, as well as taste, form, touch, and sound;
the organs of generation and excretion; and the hands, speech, nose, tongue, skin, eyes, and ears. (35)
Ego (ahaṃkāra), intellect (buddhi), mind (manas), primordial nature (prakṛti), and the individual soul (puruṣa);

destiny (niyati), time (kāla), passion (rāga), the limited power (kalā), the illusory knowledge (vidyā), and the enchantress (māyinī), as well as Pūṣan—these attend upon the supreme goddess Lalitā. (36–37)
Now, upon a couch there lies a bed of swan-down feathers, possessing a pillow made from the heads of supreme swans as its auspicious support;
it is enriched with service as its foot-pillow and provided with joy as its upper coverlet. (38)
Richly adorned with the cords of all the Vedāṅgas, with the Śānti hymns as her pillow—within this [bed], the illustrious Mahālakṣmī, together with Mahāviṣṇu, shines forth;
the graceful mistress serves her own husband. (3.119.40)
Compassionate, sixteen years of age, and adorned with elegant attire;
possessing a splendor equal to the rising sun and perfumed with the fragrance of the finest sandalwood;
he was decorated with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, and other ornaments.
With a lovely smile and a face full of moonlight, she was most beautiful;
Mahālakṣmī, radiant as the young sun, always sixteen years of age and proud of her fresh youth. (42–43)
Possessing the luster of polished rubies, with sandalwood paste and lotuses for the radiance of her toenails,
the beauty of her lac-dye flowed freely, carrying the crimson glow of her feet;
enchanting with the sweet resonance of her anklets and the tinkling of her falling bracelets.
Her shanks destroy the pride of the excellent quivers of the bodiless god of love;
her thighs possess a beauty equal to the luster of an elephant’s trunk and a plantain tree;
she is enriched by the splendor of her waist and girdle, and she shines with the full expanse of her hips. (45–46)
Adorned with a jeweled girdle, her deep navel beautified by the three folds of skin;
her chest endowed with the swelling buds of breasts like pearls;
shining intensely, she is resplendent with arms beautiful as red lac-dye. 47.
Adorned with armlets, bracelets, rings,

and finger-guards, her chin was round like a mirror for her face; she possessed a beautiful forehead and lower lip, and displayed her radiant smile through teeth possessing the splendor of jasmine buds.
Her eyes, with their lotus-like outer corners, possess the luster of red lotuses;
on her forehead, lovely with its fine hairline, a mass of curls is perfectly arranged;
and her ears are adorned with blossoming ear-ornaments and rubies set in earrings.
Her betel-roll was perpetually fragrant with fresh camphor and musk;
her face was as sweet as the orb of the shimmering autumn moon;
and her beautiful crown was fashioned from the essence of wish-fulfilling gems.
She is resplendent with the crescent moon upon her forehead situated in the center of a shimmering tilaka;
she possesses a mass of curved, swaying, thick, and slender locks of hair,
beautified by a line of vermilion applied along the parting of her hair.

Richly adorned with every elegant attire and decorated with all ornaments, her limbs are divine and super-divine; she increases the joy of Hari. She is Mahālakṣmī, the Mother of all the worlds, the Supreme Sovereign. (54–55)
She serves her own Lord upon the couch and is served by all the Śaktis;
by the mere act of serving her, the worship of all the gods is accomplished.
O Rame! Such is the description of the qualities of that very Lalitā-devī.
Indeed, even in thousands of millions of kalpas, it could never be described.
O Rame, such is the glorious city of Lalitā that exists!
Those who hear of it, speak of it, or go there attain the supreme goal.
Having had a divine and magnificent temple for Mahālakṣmī, endowed with all powers, constructed by artisans, the devotee goes to that supreme state.
In this way, there are other cities where the Goddesses and deities reside.
And they dwell with and serve Lalitā, the Supreme Sovereign;
the beginningless Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the supreme mistress Kambharāśrī,
the virtuous beloved of the glorious Gopālakṛṣṇa, the Great Viṣṇu.
O Śivarājñīśrī! O Nārāyaṇī! Worship my mother, your auspicious daughter-in-law, the source of all blessings, the glorious mistress of Kuṅkumavāpikā, who is filled with the passion of love for me. 62.

O Goddess of Kṛṣṇa, you who possess a form, chant that supreme mantra which is the auspicious, divine desire of the Supreme Lord, centered in the Parabrahman and yet formless; and worship the yantra which bestows enjoyment, prosperity, and liberation. (63–64)
The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
"O Blessed One, tell me this which is desired by all the worlds: what is that mantra, and what is its method of recitation?"
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! The objects of experience are conveyed by words;
the Veda is of the nature of eternal sound, and among those, the mantras are considered the most excellent. (66)
Among them, the mantras of Hari are the most excellent, and the mantras of Lakṣmī are always supreme.
The mantras of Durgā, Gaṇeśa, Ravi, Śambhu, and Vibhāvasu are also excellent;
indeed, the mantras of Mahālakṣmī are the best among all mantras.
I shall indeed tell you of Śyāmā Kambharā; listen to me.
Having risen early in the morning, having bowed to me, and having bathed, sit upon an auspicious seat and remember, O Lakṣmī, the divine and radiant lotus upon your own head.

Having meditated there upon the illustrious true guru, who is gracious and full of compassion, adorned with the beauty of a thousand petals and possessing filaments and a pericarp— the supreme father known as Śrīmad Gopālakṛṣṇa.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and then applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) together with the lunar dot (sacandra), thereafter,
having placed the Lord’s consort upon a cloth on one's shoulder and holding her in the heart,
and having become inwardly pure, perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana).
Offer that *arghya*— consisting of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice, flowers, and sandalwood— to Mahālakṣmī using a vessel shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree.
Then, having presented the *arghya* three times and having gratified [the deity] with water, [proceed].

Having gone to the site of the fire sacrifice, adorned with all ornaments, and provided with all the requisites for worship and the like, sit upon your seat, O Lakṣmī. Perform the ritual placements of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*); learn them as they are proclaimed by me. (74–75)
Salutation to Omana-ādi Parabrahmeśvarī on my head;
salutation to Omana-ādi Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇī on my forehead.
Salutation to Omana-ādi Vāsudevī Lakṣmī on my eyes. (76)
Salutations again and again to you, O Lakṣmī of Brahmā, beginning with Oṃ, at my mouth. May there be salutation to me for you, O Lakṣmī of Kaṃbharā, beginning with Oṃ, at my throat.
And salutations to you, O Mahālakṣmī, beginning with Oṃ, at my heart. (77–78)
Obeisance to you, O Śrī Narāyaṇī, beginning with *Oṃ*, in my belly;
obeisance again and again to you, O Vaiṣṇavī, beginning with *Oṃ*, in my navel. Obeisance to you, O Lalitā, beginning with *Oṃ*, in my hips.
May there always be salutation to Omana-ādi-Śrī at my two thighs;
may there be salutation to you, Omana-ādi-Kamalā, at my two knees; and may there be salutation to you, Omana-ādi-Ramā, at my two feet.
Obeisance to you, Omaṇādihariṇī; obeisance be to you in my two hands.
Obeisance again and again to you, Omaṇādimahāmātrī, on all sides.
Obeisance to you, Omaṇādipadmā, on the palms of your two hands.
Salutations again and again to you, Oṃmānādirakṣitrī, in the region of your back. Salutations to you, Oṃmānādi-hiraṇyā, in your beautiful limbs.
Salutations to you, Oṃmānādi-suvarṇā, in the lines of fortune on your palms.
Homage again and again to you, Oṃ Anādikumārī, in the form of the precept-dharma; homage again and again to you, Oṃ Anādijananī, in all your limbs.
Having thus performed the ritual placements (*nyāsa*), meditate upon the Sovereign of Śrīpura.
Meditate upon Śrīpura and me, the Lord of the Queen of Śrīpura.
Thereafter, invoke my form fashioned of gold;
then offer a seat, followed by water for the feet and the arghya offering.
Perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
and massage the Supreme Goddess with fragrant oils, essences, and the like.
Having performed the consecration (abhiṣeka), offer garments and ornaments.
All manner of ornaments, the finest auspicious incense, and lamps;
prostrations performed like a staff, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and circumambulation;
various kinds of food offerings—edibles, chewables, suckables, and lickables. (89–90)
Offer water, vegetables and the like, as well as milk-based preparations such as *pāyasa*;
offer drinking water, betel leaves with *tāmbūla*, and fruit.
Grant these to Śrī Mahālakṣmī and choose forgiveness for any offense.
Having performed the offering of a handful of flowers as a prostration, carry out your own exertion.
Then, O beloved, having donned a garland of *tulasī*, recite the mantra;
recite the great mantra of Mahālakṣmī, my dear Lakṣmī.
The Lord who accomplishes all goals and destroys all misfortunes;
facing north or east, one should always remain in the presence of the glory of the recitation:
*Oṃ, we know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon the wife of Mahāviṣṇu.* 94.
May that Mahālakṣmī inspire us.
Oṃ śrīṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī; oṃ hrīṃ klīṃ śrīṃ phaṭ svāhā.
(95) By reciting this thirty-six hundred thousand times, perfection shall be attained.
The fire oblation (homa) should be one-tenth of that [number], and the libation (tarpaṇa) one-tenth of that;
likewise, provide food for devotees as one-tenth of that.
In this way, the mantra becomes perfected; thereafter, perform the recitations for specific desires.
Having recited it one hundred thousand times, one may bring human beings under control;
women by two hundred thousand recitations, and likewise kings by three hundred thousand.
By four hundred thousand, one brings the daughters of the *nāgas* under control, and the women of the underworld (*pātāla*) by five hundred thousand.
With six hundred thousand [beads], one obtains Bhūsundarīs; with seven hundred thousand, the Surāṇīs;
with eight hundred thousand, the Devatās; with nine hundred thousand, the Gīrvāṇas; with ten hundred thousand, the Pitṛs; and with eleven hundred thousand, the Sureśvaras. (3.119.100)
And by twelve hundred thousand recitations, one may likewise bring the powers (siddhis) under control;
he shall become possessed of fortune, wealthy, and prosperous.
Thus, he obtains everything according to his desire, as well as divine sovereignty.
Meditating upon her and chanting her mantra, they obtain great prosperity.
This perfection is attained, but never by the wicked;
it is obtained by those people who have performed intense austerity.
Whosoever’s lineage may have a person who is a knower of mantras and a reciter [of them],
all those born in that lineage shall become liberated, satisfied, and yogis.
O Rame, this Lalitā herself is the Supreme Self accompanied by the mantra.
The virtuous always meditate upon this very great sacred ford (mahātīrtha).
It is not attained by those of evil conduct, by revilers, or by those devoid of true feeling—
she who is Kāmākṣī, Vaiṣṇavī, Mahālakṣmī, and Śrī Laliteśvarī.
"Because she caresses the Supreme Brahman, Lalitā is the most graceful one;
she who caresses Mahāviṣṇu, my Mother, is truly victorious.

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Service Rendered by the Divine Brāhmī Attendants Residing in the Cintāmaṇi Abode, the Mahālakṣmī Mantra, and the Fruits of its Recitation," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī! I shall tell you another mantra of Mahālakṣmī, by the worship of which the practitioner shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1)

Oṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī, the Great Illusion, the Great Nārāyaṇī, the Dweller in the Lotus, the Beloved of Mahāviṣṇu; Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Ṇīṃ Mlīṃ Ṣṇīṃ, salutation to the Great Sovereign who showers the goals of human existence, Svāhā. 2.
One should always recite the divine fifty-syllable great mantra.
I am its seer, Nārāyaṇa, and Mahālakṣmī is indeed its deity.
[She is] possessed of the luster of the form of a golden campaka flower and adorned with all ornaments.
Her face radiant with compassion and a smile, she is intent upon bestowing grace upon her devotees;

(4) she is fully endowed with all sovereign powers and other perfections, resplendent in every garment, as beautiful as ten million suns and moons, and wearing jeweled necklaces and other ornaments. (5)
One should meditate upon the venerable Mother Ramā, the glorious Mahālakṣmī who takes the form of the illustrious Gopāla, the great power (mahāśakti) of Mahāviṣṇu.
One should then recite the mantra ten thousand times, or one hundred thousand times, or else one-tenth of that amount.
One should perform an oblation with milk-rice (pāyasa) and worship with auspicious sandalwood paste (śrīcandana).
One should perform the installation, worship, the waving of lights (ārātrika), and the offering of food (nivedana).
One should offer water, betel-leaf (tāmbūla), the request for forgiveness (kṣamāpana), and the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
One should worship the nine Śaktis who are the very embodiments of Mahālakṣmī:
Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, Sannati, Vyuṣṭi, Utkṛṣṭi, and Ṛddhi; and on the right, Gajānana.
To the left, one should worship the Flower-Bowed One (Kusumadhanvan) with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should worship Umā, Śrī, Bhāratī, Durgā, Dharaṇī, Vedamātṛ, the goddess Uṣas, Gaṅgā, and Yamī in the eight directions.
One should worship the water brought for washing the lotus feet;
one should also worship the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, holding chowries at the sides.
Likewise, one should worship Varuṇa, who holds a parasol, in the west.
One should likewise worship the zodiac signs, the nine planets, and the elephants of the quarters;
one should also worship the world-protectors and their weapons in the fire.
For the sake of longevity, a person should offer oblations of dūrvā grass sprinkled with clarified butter.
He who should offer oblations of guḍūcī sprinkled with clarified butter for seven days,
one thousand and eight times, shall indeed live a full life.
Having offered sesame seeds smeared with ghee, one shall attain long life.
For one who constantly offers oblations of rice grains one thousand and eight times,
great prosperity will certainly arise before long.
By offering oblations of coconut, ghee, and other substances, one shall become like Kubera.
By offering oblations of jaggery and ghee, one becomes possessed of abundant food.
Thus, for whoever worships Lakṣmī—Kaṃbharā, Lalitā, Śrī—his riches are known [to all], and Mahālakṣmī is well-pleased with him. (18)
At the end of the body, she attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
In the divine world of Śrīpura, she is that mother Lakṣmī, the supreme sovereign,
who constantly manifests various incarnations throughout the three worlds.
Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Mūlaprakṛti, Īśvarī, Pārabrahmī, Akṣarī, Pareśī, Puruṣottamī, Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Gaṅgā, Virajā, and Sarasvatī. (21)
She is indeed known as Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Kamalā, Padminī, and Ramā;
likewise, she is celebrated as Tulasī, Mādhavī, and Padmā.
As Mahālakṣmī, she dwells upon the girdle of Viṣṇu as the virtuous Lalitā.
In Śivakañcī, that very goddess Kāmeśvarī, the beloved of Śiva,
exists as the supreme and worshipful Kaṃbharā, who indeed possesses manifold forms.
Śrī Nārāyaṇīśrī said:
"O Lord, grant me that supreme Śakti, Mahālakṣmī, who dwells in the city of Kāñcī and exists herself in two forms. Śrī Puruṣottama said:
In ancient times, in the sacred field of Kāñcī, Brahmā performed most difficult penance, intent on the one-pointed meditation of the Self, in order to behold Mahālakṣmī.
Before him appeared Mahālakṣmī, with her hands like lotuses.
Shining upon a lotus seat together with the great Viṣṇu—
having beheld Ādilakṣmī, the mother of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, who is enriched by every graceful ornament and adorned with all jewelry. (27–28)
The Creator of the Universe himself praised that divine goddess Kāmākṣī,
the mother of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa on this earth.
Brahmā said:

Victory to you, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Mother of the World, Supreme Sovereign! Victory to you, the co-born sister of Śrīnātha; victory to you, the auspiciousness of all! Victory to you, O mass of compassion; victory to you, who are adored by the Vaiṣṇavas!
Victory to you, O Goddess worshipped by the world; salutations to you, the creator of the world.
(3.1) Salutations again and again to you, who are to be known by those whose devotion consists of undivided contemplation.
You are the Supreme Sovereign, known and proclaimed by the hosts of sages of the Vedas. (3.2)
Salutations again and again to you, the Mother, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman;
salutations to you who reside in the heart, O Sovereign Lady of imperial prosperity;
the Vedas are indeed your breath—salutations again and again to that Mother.
By whose command even the thousand-headed god bears the earth,
and by the splendor of whose rays the sun, moon, and fire always shine—
to that Mother Lakṣmī, who possesses twenty-five forms, salutations again and again.

I bow again and again to you, Śrīvidyā, Śrī Mahālakṣmī, who abide within the inner self of all beings and whose nature is supreme bliss— even those who are lords, having attained their sovereignties, [seek you]. (35–36)

You are the essence of all-knowledge, the essence of the sacrificial pillar, and the essence of gold; you are the form of the instruction in reality, the embodiment of prosperity, and the showerer of peace.
You are the essence of place, time, and objects, and the essence of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs.
Salutations again and again to her who is the essence of the elements and the form of light; salutations to her whose measure is perfect.
(38) She is endowed with auspicious qualities, radiant with the splendor of Kambharā, the mother of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the mother of Bālakṛṣṇa, and the goddess Ramā. (39)
"O imperishable one, adorned with the mark of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, you come again and again to Surāṣṭra; salutations be unto you!
Thus praised, that Mother, seeing the Creator (Brahmā), was well-pleased.
Then Brahmā said, "Choose [a boon]," and he requested a favor:
"By the sight of you today, I am in every way fulfilled;
nevertheless, for the sake of protecting the world, I desire this—grant it to me. (41–42)
"O Creator, the people in this land of action are deluded and shrouded by the latent impressions of saṃsāra;
for their sake alone, take up residence here on this earth.
Having heard this, Mother Rāmā then said to the Creator, "So be it."
Brahmā also quickly had a magnificent temple constructed.
He remembered the Supreme Lord, the lotus-eyed one, the Lord of the lords of lords, so that he might dwell together with Mahālakṣmī.
He too arrived in person at the request of Brahmā;
he said, "So be it," for the purpose of dwelling there with Lakṣmī.
Thus, in an auspicious mansion upon a ground resembling gold—
The mother Mahālakṣmī remained there, joined by Mahāviṣṇu.
Then Brahmā spoke again: "O Mother, O Father, let those who are devotees of Viṣṇu and others, as well as Śaṅkara himself, always dwell here."
"Endowed with your own Vaiṣṇava power, fulfill this desire.
"So be it," Hari replied; Hari then assumed the form of Śiva.
Mahālakṣmī became Mahāgaurī, resplendent with great luster.
Richly adorned with every kind of beauty and a treasure-trove of great loveliness,
Śiva and Gaurī were then worshipped by Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and the gods with supreme devotion; they installed the Goddess.
The Creator fashioned with his mind an excellent city in the center,
and for the sake of those two, a temple as beautiful as Śivakāñcī;
at that time, Śaṅkara was stationed in the wind-quarter of Mahālakṣmī.
In the portion belonging to Agni, Viṣṇu himself shone forth as the unmanifest Brahmā.
Ādi-Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mātā Śrī were the Supreme Sovereign;
she is indeed Vāṇī, and she is Kamalā—those two are one with her. 53–54.
With her left eye she beheld the Lord Hari,
and with her right eye she beheld Śaṅkara and Brahmā;
therefore, she was called Kāmākṣī by the foremost of the gods.
Then the presiding deities of all the holy fords, beginning with Gaṅgā and Yamunā—
three and a half crores in number— arrived to offer service. At that time, Śrī and Sarasvatī took up chowries in their hands.
Mahālakṣmī and Vijayantī stand comfortably by her two sides;
they were born from the eyes of Ādiśrī and are adorned with all the graces of beauty.
Thus, her daughter Santoṣiṇī stands behind her own mother.
Holding a golden parasol, she of divine form shone resplendently.
Then, by the command of Mahālakṣmī, Sarasvatī herself, self-luminous,
entered the body of the Creator while all the gods were looking on.
Then, by his command, Indirā-Śrī entered the body of Viṣṇu;
likewise, Gaurī then entered the body of Śaṅkara.
And she, ever devoted to the vow of Brahman, entered contentedly into the body of Mātṛ.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, those deities dwell there in Kāñcī.
Then Brahmā said to the gods: "Every year, a wedding must be celebrated here in this abode for Mahāgaurī and Maheśvara."
Likewise, O Great Lord, the marriage of Mahālakṣmī must indeed be performed;
a great festival should be celebrated here with royal honors.
For those who perform the marriage festival, there shall be eternal good fortune.
In Kāñcī or at Kuṅkumavāpī, the fruit of the great festival is equal.
In the golden temple at the sacred site named Kuṅkumavāpī,
I have installed my own mother, the Supreme Sovereign Mahālakṣmī.
Those who perform worship to that [deity] together with Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa Mahānārāyaṇa shall attain a great fruit;
those who partake of the food offering (naivedya) shall go happily to heaven.
Those who shall practice devotion to them will go to the immortal state—
Śrīpura, the divine abode of the great-souled Mahāviṣṇu.
She herself is Mahālakṣmī, the illustrious Supreme Goddess.
She also created the three pairs consisting of Lakṣmī and Viṣṇu,
Sāvitrī and the Creator (Brahmā), and Śivā and Śiva;
and Jayā, Vijayā, and Vidyā serve the Supreme Goddess.
The illustrious Great Goddess, who bestows prosperity, always attends upon the Glorious One.
One should mutter the mantra and worship the Śrīcakra with all available materials;
by worshipping the Śrīcakra, even when it is held in the mind, one attains perfection.

The Śrīcakra is indeed the concealed form of Mahālakṣmī; of this there is no doubt. Having become a devotee and having cast the entire burden consisting of both worldly and otherworldly concerns upon the Goddess Śrī, one should abide in her refuge.
Favorable to Mahālakṣmī and free from all opposition,
he should always choose service with full confidence, thinking, "Protect me.
Even if he becomes dependent on the lowly, he attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, forbearance, straightforwardness, service to the true guru, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint;
dispassion toward the objects of the senses, and being devoid of egoism. (76)
Reflecting upon the defects of suffering inherent in birth, death, old age, and disease;
non-attachment and lack of clinging toward illusory objects; equanimity toward pleasure and pain; and devotion to the illustrious Lord Laliteśvara. (77–78)
Exclusive adherence to moral conduct, freedom from attachment to others,
inwardness, and immersion in the supreme knowledge—
practicing in this way with devotion, one becomes a true seeker of refuge for Mahālakṣmī.
One attains supreme liberation, as well as unsurpassed enjoyment and heaven.
O Lotus-born one, listen as I describe the initiation for the vision of Śrī Lakṣmī:
having meditated upon the city of Śrī in the hand, which is the supreme, highest abode. (3.120.80–81)
The preceptor, while reciting the mantra of Mahālakṣmī for Mahāviṣṇu, should touch the body of the disciple with the beautiful golden [image] of Mahālakṣmī.
This initiation by touch destroys all sins and bestows merit.
Having given [the gift] and closed his eyes, the Guru should meditate upon the venerable Supreme Goddess;
he should then look at the disciple—this is the purifying and auspicious initiation by the gaze (*dṛgdīkṣā*).
Through the touch of the Guru’s gaze, through his speech, and through service, [the disciple is purified]. (83–84)
There shall be the destruction of evil and the attainment of divine knowledge and a divine body.
Having obtained the grace of the Guru, the disciple becomes one with his very form.
For the Guru, being satisfied by the long-standing service rendered, bestows that blessing.
Initiation is said to be mental, and the offering of everything is its highest form.
(86) Having bathed at an auspicious time during the bright fortnight and performed the twilight prayers, one should bow to the Guru and proceed toward the sacred temple. (87)
Then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should worship Mahālakṣmī.
One should perform the invocation (āvāhana), the offering of a seat (āsana), the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the ritual sipping (ācamana).
[Verse 88] There is the bath consisting of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the consecration with pure waters.
[One should offer] clothing, ornaments, fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp;
food offerings, water, betel leaf, circumambulation, and praise.
Oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ oṃ namo mahālakṣmyai.

To Kambharā, to Kāmākṣī, to Lalitā, to Śrīcakrā, to Mahānārāyaṇī, to Mahāparameśvarī, to the consort of Pūrṇabrahma-Mahāviṣṇu, to the wife of Śrī Gopālakṛṣṇa, to the fulfiller of all prosperity, and to the [goddess] of the two hundred and eight [names]— mahā...
"Obeisance to you, who are composed of power: *ka eṃ īla hrīṃ hasa kahala hrīṃ sakala hrīṃ aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ sauḥ klīṃ aiṃ śrīṃ svāhā*.
(3.120.90) Thus one should offer a handful of flowers; thereafter, [on ground] smeared with cow dung...
On the ground or upon a pedestal of rice, one should place a water-pot containing jewels,
joined with the five sprouts and accompanied by a coconut fruit.
Having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should then repeatedly recite the mantra.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and having indeed presented a lamp, the Guru should cause the disciple to perform a prostration with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) and an offering of handfuls of flowers;
there, he should repeatedly cause him to offer prayers for the attainment of all desired goals.
You are the supreme abode, the supreme Brahman, and my own chosen deity.
Protect me along with my family; protect me solely for the sake of liberation.
Placing my head at the feet of the Guru, endowed with devotion— ||94-95||
Then, having washed both hands, one should offer the most excellent and sweet food offering— consisting of various foods,
fruits, and the essence of milk— to Lakṣmī.
Having imparted the mantra into the ear of the disciple, one should consecrate him with the water from the ritual pitcher.
Thereafter, being purified, he should always perform the worship of Mahālakṣmī.
He should eat only what remains after Lakṣmī, and he should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to his guru.
He should feed Vaiṣṇavas, virtuous men, virtuous women, children, and young girls.
One should offer one’s body, wealth, and life to that venerable Guru.
One should always remain subject to him and never transgress his word. Such a disciple, subsisting on the Guru’s grace, becomes the purifier of those who purify the assembly.

One should recognize as rare that Guru who, when pleased, bestows the glory of liberation in half a moment— he who delivers one from saṃsāra. From him one should receive knowledge and should serve him constantly.
Devotion to the Guru arises in the disciple; hostility toward him is the supreme sin.
Service at his feet is considered equal to liberation and the bestower of liberation.
Because he abides by the Guru’s instruction, he is designated as a "disciple" (śiṣya).
One should perform recitation and meditation, recitation and meditation, in order to eliminate exhaustion.
Through meditation, even a worm may become a bee; likewise, a disciple may become Hari.
For one who realizes identity with the Self, the fruit of the vision is the state of becoming Brahman.
When the sense of "I" has vanished and the Self is known as the Supreme Self, whatever state the mind goes toward— all those are indeed states of *samādhi*.
For the yogi who has realized that Brahman is the Self of all and whose form is Brahman, [all states are equal].
For him, nothing remains to be attained or known.
(106) A hymn of praise is equal to ten million acts of worship; recitation is equal to ten million hymns of praise;
meditation is equal to ten million recitations; and absorption is equal to ten million meditations. (107)
The body is declared to be a temple, and this living soul is remembered as its servant.
Through service, one should always satisfy Kṛṣṇa who resides within, more so than through all possible gifts.
Service to the guru is superior to ten million gifts, vows, and sacrifices.
Whatever has issued from the mouth of the Guru, all that is indeed his scripture. One should perform even that which is forbidden; one must never transgress the Guru’s command.
Even if one is distinguished by birth, learning, or wealth, one should behave toward the Guru as if prostrate before him.
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a guru with empty hands;
one should offer fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth according to one's ability.
Even Mādhava, the divine god, exists solely for the protection of his true devotees.
Having become a teacher who is a treasure-house of compassion, he acts like an ordinary worldly being.
(1.12) There is no reality superior to the Guru; there is no happiness superior to knowledge; there is no worship superior to devotion; and there is no fruit superior to liberation. (1.13)

"From remembering, worshipping, hearing, or even reciting this, a divine fruit is produced that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.14) Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Another Mantra of Mahālakṣmī, the Two-fold Form of Mahālakṣmī in the City of Kāñcī, the Residence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa Therein, and the Procedure for Initiation," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (120)

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "O Lord, although the names of the Great Lakṣmī known as Lalitā are indeed innumerable,
please nevertheless recite one hundred and twenty-five of them."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"By the recitation of the principal names, the fruit arising from all designations will surely be attained;
therefore, I shall speak of those principal names—listen."
Lalitā, Śrī, Mahālakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Ramā, Padminī, Kamalā, Sampadīśā, Padmālayā, Indirā, Īśvarī,
Parameśī, Satī, Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, and Vaiṣṇavī. (3)
The Supreme Sovereign, the Great Mistress, the Mistress of Power, the Most Excellent Being;
the Pervasive One, Māyā, the Great Māyā, the Root Nature, the Infallible One;
the Consort of Vāsudeva, the Golden One, the Deer-like One, and the Golden-hued One. (4–5)
Kārṣṇī, Kāmeśvarī, Kāmākṣī, and Bhagamālinī;
Vahnivāsā, Sundarī, Saṃvit, Vijayā, and Jayā;
Maṅgalā, Mohinī, Tāpī, Vārāhī, Siddhi, and Īśitā.
Bhukti (Enjoyment), Kaumārikī (The Maiden), Buddhi (Intellect), Amṛtā (Nectar), Duḥkhahā (Destroyer of Suffering), Prasūḥ (The Progenitress),
Subhāgyā (The Fortunate One), Ānandinī (The Gladdener), Sampat (Prosperity), Vimalā (The Pure One), Bindvikā (Named after the Drop),
Mātā (The Mother), Mūrtiḥ (The Embodiment), Yoginī (The Yoginī), Cakrikā (The Wheel-like One), Arcā (The Worshipful One), Ratiḥ (Delight), and Dhṛtiḥ (Fortitude). || 7–8 ||
Śyāmā, Manoramā, Prīti, Ṛddhi, Chāyā, Pūrṇimā,
Tuṣṭi, Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Durgā, Līlā, Māṇikī, Udyamā, Bhāratī, Viśvā, Vibhūti, Vinatā, and Śubhā. (9)
Fame, auspicious action, knowledge, art, and saffron;
the meritorious, ancient Mistress of Speech, the giver of boons, the embodiment of prosperity,
Sarasvatī, the auspicious Sound, the Foundation, the refined, and the Triple Veda.
Āyurjīvā, Svarṇarekhā, Dakṣā, Vīrā, Rāgiṇī, Capalā, Paṇḍitā, Kālī, Bhadrā, Ambikā, Māninī,
Viśālākṣī, Vallabhā, Gopī, Nārī, and Narāyaṇī.
Santuṣṭā, Suṣumṇā, Kṣamā, Dhātrī, and Vāruṇī;
Gurvī, Sādhvī, Gāyatrī, Dakṣiṇā, and Annapūrṇikā; Rājalakṣmī, Siddhamātā, Mādhavī, Bhārgavī, and Parī. (13–14)
"Hāritī, Rāśiyānī, Prācīnī, Gaurikā, and Śruti"— thus, O beloved,
the one hundred and eight names, as well as the twenty-seven,
headed by Lalitā, have been told to you.
For one who recites this constantly, enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of their hand. Indeed, there shall be prosperity, the expansion of the lineage, and all forms of bliss.
Om Śrī Lalitā Mahālakṣmyai Namaḥ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Svāhā. (16–17)
By reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, she will certainly be seen.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the great mantra of the Guru:
Om, salutation and Svāhā to the Guru who is the inner Liṅga, residing in the forehead, the Self of all.
One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; success arises that is equal to that of Brahmā.
One should meditate upon the Guru, bathe him, and worship him with many articles;
one should feed him, serve him, and satisfy him with all kinds of gifts. (3.121.20)
The Guru is Brahmā; the Guru is Viṣṇu; the Guru is Śrī Śaṅkara himself.
The Guru is Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa; the Guru is the Supreme Lord, Brahman.
The Guru is father, husband, son, kinsman, mother, and protector.
The Guru is the giver of liberation, the savior, and the bestower of great bliss.
"The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is the manifest Guru, Hari"—having spoken thus, one should bow to the Guru and then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for him. ||22-23||
One should also offer a handful of flowers and prostrate like a staff;
one should give to the guru a gift of whatever object is most dear to oneself.
For the conscious Lord is indeed the guru, the Supreme Sovereign himself.
It protects one from multitudes of calamities and leads indeed to the imperishable state.
Indeed, seeing the Guru first thing in the morning is always the highest [duty];
one should drink the water from the big toe of the Guru’s foot, which is supremely purifying. (25–26)
The nectar of the Guru’s feet destroys even sins such as killing;
the feet of the Guru sever even the bonds of *māyā* and the like.
Indeed, the remembrance of the Guru is capable of liberating one from the noose of *yāmī*.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme teacher, the eternal protector of the helpless.
Because he obstructs (ruṇaddhi) the dense (gaḍha), deep (gāḍha), and hidden (gupta) darkness (tamaḥ), he is considered the Guru.
Having fashioned an auspicious image of the Guru, one should preserve it in the home and around the neck.
"One should worship the non-duality of the Guru; thus one attains the unsurpassed nectar.
O Lakṣmī, this which has been told is the supreme essence of essences.
The sacred ford of the Guru is greater than the sacred ford of the mother and the sacred ford of the father.

The sacred site of the guru is far greater than the sacred site of the mother-in-law, and greater than the sacred site of the husband. (3.1) The sacred site of the guru is far greater than the sacred site of the chaste wife, and greater than the sacred site of the beloved.
(3.2) The sacred site of the guru is far greater than the sacred site of the deity, and greater than the sacred site of the dull-witted. (3.2)
The sacred ford of the Guru is greater than the sacred ford of sacrifice and the sacred ford of ritual;
the sacred ford of the Guru is greater than the sacred ford of vows and the sacred ford of austerity.
The sacred ford of the Guru is greater than the sacred ford of knowledge and the sacred ford of yoga.
The sacred ford of the Guru is far greater than sacred fords such as those dedicated to helping others.
This very sacred ford of the Guru is being authorized by me, the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, as authoritative.
The sacred ford of truth, the sacred ford of goodness, and I, the Supreme Lord, am the sacred ford;
indeed, these three sacred fords enter into the sacred ford that is the Guru.
Thus, O Śivarājñī, this heart-essence has been told to you.
"By reading or hearing this, one shall partake in the four goals of human life.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the One Hundred and Thirty-five Names of Lalitā Mahālakṣmī, the Greatness of Gurus as Holy Places of Pilgrimage, and so forth," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
