Chapter 122 [Author: Chapter 123 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: Śrī said:
O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy! Having heard again and again of the auspicious birth of Mahālakṣmī,
her manifestation, the cause thereof, her majesty, and her mandalas,
my heart rejoices and yearns for a daughter.
Blessed is that mother whose daughter on this earth is such as this;
in whose house the supreme sovereign Mahālakṣmī shines resplendent.
By what merit is a daughter equal to Mahālakṣmī obtained?
"Tell me, is it through vows, propitiation, service, or recitation; or by charity, austerity, sacrifices, or indeed by devotion?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, for there are indeed many causes here.
In this world, nothing whatsoever is obtained by anyone without [the exhaustion of] past karma.
Sons and daughters are obtained through the conjunction of the bonds of karma.
This world, possessing a continuous lineage through successive generations, is a flow of the threads of karma.
Indeed, from the subtle atom (aṇu) of its own nature, the father is born in the form of a son;
and from the subtle atom of its own nature, the mother is born in the form of a daughter.
Indeed, for him by whom the gift of a daughter was previously bestowed,
another girl— impelled by his great merit— is born somewhere else;
she becomes his own daughter, while the boy likewise remains elsewhere as before.
Their marriage in this world shall become a lawful union with that wife.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the birth of a daughter occurs through the merit of the husband;
it is the debt of the husband toward his father-in-law and mother-in-law from a previous existence. (3.122.9–10)
Therefore, a daughter is given after having been raised on that debt;
thus, even though she is indeed another's property, she is called "daughter. O Rame! I have thus described to you here this daughter who is bound by debt.
For daughters generally arise as a debt to their father;
indeed, the fruit of the gift belongs to the giver who first offered her to a husband.
It is held that the giver alone is the enjoyer of the fruit, and thus the giver is considered the enjoyer from the outset.

O Lakṣmī! Indeed, by whatever king the gifts of daughters are bestowed with righteous expenditures, for whichever girls those auspicious wedding ceremonies are performed and caused to be given away through the outlay of wealth. (14)
For in this world, those kings indeed possess many wives;
or else, in heaven, he becomes a great deity possessing many wives,
rejoicing while being attended by numerous apsarases.
One who gives a maiden finds a wife; it can never be otherwise. For as many maidens as are given away without a bride-price, so many wives endowed with corresponding virtues shall he obtain.
In the Kṛta Yuga, one who gives a wife obtains a wife; such is the gift of a wife.
In the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, righteousness does not bring such supreme excellence anywhere as this.
Chastity toward the husband is the highest dharma, and devotion to a single husband is supreme. (18–19)

The vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is declared to be the supreme state of having only one husband. Its violation occurs through the taking of another's wife; therefore, the giving away of a woman [to another] must certainly not be done.
[This applies even] when a man possessed of great power and of a fiery nature might be encountered somewhere.
The gift of a wife should be given without obstruction and for the benefit [of the recipient]; this is also the rule.
(21) In a case where dharma is not violated and the maiden’s status remains intact, he who has many wives may indeed give his wife. (22)
In that regard, the fruit of giving away one's wife is that she becomes [one's own] in another birth;
this duty is intended for one who is childless, with the hope of obtaining the fruit of a son.
However, the giving away of another's daughter along with wealth is considered superior.
He should perform [the rite] for her as he would for his father, and he shall obtain the fruit [of the merit] through his wife.
This alone is the most excellent rule; the gift of a wife is not the highest.
That the fruit of giving a daughter is obtained through wives has been established by all.
Service to one's father and the performance of *śrāddha* rites are traditionally held to yield fruit in the form of a son.
The *putreṣṭi* sacrifice grants the fruit of a son, while the *putrīṣṭi* sacrifice grants a daughter.
A son should be given as a gift when he is auspicious; never, however, should an inauspicious one be given.
Indeed, a gift given by means of taking wealth yields inauspicious fruit; it is not so.
A girl should be given adorned and free from the taking of wealth. She may be another's daughter, provided she is highly suitable and devoid of all defects. (27–28)
Having brought about a union between the parents and having given them great wealth,
he should then take [the child] as his own, bathe him, and give him ornaments and garments;
having adorned him with cosmetics, perfumes, and garlands, he should worship him.
Then, having observed the auspicious signs such as the lineage, birth star, and time,
and having sought out a worthy groom for the girl who possessed suitable qualities and other virtues—
and having perceived that there was mutual love between them known as *prema*— (3.122.30–31)
Having honored both according to the prescribed rite in the wedding festival pavilion, the daughter should be given to a worthy bridegroom who is most devoted to Brahman, an ascetic,
learned, endowed with excellent qualities, and capable of protecting the girl.
One should offer male and female servants, wealth, ornaments, garments, and vehicles.
One should assign fields, gardens, riches, grains, and groves;
likewise, one should assign and cause to be given houses and household utensils. (33–34)
One should bestow a wish-fulfilling cow, a buffalo, elephants, horses, and bulls;
one should grant every suitable means of livelihood that sustains a family.
Such indeed is the fruit for the donor of a daughter and for the wealthy man who gives her away in this world.
Indeed, there shall be countless enjoyments born of merit even in heaven.
Furthermore, for as many hairs as there are on the body of the girl and her offspring,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
In that very pavilion, one should perform the unsurpassed gift of Lakṣmī,
which bestows all prosperity, happiness, and increases great sovereignty.
Having fashioned the incomparable Śrī-Lakṣmī out of gold according to the prescribed rite, [one should offer it].
Or again, with a thousand, half of that, or half of that once more;
or even with one hundred and eight [beads], [one should worship] Lakṣmī, who is endowed with all auspicious marks,
adorned with every ornament, and beautified by all her finery.
Having placed the auspicious four-armed Lakṣmī and the eight-armed Mahālakṣmī within the mandala, and likewise Viṣṇu Hari to her right,
one should worship Śrī and Hari with services such as the royal offerings.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should worship [the deity], feed [the guests], and cause them to drink [beverages].
Then, having offered betel leaf (tāmbūla), one should perform the lustration rite (nīrājana) and prostrations.
Thereafter, one should offer handfuls of flowers while performing full-length prostrations (daṇḍavat). 42–43.
One should bestow wealth upon a worthy recipient, a virtuous person, or a celibate student (brahmacārī),
whether in the presence of water, fire, or Brahmins; in public,
in the presence of a guru, the sun, the gods, or before Lord Hari.
In this way, all prosperity arises for the donor of Lakṣmī.
As the fruit of that deed, he obtains wives with a complexion like the color of the golden campaka flower;
he also obtains daughters, excellent sons, and sisters. (45–46)
Through this gift, one becomes a male servant, a female servant, an attendant, or a personal assistant;
in heaven, one becomes the master of the *apsarases*, and in liberation, the powerful lord of the *śaktis*.
By the granting of Mahālakṣmī, one becomes a sovereign emperor and the husband of beautiful women.
By the gift of a female buffalo, one becomes a self-ruling monarch endowed with all happiness.
By the gift of a pair [of animals], one is born as the soul of a couple;
in ancient times, all the great seers were born from such pairs. (48–49)
Then, indeed, creation became diversified through the state of pairing;
for in ancient times, there was a state of matrimony between two sages who were born together.
In the course of time, however, marriage took place between those born of different lineages.

For the sake of assisting all creation, for the purpose of consolidating affection, and for the sake of attaining the state of being interwoven (as warp and woof) and so forth, all the great seers established [the rules]. For indeed, virtues may become non-virtues, and non-virtues, moreover, may become bulls of virtue (vṛṣāḥ). || 51–52 ||
In another age, humans among gods and men are born with the nature of beasts;
in yet another age, humans have the nature of birds.
In another age, however, humans possess the nature of sages and the nature of gods.
In another age, humans indeed become possessed of the nature of Daityas and Dānavas;
yet again and again, they become the opposite of that.
Therefore, the fruit of giving is obtained there according to the specific era.
That which is to be obtained becomes given; it is never not given.
Thus, the auspicious fruit of giving away one's son is the attainment of a husband.
In Ketumāla, mothers perform the ritual gift of their sons.
By that [act], the Gaurīs indeed attain their husbands of beautiful form;
and by the gift of a sister, auspicious sisters are obtained in splendor.
The supreme fruit of service to one's mother is that one is born in the lap of a virtuous being.
Thus, O Kamalā, these very dharmas remain hidden on earth;
those who do not know the truth do not perceive them, but instead become deluded here and there.
They encounter supreme suffering and indeed undergo affliction.
"Indeed, they give gifts only after considering it as merit or demerit.
O ladies, even though you are my wives, that was the fruit of what was given previously.
Listen, Lakṣmī, and hear also the other cause for the obtaining of a daughter."
The vow is called the *putrīvrata*, for that is indeed the *kambharāśrīvrata*.
When, in the world, the share and the authority were indeed equal, the inheritance of sons and daughters was formerly equal. (62)
Then the mother performed the Putrīvrata and the father performed the Putreṣṭi sacrifice.
This became the supreme duty everywhere in all the worlds:
"My mother Kambharāśrī [performed] the Putrikāvratam for the sake of a daughter."
From that [act], a daughter named Santoṣā was born;
she was Vāsudevī herself, Lakṣmī manifested in the form of a daughter, who is called the virtuous sister of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (65)
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
What kind of vow is that which is called the Putrī-vrata, consisting of a sacrifice?
Tell me its procedure exactly as it is, so that it may be fruitful from beginning to end.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O son, to the vow of the mother Kambharā which she performed;
through it, she became Mahālakṣmī, Lalitā, Śrī, and possessed of sons. (67)
On the first fifth lunar day (pañcamī) of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
the vow of Putrīvrata should be observed by a mother endowed with the wealth of good fortune.
On the night of the fourth lunar day (caturthī), she should indeed be intent on drinking milk.
She should be devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and sleep upon the bare ground.
Having slept in such a way that no evil dream may occur, she should rise for a moment after recollecting Lalitā, Śrī, and Mahālakṣmī. (3.122.70)
Having meditated upon the four-armed Lakṣmī, who is the luster of golden campaka flowers and yellow pigment (rocanā),
a young woman clad in green garments, adorned with gold,
anointed with sandalwood and other unguents, and fragrant with the essence of perfumes.
With a serene countenance, her hands and feet possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus;
her limbs proportionate to her form, her face beautified by the brilliance of the moon;
she shines with the splendor of lips reddened by the chewing of betel.
Having meditated upon her whose body is resplendent with the fullness of youth and who possesses a robust form, and having bathed, the virtuous woman should then worship her in a golden image.
She should then make this formal resolve: "O Mahālakṣmī, for the sake of obtaining a daughter, I shall observe the vow of the fifth lunar day."
Today I observe a fast; may it be fulfilled without obstacle.
O Mother, for that purpose I perform this auspicious worship for you.
Come here, sit upon this seat, and accept this water for the feet and the auspicious offering (arghya).
Then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and the bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Conduct the consecration (abhiṣeka) with fragrant waters mixed with the essence of perfumes.
Offer garments, ornaments, decorations, finery, and elegant attire.
Apply auspicious substances, vermilion, and flower garlands.
Offer incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of the essence of milk, milk-rice, various kinds of sweet foods, as well as vegetables and fruits. (78–79)
Then take the water for drinking and accept the excellent betel leaf;
perform the waving of lights, accept the flower garland, and offer your constant prayer.
Then perform circumambulations, prostrations, and obeisances like a staff.
"Give me a daughter who resembles you,
endowed with all auspiciousness, beautiful in every limb, lovely, a lotus-like woman of slow gait,
a servant who is a cause of delight, possessing divine prosperity, and the moonlight of peace. (81-82)
Grant us a virtuous daughter who is long-lived, free from disease, a mistress of prosperity,
the ornament of her lineage, blessed with the fortune of a husband and sons, endowed with excellent qualities,
and a devotee of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus made this request, one should then perform devotion in the form of kīrtana (chanting).
With a mind full of devotion, one should rotate the prayer beads according to one's capacity.
At midday as well, one should offer excellent food offerings, water, and betel leaf.
Then one should cause [the deity] to sleep, cause it to rise, and offer the fruit;
one should offer water at night and perform the excellent worship of the *ārātrika* with saffron,
*abīra*, musk, camphor, flowers, and other such items.
Then, having caused her to partake of a meal consisting of milk-rice and other delicacies,
she should perform dancing, recitation, singing, and keep a vigil throughout the night.
Thereafter, the observer of the vow, having bathed in the morning, should bathe her mother.
Having worshipped Mahālakṣmī and fed [the guests], and after performing the *ārārtika* ceremony, one should pray:
"Grant me a daughter; the vow has been completed, so grant me forgiveness for the vow.
O Supreme Goddess, by Your majesty, may that which was incomplete reach completion."

Having thus petitioned and paid obeisance, she should thereafter dismiss him. Having fed her own husband and drunk the nectar-like water from his big toe—accompanied by the grace of Lakṣmī—she should then partake of her own meal. (3.122.90–91)
One should give gifts according to the prescribed rite, according to one's capacity and wealth—
including all such things as garments, ornaments, and cosmetics suitable for the maiden.
One should feed at least eight maidens and give them excellent sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
O Lakṣmī, one should perform this vow which bestows the attainment of a daughter.
Just as on the dark fortnight, so too on the light fortnight, a woman observing the vow should perform the twenty-four fifth-day rites in the manner described, which grant her a daughter. (93–94)
In a dream, Mahālakṣmī will come and say to you, "O virtuous one, after the conclusion of your year-long vow, a beautiful daughter shall be born to you;
then you should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) accompanied by the gift of a bed. ||95||
One should have the worship of Mahālakṣmī performed during the Sarvabhadraka festival;
one should also celebrate a great festival, give a cow together with its calf,
and cause the gift of a maiden to be given according to one's capacity and wealth.
Homage to Lakṣmī, homage to Dhiṣṇyā, homage to Putrī, homage to Śrī;
homage be to you, Ramā, Lalitā, and Mahālakṣmī.
Just as [one honors you] with flower garlands appropriate to the seasons and with the delicious fruits of the seasons...
"May Mahālakṣmī be pleased with me; may you be the giver of a daughter to me.
Thus one should always worship the goddess Kambharāśrī during the vow.
One should certainly not practice stinginess regarding wealth; otherwise, a daughter will not be born as deceitful. (3.122.100)

A pregnant woman, a woman who has recently given birth, one who is ill, or one who has not yet undergone purification—such women, when in distress, may have [the rite] performed by another; otherwise, she herself should perform it with great care. For a woman possessed of extreme misfortune, [the goal is attained] certainly through vows observed for three years.
The attainment of a daughter shall surely occur through a single drop of the grace of Lalitāśrī.
(102) Upon seeing the birth of a daughter, one should offer the vow to the Goddess;
indeed, the vow must be observed for a long time until the fruit of a daughter is realized. (103)
The commencement of this vow for the acquisition of a daughter took place in the dark fortnight of Phālguna, and its completion was performed by Śrī Kambharā Mahālakṣmī. By that [vow],
a daughter named Vāsudevī, known as Santōṣā, was born to her.
Thus has been described, O Lakṣmī, this most purifying vow.
By performing the Putrī-vrata, a man or a woman shall obtain a daughter.
Samudra performed this very vow, and he obtained Lakṣmī as his daughter.
Sadāśiva performed the vow and obtained his daughter Jayā;
Brahmā performed the vow and indeed obtained his daughter Lalitā.
The quarters of the sky performed the vow and obtained their daughter Padmāvatī.
The Sun, having performed a vow, obtained Prabhā as his daughter;
the Kalpa-trees, having likewise performed a vow, obtained Śrī as their daughter;
and Divyavibhūti, having performed this same vow, obtained Māṇikī as his daughter.
Vairājī, having performed this vow, obtained Kamalā as her daughter;
Khyāti, having performed this same vow, obtained Śrī Bhārgavī as her daughter;
and Dharaṇī, having performed that vow, obtained Padmāvatī as her daughter.

Thus it is, and not otherwise; that which has occurred therein is certainly fruitful. One who desires a daughter should indeed unite with his wife during the fifth, or the seventh, ninth, eleventh, or thirteenth [lunar days]. || 112 ||
On the fifteenth auspicious day, when that number of days has passed into the night,
by the depositing of the seed, that girl is born from the conception of the womb.
At the time of the depositing of the seed, the deity Vāyu, moving through the left side, provides the movement [of the embryo].
Then she shall indeed become a maiden, bestowing sons upon her right side.
This is so; there is no doubt. Having understood this, one should then approach her during her fertile period.
By reciting or hearing this, there shall be the excellent fruit of progeny for one's lineage.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Giving of a Daughter, the Giving of Lakṣmī, the Vow for a Daughter, and so forth, for the Purpose of Obtaining a Daughter," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 123 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) — Chapter 123.
[The Author: Chapter 124.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Beloved One, Teacher of the World!
The foremost of all vows, bestowing all forms of ultimate liberation;
the remover of all calamities and the warder-off of all obstacles;
the dispeller of all distress and the destroyer of all diseases. (1–2)
Tell me that supreme vow, which brings all fortune and higher states, which bestows all prosperity,
and by the performance of which alone all vows are, in every respect,
as if already performed.
By the performance of which all evils are indeed destroyed;
by the performance of which all expiations are accomplished;
which bestows all goals, is the highest of all dharmas, and is supreme beyond the supreme. (4–5)
Tell me that [vow] at the beginning of which all other multitudes of vows seem as mere blades of grass,
and into which all meritorious acts such as sacrifices enter once it has been performed.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:

Listen, Lakṣmī! Even by performing all religious duties, gifts, pilgrimages, rituals, and vows, that which cannot otherwise be accomplished— for the sake of attaining that which is higher than the highest—
I shall tell you of such a vow that will certainly grant success.
I have spoken of this in many ways, yet I shall state it clearly once more:
the vow of service to the Lord is a virtuous vow that accomplishes all goals;
it is the foremost of all vows and the bringer of all auspiciousness. (8–9)
It removes all suffering, removes all obstacles, and is the abode of happiness; it dispels mental anguish, external conditions, and physical disease, and bestows the rise of all fortune.
It grants all prosperity, removes all sins, and destroys all impurities.
For that merit consists of the essence of all dharmas and indeed the essence of all sacrifices.
One should constantly worship the virtuous; for that is the vow of honoring the virtuous.
One should satisfy the lords of sages with whatever offerings are obtained. 11–12.
One should always perform the auspicious act of seeing them in the morning;
that vow of beholding the virtuous is the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
One should also constantly and auspiciously perform the service of massaging the feet of the holy ones in the evening.
The vow of massaging the feet bestows merit and grants all forms of prosperity.
(14) Every day, milk and other drinks should indeed be given to a virtuous person in the morning;
according to one's ability, this vow of offering delicious, nectar-like drink to a holy man is excellent. (15)
One who desires their own welfare should give fruits and other such items to holy men in the morning.
Ripe fruits of desirable flavors should be given; this is the vow of offering fruits to the virtuous.
Grains and other foods may be ripened by the sun, ripened by fire, or ripened by the seasons.

These should always be given to the virtuous; this is the vow of offering wholesome grains. (17) Leafy vegetables and various kinds of edible foods, such as sugarcane, tubers, sprouts, and so forth, should be given; this is the vow of offering wholesome vegetables. (18)
Raw substances such as ghee, flour, and milk should be given, along with sweets, salts, and fermented gruel; this is the virtuous vow of offering uncooked food.
Likewise, various kinds of delicious, sweet, and delightful cooked foods [should be offered]. (19)
One should constantly offer, with sincere devotion, wholesome food as part of the vow of offering to the virtuous.
Cold water should also be given for the purposes of bathing and drinking;
this is the vow of offering pure, fragrant, and delicious water fit for drink to the virtuous. (3.123.20–21)
Betel nuts and leaves suitable for mouth-freshener, along with seeds and other ingredients, should be offered; this is the vow of providing excellent fragrance.
Or, in the evening, whatever foodstuffs and drinks there may be [should be offered].
One should give gifts according to one's ability, for that is indeed the virtuous vow of the evening.
One should also perform a massage of the body to alleviate fatigue;
an oil massage should be performed, which brings about the destruction of the exhaustion of the virtuous.
The gift of clothing should be bestowed, as well as the giving of blankets and the like;
the vow of offering fine garments includes the giving of beds, seats, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is the gift of cooking pots and gourds, as well as vessels, leaves, rows [of bowls], and baskets.
Those [offerings] should be given daily; this is the vow of offering to a worthy recipient (sādhupātra).
Flowers, flower-garlands, and fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like should be offered; this is the vow of offering fragrance to a worthy person (sādhugandha). || 26–27 ||
Firewood, sacrificial fuel, and gifts of mats, coarse cloth, and fine cloths;
stools, four-legged couches, beds, and the like—this indeed is the vow of the virtuous regarding sacrificial fuel (samidh-vrata).
Furthermore, there is the gift of books of knowledge, the gift of halls, and the offering of houses.
The vow of bestowing the knowledge of Brahman is the vow of imparting excellent learning.
(29) The offering of astrolabes, water-clocks, and inkstands, as well as the offering of ink, paper, and so forth, is the vow of offering virtuous instruments. (3.123.30)
The provision of thread and needles, the provision of footwear,

and the provision of garments such as jackets— this indeed is the vow of protection for the virtuous (sādhutāraṇavrata). Furthermore, having constructed a hermitage adorned with trees and other features, its dedication to the recipient [is part of this vow].
This vow of the virtuous hermitage is excellent, bestowing both heaven and liberation.

(32) A well, a large oblong pond, a lake, a long tank, a canal, or a small reservoir should be constructed with wealth if possible; this is the auspicious vow of providing water for the virtuous. (33)
A gateway, a hall of Dharma, a moon-chamber, a balcony, a sacrificial mound, and a water-reservoir should be constructed;
a cave should be made that provides shelter from the sun, and a fire-hall and a kitchen should be built for the sake of the virtuous. (34)
This vow consists of a hall for bathing, meditation, and recitation, as well as a hall for holy men (sādhu).
Cows that yield milk along with their calves should be given to the holy men, as well as bulls for the purpose of transport; this indeed is the Sādhudhenu-vrata. || 35–36 ||
Elephants, camels, horses, lions, tigers, deer, and other such animals should be given;
however, to a capable and virtuous person, one should give the excellent vow of providing a vehicle for the righteous.
Furthermore, [one may give] wind-swift chariots, celestial palaces, swan-drawn vehicles, and boats for crossing the water.
A cart drawn by men, a palanquin,
a protective vehicle, a wagon, sandals, a lion-throne, and an elephant-throne— these, as well as a wooden seat, constitute the vow of the virtuous vehicle (sādhuyāna-vrata). ||38-39||
A garden, a grove, a field, a livelihood, and a seasonal occupation; a share of income and what is to be given—this is the vow of virtuous conduct.
Musical instruments include bronze, the jhallarī, the paṭaha, and the auspicious lute (tantrikā).

The flute, the lute, the mṛdaṅga drum and others, the mūraja, the tāratumbikā, the water-instrument, the musical instrument of sound, the hand-clap, and the kettledrum—these should be provided as musical instruments; this indeed is the vow of the "Good Instrument" (sādhuvādya). ||41-42||
The skin of a lion, the skin of an elephant, the skin of a tiger, and that of a deer—this pure hide should be given; this indeed is the vow of the virtuous regarding skins.
Pearl, diamond, gem, ruby, glass, and the finest stone.
A mardalī drum and a pestle should be given; this is the excellent vow of the Sādhusādhana.
A box, a granary, a water-skin, a gourd, a pitcher, as well as a binding rope—these should be given; this indeed is the Jolī-vow of the Sādhus. 42–44.
Alms should be given like those of a honey-gatherer, and a *tulasī* garland for the neck;
the materials for worship should be offered—this indeed is the vow of the worship of the holy one.
A fan, a fly-whisk, a tripod stand, and an upper garment should also be given.
A cloth and a water-dripper should be given; this indeed is the virtuous vow of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā-vrata).
Medicines, powders, pills, and likewise globules, as well as decoctions and electuaries should be given; this indeed is the virtuous vow of health (svāsthya-vrata).
An umbrella, a sickle, a helmet, sandals, a loincloth, and a garment, as well as a loin-cloth and a small cloth, should be given; this indeed is the vow of protecting the virtuous.
Sacred ash, a tooth-stick, and even a sacred thread [should also be provided].
A waistband and a bodice should be given as the vow for the virtuous bull (sādhuvṛṣavrata).
That which consists of giving what is desired by the virtuous is the vow of providing for the needs of the virtuous (sādhvapekṣitavrata).
The word of the virtuous is to be accepted; the observance of their command is the vow.
The nectar of the virtuous’s grace is to be enjoyed; the vow is the nectar of the virtuous’s merit.
The water from the feet of the virtuous is to be drunk; the vow is the nectar of the virtuous’s speech.
The favor of the virtuous is to be obtained; the true vow is the virtuous’s grace.
The virtuous person should accept that which is pleasing and undertake the vow of relying upon the virtuous.
(53) Thus, O Lakṣmī, these vows of the virtuous have been explained to you in their true nature;
now I shall describe other vows as well, namely those consisting of service. (54)
But for those embodied beings who achieve complete success in this practice,
when suffering has arrived, they should adopt a state of humility toward the virtuous for the sake of service—
taking the form of servitude or even the form of slavery. (55)
That which consists of the offering of everything, or that which consists of the offering of material substances;

that which consists of the offering of lamps, or that which takes the form of the offering of food; or that which consists of the offering of oil, and that which consists of the offering of ornaments. (56–57)
That which consists of the offering of clothing, that which consists of the offering of daughters and sons,
and the honor consisting of service rendered to a virtuous woman and a virtuous man—
all this is the vow of offering to the virtuous, which destroys suffering and poverty.
A woman should practice that auspicious form of honor which consists in service to virtuous women;
a man, however, must practice that auspicious form of honor which consists in service to virtuous men, so that dharma may be protected, merit may increase, and happiness may be granted. (3.123.60)
Just as a woman or a man may attain supreme merit,
so too [one attains it] through the service of a guru or a female guru, and of a saintly man or a saintly woman,
performed with faith and by a path free from doubt.
One should serve a true guru by means of that very pride which was previously cultivated.
For that is declared to be service to the virtuous, the supreme and auspicious vow of the saintly.
Indeed, when a bad dream occurs, this auspicious form of pride should be practiced.
I shall seek the sight of the virtuous and attend upon them for even a moment;
may the fruit born of evil sleep never befall me.
Even when an ill omen occurs, one must maintain a state of mindfulness.
Having sought the sight of the virtuous and received their auspicious words of blessing, [I shall pray]:
"May the fruit of this ill omen not befall me.
When fear of an enemy has arisen, one should practice auspicious humility.
"By staying for two auspicious days in the hermitage, I shall perform the sight, worship, and service of the virtuous; thus, there will be no fear of the enemy for me.
But when danger from the king has arrived, one must show proper respect."
"I shall behold and serve the virtuous for five days;
I shall feed the good and give abundant wealth to the worthy.
I shall perform service to the gods and the gift of Dharma; let there be no fear of the king."
When fear has arisen among the subjects, auspicious honor should be shown;
I shall provide for their welfare and grant them excellent means of livelihood, such as fields, gardens, and the like.
For one month I shall serve the virtuous; there is no fear for my subjects from me.
When the danger of malevolent magic arises, an auspicious vow (mānatā) should be undertaken:
"Whenever this malevolent magic, such as possession by spirits, should perish for me, then I shall serve the virtuous for five days and likewise perform worship. ||71-72||
When an affliction has arisen that is as fatal as the destruction of life,
one must then maintain respect for the virtuous hermitage and the monastery day and night.
Having dwelt there for the duration of a month, I shall serve the holy people.
I shall perform devotion and I will indeed become free from affliction.
(74) While the transformations of nature arise, a sense of humility is auspicious;
it must be practiced, and I shall cultivate the company of the virtuous and serve those who possess the right perspective. (75)
"May my nature become healthy so that I may feed virtuous people;
in the case of a wind disorder, I must practice humility and seek the company of the wise.
If I do this for ten days, my madness will perish."
When bitten by a venomous creature, this supreme vow should be undertaken:
"May the poison be destroyed, and may my life remain firm for that purpose;
I shall serve holy men constantly, day and night, for one month. (77–78)

When suffering arises from the blow of a weapon or similar causes, it is auspicious to maintain the following thought for the sake of destroying that pain: "I shall perform worship of the virtuous, as well as the distribution of material goods, food, and other offerings. (79)
"I shall dwell for just one month in a virtuous residence, eager for service.

When there is pain in the heart, fainting, a disturbance of the three humors, or the cessation of bodily functions, the best course of action is to maintain self-respect, thinking: 'I shall live even if I am struck down.'"
Having become a virtuous person, I shall dwell in the monastery of the virtuous for the sake of attaining devotion; or else, I shall perform auspicious service to the holy ones for a year,
day and night, with my mind, with material resources, and with my body, being absorbed in them.

For the sake of destroying diseases such as fever, one should perform auspicious observances (mānatā). (83) "I shall dwell among the virtuous for two days to dispel my illness; likewise, I shall have a great worship performed and a Sarvatobhadra mandala consecrated. (84)
I shall have a maṇḍala constructed for the removal of cruel diseases;
I will give various kinds of food to the virtuous for the removal of suffering.
In cases of pain such as broken limbs and the like, an auspicious act of worship (mānatā) should be performed.
"If my limbs regain their health, I shall offer silver coins;
I shall offer my home, I shall offer my livelihood, and I shall serve the virtuous.
Once medical treatment with surgical instruments has been performed upon my body by the best of physicians," [86–87]
If I am to be honored as one who is alive and free from disease,
then for six months I shall remain engaged in the service of the virtuous, becoming a bestower of food and wealth.
Whether in the flow of a river, in the middle of a flood, in a cavity, or even in the mud—
In such circumstances, one should maintain a virtuous sense of propriety.
(89) "If I were possessed of wealth, then, in the face of this unavoidable calamity, I would offer my entire fortune—or even half of it—to the temple of the Lord. (90)
For six months, day and night, I shall serve the virtuous in the monastery with my food, wealth, clothing, body, mind, and strength.
For the sake of attaining victory in battle, auspicious honor must be rendered.

I shall offer to Śrī Hari, and likewise to the virtuous, villages, regions, and riches— gold, silver, diamonds, and so forth— as well as vehicles, mounts, ornaments, umbrellas, chowries, and silk cloths, each according to its proper measure. (92–93)
I shall serve the virtuous for five months like a slave;
I shall feed the holy men at the sacrifice and cause a temple to be built.
One who is bound by nooses and placed in fetters must show such humility.
If I am released from this, I shall serve virtuous people.
Having stayed in a monastery for two months and provided food according to my ability, one who is surrounded by enmity should indeed practice humility for the sake of survival. (95–96)
If I were alive, I would give my own body weighed down with gold, or a body weighed down with silver, or even a body weighed down with sugar;
indeed, for the sake of recovering wealth and other goods stolen through theft. (97)
If that wealth were obtained, it would be right to show the highest respect for it;
I would give half to the Supreme Lord, to the virtuous one who performs righteous deeds, and I would also perform sacrifices, acts of charity, and so forth with that wealth. (98–99)
If the wife, son, daughter, father, mother, sister, or family members have been abducted by enemies, the highest form of expiation (mānatottama) must be performed;
provided that they return here alive and unhurt. (3.123.10)
Then, for the duration of a year, I shall serve the virtuous;
I shall give wealth, food, and the like, and perform auspicious sacrifices.
I shall effect the supreme pacification of misfortune, which consists of protection.
Thus have these vows of service to the virtuous, known as Lakṣmī-vrata, been described to you;
they should indeed be performed by men and women alike, for they truly remove all suffering.
Furthermore, I shall now describe all other [vows] in brief.
For those who perform it, obstacles and afflictions go far away.
(104) There is no vow in creation superior to the service of the virtuous;
by their blessing, even incurable affliction is swiftly destroyed. (105)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Supreme Vow among All Vows, Consisting of Service and Humility toward the Holy," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 124. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*).
Chapter 124.
[The Author: Chapter 125. Śrī Puruṣottama said: "O Śivarājñīśrī! Listen; O Nārāyaṇīrame! Hear."
I shall now describe the numerous vows of service to the virtuous that bring about supreme benefit.

(1) If another person performs a malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) to obstruct the milking of cows, buffaloes, goats, sheep, or camels that yield milk, one should take recourse in the vow of the virtuous. (2)

Having obtained the dust from the feet of a virtuous person and saying, "May [the power] flow forth," one should place it upon the back of the bound animal (paśu); by that means, the malevolent spell (abhicāra) is certainly destroyed.
A woman who milks the animal suddenly provides the milk for the animal.
Or else, if one should provide all the milk for a virtuous hermitage for even a single day,
and perform service for the holy ones, then one should offer it to the milker;
likewise, when cattle are afflicted by disease, one should show them honor.
"I shall perform animal sacrifice if the disease is destroyed;
otherwise, I will serve the holy men day and night like a servant in the monastery.
[6] [He spoke of] elephants, horses, and Garuḍas, as well as swans, bulls, and birds.
If there is suffering for the mounts, an auspicious expiation (mānatā) must be performed.
Once the suffering has ceased, one should then have the mount restored by the virtuous;
otherwise, I shall respectfully return that mount day and night.
I shall serve virtuous people at the monastery of the wise at my ease; having seated the holy ones upon my vehicle, I will lead them toward the garden.
And having brought them to my own home, I will honor them with the offering of garments.

I shall bestow wealth and grain if there is protection for the cattle. For the sake of destroying those malevolent spirits who roam about in the corners of my house, in the courtyard, and on the street, auspicious honors must be performed.
In this place, I shall cause the feeding of the virtuous, their worship, and the chanting of Hari’s glories; I shall perform the sprinkling of water, which is a rain of the nectar of divine grace.
However, when there is a paralysis of the vital breaths, senses, and so forth, one should practice the auspicious posture of humility.
Having stayed in the monastery for one month, I shall serve the most excellent of holy men;
I shall feed them, worship them, and abide by their word.
For if disease arises in a living being even through contact with the awns of grain, [how much more so from other causes].
In that regard, respect should be shown for the sake of removing the diseases of living beings;
a tenth part of the grain should be given to the temple of the deity, as well as food for the virtuous and the giving of food to guests and the poor. (15)
I must likewise perform the most excellent festival of the food-mound (annakūṭa).
My field must be made prosperous through well-prepared cooking, and the trees and other plants in the gardens must be freed from disease. || 16–17 ||
If the disease is destroyed, one should maintain the highest respect;
indeed, I shall offer the excellent fruits to the virtuous as a tenth part [of the merit].
If a loss is observed in the proper cooking of bulbs, roots, and other such items—
When cooking leaves, flowers, and so forth, as well as when cooking vegetables, she should then perform the ritual of measurement with auspicious intent, thinking:
"May my cooking be abundant.
She should always first give roots, tubers, leaves, and the like to virtuous people.
I shall cause a virtuous dwelling to be established within this field, a beautiful refuge;
for when the ripening of the sugarcane is threatened by the destruction wrought by jackals, rats, and the like,
one must show honor there in order to pacify those disturbances.

"I shall indeed give excellent pieces of sugarcane to virtuous men every day—five, ten, or eleven; likewise on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī). Furthermore, from the produce of my secret orchard, I shall give a tenth part to the auspicious holy man."
I shall offer sugar and other gifts and cause a great festival to be held. If there should be an excellent and abundant share of profit in my business,
then I will certainly give a tenth part to virtuous people or to the deity.
If there should be a profit exceeding the amount lent,
