out of partiality, he constantly ate without giving anything to fill his own belly.
Due to that sin, his merit was entirely exhausted.
On the contrary, he became a sinner, afflicted by the suffering of poverty;
the fortune of his home perished, as did his wife, sons, and others;
his fields and garden were lost, and he became a debtor.
Overcome by hunger and exceedingly wretched, he became a beggar.
Blind and devoid of righteousness, famished at every step, he fell into sinful conduct and entered the jaws of death. (92–93)
Having experienced the sufferings of Yama, he then fell into the state of a dog-cooker (outcaste);
after a lapse of time, he was again born among the animal species and so forth.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, [is the wealth] of a virtuous woman, of a goddess, of a god, and of a yogi.
Alas, this [sin] should not be kept at home, for it brings about total destruction from the very root.

Indeed, by means of the ritual of the gift of the scales (tulādāna), whatever wealth or burden one possesses, the man who gives it away in this manner shall attain the station of Mahendra and other celestial realms. ||95-96||
He shall become the sovereign lord of the world-protectors and attain eternal heaven.
Riding in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
he will enjoy heaven for a very long time while being honored by the deities.
He shall go to Satyaloka, Mahālakṣmīloka, and Śrīnagara;
likewise, he shall go to Viṣṇupura, the world of Hari, and Goloka.
The devotee goes to Vaikuṇṭha and attains the imperishable, supreme state.
One who beholds a great gift being given, praises it, proclaims it to the worlds, remembers it at a later time,
or hears or recites it while imbued with a spirit of devotion— (3.125.10) — [attains the highest state].
Whether it be a woman endowed with devotion, a king, a queen, a friend, or a female friend;
a brahmin, a female brahmin, or anyone else—a servant, a servant-maid, or even another person—the one who praises the gift obtains a tenth part of its fruit there. (101–102)
Having enjoyed the fruit of his gift in heaven, he shall go to my abode through devotion;
indeed, the fruit of the Tulā-dāna is thus distinguished above all else.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Tulāpuruṣa Gift," within the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*) in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 125: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 126 [[Author:
→ Chapter 127
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the great gift known as Hiraṇyagarbha;
it removes all sins, bestows merit, and should be given for the attainment of auspiciousness. (1)
Having observed an auspicious day for the Tulāpuruṣa gift,

one should collect the officiating priests, the sacrificial pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, vessels, and garments; then, having fasted, one should perform the invocation of the deities in the morning.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should have the Brahmins recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) formula.
One should place a golden image of Dharma, the supreme deity,
as well as a golden pitcher— or likewise a silver one— within the pavilion.
It should be seventy-two finger-breadths in height, with a golden lotus at its center;
its width should be reduced by one-third, and it should be filled with ghee, milk, and other substances.
It is adorned with jewels, sprouts, rice grains, cloth, and fruits.
Beside that, one should place a razor, a needle, and a golden stalk (6).
Also, a small seat, an outer garment, a sacred thread,
a golden staff, a cover, and an auspicious, new water-pot (7).
One should place a string of pearls and rubies near the jar.
One should also place a vessel containing one *droṇa* of sesame seeds upon the jar.
Having established the jar in the center of the altar within the pavilion, one should worship it.
Sprinkled and bathed with water infused with all medicinal herbs, performed with care amidst auspicious rites, Vedic mantras, the chanting of the Vedas (*brahmaghoṣa*), and beautiful hymns;
the patron of the sacrifice (*yajamāna*) wore white garlands and garments and was adorned with ornaments. (3.126.10)
Having bound a handful of flowers, one should recite this hymn of praise: "Obeisance!

Obeisance to You, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign Lord of the syllable *namas*. Obeisance to the eternally golden One, to Him who is of golden hue. (1.1) Obeisance! Obeisance! To the eternally golden One, to Him of golden complexion! Obeisance!
Salutations to the one with golden hair, whose essence is the golden *praṇava*.
Salutations to the Lord of the golden ones, salutations to the husband of Hariṇī.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha and to the one clad in golden armor.
Salutations to the one of golden complexion, who is beautifully adorned with a golden beard;
salutations to You, the Lord of Mahā-Mahā-Nārāyaṇī;
salutations to the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to you, the god of Dharma, and salutations to you, the creator.
Salutations to you, the sovereign lord of the three worlds, and to you, the sustainer of the universe.
All the worlds abide within the womb of you, the all-pervading one.
All the gods are established within your body, O Mādhava;
all the goddesses are situated within your body, which is the very essence of Lakṣmī.
Salutations to you, whose form is the universe; salutations to the supreme lordly body.
Salutations to you whose form is the world; salutations to you, the support of the world.
(18) O refuge of the world, O Soul of all, salutations to you who exist in the form of the embryo.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to you, the womb of Brahman. (19)

Salutations to You, whose essential nature is the womb of all perfections; salutations to You, Kṛṣṇa, the womb of merit; salutations to You, the womb of liberation and the womb of heaven. Salutations to that Divine Being, within whose womb the three gods reside.
"O Śrī Hari, you are indeed the soul of all, residing within every single being.
O Soul of the Self who has become the self of all beings, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence.
Having thus performed the salutation, he then offered this golden hymn of praise.
Having grasped Dharmarāja and Caturmukha with both hands and placing his head between his knees, he should remain there for five breaths.
Then the twice-born man should perform the auspicious Vedic consecrations (*saṃskāra*) therein.
The *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*,
and likewise the *sīmantonnayana* [are performed] there for the god Hiraṇyagarbha, the supreme Brahmā Parameṣṭhin, and for the god Dharma who is situated within the water-pot vessel.
Then the Guru should cause [the image] to rise with auspicious songs, mantras, and so forth. The sixteen sacraments, beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), should also be performed.
Thereafter, one should bow to the pure, perfect form of the Creator and to the Bull.
One should indeed give the needle and other items to the preceptor or to a virtuous person.
While offering salutation, one should perform this auspicious praise:
"Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha; salutations to the Lord of Sāvitrī."
Salutations to the supreme lord of Mahālakṣmī, the husband of Hariṇī;
salutations to you, the womb of the universe; salutations to you, the womb of gold.
Salutations to you, who have become the abode of the world of moving and unmoving beings.
Salutations to you, the divine one who is the very form of witness and whose nature is Brahman.
Just as I was previously born with the attributes of a mortal, so too,
through being born from your womb, I shall possess a divine body.
O twice-born ones, thus entreating him, they should bathe the patron with four jars, being intent upon the mantras and benedictions:
"Today we shall behold the limbs of you who have been born."
With this divine body, live long and be happy.
Free from sin and a treasury of merit, become one who possesses the right to heaven.
At the end, being full of devotion and liberation, may you partake in eternal bliss.
And one should bestow sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon the Brahmins consisting of gold and silver,
as well as those made of jewels, wealth, clothing, food, and drink. Then, one should offer the supreme *Hiraṇyagarbha* [image] to the venerable Guru.
One should bestow the Dharma upon the virtuous and give water-pots to the mendicant. To the Brahmins, one should likewise give gold coins, silver jars,
alms-bowls, garments, and even the finest foods.
Brahmins and virtuous men should be honored by those devoted to giving many gifts;
there, one should offer all the necessary implements to the preceptor,
including sandals, wooden shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a vessel.
A village, a district, a hall, a house, or an auspicious temple—
by giving such things as the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) through the gift of the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa),
one becomes a giver of special merit and is eternally honored in the world of Brahmā.
For as long as a hundred billion eons he is honored in the world of Brahmā;
he shall dwell in the cities of the world-protectors throughout each successive Manvantara. Having attained the supreme sovereignty of Indra, he likewise attains the sovereignty of the Sun.
Having first attained the kingdom of Candra, and after that the kingdom of Dhruva,
and having enjoyed the station of Parameṣṭhin, one becomes a possessor of the Vairāja kingdom;
then, having obtained the eternal kingdom of Mahālakṣmī known as Śrīpura.
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of Bhūma and the sovereignty of Vāsudeva thereafter,
he indeed goes to the imperishable abode of the beginningless Supreme Self,
at the lotus feet of Lalitā, Śrī Mahālakṣmī, the consort of Nārāyaṇa.
Having become a devotee of me, the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
he attains [me] and enjoys all desires together with Nārāyaṇa.
O Rame, that gift of Hiraṇyagarbha bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It is the savior of the ancestors, the bestower of lineage, and the giver of sons and grandsons;
it is the deliverer of those in hell and the destroyer of all obstacles. It is the eradicator of misfortunes as well as the destroyer of ill fortune.
It is the destroyer of afflictions and bestows accomplishment, wisdom, and happiness.
For the reciter, the listener, and likewise for one who is reading it, it yields fruit equal to honey and equal to nectar, granting success and joy. (48–49)
One should indeed set one's mind toward the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha for the sake of the embodied soul;
he, becoming a leader, is honored by gods and celestial nymphs.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to another unsurpassed great gift as well.
This gift of the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍadāna) is the destroyer of all sins;
it bestows all prosperity, as well as the glory of universal sovereignty.
It grants the station of Brahmā, bestows heaven, and provides happiness. (51–52)
Having reached an auspicious day, one should then have a pavilion constructed;
one should then summon the officiating priests and prepare the necessary materials:
ornaments, garments, wealth, gems, gold, silver, and diamonds.
One should place golden jars and the like there for the purpose of giving;
one should likewise place fruits, water, a golden garland, whatever materials are to be given,
and all sacrificial offerings in that pavilion.
One should cause various kinds of foods and likewise various flavors to be offered,
and perform the invocation of Śrī Hari and Śrī Mahālakṣmī;
one should also invoke the world-protectors, the hosts of gods, and the incarnations.

One should worship all [the deities], including those made of golden images, according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, nectar-water, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), sandalwood, and saffron. Then,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the glorious deities.
A Brahmāṇḍa made of gold or silver weighing more than twenty palas should be fashioned and placed auspiciously within that pavilion;
it should be joined with two water-pots and adorned with the figures of Śeṣa and the Tortoise.
It was joined by the eight elephants of the quarters (diggajas) and endowed with the six Vedāṅgas;
it was accompanied by the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), with the four-faced one (Brahmā) situated in the center,
and it shone with the abodes of Śiva, Acyuta, the Sun, the Moon, and other deities.
Accompanied by Umā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Brāhmī, Sāvitrī, and Māṇikī;
joined with Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Kṛṣṇā, Rādhā, Śrī, and Bhū;
and supported by the Vasus, Ādityas, Maruts, Rudras, Nidhis, and Siddhis. (62)
It has fourteen storeys within its interior and is adorned with a central pillar like Mount Meru (63).
It shines with a treasury of jewels and is endowed with great minerals;
it measures from one span up to a hundred finger-breadths in length and breadth (64).
One should place [the image] wrapped in silk cloth upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds;
likewise, one should arrange the eighteen kinds of grain all around it.
To the east, one should place Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, who reclines upon Ananta.
One should place Pradyumna, the God of gods and Supreme Lord, in the fire;
in the south, one should place Prakṛti, Māyā, Mahālakṣmī, and Kambharā; and in the southwest, one should place the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa, the Great King Śrī.
In the west, one should place the four Vedas together with the Vedāṅgas;
in the northwest, one should duly place the god Aniruddha, the Lord of Śrī.
One should place the golden god Agni in the north, who is served by Śrī.
In the fire, one should install Śrī Vāsudeva accompanied by Vāsudevī;
in the center, Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Ramā; and on all sides, Śrī Rādhikākānta, the beloved of Śrī, accompanied by Nara. (3.126.70)
One should place images of Vāsudeva made of gold;
one should place ten water-pots (kalaśas) all around on pedestals of jaggery,
enriched with the five sprouts and gems, and provided with fruits and unbroken grains (akṣata).

One should establish ten cows, each accompanied by a coconut, covered with cloth, and filled with water; they should be adorned with gold, silver, and sugar, or according to one's means, they may be fashioned in form together with their calves, being excellent givers of milk. (72–73)
Adorned with golden horns, silver hooves, and cloth coverings,
possessing copper-colored backs and accompanied by bronze milking vessels;
provided with fodder and grass, they were decorated and duly honored.

One should worship all the gods with sandals, shoes, umbrellas, chowries, seats, and mirrors; and one should also honor cows and Brahmins with various kinds of food—both solid and soft—as well as with lamps, sugarcane, fruits, garlands, and ointments. (75–76)
One should honor virtuous men and women with all objects of worship—
such as sandalwood paste fit for royalty, garlands, food, garments, and so forth—
and one should perform the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and circumambulate the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*).
One should perform salutations to the cows, the gods, the virtuous, and the twice-born. Then,
having performed one hundred and more oblations of rice grains enriched with ghee, sesame seeds, and flowers,
accompanied by mantras at the conclusion of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), [one should proceed].
O Brahmins, the bathing of the patron with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha) destroys sin;
they should properly perform it with the waters of the jars, which bestows great merit.
And the patron should perform the circumambulation three times.
Then one should pray to the Lord Narayana, known as the Cosmic Egg (Brahmāṇḍa):

"Obeisance to you, O Infinite One, whose womb contains the great creation; O Abode of the Soul of the Universe, O Support of the Universe, O Field of the World! O Cosmic Egg, salutations, salutations to you! (8.1–8.2)
The upper half of you is the Supreme Brahman, and the lower half is Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Between these two is the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma), which contains all creation.
All the abodes of the incarnations and all the manifestations of the Lord of All reside therein.
All the abodes of the gods and all the forms of human beings (84),
all dwell within [her], residing in the interior of the cosmic egg.
The supreme sovereign Nārāyaṇī is the form consisting of the entire creation (89).
O Cosmic Egg, you shine here; I bestow this gift upon you.
May all my sins be destroyed, and may meritorious deeds accrue to me.
By means of this gift, may my ancestors certainly become liberated.
May those who suffer be happy, and may poverty be destroyed.
May all diseases perish, and may riches abound in the home.
May there always be prosperity, and may blessings ever dwell in my house.
May gold, silver, great jewels, and diamonds be in my home;
may I also become one whose lineage expands through your gift.
May the faults of sin perish for my family members and for me as well.
"May there always be good fortune for the women in my family.
Having said, "Obeisance to You, Nārāyaṇa, whose form is Brahman; Svāhā!", one should prostrate like a staff with either a golden or a silver [image].
One should give to the preceptor, to a virtuous person, to a worthy recipient, or to a twice-born brahmin;
likewise, one should give other articles of utility to the venerable guru.
One should give other jewels and gold coins to the twice-born.
And one should also give silver coins to the mendicants according to one's wealth.
Or else, having divided the Brahmāṇḍa into ten parts thereafter,
one should give two portions to the venerable Guru and the remaining portions to the twice-born.
And one should bestow further wealth upon the Brahmins and other mendicants.
Having thus performed the gift of the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍadāna), one should indeed feed the virtuous;
one should feed the holy men and holy women, as well as boys and girls.
One should feed the poor and the helpless, as well as widows and female mendicants;
one should feed female students and also male students;
one should feed those most devoted to Brahman, and likewise feed one's own devotees. (96–97)
Thus, by the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa, one obtains the merit born of the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa:
sovereignty over heaven, great kingship, the supreme station of Brahmā,
and empire over many celestial chariots, endowed with the bliss of divine siddhis.
Having attained the station of Vairāja, or reached the eternal Goloka,
or the supreme world of Vaikuṇṭha filled with liberated male and female deities,
or the eternal Kailāsa world— having reached the eternal Goloka. (3.126.100)
There, having brought his ancestors, the lineages of his mother’s family, and thousands of his kinsmen to infinite time,
the person who performs such giving reaches the imperishable abode after having delivered them all.
Whoever hears, recites, or even remembers this ritual procedure,
for him there arises the merit of giving that leads to the highest heaven;
as does he who gives his mind to the act of giving for another.
In the end, he shall attain heaven through his share of merit and a share of sovereignty;
by giving this supreme gift once again, he indeed goes to the highest state.
Thus, O Śivarājñīśrī, is the supreme gift of the Brahmāṇḍa.
This has been told to you, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grants the supreme state.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Gift of Hiraṇyagarbha and the Gift of the Brahmāṇḍa among the Great Gifts," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 127 [Author:
Chapter 128 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to another great gift known as the gift of the Kalpa-tree, which destroys all sins. Having reached a sacred day, it should be performed like the Tulāpuruṣa gift.
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, well-adorned with jars and other ornaments;
it should be decorated with flowers, cloths, plantain pillars, and arches, provided with an altar and sacrificial pits, and graced by seats for the Brahmins. (2–3)
It was provided with all kinds of requisites and jars filled with water from sacred fords (tīrtha),
complete with the materials for the ritual of worship and adorned with banners;
[he worshipped] the deities at the gateway and the archway, as well as the guardians of the directions (dikpāla-devatās).
One should invoke the gods of the various branches, the incarnations of the Supreme Lord,
and all the Śrī-devīs beginning with Mahālakṣmī,
each in their proper place, preceded by the proclamation of a "holy day" (puṇyāha).
A beautiful tree of gold, endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits; beautified by flocks of birds and adorned with clusters of blossoms and sprouts;
and provided with creepers of thread for garments, ornaments, and coverings. (7)

According to one's capacity, [the quantity] should be from three *palas* upwards up to a thousand *palas*. (8) Having thus planted that *kalpavṛkṣa* in a measure of one *prastha* of jaggery, one should offer an excellent pair of white garments upon its branches. (9)
O tree, you are beautifully adorned by the gods beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
you possess five main branches and numerous secondary branches, radiant and colored white and red,
rich with green leaves and endowed with crimson sprouts.
Having adorned [the deity] with a white root and a stalk-section colored yellow and so forth,
one should place Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the fulfiller of all intentions, upon a beautiful great golden throne below. || 11-12 ||

May he establish me as Kamaleśa, made of gold, together with my wife; and may he establish all my incarnations, as well as my father and my mother. May all the forms of Lakṣmī likewise establish Kāmadeva along with his wife.
One should establish the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhi) and fashion the wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī).
One should arrange clusters of blossoms all around and nine new sprouts;
one should adorn them all with saffron, barley, and sandalwood.

One should fashion small, beautifully adorned trees called "sons" from the Mahāvṛkṣa, representing its progeny, on all sides using one-fourth of the material. Having placed a lump of ghee or a broad vessel of ghee [at the base], ||| 16 ||
Having first placed a small, auspicious wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) in the eastern part,
one should indeed place it upon ghee, adorned with wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpavallī*).
One should also place the *mandāra* tree on the southern side together with Śrī.
In the collection of wheat, adorned with the Kalpastamba and other such features,
one should then place on the auspicious western side a beautiful golden Pārijāta tree, joined by creepers rich with *kalpa*-flowers.

In a heap of rice adorned with sprouts of grass and the like, one should place [the image] together with Sāvitrī, who is situated upon a cluster of cumin seeds. Then, to the north, one should place it beautifully upon a heap of fragrant sesame seeds.
One should place excellent yellow sandalwood joined with clusters of *kunda* flowers,
adorned with heaps of rice and provided with all the requisites for worship,
in the corner regions; and the *bakula* tree belonging to the northeast direction.

Having established a most beautiful garden, one should place a lovely *campaka* tree in the southeast (*agni*), a coconut tree in the southwest (*nairṛti*), and a betel-nut tree together with a betel vine and clusters of cardamom and other plants in the northwest (*vāyavya*). (23–24)
One should plant stalks of sugarcane provided with fruits, garlands, and cloths;
having thus made an auspicious grove rooted in silk garments,
it should indeed have mango trees at its borders and be frequented by peacocks and cuckoos.
Having beautified that place, which is provided with cows, cowherds, bulls, and water-pools, one should place eight auspicious full jars there,
enriched with gems, sprouts, and cloths, and filled with fruit and water.
One should place near that [image] the two sandals, the fly-whisks, the parasol, the staff, the canopy, the chariot, the celestial vehicle (*vimāna*), and the mount;
as well as a vessel for the offering of food and a cooking pot or eating bowl.
One should place a water-pot for drinking near the foot of the tree.
One should also prepare a lamp and incense, and set out fruit, sweetmeats, and various flavors,
as well as all kinds of grains, namely the eighteen varieties.
One should place there, according to one's ability, in that pavilion at the foot of the tree:
wheat, rice, millet, *jvārikā*,
and *barjara* (31), as well as *baṇṭikā*, *śīṇikā*, mung beans, chickpeas, and kidney beans.
One should place before [the deity] sixteen types of grains: *kulatthikā*, *vaṭāṇa*, *māṣa*, and *kodrava*; likewise *yava*, *tuvarī*, and other cereals;
as well as *nivāra*, *rājaguruka*, *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and *cirbhaṭa*. (32–33)
One should place mangoes, sugarcane, coconuts, immortals (amṛtā), bilva fruits, jackfruits, rose-apples, licikās, and kaliṅgaras; as well as sugars, watermelons,
and sixteen types of cucumbers.
Then one should perform one hundred and eight oblations in the fire of the sacrificial pit (35).
With milk-rice, various fruits, and substances rich in flavor,
one should worship Gaṇeśa made of gold, together with his consort (36).
One should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of my image and of the tree;
one should bathe the tree and me, and perform three circumambulations.
One should offer salutations, recite hymns of praise, and then offer prayers.
Salutations to you, the Supreme Lord, who are the very essence of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma);
salutations to the sovereign of the wish-granting creeper (kalpavallī), the bestower of desired objects;
salutations to the embodiment of the splendor of all tastes, fragrances, and forms.
Salutations to you, the divine Sustainer of the universe, whose form is fulfillment.
Salutations to you, the god who is full of all food, the embodiment of all nectar. Salutations to the abode of all immortality, whose nature is the essence of the moon.
You alone are the Supreme Lord; you are Nārāyaṇa, you are Mādhava.
You are Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna, and you shine forth.
You are the sun, the moon, fire, and Indra; you are the eternal digestive fire within all beings.
You are the Lord of Brahmā’s mental garden and you are the lord of the forest;
though possessing a manifest form, you are also formless, and you consist of both the seed and the tree.
You are the embodiment of man and woman, and you are united with Mahālakṣmī.
You are the eternal essence, the performer of creation, preservation, and destruction.
Protected by the creepers and trees of the lineage, protect us from all sides.
Grant us heaven, bestow powers, and give us auspicious riches.
Grant me spiritual perfections and celestial chariots; likewise, bring about the upliftment of my lineage.
You are indeed the bestower of liberation upon the ancestors; grant them satisfaction as well.
At the end, grant me the state of the most blissful Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Having thus entreated him, one should give the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) to the preceptor;
then, one should present the progeny and other gifts to the four officiating priests (ṛtvij),
and all other gifts to virtuous twice-born men.
One should provide delicious food and cause it to be served to the monks and yogins;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, but should give money as is appropriate.
One should indeed give fruits, roots, and grains only to those who are worthy.
One should pay obeisance and, having propitiated him, personally dismiss him.
Then the man who bestows the gift should partake of the food offered as a favor (*prasādabhojana*).
Thus, he becomes liberated from all sins and attains the merit arising from ten thousand horse sacrifices (*aśvamedha*).
The righteous soul, together with his wife and kinsmen, and along with his family, obtains merit;
having enjoyed great sovereignty here on earth, he shall then go to heaven.
Having indeed enjoyed the great celestial realm, he shall thereafter proceed to Satyaloka.
Having enjoyed the state of Vairāja, he shall go to Vaikuṇṭha itself. Indeed,
he shall deliver hundreds of lineages of men—
past, present, and future— along with their fathers, sons, and grandsons, as they are being praised upon the heights of heaven.
By means of celestial chariots equal to the sun, he is sent by those merits to the world of Viṣṇu, which is higher than the highest;
thereafter, by those same merits, he is sent to the imperishable abode (akṣara-dhāma) beyond that.
Endowed with the power of Nārāyaṇa and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa, [he attains it].
One who is devoted to the stories of Nārāyaṇa and is a servant of Nārāyaṇa,
performing sacrifices, shall go to the state of Anādikṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, the listener, the speaker, and the rememberer of these [stories] will certainly be born as Mahendra.

Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī, to another great gift, the Great Gift of a Thousand Cows, which bestows all merit. Having reached an auspicious lunar day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or a Manvantara, [one should perform it]. (58)
Having constructed a beautiful pavilion for the gods and goddesses, as well as for me, Nārāyaṇa, and having likewise prepared an auspicious sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
one should then collect the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and invoke the deities.
One should worship me, Hari, as well as my incarnations and the goddesses;
one should worship all forms of Lakṣmī and a cow-image fashioned from gold. The patron of the sacrifice (yajamāna), observing a vow of milk, should worship her for three days.
Or for one day, he should then have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* [formula];
and he should perform an oblation in the fire with ghee, rice, fruits, and so forth.
Having performed the oblation a thousand times, [he should give] a thousand cows.
One should worship and circumambulate [the cow] standing outside, honoring her with cloths, garlands, garments, ornaments, horns, hooves, and excellent milk; thereafter,
one should worship her with chains, saffron, and coverings for her back.
Adorned with golden horns and ornaments, equipped with silver hooves, joined with small golden bells, and provided with bronze milking vessels;
endowed with golden forehead-marks and decorated with gold bands and other ornaments. (65–66)
Clothed in silken garments, honored with garlands, perfumes, and other offerings,
provided with mouthfuls of fodder, and adorned with staffs and chowries;
they were equipped with sandals, wooden shoes, umbrellas, vessels, and seats.
They should be accompanied by Nandikeśvara, along with a bull and a heifer;
or else, in the midst of golden cows, there should be a bull made of gold as well, standing among ten cows and adorned with garments, ornaments, and the like. (68–69)
On the peak of the Lavaṇadroṇa mountain, it should be joined with garlands, sugarcane, and fruits; made of gold weighing fifty palas, or three hundred,
or even produced from three thousand palas according to one's capacity.
He should be established and worshipped, as well as ten auspicious cows.
Indeed, a golden image should be worshipped, or one should worship ten parts [of the deity].
Having bathed [the deity] with nectar-like waters accompanied by the sounds of songs and auspicious music, [one should proceed]. || 71-72 ||
Having circumambulated [the herd] three times and holding a handful of flowers, one should worship the assembly of cows, pay homage, and then make this request:
"Homage be to those who are the embodiments of Brahmā; salutations to the Mothers of the Universe."
Salutations again and again to the Rohiṇīs who dwell in the worlds.
(74) The three creations indeed abide within the limbs of cows;
so too do the fourteen abodes of Brahmā’s creation. (75)
There are twenty-eight levels of worlds belonging to Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva,
and fifty-six worlds of Māyā reside among the cows.
May Rohiṇīs, Drogdhrīs, Īśvarīs, and Mātṛs protect me always.
May cows be before me, and may cows be behind me;
may cows always be upon my head, and may I dwell in the midst of cows.
This bull is the very form of Dharma and is indeed eternal.
Dwelling within the form of Hari, may He always protect me along with my family—
[the realms of] heaven, truth, the Vairāja, the earthly, the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, the city of Śrī,
the immortal, the unmanifest, and the imperishable Goloka.
"May the Bull of Brahman bestow auspiciousness upon me, even as he grants cattle.
Having thus prayed, one should offer a golden cow to the venerable Guru;
likewise, one should present Nandīśvara, the embodiment of Dharma, to the virtuous one.
One should give a single auspicious cow, adorned with ornaments, to each of the officiating priests (ṛtvij).
One should also give other cows to the Brahmins as is appropriate.
A single cow must not be given to many, for it would surely cause them distress.
A wise person should give many [images] for the increase of one's health;
auspicious ones, adorned with all ornaments, should be given to the Guru.
Many should be given to the illustrious Guru if no obstacle exists.
Various kinds of wealth, as well as grains and garments,
gold, silver, and coins— these should be given to beggars and others.
One should observe the milk-vow, remain celibate, and be solely devoted to the worship of Hari.
One should cause others to hear or listen to the story of Dhenu, and perform the recitation (*japa*) of Hari.
Thus, one attains abundant prosperity and becomes free from sin;
endowed with great merit, one travels by means of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) as resplendent as a thousand suns.
At the end of the body, having gone to the vault of heaven, he attains the Truth beyond that;
honored by the world-protectors and adorned by the expansion of his lineage,
he enjoys divine pleasures while residing in the realm of Vairāja.
Having established himself in the Vaiṣṇava yoga, he then goes to the imperishable state.
That wise man may deliver one hundred and one ancestors; likewise, he may deliver his maternal grandfathers and those born of a hundred lineages.
The ancestors rejoice over a son who gives away a thousand cows, thinking:
"May there be such a son or even a grandson in our lineage;
having become a giver of a thousand cows, he shall deliver us from hell. (91)
Even his servant, or one who merely witnesses or approves [of such a gift], shall rescue him from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Cows go before the deceased even on the path to the world of Yama. (92–93)
They cause one to cross the Vaitaraṇī river and even in the abode of Dharmarāja;
whether in heaven, in Satyaloka, or in the dwelling of Maheśvara;
likewise in the abode of Viṣṇu, in the abode of Īśānī, or in Śrīpura.
In the abode of Mahālakṣmī and the dwelling place of the incarnations,
cows— those auspicious carriers and nourishers— go everywhere. Wherever there is a cow, there indeed are the gods, the lords, and my own attendants.
Where all fortunes and the wives of Brahmā dwell, where the cows indeed reside,
where the imperishable Brahman also abides— there Goloka exists.
Through the yoga of the cows, Goloka was manifested by me, Kṛṣṇa.
Where there are cows, there am I, Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and Māṇikī;
Prajñā, Padmāvatī, Śrī, Mahālakṣmī, and the Supreme Sovereign.
There is the divine city of Amṛtā, the auspicious Śrīpurī, the abode of light. (98–99)
Eternal, enriched with all enjoyments, endowed with divine implements,
crowded with hosts of divine powers, and resplendent with divine majesty;
an abundance of perpetual bliss, possessing divine food and excellent vessels.

One who gives a thousand cows obtains such a glorious city, furnished with celestial garments, gardens, groves, couches, and pleasure-parks. Furthermore, he attains Goloka and reaches the imperishable state (akṣara-pada). || 101-102 ||
O Queen of Śivā! He obtains my entire sovereignty;
O Nārāyaṇī! he obtains all flavors, of this there is no doubt.
O Dispeller of Suffering! He obtains various powers replete with happiness.
And he enjoys all desires together with Brahmā in the divine abode.
(1.04) By reciting, hearing, remembering, teaching, and inspiring others to this [text], the patron obtains both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (1.05)
Whether a man, a woman, a virtuous wife, a saintly person, a god, a preceptor, or a lord, one who bestows the gift of a cow goes to my eternal abode, the state of Brahman.

(106) Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Great Gift of the Wish-Fulfilling Tree and the Great Gift of a Thousand Cows," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (127)
← Chapter 127 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā / Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 128 [[Author: Chapter 129 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī! Such is the great gift of the golden wish-fulfilling cow (hiraṇyakāmadhenu), which accomplishes all one's desires. || 1 ||
One should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, adorned with sacrificial pits and archways,
and provided with seats, ritual implements, oblations, fire, and other necessities;
[therein one should worship] the world-protectors, the deities, the Supreme Lord, and the Lord of Ramā.
Having likewise invoked Lakṣmī and all [the other deities], one should perform the worship and the fire-oblation (homa).
Then, the patron (yajamāna) should carry out the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) there;
and virtuous Brahmins should chant the proclamations of the Vedas and auspicious hymns.
One should have a cow and a calf fashioned from highly purified gold;
the best [cow] should weigh one thousand *palas*, the middling half of that,
and the smallest half of that again, though it should be no less than three *palas*.

Having had [the image] fashioned, he should have it brought into the pavilion and placed upon a deer-skin on the sacrificial altar (vedi) atop a mound of jaggery; likewise, it should be adorned with great jewels and other auspicious items,
as well as golden ornaments for its horns, hooves, back, and backbone.
One should worship that cow together with her calf on the forehead using saffron and other substances.
One should place eight water-pots, adorned with jewels, leaves, water, and rice,
in that pavilion, as well as all eighteen kinds of grains.
Likewise, eight stalks of sugarcane and various fruits;
vessels, a milking bowl, a rope, and an auspicious chain;
as well as eating bowls and delicious fodder—these he should place in the pavilion. (3.128.10)
One should place a pair of silken garments, ornaments, an umbrella, lamps, earrings, chowries, bells, golden horns, and the like;
as well as decorations, silver hooves, and all auspicious substances.

Turmeric, fruits, flowers, musk, sandalwood, camphor, sugar, gentle [incense], canopies, and likewise garments— all these auspicious and divine materials, as well as water from sacred fords (tīrtha)— [should be offered]. 12–13.
Having placed darbha grass, unbroken grains of rice, and tulasī leaves there in the pavilion, the sacrificer himself, being pure,
with flowers in his hands, should worship the cow and the Brahmin should recite the Vedas. (14)
Accompanied by auspicious hymns, one should perform three circumambulations.
Then, standing in the presence of the cow, one should indeed offer this praise:
"O Mother, you are the abode of all the gods and of all yogis. (15–16)
You are indeed the savior of embodied beings, the auspicious refuge of all powers;
you are the bestower of the path to heaven, the bestower of liberation, and the bestower of prosperity. You exist as the destroyer of sin; O giver of happiness, I bow down to you.
O Mother, who bestows desired fruits and destroys the torment of suffering;
O Kāmadhenu, O Supreme Goddess who grants great bliss;
O Giver of liberation to Hari, you who eternally cause him joy—salutations be to you! (18–19)
You are Kānakī, you are Hariṇī, and you are Hiraṇyā; you are Candrikā, you are Śrī, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Kamalā, and the beloved of Hari. You are Nārāyaṇī, Rasadā, Saṃkalpapūrikā, and Ramā.
You are Padmā, you are Dhāmaśakti, you are Jayā, you are Laliteśvarī;
you are Śāradā, you are Māṇikī, you are Prabhā, you are Parameśvarī;
you are the destroyer of suffering, you are Pāśavatī, you are Padmajā, and you are Tulasī.
You are Mādhavī and you are Gāyatrī; you are Kārṣṇī and you are the virtuous Śāṅkarī.
You are Vaikuṇṭhā and you are Akṣarī; you are Brāhmī and you are Kanakeśvarī.
You are Svargiṇī and you are Tāpasī; you are Satyā and you are the beloved Vaiṣṇavī.
You are the earth, you are the progenitor, and you are indeed the eternal garden.
You are the protector, the bringer of eternal merit;
you are the liberator from sins, the giver of liberation, and the purifier.
O Cow, having rendered me sinless along with my family,
and having granted us the prosperous heaven forever, you shall thereafter bestow liberation.
By your grace, my ancient ancestors have already gone to heaven.
Other pretas shall go to heaven through the merit of giving;
and you, O lady, have been given as a gift to the Guru, to the Brāhmaṇa,
to the divine and virtuous Satpuruṣa, and even to Hari.
Having spoken thus and offered water, he should then give a cow to his preceptor,
as well as gems, jewels, coins, silver, grains,
various kinds of cereals, and garments; these he should give to others with devotion.

One should feed those separated from their loved ones various foods, including excellent sweet dishes and fragrant milk-rice (pāyasa). One should also feed the poor, the helpless, virtuous wives, holy women, and children.
One should give many other gifts as well, according to one's wealth.
Thus, the giver of a golden cow goes to the eternal Brahman.
He who is capable of giving a golden cow but does not do so [should give] a silver one.
One should give a cow along with its calf; however, one who is unable to do that may give a young heifer.
As for the man who is unable even to give a young heifer, he should praise the act of giving, instruct others about it, and urge them toward it.
One who hears it, causes it to be heard, or recites it shall attain that fruit.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare another unsurpassed gift:
the great gift of gold and horses, which bestows the kingdom of heaven.
Having reached an auspicious day, one should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed for those who grant liberation and bestow celestial chariots;
there, one should have an altar or an auspicious sacrificial pit made for the purpose of the fire-oblation.
Likewise, one should keep all necessary implements nearby;
all materials for giving, such as gold, silver, and diamonds,
as well as food, clothing, and vessels intended for worship, should be set aside.

Then, one should place all the ritual materials— sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, and garlands— as well as the items for the food offering (naivedya) and the waving of lights (ārārtika), by one's side. Furthermore,
one should place a pitcher filled with water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) within the pavilion.
There, one should have the *puṇyāhavācana* performed by the most excellent brahmins;
likewise, one should cause the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the world-protectors and other deities,
as well as that of the Lord of Śrī, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
One should perform the invocation and worship, according to the prescribed rite, of all the female deities who have been released from their incarnations;
one should establish them in the center of the altar upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds.
A golden, excellent horse, clothed in silk garments,
weighing from three palas up to a thousand palas,
with its back covered by a golden saddle-cloth and adorned with a golden necklace and beautiful bridle.

It was equipped with a golden girth, adorned with golden bands, possessed a network of golden reins, and was resplendent with diamond whips; it was provided with a parasol, fine foot-restraints, and excellent hooves, and was truly enchanting. (45–46)
Alternatively, one should place a golden image of Aśvinī, adorned with ornaments, or one of gentle complexion, upon sesame seeds in the pavilion for the purpose of giving;
as well as sandals, wooden shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a vessel.
One should place eight water-pots in the pavilion there,
made of gold, silver, or copper, filled with water and joined with garlands, rice, leaves, and the like, as well as gems and bilva fruits. (48–49)
Other objects suitable for giving, even those that are beautiful—
diamonds, rubies, various gems, and many kinds of grain—
as well as garments, ornaments, and vessels, should be placed there for the purpose of charity.
One should place a bed equipped with a couch, provided with a headboard and so forth,
adorned with side-screens, pillows, and various furnishings; one should also place a cooking pot, a beautiful water-jar, and a small garden plot.
One should also place sweet foods and drinks such as milk and the like;
one should also place many kinds of desirable, well-ripened fruits;
and one should set down bulbs, root-tubers, and leafy vegetables.
In such a pavilion, the sacrificer— pure and auspicious,
bathed by the brahmins with a ritual bath of all medicinal herbs, and holding a handful of flowers—
should circumambulate three times the fire, the horse, and the preceptor. ||54-55||
One should pray to the Supreme Self, who is resplendent with all horses:
"Salutations to you, O Lord enriched by all horses, O Soul of All, who resides in the hearts of the horses!
You are the one who brought down the Vedas; salutations to you, O Son of the Aśvins! (56)
Salutations to you whose form is that of a golden horse, and salutations to you of divine form.
(57) Salutations again and again to you whose form is the horse of the Sun, and whose form is the horse of Kalki;
salutations again and again to you who have the form of Uccaiḥśravas, the divine horse. (58)
Salutations to you whose nature is the horse of the senses, and salutations to you, the horse of the mind.
Salutations to you, the Great Horse, whose form is identical to the *aśvattha* tree.
Salutations to you who assume the form of the white horse, and salutations to you, the destroyer of sin.
O Hari, you who take the form of a horse, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra!
Grant me heaven, liberation, great sovereignty, and eternal prosperity. Bestow upon me all riches, and thereafter grant me liberation.
"By your gift, may Mādhava, the Soul of the Universe, be satisfied.
Having uttered this, one should perform a single circumambulation around [the deity].
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should dedicate the horse to the act of giving.
Having paid homage to the preceptor, one should indeed present that horse.
(63) One should also give other objects as gifts according to what is appropriate.
One should bestow wealth upon the officiating priests, and food, money, and so forth, upon the mendicants. (64)
By giving [this], the sacrificer is born divine through the destruction of evil;
he proceeds to the world of the Sun, the world of Truth (Satyaloka), and Vaikuṇṭha.
One should listen to the Saṃhitā and arrange for the serving of food and other provisions.
One should also offer food to virtuous Brahmins and virtuous women;
one should give grass to the helpless, children, the aged, cows, and horses.
Becoming filled with devotion, one should feed those who desire food.
O Lakṣmī, he who gives a gift of a golden horse according to his means,
being honored by the lords of the gods, goes to the liberated state of Hari.
Mounted upon a golden celestial chariot, he goes to the supreme world of the Sun.
Or he who hears this narrative also goes to the excellent abode of the Sun;
he who reads it or causes it to be heard likewise goes into the presence of the Sun;
and he who offers praise also goes to heaven, the refuge of happiness.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the great meritorious gift consisting of a horse-chariot.
Having reached a meritorious day, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed.
One should also have an altar and a sacrificial pit made, and procure the materials for worship.

One should invoke the world-protectors (lokapālas), the deities, and those who are incarnations of the Supreme Brahman, as well as the lords (īśvara) and the sovereign goddesses (īśvarī), within the auspicious pavilion. One should also provide eighteen kinds of grain, vessels, and riches.
One should place garments, ornaments, and silver on all sides within the pavilion; likewise,
one should install Gaṇeśa and the other deities, Śrīpati, myself Janārdana,
Bālakṛṣṇa, as well as Kṛṣṇā, the beloved of Brahmā, and the beloveds of Hari.
One should invoke and worship [the deity], and then procure a golden chariot yoked with seven horses, provided with four wheels and more than that [in size],
equipped with a sapphire pitcher, a protective fender, and a banner. (75–76)
One should place me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Kamalā and the principal queen, resplendent with the charioteer Sūryamukhya at the pole of the chariot,
in the middle of the chariot.
He should also station my attendants, adorned with parasols and chowries,
as well as staff-bearers and weapon-bearers who are intent on worship and service;
likewise, he should station virtuous men and women at my side upon the chariot.
One should establish the hosts of gods, sages, and ancestors upon that best of chariots;
likewise, one should install Mahālakṣmī, Kaṃbharā, and the illustrious Gopālakṛṣṇa,
as well as all the auspicious goddesses who are ever-contented and provide a refuge for all.
One should place Lalitā there, endowed with all her powers (Śaktis).
One should place gems, diamonds, necklaces, and golden ornaments upon the chariot;
and upon a lion skin, one should place a Droṇa measure of sesame seeds, or even more than that.
Having prepared supporting cloths, one should place the chariot upon them;
sixteen or four jars, filled with gems, sprouts, unbroken rice,
cloth, water, and fruit, should be arranged there.
One should worship the gods with devotion, offering them garments of silk.
One should worship me in the chariot, O Lakṣmī, and perform the consecration (adhivāsana) under my name;
furthermore, one should procure other articles specifically for the purpose of giving as gifts.
An umbrella, yak-tail whisks, and even silken garments; sandals, wooden shoes, cows, a bed, and even a vessel;
a couch and other such beautiful objects.
One should have a beautiful golden lion fashioned together with a chariot;
the chariot should be accompanied by either two or four horses.
Likewise, there should be two attendants at the sides, each with a horse, acting as protectors of the wheels and bearing weapons.
He should worship a chariot made of a thousand pieces of gold, or another according to his wealth;
or else, he should worship a chariot weighing at least three palas, performing three circumambulations.
Being pure himself, the patron, holding a handful of flowers in his joined palms, [should perform this].
Wearing white garlands and garments, having performed my oblation with clarified butter,
and then with other fruits, flowers, and so forth, one should circumambulate the chariot and pray to the Lord, the abode of Śrī, regarding the chariot and myself as non-different.
Homage to You who have attained the supreme abode; homage to You, O Nārāyaṇa!
Homage to the Yogi whose form is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa!
Homage to You who transcend even the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and are the self of all worlds!
Salutations to You, the Lord of all abodes, the chariot of the Sovereign of All!
Mahākāla and Mahāmṛtyu are its two solstices, and the seasons are indeed its spokes.
All these are known as the wheels of Your movement; You ought to protect me from them. (93–94)
Grant me eternal heaven, and grant me a righteous destination;
grant me the supreme abode, free from time and illusion.
O best of chariots, effect the liberation of my ancestors and my family.

Having become a divine form in the shape of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), lead [us] to the imperishable state (*akṣara-pada*). Pearls are situated upon your banner; the imperishable abode (*dhāma-akṣara*) is on the tablet.
The *Īśvaras* are in the body of the staff, and all the *Śaktis* are in the fender (*varūtha*).
Within the interior are the heavenly worlds; in the center is Nārāyaṇa Hari.
All the deities are around him, and all the gods are situated on the outside.
Below are the inhabitants of the seven netherworlds, and between the two wheels are Yama and his bull.
"May merit be foremost, as well as devotion; may those gurus dwell within you.
In their witness, I indeed give [this gift]; protect me from the ocean of worldly existence.
Having spoken thus, a chariot and other riches should be given to the guru. (3.128.100)
All other gifts should be given to the destitute as appropriate;
one should feed all the virtuous, the Brahmins, and the boys and girls.
Then, one should dismiss them all and grant them leave to depart.
He should cause the *Saṃhitā* to be recited and likewise instruct others in the stories of giving.
For both the instructor and the one who gives consent obtain an equal share of the fruit;
indeed, having ascended a divine chariot, he goes to my imperishable abode.
Having enjoyed all the various celestial realms for a long time along with his family,
and having become a great lord himself, the donor of the chariot goes to the divine abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Procedures for the Gift of the Golden Wish-Cow, the Gift of the Golden Horse, and the Gift of the Golden Chariot among the Great Gifts," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
