Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall now describe here the gift of the golden elephant-chariot, by the offering of which a person attains the divine Vaiṣṇava abode. (1)
Having reached an auspicious day, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
within that pavilion, one should arrange the altar, the sacrificial pit, and the materials for the oblation.
Having invited the Brahmins there, one should also provide seats and water-pots.
He should also invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) as well as the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana). The patron of the sacrifice should have all the auspicious hymns sung;
he should perform the invocation of the deities and worship them according to the prescribed rule.
One should have constructed a golden elephant-chariot shaped like a flower, adorned with jewels and other precious things,
featuring ten wheels and variously decorated gables;
it should be provided with banners, a protective fender, and all necessary equipment, and be most beautiful.
Richly adorned with parasols, chowries, and jewels, and graced by those holding canes and other attendants;
resplendent with the radiance of the moon, mirrors, and other objects placed before it—one should place the sesame seeds upon a tiger skin or a leopard skin. (6–7)
There, one should station the chariot and indeed the articles to be offered.
Upon the chariot, one should place Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, me, the Lord of Ramā;
as well as my incarnations, the lords, and the ruby that destroys suffering and bestows prosperity.
And Rādhikā, Prabhā, Pāśavatī, Lakṣmī, Jayā, and Ramā;
Lalitā, Kamalā, Padmā, Padminī, Tulasī, and Satī; Sāvitrī, Kaṃbharā, Līlā, Gāyatrī, Mañjulā, and Bhū. (3.129.10)
Mahālakṣmī, Mahāviṣṇu, Sarasvatī, and Mādhavī; Bhārgavī, Suguṇā, Haṃsī, and likewise Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
as well as Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Śrī-Kṛṣṇa, and Mādhava.
One should place me there, accompanied by Brahmapriyā and Haripriyā, and served [by attendants].
One should also station my liberated attendants (pārṣadas) there on the chariot,
as well as all divine weapons and whatever divine grains there may be.
Various vessels, sandalwood, unbroken grains of rice, and *darbha* grass;
water-pots filled with jewels and adorned with five sprouts;
as well as a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, a mirror, and wooden shoes. (14)
One should place there for the purpose of giving a bed, a couch, a water-pot, various garments, diverse fruits, foods fit for consumption,
and wealth consisting of gold and silver. (15–16)
One should fashion a banner with Garuḍa, a chariot-pole with Vināyaka,
and a canopy beautifully adorned with rows of bells, containing an inner sanctum. It should be joined with sixteen jars and accompanied by sixteen cows.
With sixteen golden elephants adorned with strings of pearls,
their backs covered with golden saddle-cloths, possessing beautiful wheels on their golden tusks,
with golden frontal globes upon their backs, and resplendent with ornaments for their feet and other parts; (18–19)
Having prepared an auspicious chariot adorned with the beautiful resonance of tinkling bells,
one should worship Śrī Hari— who is I— stationed therein, as well as the deities and others.
Having performed three circumambulations, one should indeed offer prostrations and other rites.
One should offer praise while placing a handful of flowers before [the deity]:
"Salutations to You, whose form is Brahman, who are the refuge of Nārāyaṇa, the abode of the Lord of All, and who consist of ten million liberated souls. (22)
Salutations to you, whose form is the imperishable Brahman, who are the refuge of ten million powers, the abode of Brahman, and the very essence of heaven and liberation.
Through your gift [of knowledge], [the merit of] sacrifices, holy fords, and those consisting of vows [is attained].
May the merit of all my moral conducts and all my gifts arise for me here.
You are indeed composed of all the gods, you are also composed of all sacrifices;
you are the abode of the gods graced by all prosperity—protect me!
Purify me from the multitudes of my sins; protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Grant me through your gift a destination in heaven and thereafter the imperishable state—[that destination] at whose feet the lords of the gods, the lords of lords, bow down.
Likewise, the incarnations have been liberated; therefore, O Jaya, you are indeed graced by Him.
You are the one who leads to the further shore of the path through the forest of worldly existence for those who take refuge in Hari;
you alone exist as the bestower of prosperity upon those devoted to the Lord.
"You are the savior of the ancestors and indeed the increaser of the lineages;
you are the bestower of happiness, O Kṛṣṇaratha! Salutations to you!
Having thus entreated him and performed a fourth circumambulation, one should bow down.
One should perform an oblation (havana) into the fire one hundred and eight times for Lord Hari.
Thereafter, one should offer gifts to the illustrious and virtuous Guru;
then, one should also give other appropriate gifts to the holy man at that time.
He should give various gifts to the Brahmins, to mendicants, to children, and likewise to the virtuous; he should also give garments to young girls,
as well as diverse sweet foods and those which are the essence of milk.

One should give bowls, foods, grains, and silver according to one's wealth; likewise, a house, a hall, and a garden. A chariot constructed from a thousand palas of gold is considered to bestow imperial sovereignty.
One made of a hundred thousand pieces of gold bestows the station of Indra and grants a birth from the Unborn (Aja). Even when given as little as more than ten palas, it bestows all prosperities.
When dedicated to me, Nārāyaṇa, it grants the imperishable abode.
Bestowed upon a great virtuous person, it grants a state of sovereignty;
but bestowed upon my devotee who is devoid of [worldly] qualities, it grants my own station.
Having thus given and enjoyed heaven, the giver finally goes to my station. (36–37)
By hearing of this, by reciting it, by remembering it, by causing it to be heard,
and likewise by expressing approval, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a chariot.
Listen further, O Lakṣmī, to another unsurpassed great gift.
The gift of five ploughs destroys sin and bestows all merit.
On an auspicious day, the patron should then have a pavilion constructed, as well as sacrificial pits, altars, seats, and the materials required for the fire-offerings and gifts. (3.129.39–40)
One should place there in the pavilion various objects such as diamonds and gems for the purpose of worship,
as well as sandalwood, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and all other ritual requisites;
and one should set out water-pitchers containing jewels.

One should place five golden vessels, both with stalks and with fruits, in that pavilion; likewise, one should set down various kinds of grain, as well as food for eating and desired delicacies according to one's capacity. (42–43)
One should set aside garments, ornaments, and materials intended for distribution as gifts.
Having had five auspicious plows made of strong wood, they should be equipped with yokes,
bound with ropes, and adorned with white and black soles.
Beautiful [chariots] equipped with hand-grips and reins, yoked to bulls or men, and provided with poles,
lash-ropes, and other fittings, made either of gold or silver,
beginning from five palas and extending up to a thousand palas or more. ||45–46||
Having thus caused ten bulls to be made as yokes,
and having had them fitted with yokes, adorned with every ornament,
with silver hooves and forehead-marks, and draped in red silk cloths; 47.

One should place in the pavilion cows whose necks are adorned with excellent pearl necklaces and ornaments such as *ghurghura* bells, which possess beautiful golden horns and are exceedingly splendid;
one should also provide suitable carts according to one's capacity. 48–49.
One should cause a market town, a hamlet, a village, and a field abounding with crops,
as well as a beautiful house or a garden, to be fashioned out of gold. Thereafter, one should preserve them in their presence within the pavilion.
And one should have those learned in the Vedas recite benedictions for well-being and the proclamation of an auspicious day (svastipuṇyāha).
One should invoke me, Hari, as well as Kṛṣṇa, the ploughman;
and one should also invoke Rādhā, the daughter of Karṣṇa, and Mahālakṣmī, the female ploughman.
One should invoke the incarnations, the liberated ones, the sovereign goddesses, the gods, and the world-protectors such as Dharaṇī, Āditya, Rudra, and others,
with sacrificial fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, desired fruits, leaves, and milk-rice.
One should perform oblations into the fire one hundred and eight times while remembering me; likewise,
the preceptor should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) made of milk-rice to the Earth, the Sun, and the Rudras,
as well as palāśa fuel-sticks and clarified butter to them.
Black sesame seeds, sugar, rice, and fruits—white sugar is Mahālakṣmī herself, the Earth personified; Lakṣmī is truly pleased by it.
The goddess White Sugar is the daughter of the Earth, the one who rends the earth asunder.
Indeed, that maiden or girl emerged having burst through the womb.
Then, for her satisfaction, milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered during the oblation.
After the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should invite a Brahmin couple and worship them. || 57–58 ||
One should worship the virtuous man and the virtuous woman with divine garments, ornaments, and the like, as well as golden necklaces and rings, and by providing appropriate gifts.
In the pavilion, one should also offer eighteen kinds of grain and a milch cow.
One should place a bed with its furnishings, adorned with sugarcane stalks and other items.
Having circumambulated the ploughs while holding a handful of flowers,
one should pray to the Supreme Self, who dwells in the plough as the one who rends [all obstacles].
On the white and black plow, Śiva and the wielder of the plow (Balarāma) are stationed;
on the yoke is Viṣṇu, the upholder of dharma, and on the rope is his beloved Nārāyaṇī.
On the bulls is the god of dharma, and devotion is established upon the staff.
Śrī Hari dwells everywhere; salutations to you, O Supreme Lord!
(63) All the gods reside within you, who are rich in all powers; salutations to you!
I meditate upon the white [Goddess], the knower of the essence of the roots of the lords of the worlds. (64)
Salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the ploughman, the glorious wielder of the plough;
salutations again and again to You, the all-pervading Brahman whose very self is the plough.
You have been offered here as a gift, assuming the form of the five-fold plough.
"Grant me heaven, truth, great sovereignty, and even the earthly sovereignty of Vairāja;
grant me the essence of those fruits, and likewise, at the end, supreme liberation.
Having spoken thus and bowed down, he applied five plough-marks upon his face.
One should offer [these] adorned with implements and yoked to bulls,
and indeed one should give other gifts as well to the community of mendicants;
likewise, one should present them to the Brahmins and the officiating priests according to what is appropriate.
One should give land fit for cultivation with five ploughs, consisting of five hundred *vighāṭikās*, or even a smaller portion together with its groves;
or one should give land yielding gold, or indeed a house, for the sake of peace. (3.129.70)
Then, according to one's wealth, one should give food, water, and other such gifts; thereafter,
one should have meals prepared there for the twice-born and the yogis,
as well as for virtuous women, holy men, children, young girls, the squint-eyed, the blind, and other such women.
In this manner, one should give a gift according to one's capacity, which destroys sin.
It shall grant heaven, it shall grant a kingdom, and it shall bestow the station of Parameṣṭhin.
For as many grains of harvest as there are upon the earth, for that many ages one indeed dwells in heaven.
He rejoices together with his family and thereafter goes to the abode of Hari;
there is no doubt that the liberation of his ancestors is likewise accomplished.
By the gift of five ploughs, one indeed gains the merit born of five kalpas.
By that [merit], one is indeed born in heaven and may repeatedly become a lord of the gods.
One who bestows cows, land, a plow, or a bull shall attain Vaikuṇṭha;
by reading or hearing this, one obtains a reward equal to that.
Now I shall describe to you the great gift of the island of Lakṣmīdhara,
which destroys sin, bestows merit, dispels inauspiciousness, and brings happiness.
(77) Having reached an auspicious day, one should cause a beautiful pavilion to be constructed.
One should have a sacrificial pit and an altar constructed, and place water-filled jars adorned with jewels, sprouts, and cloth— eight of them fashioned from gold—
as well as articles suitable for distribution and those suitable for the fire-oblation (homa). || 78–79 ||
One should place all grains suitable for worship,
as well as a golden representation of the earth consisting of Jambudvīpa, adorned with its boundary mountains,
beautiful in the center with Mount Meru, and divided into nine regions.
It is surrounded on its borders by oceans and endowed with rivers, streams, and lakes;
it contains mines of all kinds of gems and stands beside the god Vārāha.
[One should fashion it] with a thousand palas of gold, or half of that, or with portions of that amount.
Having caused it to be made with five *palas* of weight, one should indeed install it;
in the center, one should place me, Śrī Hari, the Lord of Ramā.
Likewise, one should install my liberated incarnations and the liberated women (*muktānikās*).
All those who were dear to Brahmā and likewise those women dear to Hari;
the lords and their consorts, the gods and goddesses, as well as the sages;
Mahālakṣmī, Śrīgopālakṛṣṇa, and Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He should likewise cause the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and my auspicious temple to be constructed, as well as the hermitage of Lomaśa;
and he should provide ornaments, coverings, garments, and various kinds of wealth.
One should place there in the pavilion items suitable for the gift of food;
one should spread a lion’s skin or a deer’s skin there,
as well as grains among the sesame seeds, along with liquids and auspicious sugar.
One should also place fruits, silk cloth, and a canopy;
one should invoke the world-protectors, the guardians of the directions, and the lords of the gods.
Wearing white garments and remaining pure, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having circumambulated the earth and holding a handful of flowers, one whose inner self is purified by contemplation should worship and also pray:
"Salutations to you, O Soul of all worlds, O Blessed Hari, Soul of the earth! (3.129.90–91)
You are the earth, you are the sustainer, you are the nurse; protect us, O Vasundharā!
Salutations to you here, O Vasumatī; grant me always the treasures (vasu).
Salutations again and again to you, Anantā, who reside upon the head of Ananta Śeṣa.
You are Lakṣmī, you are Mahālakṣmī, and you are the contented Narāyaṇī.
You are Gāyatrī, you are Śivā, and you are Māṇikyā in my presence.
You are the destroyer of the suffering of the worlds and the bearer of their embryos; protect me!

You are moonlight, you are radiance, intelligence, wisdom, and the virtuous supporter of the universe; you are fortitude, stability, forbearance, the earth, the broad one, the netherworld, and the giver of birth.
Protect heaven, grant me the great kingdom, and bestow upon me the eternal state.
"O devoted one, grant liberation to all my ancestors who have been offered [to you].
Having thus bowed, he should offer that golden earth to a worthy preceptor;
or he may give half of it to the Brahmins, as well as jewels and other things.
Then one should feed the monks and virtuous, upright people who have assembled;
one should give gifts of grain, clothing, and fruits.
One should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) one hundred and eight times, which bestows happiness.
By that very act, evil is destroyed and merit is obtained through giving.
A man who bestows a gift of land attains the prosperity of Viṣṇu;
accompanied by the liberation of his ancestors, he travels in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun. (3.129.100)
He goes to Śrīpura and the eternal city of Nārāyaṇa;
by reading and hearing this, one becomes liberated in body and is reborn there.
Having enjoyed the sovereignty of Vairāja, he goes to my imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has been described to you the great gift consisting of the earth.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Gift of the Golden Elephant-Chariot, the Great Gift of the Five-Plow, and the Great Gift of the Golden Earth," in the third section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 129. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 130 [Author:
Chapter 131 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī! Hereafter is the Great Gift (mahādāna), the most magnificent Great Gift of the Universal Sudarśana Discus (viśvasudarśanacakramahādāna).
The best is made with a thousand palas, while that which is half of that is middling.
Or one should have a brilliant wheel made with half that size as the smallest;
it should have sixteen spokes and eight rims, adorned with silver bands.
One should have the best wheel made with twenty or more petals.
Upon His navel, one should fashion me, the auspicious Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa,
four-armed, wearing a crown, and adorned with four weapons.
On the first spoke, one should place the golden and auspicious Brahma-priyeśvarīs.
One should install Rādhikā, Lakṣmī, Prajñā, the virtuous Padmāvatī,
Māṇikyā, Lalitā, Haimī, and Jayā— these are my beloveds.
Likewise, on the second rim, starting from the east, one should place the Lord reclining upon the waters.
The glorious Lord Gopālakṛṣṇa, accompanied by Kambharā; the Guru Narāyaṇa, who is devoted to his wife and accompanied by his faithful consort;
and the auspicious true Guru Lomaśa, together with Kuṅkumavāpī.
A goat accompanied by Sāvitrī, and likewise Śiva joined with Śivā;
[he saw] the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana;
Rāma bearing the axe, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki.
On the third rim, one should cause to be fashioned the seven Mātṛkās, the eight Vasus,
and Gaṇeśa together with his family and accompanied by his vehicle.
On the fourth [rim], the twelve Ādityas and likewise the four Vedas.
In the fifth [enclosure], one should cause the five elements and the eleven Rudras to be fashioned;
in the sixth, the eight world-protectors and the elephants of the directions;
and in the seventh, all the weapons as well as the svastikas and other [auspicious symbols].
One should install the eight Siddhis and the eight Aiśvaryas in the eighth [section].
Having thus caused the Sudarśana-cakra to be fashioned within the pavilion,
one should bring it into the great hall adorned with plantain pillars and other ornaments.
Near the altar, one should place the discus upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds;
likewise, one should arrange all the ritual materials, ornaments, and coverings,
as well as the eighteen kinds of grain and the flavors, such as salt and the rest.
Eight full jars, as well as gems, jewels, and garments; garlands, sugarcane, fruits, flowers, and whatever items are fit for giving;
excellent foods and drinks, sugar, and wealth.
One should likewise protect the cow, the maiden, the *tulasī* plant,
and the fire. Then, having become purified by bathing and wearing white garments, the patron (*yajamāna*) should cause auspicious musical instruments to be played within the pavilion.
Having sat upon his seat together with the officiating priests,
and having respectfully performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and other preliminary rites, he should then invoke the deities;
having worshipped them according to the prescribed rule, he should then perform one hundred and eight oblations (homa).

Having performed the ritual consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should also offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Having circumambulated the fire-altar (*homacakra*) clockwise, one should also offer this prayer:
"Salutations to the one whose form is the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*); salutations to the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all. (3.130.20–21)
Salutations to You, the Sudarśana, whose very nature is the universal wheel (viśvacakra).
Salutations to You who reside upon the fingers of the hand of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Salutations to You, the compassionate one, who acts as a flame for the masses of sins.
By the gift of the golden discus, grant me worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O embodiment of supreme bliss, salutations to you, whose self is Nārāyaṇa;
to you who are composed of splendor, divine, and possessed of the power to destroy the asuras.
Salutations again and again to You who abide in the heart and have transcended all qualities.
The Discus is situated within Nārāyaṇa, and Hari is situated within the Discus;
between the two is Mahālakṣmī—to that Goddess, salutations again and again.
"Your weapon exists for the protection of devotees; protect me!
Having spoken thus, one should offer the Sudarśana discus to the guru, and likewise present other items suitable for donation to the twice-born.
At that time, one should indeed bestow gifts upon the distressed, the blind, the wretched, and likewise upon women;
one should give to boys and girls as well.
One should feed them all kinds of edibles and likewise perform the *ārātrika* rite.
One should perform the concluding rite and dismiss the Brahmins and others.
Thus, the giver of the discus is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence,
[residing] in the supreme heaven of Viṣṇu’s world, in Satyaloka, on the ground of Vairāja.
Having enjoyed infinite pleasures and having become one with the essence of Nārāyaṇa,
he reaches the eternal Vaikuṇṭha realm as a four-armed being;
after dwelling there for a long time, he then goes to Goloka, the supreme abode.
From there, he goes to the city of Brahmā, my supreme and imperishable abode.
Having had the eternal golden Sudarśana discus, which is the refuge of Hari,
fashioned for his home, the devotee should worship it with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
Even he who crosses the wheel of worldly existence does so by worshipping the discus of Hari.
In whosever home the Sudarśana resides, his wheels of sin are surely destroyed;
they do not arise again, but rather mountains of merit are born.
The Sudarśana [discus] constantly provides protection to the householder;
it increases his lifespan and bestows abundant prosperity,
as well as the wheel of sovereignty or even the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Now, O illustrious Queen Śivā, I shall tell you that most excellent and secret majesty of my *cakra*, which is superior in every respect.
[It is that] in whose body, house, hand, garment, courtyard, or possessions—
The Sudarśana discus shall be present there; no evil remains therein.
The messengers of Yama do not approach, and the Rākṣasas flee away. Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, and the like also take flight to a great distance.
All diseases, such as fevers and the like, never remain;
through the Sudarśana [mantra], even latent impressions (vāsanā) reach total eradication.
Obstructions caused by kings, deities, and others are likewise destroyed by the Sudarśana.
The afflictions caused by snakes and scorpions, as well as other poisons,
are swiftly destroyed by the splendor of the Sudarśana discus of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
All supernatural powers dwell there, perfectly protected in every way.
Child-seizing spirits and other such beings do not afflict that house;
nor does untimely death occur there because of the Sudarśana.
A household where the Sudarśana resides shall never be childless.
Wherever my Sudarśana is present, portents do not occur at all.
Wherever my Sudarśana is indeed present, there shall be no sudden calamities;
and through my Sudarśana, victory shall always and in every way be mine.
Furthermore, fears of thieves and tigers do not arise at all,
nor indeed fears of water or fire, nor even fears of earthquakes—
none of these occur where my Sudarśana resides.
Furthermore, through the *Sudarśana* [rite], there arises no fear of miscarriage, nor fear of widowhood for women, nor any fear concerning the failure of one's undertakings;
afflictions do not arise, and no fear of living beings occurs. (47–48)
Where my Sudarśana resides, there shall be no fear of weapons, no fear of being struck down, and no affliction from the planets;
nor shall there be [a lack of] beauty of form, fortune, prosperity, excellent flavors, and the like. (49)
Through the power of Sudarśana, many inconceivable things arise.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to that which is the great Cakra-mālā:
a golden garland or a garland of Tulasī is the supreme Cakra. (3.130.50–51)
This is declared to be the Brahma-wheel, indeed that supreme Sudarśana;
it has one hundred and eight spokes and is the most excellent wheel of the virtuous.
A rosary held in the hand of a virtuous person truly cuts away all sins.
It cuts away all the fortresses of illusion (māyā) along with their very roots;
it lifts the burdens of birth and death from the head.
He who wears the garland around his neck—his head is worshipped.

If a garland is held in the hand, Lakṣmī always dwells in that hand; if it is worn on the arm or the forearm, Ramā is produced there. His forearm shall always be the abode of Lakṣmī and remain dear to her.
That house where the *mālācakra* is present shall be protected by me,
Nārāyaṇa, who am the Self of all,
through the recitation of the garland-mantra (*mālājapa*), [which subdues] the Daityas dwelling within the wicked senses. (56–57)
The dissolution of all impurities certainly occurs [by this].
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the supreme Great Wheel of Brahman, the Sudarśana garland, is a protector at all times; it should especially be given as a gift.
One should offer a garland made of gold, silver, crystal, or pearls, or one made of *tulasī*, as a gift;
for that indeed bestows heaven and grants liberation.
One should give it to a virtuous and great-souled teacher who is a practitioner of silent recitation (*jāpaka*).
Having worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should wear a heart-pleasing garland;
for a garland made of crystal rests upon the heart of Śrī Hari.
A garland of *tulasī* held in the hand attains honor even from Lakṣmī herself.
She is this Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Mālikā, the destroyer of impurity;
she bestows the garland of heaven, grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and is brilliantly radiant.
She is adorned with one hundred and eight jewels strung upon the thread of heaven.
Adorned with Meru beads made of crystal or silver,
and bound with the *brahmagranthi* and other knots, the auspicious and virtuous Śrīvāsinī—
she who is the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss— is to be offered as a garland according to the prescribed ritual.
Having established [the image] upon a water-pot (kalaśa) in the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala,
the Gomukhī [image] should be offered together with sugar and other substances, adorned with cloth,
provided with a seat, and accompanied by a covering cloth. ||65–66||
A divine bed-cover, fragrant with fruits and endowed with divine jewels, adorned with threads of pearls, should be offered;
indeed, it should be presented along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and accompanied by wealth and grain.
Having placed that garland upon a deer-skin, a jar, or a vessel, and having offered it into the hand of my image of Śrī Hari, one should worship it.
One should bathe my garland with sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and other offerings. (68–69)

Having worshipped with sandalwood paste and other offerings, he should again place them in my hand. Then, having performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), the incense, and the lamps, and having bowed to me,
he should offer the food (*naivedya*) to me and then feed the garland.
The Goddess of Consciousness is my garland; the graceful woman is mine.
She is the eternal power, most divine, the bestower of all merit.
Together with the svastika, she grants wealth, grain, and other blessings.
Having bowed to the guru and prostrated before him again and again, one should pray to the guru there: "Whatever offering of the garland I am making to the guru,
may the Supreme Self, Kṛṣṇa, be pleased with me by that merit."
May I always be protected by Mālā, Rādhā, and Lakṣmī.
O true Guru, may my sins be destroyed by the offering of this garland;
may Mādhava, ever pleased with me because of the garland, grant me happiness.

Thus one should give this garland-wheel, which removes fear when given as a gift. Where there are twenty-seven beads—either auspicious ones or a protective silver one—that constitutes a quarter of the garland. (76)
Or else, because of doubt and hesitation, he protects her by means of a number.
Thus, this son of hers is her protector; one should entrust even him [to her].
The offering of the garland is a great gift that destroys all sins.
O my beloved, the constant recitation with a rosary (mālā) should be dedicated to Nārāyaṇa;
by that, wicked sins are destroyed moment by moment.
For one who has surrendered everything to Me and performs japa, there is no sin whatsoever.
It is said that there is no sin for one who gives these two wheels:
the great pair of wheels known as the Sudarśana and the Mālikā.
The Mālikā is the destroyer of worldly existence, while the Sudarśana is the slayer of demons.
Moreover, the third wheel is indeed the finger ornament;
the ring-wheel made of gold jewelry should especially be given as a gift. Indeed, the giver of the ring becomes a sovereign emperor upon the earth.
The giver of all types of finger-rings becomes a king in heaven.
The giver of signet rings, finger-rings, and the like becomes a creator of the universe.
Having fashioned [these] from gold, silver, and other materials, one should honor the preceptor and the twice-born.

Having offered salutations to the virtuous, chaste, and great saintly woman devoted to her husband, to the true guru, to the teacher learned in the Vedas, to the virtuous son of Nārāyaṇa, or even to one belonging to the lineage of Acyuta, he should then offer [the gift]. 85.
Having worshipped the rings and finger-rings with excellent saffron,
one should offer this ornament upon the thumb of the right hand;
for there always resides Kamalā-Ramā, the one who takes away gold.
Having worshipped it, one should pray to that ring, the ornament for the finger:
"Protect me always from the waves produced by the ocean of saṃsāra;
O golden one, may there always be liberation in my hand. (88)
"O Blessed One, grant [this] to me, O Blessed One, O beloved one!
O Urmi, having destroyed all my heaps of sin, submerge me in the wave of the bliss of Brahman, O Beloved of Kṛṣṇa! (3.130.89–90)
Having thus worshipped and made supplication, one should give as a gift a beautiful ring made of gold—
either one or ten— possessing three, five, or seven auspicious ridges.
If he is capable, he should give twenty [gold pieces] as a gift to a virtuous twice-born devotee of Viṣṇu with great devotion;
and he should also offer a fourth item, such as a bracelet or a ring made of gold, upon his hand.
One should also offer a lion-throne that resembles a wheel, inlaid with jewels, adorned with gems and diamonds,
set with pearls and rubies, and encrusted with the Kaustubha gem;
it is the destroyer of all poverty.
It bestows all prosperity, bestows Lakṣmī, and likewise bestows a wife;
it bestows the kingdom of heaven and likewise bestows Satyaloka;
it bestows Brahmaloka and likewise bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this manner, O Lakṣmī, one should offer ornaments for the feet and the forearms, as well as bracelets,
bangles, anklets, and waist-bands,
fashioned from gold and silver and adorned with gems and pearls. (97)

It bestows all splendor and resounds with the tinkling of a network of small bells. O Lakṣmī, one should likewise give a golden necklace (*natthikā*) and a beautiful, circular golden chain adorned with jewels. (98–99)
O beloved, all these wheels have been described by me to you;
they should indeed be given according to one's capacity, for they bring merit through the act of giving. They bestow heaven, grant great prosperity, and even grant liberation.
They destroy poverty, disease, and discord, and bring about happiness;
they cause the expansion of one's lineage through divine progeny and the like, and increase the fortune of having celestial women, husbands, and sons. (10.1–10.2)
"From reciting, hearing, remembering, and even from rejoicing in these gifts,
all of them indeed bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends [the section on] the gift of the Great Discus Viśvasudarśana, the gift of the Mālikā Great Discus, the gift of the Vārakṣaka, and the gifts of the ring, the finger-ring, the armlet, the bracelet, the chain, and the *biṅgī*— in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīyasaṃhitā*.
Chapter One Hundred and Thirty: An Exposition on the Bestowal of Great Wheels, Such as the Ḍī, Kaṅkaṇa, and Nāstika;
Chapter 130 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section Three (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 131.
[Author: Chapter 132.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, to the unsurpassed great gift (mahādāna).

And [he should perform] the gift known as the Mahākalpalatā, which is like a golden creeper. (1) Having reached an auspicious lunar day, he should have a beautiful pavilion constructed; he should also have an altar and a sacrificial pit made, and install them for the purpose of the fire-sacrifice. (2)
He should have the Brahmins perform the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*) for the sake of the ritual substance.
Having taken up the materials for the gift, he should place them there in the pavilion.
The officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) [should receive] all the requisites, ornaments, clothing, and so forth.
And upon the seats of the gods, of Nārāyaṇa, of mine, and of Śrī,
as well as of the goddesses, he should perform the invocation and worship.
There in the pavilion, one should [place] ten golden creepers known as Kalpavallīs.
One should place ten golden trees, produced from gold weighing ten *uttara*s, adorned with fruits and flowers;
they should be provided with jewels, silken garments, and the like, and likewise decorated and beautified.
They should be accompanied by *vidyādharī*s and similarly graced by *suparṇa*s.
And one should fashion the wives of the eight guardians of the directions (dikpāla) according to their respective creepers.
On the mountain of sugar, one should cause all the creepers to ascend;
[specifically] the Aindrī [creeper], representing the spear mounted on an elephant, and the Āgneyī [creeper], representing the spear mounted on a ram.
In the south, she is seated upon a buffalo; in the southwest, she is seated upon a donkey;
in the west, she is seated upon a crocodile; and in the northwest, she is seated upon a deer.
In the north, she is seated upon a golden vehicle; and in the northeast, she is seated upon a bull.
Likewise, one should place sixteen grains there in that pavilion:
Lakṣmī, Śivā, Sāvitrī, Māṇikyā, Duḥkhahātmā, Kambharā, Śrīmahālakṣmī, and the contented sister of Hari.
One should likewise place juices, fragrances, sweet-tasting substances, and jars of ghee;
having fashioned them with gold weighing a thousand [units], one should indeed place them in the pavilion.
One should also place eight cows and eight jars filled with water containing gems.
One should also place them adorned with cloth, rice, leaves, and so forth.
One should worship them according to the prescribed rite, and likewise worship the creepers.
Having worshipped them with the chanting of the Vedas and having performed three circumambulations, [one should proceed].
One should pray to those creepers accompanied by Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa—to those who destroy the sins of others and protect their own devotees.
"Salutations to you who grant fruits; salutations again and again to you who are like the wish-fulfilling Kalpa trees. (15)
Salutations again and again to those who bestow all prosperity and possess every supernatural power;
salutations indeed to those whose very nature is Mahālakṣmī and who are the self of all.
[They are] Svarga, Amṛta, Śrīpura, Vairāja, and Gavāyana.
"May you, who are the personification of charity, grant us Vaikuṇṭha, the imperishable abode, forever;
and having been bestowed, may you always protect us.
Having prayed thus and performed another circumambulation, one should offer [the gifts].
One should give half to the preceptor and half to the virtuous teacher, while giving portions to others as well.
Indeed, one should bestow gems, diamonds, silver, cows, and whatever garments there may be upon mendicants and those who are destitute or helpless. (3.131.19–20)
One should perform the oblation according to the rules, feed virtuous Brahmins,
and also feed boys and girls, and bestow wealth. Then, O Dear One, one should perform the ritual dismissal, bid them farewell, and prostrate.
In this way, one should perform the gift of the wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā); its fruit is great.
Sovereignty arises, there is liberation for one's ancestors, and the earth, ever abundant with crops and other resources, remains at his disposal. (22–23)
Indeed, the supernatural powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā) arise for the giver of the creeper;
in heaven, those desire-granting creepers (kalpalatās) become his celestial nymphs (apsarases).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this great gift of yours truly fulfills every wish.
It has been declared throughout all the worlds that this auspicious rite bestows great sovereignty.
Likewise, one should perform the gift of a Kalpapriyā; hear now its procedure.
An auspicious image should be fashioned from a thousand bhāras of gold. (25–26)
Adorned with garments and ornaments, beautified by every kind of finery,
she was a beautiful young woman graced by sons,
daughters, and others; she possessed cows, buffaloes, elephants, and horses, and was further adorned with beds and other furnishings.
Endowed with wealth, grain, and the like, and provided with juices, foods, and fruits—
having placed that great Rāmā there in the pavilion in the form of his wife,
one should invoke her before the altar and worship her with all kinds of offerings.
One should perform the nightly lamp-offering and present excellent food offerings and water.
Whatever kind of wife one desires, provided she is endowed with the necessary materials,
she should be made to appear thus, adorned with articles of beauty.
Accompanied by male and female servants and friends, and graced with the prosperity and splendor of her household,
she should worship that [deity] and perform oblations into the fire one hundred and more times.
Having circumambulated the fire, she should take it into her own hands and offer it.
Then, one should further entreat a preceptor, a virtuous Brahmin, Lord Hari, Kumāra, or even a holy person:
"This wife has been given by me as a gift to a twice-born."
Endowed with all the requisites of household life and adorned,
you alone are Mahālakṣmī, the consort of Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Goddess. O Rame, grant me forever the fruit of giving and the state of wedlock.
"In heaven, in truth, in Vairāja, and in Vaikuṇṭha, let my wife be united with me and go along with me; likewise, grant me this fruit.
Having spoken thus, he should place his beloved in the hand of the brahmin preceptor.
This beloved golden statuette shall be the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
Through thousands of future births, one's conjugal union shall remain unbroken.
O Lakṣmī, it grants all prosperity and bestows eternal bliss. (37–38)

Bestowing all enjoyments and increasing the lineage of sons and grandsons— this great gift of the Kalpa-woman has been described by me to you. According to the number [of women given], they shall be desired in heaven or on earth.
Likewise, that same number of effigies of his own wives should be provided.
Having placed them within the pavilion near the fire,
he should first have all of them married according to the marriage rite by the twice-born.
Adorned with garlands of choice flowers, holding them in their hands,
radiant with all ornaments and endowed with every decoration—
the wise man should then offer them all as a gift, having made them his own wives.
For in this way, when women are given here according to the prescribed rite, they certainly become so in the next world; of this there is no doubt. This is a supreme and great gift;
it is indeed the gift of a golden woman, taking one's own wife as a representative.
A woman should certainly not be given as a gift; rather, a golden image should be given.
Indeed, the Creator has declared that the gift of a woman is a great gift.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, one should also offer the Lord of Gold in the act of giving.
Adorned with every ornament and beautifully graced by all prosperity,
that great gift of gold is indeed the bestower of a husband and good fortune.
I shall now describe to you the procedure for this, by the performance of which [the goal] is truly attained at all times.
She shall never experience widowhood; rather, she attains the good fortune of a husband.
Having fashioned a golden image, she should worship it there in a pavilion.
Therein, she should invoke Nārāyaṇa, the Lord and Consort of Śrī.
Then, according to the marriage rite, she should place him within the pavilion.
Thinking him to be her own husband, the woman should marry that golden bridegroom, who possesses the splendor of a husband, after placing the wedding garland upon him and taking his hand. (3.131.50)
Then she should offer her husband, who has circumambulated her, for the sake of a gift;
at that time, she should also offer all other various objects.
She should offer him as the beloved husband she desires to have in birth after birth.
Such a gift, endowed with all perfections, should be given to a woman whose husband has died.
This gift is proclaimed as a great gift, the gift of a husband;
it bestows all good fortune and is auspiciously conducive to the perpetual state of household life. (52–53)
Bestowing both heaven and liberation, and granting eternal bliss,
the gift of a son and the gift of a brother produced from a golden statuette—
these should be performed in this very manner, having invoked me, the Supreme Lord.
That which is given according to the prescribed rite bears fruit even in the form of a son;
that which is given in the form of a brother surely bears fruit as progeny.
By the gift of an image of Hari, Mādhava, who is Hari himself, becomes united with one.
By the gift of a beloved wife, even Kṛṣṇa becomes beloved.
Therefore, these gifts should be given according to the prescribed rule.
By the gift of male and female servants, male and female servants are obtained.
Nothing that has not been given is obtained; therefore, one must indeed give on this earth.
What is given here remains present both in this world and in the next.
One who gives happiness shall become happy, and one who gives suffering shall become miserable.
A gift of merit should be bestowed upon a householder, excluding water,
as well as upon the sick, the poor, and those who have knowledge of the world beyond;
merit born of vows and other such acts should be given to one whose life is on the verge of death.
In this way, there are other meritorious acts consisting of asceticism (tapas),

as well as merits consisting of sacrifices, those arising from great festivals, merits from the recitation of the Vedas (pārāyaṇa), and whatever merits arise from the chanting of mantras (japa). || 61–62 ||

All merits arising from giving, those born of providing hospitality, those resulting from the worship of the gods, those produced by service to the guru, and those arising from service to one's husband—
all these should be offered through the act of giving according to the prescribed rite. (63)
Virtues such as devotion to one's husband, which bestow happiness when given as a gift, should be bestowed.
(64) Virtues such as fidelity to one's wife, virtues of the righteous, and virtues of altruism, which bring about happiness, should also be given as gifts according to the prescribed rules. (65)
The merit of knowledge, the merit of digging wells, the merit of *iṣṭāpūrta* and other such rites,
the merit arising from assistance such as providing medicinal herbs, and the merit of giving which bestows happiness;
the merit of providing refuge, that born of truth, and likewise the auspicious merit arising from compassion.

The great merit arising from non-violence should especially be bestowed in the act of giving. Likewise, the merit arising from giving with the neck, the merit arising from giving with the waist, and the merit arising from giving with the heart should especially be bestowed in the act of giving. (67–68)
The great merit of granting life, which arises from protecting those who have come for refuge and from providing a support for the supportless, should be especially bestowed among all gifts.
The gift of the Veda is the greatest of all gifts and is supreme beyond the supreme.
The gift of knowledge is the gift of Hari; the gift of liberation is even greater than that.
Indeed, the granting of fearlessness is the most excellent among all gifts, for there exists nothing superior to it that should be bestowed with every form of devotion. (3.131.70–71)
Indeed, the gift of the moon and sun bestows brilliance upon the eyes;
the gift of higher knowledge (vijñāna) bestows radiance upon the heart.
Furthermore, the gift of liberation to the self bestows eternal bliss.
This gift of fearlessness alone should be given by one desiring liberation.
(73) The gift of the body should be performed for the sake of obtaining an auspicious body and so forth;
the gift of the house should be performed for the sake of easily obtaining a dwelling and so forth. (74)
The gift of clarified butter should be performed for the sake of easily attaining nourishment of the body; the gift of seeds should be performed for the increase of dharma and progeny;
the gift of water should be performed for the satisfaction of one's ancestors and oneself.
The gift for the guru must be performed; having fashioned an image of the guru out of gold according to the prescribed rite, and having worshipped it along with its ornaments,
one should invoke the guru and pray for the sake of one's own liberation.
One should give that [image] to a righteous, virtuous person who is a worshiper,
and specifically to one who is indeed capable of performing its worship constantly.
To him the form of the Guru should be given, for by this the fruit of worship is obtained.
If she is not worshipped, the one who gave her in marriage would incur sin.
(79) Furthermore, the images of the gods may be made of gold or silver, or produced from gems and jewels, or fashioned from wood, cloth, and so forth. (3.131.80)
Indeed, these [images] should be bestowed according to the prescribed rite, preceded by their formal installation;
they should be enriched with the splendor of all ornaments, endowed with every type of attire,
possessed of all auspicious decorations, gentle, and beautiful in form.
They should be presented together with vessels, perfumes, articles for worship,
and garments; accompanied by necklaces, strings of pearls, ornaments, festive items, and appropriate weapons— [these offerings] for Gaṇeśa, Hanumān, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, and likewise for Ravi.
Beautiful and auspicious images should be offered to Vāstu, to the world-protectors (lokapālas), to their hosts, to their lords, and to the virtuous attendants;
they should be adorned with all ornaments and graced by every kind of finery.
Endowed with appropriate attire, equipped with suitable weapons, provided with fit mounts, and accompanied by worthy servants;
likewise possessed of their own strength, they should be given as gifts, for they bestow happiness. (85–86)
Mahānārāyaṇī, Brāhmī, Mahālakṣmī, Ramā, Amṛtā, Kamalā, Śrī, Prabhā, Deyā, Kānakī, and likewise Māṇikī;
Sauvarṇā, Kaṃbharālakṣmī, Lalitāśrī, and Śubhānanā.
Gajānanā, Mahālakṣmī, adorned with splendors, should be given;
Gaṅgā, Durgā, Pāśavatī, Satī, Kanyā, Kumārikā, Santuṣā, Jānakī, Ramā, Jayā, and Padminī should be given. (88–89)
Sāvitrī, Vijayā, and Duḥkhahā—the Mother of the Vedas—should be given.
Saṃjñā, Svāhā joined with Vahni, and the adorned Caṇḍī should be given. Kātyāyanī and Mahākālī, beautified by their respective attire, should be given.
Gaurī, Devyā, Tulasī, and Vṛndā, resplendent in her marriage;
these and other goddesses of the gods, as well as the Mothers of Īśāna, the Yoginīs, and the liberated women—these should be given as gifts to Janārdana. (91–92)
These well-established images should be given with great enthusiasm for the purpose of worship to a virtuous, devoted twice-born man;
they should be adorned with dress, ornaments, food offerings, vessels, garments, and the like.
Temples suitable for their residence should also be provided, as well as gardens of great prosperity filled with fruits, garlands, and honey;
groves endowed with crops, and indeed fields of sugarcane. ||94-95||
Various kinds of food, including vegetables such as leaf-greens and the like, should be given.
Forests should be bestowed, as well as wells, tanks, and lakes.
All things for enjoyment, including perfumes, juices, and edibles, should likewise be provided.
Grains, treasuries of wealth, male servants, and female servants should be given.
Whatever is given is obtained; that which has not been given is never obtained anywhere.
Therefore, having fashioned images, wives and female servants should also be given as gifts. (97–98)
Having given thus, one may also obtain supreme happiness in the householder's stage of life;
having become happy in this world, one further attains sovereignty.
[One dwells] in heaven, in Satyaloka, in Vairāja, in Vaikuṇṭha, in Śrīpura, and in the Imperishable.
He is born in the abode of Goloka, possessing the splendor of Dhāmeśvara Nārāyaṇa. Endowed with every charm and enjoying all forms of pleasure,
he becomes eternal, overflowing with all bliss and supreme bliss.
"By reading this, by hearing it, by remembering it, by rejoicing in it,
and even by encouraging others to give it, one shall become a repository of equal merit.

(3.102) Thus ends [the section on] the gift of the Great Kalpa-creeper Suvarṇavallī, the gift of Kalpapriyā, the gift of Svarṇakāntā, the gift of Puṇyā, and the gifts of Abhayā and so forth, [concerning] the Guru, the Deity, and the Goddess, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 131: The Description of the Rituals for Great Gifts, including the Great Gifts of Temples, Lands, Gardens, Ornaments, and so forth.
[The end of] Chapter 131 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age.
Chapter 132.
[The Author: Chapter 133.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the gift of the seven oceans.
This great gift destroys all sins and bestows the abode of heaven.
(1) Having reached an auspicious day and month, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed;
one should also have a lovely altar made and procure the materials for the gift. (2)
One should have those learned in the Vedas recite words of "Svasti" and auspicious verses on that holy day.
One should invoke the guardians of the world (Lokapālakas) upon their seats within the pavilion,
as well as the Supreme Lord, Hari, and myself, Śrī Rāmā, the daughter of the ocean.

One should indeed have seven beautiful sacrificial pits constructed within the pavilion. They should be made of gold, weighing more than seven palas and up to a thousand palas, and they should be as splendid as the vessels used for the oblation.
First, one should fill the golden pit with salt;
likewise, the second with milk, and the third indeed with ghee.
The fourth should be filled with molasses, and the fifth likewise with curd.
The sixth [ocean] should be with sugar, and the seventh with sweet water.
These seven oceans indeed should be especially worshipped.
One should place an auspicious golden Brahmā in the first ocean.
In the second [day] Keśava and me; in the third likewise Hara;
in the fourth Bhāskara as well; and in the fifth the Moon.
In the sixth Lakṣmī, my wife; and in the seventh Pārvatī, the virtuous Satī.
One should establish male and female servants, as well as jewels, diamonds, and pearls;
all the finest grains and whatever items are suitable for gifts.
Having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the Varuṇa mantras, one should worship the gods.
Having circumambulated me three times to the right, he should pray to me along with the oceans:
"O Oceans, having produced all flavors, you always bring happiness to the entire creation;
likewise, grant happiness to me."
By your waters, all my sins go to destruction;
may my prosperities increase. Bestow prosperity upon me, and you who are established in giving, may you cause my fortune to flourish.
May my treasuries, consisting of gold and silver, be like the oceans;
may my happiness be inexhaustible both in this world and the next.
May you all, possessing divine bodies, be offered here for my sake.
All of them bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and grant the status of a great sovereign empire.
At the end, they bestow the realms of heaven and truth, as well as the earthly, heroic, and royal worlds;
they grant the city of Śrī, the abode of nectar, the unmanifest, and the imperishable state.
O sons of Rādhā, may you indeed grant us Goloka;
and may you always grant me oceans of bliss.
May you also bring satisfaction to the ancestors and act as their deliverers.
"May they be the bestowers of happiness upon all those who cause the destruction of lineages.
Having thus entreated, these seven golden oceans should be given to the preceptor, to the virtuous one, and likewise to Hari, the Lord. (3.132.20)
Various things should be given to the poor, the blind, and the wretched— food, jewels, garments, vessels, and wealth, each as is appropriate.
One should feed Brahmins, holy men, virtuous women, and chaste wives.
O Lakṣmī, one who gives gifts in this manner— even to boys and girls— goes to the abode of Vairāja;
thereafter, to Śrīpura, the immortal abode, and then to Goloka, the imperishable realm.
He departs for the supreme world of Brahmā, the eternal abode,
traveling in a golden-colored celestial chariot attended by apsarases;
honored by my attendants, he goes to my own beloved, eternal station.
There, in that great ocean of bliss, he rejoices and exults greatly.
Listen, Lakṣmī! Furthermore, hear of another unsurpassed great gift:
the jewel-cow, which bestows the world of cows and grants happiness. (25–26)
Having reached the day of the Pavitra rite, one should have an auspicious pavilion constructed;
one should likewise have an altar and a sacrificial pit made, and deposit gems there.
One should also deposit all the materials for the gifts as well as the jewels.
A wise man should place upon a black antelope skin those items suitable for the purpose of the gift of a cow;
then, he should likewise establish the jewel-cow, adorned and accompanied by her calf, upon a heap of salt as large as a *droṇa* and upon a deer-skin.
The king should indeed fashion a great cow that grants all desires and purposes;
he should place eighty-one rubies in the mouth of the cow,
and he should likewise arrange one hundred topazes in her nose.
On his forehead was a golden tilaka, and on his two eyes were a hundred pearls;
likewise, on his two eyebrows were a hundred corals, and on his two ears were two shells.
His horns were made of gold, and his head was fashioned from diamond-jewels.
On the neck, there is also a cloth made from a hundred *gomedaka* gems and other such stones; on the back, a hundred *indranīla* sapphires; on the sides, beautified by *vaidūrya* cat's-eyes;
the belly with crystals; and the waist with a hundred *saugandhika* gems.
One should have the hooves made of silver, the tail fashioned from strings of pearls,
the sun-stone and moon-stone for the nostrils, camphor and sandalwood for the scent, saffron for the body hairs, and a silver navel. (34–35)
One should fashion a hundred *gārutmata* gems at the base of the tail and fine jewels upon the breasts;
likewise, one should arrange other gems according to one's capacity.
One should also represent the tongue in the form of sugar and molasses in the form of cow dung.
Ghee and urine are in their natural forms, as are curd and milk. At the tip of the tail is a fly-whisk, and nearby is a copper milking vessel.
There are golden earrings and ornaments according to one's wealth. (37–38)
One should keep fodder and grains nearby for their protection;
one should set aside a fourth part for the calves and store all the grains there. One should also have sugarcanes planted and a five-colored *jhullarī* (swing) constructed.
Likewise, one should place various beautiful fruits within the pavilion.
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa), O God, one should likewise perform the invocation of the deities.
One should worship me and the gods according to the prescribed rite, and circumambulate the cow.
Having performed [the ritual], the donor, having bowed to the Brahmins, Hari, and the cow, should make this request:
"O Goddess, you are the embodiment of all the gods and the savior;
salutations to you, the image of all the wish-fulfilling cows. (42)
O Mother, bestower of all desires, dweller in Goloka, beloved;
O Mother, destroyer of sin, giver of merit, and bestower of liberation, salutations to you!
O Lakṣmī, in your form, deliver me in every way from this ocean.
O bestower of all prosperity, O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, deliver me from the ocean!
Grant me the heavenly realm of Vairāja, the city of Śrī, and likewise immortality.
O Kamalā, indeed grant me Goloka and the imperishable abode.
Having thus made this earnest request, it should indeed be given to a virtuous guru;
it should be given to a Brahmin who is a worthy recipient and a Vaiṣṇava.
Other jewels, grains, and whatever other things are fit to be given [should also be offered]. ||46-47||
All those things should be given to the mendicants with great devotion;
likewise, virtuous Brahmins, boys, and girls should be fed. By thus bestowing gifts, one becomes a partaker of heaven as well as liberation.
He is always born endowed with worldly enjoyment, liberation, and the great liberation;
he becomes a savior of his ancestors and a savior of his family members. Indeed, he becomes a most meritorious vessel and one who consists of the bliss of Brahman. (3.132.50)
Now I shall describe another great gift with which I likewise delight:
that known as the Great Elemental Vase (*mahābhūtakalaśa*), the supreme means for accomplishing all aims.
Having selected an auspicious lunar day and month, one should construct an excellent pavilion.
Then, one should have the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*) and the declaration of a meritorious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) performed.
In the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should place clarified butter, rice, and other materials;
as well as the implements for the gift, ornaments, clothing, food, fruits, and so forth.
Having established the world-protectors (lokapālas), he should perform my invocation;
he should worship them all according to the prescribed rite and place a golden pitcher adorned with five sprouts and endowed with great jewels and other ornaments. (54)
Measuring one hundred finger-breadths from a span (prādeśa), it should be adorned with beauty;

filled with milk and clarified butter, and provided with garments, flowers, and other offerings of the prescribed type, one should install it, worship it, and likewise invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) therein. || 55–56 ||
One should place the Earth, accompanied by Varāha and adorned with Kamalā and others, within that pavilion; there, one should worship Vināyaka.
[Then] Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and likewise Anila—
One should worship Kubera and Maheśāna upon a heap of grain.
There, one should likewise worship the Ṛgveda accompanied by a rosary,
the Yajurveda accompanied by a lotus, and the Sāmaveda accompanied by a lute.
One should likewise worship Atharvaṇa, who is enriched with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and adorned with lotuses;
then one should fully worship Brahmā, Rudra, and Viṣṇu as well, and finally me,
the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, together with Māṇikī.
One should worship with a spirit of devotion and then perform the *ārātrika* ceremony.
[One should offer] all kinds of grains, ornaments, various gems, sandals,
wooden shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a mirror.
Having prepared the bed, water-jars, lamps, and various articles—
all intended for the purpose of giving— and having circumambulated me three times,
one should offer them according to the ritual rules and then request the jar.
Salutations to you who are the form of the universe, who are clothed in black, the creator;
salutations to you, Viṣṇu, who are Rudra in form, the peaceful one, and the water-jar; salutations to the abode of all, the giver of liberation, salutations again and again.
Salutations to you who are the abode of nectar and the bestower of golden heaven;
salutations to you, O golden pitcher, the giver of the imperishable Śrīpura.
You are the dwelling place of all gods and are resorted to by all goddesses.
Endowed with all supernatural powers, prosperity, and perfection—to you, I offer salutation after salutation. (67) You are the very essence of the five elements; I give myself as an offering.
Grant me sovereignty in this world, and thereafter, liberation in the next. (68)
Having thus prayed to the virtuous guru, who is likewise a yogi, [I declare]:
"This auspicious golden jar must be given by me to Hari;
furthermore, all other gifts and offerings should be given as is appropriate. (69)
Food should be offered to all near the pavilion.
For one who thus performs this great festival consisting of the offering of the jar,
his kingdom and great sovereignty shall certainly be established on earth and in heaven.
In the world of Truth, in Vairāja, in Vaiṣṇava, in Śrīpura, in the immortal [realm], in Vaikuṇṭha, in the unmanifest abode, and also in the imperishable Goloka,
one attains great liberation after having enjoyed the most excellent of enjoyments.
He shall liberate all his ancestors and shall always travel in a celestial chariot.
He should make a gift of even a very small water-pot according to his wealth;
likewise, he may offer a large jar, a pitcher, a wooden trough, or a cow.
One should perform the gift of a water-pot and the gift of a treasury;
by that, there shall be enjoyment and liberation, bestowing happiness.
Through reading, hearing, remembering, and rejoicing [in this], [one attains these fruits].
The fruit of the gift of a water-pot is indeed the destruction of all sins.
(76) Now I shall declare another gift to you; listen to me, O Lakṣmī!
One who desires prosperity should perform the great gift of Lakṣmī. (77)
One should cause an excellent pavilion to be constructed, adorned with jewels, gems, and the like;
beautified by pillars of plantain trees with all manner of sprouts, and by archways;
provided with variegated cloths and mirrors, and graced with golden water-pots.
It was adorned with banners and provided with an altar, resplendent with sacrificial pits and seats;
it shone with grains, ornaments, garments, jewels, gems, and rubies;
it was fully supplied with the articles to be given away, and the place for the officiating priests and others had been prepared. (79–80)
Accompanied by a water-pot and provided with the necessary materials for the ritual,
one should place there in the center, upon a golden seat, the beautiful Lakṣmī Mahāsatī,
fashioned from gold according to one's wealth.
Adorned with all ornaments and graced by every mark of beauty,
endowed with all finery and garments, she was accompanied by Nārāyaṇa;
[he was] the golden image of Nārāyaṇa, four-armed and decorated with ornaments.
One should establish the bride as being worthy of selection and perform the recitation of the *svasti* benediction.
Likewise, one should worship Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī according to the prescribed rite.
Indeed, beginning with the ritual bath, one should perform the entire service of honor up to the final offering of handfuls of flowers.
One should perform the entire rite according to the marriage ritual as is appropriate.
One should cause the bridegroom’s garland to be placed upon the neck of Hari by the hands of Śrī.
And one should offer food, water, betel, and the waving of lamps (ārārtika).
Having performed a circumambulation, one should offer oblations of ghee and other excellent substances such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Then, one should indeed give a gift to Nārāyaṇa for the sake of Mahālakṣmī.
One should then supplicate Lakṣmī and the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed rite.
"You two are my mother and father; you are my protectors, guardians, and lords.
(88) "O Blessed One, by the granting of [this] fortune, may my prosperity increase;
may there certainly be the dissolution of all portions of my sins. (89)
By offering this to you, may I attain great sovereignty and supreme lordship;
may there be liberation for my ancestors, and likewise may there be the increase of my lineage. May I attain the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, and thereafter, may I reach the imperishable state.
"May all kinds of prosperity be in my home through the power of Your grace.
Having thus prayed, Lakṣmī should indeed be given to Nārāyaṇa;
thereafter, the image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa should be given to that virtuous seeker.
It should be given to the virtuous guru and to the temple seeking auspicious purposes;
all other jewels and such should be bestowed upon the community of mendicants.
One should also feed the virtuous, the brahmins, children, the destitute, and young girls.
The bride should feed the helpless, the blind, the twice-born, devotees, and yogins.
She should provide gifts of food and so forth, as well as gifts of clothing and so forth;
she should provide gifts of wealth and so forth according to her faith and her means. (94–95)
Thus, by the gift of *lakṣmī*, one obtains the fruit of the gift of *lakṣmī*;
likewise, one attains the fruit of the gift of a daughter and the fruit of the gift of a wife.
One also obtains the fruit of vows and sacrifices, as well as the fruit arising from *satras*, *iṣṭas*, and *pūrtas*.
One shall also attain the fruit of all forms of giving as well as the fruit of the Cāturmāsya vow.
Having enjoyed imperial sovereignty even in this world through the grace of Lakṣmī,
one shall attain the kingdom of heaven, the kingdom of truth, and the station of Vairāja.
Then, having enjoyed the kingdom of Śrīpura, he shall attain Goloka;
and having enjoyed the supreme Vaikuṇṭha, he thereafter goes to the imperishable abode.
Immersed in the lake of Brahman-bliss, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
The giver of gifts likewise obtains enjoyment and liberation according to his desire.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have those great gifts been described to you;
there are also other various kinds of gifts here as well.
The gift to Sūrya, the gift to Candra, and likewise the gift to Mahendra; the gift to Brahmā, the gift to Viṣṇu, and the supreme gift to Śambhu;
as well as the gift to Kubera and the gift to Yama, which is the abode of auspiciousness.
One should give the gift of life, the gift of the senses and so forth, and a golden image (10.3).
In that very context, as well as everywhere else, one should give the gift of the yantra as is appropriate;
likewise, the gift of the imperishable Brahman and the gift of Goloka (10.4).
One should likewise give the gift of Vaikuṇṭha as well as the offering of Śrīpura,
and other such gifts as one desires,
all of them in their entirety, for the sake of attaining [the goal] in another birth.
Or one may give the most excellent gift of devotion for the sake of liberation.
By reciting, hearing, remembering, and approving of this, one shall obtain the entire merit of giving, according to one's faith and purity. (106–107)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for the Great Gift of the Seven Oceans, the Great Gift of the Jewel-Cow, the Great Gift of the Vessel of the Great Elements, the Great Gift of Lakṣmī, and Other Such Great Gifts," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 133 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 133: The Description of the Ritual for the Great Gift of the Golden Egg (*Hiraṇyāṇḍa-Mahādāna*). Śrī Nārada said: O Lord, please describe to me the procedure for the great gift of the golden egg (*hiraṇyāṇḍa-mahādāna*), which is the most excellent among all great gifts. Śrī Bhagavān said: O sage, I shall explain to you the ritual procedure for the great gift of the golden egg, which bestows all desired fruits. One should perform this great gift on the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, or on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) of any month. Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) and observed the vows, the donor should prepare a golden egg according to his means. It should be made of four *maṇḍalas* (palas) of gold, or even half of that, or a quarter, or even a sixteenth part, according to one's capacity. Alternatively, it may be made of silver, copper, or clay, adorned with various gems. One should fashion a beautiful image of Brahmā upon the golden egg. He should have four faces, four arms, and be seated upon a lotus. He should be adorned with a crown, earrings, necklaces, bracelets, and other ornaments. He should hold a staff (*daṇḍa*), a rosary (*akṣamālā*), a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and a book (*pustaka*). He should be depicted as peaceful, seated comfortably, and surrounded by the Vedas. Having prepared the golden egg and the image of Brahmā, the donor should place them within a pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) decorated with flowers and banners. He should then perform the ritual worship (*pūjā*) with fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*). He should recite the hymns of the Vedas and the *Puruṣa-sūkta*. Then, having invited learned Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, he should present the golden egg along with the image of Brahmā to them. He should say: "O Brahmins, accept this golden egg, which is the source of the universe, for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors and myself. By giving this great gift of the golden egg, the donor is liberated from all sins and attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. This is the eternal rule for the great gift of the golden egg. Thus I have described the ritual for the great gift of the golden egg. One who hears or recites this obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Great Gift of the Golden Egg," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
