[The Author: Chapter 134.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O beloved of Kṛṣṇa, my dear one, I have heard of the great fruit of giving.
"O Lord, that which was spoken by you—that it should be given on an auspicious day—[is understood].
All auspicious days have been known to me as described by you; yet I wish to know which among them is the most auspicious day. Please tell me that."
Śrī Puruṣottama said: That day on which my manifestation as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa occurred upon this earth is indeed the most meritorious of days. (3)
This very eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika is the most excellent for making gifts;
likewise, the donor’s birthday is considered preeminent for the sake of the giver.
Furthermore, days bearing auspicious names are also most excellent.
The days of the month of Brahmā are most excellent for the giving of gifts.
(5) I shall now declare the names of the thirty months; listen to me, for by the mere recitation of them one is endowed with the merit of the Vedas. (6)
The first is the Śvetakalpa; the second is Nīlalohita;
the third is Vāmadeva; the fourth is named Rāthantara;
the fifth is called Raurava; and the sixth is named Devadinna. (7)
The seventh is named Bṛhat, and the eighth is called Kandarpa.
The ninth is named Sadya, while Īśāna is considered the tenth.
The eleventh is named Tamas, and the twelfth is Sārasvata.
The thirteenth is called Udāna; the fourteenth is Gāruḍa; the fifteenth is Kaumārya; the sixteenth is Nārasiṃhaka;
the seventeenth is named Samāna; and the eighteenth consists of Āgneya.
The nineteenth is named Soma, and the twentieth is considered Mānava;
the twenty-first is that Puruṣa, remembered as the day of Brahmā.
The twenty-second is Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise the twenty-third is Lakṣmī.
The twenty-fourth is Sāvitrī, the twenty-fifth is Aghoraka;
the twenty-sixth is Vārāha, and the twenty-seventh is Vairāja.
The twenty-eighth is Gaurī, and the twenty-ninth is Maheśvara.

The thirtieth lunar day, which is considered by Brahmā to be the *kuhū* (new moon), is indeed a *pitṛkalpa*. Among these days, those which are the days of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*), the days of Śrī, and the auspicious lunar days (*atithi*) of Śiva, are meritorious for the giver of gifts.
O Rame, the days of Hari’s birth and the zodiac signs of Hariṇī’s birth are indeed meritorious; they are auspicious days for vows and always suitable for giving gifts.
Indeed, all people of small hearts are not capable of performing them.
Those of noble mind perform the acts of giving that have been prescribed.
Whenever a person’s intellect becomes intent upon the duty of giving,
on that very day the donor must swiftly perform the act of giving.

Faith has departed, time has passed, and enthusiasm too has gone; the worthy recipient is gone and the object [of charity] is gone—these will never return again. All prosperities are transitory, and life itself is likewise fleeting.
One should also direct those wandering volitions toward virtuous actions.
One should thoroughly satisfy Nārāyaṇa, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, my Lord who is the Master of the Imperishable,
as well as the incarnations, the lords, the gods, and the sages.
One should satisfy the planets with gifts, O Lakṣmī, for they are my own forms;
for the attainment of all desires, one should always cause the planets to be pacified.
One who desires prosperity or peace should perform the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).
Or one who desires the nourishment of his own life-span, who wishes for a lineage, and who is intent on happiness—

on an auspicious day declared by a Brahmin, having performed the *brāhmaṇavācana* rite and having installed the planets and the deities presiding over the planets, he should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*). (23–24)
The sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña) is considered to be the ten-thousand oblation (ayutahoma), the hundred-thousand oblation (lakṣahoma),
and likewise the ten-million oblation (koṭihoma), performed according to the strength of the purpose at hand.
Indeed, the sacrifice to the nine planets (navagrahamakha) is considered to consist of ten thousand oblations (āhutis).
To the northeast of the pit,

having constructed a square altar measuring two *vitastis* in width, surrounded by two Brahmins, elevated by one *vitasti*, and beautiful, and facing north, he should then perform the "leading of the fire" (*agninayana*).
One should invoke the deities into it: Sūrya, Soma, Maṅgala, Budha, Guru, Kavi, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu.
[28] Sūrya is in the center, Maṅgala in the south, and likewise Guru in the north.
One should likewise install Budha in the northeast and Śukra in the east;
Candramas in the southeast, and Śani in the west;
Rāhu in the southwest, and Ketu in the northwest.
Or one should place the auspicious subordinate deities within the rice grains:
Īśa for the Sun, Pārvatī as the subordinate deity for the Moon;
Skanda for Mars, and Hari as the subordinate deity for Mercury.
One should install Brahmā as the presiding deity of Jupiter, Indra as that of Venus,
and likewise Yama as the presiding deity of Saturn; similarly, one should install Kāla as the presiding deity of Rāhu, and Citragupta as the presiding deity of Ketu.
Then, one should install the counter-deities (pratyupadeva) here and there in their respective places:
in order, Agni, Jala, Pṛthvī, Viṣṇu, Indra, Śacī, Prajāpati, the Bhogins, and Brahmā; one should thus establish them.

One should invoke Vināyaka, Durgā, Vāyu, and Ākāśa as well, using the *vyāhṛtis*; likewise, one should invoke Aśvin and Kumāra. One should meditate upon Ravi as being red in color, and likewise Maṅgala as being red.
One should then contemplate Soma and Śukra as white in color, Budha and Guru as tawny, Śani and Rāhu as black, and Ketu as smoke-colored.
Flowers and garments of the colors corresponding to these planets should be offered.
In this rite, fragrant incense alone serves as the canopy above;
likewise, one should offer everything worthy of worship, such as fruits and flowers, during the ritual of honor.
To Sūrya, one should offer rice cooked with jaggery, and to Soma, milk-rice with ghee.
For Maṅgala, however, [one should offer] saṃyāva; for Budha, kṣīrakullarī;
for Guru, curd-rice (dadhyodana); for Śukra, jaggery-rice (guḍaudana);
for Śanaiścara, kṛśarā; and likewise for Rāhu, beans (māṣa).
Then one should worship the deities of the banners with variegated rice.
To the northeast, one should place a water-pot provided with curd and unbroken grains,
joined with mango sprouts, and accompanied by a pair of garments and fruits.
One should place [the vessel] endowed with the five jewels and install Varuṇa;
one should indeed invoke the sacred fords (tīrthas) and the oceans there in the water.
[One should take earth] from an elephant, a horse, a road, an anthill, a crossroads, a pond, and a cow-pen.
Having brought earth combined with the water of all medicinal herbs,
the Brahmin should place it there for the purpose of bathing the patron.
He should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with clarified butter, barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth.
Arka, palāśa, khadira, apāmārga, pippala, audumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) in sequence;
for each of these, one should offer one hundred and eight or twenty-eight oblations.
It should be offered with honey, clarified butter, curd, and likewise with fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
One should prepare fuel-sticks from those branches, a span (*prādeśa*) in length, without side-branches or leaves; there, one should offer them while reciting the deity-mantras.
Having offered ten oblations of cooked sacrificial rice (caru), fuel sticks smeared with ghee, and various kinds of food, one should likewise offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis. Then,
one should present the consecrated caru to each respective deity.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and bathe the patron (yajamāna).
"May all the gods who have been worshipped here protect you;
likewise, may others worthy of worship protect you on all sides. (3.133.50–51)
Thus, having been bathed along with his wife, the sacrificer should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins and likewise to the householders as is appropriate.
He should offer a tawny cow to the Sun and a conch shell to the Moon.
One should give a red bull to Bhauma (Mars), and gold to Budha (Mercury).
To Guru (Jupiter) one should give yellow cloth, and to Śukra (Venus) a white horse.
One should give a black cow to Śani (Saturn), and likewise iron to Rāhu.
One should give a goat to Keśava, or as many cows as [required],
or one should give gold so that the Guru is fully satisfied.
Regarding the object to be given, it should be preceded by my own propitiation of the Lord.
O Ramā, charity is born as the bestower of the most excellent merit.
O Mother, you are the cow in the form of the earth, affectionate toward Kṛṣṇa;
may you be my source of merit and the remover of my sins; grant me eternal peace. (56–57)
You are the conch of the multitudes of merits, an embodied form of auspiciousness;
residing eternally in the hand of Kṛṣṇa, grant me peace incessantly.
You, the bull of Dharma, are established within the very form of Kṛṣṇa.
May he grant me the empowerment of all bliss and joy.
(59) O Gold, son of Fire, seed of gold belonging to the Radiant One;
you who bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace and prosperity. (3.133.60)
O Lord who always wears the excellent yellow garment, divine and beloved of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
grant me peace and prosperity, and make me beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
You are Hayagrīva, Viṣṇu, the consumer of the potency of the nectar-herbs.
"O Lord, Sovereign of the Maṇikya horse, grant me immortality and peace!
O Kṛṣṇā, you were born as a cow, as the wife of Kṛṣṇa, and as the daughter of Kṛṣṇa (Kārṣṇī);
you remain the sustainer of Kṛṣṇa—nourish me forever! (62–63)
O Iron, servant of the elements, you who perform every task for your master; O White-Deer, beginning with the arrows and the gods, grant me eternal peace.
O Goat, you are the form of Time (Kāla), seen in a dream as terrifying.
O carrier of the fire, being duly worshipped, grant me perpetual peace.
(65) May cows, who are indeed the very form of Kṛṣṇa, the refuge of all lords and gods, and capable of uplifting all beings, be the source of my prosperity in every way. (66)
O bed, you have been enjoyed by Kṛṣṇa; you are purifying and the bestower of sons.
May you always grant me prosperity, and may my wife never be separated from me.
Since all the jewels of the gods indeed reside within you, [may they be mine].
"May they indeed place my dwelling of jewels here in this house!
O you who have been offered to me, grant me the supreme gift of land, as well as the gift of gold; and grant me the abundance of food and the abundance of wealth! || 68-69 ||
Having thus entreated and made a formal request, one should especially give in charity;
he attains all his desires and is glorified in heaven after death.
But as for that seizure which constantly causes pain to one who has little wealth—
Having honored that [deity] with effort, one should satisfy it along with Śeṣa.
Through worship, there is pacification of afflictions, just as by means of armor.
One should give a complete sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
At weddings, festivals, sacrifices, consecrations, and other such rites,

one who is devoted should perform the auspicious *navagrahamakha* consisting of ten thousand oblations (*ayutahoma*), for the sake of removing obstacles, for the sake of peace, and to pacify all agitation. (73)

The lawful wives, all together, and the nine planets beginning with the Sun;

I am to be worshipped in the Aśvattha tree, and I am the treasure within the ear-cavity.
I am Gāyatrī together with Brahmā, and Pārvatī in the presence of Śiva;
likewise, I am Indrāṇī in the world of the gods, and I am Sarasvatī in the mouth of Brahmā. (38–39)
In the solar orb I am radiance, and in steadfastness I am Vaiṣṇavī, the noose-bearing goddess;
in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I am the joy-bestowing Ramā. I am Arundhatī among the virtuous women, and Tilottamā among the hosts of Apsarases.
I am the digit of Brahman (Brahmakalā) in Citta, and in all beloved ones I am Kāntā.
I am Bhaṅgā on Mount Nīla, and Vijayā on the land of Āsāma.
In Kāmarūpa I am Kāmākṣī, and in the region of Brahmā I am Irā.
In the Khāsī regions, the Brahmaputrī is the purifier falling upon their bodies;
in this ancient Śyāma region, she is the daughter of Menakā;
in Uccīna, she is the mistress of sacrificial rites; and in the three Aṅgulas, she is Kāramī.
In Kārākāra I am Kṛṣṇavarṇā; in Eluna and Khanira I am [Kṛṣṇavarṇā]. In Mūka I am Maṅgolakī, and in Khiṅgaṇa I am Mañcchikā.
In Stenāvāsa I am Pāraśavī, while in Rāśana I am Rāśiputrī. (44–45)
I am Uralā on Mount Coralā, Raktā on the ground of Cāraktabhū,
Nārāyaṇī in Sudāna, and Alpā on Mount Alpa. I am Iṅgitajñā in Ketumāla, and I am Parī in Balāyata.
Hāritī is in Piṅgadeśa; Amarī is in Kiṃpumātman.
Rākarī is in Mānakaṅga; Parinārī is in Dakṣaka.
Saṃhārā is on Mount Najarādri; Kāmarūpā is in Kamāraṇa.
I am Māsāmbā on Mount Sāmba; I am Kalihārā in Mitrapa; I am Hotriṇī in Trihotra; and I am Māṃjhāmbikā in Jhamba. I am Maṇikāntā in Navadeśa, and Mahordhvikā in Uṣṭrālaya.
O Dakṣa! I dwell upon the earth in such forms as Kalagaralī in a female dog and Cāliśī on Mount Kātha. Perform my worship everywhere; it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus spoke the illustrious Mahālakṣmī then to Dakṣa, the Prajāpati.
Therefore, the worship of Mahālakṣmī brings about all peace;
he who recites all your names during that worship—two hundred in total—[attains his goal].
May all accomplishments (siddhis), which grant whatever is desired, attend upon him. Furthermore,
may the afflictions of the planets, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and likewise of enemies,
go to their destruction through your peace-offerings, sacrifices, and other rites.
Having caused an excellent pavilion, auspicious on all sides and shaped like a lotus,
to be constructed as circular, and likewise having a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) like a lotus,
one who recollects you, the Supreme Goddess, by means of the two hundred names— ||55||
Having invoked [the deity] into rice grains, one should worship with lotuses and other offerings.
By my grace, all his afflictions shall indeed perish.
Having performed eight oblations, each accompanied by its respective name. (56–57)
Then one should offer the great oblation with ghee, milk-rice, and sweet foods;
likewise with streams of ghee, fruits such as rice and the like, coconuts and other fruits, sacrificial fuel-sticks, sugar, and so forth. (58)
Whatever is desired by his mind, all that shall indeed come to pass.
Kingdom, heaven, and liberation—all these shall be his.
Through the attainment of wife, son, and husband, as well as wealth and fame, they shall be his. (3.135.60)
I shall describe the proper arrangement for that Lakṣmī sacrifice as it truly is:
one should take a circular pavilion measuring one hundred and twenty cubits in circumference,
auspiciously constructed with ten pillars.
One should construct a pavilion there, beautifully adorned with four doors,
with archways, a fine canopy, and a circular pinnacle, as well as with golden jars and a splendid banner. (62–63)
One should cause it to be made auspicious, adorned even with a banner of red cloth;
likewise, one should depict various weapons all around upon the arches—
eighteen distinct types, proceeding from the east to the south.
A sword, a shield, a scimitar, a staff, a noose,
a thunderbolt, a bow, an axe, an arrow, a discus, a mace, a conch, a great goad,
a lotus, a garland, a spear, a missile, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness.
In this manner, one should have these weapons placed upon the archways;
and at every pillar, one should likewise have water-pots and banners installed.
One should also establish the eight goddesses on the door-frames as the presiding deities of the limbs.
Likewise, one should establish Śrī and Māṇikī on the two eastern branches;
likewise, one should establish Ramā holding a noose on the southern [branch];
and likewise, one should establish Maṅgalā and Amṛtā on the western [branch].
Furthermore, one should install Vijayā and Jayā in the north;
on the central pillars, one should place Durgā and Satī in the northeast.
Likewise, one should invoke Svāhā and Svadhā upon the two fire-pillars.
In the southwest (nairṛta), one should likewise install Saṃhāriṇī and Vaśinī.
In the northwest (vāyavya), one should install the beautiful and auspicious Śāradā Vāṇī,
as well as Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Sarasvatī, and Yamī.
One should install the sixteen Śaktis— Vaiṣṇavī, Varāhī, Caṇḍikā, Aindrī, Vāruṇī, Bhuvā, Saṃjñā, Kaumudī, Nandā, Nārāyaṇī, and Ramā, along with Santuṣṭā— upon the canopy.
Adorned with exquisite beauty at the locations for the sacrificial offerings between the pillars,
measuring two cubits in height and richly decorated with all ornaments, one should worship them with the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites,
with saffron, unbroken grains of rice, oil, and other fragrant substances such as sandalwood. (74–75)
The pit (kuṇḍa) should indeed be circular and ten cubits in size;
likewise, one should have it fashioned in the form of a lotus with sixteen petals.
One should also construct a yoni there, as well as the three-fold girdle (mekhalā).
One should cause the performance of Lakṣahoma and Koṭihoma sacrifices, which bestow the attainment of one's desires.
One should invoke and worship two hundred forms of yours—
the exalted and auspicious-faced image of Mahālakṣmī that is your very self.
One should have [an image] made measuring fifty-six finger-breadths, complete with a crown and adorned with necklaces;
it should be seated upon a golden lion-throne and fashioned from gold or another metal.
One should likewise fashion the companions in a manner appropriate to them.
Having bathed the Supreme Goddess with the five nectars and waters from sacred fords,
he adorned her with fragrant perfumes, ornaments, garments of pure consciousness, and beautiful floral decorations for the various parts of her body. (3.135.80–81)
Having worshipped with sandalwood, unbroken grains, tulasī, musk, and fragrant essences, one should offer various types of food offerings (naivedya),
including all kinds of sweetmeats and milk-rice preparations. ॥82॥
One should indeed offer sweet juices along with vegetable dishes as the sacrificial food (naivedya).
Then one should give water and betel leaf, and thereafter perform the waving of lights (ārātrika).
Having performed circumambulation, one should then pray and likewise prostrate.
O destroyer of birth, O destroyer of worldly existence, O destroyer of disease, O Supreme Goddess!
O Vāsudevī, O Kṛṣṇadevī, O Mahālakṣmī, salutations be unto you!
O Pārabrahmī, who dwells in the hearts of all beings, O you who are higher than the highest!
O you who possess the form of all goddesses, O Protectress, salutations to you again and again!
May suffering—whether from fate or from humans, born of karma or born of time, arising from past actions (*prārabdha*) or produced by malevolent spirits—not come to me, your devotee. (86–87)
Whatever mental suffering there may be— whether born of one's own nature, already arisen, or yet to arise— from a curse, from malice,
from negligence, from ignorance, or whatever ill-conceived undertaking I may have undertaken; || 88 ||
May my lack of lineage, childlessness, lack of female progeny, and dishonor—
along with every fear of disease— come to an end through Your grace; may there be only happiness for You, and may joy prevail forever.
"May there be for me the eternal Śrīpura, heaven, and the immortal state;
at the end, may the imperishable supreme abode be my highest goal.
Having thus prayed, one should then offer a handful of flowers.
Having propitiated the Great Holy One (Mahāsatī) in order to have his offenses forgiven, he should dismiss him;
likewise, he should dismiss the female attendants and dismiss the secondary deities.
And he should give the deity Lakṣmī to the Guru, who is the embodiment of Brahman.
Or one may install Mahālakṣmī in a temple that is stable and firm,
either together with Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
or joined with Śrīmad Gopāla Kṛṣṇa, who is the very self of Mahāviṣṇu.
One should establish [the image] in a temple of the deity adorned with golden pinnacles (95).
Likewise, one should offer gifts of gold coins and silver;
one should also offer ornaments and garments made of rubies, diamonds, and other precious gems (96).
One should also distribute sweet foods and offer garments for women;
one should present beautiful ornaments and various articles of utility.
One should cause all kinds of wealth, grain, and gifts of houses to be bestowed.
Having thus performed the expiation, one should then partake of food.
One should feed virtuous Brahmins, as well as the poor, the blind, and the wretched; likewise children, young girls, and women who are helpless and destitute. (98–99)
One should feed and likewise honor virtuous, chaste, and noble women;
one should also constantly worship Lakṣmī and feed her according to the prescribed rite.
For one who acts in this manner, there shall never be any suffering or distress whatsoever.

There shall always be enjoyment, perfect great liberation, and universal sovereignty (101). Through the grace of Śrīpati and Śrī, there shall be the state of being an enjoyer of unbroken bliss, the state of being more beloved than the host of goddesses, and equality with Kṛṣṇa (102).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, has this worship of yours, which bestows tranquility, been described.

By reading or hearing this, great happiness shall always arise. (103) Thus ends [the section on] the two hundred names and forms spoken by Mahālakṣmī to the Prajāpati Dakṣa in the Śrī-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā, within the third book, the Dvāpara-Santāna, concerning the peace-offering and worship in the Lakṣmī-sacrifice and the image of Mahālakṣmī.
The one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Their Mandalas and So Forth," from the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section Three (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age),
Chapter 136.
[The Author: Chapter 137.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to these two hundred names of Lakṣmī.
Formerly, having performed penance and propitiated you with prayers,
the auspicious maiden of the Pitṛs named Acchodā, who was born from their mind,
obtained the powerful Amāvasu as her husband. (1–2)
She received the blessing of the ancestors and Mahālakṣmī:
"Born from the womb of a fish, the daughter of King Vasu born of Suvīrya,
you shall be a maiden nurtured by fishermen and you shall be rich in grain."
"By the power of Parāśara, you shall obtain one son.
On an island abounding in jujube trees, having yourself become the mother of Viṣṇu, you will thereafter be wedded to Bādarāyaṇa, the infallible one. (4–5)
By King Śāntanu, a portion of the Ocean,
you shall become a mother of two sons, Citrāṅgada and Vicitravīrya;
and having produced them, you will then swiftly depart for the world of the ancestors.

In the world of the ancestors (pitṛloka), you shall exist in the form of the Aṣṭakā rite performed in the month of Prauṣṭhapada. By name you shall be Satyavatī in this world, and likewise Aṣṭakā in the world of the ancestors;
you shall eternally bestow long life and health, and grant the fruit of all desires.
"From that point on, you shall become a river;
you will be known as Acchodā, eternally bringing about the liberation of your ancestors.
Thus did that daughter of the Pitṛs [attain her state] through the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow.
Vyāsa’s mother, Khyātimatī, indeed obtained a boon.
(10) It is sung that by one who recites two hundred names on the eighth day during worship, or at the giving of a cow, or at the offering of a *śrāddha*, he shall indeed have many sons. (11)
O Lakṣmī, there are likewise two hundred such sacred fords (tīrthas) even within the three worlds; by bathing there, one attains Brahman.
His ancestors become fully satisfied, they cross over [saṃsāra], and they too go to Brahman.

Furthermore, there are hundreds of other Barhiṣads, the sons of Pulastya, who dwell in heaven as Pitṛs. Among them was a virtuous maiden named Pīvarī, the mind-born daughter of one of them; she performed your vow, O Lakṣmī.
Having performed a vow and severe austerity that brought peace to Lakṣmī, you obtained me as your divine consort in the forest, accompanied by Hari and Kṛṣṇa;
and there, from me alone, you received this boon: "Become one who possesses a husband."
"O Śukradeva, you shall indeed become a great yogi.
You will obtain Kṛtī as your wife—the daughter born of his mind—and she shall be a yoginī of divine beauty. (16–17)
"You shall indeed give your daughter to the King, the Lord of Pañcāla;
then your four sons, who are like great lords, will become Kṛṣṇa, Gaura, Prabhu, and Śambhu—bestowers of liberation. (18)
"Accompanied by your husband, sons, and others, you shall attain liberation after a long time.
Thus did Pīvarī obtain this boon from you through her vow.
And furthermore, there were other ancestors as well, named Marīcigarbha. (3.136.20)
The auspicious daughter of these [sages], known by the name Yaśodā,
having performed a vow for you, O Lakṣmī, became the wife of Aṃśumat;
she was also the mother of Dilīpa and the grandmother of Bhagīratha.
From that, the beautiful woman was born; though she had attained liberation, she went to heaven.
Then, in former times, there was a daughter of the Ājyapas named Virajā, who, having performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, became the beloved wife of Nahuṣa.
And she who was the mother of Yayāti became the Aikāṣṭakā thereafter;
having gone to the world of Brahmā, she rejoices there for eternal years.
Now, the daughter of the mind-born Pitṛs was the virtuous Narmadā.
Having performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, she rejoices in the form of a river.
She always rejoices in heaven and also rejoices in the world of the ancestors;
she is honored in the three worlds as the playful companion of Hari.
Then Gaurī, though the daughter of the Pitṛs, indeed shines as the beloved wife of Śukra, the mother of the Sādhyas, by virtue of her Lakṣmī-Śānti vow.
Thus she is present in heaven, in Satyaloka, and in every place upon the surface of the earth.
By the very Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, they rejoice in the abundance of prosperity.
Now, O Lakṣmī, there was a Yoginī named Kṛtvi, the daughter of Pīvarī, who was the granddaughter of Mānasā. (28–29)
The king, the lord of Pañcāla named Anagha, a descendant of Vibhrāja, performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow together with Nārāyaṇa for the sake of obtaining a son, as did his wife,
Hari, Nārāyaṇa, and Ramā.
Then, by means of the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow alone, she indeed gratified them;
and Lakṣmī and Janārdana, being pleased, spoke to her regarding a boon.
She then chose as a boon a son equal to Nārāyaṇa.
One who has reached the further shore of all scriptures, a righteous and excellent yogi,
a knower of the cries of all beings, and possessed of great strength and prowess—
having granted this boon with the words "So be it," he vanished from sight.

Then this very Nārāyaṇa himself became his son, known by the name Brahmadatta, compassionate and possessing the true strength of goodness (sattva). His wife was Lakṣmī, who was then named Sannati. ||34-35||
Her son was Viṣvaksena himself, the Blessed Lord.
Thus, the merit of the Lakṣmī-vow always bestows great fruit.
Now, she who was formerly Sinīvālī became the wife of Kardama.

Having performed the Lakṣmīśānti vow, Devahūtī then became the mother of Kapila, who is Śrī Hari, by means of that vow. In ancient times, Dyuti, having performed austerities and practiced the Lakṣmīśānti vow, [attained her goal].
Tuṣṭi obtained Vibhāvasu as her husband and bore sons beginning with Pavamāna;
she also performed austerities and observed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow,
whereby she indeed obtained Dhātṛ as her husband, who is honored by all the worlds.
Prabhā, having performed the vow, obtained Hari as her husband, Prabhākara;
Kuhū, having performed the vow, obtained the auspicious Haviṣyanta as her husband;
Kīrti obtained Jayanta as her lord; and Vasu obtained Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
Urvaśī obtained Purūravas as her husband, who was a source of joy;
once, Urvaśī danced at the Svayaṃvara of Lakṣmī.
Lakṣmī performed the Śānti-vrata and gave birth to eight sons.
Āyu, Dṛḍhāyu, Aśvāyu, Dhanāyu, Sadhṛti, Vasu,
Śucividya, and Śatāyu— after that, she indeed went to heaven.
Then, O Lakṣmī, the auspicious Śarmiṣṭhā, daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, [remained].
Having performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, Devayānī, the daughter of Śukra, obtained Yayāti as her virtuous husband; thereafter, she performed the Lakṣmī-vow and restored Kaca,
the son of her preceptor, to life after he had been devoured by the wild beasts of the Daityas.
Furthermore, the Daityas ground Kaca in wine and made him drink it.
Śukra gave the *sañjīvanī* [life-restoring] mantra to Kaca; and Śukra also gave it to Devayānī, who was still within his womb, out of his auspicious concern for her.
Having performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, Kaca went to his father’s house;
by the power of that [vow], he taught the Sañjīvanī [vidyā] to his own disciples.
Then indeed, Jyāmagha’s wife, Caitrā, through the Lakṣmī-vrata...
And she obtained a son named Vidarbha, who was endowed with excellent virtues.
Then the daughter-in-law likewise obtained that husband through the Lakṣmī-vrata;
she who had been conquered in the midst of battle by Jyāmagha and made his daughter-in-law.
Indeed, Dṛśadvatī performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow for Uśīnara and obtained Śibi,
the son of Uśīnara, as a universal emperor (cakravartin).
And in former times, Bali’s wife Sudeṣṇā, having performed the Lakṣmī vow—
Dīrghatamas obtained as sons Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, Puṇḍra, Suhma, and Śūdra— auspicious Brāhmaṇas who enjoyed royal power. Śakuntalā, having performed a vow, obtained Bharata as her son.
Mamatā, having made a vow, obtained the auspicious son Bharadvāja from Bṛhaspati and gave him to Bharata.
He was a disciple of the high-souled Kauśalya Hiraṇyanābhi.

Having prepared the way and undertaken a vow, he then, by the grace of Lakṣmī, divided the divine Sāma-saṃhitās into twenty-four parts. Ahalyā, however, was the sister of Divodāsa; she [was born] from Śaradvat.
It is said that she obtained the sage Śatānanda as her son through the Lakṣmī-vrata;
likewise, the Kāverī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Narmadā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Vitastā, Candrabhāgā, and Irāvatī [arose]. (57)
The Vipāśā, the Kauśikī, the Śatadrū, the Sarayū, as well as the Sītā, the high-minded Manasvinī, the Hradinī, and the purifying river [Gaṅgā],
having performed the Lakṣmī-Śānti vow, indeed obtained sons who were worthy of their stations.
In this way, other women as well, having performed this Lakṣmī-vrata,
obtained wealth, daughters, sons, heaven, and liberation. Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the most excellent vow known as Saubhāgya-śayana.
This was performed by you in the past, bestowing the fruit of all desires.
Formerly, when the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, and Mahas were consumed by fire,
the collective good fortune of all beings then became concentrated into a single mass.
Having reached that Vaikuṇṭha situated upon the chest of Viṣṇu,
and desiring to go once again to that state of auspiciousness among created beings at the time of re-creation,
she manifested from the chest of Hari in the form of Lakṣmī.
And by the command of Hari, that [nectar] became the bestower of all happiness;
having abandoned her form as Lakṣmī, she took on the form of *rasa*, consisting of nectar.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—those who are the sustainers of creation—[partook of it]. (64–65)
There, accompanied by the goddesses, they drank that essence which increases beauty,
charm, fortune, splendor, strength, and other qualities.
What remained was divided into eight parts for the sake of all created beings.
From the essence (rasa), seven joys arose that bestow good fortune:
sugarcanes, balls of molasses, flat beans, cumin seeds, cow’s milk and the like, safflower, vermilion, and likewise saffron. (67–68)
Including salt—these increase one's good fortune through that vow.
Nārāyaṇa himself protected her, who was the very embodiment of auspiciousness.
Because of his fondling, she became his beautiful daughter named Lalitā.
She always caresses the worlds with her form of auspiciousness. Having attained the worlds through her grace, she is called Lalitāśrī. The Great Lord married this Trailokyasundarī.
O Lakṣmī, you alone have become Mahālakṣmī, the bestower of good fortune, who is composed of auspiciousness in this world and grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
What is there that a man or a woman does not obtain by worshipping you with devotion?
I shall now describe to you that vow for propitiation which brings about welfare;
having reached the month of Vaiśākha, on the third day of the bright fortnight, the sacrificer should perform a bath with sesame seeds in the forenoon. (73–74)

Then the goddess Lalitā, the embodiment of good fortune, chose Nārāyaṇa as her husband. One should worship me, Nārāyaṇa, together with her at dawn on the third lunar day, using fruits, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
One should bathe Śrī with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with waters from sacred fords (tīrtha).
"Obeisance to Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, and Lalitā on the head;
obeisance to the Goddess, Mahādevī, and Lalitā on the face. (76–77)
Homage to Brāhmī, to Mahābrāhmī, and to Vaiṣṇavī in the heart; homage to Mātṛ, to Mahāmātṛ, and likewise to Nārāyaṇī in the belly.
Homage to Śrī, to Mahāśrī, and to Vāsudevī at the region of the hips.
Salutations to Bhāgyā, Mahābhāgyā, and Saubhāgyā; salutations to Urū.
Salutations to Bhūmnī, Mahāśūnyā, and Vyāpikā at the feet. Salutations on all sides to the wife of Anādikṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (3.136.80)
Salutations to you, the abode of good fortune; salutations to you, the manifestation of beauty.
Salutations to you who possess a dual form; repeated salutations to you, the divine couple.
Salutations again and again to Lalitā, who is endowed with all auspiciousness.
Having thus bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, one should offer garments and ornaments.
One should present all the decorative jewels and articles of adornment.
Likewise, one should offer ghee, vermilion, milk, saffron, and salt.
Cumin, collyrium, sandalwood, red sandalwood, turmeric, camphor, musk, and bracelets;
a chain, a necklace, a string, together with anklets and rings. (84)
One should place before [the deity] flat beans, betel leaves, areca nuts, and betel,
as well as sugar, cloves, and cardamom.
One should offer incense, a lamp, food offerings, and fragrant water.

One should indeed perform the *ārārtrika* rite, circumambulate Lalitā, offer salutations, and present a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). One should pray to Lalitā and Kṛṣṇa: "May supreme fortune be granted to me. (87)
Indeed, even the form of a married couple brings unbroken happiness.
In the home there should always be flavorful grains and other edibles, sweet foods, soups, boiled rice, vegetables, and curd-rice. (88–89)
All things produced from milk and those produced from sugarcane,
as well as seasoned meat preparations (*veśavāra*) and other such items used for perfuming the mouth; beds, coverlets, vehicles, and articles of dress and ornamentation— [all these are forbidden].
All ornaments and garments, as well as various kinds of jewelry;
vehicles, mounts, chariots, cows, horses, elephants, and excellent bulls; groups of male and female slaves, servants, and female companions; and likewise golden dwellings. (91–92)
Varied dwellings, fields, and gardens;
all great parks, as well as lineage, sons, and daughters;
daughters-in-law and kinsmen; and fame, renown, and prosperity. (93)
May supernatural power, peace, the jewel-elephant, health, and the supreme Dharma [be granted].
May devotion and knowledge be bestowed; thereafter, O Kṛṣṇas, grant the imperishable abode.
Having thus worshipped them, one should then install them there in the pavilion.
One should indeed perform the fire sacrifice (havana) consisting of one hundred and eight oblations;
then one should give the priestly fee (dakṣiṇā), feed the virtuous Brahmins,
feed the poor and the helpless, and then bestow gifts.
One should again perform the ritual service at midday.
One should offer various kinds of food, and provide water and betel leaf.
One should cause Kṛṣṇa, the Nārāyaṇa, to rest for one ghaṭikā and then awaken him.
One should offer water and fruit, and worship [the deities] in the evening at night;
one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with festivities and then feed them.
Thereafter, one should lay those two Lords to rest upon a soft and auspicious bed.
This vow consists of sleeping together on this very bed, known as the "Bed of Good Fortune.
Then, having risen in the morning, one should awaken the two deities and worship them according to the prescribed rite;
likewise, one should honor a Brahmin couple with garments and ornaments.

Tulasī, lotuses, and so forth are indeed prescribed for every month;
having thus performed the vow, a woman— whether a maiden or even a widow—

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this Ghaṭalakṣmī vow of yours.

For those observing the Ghaṭalakṣmī vow, however, heaven shall come to be gradually over seven days. This world of earth (bhūrloka) is called heaven because of its abundance of wealth, happiness, and joy;
and even the atmospheric world (bhuvarloka) is heaven for the accomplished yogins.
All those realms beginning with Svarga exist within the heavens, ending with Satya;
for these are indeed the seven worlds of the gods, since they grant access to the divine state. By virtue of your vow, however, you shall exercise sovereignty over all of them in succession.
From this very Ghaṭalakṣmī vow, [these] arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
In this world, through this vow, auspicious form, excellent longevity, supreme good fortune, abundant prosperity, and vast wealth arise for you here.
Listen here to the divine story of the high-souled Agastya.
Formerly, Vahni was commanded by Mahendra for the sake of destroying the enemies of the gods;
thereupon, Vahni consumed ten million dānavas.
Of those thousands of Dānavas who remained after being consumed by fire,
the wicked ones, fleeing in terror, entered the ocean.
Among them were Tāraka, Kamalākṣa, Kāladaṃṣṭra, and Parāvasu.
Virocana and they established themselves in the ocean;
and thinking them to be powerless, they were neglected by Agni.
Then, after some time, the Daityas indeed regained their strength once again.
They torment the gods and humans, along with all moving beings;
having thoroughly oppressed the brahmins and the virtuous,
they enter the water again for five and seven thousand years, O heroes.
"O Lakṣmī, by the strength of their watery fortress, they oppress the three worlds;
therefore, even Mahendra instructed Vahni:
'Let this ocean dry up before long for the sake of destroying the Daityas. (12)
"Since this ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, is the refuge of our enemies,

for within even a single *yojana* of this [ocean], there dwell hundreds of millions of living beings, and thus a great destruction of creatures would surely occur. (15)
"And how shall I perform that which would result in sin for me without end?

"You are the god who causes burning and are free from the stain of sin; nevertheless, you do not carry out my command—therefore, I declare: become a human!

Urvaśī, the daughter of Śrī Nara-Nārāyaṇa, was the most excellent of the Apsarases.

"I was previously chosen by Mitra; I am indeed his wife according to dharma, and not yours now, O Lord Varuṇa.

At that very time, however, Nimi [confronted] the illustrious Vasiṣṭha.

from that jar, the fire Agastya was born as a young boy.
Vasiṣṭha was born as Vāyu; there a boy was produced.

With joy they fed him with sweet food and milk-rice,

Endowed with the five jewels and accompanied by a vessel of clarified butter,

Richly adorned with all kinds of ornaments, born of gold in its horns and hooves,

Then the gracious mother, the great and virtuous Śrīghaṭalakṣmī,
appeared visibly before them and urged them to choose a boon.
They both chose an excellent boon, saying, "O Mother, by your grace..."
"Therefore, act in such a way that there may be liberation from this human birth.

after you have drunk the ocean, liberation from them will come about through a human birth."
"This Vasiṣṭha shall possess a divine body together with you.

Vasiṣṭha then requested the auspicious Ghaṭalakṣmī-vrata.
On the day of Agastya’s rising, at dawn,

having performed his bath with white sesame seeds and other materials using water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and wearing white garments, the householder who worships you, Lakṣmī, in either an earthen jar or a golden jar— || 3.137.50 ||

should indeed offer them worship and present the arghya water to them in due order.
In the Bhūrloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka,

[The two who] resemble kāśa flowers and are born from fire and wind... (55–56)

"For twenty-five billion Brahmās,

Having thus accomplished this great task, those two sages went to heaven.
Thus has this Ghaṭalakṣmī-vrata been described to you, O Lakṣmī;
for seven days, it consists of subsisting on fruit and performing worship.
It should be performed at the rising of the star Agastya, and it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
or likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa, Vaiśākha, or Kārttika,
perform your worship complete with a pavilion and a garden, and accompanied by the concluding rite (udyāpana).

Then one should perform the ritual dismissal and feed young boys and girls.
This is the supreme Lakṣmī-vrata, the most auspicious of all auspicious rites.

This vow brings about the destruction of all sins and increases good fortune and health;

Furthermore, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe another vow pertaining to Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

In all months, having fashioned an auspicious-faced Lakṣmī out of gold—
one who wears red garments, has red unguents, and is anointed with red sandalwood—

garments, red necklaces, red fruits, and the like.
One should worship me, Nārāyaṇa, who am red, with red flowers.

The female worshipper, established in the vows of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, should pray to you:
"O Mahālakṣmī, you are clad in red garments; Nārāyaṇa is established in the red. || 91-92 ||
Grant me health, renunciation, great peace, and union with Hari;

Here, I perform for you the Sāṃkhya-yoga-Mahālakṣmī-vrata.

Having thus entreated, one should likewise offer a golden image of Lakṣmī to the preceptor;

This vow of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, accompanied by fasting, should be performed;
it removes all sins, bestows a divine body, and is dear to Hari. (97–98)
She shall become a virtuous wife beloved by Hari, a performer of vows who has cast off her body;
she shall become wondrous, divine, and established in the abode of the Imperishable.

however, those performed for the sake of my grace truly grant liberation.
Eating only at night for one year is declared to be the *nakta-vrata*.
The observer of that vow should begin it either from the month of Kārttika or from Āṣāḍha (4).
Beginning on the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī), when the year is complete, he should give a golden Sudarśana discus together with a cow as an offering to his venerable guru (5).
One should also feed virtuous people and perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the vow;
by giving gifts of clothing, one rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should observe the vow of eating only once a day, consisting of a meal at midday.
Having offered everything to the God, one should eat, and never with anyone else.
This shall be the vow for a year, and at the end of the year, there should be a great festival.
One should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and donate a golden bull.
One should also bestow food upon the virtuous and even give a cow;
one should observe the vow of eating every other day for the duration of a year.
One should eat only on alternate days, and at the conclusion of the vow, there should be a great festival.
One should bestow a golden lotus during the gift-offering and perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
One should give a vessel filled with sugar and feed the virtuous.
The observer of the vow attains great merit and, at the end, indeed reaches the state of Viṣṇu.
During the four-month period, one should avoid anointing the body with excellent oils;
this avoidance of anointing is declared to be the supreme vow of austerity.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give gifts of oil and other such items, as well as various foods for the meal.
This, however, is pleasing to me, for by it one goes to the abode of Hari.
(1.3) Furthermore, the avoidance of flavors is proclaimed as the "vow of flavors" (*rasavrata*).
[These are: honey, coconut water, curd, milk, ghee, and sugarcane juice. (1.4)
At the end of the year, one should either complete the vow or perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
One should give gifts of mercury and other substances, and offer fine garments.
One should also perform the Kāmavrata, which always destroys sorrow.
During the four-month period, one should always remain devoted to celibacy.
When the vow is completed, one should offer a golden Ashoka tree;
one should also offer sugarcane and likewise offer garments.
Having enjoyed these pleasures, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and go to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Indeed, the observer of the vow during Cāturmāsya should avoid clipping the nails;
he should also avoid shaving the hair during Cāturmāsya.
Having observed this vow with the consciousness that nothing has been cut, and having performed a great festival,
one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) at the end and feed the virtuous with milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should give to a twice-born man as a gift golden nails and hair.
O Lakṣmī, one should offer my gentle form to you every day;
this is proclaimed as the Saumya-vrata, lasting for a full month. By this, one becomes gentle in Vaikuṇṭha and indeed becomes the moon here on earth.
At the end of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should give many gifts of jewels.
In the month of Kārttika, having performed worship, one should give to the preceptor a golden image adorned with household utensils; this is called the Saubhāgyavrata.
Then one should offer an image of Viṣṇu and an image of Śrī to the venerable guru; on other occasions, one should perform various acts of giving while reciting, "May Śrī Hari be pleased.
At the time of twilight, one should observe the Sārasvata vow, which consists of maintaining silence.
Having observed the vow for one year, one should give a jar of ghee, a vessel of sesame seeds,
a pair of garments, a bowl, and a bell to a twice-born man. One should present the gift of a cow to the preceptor and the donation of books.
And this Sārasvata vow bestows knowledge, beauty, and other such qualities.
Then, on the fifth lunar day, one should perform the Sampad-vrata, honoring the virtuous Mādhavī;
one should worship Lakṣmī constantly, and at the end of the year, offer a golden lotus.
One should give a lotus to the Guru, as well as a milch cow together with her calf;
such a person, endowed with prosperity, attains the station of Viṣṇu birth after birth.
One should always sweep the entire temple of the Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
At the end of the year, he should bestow a milch cow as well as a water-pot;
by that act, he shall become a king for ten thousand births and thereafter go to the city of Viṣṇu.
This is known as the Āyur-vrata, which effects the cleansing of sins.
Then one should perform the Kīrti-vrata; one should always practice eating but a single meal [a day].
At the end of the year, one should give ten cows and a golden tree.
There shall be the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, and prosperity and fame shall be the result.
Now, the vow of the Sāman is declared: one should constantly recite the hymn before Hari at the three times of day, and always offer sesame seeds;
one should also offer flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata) for the purpose of worshipping Hari.
When the full year has elapsed, one should give a great golden lotus;
by giving a sesame-cow eight fingers in height, one goes to the supreme state.
Then, on the ninth day, one should observe the Vīra-vrata while eating but a single meal.
For one year, she should feed young maidens, and at the end of the year, she should likewise give to the venerable Guru golden bodices, garments, and a golden lion; furthermore,
she should bestow ornaments, clothing, and other gifts upon the maidens according to their merit.
One will be handsome from birth and, at the end, shall go to the abode of Hari.
Likewise, one should observe the milk-vow on the full moon day for an entire year;
at the conclusion of the year, one should give five milch cows along with their calves.
He who gives saffron-colored garments along with water-pitchers goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and shall deliver a hundred ancestors;
he should also perform the Śrāddha for his ancestors, for this is considered the vow of the ancestors.

Then, during the four months beginning with Caitra, one should cause all people to drink cool water; at the conclusion of the vow, one should present a water-jar (maṇika). One should also give food, clothing, a vessel of sesame seeds, and gold.
This is the Jalānanda-vrata; by it one becomes a sovereign at the end of a kalpa.
Then, one should perform the Dhṛti-vrata, [worshipping] me as Śrī Hari every day, and thereafter cause the auspicious one to be bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
At the end of the year, one should perform the gift of a conch shell and goes to the abode of Hari.
(43) A person who has observed the vow should not harm any living beings at the end of the year;
rather, he should perform this gift of a cow and the gift of a golden deer. (44)
By this vow of non-violence, he shall become a sovereign at the end of the kalpa.
Then, he should perform the ritual bath in the month of Māgha with cold water,
worship the Sun daily, and bestow gifts upon the twice-born.
Grain, clothing, ornaments, and so forth—this is called the Sūryavrata.
During the Cāturmāsya, one should worship Mahāviṣṇu and Mahālakṣmī;
the observer of the vow should also bestow gifts of cows and food according to his capacity.
He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu through this auspicious vow of Viṣṇu.
Now follows the vow named Śīla, which bestows the fruit of character and health.
For a full year, whether a woman or a man, one should observe celibacy.
One should give a cow made of ghee and always offer garlands of flowers.
Likewise, one should feed excellent ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa) to virtuous people.
At the end of the year, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) and bestow grain and wealth.
He attains the imperishable realm of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, one should not consume oil for a year, but should instead offer a lamp;
one should give a golden lamp, gold, and a discus to a twice-born brāhmaṇa.
He who gives a pair of garments indeed goes to the abode of Brahmā.
This is declared to be the vow of the lamp, which bestows radiance as well as beauty.
Now, beginning from the month of Kārttika, one should eat milk-rice (pāyasa) only at night.
At the end of the year, one should give a cow; this is indeed the vow known as Pāyasa.
It brings about auspiciousness for the earth, bestows sovereignty, and grants liberation.
Now, one should always avoid perfumes, ointments, and the like for the duration of the year.
The vow known as Nirgandha is proclaimed; at the end of the year, one should give gifts of fragrant substances.
(55) Then one should perform the Kānti-vrata; every day one should offer a gift of a cow, and for a full year thereafter, one must not eat salt. (56)
One should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), which bestows the fruits of beauty and fame;
having become a king for a full kalpa, one shall dwell eternally in the world of Viṣṇu. Then, one should observe the vow of Brahmā and fashion an auspicious golden Brahmāṇḍa.
On an auspicious day, one should give even a small amount of sesame seeds to a brahmin;
likewise, the observer of the vow should subsist on sesame seeds for three days.
Furthermore, the observer of the vow should make a gift of garlands, garments, and ornaments.
He goes to the world of Brahmā and shall attain the state of Nirvāṇa. Beyond three *palas* of [mercury] according to one's capacity, it is proclaimed as the *brahmāṇḍa*.
Now, one should perform the *dhenuvrata*; for three days, one should observe the vow of subsisting on milk alone.
One should give a golden bull and a cow with two faces;
one should also bestow rice and a golden bull weighing half a pala.
Having given these through the excellent vow of the cow, one goes to the station of Brahmā and to Goloka.

Then one should perform the Kalpa-vow: having fashioned a wish-fulfilling tree out of materials weighing more than a *pala*, one should give it to a virtuous person along with rice grains containing double-seeded pulses.
By this gift of the Kalpa-tree, at the end of the aeon, one goes from heaven to my own abode.

Now, one who has observed a month-long fast should present a beautiful, milch buffalo to the venerable Guru; this is called the "Buffalo Vow. One should also give a beautiful golden image of the Earth weighing more than twenty palas.
This is declared to be the Dharā-vrata: one should eat only a single meal during the day.
Such a person dwells in the abode of the Lord of Śrī for seven hundred kalpas;
thereafter, the man who performs the Dharā-vrata goes to the imperishable realm.
My devotee surely attains Me and, as My attendant, serves Me.
(67) In the months of Māgha and Caitra, one devoted to the *guḍavrata* should give jaggery;
eating jaggery and drinking jaggery, he should worship with sesame seeds and jaggery. (68)
One should offer me and Lakṣmī, and at the gift of jaggery, one should give an image made of jaggery along with the jaggery itself.
This is declared to be the Guḍavrata, which bestows liberation and grants salvation.
Then, one who observes a fast for a fortnight should present a pair of Kapila cows.
And one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), which brings about supreme bliss.
That indeed is the Kapila-vrata; at the end of the kalpa, one shall become a king of kings.
Furthermore, for one year, one should eat but once a day and constantly provide food and water.
One shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu at the end; this is considered the Prāpti-vrata.
One should eat only at night on the eighth lunar days (aṣṭamīs), and at the end of the year, one should give a cow.
Thereafter, one goes to heaven, and finally, one attains the station of Brahmā.

This very vow is called the Sugativrata, which bestows a happy rebirth. He who gives fuel to a Brahmin for a year, as well as one who gives a cow, performs this Vaiśvānaravrata; its performer goes to Brahman.
On the eleventh day, the observer of the vow gives a beautiful golden image of Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa on the twelfth day;
and at the conclusion of the year, the practitioner of the vow gives a golden Vaiṣṇava discus.
Having performed this Kṛṣṇa-vow, one shall become a sharer in a kingdom at the end of a kalpa.
By offering me [this vow] at the end of the year, one shall indeed attain my abode.
Eating only milk-rice (pāyasa), one should give a pair of cows to a Brahmin at the conclusion of the year.

One attains the world of Lakṣmī; this is called the Śrī-vrata. He who, on the seventh lunar day, gives away a beautiful, milch cow, surely goes to the world of the Sun; that is called the Bhānu-vrata.
On the fourth lunar day, one should eat only at night and, at the end of the year, offer a golden elephant.
This vow, known as the Vaināyaka, bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
During the Cāturmāsya period, the practitioner of the vow should offer fruits made of gold and silver.

This fruit-vow (phalavrata), which bestows the world of Viṣṇu, is indeed of great power. He who fasts on the seventh lunar day and, at the conclusion of the year, gives a golden lotus along with cows in a golden vessel, this is proclaimed as the Saura-vrata.
One should also bestow this gift of the sun, which grants access to the solar world.
Having completed twelve Dvādaśīs by means of fasting,
the observer of the vow should give cows, garments, gold, and ornaments to the venerable Guru.
O Rame, by performing this vow of Viṣṇu, one attains the supreme state;
having performed the rite of releasing a bull on the full moon of Kārttika, one should observe a fast at night.
This is considered the annual vow that leads to the attainment of the state of Śiva.
One should give golden cow-prints; this is the vow of the footprint (padavrata).
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of clarified butter to a virtuous person.
This is declared to be the vow of clarified butter (ghṛtavrata), which bestows the fruit of the world of Brahmā.

Sleeping in the open air during the rainy season, one should at its conclusion give a milch cow; this vow, known as Ākāśa, bestows the station of Indra. Thereafter, one should eat only food not cooked by fire on the third lunar day.
Indeed, at the end of the month, one should perform the gift of a milch cow;
this is declared to be the "Auspicious Vow" (Śreyovrata), which bestows Goloka and grants happiness.
One should also provide an auspicious chariot drawn by horses, made of gold weighing more than two palas.
One who observes the Rathavrata while giving gifts shall dwell swiftly in heaven for a hundred kalpas;
at the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king of kings, and thereafter proceed to the supreme state.
He who performs fasts for six months, with a day of eating every other day, [attains the same].
At the end of the year, one should be a giver of cows; this is declared to be the Vāruṇa vow.
Having attained the kingdom of Varuṇa, one then goes to the supreme state.
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow and bestow a golden moon upon a virtuous person.
This excellent Candra-vrata bestows the fruit of the lunar world. In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should constantly perform the penance of the five fires and become a donor of gold and a cow.
This is declared to be the Tapo-vrata; from it, one attains sovereignty.
Thereafter, one attains Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Imperishable Abode (Akṣara).
One should offer a canopy made of cloth and other materials in the temple of the Lord;
by the excellent fruit of the Vitāna-vrata, the giver of the canopy goes to heaven.
In the month of Māgha, one should remain with wet clothes; on the seventh day, one should become a giver of cows.
The observer of the Ārdra-vow becomes a king, goes to heaven, and attains liberation.
Furthermore, he who gives a preeminent dwelling as a gift in Phālguna—
One who observes the *dhāmavrata* surely proceeds to the temple of the Supreme Lord.
Having worshipped a virtuous man or a virtuous woman, one should feed them excellent sweets;
one should then eat the *prasāda* oneself—this indeed is the vow called *prasādavrata*. ||97-98||
It removes all sins, bestows merit, and likewise grants liberation;
it is purifying, most excellent, and indeed the supreme sanctifier of the assembly.
By eating only one meal on the first lunar day (pratipad) and gifting a tawny cow at the end of the year, one attains these rewards.
One who constantly performs the worship of Vaiśvānara goes to the Fire-god.
This vow of Vaiśvānara bestows divinity and grants happiness;
at its conclusion, one should eat only a single meal on the tenth lunar day and give ten cows as a gift.
One should give a golden leaf; one shall become the sovereign of the Brahmāṇḍa.
This is indeed proclaimed as the Viśvavrata, O Lakṣmī, an ocean of merit.
One should always perform the recitation; this is the vow known as Kīrtana.
One should always engage in discourse; this indeed is the vow known as *kathā*. One should always perform worship; this indeed is the vow known as *bhajana*.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these sixty-one vows have been described to you.
For the sake of benefiting the worlds, since the world possesses three limbs—
through the recitation, hearing, and remembrance of this,
as well as through its performance, rejoicing, giving, and even by providing assistance. (105)
One shall surely obtain the merit of the vow and attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "A Brief Description of the Sixty-one Miscellaneous Vows," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Chapter 140: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age)*
Chapter 141 [Author:
Chapter 142 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Lord of the syllables, O Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, my Lord!
O Sovereign of Goloka, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, O Nārāyaṇa!
O Bhūman, O Lord of the unmanifest, O Vāsudeva, O Lord of the Immortal!
O Lord of Śrī, for one who is truly unable to perform those very vows prescribed for the residents of Śrīpura—how can there be liberation for such a person?
[This applies to] women, children, the elderly, the sick, as well as beasts and birds. (2–3)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Rame, by the remembrance of My name, his liberation shall come—O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the True Lord! (4)
O Śrīkṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O glorious Nārāyaṇa, O Narāyaṇa!
O Govinda, O Mādhava, O Viṣṇu, O Master, O Sovereign of Men, O Acyuta!
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, O Blue-throated One, O Bringer of Bliss to Mahālakṣmī!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, ocean of compassion, son of the illustrious Gopālā;
O son of Śrī Kaṃbharā, you who are the sovereign of Aśvapaṭṭasara, whose dwelling is established at the holy site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, abide within my heart. (6–7)
"O Rāma, O Śrī Puṇḍarīkākṣa, O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O All-pervading One, O Sovereign of the beloved of Hari—protect me and release me from bondage!
Thus, the chanting of these names of mine shall indeed grant liberation. (8)
Moreover, one should hear and recite the greatness of my abode known as Akshara, of Ashvapatthasara, of the land of Kumkumavapika, and of this sacred ford (tirtha). (3.141.10)
One should indeed listen to the stories of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
which consists of one hundred thousand verses, twenty-five [thousand] more, and thousands— that is,
one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses in this compendium.
I am the fulfiller of the desires for dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, abide upon this earth in the form of the *Saṃhitā*, which is my second manifestation as scripture. (12–13)
In all the worlds of living beings as well as in the worlds of the Lord,

and even in the Imperishable, I abide as the essence of the collection [of the Vedas], having sound as my form. Whether it be an entire chapter, a section, a continuous passage, or even a single verse, [I am present].
He who shall recite this will become one whose self is the elements and whose self is liberated.
He who shall hear it with a steady mind will become one whose self is Brahman.
Those who pay homage to my reciter shall become purified.
They who shall perform worship to him will go to the highest heaven;
those who, having gone to the sacred ford of Lomaśa’s hermitage, shall dwell there constantly—
for them, through my grace, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to hand.

Those who offer praise shall go by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot (vimāna) to the supreme, imperishable state. Those women who perform pilgrimage at this sacred site (tīrtha) shall go to the city of Lalitā. || 18–19 ||
Indeed, they shall rejoice with Śrī Nārāyaṇī in the imperishable realm;
likewise, they shall abide in the abode together with Lakṣmī, the queen of Śiva.
Having obtained me as their beloved Kṛṣṇa, they shall rejoice perpetually.
O Lakṣmī, I am the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha), and you are a sacred ford equal to me.
Our dwelling place is a sacred ford resembling the Imperishable (Akṣara) itself,
located in Saurāṣṭra, in the region of Ānarta, all around the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake.
To the south of Bhadrāvatī, to the west of Śatruñjayā,
on the eastern side of Mount Raivata, and within the northern region of the Vyāghrī forest,
there is my own circular field, extending for a hundred *krośas*.
O Lakṣmī, it bestows liberation, destroys sin, and grants all the goals of human endeavor.
Having bathed in the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, people indeed go to heaven and attain liberation.
I am Hari myself in the form of the Maṇḍala, which consists of the Kuṅkumavāpī field.
I protect it in every way, even from millions of liberated lords among the gods;
I protect my beloved Badrī at Kuṅkumavāpikā.
By remembering her, a human being indeed becomes capable of burning away all evil.
By seeing Badarī, or even by chanting her name,
and by touching its soil, a person is liberated from sin. Even for thousands of yojanas away from Badarī, a person is freed from evil simply by remembering it.
Whether a woman or a child, one attains the supreme goal;
by the mere touch of the leaves and flowers of the Badarī tree, one finds auspicious blessings.
Having bathed in and drunk from it, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.
Meditating upon Badrī in his mind, one obtains abundant desires.
Having gone to Kuṅkumavāpikā, which is equal in splendor to the glory of Badrī,
one who observes celibacy should dwell there for a month and gratify the ancestors and the gods.
Wherever he is born, he obtains his desired objects. Having seen Badrī and drunk its water, the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, siddhas, and cāraṇas have departed for my imperishable abode.
For those who are afflicted, for the poor, and for those of firm resolve, there is nothing else that bestows liberation equal to Badrī in Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Whether one is diseased, wretched, or old, through the service of Badrī [one attains it]. || 33-34 ||
Or, if one should abandon one's life-breaths by fate in the vicinity of Badarī,
one goes indeed to the abodes of Kṛṣṇa in celestial chariots possessing the luster of glowing gold and resembling the sun,
and rejoices there for eternal years.
He obtains all his desired objects of enjoyment and the like;
in the eternal state, he rejoices in celestial palaces composed of every kind of jewel, adorned with various banners, and filled with beautiful women. (36–37)
In that world, the trees bear all desired fruits, the earth is made of gold, and the soils possess every flavor; there one is glorified.
Even by merely remembering Badarī as well as Kuṅkumavāpikā, [one attains such a state].
Having abandoned his life-breath, he surely goes to the world of Brahmā, which is higher than the highest.
He who, supported by dharma and truth, bestows a cow in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā—whether by deed, thought, or word—[attains that supreme state]. (3.141.40)
Gold, gems, pearls, wealth, grain, and likewise clothing—
one should bestow these for one’s own sake, for the sake of the ancestors, or even for the worship of the gods; for him,
these become multiplied infinitely in the imperishable state.
One should give a single milch cow in exchange for hundreds of thousands of other cows;
a cow thus given saves one's sons, servants, and dependents right here.
Furthermore, he who bestows a daughter in marriage at the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā [attains the same merit].
By means of the marriage rite in his abode, there is infinite merit.
And this jewel from Saurāṣṭra is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself, eternally embodied;
even at the time of dissolution, there is no destruction of it due to my dwelling therein, O lotus-born one.
Just as at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake during the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices,
one obtains eternal fruit and freedom from rebirth by bathing there.
O Rame, ten thousand holy sites and sixty crores of others are present here.
All of them dwell here within my own abode; therefore,
the giver of a golden woman goes to heaven from this place,
and he obtains a hundred maidens resembling Urvaśī.
He shall become the husband of many thousands of women in their midst.
For that place where the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is located is my field of spiritual perfection (siddhakṣetra);
having plundered there, even a sinful soul becomes a sanctifier of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).

The site of Kuṅkumavāpikā is the most sacred of the sacred, the most auspicious of the auspicious, and the bestower of liberation among those that grant liberation. To the north of the lake flows the inexhaustible river from Pātāla.
The great Gaṅgā of Śvetadvīpa, impelled by Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa,
flows as the white river within the waters, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The Viṣṇupadī herself descends from heaven and disappears here, becoming invisible.
The Brahmahrada lake is always present at my feet,
and it flows as a river of nectar from its celestial source into these waters.
By means of that, all the immortals indeed subsist upon this earth known as Aśvasaras.
And here, the person who performs a pilgrimage obtains the fruit of fasting unto death.
(54) But he who bathes for one month in the waters of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state. (55)
But he who, out of ignorance, undertakes a pilgrimage to sacred sites and the like in this world,
is honored in the heavenly realm, with all his desires fulfilled.
Once, the divine Lomaśa went to the ground of Prayāga.
Prayāga was indeed not there; instead, the sage Bharadvāja resided there.
Lomaśa, the king of holy places, questioned Bharadvāja:
"O sage, where has he gone today? I have had no sight of him."
Then Bharadvāja said:
"Prayāga has gone to the Aśvasaras lake to wash away those great sins and heinous crimes which were offered by men through the Kumbha-yoga after bathing. (59)
Where the sacred site known as Kuṅkumavāpī exists, where Lakṣmī herself resides,
and where Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa also dwells— there Prayāga has gone; behold, he will arrive swiftly.
Lomaśa, having seen the enclosure there, stayed for a moment;
meanwhile, Prayāga arrived, having completely shaken off all his sins.
Lomaśa, having honored him, departed for the Badarikāvana forest.
There, the divine Badarī, the abode of Nārāyaṇa, was not present;
it had not been seen by Lomaśa at that time. Then the sage himself was asked:
"Where is the pilgrimage to Badarī, and when will one ever go there?"
The slender lady replied, "She has gone to the Aśvasarovara lake in Saurāṣṭra,
in order to serve the Lord of her life, the beloved Master Bālakṛṣṇa, who is Śrīpati Puruṣottama in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā."
She exists there in the form of a maiden among the beloved wives of Brahmā;
having become the daughter-in-law of Hari, she shines resplendent together with Lakṣmī.
At times, she appears there as an ascetic on the bank of the Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Muktakoṭikā exists in the form of a jujube tree,
spreading her celestial palace directly above the oblong pond;
she stands upon the northern ground, her branches extending over the pond.
Indeed, they always exist in the form of umbrellas, impelled by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
O Sage, she who is the large-eyed wife of Hari shines there;
she who is Badarī herself shines there.
Even here, she exists in another form for the sake of the Blessed One;
at the time of Hari’s residence, she becomes a provider of shade.
She will arrive here swiftly at the hour of midday.
Having thus understood the state of the great sage’s body, the venerable sage Lomaśa remained there until midday. That virtuous girl,
Badarī, quickly arrived by way of the sky and became Badarikā.
Having honored her and likewise having worshipped Śrī Narāyaṇa beneath it, Lomaśa proceeded to the great Bālakṛṣṇa-sarovara. After bathing in Lake Mānasa, he traveled through the sky to Saurāṣṭra.

Having made this certain, he then resided eternally in my abode on the grounds of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, perceiving the majesty of the earth. Indeed, that Badarī is Mahālakṣmī, who is truly one with me, Nārāyaṇa.
Commanded to remain forever, she dwells upon the bank of the pond;
though her form may become invisible at other times,
she will become visible again when there is an assembly of devotees.
Likewise, other beloved wives of Brahmā, assuming the form of jujube trees,
will become thousands of ponds subsisting on that water;
they shall be visible there, for the earth never becomes empty.
Likewise, the goddesses dear to Hari exist here as creepers;
the one named Anārakalikā exists in the form of a pomegranate tree,
and my wife Uttejinī exists in the form of a tamarind tree.
There are two types of *hiṅgudī*: the *snehilī* and the *subhagā*.
My wife Jāmbavatī is there as Jāmbikā; Rāviṇī the singer is also there, as is Rāvaṇikā. 81–82.
In this way, my other beloved friends and their respective companions are there;
likewise, the milk-plant creeper and the maiden reside there.
Indeed, there are many flower-like groves in the form of gardens, as well as numerous rows of trees.
The liberated women, possessing divine and beautiful forms, always serve me. (84) Sometimes they appear as trees and creepers; sometimes they appear as lovely women with beautiful forms.
Sometimes they become visible, and at other times they become invisible. (85)
In some places they are with me on my bed, in some places indeed upon my elephant-throne; in some places they sport with me in my celestial vehicle.
In some places they are by my side on the ground of the *rāsa* dance, and in some places even within my pavilion.
In some instances, they become merged within my heart, consuming bliss;
at other times, having attained a state of uniform flavor, they rejoice as beings intoxicated by that very self.
They remain distinct during eating, sporting, drinking, and service.
O Lakṣmī, just as you abide in my heart, at my side, and in my presence,
so too do those auspicious lotuses like you abide for me.
That land where they dwell is my imperishable abode.

O Lakṣmī, the Kuṅkumavāpikā-tīrtha is the best of all holy places, the most excellent pinnacle among tīrthas. In every kalpa, within Surāṣṭra, it comes into being by my will alone; it was created by me at the beginning of the cosmic egg.
Surāṣṭra is your kingdom, independent and like unto a subcontinent.
The land of Kṛṣṇa is equal to Kṛṣṇa himself; she belongs to the lineage of Kṛṣṇa and is my very own form.
The land of Mokṣadvāravatī is purifying in every age.
There is a river named Subhadrā-Bhadrī, which was created by me;
by the mere remembrance, touch, or drinking of even a drop of its water, the destruction of sin certainly occurs, and one likewise goes to heaven and the imperishable state. (93–94)
Even for me, a man of such power, when separated from me for a moment,
my sovereignities dissolve and my feminine splendors are cast down;
then, O auspicious one, even the most excellent river Subhadrā is plundered by robbers.
The wife of Nara exists in the water as the very embodiment of a great *tīrtha*.
She constantly bestows auspiciousness upon those who bathe there, manifesting every form of well-being.
In Śrī Puruṣottama, she stands as the river in the form of action, the personified form itself. (96–97)
Possessing a divine form, my sister is well-pleased in Badarī;
in my abode, Muktānikā manifests in five forms.
The oceans, lakes equal to the ocean, and likewise the rivers [are her manifestations].
In my Kuṅkumavāpī, there dwell meritorious ones in the form of Brahman.

Indeed, all the Vedas and sacrifices are present here in embodied form within this imperishable place; likewise, the great ṛṣis, the ancestors, the Siddhas, and the stainless holy men reside there. (3.141.99–100)
The truthful, the virtuous, the wielders of the discus, and the attendants who bear the discus worship me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person, who am without beginning.
This is a great field of perfection, a realm of light higher than the highest.
This is auspicious, this leads to heaven, this is truth, this is happiness;
this is merit, this is righteous, this is purifying—the supreme teaching of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard even this, which is the best of sacred fords among sacred fords, one rejoices in the heights of heaven.
One attains the memory of past births, as well as the power to remember everything; one comes to know that which pertains to the three periods of time and also acquires omniscience.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of How Even Sinners Are Liberated through the Remembrance and Vision of the Kuṅkumavāpikā Tīrtha," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-santāna) of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
