The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Nārāyaṇa, beloved of the world, protector of all, omnipresent one! How does a human being on earth conquer death that arises from the three periods of time? (1)
By what means can powerful death, which has turned back no one, be warded off?
Or in what form does death pursue human beings?
(2) Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, O Rame, O Lakṣmī, O Samudrajā, and listen also, O Akṣaramāṇikī! Garuḍa, indeed my devotee, was seated in my house.
Meditating upon my rosary and my own divine form, [he remained thus].
(4) Then his own son was questioned by his father Kaśyapa:
"O son, O great devotee, O yogin, how can death be averted? (5)
"In what form does death indeed arrive and carry one away?
How is it that it moves here without touching the embodied being?
Having heard this, the bird spoke to his father: "I shall tell you that."
Through devotion, death is warded off by taking refuge in the Supreme Self.
(7) The messenger of Death approaches, bearing a staff or a weapon, appearing as a naked mendicant or in other forms;
having seized the body, one does not live because of his bite. (8)
If three fangs are found embedded in a bite on a funeral pyre, an anthill, a mountain, and so forth, or in a well or a hollow of a tree, the bitten person does not live. Furthermore,
[one bitten] on the sixth lunar day, under the signs of Cancer or Aries, or during the asterisms of Mūla, Āśleṣā, Maghā, and others [is likewise lost].
One bitten in the armpits, the hips, the throat-joint, the temples, the ears, the belly, and so forth;
in the mouth, the arms, the neck, or on the back—such a person is not spared by the Lord of Fortune (Śrīpati).
Śeṣa, Arka, Phaṇipati, Candra, and Takṣaka are said to correspond to Mars (Bhauma). (3.142.10–11)
Karkoṭaka is Mercury, Padma is Jupiter, Mahāpadma is Venus,
Śaṅkha is Saturn, Rāhu, and Kulika are these [other] planets.
One bitten by a snake belonging to the species corresponding to whichever planet it is under does not survive.
The big toe of the foot is the first lunar day (pratipad); the two backs of the feet are the second;
the two ankles are indeed the third; the two knees are the fourth; the penis and the vulva are the fifth; and the navel is considered the sixth lunar day (tithi). 13–14.
The heart is said to be the seventh [tithi], and the two breasts the eighth day;
the throat is said to be the ninth, and the nostrils the tenth.
The eyes are to be known as the eleventh, and the ears are considered the twelfth.
The two eyebrows are the form of the thirteenth [tithi], and the conch [shell] is considered the fourteenth.
The head is the fifteenth; on that lunar day, one should bite that spot.
Then, bitten by the maw of Time (Kāla), the embodied being does not live.
It is held that for a man this occurs on the right side, while for a woman it is on the left;
one bitten at such a moment never lives.
However, one should perform the recitation of "Oṃ Garuḍa Svāhā" one hundred thousand times.
One should touch [the deity] at the big toe, the sole, and the heel;
at the shank, the knee, and the thigh; at the penis, the vulva, and the waist;
at the hips, the region of the navel, and the buttocks; and at the belly and the heart. (3.142.19–20)
In the regions at the sides of the breasts, in the arms, on the palms of the hands, in the fingers, at the elbows, in the throat, the neck, and the nape of the neck;
in the jaw, the mouth, the cheeks, the nose, and the temples. (21)
One should repeatedly place [the mantra] upon the two ears, the back of the ears, the forehead, the two eyes, the two eyebrows, the skull, the head, and also the crest;
by the recitation of the mantra, that embodied being becomes Garuḍa himself. (22–23)
Even in dreams, venomous serpents do not step upon his shadow;
even snakes that are the very form of Time flee from him out of fear.
By the application of this mantra, all poison is destroyed and dissolved.
"Oṃ, O Śeṣeśvara, Lord of the Nāginīs, you who ride upon the back of Garuḍa!
O Śrī Hari, who grants the fruit of Āstīka’s words, remove the poison, remove the poison!
One should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times; thereafter, it becomes perfected.

Even Mahākāla would flee far away out of fear from my constant chanting of the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, which has been practiced by me since time immemorial. Even Mahākāla retreats to a great distance out of fear of me.
Even one who is unfit for liberation lives here as a possessor of a body; of this there is no doubt.
One should perform the worship of me, Śrīdhara, together with my retinue, having meditated upon oneself as the one named Śrīdhara, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. (28–29)
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Puruṣottama, the Supreme Self;
salutations to the Imperishable One, and repeated salutations to Māṇikyā.
Salutations again and again to Padmāvatī, Jayā, and Lalitā.
Salutations again and again to the giver of happiness, to Wisdom, and to Lakṣmī. Salutations again and again to Rādhikā, to Action, and to Knowledge.
Salutations again and again to Will, to Kamalā, and to Mahālakṣmī.
Oṃ Hrīṃ! Salutations again and again to Viṣṇu, the bearer of Śrī.
Then [offer] the consecration (abhiṣeka), as well as clothing, the sacred thread (yajñopavītaka), sandalwood paste (gandha), flowers, incense (dhūpa), a lamp, food, and circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa).
One should give [these], recite my mantra, and meditate upon me residing in the heart—
resembling pure crystal, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
with a gracious countenance, gentle, and adorned with a shimmering crown and earrings. (34–35)
One should meditate upon my supreme, auspicious form: the wearer of the crown, with noble limbs, adorned with a forest garland, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
Salutations to Śrīnivāsa, to Kṛṣṇa; salutations to the Lord of Śrī.
Salutations again and again to Śrīdhara, who holds the Śārṅga bow and bestows prosperity. Salutations again and again to You, the beloved of Śrī, the peaceful one, and the possessor of glory.
Salutations to the dweller on Śrīparvata and to the granter of ultimate welfare.
Salutations to You, the source of all that is auspicious, and the resting place of Śrī; salutations to the embodiment of supreme well-being, and repeated salutations to the bestower of prosperity.
Salutations again and again to the one who reclines with Śrī and who is the refuge for all.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should indeed bid farewell to Śrīśvara.
One who performs worship in this manner certainly becomes free from poison;
he is shaken free from sins and attains my supreme state.
"Oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Śrīdhara, to Śrī Viṣṇu, the Victorious One.
This mantra removes all diseases, removes all afflictions,
destroys all sins, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
It is indeed the destroyer of all poisons and the eradicator of malevolent spells (abhicāra). It fulfills all desires and bestows my own abode.
Having become my very self, one should perform the recitation; one shall live, of this there is no doubt.
One should administer an oath by the name of that serpent which dwells in a particular month, in a particular season, and which shares its course with the sun;
by that means, the snake venom is quickly pacified, without a doubt.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the sevenfold manifestation beginning with Māsa, Sarpa, and Arka,
which dwells together as the solar self of Hari.
Just as the one Sun is described in many ways through various ritual procedures, so too is he.
Dhātṛ, Sūrya, the Apsaras Puñjikasthalī, the Rākṣasa Heti, the Nāga Vāsuki, the Yakṣa Rathakṛt, the lordly Ṛṣi Pulastya,
and the Gandharva Tumburu— these attend upon him in the month of Caitra.
Sūrya, Aryaman, the Apsaras Puñjikasthalī,
the Rākṣasa Heti, the Nāga Kacchanīra, then Ojas, the Yakṣa Pulaha the sage, and Nārada the Gandharva— these dwell in Vaiśākha. (3.142.50)
Mitra, Sūrya, the Apsaras Menakā, the Pauruṣeya Rākṣasa,
the Nāga Takṣaka, the Yakṣa Rathasvana, and likewise the sage Atri,
as well as the Gandharva Hāhā— these attend upon Jyeṣṭhā.
Varuṇa, Sūrya, the Apsaras Rambhā, and the Rākṣasa Citrasvana;
Śukra, the Nāga Sahajanya, the Yakṣa Vasiṣṭhaka, and the Ṛṣi Hūhū—these Gandharvas preside over the month of Āṣāḍha. (52–53)
Indra, Sūrya, the Apsaras Pramlocā, the Rākṣasa Vaya, the Nāga Elāpatra, the Yakṣa Śrotra, the Ṛṣi Aṅgiras,
and the Gandharva Viśvāvasu— these are the ones who preside over the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Vivasvān is the Sun, Anumlocā is the Apsaras, and Vyāghra is the Rākṣasa.
Śaṅkhapāla is the Nāga, Āsāraṇa is the Yakṣa, and Bhṛgu is the Ṛṣi. Ugrasena is the Gandharva; these are the ones who preside over the month of Bhādrapada.
Pūṣan, Sūrya, the Apsaras Ghṛtācī, Vāta as the Rākṣasa,
the Nāga Dhanañjaya, the Yakṣa Suruci, the Ṛṣi Gautama,
and the Gandharva Suṣeṇa— these are the ones who preside over the month of Māgha.
Parjanya, Arka, the Apsaras Senajitī, Varcas the Rākṣasa,
Airāvata the Nāga, Ṛtu the Yakṣa, Bhāradvāja the Ṛṣi,
and Viśva the Gandharva— these indeed follow after Phālguna. (58–59)
Aṃśu, Sūrya, the Apsaras Urvaśī, the Rākṣasa Vidyutchatru,
the Nāga Mahāśaṅkha, Tārkṣya, the Yakṣa Kaśyapa, and the Ṛṣi Ṛtusunā—
these are the ones who preside over the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Bhaga, Sūrya, Pūrvacitti, the Apsaras, Sphūrja,
the Rākṣasa, the Nāga Karkoṭaka, the Yakṣa Ūrṇa, the Ṛṣi Āyus,
and the Gandharva Ariṣṭanemi— these attend upon him in the month of Pauṣa.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Sūrya, the Apsaras Tilottamā, Brahmā, the Rakṣas Apeta, the Nāga Kambala, the Yakṣa Śatajit, and the sage Jamadagni— these,
along with the Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra, abide in the two Aśvinī constellations.
Viṣṇu, Sūrya, the Apsaras Rambhā, and the Rākṣasa Makha-peta;
the Nāga Aśvatara, the Yakṣa Satyajit, and the sage Viśvāmitra;
and the Gandharva Sūryavarcas—these preside over the month of Kārttika.
For these groups, numbering twelve and seven, are indeed proud of their stations;
they are distinct solar splendors that bring about ripenings.
And the Apsarases and Gandharvas truly perform dance and song.
The yakṣas known as Vidyāgrāmaṇīs yoke the chariot;
the serpents, having become its ropes, indeed proceed to fasten the chariot.
The rākṣasas, traveling behind, certainly urge the chariot forward.
The sages, such as the Vālakhilyas and others, praise the Lord, the charioteer, with Vedic mantras; they indeed lead him toward his setting.
This occurs according to the prowess and the austerity of these very gods.
According to what is appropriate, according to dharma, according to reality, and according to his power,
so does that Sun shine; indeed, having attained success through his splendor,
he dispels all the inauspiciousness of living beings by means of his own radiance.
By these auspicious acts of men, evil indeed is carried away;
by my command, evil is dispelled for those who practice virtuous conduct.
They perform austerities, they recite prayers, and they truly gladden all living beings.
For beings protect one another out of compassion;
therefore, O Lakṣmī, the suns remembered [by them] protect from the passage of time, and the Apsarases protect from the delusions of intoxication. || 73-74 ||
At night, the *rākṣasas* protect [the practitioner] from the hosts of demons and from evil times;
when worshipped, the *nāgas* then protect him from the poisons of serpents and the like.
The *yakṣas* always protect him from the dwellings of *yakṣas* and other such subterranean openings.
The sages, being honored, protect [the world] through austerity and mantras.
The Gandharvas, being honored, protect the worlds and bestow prosperity.
Thus, all are composed of time and are joined with their respective times.

When worshipped and saluted, they, being pleased, protect you. Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare the excellent Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, by the recitation of which death is overcome for those who are born. (78)
"I am Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Supreme Lord; my body is Mahākāla, who is my Śakti. His daughter is indeed Mṛtyu.
That Mṛtyu was created by me as the daughter of my own sovereignty. (3.142.80)
"I am the Lord Kālajit; I am Mādhava, the conqueror of death.
One should constantly recite my name, bowing while saying, 'Mṛtyuñjaya' (Conqueror of Death).
One should recite day and night: 'Oṃ namo mṛtyuñjayāya svāhā'."
By that, death itself turns away from him; of this there is no doubt.
(82) Bad dreams perish, as do evil omens of enemies.
Malevolent planets are averted, and even misfortune dissolves away. (83)
Great fear dissolves and the senses indeed go to their dissolution;
calamities perish—both those caused by fate and those arising from material elements. Internal diseases, mental anxieties, and all limiting conditions are destroyed.
Sudden misfortunes dissolve and melt away where I am;
there is not even the slightest suffering there, much less any great. O Lakṣmī, when I am constantly remembered and worshipped, I dwell there.
In that heart there is indeed eternal bliss with Me;
for among devotees, wherever there is Śrī, there is joy.
Both I and you—the Imperishable Brahman—dwell in the hearts of those who are liberated.
Indeed, in that place, even Time, Death, and sins become purifiers;
they arise as givers of happiness and become true blessings.
However, for one who is devoid of devotion in this world, there is suffering arising from the planets and other such influences.
Arising from serpents and the like, as well as arising from suffering and poverty,
these wicked afflictions torment those who do not take refuge in me;
yet, O Rame, the afflictions flee swiftly from those who have taken refuge in me.
The messengers of Yama flee, as do the omens of death.
One who has devotion as their armor should unite the self with the Self;
having become the inner self, one should remain established in identity with It.
For me, who has attained identity with that [Reality], there exists not even a trace of time through action, mind, speech, body, or the stream of the senses.
There is no scent of *māyā* for him; how, then, could there be any scent of death?
This one rejoices at my side; he is my own portion and has attained the state of being "mine.
Just as Śrī rejoices in the world, and as Ramā and Lakṣmī rejoice, just as Ananta rejoices and Garuḍa also rejoices.
Sanatkumāra always rejoices as does Śaṅkara;
as Viṣṇu rejoices, so too Nārāyaṇa exults.
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa also rejoice.
In that way, the devotee who is freed from the noose of time rejoices.
That woman who performs the recitation of my name becomes like Māṇikyā;
O Lotus-born One, the glory of Māṇikyā is eternally of the nature of my own abiding presence.
Wherever I am, there indeed all sovereign powers belong to me;
there, in that place, time, māyā, and the like do not exist, nor does karma or suffering.
"Oṃ, salutations again and again to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."

"O Lakṣmī, for one who recites thus, sin shall never touch them. (3.142.100) Thus has the power of my mantra been declared; it cannot be overcome by force, for it is difficult to surpass. The power of my name exists as superior to all other powers. (101)
O beloved, the power of my form is always superior to all other powers;
indeed, my own power is also greater than all powers.
Taking hold of that, one may conquer Time, Māyā, and sinful karma.
Having conquered all poisons— both the poison of saṃsāra and the enemies that are the objects of the senses—
and having drunk the nectar consisting of Me,
a mortal attains both worldly enjoyment and liberation; he becomes immortal in the Imperishable.
"By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this, one who has taken refuge in Me rejoices, having abandoned the fear of Time and Māyā.

(105) Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature and Power of Time and Death, and the Method for Conquering Them through the Recitation of Their Respective Mantras and the Worship of the Supreme Lord," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (142)

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, you have previously described various types of dharma for the Kṛta age, and others even different from those for the Tretā age. (1)
What are the people like in the Dvāpara age, where those who proceed with faith indeed attain dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa?
What is the nature of those who perform mantras, [recite] names, and practice devotion?
"Even those devoid of truth will attain liberation or go to heaven.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; let truth and dharma be the givers of liberation."
The dharmas of the Tretā age, by their very nature, bestow great sovereignty;
they grant the worlds of Īśvara—those of Bhauma, Vairāja, and Vaiṣṇava.
O Lakṣmī, the dharma of the Dvāpara age is inferior, being touched by impurity.
For the sake of destroying that [evil], I repeatedly assume the form of Kṛṣṇa during the Dvāpara age.
Indeed, through my yoga and by association with the virtuous, even sinners cross over [to liberation].
Listen to the duties of the Dvāpara age, which have declined from what they were previously.
In that [age], those whose primary quality is devotion indeed cross over, and not other people.
All the accomplishments of the Tretā age perish in the Dvāpara age;
there is greed, a lack of fortitude, trade accompanied by deceit, and hypocrisy.
Furthermore, the non-ascertainment of reality and the destruction of the castes [occur];
however, for all actions associated with their respective agents, there is the opposite:
travel, slaughter, supreme punishment, pride, arrogance, power, and injury. (9)
In the Dvāpara age, there is further lack of forbearance, passion, and darkness;
even the stages of life (*āśrama*) that serve the purposes of dharma become confused as the bull [of dharma] declines.
There is disagreement regarding the revealed scriptures (*śruti*) and the treatises (*śāstra*), and people find their purpose in excessive reasoning.
Doubt arises because of that, and certainty is not attained;
through the persistence of an unresolved matter, even the true nature of dharma perishes. Dharma established through disagreement becomes confused and comes to grief.
Then the Veda is divided into four parts by Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa. Furthermore, the Vedas are subdivided by the sons of the sages due to variations in their perspectives;
new Saṃhitās also come into being through the great seers.
In the Dvāpara ages, they proceed with their own philosophical systems having divergent meanings.
Thus, the ritual of the Adhvaryu priest proceeds through various methods,
as well as through options, omissions, secondary and primary alternatives, and principal variations.
In various places, [the Dharma] proceeds with differing qualities.
(16) Thus, faith, trust, retention, contemplation, and veneration perish through the passage of time, and even truth itself perishes. (17)
In this [Dvāpara age], the state of being governed and stability vanish;
deceitful conduct perishes, while hypocrisy, untruth, and the act of deceiving others increase.
Thus, in the Dvāpara age, there arises the false view born of perversion.
Death, various kinds of obstacles, and calamities arise again and again;
afflictions, diseases, and anxieties that emerge unexpectedly, as well as attachments to sense objects, occur more frequently in the Dvāpara age. (3.143.20)
Then, in the Dvāpara age, trees, shrubs, and medicinal herbs, as well as their own offspring, would forcibly produce [their fruit] according to their strength;
but upon seeing this, the medicinal herbs entered into the earth.
In the Dvāpara age, [crops] indeed sprout from what has been ploughed;
beyond that, however, in the middle of the Dvāpara, the various groups of herbs do not sprout.
At that time, agriculture by means of seed occurs everywhere even without [previously sown] seed.

Then they plant in the earth the seed, the root, the branch, the bulb, the stalk, the tube, the fruit, the leaf, the cluster, the knot, or its sprout, as well as the matted roots, the bark, and the stem. (24)
In the Dvāpara age, plants of that lineage are born from that [earth];
at that time, the livelihood of all people becomes dependent upon them, and subsequently, in the Dvāpara age, the various commercial dealings involving those plants arise. (25–26)
Otherwise, their very livelihood would cease at the end of the Tretā Yuga. At that time, they will resort to the occupations of trade, agriculture, and commerce;
moreover, water will arise from the hands [of men] due to the digging of the earth.
Then wells and oblong ponds also appear everywhere on all sides.
At that time, powerful lords are born who possess rightful ownership,
while those who are weak become destitute and deprived of their property.
The powerful ones plunder the livelihoods derived from trees, creepers, and so forth—
women, fields, daughters, sons, wealth, and cows.
For the sake of establishing the boundaries of social order, Brahmā created the mighty Kṣatriya class.
To protect the subjects from harm, he establishes a king upon his head;
at that time, he makes the system of castes and stages of life secure and free from fear.
Yet, even then, drought, death, and disease prevail on all sides.
Just as the creation of dharma exists, so too does the creation of adharma;
indeed, in the Dvāpara age, they proceed with equal measure among human beings.
Up until the end of the Dvāpara, the dharmas of the Tretā age persist here and there.
Even those [virtues] exist no longer; they perish when the second half of the Dvāpara age has passed.
Truth is accompanied by falsehood, non-stealing is mixed with theft, non-violence is mingled with violence, and virtuous conduct is joined with immorality.
Possession is joined with greed; policy is touched by injustice; purity is touched by impurity; contentment is accompanied by craving;
austerity is mixed with praise; and self-study is motivated by the desire for wealth.
Meditation on the Lord serves to destroy suffering; devotion seeks one's own welfare.
Children, wives, and so forth serve half for one's own sake and half for the sake of the bull (the husband).
Likewise, servants are of such a nature that they serve half for their own sake and half for the sake of others.
Even kings arise who pursue half their own interest and half the interest of others;
likewise, even sages become devoted to asceticism for half their own sake. In the Dvāpara age, social relations also come to be half based on blood ties.
Religious duties and sacrifices are performed for the sake of achieving one's own goals.
Half of the food to be eaten is obtained from rain, and half from the water of wells.
Indeed, in the latter part of the Dvāpara age, a fixed lifespan no longer exists.
Since even while an elder lives, sons and others may die,
trees bear fruit only during the latter half [of their life], and likewise creepers and women; so too,
men become possessed of only half their strength during the age of Dvāpara.
People conduct their mutual dealings with only half-hearted trust;
yet, when an auspicious undertaking is begun, it certainly bears fruit for that purpose.
Likewise, the currents of rivers consist of half-water, and the seasons yield half of their true fruits.
In some places, among people whose lifespan is half that of the Tretā age,
creation occurs through mere volition (saṃkalpa) in every location during the Satya Yuga.
Furthermore, in the Tretā age, the process of creation proceeds through visual perception.
At the end of the Tretā age, creation occurs through physical touch; in the Dvāpara age, it occurs even from sexual union.
When half of the Dvāpara age has passed, creation from sexual union becomes fruitless in some places.
Thus, indeed, all lineages come to be through the depositing of seeds.
Men of futile vigor, whose latent impressions (vāsanā) function only partially, who have formed attachments to objects only half-fully, proceed with only half-intense passion;
likewise, their offspring are only half-afflicted by disease and possess only half-strength. Thus it is said.
In the two preceding ages, [the lifespan] proceeds at half its length;
mantras yield only half their fruit, and gurus possess only half-enlightenment.
Indeed, charity, vows, compassion, and righteousness attain only half their true nature. (3.143.50)
In this Dvāpara age, disciples abide by only half of their instructions and consider themselves to possess only half of their master's stature;
likewise, young women maintain only half of wifely devotion.
Indeed, in this age, the entire household accomplishes only half of its intended purpose.
The hermitages possessed only half of their sages, and the social classes possessed only half of their own renown.
The gods bestowed only half of their fruits, and their lords provided only half of their protection.
In battles, there was only half-victory, and the warriors were only half-capable of conquering through truth.
The primary [virtues] and those that are half-subordinate manifest as half of the kingdom;
fortune indeed bears fruit as half, while the determination of truth sustains half.
Those who possess only half-essence are born with roots rich in full essence.
In the Dvāpara age, O Lakṣmī, oaths as well as the words of merchants are only half-true;
likewise, the trust placed in great men is established only on a partial basis. (55–56)
For from Satyaloka, the Siddhas go everywhere as far as half [the distance];
the Pitṛs likewise go as far as half;
and the gods also come to the earth by that same measure of half.
Likewise, those dwelling in the netherworlds (pātāla) and elsewhere remain only half-present;
in the Dvāpara age, O daughter, all beings there are entirely powerless.
Medicinal herbs possess only half their strength, and physicians are but half-examiners.

Astrologers are half-awake, physicians are half-treaters, and mechanical devices are half-mechanisms; indeed, they grant only half their intended results. They become broken in the middle and hang suspended in between.

Even when there is no firmness due to old age, their power of vision declines; they become diminished in their capacity for receiving, moving, and experiencing joy. Their powers of hearing and touch fade away, as do their abilities for tasting and smelling. (61–62)
In the Dvāpara age, beings arise with diminished strength and vitality;
the abodes of truth, the dwellings of the gods, the schools of the teachers,
and the righteous— for the most part— perish by half when half of the Dvāpara has passed upon the earth.
Sacrificial halls, festivals, temples, and virtuous people—
those jewels of truthful minds and those sacred fords that exist on earth—
half of them perish when half of the Dvāpara age has passed.
The destruction of half the purity and the destruction of half of what is touchable and untouchable;
the destruction of half the venerable and the non-venerable, and the destruction of half the worship of those worthy of worship;
the destruction of half the enjoyment of objects of enjoyment, and the destruction of half the drinking of what is to be drunk. (66)

When half of the Dvāpara age has passed on earth, there is the destruction of half of the object of meditation and the meditation itself; when half of the Kali age has passed, there is the destruction of half of the goals of human endeavor (puruṣārtha), the destruction of half of what was conceived, firmness results from the existence of only half [of one's resolve], and undertakings concern only half [of their original scope]. (67–68)
Intelligence yields half its potential through reflection; effort brings about half its fruit. Friends possess only half their true nature, and servitude proceeds with only half its intent.
Livestock have only half their trust, and birds offer only half their devotion.

When half of the Dvāpara age has passed, there will be only partial understanding of languages. When half of the Dvāpara age has passed on earth, things will consist of only half-attractiveness, beings will possess only half-attractive powers, and the sources of affection and so forth will be reduced to only half.
Restrained by royal punishments, the subjects abide according to the law;
even half of an action that is manifest is counted as such an action.
But that which is concealed is not counted at all as half by people of the Dvāpara age.

In the Dvāpara age, fear of fate indeed prevails among living beings for half [the time], while fear of sin likewise prevails for the other half; yet that [fear] is not even reckoned in that age. Similarly, fear of malice and fear of falsehood prevail for half [the time], but they are not reckoned [as significant].
In the Dvāpara age, O Lotus-born One, fear of evil deeds does not even enter the mind, nor is sin considered as such; thus, indeed, only half [of dharma] remains.
But in the subsequent period, the Tretā age, truth survives as a third part.
In the final two ages as well, three-quarters of the [virtues] such as truthfulness perish;

indeed, at the end of the Dvāpara age, embodied beings possess only a fourth part of their lifespan. At the beginning of the [Dvāpara], it was five hundred years, and in the middle of the Dvāpara, it was half of that.
O Rame, when one-third of that period has passed and one-fourth remains, the lifespan of all embodied beings undergoes a reduction by half. Indeed,
in the Satya Yuga, human beings are eight *tālas* in height.
In the Tretā age, those six-tāla trees were twice as high; in the Dvāpara age, they were four times as high.
In the latter half of Dvāpara, they were half that size, and then half again, until they were ten cubits tall.
The trees were four times higher than that, and the elephants were half the height of the trees.
Horses are half the size of elephants, while oxen and other such animals are not equal to them;
in the Dvāpara age they exist with their strength reduced by one-third. At the end of Dvāpara they become powerless, having lost four parts of their strength from the beginning.
Those who possess supernatural powers (*siddhimanta*) become tall and long;
then they become short, with small bodies and consequently little girth.
Their food consumption is ten measures, then five measures, and then half of that.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, it will then be one *māna* and half of that;
indeed, travel by day occurs [only] in the Satya Yuga, while [the sun] remains in the sky.
[This applies] throughout the fourteen worlds, on the earth, and even in other continents.
In the Tretā age, however, travel indeed depends upon celestial chariots (vimānas).
On that day, human beings travel a hundred yojanas;
in the Dvāpara age, it is half of that, and in the latter half of Dvāpara, it is half of that again.
At the end of the Dvāpara age it is half of that, and after that, half again;
thus, for those with short bodies, the sequence of the quarters becomes distorted.
Without breath-control (prāṇāyāma), they possess no power of movement through the sky.
They were supported by the earth, they dwelt upon the earth, they moved upon the earth, and they were devourers of the earth.
O Rame, at the end of the Dvāpara age, the subjects there were thus the children of the earth;
O Rame, at the end of the Dvāpara, people were filled with hunger, thirst, and extreme distress.
Abounding in wickedness, endowed with deceit, filled with selfishness and egoism,
and possessed of many impurities, they are born at the end of the Dvāpara age;
they are small-minded, lacking in fortitude, and likewise devoid of depth.
O Lakṣmī, at the end of the Dvāpara age, all human beings are born [deprived of virtue];

even women are bereft of prosperity and are destroyers of half the moral boundaries. Likewise, they are arrogant with pride, egoism, and the sense of ownership over their own half [of the husband]. || 91-92 ||
They indeed become slaves to the afflictions and likewise devoid of even a portion of the Dharma;
consequently, fortunes abandon them, splendors depart from their home,
prosperities vanish, and riches flee away.
And even the refined appear as mere semblances of prosperity, for they are indeed false prosperities.
In the Dvāpara age, refined people abandon half of their refinement;
at the end of Dvāpara, that state of refinement is destroyed by impurities.
And that Kāla who existed in the past, whose nature is half-kleśa, now proceeds;
the messengers of Kāla overwhelm men within their dwellings.
The fires, having gone to the left half, move clockwise.
At the end of the Dvāpara age, half of the substance offered for worship dissolves;
all that is one's own becomes twofold, while the supreme and most excellent is that which is for the sake of another.
Indeed, the Dvāpara state of the mind is that which is permeated by the consciousness of the other.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, human beings indeed resort to various kinds of dharmas;
their progeny perform half that which is sinful and half that which is meritorious.
Even while seeking wealth and pleasure, their progeny undergo decline.
There, one should recite my mantra known as the Gāyatrī continuously:
"Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, śrīghanaśyāmāya vidmahe | nīlakaṇṭhāya dhīmahi, tanno hariḥ pracodayāt. (1.143.10)
"Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, may we know the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa; may we meditate upon the beginningless Kṛṣṇa; may that Kṛṣṇa inspire us.
(1.02) "Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ, may we know the glorious Nārāyaṇa..."
"Let us meditate upon Vāsudeva; may that Viṣṇu inspire us. (1.03) One should mutter: "Oṃ, salutation to the Beloved of Śrī Brahma-priyā, Svāhā!
(1.04) Likewise, one should mutter: "Oṃ, salutation to the Beloved of Śrī Hari-priyā! (1.04)

One who performs six hundred thousand recitations of this mantra indeed crosses over the ocean of worldly existence. Therefore, in the Dvāpara age, one should recite this mantra for the sake of liberation:
"O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī!"
O Lord of Rādhā, Supreme Brahman, Lord of the Gopīs, Lord of Jayā;
O Lord of Lalitā’s Śrī, Lord of Prajñā, Lord of Padmāvatī;
O Lord of Sukhadā’s Śrī, Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Śrīmāṇikī! 106–107.
O Lord, sovereign of swans, garuḍas, elephants, and horses;
O Lord of the virtuous, Lord of chaste and faithful wives, Lord of all, All-pervading One!
O Blessed One, lotus-eyed one, deliver us from the ocean of worldly existence.
From the Dvāpara age of terrible form, indeed characterized by the final epoch—thus one should petition the Blessed One, the eternal Supreme Lord;
one should worship me, wear me [as a mark] upon the heart, and offer everything unto me. (3.143.110)
"O Rame, in this way men shall attain liberation at the end of the Dvāpara age through the recitation and hearing of my *Saṃhitā* as well.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Dharmas, Rituals, and Natures of the Dvāpara Age, and the Demonstration of Devotion to Mantras and Other Means for the Liberation of Men of That Kind," in the third section, the *Dvāparasantāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 144 [[Author: → Chapter 145
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: O Hari, are the duties of the ages eternal, or are they subject to change?
Do the virtues arising from one age not prevail in another age?
Śrī Puruṣottama said: "O Rame, the duties of the ages (yuga-dharmas) are eternal, for the age itself is indeed composed of dharma.
Nevertheless, those duties appropriate to other ages are overturned by powerful men."
Indeed, the impure qualities of the Kali age are overturned by those who uphold the Truth (Ṛtambhara);
likewise, the attributes of the physical body are overturned by powerful yogis.
The laws of time are overturned by virtuous women, such as Sādhvīkā and others.
The laws of defects are overturned by perfected beings and holy men;
(4) the laws of regions are overturned by capable and eminent teachers;
the laws of subjects are overturned by kings who rule with justice. (5)
The duties of ascetics are subverted by those who produce wonders; the duties of maidens are subverted by assemblies honored by the world;
and festivals and the like are subverted here by people with the speech of perfected beings.
The qualities of caste are transformed by those who know the conduct and the highest principles of the castes;
(7) the physical bases [of existence] are transformed by people who have renounced the body; and the mental faculties are transformed by people intent on attraction. (8)
Where truth exists in a person, there indeed are the qualities of the Satya-yuga;
where the quality of *sattva* joined with *rajas* prevails, there are the qualities of the Tretā-yuga;
and in the Dvāpara-yuga, *tamas* slightly joined with *rajas* prevails.

The qualities of the Kali age are indeed characterized by darkness (*tamas*), for therein darkness prevails. In the *sāttvika* [age], there are indeed the qualities of *sattva*; in the *tāmasa* [age], those joined with *kali* prevail.
When *sattva* and *rajas* are combined, it is *tretā*; when *rajas* and *tamas* are combined, it is *dvāpara*.
In the Kṛta-yuga, O Lakṣmī, Dharma indeed exists in its four quarters;
by means of that, the Blessed One—who bestows virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation—is attained.
For the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is Dharma itself; Kṛṣṇa is the worship and Kṛṣṇa is the libation.
The fire sacrifice, the twilight devotions, as well as meditation and concentration—all these are Hari.
(13) There are four feet of Dharma: truth, charity, austerity, and compassion.
I am Hari, the protector of Dharma; truth and the others are my feet. (14)
In the Tretā Yuga, Dharma stands on three feet, consisting of truth, charity, and compassion;
and in the Tretā as well, I delight in all things such as sacrifices and offerings.
In the Dvāpara [Yuga], it consists of two feet, namely charity and compassion, and I am that very essence.

In the Kali age, I am one-quarter [of my essence] as charity; I delight in being composed of charity. In the Satya age I am indeed white, in the Tretā age I possess a red color, in the Dvāpara I am tawny, and in the Kali I become black.
The qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* exist within the person (*puruṣa*). Impelled by the person, they also revolve within the selves.
But when *sattva* is predominant, as are the mind, intellect, and senses... [18]
Then one should know it to be the Kṛta Yuga, when there is delight in knowledge and austerity.
When embodied beings possess the power for optional rites and their fame, then it is indeed considered the Tretā Yuga; passion arises within the heart while outwardly it is diminished. (3.144.20)
When greed, discontent, pride, hypocrisy, and envy prevail,
as well as a delight in ritual acts performed for desire— that is the Dvāpara age, characterized by rajas and tamas.
When there is constant falsehood, sleep, violence, affliction, and lethargy—
Grief, delusion, fear, and wretchedness— these are then considered to be *tamas*,
O Lakṣmī, when the Dvāpara age has passed. People become harsh in speech, their dispositions are dominated by desire, and the lands are filled with various kinds of bandits.
At that time, religious practices will be filled with heresy, and kings will be devourers of their subjects;
the people will be satisfied only by the touch of genitals and bellies, while rulers will be motivated solely by wealth.
Students will be devoid of vows and impure, and householders will be destitute.
In the Kali age, ascetics will dwell in villages, renunciants will be greedy for wealth,
and holy men will have great appetites and great cravings;
then servants will abandon their masters, and ascetics will abandon their vows.
In the Kali age, Śūdras indeed accept gifts, while Vaiśyas are devoted solely to asceticism;
the people will be anxious and their offspring will resemble Piśācas.
They will consume food unjustly and be devoid of worship for the gods and guests.

In the Kali age, all men become devoted to women and are deprived of ancestral rites and water offerings. Women, though having many children, possess little fortune; they are intent on scratching their heads and utterly disregard commands. (28–29)
Likewise, those intent on their own self-interest, their senses agitated by sin, practice deceit, malice, and even the slaughter of ascetics.
In the Kali age, there will be negligence, disease, and constant fears of hunger.
There will be a terrible fear of drought and the upheaval of nations.
Greedy people will speak untruths, and sacrifices will be performed with improper rites by those of wicked conduct.
Furthermore, there will be social intermingling among all men across all castes.
In every way, their beds, seats, and food were scattered about;
here and there occurred the killing of embryos, the killing of heroes, and the killing of the virtuous.
Even while still young in life, the members of the family died out of order.
They will possess little luster and strength, be mostly untruthful, and unrighteous (34).
Kings will abide by the conduct of thieves, and monarchs will act according to their own lusts.
Wives faithful to a single husband will no longer remain; instead, those who practice malevolent magic will increase (35).
Wearing saffron robes yet free from restraint, these men who bear the outward marks of divinity act for their own livelihood;
having offered away the food and provisions of others, they accomplish their own selfish ends.
Outcasts have become the rulers of kingdoms, and Brahmins are indeed their servants.
Brahmins, whose learning, fortune, strength, and vision have been exhausted, serve outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas).
O Rāma, in the Kali age, the Vedas, Śāstras, Āgamas, and Dharmas become obstacles;
they are indeed utterly destroyed here through the intermingling of dharma.
In the Kali age, there will be neither sacrifices nor marriages;
rather, the cause of domestic happiness will be the fulfillment of one's own desires.
Indeed, all people in the Kali age will declare the conduct of barbarians to be the most excellent.
Then the god sent down a rain of variegated colors, and the crops ripened in various hues.
All followed the profession of greedy merchants, seeking profit through deceitful sales;
there was no one who did not utter cruel speech, nor anyone who was upright or free from malice.
In this evil age, there is neither benefactor nor one who returns a favor;
the earth is devoid of kings and is not covered with grain or wealth.
In the Kali age, those who revile others and those who are fallen exist in every way.
In the Kali age, mandalas exist indeed in various regions and cities,
serving only the affairs of kings and destroying righteousness;
the earth possesses little water, yields little fruit, and is devoid of wealth.
There will be protectors who do not protect, plunderers who do not punish,
and those who seize the wealth of others, as well as the wives and children of others;
people who delight in violence, whose desires are wicked, and whose consciousness is utterly lost.
In the Kali age, friends are sweet in speech but malicious at heart;
thieves steal the property of other thieves, and in the Kali age, there is yet another who steals from the thief.
Indeed, in the Kali age, insects, mice, and snakes even attack those [thieves].
In the Kali age, there will indeed be many paths and traditions;
they will be enjoyers of dharma in secret while displaying outward conduct,
consuming the wealth, food, and enjoyments of gods, holy men, ascetics, yogis, and virtuous women.
Satiated by hunger, men indeed cultivate the path of evil.
(49) In the Kṛta age, dharma lasts for a hundred years; in the Tretā, it lasts for a year;
in the Dvāpara, it lasts for a month; and in the Kali age, it lasts for only a single day. (50)
In the Kali age, people indeed abandon even that daily religious duty (*āhnika-dharma*);
they are distracted, wandering aimlessly, and afflicted by fear of one another.
Protecting only their own lives, they are merciless and deeply distressed.
In the Kali age, people will be devoid of moral boundaries, lacking in self-restraint, without affection, and shameless; they will be devoid of effort, eaters of meat,
dwell on the shores of the ocean, and subsist entirely on fish.
At that time, men were homeless, clothed in bark, and slept upon the ground.
Men, animals, gods, birds,
and aquatic creatures were for the most part equal in their conduct, living together in a state of social intermixture during the Kali age.
I, Nārāyaṇa, impel my own dependents there—
my divine-bodied attendants who appear in the form of sages and ascetics. Indeed,
for the sake of establishing righteousness, they dwell there beyond the reach of ordinary perception.

On the mountains, couples of virtuous conduct who subsist on wild roots and fruits are born; from them arise beings composed of dharma, capable of all sovereign powers and endowed with devotion to the Vedas. (57)
By my incarnations, many wicked races are slain;
those dwelling on the shores of the ocean perish through excessive winds, excessive rains, and other calamities.
Consequently, the sages of the forests, who are my sons and attendants, [perish]. (58–59)
The descendants of Kārtavīrya continue to exist on earth, perpetuating their lineage.
Thus, there is the continuation of the Kṛta age and likewise the destruction of the Kali age.
Endowed with the fitness of the Kṛta age, the Ṛṣis who were his attendants are born.
Possessing divine bodies capable of enjoyment, they were steadfast in their vows;
all were yogis endowed with dispassion and likewise devoted to the realization of the Self.
They were contented, established in austerity, most righteous, and characterized by devotion.
Then the Seven Sages, having come from heaven, dwell among them;
and the Seven Sages truly proclaim the Dharma here among them.
Those perfected ones who remain in the Kali age move about unseen.
They indeed come into the light and become those very teachers;
as gurus worthy of protecting the world, they move among the subjects and even bestow sovereignty upon those born of a noble lineage fit for the Veda.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the Kṛta Yuga begins once again there;
you, who had reached a state of decline in the Kali age, flourish once more in the Satya age.
O Lakṣmī, you attain purity through association with virtuous men and virtuous women.
The Āsurī, the Yātudhānī, the Paiśācī, the Yakṣarākṣasī,
and the Tiṣyā— you are indeed Satyarūpā, the divine Lakṣmī who is born.
At that time, in the Kṛta age, couples were for the most part devoted to the duties of the household.
And those ascetics who are equal to [true] ascetics are devoted to celibacy;
they are free from desire and utterly devoid of longing, sporting in the bliss of the Self.
Through the mere yoga of mental resolve, they are joined with the mere sight of women.
Furthermore, their progeny, as well as sons, grandsons, and so forth,
become virtuous men and women when the Kṛta age has arrived.
Gods, asuras, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas [all become virtuous].
For by the power of the Satya Yuga, they are born as observers of dharma and vows;
they are born again as before, equal in circumference and height.
[They are likewise equal] in strength, yoga, sovereignty, prosperity, and meditative absorptions.
Those who have gone to the sky or to the waters are born again as before;
likewise, in clouds, in blossoms, and among material beings, they are produced just as in the past,
arising from my creative will.
The beasts and birds, as well as the cows and wish-fulfilling cows;
the trees and wish-granting trees, the creepers and wish-granting creepers;
the humans with divine bodies and the women who are celestial maidens.
When it is performed in this manner, the results arise just as they were when performed by those of old.
However, O Lakṣmī, from the muhūrta called Brāhma until the end of the morning [period], there is the Prātaḥkāla; after that comes the Saṅgava, and likewise the Madhyāhnaka.
Then the period of half of the latter half is evening, which possesses diminished strength;
thus all the ages (yugas) are established, each being progressively weaker than the one preceding it,
possessing ever slightly less strength and being ever slightly more afflicted by decline.
Consequently, they are characterized by a progressive decline and are not equal in every respect.
Indeed, compared to the Satya-yuga existing at the beginning of creation, the subsequent Satya-yugas possess less strength; they are certainly not equal to that primordial Satya.
My yogic power is complete; wherever it is present, [beings] are like the primordial age (Kṛtayuga). When manifested in an individual with power inferior to mine, the Yuga is made inferior.
Know it thus: without me, the world is powerless.
Wherever I am, O Lakṣmī, there is goodness everywhere—even in the state of a householder. Wherever I am not, O Lakṣmī, there is no goodness, even if it possesses the marks of virtue.
In whichever age, O Lakṣmī, by whomsoever I have been acquired, [therein lies true merit].
By him the Kṛta Yuga has been won; by him all that is dear has been won.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now describe the virtuous ones, and then indeed the holy ones (sādhus).
For they have united with Brahman within; therefore, the virtuous call them such.
Those who manifest the peaceful Supreme Self within all living beings are the virtuous;
such saints accomplish their own goal, which is liberation, and they also bring about the work of liberation for others. (85–86)
O Lakṣmī, one is called a *sādhaka* (practitioner) by virtue of accomplishing divine deeds;
O Lakṣmī, he alone is a *brahmacārī* (celibate student) who conducts himself within Brahman.
He is beneficial to his guru, acts for his own welfare, and is always devoted to truth and what is wholesome.
The celibate student is indeed virtuous, and the benefactor is the most excellent of the virtuous. Because of his purpose and his practice, the householder is called virtuous;
for in the Satya Yuga, those householders were indeed virtuous, equal to the truly virtuous.
Those virtuous ascetics in the forest are indeed Vaikhanasas;
and striving ascetics are virtuous through the practice of yoga. Dharma is declared to be the means to higher states and the bestower of well-being upon those who act rightly.
The bull [of Dharma] was created by the seer Nārāyaṇa and by Brahmā.
Marriage, the *agnihotra* sacrifice, worship, and so forth, according to the divisions of caste and stage of life, as practiced by the virtuous— that is called his *ācāra* (conduct of the refined).
My remaining attendants, sons, disciples, and great sages likewise remain here for the sake of dharma, continuing the lineage of the world;
they are practiced again and again by the disciplined ones of former and even more ancient times.
And because it has been so considered by each successive generation of the ancients, that conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is eternal.
Giving, truthfulness, austerity, devotion, learning, sacrifice, worship, and self-restraint—
these eight are the practices that are indeed recognized as the conduct of the learned.
Celibacy, austerity, silence, fasting,
service to one's parents, and likewise taking refuge in a guru—
this sixfold set constitutes the dharma of the virtuous; therefore, householders are virtuous.
Having reached the current of Māyā, he is neither carried away by it nor does he merely cross over;
for this virtuous man is indeed a true deliverer, even though he is a householder.
Abounding in the conduct of the refined, he is truly a bull among men (a leader), esteemed by the holy.
The renunciation of actions unto Me is true *saṃnyāsa*, the duty of the virtuous.

The hymn to Brahman, the hymn to the Ritual, and the hymn to the qualities of Hari—these are performed by me according to the ancient tradition by the cultured, the righteous, and the truly pious. (99)

Knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue— these four are innate (*sāṃsiddhika*) in those who are indeed virtuous sages (*ṛṣi*). Because they perceive (*ṛṣanti*) the supreme Brahman, they are considered *ṛṣis*.
Indeed, among the virtuous, the root *ṛṣ* in the sense of "going" is rightly established as meaningful.
Those who are the mind-born sons (*mānasa*) and the legitimate sons (*aurasa*) of the lords,
as well as the sons of the sages (*ṛṣiputra*), the *ṛṣīkas*, and those sages whose wealth is their austerity (*tapodhana*).
The sons of Brahmā are the Brāhmaṇas, the Kṣatriyas, and likewise the Vaiśyas;
the sons of the sages are the sages themselves, who are the cause of the continuation of the worlds.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the virtuous are indeed manifold in their adherence to truth and righteousness.
Moreover, even virtuous householders engage in truth;
by taking refuge in them, liberation and worldly enjoyment certainly arise.
[This occurs] through reading, hearing, remembering, and association with the virtuous.
The fruit, consisting of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
(106) In all the ages indeed, O Rame, there is one great quality: through the chanting of my name, Kṛṣṇa, liberation shall surely come to pass. (107)

In the Kṛta age, Hari is attained through sacrifice; in the Tretā age, He is won by chanting; in the Dvāpara age, Hari is reached through service; but in the Kali age, He is attained through glorification.
Though the Kali age is a treasury of defects, its virtue is the glorification of Hari.
The Dvāpara age, though half-defiled, is virtuous compared to my birth;
I was not born in such abundance during the Satya-yuga and others because all subjects were already perfected.
Yet, I am born again in the Kali-yuga in greater measure than in consideration of the other ages.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Analysis of the Transformation of the Duties of the Yugas," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 145 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 145
[The Author: Chapter 146.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
O Blessed One, tell me how your glorification (kīrtana) should be performed.
"By that very act of humble devotion, may you find clarity of mind.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"One should perform my kīrtana with a beautiful voice and a sweet inner resonance."
O Rame, may they praise me with savory food, with songs of the Tathāgatas, and with musical performances;
with rhythmic beats and measures, with dances, and with the tinkling of small bells and the like;
and with many passionate songs and so forth.
I shall explain the science of music (*gāndharva*) to you according to its true nature; listen attentively.
There are seven notes, three scales (*grāma*), twenty-one melodic modulations (*mūrcchanā*), and forty-nine micro-intervals (*tāna*);
this constitutes the circle of musical notes (*svaramaṇḍala*).
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama,
dhaivata, and niṣāda— these are proclaimed as the seven notes (svaras).
Sauvīra, madhyama, and hariṇa are indeed the three grāmas.
I shall now describe here those divine *mūrchanās* which produce a state of ecstatic absorption (*mūrchā*).
The first is proclaimed as Hayamedhā, indeed the Hreṣiṇī;
the second is proclaimed as Agniṣṭomā, the Āgneyī. (7)
The third is proclaimed as Vājapeyā, which is Śyenī.
The fourth is proclaimed as Rājasūyā, which is Rāṇikā.
The fifth is proclaimed as Yavarātā, which is Vaṃśinī.
That which is born of gold and is golden is proclaimed as the sixth *mūrcchanā*.
The seventh *mūrcchanā* is considered to be *gosavanā* and *rāmbhaṇī*.
That which is accompanied by whirlwind and rain is indeed considered the eighth *mūrcchanā*.
The ninth *mūrcchanā* is considered to be *garjinī*, belonging to Brahmā (*brahmadā*). The tenth *mūrcchanā* is considered to be *lālinī*, belonging to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā*).
The eleventh *mūrcchanā* is considered to be *kṣautī*, belonging to Dākṣāyaṇī (*dāgayākṣī*). (11–12)
Pānakrāntā, the bhaṣiṇī, is indeed the twelfth mūrcchanā;
mṛgākrāntā, the citkarī, is the thirteenth mūrcchanā;
and viṣṇukrāntā, the dhāriṇī, is the fourteenth mūrcchanā.
The fifteenth [day] is Santakokilikā and Unmādinī;
the sixteenth is Sūryakrāntā and Kālarohiṇikā;
and the seventeenth is Sarvatobhadrikā and Modamādinī.
Pūrvabhadrā, Bālakaṇṭhī, and indeed the eighteenth *mūrcchanā*;
Ālambuṣī, Hāṃsinī, and indeed the nineteenth *mūrcchanā*;
Sāgarā, Vijayā, Kokilikī, Viśā, and Manoharā.
The Nāradī and the Mānavī are the twenty-first mūrcchanās.
O beloved, there are also other secondary mūrcchanās;
there are many Mānavyas, Pākṣiṇyas, and Pākṣavyas as well. (17–18)
Śāradā knows all of them— Sarasvatī, Bhāratī, the Brāhmīs, the Gāṇyas, the Paryas, the Apsarases, those of the form of peacocks,
the Yākṣīs, the Kinnarīs, the Hāṃsyas, the Nāginīs, and the Vāḍavas. (19)
The *paitrya*, *daivya*, *kṣautya*, *tāḍinya*, and the various *bhauṃkinī* types;
the *mainākya*, *paikya*, *śaukya*, and the *kilāyikās*—
having understood these according to their respective characteristics, one should perform the song (*gīti*) as a singer (*gāyikā*).
Having understood the short, long, and protracted [vowels], one should employ the musical note (*svara*) in singing.
Then, one should repeatedly apply the *tānas* continuously during the flow [of the melody].
(22) The *tānas* are called *starās*; they are joined with moments during the flow.
Those which follow the expansion of the *sphoṭa* are differentiated according to their momentary distinctions.
The first is the *brahmatāna*, while the second is the *garbhatāna*. Furthermore, there are the *vyajya*, the *sañcaraṇa*, the *aṇu*, the *yoga*, and the *ārohaṇa*. 23–24.
Tanu, Puṣṭa, Viśāla, Vikāsa, Stanapa, Kumāra, Vāmana, Dvistara, and Vikṛta;
Dṛḍha, Dugdha, Kalāpa, Āvartaka, and Taraṅgaka. (25)
The depressed, the level, the elevated, the horizontal, and likewise the timid;
the measured, the pointed, the desired, and the heated—these constitute the thirty.
Furthermore, there are the horned, the arched, the pillar-like, the thief-like, and the merged. (26–27)
Udbhava, Aṅkuraka, Granthika, Śākhika, Bahumūla, Hasta, Vartula, Ucchraya,
Śṛṅga, Guru, Avaroha, Vega, Sthiti, and Ghaṭodara. ||28||
These *tānas* of yours have been declared; now hear likewise the secondary (*gauṇa*) *tānas*:
Skanda, Kāku, Puṣkala, Ropa, Santāraka, Taraṇi, Saṅgama, Ati, Vigama, Kṣepaṇa, and Mṛdha. (3.145.30)
Prokṣaṇa, Miśraṇa, Galika, Kartana, Ullekha,
and Raya are proclaimed as the sixteenth;
Uccara, Śaśavinyāsa, and Lakṣadhāra are the twentieth.
With liquor, with vehicles, moving downwards, and likewise moving upwards;
in the womb, transposition, reversal, and wandering about;
the bridge-construction and the support-construction—this is proclaimed as the thirtieth [chapter].
The mountain (aga), the sleeping, the swooning, the trembling, the leaping, the "itkṛta," the unmade, the withdrawn, the life-giving,
the bodiless (videhaka), the rescuer (uttāraka), and the palm-leaf-clad (tālavāsa)— these are considered the forty-two [mudrās].
The *piṇḍaka*, *kīrṇaka*, *yukta*, *bhaṅgī*, and that which is called *lahara*;
*samavāya* and *anuvāya*—thus are the *tānas* characterized by their qualities (*guṇas*).
Furthermore, there are others such as *tāra-tāra* and so forth, as well as *tāra-tama* and so forth. (35–36)
O Lakṣmī, those who lack a [pure] continuum, who utter cries of lamentation or joy, and whose dispositions are fragmented— having recognized them as such, one should thereafter proclaim them.
One should employ the appropriate places and efforts, following the various sequences of breath.
O Rame, one should proclaim those [manifestations] that follow the *hāva* and *bhāva* emotions, as well as those joined with bodily movements,
those joined with movements of the limbs, those engaged in the actions of the minor limbs (*pratyaṅga*),
and those impelled by the flash of inner knowledge and so forth. || 38-39 ||
These names differ in every kalpa and in every cycle of four yugas;
I know them all through their designations according to their true nature.
Long ago, the yogi Śrī Nārada approached me for the sake of singing [their praises].
I have heard everything from him, yet it was indeed incomplete.
Then, O Lakṣmī, he was instructed by me again and again for the sake of his training; he became your disciple and was taught by you for a long time.
O Lakṣmī, in your presence and within the assembly of the beloved wives of Brahmā, he sang before me with all his limbs and minor members perfectly complete; indeed,
he became the remover of the pride of ten million times a hundred billion women.
With a serene mind, I gazed upon the venerable sage Nārada;
thereafter, he was brought by me into the form of a singer. You know all of this, for you are indeed Nārāyaṇī.
Then Śāradā, the goddess of speech, having heard that song by Nārada, stood motionless for a moment; what then can be said of other women?
She, a connoisseur of aesthetic flavor, shook her head repeatedly.
All the Sarasvatīs became momentarily bewildered for a moment.
Indeed, there was much praise for the Guru’s Lakṣmī there.
I presented a worthy reward to Nārada on that occasion.
Likewise, the wish-fulfilling gem, the necklace, and my Sudarśana discus—
this divine Śakti, which distinguishes my sovereignty, was bestowed by me.
Then Śrī Nārada was born as an incarnation in the form of a partial manifestation (aṃśa-rūpaka).
Nārāyaṇa and Nārada indeed did not treat you with contempt out of compassion.
Furthermore, in the assembly, Nārada praised your compassion;
he extolled you in every way as the one by whom he was instructed in that knowledge.
From that time on, O lotus-born one, my wives and even the Apsarases repeatedly practiced the method of singing in your presence; thus, O beloved,
that art of music spread manifold throughout the world.
Śaṅkara, having become a Vaiṣṇava, learned a portion [of the art] from you;
thereafter, he performed a dance adorned with song.
Being pleased, I bestowed upon him the ornament of yoga.
"Remember, Lakṣmī, everything that was previously possessed by you.
Thus addressed, she remembered and beheld within herself a vast music hall extending for a thousand yojanas.
And in the divine abode at Śrīpura, he beheld himself within a palace of a thousand chambers;
there he saw himself assuming a thousand forms,
acting as a teacher who had ascended to the state of instruction, performing instrumental music and song.
There, the cowherd women, the female attendants, and those who are liberated;
the beloveds of Brahmā, as well as the consorts of the Īśas and the daughters of the Īśvaras—
these groups of Apsarases train while engaging in conversations with them.
The goddesses, the Siddhas, the Yoginīs, and the hosts of Śāradā;
the Gāyatrīs, the Sāvitrīs, the Brāhmīs, and the celestial maidens; the Gandharvīs, the Yakṣīs, the Kinnarīs, and the various classes of attendants. (3.145.59–60)
The sons of Kaśyapa were taught the purpose of bestowing wealth;
there, many Gandharvas born of the former creation were also instructed.
Furthermore, the daughters of the Daityas, the Dānavīs, and the daughters of the Asuras [were taught].
He also saw daughters of the Mānavyas and Ṛṣis who live until the end of the kalpa, being instructed in the music hall by their own female teachers;
he beheld all the daughters of the Nāgas as well, desiring instruction. (62–63)
Having thus suddenly beheld the divine schools herself, she was filled with great wonder; there she was honored by all the deities.
Standing in the place of honor for all of them, she remained there, having accomplished her purpose.
She did not consider herself worthy of excessive pride, yet she realized my greatness.
There, seeing me, her husband Kṛṣṇa—even as I was singing a song—she beheld her own Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (65–66)
Rising up, Lakṣmī fell at his feet and spoke:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O Kṛṣṇa, who are endowed with grace toward your own consort! O Hare, ocean of mercy, my beloved, great honor has been shown to me. (67)
O Janārdana, by your grace I behold all this:
in Śrīpura I am indeed a teacher who composes songs of music;
whatever women, men, Gandharvas, or celestial nymphs there are in the world—[I see them all]. 68–69.

Indeed, those who are Śāradās and Sarasvatīs are my disciples; all of them, by the millions, learn from me in the concert hall. From my own nature emerge the musical notes, the scales, and the melodic modulations.
They dissolve into Brahman alone, just as I abide within the heart.
All this exists within me, and there is a desire for song in me;
if there is the command, [there shall be] singing complete with all its primary and secondary limbs.

"O Supreme Lord, I wish to perform [this rite] together with all my friends. Thus addressed, I, the Lord of Śrī, spoke; O Kamalā, I then prepared an auspicious, very spacious pavilion and provided seats as well.
Having gathered musical instruments, I placed them in the auspicious pavilion.
Then all of you, Lakṣmī and the others— the beautiful beloveds of Brahmā—
arrived at that pavilion and took their respective seats as was fitting.
O Lakṣmī, they performed a musical concert, and I became pleased by that;
I granted them a boon again and again upon the earth:
"You shall perform excellent music, and you shall become my wives."
By this truth, O lotus, in the Aśvapaṭṭa lake, all those beloved of Brahmā as well as women beloved of Hari exist;
likewise, my own beloved ones reside in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā. || 77–78 ||
While this news was thus unfolding before the divine vision, everything then vanished;
only the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and his own golden temple were visible. (79)
Seeing her own friends and her beloved as they were situated in the temple,
Lakṣmī rejoiced and was struck with great wonder.
Filled with joy, she rose up toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Person.
Embracing the *saṃgītikā*, she performed it filled with joy;
then Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa Hari ceased [speaking].
Then Lakṣmī desired to drink water, and he gave her water.
Māṇikyāśrī prepared delicious food, as well as soup and rice;
Śrīhari-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa ate it, while Nārāyaṇī gave him water.
Padmāvatī gave him betel-leaf, and Prajñā gave him a garment.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa rested on a couch made of gold;
Lakṣmī and Padmāvatī massaged his feet,
while Prajñā and Māṇikī massaged his body.
And other beloved wives of Brahmā likewise served Hari as their husband in their respective homes; thus Hari attained rest. Then they all indeed accepted the food of his grace.
At midday, they drank water and attained supreme joy;
they obtained a fraction of their husband’s grace and performed their household duties.
Thus, O illustrious Queen of Śiva, I have related this ancient account to you.
Everything here concerning the practice of song, instrumental music, and so forth has been told.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reciting this, one shall obtain enjoyment and liberation, and become filled with all bliss. (3.145.89–90)

O Lakṣmī! Those beloved of Hari, as well as those beloved of Brahmā, who perform kīrtana while remembering me and you, will undoubtedly cross over [the ocean of worldly existence], even if they have cast off this illusory body through knowledge. (91)
Having separated the senses and made them divine anew,
having performed the internal divine meditation and burnt away latent impressions (vāsanā),
[one should listen to] my divine life-story accompanied by the chanting of the Praṇava. ||92-93||

Whosoever—whether a god, a Daitya, a Yakṣa, a Rākṣasa, or an Asura; or even a serpent, a beast, a bird, a Kinnara, or a Guhyaka—performs [this] by means of the self in the form of Brahman, [shall attain the supreme goal]. (94)
Having offered themselves into me, who am consciousness and bliss, and having established union with me,
those others who shall perform the chanting of my names, O Lakṣmī, they all— by virtue of their devotion to me alone— shall attain the supreme state.
O Lakṣmī, even a brief glorification performed through the remembrance of my form becomes divine; it bestows liberation and destroys sin.
Indeed, one should perform this glorification by becoming entirely one with me.
That indeed becomes fruitful, bestowing complete bliss.
For those possessed of intense fervor, my chanting yields intense fruit.
O Lakṣmī, I dance at that time when the female singers dance.
I sing together with the Gandharvas, yet those who bear shields do not see me;
I increase the joy of my devotees and I acquire it for them. Having increased their affection, I lead them at last to the imperishable state.
"They come to me by force and do not leave me, O Giver of Desires.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Melodic Scales, Grāmas, and Mūrchanās in Saṅkīrtana, and Lakṣmī’s Vision of the Divine Music Hall," etc., in the Third Section on the Dvāpara Age of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
