Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, you who are devoted to me, my singer;
as I chant my own names, a divine state arises within me here. (1)
O Lakṣmī, where there is singing of Me, worship of Me, and chanting of My glories,
no great calamities ever arise there at any time.
Indeed, for those devoid of devotion to Me, great calamities certainly do occur.
Peace must be established for them; otherwise, human beings will perish.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
When great portents have arisen, what peace can be found for them?
"For the benefit of all embodied beings, tell me of such peace.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Listen, Lakṣmī, to the great portents arising from the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth."
I shall describe in truth the pacification for those beings who are born therein.

O Lotus-born One, gentle pacification is prescribed for celestial portents, while fearlessness is for those in the intermediate space; and the Vaiṣṇava pacification is desired for terrestrial calamities.
One who desires victory over an enemy, one who seeks prosperity, one who has been subjected to malevolent magic by others, and one who wishes for the destruction of an enemy—
such a person should practice the peace rite of *Abhayā* for the sake of eliminating great fear.
One should also have the highest propitiatory rite (śānti) performed by virtuous Brahmins.
One who is afflicted by consumption (rājayakṣman), one emaciated by wounds, or one suffering from severe illness,
yet desiring to perform sacrifices or seeking dharma, should cause a gentle propitiatory rite to be performed.
In the event of an earthquake, the destruction of food supplies, famine, excessive rainfall,
the arising of fear from locusts and the like, or danger born of heedless thieves—
a devotee of Viṣṇu should perform the Vaiṣṇava rite of pacification (śānti) therein.
When the killing of animals has occurred, or even the killing of human beings,
one should perform a fierce propitiatory rite for the terrible death of embodied beings;
one should also carry out sacrifices, oblations, and the worship of Rudra and the other deities.
When there is a decline of the Vedas, a destruction of the scriptures, among people who have become nihilists,
and when the unworthy are being worshipped, one should perform the Brahma-śānti rite.
One should cause the worship of Parameṣṭhin and other rites to be performed by those who are knowers of the Vedas.
It shall be effective during consecration, as well as in times of fear from an enemy army;

one should perform the Raudrī-śānti rite in cases of internal dissension within one's own kingdom or for the destruction of enemies. [This applies] when the wind has persisted for more than three days, or during a most violent storm.
When food is censured by all, when there is a disorder born of wind, or when fear arises,
or when a disease born of wind has occurred, one should perform the pacification of Vāyu.
When the fear of drought has arisen, or even the fear of excessive rain, [one should likewise act].
When abnormal rain has occurred, when a body of water has become corrupted,
or when there is danger arising from water, one should perform the Vāruṇī propitiatory rite (śānti).
When fear of a curse arises, or even fear of a curse uttered through mantras, [one should likewise act].
When the fear of a false curse has arisen, one should perform the *bhārgavī* pacification (*śānti*).
When there occurs a deformity at birth, a disease of the fetus, or miscarriage;
and when the birth is stillborn, O Rame, one should perform the *prājāpatī* pacification.
In the event of damage to household utensils, as well as to houses,
one should perform the *Tvaṣṭṛ-śānti* (the propitiatory rite for Tvaṣṭṛ) for carts and vehicles;
likewise, in the case of deformities or even fear concerning boys and girls.
In the event of destruction or failure to thrive, one should perform the Kaumārī Śānti;
in the event of fear of forest fires or fear of fire, one should perform the Āgneyī Śānti.
Furthermore, when a violation of commands occurs or when there is loss among servants and the like, [one should perform the appropriate rite].
When a disorder of horses and other animals arises in the form of disease,
and when there is a disorder such as a singing defect (gītikā) or a falling out of the throat and so forth,
and in cases of throat diseases, wounds, and the like, one should perform the Gāndharva-śānti rite.
One should perform the Āṅgirasī rite of pacification even when there is an affliction caused by elephants;
likewise, when fear of Piśācas and the like arises, or when there is the manifestation of Bhūtas, Pretas, and so forth,
or when suffering is caused by Ḍākinīs and others, one should perform the Nairṛtī rite of pacification.
When the fear of untimely death has arisen, or when a bad dream is observed;

or when such suffering as that of hell, or by Yama and others, has been encountered; or when one has fallen into an evil rebirth or the abode of Yama—one should cause the rite for peace from Yama to be performed. (26–27)
In the event of the loss of wealth, the loss of property, the loss of ornaments, gems, and the like,
or indeed the destruction of prosperity, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti) dedicated to Kubera.
Likewise, [one should perform it] in the case of the loss of trees, crops, bulbs, and fruit-bearing plants.
In the event of abnormalities regarding the fruits of creepers, grains, and roots,

or upon the destruction of wealth and sources of prosperity, one should cause a terrestrial pacification (pārthivī śānti) to be performed by those learned in the Vedas who are well-versed in the rites of propitiation.
During the first watch of the day or at night when there is a great calamity;
under the asterisms of Hasta, Svāti, Citrā, Āditya, and likewise Aśvinī;
or when born under Aryaman, as well as during other such afflictions.
Even when portents have occurred, one should perform the Vāyavya propitiatory rite (32).
During the second watch of the day, or at night during a calamity,
under the asterisms of Puṣya, Āgrahāyaṇī, Viśākhā, Maghā, and Bharaṇī (33).
Likewise, in the event of portents or misfortune, one should perform the Āgneyī propitiatory rite;
during the third watch of the day or at night when there is an affliction,
[one should act] under Rohiṇī, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, Vāsava, or Vaiśvadevata.
Likewise, during Jyeṣṭhā and Maitrī, and in all types of calamities,
one should have the Aindrī Śānti performed by Brahmins who are experts in the mantras.
This should be done at the fourth division of the day or during the night when a disaster occurs.
One should perform the Varuṇa-śānti rite during the asterisms of Āśleṣā, Revatī, Ārdrā, the fierce Ahirbudhnya, Mūla, and the one presided over by Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj),
when a calamity arises during the periods of the Mitra-maṇḍala.
In the midst of wonders and marvels, one should perform the two kinds of *śānti*.
*Śānti* is indeed armor; it protects one from calamities and the like.
For *Śānti* is considered the wife of Dharma and the daughter of Dakṣa. (38–39)
Endowed with righteousness by me and joined with my power,
she is the very embodiment of my strength and has been infused with my own might.
Nourished by the powers of various deities, she now removes all calamities.
Calamities flee away through rites known as *śānti*.
The deities inevitably become displeased due to the misconduct of people;
and from the displeasure of the deities, indeed, portents arise.
It is known as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial; among these, the one that bestows peace is the pacification of those [disturbances].
A celestial affliction is proclaimed to be an anomaly of the planets and constellations, such as the falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and likewise halos around the sun or moon.
There was also a city of Gandharvas, as well as distorted rain;
rain of blood, the heat of poison, and atmospheric portents;
and terrestrial disturbances affecting both moving and stationary beings, as well as earthquakes born from the earth.
An abnormality in reservoirs of water is also a terrestrial portent;
however, when it occurs on the earth, its fruit is known to be small, and it ripens only after a long time.
A cloud-born portent yields middling results and grants its fruit during the middle period.
But if, when a portent has arisen, the rain should become auspicious,
the portent should be known as fruitless within seven days. However,
the cessation of portents does not occur except through their destruction.
For three years, there shall be a wondrous and most great cause for fear,
affecting the body of the king, the world, the city gate, or the royal priest; likewise,
it will ripen upon his sons, as well as his treasury and his mounts.
For extraordinary portents arise from the very nature of the seasons. (50) When pacified by rites of propitiation, they become bringers of auspiciousness;
however, according to the specific divisions of time and month, they remain auspicious even without such pacification. (51)
Thunderbolts, earthquakes, the crashing sounds of falling bones, halos around the sun, dust, smoke, and blood-red sunsets and sunrises;
the premature budding of trees, excessive moisture, and trees bearing fruit out of season—[these are the omens]. (52)
The increase of cows, birds, and honey is auspicious during the months of Phālguna and Caitra.
[However, these are unfavorable] if the sky is defiled by comets, meteors, and falling stars, or if the orbs of the sun and moon appear tawny, black, white, yellow, grey, or dark red. (53–54)
Blood-red, crimson like a twilight sky, resembling a turbulent ocean,
and the drying up of the waters of rivers— these are auspicious in the summer.
So too are a rainbow, a halo, lightning, and the appearance of meteors.
Trembling, upheaval, and deformity of the earth, as well as fierce laughter from the ground;
the shaking, crossing, and floating of rivers, wells, and lakes—these are indeed auspicious during the rainy season for horned animals and wild boars. (56–57)
Cold winds and frost, the crying of beasts and birds, the sight of *rakṣasas*, spirits, and *piśācas*, and the speech of non-human beings;
the quarters of the sky shrouded in the darkness of smoke, along with the clouds, forests, and mountains. (58)
If the rising and setting of the sun occur at a high altitude during the winter season, they bring about auspicious results.
There is the sight of divine women, forms, Gandharvas, and wondrous celestial chariots (vimānas),
as well as the vision of planets, lunar mansions, and stars, and the hearing of superhuman speech.
The sound of singing and musical instruments on the forested mountain ridges,
the growth of crops, and the emergence of flavors during the autumn bring about auspiciousness;
whereas the falling of snow, the rising of violent winds, and the sight of deformed or wondrous portents [indicate otherwise].
The sky appears like black collyrium, yet it is tinged with a reddish-brown hue by falling stars and meteors.

The birth of variegated offspring among women, cattle, goats, horses, deer, and birds, as well as the budding of leaves and the growth of sprouts on creepers, are auspicious signs during the winter season.
The images of the deities dance, tremble, and blaze;
they emit fire, smoke, oil, blood, and fat. They move about, weep, perspire, and even laugh. (64)
They rise up, sit down, run about, and blow [their trumpets];
they brandish, eat, or handle their quivers, weapons, and banners;
they indeed turn face downward and wander from place to place. (65–66)

For such portents as these are seen arising suddenly in the temples, sanctuaries, and fortifications; one should not take up residence there. Or if the queen meets with misfortune, that country perishes.
If one observes portents during divine processions, one should declare fear for the country.
One should not find pleasure in dwelling there in the palaces of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
For cattle, there will be suffering born of Rudra; for kings, suffering born of the World-Guardians (Lokapālas).
The suffering of army commanders arises from Skanda, Viśākha, and others; that of the people arises from Viṣṇu, Vāsava, Indra, and Viśvakarman; and that of leaders and rulers arises from Vināyaka.
For those sent by the gods, those sent by kings, for goddesses, and for royal women,
suffering arises from Vāsudeva or from the planets, and not otherwise.
Regarding sufferings that have befallen deities, the domestic priest is the knower of the Vedas.

One should bathe the image of the deity, clothe it, and adorn it; one should worship it with the excellence of perfumes, garlands, food, honey-mixture (madhuparka), and other offerings. One should perform ritual attendance according to the rules and offer oblations for seven nights.
Then, one should always feed virtuous Brahmins in the sacred fire;
one should honor the virtuous men and women with delicious foods and desired drinks, along with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
When the eighth day arrives, one should perform the gift of a cow, land, and jewels.
One should give gifts of gold and complete the pacification of the planets;
by having the recitation of peace-mantras performed, one shall bring about the total subsiding of evil.
When this is done, those obstacles will undoubtedly come to rest.

Now, if fire blazes without fuel in the kingdom of one [king], or if fire possessing fuel does not blaze, that kingdom is oppressed by enemies. Or if meat, or anything else that is moist, should burn in water; ||| 77–78 ||
If the walls, archways, gates, the royal palace,
or the temple of the gods are ablaze,
or if they are consumed by lightning, then there will be fear for the king. (79)
Where there is fire on dry ground, there is danger to one’s master.
Where there are shadows without a source, or dust without a cause,
or smoke without fire, one should know that great danger exists there.
If lightning strikes when the sky is cloudless and devoid of stars, there will be danger;
likewise, if the sky is bright with stars during the day, danger likewise arises.
When there is an anomaly among the planets and constellations, or when the stars appear irregularly, [danger follows].
If there is a fire in the city, on vehicles, among quadrupeds, wild animals, or birds; or if weapons are blazing or even smoking,
and if they emerge from their sheaths, a tumultuous battle will occur.
Where sparks are seen appearing here and there even without fire,
and bows become full and deformed by their very nature,
and where there is a transformation of weapons— there one should predict battle.
Having fasted there for three nights,
the domestic priest should indeed offer oblations with fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees, mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
Through the offering with fire-mantras, peace is produced for them.
One should feed the virtuous, the chaste, the Brāhmaṇas, children, girls, and women; one should worship the gods and organize a great festival.
One should give gold, wealth, jewels, cows, land, and clothing.
Then there shall be the pacification of calamities caused by fire and weapons.
In those cities where they are seen walking step by step—whether weeping, or laughing, or exuding many fluids—[there shall be peace]. (3.146.90)
Even without wind, trees shed their branches while remaining free from disease; likewise, three-year-old trees display fruit and roots at the proper time.
In this very way, they manifest their own fruit and flowers within the interval.
They exude milk, fat, blood, honey, and water;
they suddenly wither yet remain free of disease, or having withered, they grow again.
Here, those who have fallen rise up, and likewise, those who have risen fall down. (92–93)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you of the distinct results that occur there:
from weeping, disease arises; from laughing, the ruin of the country occurs;
and from the falling of a branch, there will indeed be a battle that destroys the warriors.
The flowering of the *bālavallī* plant brings death to children;
its fruit and flowers cause dissension within one's own kingdom.
There shall be a decline in cow’s milk, and in the case of oils, a famine will descend. (95–96)
A decrease in mounts occurs when [the tree] exudes alcohol; if blood flows, a battle will break out.
When it exudes honey, disease shall arise; when it exudes water, there will be no rain.
Trees that have withered despite being free from disease truly indicate a famine.

If there is sprouting in dry places, it destroys the potency of food. (98) For those who have fallen, rising up will bring fear and cause division. When moving from one place to another, there will then be the ruin of the country. (99)
Even when the trees are blazing and even as they weep at the loss of their wealth,
all this misfortune befalls the king regarding those trees that have been worshipped.
If there is an abnormality in the flower or the fruit, the tree shall indicate the death of the king.

When the trees have thus grown, one should quickly cover those trees and adorn and worship them all with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings. One should place a large umbrella over the trees for the pacification of evil.
One should indeed worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śrī, and Śivā among the trees;
one should offer animals and food, and perform the propitiation of Rudra (rudraśānti).
Having offered oblations into the trees with the mantra "To the Rudras," Rudra should then recite the prayer.
Having worshipped with offerings rich in milk-rice, clarified butter, and honey, one should perform the gift of land (bhūdāna).
One should also engage in song and dance; thereafter, there will be peace for Rudra.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, it dispels all fear of the subjects and the king. (104–105)

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rituals for Pacifying Celestial, Atmospheric, and Earthly Portents," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 147 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*)
[The author: Chapter 148.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Excessive rain, drought, and the fear of famine and other such calamities are considered [the results of such actions].

But if there is endless rain during the day outside the proper season, it should be understood as bringing fear. (1) Furthermore, unnatural phenomena occurring even when there are no clouds should be known as portending the death of the king.
When there is a reversal of cold and heat, there is danger for kings arising from enemies. (2)
Where blood rains down, there shall be fear of weapons;
with a rain of embers and dust, there is the destruction of the city.
With a rain of marrow, bones, fat, and flesh, there is great danger to the people and to the king.
Likewise, there will be great fear of enemies regarding grain, flowers, fruits, and food.
(4) A rain of dust from fruits is considered to cause fear of disease;
and when there is a rain of food out of season, danger shall befall the crops. (5)
When the sun is free from dust and the sky is cloudless, if no shadow is seen—
or if it is indeed seen in the opposite direction— then there shall be danger to the country.
If there is an unseasonable rain of hailstones, there will be fear of famine.
Or likewise at night when the sky is cloudless, [seeing] something white to the south or north;
or a rainbow, the fall of a meteor, a city of the Gandharvas, a conflagration of the quarters,
a halo around the sun or moon, or even the darkening of the directions.
There will indeed be fear of an enemy army as well as calamities within one's own country.
(8) For the sake of pacifying those, one should perform a sacrifice to the Sun and a sacrifice to the Moon;
likewise, one should perform a sacrifice to Parjanya and a sacrifice to Marut. (9)
One should give wealth, goods, gold, and cows as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) there;
thus those portents, having attained pacification, will certainly not yield their [ominous] fruits.
Listen, Lakṣmī, likewise to other portents that announce suffering.
Rivers, lakes, and springs approach or draw near to the city; or they become tasteless, discolored, turbid, heated, frothy, and infested with living creatures. (11–12)
If rivers carrying oil, milk, wine, or blood flow toward it,
there will be fear of an enemy army within six months.
Or if reservoirs roar or blaze like fires, [the same result follows].
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, they emit flames, smoke, and dust;
or else, if water appears within them, or if there are reservoirs of excellent water, or if the sounds of music are heard, there will be danger to people. (14–15)
For its pacification, O King, one should perform oblations with honey, oil, and clarified butter;
one should recite the Vāruṇa mantras and have them recited by Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
There should be an offering into the water and an ablution in the water with ghee and other substances.
One should offer honey, clarified butter, and milk-rice as food for the virtuous yogis.
Likewise, one should give white-robed cows to the venerable Guru;
indeed, one should present water-pots and offer gems and pearls.
Listen, Lakṣmī, and hear further how there is a transformation among women:
women who give birth prematurely, as well as those whose offspring are born past their time;
and those who have deformed births, or who give birth to twins or triplets.
For women have given birth to non-human beings and those without mouths, as well as those afflicted by calamities;
they give birth to and bring forth those with missing limbs and those with extra limbs.
This is likewise true for beasts, birds, and all crawling creatures.
In whatever country, village, or family such persons may reside,
there shall be the destruction of that country, village, or family.
Therefore, the king should banish men and women who possess such deficient limbs.
One should pacify the female classes being oppressed within one's own kingdom with oblations.
Indeed, one should perform the "sacrifice of women" (nārī-yajña), consisting of fire-offerings, feeding, and so forth,
as well as the bestowing of garments and ornaments upon women and young girls.
Likewise, one should perform the worship of the Mothers, of the gods, and of the goddesses;
likewise, the worship of the Yoginīs, of the virtuous women, and of the chaste wives.
One should perform the worship of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, Prabhā, and Pārvatī.
One should perform the worship of Māṇikyā, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, and Mahālakṣmī (26).
One should perform the worship of Lalitā, Yamunā, Gaṅgā, Rati, and Bhakti,
as well as the worship of the family deity (kuladevī), and likewise cause it to be performed (27).
One should also perform the libation for the Brahmins according to one's desire;
then, O Lakṣmī, peace shall prevail and no misfortune shall arise.
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to that which indicates the onset of misfortune.
Vehicles that were unyoked move forward, while those that are yoked do not move at all.
Even when urged from behind, they do not go; there is great danger in that state. When being driven, they do not pull, yet they pull even when not struck. (3.147.30)
The immovable indeed move, and the movable do not move;
in the sky there are sounds of musical instruments and the resonant strains of song and music.
If wood, ladles, axes, and so forth were to undergo transformation, [it would be as if they moved].
One should strike cows by hitting their tails, and women by striking them with other women.
(32) When household utensils and the like are damaged, there will be terrible fear of weapons;
for the sake of pacifying that, one should perform the worship of Vāyu and the honoring of Brahmins. (33)
One should offer parched grain (saktu) and sweet foods such as ambara to Vāyu;
one should recite the great Pavamāna mantras and the mantras dedicated to the Maruts.
One should feed [the deity] with supreme rice-pudding (paramānna) and perform oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) and other offerings.
One should give more abundant sacrificial fees; by that, O Rame, there shall be peace.
Listen, O Śrī-Śivarājñī-Śrī, to another indication regarding animals:
when wild forest birds enter the village. (35–36)

Village-dwellers go to the forest, aquatic creatures go to dry land, and land-dwellers go to the water; they howl fiercely and without fear. At the king’s gate and at the city gates, jackals, owls, and dogs [howl].
If day-roaming creatures roam at night, or likewise if night-roaming creatures roam during the day;
if village animals abandon the village, then emptiness is indeed the result there.
Or if they howl fiercely during the twilights and form circles.
Wherever crows and owls cry out discordantly, even there the fruit is emptiness. If crows and owls cry out above one's head during the day,
a time of calamity will come upon him, or fire may break out suddenly.
There may be death, ill repute, or even the loss of his position;
a time of calamity brought about by the subjects and householders shall befall him.
Where a cock crows at night, or where a cuckoo sings in winter.
If a female jackal cries facing [the house] at sunrise, it shall indicate danger;
if a carnivorous pigeon enters the house or settles upon the roof;
or if flies produce honey—there shall be death for the master of the house.
If a carnivorous creature should fall upon the walls, gates, houses, arches, marketplaces, or streets;
or if anthills should arise, or if honey should flow from them [the weapons and so forth]—such as banners, umbrellas, and arms—[these are omens of ill]. 44–45.
That region goes to ruin and the king likewise dies; furthermore,
mice, locusts, parrots,
and small grass-eating insects appear there in countless numbers, and the fear of famine and Māra shall descend.
In that city where dogs abound with wood, firebrands, bones, and horns, and where monkeys cause distress;
where venomous dogs roam about on all sides; and where crows, with their beaks full of grain, fall upon the threshing floors or within the city itself. (47–48)
In that case, there will be the experience of famine, which brings about the exhaustion of the body;
furthermore, there will be fear of armies in battle for the people there.
If a crow is seen on the day [of the query] intent upon mating, [the same results follow].
Either the king dies there, or that country perishes.
Crows fly about at night, and indeed there will be the ruin of the house.
Likewise, where an owl is seen at the king’s gate or within the home, [the same calamity follows]. (3.147.50–51)

The death of a householder, as well as the loss of wealth, is to be known [as a portent] from the aberrations of wild animals and birds; one should perform a fire-oblation accompanied by sacrificial fees.
May the gods, in the form of pigeons, protect the village, the house, and the family.
Five or six twice-born men should mutter the mantras of Rudra and the mantras of Indra.
At the conclusion of the protection rite, cows should indeed be given as gifts; one should perform a sacrifice for the pacification of the planets (grahaśānti).
One should perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu, or alternatively, one should perform a sacrifice to Rudra.
One should also cause the pacification of elemental disturbances (bhautikī śānti) to be performed by the best of the twice-born.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another matter regarding elemental matters such as the consecration and so forth of temples, arches, watchtowers, gates, walls, and dwellings. (55)
But a falling of firm objects without a visible cause portends the death of the king.
Or, where the quarters are overwhelmed by dust or smoke, and the sun, moon, and stars appear discolored, they bring about an increase in fear. (56–57)
Where Rākṣasas are seen, where Brāhmaṇas act contrary to the Dharma, where the seasons indeed become fruitless, and where the unworthy is honored by people;
where the constellations appear disjoined, portending great danger—[in such places, one should not stay]. (58)
When there is the rising of comets, eclipses of the moon or sun, or a solar eclipse,
and wherever there is an abnormality in the planets or constellations, in that region there will be great fear.
Women will engage in quarrels, and children will kill other children.
Where there occurs an interruption of appropriate ritual acts,
the sacrificial fire, though being offered oblations, does not blaze even during rites for peace;
likewise, ants and carnivorous creatures move toward the north.
Where full jars leak, or the sacrificial oblation is spilled;
where auspicious words are not heard on all sides;
where sneezing afflicts one, and dolls laugh. (62–63)
The various kinds of food spoil, and the milk flows out from the vessels;
though the gods and the Brahmins are present, no divine power is perceived.
The subjects are devoid of devotion toward the gods, the virtuous, and the Brahmins.
Musical instruments are played with dull sounds and out-of-tune notes.
(65) There, people hate their teachers and friends and are devoted to the worship of enemies;
there, people show contempt for those who are worthy of worship, those who are honorable, and the most excellent persons. (66)
Where atheism arises during rites for peace, auspiciousness, or fire-offerings,
either the king dies there or that country perishes.
Listen now to the signs where misfortune befalls a king.
The king hates his own subjects and comes into conflict with the people.
He seizes the property of the subjects by force and seeks to kill them. He displays ingratitude and becomes enraged when entreated. (68–69)
He reviles the virtuous and does not respect their praise;
out of greed, he forcibly imposes unbearable taxes upon the people.
When his disposition has thus become perverted, he should perform the sacrifice to Śakra.
One should likewise gratify the Lord of the Gods together with his consort, as well as the other deities.
Food should be offered to the twice-born, oblations to the gods, worship to virtuous men, and the presentation of ornaments and such to virtuous women. (71–72)
Food should be given to young girls and auspicious items to children;
gifts such as cows, land, gold, and the offering of garments should be made.
An excellent fire sacrifice (havana) must be performed, for by that, peace will surely be attained.

In whatever region or village cooked food appears like meat, or if curd is seen to have a blood-like hue, that village or district shall perish. Furthermore, the residence of the village headman shall fall down without any apparent cause. (74–75)
If a house should collapse, or if there is the destruction of the king at that time;
if there is a rain of red stones and the howling of dogs on all sides, there will be the ruin of the country and the village. One should then perform a sacrifice to Viṣṇu.

An earthquake accompanied by thunder is a precursor of famine. (77) If it moves from the south to the north, there will be great fear for the empire; if it moves from the east to the west, the death of the king will certainly occur. (78)
If it moves from the east to the west, a battle arises among kings;
if it moves from the north to the south, then there will be abundance of food.
In the first watch of the day there will be disease, and in the second, it causes the loss of wealth.
In the third [watch], it brings grain and wealth; in the fourth, it bestows moderate results. (3.147.80) If there is an earthquake at twilight, it indicates the loss of all one's possessions.
If a crow caws upon setting out on a journey while perched on a thorn bush or a tree, it causes distress. (3.147.81)
If a crow comes facing one during a journey while perched on a vehicle, or if it does so in the sky, then death awaits; one should not undertake a journey at all.
If it flaps its wings on the right side, one must not travel in that direction.
Once gone, it does not return; death is certain, O Rame.
If the crow flies from the left to the right, there will be slaughter and imprisonment.
If its flight toward the north is accompanied by the sound of *tāra*, there will be a great famine.
There will be the outbreak of a great pestilence, the great slaughter of the people,
and a battle resulting in destruction when two comets appear face-to-face.
When a comet with a crest rises, there is the falling of royal umbrellas and the destruction of children and others.
If the rising occurs with the tail [of the moon], the destruction of cattle will surely befall the earth.
During an eclipse in the mouth of the sky (the solar eclipse), there will be war or famine on the ground.
At the time of departure, there will be black grain and cotton for the embodied being who possesses medicinal herbs.
Dry grass, dried cow-dung, and dry wood;
ashes, oil, and molasses—these belong to a man devoid of fortune who carries oil with him.
A naked man, a woman with disheveled hair, and likewise a sick man wearing saffron-colored robes.
A variegated cloth, a tattered rag, and so forth; an outcaste, a vessel for impurities;
a dead bird, iron objects, a widow, and likewise mud; leather, a leather-worker, buttermilk, a corpse, and a pregnant woman. (3.147.89–90)
A prison-dweller, a black bull, a snake, and also a frog;
a chameleon, a forest lizard, a hare, and a boar;
grass, bone, a red flower, a cat, and a predatory beast. (91)
A blacksmith, one ground by a machine, a shaven-headed man, or even a wicked person;
one with matted hair, a lame man, a buffalo, one who is deformed, and likewise a donkey; a weeping person, an ascetic, an enemy, and a person who has been imprisoned. (92–93)
A dog fight, a large web of spider silk, ants and the like,
the migration of ants, a stone, salt, sneezing, a cow-sneezing,
a barren woman, a washerman, and something unpleasant. (94)
If [the bird] closes its eyes on the path, one should certainly not go anywhere there;
death, great suffering, failure of the task, or humiliation [will follow].
For a man, these are the left limbs, but for a woman, they are the right limbs. 95–96.
If these [omens] should manifest, one should indeed know them to be a great calamity and destruction.
Whether there be the falling of a staff during travel, or the falling of a weapon,
or the falling of a crown and such, they are indicators of a fall.
If one falls from the top of one's own palace or from a staircase and so forth,
there will quickly be defeat, death, or even suffering.
When such things occur, one should immediately perform rites of pacification.

One should perform the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the sacrifice to Rudra, the worship of the gods, the propitiation of the planets, and the practice of recitation, charity, vows, and so forth; thus, peace shall certainly prevail.

(3.147.100) Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Peace-Rites and Other Measures for Various Portents," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (147)

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the disturbances arising from the heart,
as well as those arising from the body, and the various portents and twitchings.
If the body vibrates at the head, there will even be the acquisition of land;
if it vibrates at the forehead, there will be an increase in status; and if at the eyebrows or the nose, there will be union with beloved ones.
(2) If the eyes vibrate, there is the gain of servants; if at the corners of the eyes, the arrival of wealth.
In the upper and middle [parts], the disappearance of the object itself occurs.
(3) O Lakṣmī, when the root of the eye throbs, victory shall swiftly come to pass;
if it throbs below, there is enjoyment with a woman, and at the end of the ear, the hearing of pleasant news. (4)
In the nose, there is the attainment of joy and happiness; in the lower lip, the attainment of pleasure.
From the throbbing of the throat comes the acquisition of enjoyments, and likewise, from the shoulders, the increase of enjoyments.
From the throbbing of the arms comes affection for friends, while from the hands comes the arrival of wealth.

If the back throb, there is no victory; if the chest throbs, there will be victory. (6) If the flanks throb, there is the gain of affection; if the breast throbs, the birth of a daughter occurs. If the navel throbs, there is loss of position; if the intestines throb, there is the arrival of wealth. (7)
If there is throbbing at the joint of the knee, it indicates an alliance with enemies; if it occurs in the powerful [parts], it signifies a meeting with the strong.
If there is throbbing in the calves, there will be destruction in one's portion of land, without a doubt.
O Lakṣmī, if there is throbbing in the feet, one shall attain a position in the celestial sphere.
If there is a throbbing at the soles of the feet, it will result in travel on a journey that brings gain.
(9) In the case of a woman, throbbings on the left side always bring gains; for a man, such throbbings on the right side do so.
If these occurrences are reversed, they grant no gain; of this there is no doubt. (3.148.10)

When the manifestation of the undesirable occurs, one should perform fire-offerings (*havana*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), as well as gifts of gold, feeding, and so forth. For the attainment of happiness, a Vaiṣṇava or Raudra rite of pacification (*śānti*) should be performed there.
Now, hear of the sleep-related disorders arising from abnormalities originating in the heart (1.2). Upon seeing undesirable signs that yield evil results, one should perform pacificatory rites.
The sprouting of grass, trees, or shoots upon any part of the body other than the navel [is a sign of death] (1.3).
The powdering of the head with the dross of bell-metal, shaving the head, as well as nakedness;
wearing soiled garments, anointing the body, and wallowing in mud;
sinking in mud, falling from a great height, and mounting a swing. (14)
The smelting of refined metals, the slaughter of horses,
the climbing of trees with red flowers, the ascending of a mandala, and likewise the act of riding boars, bears, donkeys, and camels. (15–16)
The eating of cooked meat, oil, and *kṛsara*; dancing, laughing, marriage, and singing;
as well as the salutation of musical instruments that lack stringed accompaniment. (17)
Plunging into a stream, bathing with cow-dung water, bathing with mud or even with dust-water;
entering the mother’s womb, and even ascending the funeral pyre—(these are equal). 18–19.
The falling of Indra’s banner, the falling of the moon and the sun,
and the appearance of portents celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial; likewise,
the provocation of anger by gods, the twice-born, kings, and teachers.
Embracing young girls, sexual intercourse with men, the wasting away of one's own limbs, purging, vomiting, and the like;
traveling toward the southern direction, and being overcome by disease. (21–22)
The loss of merit, the loss of fruits, sweeping the house in a dream,
the collapse of the house, playing with *piśācas* or monkeys,
as well as dalliance with bears, carnivorous beasts, dwarfs, and wicked women. (23)
There is also defeat by others and the arising of suffering from others.
Wearing saffron-colored garments, association with women clad in saffron, drinking oil, being immersed in oil, and anointing oneself with red flowers. (24–25)
The spoiling of foods, the sight of wooden logs,
the straying of carts from the path, the eating of much fried flour-cake (saṃyāva),
the sight of prostitutes, and indeed the drinking of their breast milk.
The bursting of *śataghnī* weapons and the like, as well as eating the remains of food and so forth;
the sight of theaters, brothels, and executioners;
falling into the currents of lakes, and the burning of crops. (27–28)
Quarreling with water, the ornamenting of a boat, seeing the blind,
sitting upon the hips of a dark woman, shoes placed upon the head,
the arrangement of contradictory syllables, and seeing one's own self while traveling abroad.
The invisibility of Citramūrti, the head of Gaṇeśa’s corpse, the sight of a camel, obstacles encountered while eating food,
the shaving of the head, the falling into the ocean, and likewise the flow of blood from the *liṅga*. (3.148.30–31)
Wearing worn-out garments, the anger of a brahmin preceptor,
looking at a barking dog, being seized by a hooded serpent, death,
and likewise falling from a rooftop terrace onto stone slabs— [these are the omens]. (32)
The gaze of a cat in a forest, a black male [bird] as a target,
the sharpening of weapons by the wicked, the bursting of a false weapon, the eating of rice-milk porridge with buttermilk, and even the disappearance of objects. (33–34)
Furthermore, there is the sight of enemies, the falling down of feet during *viṣṭi*,
and likewise the sight of six-legged insects during *viṣṭi*;
as well as the cutting off of the ears and nose performed by Yavanas and others.
One's own naked vision, anointed with oil and joined with a red woman;
(36) the turning over and the falling down of the five parts of the crown and so forth;
the falling of the crest-lock, the falling of the throat, and also the falling of the teeth. (37)
The falling of the *liṅga*, as well as the blazing of the consort;
the sight of a noose around the neck, and likewise death upon being struck;
the killing of cows, women, and so forth in a dream, and the vision of great portents and the like.
Seeing one's ancestors, fleeing to a foreign land,
being insulted by everyone, likewise climbing onto a corpse, and being seized by enemies from the surface of the earth for the sake of wealth. (3.148.40)
If one becomes an ant or a scorpion serving as a vehicle,
or if there is the fleeing away of one's wife, these indicate the destruction of all one's possessions.
Furthermore, the widowhood of a daughter and the ruin of a temple [are likewise omens].
The discharge of blood, diseases of the blood, the appearance of wasting diseases (kṣaya),
the birth of a stillborn child, as well as the death of a pregnant woman,
the falling of a celestial chariot, and even the breaking of a cart— these are [omens]. ||42-43||
In the forest, he was seized by a tiger, killed by a lion,
and likewise harassed by crocodiles and fell into a deep abyss; furthermore,
he was confined in his own pit and imprisoned within his own palace.
Furthermore, there may be the binding of the feet by many people;
the enjoyment of a Cāṇḍālī woman, or even the enjoyment of a Cāṇḍāla; the sight of spirits in a dream; and the sight of a terrifying forest. (45–46)
Furthermore, there is the sight of predatory beasts, entering into the midst of fire,
traveling to heaven by vehicle, as well as going to the cremation ground;
there is also the vision of Yama and the sight of the Person of Time (Kālapuruṣa).
Seeing a ghost in a dream, seeing a bearer of nooses, beholding a royal messenger, or even seeing Garuḍa;
likewise, eating *tulasī* and smearing the ground with cow dung. (48–49)
Being carried away by a violent storm, being dragged by a machine,
being pulled about in a public assembly, and likewise being trampled underfoot;
vomiting blood mixed with worms, and seeing insects during the act of vomiting.
The bite of a black cobra, the sight of worms in one's food,
the shaking of mountains, the shaking of houses,
the birth of children by virgins, and the birth of deformed offspring by women. (51–52)
The falling out of facial hair among men and the growth of facial hair among women;
men wearing the dress of women and women wearing the dress of men;
likewise, the absence of breasts in women and the possession of breasts by men. (5.3)
If this is seen in a dream, there will be loss of territory and great fear.
If a king is seen killed in a dream, the destruction of the kingdom will certainly occur. Likewise, the movement of trees and the movement of creepers [are also inauspicious]. (54–55)
The departure of maidens toward foreign lands is also observed;
there will undoubtedly be a loss of fortune and famine—of this there is no doubt.
There will also be the movement of rivers and the overflowing of the ocean on all sides.
There, by means of water, there shall be the dissolution of that continent and even of the earth;
or else the dissolution of the entire earth may occur—no deliberation is required on this point.
Likewise, there shall be the movement of temples and the movement of mountains. (57–58)
And the Śilāsainya monastery shall become fruitful in its teaching.
If sounds arise in the fortress that are unknown and bring fear, there will be danger of the destruction of the fortress and danger of the destruction of the kingdom. (59)
If a sudden roaring should occur in the armpits at night,
there will arise the spread of disease, a great pestilence, and the destruction of the people.
If monkeys and bears laugh in the corners of houses, [the same calamities follow].

At the end of the month, the house will surely become empty; of this there is no doubt. If, in a dream, one sees a shaven-headed man wearing red garments and holding a staff, death will occur there, and even one's prosperity will perish.
If, in a dream, forest goddesses are seen who are withered, emaciated, and aged maidens; or those who are pregnant yet have dried-up bodies;
or those with broken legs, who are lame, mutilated, or possessing horns and humps—(63–64).
The worlds are struck by drought and people die there, of this there is no doubt;
where cattle are slaughtered by barbarians, even if seen in a dream, there afflictions from barbarians arise, of this there is no doubt. (65)
Where flesh-eating beasts are seen in packs above a city, there shall be the destruction of that city; its protection may be achieved through sacrifices to Rudra.
Where bright, radiant maidens weep and depart from a place, [that place will meet with ruin].
In that place, there shall be the destruction of knowledge and the ruin of undertakings;
the loss of artistic skill and the onset of poverty and wretchedness shall prevail.
Furthermore, circles of widows are seen everywhere around it.
There, circles of headless trunks [roll about], for destruction indeed comes from battle.
(69) Where animals stray from their proper seasons due to the snares of the beastly, there shall be a violation of dharma in that land and an increase in the conduct of barbarians. (70)
Other such things as well, including the appearance of leprosy and the like, as well as evil dreams, may occur; it is better to report them immediately.
Furthermore, one should perform a ritual for inducing sleep and a bath with medicinal paste made from sesame seeds.
In the sacrificial fire, the honoring of Brahmins and the true, the worship of the gods, (72) the praise of Śrī Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the worship of Vāsudeva,
the hearing of the liberation of the Lord of Nagas, and the worship of Bāla-Kṛṣṇa. (73)

One should perform the sacrifice to Rudra and the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, hold festivals, and chant the praises of Hari; one should cause the story concerning Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī to be recited in one's own home,
and undertake the great complete reading (*pārāyaṇa*) of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
When great danger has arrived, one should perform that which removes fear.
A dream seen in the first watch [of the night] yields its fruit within a year;
in the second watch, after six months; and in the third, after three months.
Within four months, the fruit of what was performed during the ten-day period will appear;
likewise, the auspicious or inauspicious results of two dreams occurring at night will manifest then.
Furthermore, that which is seen later will come to pass, while that seen earlier will be lost.
When these non-existent [omens] appear in a dream, one should perform their neutralization:
the sacrifice to the planets, the sacrifice to Viṣṇu, the sacrifice to Rudra, the sacrifice to Satī, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice of feeding, and the merit of giving gifts. (78–79)
A king devoted to righteousness and desiring the welfare of his subjects should perform sacrifices to the planets accompanied by a hundred thousand oblations,
both at the confluence of rivers and in the presence of the gods.
One should examine the ground at a sacred bathing place near a pond.
One should dig a pit one cubit deep and perform one thousand and eight oblations there; by that, peace is produced.
In the case of a *lakṣahoma*, it should be doubled, and in a *koṭihoma*, it should be quadrupled. Eight officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be appointed, subsisting on roots, milk, and fruits.
One should place jewels suitable for donation within the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
One should offer ten thousand oblations with the Gāyatrī mantra; six times that number with the Mānastoka mantra (84).

Thirty oblations should be offered with the mantras beginning with "graha," four with those having Viṣṇu as the deity, five with the Kuṣmāṇḍa mantras, and sixteen with flowers and other such offerings (85).
Ten thousand oblations of *bādara* fruits should be offered into the sacred fire with the *Śrī* mantra;
fourteen thousand should be offered with the mantras dedicated to Indra;
and the remaining five thousand should be offered with the mantras dedicated to Indra as well.
Having performed a hundred thousand oblations, one should perform the Puṣya-bath (puṣyasnāna).
With sixteen auspicious jars containing gold, one should bathe the patron; then peace will certainly prevail. (87–88)
One should give elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, land, garments, and wealth;
one should also give a hundred oxen and cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) on this occasion.
When the month is fully completed, the Lakṣahoma is proclaimed.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the procedure for the *koṭihoma* sacrifice on a riverbank.
Sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are required there, and the initiation (*dīkṣā*) is considered to last for one year.
Having commenced the oblations (*homa*) in either the month of Caitra or Kārttika, the year [is spent]. (3.148.90–91)
The patron of the sacrifice should have [the rite] performed while subsisting on milk or eating fruits.

Palāśa wood is recommended for the sacrificial fuel (samidh), as are barley, rice, mung beans, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds; likewise, there should be a continuous stream of clarified butter (vasordhārā) poured over it.
In the first month, one should indeed give a meal of milk to the officiating priests;
in the second, one should give *kṛsarā*, which accomplishes virtue, desire, and wealth;
in the third month, *saṃyāva*; and in the fourth, auspicious *modakas*.
On the fifth day one should give curd-rice, and on the sixth, a meal of barley meal;
on the seventh, one should give cakes, and on the eighth, ghee-cakes;
on the ninth, sweet rice, and on the tenth, a desired offering of barley.
In the eleventh [month] one should offer *māṣavaṭas*, and in the twelfth, the six flavors (*ṣaḍrasas*).
Clad in unwashed garments, purified and well-veiled, one should perform oblations for half the day;
this brings satisfaction to the gods beginning with Indra and fulfills all desires. (96–97)
One should cause all the gifts for the gods to be made and have the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice performed.
There, one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rule at every hundred;
at a thousand, twice as much should be given, continuing up to a hundred thousand.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is to be offered to the deities; one should honor the twice-born.
One should satisfy the gods and the ancestors with the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the prescribed rule.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa), one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a scale equipped with two sets of strings.
Having weighed oneself, one should likewise weigh one's wife with gold,
silver, sugar, and diamonds;
by giving such gifts, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and the destruction of obstacles.
"May the Lord Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the master of all sacrifices, be pleased.
Having spoken thus, one should bow to the brāhmaṇas and feed a hundred thousand men;
all calamities will perish, and merits shall accrue to him.
One should not grieve over birth and death, nor over deliberations regarding what has been done or left undone;
rather, one should perform the supreme sacrifice to the planets and other deities according to one's ability.
[This yields] the fruit of all the prescriptions for sacred fords and the performance of all sacrifices.
By doing so, O Lakṣmī! one shall obtain [the fruit] from hearing or even from reciting it.

(105) Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Planetary Sacrifice and Other Rites for the Purpose of Pacifying the Harm Caused by Bad Dreams and the Like," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
(Chapter 148, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Part 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga)
Chapter 149 [Author:
Chapter 150 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:

Listen, O Śivarājñīśrī: when an auspicious dream is seen, it produces an auspicious result for the dreamer; however, one should not return to sleep. Ascending a mountain, a palace, an elephant, a horse, or a bull is auspicious.

Climbing upon trees with white flowers is considered auspicious. Likewise, the appearance of trees or grass sprouting from the navel, as well as having many arms or many heads, and the appearance of trees bearing fruit [from one's body], are likewise [inauspicious]. (2–3)
Wearing white garlands and garments, rubbing all one's limbs clean,
touching the moon, the sun, and the stars, and touching the banner of Indra and other such objects;
(5) performing the rite of raising Indra’s banner, and witnessing the slaughter of enemies.
The swallowing of the earth, water, and oceans; victory in debate, gambling, and battle;
the eating of raw meat, fish, and milk-rice;
and likewise the sight of blood or bathing in blood. (5–6)
The drinking of liquor, blood, wine, and even milk;
being wrapped in intestines on the ground; seeing the stainless sky;
and milking a cow, a buffalo, or a female elephant with one's mouth.
The milking of lionesses, mares, and tigresses is auspicious.
So too is the favor of gods, holy men, teachers, and qualified yogis;
as well as the favor of brahmins and virtuous wives devoted to dharma.
Furthermore, there is the consecration (abhiṣeka) performed with water resting upon the horns of cows,
or with lunar water, or with the waters of the Gaṅgā, or with rainwater from the sky.
This very consecration should be understood as bestowing sovereignty and bringing about auspiciousness.
In a dream, the consecration to kingship and the supreme consecration to a celestial abode [are auspicious].
Furthermore, the cutting off of one's own head indicates the destruction of obstacles.
Obtaining the insignia of royalty and the sounding of stringed musical instruments [are likewise favorable].
Likewise, crossing waters, leaping over uneven terrain,
the birth of female elephants, mares, and cows in the home,
as well as the mounting of horses and the riding of elephants; ||| 13 ||
Mounting a bull and mounting a beautiful celestial chariot;
likewise, the acquisition of excellent women and the embrace of a virtuous wife; the worship with gold and the smearing of excrement upon one's body. (14–15)
For those who are living, the sight of sovereigns, parents, and gurus;
the gentle and supreme sight of virtuous people, of chaste wives, and of one’s own beloved;
and the sight of deities and of pure yogis—[all these bring great benefit].
The sight of pure waters and festive celebrations is auspicious;
the sight of trees endowed with fruits and flowers is excellent; the sight of creepers is preeminent, and the sight of gardens bestows well-being. (17–18)
The sight of gardens containing grain, of fields, of water-filled rivers, clouds, and lakes is auspicious.
Likewise, the sight of swans and cuckoos is also auspicious. (19)
The sight of cātakas, peacocks, and garuḍas; the sight of peahens and white birds with variegated plumage is auspicious.
So too is the sight of deer, monkeys, and gavayas.
The sight of rhinoceroses and likewise of gaṇḍakas is auspicious;
the bite or the sight of red serpents is excellent.
The sight of coins, silver, and gold is likewise auspicious.
The sight of ornaments, necklaces, and divine garments;
the auspicious sight of sandalwood, saffron, unbroken rice, darbha grass, and the like;
as well as the sight of objects of adornment and auspicious items—[these are favorable omens]. 23–24.
Beholding a courtesan, beholding a female dancer, likewise beholding queens, beholding goddesses, and the sight of a Brahmin woman;
beholding a maiden, beholding a holy man, and beholding a deity. (25)
Indeed, the sight of temples, shrines, and palaces is auspicious;
so too is the sight of devotees, the sight of divine palaces, the sight of festivals such as the *ārātrika*, and the hearing of sacred hymns (*kīrtana*). (26–27)
Hearing this discourse, seeing pavilions and the like,
seeing venerable persons in a dream, having one's feet massaged by venerable persons,
or even having one's own body massaged by the Guru or by one's father; ||| 28 ||
Massaging the feet also bestows victory in all undertakings.
(29) So too does the sight of Gaṇeśa, the sight of the attendants of Hari, the sight of the bridal procession, and the sight of sacrifices, rituals, and the like. (30)
There was the witnessing of the installation festival and the honoring performed by the subjects;
there was repeated prosperity through the womenfolk with unbroken rice grains and the like, as well as blessings;
and the wearing of gold, garments, and other ornaments, along with the putting on of divine garlands and such.
Writing, worship, the display of pleasure with a beloved,
and likewise a shower of flowers— these auspicious things seen in a dream,
and observations such as these in a dream, indeed accomplish all goals. (32–33)
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, I shall declare to you the omens regarding a journey;
thus the journey of subjects and even of kings shall indeed be fruitful.
It shall also be successful for holy men, for women, and for everyone.
It shall likewise be free from suffering, grant desired fruits, and bestow supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
White jasmine flowers are excellent, as are full water-jars, women, maidens, ornaments, lotuses, and birds. (35–36)
A pregnant sapharī fish, meat, and fish—these three; a pair, a bride, cattle, horses, and elephants; the Buddha alone is a beast, yet the bull is a sacrificial animal.
The goat alone is the king of excellent animals; the thirty gods are friends, and women are [the source of] pleasure.
Brahmins who are devoted to Viṣṇu and virtuous, wearing their topknots and sectarian marks;
fire accompanied by its blazing flame; a king who is a true guru;
a learned man, a follower of dharma, one observing vows, a merchant, one free from hypocrisy, and one skilled in giving gifts. (38–39)
A courtesan who is virtuous and chaste, durva grass, fresh cow dung,
gold, silver, copper, rubies, gems, diamonds, pearls,
crystals, ornaments, and new garments.
A new vehicle, a new woman, and also a new carriage;
fresh food, barley, white mustard seeds, and medicinal herbs;
a palanquin for men, a throne, and objects made of gold and silver. || 41-42 ||
The divine chariot, instrumental music, singing, circles of dance, and festivals;
the sword, the parasol, the banner, the whetstone, and the kettledrums and other such instruments;
weapons, clay [images], and trees laden with grain and fruit.
All royal insignia and whatever are the insignia of the preceptor;
ghee, curd, and milk, as well as various fruits; a person of honor adorned with ornaments, a svastika, and a vardhamānaka. 44–45.
The sight of betel, the *nandyāvarta* design, the *kaustubha* gem,
necklaces, beautiful vessels, and the hearing of musical instruments;
the notes of *gāndhāra*, *ṣaḍja*, and *ṛṣabha*, and sweet songs.
On one's back, the currents of wind are always favorable and bring happiness;
likewise, carnivorous animals have melodious voices, the clouds thunder, lightning flashes, Indra’s bow appears, and there is even the trumpeting of elephants. (47–48)
Serenity, hearing auspicious teachings, saluting those worthy of worship,
the words of the guru’s blessings, contentment of mind, and what is pleasing to the mind—
on one side are all these signs, and on the other side is contentment of mind alone. (49)
The sight of auspicious objects, saffron, and unbroken grains;
a cow with her calf, a horseman, and even a black antelope; a peahen, a parrot, a maina, a cuckoo, and the sound of frogs. (3.149.50–51)
He disregarded the words of his parents as well as the instructions of his preceptor;
he consumed flowers, garlands, leaves, and vegetables as food,
along with various kinds of sweetmeats, acting as both a worshiper and a storyteller.
Even the servant who is a supreme devotee [is distracted] by curd, lamps, and fine incense;
by the chanting of the Vedas, hymns of praise, and the play of children; by the playful laughter of maidens and the gazing of young wives. (53–54)
The sounding of hand-claps, hearing the cry of "Victory!",
receiving honor from the assembly and the community, being summoned by one facing him,
seeing sprouts of wheat and young grass, and the full vessel (pūrṇapātra).
Prostration, a cry of joy, the arrival of raindrops from a cloudless sky,
and likewise the falling of flowers and flower-clusters from a tree upon one's own head at the time of departure are auspicious signs indicating gain. (56–57)

The raining down of parched grain, the display of the sacrificial vessel, the leaping of horses, and auspicious signs indicative of victory; the hearing of pleasant news, the arrival of gods and preceptors, and the performance of oblations—[these are signs of success]. //58//
The sight of banners, as well as the hearing of divine music;
the hearing of the music of the *gālava* bird, and the sight of fresh sprouts;
the sight of ritual hand-gestures (*mudrās*), and the beholding of women abounding in good fortune. (3.149.59–60)
The sight of her beloved by the wife, the calling of her beloved, dear speech, even the word of command, and the hearing of the name Nārāyaṇa;
[these are the nourishment and sustenance for all beings of every species during their childhood]. (61)

Seeing a child, a calf, an animal, or a bird drinking milk, or eating grains and the like together with its mother; and witnessing the sexual acts of village-dwellers, spirits, animals, birds, or living beings. (62–63)
Gifts being distributed, and festive decorations at the city gate;
festive decorations also upon the rampart, and colorful rangavalli patterns at the front of the houses;
and a rooftop pavilion (candraśālā) adorned with a banner—this indeed is seen as auspicious.

There were sacred trees adorned with banners, and the grounds of the shrines were made of clay. There were triumphal arches of fresh leaves that were truly auspicious, and the walls along the royal roads were smeared with sandalwood paste. (65–66)
For the sprinkling of fragrant water is indeed a source of auspiciousness;
so too is the sight of sandals and the beholding of the form of the Guru.
Likewise, there is the sight of the ocean and the sight of the full flow of rivers.
Beholding divine youths and gazing upon divine maidens;
(68) beholding new machines, as well as the guru’s mantras and the scriptures;
hearing narratives and likewise remembering one's ancestors. (69)
There was also the recollection of his descent and the witnessing of great festivals;
all the fruits were ripe, along with their branches, even those that were unripe;
and the trunks and branches of the trees were indeed rich with pods and ears of grain.
The beauty of fresh sprouts, when seen, bestows prosperity.
(71) The flowing of ink from an ink-pot, the falling of ink, the oozing of saffron, and likewise the throbbing of the hips; (72)
Even the offering of betel leaves, the presentation of vessels and bowls, and all that is sweet in the form of morsels in the mouth during a journey—
this brings about auspiciousness, bestows gain, and likewise grants victory. (73)
The skins of lions, deer, tigers, elephants, and so forth;
golden bands, ribbons, and bells; and the roaring of lions and the trumpeting of elephants—these indeed constitute auspicious signs. (74–75)
Others have performed the offering of substances into the hand, such as the offering of jewels and so forth;
likewise, the giving of saffron and unbroken rice, as well as the clapping of hands.
The giving of the hand is excellent, and the giving of the mind is likewise supreme.
In such auspicious and favorable circumstances, there shall indeed be auspiciousness:
victory, gain, increase, honor, stability, fame, strength, rising prosperity, exaltation, fortune, happiness, wealth, and offspring. (77–78)
Such things as these arise, especially in the state of a householder.
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe the opposite conditions that bring about fear:
the wind blows harshly, dry, and filled with grit, blowing directly against one and causing distress.
If an enemy, a base person, or a wicked individual is seen, it portends fear.
Rain with the force of a pestle (musaladhārā) falling against the grain is not auspicious.
Planets moving in their direct course (anuloma) are praised, Jupiter especially so. (3.149.80–81)
The moon is most auspicious when facing forward, as is a maiden facing forward.
During a journey, the falling of banners, garments, a staff, a parasol, sandals,
or ornaments is considered a source of sorrow.
The falling of weapons and the like, and the mishandling of implements and the like;

[the occurrence of these] at the gateway for one who has departed, as well as the striking of the head, the trampling with the tips of the feet, sneezing, and being asked contemptuous questions. (83–84)
Inquiry regarding where one has come from and so forth is inauspicious, for it indeed bestows suffering.

Husk-powder, ashes, skulls, bones, broken vessels, and rags;

Likewise, oil-cakes and the like from which the essence has been extracted; fruits and such that have been broken; leather used for binding hair;
iron, mud, a eunuch, one who is insane, and even a skeleton. 91.
With disheveled hair, afflicted by pain, and clad in garments of red ochre;

Black grain, medicinal herbs that have been parched or spoiled, the sight of a miser, the sight of damp or wet objects,

Theft of the ritual implements, the disappearance of the principal object,

humiliation, shedding of tears, stumbling, being plundered, sleeping [inappropriately], fever, obstruction, the breaking of the wheel and other [implements], and likewise the leaking of weapons. (95–96)
Seeing one's own anus, as well as seeing young grass and the like—
all such things during the journey are givers of suffering.

Peaceful rites (śāntikarma) should be performed: fire oblations (homa), recitation (japa), worship (prapūjana), feeding of virtuous Brahmins, gifts, and a great festival;

The performance of sacrifices for the sages and the complete satisfaction of worldly beings—
such activities as these, as well as the chanting of the names of Hari, sacrificial discourses, and whatever rites for peace are to be performed, [should be undertaken]. 101–102.
O Lakṣmī, when this is performed, indeed all evils go to destruction;
through recitation and even through hearing, evils truly depart.
Through rites for peace and so forth, there shall always be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Auspicious Omens, Dreams, and the Like, as well as Worship, Peace-Rites, Sacrifices, and so forth, for the Purpose of Turning Back Adverse Signs during the Departure for Pilgrimage," in the Third Section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Ḍākinīs, śākinīs, bhūtas, bhairavas, and piśācas;

Chapter 152 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, you are Hari himself, the incarnate one.
I know in every way that you have been born for the sake of uplifting the worlds.
How can there be the upliftment of those who have not attained your yoga— those unfortunate ones who are sinners burdened by the five great sins?
"O Kṛṣṇa, tell me here: how can You deliver those who are associated with the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, and sexual intercourse with a chaste wife?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the means for their upliftment.
It is certain that my compassion for even the most sinful of sinners blazes forth like a flame.
Indeed, out of compassion, I have established sacred pilgrimage sites (tīrthas) in this world.
There are indeed marvelous things, both animate and inanimate;
by the mere touch or sight of which sins truly blaze forth.
The Aśvapaṭṭasara Tīrtha is the destroyer of all sins.
The Narmadā Śuklatīrtha, as well as the supreme Bhagukṣetra;
the great Oṃkāra Tīrtha, which destroys all sins;
Somanātha, Dvārikā, the Gomatī, and the Svarṇalekhikā.
The Nārāyaṇahrada is a sacred ford that destroys all sins.
(8) So too are Bhadrāvatī, Sābhramatī, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Kāverī, Tāmraparṇī, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā. (9)
Gokarṇa, the sacred field of Mādhura, as well as Kapālamocana;
Haridvāra, Viśālā, Kaurava, and likewise Puṣkara;
Saṃbhala, the Brahmaputrā, the Gaṇḍakī, and the river Kāñcanī.
Gāgarā, Sindhurā, as well as the Pampā lake;
Setubandha, Jagannātha, and the supreme holy site of Kāpila; and also the lake named Mānasa, which destroys all sins. || 11–12 ||
Kedāra, where the body falls, and the great river Irāvatī; Menakāṅgī, Śikṣāṅgī, and Bālakṛṣṇa Sarovara;
the Kṛṣṇā River, Kaubera Lake, and the river named after me (Mannāmikā). || 13 ||
The Cāṅga, Śikṣāṅgikā, Śālavīnā, Triaṅgi,

The Supāravaryaka lake, the Mekāñjī, the great river,
the Vinipāda lake, and the lake named Sulavā— O Lotus-born one, such sacred fords as these were created by me.
On the surface of the earth, for the destruction of great sins and other evils,

those people who bathe there attain purity and my supreme liberation.

Where there is the ritual bath of the *avabhṛtha*, one is liberated from sins there;

Where there are people practicing celibacy, where ascetics reside, and where there are virtuous ones whose character is that of Brahman—there one is liberated from sins.
