Where the Videhas dwell, those embodied beings are virtuous and established in Brahman.
Where there is congregational chanting (*kīrtana*) and a temple, there people are liberated from their sins.

Where austerity (*tapas*), meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) exist, and where cows are worshipped, there people are liberated from all sins. (3.151.29–30)
One should sacrifice one’s life for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, or for the sake of the righteous;
likewise, one should sacrifice one’s life for the sake of the gods, for the sake of the ancestors, or for the sake of one’s mother.
One should also sacrifice one’s life for the sake of one’s master, for the sake of one’s husband, or for the sake of truth.
One should renounce one’s life for the sake of Dharma, for the sake of sacrifice, and for the sake of liberation.
Then all sins are surely destroyed; of this there is no doubt.
One may also practice fasting or even cast oneself down from Mount Bhṛgu.
Or one may enter a blazing fire, or enter the water at a sacred ford;
then all sins are destroyed, there is no doubt.
And he who gives food to a learned man for as long as he lives...
His sins are destroyed; he is cleansed even of the murder of a Brahmin. By bathing at the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of sacrifices, one is liberated from transgressions.
One should give one's entire possessions to a virtuous and learned person who is an embodiment of Hari.
His sins are destroyed by giving and by serving the virtuous;
by merely bathing at Triveṇī, all his transgressions perish entirely.
He bathes constantly at the three times of day and bows down to all the deities.
By subsisting on a single meal a day, his sins are destroyed in every respect.
By bathing in the water from Hari’s feet, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
by drinking the five products of the cow for the duration of a year, a drinker of intoxicants is liberated.
A thief of gold is liberated from sin when struck with a wooden pestle by kings;
one who has had sexual intercourse with a woman forbidden to approach should perform five or six *cāndrāyaṇa* penances.
Furthermore, one who associates with those who have fallen from their status must indeed perform those same vows.
Or, indeed, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for one year without sloth;
or he should give away his entire property as a gift, which purifies all sins;
or he should go to a sacred field such as Gayā and the like, which destroys sin.
Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), whoever worships me as Hari after feeding virtuous brāhmaṇas is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight for the sake of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow...
To Vaivasvata Kāla, to the Destroyer of all beings,
to Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka—
one should offer eight handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds to each of them respectively.
One should worship the God of Dharma and is liberated from all sins.
One should practice celibacy, sleep on the ground, observe fasts, and honor the virtuous. By remembering Kṛṣṇa, one is released from all transgressions.
Having fasted on the sixth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship the Sun on the seventh;
then, having also fed [the brahmins], one is liberated from all sins.
Having fasted on the eleventh day and worshipped me, Hari, [one attains the same]. (47–48)
On the twelfth lunar day, one should feed the virtuous; thus one is liberated from all sins.
One should constantly recite prayers, frequent sacred fords, and perform the worship of gods and the virtuous.
Indeed, by doing this always with faith, one is liberated from all sins.
Furthermore, he who gives gifts at the beginning and at the end of an eclipse—
whether of diamonds, gems, grain, other articles,
lands, houses, or food— is liberated from all sins.
Even one who is joined with great sin, if purified at sacred fords (tīrthas) and should give up his life according to the rule, is liberated from all transgressions—
whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or defiled by a great sin (mahāpātaka). (52)
A virtuous and auspicious woman who is devoted to her husband shall uplift her husband.
For that woman who is devoted to her husband and is ever eager to serve him, no sin exists either in this world or in the next.
The virtuous man who is devoted to the Supreme Brahman, the virtuous woman who is intent upon Lakṣmī,
and the disciple who serves the Guru as Brahman, are liberated from all sins.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and other sacred sites, one obtains the fruit of all merit.
But he who, having bathed according to my command, delivers himself from great sins;
who gives his entire wealth to a holy man, and gives it to Śrī Hari for my sake,
and gives it to Lakṣmī and Mahālakṣmī— he is liberated from all sins.

One should offer wealth in the form of treasures to the god Viṣṇu, and one should also give for the sake of sacrifice; thus one is liberated from all sins. Indeed, one must never go outside the house of a brāhmaṇa under any circumstances.
One who is content with whatever comes by chance is not touched by sins.
He who, having endured hardships himself, brings happiness to others, becomes a vessel for all blessings and is indeed never touched by sins. (3.151.60)
He who eats the remains of food, who partakes of what is graciously offered by his guru,
and who is content with a diet of alms— no sin exists for him. Furthermore, he should be of virtuous conduct and maintain a livelihood that is not solicited.
One who is content with whatever is obtained by chance is never touched by sins.
A person who is always immersed in the stories of Kṛṣṇa and bestows the knowledge of Brahman is liberated from all sins through the desired awakening found in the company of the virtuous.
He who is Brahman himself, a knower of Brahman, a devotee of Brahman, and likewise served by those most devoted to Brahman—
he who possesses discrimination regarding the Self— is never touched by sins. Just as one may have a false perception of expectation, so too may there be a mockery of renunciation.
Just as one who is devoted to meditation is not touched by sins:

free from thirst for the desirable and the undesirable, with hunger extinguished by gain and loss, and devoid of activity regarding what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped—he is indeed not touched by sins. (65–66)
Whether one is wretched, penniless, wealthy, or even a king,
by serving the virtuous according to one's ability, one is liberated from sins. Indeed,
by bestowing the nine treasures in a sacrifice, one is liberated from sins.
One should assign the Padma, the Mahāpadma, the Makara, and the Kacchapa;
one should likewise offer the Mukunda, the Nanda, the Nīla, and the Śaṅkha.
One should also present the Mahāśaṅkha, and by doing so, one is liberated from all bonds.
A treasure is not to be recognized by its number, but by the act of giving;
even a pauper, having given to the Divine, is considered the Lord of Padma, the Master of Treasures.
Conversely, one who possesses great wealth, such as a conch-shell hoard, yet does not give, is called a miser.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall describe the giver who is the lord of treasures (71).
Even one of meager means who should diligently give his own wealth for the sake of the gods, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of truth, or to a virtuous ascetic (72).
To a virtuous person devoted to Viṣṇu and established in Brahman for the sake of merit—
that substance known as the lotus belongs indeed to him, for he is the lord of the Padma treasure.
Whether the substance be small or great, it is his own entire wealth.
But he who, setting aside the mere maintenance of his journey,
should offer wealth to the gods and others— for him, the Great Lotus Treasure (Mahāpadmanidhi) is intended.
That wealth is declared to be *sāttvika*, for such a donor is indeed *sāttvika*.
In the world beyond, Lakṣmī indeed makes his wealth immeasurable;
for the sake of my devotees, being well-pleased, you grant him everything. Therefore, these two treasures belong to those who are devoted to the gods and free from greed.

The two named Divya are inexhaustible and filled with lotus-like compassion. (77) Listen indeed; I shall speak of Makara: he has acquired wealth through hardships, yet, intent on his own self-interest, he enjoys it himself and does not give anything at all in charity. (78)
Desirous of gain, one should give for the sake of interest at the end of the year for the purpose of increasing it,
having abandoned the old friendship and established ever-new friendships.
In this way, indeed, the destruction of wealth occurs through successive generations.
Even when one gathers weapons such as swords and arrows, they perish.
That treasure which consists of wealth kept for one's own sake alone is a "makara" hoard;
at the time of death, that entire possession is lost and falls into the hands of others. (3.151.80–81)

Listen, O Lakṣmī, to the story of the tortoise who, having acquired wealth through great effort, neither enjoyed it nor gave it away; out of greed, he did not trust anyone, but instead cast that useless treasure into a hole in the ground. (82)
When it has been accumulated, at the end of life, even by others—whether by kings or by groups of thieves—it is carried away like a tortoise;
for that [accumulation] is said to be of the nature of passion (rājasa), while the tortoise-like [state] is always of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). ||83-84||
The *mākara* contains half a sin, while the *kacchapa* contains a full sin;
O Lakṣmī, listen, one should diligently acquire the *mukunda* treasure.
However, even after depositing it repeatedly in a treasury or in the earth—
Again and again, she squanders her wealth upon prostitutes, dancers, and singers, as well as upon performers,
vices, and hardships; thus,
this woman devoted to sin wastes away the riches known by the name of Mukunda.
Even one who has committed evil is indeed to be awakened; he is the treasure-trove containing the sheath of Mukunda.
Listen, O Nanda, for I shall describe to you the treasure within the lotus-born [Brahmā]:
he is the great blissful one, characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, and he is truly the support of the lineage.
All members of the family enjoy wealth out of a spirit of affection;
praises are also bestowed upon them, and they come to have many wives. Their enjoyment of wealth serves both their own interests and for the benefit of others. (3.151.90)
He shows indifference toward former friends and forms attachments with others;
such is his own wealth, which consists of the *nandana* treasure.
Listen, O Lakṣmī, I shall likewise describe the *nīla* treasure and the one following it.
One who possesses blue wealth is indeed always of a sattvic nature.
He collects clothes, grain, and so forth, constructs tanks and similar works, maintains a treasure for three generations, and establishes mango groves and the like. (92–93)
He indeed performs religious duties and gives a garden to Viṣṇu;
O Lakṣmī, listen as I describe the conch-treasure (śaṅkha-nidhi), which brings about calamity.
The conch-treasure consumes the wealth of a single person and brings about the end of that wealth.
O Rame! Neither his family nor even his lineage enjoys his wealth.
His attendants eat poor food and do not wear beautiful clothes;
desiring only to nourish his own interests, he gives to other men in vain. (95–96)
Listen, Lakṣmī, the great conch-treasure is for the sake of enjoyment alone;
for wealth exists only with others and not even slightly in one's own home.
Thus indeed are treasures to be understood, and having known them, one should employ them.
One is liberated from all sins by performing service for the deities at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Means for Destroying All Great Sins and Other Evils, and the Explanation of the Names and Purposes for the Employment of Wealth Pertaining to the Nine Treasures," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*). Chapter 151.
Chapter 152 [Author:
Chapter 153 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to [the account of] those sons who effect the removal of sin,
who are endowed with the power of Dharma, and by taking refuge in whom there is liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Śraddhā indeed gave birth to a son named Kāma.
Desire, when applied for my sake, is ordained for liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Śrī gave birth to an auspicious son, Darpa;
and Darpa, when applied for my sake, is ordained for liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Dhṛti gave birth to a son, Niyama;
he was appointed for my sake and is intended for liberation.
Likewise, from Dharmadeva, Tuṣṭi gave birth to a son, Santoṣa.
And this [Dharma], being employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (5) From Dharmadeva, Puṣṭi likewise gave birth to a son, Lobha;
Lobha, being employed for my sake, is intended for liberation. (6)
Likewise, Medhā bore a son named Śruta to Dharmadeva;
he was appointed for my sake and is intended for liberation.
Furthermore, Kriyā bore a son named Daṇḍa to Dharmadeva.
The rod of punishment, when applied for my sake, is intended for liberation. Policy follows the rod, and discipline follows policy;
these three, when applied through me, truly lead to liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Buddhi likewise gave birth to a son named Bodha;
Bodha, when employed for my sake, is intended for liberation.
From Dharmadeva, Lajjā likewise gave birth to a son named Sunaya.
The path joined to Kṛṣṇa is ordained for liberation.
Likewise, from Dharmadeva, a body was born of resolve;
and that resolve, directed toward me, shall grant liberation. (11–12)
From Dharmadeva, Śānti gave birth to a son named Kṣema;
Kṣema, being employed for my sake, is destined for liberation.
Likewise, from Dharmadeva, Siddhi gave birth to a son named Sukha.
Sukha, when united with Kṛṣṇa, is ordained for liberation.
Likewise, Kīrti gave birth to a son, Yaśas, from Dharmadeva;
Yaśas, when united with Kṛṣṇa, is ordained for liberation. (14–15)
If all the grandsons of Dharma are indeed engaged for my sake,
they shall all lead to liberation and destroy all sins.
Kāmaputra is Mahānanda, and Harṣaputra is Atimānaka.

The cessation of restraint is the satisfaction of contentment. Accumulation is the son of greed; decisive judgment is the son of sacred learning. The one known as hardship is the son of punishment; prosperity is the son of statesmanship. (17–18)
Abhyudaya was the son of Vinaya; Śantanu was the son of Bodha; Tejas was the son of Sunaya; Āyaka was the son of Vyavasāya;
Rakṣaṇa was the son of Kṣema; and the one named Moda was the son of Sukha.
My son is a festival of glory, and my grandsons are indeed the sons of Dharma.
O Rame, all these [mantras] bestow liberation and destroy sins;
they should be joined with yoga by the virtuous, for those divine ones truly deliver them.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to those who indeed bestow sin and cause the exhaustion of merit:
the sons of Adharma, who promote wicked deeds and conduct.
Hiṃsā was the wife of Adharma; from her was born a son, Anṛta.
Untruth was declared to be falsehood; it causes suffering and brings about sin.
Nirṛti was his sister, and his two sons were Naraka and Bhaya.
Furthermore, two daughters are likewise considered to be Māyā and Vedanā.
Likewise, Māyā’s son was Death (Mṛtyu), the snatcher away of all beings;
and from Vedanā was born a son named Suffering (Duḥkha).
From Death were born Disease, Old Age, Sorrow, Thirst, and Anger.
And Nirṛti gave birth to a son named Vināśa, who was difficult to endure.
Brahmā then spoke these beneficial words to Nirṛti’s son, who was difficult to endure, hungry, emaciated, having the voice of a crow, and with a sunken face: |||27||
"Do not devour this world, my son; I shall provide you with a livelihood.
May your dwelling always be that of the unrighteous—one that is stale, infested with insects, and likewise looked upon by dogs. (28)
That which is in a broken vessel, or touched by the breath of the mouth;
that which is leavings, or even steaming, or licked, or unconsecrated; that which is defiled by a woman in her courses, or eaten by a woman in her courses—that shall be yours. (3.152.29–30)
"O Yakṣa, whatever has been offered or given without faith, by those who have not bathed, with contempt, or that which is abandoned and wicked— all that has been surrendered by me to you.
[I also surrender] that which involves breaking the line of guests, deceit, partial cooking, and deception."
Your dwelling shall be in quarrels and in misery.
(32) Indeed, you will always reside in a house where the aged are not nourished, where the cow is bound and neglected, and where there is a lack of sustenance for children. (33)
You shall overcome those mortals who fast in vain, those addicted to gambling and women, those of cat-like conduct, and the deceitful;
as well as the wicked who inflict suffering and those who betray trust.
Your dwelling shall always be in the houses of those who oppose those seeking refuge.
O merciless one, you must indeed always remain in such a home, for it is difficult to endure;
you must never stay in the house of a righteous person or in a temple of the gods. (35–36)
Abandon that house where one who is pure within and without, having performed the purificatory rites according to rule, is free from greed and has conquered desire;
and where there is loving-kindness toward children, the elderly, women, and men alike.
Likewise, abandon that house among your circle of kinsmen where women are indulgent, not eager to go outside, and always full of modesty; O Yakṣa, avoid that home entirely. (38–39)

Avoid that house where beds and foods appropriate for one's age are provided, yet service to the virtuous is lacking. (3.152.40) [But rather] that house where compassionate ones are always established in virtuous deeds.
Avoid that house which is furnished with common utensils;
avoid that house where those seated on their thrones rise up suddenly in the presence of their teacher or even in the presence of the elders.
That house whose door is not pierced by young trees, shrubs, and the like, and which possesses the beauty of a garden—that dwelling is auspicious; avoid the others.
Where no sound arises within the house that pierces the vital points of men—
Or if there is no such speech [of virtue], avoid that house.
(44) Avoid that house where there is no worship of the gods, the ancestors, mortals, and guests, and where one eats only what remains from their favor. (45)
You should avoid men who speak untruths, those lacking in forgiveness, those who are harmful, and those who feel regret;
you should also avoid women who are envious,
as well as those women who are devoted to serving their husbands and who avoid the company of unchaste women.
Abandon that woman who is nourished by the remnants of food belonging to her husband and family.

Always abandon the auspicious Brāhmaṇa who possesses Vedic knowledge, is characterized by goodness (*sattva*), worships the gods, is devoted to sacrifices and other rites, and is contented and peaceful. (47–48)
O Duḥsaha, abandon the Kṣatriya who is a protector, a donor, one who follows the path of dharma, devoted solely to justice, and loyal, even if he possesses a strong army!
Abandon also the Vaiśya who is established in business and is dedicated to truth and dharma!
Abandon the Śūdra who is non-violent, devoted to giving, faithful, and a servant of cows;
abandon the Śūdra who is intent on service, devoted, peaceful, and free from deceit.
Wherein the husband and wife are mutually supportive in their devotion, [there is no fault]. 3.152.50–51.
Abandon that house in every way where the two are devoted to dharma and liberation;
do not dwell, O unbearable one, in a place where the son performs worship for the guru, the gods, and likewise for the father, and where the wife performs it for her husband. (52)

In the morning and evening, your house is anointed with unguents, consecrated by the worship of the gods, and purified by the feet of the virtuous; yet you are unable even to look upon it. Furthermore, its beds are unseen by the sun, and it is constantly provided with fire and water. (53–54)
The lamps that illuminate the sun possess the power of the gateway of giving;
they are vessels for the grace of the virtuous, abodes of fortune, and worthy recipients [of merit].
Wherever Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī are also worshipped, [there such things exist].
Where there are virtuous men and virtuous women, whence can there be fear of misfortune?
(56) That house where there is a bull, sandalwood, a lute, a mirror, honey, clarified butter, sweet food, ghee, and copper vessels—that is not a place for you to take refuge. (57)
O anthill! Dwell there where there are thorny trees, where there are intoxicating creepers, and where the wife is devoid of marriage.
Wherein a house has five men, three women, and likewise three lineages.
It is dark and without fire; that is your dwelling place.
O unendurable one, dry up this house: it has one goat, two ewes, three cows, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants. (3.152.60)
The hoe, the sickle, and the basket; likewise, vessels such as cooking pots;
all implements, as well as the pestle and the mortar;
the bedstead for women, and whatever else was scattered here and there.

Your house, your dwelling place, is unclean and filthy. In it, the pestle and mortar are the women's seat, and the threshold is their place for counsel. Dwell in that house, O you who are so difficult to endure! (62–63)
O Duḥsaha, just as grains, both ripe and unripe, are trampled where they are kept in a house, so too should you roam at will among the students there.
Where fire is applied to the lid of a cooking pot by means of the handle of a ladle or a fruit-stick—
For in that house is the abode of all misfortunes without exception.
In whose house there is human bone, death dwells therein day and night; there your stay will be unbearable, as well as that of other rākṣasas.
Where Padma and Mahāpadma dwell, where there is a young woman who eats sweetmeats,
and where there are Vṛṣabha and Airāvata— abandon that house by all means.
Where there is a deity without weapons, yet [the protector] is armed without a battle.
They are imagined by men as objects of worship; therefore, abandon that temple.
Do not dwell in that house where the citizens and country-folk perform their long-established great festivals as they did before.

Go to those whose auspicious marks have been destroyed by bathing with water from a winnowing-basket fan, by the droplets of water used for washing clothes, or even by the water on the tips of their fingernails; they who observe local customs,
family duties, and festive rites.
A house devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, endowed with auspicious sacrifices;
a home possessed of purity and right conduct, esteemed by the world, always a refuge for worship—do not touch that house, O unbearable one, nor gaze upon those who dwell therein. (71–72)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, at the beginning, Brahmā gave a house to Duḥsaha for the sake of his residence;
indeed, Duḥsaha was accompanied by Adharma.
Duḥsaha’s wife was known by the name Malinī.
The daughter of Kali is skilled in strife and clings to the nature of affliction. Her sons are eight in number, and there are eight daughters who inspire fear:
Dantākṛṣṭi, Ukti, and Parivarta as the third.
Aṅgadhṛk, Śakuni, Gaṇḍaprāntarati,
Garbhahā, and Sasyahā— listen also to these names of the Kanyās.
Niyojikā is the first, and Virodhinī is the second.
She who seizes [the soul] herself, she who causes wandering, she who steals the seasons,
she who destroys memory, she who destroys the seed, she who creates enmity— the eighth—
and she who bestows fear; hear from me their respective functions among these.
The "tooth-puller" (*dantākṛṣṭi*) resides in the teeth of infants who have been born;
it causes the onset of fever. Its pacification is achieved by scattering white mustard seeds upon the bed and by wearing a linen garment.
Thus, one named Tathokti says: "Let there be the establishment of Duḥsaha;
however, for the sake of his pacification, Janārdana should be glorified with auspicious hymns.
Parivarta indeed effects the turning of embryos.
One should perform protection with Rakṣoghna mantras and white mustard seeds.
Indeed, when there is evil throbbing of the limbs, it causes trembling;
then, by the touch of Kuśa grass to that spot, cessation occurs.
And when a bird perched on a crow or other such bird always utters an evil omen, one should abandon the task and turn back.
Furthermore, at the end of the mark known as Gaṇḍaka, the Gaṇḍaprānta bird also dwells there.
All undertakings are indeed destroyed by the obstruction caused by the worship of the gods.

For one afflicted by the *gaṇḍa* [muhūrta], there is indeed dissolution through bathing with cow’s urine and mustard seeds, through the worship of the corresponding planets, and by performing festivals for the Dharma and other such rites. (84–85)
A destroyer of embryos or one who causes the destruction of embryos perishes through constant purification;
he is destroyed by means of divine mantras, garlands, and other protective rites.
A destroyer of crops, moreover, destroys the abundance of grain within the field.
Therefore, one should provide protection by wearing worn-out sandals; likewise,
by walking with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), by the entrance of a Caṇḍāla,
by offering the external bali-oblation, and by dwelling at the feet of the virtuous.
That which impels human beings toward theft, sexual misconduct, intoxicants, and the like,
one should pacify through association with the virtuous;
[this is achieved] by undertaking dharma such as initiation and the like, through vows, and by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites.

She indeed creates discord between husband and wife, and always causes strife among kinsmen, friends, parents, and sons. One should perform a propitiatory rite for her by following the conduct prescribed in the scriptures. 3.152.90–91.
A daughter who steals for herself even carries off grain from the threshing floor;
likewise, she takes away the milk from the cows and even the ghee from the milk;
she plunders the prosperity from the abundant wealth in the kitchen.
Likewise, she steals food that is half-cooked, as well as that which remains in the kitchen;
she steals the food while it is being served, and while one is eating, she eats half of it. Indeed, she likewise carries off the leavings of men.
She also steals the perfected elixir from the workshops of the manufactories;
she is a stealer of milk from the udders of cows and women at that very moment.
Likewise, she takes the ghee from curds, the oil from sesame seeds, and the liquor from the taverns.
One should also [prepare] the dye for safflower and other materials, as well as thread from cotton (96).
For the sake of pacifying that [obstacle], one should arrange an auspicious pair of peacocks and place an artificial woman there, both in the house and on the site (97).
Likewise, one should recite the protective mantra for Lakṣmī:
"O Lakṣmī, Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī, Lalitā, Kambharā, Sati!
Strike down the wicked thief; let the thief meet with destruction! (98)
Having prayed thus, one should cause [the substance] to be placed in the house, on a spot of ash, or in a cow-pen.
It is destroyed by the smoke, ashes, and other offerings of the fire-deities used in the *homa*.
Furthermore, another [substance] causes agitation among those dwelling in the same place.
For a man, however, that [spell] becomes a deluder that bestows suffering.
Therefore, one should provide protection for him with scattered white mustard seeds,
wherever that man sits— whether on a seat, a bed, or upon the ground.
Furthermore, that woman who steals the flowers of other women is a debtor-stealer;
she should perform ablutions at sacred fords, temples, shrines, and on mountain peaks,
as well as at river confluences and natural pools, for the sake of her pacification.
The physician should administer the best medicine appropriate for the season.
[This] indeed destroys the memory of women, for she is a destroyer of men's memory;
likewise, it is through resorting to secluded places and the worship of Lord Hari.

And by means of unctuous food and drink, there shall be a subsiding of that [disease]. Another [type], born from the transformation of the seed and the food, also takes away the virility and the *rajas*.
[One may overcome it] through the grace of Hari, by eating pure food, and by pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrtha*).

And its pacification is declared for one who holds the fruit of desire in his hand. One who is hated should offer sesame seeds mixed with honey, milk, and ghee into the fire for the sake of peace; one should perform the sacrifice to Mitravindā.
O Lotus-born One, I shall now describe the names and other details, such as the naming ceremony, for these sons and daughters, as well as their other offspring:
two daughters, Vijalpā and Kalahā, were born from the drawing out of teeth.
Both [of these] produce afflictions; peace must be established through the performance of fire oblations (homakarma).

(109) In the rite of offering (balikarma), one should scatter sprouts of dūrvā grass smeared with honey, ghee, and milk, and likewise offer them into the fire while reciting the name of Mitra. (3.152.110)
From Tathokti was born a son named Kālajihva, who oppresses the wicked.
Furthermore, from Rama were born two sons, Parivarta and Suta, who were deformed and hideous.
They took refuge in trees, moats, walls, and the ocean.
Therefore, one should not cause a pregnant woman to mount a tree,
a tower, a moat, a rampart, or the great ocean, for these things cause the destruction of the fetus.
O Lakṣmī, the son of Aṅgadhṛk was known by the name Piśuna.
For men who have conquered their minds, the strength resides in the marrow of the bones.
Among birds, there are those with five types of offspring: the hawk, the crow, the pigeon, the vulture, and the owl;
of these, the hawk is considered to bring about death.
The owl brings about death and bestows the state of a *rākṣasa*;
the vulture brings disease, and the dove leads one upon the path of Yama.
Furthermore, if hawks and other birds perch upon his head, [the same result follows]. (1.15–1.16)

A man should avoid a house whose roof is occupied by a pigeon. O beloved! if a hawk, a pigeon, a vulture, a crow, or an owl enters and dwells in that house, it shall announce the end for those living there.

Indeed, even in a dream, seeing a pigeon or similar bird is not auspicious. One should not approach a woman for sexual intercourse during the following times: when she is fond of the region of her cheeks, when she is menstruating, while residing on a Śrāddha day, or while residing on a festival day (parvan). 1.18–1.19.
The son of Garbha-ha is Nighna, and Mehinī is the daughter.
One enters the womb and devours it, while the other, having eaten it, causes delusion.
From that, children are born as frogs, tortoises, and reptiles.

Or else she indeed becomes feces; therefore, while she is pregnant, she should avoid the cremation ground, the burial site, and crossroads at night. She should avoid the shade of trees and must not discard her upper garment. 121–122.
And the son of Śasyahaṃsa, Kṣudraka alone, destroys one who desires prosperity.
On an inauspicious day, the field of the sower bears no fruit at all.
[Likewise] the daughters of Niyojikā—Mattonmattā and Pramattikā.
And these nine enter for the destruction of all embodied beings:
[the three] who, through unrighteousness and other vices, join others with the wives of men;
and the three sons of Virodhinī: Nodaka and likewise Grāhaka. || 1.24–1.25 ||
And that which is called "the obscurer of darkness" exists in a household devoid of right conduct;
the first [of these] sows slander, while the second, the "seizer," indeed takes hold of it.
The third generates anger through darkness, and these are all exceedingly painful.
O Rame! These three sons, begotten through theft, are themselves to be taken away:
the one who takes everything, the one who takes half, and likewise the one who takes the virility.
They dwell forever in a house of misconduct, a house of suffering.

The son of Bhrāmaṇī, named Kākajaṅgha, who was devoid of righteousness, took pleasure in it; he sang, ate, and indulged in laughter. Furthermore, there were three daughters: Kucahā, Vyañjanahā, and Jātahā.
If for a woman the proper marriage rite is not performed,
or if it is delayed beyond the proper time, then a certain [female spirit] seizes her two breasts;
likewise, if the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* has not been offered and the mother has not been honored.
Another [woman] steals the garment of a married maiden;
the third, however, [is found] amidst the fire, in a smokeless place, in a maternity chamber, devoid of lamps, weapons, pestles, living beings, and mustard seeds. (1.32)
Having entered, she seizes the newborn child, and that [child] perishes.
She is known as Jātahāriṇī, a most terrible flesh-eater.
Therefore, one must take great care to provide thorough protection in the lying-in chamber.
Smṛtihā was known by the name Pracaṇḍa, and Āttukāmana; Līka and Caṇḍaputra—they were all born from the womb of a Cāṇḍāla.
Indeed, the Līkas cause the lineage of unrighteousness to dwell and they carry it away.
One who destroys seeds strives for the destruction of seeds while devoid of purity.
The sons of an enemy reveal harm to men;
yet even a sinner may reveal his own virtues in the world. (1.36–1.37)
But the second [type] draws down the virtues and the benevolence established in the world.
Thus, all these are malevolent, by which the subjects encounter suffering.
Their pacification must be performed through various offerings and ritual honors.
Through sacrifices to the Raudras, Vaiṣṇavas, Daivas, Bhautas, and Cāṇḍikas;
through the worship of Hari with devotion, as well as by vows and propitiations; and through the special service of the virtuous and through wonderful, worthy offerings.
Thus has been told, O Lakṣmī, that which destroys the sins of the wicked,
as well as rites for pacification and other matters, and the portents occurring in connection with them.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Lineage of Dharma, the Description of the Lineage of Adharma, the Abodes of Duḥsaha, and the Description of the Calamities of the Descendants of Duḥsaha," etc., in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Which direction is considered best for a journey, and which is considered inferior? When is it deemed [auspicious]?
When is setting out most excellent, and at what time is what action auspicious? (1)
"When might there be an inauspicious conjunction of asterism, day of the week, and lunar day?
Tell me all that for the sake of the welfare of the world.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Kṛttikā has Agni as its deity; Rohiṇī has Brahmā as its deity;
Mṛgaśiras has Soma as its deity; and Ārdrā has Rudra as its deity.
(3) Punarvasu has Sūrya as its deity; Puṣya, however, has Guru as its deity.
Aśleṣā has the serpents as its presiding deity; Maghā, however, has the ancestors as its deity.
(4) O Lotus-born One, Pūrvāphālgunī should be known to have Bhaga as its deity; O Lotus-born One, Uttarāphālgunī should be known to have Aryaman as its deity. (5)
Hasta has Savitṛ as its deity, while Citrā has Tvaṣṭṛ as its deity;
Svātī has Vāyu as its deity, and Viśākhā has Indra and Agni as its deities.
Anurādhā has Mitra as its deity, while Jyeṣṭhā has Śakra as its deity.
Mūlā has Nirṛti as its deity; Pūrvāṣāḍhā has the Waters (Āpa) as its deity.
Uttarāṣāḍhā is proclaimed to have the Viśvedevas as its deity.
Abhijit has Brahmā as its deity, and Śravaṇā has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Dhaniṣṭhā has Vasudeva as its deity; Śatabhiṣā has Varuṇa as its deity;
Pūrvabhādrapadā and Uttarabhādrapadā have Aja-Ekapād as their deity;
Revatī has Pūṣan as its deity; and likewise, Aśvinī has the Aśvins as its deity. (9)
Bharaṇī and Yamadevā are declared to be the presiding deities of those constellations (ṛkṣa).
Brahmāṇī is established in the east on the first and ninth lunar days (tithi),
and Māheśvarī is in the north on the second and tenth lunar days.
On the fifth and the thirteenth, Vārāhī is situated in the south;
on the sixth and the fourteenth, Indrāṇī is situated in the west;
and on the seventh and the full moon day, Cāmuṇḍā is in the northwest.
On the eighth and new moon days, Lakṣmī is considered to reside in the northeast (īśāna).
On the eleventh and thirteenth days, Vaiṣṇavī is in the southeast (agnikoṇa);
on the twelfth and fourth days, the virtuous Kaumārī is in the southwest (nairṛta).
One should never engage in going or other such activities in the presence of the Yoginīs.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla,
Punarvasu, Puṣya, Hastā, and likewise Jyeṣṭhā— these bestow excellence upon setting out on a journey.
The five constellations beginning with Hastā, as well as the three Uttarās, are indeed [auspicious].
Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Punarvasu are excellent for putting on new clothes and also increase good fortune. (16–17)
Kṛttikā, Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Maghā, Mūlā, Viśākhā, and the three Pūrvās—these have their faces turned downward; indeed, tasks directed toward the lower regions should be performed under them.
These include the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as digging the earth and creating caves.

Dugging up a temple, digging for treasure, grass, calculation, the commencement of astrology, and entering a subterranean hole—one should perform these very acts; they will certainly succeed as undertakings directed toward the underworld. (3.153.20)
Revatī, Aśvinī, Citrā, Svātī, Hastā, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭhā— these are considered to be side-facing (pārśvamukha).
[Under these, there is] the taming of elephants, camels, horses, bulls, buffaloes, and cows.
One should perform the sowing of seeds and the launching of boats and the like;
likewise, the movement and arrival of wheeled vehicles, machines, and chariots [should be undertaken under these asterisms]:
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, Puṣyā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the three Uttarās. (22–23)
Śatabhiṣā and Śravaṇa—these nine are considered to be upward-facing.
Under these, one should cause the coronation for a kingdom and the binding of the royal fillet to be performed.
One should have all these [rituals] carried out under the upward-facing [asterisms].
The fourth, the sixth, the eighth, and likewise the ninth;
the new moon, the full moon, the twelfth, and the fourteenth—these are inauspicious. However, the first day of the dark fortnight and the second day on a Wednesday are auspicious. (25–26)
The third lunar day joined with Mars, the fourth with Saturday;
the fifth with Jupiter, and the sixth is auspicious when joined with Mars or Venus.
The seventh is situated with Mercury or the Moon, and the eighth is joined with Mars or the Sun. (27)
The ninth lunar day falls on Monday; the tenth, on Thursday.
The eleventh is pervaded by Thursday; the twelfth, on Wednesday.
The thirteenth falls on Friday and Tuesday; the fourteenth is excellent when it falls on Saturday. (28–29)
On a Thursday, both the full moon and the new moon days are to be understood as most auspicious.
The sun burns away the twelfth lunar day, while the moon burns away the eleventh.
Mars burns away the tenth, and Mercury burns away the ninth.
The preceptor (Jupiter) burns the eighth lunar day, and Venus burns the seventh;
Saturn burns the sixth, and indeed there is no journey on these days. [One should avoid travel] on the first, ninth, fourteenth, and eighth lunar days.
One should avoid setting out on a journey from afar on Wednesday. The sixth lunar day falls in Aries and Cancer; the eighth in Virgo and Gemini;
the fourth in Taurus and Aquarius; and the twelfth in Capricorn and Libra.
The tenth lunar day in Scorpio and Leo, and the fourteenth in Sagittarius and Pisces—these are "burnt" (dagdha) days; living beings, including humans, must not travel on them.
When the Sun is in the three stars of Viśākhā and the Moon is in the three stars of Pūrvāṣāḍhā... [34–349]
O Ramā! One should avoid the triad of Dhaniṣṭhā on Tuesday, the triad of Revatī on Wednesday, the triad beginning with Rohiṇī on Thursday, and the triad of Puṣya on Friday;
furthermore, one should avoid the triad of Uttarā-phālgunī on Saturday.
This is an ominous conjunction that brings about death, disease, and other calamities.
(37) The Sun is in Mūla, the Moon in Śravaṇa, Mars in Uttaraproṣṭhapadā, Mercury in Kṛttikā, and Jupiter, O Lakṣmī, in Punarvasu. (38)
Pūrvaphalgunī with Venus and Svātī with Saturn—
these are indeed the Amṛta-yogas, which accomplish all undertakings.
Five ghaṭikās in Viṣkambha and seven are proclaimed for Śūla.
In *ṣaḍgaṇḍa* and *atigaṇḍa*, and nine [units] in *vyāghāta* and *vajra*;
in *vyatīpāta*, *parigha*, and *vaidhṛti*— on every such day,
these *mṛtyuyoga*s must be avoided, for they cause the destruction of one's undertakings.

The Sun is auspicious in Hastā; Jupiter in Puṣya; Mercury in Anurādhā is favorable; Rohiṇī is excellent for Saturn; and Śatabhiṣaj is auspicious for the Moon. Revatī is excellent for Venus; and Aśvinī is favorable for Mars.
These are the Siddhi-yogas for you, which destroy all defects:
Bharaṇī on a Saturday, Citrā on a Monday,
Uttarāṣāḍhā on a Tuesday, and Dhaniṣṭhā when it falls on a Wednesday.
When Śatabhiṣā falls on Thursday, Rohiṇī on Friday,
and Revatī on Saturday, these are indeed considered Viṣa-yogas.
Puṣya, Punarvasu, Revatī, and Citrā [are likewise considered such].

Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Hastā, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśirā, and Śatabhiṣaj are also suitable for rites such as the birth ceremony (jātakarma). Likewise, Viśākhā, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Ārdrā, and Bharaṇī [are suitable]. (46–47)
Aśleṣā and Kṛttikā—these [nakṣatras] bring death during a journey.
Six periods (daśās) are to be understood for Āditya; fifteen are recorded for Soma.
Eight are to be understood for Maṅgala; seventeen are recorded for Budha.
The period of Saturn should be understood as ten years, and that of Jupiter as nineteen.
The period of Rāhu is twelve years, while that of Venus is twenty-one. The period of the Sun brings suffering and causes agitation and the destruction of the king. (3.153.50)
The period of the Moon bestows prosperity and likewise grants the enjoyment of desired food;
the period of Mars brings about suffering and leads to the destruction of sovereignty and other blessings.
The period of Mercury grants celestial women, bestows kingship, and increases the treasury.
The daśā of Śani causes the loss of kingdom and brings suffering to kinsmen.
(52) The daśā of Guru bestows sovereignty and grants happiness, dharma, and other blessings.
The daśā of Rāhu causes the destruction of kingdom, brings disease, and results in suffering. (53)
The period of Venus bestows elephants, horses, and the attainment of kingdom and women.
Aries is the domain of Mars, while Taurus is proclaimed to be the domain of Venus.
Mercury is the domain of Gemini, and the Moon is the domain of Cancer.
Leo is the domain of the Sun; Virgo is the domain of Mercury;
Libra is the domain of Venus; Scorpio is the domain of Mars;
Sagittarius is the domain of Jupiter; and Capricorn and Aquarius are the domains of Saturn. (55–56)
Pisces is the desired sign for Jupiter, yielding profit in trade;
when two full moons occur where there are two Pūrvāṣāḍhās,
that is known as Dvirāṣāḍha, and Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are auspicious for adornment.
For a journey, the deer, snake, monkey, cat, dog, pig, birds, mongoose, and mouse are auspicious when on the right side. ॥58-59॥
A Brahmin maiden, a corpse, an elephant, a conch shell, a kettledrum, the earth, a flute, a woman, and a full water-jar are auspicious sights during a journey.
Jackals, camels, donkeys, and the like are auspicious when appearing on the left side during a journey.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, oils, cooked food, charcoal, and serpents;
a woman with disheveled hair, one wearing a red garland, and a naked person—these are inauspicious omens.
A hiccup occurring in the east yields fruit, while in the southeast it bestows fever and grief.
In the south she is the giver of loss and the bringer of grief and torment;
in the southwest she is the giver of sweet food; in the west she is considered the bestower of wealth;
in the north she is the cause of quarrels; and in the northeast she would be the giver of death.
Having drawn the Sun in human form, one should place his asterism and the triad beginning with that [asterism] upon his head; three [stars] upon his face;
one each upon the two shoulders, the pair of arms, and the two hands.
One should place five in the heart, one in the navel, and also one in the secret place;
one each in the two knees, and the remaining ones one should apply to the feet.
A man whose nakṣatra is situated on the feet becomes short-lived.
If [the breath] is known to be located in the genitals, one travels abroad; if in the private parts, one has illicit relations with another's wife.

If it is situated in the navel, one is content with little; if in the heart, one becomes a great lord. If it is in the hands, one becomes a thief; if it has fallen from its place into the arm, one becomes a wanderer.

If the Moon is situated in the shoulder (skandha), one obtains sweet food in the mouth; if on the head (mastaka), one is enriched with silk garments—thus is the result according to the respective asterisms. The Moon in the seventh house of prosperity (upacaya) is excellent, as is the second-born [Moon] during the bright fortnight (śukla).
The fifth and the ninth [houses] also become givers of gain.
O Lotus-born One, listen: there are twelve conditions (avasthās) of the Moon;
indeed, the periods (daśās) occur in groups of three constellations, beginning from Āśvinī. 3.153.70–71.
In two and a half [periods], the first [daśā] brings about departure from home;
the second is considered to bring loss, and the third brings death.
The fourth daśā bestows victory, while the fifth brings laughter.
The sixth [stage] bestows the delight of play; the seventh bestows happiness and joy.
The eighth stage brings grief, while the ninth bestows enjoyment.
The tenth stage brings fever, and the eleventh stage brings trembling. (73–74)
The twelfth [lunar day] bestows stability, and its fruit is considered equal to that of the tenth.
[If Venus] is situated in the first house, it produces contentment; in the second, it destroys happiness.
In the third, it grants royal honor; in the fourth, it brings about quarrels.
In the fifth [house], he bestows a wife; in the sixth, he becomes a giver of wealth and grain.
In the seventh, he bestows pleasure and honor; in the eighth, he causes doubt regarding one's life.
In the ninth, he bestows the accumulation of a treasury; in the tenth, he grants success.
In the eleventh [lunar mansion] the moon bestows victory, and in the twelfth it brings death.
One should undertake a journey toward the east during the seven asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā;
one should go toward the south when starting from Maghā, and toward the west when starting from Anurādhā.
A journey during the seven asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā is always considered excellent for the northward course.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Citrā, and Dhaniṣṭhā are auspicious for assuming a disguise;
Mṛgaśirā, Aśvinī, Citrā, Puṣya, Mūla, and Hastā are indeed auspicious.
In the giving away of a daughter in marriage, on journeys, and in rites such as consecrations,
Venus and the Moon situated in the birth sign are always considered to bestow auspicious results.
The Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus indeed bestow auspicious results when situated in the second house.
In the third house, Mars, Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon are considered to grant auspicious results. Mercury is excellent in the fourth house; Venus and Jupiter are excellent in the fifth house.
Likewise, the Moon and Ketu are proclaimed to be excellent in the fifth house. (82–83)
Saturn, the Sun, and Mars are always considered excellent in the sixth house;
Jupiter, the Moon, and Mercury in the seventh; likewise Venus in the eighth;
Jupiter is excellent in the ninth; and the Sun, Saturn, and the Moon in the tenth. (84)
In the eleventh house all the planets [are auspicious], and in the twelfth, Mercury and Venus.
Capricorn is best with Leo, Aries is excellent with Virgo, Pisces with Libra, and Cancer with Aquarius. (85–86)
Taurus is favorable with Sagittarius, while Scorpio is favorable with Gemini;
in this way, everything indeed becomes conducive to affection and bestows auspicious results.
Starting from its very rising, the Sun establishes itself in each zodiac sign.
It proceeds for six [ghatikās] during the day and for six during the night.
In Pisces and Aries, there are likewise five ghaṭikās;
in Taurus and Aquarius, four; and in Gemini and Scorpio, three. (88–89)
Five *ghaṭikās* are proclaimed for Aries and Cancer, six for Leo and Scorpio, and seven for Libra and Virgo.
If the ascendant is Aries, she will be barren; if it is Taurus, she becomes a woman of passion.
In Gemini, she is fortunate; in Cancer, she becomes a courtesan.
In Leo, she has few sons; in Virgo, she is endowed with beauty. In Libra, she possesses beauty and prosperity; in Scorpio, she will be harsh.
In Sagittarius there will be good fortune; in Capricorn she will be one who goes to the lowly;
in Aquarius she will have few sons; and in Pisces she will be endowed with detachment.
Libra, Cancer, Aries, and Capricorn are the signs that move steadily.
Leo, Taurus, Aquarius, and Scorpio are considered fixed signs;
Virgo, Sagittarius, Pisces, and Gemini are of dual nature.
Departure should be made under a dual sign, while entry should indeed be made under a fixed sign. (94–95)
One should have the installation of a deity and the marriage ceremony performed on days of a dual nature.
Among the lunar days (tithis), Nandā, Bhadrā, and Jayā are excellent, while Riktā should always be avoided.
Nandā consists of the three lunar days: the first, the sixth, and the eleventh.
The second, seventh, and twelfth lunar days constitute the triad known as Bhadrā.
The eighth, third, and thirteenth lunar days constitute the triad known as Jayā.
The fourth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days constitute the triad known as Riktā. (97–98)
The fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days are considered auspicious when full.
Mercury is classified as *cara* (movable), Jupiter as *kṣipra* (quick), Venus as *mṛdu* (soft), and the Sun as *dhruva* (fixed).
Saturn is *dāruṇa* (terrible), Mars is *ugra* (fierce), and the Moon is *sama* (neutral).
One should set out with the *carakṣipra* (swift-moving) planets and enter [the city] with the *mṛdu-dhruva* (gentle and fixed) ones.
One should fight with the *dāruṇa-ugra* (terrible and fierce) ones; victory will surely follow, without a doubt.
The consecration of a king and fire rituals are recommended on a Monday.
Traveling, setting out on a journey, acquiring a home, and building a residence;
command of an army, heroic combat, and the practice of weapons—these are auspicious under Mars.
Accomplishing one's goals, counsel, and embarking on a journey—these are auspicious under Mercury.
Reciting [the Vedas], worshiping the gods, and providing clothing and ornaments for the preceptor;
giving a daughter in marriage, mounting an elephant, and sexual union with a woman—these are auspicious during the period of Venus (Bhārgava).
Installing [deities] and entering a new house, as well as tethering an elephant—these are auspicious during the period of Saturn (Śani).
Having thus observed all these factors, one should proceed with the commencement of any undertaking.
O Rame, through reading or hearing this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, the lunar days, and the astrological conjunctions [are likewise encompassed].
The ten houses, the omens, the hiccup-stations, the ascendants,
and the ghaṭikās— all these, contemplate them as my own form.
Indeed, for an embodied being, everything arises in accordance with their merit.
O Lakṣmī, when I am remembered there, and even when I am worshipped, fed, served, saluted, propitiated, and attended upon,
I bring about all good fortune; I make the distressed well-settled.
And having known Me, there is no destruction of one's purpose anywhere. (10.9) Everything is fruitful for the devotee, but for the atheist it is fruitless.
For the self-possessed, the fruit is supreme; for the one lacking self-mastery, it is inferior. (3.153.110)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Success or Failure of Actions Based on Specific Constellations, Yoginīs, Lunar Days, Planetary Periods, Omens, Hiccups, Locations, Ascendants, and Ghaṭikās," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

[The Author: Chapter 155.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of Sarojinī.
Formerly, there was a daughter of a potter who desired clay.
She would bring suitable earth for the making of all vessels, such as jars and the like, using donkeys and other beasts of burden. (1–2)
Accompanied by her mother, father, brother, and occasionally her sister,
that virtuous maiden, though fit for marriage, was not sought as a bride anywhere;
thus she remained in her father’s house, devoted to the life of celibacy.
Devoted to serving the elderly and dedicated to virtuous conduct and Dharma,
she was intent on her own duties and content with even the smallest things.
Having become such a presence in the home of the poor man, his desire did not increase.
Indeed, that virtuous woman lived endowed with natural contentment.
Then, in the course of time, her mother named Ghoṇāvatī, having been afflicted by fever, passed away and went to heaven; Sarojinī then lamented for her.
There is no happiness equal to that of a mother; there is no support like the birth-giver.
(7) For daughters, the mother always shines as heaven within the home.
Even for children who are destitute, the mother is considered their supreme wealth. (8)
Without first giving to her own children, the mother does not eat or drink;
she does not let the day pass without remembering her own offspring born of her.
Even when they are forgotten or during sleep, she calls out to her children.
Like gods, the mother nourishes [her offspring] and serves her own;
they remain right in the lap of the mother, for even among birds, nectar indeed resides there.
Even their eggs are nurtured at all times by the warmth of the mother's belly.
Even for a mere moment of separation, a mother finds no happiness;
yet that mother shall go to heaven today, even though her father is old.
He too, whose livelihood is dependent upon his son, shall likewise ascend to the celestial realm.
Therefore, I must always remain here, for it would be like dwelling with one's brother's wife. Indeed, even staying here without affection is perceived as hell.
What should I do now, and what must be done by me hereafter?
Thus, she remained perpetually sorrowful and devoid of passion.
Then, at the twelfth *śrāddha*, the venerable elders arrived,
along with their relatives, kinsmen, and those connected by marriage.
There, a desire was formed by one [man] specifically for the sake of Sarojinī.
Her father was informed, and he too gave his consent.
By the formal betrothal, that maiden was given to the potter.
Then, at an auspicious moment, the girl was married with great blessings by her father, named Cakradhvas, to one called Nāladharāya.
That maiden also became joyful and abandoned all sorrow entirely.
She went indeed to her husband’s house and, dwelling in happiness, enjoyed pleasures;
however, there were bodily marks on the girl that portended the loss of her beloved:
a beard, the length of her lips, and likewise a flat nose. (3.154.20)
When a woman with squinting eyes comes to the house and does not touch the ground with her big toes or her ring fingers, then at that very moment,
the husband falls ill with fever; having become emaciated, he indeed dies.
And she became a widow due to the defects of her physical marks.
Then, having reached her father’s house and protected by her brothers, childless and without support, she grieved for herself repeatedly. (22–23)
Again, after a year, requested by another potter,
she was married by her father and went once more to her husband's house.
There, in that happy home, she enjoyed even greater happiness than before.
But furthermore, due to the power of portents and the malefic influence of the planets,
her second husband, named Ratnaka, also died. Childless, she grieved repeatedly for that virtuous husband.
Lamenting her own misfortune, she returned once more to her father’s house;
then, her father also, his time having come to an end, fell under the power of death.
Thereafter, Sarojinī became dependent upon her brother.
After a year had passed, the third potter, her brother, gave her his desired daughter-in-law, Sarojinī;
she went to her husband’s house and spent that year there in happiness even greater than before. (28–29)
Then her third husband, named Lāladāsa, also died;
she grieved exceedingly in her mind, indeed reviling her own fortune. Then, having reached her brother's house, she lived there in constant sorrow.
Again, after another year, requested by yet another potter,
she was given away according to the prescribed rite by her elder brother and went indeed to the house of that husband.
She enjoyed happiness for only one year, and then even the fourth husband died.
Having returned once more to her brother’s house, childless and deeply distressed,
she spent her days in misery, dependent upon others.
Then one day, her brother’s wife, seeking refuse, gave her an order.
"Indeed, go to the boundary for the sake of fuel to cook the earthen vessels; bring together firewood, sacrificial logs,
leaves, stalks, pieces of wood, and stems for the purpose of the cooking pot."
At that very moment, Sarojinī became afflicted with fever and chilled by the cold;
she forbade her departure and fell asleep upon the ground.
Then her brother’s wife, becoming enraged, uttered insults.
Having heard this, she did not reply, for she was suffering from the pain of a fever.
When Sarojinī did not come even though she had been summoned,
then the brother’s wife went to the hut, took Sarojinī by the hand, and [led her away].
She also dragged her by force and commanded her to fetch firewood;
but the lotus-pond, afflicted by fever, cried out, "I will not go!
Then she struck her brother’s wife, and she in turn struck her, as they fought one another.
Then their battle took place, hair-to-hair and accompanied by shouting.
Even the neighbors, having heard of it, gathered at that house;
the family members arrived, as did the villagers and friends.
By means of various conciliatory words, they all pacified their distress;
yet then, enmity arose between them, ever increasing with the fury of their eyes. Indeed, from that point on, a constant battle of glares broke out between their two eyes.
Verbal quarrels with the Gālikās and even physical altercations arise.
Thus, as the days passed, her brother fell under the power of Time (died).
There was no protector for him; his brother’s wife, who had excellent sons, remained [without one].
He then forcibly expelled her from his own house;
she too, having abandoned the village while remaining in her mature state, lay down on the riverbank.
There, she saw a dream that was the cause of her former suffering.
In a previous birth, she saw her own mother, a rider on horseback, acting as a slayer.
In her own home, for the sake of sale, she would indeed kill a young goat;
having killed many such goats, she sustained herself.
Seeing herself as such a slayer, she died;
thereafter, she went to the city of Yama and experienced sufferings there.
Then, having become a female *piśāca* for exactly a thousand years, she remained so.
"I shall become Sarojinī, born in the house of a potter.
Having seen this very dream on the riverbank,
she then arose and understood it to be the fruit of her past actions.
For indeed, everything done previously is obtained later by all embodied beings.
Since goats were killed by me in the past, my boons are perishing;
all my husbands are dying because of my own actions.
"Therefore, having become a female mendicant, I must certainly go.
Having reflected thus upon the affliction of karma, the affliction of the planets, and that born of one's own nature,
and considering such suffering to be the fruit of past actions, she went to a hermitage of virtuous women in the forest.
There shines the divine renunciant Śrī Satīśvarī, a Vaiṣṇavī and celibate woman, accompanied by a thousand disciples;
her form consists of divine splendor and destroys sins through the mere sight of it. (54)
She was devoted to the worship of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
she was auspicious, endowed with the wonders of hearing and seeing from afar, and a remover of the suffering of others. She was intent on the practice of yoga and had conquered her senses. (55–56)
At that hermitage, men never enter at any time.
Some maidens are devoted to the fire-oblation and wear the sacred thread;
others are intent on meditation, dedicated to the offering of garlands and the chanting of prayers.
Some virtuous women were devoted to asceticism, their beauty enhanced by matted locks; some were naked, while others were devoted to dwelling among trees or clad in bark;
likewise, some wore garments of leaves, bamboo, or mats, and others were devoted to woolen blankets and the like.
All were devoted solely to Brahman, truthful, virtuous, and observant of vows dedicated to Kṛṣṇa;
they possessed manifest love for Kṛṣṇa and were intent upon the path of liberation.
Even the gods Vāyu, Sūrya, and Śaśin, as well as the fires, could not touch them.
Daughters accompanied them, and servants were in their dwellings.
Indeed, there was no natural enmity between the deer and the king of beasts;
there, desire, anger, and the like truly abandoned their inherent nature.

In that auspicious hermitage of virtuous women, youthfulness does not exist at all; rather, that which is present there is sattvic. In this place, they abide in a state devoid of the qualities (guṇas).
Indeed, the menstrual flow of these virtuous women has been dissolved through their ascetic penance.
The goddesses shine with divine bodies, like [the powers] in the sky of consciousness (cidambare).
There, the vessels of water, fire, and steam possess the union of cold and heat;
there, the supernatural powers (siddhis) exist through speech, resolve, and the mind. 64–65.
Some goddesses dwell in mountain caves, while others reside in huts;
some have made their abode in the sky and even sport in the firmament.
Some are knowers of the Vedas, and others are likewise performers of ritual actions.
Some were devoted to the Sāman hymns, some were awakened by the Ṛg verses;
some were constantly intent on knowledge, while others assumed many forms.
Still others remained established in meditative absorption; thus these virtuous women shone forth.
Having gone there, [he saw] Virūpākṣī, Kumukhī, Dīrghakādharā,
Romajaṅghā, Cipiṭikānāsā,
Cipiṭapādikā, Sthūlaghoṇā, Raktakeśā, Sūkṣmamukhī, and Kṛśastanī. (69)
Sarojinī, the daughter of the potter, being without refuge,
wandered at the very entrance of the hermitage where the deer roamed;
there, on the dust-covered ground, she rolled about, endowed with great majesty.
That sacred dust had indeed been rubbed upon her body;
seeing that holy devotee, yet with limbs that were inauspicious,
O Lakṣmī, the young maidens approached the sorrowful young woman.

Having bowed to all the young women, she went together with them to another hermitage where the virtuous Satīśvarī, the Guru, resided. Having offered her salutations, she wept and fell at the feet of the Guru.
Seeing her distressed and miserable, the virtuous mistress felt compassion and said to her,
"Do not fear," and likewise gave her bark garments.
When questioned regarding her circumstances, she understood that [her husband] had taken refuge in dispassion.
And having been protected among virtuous women, she manifested the purity of her body.
The mistress of virtuous women (Satīśvarī) granted her a monthly vow, as well as the practice of heating herself with five fires and subsisting on a diet of fruits and roots. || 76–77 ||
She constantly performed the recitation of my mantra a thousand times, always with one-pointed mind, thinking: "The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is my Lord and my husband. (78)
At the end of the month, having been satisfied by thirty thousand recitations, Śrī Satīśvarī summoned her and said, "Drink this water born of my grace.
Sarojinī drank the water, which was the nectar of the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (3.154.80)
Then she indeed manifested a divine form, equal to the sun;
she was like Lakṣmī, like Durgā, like Sāvitrī, and like Śacī.
She became endowed with the wonder of divine power and great sovereignty.
With the perfection of the divine eye, the divine ear, and the divine mind,
she shone in the midst of the virtuous women like a supreme string of pearls;
her entire body became like a divine lotus plant.
A most auspicious and supreme body, adorned with the marks of all the best six lines on its limbs, capable of traveling through the sky, and obtained through grace,
was born; indeed, by that very grace, she became the creator of the jar and the sustainer of Brahmā.

Then she constantly served the venerable Gaurī, the sovereign lady of the virtuous, through divine yoga and asceticism, by means of heaps of merit, and with many acts of service; thus she gratified Gaurī. (85–86)
Then Satīśvarī asked her, "Tell me your heart's desire;
O upholder of Brahman, what do you wish? I shall grant it to you.
Sarojinī then replied, "Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my husband."
May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be my Supreme Lord.
Standing at the soles of Lakṣmī’s feet, I shall serve the Supreme Lord;
wherever Lakṣmī is, there I shall dwell as her companion in yoga.
Without my beloved Lord of Lakṣmī, nothing else pleases my heart;
indeed, I desire only that liberation which consists of the state of being a servant through service. May I become fulfilled by attaining Him; therefore, act accordingly.
Then the virtuous Goddess said, "So be it," to Sarojinī.
She gave her two great mantras for the purpose of recitation:
"Oṃ, we know Mahālakṣmī; we meditate upon the wife of Viṣṇu."
May Lakṣmī inspire us.
(92) "Oṃ, let us know Nārāyaṇa; let us meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May Viṣṇu inspire us. (93)
Having obtained both mantras, she constantly recited them and worshipped them;
devoted to meditation and service, she was ever intent upon Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
At the end of a year, the two of them, being well-pleased, appeared before her within the range of her direct perception.

Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, having been born, said to Sarasvatī: "Tell us, what is it that dwells in your mind? That very thing shall be granted as a pair. Having heard this, she bowed with devotion and chose him as her boon.
"Standing at the soles of Lakṣmī’s feet, I shall always serve Hari.
"So be it," they both said, and they accepted the lotus.
Śrī and Rameśvara then created two forms of the lotus.
There was one divine lotus, rich with stalks and flowers, fragrant and celestial;
the second was in the form of a maiden, described as a *padminī*.
There, Hari indeed took that *padminī* by his own hand.
Then Sarojinī and Vallikā became his divine wives, equal to Lakṣmī and possessing the very form of Lakṣmī’s sister; they dwelt there in the midst of the water,
abounding in stalks and lotus petals, while Lakṣmī herself resided there forever.
Sarojinī was always rich in serving the feet of Lakṣmī.
From that time forward, O Ramā, Lakṣmī has always shone within the lotus;
purified by the dust of Lakṣmī’s feet, she serves Śrī Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, in former times Sarojinī became the sustainer of the world through constant devotion to her guru;
then, by devotion to her guru, she became the maker of the water-pot (the earth) and the upholder of Brahman.
By devotion to the Lord of Satīs, the planets and other celestial bodies were rendered free from affliction.
All the bodily marks, even those that bestow misfortune,
attained a reversal and subsequently became divine forms.
Thus, through constant devotion and the daily service of the virtuous, || 105 ||
Through the grace of virtuous women who know Brahman, one attains divinity;
through the sight of holy yogis, sins are destroyed on the spot.
By serving them, divine qualities that grant supreme liberation are obtained.
Furthermore, all obstacles such as untimely death and adverse karma that cause suffering—
indeed, they all come to dissolution through the fruit of service to the Guru.
Thus, malevolent planets become auspicious, and unfavorable times likewise become favorable.
The unfortunate becomes fortunate, and even the earthly body shines divinely;
the short-lived gains long life, and the poor attains wealth. Indeed, through service alone, even sins are transformed into merit.
"By reading, hearing, or even remembering this, that fruit [is attained]. (3.154.110).

Thus ends the chapter titled "The Description of how Kamalinī Vallikā—who was formerly the daughter of a potter named Sarojinī—after the death of her four husbands due to the sins of her previous birth, departed for the hermitage of the holy Satīśvarī out of renunciation; and there, through devotion to Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and service to her guru, after the destruction of planetary afflictions and physical defects, attained the true form of Kamalinī Vallikā as well as the state of the goddess named Padminī," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
Are those Manus who have been mentioned by you worshipped by the world?
"Tell me here, O Kṛṣṇa, how those fourteen [Manus] originated.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"The Manus are indeed portions of Me; in every Kalpa, there are fourteen."
They become lords of all kingdoms and promoters of the Dharma; even the sovereigns of the fourteen levels, who promote justice,
have all been appointed by me alone, and they carry out their respective duties.
Svāyambhuva, Svārociṣa, Auttami, Tāmasa,
as well as Raivata, Cākṣuṣa, and Vaivasvata is the seventh;
Sāvarṇi, Dakṣasāvarṇi, and Brahmasāvarṇi as well.

The lifespan of each Manu is said to be seventy-one [yugas] plus a fraction.

and the day of Brahmā is also more than a thousand [yugas].

At the end of more than two thousand [years], at dawn, the creation of the Dānavas shall occur;
from Pātāla up to Svarga, it shall consist of the ten worlds.
To the east, on the bank of the celestial river, there is indeed the Vaiṣṇava [abode] with many assemblies.
The righteous-souled and great ṛṣi Dharmatapā performed a sacrifice. I, Narāyaṇa, being pleased with that Dharmatapā,
granted him an excellent boon according to his desire.
Even within the state of worldly activity, he desired that auspicious cessation;
therefore, I first bestowed upon him the fruit of my asceticism, the fruit of my sacrifice, and the station of a Manvantara—he indeed became this Svāyambhuva Manu. (11–12)
The mind-born son of Brahmā, who was devoted to the protection of his subjects,
took the virtuous woman Śatarūpā as his wife.
Priyavrata and Uttānapāda were born as their two sons.
Then, on the bank of the river Varaṇā, there was a brahmin named Vāraṇa.
He had this thought: "I shall see the entire earth. Just then, a virtuous guest who traveled through the sky arrived at his house.

Having said this, he gave the medicine, ground into powder, upon his two feet.
Within half a day, the twice-born one traveled a thousand *yojanas* through the sky;
he went to the snowy mountain and descended onto the earth and water.
The foot-ointment produced from the supreme medicinal herb was washed away;
rendered unable to travel through the path of the sky, he remained upon the surface of the earth.
The preeminent Apsaras named Varūthinī beheld him.
She was bewildered and reflected within her heart on how she might serve him.
Having gone before him with supreme devotion, righteousness, vows, good character, and the conduct of a virtuous woman, she indeed served him.
The brahmin, being pleased, granted her a boon:
"O Prajāvatī, become possessed of sons and grandsons, honored by the three worlds.
Having thus bestowed this blessing, the brahmin likewise remembered me.
Having prostrated before the Gārhapatya fire, he spoke to it in a low voice:

Just as virtuous and saintly persons who have arrived as guests were served by me,
and just as Vedic rites were not neglected by me at their proper time;
and just as my mind never turned toward the wealth of others or the wives of others.
"By that truth, O Fire, through which the Supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa is eternally worshipped, carry me now indeed to my own home. As he was speaking thus, the Gārhapatya fire itself [appeared].
Then a ram-like being with wings appeared before him;
the twice-born one, having mounted its back, quickly reached his own home.
The army as well, having bowed to that brahmin, was accompanied by his blessings.
He obtained a divine Gandharva named Devakeli;
from him she conceived a child endowed with the luster of the Brahmins' blessings.
That boy was born radiant, like a blazing fire.
Because he shone with his own radiance (*svarocis*), he became known by the name Svarocis.
And Svarocis indeed ascended into the sky in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*).
As for that river Manoramā which belonged to the blue-lotus-eyed maiden—
In former times, O Goddess, the Vaiṣṇavī became [the wife] of the Gandharva through her ascetic penance.

having made him her lord, the river went to his abode with him.
Together with her, by means of a celestial chariot, [he traveled] through forests and groves.
