As she approached his side, he touched her with his right hand. (35–36)
That doe, having vanished, was indeed born as a divine goddess;
then, overcome with wonder, he addressed her, saying, "Who are you?
And she said to him, "I am the deity of this forest."
"I have been requested by the gods and sent to you; I stand here before you. "O great-minded one, Manu must indeed be produced by you through me.
Having been addressed thus, Svarociṣ himself took her as his own beloved.
And upon her, he then begot a son of great splendor.
At the very moment of his birth, celestial instruments resounded;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the throngs of Apsaras danced.
The father gave the boy his own name, Svārociṣa.
O Lakṣmī, Svārociṣa shall be the second Manu;
he whose presiding deity is the knowledge named Padminī is indeed Lakṣmī herself.
He learned from her entirely those foundations and treasures,
by which the treasures such as the *padma* and others on the earth are clearly known through the grace of the deities and by attending upon the virtuous. (43)
And wealth bestowed by the treasures increases even in the human realm.
Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Kacchapa,
Mukunda, Nandaka, Nīla, and Śaṅkha— these are the treasures of Manu.
In his very home, there were always those who fulfilled every desire:
wealth, jewels, weapons, elixirs, musical instruments, and minerals;
grains, articles of enjoyment, and ornaments—these divine things were ever present for Manu.
Now listen to the beautiful third mantra, that of Lakṣmī.
There was a son of Uttānapāda named Uttama by name;
he was the renowned son of Suruci, who shone with the prowess of the sun.
That knower of dharma married a woman of the Bābhravya lineage named Bahulā;
devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, he went together with her to see Śeṣanārāyaṇa and worshipped the illustrious Narāyaṇa.
She also worshipped the rest, and she indeed worshipped Śeṣa’s daughter.
She gave ornaments to that auspicious lady, and she was truly pleased.
Kalyāṇī, the daughter of Śeṣa, then bestowed an auspicious blessing upon her.
"A son of great heroism shall be born to you from this wife;
he will be a wise lord of a Manvantara, possessing an unimpeded and excellent wheel.
Then, when the time had come, the king obtained a son, the best of sons.
The celestial drums resounded and a rain of flowers fell.
The assembled sages gave him the name Auttama;
since he was the son of Uttama, he became renowned by the name Saudauttama.
The sages and gods shall establish him in the status of Manu.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall speak of the fourth Manu; listen to him.
There was a king on earth, renowned and powerful, named Svarāṣṭra.
Indeed, he performed austerities for a long time on the banks of the Vitastā.
His wife, a virtuous queen who was a yoginī capable of assuming any form,
became a doe and dwelt constantly in the forest in the vicinity of the king.
Devoted to the life of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the king heard a voice from the sky:
"O King, by the power of her asceticism, a divine son shall indeed be born to you from this woman Utpalā; he shall be named Tāmasa Manu. (568)
"Therefore, bestow seed upon her for the sake of benefiting the world.
Upon hearing this, the king granted union to the menstruating Utpalā; yet, by mere touch, Utpalāvatī conceived a child.
Then that Utpalāvatī, having the body of a doe, gave birth to a son. Then all the sages, having gathered together in the forest at that time,
beheld his mother, who was indeed a dark-colored doe.
"Let this fourth Manu be known by the name Tāmasa.
Having quickly propitiated the Sun,
he obtained all the divine weapons, including those of destruction, in their entirety.
O Rame! Manu, known as Tāmasa, will shine forth having become a Manu.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I tell you of the fifth Manu.
There was a highly fortunate sage named Ṛtavāk.
At the end of Revatī, he had an unfortunate son whose diseases increased.
Because of him, even that king of sages contracted a long-lasting illness. Ṛtavāk said to Revatī: "By means of your yoga, my son [has been afflicted]. (65–66)
"O Revatī, you who have been born as a giver of disease due to your immoral conduct, fall down quickly! When he had thus uttered this curse,
the constellation Revatī fell indeed upon my region of Vastrāpatha, on Mount Kumuda in Saurāṣṭra.
And due to its falling, that mountain Kumuda became known as Raivataka.
On Mount Raivata, that maiden Revatī was born from a lake;
and the king of sages named Pramuca [found] the girl near his hermitage.
He indeed took up and nourished the girl as soon as she was born. Then, after some time, a king named Durgama arrived there and summoned his beloved, Revatī.
Then Pramucu gave his daughter to Durgama.
There, by the power of his asceticism, he made the constellation Revatī join with the Moon in the sky, just as before; and then he spoke to his son-in-law: ||| 71–72 ||
"O protector of the earth, let that which pertains to your marriage be told; what may I give you?
The king said, "Out of favor toward you, O sage, I choose a son as my mantra.
The sage replied, "So be it; thus shall a son become your mantra."
Taking her with him, the king went to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake.
Having bathed there, worshipped me, and bowed to the sage Lomaśa,
he proceeded from Durgama to the city of Durganagara on the bank of the Gaṅgāvatī.
Then, from Revatī, a son was born named Raivata Manu;
in another kalpa, the son of the Sun, Revanta, will also come to be.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, this Raivata shall be the fifth Manu.
Thus has the sixth Manu been described to you; now listen as I speak of him.
O beloved, he was born in a previous birth from the supreme Cakṣuṣa, and for that reason, he is known as Cākṣuṣa even in this present birth.
Remembering his past lives, he was born there, resting upon the lap of his mother,
the wife named Giribhadrā, who belonged to a kṣatriya lord of the earth.

Having placed that child born there in the house of the queen named Vikrāntā, the wife of King Haimi, she took him and departed. Having placed the royal boy in the house of the Brahmin Bodha, she took that infant [of the Brahmin].
The Rākṣasī even carried off the child of the Brahmin and devoured him.
Thus, although he had been raised on the queen’s couch in the royal palace,

Brahmā, having approached him while he was performing most intense austerity, spoke to him as he turned him away from his penance: "O Cākṣuṣa!
He then appointed him as the sixth Manu; thus, he shall become the sixth Manu.
Now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I declare to you the mantra of the seven [names]:
Ravi’s wife, renowned as Saṃjñā, was the daughter of Viśvakarman;
he begot upon her the auspicious son Vaivasvata. (85)
O Lakṣmī, this Vaivasvata shall indeed be the seventh Manu;
because he is born of a woman of the same lineage (savarṇa) as his predecessor, he is renowned as Sāvarṇi.
Now, O beloved Nārāyaṇī, listen as I speak of the eighth Manu.
In the previous Svārociṣa Manvantara, there was a king named Suratha.
Defeated by his enemies in battle, he went to the forest in sorrow.
Then, a sorrowful Vaiśya named Samādhi arrived there.
Seeing him distressed, the king asked, "Why do you grieve?
The Vaiśya replied to the monarch: "I lived happily in your kingdom;

Deprived of wealth, wives, and sons, having taken my riches,

"Is there well-being or is there ill-fortune now in the homes of my women, my kinsmen, my daughters, and my householders? How are they?

The king said: "Since you have been cast out by those—your wife, children, and others—why does your mind continue to cling with affection to them?
The merchant said: "It is so; nevertheless, my mind is still pained."

What indeed can I do? For even my illusory mind runs toward them—those who, greedy for wealth, cast me out after abandoning affection for their father and the love due to a husband and kinsmen, even though I was devoted to them. (95–96)
I know them to be perverse, yet even knowing this, I do not abandon them;
for my heart is inclined toward love even for kinsmen who are devoid of virtue.
On their account, sighs and dejection arise within me.
What cruel act could I possibly do toward those who are displeased with me?
(98) Some living beings are blind by day, while others are blind by night;
some living beings have equal vision both by day and by night. (99)
Even those possessed of knowledge are born blind with delusion and suffer from misery upon misery;
even beasts and birds are likewise devoid of self-interest.
Men, like deer, undergo suffering for the sake of wives and children.
Indeed, through illusion (māyā), they wander in the pit of possessiveness and the whirlpool of delusion.
But this very [illusion], when directed toward the devotees of Viṣṇu, is considered the bestower of boons for the sake of liberation.
That is the supreme, eternal knowledge which serves as the cause of liberation.
She is indeed the cause of bondage to saṃsāra for those who lack devotion, and she is the deluder of the ignorant.
She is eternal; she is truly the Mother of the World and will become the Soul of the World.
And in the form of yogic sleep (yoganidrā), she also manifests within the realm of Viṣṇu.
"Through austerity, Māyā is mastered and she even becomes a bestower of liberation.
Thinking thus, O King, those two Vaiśyas, acting together for the sake of knowledge,
performed intense austerity while remembering Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī.
And Lakṣmī, accompanied by Nārāyaṇa, granted them her vision;
she bestowed a boon upon the king, saying: "After you die, you shall obtain birth from Sūrya as the Manu named Sāvarṇika."
"This Vaiśya shall be possessed of knowledge, as well as wealth and happiness.
Having thus granted them the boon they desired, Lakṣmī,
being praised by them with devotion, immediately vanished from sight.

Thus, having obtained this boon from Lakṣmī, Suratha, the best of Kṣatriyas and son of the Sun, shall become Sāvarṇi, the eighth Manu. Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Birth and Other Details of the Eight Manus," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 155, Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā/Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga),
Chapter 156 [[Author: → Chapter 157.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O beloved Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the ninth mantra.
There was once a king named Dhanavarman in the small kingdom of Surāṣṭra.
Seeing other great kingdoms, my mind was always filled with anxiety:
"I am not a sovereign king adorned with ornaments; I am but a petty ruler of a small village.
Without fame and imperial sovereignty, there is truly no peace in my heart. (2)

"Therefore, I shall indeed exert effort incessantly for the sake of sovereignty. (3) Having reflected thus, he departed from his own village together with his wife, sons, and kinsmen, proceeding to the banks of the Aśvapaṭṭa for the purpose of a pilgrimage and likewise for ascetic practice. (4)
Having gone to the hermitage of Lomaśa, he bowed at his feet before him;
once a seat was offered, he sat down and was asked about his welfare.
He replied to Lomaśa, "I am well by your grace."
The village, sons, daughters, wife, cattle, fields, and farmers—
may all these indeed be well through your grace, O Guru.
Yet my heart remains unsatisfied with this petty kingdom of a village, as if it were a mere trifle.
He desired a great kingdom and requested a vow for its attainment.
Having heard this, Śrī Lomaśa first gave him the body-purifying vow,
and then bestowed upon him the supremely meritorious mantra of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He said: "O King, perform supreme penance here in this mango grove at the foot of a tree, worshipping the Lord.
Possessing good austerity, good recitation, and great devotion, endowed with long-standing fortitude, together with your wife, sons, and others, perform the highest penance! (3.156.10)
Homeless, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits, free from passion, sleeping upon the ground, possessing the character of Brahman, and living without possessions;
they constantly performed their ablutions at the three periods of the day and offered worship daily.
"Oṃ anādi-śrī-kṛṣṇa-nārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
(12) May all those devoted to this mantra perform their penance here for one year;
thereafter, for another year, may they be reciters of the Lakṣmī-gāyatrī here. (13)
"Oṃ, may we know Mahālakṣmī and meditate upon the consort of Viṣṇu;
may that Lakṣmī inspire us. Let this [mantra] be recited for a year.
Śrī Hari will swiftly grant the accomplishment of one's desired goals.
Having been addressed thus, they bowed to their preceptor and worshipped him with pure devotion.
(15) Having bathed at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, they went to the mango grove.
There, in the forest, they spent a month, a year, and likewise another half-year, performing austerities. (16)
O Lakṣmī, being pleased at that time, I went toward them along with you; I came into their sight before them, and Dhanavarman attained great joy. His entire family bowed to me with great haste.
Urged by me for the purpose of granting his desired boon, the king quickly honored him according to the custom of hospitality and requested an excellent boon:
a supreme sovereignty that surpassed all other human kings. (18–19)
"I have granted you the sovereignty renowned among men, saying 'So be it.
O Dhanavarman, together with your family, you shall become the great Manu. For you will be Sāvarṇa, the son of Dakṣa, who is to be the ninth Manu."
"Indeed, you shall be known by the name Dakṣasāvarṇi for seventy-one [kalpas];
dwell for that long in the heavenly world with your own independent realm.
As soon as this was said, right there appeared a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the sun.
Resounding with the songs of gods and apsarases, that beautiful [place] came to you on earth;
meanwhile, out of compassion for me, the king passed away along with his family.
Possessing a divine body, he went to heaven as the independent lord of the stars.
"When the time has arrived, he will indeed become Dakṣasāvarṇi Manu.
(24) Thus, O Lakṣmī, the ninth Manu has been described to you;
now I shall describe to you the tenth Manu, Brahmasāvarṇika. (25)
She set her mind upon a certain dull-witted Brahmin named Brahmasāvarṇi, who was living on the shore of the Bālakṛṣṇa lake:
"I shall perform extensive penance; what happiness indeed is there here in the state of a Brahmin? (26)
"The kingdom exists in supreme happiness, filled with all enjoyments.
Having reflected thus, the dull-witted Brahmin named Balīśvara himself remained constantly dwelling in the water of a lake for ten years.

While meditating, he became [aware of] me, the Lord of Śrī, his beloved master. I, seeing him established in samādhi—my devotee whose veins had been consumed by a fish and whose entire skeletal frame was covered with moss—[approached]. (29)
And in order to rescue him, I went into his presence together with you.
Having entered within, I raised up that lord of the Bālīs;
he possesses neither skin, nor a network of vessels, nor sense organs. || 3.156.30-31 ||
How would he see, hear, touch, or speak?
How would he stand or move? Whence would there be the movement of the vital breaths?
There is no blood, nor marrow, nor belly, nor cavities.
Having entered the body of this devotee who is thus situated within me at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra),
I established the constituent elements within that cage;
nourished by me, they became the sinews, marrow, and so forth.
All the channels (nāḍīs) there were also renewed by me;
blood was filled therein, and subsequently, the hair grew forth.
His body was covered with skin and endowed with the senses, vital breaths, and the mind.
Having perfected his meditation, he emerged from within and went outside.
As soon as he rose from the water, he saw me standing before him—
the glorious Supreme Self— bestowing that [boon] upon him.
He too, beholding me as Hari, requested the fruit of his asceticism;
he indeed worshipped me repeatedly with mere water and with his heart, saying:
"O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Siddhi, O Lord of the Universe!"
"O Lord of Māyā, O Lord of lords, O Lord of kings, O Master!
Grant me here a great kingdom and also the status of a Brāhmaṇa forever.
"So be it," I said, and this boon was granted to that high-souled one.
He fell at our feet and offered auspicious lotuses at our feet;
he drank the nectar of our feet.
Indeed, food consisting of milk was prepared and offered by us both.
Having quickly drunk water like the King of Videha,
that sovereign of devotees, having cast off his body, indeed arrived in the sky with me and you in a celestial chariot, for he possessed a divine body. || 42-43 ||
Offered by me to the gods, he dwells even in the world of the gods.
Then, after some time, having attained the status of a son to Brahmā,
he himself will become the Manu known as Brahmasāvarṇi.

"O Lakṣmī, by the power of my worship and through austerity, he shall indeed attain supreme humanity, endowed with both Brahminhood and kingship. Now, O Lakṣmī, listen as I declare the eleventh mantra. 45–46.
Formerly, there was a farmer belonging to the Vaiśya caste named Dharmasāvarṇi, who was devoted to righteousness and supported a family consisting of a host of deities.
Born in the land of Surāṣṭra, he was renowned by the name Ānandavarṇin.

He practices devotion to the Blessed One and exerts himself in celibacy (brahmacarya). Always remaining one whose vital energy is drawn upward (ūrdhvaretas), he dwells even in the tiger-infested forest on the bank of the Soḍhu river, seeking refuge under a śiṃśapā tree.
With great dispassion, he performed the recitation (*japa*) of Śrī Hari;
for ten years there, he consumed only sugar-cane stalks as food.
Then, indeed, through fierce austerities, he propitiated me, Acyuta.
He finds no sleep and even abandons deluding illusion.
"Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe!
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrī Puruṣottama! (51–52)
Thus he constantly cried out and chanted the name of the illustrious Narayana.
Twenty years passed happily for him as he performed this recitation.
Then that farmer, Devanika, became intent upon meditation.
On the full moon day of the month of Śārada,
when the lunar splendor was exceedingly beautiful, he beheld me— divine, with a face like the full moon— arrived there in that forest of level ground near a śiṃśapā tree.
Rising suddenly, the Vaiśya fell at my feet;
he worshipped me with auspicious flowers and such, as well as sugarcane, tubers, and roots. Urged by me, he also requested a boon.
"May you attain the status of a Brahmin, divinity, great sovereignty, and all prosperity.
When he had been addressed by me thus, he was dissuaded from the exhaustion of ascetic toil and went to the great sacred field of Aśvapaṭṭa, the hermitage of the venerable Lomaśa.
I and Adṛśyabhāva both returned to our own abode.
Then Devānīka, dwelling in the family of a sage, took refuge in me;
and in due time, casting off his body, he went to the auspicious realm of Truth.
That highly meritorious Brahmin,
the son of Dharma, was born in the abode of Dharma as the mind-born son of Brahmā, who upheld righteousness;
he belonged to that lineage of mine in the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
Worthy of your worship, they dwell indeed in the vast region of Saurāṣṭra;
likewise in Jālāyana, Sauvīra, Sārakaṭa,
Gairika, Gokṣura, and Kṣārapāṭa— there my ancestors truly reside.
That Devānīka, the son of Dharma, by his own masses of merit and through my will,
shall indeed attain the status of a Brahmin and the rank of Dharmasāvarṇi;
having thus attained these, he shall become the eleventh Manu, a lord of kings.
For that duration of time, he shone in the Hall of Dharma in Satyaloka.
Now, O Lakṣmī, my dear, listen as I speak of the twelfth Manu.
On the unbroken surface of the earth, on the bank of the Nārāyaṇī, the compassionate one dwelt.
There was a Śūdra named Ghṛṇeṣika, who was devoid of righteous deeds;
he was intent on maintaining his family and especially subsisted by catching fish.
Once, there occurred a rain that caused the waters to overflow their banks.
Then, like the great river Nārāyaṇī spreading out here like the ocean,
the floodwaters indeed swept away house after house and village,
carrying them off; even a Śūdra, together with his wife and sons and accompanied by his home, was being carried along.

Then, as if upon a boat in the midst of water, that small wooden house floated in the water with its foundation intact. At that time, he offered praise to Rudra for the sake of his own protection. (3.156.69–70)
If, having regained my life, I should obtain the state of being at home,
I shall indeed always perform the auspicious worship of Rudra together with my kin;
I shall avoid fish and I shall certainly not commit violence.
"Out of devotion to Rudra, I shall subsist on wild roots, fruits, and the like;
I shall perform only my religious duties. May the husband of Satī protect me!
Having thus made this vow, he remained with his family at home by the water.
She performed worship to Rudra, who was in her own form:
"O Hara, remove my distress; O Lord of Satī, remove my suffering and protect my life!
O Mahādeva, O Mahākāla, you who possess the nature of Brahmā and Viṣṇu! (74)
"Victory to you, O Śambhu! Victory, O Rudra! Victory, O Lord of Śrī Pārvatī! Victory!
You are the protector at the time of death; I am yours, so grant me life! Thus did he perform his worship, absorbed in Him along with his family. (75–76)
By the will of Rudra, his boat, which was upon the water, reached the shore.
When the floods subsided, he too emerged from the house onto the ground;
having descended, he went a great distance to where the city of Śrīvana was located.
Then he sustained his livelihood by begging for alms such as vegetables and other food.
Thereafter, accompanied by his family, he went to a forest region on the outskirts and propitiated Rudra, setting aside his own wicked qualities.
Thus five years passed for him while he subsisted solely on fruits and roots; then Rudra arrived,
accompanied by Satī, exceedingly gentle, like a great forest-dwelling yogi.
He said, "O compassionate one, how do you fare in the forest? What is your desire?
[The other replied,] "I am Rudra; speak, and I shall grant you whatever you wish, for I am pleased by you.
Then Ghṛṇeṣika chose the status of a son and also sovereignty.
"So be it," Hara replied, and having received the worship,
he vanished. At the end of the year, Ghṛṇeṣika, along with his family,
abandoned his body due to fever and, becoming a divine attendant, went to the Kilaśaka [heaven].

Where Rudra Mahādeva, the husband of Satī, shines resplendent—there the son of Rudra was born and always dwelt in the abode of Rudra. He shall become Manu Rudrasāvarṇi, the possessor of imperial sovereignty and its enjoyments. (84–85)
Thus has this twelfth Manu been described to you.
O Lotus-born One, hear now of the thirteenth Manu, Devasāvarṇi.
Formerly, there was a Brāhmaṇa on the bank of the Dīnā river in Ketumāla.
The Vaiṣṇava is devoted to the portions of the sacrifice and other such rites, and is a worshiper of the gods.
With the sixteen and other ritual services, he indeed worships Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Satī, Hara, and Gaṇeśa; he likewise gratifies the ancestors with libations.
In sacrifice, he constantly gratifies the gods with clarified butter and other offerings;
I am pleased with him, and I became present within the scope of that sacrifice.
To grant him a boon, I restrained him, and he requested the most excellent of boons.
"Grant me sovereignty for the sake of your worship, and likewise for the sake of the worship of the gods;
and at the end, grant me the station of Brahman for my sacrificial journey.
"So be it," I said, and the boon was granted to that great-souled one.
Having granted a boon to him named Sudharman, I indeed vanished. He too, having cast off his body, was born as a son named Deva in the house of the patriarch Ruci by Mālinī. ||92||
O Lakṣmī, he will become the Manu named Devasāvarṇi, the son of Raucya.
Then, all the deities together shall establish him in the office of Manu for this thirteenth Manvantara.
Ruci was indeed the son of Brahmā; he lived the life of a religious student (brahmacarya).
Then his ancestors said to him, "O dear son, enter the householder's state (gārhasthya).
For by means of a son, there shall indeed be the deliverance of the ancestors, as well as their satisfaction. (95)
Then he performed the *śrāddha* rites and indeed established the life of a householder.
Upon Mālinī, he begot a son, the Manu Raucya;
this very one shall be the thirteenth Manu, possessed of great strength.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Previous Birth Stories of the Manus from the Ninth to the Thirteenth," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 157 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) — Chapter 157
[The Author: Chapter 158.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: The wise Prajāpati Ruci, though unwilling, [approached] the beautiful woman.
He undertook the life of a householder; tell that to me in detail.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, how he attained the state of a householder.
He protected the virtues of the ascetic while yet attaining the duties of the householder.
O Lakṣmī! Ruci lived free from all attachments, devoid of possessiveness and egoism, sleeping little and eating sparingly. (2–3)
Seeing him without a fire, without a dwelling, taking food only once a day, without a hermitage,
and free from attachment, his ancestors spoke to Ruci: "O child,
why do you not take a wife?"
It is meritorious, purifying, bestowing happiness, righteous, and the means for attaining heaven and other realms.
(5) It is auspicious, destroying debts, granting liberation, bestowing family fame and gain, the destroyer of bondage, and that which causes the exhaustion of all latent impressions. (6)
Accompanied by his wife, through service to all the gods, the ancestors, the virtuous, the sages, and guests, one attains heaven. Therefore,
you [must discharge] that debt to the gods, the debt to the ancestors, and likewise the debt to the sages.
Day after day, you shall incur bondage even without a wife.
O son, without the birth of a son, without the gratification of the gods, and without the satisfaction of the sages, you will certainly not attain the supreme goal. (8–9)
The affliction that exists in taking a wife is greater than that which exists without a wife;
this is true both in this world and in the next. Therefore, my son, become a householder.
Even for one who has no wife, performs no sacrifices, and lacks a lineage, [there is still suffering].
"The deceased surely goes to hell; therefore, my son, become a householder.
Having heard this, Ruci replied to his ancestors with auspicious and righteous words:
"O ancestors, I consider your command to be authoritative; I shall do as you say, even as I offer my salutations to you."
"Celibacy is the very form of Brahman, equal to Brahman, and the giver of liberation.
Therefore, I desire liberation; heaven does not appeal to me at all.
Having thus attained this realization, I took a wife.
It is held that [the worldly life] leads to evil, afflictions, extreme suffering, distress, disease, and a downward rebirth.
(14) The restraint of the self, the senses, and other principles is considered the giver of liberation;
this [restraint] would not exist for one who has taken a wife and is overwhelmed by lust and passion. (15)

The mire of karma, born from the union of the doer and the deed, increases as a latent impression (*vāsanā*). This mud of action, accumulated over many births, remains satisfied even when this self is cleansed by bathing in the sacred ford of Brahman (*brahmatīrtha*) and other such means. (16)

The wise should indeed wash [the mind] with the water of meditation, devotion, and so forth. O ancestors, I wash away the long-accumulated mud consisting of latent tendencies; being devoted to celibacy, I make myself fit [for liberation]. 17–18.
"Indeed, I am able to effect your deliverance;
by the power of celibacy alone, I shall cast off my bonds and my faults.
When this was said, the ancestors replied, "O son, that is indeed fitting and so it shall be."
The path to liberation is indeed celibacy; of this there is no doubt.
(3.157.20) In the past, obstacles were encountered on that path: sins, inauspiciousness, and evil impulses;
as well as egoism, possessiveness, illusion, and countless other karmic actions. (21)
All deeds performed in the past, whether meritorious or non-meritorious, which were intended for experience, must be completely washed away right here.
While experiencing those [fruits], washing them away, and performing no new karma that is devoid of qualities, one should proceed.
Abandoning bondage for the sake of liberation by surrendering everything to Kṛṣṇa—(23)—for one who conducts their journey here [in this world], no further bondage arises;
there is the completion of past karma and the fruit of unimpeded liberation. (24)
In this way, O son, the cleansing of actions is appropriate through gradual performance.
This lack of discernment, which produces the mire of sin, is certainly not to be counted [as a virtue], my son.
Therefore, having taken a wife, enjoy [life], renounce [worldly attachments], and liberate yourself.
"Having performed the supreme service, go to the eternal, imperishable [state].
Having heard these words of her father, Ruci said to the ancestors:
"The path of action is indeed ignorance; do not involve me in that. (26-27)
"Ignorance and action are both equally hellish;
freedom from action is declared to be perfection, and I shall achieve that freedom from action.
Having heard this, his ancestors spoke this true reply:
One should perform such action by which knowledge is acquired.
Through knowledge, that which is called ignorance or lack of wisdom shall go to dissolution.
O son, by the non-performance of prescribed duties, one nourishes ignorance and lack of wisdom.
Furthermore, the non-performance of what is prescribed and the performance of what is forbidden leads to bondage.
If one were to maintain restraint regarding the non-performance of the prescribed, that too would be a destruction of dharma.
It would not lead to liberation; rather, in the end, it causes a downward rebirth.

It is not a washing away of sins; on the contrary, it is merely their acquisition. (22) One is completely consumed by the sins arising from the non-performance of prescribed duties. Therefore, one should perform auspicious acts that are prescribed for the purpose of preventing the occurrence of such transgressions. (33)
Since the householder's life is ordained to follow the life of celibate study, O son,
if that duty is like poison, then it is a remover of poison;
by means of the "poison" of the householder's state, destroy the "poison" of transgression.

Having fully fulfilled the life of a householder, O son, destroy that poison of the forest-dweller by means of renunciation; thereafter, always destroy the poison of the forest-dweller through the attainment of self-surrender to Brahman, and abandon the body, senses, and so forth.
"Therefore, abandon the sense of self-identity through absorption in the Supreme Self.
Having ascended this sequence in this manner, achieve the supreme ascent.
Having spoken thus, all the ancestors became invisible and departed for their own abode.
Having reflected with a resolute mind, Ruci set his heart upon taking a wife.
Remembering his father Brahmā, he performed further austerities.
Brahmā, having approached him, said to Ruci: "You shall become a Prajāpati."
Having created progeny, obtained sons, and performed Vedic rites;
having entered the four stages of life and established that system among his subjects;
and having enjoyed the ever-renewing fruits of his actions following the union with his wife— (3.157.40)
Then, having satisfied your ancestors, you shall attain supreme perfection.
Once your ancestors are pleased, they will grant you a wife and sons as you desire;
when your grandfathers are fully satisfied by your command, what would they not give?
O Lakṣmī, having heard these words of the Creator, Ruci herself was delighted;
she praised the Creator and worshipped him with water and flowers.
Then, Brahmā vanished there on the riverbank, and Ruci [remained] thereafter.
Having gratified the ancestors, he bowed down with profound devotion and offered praise:
"I pay homage to Śrī Harikṛṣṇa, the eternal Grandfather;
to Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama. (44–45)
I bow to the imperishable abode of Śrī-Brahmā and to the liberated Maheśvaras;
I bow to all powers, sovereignties, qualities, and the Pitāmahas. I likewise bow to the weapons, all prosperities, the manifestations, and the lords.
I bow to the Muktānikās, the Avatāras, and the Mothers such as Śrī, Ramā, and others; I bow to those known as the Vyūhas, and I bow to the Virājas.
I bow to the virtuous knowers of Brahman who dwell in Satyaloka.
I bow to those ancestral spirits honored at the *śrāddha*, and to those who are the presiding deities of the *śrāddha*;
I bow to those who are gratified even by the gods during the *śrāddha*.
And I bow to those in heaven who are gratified by the great seers (*maharṣis*).

I bow to those who are likewise gratified by the Siddhas; I bow to those who are worshipped even by the Guhyakas for the sake of supernatural power. And I pay homage to those ancestors who are honored by human beings on earth.
I bow to those ancestors who bestow their own desired worlds,
who are worshipped with faith by Brahmins during śrāddha rites and are thereby gratified. I bow to those who grant the station of Prajāpati, who are gratified by the offering of water.
I bow to those who grant the fruits of lifelong asceticism and are highly honored;
I bow to the Pitṛs gratified by Kṣatriyas and worshipped at sacrifices;
I bow to the Pitṛs worshipped by Vaiśyas, who consume the *kavya* offerings.
I bow to those ancestors who are honored by Śūdras, those honored by food during auspicious times (sukālina),

those honored by Asuras, those honored by the Pitṛs, and those whose food consists of blood. I also bow to those who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) and who are gratified during the performance of Śrāddha rites.
I bow to the Svadhā-eaters, who are worshipped by the inhabitants of the netherworld (Rasātala),
and who are honored with all enjoyments by the Nāgas and others.
I bow to the Pitṛs— those dwelling in heaven, those in the intermediate space, and those established upon the earth.
I always bow to the Pitṛs who reside in celestial chariots, who possess embodied forms,
who are honored by practitioners of yoga, who are auspicious, and who bestow liberation from suffering.
I perpetually pay homage to those Pitṛs who have taken form and who partake of the *svadhā* offering.
May all those who bestow the fruits of desires, those who grant liberation while residing in heaven,

those who satisfy the wishes of seekers, those who grant celestial status and sons, those who bestow the station of Indra or Sūrya, and those who grant cattle, one’s own home, and power— may they all be satisfied. (3.157.60)
May all those who dwell in the moon and the sun, clothed in rays and stationed in celestial chariots, be satisfied with water, food, perfumes, flavors, and the like, and may they bestow nectar.
May also those others who consume the food offered into the fire and who subsist on sacrificial oblations be satisfied.
May those who dwell in the bodies of Brahmins and those who reside in the bodies of holy men,
as well as the ancestors who subsist on funeral cakes (piṇḍa), attain satisfaction through the water, sesame seeds, and other offerings presented by me;
and may they, gratified by black sesame and vegetable leaves, experience joy.

In that situation, a means must be employed for the pacification of the offense;

with *pīlu*, *dhātaki*, *cirabilva*, and *lodhra*;
with *kṣīrikā*, *aśmaka*, *navaraṅga*, and *trikhaṭvaka*.
With *bhallātaka*, *indrayava*, *guñjā*, and *karamardaka*;
with *aviṣṭaka* together with *drākṣā*, and with *putrajīvaka*;
with *kaṅkola*, *lavaṅga*, creepers, and betel vines.
With *marīca* peppers, jasmine flowers, loose-flowers, and *trapusa* cucumbers; with *kuṣmāṇḍa* gourds, *cirbhaṭa* melons, *paṭola* vines, and *kāravella* gourds;
with *karkoṭaka* cucumbers, eggplants, radishes, and sweet thorny fruits.
They were adorned with *śṛṅgāṭaka*, *kalhāra*, and mustard flowers,
as well as with *somavallī*, *saṃdhinīvallikā*, and *sañjīvanī* herbs;
and likewise with *kākālī*, *kāsamardī*, and *śakandala* plants.
With forests of pulse-bearing plants, grain fields, bamboos, and *kīcaka* reeds;
with thickets of *śara* grass, cotton plants, golden trees, and *bhūtṛṇa* grass;
and with *śṛṅgavera*, *ajamodā*, *kuberaka*, and *priyālaka* trees.
The beloveds of Hari beheld the forests adorned with white water-lilies, blue lotuses, land-lotuses,
kaseruka roots, lotus stalks, wheat, mustard seeds,
and wild rice. (66–67)
Likewise, they saw there birds of various forms:
peacocks, woodpeckers, sparrows, and cuckoos;
kādamba ducks, swans, lapwings, and wagtails.
Kuraras, kālakūṭas, khaṭvāṅgas, and likewise lubdhakas;
gokṣveḍakas, kumbhas, dhārtarāṣṭras, śukas, and bakas; dhātukas, cakravākas, kaṭukas, ṭiṭṭibhas, and bhaṭas. (3.159.70)
Pigeons, lotus-birds, sarikas, and hallaras, as well as lavas, prabhadrakas, garudas, and copper-crested cocks;
chickens, black sparrows, partridges, and kalahamsa swans.
They beheld woodpeckers, sparrows, francolins, and *ḍiṇḍima* birds;
they saw *bhūliṅga*s, *sīrapāda*s, and *bhṛṅgarāja*s;
as well as gallinules, sparrows, *kāraṇḍava*s, *caṣa*s, and *cātaka*s.
They beheld parrots, peacocks, cranes, and swans;
they beheld flocks of birds born of many species;
and they also beheld beasts of prey of various forms and deer. (74)
Tigers, maned lions, leopards, śarabhas, and wolves;
bears, hyenas, monkeys, golangulas, and pragaṇḍakas;
vanaras, hares, cats, wild dogs, and bhallukas. (75–76)
Mataṅgas, buffalo, gavayas,
yaks, bulls, white asses, sṛmaras, rams, and even sāraṅga deer;
as well as kukuras, nīlakas, karālas, and śambaras.
The women beheld Rāma-śarabhas, Toraṇas, Kāla-pucchas, Varāhakas, horses, donkeys, Reṇḍīyaras, and Citrakas; they looked upon lakes and rivers with white waters. (78–79)
The beloveds of Hari beheld the mountain’s caves, which were warm in some parts and cool in others, along with their various conduits; then,
they saw before them the auspicious hermitage of the seer Atri.
Endowed with natural radiance and free from the defects of violence and the like,
there was no falling of snow for five yojanas in every direction.
Worshipped by Atri, Kṛṣṇa and the Kṛṣṇās went before him.
In its vicinity stands a beautiful, great, white peak,
where indeed the clouds gather together and let fall snow.
Furthermore, ahead of it lies another exceedingly lofty peak.
The clouds constantly and repeatedly rain down water and snow.
Between the two peaks stands an exceedingly lofty summit;
on its western slope dwell auspicious groves of trees. (84–85)
Pervaded by darkness and dense with the abundance of fruits, flowers, and the like,
the sun does not shine there, nor does the moon gleam.
Nevertheless, a light resembling that of day indeed exists there.
The Badarī trees are found there, and the great seers dwell therein.
Then a celestial chariot, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns, descended from the sky into Viśālā, illuminating all directions. (87–88)
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as the great sages devoted to the Dharma,
quickly approached the celestial chariot,
overcome with wonder upon seeing the Lord, the beloved Śrīpati, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa.

They all suddenly worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Brahmā, the Supreme Lord, with water, sandalwood, and excellent fruits; and Nara and Nārāyaṇa were also worshipped by that Supreme Soul.
Both brothers were honored by all the Nārāyaṇī goddesses;
the great sages were likewise honored, saluted, and asked for their forgiveness.
Then, having given gifts and served them with heartfelt devotion, [they departed].
Having bowed to those foremost of the virtuous, to Bhakti, to Vṛṣa, and to Hari,
they then ascended the celestial chariot and proceeded before Him.
Then Himācala himself, accompanied by Menakā, became the lord of kings.
Eagerly, he went toward Kṛṣṇa’s celestial chariot for the purpose of worship;
having bowed and performed the rites of worship, he requested permission to return home. Hari also, desiring his wish, went to his abode.
Indeed, all around the mountains are walls made of white snow;
in the center is a vast valley, beautified by lakes and the like,
provided with gardens and such, and there stands a palace accompanied by a city.
The beautiful and most enchanting abode of the Himalayas exists;
indeed, the celestial chariot descended there upon the ground of the enclosure, at the home of the primordial Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa within the Himalayas. ॥98॥
Menā and Himālaya likewise offered a welcome and worship to Hari, Haripriyā, and the others as was appropriate. The mountain experienced supreme bliss from the sight of Nārāyaṇa. (3.159.100)
They settled the Supreme Lord together with his beloved in a magnificent palace and quickly prepared various nectars and excellent foods.
He fed him promptly and thereafter performed the ritual waving of lamps (*ārātrika*).
And Śrī Hari rested there, joyfully served by His beloveds.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Brahmapriyā and others, traveled in a celestial chariot while beholding the earth and went to the home of Himālaya," in the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga)*

Then Himādri indeed arrived for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Soul,

"The Guru of all the Nārāyaṇas has come to my house!

All those attendants who dwell in Vaikuṇṭha are dear to me.

Armed with weapons and tireless, they were utterly devoted to their master;
(5) wearing crowns and dressed in auspicious attire, they were adorned with jewels and gems;

"Let them go slowly, let them go slowly; let them not cause a crush here.

His weapons and other gear likewise fell from his hands.
When this fall occurred, Bala indeed gave way to anger.
Then Jayā, with her two elbows, her two hands, her two sides, and likewise her chest, rose up from her circle of friends including Prajñāpāśavatī and Māṇikyā,

Having uttered cries of reproach at her fallen companions,

uttering cries of "fie!", shouting "shame!", standing ready to drive them away,

"Fly away! Fly away! Jayā and the others cried out to him:
"You are not fit to remain here, filled with wrath at the women's gate.
One who is powerful, ever-attentive, gentle, and repeatedly patient is always fit for this place. (32–33)
He possesses a handsome form and sweet speech that is pleasant to hear; he is humble and patient, and in him no harshness is found.
Though powerful, he is as weak as a woman and remains a devoted servant.

"Indeed, you shall soon fall from the creation of the Creator in this cosmic egg;

Thus addressed, he instantly turned pale and was on the verge of falling.

Filled with rage and bolstered by the strength of Nārāyaṇa, he considered himself superior; and with anger, he replied with these words to Jayā, Aprajñā, Pāśavatī, Māṇikyā, and the other women. (38–39)
"Those who have indeed told me, 'Fall upon me,' let them fall even upon the wise;

Thus, when these words consisting of curses had been uttered to one another,

Then Bala, Jaya, and the others also intensely entreated her for release from that fall and for the cessation of the curse.
Lalitāśrī replied, "Indeed, this has come about by my own will."

I too must go to that place where you, my female friends, are—

for the sake of the task of uplifting the world and to fulfill the heart's desire of his friend.
"This is Prajñā," "This is Jayā," and "This is Pāśavatī"—[thus he shall recognize them].
"O Māṇikī, you shall become the wives of Kṛṣṇa along with me.

Furthermore, this attendant Bala, who was mentioned by Hari, was appointed to guard my city gate; however, out of anger, he incurred a curse.
By the will of Kṛṣṇa he indeed became small, and likewise by my will as well.
"This fool, indeed filled with wrath within the cosmic egg of the Creator,
was born with an asuric disposition and accompanied by anger.
Thinking that he would seize [the world], he shall attain liberation upon his death at the hands of the gods and others."
The elements arising from his body shall exist on earth as transformations;
likewise, in heaven, there shall be excellent jewels and material gems.
Thus, they will be worthy of worship everywhere and in every respect.
Thus, for the sake of accomplishing this very great task, I,
as well as Nārāyaṇa, have desired the downfall of the Goddess,
and the downfall of Bala has been desired for the sake of the jewel.
Whatever I have desired shall come to pass exactly so;
for this divine attendant is a king among devotees of Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent of great Bhāgavatas, purifying and sanctifying the world. (55)
Even the jewels arising from his purifying body are themselves purifying;
when worn, they shall cleanse the worlds of sin and protect them from miseries and calamities as well. (56–57)
And ornaments shall indeed arise from the body as jewels;

Thus, the liberation of Bala was brought about by the gods and by Nārāyaṇa.
Furthermore, from that [state], she will quickly and swiftly become a friend on earth once more.
I too shall exist on the surface of the earth in the form of Lalitā, as the princess and the servant of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (3.161.60)
"In the south, at Kāñcī, I shall become Lalitālakṣmī;
for the sake of performing many acts of upliftment, everything will be suitable.
Having spoken thus, Lalitālakṣmī [resided] in the gateway of the abode at Śrīpura.
Having spoken thus, he went to his own seat, and Jayā and the others quickly descended;
they obtained births as they desired here on the surface of the earth within the cosmic egg.
Bala, too, was born here in this world with the nature of an Asura.
From Kaśyapa and Diti, a son indeed named Bala was born;
he was a great Asura, a Daitya, the elder brother of Sukeśī and others.
Having been born, he remembered his former lives and, filled with great joy, performed austerities.
Having meditated upon Viṣṇu for a hundred years on the summit of Mount Meru,
he placed his head upon the earth and his feet in the sky;
covered by a network of creepers, he entered as it were into a state of profound meditative absorption (samādhi).
A bird’s nest was formed upon the back of the creeper at his feet;
bound by the creeper, he remained motionless for a hundred years,
his flesh withered away as he remembered Nārāyaṇa in his heart.
Then I went before him for the sake of his liberation from the curse.
By my own hand, I cleared away all those creepers;
and by my two hands, he was granted a measure of knowledge.
He recognized my two hands by their mere touch;
instantly bathed by me,
he raised his face and fell prostrate like a staff, weeping as he shed tears.
With his limbs overwhelmed by love, he prayed for liberation from the womb.
Viṣṇu said: "You have always been my devotee and likewise my purifier;
O devotee, by granting you my vision, you have become even more purified than before."
Listen quickly, for you shall be released from this womb of a demoness.
Abandoning your asceticism, go to the world of Indra and display your strength.
Indeed, even millions of gods are not capable of conquering a Daitya who is devoted to his purpose.
When they perform service [to you],
you shall then be pleased and will grant them an excellent boon; indeed,
you will be requested by them in the form of sacrificial fuel at a sacrifice.
All of them together shall indeed carry out that slaying of yours,
and from your body there shall arise diamonds,
various gems, and diverse jewels.
"Then your liberation will swiftly come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus and given me the discus, he indeed became invisible.
Abandoning his asceticism, he went to heaven and requested a battle with Indra and the other gods.
In battle, Mahendra gave him combat and was defeated by him;
both the Sun and the Moon were also conquered, as were the guardians of the quarters.
Even Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana discus was indeed defeated.
Indra and the others were conquered by him; they are not able to conquer him.
Having become subject to another's will, the gods performed service to Bala.
By that service, Bala was exceedingly gratified and [offered] them a boon.
He dispatched the gods, and those gods, having reflected upon Viṣṇu’s words and remembering them well, then requested their own beneficial gain:
"If a boon is to be granted to us, and if you are one whose word is true... (82)
"If you are pleased with my service and if you are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, then grant me one supreme boon, the most desired of all the gods:
let Yajña be Nārāyaṇa himself in person, and may you yourself become the sacrificial fuel (samidh) therein. (83–84)
"Having joined together with us— the gods, Daityas, Nāgas, serpents, and Dānavas— you shall indeed attain liberation through this oblation.
Thus addressed, the Daitya Bālaka became exceedingly joyful.

For the sake of Viṣṇu, he offered a fuel-stick, which was my supreme good fortune. (8.6) Death for the sake of the gods and total self-surrender would be the highest state here in this world; for transmigratory existence is by nature subject to death, yet death for the sake of the deity is [liberation]. (8.7)
If it can be obtained for the sake of cows, for the sake of my preceptor, for the sake of Mādhava, for the sake of dharma, or for the sake of a religious duty—what gain could be greater than that?
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what supreme fortune stands before me today!
"Since I have been appointed by the gods to stand at the mouth of Lord Viṣṇu,
my self-offering today shall become most auspicious.
Having reflected thus, he then granted the boon, saying, "So be it."
And the gods, having obtained that boon, eagerly caused a sacrificial ground to be prepared on the western slope of Mount Meru.
There, the gods, Daityas, Dānavas, and birds were summoned.
The great seers, the ancestors, human beings, trees, and creepers;
the yakṣas, the rākṣasas, and also the piśācas, the sources of all beings;
the kuṣmāṇḍas, the kinnaras, the nāgas, the gandharvas, and likewise the serpents.
The serpents, the foremost of the Asuras, the Apsarases, and likewise the rivers;
the oceans, as well as the forests and lofty mountains;
the clouds, the lightning, the caves, and the multitudes of medicinal herbs.
The principles (tattvas), having been invited, arrived there at that great sacrifice.
At that moment, the sacrificial rite was set in motion by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others; Bala then offered his own form as the sacrificial fuel (samidh).
He sat down at the sacrifice as soon as he was sprinkled with the waters of the *vardhinī* vessel;
at that moment, having taken the form of a sacrificial fuel-stick (*samit*), he became like a great mountain.
He appeared like a vast heap from which trees, creepers, and crops are produced.
Abounding in rice, flowers, and fruits, the mountain possessed a desirable taste like clarified butter.
At that time, it was not perceived as having the form of a living being; rather, it took the form of an oblation.
Indeed, all sacrificial offerings were seen there upon the mountain at that time.
Considering the mountain-like mass of the oblation to have been turned back,
the gods performed a purificatory rite, sprinkled it, and then offered the oblation. At that time, there were indeed hundreds of thousands of offerings poured into the fire for him.
Possessing the essence of seeds, grains, clarified butter, and fruits, and being fragrant—
these auspicious components of that army of pure beings became sacrificial fuel when cast into the fire, and they turned into jewel-seeds. (101–102)
Then, seeing those seeds in the vessel, which were as radiant as the sun and the moon,
the gods and others, who knew their value, took them.
[They were taken] by the gods, the yakṣas, the siddhas, and those who subsist on air.

Then, a vast crocodile consisting of jewels and seeds appeared all around the human beings, great sages, and officiating priests. Leaping up from the sacrificial pit through the path of the sky, the gods and others seized it.
Seizing one another, they traveled far in their celestial chariots toward their own homes; there was then a great commotion due to their mutual pulling and tugging.
In the sky, a great scramble occurred for the sake of the seeds of jewels.
And those seeds which fell from the path of the sky during the assault,
as well as those dropped by the hands of those falling swiftly from their celestial chariots—
[they fell] upon mountains, into oceans, into rivers, and even into forests.
Then, by means of their respective qualities, seeds and gems came into being upon the trees, in the paths of the clouds, upon the earth, and even in the lakes;
they became various kinds of things endowed with the qualities of that which they were to occupy.

Thus has the origin of the various kinds of jewels been proclaimed to you. (3.161.11) Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fall of the *pārṣada* named Bala from the Abode of Śrī-pura due to a mutual curse with Jaya and others; the fall of the Daitya Bala at the sacrifice; and the production of jewels from the bodily elements of the sacrificial fuel-sticks," in the *Dvāparasantāna* within the third book of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 162]
[The Author: Chapter 163.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī, Ramā, and others, as well as my beloveds, Jayā and the rest.
All those jewels indeed possess great qualities.
They are destroyers of evil spirits, demons, poison, serpents, and diseases, and they are beneficial;
likewise, some may be endowed with qualities while others may be devoid of them.
Diamonds, pearls, rubies, emeralds, sovereign gems,
sapphires, lapis lazuli, topazes, and various species of birthstones;
karketanas, pulakas, rubies, and likewise crystals.
Coral, pearls, glass, and gems—these indeed are what they are.
Having examined their shape, color, quality, defect, and their resulting effects, their value is determined; it is not otherwise.

Those gems which are employed on auspicious family occasions or on days when the sun is eclipsed become indeed full of defects and deprive one of prosperity. Therefore, having examined them, one should accept and even wear [gems].

At an auspicious time, one shall obtain supreme prosperity through auspicious deeds alone. Wherever the seeds of *balā*, bone, and sacrificial fuel fall, there the diamond-gem (*vajramaṇi*) becomes possessed of great power among all things. (7–8)
Various kinds of diamonds, bearing the name "vajra," have arisen;
namely those from Haima, Mātaṅga, Saurāṣṭra, Pauṇḍra, Kaliṅga, Kosala,
Veṇātaṭa, and Sauvīra— these are the regions endowed with the production of diamonds.
Those originating from the Snowy Mountains (Himālaya) are slightly copper-colored; those from Mātaṅga are tawny;
and those born in Saurāṣṭra are copper-red. Those produced in Puṇḍra are considered dark-complexioned; those from Kaliṅga are golden-hued; and those from Kosala have a yellowish luster.
Those from the banks of the Veṇā are moon-like; those from Sauvīra have the luster of clouds.
It is perfectly even on all sides, excellent in its qualities, and light like a beautiful color.
It is free from lines, spots, crow-feet, stains, and breaks.
Even if it is only the size of an atom, that is indeed the supreme vajra.
If it has a sharp point and edge, it is the refuge for the gods;
when worn, it grants gain, is unfailing, and bestows all happiness. (1.3–1.4)
Just as the color [of a diamond], so is the celestial abode;
just as it is luminous, so is its name among the gods conceived.
Indeed, according to the distinction of color, different deities dwell within the diamonds.
Hari himself resides in green [leaves], Varuṇa himself in white ones;
Śakra resides in yellow ones, while Hutāśana resides in reddish-brown ones.
The Pitṛs are present in dark [leaves], and likewise the Maruts in copper-colored ones. (16–17)
A Brahmin should wear a beneficial gem that has the luster of a white water-lily, crystal, or conch shell;
a Kṣatriya should wear a gem resembling the color of a hare or a tawny eye;
and a Vaiśya should wear a gem with the hue of a plantain leaf, which bestows prosperity.
A Śūdra should wear a gem resembling the blade of a clean sword.
Or it may be as red as the Japā flower or coral, or like the juice of turmeric.
Kings should wear two gems of diamond-like color, which bestow welfare.

A king indeed should wear a diamond (*vajra*) consisting of all colors, or a gem that is circular both above and below and endowed with many hues. Such a gem is suitable for a king and not for others, for it brings hardship to other castes.
A diamond is a source of prosperity for those possessed of merit, but for others, it brings misfortune.
(22) If its point is seen to be crushed or shattered, then even if it possesses other qualities, it should never be worn by those seeking their own welfare. (23)
A diamond with shattered or cracked points, containing specks of impurity in its center, destroys prosperity; it should never be kept in the house.
Likewise, one whose single part has a reddish luster, or which is entirely red in color, [should not be kept].
This indeed is death; this jewel should never be worn anywhere.
Its crores, its sides, and its facets are six, eight, or twelve;
with high, even, and sharp points—these are the qualities of a diamond produced from a mine.
Pure according to the six criteria, stainless, with a clearly manifest and sharp edge, light, endowed with the correct color, free from defects, and likewise possessing excellent sides;
it is richly adorned with the rays of a rainbow, filling the entire circle of the sky. (27)
One should wear this vajra, which is difficult to obtain, for it increases longevity, women, and wealth;
it protects cattle, grain, and prosperity, and causes all forms of prosperity to flourish;
it removes the fear of predatory beasts, fire, poison, tigers, thieves, and water. (28–29)
This diamond, a jewel that wards off the malevolent spells of the Atharvans from afar, is worth twenty loads of rice; it possesses the highest quality and value.
In its fibers, luster, oiliness, and weight, it is not lacking even a fraction [of perfection].

A vajra that is deficient is considered to have [reduced] value, profit, and so forth. If it is half [the size], it is said to possess half the quality; if it is a quarter, it shall possess a quarter of the quality. Furthermore, if it possesses a quarter of the quality, its value shall be a quarter. (3.1–3.2)

Indeed, a diamond may consist of a thirtieth part, a hundredth part, or even an eightieth part; likewise, it may be a thousandth part, yet it remains subtle and possesses power according to its quality. Furthermore, the weight of diamonds is determined by eight mustard seeds.
That diamond which is endowed with all qualities floats upon the waters;
even among the entire range of gems, its wearing is prescribed.
Even in a very small measure, its weight is inferred when it is worn.
Therefore, one must certainly uphold even a single atom [of the Dharma].
Even a diamond with a slight flaw may be worth a tenth of its value;
however, one that is manifestly full of many flaws is worth only a hundredth of its value.
The value of a diamond with many defects is very small when used as an ornament.
Such a flawed stone, which brings about slight loss, is worn only after being encased in a setting.
Indeed, it is enough to say that even the wearing of a defective diamond for the sake of adornment is futile. (37–38)
A woman should never wear a diamond, even one possessed of excellent qualities;
she who desires the birth of a son must never wear it at any time.
However, a long, flat, short, or quality-less diamond may be worn.
With iron, topaz, and likewise with gomedaka,
with lapis lazuli, crystal, and various kinds of glass,
counterfeit gems are produced by skilled artisans that resemble diamonds.
Their testing should be performed with a laboratory for alkaline abrasion.
Whatever gems exist on earth, as well as other metallic ores—all these may be scratched by the diamond, but the diamond is not scratched by them. (42)
Heaviness, excellence among all gems, and the clarity of luster are the causes [of its value].
In the case of a diamond, lightness and the clarity of luster are the reasons;
indeed, diamonds of superior birth completely scratch those of inferior birth on all sides. (43–44)
Diamond is engraved by diamond; diamond is not engraved by anything else.
As for diamonds, pearls, gems, and whatever other species there may be, when they are set [in a setting], their luster does not radiate upward. (45)
If, due to being scratched obliquely, it appears in some way on certain [parts], then for those being drawn obliquely, it is impaired at the sides;
its edges are shattered like a vajra, discolored, and marked with lines and dots. //46-47//
If that king possesses the rainbow weapon and bestows sons, wealth, and grain,
he indeed wields the lightning-like thunderbolt of Indra;
by his very prowess, he attains imperial sovereignty upon the earth.

The Vajra-ratna has been described to you; O beloved of Brahmā, hereafter I shall describe the pearl-jewel (muktāphala-ratna); listen and understand. They are distinct from one another: some are clear, some are translucent, some possess dense luster, and others are stained with impurities.
Pearls are indeed produced from elephants, clouds, boars, conch shells, fish, serpents, oysters, and bamboo;
among these, those born from water and earth are the gems.
However, the pearl originating from an oyster is considered the best among all.
That which originates from mother-of-pearl is to be pierced; indeed, all the remaining types are unpierceable.
(52) Although that which comes from bamboo, elephants, fish, corals, conch-shells, and boars lacks luster, it is praised as auspicious. (53)
The pearl originating from a conch and that produced from an elephant are considered the lowest grade.
Likewise, one that has the color of the center of an elephant's frontal globe, or is yellow, or lacks luster, is inferior.
Furthermore, a conch-pearl measuring a large *koṇapala* is also of the lowest quality.
In those conch shells and elephants that are considered to be of pure lineage,
the whorls (vṛtta) are yellow even if they lack luster;
whereas in fish, those whorls that are produced are well-formed even if they are small.
Extremely minute and the color of the back of a pāṭhīna fish, they indeed arise within the mouths of fish in the midst of the ocean.
Their luster is like the power of a boar’s tusk, resembling the sprout of a tusk.
That which arises from the earth is called "pearl-like" (muktākhya), and in some cases, such auspicious [pearls] are considered similar [to those found in shells].
That which arises from stones is of the same color, and that which arises from bamboo possesses a luster equal to it.
Even bamboo [pearls] are to be enjoyed by noble people everywhere; they are certainly not [ordinary]. (58–59)
The round and brilliant gems born of serpents become as if washed by the luster of the edge of a sword;
one who wears such serpent-born pearls becomes virtuous and endowed with splendor.
He shall indeed possess royal splendor and shall also be rich in power.
(61) One who desires to know the value of a jewel should, at an auspicious moment, place it upon the roof of his house after having made great protective rites. (62)
At that time, indeed, there arise great sounds of kettledrums in the sky,
flashes of lightning, and clouds as well.
Such a pearl as this, wherever it may be— whether in a casket or in a house— [brings prosperity].
Therein there are no serpents, no obstacles, no *yātudhānas*, nor mental afflictions;
there are no calamities or diseases where the pearl originates from a serpent. But as for that pearl which arises from a cloud, O deities, it is [of a different nature]. (64–65)
They indeed carry away from the path of the sky that which possesses a luster like the rays of the sun;
it shines at night just as it does by day wherever it stays with its own radiance.
For such a jewel, the price is the earth made of gold.
Yet it is not at all sufficient, since it bestows gold and jewels.
He before whom this jewel shall appear enjoys the circle of the earth;
furthermore, the fortune and splendor of both his subjects and the king increase. (67–68)
Indeed, even at distances of thousands of *yojanas*, misfortunes do not reach him.
Such were the ivory ornaments on Bala’s [elephant] that were released;
they served as sacrificial fuel in that sacrifice from time to time. (69)
Those seeds which were born in various colors and forms,
which indeed fell into the waters of the oceans while pure,
and which are beautiful with the luster of moonbeams— those are indeed the ones produced from oyster shells.
Indeed, those born from oyster shells are produced on the island of Siṃhala, in Saurāṣṭra, Tāmraparṇaka, Pāraśava,
Pāraloka, Kaubera, the Pāṇḍya country,
Hāṭaka, and Hemaka.
Produced from oyster shells, it possesses a color that is not too dark, is endowed with excellent qualities and luster, and is characterized by its shape and dimensions;
it is found in Vardhana, Pārasīka, Pātāla, and Siṃhala as well. (73–74)
Indeed, for a single pearl produced from a mother-of-pearl oyster that has been processed on a whetstone,
a value of two thousand silver coins (mudrās) is possible;
however, for a gem deficient by half a māṣa, the price is reduced by one-tenth.
That which weighs three *māṣakas* and is worth two thousand [coins],
that which weighs two and a half *māṣakas* is worth one thousand five hundred;
and that which weighs two *māṣakas* is worth one thousand.
The price of agallochum weighing one *sārdhamāṣaka* is indeed five hundred;
that of agallochum weighing six *guñjās*, which is a jewel, is two hundred and fifty. That agallochum which weighs four *guñjās* is considered to have a price of two hundred.
That which is heavy by two *guñjās* is considered to have a value of one hundred;
likewise, the value of that which is heavy by one *guñjā* is indeed fifty *mudrikās*.
That which possesses sixteen *guñjās* is known as a *dharaṇa*, specifically called *dārvika*.
A string of thirty *gruñjas* is called a *dharaṇa*, which is termed a *ratna*;
however, those inferior gems are worth thirty [coins],
or twenty, or likewise ten.
Now, its examination is as follows: having placed the juice of a citron (*jāmbīra*) in a vessel, the gem is heated;
it is then rubbed with *piṇḍamūlaka* roots.
If it leaves a streak, it is indeed artificial or of inferior quality.
Having placed it inside a clay-coated crucible, one should cook it in fire;
then in milk, then in water, then in ghee, and again in waters.
Then, by rubbing with cloths, it becomes endowed with excellent qualities and luster.
That which is the best is indeed true pearl, flawless and resembling white glass;
it should be worn as an ornament set in gold.
If there is doubt that it is artificial, further examination must be performed.
One should soak that [substance] in warm, salty oil overnight in water;
it should then be rubbed with rice grains while placed between two dry cloths.
If discoloration does not occur, it should be known as genuine.
White, possessing the correct proportions, glossy, heavy, transparent, and perfectly pure;
(88) with an abundance of luster and well-rounded—that pearl is indeed endowed with all virtues.
Not even a single defect in it brings misfortune to its owner. (89)
Thus have I described to you the pearl-gems, which are dear to Hari. Now I shall speak of the rubies; listen to them according to their origin.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Origin, Value, and Excellence of the Diamond and Pearl Gems," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
