Chapter 163.
[The Author: Chapter 164.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having obtained the seed of Bala’s blood as fuel, the Sun-god...
The lord of Laṅkā traveled by way of the sky and besieged him.
And in the ocean, indeed upon the Gaṅgā of Rāvaṇa, seeds fell;
from them, radiant jewels were born.
Those gems produced from lotuses are brilliant and possess beautiful colors;
likewise, those originating from *saugandhika* flowers are virtuous in quality, as are those arising from *kuruvinda* stones.
Furthermore, there are others made of crystal that are radiant and come in many colors.
They were born resembling the bandhūka, guñjā, indragopa, and japā flowers, as well as blood;
they resembled the pomegranate, the kiṃśuka flower, vermilion, and the utpala lotus;
they possessed a radiance with the color of the padma lotus, saffron, and lac-dye. || 4–5 ||
Those made of crystal, which shine intensely with their own luster and are clearly visible, color their sides with the rays of the sun;
they possess a hue blended of safflower and blue, with the brilliance of fierce red lotuses. (6)
Some have the luster of lotus flowers, while others have the brilliance of vermilion;
some possess the hue of the eyes of cakoras, pigeons, and cranes,
and others even have the splendor of the finest red lotuses.
These crystals originating from *sphāṭika* (rock crystal) and *padmarāga* (ruby) are generally similar in their brilliance, hardness, and weight; they are endowed with blue and red lusters.
However, these gems arising from *saugandhika* (ambergris) are for the most part similar [to the former].
Jewels produced from Kuruvinda are inferior in color to these;
they lack internal luster, possess little brilliance, and are not endowed with great power.
Those similar to them are found in the Andhra country as well as in the Tumburu region.

Those of similar quality are born [as common stones], for they are considered to be of little value. An abundance of color, weight, oiliness, evenness, transparency, brilliance, and size—these are the indicators of the excellence of gems. (12)
But those which are like gravel, possessed of flaws, impurities, and the like;
lacking luster, rough, and discolored—they are not excellent.
By wearing such a flawed gem, one likewise incurs grief, anxiety, and disease. (13–14)
One incurs death, suffering, and loss of wealth; of this there is no doubt.
Five types of [gems] that are of different species become equal to rubies (padmarāga).
Those originating from Kalasapura as well as those born in the region of Tumburu [are such].
Those originating from Muktapāṇīya and those from Siṃhala are called Śrīpūrṇakas;
indeed, those gems arising from Kalasa are characterized by a combination of *tuṣa*.
Those from Tumburu are copper-colored, while those born in the land of Siṃhala are black.
Pearls that are by nature devoid of luster and lacking brilliance become copper-colored when combined with husks, even if they are oily. Those which,
when rubbed, lose their luster are of inferior birth.
That pearl which has its top pressed by a finger and bears a dark tint on its side,
and which, even if it possesses qualities similar to another pearl situated nearby, remains of inferior value— even if it is indeed equal [in other respects]. (3.163.20)
When artificial doubt has arisen, one should rub it on a whetstone;
it should scratch against [the genuine stone] produced from its own species, and they should scratch each other.
This applies to either a diamond (*vajra*) or a *kuruvinda*, provided no other [substitute] is used. (21)
It is not possible to produce a line on rubies and sapphires.
Where there is a line, that gem is indeed inferior and is not called the best;
or rather, it may even be artificial if it possesses a line.
A jewel that is artificial or flawed should never be worn,
even if it were equal to a genuine jewel or the Kaustubha gem.
A single Caṇḍāla, however, [is more dangerous] than even many twice-born Brahmins.
In the same way, a corrupt person surely defiles others and even destroys their virtues.
One who wears the ruby of truth, even while dwelling among enemies,
shall not be overcome by calamities nor overwhelmed by obstacles.
It is not overcome by calamities, misfortunes, or defects;
endowed with the brilliance of its color, it is excellent, whereas that which lacks these is indeed inferior.
An excellent gem should always be worn, but an inferior one never.
It renders valueless that which holds what is valueless. 28.
Now, O beloved of Brahmā! I shall speak here of emeralds.
While Vāsuki was grasping the seeds of the *balapitta* wood in the sky, 29.
When Garuḍa pursued him there, he blocked his way;
and seeds fell upon the ground of the Māṇikya mountain,
as well as among the Turuṣka trees and the creepers of the Nalika forest.
And on the shore of the white ocean, emeralds then came into being.
Seeds also fell from the opening of Garuḍa’s beak;
from them grew trees with the hue of the Śirīṣa flower and the throat of a parrot.

Those gems produced from bile are considered to have a luster resembling the back of a firefly, the sheen of moss or water-grass, and the brilliance of a white water-lily or young grass-blade, as well as the radiance of a serpent’s hood. They are also known as *patraraṅga*.
All poison arising from the seed of the coils of serpents is pacified [by these].
That which cannot be treated by any collection of medicinal herbs or mantras—
the poison produced by the fangs of great snakes— is, however, pacified by these.

That gem which is intensely green, soft, radiant, and possesses a luster like the midst of gold powder is considered the most excellent. It is endowed with all the qualities of its configuration and possesses a uniform appearance.
Through contact with the rays of the sun, the Guru inflames the hermitage;
and through union with the radiance of lightning, that which becomes endowed with internal luster should be green like a grassy meadow—that indeed is the most excellent. (37–38)
Where there are many colors, yet with a clear core in the center,
and which is cloudy, glossy, pure, and possesses the luster of a peacock feather on all sides—
that is to be understood as inferior to the former; for it is considered slightly superior [to that].
Variegated, rough, dull, hard, and gritty— just as emerald is not considered superior when mixed with stone-born copper,
so too is that which is fashioned from fragments of emerald or joined together in such a manner. (3.163.40–41)
Those who desire their own welfare should never wear it, nor should they ever seek to conquer it;
for by its power, even the rays of the *bhallātaka* fruit undergo a transformation.
Those emeralds that are artificial must never be worn at any time.
Likewise, pearls equal to diamonds, and emeralds as well—
[these are the best]. Indeed, for those whose luster rises upward, or is straight, or moves in a curve,
that [luster] immediately vanishes when they are viewed from the side.
These emeralds of mixed origin should be understood as bringing auspiciousness;
they are used for bathing, sipping water, and recitation, as well as in rituals involving protective mantras,
in the giving of cows, gold, and other gifts, and even when the means of practice have been performed.
In rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests, and in the worship of gurus,
when [the body] is afflicted by various kinds of defects arising from poison—
[it becomes] free from defect, endowed with qualities, and joined with gold. (46–47)
Emerald should always be worn during battle and in the pursuit of victory.
Emerald is proclaimed to have a value exceeding that of ruby.
Even in the case of an emerald, a loss of value occurs when defects are excessive.
Thus have the emeralds been described; now I shall speak to you of the sapphires.
That seed of the *samid* [sacrificial wood] belonging to Bala, which fell upon the land of Siṃhala and the region of Kaccha, became that earth in many places on all sides. (3.163.50)
They were born as sapphire-blue, yet they were of many varieties;
some had the luster of blue lotuses, bees, or the bow of Śārṅga, while others were like the throat of Hara.
Some resembled mountain peaks, some the water of the ocean, and some the plumage of peacocks.
Those of great quality possess a blue hue, resembling the color of a peacock's throat.
However, those that have cavities in clay, stone, or rock, that are gritty, cracked,
or possess the luster of mica-sheets, are indeed defective in color.
One who wears an indranīla obtains all the qualities of a padmarāga;
the very same examination that applies to a padmarāga applies to an indranīla as well.
When thrown into fire, a padmarāga will ascend through the fire for as long as [it remains unscathed].
If an even larger sapphire were thrown into the fire, it would pass through;
that alone should be understood as the auspicious test for a genuine gem.
Nevertheless, [this method] is not intended as a test for those qualities that cause destruction. (59–60)
A gem should be placed in fire, for it may indeed be counterfeit; such a gem brings misfortune to the wearer, as well as to the one who made it and the one who caused it to be made.
Glass, blue lotus, oleander, lapis lazuli, crystal, and the like—these are the imitations.
Indeed, these gems are also like sapphire (indranīla).
When there is an excess of hardness and weight, their excellence arises.
The sapphire is copper-colored, with the luster of a karavīra flower or a blue lotus.
That which shines with the luster of a rainbow within its dark blue center is called an *indranīla*; it is highly precious and very difficult to obtain.
That gem in which beauty resides with a hundredfold intensity due to the predominance of its color—
If it should lead everything to a state of blueness, it is called Mahānīla (Great Blue).
Whatever price is set for a *padmarāga* (ruby) weighing one *māṣa*,
that same price is set for an *indranīla* (sapphire) of equal weight due to its superior qualities.
Now, regarding the Lakṣmīs! I shall explain the origin and other details of Vaidūrya.
For they arise from the seed-mantras of the *samidhs* whose essence is the sound of the demon Bala.
Indeed, they possess many colors and are endowed with beautiful and charming splendor.
On the distant mountain, in the land of Kāmarūpa where Kāmākṣī resides,
there are vaidūrya gems that shine like monsoon clouds;
though they are radiant, they have become auspicious, resembling sparks of fire.
Those with the luster of a peacock’s neck, as well as those resembling bamboo bark and those like the feathers of a bow, are excellent and bestow superior fortune.
Likewise, those made of girika, śiśupāla, kāca, and sphatika are also praised.
And the smoky-colored ones are equal to the varieties of *vaidūrya*.

Due to the absence of lines and because of its lightness, it is called "glass" (*kāca*); Śiśupāla [is so named] because of its lack of luster, while *girikāca* is so called because of its dullness and *sphaṭika* because of its brilliance. 67–68.
The price of two *pala*s of heavy [sapphire] is considered equal to that of an *indranīla*.
Indeed, differences in name, color, and quality give rise to differences in price.
Oiliness, lightness, and softness are always the diagnostic marks for distinguishing varieties.
If worn on the wrist, it bestows gain, provided its value is sixfold [the cost].
This price, however, would be much higher in mines or in the land of Bhūdeśa.
A gold *suvarṇa* consists of sixteen *māṣas*, and one-seventh of that is known as a *saṃjñaka*.
A *śāṇa* consists of four *māṣas*, and a *māṣaka* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*. A *dharaṇa* is proclaimed to be the tenth part of a *pala*.
When the weight exceeds a *dharaṇa*, the price increases due to the added burden.
Now, O Lakṣmī, I shall describe the *puṣparāga* gems; listen with understanding.
The bark, fuel-sticks, and seeds of the *balā* plant fell upon the Himālaya mountains, and from them were born the highly virtuous *puṣparāga* gems. (73–74)
The ruby varieties of stone that are yellowish-white are called *padmarāga*. Those that are yellowish-red are designated as *kauruṇḍaka*.
However, those that are transparent, red, and yellow are known by the name *kāṣāyaka*.
Those that are slightly blue and white and glossy are designated as *somānakas*.
Those that are extremely red are considered to be *padmarāgas*.
Those that are deep blue are *puṣparāgas*, known by the name *indranīlas*.

Pure *vaidūrya*, which resembles [the color of] lapis lazuli, always bestows upon women the pure fruit in the form of a son through its wearing; of this there is no doubt. (78) Now, I shall describe here the *karketana* gems, which are the jewels of fortune (*lakṣmī*).
The wind then approached the seeds of the *nakha* fuel-sticks belonging to Bala;
he scattered them in the lotus groves, and from them there arose *karketana* gems, possessing the luster of honey, soma, and blood, resembling copper-colored and yellow fire. (3.163.79–80)
Those that are blue, white, or rough remove defects such as disease;
those that are glossy, pure, uniform in color, yellow, variegated, and heavy;
and those free from the defects of lines and scars—such *karketana* gems are purifying.
Having wrapped it with a gold leaf, one should heat it with fire.
If it becomes radiant like a karketana gem, it destroys diseases;
it also eliminates afflictions, bestows long life, and grants a lineage of happiness.
When worn as an ornament, this [gem] bestows wealth,
grain, honor, kinsmen, and even radiance.
Some, however, are blue, deformed, faded, and likewise turbid.
Devoid of brilliance and luster, they become like white crabs;
lacking in virtue, they are indeed sources of suffering and must never be worn.
Having encountered the rays of the sun, they come to possess a halo of light. (85–86)
Those which are born as such become indeed the most precious *karketana* gems.
Now, O beloved of Brahmā, I shall describe to you here the *bhīṣmaratna* gems.
The seed of the *samid* tree, born from the vital energy (*vīrya*) of the demon Bala, exists upon the Himalayas.
Then, in the region to the north of that, there fell indeed formidable [seeds]:
those resembling conchs and lotuses, and those appearing like Syonāka flowers;
when worn around the neck, they truly bestow prosperity. (88–89)
Upon seeing one who wears the Bhīṣma jewel,
wolves, leopards, śarabhas, tigers, panthers, and elephants flee from afar.
If the Bhīṣma jewel, endowed with excellent qualities, is worn as a finger-ring, [it grants protection].
In the rite of libation for the ancestors, it indeed bestows great satisfaction.
Likewise, the poisons of serpents, birds, rats, and scorpents are pacified;
and by wearing it, fear of water, fire, thieves, and enemies is surely destroyed. (91–92)

One should avoid from afar that which resembles a cloud or water-moss, or that which is rough, yellowish, lusterless, discolored, or soiled, for such a stone brings loss. The price should be determined according to its qualities, taking into account the excellence of the place, time, and other factors.
Now indeed, O beloved of Brahmā, I shall speak of the *pulaka* gems for you.
O serpents, the seeds of the *samidh*-wood from the claws of the demon Bala were cast upon the mountains, as well as upwards and even into the northern rivers. (94–95)
From that region, indeed, gems and *pulaka* stones were produced in Daśārṇa,
Vāgade, Melakaka, and also in Kālakaka.
They were the color of *guñjā*, collyrium, and honey, as well as having the luster of lotus stalks.
Those with the luster of a gandharva, fire, or plantain tree are likewise considered excellent.
Those with variegated patterns resembling a conch, a lotus, a water-pot, or the sun, and which are free of lines, are proclaimed as auspicious "pulakas" that bestow prosperity. (17–18)

If these are held, they take on the fierce forms of crows, donkeys, oxen, jackals, and wolves; with faces like vultures covered in flesh, they bestow death. The price for a load of their flesh is five hundred coins.
Now, O Lakṣmīs! I shall describe to you the jewel called Rudhira. Agni took the seed of the *samid* wood known as Rūpa belonging to the demon Bala;
he cast it into the Revā river, and certainly also into the low-lying ground.
Some resembled the indragopa insect, others were like the beak of a parrot; those who were well-nourished were of a blood-red color, and they indeed became crimson.
In their midst, some were as white as the moon, possessing pure complexions and balanced proportions.
Those resembling sapphire (indranīla) indeed bestow servants and sovereignty.
Those called "divine diamond" (suravajra), when baked, grant gains and provide prosperity.
Now I shall describe the auspicious gems known as crystal (sphaṭika), which bring fortune.
In the lands of Kāverī, Vindhya, Yavana, Cīna, and Nepāla,
he cast the seeds of the *samid* known as *medā* belonging to Balāsura, along with *lāṅgalī*,
into the path of the sky; that oil indeed became crystal.

White as lotus stalks and conch shells, yet possessing slight variations in hue, they were indeed capable of destroying sins and possessed the value of excellent qualities. Then Śeṣa [offered] the entrails of Bala, which were in the form of sacrificial fuel and seeds. (10.6–10.7)
He first cast them into Kerala and other regions; from that they became corals, possessing the color of a rabbit's blood and resembling the hue of *guñjā* and *japā* flowers.
Indeed, those [corals] were produced as distinct varieties, such as the *devakaroma*.
Clear, soft, glossy, and beautiful in form, coral is beneficial;
it brings wealth and grain to the world and destroys the fear of poison and affliction.
Thus, these gems are born from their respective seeds and lineages.
Minerals are produced, as well as gems belonging to the fire-element;
all these gems, dear to Brahmā, have been described by me to you.
They arise through the instrumental cause of my devotee Bala. (111)
Those who cause me to be remembered through the retention [of my teachings] and their recitation,
from that power he went by means of a celestial chariot to my very abode.
And you, Jayā and the others, are women who abide here as mine.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Origin, Qualities, and Other Attributes of Padmarāga, Marakata, Indranīla, Vaidūrya, Puṣparāga, Karketana, Bhīṣma, Pulaka, Rudhira, Sphaṭika, and Vidruma Gems," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
[Compare with *Padmapurāṇa* 6.6.24; next page.]
A constituent part of the body; an instrument; the name of a gem; application; other than blood; blood; the sun; a ruby; a rival; love; bile;
Vāsuki; emerald; the pacification of poison.
The pair of eyes are sapphire,
the voice is lapis lazuli, the skin is topaz, and it bestows sons.
The *nakha*, *vāyu*, and *karketana* destroy diseases; the claws of the *bhīṣma*, *vyāghra*, and others cause [enemies] to flee;
and the *bhujaṅgama* increases horripilation.
Form is the sacrificial fire; blood is the servant; sovereignty is the fat; the plow is crystal; the destroyer of sin is the entrails;
the remainder is coral; and wealth and grain are the hands.

Chapter 164 [[Author: → Chapter 165

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "O Beloved! Regarding the fourteen Manus proclaimed by the Blessed One, tell me of those among them which were your incarnations, along with their respective deeds."
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Śivarājñī! I shall describe there the incarnations that destroy the Daityas, along with their causes, which protect the Dharma. (2)
At that time, Svāyambhuva Manu was the Indra known as Viśvabhuk;
likewise, the Daitya Bāṣkali performed severe penance.
Indeed, that Daitya brought under his control the sons of Manu, beginning with Agnidhra.
He brought under his control the seven ṛṣis— Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and Vasiṣṭha—
as well as the invincible Śukras and the Yāma gods.
Furthermore, Viṣṇu, having been urged by Nārada for the sake of slaying the Daitya,
dispatched his great discus, Sudarśana, to the forefront of the battle.
He then severed the head of the Daitya and liberated the gods.
O Rame, this is my first incarnation as Viṣṇu.
Then, again, in the second Manvantara, that of Svārociṣa, the Daitya Purukutsa [oppressed] Vipaścit, who was Indra, and the gods. (7–8)
In that manner, he oppressed Oja, Sthamba, and Niścala;
he also oppressed Ṛṣabha, Ārva-vīra, and Dambholi.
He further oppressed the Seven Seers, the Tuṣitas, and the Pārāvata gods.
He afflicted Manuputra, Ekala, Vinata, Vidyota, Ravi,
Bṛhadguṇa, Karṇānta, and Nabhasa as well; and he tormented him while he was dwelling in the midst of the waters, or sometimes in the form of a cloud.
"Even though I was entreated by Mahendra himself,
I assumed the form of a white elephant with wings, resembling a mountain,
possessing four tusks and two trunks, and suddenly appeared in the forest to destroy that which was present. (12)
When that Daitya, armed and fighting with force in battle,
I shall slay him with my tusks, my two trunks, and the trampling of my feet; at that time, I shall become Gajanārāyaṇa upon the earth.

Renowned and worshipped by the worlds, bestowing both liberation and worldly enjoyment— O Rame, my second incarnation is said to be named Gaja. And during the third Manu, Auttama, there was the Dānava Pralamba.
The one of great strength will cause distress to Mahendra, as well as to the one named Svaśānti,
Rathaujas, Ūrdhvabāhu, the sinless Śaraṇa, Maṇi, Śaṅku, Sutapas, and the Seven Sages.
Having fought those gods— the Vaśavṛttas, Svadhāmas, Śivas, Satyas, and Pratardanās— he will bring them under his own control.
He will also [subdue] the sons of Manu, Paraśu, Vinīta, and Āja.
Śuci, Suketu, Suvala, Devāvṛdha, and Sumitraka—
having acquired great energy, he will conquer all of them in battle.
Having gone into the midst of the great waters, the Dānava will take up his residence there.
Then, requested by Manu, I shall become the Lord in the form of a fish within the waters; indeed, I shall destroy Lambaka. This is my third incarnation, assuming the form of a fish.
In the time of the fourth Manu, known as Tāmasa, on this earth,
the Asura Bhīmaratha— strengthened by the Bhaimaratha Asuras—
set out to conquer Indra, who was named Śibi, as well as the sons of that Manu. (22–23)
He brought under his control ten more: Jānujaṅgha, Nirbhaya, Navakhyāti, Naya, Vivikṣipa,
Priyabhṛtya, Haviṣkandhi, Kṛta, Kṛtabandhu,
and Prastalākṣa.

At that time, he indeed brought under his control the sages Jyotirdhāmaka, Dhṛṣṭa, Kāvya, and Hemaka; as well as Agni, Ceta, and Caitraka. He likewise brought under his control the gods Surāgas, Svadhīs, Haris, and Haritakas.
Then, requested by the gods, I, Rāma, said:
"I shall slay that great asura Bhīmaratha, who dwells at the bottom of the ocean, with my massive body in the form of a tortoise in the midst of the waters. (27)
And this is my fourth incarnation, assuming the form of a tortoise.
During the time of the fifth Manu, Raivata, on earth,
he who has conquered his enemies bound the one named Vibhu as Indra.
The two Daityas, accompanied by their hosts of Daityas, [attacked] the sons of Manu as well as Mahāprāṇa, Sādhaka, Pratyaṅga, Naramitraka,
Śuci, Paraghna, Vanabandhu, and Dṛḍhavrata.
He conquered Ketuśṛṅga and also oppressed the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis).
[He likewise subdued] Devaśrī, Vedabāhu, Ūrdhvabāhu, Svadhāmaka,
Hiraṇyaromaka, Parjanya, and Satyanāmaka.

In this manner, he oppressed the gods— who were free from passion and had performed the horse-sacrifice— as well as the Vaikuṇṭhas and the immortals, in many ways on all sides. Then, requested by the sages, I, who was dwelling in the forest, spoke.
Having assumed the form of a swan, he slew Śāntaśatru.
This is my fifth incarnation, bearing the form of a swan;
thereafter, during the time of the sixth Manu, Cākṣuṣa.
The great Daitya Mahākāla became the bringer of sorrow to the gods;
having conquered Indra, as well as the sons of Manu known as Manojava, Uru, Puru, Śatadyumna, Tāpasa, and Satyabāhuka. (36)
Having conquered Kṛti, Agniṣṇumati, Rātri, Sudyumnaka, and Nara;
likewise having defeated the Āryas, Bhāvyas, and Pralekhakas among the gods, as well as the Pṛthukas and Prasutas, and even the Ṛṣis. (37–38)
Having conquered Haviṣmān, Sutanu, Svadhāman, Vairāja, Abhimāna, Sahiṣṇu, and Madhuśrī— these seven— he, Mahākāla,
will indeed rule over the sovereignty of the three worlds. (39)
Then, O Lotus-born One, requested by the worlds, I shall assume the form of Hayagrīva and destroy the Daitya Mahākāla. This is my sixth incarnation, possessing the form of Hayagrīva.
And in the seventh Manvantara, O Lakṣmī, under Vaivasvata Manu,
the great Daitya Hiraṇyākṣa, a truly wicked one, conquered all the gods: the Maruts,
the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the hosts of Sādhyas.
The king of the Daityas conquered the Viśvedevas, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Āṅgirasa gods,
and likewise the god Indra named Tejasvin;
he also oppressed the sages, including Bharadvāja and Gautama.
He brought Viśvāmitra, Kaśyapa, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and Atri, as well as the sons of Manu, under his control. He likewise subdued Ikṣvāku, Laviṣyanta, the one named Nediṣṭha, and Nabhas.
He made Pāṃśu, Viṣṭi, Sarjāti, Karūṣaka, Pṛṣadhra, and Sudyumna— all of whom were Vaiṣṇavas— his own followers. At that time, I, Hari myself, was personally entreated by the Earth with devotion.
"Assuming the form of a boar, I shall indeed slay Hiraṇyanetra;
this is the seventh incarnation, the Boar, the protector of the earth and other realms.
And in the eighth Manvantara, named Sāvarṇya, King Bali will be Indra."
The Daitya Virocana’s son became a great devotee.
At that time, the gods—the sons of Aditi, the performers of great austerities, and all the principal hosts—remained under his control as if by force. (3.164.49–50)
Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, Vyāsa, Gālava, Dīptimān,
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, and Paraśurāma— even those sages were under his control.
The sons of Sāvarṇi were Arvavīra, Vijaya, and Satyavāk.

He is the creator, the bodiless, the one who possesses movement, the most excellent, and the most venerable. (52) When all the words of Bali were under his control and he was filled with sorrow, I, at the request of the gods and the sages, assumed the form of a dwarf. (53)
Having become a Brahmin beggar, I shall seize the abode of Śakra;
I shall send Bali to liberation and dispatch him to heaven, and I shall grant [the earth] to Jiṣṇu.
O Lotus-born One, this is my eighth incarnation, indeed Trivikrama.
In the ninth Manvantara, under Dakṣasāvarṇi Manu,
Kālakākṣaka led the enemies of the gods against Indra, who possessed a wondrous name;
he was an Indra who was a portion of Kārttikeya, and these were the sons of that Manu.
He brought under his control Dhṛṣṭaketu, Dīptiketu, Padmahasta, Nirākṛti,
Pṛthuśravas, Ṛcika, Bṛhaddyumna, and Bṛhadguṇa; likewise,
he brought the Seven Sages, as well as Medhātithi and Vasu, into subjection.
Jyotiṣmat, Sabala, Dyuti, Kavya, and Havyaka;
likewise the Pāras, those called Sudharmas, and the Marīcigarbhas— then,
being entreated by the gods, I become Padmanābha.
"I shall slay Kālakākṣa and make the gods happy.
O Lotus-born one, this ninth incarnation of mine is indeed Padmanābha. In the tenth [Manvantara], during the period of Brahma-Sāvarṇi, there will be the great Asura Baliśatru."
He brought under his control the Indra named Śānti, as well as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis):
Āpomūrti, Haviṣmat, Satya, Sukṛtin,
Nābhāga, Apratima, and Vasiṣṭha— these were the ṛṣis.
The great asura brought under his control the sons of Manu, Sukṣetra, Bhūmisena, Jayadratha,
Anamitra, Vṛṣabha, Śatānīka,
Suparvaka, Suvīrya, and Auttamaujas.
He brought the gods, who were sitting at ease with their vital breaths restrained, under his control.
Then, requested by the gods, I myself, assuming the form of Hari, said:
"O Rame, I shall indeed cause that enemy of Bali to be slain with my mace."
O Lotus-born One, this tenth incarnation of mine is in the form of Hari. In the eleventh [incarnation], as Dharma-Sāvarṇi Manu,
the great Daitya Daśagrīva brought Indra and the gods under his control.
[He created] birds that travel at will and take delight in their own emanations;
likewise, he created gods who each took delight in individual things, as well as the sons of Manu:
Sarvatraga, Suśarman, Devānīka, Puru, and Guru.
He brought under his control Kṣetravarṇa, Dṛḍheṣu, Ārdraka, and Putraka, as well as the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), Agnitejas, and Haviṣyaka;
and Viśva, Viṣṇu, Vistara, and Haviṣmant of the lineage of Varuṇa.
Requested by the sages, I shall assume the form of Śrīrūpa, the deluder;
having become thus, I will slay that great asura who seeks to deceive and seize me.
My eleventh incarnation, delighting in the form of a beautiful woman, is Śrīnārīrūpa.
In the twelfth [manvantara], during the Sāvarṇi period of Rudra, the preeminent asura named Tāraka brought Indraka, whose domain is Truth (Ṛtadhāman), under his own control;
he likewise subdued the sons of Manu: Devavanta, Upadeva, and Vidūratha.
[He gave] Devaśreṣṭha, Mitravanta, Mitradeva, and Savīryaka;
likewise Mitrabindu, Mitravāha, and Pravāha;
as well as the Svadharmanas, Rohitakas, and Haritakas among the gods.
Then the gods [worshipped] Surāri, Sutapas, and the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis);
likewise, Tapasvin, Sutapas, Tapomūrti, and Taporati;
as well as Tapodhṛti, Dyuti, and Vidyuti. Thus indeed did the gods [proceed].
They offered prayers for my sake and for the destruction of Tāraka.
Tāraka, moreover, was possessed of great strength due to a boon from Śaṅkara;
for man is indeed the conscious principle (tattva), while woman is illusion (māyā), which is insentient.
Having obtained those two boons, he was indeed free from disease; death would not come to him from either of them.
He conquered all beings and ruled over the kingdom born of the three worlds.
Therefore, for the sake of his destruction, I assumed the state of a eunuch.
In that form, O Kamalā, I shall indeed destroy Tāraka.
This is a new incarnation as a neuter Hari;
from that, a creation consisting of neuter beings arose, superior even to me.
O Lakṣmī, this twelfth incarnation of mine has been proclaimed.
By meditating upon and worshipping the Neuter Hari at that time,
human beings shall attain supreme liberation, which is devoid of both female and male gender.

In the thirteenth [manvantara], during the period of Devasāvarṇi, the one known as Ṭiṭṭibha, a Daitya, brought even Divaspati Indra under his control. He also subdued the sons of Manu: Citrasena, Tapas, Dharma-rata, and Dhṛti.
He brought under his control Vicitra, Gharma, Kṣetravṛtti, the steadfast Sunetraka, as well as the Ṛṣis, Sunaya who perceives reality,
Dhṛtimat, Avyaya, Niśārūpa, and Nirutsuka.

Then, by means of his power of transformation, the Ṭiṭṭibha brought under his control the gods who dwell in heaven, those who follow their own dharma, and the immortals who perform their respective duties. The gods and others sought to destroy that Ṭiṭṭibha, who resided upon Mount Meru.
Desiring me, I assumed a long peacock form;
in that peacock form, I shall cause the *ṭiṭṭibha* bird to be killed.
This, O Lakṣmī, is proclaimed as my thirteenth incarnation.

"I shall be a peacock, O Great King, and then I will receive worship in that age. In the Bhautya Manvantara, during the fourteenth period of Indra-Sāvarṇi, the great Asura Śuci, having become Indra, exercised sovereign rule over the three worlds.
He brought under his control the sons of Manu— Gabhīra, Dhṛṣṭamūru,
Tarasvin, Abhimāna, Gabhīra, Grāha, Jiṣṇu,
Pravīraka, Durlabha, and Saṃkrandana.
He himself brought the Seven Sages, Agnibāhu, Agnidhra, Śuci, Māgadha, Śukra, Ajita,
and Mukta under his control;
as well as the Cākṣuṣas, the Karmaṭhas, the Pavitras, and the radiant Suras.
By his mere word, he brought the hosts of gods under his control; likewise,
at the time of evening, when I, Hari, was requested by Brahmā for the sake of the dissolution and destruction of the demon Indra.
With the Sudarśana discus, I shall slay Śakra.
This incarnation as Sudarśana-Hari is my final one;
O Lakṣmī, it is said that at the end of the Kalpa there will be many others besides this.
By the force of necessity, my incarnations indeed become innumerable.
On whose hand or on the sole of whose foot there appears a fish, a bow, a banner, an arrow, a trident, a svastika, a discus, a lotus, or even a jar— [he is one of my devotees]. (96)
Thus, I am Nārāyaṇa himself, existing in a concealed form.

I abide as one whose nature is virtuous, whose actions are virtuous, and who is all-knowing; though possessing sovereignty, I am without the pride of power, and though divine, I conduct myself like one who is not divine.
Through association, meeting, union, sight, or even touch;
through living together, remembering, or serving—He certainly bestows liberation.
Fortunate embodied beings, having known Me and propitiated Me through service, [attain this].
And on the path to liberation, they acquire my extraordinary bliss. But those who are devoid of devotion, considering me to be a mere human, flee far away;
they are asuras, full of sin, intensely envious, and transgressors. (3.164.10–11)
Even those established on the path to liberation will go to many hells;
however, those who, having known Me, take refuge in Me, shall go to My imperishable state— [distinguished] by the marks of omniscience as well as by divine qualities and the like.

Men, women, animals, birds, and those born of the Śūdra caste—even those devoted to unrighteousness—are indeed purified through my yoga. Desire, anger, greed, pride, intoxication, and envy—[are likewise overcome]. (10.3–10.4)
Through my yoga, both evil qualities and merit and demerit are devoid of attributes for me;
those who are united with me by whatever disposition are indeed eternally united and are never separated.
My yoga indeed bestows liberation upon gods, humans, and rākṣasas;
(106) and even for śūdras, birds, animals, and the women of the daityas and dānavas—by my mere will, multitudes of eggs are delivered across [to liberation]. (107)
By my mere association, even those who perform evil deeds are purified;
for that very action which is sinful by name becomes purifying when performed toward me.
I am independent, and my sacred traditions indeed teach the highest virtues.
"Let this bull be so; I maintain that he is indeed a bull.
Even one who is not a bull may become a bull for me through my resolve, or a bull may become a non-bull.
Having reflected thus, they serve me, the Supreme Lord, in embodied form. (3.164.110)
Their liberation rests in His hand for all actions, both here and hereafter.
By reading or hearing this chapter, there shall be liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purpose and Nature of the Fourteen Incarnations of Hari during the Fourteen Manvantaras," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.

The illustrious Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: "What kind of auspicious and virtuous deed should be performed here by a living person, so that he may be happy everywhere and in the next world? (1)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: My worship must be performed, for it bestows supreme happiness in the hereafter.
The worship of the ancestors must be performed, and by that, the worship of the gods becomes auspicious.
One should perform the most excellent gift as well as the auspicious *jīvacchrāddha*;
by performing it here with one's own hand, its fruit is obtained in the hereafter.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
Tell me the procedure for how and what kind of *jīvacchrāddha* (funeral rite for the living) is to be performed;
O Lord, tell me everything that must be offered therein.
Śrī Puṣkottama said:
In a temple, in the abode of the virtuous, in a monastery, or in the presence of the Lord;
in a school, on a sacrificial ground, on a mountain, or on a riverbank (5);
in a forest, at a sacred ford, in a place of worship, or even in any other pure location.
One should perform the *jīvacchrāddha* in one's own new home, which bestows happiness.
(6) When one contemplates dharma, the *śrāddha* should be performed with reverence;
it is offered with faith by one’s own hand, through the heart, and with meditative visualization. (7)
That *śrāddha* is to be understood in every respect as being proclaimed fivefold:
the *pārabrāhmika*, the *paitrya*, the *daiva*, the *aiśvara*, and the *bhautika*.
Whether in childhood, youth, old age, or at the proximity of death, [it should be performed].

This should be performed at any time, in five ways, by auspicious people. When the *jīvacchrāddha* is performed, the living person is liberated while still alive—whether performing actions or not, whether ignorant or possessed of knowledge. (3.165.10)

Whether he be learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) or not learned in them, whether he belongs to one of the four castes, or even if he is a renunciant (*tyāgin*) established in a stage of life (*āśrama*), he should indeed perform the *śrāddha* in five ways,
having first remembered Hari, the Supreme Brahman, within great temples.
A person living on this earth should offer daily food offerings (naivedya) to Hari.
One should offer ever-fresh great food offerings (mahānaivedya) to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, consisting of fifty-six varieties of enjoyments; that leads to the fruit of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Every morning, one should likewise offer to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa mung-bean sweets, milk, sugar, and so forth; furthermore,
one should give betel leaves and nutmeg for His satisfaction.
The fruit of that shall be inexhaustible happiness for the donor himself in the next world.
(15) One should also offer auspicious sweet foods even at midday;
one should present cooked foods seasoned with ghee, clarified butter, and sugar. (16)
One should offer vegetables, split pulses, soup, various kinds of cooked rice,
*polikās*, *pūrikās*, milk preparations, and milk products; as well as delightful *āranālas* (fermented gruel) mixed with *veṣavāra* spices.
One should offer foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked, as well as fruits,
bulbs, flowers, petals, leaves, and stalks for the meal,
to Kṛṣṇa, the God of gods, who is accompanied by all forms of prosperity.

One should always offer royal enjoyments in vessels and bowls made of gold and other materials; that is indeed a *śrāddha* performed visibly. A livelihood in the form of a means of subsistence was given by the living [king] to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
That [offering] indeed bears fruit in the imperishable abode, in Goloka, and also in Śrīpura (21).
Whatever is given to the Supreme Lord becomes inexhaustible;
even when returned by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow upon his state of liberation, it is still attained [as a reward] (22).
Whether in Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, the unmanifest, or even in the immortal realm,
whatever is given here to the Lord is obtained with infinite merit.
Thus, these waters are sweet, cool, and delicious.
All things desired in every season should be offered to Śrī Hari.
When given as a means of subsistence, they are obtained for the sake of His satisfaction.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, mouth-fresheners should be presented for the sake of purification.
These also include betel leaves, cloves, cardamom, camphor, and betel rolls,
as well as areca nut powder, khadira wood powder, and other desired fruits.
Furthermore, at the time of rising, one should likewise offer water, fruit, and leaves.
Whatever things are to be given for the sake of food, whether they be hot or cold;
all those cooked in ghee, those cooked in oil, all those cooked by fire, and those cooked by the sun. (27–28)
Edible foods that are ripened in their proper season and possess fragrant flavors should always be offered to Śrī Hari during the third watch of the day. Furthermore,
for the sake of the evening meal and drink, one should likewise offer *pūrikās* and *polikās*.
One should offer milk, vegetables, buttermilk, and water to Śrī Hari.
Indeed, one should always present these, or else provide a garden for His sustenance; one should likewise offer fields, palatial mansions, and dwellings.
One should offer villages, houses, and land that provide a means of livelihood to the Supreme Self,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
One should also secure a source of income with wealth for the purpose of maintaining a continuous flow of worship.
Thus, that which one performs with faith is called a *jīvacchrāddha*.
Every year, once a year, one should provide a meal accompanied by water,
or otherwise, one should offer a vessel of food (*sthālanaivedya*) along with a coin (*nāṇaka*).
One may give [the means of subsistence] every month, or likewise offer it at every festival; one may also bestow it every fortnight, or even grant it on every sacred occasion (parvan).
Thus, an excellent livelihood has been provided for Śrī Hari.
This [śrāddha] leads to inexhaustible fruit and bestows eternal satisfaction.
O Lakṣmī, this śrāddha pertaining to the Supreme Brahman has been described by me to you;
now listen as I describe the śrāddha pertaining to Īśvara.
In whichever temple there are my incarnate images—
the manifestations such as Vāsudeva and others, the perfected sages such as Kapila and others,
the Śrīs and Lakṣmīs, and the auspicious male and female attendants— [there I am present]. (38)
One should offer the sacrificial food (nivedya) to Vairāja and the other lords;
one should also give sweet food, water for drinking, fruit, bulbous roots, leaves and so forth, betel-leaf preparations, milk, and here, honey that is still living.
All that is declared to be for the Lord; when given, it is for the sake of a return fruit.
O Lakṣmī, I shall now tell you regarding that which is offered to the ancestors:
whether in water, at the root of a *darbha* grass, at the foot of a tree, or upon the bare ground.
One who is alive should give [offerings] into the hand of a Brahmin or into the mouth of a Brahmin for the sake of satisfaction.
For the meal, one should give raw rice balls (*āmapiṇḍa*), cooked savory foods,
vegetables, leaves, fruits, roots, and milk for the sake of satisfaction.
And one should also respectfully offer the *daiva* śrāddha to the gods— to the Ādityas, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Vasus—
as well as to other deities, offering what is auspicious according to one's preference.
That is indeed declared to be the *daiva* śrāddha; listen as I describe the procedure.
Having examined the ground according to rule by means of its smell, leaves, sap, and so forth, one should prepare an auspicious sand mound (*sthaṇḍila*) on a site free from thorns or debris.
In the center, having smeared with the prescribed rite a most beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit at most, and having established the fire;
having performed the ritual fuel-adding (anvādhāna) according to the scriptures and having enclosed it on all sides.
Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] according to the scriptures as handed down through the traditional lineage (48),
and having completed everything up to the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) and worshipped the fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should offer oblations separately with fuel-sticks and the like, and separately with the sacrificial porridge (caru). (49)
One should also offer oblations with clarified butter, having extracted [the essence] for oneself among the gods and other beings.
Then, for the sake of their satisfaction, one should offer all the constituent elements (tattvas).
*Oṃ bhūḥ, salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.*

and thereafter offer it also for the satisfaction of the consort of the Supreme Self.

One should also give vehicles, beds, carriages, vessels of bell-metal, copper, and so forth;
[objects] made of gold and silver, a cow, sesame seeds, fields, and riches;
as well as groups of female and male slaves, and even a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should offer flavorful food balls (*piṇḍa*) separately in eight varieties.
For three days, one should offer sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and a meal of milk to Śrī Viṣṇu.
Whether one performs this for the deceased or not, if one performs it while living, the deceased shall receive [the merit]. (88–89)
Having acted in this way, there is neither purity nor impurity for one who has died here;
since he is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is indeed no birth-impurity (sūtaka) for him.
For those who perform the cremation, there is merely the ritual bath; beyond that, there is no further impurity.
In that lineage, whether it be a daughter or a son who increases the family line,
he too shall certainly be liberated and become a savior of his ancestors.
Even while living, the ancestors are released from hell through the performance of *śrāddha*.
By this rite, he is released from his debt to his mother and father;
when the time arrives, his dwelling in the pit, his cremation, and his immersion in water—all these shall be for the sake of his liberation, free from all defects. (93)

One should give [offerings] to the elements, to cows and cattle, and to birds such as parrots;
one should also bestow them upon insects, moths, other living beings, and fish and the like.
One should give water to trees and the like, and grains to embodied beings;
one should offer food to mendicants and present them with clothing and a bowl.

For this deceased person, there is no waiting for twelve days at all.
Seated upon a bull, he quickly departs by means of a celestial chariot to the world of merit;
or else, the divine *ātivāhika* deities who move upward lead him there. (97–98)
O Lakṣmī, in this manner the Śrāddha that bestows life should be performed;
it shall grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation when one offers what has been earned by one's own hands.
Cooking with one's own hand and eating with one's own hand [are essential].
He who acquires wealth with his own hand and gives it away with his own hand conquers in this world and also conquers in the next;
by merely hearing this, one likewise becomes endowed with merit.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Jīvacchrāddha," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 165. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 166.
[The Author: Chapter 167.
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said: "In this world, two things prevail: nectar and poison."
Nectar (*sudhā*) and ambrosia (*amṛta*) are indeed the same as poison (*gara*) and venom (*viṣa*) in terms of their taste.
Or rather, O Hari, if that [taste] were not there, what would it be?
Knowing which, these people of the world might either become detached or take hold [of it]. (1–2)
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Formerly, during the churning of the ocean, a great poison arose; the yogi Śrī Śaṅkara drank it, while the great sages offered him praise. (3)
O Blessed One, O Hara, you have swallowed the most terrible poison known as Kālakūṭa;
O Treasure of Compassion, everything has been well-protected and established by you.
You are capable, you are the Great Lord, and you are the protector who removes all poison.
"O Suyogin, may you always be victorious! You are Brahmā, free from all attachment.
Upon hearing this, Śambhu laughed and said to the other sages:
"The poison called Kālakūṭa is not the true poison; the world is the fierce poison."
What indeed is the use of this [power] for one who is already capable of neutralizing that poison?
A yogi should, with every effort, neutralize the illusory poison.
Those who are the removers of illusory poison are indeed Śaṅkaras.
The gurus, the gods, or the exceedingly pure holy ones bring about well-being;
for those great-souled yogis are indeed the bestowers of peace and liberation.
For those virtuous ones are truly capable of removing the poison of saṃsāra.
The virtuous ones such as Sanaka and others, as well as the yogis such as Śuka and others, and the chaste women who effect the destruction of latent impressions—they are all [liberated].
This saṃsāra is of two kinds: indeed, both embodied and unembodied.
The embodied [Self] indeed takes the form of husband and wife, while the unembodied consists of latent impressions (vāsanā).

False knowledge is the cause of these impressions; and by the power of impressions, there arises for those possessed of passion the state of householdership and the enjoyment of sense objects. (11–12)
Hatred toward passion takes the form of a friend, even while providing assistance in what is undesirable;
these two defects are the motivators for engagement and withdrawal.
That engagement and withdrawal, accompanied by qualities, bring about action.
The arising of that which is active is its connection with the first moment.
Growth, nourishment, and firmness, as well as decline, decay, dissolution, and so forth—arising followed by dissolution at the end occurs again in accordance with karma. (14–15)

Thus, even while wandering here in the wheel of saṃsāra, one possessed of discrimination and free from attachment, aversion, and the like, becomes liberated from bondage. (1.6) There are many poisons; listen as I speak of them, O Lotus-born One.
Sweet poison is the sense of "mine" regarding one's family; such pride exists from birth. Mother, father, friend, and relative—the great poison is the sense of "mine.
"This house is mine," "this garden is mine," "this field is mine," and "this chest is mine. (17-18)
"Mine is wealth, mine is gold, mine is clothing, and mine is the most excellent food.
My word is always to be honored; that which is spoken by me is indeed the truth.
My foremost speech is invincible, and it alone is to be revered. (19)
Victory is mine, my resolve is firm, and I am to be honored by no one else.
(3.166.20) Whatever has been determined by me must be accepted in every way by the people;
for this intoxication, by which one is tormented, is said to be a great poison. (21)
Power is declared to be the supreme poison, for it produces affliction and incites conflict; knowledge of the arts is also a poison, as is wealth, for it brings about destruction.
O Lakṣmī, sense objects are indeed poisons that cause one to fall into the great hells.
Sense objects are indeed like poison, for their possession is incurable.
O Lakṣmī, thirst is the supreme poison; passion is a most great poison;
hatred is a poison in the form of fire; but anxiety is a poison that brings about destruction.
Desire is the most potent poison among all poisons;
it arises from hell, bestows hell, and grants residence in hell.
Likewise, delusion is a great poison that brings about the undesirable and yields immense suffering.
The deluded man does not know what ought to be done; consumed by infatuation, he perishes.
(26) Existence itself is a supreme poison, and sovereignty is a deadly poison.
Greed for the tongue, the genitals, and the belly is a poison that is like a lethal brew. (27)
Atheism, and the dishonor of one's teacher and parents, are poisons as grave as any;
by these one is suddenly struck down and falls into ruin and a downward path.
A curse is poison to those who are suffering, and lack of affection toward the virtuous is poison.
Unrighteousness is poison; it burns one from heaven and destroys prosperity.
(29) Blame, theft, and violence—these are poisons at their root; they cut away the doer’s merit and bring about his destruction without delay. (3.166.30)
Miserliness, intolerance, and envy are the eyes, while the heart and mind are made their respective abodes;
by these, the person is burned.
Thus, this [person] is enveloped by poisons and surrounded by ignorance.
The hell-being exists in every way; this is a difficult and endless poison.
(31) Whether born from a sprout, born from sweat, born from an egg, or born from a womb, they wander indeed due to the absence of renunciation and through the impressions of ignorance and karma. (33)
The body, consisting of the six sheaths and containing the vital fluids, certainly undergoes transformation.
The first birth is considered to be from the father, consisting of the bestowal of seed;
the second birth is from the womb, which is regarded as the state of infancy.
The third [birth] is from the investiture with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), and marriage is the fourth.
The fifth is from the renunciation of all worldly ties, while the sixth occurs after death.
The seventh is the attainment of liberation; thereafter, no further birth exists.
The bondage of action arising from the seed, from animals, and from humans;
that which is unfallen, that which pertains to spirits, and the seventh, which is indeed without rebirth—
thus do these births become smeared with poison.

The mere implantation of the seed is called the "seed-birth" (baijika). That which is obtained through the birth of an embryo like that of an animal is the "animal-birth" (pāśava), namely the birth of a child. [One should receive] the Manu, the mantra, the Gāyatrī, and also the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). || 38–39 ||
It approaches men as bulls and enters human birth; marriage and the bond of ritual action are a state equivalent to a prison.
That birth, which takes the form of a bond of action, assumes the form of a marital union.

But he who, having renounced everything and being free from passion, attains renunciation— for him who has gone for refuge to Hari, birth is declared to be ended. At the time of casting off the body, while in the state of a departed spirit, he effects the union with the subtle body.
The embodied soul, joined with merit and demerit, wanders; that is birth.
It is called *praitaka* when it occurs anywhere for the sake of rebirth.
For the sake of liberation, one should practice disinterested devotion (*nirguṇā bhakti*) and discharge one's debts.
Having severed his bonds, dissolved [his impurities], and destroyed all poisons,
he who departs for the abode of Hari never returns to birth;
he is indeed one who has attained unsurpassed sorrowlessness and is a consumer of the great nectar.
Having attained the seventh birth, death no longer exists for him.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these six poisons indeed become vast;
they are cruel, burning, and cooking [the soul] on all sides.
There are indeed many sufferings in the womb, as well as on the path through the birth canal;
likewise upon the earth, and while lying in bed, during childhood and youth, in enjoyment or in disciplined practice, in worldly affairs, in old age, and in a state of dependence.

For the wise, there are only sufferings in states of incapacity, poverty, disease, death, and likewise in the state of a departed spirit; as well as in the realm of Yama, in the earth, in poison, among animals, humans, yakṣas,
piśācas, rākṣasas, and gods.
In the assembly of the Pitṛs who enjoy pleasures, among the Gandharvas and the hosts of Apsarases;

in the realm of Indra, in that of Brahmā, in the natural world, in the Vairāja heaven, in the abode of Prajāpati, in the domain of Puruṣa, and in the maw of Time—therein lies suffering, a most great poison. (3.166.50–51)
Poison is of the nature of earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego;
it is elemental and its suffering exists in the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Present sufferings and future poisons,
as well as various sufferings regarding place, time, and action—
just as a tree whose roots are severed falls helplessly to the earth, so it shall be. (53–54)
Due to the exhaustion of their merit, even the gods fall to the earth;
likewise, the suffering born of sin is forcibly experienced as mere pain.
This is true even for those in hell and for kings who have not attained their heart's desire.
Furthermore, suffering arises for ascetics and those of the [four] castes who fail to perform what is prescribed; likewise, even for the dispassionate who are submerged in the fear of saṃsāra,
as well as for insects, birds, wild animals, domestic beasts, elephants, and horses.

Poison is suffering, and for one who does not abandon what is like suffering, that [poison] is indeed suffering. For all the denizens of celestial chariots (*vaimānika*) who hold office for a kalpa, as well as for those such as Manu who take pride in their stations, the terrestrial realm is poison. (58)

Due to their mutual desire for victory, among the gods, the Daityas, the Rākṣasas, and kings, there is poison and suffering throughout the three worlds. Hermitages exist for the sake of rest; through knowledge, one may find repose. (3.166.60)
Knowledge is a source of suffering when imparted to an unworthy recipient; therefore, one should seek to attain the status of a worthy vessel.
Through constant association with the virtuous, the state of being a worthy vessel arises.
By means of that, O Rāma, the Brahman may be sustained even through the grace of the good.
The Supreme Brahman is to be held in the eyes; likewise, Hari is to be held in the ears.
Kṛṣṇa is to be held in the sense of touch; Viṣṇu is to be held in the locus of taste.
The Supreme Lord is to be held in the nose; the Lord himself is to be held in the feet.
The pervasive Lord (Īśvara) should be held within the anus and the genitals;
Māyeśa should be held in the mind; Narāyaṇa should be held in the heart;
Mādhava should be held in the intellect; and Ṛṣīkeśa should be meditated upon in reflection.
The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is to be meditated upon in the earth; the One who reclines on the waters (Jaleśaya) is to be meditated upon in water;
the Lord of Light (Dhāmeśa) is to be meditated upon in fire; and the Lord of the Cosmic Virāṭ (Virāṭpati) is to be meditated upon in the wind.
Mahāviṣṇu is to be meditated upon in space, and I myself am to be meditated upon within one's own self.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, I am to be seen, and likewise Hari is to be heard;
I alone am to be smelled, tasted, and touched;
I am also to be reflected upon, understood, and acted upon—I am Hari.
"I am indeed that which is to be willed; I am that which is to be spoken; likewise, I am the Lord.
I am that which is to be grasped, that which is to be traversed, and that which is to be manifested in creation.
I am indeed that which is to be gladdened; I abide within every single reality."
I am established in the vital breath, in departure, in movement, in drinking, and in stability.
One who possesses self-mastery should worship me as the Self of all, moving everywhere—abiding in food, in water, in the vital breath, and situated in the mind. (3.166.70)
One should worship me, Hari, the Supreme Person, as abiding in consciousness;
and as abiding in the senses, as abiding in the objects of the senses, as abiding in time, and as established in the individual soul.
One should worship me, who abide in all things, for the sake of cutting through the poison of saṃsāra.

Abandoning ignorance— the impurity and the poison— approach me, who am the nectar, the Lord of the Imperishable, the inner Supreme Self, the gracious Hari, the Lord of lords, the innate Master residing within. || 72–73 ||
Having known [Me] directly, one shall indeed attain the vast state of immortality.
One should constantly practice that knowledge which pertains to My domain as the primary focus.
Endowed with this singular knowledge and joined with the affection of devotion, [one attains liberation].
Having abandoned the poison of attachment, he is liberated and attains Me; of this there is no doubt.
Whether in this world or in the next, nothing remains for him to be done, because as one liberated while living, even his latent tendencies have dissolved.

Devoted to knowledge and devotion, he is a knower of Brahman in the ultimate sense. Thus liberated from saṃsāra and freed from the poison of suffering, he, established in the refuge of the Guru, goes to the imperishable abode of the Supreme Self.
The sins and poisons of the yogi are digested;
even while playing, he is not tainted by various kinds of poisons.
O Rame, the meditation on Śrī Hari remains forever truly free from poison.

One whose character is that of Brahman should practice meditation through association with a Guru; he attains a state of total absorption in me, and finally even dissolution into me. Indeed, my devotee certainly finds this; for him, even poison becomes nectar.
In this way, all poisons indeed shine as nectars for him.

The elements, the subtle constituents, the objects of the senses and those arising from the objects, the qualities and the absence of qualities, as well as the actions and whatever poisons there may be—[all these become nectar]. (8.1–8.2)
All those [elements] are imagined as nectar within me, the Supreme.
Thus indeed is the devotee a consumer of poison; he alone is capable, and no other anywhere.
He would indeed be able to sustain the earth, water, and fire.
He shall be capable of supporting the wind and the ether, as well as the eightfold functions and the lords;
he shall indeed be able to support both Prakṛti and Puruṣa,
and being identical with Me, he shall be competent to support Time as well.
He would also possess the nature of the imperishable (akṣara) and be capable of sustaining even the liberated ones;
for as I am, so is he— capable of bringing about the destruction of the very beginning of worldly existence,
possessing the divine state that is my own self.
Having attained the state of the Supreme Lord, one becomes capable of performing everything.
Through direct experience, one should recognize poison and contemplate its remedy;
or, having consumed even non-poisonous or virulent poison, one should destroy that poison [through this power]. (87–88)
The virtuous are said to be non-venomous, whereas I, Hari, am fierce venom.
Yet, through contact with the virtuous, even one who is poisonous becomes non-venomous by drinking from me.
Through affection for me, who am non-venomous, and through devotion, one attains my grace.
"Through grace, liberation comes swiftly; this is my solemn promise, O Rāma.
Whether situated in the womb, being born, a child, a youth, or even an old man, the embodied soul is liberated through the grace of the Supreme Self. (3.166.90–91)

Whether born from an egg, born from a sprout, or even born from sweat, a man or a woman who possesses my grace is liberated. Even embodied beings are but portions of myself, distinguished by my yoga. (92)

Endowed with my nature, they go to the supreme goal. Beheld by me, my devotees—who are portions of myself and have taken refuge at my feet—cross the poisonous ocean of saṃsāra as objects of my compassion. (93–94)
Just as oil, when mixed with water, rises upward and floats, so too the embodied soul,
through union with Kṛṣṇa, rises upward and crosses over.
Just as fire, being kindled, naturally moves upward, so it is.
In the same way, the embodied soul, greatly nourished by my supreme devotion, ascends upward;
just as a yogi reaches the door of Brahman through great powers of yoga,
so indeed does this soul reach the Supreme Brahman through my sovereign powers.
Just as Gopī, having attained the Unborn, became Gāyatrī, so too the cowherd, having attained Hari, shall reach Goloka. Just as Lakṣmī, having attained Hari, obtained a dwelling within his heart.
In the same way that a devotee, having reached Hari, attains residence in the Imperishable;
and just as Māyā, having reached Hari, is dissolved within Hari—so too the devotee, having reached Hari, is completely dissolved within Hari. (3.166.99–100)
Just as a wife clinging to her beloved does not perceive herself as separate from him,
so too the devotee, absorbed in Hari, does not perceive his own distinctness. And just as sugar attains the state of being the very essence of milk, [so does the devotee become one with Him].
Likewise, when one performs dark deeds toward Kṛṣṇa, devotion attains the state of milk.
Just as a moist mind indeed merges into a vessel of oil,
so too my affectionate devotee merges into me as non-different.
Just as bliss (*ānanda*) and joy (*pramoda*) are not separate from the Self,
so too is the devotee of divine form not separate from the Supreme Self.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I described to you this state of being a "poison-destroyer" (*viṣahāra*).
By reading or hearing this, all poison is dispelled.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Poisons of Saṃsāra and the Means for Their Removal," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 166.
Chapter 167 [Author: Chapter 168 → Śrī Nārāyaṇī said: Śrī said:
"O Keśava, for you who are devoted and have fallen into distress—
how may there be an end to this calamity, and how may there be the destruction of my sins?
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
For an embodied being who lacks vows, is incapable, and is devoid of knowledge,
this hymn known as the *Vyāpaha* is intended for the destruction of calamities, sins, and the like.
Having become one-pointed in mind, one should praise the Supreme Lord.
One should praise the incarnations, the liberated ones, the lords, the ancestors, the gods, the sages, the gurus, the devotees of the Lord, and the virtuous.
Having become one who seeks no other refuge, one should pray; thus one shall become happy. (3–4)
O Rame, I shall recite for you this divine hymn that bestows all spiritual accomplishments;
it swiftly grants every desired object to the listener, the speaker, and the reader.
*Salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Self.*
Salutations to the Great Blessed One, the Lord of the Immutable Syllable, the Supreme Self;
salutations to the Sovereign of the three creations, the Inner Controller of all, to the Supreme Brahman,
the Puruṣottama, and the Incarnate One.
The all-knowing, the abode of all, the dwelling place of Śrī, established in all things,
situated in the supreme imperishable, and the Lord of liberation— may He dispel my sin.
May the incarnate Supreme Brahman, the divine-souled Śrī Narāyaṇa, [grant this].
May the Blessed Supreme Lord indeed dispel my sin.
(9) May Hari—the beginningless and endless Lord of all, the possessor of all knowledge, the bestower of all and the giver of happiness—dispel my sins and calamities. (3.167.10)
Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, worshipped by the universe—
may the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa dispel my sin.
He who is beloved by the Consort of Brahmā, the lover, the peaceful one, the Lord overflowing with affection.
May the one who is dear to Hari and captivating to the mind dispel misfortune and calamity.
(12) May the supreme beloved, who is served by the circle of liberated souls, who is attended by the multitude of emancipated ones, and who is most desirable, dispel sin and misfortune. (13)
May the Supreme, the Avatārī, who is complete, the Brahman beyond the supreme, the Lord of the high and the low, the Highest, remove my sins and calamities.
May the Lord of Śrī, the Bearer of Śrī, the Heart of Śrī, the Possessor of Śrī, the Giver of Śrī, and He who is endowed with Śrī [grant this].
May the venerable Śrī Hari Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Fortune, dispel my sins and misfortunes.

(15) May the Lord of Lakṣmī, the bearer of Lakṣmī, the one who takes Lakṣmī as His heart, who is endowed with the granting of fortune, and who is exceedingly pleased by the service of Lakṣmī, dispel my sins and misfortunes. (16)
May the Lord of Rādhā, who bears Rādhā, who is the heart of Rādhā, and who is united with Rādhikā;
may He whose soul is Rādhā, the Kṛṣṇa of Rādhikā, remove our sins and calamities.
(17) May He whose vehicle is Māṇikī, the Lord of Māṇikī, and the Master of Māṇikī [grant us protection].

May the Lord of Goloka, the Lord of the Gopikās, worshipped by the Gopīs and the cowherds, the protector of the cows and the cowherds—Kṛṣṇa, the guardian of the cattle—dispel my sins and calamities. 19. May the new necklace of rubies dispel my sins and calamities. 18.
May the Lord Nārāyaṇa— the best of men, the king, the protector, the supreme among humans,
the dweller in Vaikuṇṭha— dispel our sins and calamities.
May Vasuda and Vāsudeva, the bestower of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation, [grant us grace].
May the consumer of nectar, the giver of nectar, dispel all sins and calamities.

(21) May the giver of the earth, who dwells upon the earth, who is the Infinite, who increases the fortune of those who possess the earth, and who is the Lord of the existence of the earth and the Unmanifest, dispel all sins and calamities. (22)
May Hari— the knower of the Vedas, the upholder of the earth, the bearer of the deep-toned drum, the possessor of wisdom, the one who sustains the cows,

the milker of the cows, the swan, and the remover of the calamities of sin— ward off my misfortunes. May he who is an ascetic, who is affectionate toward his devotees, who is virtuous, a mendicant, fierce, the sacrifice itself, and the forest-dweller [protect me].
May Bāla, the best of physicians, the one who suffers for others, dispel sins and calamities.
May Samrāṭ, the teacher, Kṛṣṇakānta, the wise one, the cause of incarnations, the possession, the partial incarnation, the digit, and the manifestation dispel sins and calamities. (24–25)
May Pūrṇa, Para, Vyūha, Aiśa, Antaryāmin, Arcā, Svarūpakṛt, Vibhava, Caitya, and Sunyāsī dispel my sins and calamities.
May He who dwells in all abodes, who possesses manifold forms, and who is the Supreme Lord [grant me grace]. //26//
May the Teacher of the insentient and the sentient dispel my sins and calamities.
(27) May Nārāyaṇī, the Mistress of Śrīpura, Mādhavī, and Puruṣottamī;
may Kārṇī, Śrī Lalitā, and Lakṣmī dispel my sins and calamities. (28)
May Bhārgavī, Duḥkhahā, Lakṣmī, Śivarājñī, Vaiṣṇavī, Padminikā,
and Padmajā dispel my sins and calamities.
May Kaṃbharāśrī, Mahālakṣmī, Vāsudevī, and Pareśvarī [grant me protection].
May the imperishable, divine Śrī remove my sins and calamities.
May Pauruṣī, Prākṛtī, the Goddess, Māyeśī, Pārvatī, Prabhā,
Pārabrāhmī, Ramā, and Mātā remove my sins and calamities.
May Padmā, Vairājī, Gaṅgā, Revā, Sarasvatī,
Gāyatrī, Gomatī, and Gopī— who abide in abundance— dispel sins and calamities. May Sādāśaivī, Māheśī, Brāhmī, Brahmapriyā, and Satī likewise do so.
May the virtuous, sovereign Lady of the Moon dispel sins and calamities.
(33) May the golden, gilded, deer-like one of golden form, Vaikuṇṭhā, Tulasī, and Vṛndā dispel sins and calamities. (34)
May she who is perfected, whose form is the ancestral *siddhi*, the wonder of the Sudhanvans, the nectar, the immortal,
and the one possessing nooses, remove sins and calamities.
May she who is the solar radiance, the attendant of Parshada, the goddess of Ishvara, and the delight of Rati [grant protection].
May Prīti, whose form is devotion and vows, dispel my sins and calamities.
May the gentle, ancient, divine, contented, and satisfied Abjikā, Kamalāmbā, and Śāradā dispel my sins and calamities. (36–37)
May Aindrī, who consists of pure bliss, whose power is consciousness and whose form is knowledge,
the Yoginī established in the heart, remove my sins and calamities.
May Mohinī, Nandinī, Padmekṣaṇā, Urvaśī, and Pativratā [grant me protection].
May my mother, who is golden-hued, dispel my sins and calamities.
May the meritorious, purifying, and learned daughter of the ocean— who bestows wealth, sustains riches, removes distress, and is peaceful— dispel my sins and calamities.
May Śrī— who knows the true nature of beings, who bestows enjoyment and liberation, who grants fearlessness to her devotees,
who occupies half the body of [Śiva], and who is the very life-force— dispel all sins and calamities.
May she, endowed with good fortune, rich in splendor, and adorned with every ornament, [grant protection].
May Gaurī, whose limbs are radiant with every ornament, dispel sins and calamities. May Gaurī— the Fortune of crops, the Fortune of jewels, the Fortune of prosperity, the mistress of the household,
and the bearer of grain and food— dispel sins and calamities.
May Rohiṇī, the nourisher, the maiden in the bloom of youth,
the delighter of the gods, and the beautiful woman, dispel my sins and calamities.
May she who consists of *sattva*, who bestows *sattva*, who upholds *sattva*, and who is united with *sattva* [protect me].
May she who is composed of *sattva*, who is existence-consciousness-bliss (*saccidānanda*), dispel sins and calamities.
(45) May the liberated attendants, the devotees, the other devotees, the lords to be attained (*sādhya-īśvarāḥ*), the goddesses, and the great liberated ones dispel all sin and misfortune. (46)
The conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the Kaustubha gem, the crown, the forest garland, and the flower garland of Hari dispel sin and calamities.
Likewise, the staff, the umbrella, the chowrie, the armlet, and the bracelet [dispel them].
The chain, the girdle, and the black antelope skin remove sin and misfortune.
(48) All the qualities, sovereignties, wonders, perfections, and powers of Śrī Hari remove sin and misfortune. (49)

Śālagrāma, as well as the sage Śālāṅkāyana, the Gaṇḍakī river, Triveṇī, and the Śāla tree— these dispel sins and calamities. Badarī, the one who dwells in Badarī (Viṣṇu), the sages, Nara, and Hari [likewise do so].
The Gaṅgā, the Himālayas, gold,
Śeṣa (the serpent upon whom Viṣṇu reclines), the Ocean of Milk, Lakṣmī (born from the milk-ocean), and the white king of serpents (Śeṣa)— these,
as well as fasting and being released from one's food, dispel sins and calamities. 51–52.
May Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and the Sun;
the Gaṇas, the Rudras, and the Rudrāṇīs—dispel my sins and calamities.
May the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, the Moon, the stars, and the luminous beings [grant me protection].
The planets and the comets likewise dispel sins and calamities.
The swan, Garuḍa, the bull, the lion, the deer, the elephant,
Śeṣa, the peacock, and the celestial vehicles dispel sins and calamities.
Kārttikeya, Mahākāla, the great vajra, and the trident;
Kāladaṇḍa—may these weapons dispel your sins and calamities.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Lords of the Lord.
May the guardians of the quarters and the protectors of the worlds dispel sin and calamities.
(57) Likewise, may the ether, touch, fire, taste, earth, as well as the subtle elements and the vital breaths, dispel sin and calamities. (58)
May the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Kinnaras, and likewise the Guhyakas,
the Gandharvas, and the Kiṃpuruṣas, drive away sin and calamities.
May also the mothers of the gods and the mothers of the Gaṇas [grant protection].
May all the Mothers of beings dispel sin and calamities.
(3.167.60) Likewise, may the Apsarases, the goddesses, the lunar mansions, the lunar days, the fortnights, the months, and the years dispel sin and calamities. (3.167.61)
Fever, diseases, the seasons, debts, as well as Rākṣasas,
Daityas, and wicked Dānavas— may they dispel sin and calamities.
May the oceans, rivers, wells, tanks, and oblong ponds [grant protection].
Varuṇa, through his ponds and lakes, removes sin and misfortune.
(63) The cows that rain down all desires, the creepers that fulfill every wish, and likewise the wish-fulfilling trees—these remove sin and misfortune. (64)
Sacrifices, sacrificial rites, injunctions, and even the Vedas;
the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the meters—may these dispel sin and misfortune.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet.
May the thousand-armed, omniscient one dispel sins and calamities.
May the purifier, the fire, the bearer of oblations, the seven-flamed, the seven-tongued, the golden-colored, the mouth of Brahmā, dispel sins and calamities. (66–67)
Charity, self-restraint, compassion, the divine, the gods, the goddesses, the virtuous, the saintly, the noble men, and the meritorious—these dispel sin and calamities.
The elderly, those worthy of worship, the devotees of the Lord, and the single-minded devotees of Hari [are likewise protectors]. 68.
Astrologers and divine beings dispel sin and calamities.
(69) Vows, meritorious deeds, the practice of good works, service, faith, and spiritual cultivation dispel sin and calamities. (3.167.70)
Yoga, all forms of knowledge, truth, dispassion, and mastery— these,

as well as the worship of Hari and His command, dispel sin and calamities. The household deities, the village deities, the field deities, and those dwelling at the boundaries [are likewise to be honored].
The deities of the doorways and the deities outside dispel sins and calamities.
(72) The deities of the site, the deities of the ancestral rites, the deities of the sacrifice, and the great festivals;
the sacred fords and the abodes of the gods—these dispel sins and calamities. (73)
Temples, shrines, monasteries, and places of sacred discourse—
all sacred sites of liberation dispel sins and calamities.
Mothers, fathers, excellent kinsmen, and virtuous wives [likewise do so].
Devotees, boys, and girls dispel sins and calamities.
(75) All expiations, *darbha* grass, and the weapons of the gods, as well as the divine offerings to the gods and ancestors, dispel sins and calamities. (76)
The divine chariots, the paths of the gods, the celestial ways, the deities,

and the divine guides who carry one across— may these dispel sin and calamities. May the lightning flashes, the clouds, the rain-bearing mists, the earthquakes, and likewise all misfortunes [be warded off].
And those gods who receive sacrificial offerings, may they dispel my sin and misfortune.
(78) The treasures, the quarters of space, the Manus, and likewise the Kalās—may these fourteen abodes dispel my sin and misfortune. (79)
The *vyāhṛtis*, the breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*), the attendants of Yama born of the lineage of Dharma,
Dharmadeva, and his wives— may they dispel sins and calamities.
May the deities of the sacrificial pits and pavilions, who dwell upon the banners and branches, [likewise protect us].
The deities of the sacrificial ladle and other implements dispel sins and calamities.

and the consecrated remains (prasāda) consumed by the guru dispel sins and calamities.
The water from the feet of the virtuous, the water from the feet of the holy,

and the meritorious water from the feet of Viṣṇu dispel sins and calamities. Association with the good, service to them, seeking refuge in them, and following their commands [bring about this result].
Serenity and blessings dispel sins and calamities.

(84) The sacred ford of the mother, the sacred ford of the father, the most excellent sacred ford of the guru, the sacred ford of the fallen, and the sacred ford of the virtuous wife dispel sins and calamities. (85)
The *gotīrtha*, the *avabhṛthatīrtha*, the *paṅktitīrtha* on the right,
the *saṃnyāsatīrtha*, and the mantra— these dispel sin and calamities.
[Likewise do] the sacred thread, the *kaṇṭhī* [rosary], the *taulaseyī* [garland of basil], and the act of surrender.

"I am surrendered to him; may he purify me, his devotee, in this world.

This merit, when recited, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another for whom it is recited,

Having cast off all evils, he who recites this becomes pure.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the third section, the lineage of the Dvāpara age, wherein the *Vyapohana-stavana*—which serves to destroy all calamities, sins, bonds, and the like—is declared.

Chapter 169 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, to this meritorious account which destroys all sins and bestows all merit: the gift of a daughter at a sacrifice.
