Having given alms to mendicants, girls, and children,

One should satisfy the ancestors and the deities with sweet foods, grains such as *kaṇa*, auspicious sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter, and continuous streams of ghee. Then,
one should invoke the Youth (*kumāra*) there in the pavilion.
One who is learned, handsome, renowned, and born of a noble lineage;
one who is prosperous, youthful, and a delight to the mind of the maiden; one who is fortunate and whose character, dharma, virtues, and so forth have been previously ascertained. (5–6)
Having seated him in the presence of the assembly near the fire,
with the Brahmins as witnesses for the rite and the Fire-god as witness in the pavilion,
the father of the girl then acted in the presence of the gods who partake of the sacrifice.
One should worship with water, flowers, and other offerings, and proclaim their names, lineages, and so forth.
Having observed their fitness as recipients for the sake of the gift, one should cause the recitation of the *svastivācana* (benediction).
One should also perform the purification of the body and bestow the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
One should cause the Vaiṣṇava and Pārameśvara mantras to be imparted during the sacrifice;
one should protect the tulasī there, and then have the tilaka mark applied.
One should fashion the crescent moon (candraka) with unbroken grains of rice, saffron, and sandalwood.
Wearing beautiful flower garlands and auspicious attire, he should be most excellent in appearance.
He should offer ornaments to him and then worship his feet.
He should cause the madhuparka to be given and should cause the one who is well-pleased to partake of it.
One should also cause the oblation of sacrificial milk-rice and other offerings to be performed;
or else, one should have delightful musical instruments played and likewise have songs sung.
One should have Vedic verses and mantras chanted by twice-born Brahmins learned in the Vedas.
Having paid homage to all the gods, to Hari, Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and Nārāyaṇī, to Agni, and to the Brahmins, the father approached his daughter,
who was adorned with many ornaments and embellished with excellent essences. (14–15)
Adorned with divine garments and other finery, gratified with honors and gifts, and propitiated for the sake of marriage, he should place her— who has been brought to the pavilion—
in the presence of all people, at the left side of the bridegroom.
One should salute the fire, the twice-born, the virtuous, the sages, the elders, and the assembly.
One should also bow to Kumāra and honor him with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should apply saffron, unbroken grains, and sandalwood paste to the forehead of the boy.
"May Nārāyaṇa be pleased with me; may Gaṇeśa be pleased with me;
may all the deities be pleased; may my desired rites be accomplished.
Then, having sat upon the seat offered by the Brahmin, the girl should speak thus.

"Whomever my father shall bestow upon me, I will become his lawful wife in the presence of the sacred fire; may there be no obstacles for me in this world. Having spoken thus, that maiden should indeed release that water upon the ground.

should take water into his own hand according to the manner previously described;

In the presence of the gods, [this act] is indeed the most excellent, the highest of the high.
(38) By the gift of a casket and so forth, the fruit of giving heaven shall be attained;

By the gift of a water-pot (gagaṛī), one obtains the fruit born of the gift of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
likewise, by the gift of cows, land, grain, gold, and so forth during the sacrifice,

A milch cow with golden horns and silver hooves, covered with a divine cloth, accompanied by a bronze vessel and her calf, should be given along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); [this yields] the fruit born from the gift of the world of cows (Goloka). 41–42.
As long as the calf’s face, complete with its feet, is visible within the birth canal, for that long the cow should be known as the Earth; the donor shall attain universal sovereignty.
Massaging those who are weary, nursing the sick, and the worship of the gods—
Worship of the ancestors, honoring the elders, service to the virtuous, and service to one’s husband;
likewise, worship of chaste women, the sweeping and cleaning of the temple, and the clearing away of the vessels and remains of food for holy men and yogis. (44–45)
And the pleasing of the Brahmins—all that is like the gift of a cow;
it destroys sin, bestows merit, grants heaven, and likewise grants liberation.
By giving one’s own desired object to a virtuous person, one shall attain liberation.
By giving one's own desired object to a twice-born man, one shall attain heaven.

By giving land, lamps, food, clothing, and clarified butter, one shall go to prosperity.
By giving a house, grain, an umbrella, garlands, trees, vehicles, clarified butter,
water, a bed, and ointments, one attains heaven.
A giver of the Veda reaches the world of Brahmā, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
By giving the Vedas, their meanings, the treatises on sacrifice, those which are the treatises on Dharma,
as well as the Saṃhitās, one attains the world of Brahmā.

One should accept what comes unasked, even from those who have performed evil deeds.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, clarified butter, curd, and purifying water;

Even though he is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, he is considered the excellent recipient.
At that time, in the sacred field of Ācyuta, within the sacrificial hall,
a gift given indeed becomes imperishable when witnessed by the gods and others.

All sins are destroyed, and the arising of all merit occurs.

Or, if one should speak of the faults of a Brahmin, a guru, a deity, or a king,

He who gives away everything, including his very life, for the sake of the gods— his karmas, even those born of fierce deeds, are indeed destroyed.

which destroys time, illusion, evil karma, Yama, fear, and the like.
Having performed a sacrifice, one should indeed take up the supreme Vaiṣṇava renunciation.
Having attained the state of a knower within the self, one dispels all sins.

Now I shall describe to you another [rite] concerning the attendants of Vināyaka,
which wards off the sufferings of the wicked and the extremely wicked and bestows happiness.
(67) One dreams of plunging excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men.
Furthermore, even when one's undertakings are fruitless, one desponds due to the absence of a [favorable] sign.

In ancient times, the ṛṣis bathed Indra and liberated him from evil;

Śrī Nārāyaṇī said:
How is it that even though they are eternal and possess knowledge, living beings are embodied?
"Even though they know it to be the abode of death, they still go there; tell me the reason for this.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
"Everything crooked is the abode of death; indeed, those who are crooked go to death."
For those Māras—desire and the rest—indeed practice a crooked way of life.
They alone, residing within one's own body, are the enemies and slayers at all times.
O Rāma, for those yogis who are virtuous and free from them, there is truly no death.
Death is indeed declared to be hell, and it is produced by birth and so forth.
Birth is obtained through the power of karma, and karma is acquired through latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
If those impressions are utterly consumed by peace, self-restraint, and service to the virtuous, [then liberation is attained].
Through devotion to Hari, one should wash away the self and attain purity.
Then, that death known as "dying," which is so painful in form, does not occur;
having attained a divine state, one goes to the eternal Brahman.
He shall indeed become long-lived and possess eternal sovereignty;
by my power, his bodily elements, which are otherwise subject to death, become divine.
Furthermore, both negligence and delusion perish for him in every respect.
Indeed, those two forms of Mṛṣi never enter into him at any time.
For the devotee who is free from *māyā* and established in my yoga,
even divine *māyā* arises for him, entirely devoid of bondage and the like.
Then that eternally liberated self proceeds into Brahman alone.
O Lakṣmī, you likewise become thus, just as you are born from the ocean;
through my yoga, you abide as divine and free from illusion.
She is eternal, perfectly symmetrical in form, and devoid of increase or decrease.
As I am, so indeed are you; likewise is the devotee as well.
My will is such that Lakṣmī is born exactly in that same manner through her.
In the past, a war took place between the Self and the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
By means of that ego-sense, this body was made into its own kingdom;
and by it, every fragrance arising from that kingdom was seized. (13)
Foul-smelling, residual, death-dealing, and painful, it is indeed poison.
Having observed this evil deed, which consists of the destruction of knowledge,
and having observed the practice of non-selfhood, the conscious Self took up the weapon of discernment.
He cast off that wicked ego, which bestows death;
yet even as it was being struck by that exceedingly swift weapon,
the ego abandoned its watery portion and entered the earth, free from affliction.
By him, all the nectar born of his own kingdom was seized;
only the poison remained, its flavor perceived as bringing death and misery.
Then, for the sake of slaying him, he hurled his very self as a weapon.
Being struck down, the ego entered the region of light;
there it assumed its beautiful form belonging to its own kingdom,
while the remaining ugly form was taken up again by the conscious self.
Then he discharged against him a sharp weapon called discernment (*viveka*). Although being struck, the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) entered the realm of wind (*vāyubhūta*);
there it seized its own kingdom, known as touch (*sparśa*), which is characterized by pleasure.
Seeing him still there as before,
the remaining Kutsaparsva then discharged a weapon at him for the sake of his destruction.
Ego (Ahaṃkāra) entered the ether and seized the sound residing therein.
Seeing that the word *ku* and the remainder [of the name] were still present,
the conscious self (cidātmā) seized a weapon and struck him down. At that moment, egoism (ahaṃkāra), which was previously without support, entered into the conscious self.
The Guru, being the conscious self (cidātman), instructed even the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti) [in this way]:
"I am of the nature of Brahman. That ego-sense also maintained that [conviction]. Then, through the realization of its own nature as Brahman, it attained the state of Brahman.
Even Māyika attained the state of Brahman through the worship [of the Self] according to the word of his guru.
The conscious self (cidātman) struck him with discernment, yet it did not truly undergo destruction;
because he remained established in the Self, he became one who was freed from death.
Having abandoned his own individual nature, he attained the state of the conscious self;
having reached the condition of being invulnerable, he took recourse in the divine sense of "I.
Having relied upon divine intellect, he attained the Supreme Self.
He is always born invincible, established in the self through divine intellect.
O Supreme Lord, having attained the state of liberation through supreme devotion,
no obstruction whatsoever arises for those liberated ones who possess the divine reality.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, destruction indeed follows from the surrendering to death.
The surrender of the self, along with all the senses, their functions, and their activities,
together with the self and its mental states, is the offering unto Brahman, which is beyond all qualities (nirguṇa).
In me, who am devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), there is no death at all that causes suffering to the world.
O Lakṣmī, diseases are of two kinds: physical and likewise mental;
their arising is mutual for those which depend upon one another.
For these [humors] are born of the body when there is an imbalance of wind, bile, and phlegm;
indeed, their state of equilibrium is proclaimed as health and well-being.
Just as a substance is crushed by a medicinal agent that is its opposite, so too [is the body affected].
Cold is countered by heat, and heat is countered by cold.
(35) Likewise, when there is a mental affliction, the mild is countered by the sharp;
sorrow is overcome by joy, and joy is overcome by sorrow. (36)
If there is equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, that is the self’s state of health;
their imbalance is indeed disease, for which massage is prescribed.
One who suffers strives for happiness, while one who is happy even remembers suffering.
Both of those states arise from the qualities (guṇas) and belong to the mind, not to the self.

If one obtains from the mouth of a true guru that ancient wisdom which consists of the nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, then the mind desires its own destruction;
it strives for its own dissolution by means of the weapon of that very wisdom.
The Self alone shall be the warrior, having indeed mounted the chariot of Brahman.
Then, O Lakṣmī, the Self will conquer the supreme state of Brahman;
one should cast away all external equipment, like wealth belonging to a Vaiśya.
Being free from attachment and without possessiveness, one will then attain perfection.
As long as the thought "this is mine" arises, death remains present.
When the state of "this is not mine" occurs, death has passed away for him.
"For him, the eternal realization 'I am Brahman' shines forth clearly.
O Lakṣmī, for such a person of discrimination, there exists the infinite sovereignty over the entire universe, consisting of both the moving and the stationary. (44-45)

Having placed the state beyond death at his feet, he shall go to the eternal Brahman.

Having fallen from the body, enveloped by his own actions—
accompanied by immeasurable sins and merits, and possessing a subtle body—
he proceeds to another state of existence, which is fashioned in three ways according to his deeds. (3.171.30)
A human being goes to a destination where merit and sin are attained in equal measure;
even in this very world, one surely experiences high and low enjoyments according to one's own actions.
Indeed, by means of inauspicious deeds, people go to a lower state.
They go to that hell where they are cooked by the fruits of their actions.
Those who possess merit, however, go to the upward path consisting of stars,
even to the orb of the moon and the orb of the sun.
Having enjoyed such delightful things as these, upon the exhaustion of their merit, they fall again;
they go to the earth, experiencing rebirth and repeated death.
Driven by their karma, they go once more to heaven or to hell.
And even in heaven there is no contentment upon seeing the most radiant splendor;
gods who are low, high, or middling both covet and seize it.
Having reflected thus, a wise person [should offer] his subtle body to the Lord Hari. (35–36)
Having made this offering, he indeed departs, becoming divine, for the imperishable state.
[He offers] the eye, the function of the eye, the eyeball, and likewise the deity;
as well as the object, which is form itself, the knowledge, the consciousness, and the knower. (37)
[One should offer] reflection, determination, intention, and all enjoyment;
likewise, the self and the mental impressions, as well as memory, to Keśava.
Having offered everything that has been offered to the Self, one should offer it all [to Him]. (38–39)
Having fashioned or even abandoned a subtle and divine body, having cast off union with *prakṛti* and established myself in the yoga of Brahman,
I rejoice, having utterly consumed all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through meditation upon me.
He indeed proceeds to the Supreme Brahman, to me, Hari, the Puruṣottama.
Thus, having abandoned the three bodies, he attains the eternal Brahman;
[he abandons] all objects such as fragrances and the external sense-streams in every way.
Likewise, having surrendered everything— the internal channels, as well as the fruit and enjoyment—
into Me, and having abandoned the triad, one goes to Me, the Supreme Lord.
O Lotus-born One, upon the exhaustion of karma, the destruction of the gross body occurs.
Upon the exhaustion of merit and demerit, the destruction of the subtle body occurs.
Through the flow of the bliss of Brahman, there is indeed the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).
This subtle body, which consists of latent impressions, dissolves through the realization of "I am [Brahman]. (44–45)

There is also the dissolution of the body, which is known as the cause of ignorance. Listen now to how the attainment of the Self occurs for that which is of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss—neither a god nor an embodied being. (46)

O Lakṣmī, through various causes the conjunction with a body arises. This Self is pure and divine; it resides either in the Imperishable (akṣara), or in a region of the Imperishable, or at its boundary, or in the vicinity of the objects of Māyā. ||47-48||
By its very nature, it assumes the qualities of proximity like a crystal;
those very qualities, belonging to others, become subject to the designation "belonging to others.
These are the laws of manifestation and restriction, which are the properties of *māyā*.
"Having attained me and having manifested me, I have become engaged in those endowed with self-restraint"—thus does the Self conceive through the functions of the principle of *māyā* and the rest;
whether it be a conclusion, or conceit, or reflection, or cogitation. (3.171.50–51)
He indeed perceives that which consists of the radiance of *māyā* as consisting of his own radiance;
he perceives even his own [perception] as being mixed with the radiance of *māyā*.
This mixing and this delusion is indeed what is designated as *avidyā*, ignorance.
By means of that [intellect], the self engages in actions consisting of merit and demerit.
Through its illusory power (māyā), however, auspicious and inauspicious actions arise for it;
and through the perception of those auspicious and inauspicious [actions], the taint (lepa) arises for it.
Through the taint upon knowledge, it also becomes tainted by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced thereby;

and that taint which exists within the impression in the form of *dharma* arises in the substrate, the living soul (*jīva*), which is transparent in nature. By means of these, the living soul transmigrates.
Even though he is joined with the subtle [elements], he still yearns here for the attainment of his own desired enjoyments and so forth.
Because of that, being accompanied by the subtle elements, he obtains the gross material body.
Having encountered gross dullness, and being ripened by the gross elements, he becomes exceedingly dull.
Possessing gross states, he becomes greedy for action and enjoyment;
repeatedly attaining various fields of experience again and again,
he enjoys enjoyments consisting of pleasure, which are granted by the impressions of his past fortune.
And from that, they obtain a long-lasting fruit to be enjoyed for a long time;
indeed, O Lakṣmī, one obtains inexhaustible fruit to be experienced through many births—even though one is unattached, by the very nature of attraction. (3.171.59–60)

Just as a powerful man who is not yet a king, having seized a kingdom, becomes a ruler, so too this embodied soul, possessing the yoga of attraction, draws in other qualities and establishes its own sovereignty. (61)
Though free from illusion, this person becomes possessed by illusion; he is neither born nor does he cease.
He enters into states of being that become ever more intense and is not released, just as a leather-worker never abandons his foul-smelling vat.
Enveloped by its own actions (karma), this [self] does not abandon the wretched body;
rather, it encounters auspicious, inauspicious, or mixed karma.
Just as a fruit-bearing tree, when it comes into bloom, yields abundant fruit.
In this way, he would have much merit performed with a virtuous mind;
likewise, he incurs sin performed with a sinful mind. Therefore, being joined with the mind, this [individual] proceeds as one who is greatly indolent.
Just as a servant gives to his master, so does he [the mind] give, and he [the self] indeed consumes it;
yet if he desires further enjoyments, his lifespan comes to an end.
Impelled by desire, he is led into dwelling within the womb.
Through his mind, and burdened by merits and sins, he sleeps within the womb, powerless.
The semen mixed with blood becomes the *kalala*, the precursor of the body; it enters the womb, assuming a form corresponding to its auspicious and inauspicious [karmic] qualities.

One enters the *kalala* stage according to the influence of past karma; another enters the *budbuda* stage according to his own karma. One enters the *māṃsa* stage, and another the *peśī*, due to their respective actions. (3.171.70)
One enters into a basket, another into a statue rich with limbs;
one enters into a figure possessing every limb, and yet another even into an embryo—either swiftly or after a long time, according to the sequence of their past karma. (71–72)
When the puppet has been fully nourished by the flow of juices and sustained over time by heat and other factors,
and is endowed with breath, the individual soul (jīva) indeed enters it according to its own karma.
Due to its subtlety and unmanifest state, the soul, possessing a subtle body, [remains there].
It enters indeed through the internal arrangement [of the body] and becomes attached there by means of karma.
Therein dwells the Great Brahman, the protector even of the seed;
I too reside together with that Supreme Brahman, the seed of seeds.
He is the doer, the instigator, the nourisher, the creator, the protector, and the observer;
He is the witness, the unattached one, and the bestower of the fruits of action.
I am the eternal seed of the seeds for all embodied beings.
I dwell as the impeller of the principles that bring about fulfillment.
Living beings live by means of me, who am the life-sustainer of the vital breaths, the senses, and so forth.
At that time, that individual soul (jīva), having indeed entered all the limbs of the embryo, [animates it].
Established in the seat of the vital breaths (prāṇādhāra), it immediately bestows consciousness through wisdom;
by means of that, it causes the limbs and so forth to move, and thus this [self] is called "endowed with life" (sajīva).
Just as a small amount of molten gold [pervades] an entire bronze statue...
Indeed, he creates a body made of gold as well as one made of living soul. This conscious being performs this entry into the living soul,
just as fire, having entered a lump of iron, transforms it into its own nature.
Likewise, having entered the insentient, this [consciousness] should define it through its own sentience, just as a lamp, though shining within a house,
illuminates both itself and others while remaining in a single place. (82)
Thus, although situated within the heart, the Puruṣa shines forth toward the three bodies.

There, in the womb, he experiences until the ninth month that which was previously performed and is suitable for the state of gestation. Then, in the tenth month, [he experiences] the fruits of his actions from that previous birth.
Knowledge arises, and then he goes outside;
the karma of the womb has reached its exhaustion, and the karma of childhood has arrived.
Under its influence for the sake of experience, the child enjoys what was done by himself.

Now, being born as a youth, naturally desiring sense objects, he engages in excessive pursuit of those objects and thus sin is produced for him again. When he turns away from sense objects, merit is produced for him. (86–87)
Charity, religious observance, celibacy, service, the concentration on Brahman, self-restraint, tranquility, compassion, pilgrimage, vows, self-control, and discipline;
as well as the avoidance of falsehood and the refraining from taking the property of others. (88)
Service to one's mother and father, worship of deities and guests,
reverence for teachers, non-violence, purity, restraint of the senses, the practice of auspicious deeds, and conduct in accordance with the way of the virtuous. (3.171.89–90)
If one should perform these [duties], righteousness flourishes;
and righteousness, when well-protected, protects both this lineage and the celestial realm. One should practice service toward the virtuous and maintain a firm standing among the righteous.
One should observe every conduct in which peace is uninterrupted.
He who protects this Dharma shall not fall into an evil state;
he constantly attains the prosperity of both righteousness and consciousness.
Indeed, the rules of conduct and observances have been declared solely for the sake of spiritual prosperity.
In this way, the world is disciplined by teachers who are knowers of the scriptures.
And while abiding in these observances, the embodied being becomes a yogi in this very life.
Just as poison does not touch one who knows the science of poisons,
so indeed worldly existence does not touch one who abides in the observance [of yoga].
Māyā and the fruits of action do not touch one who is established in yoga.
The yogī, having become liberated while living (jīvanmukta), is released from the body.
Established in yoga, the liberated embodied soul is distinguished throughout all worlds.
He is the giver of liberation in the world, for he is indeed free from attachment.
If, however, merit has been acquired by an embodied being through the path of Dharma,
then either after the enjoyment of that merit or after a long period of time,
his crossing over from saṃsāra may occur through association with the virtuous.
Alternatively, after the exhaustion of the fruit of evil karma through births as animals, birds, and so forth,
the destruction of sin occurs suddenly for the virtuous through their association with others.
[This occurs] by means of contact with vehicles, mounts, shade, and the like, or through the offering of leaves, flowers, and other such things.
Through the practice of serving the virtuous, merit is produced for him.
From that, he attains a good birth, or heaven, or the higher realm;
from that, the world of Īśvara, and from that, he proceeds to liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, having performed and experienced one's karma, one is liberated.
Long ago, at the time of creation, by my very command, a person was indeed born.
Having fashioned a body for himself, he created the three worlds.
Having created Prakṛti, which consists of the three guṇas, both immobile and mobile,
and which is the very nature of my Māyā, he then bestowed it upon the Puruṣa.
That Prakṛti is that by which this entire world of bodies is pervaded.
The Puruṣa, variegated by Māyā, then created Pradhāna; and from Pradhāna, through union with the Puruṣa, various principles (tattvas) indeed arose,
consisting of golden forms, from which the Virāṭ was born.
From that [came] Brahmā, from him the gods, and these creatures beginning with humans.
All this is composed of *māyā*, perishable; beyond that is the imperishable, the immortal abode, and above that stands my supreme abode.
Commanded by me, those lords created a creation numbering ten million worlds;
even after observing that, Brahmā created the fourfold beings.
Having established the measure of time for them, the Grandfather—

He fashioned both creation and dissolution for the sake of happiness. Yet that happiness is mixed with suffering; the body is impure, all bodies are headed toward destruction, and worldly existence bestows terrible misery.

Abounding in the bonds of birth and death, it is difficult to cross for those who are greatly deluded; yet it is easily conquered by the unattached, even by the virtuous who are possessed of doubt. Through discernment, they become disenchanted while seeking the supreme state.
Having abandoned this very body, which has indeed been attained, they depart; O Lakṣmī, thus has the liberation from the body been described to you here,
as well as how the body is acquired, and how liberation is attained.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Causes of the Dissolution of the Body, the Causes of the Acquisition of the Body, and the Causes of Liberation from the Body," within the section on the Dharma of Liberation in the third *dvāpara* cycle of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 171. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*).

Chapter 173 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, to how the dissolution of Māyā comes about:
by means of knowledge (vidyā), a living being crosses over, since one thereby conquers ignorance (avidyā).
That which is considered the knowledge of Brahman, the supreme knowledge, and the knowledge of the Self—[is this very thing].
For by the worship of the Supreme Self, that ignorance is indeed shattered.
(2) The conclusion, accompanied by affection, as well as reflection of that same nature, and likewise meditation upon Śrī Hari, accompanied by the knowledge of His majesty. (3)
The knowledge of one's own true nature, which is repeatedly joined with the realization of perfection,
consists of wisdom (*vidyā*) and is said to lead to the attainment of the Supreme Brahman.
O Rame, that indeed is wisdom by which the Supreme Brahman is realized.
For it is indeed by casting away ignorance that she bestows the Supreme Brahman.

Just as the purification of gold is accomplished by four means—namely, by cutting with a stone, by heating, and by hammering—so too is the purification of the Self achieved through these methods. || 5-6 ||
Likewise, the departure of one's own illusion occurs through the fourfold means:
by association with the virtuous, by knowledge, by dispassion, and by supreme devotion.
Through association with the virtuous, there indeed arises the cessation of the flow of the material qualities.
By means of discernment (*vijñāna*), there is the gradual reversal of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), there is the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the engagement with Hari.
Through affectionate devotion (*sneha-bhakti*), there is attachment to Hari; thereafter, through that [devotion], there is non-attachment to *māyā*.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, may there be the departure of Māyā through the grace of the true guru;
by the favor of Kṛṣṇa, the destruction of Māyā shall swiftly occur.
Through residence with Hari, the cessation of Māyā takes place within one's own self.
Just as all deer depart upon the arrival of a lion, so do lowly beings depart upon the arrival of a king;
and just as the organs residing within the body depart upon the arrival of death. (11–12)
Just as mice depart from a hole due to the presence of a snake,
and just as festivities depart from the heart due to the presence of fear,
so too does the departure of anxieties occur during a great festival.
Likewise, through the residence of Hari, the disappearance of Māyā occurs.
(14) Wherever I dwell, there Māyā does not remain;
I dwell in my devotee, and there Māyā is not found. (15)
He who is absorbed in the One Way, the Dark One (Kṛṣṇa), contemplating Brahman; who remains silent, free from all modifications, and holds nothing other than Me— he,
by gradually renouncing each preceding stage, shall cross over the bondage of worldly existence.
Free from malice, patient, tranquil in mind, and having conquered the senses;
devoid of wretchedness and hatred, fearless in the pursuit of Brahman;
with mind and disposition mastered, my devotee is liberated and rejoices in Me. (17–18)
Endowed with a pure disposition toward all living beings as if toward oneself, free from egoism, pride, and the like, he is liberated in every respect.
Whether in life or death, in stability or suffering, in happiness or fainting—[he remains thus]. (19)
He who is the same in gain and loss, in the pleasant and the unpleasant—he indeed is liberated. (3.172.20) He does not covet anything, nor does he despise anyone;
free from the pairs of opposites and devoid of passion and the like, he is in every way truly liberated. (21)
Ajātaśatru, though without kinsmen, without offspring, and even without a wife,
having renounced dharma, artha, and kāma, and being free from all desire, is liberated.
Free from both merit and demerit, he exhausts only that which has already begun (prārabdha).
One who has brought about the destruction of the principles that initiate the body, whose mind is peaceful,
who delights in the non-dual Śrī Hari through service with a spirit of love,
and who has attained self-knowledge— that person, being my very self, is liberated. (23–24)
One whose abode is hope and who possesses divine vision should behold the world as impermanent—
resembling a *aśvattha* tree, fraught with birth, death, and old age.
Endowed with detachment, tranquility, and such states, one is freed from all defects.
He indeed abandons the bondage of the self and attains liberation without delay.
Having seen me—who am devoid of a body composed of illusion and who delights in divine fragrance, taste, touch, sound, and form—he is swiftly liberated. (26–27)
Having seen Me— the Lord who is neither gross nor subtle, causeless, supreme, devoid of qualities, yet the enjoyer of qualities— one is instantly liberated.
Having abandoned all desires through the intellect, even while remaining within worldly existence, one is freed.
My devotee, imbued with devotion, gradually attains nirvāṇa.
Freed from external and internal purificatory rites, devoid of the pairs of opposites, truly without possessions, and free from attachment—he is indeed liberated. (3.172.30)
The ascetic, rich in devotion to me and devoid of other mental impressions,
having attained the eternal Brahman— everlasting, imperishable, and upward-tending—
becomes tranquil and approaches me, the Supreme Brahman, who is higher than the highest.
Seeing the Self within himself, he indeed attains the supreme state.
Having withdrawn all the senses, one should fix their functions in the mind;
having fixed the mind in the sense of "I" (the ego), one should then fix that in the intellect.

Having constantly restrained the intellect and likewise its corresponding memory, and having firmly established the mental impressions within those very impressions, one should offer the impressions into the Self.
One should offer the Self into Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless and glorious Supreme Person.
Thus, having attained union with Me, he is fit for eternal liberation.
(35) Such a supreme saint is one whose conduct is solely devoted;
existing while perceiving Me in his own true form, he enjoys My bliss. (36)
With an irreversible light accompanied by the inner eye,
he perceives the Self within himself as Me, his Lord, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Thus, being joined with his own self, he beholds Me, the Self, therein.
Just as a person indeed perceives himself as "this is I" in a dream,
so too does this [person] properly perceive Me, the Self, within his own true nature. It is like the film of water that remains on the body of one who has bathed.
If some skillful person were to extract it and display it separately,
so too could one extract the body and display it as distinct from the subtle [body];
and having extracted the subtle [body] from the causal [body], one would display it in its separateness.
One might demonstrate the cause by separating it from illusion (māyā).
Likewise, someone might demonstrate illusion by separating it from the individual soul (jīva); and similarly, a yogi might demonstrate the individual soul by separating it from Hari. 41–42.
Just as a yogi might demonstrate himself by making himself appear distinct,
so too should one demonstrate me, the Supreme Self, by making me appear distinct. Nevertheless, he whose mind is disciplined does not become separate from me, who am the Plenum.
I am the pervader of all things, yet I am the one who restrains even His sovereignty. By manifesting Him within myself, I govern Him in every way.
Having attained Me, he is liberated from me and enjoys My sovereign powers.
His illusion has indeed ceased; he has gone to Me, the supreme imperishable.
Just as illusion does not exist there, so it does not exist here [in this state].
Wherever My devotee may dwell, he is indeed free from illusion.
Free from qualities yet possessing divine qualities, he becomes a vessel for the state of Nirvāṇa.
For when the embodied soul perceives the Self as united with Me, there is no lord over him in this world; he is the master even of the three worlds. (47–48)
He becomes one-fold, two-fold, three-fold, ten-fold, or a thousand-fold;
he assumes various other beautiful bodies according to his will.
For him there is no disease, no old age, no death, nor even sorrow.
This self-controlled one causes even the gods to exercise their godhood;
indeed, he attains the Supreme Brahman, having abandoned the notion of a physical body.
For him who has attained the state of Brahman, no fear of destruction arises.
When beings are afflicted or destroyed, he indeed has no fear;
nor is he shaken by afflictions, sufferings, and terrible sorrows arising from attachment and the like—
the self-disciplined one who is free from desire and filled with peace.
Death does not pierce him, nor does time devour him.
Nothing else in this world is seen to be more blissful than this:
having properly yoked one’s own self, it becomes established in me, Kṛṣṇa.
With the suffering of thirst having ceased, he sleeps happily within himself;
casting off this human body, he attains his form as he desires.
Therefore, once liberated, detachment should be maintained; it is not prescribed [as a new duty].

The seer of the Self does not desire even great lordly enjoyments. Established in the Self, the great liberated one—liberated while living and possessing a body—is seated even in a city, yet his mind does not abandon the external world. (56–57)
Though staying within the city, he dwells in his own abode;
even while in that abode, the mind of the liberated man does not release itself toward the external.
Even if he should dwell in a hut on the outskirts, his mind does not abandon its focus.
Even where it dwells within the body, its own mind remains outside;
even toward objects consisting of the body itself, it does not let go for even a moment. It does not let go of the sense organs, their physical seats, or the subtle elements. (3.172.60)
The mind does not leave the cakras, beginning with the mūlādhāra, for even a moment;
nor does the mind leave any other subtle principle (tattva) for even a moment.
This is because he is free from latent impressions (vāsanā) throughout all three kinds of bodies.
Within and without, he perceives me, Hari, as a single essence.
Since everything here is entirely filled by him, he sees me as identical to that; indeed, he beholds me as the Supreme Fullness (paripūrṇatama) and nothing else.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and possessing ears everywhere— perceiving Me as such, he beholds Me;
even while maintaining his own body, he indeed perceives only Brahman.
Then, having attained a celestial chariot (vimāna) and being filled with joy,
he takes that chariot as his support and goes from there to liberation in Me.
This is not easily understood by one whose inner self is confused.
For those who perform ritual actions, there is the world of the gods; for the wise, the eternal ether;
for the perfected ones, the abode of truth; and for the devotees, the eternal Brahman.
Indeed, O Lakṣmī, that supreme goal is the eternal Brahman.

Wherein there is immortality, well-being, happiness, and constant joy—by relying upon this means of accomplishment, even sinful women in their final state all attain the supreme goal; how much more so, then, those who are deeply learned? (68–69)
Those who are devoted to their own duty, faithful to the virtuous, seekers of the welfare of others,
knowers of Brahman, steadfast, and eternally dedicated to Brahman— for them,
there exists no other happiness whatsoever beyond my world.
Having known and having abandoned delusion, one shall attain the supreme goal.
This dissolution of māyā and liberation have been shown to you;
through the yoga of my very self, which is the goal to be attained, one is joined to the highest state.
"O Lakṣmī, his thirst does not dwell upon any other object apart from Me;
for that very reason, this devotee shines in My supreme state.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Dharma of Liberation, the Means for the Dissolution of Māyā, and the Attainment of the Abode of the Supreme Brahman," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. Chapter 172.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; I shall here relate the conversation between a husband and wife who were practitioners of yoga in the past—a discourse worthy of being heard and bestowing the supreme goal.
In ancient times, a yoginī named Śrutiphalā,

having ascended to a state of doubt, questioned her husband, a yogi named Sadvidyāyana, who had reached the further shore of both spiritual knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), solely for the purpose of instructing the world.
O Lord, I always abide in the meditative absorption of the three bodies;
I am devoted to the service of my husband, yet I am also a servant of Hari. I am intent on the duties of the body, yet I also possess the nature of desire.
Devoted to the service of the gods, I live with pure intention;
awakened by my husband, I live free from attachment, intent upon the knowledge of liberation.
Nevertheless, O beloved, my mind still wanders along the path of the body and its sensual objects.
For here and there, by the nourishment of the elements, the downward-flowing river proceeds;
that mind of mine, having the nature of a downward stream, drags me along.
O Lord, when shall I then become one who possesses an upward flow?
"When shall I attain liberation? When indeed shall I find eternal happiness? To which world shall I go, having taken refuge in you, my beloved?
You remain here with all actions abandoned, though you are capable and possessed of desire."

But a wife, having no other refuge, always depends upon her husband. (9) Thus, I maintain both spiritual discipline (*yoga*) and desire (*kāma*), as well as virtue (*vṛṣa*), through union with my husband;
nevertheless, this bondage of karma remains mine. (3.173.10)
No one who has entered into the enjoyment of worldly pleasures attains liberation.
O Lord, you know all that; how then can there be liberation through action?
We have heard it said that wives attain the worlds won by their husbands.
"If the husband here is devoid of merit in this world, what recourse is there for the wife?
Having obtained a husband such as you, what state indeed shall I attain?
Thus was the best of sages, named Sadvidyāyana, questioned.
With a tranquil mind, yet smiling within his heart, he said to his wife, who was the fruit of his sacred learning:
"I have no desire, nor do I have any bondage; I do not consider the nature of the body to be mine.
This self is not the wife, nor is this self known as the husband. (14)

The body of the man is called "husband" (pati), while the body of the woman is called "wife" (patnī). Such is the worldly convention established; this is known as *bhava*. Furthermore, the bond of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-bandhana*) is especially characterized by the state of matrimony (*dāmpatya*).
Even more than that, the state of having offspring leads to bondage.
Desires, attachments, latent impressions, and the like are attributes of the body, not of the Self.
Behold me, possessing a divine body, in the form of Nārāyaṇa.
The husband is Brahmā, the husband is Viṣṇu, and the husband is the god Maheśvara.
Thinking him to be the Supreme Brahman, she who serves him is liberated.
Out of love, the gopīs are liberated again and again at the beginning of every kalpa.
By the grace of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa’s Lakṣmī,
O beautiful woman, serve me, regarding me as the form of Brahman;
then you will certainly attain the world of the virtuous Yoginīs.
"Or, having resorted to freedom from qualities (nairguṇya), worship me, the Supreme Lord.
Then you will undoubtedly attain the liberation of Brahman (brahmanirvāṇa).
Having spoken thus, that yogi [emitted] Kāma in beautiful form from his own body.
Having separated [the body], Kāma indeed consumed it with fire and became like ashes;
he then gave the well-formed, yet quality-less, lump of Kāma to his wife.
By the touch of that, he became divine, liberated, and truly embodied.
Kāma assumed a divine form out of a desire for the knowledge of the six systems.
Having witnessed his supreme wonder, Śrutiphālā said to her husband:
"O Lord, you who have conquered indignation, conquered passion, and conquered the senses! (24–25)
"O you who have conquered all wealth, I now recognize that you are divine.
My suspicion, born of desire, has ceased through this divine vision.
I behold you as the Lord in the form of Kṛṣṇa, possessing four arms."
I perceive all your divine activities without a doubt.
My restlessness has vanished and my feminine intellect has departed today;
having attained divine delight, I have become divine through your power.
"Tell me, however, that knowledge which is appropriate for me and brings happiness.
Having spoken thus, she prostrated herself; and Kāma, possessing a divine form, suddenly entered her body with the desire to impart true knowledge.
Having seen this, she became free from doubt regarding the fruit of her hearing [the scriptures].
Thus, in one who is devoted to Kṛṣṇa, all divine qualities reside within the body;
indeed, even all base qualities become virtuous qualities.
Desire, affection, happiness, service, nourishment, pleasure, and auspiciousness—
when directed toward Śrī Hari by a devotee, these become divine among the saintly.
Those attachments which are formed toward women, sons, kinsmen, daughters, and family members [become otherwise].
These very [deeds] performed toward the virtuous have opened the door to liberation.
I have attained the Lord of Yoga; I am blessed, having attained divinity. I have no bodily activity, for I am a divine woman, O beautiful one.
I am indeed not the woman; I am liberated and eternally joyful.
The body is endowed with the objects of the body, while the Self is adorned with the objects of the Self.
The paths of these two are distinct; what natural connection could there be?

Thus, in a mere moment, that beautiful woman became a Brahmani who had realized Brahman and was free from all attachments. Then Vidyanaga spoke thus to his wife, who had attained such knowledge: || 36-37 ||
O fortunate one! All activity is attached to the body and not to the Self.
In this world, action—whether as an object of perception or a visible phenomenon—is grasped by the organs of action and the organs of knowledge.
To determine that "the body is the Self" and "this is action" is bondage.
Even in that state, one falls into delusion because of the predominance of karma.
Every person devoid of knowledge is possessed by the delusion of bondage to the body;
as long as there is identification with the body, freedom from action (naiṣkarmya) will not arise for him.
Through the body, the senses, the mind, and so forth, one experiences auspicious and inauspicious results—causes of birth, enjoyment, old age, and disease—which bestow bondage.
Indeed, this is the inherent nature of the principles (tattvas); they certainly do not abide in the state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
Actions remain joined with living beings, and action persists within them.
Indeed, actions born of creation lead to various bodily forms:
for the Brahmin, these include the Agnihotra sacrifice and the like, as well as the study of the Vedas. (42–43)
For a Kṣatriya, the duty is governance; for a Vaiśya, trade as well as agriculture;

for a Śūdra, service. For one of Brahmanic character, there is the study of the Vedas, the performance of oblations and so forth, honor toward one's wife, charity, the acquisition of wealth, and the nourishment [of dependents]. (44)
In forest after forest, one follows the forest-dweller's way; for the virtuous, there is the wandering for alms and so forth.
Even the practice of Brahman does not constitute freedom from action (*naiṣkarmya*).
This innate nature, embodied as the body, is indeed fickle. (49–50)
The transformations are flickering, and the mind is likewise unsteady;
the intellect is a cluster of senses, and the consciousness is restless toward sense objects.
The latent impressions are as turbulent as a churning vessel, and even the stream of knowledge is unstable.
Knowledge, desire, and volition, as well as hatred and the like, depend upon their respective objects;
they follow after their objects, and restlessness resides in the underlying nature. Indeed, all this, born of the principles (tattvas), is by its very nature active, like a monkey. (48–49)
How could that which is devoid of activity remain so as to attain peace?
Therefore, for the sake of its transformation, one should resort to unwavering steadiness.
By entering into unwavering steadiness, one attains immobility.
That Supreme Brahman is of such a nature, perfectly complete everywhere;
it is eternally motionless and serene. One should take refuge in that goal with body, mind, speech, heart, and soul—in every way. (51–52)
Just as a lamp placed in a windless spot within a granary,
though flickering, indeed becomes extinguished by itself due to the oil;
so too, one may for a moment become free from flickering.
Or it may dissolve there, attaining a state of inactivity within that ether.
Thus, although this conscious self is enveloped by the flickering [senses], it becomes inactive upon reaching cessation within the ether of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 54-55 ||
And it should become steady like a gem, possessing the luster of a jewel-lamp;
just as a jewel-lamp is steady when endowed with its natural radiance.
Whether there be wind or oil, or even if they do not exist, it still shines.
Thus, this infallible one always remains bestowing radiance.
For the objects of the senses residing within the body, O gentle one, are always like the wind;
they may be enjoyed or not enjoyed, but the jewel remains indifferent. (67–68)
O wife, the attributes of the body are either experienced or not;
but the Self is like a jewel—indifferent to both you and me, and devoid of karma.
Having attained the Supreme Brahman, why do you fear the worlds?
O Supreme Goddess, abandon the doubt, "Where shall I go? for you are liberated.
I am eternally Brahman, and I shall go to the supreme state;
through knowledge, worship, devotion, and other means, you shall go with me.
For those household duties are indeed dharma; they are not adharma, nor do they lead to hell.
Through the seasonal duties and the duties of the mind, they attained divinity through union with Me.
By means of the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of Brahman, the Supreme Self— |||62||
"I am divine; by my yoga, you, my wife, have attained divinity.
Who else will proclaim this supreme, secret, and esoteric state of one's own being—which bestows liberation and is free from bondage?"
The enjoyer does not attain the supreme and most excellent state of the non-enjoyer.
O beloved, how could one describe that which has been declared by me to you?
For all embodied beings, the *rākṣasas* become all obstacles.

Having abandoned those [desires] on the path to Brahman and the path to heaven, one shall become happy. O beloved, by taking refuge in the Supreme Self abiding within the self, I have brought the Rākṣasas, who can assume any form at will, under my control in every way.

In the middle of the eyebrows, one attains the meditation upon the Guru, the venerable Supreme Self, wherein resides that Supreme Brahman, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. He is always visible in the vision; therefore, O you who are beyond the material qualities (*nirguṇā*), worship Him.
The *iḍā*, the *piṅgalā*, and the *suṣumṇā*—these are the pathways.
Even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, having united with their beloved [the Supreme], worship that Kṛṣṇa who is beyond the Imperishable, whom the great seers likewise revere. (3.173.70)
Worship Him whom the wise, who are firm in their vows, peaceful, and have conquered all objects of sense, constantly worship; O fair-browed one, abandon concern for the body.
That [Supreme] cannot be smelled by the nose, nor can it be tasted by the tongue.

It cannot be touched by the sense of touch, nor can it be seen by the eye; indeed, it is beyond hearing. Therefore, worship that Supreme Brahman with the self together with the mind and the intellect firmly grasped in Brahman.
That Supreme Brahman is attained through His grace by serving Him—[the Brahman] which is without smell, taste, touch, form, and devoid of sound;
from which the Tantra proceeds and in which it is finally established. (74)
And those vital breaths, such as prāṇa and the rest, proceed by depending upon him;
therefore, O beautiful lady, worship that witness of all, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord, the most excellent Master, the Lord of Śrī, the infallible One.
"I am not your husband, nor are you my wife; you are Śrī Puruṣottama, the Supreme Person.
Worship that Puruṣottama, the divine Self of us both.
[Know] Prāṇa in the heart, Apāna in the anus, and Samāna situated in the navel."
Udāna resides in the region of the throat, and vyāna pervades the entire body.
Having mastered the self within these, contemplate the Supreme Lord.
Vaiśvānara, the sevenfold fire, indeed moves within the vital breaths that traverse the body.
The smeller, by means of the sense of smell, experiences the object of smell—fragrance—in the earth; the drinker, by means of the tongue, experiences the object of taste—flavor—in water;
and the seer, by means of the eyes, experiences the visible object—form—in fire.
The toucher perceives the tangible object, touch, through the skin, indeed within the wind;
the hearer perceives the audible object, sound, through the ear, within space;
the thinker perceives his own mental object through the mind.
The knower, through the intellect, indeed causes the object to be known;
likewise, the Self, by means of the supreme Self, experiences everything that is to be experienced.
That which is experienced by the supreme Self is divine, and not worldly.
The mundane [body] is for bondage, while the divine [body], when offered, is for liberation.
(84) In this very manner, movement is performed by the two feet;
grasping is done by the two hands; and conversation and speaking are carried out by the voice. (85)
The evacuation of excrement through the anus, the experience of pleasure and so forth through the generative organ,
as well as going, grasping, speaking, emitting, and causing delight— he indeed performs all that;
for Vaiśvānara is the inner self, the Supreme Self.
I am not the agent, nor are you the agent; therefore, there is no bondage of karma.
One should indeed surrender the conceit of being a knower into the Supreme Self, and one should also surrender the notion of being an enjoyer into the Supreme Self.
In this state of being, I am never a man, nor are you ever a woman;
for he who is I is indeed you, and we two both abide in the Supreme.
There is not the slightest thing that exists apart from the Supreme Self for us two.
"You are the Self and I am likewise the Self; we both abide in the Supreme Self.
Since everything that must be sustained is offered into this [Supreme Self] in which we dwell, how could there remain for me or for you even the slightest karma? (3.173.90–91)
When everything is completely surrendered to the Lord of Gods, whose nature is actionless,
then whatever world belongs to Him is also eternally ours.
For the supreme state is the sky of consciousness, the imperishable and eternal abode.

That which belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone is ours as well. (93) Where Anādi-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the illustrious Puruṣottama, resides, there I am, and there you shall go; of this there is no doubt. (94)
Worship that Supreme Self, the Lord and Master who is your husband;
abandon wretchedness, doubt, and fear, which lead to a low rebirth.
Accept knowledge, detachment, righteousness, and flawless devotion.
"Be indeed fearless and grant [me] the supreme abode itself.
Thus addressed, his wife Śrutiphālā, who was deeply learned,
attained the highest joy, for she delighted in the awakening of Brahman.
She bowed at the feet of her husband and became like Lakṣmī to Lakṣmīpati.
From that time on, she performed all her rites solely through dedication to me;
she acted eternally according to the Vedas and worshipped me, the Supreme Lord.
She attained supreme bliss and partook of the essence of Brahman.
Though she remained within a household, she was constantly free from attachment to the home;
though joined with her husband, she was always united with Kṛṣṇa. (3.173.100)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Reply—beginning with the attainment of the world of the Supreme Brahman through the method of total renunciation and actionlessness—in response to the questions concerning the departure to the world of Kava and other matters, posed by the wife Śrutiphala to the sage Sadvidyāyana," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 174: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Continued]
[The Author: Chapter 175.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, how one attains a body.
I shall relate exactly as it is how even the soul alone becomes laden with karma.
(1) The soul exists in the ether together with its own subtle karma.
From volition arises joy, and by that, one engages in desire. (2)
Then, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) proceeds from the union of semen and blood;
when the semen is held by the *prāṇa*, the downward breath (*apāna*) proceeds there.
Driven by the *apāna*, the semen is impelled and it also draws forth the female seed (*rajas*).
And by being mixed with that [apāna], the samāna becomes the lower seed-state (bījatā).
The udāna leads the mixture toward the embryo in the abdomen.
It certainly joins the mixture at its place, the navel, for the sake of the umbilical cord.
And *vyāna* is involved in the mixing [of elements] therein; it pervades for the sake of digestion.
Once digested, it indeed takes the form of offspring, nourished by the woman's *nāla*.
Having attained birth, it goes outside; that is considered to consist of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*).
From the mother come the body hair, blood, and flesh; therein indeed they exist.
From the father come the sinews, bones, and marrow; therein they exist, endowed with strength.
In such a material body as this, "māyā" is defined.
The body is said to be the *māyā* of the Self, whereas that which is bodiless is indeed free from *māyā*.
The Self always resorts to me—the senses and so forth—for its own nourishment.
Therefore, I am the body, characterized by the quality of being nourished, and I am indeed of the nature of *māyā*.
Through the existence of my body, the living self (jīvātman) experiences [existence].
Therefore, the body is always *māyā*, which provides all objects of experience.
By means of its own karma, the self undergoes bondage to the body through the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
The Caturhotṛ is the summit; if the Hotṛ reaches this bond, there is this quartet:
the instrument, the action, the agent, and the liberated one. These four Hotṛs each indeed consist of seven [factors].

The nose, the tongue, the eye, the skin, the ear, and also the mind, as well as the intellect—these seven are the instruments; they are the causes of the qualities. Likewise, odor, taste, form, touch, and sound [are the objects]. //13-14//
That which is to be thought and that which is to be understood—these are the actions and the causes of action.
Likewise, the smeller, the eater, the seer, the toucher, and the hearer;
as well as the thinker and the understander—these seven are the agents and the causes of agency.
Such beings devour and offer up their own constituent elements.
He who is unattached to these seven is indeed liberated in a sevenfold way;
I am devoid of causes and the like, and I remain untainted by karma.
I have no agency whatsoever; therefore, I am eternally liberated.
Devoid of the notions of "I" and "mine," I abide in the state of liberation.
Otherwise, through the fourfold officiating priests, I would remain bound by illusion.
The ignorant man is afflicted by the sense of "mine" regarding food that is not his own.
(1.9) Consuming food for the sake of the body, nourishing it while possessed by the notion of "mine," he—by eating what is not the Self—is afflicted by illusion. (3.174.20)
Illusion, thirst, and the form of craving increase one's desire for sense objects; by drinking what should not be drunk through illusion, this person is destroyed.
Indeed, that which is unfit to be drunk is not offered to the Lord, nor is that which is unfit to be eaten presented as an offering.

Or rather, this water that is for the body and perceived by the senses—though it be drinkable and delicious—is indeed unfit for consumption, even if it is sweet and composed of the elements. One who cooks for the sake of the self is neither bound nor liberated. (22–23)
That which is subtle—whether food or drink, auspicious or inauspicious—is perceived by the mind;
likewise by speech, the eyes, the ears, and the skin.
That which is grasped by the tongue and that which is grasped by the sense of smell [are also perceived by the mind]. (24)
Whatever is traversed by the hands, the feet, the genitals, and the anus;

whatever is perceived or experienced by the intellect (*buddhi*), the mind (*citta*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), or by the external sense-spheres—whether individually or collectively, whenever it occurs. (25–26)
Whether in dream or waking, at the end or in the middle, or at the beginning—
whatever is eaten or drunk for one's own sake is indeed composed of illusion (māyāmaya).
It truly destroys the embodied being as he is being cooked by means of nooses, whips, and the like.
All that is abandoned by leaving self-interest behind in the Supreme Self.
Indeed, even what is eaten and drunk becomes truly devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
Thus, for one who knows the yoga of the qualityless, the fire of knowledge blazes forth.
It is the reducer of all ashes and the destroyer of the bonds of illusion;
it is the sacrifice of union with Hari, for which the renunciation of all one's possessions serves as the sacrificial fee.
It has service to the virtuous as its concluding purificatory bath and plunging into the river of liberation.
For him, this cycle of existence born of food and drink does not exist. Although active while remaining in the world, that Puruṣa is indeed inactive;
through union with the Supreme Puruṣa, he bestows liberation here upon ten million beings.
Even while living with a lover, his desire is not illusory; and even while living with her husband, her passion is not illusory.
It is for the sake of the Self, for the sake of Kṛṣṇa, and indeed for the sake of the Supreme Brahman.
The transition to another body for one's own sake brings about the experience of auspicious and inauspicious results.
O Lakṣmī, that which is for the sake of Kṛṣṇa leads in every way to the abode of the Supreme Brahman.
[This applies] when the individual soul, whose nature is thirst for its own self, remains possessed of latent impressions and attachment. (34–35)
Karma previously accumulated remains, yet it perishes by taking refuge in me;
indeed, by surrendering everything to me, the fruit of action is destroyed.
By taking refuge in the holy ones and in my own form, one attains divinity.
Just as my yoga progresses, so too does my divine nature [unfold].
(37) Just as a wife attains auspicious worldly divinity through union with her husband, and the sky attains a radiant divinity through its connection with the sun; (38)
Through the application of gold, copper attains divinity and loveliness;
through the application of virtue, the divinity of people is created by knowledge;
and through the application of dress, the divinity of kings is produced by ornamentation.
Through the union with gold, the divinity of the gods was established; through merit, that of the ancestors;
through sovereignty, that of the Siddhas; and through austerities, that of the ascetics.
The divine nature of the disciples and the groups of servants was brought about by their service.
The divinity of the Gandharvas comes from their songs; that of the virtuous, from offering everything to Acyuta; that of chaste women, indeed, through truthfulness and their vows;
and for those practicing celibacy, divinity everywhere arises through the vow of Brahman.
Through the attainment of the station of the lords and through my yoga, liberation belongs to those who are freed;
yet divinity always resides in me, as does the splendor (lakṣmī) that issues from my limbs.
O Lakṣmī, that divinity of mine is eternal and inherent to my own nature.
Having attained such a state as this, my devotee, endowed with divine nature,
attains eternal divinity and rejoices in my abode.
Furthermore, his illusion, senses, internal organ, elements, and subtle constituents [are likewise transformed].
Through my yoga they became divine; therefore, I am indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Through my yoga, infinite living beings have attained the state of Śiva.
Through my yoga and through devotion, men have become countless Nārāyaṇas.
Those who have been born and those who are being born are indeed inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha;
they are also inhabitants of Goloka, inhabitants of the Supreme Abode (Paradhāma),
residents of the Imperishable (Akṣara), as well as inhabitants of other abodes.
And those dwelling in the world of Īśa are inhabitants of the world of Māyā. Countless crores of Viṣṇus, possessing the form of Viṣṇu, are born;
and countless Vairāja Brahmās are also born. (3.174.50)
Furthermore, principal puruṣas are born in infinite numbers;
and even those who are liberated are born in infinite numbers, having gone to the Abode.
They sing, rejoice, and dance with joy for Hari.
What need is there to speak of a mere touch of Māyā, O Lakṣmī?
Even Māyā, the Great Goddess, rejoices there upon attaining Me;
she, the imperishable supreme Vidyā, and even Māyā herself, undergoes transformation.
If a supreme devotee knows such a divine procedure, his yoga will always be divine; what cause for lamentation could there be in that?
Thus, through my power consisting of yoga, divinity [is attained].
One who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa indeed becomes preeminent among all.
There is but one Teacher dwelling within the heart; I am that supreme Nārāyaṇa.
United with me, my devotee carries out and accomplishes [all things].
The one Guru residing in my heart is I myself, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
instructed by me, the devotee carries out and performs [his duties].
The one kinsman residing in my heart is Śrīpati, Puruṣottama.
Instructed by me, he now carries out [the work] and performs it.
There is but one Lord dwelling in the heart, the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
embraced by me through him, the devotee enjoys bliss.
I alone am the inner controller, the Supreme Self dwelling in the heart;
impelled by me, this [individual soul] proceeds and acts. I alone am the single hearer, the eater, the knower, and the thinker.
I alone am the smeller, the toucher, as well as the seer and the taster;
I alone am the one who causes bliss, the grasper, the goer, and the emitter.
It is by me alone that this world is experienced—it eats, it knows, and it rejoices.
I am the Guru, the Supreme Brahman; in me, his dwelling is complete in every way.
By performing this act of offering to the Guru, he is not tainted by action.
Thus, while living here, there shall be for him the state of liberation while alive (jīvanmukti).
At the end of the body, may there be eternal liberation for him in my very abode.
I grant him my own indivisible, imperishable abode, which is the refuge of bliss;
and may he possess an eternal dwelling in the Imperishable, enriched with all happiness.
"By my meditation, he is liberated and attains similarity with me;
through my grace, he obtains all my divine powers.
O Lakṣmī, this great lore of Brahmā has been revealed here to you."
Upon attaining which, a man or woman becomes one whose very form is Brahman.
For this purpose, I previously established my own Vidyā here in this sphere—the single-syllabled Brahman "Om," known by the name of the letter 'Da'. (67–68)
Having obtained her, who bestows the highest good, all the serpent-sages, celestial seers, and enjoyers of worldly pleasures fled with zeal, each according to his own nature;
all the serpents, celestial seers, and dānavas were intent upon their various respective goals.
Having understood the letter *da* in its various forms, they remained established in their respective natures.
Through the letter *da*, the disposition for biting arose in serpents, while among the asuras, the disposition for deceit, born of their own nature, came forth. (3.174.70–71)
At that time, the disposition toward giving arose naturally among the gods;
through their very nature, the disposition toward self-restraint arose among the great seers;
and thereafter, a state of compassion arose within the virtuous.
From the letter *da* in the word *dakṣiṇā*, the disposition of men arose;
from the letter *da* in the word *darśana*, the disposition of women arose.
They all naturally practiced the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the foremost of all [rasas].
The disposition toward milking [the earth] arose among kings, as did the disposition toward the earth and the kingdom;
the disposition toward punishment arose among the Rākṣasas and the Daityas;
and the disposition toward skillful conduct arose among the elders by their very nature.
For those engaged in action, the state of being dependent on fate arose from their destiny; for the industrious, it was through the letter *da*.
For the wretched, the state of misery arose from their nature through the letter *da*; for the lords, the divine state likewise arose from their nature through that same letter. (76–77)
The disposition of the piśācas toward foul odors was innate; the disposition of gamblers toward wickedness was innate;
and the disposition of teachers toward instruction was innate.
Among the Dānavas, there arose a desire for victory through the strength of their arms;
among householders, a desire for a virtuous son in their longing for pregnancy; and among animals, that same desire was directed toward food in the matter of their tusks. (3.174.80)
From that, the disposition toward performing śrāddha rites for the ancestors on the Darśa festival and other occasions arose;

likewise, among the people dwelling in their respective lands, the contemplation of the Divine (Brahman) emerged. Thus, O Lakṣmī, various forms of contemplation upon Brahman indeed came into being at that time.
For she was born of the inherent nature (svabhāva) of all beings and acted according to their karma;
yet for some, she did not lead toward divine liberation.
Therefore, the Brahman "Sa" was taught by me once again. 82–83.
At that time, for those seeking liberation, service to the virtuous became natural through the syllable *sakāra*; for householders, a virtuous disposition became the giver of liberation;
and from that, the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of all duties such as ritual action arose. (84)
Truth is his vow, truth is his dharma, truth is his world, and truth is his eternal nature.
(85) Likewise, he is eternality itself, as well as being existence-consciousness-bliss;
he is the self of all, possesses a formal embodied form, and is endowed with attributes. (86)
Good fortune, a well-disposed mind, wifely fidelity, equanimity, as well as impartial vision, the grasping of the essential,
possession of spiritual accomplishment, and likewise the vow of celibacy free from emission. ॥87॥
Worship of the Lord of the Gods, service to Śrī Hari, the all-seeing;
I am that [service], as well as recitation (*japa*), the golden worship of Sūrya, the eternal practice of the seers (*ṛṣi*), and also union (*sāyujya*) and equality of power (*sārṣṭi*). 88–89.

Mankind, gods, sages, and even the ancestors likewise accepted all these qualities born of action: union in the same world (sālokya), similarity of form (sārūpya), co-existence (sahabhāva), and the relationship of master and servant (svāmisevakabhāva).
The sages and the souls who are devotees have indeed taken up the path to liberation.
They performed hearing, service, total surrender, and complete offering;
thus, having attained the Guru, who is the Supreme Brahman and the giver of liberation, one reaches it from that.
Having realized their own self as having attained the state of Brahman, they worshipped; and having experienced the Supreme Lord residing within themselves, they worshipped him.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the world of living beings [worships] according to its own nature.
Even after receiving [instruction] from a teacher, one experiences both the existent and the non-existent.
Moving through the world with auspiciousness, a person becomes one whose conduct is auspicious;
he is always a true *brahmacārī* who is devoted to the conquest of the senses.
Wandering through the world with evil intent, one indeed becomes an evildoer;
likewise, one who acts according to desire out of passion is one who delights in the pleasures of the senses.
But one who acts according to dharma is one who delights in sacrifices, offerings, and the like.
But he who practices merit through austerity and is devoted to the observance of vows;
yet, having transcended the performance of such vows, abides solely in Brahman—moving through the world in the form of Brahman—he indeed becomes established in Brahman. (97–98)
Celibacy is the form of Brahman; one whose character is fixed in Brahman is always happy.
For such a person, Brahman alone is the fuel, Brahman is the fire, and Brahman is the source.
Having fully realized that everything is Brahman, he attains the Supreme Brahman.

The self is Brahman; the guru is Brahman; he is firmly established in Brahman. Composed within that supreme Brahman, possessing the character of Brahman, and devoted to that celibacy which is the supreme Brahman—he attains me.
Whether it be a man, a woman, or even a eunuch— whatever person there may be who has reached the end of birth, remembers their past lives, and possesses right conduct—
having attained the Supreme Brahman, they indeed rejoice together with me.
"Whether performed here or there, all his actions indeed grant liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Attainment of a Body Occurs, the Experience of Auspicious and Inauspicious Karma, the Attainment of Brahman, the Foundation of Karma, the Offering of Fruits, the Acquisition of Divine Status, Eternal Liberation, Dwelling in the Imperishable, and the Realization of Sārūpya," in the Mukti-dharma section of the third book, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
