Chapter 175 [[Author: → Chapter 176
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Thus, O Lotus-born One, the Lord himself, known as Sadvidyāyana, spoke these many bulls of liberation to his wife Śrutiphālā.
And he spoke thus concerning the ocean of saṃsāra, which is devoid of a bottom, where the fish of the senses find their livelihood, and which is tossed by the waves of internal agitation;
a path carved out by the boat of the elements, and bound by the hope for sense objects. (2)
Abounding with fish that are the mere elements of sustenance, with winds of grief and joy, etc.;
having crocodiles of desire, anger, and so forth; having the confusion of the quarters caused by delusion and error;
having whirlpools of attachment and aversion, and providing the coolness of the water of latent impressions (vāsanā). (3–4)
Having crossed over the shoreless ocean known as karma— consisting of merit, demerit, and the like—
and through union with Hari, I have entered the supreme realm,
which is divine, endowed with divine qualities, and resplendent with divine cows. (5)
It is eternal, golden-hued, truly fearless, and worthy of the Vedas. There, the rivers consist of bliss, the trees are filled with joy,
the wish-fulfilling creepers are full of delight, and they are the abodes of the essence of affection.
Where there are festivals for the Lord, who is endowed with all excellent qualities and possesses eternal youth, beauty, affection, and love—
there is no other giver of happiness than He, nor is there any other happiness besides this.
Having attained that, there is no sorrow, nor suffering, nor likewise fear.
Indeed, the seed of impermanence does not exist there; nor is the three-branched tree found there.
There are neither the seven secondary branches nor the sixteen inner branches. (3.175.10)
There were no matted-haired sages there, nor those practicing the yoga of mental invocation;
no enclosures of bamboo stakes, nor ground elevated by clan-trees.
Indeed, there were no sharp-edged thorns, nor gravel there at all.
There was no heat arising from the sun’s rays, nor coolness produced by moonlight;
there was neither smoke from fire, nor shade from canopies, nor clouds, nor rain, and the five fires were not present there. (12–13)
There are no colors arising from the blending of pigments, nor is there a mass of the erotic sentiment;
there is no field of bondage there, nor are there fetters that obstruct. Indeed, there are no rubies or other such gems there.
There are flowers of five colors and fruits possessing the three tastes.
There are no ordinary trees or plants there; instead, those [trees] exist there.
Padmarāga gems and sweet juices are found there, and swans dwell there.
Satiated with necklaces of pearls, they cry out, "I am he! I am he!
There, their splendors are unobstructed and devoid of boundaries.
There, the cows have many horns and are filled with every desire.
The Nārāyaṇīs are great beings who remove all suffering;
they are the deities Kṛṣṇa, guests, and dwellers in the sky.
They are initiated and are also constantly beheld by their Lord.
There, eternal festivals for her companions always take place; yet, in their unions with their beloved husbands, their amorous dalliances are devoid of satiation.
[She beholds] that supreme ground, higher than the highest, which is unshakable, changeless, and imperishable.

"I have attained [it]," Śrutiphala sang, his mind fixed on Sadvidyā. "Hā3u Hā3u! he sang again and again, remembering the auspicious place and recollecting that sacred ground which is the fruit of the Vedas. (21-22)
He danced to the rhythm, speaking and even teaching;
and then, in the presence of Śrutiphala, he attained a state of spiritual softness.
Having become composed once more, he said: "Blessed are you, O Supreme Goddess!"
"I am that which you are; he is I, and she is you. Indeed, this Self is the Supreme Lord.
(24) Those virtuous ones who realize Him have no fear anywhere—neither above, nor below, nor across; no end of Him is found on earth. (25)
Indeed, there are divine forest groves belonging to Hari there,
where even a three-faced woman does not grow if she is turned face-downward.
Mountains and hills also exist and dwell there.
They bathe at the confluence of the Brahmavahā river with the Pārameśvara,
where their desires have been thinned by the satisfaction of bathing; firm in their vows and radiant as gods,
they enter into the Self within themselves and worship the Supreme Self.
Those who know the forest of the feet dwell and rejoice here;
such is this supreme forest of the feet that those most devoted to Brahman have realized.
Through my yoga I have attained it, and you have attained it as the true fruit of the Vedas.

I have attained the Supreme Brahman, the abode of knowledge, and I am now free from fear. Immersed in the bliss of Brahman, I do not perceive harsh odors, nor do I experience harsh tastes, nor do I behold harsh forms. (3.175.30–31)
I do not touch harsh touch, nor do I hear harsh sound;
I do not form harsh thoughts, being immersed in the bliss of Brahman. I desire nothing undesirable, and there is no object of hatred for me.
I dwell in the Net of Brahmā, overflowing with the bliss of Brahman.
(33) Overflowing with the bliss of Brahman, I offer everything—whether earthly or watery—into the Supreme Lord during the sacrifice to Brahman. (34)
Whether it be of the nature of fire, wind, or space; whether it be qualities and so forth, subtlety, or even internal state, action, or consciousness;
whether it be innate nature or artificial, insentient or sentient—[it is all the same].
Or rather, overflowing with the bliss of Brahman, I offer my very consciousness as an oblation.
Having offered up my perishable nature through its imperishable state within the Infallible One, I offer myself; thus liberated, I am overflowing with the bliss of Brahman.
For one who is equanimous toward all beings, free from deceit, self-conquered,
and completely liberated on all sides, no fear exists at all. Indeed, there is only association with the virtuous and meeting with those who are liberated.
Through devotion, there arises a state of identity and non-difference from Śrī Hari.
Having thus obtained these supreme gains, I experience joy in every way;
immersed in true knowledge, I find the sweet fruit of the fruit of the Vedas in its very taste. (3.175.40)
Thus, in the very abode of true knowledge, Lakṣmī made his wife— who was of the nature of Brahman— the fruit of the Vedas through instruction in every way.
Then, once upon a time, there was a king named Alarka, a great devotee of the Lord.
The son of Madālasā, having indeed conquered the entire earth, stood beneath a tree and set his mind upon peace. For the sake of peace, he reflected: "The entire earth has indeed been conquered."
Even with sharpened arrows and weapons, there is still no peace;
for the mind is indeed fickle and wicked. Thinking, "Having conquered it, I shall attain supreme peace," I cut through this mind with sharp shafts.
"I shall cut off the senses, which are the instruments, here with my arrows.
Having reflected thus, he fixed extremely subtle arrows upon his bow;
then, the mind, having become embodied, stood before him.
O Lotus-born One, he declared that Alarka was beyond the range of arrows:
"These arrows shall not kill me, O Alarka;
being unobstructed, they will turn back fruitlessly and pierce you instead—you shall die."
"Release other arrows by which I may be destroyed.
Having heard this, Alarka replied: "O Mind, you perceive many odors in conjunction with the sense of smell; it is through its assistance that you live."
"Then I shall destroy your sense of smell with sharp arrows, and that will be your death.
Having heard this regarding his sense of smell, Alarka then replied to him fearlessly:
"O King, these arrows of yours will not kill me, for I am beyond their reach."
"Returning, they will pierce your vital organs; you shall die.
Discharge other arrows with which you might destroy me.
Having heard this, Alarka then said: "Indeed, this tongue is my helper. (51–52)
The mind is always a provider of dear service by means of bestowing flavor;
likewise, this skin is always a provider of pleasure by means of bestowing touch;
and similarly, this ear provides assistance in the acquisition of sound for him.
Likewise, even this eye is an assistant in the acquisition of form;
in the same way, all these other organs, such as the sense of smell and the rest, are indeed assistants to the mind.
This intellect, acting as a thief, seizes what has been given to the mind;
and egoism, having joined with them here, eats [the fruit] full of pride. I shall strike down all these in every way with subtle arrows.
Having heard this, the intellect, together with all [the other faculties], said to Alarka:
"O Alarka, these arrows shall not touch you, nor shall they ever touch us.
For these [arrows] are gross, while we are subtle; there is no contact for us, much less any talk of death. (57–58)
Fruitless and turned back, they will kill you in their rage;
yet even when he discharged his arrows, they returned to him fruitless.
They struck Alarka, and Alarka fell into a swoon.
He remembered me, Śrī Hari, in the form of Dattātreya.
Having manifested myself, I indeed granted him life;
the arrows were extracted from his body, and he truly rose up.
I discharged at him arrows that embodied the power of one-pointed concentration—
arrows unattached to the subject-object duality and so forth, established solely in their own essential nature;
these were the arrows of yoga, joined with my mantras and fixed with the Brahma-weapon.
Having reached those sharp, subtle, and internal [enemies] drenched by his discharged weapons,
he too quickly released them through himself toward all the senses and other faculties.
Some of them struck everyone down swiftly, while others indeed fled.
Furthermore, having bound them with nooses by means of the rays of his concentration,
he cast them into the Lake of Brahmā, and they attained dissolution there.
Then, having become divine beings, they attended upon the liberated Alarka.
Then, having assumed a divine form, he attained the highest perfection.
Together with his mother and his brothers, he indeed went to liberation.
While speaking thus, O Lakṣmī, listen to this instruction which bestows discernment.
"Alas! Everything external, conquered by arrows, was indeed entirely impermanent;
and until today, everything pertaining to the body has been practiced, yet not that which is internal.
But today, by the grace of the True Guru, those things possessed of defects have been conquered."
Indeed, all the senses and other faculties, having been endowed with qualities individually,
were cast into the lake of Brahman and brought to a divine state.
Thus, having become one of divine form, I worship Keśava.
Without total surrender, there is indeed no happiness anywhere else.
By surrendering one's own self to Kṛṣṇa, the highest and eternal happiness is attained.
Furthermore, even in a battle created by Māyā, eternal victory shall be yours.
Through the practice of yoga directed toward the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
O Lakṣmī, King Alarka thus attained eternal peace;
and Śrutiphala also attained peace by serving her husband.
Listen, Lakṣmī, to the three enemies who indeed exist everywhere as the three qualities:
*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. These grant bondage impelled by *māyā*. These three are the enemies in the world; though they are threefold, they are nine as well.
Exhilaration, joy, and bliss—these three are born of *sattva*.
Craving, anger, and the onset of hatred—these three arise from *rajas*.
Fatigue, drowsiness, and delusion—these three arise from *tamas*. (75–76)
These nine enemies indeed obstruct consciousness within the body;
they constantly cause it to remain merely within their own respective natures.
When the person, having reached the assembly of liberation, desires to conquer them, [then he attains isolation].
When he is able to abandon the city [of the body], then he should surrender those [senses] unto me.
To the extent that they are thus conquered, to that extent one becomes liberated;
for greed is a great defect which must certainly be overcome.
O Lakṣmī, for others, victory may result in fruitlessness due to craving;
yet he who is impelled by that [divine power] never encounters thirst anywhere at all.
One afflicted by thirst here runs toward low ground and falls.
He does not perceive what ought not to be done, for he follows from low to lower [states].
From that arises anxiety and fear; from that comes the passionate (rājasa) state, and from that further the dark (tāmasa) state, whereby he exerts himself in action.
When birth and karma are exhausted, there is death; then rebirth, and again death.
But when greed is conquered, there is freedom from craving, which is indeed eternal great bliss.
That is the sovereignty of the self, and it bestows the bliss of Brahman.
The great kingdom is the divine kingship, whose beloved essence is the Supreme Brahman.
King Kṛṣṇa is the supreme Lord; that kingdom is my own kingdom.
Indeed, the King himself, becoming the very Self, considers it exactly as it is. (84–85)
If indeed the individual soul (*jīva*) abandons the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the true King,
and becomes a king himself, then that [king] is rootless and a deceiver. What sovereignty can there be here for the *jīva*, inherited from his father and grandfather?

Whether it be the earth, the earthly body, action, or even dharma—whatever constitutes enjoyment is the kingdom, and whatever constitutes existence is the king indeed. There is no kingdom in the physical body, nor is there a kingdom in the mind. (87–88)
There is no sovereignty over the group of senses, nor is there sovereignty over the sense-objects.

The individual soul (*jīva*) alone is subject to everything; you do not consider the [senses] to be subject to the soul. For how could there be sovereignty for the soul, or even kingship, in the case of a bull?
For those [objects] are never entirely dependent upon the living soul at any time.
Therefore, without having obtained a kingdom and having abandoned the false realm of sense-objects,
one should become happy by taking refuge in the King, the Supreme Self.
The states of existence are always finite, for they are born of karma and produced from the body;
being material in nature, they are likewise [transient], and therein the self has no sovereignty.
Thinking "this is mine," one falsely clings to them.
When one departs without having questioned that [Self], then one realizes destruction.
"Neither kingdom nor anything else is mine; my body is not mine—how much less anything else?
Thinking thus, a man of wisdom should accumulate the divine kingdom.
One should not consume fragrance for one's own sake when that earth has come under one's control;
one should not take flavor for one's own sake when those waters have come under one's control;
one should not take form for one's own sake when that fire has come under one's control.
The wind, having come under my control, does not take contact for its own sake;
space, having come under my control, does not take sound for its own sake;
and the mind, having come under my control, does not perform mental activity for its own sake. (96–97)

I have no effort for my own sake, for my self has come under my control. All my undertakings are for the sake of the gods, for the sake of guests, for the sake of living beings, and for the sake of the ancestors; indeed, they are dedicated even for the sake of liberation.
"O Lakṣmī, for me everything is an offering to Brahman, and even my religious duty leads to my liberation.
Thinking thus, a person is released from the ocean of worldly existence.
Having spoken thus to his wife, he who was named Sadvidyāyana— 3.175.100.
Again he said: "I always abide in the fruit of the Vedas;
I am a Brahmin, I am liberated, and I am a follower of the householder’s dharma.
Furthermore, I am devoted to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. (101)
"I am not as you perceive me to be, possessed of desire.
The entire kingdom of the Lord of Kamalā [Viṣṇu] exists in me, in you, and on the earth;
you shall come to know this with such an understanding, and it cannot be otherwise. (102–103)
"O beloved, Nārāyaṇa is my wealth; therefore, I am wealthy.
There is but one path, the Supreme Brahman, by which those who know It proceed.
[104] Whether in households, forest retreats, the abodes of teachers, or as mendicants—
Likewise, in other abodes there is the kingdom of the Supreme Lord Śrī.
Having stayed there and received leave to depart, one must go further to the divine place, the celestial abode; in the midst of it, there is no fear from any other place. 105–106.
Since your beloved wife is devoted to the fruit of sacred learning, most excellent in Brahman, and a speaker of Brahman,
you shall have no fear of the next world through the application of true knowledge and discipline;
being intent on the contemplation of my own nature, you shall attain my very self.
"I am the Self; I have attained the Supreme Self, there is no doubt.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge for Crossing the Ocean of Saṃsāra and Other Matters," within the section on the Dharma of Liberation in the third book, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 176 [Author:
Chapter 177 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Having heard this fruit of her hearing, Śrutiphālā questioned her master once more:
"I am fulfilled; nevertheless, this quest for knowledge is profound.
It is not possible for one of small intellect to either understand or practice it. (1)
"Tell me here the Dharma of liberation, both extensive and concise.
(2) Having heard these words of his beloved, O Lakṣmī, the sage Sadvidyāyana—who brings benefit to all women—spoke clearly. (3)
The lower fire-drill (araṇi) is the form of the intellect of a woman, while the husband is the supreme upper fire-drill;
when these two rub together through austerity and sacred learning, the fire of knowledge is born therefrom.
The intellect is called the woman and the self is the man; thus they are declared to be a couple.
And the Supreme Self, the supreme teacher, dwells within those two.
Janārdana, the Self of all selves, is to be propitiated by all ritual actions—whether by those two residing in the bodies of women or by those residing in men. || 5–6 ||
This knowledge, the knowledge of Brahman, has been declared by me in brief.
You are that very one, eternally liberated and nourished by the intellect.
I too am eternally liberated and nourished by the intellect.
The husband is the self (ātman) and the beloved is the intellect (buddhi); through these two, Brahman is attained.
(8) Intellect is the fruit of the sacred revelation (śruti), and the conscious one is the vehicle of true knowledge (sadvidyā).
Of those two, the Self is the Supreme Brahman, I am Lakṣmī, the Puruṣottama. (9)
"By taking refuge in me, consciousness becomes liberated and divine;
and the Self, having true knowledge as its vehicle, becomes the Great Liberated One.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall tell you the auspicious story of the teacher and the disciple."
O beloved, the disciple Siddhivedhāyana questioned his own guru, the teacher known as Muktistotāyana, regarding his son:
"What is declared to be the supreme good? Who is the transcendent (para), and who is the non-transcendent (apara)?"
Whence am I and whence are you? What is the supreme truth and happiness?
From what are beings born, and by what do living creatures live?
(13) What is truth, what is austerity, and what are the qualities proclaimed by the virtuous?
Which paths would be auspicious, and what is considered eternal happiness?
O learned one, tell me all this by which liberation is produced;
for people are afraid of worldly existence and desire emancipation. (14–15)
The gurus are indeed the saviors who grant liberation, for they are compassionate,
the protectors of those who have come for refuge, and purifiers.
Having heard that from Siddhiviśāyana, [he understood] the gateway to the stream of liberation.
He indeed instructed the disciple, whose inner sheaths were possessed by the desire for liberation:
"Listen, Siddhivēśa, I shall tell you everything exactly as it is.
The worship of the Supreme Lord is, in my view, the supreme good."
He alone is the Supreme Lord, the cause of all causes;
He is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
[19] He is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Mādhava.
The Lord is the teacher of Māyā, the syllable Om, and so forth, as well as the cause of his incarnations.
The renunciants (saṃnyāsas) are the virtuous by nature; they are likewise the very forms of Hari.
The saints (sādhus), the incarnations (avatāras), the Lords (īśvaras), and the other manifestations (vyūhas) are also He.
Furthermore, the imperishable Brahman and those who are liberated are indeed the *apara* (the lower);
so too are all those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*) also *apara*. All selves (*ātman*) who are desirous of enjoyment and possessed of craving are likewise *apara*.
The supreme reality is declared to be the Self (ātman), while that which is always non-Self (anātman) is the inferior.

Indeed, the ego (ahaṃkāra)—composed of the three māyās—arose from the principle of Mahat as "I am born. Likewise, the sense of "you" (tvam-bhāva) arose from that [ego] through the perception of duality regarding what is not the Self.
The designation "I" and "you" is illusory and does not belong to the Self.
The evolving Great Principle (mahat-tattva) brought forth the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
From the ego-sense arises, in every respect, the state of duality, which is of the nature of delusion. 25.

Upon the renunciation of that [identification], and the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine," the self enjoys the bliss bestowed by the Supreme Self; that is the supreme bliss. For indeed, through union with Śrī Hari, this remains unassailable throughout the three periods of time. (26–27)
That which is born from the yoga of the Blessed One is indeed said to be truth and happiness;
it is never subject to destruction, nor can it be taken away, nor is it exhaustible, nor does it decay.
Such is that [state], consisting of a mass of great bliss.
Having obtained that other [state], it indeed becomes mindless and sapless here;
the giver of that is the Lord Śrī Hari himself, the Supreme Controller, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Infallible One. (3.176.30)
From that, the incarnations (avatāras) arise, and from them indeed the male lords (īśvaras);
from them also the female lords (īśvaryas), and from that Māyā is born.
(31) Likewise, the sages (ṛṣis), the gods, human beings, and the immobile entities and so forth [arise].
Indeed, all embodied beings,
while digging up the earth, are born from Śrī Hari; they live only when entered by Him,
having been established by Māyā through the principle of the Filler (Āpūraka).
Pervaded internally by sin, they live for a long or short time; life is indeed a collection of actions—merit and demerit earned by oneself.
As long as those unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) arising from karma persist, so long do they remain. (34)
Embodied beings always live when that [truth] exists and die when it perishes.
(35) The Supreme Brahman is indeed Truth; liberation is eternally considered to be Truth.
The Self is Truth—consciousness and bliss—and Śrī is the ever-abiding Truth. (36)
Truth is the eternal dharma of the virtuous, which is said to bestow liberation.
Indeed, austerity is the highest goodness, and renunciation is the supreme austerity.
When one has the capacity, forbearance is called the highest austerity.
Knowledge, wisdom, and austerity are said to bestow liberation; that [knowledge] shall always be so.
He who knows the dwelling within Brahman as well as the departure from Prakṛti, and likewise the distinction between the conscious and the unconscious, attains the supreme goal. (38–39)
He who desires nothing and conceives no egoistic notions,
even while remaining in this world, is fit for becoming Brahman.
[3.176.40] In me, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the supreme Consciousness and Bliss—
Having performed the dedication, one should remain; one is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
Long ago, Brahmā was questioned by the Brahman-sages regarding the supreme good:
"How should one perform action properly? How may one be released from sin?"
"What paths are auspicious for us? Which are the southern and northern routes?
Having heard this, Brahmā said to them: "One should always perform service to the guru.
The gurus are the bestowers of liberation; they are holy beings and virtuous people. (43)
All those who wash away sins and bestow a treasure of merit;
those who act for the welfare of others without being prompted—such stainless ones are true gurus.
The instructions given by them are to be accepted, for they are considered to be virtues.

Those qualities by which a conscious being attains nourishment in goodness (*sattva*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are indeed of divine form; others are considered base qualities (*durguṇa*).
Impelled by these qualities, the self performs actions that bring about happiness.
Or rather, that which bestows the next world, or bestows the supreme abode, is auspicious. (47) Action that bestows the supreme abode is considered good, the best among the good.
Action that bestows the next world is considered good, better than the former. (48)
In this world, action endowed with righteousness is called virtuous action.
Brahman is truth, austerity is truth, and service to the guru is truth.
Truth is the noble and innate duty; by that one is liberated from sin.
Visiting sacred fords, serving the virtuous, and indeed serving one's ancestors are purifying.
Knowledge of the Self, knowledge of Hari, and devotion—which destroy all sins—as well as service to one's mother, service to cows, and service to chaste women, are indeed purifying. (3.176.50–51)
Devotion to the gods, devotion to the guru, and meditative absorption destroy sin;
celibacy and renunciation are both destroyers of all sins.
Even the life of a householder bestows heaven, yet when dedicated to Me, it grants liberation.
The forest-dweller’s stage (vānaprastha) is for those free from passion; it destroys the activity of illusion.
Having understood that dharma is characterized by faith, they practice it.
[It consists of] charity, service, sacrificial fees, truth, merit, and goodness.
Service to others becomes for you sacred pilgrimage sites and divine vehicles;
knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, meditation, absorption, and self-surrender;
the chanting of mantras and supreme contentment—these become for you the means of spiritual accomplishment.
Worship, supreme devotion, love, and likewise service;
surrender, falling for refuge, and the vehicle to liberation—these are all auspicious paths. Yet Hari is always the most auspicious of them all. (56–57)
Having gone there, the steadfast one enjoys that eternal, divine bliss;
becoming one with Nārāyaṇa, he enjoys every prosperity.
Thus have the paths been described to you, as well as other and further ones.
I shall describe those who give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and bestow offspring, who possess excellent wheels.
Having taken the merit of his human state, the deity indeed remains for a long time;
then, taking the remainder, he returns to the human state on the southern path.
Taking his sins, he indeed goes to the kingdom of Yama for the sake of cessation;
taking the remainder, he is born among the animals or then somewhere among humans.
Thus, on the southern path, there are eighty-four lakhs [of species].
It revolves like a wheel; that very path is the southern one.
There, within that southern pathway of the body, the principles (tattvas) abide.
The Unmanifest (avyakta), which is indeed the root-illusion (mūla-māyā), stands established as consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa).
The prior portion is in a state of equilibrium, while the subsequent portion is in a state of disequilibrium.
The principle of *dhruva* is both filling and stable, yet possesses the nature of procreation.
From the [three] qualities (*guṇa*) in a state of disequilibrium, the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*) is born.

In the body, that nature of consciousness of the conscious self indeed takes the form of a woman. From that, the son named ego (ahaṃkāra), who exists in three states, is born; consisting of the three qualities (guṇas), it functions within all bodies.
From that, the subtle elements and the sense organs are produced;
from that, the mind is also born, and from that, space and the vital breath (prāṇa).
From that, fire is produced, from that water, and from that the earth is born.
All of these exist here in the body in the region of Dakṣiṇāpatha.
Thus, it may have nine doors opened, or likewise two doors bound shut;
or it may have one door in excess, or even one door deficient, and so forth.
It consists of six sheaths, possesses five harsh qualities, and is extremely subtle with nineteen components.
It is endowed with consciousness, possesses eight attributes, many attributes, and inherent properties;
it is characterized by dissimilar attributes, and is perpetually defiled and impure.
Furthermore, at the end, there are three streams of phenomena (*dharmas*):

Through that union, our activity is of the nature of Kṛṣṇa and is indeed beyond the material qualities (nirguṇa).
Therefore, O wife, in every undertaking, remember Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord—
not me, nor you, but Kṛṣṇa alone— both in union and in separation.
"In this world, O dear one, there is no bondage for you here, nor in this body;
nor is there any bondage for me, who acts solely for the sake of others.
Even though she was being instructed in this way, O Lakṣmī, that mendicant nun—
Then, though she was virtuous and had gained confidence even slightly, she reflected once more: "This desire is of a defiled nature;
it is indeed sin, which bestows hell and also bestows suffering. (38–39)
Thus she constantly thought and always worshipped me with devotion.
One day, I appeared before them visibly within the range of their vision.
To destroy her doubt, I touched her with my own hand.
She was bewildered by my own form, which was adorned with every kind of ornament.
The deluded woman quickly cast her gaze upon me in the presence of her husband;
for me, she did not require sexual union at all, but [was satisfied] entirely by the mere touch.
All joys were indeed bestowed upon her, and she became supremely happy;
from that time forth, she possessed a divine state of desirelessness. The mental resolve born of longing was forever destroyed within her inner self.
Free from desire, she became liberated in form and strengthened by her vow of Brahman.
Even the mendicant, touched by her, became entirely free from desire.
From that time forward, both of them, radiant as the sun, were established in the vows of Brahman and virtuous conduct.
They became extraordinary, worthy of worship by the gods and worthy of worship by the world.
Thus, through my constant service, I rendered them free from desire;
indeed, by my yoga, even the women and the men became devoid of longing.
Indeed, they all proceed to the supreme state.
Having met their end in due time, seated within divine celestial chariots and having become liberated in form, those two went to my imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, in this world, for the man and woman who thus offer themselves to Me,
I destroy all defects and bestow divine virtues.
For the compassionate Supreme Self, who is capable of accomplishing everything, [this is not difficult].
The scripture exists in the world for the sake of the devotee; indeed, I deliver the devotees.
O Lakṣmī, various kinds of alms must be given to my Lord;
through my yoga, all that becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) for him.
Listen, O Kamalā; I shall tell you various things:
whatever is most dear to oneself is considered to be entirely of the nature of alms—whether in dream, waking, deep sleep, the fourth state, or liberation.
One should never accept what has not been offered; having given it to me, one should partake of it.
One should offer me every kind of food and drink, both savory and sweet; and whatever delicious drink is desired, one who takes refuge in me should give that to me.
Whatever garments are beautiful, as well as attire, ornaments, and the like;
gold, silver, diamonds, and other jewels—let one offer these to me.
One should also offer to me massages and the like, fragrant substances, and collyrium.
He should offer me crowns and the like, beds and the like, and balls for play;
he should also offer me canopies and the like, seats and the like, and vehicles and the like;
he should offer me temples and the like, mounts and the like, and celestial chariots and the like.
One should offer me incense, lamps, flowers, sandalwood, and the like;
one should offer me elephants, horses, cattle, and so forth, as well as male and female servants.
One should offer me all forms that are beautiful and sounds that are pleasant to hear.
May he offer to me all kinds of tactile sensations and all objects of perception;

may he offer to me those things to be traversed that are full of happiness and those to be rejoiced in; may he point out to me all varieties of sweet foods and the blossoms of the *tulasī* plant. (3.178.60)
One should give me, the mendicant, the essence of oils, camphor, and so forth;
one should always offer me a son, a daughter, a husband, a wife, and one's entire possessions.
One should offer me all weapons and all mechanical devices.
One should offer to me the rites of sacrifice and worship, such as the oblations (havana) and other ceremonies.
One should also offer to me the crops, the ears of grain, and likewise the grains;
and one should offer to me medicinal herbs rich in sweet flavors, honey, and so forth.
He should also offer me the sixty-eight arts and the nine treasures;
a person should bestow everything upon me, both manifest and unmanifest.
All income, production, and the increase of wealth and goods [should likewise be offered].
May he offer unto me that which is of the heart, of the body, and of the senses.
Having given me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, may he unite me with learning,
knowledge, discrimination, skill, and the possession of virtues.
One should offer to me all that is right and all service rendered to others;
both those intentions which are fruitless and those which yield fruit in the end—
offer all such deeds and efforts to me.
May he bestow upon me all sovereign powers, all strengths,
all states of being, all wonders,
and all endowments of beauty and virtue. (68–69)

I am for the sake of others; as a monk, I bestow an infinite number [of gifts]. Having received whatever is requested through begging, I surely give it away—the eternal kingdom, heaven, the divine worlds, enjoyments, and new riches.
I bestow upon them happiness, festivals, joys, and delights. I give wealth, grain, garments, and excellent dwellings;
I grant cattle, male and female servants, sons, and daughters.
Whether it be the station of Dhiṣṇya, or that of Mahendra, Vaiṣṇava, or even Brāhma; or the status of a world-protector (dikpāla), or the sovereignty of Īśvara, or the supreme station of Vairāja;
or the lordship of the worlds, or the state of a great ṛṣi, or the rank of a Guru.
I grant you either eternal sovereignty over the sun or the moon;
or I grant you Vaikuṇṭha, the immortal unmanifest realm, Goloka, the imperishable, Śrīpura, Brahmaloka, or the supreme abode.
I beg of you all; everything is always pleasing to me.
Through giving, I receive this [world], and having enjoyed it, I give back an infinite amount.
I beg for merit and sin, for the auspicious and the inauspicious alike.
Having received what is undesirable given by people, I bestow back upon them what is desirable. Having encountered loss, O self, I give back the fruit consisting of gain.
And having received even a little, I give back manifoldly according to their wish.
I bestow abundant Lakṣmī and exceedingly vast riches;
I grant manifold powers and perpetual victory.
Whatever is mine in its entirety, all that I give to him.

"Whoever would offer everything to me, having become mine, and remains so— I am thus capable of giving all that is infinite, simply by saying 'Lakṣmī. If indeed mendicants beg for my sake and offer [it] to me," ||| 3.178.80–81 |||
And from them they enjoy [the fruits], for I grant them infinite reward.
These many kings, brahmins, and sages—
at the conclusion of their ascetic penance— begged of me alone for a son.
I became the son of mendicants, repeatedly begged for in vain;
I was Gaṇeśa to Śaṅkara, Hari Kṛṣṇa to Vṛṣa, Vāmana to Aditi, and Kapila to Kardama. (83–84)
I am Gopāla of Vasudeva and Ṛṣabha of Nābhi; I am Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa of Kaṃbharā.
Likewise, I became Datta of Atri and Paraśurāma of Jamadagni.
Rāma was the son of Śataratha and likewise of Brahmā;
such are his various births, which indeed take the form of mendicancy.
Everything exists within mendicancy, and even "I" exist within mendicancy.
The mendicants are my vessels of supreme affection, my very own forms;
you, O Supreme Goddess, were given as alms by Bhṛgu, and you are of the lineage of Bhṛgu.
Even Padmā was obtained through alms, and Nārāyaṇa likewise.
Thus, Duḥkhahāśrī was obtained, as well as Lakṣmī and Māṇikī;
likewise, Prajñā and Padmāvatī were gained, along with Bhikṣā, Kamalā, and Ramā.
By reading and hearing this, one shall become possessed of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation of the Sage Bhikṣāyana through the Offering of All Actions to Śrī Hari and Other Deeds, as well as the Greatness of Alms-gathering, Even While in the Householder State," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

[The Author: Chapter 180.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, Lakṣmī, in the city named Bhāvuka there was indeed a Vaiśya who was destitute.
Indeed, from childhood, his father died and he was nourished by his mother;
this mother, whose name is Nityāśrayā, always protects her son Veśin alone, as the very root for the increase of the lineage. (1, 9)

She was constantly a widow; she would always go to the temple of Kṛṣṇa in the presence of the brāhmaṇas to hear the sacred narratives, by which her suffering was destroyed. (9) Through the knowledge gained from those narratives, auspicious fortitude suddenly arose within her.

Her fevers vanished, her sufferings were destroyed, and she became entirely free from anxiety. (4) That beautiful woman listened to the *Saṃhitā* named *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa*; for two years, she listened to all the narratives. (5)
Having heard those various stories, she became embodied in the form of Brahmā;
that virtuous and chaste woman, endowed with righteousness, remained bodiless.
Then, she indeed understood the meaning of her own name, "Nityāśrayā" (the Eternal Refuge).
My refuge is the eternal Lord Hari, my own Master.
Hari is the husband, the lord, the master; I am His wife.
The Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is to be served by me at all times. (7–8)
The cowherd boy himself, the imperishable son of Kambharā,
the Lord of Lakṣmīs numbering in the hundreds of billions, is the Śrīpati, the Supreme Lord.
He alone is the fulfiller of all desires for his own devotees.
"Nārāyaṇa, the beloved Lord and Master, is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having attained such knowledge, she remained established in her vow and austerity,
and performed the service of the form of the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
By her, indeed, a beautiful image was caused to be made for me upon a copper plate;
the worship of that [image], consisting of self-surrender, was constantly observed as a vow.
Listen, Lakṣmī, how she performed that service.
Having risen in the morning, she recites one hundred and eight times on her rosary the name "Oṃ Śrī Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa" upon the ground;
thereafter, remaining on her bed, she performs meditation upon my form.
The feet, the calves, the knees, the thighs, the hips and so forth;
the waist, the navel, the belly, the chest, the back, and both sides;
the throat, the mouth, the cheeks, the jaws, the forehead, and the two eyes. (15)
Thinking of Kṛṣṇa’s ears and his crest-lock, she then performs her bath.
O Anādikṛṣṇanarāyaṇa, this devoted mother of the helpless constantly performs the chanting of Your names even while bathing with a water-jar.
She herself indeed gathers *tulasī* leaves and flowers from the bushes and offers them to the Sun and to the ancestors who dwell in heaven.
Having gathered and ground the sandalwood, she returns home carrying water.
Having placed my image upon the seat, one performs the invocation and the rites beginning with the offering of the seat;
then one offers me water for the feet, the respectful oblation (arghya), and water for sipping, using water,
sandalwood paste, pure water, and likewise flowers.
Even without the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one may worship using substances designated by the name "five nectars.
One should also offer clothing, a sacred thread, and myrobalan fruit for the purpose of adornment;
as well as rice grains and excellent saffron for all the purposes of decoration. (21)
That virtuous woman indeed offers me incense made from sandalwood powder (22).
She offers a lamp with oil, and for the food offering she provides chickpeas and the like;
or else, in the very morning, she offers fruit, a vessel of sesame seeds, or molasses (23).
He offers whatever water he has obtained and likewise presents it;
he performs the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) preceded by the ringing of a bell.
He performs circumambulation, prostration, praise, and the auspicious ritual dismissal (visarjana).
And every morning, she always performs [her duties] preceded by an offering of handfuls of flowers.
Then indeed she attends to the household tasks: the fondling of the child, the protection of the child, the giving of breast milk, and the feeding of the child. (25–26)
Content with the state of being a servant, she indeed provides nourishment;
satisfied with food, clothing, and the like, she serves her husband Kṛṣṇa.
Then, in the form of a maidservant, she becomes a servant for the performance of servitude.
The alms-bowl goes to the house of the merchant with the desire to apply ointments and other such things [to it].
(28) Having performed the work of a servant, at midday one receives food, fruit, and so forth from the merchant’s wife; taking that, one returns to one's own home. (29)

"Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who is attained through my worship, comes constantly to the excellent family; they hear the chanting of my names. All that became my devotee, including the elder merchant Rūpaśa. (3.179.30)
When she met her death in due time, she remained eternally present in the house.
Repeating "O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," I was drawn by her and went indeed into the presence of the merchant.
I appeared directly before him, and likewise before that woman;
having bestowed divine touch upon me, he led me indeed to that imperishable abode.
From a most divine celestial chariot, I beheld that family.
"Everything born of my devotion has been produced by that helpless woman; indeed, with her I take delight.
At midday, having performed the household duties for the merchant in this very manner, she always comes to her own home after feeding her own son. (34–35)
Having caused [me] to drink milk, she eats while remaining established in the remembrance of Kṛṣṇa;
in the evening, she also performs the ritual waving of lights (nīrājana) and my worship.
Then, having given me food and having herself eaten as well—
She would fall asleep placing the boy at her side, and likewise me as well.
Thus, the Vaiṣṇavī, who always takes refuge in me, constantly attended to me.
Even as a child, having witnessed his mother’s devotion, he became the most excellent of devotees.

Just as his mother was, so too was his son—a refined soul who possessed self-knowledge. Even in childhood, this great devotee engaged in play such as offering worship and other rites, having fashioned an artificial image of clay upon a seat of sand. (39)
He worshipped my image with paste made from *kardama* and sandalwood and other substances.
Grasping blades of grass and leaves lying on the ground, he offered them with devotion, thinking they were flowers; likewise, he regarded even water as his mother.
He respectfully offers food from a vessel broken by clay,
as well as other items such as ripe fruits cooked with neem;
he likewise performs circumambulations and prostrations like a staff, and offers garlands.
He indeed supplicates Hari for forgiveness, compassion, and favor. Then,
he dismisses all of that, even along with his friends,
and delights right there in front of his house while worshipping me, Nārāyaṇa.
As time passed in this manner, that youth became a supreme devotee, and his mother too began to worship me; I was then pleased with them both.
And Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin, arrived there.
Then she, who was constantly dependent on me, requested alms there.
She gave me a single *roṭaka* cake and provided buttermilk for my meal.
Sitting there in the courtyard of the house, I ate a little.
I likewise gave that boy half a *roṭaka* cake,
as well as a small amount of buttermilk and milk which I had prepared.
The young son, filled with wonder, spoke repeatedly to his mother.
"O Mother, by the grace of the Brahmin, this buttermilk has turned into milk;
even this flatbread, though smeared with ghee, has become sweetened. Therefore, this most excellent Brāhmaṇa is truly marvelous. (3.179.50)
Having heard this supreme marvel, the mother, bewildered, gazed upon the Lord;
as she fixed her gaze upon his gaze, he became four-armed—divine, with divine limbs and adorned with all divine ornaments. (51)
I became Puruṣottama, endowed with divine marks and accompanied by Lakṣmī.
Then, upon merely beholding me, the Supreme Lord and Consort of Śrī, she fell at my feet and cried out, "Save me! (52–53).
My son, known as Keśī, recognizing me as the Supreme Lord,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the protector of the helpless— fell at my feet.
The boy praised me, and his mother, overwhelmed with emotion, also offered praise.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of mercy, protector of the helpless, Mādhava!
O Śrī Hari, Lord of the world, deliver me from this cycle of worldly existence.
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, my Lord! || 55-56 ||
By you, in the form of a brahmin, mother and son have been delivered.
"You are the protector of the protectorless"—this word of yours is true.
Indeed, O Supreme Lord, many stories concerning you have been heard by me.
Having attained supreme dispassion, O Janārdana, you have been served by me. Having obtained knowledge and recognized you as my Lord, I worship you eternally.
This child is yours, O Protector; look after this little son.
"O Śrī Puruṣottama, lead me to Your abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
O Lord, Beloved, Friend, Kinsman, Protector, Śrī Hari, protect me!
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, she offered a handful of flowers to Me.
She grasped my feet and wept, overwhelmed with love. O Rāma, her feet were drenched by those tears of hers;
and my son, too, offering himself to me, shed tears of love.
"Grant me liberation, O ocean of mercy, Supreme Lord, Consort of Śrī!
Thus he spoke, placing his hands upon my chest and drawing me close;
he embraced me just as a son embraces his father.
I shed tears toward my most devoted son.
He was drenched by them, and thereafter he attained divine vision.
O Rāmā, I gazed upon his mother with a compassionate look.
Then that divine vision of hers also quickly turned away:
"Out of compassion for me, these two knowers of the three times have resorted to supernatural powers;
yet they have become like Lakṣmī and Muktā, moving about with divine ease. (66)
There, with divine articles of worship prepared and gathered, the two of them worshipped me; yet they did not release me.
"O Kṛṣṇa, dwell here," they said to me again and again. (67–68)
Or rather, they both then said, "Lead us together.
Then, having well-contracted my form, I again assumed the form of a brahmin. They both served me with fans made from their hands.
Having deliberated upon the liberation of those two who possessed divine forms,
I led them both together and caused them to ascend a celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun;
[I likewise led] the son Keśin and his mother Nityāśrayā, who was indeed destitute.
He swiftly brought me to my own abode, the imperishable supreme state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am the protector of the helpless and their savior;
I am the beloved of true devotees, the bestower of liberation, moved by great compassion.
"From reading and hearing this, auspicious enjoyment and liberation shall arise.

(73) Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord’s Bestowing of His Vision and Liberation upon Anāthā, Nityāśrayā, and Her Son Keśin, after Witnessing Their Devotion to the Bhāgavata," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
