Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Lakṣmī, to another auspicious story concerning my devotee.
In a city named Māyā, there lived a devotee of mine known as Vyāghra. (1)
From childhood he possessed a divine nature, was affectionate toward the virtuous, pure, and holy;
whenever ascetics, Vaiṣṇavas, or female renunciants arrived,
he would immediately go to see those saintly ones.
He performs the massaging of feet, the fetching of water,
and likewise (3) the cleaning of vessels and so forth, as well as sweeping, within the hermitage at all times.
He partakes of the food offered by grace and always serves the virtuous (4).
Thus, endowed with devotion, the devotee received a great blessing:
"Live long! Remain long! Be happy and prosperous! (5).
Then, although he was engaged in the service of the virtuous, once—
Out of childishness and greed,
he seized by way of theft the golden chain that was an ornament of Vāsudeva, which had fallen [from him].
The virtuous men went to another village, while the tiger [remained with] the chain.
Having obtained it during the cleaning and other rites while it was not yet visible, he indeed protected it;
having brought the golden chain to his own home, he placed it inside a casket.
No one at all knew of it, and thus he guarded it well.
Indeed, his mother did not know of the chain within the wooden chest;
nor did his father, a wandering bard named Kūṭadeva, know of such a golden chain within the wooden box. (3.180.9–10)
He recognizes it himself when it is held, and he sees it even in the darkness;
furthermore, he places it back there, hidden within the chest.
(11) Now, there was a virtuous man named Śyāma, a worshiper of the form of Viṣṇu.
But during the worship in another village, as long as he desired the chain [to remain],
he did not see it at the time of worship and reflected that it must have fallen.
He repeatedly made inquiries through his devotees in Māyāpura.
The devotees asked the tiger whether he had seen [the thief] or not;
out of greed and fear, he gave them a reply.
Thus, due to the tiger's state of untruthfulness and the sin of theft—
On both hands of the gold thief, however, there appeared ringworms on all the fingers,
and even on his two thumbs, leprosy broke out completely;
his body became covered in white leprosy— this was the fruit born of the sin of theft.
He devoted himself to me, the Blessed One, and likewise applied medicinal remedies;
yet his leprosy did not subside at all, and he became exceedingly miserable.
Though he partook of the fruit of serving a holy man, he also bore the burden of the sin of stealing gold. (17)
There he heard a discourse concerning Lakṣmī;
indeed, he heard that the fruit of stealing gold would be leprosy,
and he also heard of its atonement, which is the gift of gold.
If one who has stolen gold performs the Brahmakṛcchra vow as well as the Brahmakūrca vow for seven days, he is liberated from that sin. Furthermore,
this [act] involves causing internal pain through deception in secret.
Having made it known abroad, he undertook the Brahmakūrca vow.
On the first day, he drank water boiled with khadira leaves;
on the second day, he drank water boiled with kiṃśuka flowers.
On the third day, however, he drank water boiled with bilva leaves;
on the fourth day, he drank water boiled with lotus seeds;
and on the fifth day, he indeed drank water boiled with udumbara fruits.
On the sixth day he drank [water] cooked in a blade of darbha grass, and after that,
on the seventh day, he observed a fast while repeatedly worshipping me; he also performed a rite of propitiation before my image to destroy his sins.
"O Hari, while I was performing the cleaning there, I obtained gold;
that very sin has indeed manifested as leprosy upon me—forgive me for that!
(26) I shall give a golden garland back to that virtuous man."
I have also performed atonement by means of the Brahmakūrcavratam vow.
May this disease of mine come to an end; for the sake of my devotion, please show me mercy.
Save me, protect me, O Lord of the World, O Śrī Hari, O Puruṣottama!
"You are the one who effects the removal of sin; protect me, your devotee.
Thus he entreated him excessively, shedding profuse tears.
(29) He reflected that death would come when his leprosy did not vanish.

While he was thus reflecting, I fell asleep; and in a dream, I appeared in his presence, manifesting my own form bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace. Laughing, I said to him: "O devotee, why do you grieve? Speak!"
He said to me, "O Ocean of Compassion, out of greed for gold, I obtained a chain from the virtuous Viṣṇu; however, it fell to the ground.
It was preserved by me and remains in my house, and I am enjoying its fruit in the form of leprosy. (32)
"Having heard this story, I have performed the expiation for the theft of gold.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord, destroy my sin by means of the Brahmakūrca vow.
Thus did he pray in my presence. Then I [spoke].
Suddenly interrupting his dream, I brought him to the waking state;
he too, having quickly arisen there and beheld me as the Supreme Lord,
became choked with love and prostrated himself like a staff, offering praise.
He danced with fullness of love and likewise begged for forgiveness.
Then, in order to remove his fault, I said to him:
"Give me the golden chain; indeed, your sin has departed."
Then the tiger, having stood up, gave me the chain;
I then placed that chain around my own neck.
At that moment, those virtuous ones went to that very place where they had been.
She had gone to Mūrtikaṇṭha, and the saintly man saw her.
Beholding that golden garland, he rejoiced again and again and recounted to everyone the supreme wonder of Hari. || 3.180.40 ||
Indeed, for the sake of His devotee, the Blessed Lord Himself provides both acquisition and preservation;
He thinks only of His devotee in both prosperity and adversity.
Whosoever may be the devotee of anyone, for that person's sake, the Blessed Lord Himself [acts].
He indeed bestows his own entire divine sovereignty.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, Vyāghra, the king of devotees, was instantly freed from leprosy and became cleansed of all sin. 43.
He was born fortunate and handsome, just as he had been before.
Therefore, I myself, Nārāyaṇa, protect those who have taken refuge in me—
whether they be sinners, filled with impurity, or overwhelmed by the defects of *māyā*.
Though [the world] is filled with hundreds of millions of latent impressions (vāsanā) and devoid of righteous action and the like, [I am not so];

for even one who has come to me for refuge, who has renounced life for my sake, whose every activity is for my sake, and whose meditation and worship are for my sake—[even such a person is dear to me]. 45–46.
I shall protect people in every way by accepting the surrender of all their possessions to me.
Listen now to another divine story that destroys the torment of sin.
In the village of Dhanagrāma, there lived an excellent Brahmin who served as the officiating priest for the village.
The one named Uttama lived with his family and was primarily devoted to the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) of the Vedas.
He indeed facilitated the performance of rituals for people of all castes;
he was even the preceptor of the king and carried out the king's affairs as well.
The food of kings is said to be heavy, as is the food of thieves;
likewise, the food of people who do not give, and of those who have fallen from their status, is heavy.
O Lakṣmī, what is eaten does not digest, and even what is drunk does not digest.
Even when robes, alms-bowls, and other such items are accepted as gifts, they do not wear out [for him].
His possession of beds, cows, gold, and so forth never diminishes;
he is merely a village priest, yet he is called a "supreme" Brahmin.
Out of greed, he seized wealth and other possessions from all the social classes;
he ate, drank, feasted, took pleasure, and rejoiced in his home.
Indeed, his prosperity in the house became preeminent, surpassing even that of the king.

Jeweled necklaces, golden garlands, golden couches and seats; (54) variegated mansions, numerous male and female servants, as well as cattle, buffaloes, and so forth, along with elephants, horses, chariots, and the like. (55)
Everything of his became prosperous; he had sons and daughters who bestowed happiness, and his wife was endowed with devotion, righteous, and faithful to her husband.
Then, by means of the burden of his gifts and the heaps of wealth belonging to the wicked—
Due to the food, drink, and other things of sinners, *jalodara* (water-belly) arose.
Because of that, the abdomen is tormented and indeed a great belly hangs down.
What is eaten does not digest, nor does what is drunk ever decay.
At that time, not even for a single moment did he experience happiness through his supernatural powers;
nevertheless, he went to the hermitages of physicians for the sake of curing his disease.
Yet, despite the application of many medicines, his abdominal dropsy [remained].
Far from being destroyed, it indeed increased day by day.
(3.180.60) Then one day, that Brahmin went to the sage Devāyana;
having bowed deeply to the holy man, he informed him of his own ailment. (61)
The virtuous man gave him a garland of the names of Hari and a *tulasī* rosary, and instructed the Brahmin in the recitation of the mantra:
"O Hare Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, make me free from suffering.
Thus, he taught him the *japa* of one thousand repetitions.
"He too chanted thus every day with joy, [thinking] 'It is indeed eternal.
He always worships me solely for the sake of destroying his disease.
One who is afflicted worships me constantly; one who possesses worldly power does not worship me at all."
Just as he had previously worshipped me out of self-interest when afflicted by a desire for wealth, so too,
after a year had passed,
I granted him my vision out of compassion before he performed his devotion, in order to bring about the healing of his disease.
Having formed a circle of holy men (*sādhus*), he went toward his house.
He too, for the sake of pacifying the disease, joyfully gave food and other provisions;
he also gave various items such as gold, silver, and garments to the *sādhus*.
He also prayed most fervently for the sake of curing his disease.
Having become a virtuous guru, I placed my hand upon his abdomen so that a miraculous transformation might indeed occur from within his belly. (68)
The great disease of dropsy fled from him in bodily form;
hideous and terrified, it ran away and fled.
Once the disease had gone, the Brahmin became healthy within a moment. (3.180.70)
Then the water became dry and the digestive fire (jāṭhara) became auspicious;
we all, being virtuous, quickly vanished from sight.
He too, having recognized me as Nārāyaṇa, then worshipped me repeatedly.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that devotee was rendered free from ailment by me at that time;
he too, in the end, went to my abode, the imperishable realm of the Supreme Self.
By reading and hearing this, there shall be health, worldly enjoyment, and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Cure of Leprosy for the Leprous Thief Named Vyāghra, a Devotee of the Cāraṇas; the Cure of Dropsy for the Devotee, the Village Priest Brāhmaṇa Named Uttama; the Vision of the Lord, Liberation, and Other Matters," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 181: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 181.
[The Author: Chapter 182.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of Virāja.
A devotee named Virāla, a wealthy Vaiśya living in Mañjuṣṭha village, lived there together with his family. He was engaged in the trade and sale of foodstuffs, garments, and vessels. (1–2)
The donor was a man of wealth exceeding one hundred thousand [gold pieces], devoted to the service of the virtuous,
by whom this beautiful and most splendid hall of dharma was constructed;
there, arriving guests and holy men find rest.
There, travelers, ascetics, virtuous women, and those on pilgrimage were [welcomed].
By him, a most excellent and auspicious almshouse for food was established there,
wherein there was sweet, flavorful food, milk, and likewise boiled rice.
The monks always receive *pūrikās*, soups, vegetables, and other foods;
they eat constantly by the hundreds, and he bestows words of blessing upon them.
Even the Vaiśya Virāla constantly offers his own hand as a gift.
He gives gifts to the ignorant, to the helpless, and even to women. (7) He causes the chanting of the names of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Viṣṇu to be performed;
he performs my worship himself and likewise causes it to be performed every day. (8)
She had five sons, seven daughters, and two wives;
all of them worship me, Śrīpati, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Meeting together every evening before me, they also perform kīrtana.
They engaged in delightful conversation and listened to one another.
Thus, while Virāja, endowed with merit and great prosperity,
had not yet reached old age, he was seized by the mild consumption known as *rājayakṣmā*.
Having become emaciated by a disease that was constantly increasing,
many medicines were administered and likewise many mantras were recited.
Many virtuous persons were also attended upon for his sake.
The disease did not subside, and the merchant became consumed by anxiety.
His family was seized by worry: "Our venerable father will die;
what should be done? Where should we go? Indeed, for the sake of protecting our father—" (13–14).
While they were thus reflecting, the auspicious Kuṅkumavāpikā—
the sacred ford that removes disease, where the Lord of Śrī is personally present—
came to mind; and so, indeed, did Janaka’s thought arise.
Together they set out for the sacred ford of Aśvapaṭṭasara,
chanting my name and remembering me, the Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the remover of disease.
Then, having arrived at the shore of Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, they sat down beneath a banyan tree; remembering me, they drank water.
Having reached the inexhaustible pool, all those radiant ones bathed.
Then they gave gifts of gold, silver, and garments;
likewise, they gave vessels, sweet foods, and blankets, saying,
"May the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa be pleased with us."
Then, perceiving his devotion, Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin,
went to the shore of the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake into his presence.
At that time, the consumptive man named Virāla, considering death at that sacred ford [to be his goal],...
Nārāyaṇa remembered me in his own heart; may he protect me.
Then, having gone into the presence of Virālaka, I asked him:
"O wealthy one, from where, for what reason, and how have you come here? || 22-23 ||
"O Tīrthakṛt, how long has this disease of yours persisted?
Remembering death with great distress, Virālaka wept and lamented there in many ways; he then questioned me, the Brahmin.

"Salutations to you, O Brahmin! You are an elder; if you know the divine cause, tell me how this disease arose for one who has performed much merit. O god on earth, no sin has indeed been committed by me in this birth. (25-26)
Indeed, various kinds of meritorious gifts have been performed by me in many ways. Since my childhood, I have been served by the virtuous and am a worshipper of Śrī Hari.
My family, too, is always endowed with devotion toward the Supreme Lord.
"I perform my religious vows with devotion along with my family;
nevertheless, show me how this wasting disease came upon me.
Having heard this, the one in the form of a brahmin spoke everything concerning Virāla.
O Lotus-born One, he indeed related the account of his previous birth:
"Listen, O merchant; you are most meritorious in every respect in this life.
Whatever karma was performed in the past is never separated from anyone."
In a previous birth, you were a Brahmin named Gaṅgeśvara.
You lived on the meritorious bank of the Sābhramatī at the temple of Viṣṇu, where you served as a priest; nearby were fields of grain and gardens. (31–32)
The seats were indeed beautiful for the Vaiśya, yet the Vaiśya met his death.
His wife, having become a maidservant in the palace, then performed service there.
That virtuous woman also provided cows and bulls in that palace.
She likewise gave fields and gardens to the temple;
being unable to perform agricultural labor, she became a servant in the temple and dwelt in the refuge of the deity, dependent on you and without any other support.
She indeed performs the service of the bulls with grass and other fodder, as well as milking them and so forth;
likewise, she carries water and performs cleaning and other such tasks.
Always abiding by his command, she serves Gaṅgeśvara.
Whatever grains, vegetables, fruits, and so forth grow upon the earth,
you first take those and give them to the Brahmins;
and you always cook delicious food yourself and offer it as an oblation to Viṣṇu.
Having granted her grace, you then accepted food from her;
the servant, having prepared garlands of flowers and other offerings, presented them to Viṣṇu.
In this way, she constantly serves both you and the Lord Viṣṇu.
Free from hypocrisy, endowed with devotion, characterized by total surrender, and possessed of righteousness— (3.181.40)— now, since you, greedy for flavors, prepare delicious food and,
having offered the finest portion to Viṣṇu, eat it secretly within the temple; (41)
Having eaten and attained satisfaction, you then gave even that coarse food— wheat cakes— to your female servant. Thus,
you have always shown partiality toward the giver.
First, that which was to be given to the giver should have been given by you; however, that was not done then.
A breach of the row was committed there, and that sin became yours in the past.
Once, during a period of excessive rain, there was a great flood on the Sābhramatī. || 43–44 ||
Pervading the fields, the groves, and even the temple, it arrived;
indeed, with a surging and great velocity, it increased rapidly.
And the cows, the bulls, and the servants were on the ground rising up from the temple.
On the ground, in a safe place, they all climbed up, afflicted by great fear.
That terrified servant girl, the farmer’s wife, when the water approached, clung to you;
embracing you for the sake of life, she was eager to preserve her own existence.
You, as well as that farmer’s wife, Ratnamālā, the cows, and the bulls—all for the sake of their livelihood—remembered me in my embodied form.
Then I thought: "I must protect these yogis who are devoted to me."

But even when the time of death has arrived, O merchant, the mind of an embodied being remains defiled, powerful, difficult to restrain, and laden with latent impressions (vāsanā). Upon the touch of a woman's body, it quickly undergoes a transformation. (3.181.50)
Then, at that time and in that place, your mind indeed underwent a transformation; for you, overcome by desire, were embraced by the flood of water.
Having realized this, I abandoned you, and even your servant was cast off at that moment.
"Even though I had come for the purpose of protection, I did not provide you protection there.
O twice-born one, seeing the destruction of Dharma, I did not offer protection.
You were carried away by the force of the current along with the greedy woman. (52–53)
Cows and bulls were also swept away in that flood;
all of them died, being endowed with merit yet possessed of a slight amount of sin.
O Brahmin, you are Gaṅgeśvara, the one who caused the breach in the row at that time.
Now you are indeed one who possesses the merit of service to Hari and is wealthy;
the field, the gift, the plowman, and the servant are yours, and she is indeed your housewife.
This Brāhmaṇī woman who was with you at the time of your death is your second wife.
Immediately thereafter, this very woman died of grief; yet here she shines, O merchant.
Those five sons who were bulls have indeed died in the waters.
These seven daughters, O merchant, and the two cows have also died in the waters.
"Indeed, this wealth and prosperity exist for you through the fruit of my worship.
This illness, O merchant, has come upon you today because you ate desired food for your own sake while breaking the line; but she, being free from guile, rejoices. (58–59)

A female cultivator enjoys the merit of giving fields, enclosures, and the like; a Brāhmaṇa woman, however, enjoys the religious merit of devotion to her husband. Gods, cattle, and humans enjoy happiness through wealth.
"You, a worshiper endowed with wealth, grain, jewels, women, and progeny,
have incurred consumption as the fruit of the sin of breaking the line [of guests].
Yet, through the power of devotion, both I and your family [shall be restored]."
"I am Mādhava, who has arrived for the sake of the liberation of the one who has come to the sacred ford.
O Virālaka, tell me whether you desire liberation or freedom from disease.
Whatever you wish, I shall grant it here," said Hari, assuming the form of a brahmin.
"I shall by all means bring about the destruction of the sin of one who eats in secret.
O merchant, be free from disease, or else attain liberation right here.
Upon hearing this, he was suddenly thrilled; having bowed to Puruṣottama, [he departed].
He asked me, "Does my life still remain in this world, or not? I replied to him, "Not even a moment of life remains for you beyond this point;
however, you are a devotee and have come to dwell with me, O seeker of truth."
Therefore, out of compassion and with the desire to destroy your disease, I shall grant that to you.
Whether you desire long life, liberation, or even both,
I shall remove birth, death, old age, and disease for one who seeks my refuge.
Thus addressed, that eminent merchant then gave a seat, as well as water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and fruits to me in the form of a brahmin;
he also gave musk, saffron, camphor, and *kesara* flowers.
Sandalwood and the finest fragrant woods, as well as excellent jewel necklaces; flower garlands, woolen blankets, crowns, bracelets,
earrings, finger-rings, and chains fashioned of gold.

Then the merchant offered me fragrant essences, an umbrella, fly-whisks, golden sandals, various gifts, as well as sons, daughters, and both types of women; indeed, Lakṣmī, he surrendered all his wealth to me.
He worshipped me according to the prescribed rite and said, "I am yours.
"Save me! Protect me, O ocean of compassion! Do as you wish; I am indeed yours.
When Virālaka had spoken thus, I, Acyuta, [responded]. ||73-74||
He said to him, "O merchant, may you become free from disease immediately.
Stay upon the earth for only one year, and thereafter you shall attain liberation;
there is no doubt that you will go [to heaven]. Having performed this pilgrimage, return home. (75)
"Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, is my Master and my Lord.
Recite this mantra daily; worship Kṛṣṇa, your beloved.
Remember me always, O merchant, and perform the pilgrimage to the five sacred fords (pañcatīrthī). || 76-77 ||
Constantly serve the virtuous, the holy men, and the saintly women.
Perform the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, and likewise the sacrifice to all beings.
Offer gifts, perform oblations, and present to me the offering of food and worship.
In this essence-less cycle of existence, the only essence is constant service to Hari.
(79) Service to the virtuous is the supreme essence; indeed, the company of the virtuous is the medicine.
Service to Me grants liberation to the virtuous and destroys their latent desires. (3.181.80)
Through the power of serving the virtuous, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) here indeed come to dissolution;

honoring the worthy is the means for destroying the sins of infinite births. Honoring the worthy also brings about the destruction of even those karmic effects that have begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*).
The virtuous are worthy of honor; they destroy obstacles and the entire web of diseases.
The virtuous are like wish-fulfilling gems (cintāmaṇi), granting what is well-thought of; the virtuous are like wish-granting trees (kalpavṛkṣa), bestowing the highest desired object.
The virtuous are indeed like wish-fulfilling trees, for they grant the fruit of immortality; the holy ones are like cows of plenty, milking forth eternal happiness.
The virtuous bestow spiritual perfections and are indeed the givers of all prosperity.
By their blessings, they bestow great fortune even upon those of meager merit;
through my yoga, they cause me to attain divine nature and the imperishable state.
These holy ones ward off the messengers of Yama; they are my heart. (85–86)
They indeed burn away evils, increase merits,
bestow good fortunes, and remove calamities. O merchant, always perform service to them, for it grants grace.
Always perform the five sacrifices with a gentle disposition and with sincere devotion.
Practice service to cows and service to dharma, which bestows heaven.
O Gaṅgaka, always seek the practice of discourse regarding the knowledge of the Self.
O noble-hearted one, always perform my worship alone;
at the end, having granted you my vision, I shall lead you to my imperishable abode.
Even such acts as the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, sexual misconduct, and theft—[are all purified by it].
Even for those who have committed the extreme sins of foeticide and the like, there is atonement in the realm of Yama.
(9.1) He by whom service was rendered to the virtuous has likewise attained their favor;
he by whom the word of blessing was received through the total surrender of himself to the holy ones. (9.2)
The burning away of all those various sins occurs swiftly;
O virtuous one, there is no atonement whatsoever equal to service to the holy, nor any other.
For one who is immersed in service to the saints, O Lakṣmī, the world of Yama does not exist.
Even worms, moths, and the like;
even outcastes, executioners, courtesans, and thieves—have all been uplifted by service to the virtuous.
So too have beasts, birds, trees, creepers, and shrubs. (94–95)
Through the practice of the holy ones (*sādhuyoga*), they attained supreme bliss in the lotus [of the heart].
The great path of devotion to Kṛṣṇa proceeds only through the holy ones;
from the holy ones, it subsequently spreads throughout all the worlds.
People cross over saṃsāra and reach its further shore;
those who are devoted to the service of the virtuous surely go to my world,
having enjoyed infinite heavens as well as the stations of the lords.
And they rejoice in Vaikuṇṭha, in Goloka, and in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāman).
Thus instructed by me, O serpent, that Virālaka,
the king of devotees, went to his own home, joyful and wealthy, by my command.
He sent me there, and at the end of the year he met his death.
Having performed supreme service to the saintly, he went to my imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, both the listener and the speaker who possess this devotion shall go to that abode.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Previous Birth of the Vaiśya named Virāla, His Attainment of Śrī Hari in the Field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, the Destruction of His Royal Consumption, and His Liberation," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 182: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age).
Chapter 182.
[The Author: Chapter 183.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇīśrī, listen to this story and likewise another.
In ancient times, there was a king named Pṛthvīdhara in Karṇapura.
While governing a fragmented kingdom, he protected his subjects according to dharma. Every morning, more than a hundred mendicants would regularly gather in his courtyard. (1–2)
Indeed, helpless young boys and girls,
as well as helpless widows, find satisfaction by eating at this food-distribution hall (*anna-satra*) through the acquisition of your food.
Then King Pṛthvīdhara himself went to the temple of Viṣṇu.
He constantly performs the worship of the form of Nārāyaṇa with one thousand Tulasī leaves, saying "Salutation to Viṣṇu," while meditating upon,
remembering me, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person.
Having offered incense, a lamp, food offerings, water, and betel leaf,

as well as performing the waving of lights (nīrājana), hymns of praise, and circumambulation, one should prostrate like a staff. Then, one should give a gift of one hundred silver coins and likewise a hundred garments.
He always gives at least one cow as a gift, and thereafter,
having offered a handful of flowers to Śrī Hari, he returns to his own home.
Thus he worships me constantly, subsisting only on food offered to me.
He always lived as a devotee, abstaining from violence and sexual misconduct.
Indeed, devotion belongs to him whose merit was performed in a previous birth;
even amidst the splendor of sovereignty, his mind remains fixed on dharma.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, Pṛthvīdhara, having performed his auspicious daily rites, always goes to the court of justice and there delivers the verdict. Then, every evening, he invariably listens to my discourse.
From the assembly of the virtuous gathered for the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
the saintly, perfected, and steadfast ones dispel his many doubts.
Furthermore, the king partakes of the drinking of the water from the feet of the virtuous.
At the conclusion of the discourse, he performs a kīrtana accompanied by musical instruments. (13) Thousands of people—women and men alike—perform the kīrtana:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Hare! (14)
"Hare Viṣṇo! Hare Jiṣṇo! O Anādi-Kṛṣṇa! Hare!
Hare!"—in this manner they performed worship to You with cymbals and other instruments.
Then the virtuous departed for their monasteries, and after them, the king [departed].
Having performed the evening worship of the deity and obtained excellent food,
he then becomes absorbed in meditation while rotating my rosary,
repeatedly chanting "Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa."
Thinking, "He is indeed sleeping," the king also practiced virtuous conduct.
His queen, named Madhuvindā, was a devoted Vaiṣṇavī;
endowed with wifely fidelity, she was as chaste, O Brāhmaṇas, as the virtuous Satī. (18)
She worships me, the Supreme Self, perceiving the world to be terrible, a bondage rich in the defects of suffering, permeated by latent impressions, and subject to decay;
whereas she regards the eternal Supreme Self as liberation and as her very own soul. (3.182.20)
She considers people who grant liberation as virtuous and serves them;
possessing a peaceful character like that of a king, this daughter of the king worships me, Janārdana. O Lakṣmī, as is the king, so shall the subjects become endowed with virtue.
His sons and others also took refuge in me, the Lord of Śrī.
Likewise, all subjects of every caste worshipped me;
they offered gifts, performed recitations, and rendered service. (22–23)
Even when performing tasks such as sweeping for virtuous people,
the Blessed Lord remains ever-pleased with Vaiṣṇavas who conduct themselves in this manner; likewise, the rain-god Parjanya pours down rain.
The riches rejoiced as if they were sentient beings endowed with consciousness;
the cows rained down all desires, the trees bestowed fruits, the crops yielded grains, and the earth itself provided its juices. (25–26)
For that devotee of mine, there were no enemies, nor did calamities arise; moreover, that king became rich in happiness. In due time, his first son was born blind from birth.
The birth celebrations were performed by him at the proper time;
however, that son did not open his eyes at all and was known to be blind from birth.
Indeed, the king performed the rites for Viṣṇu during a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice.
For the purpose of opening his eyes, he performed worship of the sun and the moon,
and offered an unbroken lamp of ghee in the temple of the deity for one year; yet, O King, his blindness persisted even after that time had passed.
Suddenly abandoning all hope, he set his mind upon asceticism alone.
(3.1) Leaving the royal palace, he took a seat in the shade beneath a grove of trees in a garden and sat down to practice penance. (3.2)
Chanting the name of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he turns his rosary;
the king subsisted on fruit alone, eating but once a day in solitude.
Holding a Śālagrāma stone before him, he worships me and remembers me as well.
Even though he was clothed only in bark garments and sat upon a deer skin,
devoid of all enjoyments, yet longing for his son and daughter-in-law,
he attended upon me day and night there in that hermitage, dwelling in a tree-hut.
The king endures the rain, the cold, and the heat, and he serves me; with devotion, he performs worship of my Śālagrāma stone. He observes the three daily ablutions and bows down to the sun.

Pañcakeśī, who performed worship to the ancestors, remained thus for a year. When a year had passed, the king, having meditated upon me repeatedly during the night, praised me: "O Kṛṣṇa, your name is Hari; indeed, it removes all suffering. (37–38)
O Mādhava, why do You not remove the suffering of me, Your devotee?
You are entirely capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise.
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever merit exists is indeed Your gracious favor.

O Kṛṣṇa, whatever evil there is, it is indeed your hostility and indifference [toward me]. (3.182.40) If you display such indifference even toward a devotee, what then is the fate of that devotee who has been abandoned by his protector? (41)
"O Mādhava, grant protection to my son by bestowing your sight;
having shaken off his sin, restore his vision.
Having heard this prayer, I quickly prostrated myself like a staff.
Having observed my son’s asceticism, I came here for the sake of his eyes.
Wearing matted hair, carrying a staff, virtuous, smeared with ashes, and clad in a deer-skin,
I appeared within that circle of trees, holding a water-pot in my hand.
Uttering "Hare Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu" in the presence of the virtuous, he departed, saying:
"Victory to the yogin, the lord of the earth, who is in the guise of an ascetic!
Having thus spoken these words, [he offered] the auspicious water from his water-pot.
The king, having attained the highest amazement, gave [this] to him:
"From where has this sudden guest come, appearing in the guise of a holy man? Or could he be that divine Acyuta who fulfills the heart's desire? || 46-47 ||
"A guest must indeed be honored, especially one who is virtuous.
Having reflected thus, the king rose and fell at his feet;
he offered him a seat, as well as the *arghya* and the *madhuparka*.
He performed worship with flowers, perfumes, fruits, and other offerings.
Then, having offered his salutations, he inquired about the reason for his arrival:
"I am blessed; I have achieved my purpose through the sight of a holy person. (3.182.50)
The supreme water in the form of a sacred ford has been obtained from his water-pot;
its mere sight is purifying and makes all the senses holy.
Indeed, the touch of that which is the station of the virtuous has been attained as the destroyer of sin.
"By the power of my good fortune, I shall today obtain service and grace;
through compassion, divine favor, and the accumulation of merit.
Having spoken thus, he stood before him in silence with palms joined in reverence.
"I am one whose nature is virtuous; speak, may you be endowed with prosperity! Is all well with you, O King? Or tell me, what is the reason for your asceticism?
The King said: "By the grace of the virtuous, all is well with me."
"I possess sons, I possess wealth, and I am devoted to the virtuous.
Nevertheless, my son remains in a state of misfortune and does not even look upon me.
O holy one, he is as if born blind; tell me, what could be the cause?"
"O Lord, for the sake of obtaining sight for him, I am performing penance in the month of Mādhava;
it consists of worship, and I have no other desire.
For that man whose son is blind, his kingdom indeed becomes blind. || 57 ||
Blindness in the house of one who is not blind, and indeed blindness within the lineage, is a source of great suffering. (58) How may this blindness be driven far away? You know; show me the way!
By meeting with you, a holy man, I shall have fulfilled my purpose in this matter. (59)
The speech of the virtuous is divine, always true in meaning and bestowing success;
the heart of the virtuous is indeed gentle and removes all suffering.
The sight of the virtuous is meritorious, and likewise, their service grants liberation.
"The fulfillment of all hopes for the virtuous has been accomplished.
Having said this, he ceased speaking; and then, O Lakṣmī, I said:
"Listen, O King, in a previous birth your son was an ascetic."

Just as I was dressed in the garb of an ascetic, so too did that brahmin Durvoḍhaka become an ascetic; being poor and desiring a kingdom, he performed penance at the Śuklaka tīrtha on the bank of the Revā. (63)
Where many men seeking sacred fords (tīrtha) come and go,
there at that sacred ford men and women bathe and depart from its side;
Durvōdhaka, beholding this, indeed established himself in that place of austerity.
O Lakṣmī, the sense organ is powerful, and the mind is likewise powerful;
when an object comes before it, whether approaching or departing, the mind becomes fickle.
O Rame, the ascetic must always effect its restraint.
If the senses and the mind are not restrained, austerity is fruitless.
When will the turbulent mind not lead one onto a wrong path?
Furthermore, there is never any certainty or conviction regarding such a mind. (67–68)
Once, you yourself, as king, accompanied by your family and abundant with whatever provisions were required,
went with a limited retinue toward the Revā river to bathe at Śuklatīrtha on a festival day.
At that place where this virtuous ascetic, the brahmin, was performing his penance,
you then took up residence in a mango grove a short distance away.
Having recognized him as a virtuous ascetic with matted hair, you stood before him.

Together with her co-wife, she offered salutations and likewise performed worship; the queen, filled with devotion, presented fruits and other offerings. Having washed the feet of the saint, your beloved wife drank the water.

Upon seeing her, who was endowed with form, youth, beauty, nourishment, and erotic charm, delusion arose in this ascetic Brahmin; and he cast his two eyes upon her secretly, filled with desire. (73–74)
Then that brahmin,
filled with longing and intent upon the kingdom, performed austerities with desire for a queen who was a disciple, for a holy female attendant at a sacred ford, and likewise for the king’s mother.
And with his senses and mind uncontrolled, he then committed an evil act of vision.
Indeed, those who are lustful become blind from birth;
those who are infatuated with another’s wife employ a wicked gaze. (76–77)
Thus, at that time, the sin of delusion indeed arose for this brahmin ascetic who was infatuated by the beauty of her form.
Therefore, in order to prevent the arising of such delusion, beautiful women [should always be avoided]. (78)
They do not even show their faces for the sake of protecting their virtue;
noble women always maintain the covering of modesty over their mouths, concealing them for the protection of their chastity and other virtues. (3.182.80)
Because vision causes delusion, they do not even grant the sight [of themselves].
Covered by a veil, they remain unseen by the sun.
Then, O King, that ascetic passed away in the course of time.
For this son of yours was born from her, being conceived in her womb while she was deluded.
That high-souled one obtained this kingdom as the fruit of his asceticism,
and he has indeed reaped the fruit of his evil gaze known as this birth.

O you who are devoted through austerity, I, the Lord who resides in Śālagrāma, have arrived, being well-pleased by your worship and other offerings. I am that very Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, the granter of your desires.
"Speak, O King; I shall give you here whatever is pleasing to your mind.
I have come here for the sake of my devotees; if you desire anything, I shall grant it to you.
Thus addressed, that royal sage named Pṛthvīdhara then [replied]. (85–86)
He requested the sight of his son, as well as devotion at my feet, and finally, the imperishable abode and a lineage consisting solely of devotees.
Having heard this, I granted him [his wish], saying, "So be it; it shall happen exactly thus."
Having given water from his water-pot and then vanished from that spot,
the king, with a tranquil mind, completed his penance and departed for his own home situated in the village, clad in bark garments.
Honored by the subjects and recognized as a worthy recipient of boons, having attained his heart’s desire, he was further gladdened by shouts of victory; then,
accompanied by excellent musical instruments, he proceeded to his own palace.
Instruments were sounded on all sides, and the queen indeed attained a state of clarity.
The king, having gone toward his son, quickly gave the water granted by me into his son's eyes; by the touch of that water, the eye became possessed of sight.
Then, through the touch of the water, his right hand became auspicious and endowed with sight;
a great festival took place, and the fruit of their asceticism was fully realized.
Then a young son was born, who indeed possessed the memory of his past lives at all times.
Consequently, he always remembered his own fruit of having possessed evil eyes;
thus, he became a great devotee of the Lord, endowed with righteousness, a king named Citradhvaja, devoted to the virtuous and full of majesty. (94–95)
O Lakṣmī, he always honors me; he governs with justice the kingdom entrusted to him by his father and indeed delights his subjects.
Even as his father passed away in a celestial chariot, at that time I too [was present].
He indeed caused him to attain his own abode, the imperishable state of Viṣṇu.
Thus, by Viṣṇu, the fulfillment of the desire of my devotee—who had been strengthened by penance—was accomplished through the granting of the eyes of a son. (97–98)
O Lakṣmī, being pleased and becoming subject to devotion on this earth, I entirely destroy both the external and internal blindness of my devotees;
I bestow the divine light of the Self and the treasure-trove of knowledge.
By which, having crossed over the darkness of illusion, they proceed to the supreme state.
(3.182.10) From reciting, hearing, remembering, and worshipping me, there shall arise enjoyment and liberation, as well as prosperity, happiness, and final release. (101)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Previous Life of King Pṛthvīdhara and His Son Born Blind, and How the Lord Granted Him Sight," in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 183: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) [Chapter 183]
