Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, on the bank of the river Śatrūñjayā.

There was a Śūdra named Sāgara, a devotee who served as a forest guardian. (1) Devoted to the kingdom of Pālikā, he—along with his sons, his retinue, and his weapons—performed the protection of the forest throughout the expanse of Pālikā. (2)
Once, in the forest regions, King Pālikātānaja went out for the sake of hunting, accompanied by only a few servants.
Having entered that forest, the king [reached] that very ocean.
He led his servant along with him there to act as a guide for the deer and other animals.
Even though he was a Śūdra, this man was a devotee of Hari and would never commit violence;
indeed, out of fear of the sin of killing, a non-violent person avoids harming even a king.
"Indeed, he led [the king] toward a desolate region devoid of game;
'Here the deer come, go,
and even dwell,' so saying, he led the king, the lord of the earth, known as Vanapāla."
Where there was water, delightful forests, and beautiful regions;
where here and there were settlements of people— he led him to that region,
wandering from forest to forest even within the great wilderness until evening.
Pointing out here a deer and there a deer, he led the king astray while chanting the name of Śrī Puruṣottama;
meanwhile, within his heart, he prayed to me: "O Blessed One, please forgive me."
"O Lord, I do not wish to commit any offense against the king arising from hunting here;
nor do I wish to kill the forest-dwelling deer myself at any time, nor to cause others to commit such violence on my behalf."
Therefore, O King, I am being led by Udvāṭa to a place where deer are not found, so that no violence may befall me.
O Mādhava, protect me in such a way that the sin of killing does not occur.
"O Lord, may no wild animal on this path ever encounter the King. O Inner Controller, O Sovereign, ordain all things accordingly as you have willed.
Thus did that righteous and pure Śūdra devotee pray to me. (13–14)
There, a deer-skin-clad hunter goes ahead of that king, pulling him along here and there while describing [the scene] in many ways; O King, this indeed would be a sword.
Here there might be a painted deer, and here a horned antelope (sṛmara).
"Could it be a gavaya, or a hare, or a rhinoceros here? Or perhaps a hyena, a black deer, or a wild boar here?
Thus, binding himself with hope, he goes on and on, full of eager anticipation. (16–17)
He offers water and fruits to the king and even serves him;
nevertheless, that king finds no satisfaction except for deer.
Thus, evening fell within the forest.
When the deer was not captured, the king also became hopeless at that time. (19) When the sun had set, they all rested within the forest;
hungry and despondent, they stayed beneath a banyan tree on the shore of a lake. (20)
Then, by the turn of fate, another forest-dweller who had been wandering through his own forest returned toward his home;
there, beneath a banyan tree, he heard the voices of men. (21)
Although he had departed by way of the side, he returned to take refuge under the banyan tree.
There he saw the king accompanied by a limited number of attendants; he bowed to them with devotion, stood before them, and questioned the monarch.
"O King, how can there be rest for the group of servants here tonight? If there is work to be done, I shall remain at your command to serve you.
I am your servant, knowledgeable of forest paths, familiar with wild creatures, and accustomed to dwelling in the woods. (24)
"In the forest I know everything and I carry out the king's command.
Having heard this account and that his daily routine was fruitless,
the king then declared all his wandering for the sake of false hunting to be so indeed.
Then, having heard this, another forest-dweller named Dakṣagarva said to the king:
"O King, this forest is never inhabited by such deer as those;
by whom has this path been shown, which yields nothing but distress? (27)
"In this forest there are no deer, for wood-gatherers roam here.
But there is another forest for deer on the southern bank of the river;
there, success in hunting is always achieved. (28–29)
"O King, you have indeed been deluded by someone; you are proceeding here in vain.
This exertion of yours in this forest is nothing but hardship.
Thus addressed, the king then realized he had been deceived.
Indeed, Sāgara, though a Śūdra, acted in vain by wandering about [to seek his son].
Alas! Men are indeed betrayers of trust; having dragged a king onto a wrong path, they lead him toward death.
One should never place trust in strangers, whether in the forest, at home, or on the battlefield; kings may encounter great hardship by placing their confidence in those unknown.
We, seeking deer, have been deceived here by the ocean.
"We have been led far astray and rendered fruitless in this forest abounding in wild beasts.
This man, indeed, is a fit object for punishment; he exists under a deceptive guise.
He must be abandoned through the infliction of punishment, and instruction must be given here by me. || 34-35 ||
Having reflected thus, the king then spoke to the forest-dweller named Dakṣagarva: "Stay here, or go to your home;
come back here tomorrow morning with me for the sake of hunting in the forest."
"I shall indeed grant you the highest desired reward as a prize for success in hunting; go or stay, it is not otherwise.
Having thus shown his necessity, Dakṣagava paid his respects and departed.
He went to his own home at night and did not return to that place in the morning.
The king, having become enraged, questioned the ocean at the very break of dawn:
"Tell me, how is it that you led me here into this forest?"
"Since there was no hunting at all, your wandering in the forest was in vain.
You have caused me this distress; therefore, you must be punished in every way.
Indeed, you shall receive only your monthly salary from my treasury."
"Since I have indeed been deceived here by you, my servant,
therefore I shall now inflict punishment upon you, who acted with deceitful intent.
Having spoken thus, the king quickly addressed his other servants with these words.
"Let them crush the forearms and feet of this wicked man here with stones!
Let them throw this evil man down beneath the banyan tree!
Having been addressed thus, those other servants and soldiers became filled with rage.
Seizing those harsh stones, the fierce ones pulverized them;
having broken both his ankles at the foot of that banyan tree,
they all, along with the king, departed from that place after casting him down.
Then, for the sake of hunting, wicked men filled with pride entered another forest.
There, by chance, this Sāgara encountered me;
remembering me, Puruṣottama, he wept many bitter tears.
O Blessed One, why do you not provide protection for your devotees here?
O Kṛṣṇa, why do you not likewise bring about the destruction of the sinners?
For one knows that great sin lies in violence; [yet you act] by protecting the deer.
Indeed, it was I, the compassionate one, who set the king’s gate open.
O ocean of mercy, I am your devotee; how can I lead a cruel king—who is full of compassion for the young fawns—to slaughter the deer? (3.183.50)

"Alas, O Kṛṣṇa! Today I have obtained the fruit of non-violence, which is indeed violence itself; for even you must endure what has been done to one who has taken refuge in you. Yet this is a supreme wonder: that you do not protect your devotee. (51)
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Nārāyaṇa, O Lord!
O beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Victorious One, grant me protection!
If You do not come quickly here to this dense banyan tree in the forest, [I shall perish]. (52–53)
At that time, perhaps some person will say to me: "Death shall surely come to me here this very day;
because of the hardship of traveling on foot, no one will give me water.
To save my life I shall go forth, yet my destination will be miserable.
Even my family members will not know of my death here.
O Hara, O Nātha, O Hare-Kṛṣṇa, O Bāla-Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Hare!
O Hare, son of Śrī Kambharā, Lord of Rādhā, Lord of Ramā! ||55-56||
Come quickly, O Lord of Kamalā, O Lord of Lakṣmī, O Master!
O Lord of Padmāvatī, O Lord of Prajñā, O Lord of Śrīmāṇikī!
O Lord of Muktā, O Lord of Brahman, O Lord of Creation, O Lord of the World!
O Lord of devotees, O Lord of the wretched, O Lord of those dear to Brahmā, O Hari!
Come quickly, O Blessed One, assuming a body for the sake of protecting your devotees.
O Lord of Saurāṣṭra, O glorious Lord of the cowherd boys! 58–59.
"How indeed, O Blessed One, shall I endure this agony born from the crushing of my ankle joints? Here my life-breaths are surely fainting away.
Having spoken thus, he prostrated before me and fell into a state of unconsciousness.
"O Lakṣmī, as long as the ocean remains devoted to me, so long shall I quickly go to his side, assuming the form of a forest-dweller;
taking leaves of the *sandhinīvallī* plant, I shall bring its excellent juice. (61-62)
Having extracted [the fragments] with his fingers, he placed them back into the broken regions;
immediately the two forearms were joined together,
and the two bones became as they were before— sound and free from disease.
I touched him again and again, for he was both powerful and rich with blood.
I indeed prevented my devotee from fainting;
I raised him up and removed that entire suffering from him completely.
He was fed and then given excellent water to drink;
he was affectionately embraced with a loving gaze and conducted to his own home.
There, he worshipped me—who appeared in the form of a forest-dweller—with great devotion.
Having provided a delightful seat in his house, he performed service for me.
His wife, Hīrukā, as well as his sons and daughters,
O Lakṣmī, also rendered me manifold service with meals and other offerings at midday.
"I have eaten, I have drunk water, and likewise I have accepted service in the form of massaging my feet, rubbing my limbs, and so forth. Then this devotee Sāgara questioned me regarding himself.
"O Lord Hare, ocean of mercy, how has this misery come upon me?
By what sin indeed has this breaking of my feet occurred?
I have not harmed any living beings, nor have I consumed meat, wine, or similar things. (3.183.70–71)
O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, even when touched, falsehood is never committed;
nor is theft or adultery ever practiced at any time. This deception of the king was, however, for the sake of protecting living beings.
"O Lord, I have done nothing; no sin could have been committed by me here.
How did I strike your feet? How did I cause you such suffering?
O Master, tell me the truth, or explain what kind of karma it must be."
"In this birth, I have neither committed nor even remember [any such act].
If it were done by one acting in ignorance, tell me that which dispels my doubt.
Then, O Kamalā, I informed him of what had been done in a previous life.
Indeed, no such cruel deed was committed by him in this life.
Therefore, I said: "Listen, O Sāgara, to what was done in the past.
You were indeed an elephant-keeper, the protector of the king's elephant. (76–77)
"You were indeed the elephant-keeper for this king's father, Dharmapāla;
you were a Śūdra with a family living here.
Once, while performing the service of guarding the elephants,"

When the elephant displayed its rut, he then made many efforts to bring that young, intoxicated elephant under control; indeed, he placed *gokṣura* and other substances, as well as iron [spikes], upon the soles of the elephant's feet. (3.183.80)
Likewise, having pierced the feet of the elephants with iron bolts, iron chains, and the like,
and with fierce bhalla-arrows, long bamboos, and iron-tipped fruits,
they rendered them powerless.
He completely blocked his movement there, which was already devoid of any path;
he struck down the foolish demon who was attacking his feet excessively,
and at that moment, the bone of even one of the elephant's legs was shattered.
Furthermore, when that elephant desired to rise up, you,
being merciless, struck it again on its forefeet with iron clubs;
the bone of its second foot was shattered on the side.
Thus, because you broke his two leg-bones out of cruelty, you were then cursed by the elephant: "You shall be my protector and yet my executioner;
indeed, with my own trunk, your foot shall be broken."
In due time you have met your end, O Sāgara;
and today the elephant has likewise met his end. This is that very prince, and this is that elephant known as Vanapāla whose feet were formerly broken.
"Today you are a king, and today you are a forest-guardian.
Your feet were broken by him as the fruit of what was previously broken [by you].
Do not grieve; you are my devotee, and indeed you have been protected by me today. (88–89)
Action performed in the past does not abandon any embodied being;
O devotee, the action you have performed has been obtained by you in the form of its fruit. However, through my devotion and non-violence, protection has been granted to you.
"Even a slight offense against the king has arisen here as the cause [of this].
You should not grieve over the breaking of your foot in the forest.
Worship me, the Supreme Self; behold my divine form."
"I am Nārāyaṇa himself, come here in my four-armed form.
Go this very day to the king who has returned home in the evening;
tell him the entire account, which will provide protection and bestow happiness."
"Having heard this, that king will surely honor me;
through your yoga, I shall indeed grant liberation to the king.
Do not fear, O lord of devotees; I shall be with you."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished there before the lotus-born Brahmā;
the devotee, remembering Hari, went to the king’s palace during the night and related the entire auspicious account to the king.
Upon hearing this, the king was struck with wonder and repeatedly begged for forgiveness.
Having taken refuge in me, the protector of devotees, he offered praise again and again, recognizing his own previous birth as an elephant. (97–98)
Having attained supreme wonder and realizing that the body is transitory,
the king became a devotee and took refuge in me along with his family.
His father and his kinsmen also thereafter constantly worshipped me.
Having ruled their kingdoms and performed service to the virtuous, they practiced devotion at every opportunity;
thus they attained Me, the Supreme Lord, the abode of Śrī, the imperishable and true state.
O Lakṣmī, by reading and hearing this, one gains both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Śūdra named Sāgara, whose feet were broken, having his feet made free from pain by the Blessed Lord, along with the account of his previous birth," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the lineage of the Dvāpara age. Chapter 184: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 184.
[The Author: Chapter 185.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the purifying [account] of Vṛkṇadeva.
I shall relate to you, my devotee, this ancient story that destroys all sins.
(1) In the city of Dhruvālaya, there lived a man of the Śūdra caste who was exceedingly righteous;
he was named Vṛkṇadeva and served as a messenger. (2)
Of the atheistic king named Bhāvaśūra,
Vṛkṇadeva was a devotee of mine, while Bhāvaśūra himself was an atheist.
Between these two constant friends, a dispute constantly arose.
Vṛkṇadeva always says, "O King, worship the Lord Hari.
Bhāvaśūra replies, "Worship both fortune and karma.
When a great festival arrived, Vṛkṇadeva repeatedly urged the king toward his religious vow.
He says, "Perform acts of charity, worship, and religious duties";
yet the king considers all such charity and worship to be false. He believes there is neither heaven nor merit, nor indeed any such thing as dharma.
Everything arises from its own nature; as is the field, so is the growth.
Just as a son begotten by a king upon any woman whatsoever is born as a king, such is the condition that conforms to the lineage. (7–8)
One born from royal seed in a poor woman is born wretched;
for one's own nature, innate action, and destiny prevail everywhere.
A kingdom does not come to one who is devoid of fortune.

Poverty never at all approaches one who possesses royal fortune. (3.184.10) Just as a ray of the sun, having entered water, would become cool, so cold water would attain heat through contact with a great fire. (11)
Everything produced from the earth indeed attains the state of being earth upon the earth;
likewise, by the power of the mine and by nature, the heavy becomes light according to its intended purpose. Thus, there is no weightiness in devotion toward that [result].
Either there is the weight of destiny, or there is the weight of action.
Action born of nature indeed proceeds like one's inherent disposition:
a biped moves by means of two [feet], while a quadruped moves by means of four.
Śatapāda moves with a hundred [feet], and his formation is likewise;
the elephant eats with two faces, and the tree with a thousand roots. Kārtika has six faces, and Brahmā likewise has four.
Just as the ocean is the appointed portion for the submarine fire (Vāḍava), so too is it for him.
Action performed at the proper place and time arises in the form of fortune;
through that, one may obtain a kingdom, happiness, heaven, and the ancestral lineage.
"Understand this, Vṛkṇadeva: devotion has no causal role therein.
In this manner, the king constantly rebuked Vṛkṇadeva.
Then, after some time had passed in this way, once upon a time, the king—
He asked Vṛkṇadeva: "Tell me, how have you been cut down by me?
If devotion is indeed the cause of one's own well-being, then why, by the power of devotion, do you not avoid being cut down? (3.184.20)
Then Vṛkṇadeva spoke to King Bhāvaśūra:
"This state of being maimed has arisen from past action; indeed, it can be wiped away through devotion.
O King, Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu is truly the fulfiller of the desires of his devotees. (21)
If a devotee desires sovereignty, the Lord Hari surely grants it.
If a devotee desires health, Nārāyaṇa surely grants it.
Whatever desires one may long for, Hari surely fulfills them all. (22–23)
For one who has desires, the Supreme Lord is the fulfiller of those desires;
for one who is free from desire, the Supreme Lord is the bestower of great bliss.
Indeed, everything truly exists [for him], and Mādhava is pleased by devotion.
When Hari is fully satisfied, he gives everything; of this there is no doubt.
Then Bhāvaśūra said: "You speak everything falsely.
Mutilation does not depart, nor does health become established in one's lap. (25–26)
I have no confidence in devotion as I do in ritual action;
nevertheless, O Goddess who art uncut, I shall indeed make some wager here.
I am the King, uncut, while you proceed as my servant, cut.
But this is determined by karma; it does not change.
(28) If the power of devotion were the cause for such a reversal, then let there be an exchange here between us two regarding the state of being uncut or cut. (29)
"Then, recognizing the power of devotion, I shall perform worship of Hari;
otherwise, I will by no means consider your words to be true.
Having heard these words of the king, even though I was cut down, I [regarded] my Lord...
Then, with supreme devotion, he remembered [the Lord] in the presence of the king.
As the king had declared in the sight of all the people,
"May it be so," he spoke thus again and again, O Soul of All.
O Lakṣmī, having come under the sway of Vṛkṇadeva through his very devotion and affection, I remained hidden right there in that state of being cut; then,
having pulled [the body] from Vṛkṇadeva, I cast it into the two hands of the king.
Then the king was quickly cut at the forearms; likewise, his elbows became bent and his veins were pulled taut. His two hands instantly became like dry wood and appeared as if stretched out.
While everyone there was watching,

the two hands of King Vṛkṇadeva, which had previously been bent down due to their amputation, suddenly became free from their bindings and were restored to their functional state, capable of performing their respective tasks. ||36||
Deeply red, abundant, endowed with nourishment, and performing their functions as desired—
having seen such a great marvel, the people laughed; the king, however, considered it the fruit of excessive speech arising from atheism.
He considered devotion to be truly the transformer of karmas;
he recognized the supreme power of devotion and abandoned atheism.
Thus, O Rame, his birth-born disease has indeed been cut away by me.
Then, for the sake of honoring devotion, those two were exchanged. (3.184.40) Thereupon, the king became devoted, having abandoned pride in his actions;
likewise, by the power of being cut down [of his pride], he renounced pride in his own nature. (41)
Then the queen named Śīladharman lamented; indeed, her sons, daughters, servants, and subjects also grieved excessively.
Vṛkṇadeva too, seeing the king mangled, lamented.
He prayed to the Supreme Soul for the removal of the king's disease.
Then the king also received from Vṛkṇadeva this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā."
Then he recited his rosary one hundred and eight times;
at that very moment, I, the Lord who protects my devotees, appeared in an instant,
bearing the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the Vaijayantī garland.
Accompanied by Śrī Lakṣmī, the king quickly beheld me, divine, within the splendor of Brahmā in the sky; Vṛkṇadeva also beheld me,
and then all the subjects gazed upon me, the Lord.
They uttered cries of victory, bowed down, and praised the Imperishable One;
they considered themselves blessed and fortunate that they had beheld the Supreme Self.
Indeed, through the yoga of single-minded devotion, many attained the vision of Him.
Having caused my divine and auspicious form to vanish and having assumed a beautiful body,
I went into the presence of the king and touched him; at that moment,
the king's atheism was instantly destroyed, and he became devoted to righteousness.
As was the devotee, so was the king; both became righteous.
The king, his subjects, and all others attained supreme joy. Having obtained the sight of me, they celebrated with blissful festivities.
And all of them worshipped me, Nārāyaṇa, with great reverence.
Then the servant Vṛkṇadeva questioned me, the Lord:
"How did my state of being cut come about, and how was it gone? Tell me this."
Then, O Kamala, I related to my devotees the entire account of my previous birth— that very sin which brings about mutilation.
Formerly, you were a monkey-ascetic who protected monkeys.
Having made the monkeys play and having gathered people to his dwelling,
he maintained his livelihood by means of food, clothing, and other goods obtained from the villagers.
There were two bears, five mongooses, and seven monkeys.
At that time, two snakes and eight scorpions came under your control;
through their various playful antics, you maintained your livelihood as a family man.
All those members of your household were trainers of those respective creatures.
And having made those creatures play in the sky and on the ground,
they earned their livelihood and maintained their subsistence;
while they were living in this manner, established at the edge of the village.
While everyone was asleep at night, a wolf arrived from the forest. As soon as the monkey perceived its scent, he quickly leapt away out of fear; however, he fell upon your chest.
Then the two hands of that monkey fell upon your forehead and eyes;
at that moment, your forehead was torn by his claws.
Although you were suddenly asleep, you perceived a supreme fear, like a common beast.
Seeing that monkey of his own, you struck him with an iron staff;
both of his forefeet were broken, and at that moment Bhalluka also [was struck].
He let out a cry of fear, and the other animals also cried out.
Then, having risen and encountered fear, you saw a terrifying forest-dweller;
a cruel wolf, a devourer of monkeys, was indeed standing not far away.
Having let out a great cry, you [struck] that wolf with a sharp spear.
Having rushed forward, you then tore open his heart;
he fell down and died, yet you, O wolf, remained fearless.
At that time, the bears and other creatures also became free from fear.
At that time, while the monkey was still held in his own bonds, you suddenly and without reflection broke his two legs out of anger;
thus the monkey who had taken refuge with you met with great suffering there. (67–68)
Even one who had sought refuge with him, as well as those who relied on him for their livelihood,
and even those he had protected like sons, were struck with iron clubs by him;
the hands of that man who uttered harsh insults were broken.
They performed the ritual of massaging his feet with pieces of cloth, medicinal herbs, and other substances.
At the end of a month, both his forefeet became free from pain;
however, they remained permanently bent, mangled in form, and crooked. (3.184.70–71)
The fruit of that [action] has been obtained by you in this very birth as a state of being maimed;
it was only from that time until now that this suffering of yours arose.
Nevertheless, you [participated] in the play of the monkey and the bear.
You sang the verses originating in a former age concerning Jāmbavān and Hanumān,
which describe the form of the battle and include the lifting of Mount Droṇa;
they indeed consist of accounts of my own connection and are filled with the spirit of devotion.
By the merit of that recitation, even though you were maimed, you have become endowed with great prosperity;
even while under the protection of this king, you are wealthy.
You remain devoted here, and you cause others to maintain steadfast devotion.
"The power of your devotion has indeed arisen, by which I am truly under your control.
I have come for your protection, and your state of being mangled has been prevented.
Listen further: this king Vṛka here has died and been born again."
Thus this king remains together with you, yet he possesses an atheistic disposition;
by his own nature, he has been hostile toward religious duties and the like from the very beginning.
Just as the breaking of a monkey's hand was caused by the action of a wolf.
"And half of that fruit would have belonged to Vṛka himself.
Thus this king attained his mutilation, while your sin passed onto the monarch.
Listen also to how this very Vṛka indeed attained the status of a king. (3.184.80)
In his third previous birth, he was a wrathful Brahmin named Prāṇadhara,
whom people called "Life-Taker" (Prāṇahara) because he caused agitation and suffering during religious rites, rituals, and festivals. (81)
During marriages, proclamations, or acts of giving, he would forcibly seize even more than his share.
Insatiable through excessive speech, by sheer force, and even through strife, he would indeed take away wealth, food, and all kinds of goods by violence. (82–83)
Just as the asceticism of even an ascetic becomes fruitless through anger,
so too the austerity of one who is full of craving and prone to wrath becomes in vain.
Nevertheless, [he attained some merit] through the worship of the gods and other rites, as well as by a mere fraction of his penance.
In that very same way, having died due to his heap of sins, he went to the abode of Yama.
Then Citragupta reported both his auspicious and inauspicious deeds; [Yama said:
"First, what should be enjoyed by you? Speak as you wish, and I shall satisfy you. (85–86)
Having heard these words of King Yama, he became filled with intense anger and said:
"O Yama, I must first experience my own sins;
only then shall I be joined by Yama to experience the sufferings of the realm of Yama. (87)
Having experienced the sufferings of hell, he became a wolf due to the remainder [of his karma].
There, his death occurred at your hand.
Indeed, because of the merits performed by him in the past, his sovereignty lasts but a short time.
One's innate natures, formed by previous births, can never be abandoned by anyone;
moreover, due to the defects of his former nature, he takes pleasure in quarreling.
Nevertheless, O Devavrata, you instruct him every single day.
Through auspicious speech and other means for the sake of devotion, his merit increases.

Indeed, just as fruit from a tree and even ghee from milk are obtained gradually, so too is the fruit of a son obtained gradually from a wife, and purification through sacraments is achieved gradually. (91–92)
Knowledge comes slowly, wisdom comes slowly, and the acquisition of wealth and such comes slowly; for those engaged in practice, proficiency arises gradually through repeated encounters.
In this way, over time, merit also accrues to this king.
Even now, evil and mere mutilation persist to some small degree;
nevertheless, through my yoga of devotion— that is, through the yoga of devotion to me—
all that evil shall go to its destruction by means of my yoga.
And at dawn tomorrow, this king’s state of being maimed will vanish;
his cruelty and atheism as well—everything will be destroyed.
He will become my exclusive devotee, just as you are.
"And at the end, both of us shall indeed dwell in my abode.
These sons of yours, Vānara and the others, whose cruel dispositions were severed, have now been born as humans; they too shall attain liberation."
Having thus granted the boon, I indeed vanished from sight. On the very next morning, as soon as he had arisen, the king’s affliction was gone.
He performed intense devotion unto me, saying, "O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa!"
In due time, King Bhāvaśūra went to my divine abode;
Vṛkṇadeva and the others also attained liberation in their own time.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I constantly provide protection for one who is truly devoted.
Through the yoga of devotion, the welfare of living beings is surely attained.
Through the yoga of devotion, devotion arises, and likewise, union with Me occurs.
(102) There shall also be the destruction of sin; for human beings, the company of the virtuous is a treasure.
"Even a very small act, when performed, bears fruit and grants liberation to both the listener and the speaker.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Vṛkṇatā through the Devotion of the Bhakta named Vṛkṇadeva, the Liberation of King Bhāvaśūra by means of Bhakti-yoga, and his Past-Life Accounts," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (Dvāpara-yuga-santāna)*
Chapter 185 [Author:
Chapter 186 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī,
to the beautiful story of the devotee named Mañjulakeśa, a resident of the village of Halavāda.
O Lakṣmī, in the city of Halavān there was a Brahmin named Mañjulakeśa.
He lives as one exceedingly devoted to me, having exerted himself to the utmost in dharma.
Constantly bathing at the three sessions of the day, he performs the worship and salutation of the three junctions; morning by morning, he worships Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Satī, and the Sun.
Reciting hymns of praise, he constantly prays to Hari:
"O Hari, Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, may devotion to You be mine forever;
may there be the supreme majesty of Your nature and exclusive servitude."
O Kṛṣṇa, likewise, may I have no perception of fault in You or in Your devotees.
(5) May I always have the company of those virtuous ones who are Your exclusive devotees, and may I always behold Your forms as well as those of the virtuous. (6)
May my mind be firm in the Dharma; may I possess resolute determination.
May there never be for me even the slightest contact with liquor, meat, or similar things.
May I never consume forbidden foods, nor onions or garlic.
Let it not be, let it not be; may my restless mind never at any time turn toward theft. May I have no inclination even to revile your devotees, nor may I harbor even the thought of reviling the gods.
May I never have association with the Asuras or the nihilists anywhere;
may there be no passion for sense objects, but may my love always be for You.
O Kṛṣṇa, may my self-offering always be unto You.
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, may my devotion as a faithful wife always abide in You.
(1.1) Thus, together with her family, she constantly prays for Me; indeed, she does not drink even unstrained water unless it has first been offered to Me. (1.2)
He does not eat food, fruits, and the like, even if they are not offered; he does not use clothing, garments, ornaments, and so forth, even if they are not offered;
nor does he use a carriage or even a vehicle if it has not been offered.
Having indeed offered whatever ornaments and articles of enjoyment are there for his own sake, that great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata) partakes of them;
he constantly performs worship unto me, Nārāyaṇa. || 14-15 ||
Then, for the sake of alms, he goes to the city; having obtained food by begging,
he returns home, cooks it, and after offering it to me,
he eats it together with his family, accompanied by *tulasī* leaves.

He recites the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā* and indeed causes the people who have come to the hermitage to hear it. Accompanied by his wife, this god on earth, O Lakṣmī, is joined by his sons and others. (17–18)
Then, that great devotee firmly maintained his religious duty;
yet sometimes his kinsmen would even invite him to a feast for kinsmen.
However, although he was a brāhmaṇa, that brāhmaṇa did not eat at such a feast for kinsmen.
He does not eat food that has been cooked with unstrained water or that has not been properly prepared (asaṃskṛta).
Even in such cases, he never eats food defiled by onions and the like,
nor ever eats food mixed with garlic and similar substances.
For this reason, his kinsmen were performing the ritual of drying [the body] for him;
yet Mañjula, with his beautiful hair, indeed endured everything.
Then, on one occasion, Mañjula went to the house of a relative.
But the relatives said to him, "For your sake, we shall prepare a pure meal;
having cooked it, we will give you food that brings satisfaction—so eat! But first, you must inspire confidence in us regarding the food being prepared. (23–24)
Knowing this, they became filled with rage and gave him liquor during the fine meal;
Mañjulakeśa, having perceived it by its fragrance in the food contained within the vessel,
[found] a small amount mixed with wine, accompanied by sugar and saffron.
He indeed abandoned that food and left the water in that house;
then Mañjula, enraged by the betrayal of his trust, cursed him:
"This man who, having gained my confidence with food, gave me liquor! (26–27)
"Let this man become disfigured, intoxicated, and even insane.
When this was suddenly spoken in the presence of the people,
Mañjula’s son-in-law then became disfigured and insane.
His mind quickly became deranged, and he abandoned all sense of propriety.
He uttered wicked speech and engaged in wicked conduct, reducing her to a state of nakedness.
Punished by a curse, his father-in-law was known by the name Pāśupateśa.
Dejected and deprived of his luster, he caused various kinds of disturbances;
standing in the presence of people, he would urinate while naked.
He would cry out, dance, clap his hands, leap, and even run about.
He reviles, laughs, and sings incoherently;
having obtained vessels and garments, he tears them apart and even rends them.
He utters words that should not be spoken and performs bestial gestures. (32–33)
Thus, indeed, through the fault of the curse, he suddenly fell into a state of mental derangement;
he caused many afflictions, even those that were unforeseen.
Because of these afflictions, his family became greatly distressed in various ways.
Then he entreated that brahmin for the cessation of the curse.
Mañjulakeśa also said: "Let them abandon the eating of forbidden food;
let them perform purification through great penance and vows. (35–36)
Therefore, following the purification, let them perform the auspicious Vaiṣṇava sacrifice known as Brahmakūrca;
let them also give gifts of cows and recite there the Vaiṣṇava mantras of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
"Accept [this] for the sake of performing acts of devotion; from that, you will attain well-being.
(38) Thus addressed, the family members of the Lord of Pāśupata abandoned the eating of forbidden food and performed the *brahmakūrca* rite. (39)
They performed a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and gave gifts of excellent cows;
they then took up the mantra, "Omanādika Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa is my Lord and Master," as well as other mantras.
They became Vaiṣṇavas and chanted "Hare Kṛṣṇa.
Yet, even though all this was done, their mental distraction did not cease.
Then Mañjulakeśa, possessing great devotion, remained without food.
Remaining on his seat for seven days, he performed the recitation of Bālakṛṣṇa's names;
and having gathered together, he earnestly entreated his relatives.
Then, indeed, for the sake of protecting his devotees and for the fulfillment of their desires, I [appeared].
Remaining invisible, he listened to the chanting and other devotional acts.
When the seven days had passed, on the morning of the eighth day, during the worship,
at the conclusion of the waving of lights before the Śālagrāma, I appeared in my own form.
I revealed to them my divine form, attended by Śrī,
situated in the midst of a circle of splendor, resplendent with rows of golden necklaces;
clad in celestial attire, enriched with ornaments, and beautified by an excellent crown.
Holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, bestowing blessings, auspicious,
with a serene countenance and lovely form, he had arrived for the sake of protection.
Upon seeing me in such a state, they fell into a state of delusion.
The mental fluctuations of all of them were fixed upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and all their senses were absorbed in me, the Radiant One.
Just as they had attained meditative absorption (samādhi), so too did they remain absorbed at that time.
They attained from my form that supreme bliss which is difficult to obtain and most excellent.
Through my very happiness, they became happy and were joined with the bliss of Brahman.
Devoid of any memory of anything other than me, they knew only their own true nature.
Just as those [beings] became liberated, established in their own abodes with steady consciousness,
so too, after bestowing momentary happiness and then effecting the dissolution of his splendor,
I quickly became a sage in the form of a holy man, wearing saffron robes.
Holding a garland in his hand and muttering "Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa," causing the Lord's name to be heard, and bringing them outside while making them mindful—
having heard my voice, they all rose from their state of meditative absorption.
They beheld before them me, Hari, in a virtuous form;
filled with love, overwhelmed, and with divine minds, they bowed down.
Chanting "Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," they approached me.
They all prostrated like staffs and fell at my feet.
Having seen that face which was perceived in meditative absorption,
and having seen its brilliance as well as that serenity, those who sought the state of a holy man were moved.
Seeing that he was in the prime of youth, they concluded: "The Lord has arrived in the form of a virtuous man for the sake of protection and indeed to fulfill the desires of his devotees.
They offered him the guest-offering (*arghya*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), an excellent seat, and water.
They gave him fruit, suitable food, and their very hearts;
they offered up all their possessions and fell repeatedly at his feet.
They massaged his feet with their arms and embraced me closely.
Then, having washed their feet with water, they drank the milk, saying:
"We are blessed, for through the power of devotion we have approached the Blessed One.
Blessed is this Mañjulakeśa, the father of the devotee of the Lord of the Daughter."
Blessed is our son-in-law, whose father is devoted to Hari;
blessed is that virtuous and chaste daughter named Kṛṣṇalīlā,
through whom her father attained the grace of the Lord.

Aho! By the power of devotion, the liberation of hundreds of householders and hundreds of kinsmen certainly occurs wherever a devotee of the Lord, a master of the Bhāgavata, dwells, even in a village. (64)
Those villagers attain liberation through the yoga of devotion; of this there is no doubt.
In whatever village a devotee may dwell, the sins of the embodied beings do not remain there at all; they perish through the chanting of the devotee’s praises. (65–66)
Wherever a devotee travels— on the road, in a garden, or near a house—
there obstacles perish and auspiciousness prevails at every step.
In whatever village a devotee resides, within the boundaries of that place, [the same occurs].
The messengers of Yama, overcome by fear, do not enter at all wherever there is the residence of a devotee—
whether on earth, in water, or in the sky. That sacred place (tīrtha) is in every way auspicious and a deliverer for embodied beings burdened by sin.
Wherever there is devotion, there the deities arrive, duly honored.
Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, being liberated, arrive and dwell there.
So too do the supernatural powers (*siddhis*), yogic attainments, and various forms of sovereignty.
Those caravans of devotees dwell there, enriched like wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa).
The Vasus and the attendants (pārṣadas) also dwell in the house of the devotee.
A devotee is, in every respect, a moving, conscious sacred ford (tīrtha).
Victory is there, prosperity is there, aesthetic delights are there, and great supernatural powers are there;
where the devotee shines, there is dharma and supreme liberation.
Indeed, those who commit offenses against the devotee [are purified] by the grace of that devotee.

Since even sinners may become highly meritorious through devotion and compassion, our own sinful fortune has indeed been transformed into a virtuous nature. Today, by the grace of this devotee, our meeting with him is blessed. (74–75)
"Even for those who harbor hatred, liberation is indeed ordained by Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
likewise, liberation is brought about for us haters by Mañjukeśa.
Today, even our sacrifice has become fruitful, and our gifts have become fruitful."
The *brahmakūrca* vow is fruitful, and their birth is fruitful;
our prosperity is fruitful, and even our eyes are fruitful—for in whosever home Hari himself shines forth in the form of a holy man. (77–78)
O Blessed One, forgive our sins born of drinking intoxicants and the like;
O Blessed One, Supreme Person, forgive this offense of your devotees.
A curse was bestowed by Mañjulakeśa upon Pāśupateśaka.
O Lord of Ramā, let this state of madness in the elder be withdrawn.
O virtuous Hari-Kṛṣṇa, quickly show us mercy so that he may regain his composure and his mental confusion may dissolve. (3.185.80–81)
Thus they all made their request, and Mañjukeśa also then repeatedly entreated me for the sake of destroying the mental state of Pāśupateśa.
Having heard the desire of my devotee, I gave water from my *kamaṇḍalu*.
Having quickly caused the Lord of Pāśupata and the brahmin to drink [the medicine],
I then swiftly dispelled their mental derangement, O Kamalā.
Thereupon, he too suddenly became composed, radiant, and pure.
He massaged my feet and then prostrated like a staff;
with a voice of faltering syllables, he said, "Forgive me.
He said to me, "O Kṛṣṇa, ocean of mercy, grant me liberation!"
Having been granted fortitude by me, he worshipped with supreme devotion;
indeed, he offered everything suitable for a guest and pleasing to the heart.
In this way, through the practice of devotion, I removed his mental distraction.
He then bestowed devotion upon them and gave this mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
They received this mantra and chanted it with the utmost reverence.
And the villagers, having heard of the virtuous Camatkāra, arrived there.
O Lakṣmī, thousands of people, including Brāhmaṇas and others, seeing me in that manner and beholding the auspicious Camatkāra in person, took refuge in me. (3.185.90)
O Lakṣmī, all those Vaiṣṇavas, having been consecrated by me with mantras and endowed with my blessings, came to worship me.
Then I bestowed a noble boon upon Majjukeśa.
"Everything shall come to pass exactly as you wish by your word.
Indeed, even this Lord of the Pāśupatas, together with his family,
shall attain supreme liberation through my devotion at the time of his death."
In this village, those devotees who shall worship the Supreme Lord will attain all perfections and reach the ultimate spiritual goal;
here, no obstacles from Yama shall approach, for they will be driven far away.
"And through your majesty, O devotee, devotion shall abide among the worlds.
Having spoken thus, I withdrew my virtuous form and became invisible.
Then those devotees, having attained devotion and having worshipped me, [attained their goal] at the end.
And at that time, O Lakṣmī, those attendants, having become my attendants along with their retinues, went by means of a celestial chariot to my imperishable abode, possessing beautiful forms.
Mañjukeśa also, my devotee, went to my imperishable abode.
Through union with that [devotion], other humans as well have likewise attained the supreme state of Nārāyaṇa and gone to his refuge in Vaikuṇṭha and other realms.
Thus, O Kamalā, I am forever the destroyer of the suffering of my devotee.
"From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, and even from reflecting upon it,
there shall surely be both worldly enjoyment and liberation through the majesty of Śrī Hari.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord bestowed liberation from the curse and supreme emancipation upon the Brahmin Pāśupateśa, who had attained madness due to the curse of the devotee-Brahmin named Mañjulakeśa," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 186 [[Author: → Chapter 187
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this purifying story of the devotee named Bāṇāṅgaṇa, who resided in the village of Vairāḍhya.
Bāṇāṅgaṇa was indeed a Śūdra, a wicked Śūdra who was the lord of those bearing banners;
for he produced liquor from the juices of trees in many ways.
He constantly performed the work that had been handed down through his family lineage.
Having performed both selling and buying, he even sustained his family.
(3) Then once, having joined a caravan, he went to the Raivata pilgrimage site to perform the pilgrimage, as well as to conduct trade and circumambulate it. (4)
Thousands of people go to Revatācala in Kārtika,
as well as to the Vāmana Tīrtha, the Nārāyaṇahrada,
the Revatīkuṇḍaka, Bhaveśvara, and Mṛgīsthala in Saurāṣṭra.
At Dāmodara, at Nārasiṃha, at Svayaṃbhū and Parameṣṭhin;
at Rādhālaya, at the river Svarṇarekhā, at the sacred site of Śrī Hanumān;
at the Gaṅgā, at Ambā, at Dattapāda, and in forest after forest.
In Sītāvana, Rāmavana, and likewise in Pūrvajāmbūvana;
in Boriyā, Droṇikā, and Sthalyā, as well as in Kāṣṭhahārivana;
in Devasarovara, Āmravana, and again in Bhaveśvara.
Even Bāṇāṅgaṇa,
accompanied by carts and ten million men, travels along, carrying liquor for sale while circumambulating Mount Kumuda. (3.186.10)
Those who are devotees of Rudra, or Śākta followers, or those who rely upon Bhairava— being of a *tāmasa* nature—
they drink liquor in many ways during the month of Kārtika and treat it as a sacred pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*). This applies to virtuous women and men, as well as householders and ascetics alike.

Then even the Vaiṣṇavas go on pilgrimage and perform circumambulations. There are sages, holy men, truthful ones, and various auspicious stories concerning Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, as well as those concerning Śaṅkara.

In various places, both twice-born brahmins and learned scholars perform [these rites] for Sarasvatī and Vedhas, for Gāyatrī and Raivata, for Revatī and Vāmana, and also for the virtuous women and the holy ones. (14)
The wise, the learned, the elders, and likewise the yogins,
as well as the yoginīs and the Mothers, sing hymns of praise; and Bāṇa, with divine vision and devotion, offers them drink.
To those beggars who come near his own chariot,
he gives drinks with a meritorious vision and through service;
furthermore, at night as well as in the morning, he listens to kīrtanas.
There were various divine vessels that grant liberation.
There, O Lakṣmī, he heard the speech concerning Viṣṇu within that Vaiṣṇava narrative—speech characterized by righteousness, endowed with devotion, and bringing about welfare. (18–19)
Those who desire to cross over the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) should always perform pilgrimage (tīrtha).
Indeed, pilgrimage on earth is of two kinds, for a pair is found there:
the immobile and the mobile; thus, these two types of pilgrimage exist upon the earth.
Stable objects such as water-tirthas and mountains, as well as temples;
images, forests, groves, trees, sacred shrines (caityas), and grounds;
the birthplaces of the gods, and the lands of the birth and other stages of the virtuous. || 21–22 ||
The dwellings of Brahmins, the dust raised by cows,
and their pastures— indeed, all these are stationary holy places (tīrthas).
Having gone to them, one attains merit through bathing, drinking, immersion, and beholding.
Men of pure disposition who serve the immobile beings cross over [the ocean of existence].
Indeed, for those who serve the immobile beings, sins first burn away;
thereafter, the dawning of merit occurs, and from that, devotion arises. (24–25)
Through devotion, there is satisfaction of the deity; through that satisfaction, there is the vision of the gods and others.
Indeed, a direct divine state arises, and from that, divinity itself comes to be.
Through this divine disposition, the devotee attains complete detachment.
He obtains supreme affection and attains the highest devotion. Through supreme devotion, liberation occurs gradually over the course of time;
however, for those possessed of intense spiritual urgency, liberation indeed comes swiftly, even from a stationary state.
It might happen for someone at some time, but there is no liberation for all;
therefore, stationary holy places (sthāvaratīrtha) do not indeed grant swift liberation.
When there is dullness of faith, there is slowness in those [pilgrimages] characterized by slow, medium, or other velocities.
O Lakṣmī, even in liberation, there arises the attainment of long-lasting purification.
Therefore, among the immobile *tīrthas*, the mobile ones are indeed superior;
here, the mother is a mobile *tīrtha*, and the father is a mobile *tīrtha*.
The husband is a moving tirtha, and the chaste wife is a moving tirtha;
the sage is a moving tirtha, and the virtuous woman is a moving tirtha.
The virtuous man is a moving tirtha, and the yogi is a moving tirtha.
The Saṃghatīrtha is mobile, and the Yātrātīrtha is also mobile;
the Bhaktatīrtha is mobile, and the Tapasvitīrtha is supreme.
Indeed, the devotee who has offered himself (ātmanivedi-bhakta) is the most excellent mobile tīrtha.
The deities who are portions of Hari— namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— as well as Satī,
Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī, are indeed moving tīrthas.
The Yoginīs and the Sāṃkhya-Yoginīs are likewise moving tīrthas.
The cows were wish-fulfilling, and the people were observant of vows and virtuous conduct (36). Devoted to celibacy and free from the faults of meat and liquor,
the people were rich in righteousness and were indeed moving shrines through their devotion (37).
They purify themselves by the mere sight of these [places], as well as by touch and service,
in which neither liquor nor meat— forms of sin— is found;
having undertaken the vow of non-violence, they worship the Supreme Lord.
Having firmly established themselves in the vow of truth, they engage in recitations and sacred discourses. Having undertaken the vow of non-stealing, they practice the giving of material goods.
Having maintained the vow of celibacy, they serve their most excellent gurus.
Having established themselves in compassion and their vows, even while providing service to the helpless,
righteous people perform meritorious acts consisting of total self-surrender— such as serving their teachers and serving their gurus in accordance with dharma.
Having completely abandoned the sense of bodily existence, they cultivate the contemplation of Brahman.
They serve [the Lord] as their own self, and likewise as their Master;
they serve Him as liberation, and likewise as one who is liberated.
O Lakṣmī, when served in this manner, this supreme moving tīrtha quickly shakes off sins and swiftly bestows liberation as well.
It is so when [beings] are seen, touched, bowed to, worshipped, and likewise fed.
The virtuous have been caused to drink, carried away, massaged, and anointed;
they have been propitiated, clothed, and adorned;
they have been delighted, gladdened, made to laugh, and likewise celebrated. (45–46)
They were entrusted, taken up from the beginning, carried along, and laid down;
they were adorned, saluted, served, and held within the heart.
They were made kin, associated with, and embraced upon one's own breast.
For the virtuous quickly purify those who have been consecrated with the *nīrājana* rite, made green [with herbs], perfumed with fragrant liquids and the like,
bathed, anointed with oil, scented, forgiven, remembered, and sipped water for purification (*ācamana*). (48–49)
Whether they are perfumed, illuminated, smeared with saffron, or adorned with moon-like beauty;
whether they have been circumambulated or prostrated to like a staff—
even when held within one's own heart, the virtuous quickly purify.
The Sādhu-tīrtha is the supreme sacred ford, manifest as Nārāyaṇa himself.
The Agni-tīrtha is indeed purifying, and the Sūrya-tīrtha is likewise;
but the Sādhu-tīrtha is the purifier of all purifiers and the sanctifier of the assembly.
The grace of a holy person is rich in merit and destroys all sins;
the touch of a holy person is a great initiation that annihilates all evil.
Even the mere sight of a holy person destroys the sins of the senses.
The instruction of the virtuous is indeed a sacred ford that destroys one's own impurities.
The very resolve of the virtuous is the supreme resolve of Hari.
And I, O Lakṣmī, dwell in every way within the hearts of the virtuous.
Indeed, all sacred fords dwell at the feet of the virtuous;
all merits dwell upon the shanks of the virtuous;
and all merit-bestowing sacrifices dwell indeed in the knees of the holy ones.
All the gods and likewise the goddesses dwell in the thighs of the virtuous man (sādhu).
Good conduct, vows, and austerities reside in his well-guarded [private parts].
And in the waist of the virtuous man dwell the supernatural powers (siddhis) and all forms of prosperity.
In the belly of the virtuous man dwell all the ṛṣis; in his stomach reside the fires.
In the navel of the virtuous man dwell the powers of yoga in every way.
In the chest of the virtuous man dwell the most righteous ancestors.
On the two sides of the virtuous, indeed, all gifts reside;
in their two flanks, all the oceans reside; and on the hips of the holy man, all the celestial abodes (dhiṣṇyas) reside.
Even Mount Meru, the refuge of all, dwells upon the back of the virtuous man;
even all powers dwell upon the shoulders of the virtuous man;
and even the supreme abode of Brahman dwells within the throat of the virtuous man.
In the arms of the virtuous, Mahendra and the other guardians of the quarters truly reside. In the elbows of the saintly one, the celestial armies dwell eternally.
And in the hands of the virtuous, O Lakṣmī, all forms of prosperity and fortune abide.
In the palms of the hands of the saint (sādhu), both enjoyment and liberation reside;
in the collection of the saint’s fingers dwell the planets, such as the moon and the sun.
In all the channels (nāḍīs) of the saint, all rivers abide.
In every hair of the saint dwell the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpapādapāḥ).
On the back of the saint’s neck shines the Great Rudra;
in the saint’s impurity dwells Mahāmāyā, and in the saint’s semen resides the Golden One (Hiraṇmaya).
O Lakṣmī, a person shines when freed from the noose of *māyā*;
O Lakṣmī, for the virtuous man, the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) shines through his actions.
O Lakṣmī, the goddess of fortune who bestows prosperity shines upon the chin of the virtuous man.
Divine powers always reside upon the lips of the virtuous.
I myself am present in the mouth of the virtuous as the impeller of all actions; indeed, all the Vedas, which are my own words, dwell upon the tongues of the righteous. (3.186.70)
In the nose reside the realm of Satyaloka and Vairāja, who shines forth from Virāṭ;
in the cheeks reside both Vaikuṇṭha and Goloka for the virtuous;
and in the temples reside Mahāpuruṣa and Sadāśiva.
In the frown, Mahākāla and Saṃkarṣaṇa shine forth;
in the two eyes, the knowledge of Brahman and direct realization (sākṣātkāra) reside;
on the forehead is the splendor of Brahman, and all abodes are present there.
The imperishable Brahman resides in the head, and the Supreme Person in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Indeed, all those liberated from saṃsāra dwell in the hair of the virtuous.
All powers reside in their will, and the lords of the righteous dwell in their minds.
For the virtuous, worship of the Buddha resides in the mind that is dear to Brahman.
The Blessed Lord resides in the saint; Nirvāṇa is found in association with the saint.
Indeed, when the saint is pleased, all the heavens are present.
For the virtuous, dissolution occurs in sleep, while creation occurs upon awakening;
meditative absorptions (samādhi) are found in deep sleep, and for the wise, the state of Brahman is attained in meditation.
Discernment is found in the Upaniṣads, and the Sudarśana [discus] is in the rosary.
The Brahma-weapon resides in his knowledge, while the Nārāyaṇa-weapon dwells in his soul.
In all his bones, pools of nectar shine eternally for the virtuous;
divine dispositions reside in the body of the saintly one, and wish-fulfilling creepers grow upon his palms.
In the middle of the chest is the lineage of Dharma; both breasts are the two paths.
On the seat of the virtuous are the pedestals of all the deities.
Indeed, all the goddesses always reside within the ritual actions of the virtuous.
"And in that vessel belonging to the virtuous, there indeed resides the satisfaction of Hari.
Thus did the lord Dhvajīśvara hear this delightful story,
and he came to understand the sin of selling liquor from the words of the scriptures.

Thus he grieved in his heart: "The sale of liquor must be abandoned by me forever, and I must always undertake other efforts free from blemish. Just as the potter's work consists of the fashioning of earthen vessels, so too [must my labor be directed elsewhere]."
"Therefore, since there is a purpose [to be served], the sin of drinking liquor must be abandoned.
Having reflected thus, the drinker of liquor, who was a virtuous and devoted servant of the saint, bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake and offered this prayer.
"O holy man, I am a potter by caste, a drunkard who makes liquor.
Having heard your story today and having bathed in the Nārāyaṇahrada, I have come for refuge to you; purify me and wash away my sin."
Upon hearing this, the servant of the virtuous one indeed gave him Vaiṣṇava water;
he also granted him prasāda and bestowed upon him the Brahmakūrca vow.
He gave him the Vaiṣṇava mantra and presented him with a garland of tulasī.
To Bāṇa’s army, which had come for refuge along with its family, [he said]:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā" (Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā).
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, obeisance be unto You."
He gave him the mantra known as Itikīrtana and made him a true Vaiṣṇava. The Guru granted him this blessing: "Lord Hari will meet you.
Having received this supreme blessing, Bāṇāṅgaṇa went to his own abode.
He departed and abandoned his occupation with liquor;
he indeed undertook the occupation of making earthen vessels.
He took refuge in me, the Supreme Self, and performed constant glorification.
Indeed, I have observed that he, together with his family, possesses supreme devotion toward me, accompanied by purity;
for he constantly worships me, eats only what is offered to me, protects [the offering], and applies himself [to my service]. || 93-94 ||
Together with his family, he observed the Cāturmāsya vow, subsisting on fruits and other such items;
in the month of Kārtika, he performed the worship and the concluding rite (udyāpana) according to the rules of the vow.
Then, on the night of Ekādaśī, he kept a vigil.
On the twelfth day, at dawn itself, O Lakṣmī, I, endowed with splendor and bearing the conch, discus, and mace, became pleased with him and granted him my own vision. Beholding me,
he prostrated himself like a staff and worshipped me with supreme devotion.
Together with his family, he repeatedly fell at my feet for refuge and then entreated me:
"O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, deliver me from the ocean of worldly existence! (98)
Then I gave him water for his feet to drink;
he drank it together with his family, and at that moment he became a virtuous soul.
His bonds were quickly severed, and his mind was fixed upon liberation. (3.186.100)
At that time, O Lakṣmī, I quickly caused him to cast off his body;
I then caused him to ascend this most excellent celestial chariot.
Along with my attendants, I sent him to my own imperishable abode.
Then, when his own lifespan had come to an end, his family also gradually entered my imperishable abode, as he remained established in my true word. Thus,
through the association with the virtuous, the impurity of that very devotee was removed.
Having kindled it all, he bestowed upon him my imperishable abode;
Bāṇa’s entire retinue attained liberation, and his family followed after them in succession.
Indeed, having become that purifying and imperishable Vaiṣṇava state, they went to liberation.
"From reading this, from hearing it, and from remembering it, liberation shall come.

(105) Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Liquor-Seller Named Bāṇāṅgaṇa through Association with a Holy Man, and the Description of the Glories of the Holy Man’s Form," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga)*
Chapter 187 [Author:
Chapter 188 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, and likewise hear this other auspicious story.
In a city named Dhavala, there lived a leather-worker who subsisted on the dead.
He resided on the outskirts of a village, constantly dealing with the carcasses of hoofed animals.
He was a stealer of dead animals from the midst of the village;
he was a cleaner of hides, untouchable, and lived far away. Indeed, he and his family were always eaters of dead flesh and perpetually sinful. (2–3)
Having established a dwelling in some place and having sold hides,
he would purchase with the wealth obtained wheat and other grains, as well as vegetables, fruits, and so forth;
bringing these to his own home, he would cook them and eat.

In some places, that meat-eater provides food for his family with wild cats, jackals, and hares; likewise, in other places, with boars, hyenas, and the like, and in yet others, with tortoises and fish. (5–6)
Thus, by birth, by his occupation, and by his food, that most sinful leather-worker,
known as Mṛtādana, lived always far away and was shunned.
Then once, during the rainy season, when it was falling day and night...
A flood of water arrived with great force from all sides.
There, some living beings and creatures were then carried away by the trees;
both the dead and the living, as well as domestic animals, were swept along. (8–9)
Even some of those who roam in the pasture of grassy fields were unable to reach their homes during the rains due to the force of the floodwaters.
One cow, however, was carried away by the force of the current and lost her life.

Near the dwelling of a leather-worker, right by the edge of a water tank, she was seen being pulled out by the waters; at that moment, the leather-worker, moved by compassion, desired to rescue the cow. (11–12)
Fat, powerful, and sturdy, the eater of the dead was capable of swimming;
tying a rope measuring a hundred cubits around his waist, he plunged into the water. Having given one end of the rope to his family members to hold with their arms...
And he threw another strong, knotted rope around her neck.
Where the cow was suddenly falling as the current of water carried her away,
he crossed it with speed and stood before her at the lower part of the stream.
The cow is carried by the full [load], and the leather-worker is also carried;
those who stand on the bank holding the rope run along after that same bank.
By the leather-worker crossing over with the agility of his hand, [the boat is moved].
The end of the cord, which had been folded over, was placed around the cow's neck;
a knot was quickly tied and it was fixed between her two horns.
Having made the cord hang down, he fastened its other end to his waist. (17–18)
Then the householders said, "Let us pull him by force!
And that rope, held in their own hands, was pulled by the householders.
Due to the initial momentum, the leather-worker was dragged toward the bank.
The cow, tied with a rope around her waist, was pulled toward the bank;
drawn along by the householders working together,
she reached the shore alive, accompanied by the leather-worker.
Then the cow, satisfied by the preservation of her life, spoke this blessing to them:
"By my protection, all your sins have been destroyed.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the gift of a cow, and whatever great fruit is obtained from sustaining a cow's life—"
Whatever fruit there is in the service of cows, may all of that belong to you.
And whatever fruit is said to come from the gift of a cow while she is in calf—may that fruit be yours by virtue of my saving your life. (23–24)
May the fruit that comes from a golden cow, the fruit born of a tawny cow,
and the fruit that comes from a *gomedha* sacrifice— may all that be yours through my protection.
May the fruit that comes from protecting the earth and the fruit that comes from protecting the subjects likewise be yours.

May that fruit which comes from protecting a maiden be yours through my protection; may that fruit which comes from protecting a virtuous wife, that which comes from protecting children, and that which comes from protecting a Brahmin, be yours through my protection. (26–27)

May that fruit which arises from protecting the virtuous, that fruit which arises from protecting the gods, and that fruit which arises from protecting those who have come for refuge— may all that be mine through my protection [of you]. May also that fruit which arises from protecting the terrified, and that fruit which arises from protecting life, be mine.
May that fruit which comes from the gift of liberation belong to you through my protection;

may that fruit which comes from the protection of Dharma, that fruit which comes from protecting a fetus, and that fruit which comes from service to one’s mother, belong to you through my protection. (3.187.30)
May the fruit of worshipping the gods, the fruit of protection from death,
and the fruit of visiting the holy sites of the Gaṅgā— all that come to you through my protection.
May [the fruits of] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and those arising from the injury of animals [be likewise removed].

May the sins of eating meat be dissolved through my protection. For one who gives up their life for the sake of a cow, for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a virtuous person, or for the sake of a deity, there is the destruction of all sins. (32–33)
For my sake you have given up your lives; for my sake you have lived your lives. You are the protectors of me; may you live, served by prosperity.
May you enjoy worldly enjoyment, liberation, and great wealth, like that of heaven.
May your lineage always be devoted and full of devotion toward the cow, the protector of cows, the cowherd, the lover of the cowherd girls, Govinda, and the child of the cowherds;
may you have affection for the child of the cowherds and your dwelling in Goloka. (35–36)
Thus, trembling, agitated by fear, afflicted by cold, and likewise hungry, the cow then gave them auspicious blessings. Then,
she slowly approached that pregnant, white cow.

That leather-worker led her to his own home and indeed protected her. He gave her the finest morsels of fodder and served her with grass and water. No one came for her; there was no master to take her away.
Thereupon that cow took up residence in the house of a leather-worker;
having eaten grass, she would return and stand by his side in the evening.
Thinking her to be his own, the leather-worker tended to her according to his ability.
Even though he was poor and a mendicant, for the sake of the cow he repeatedly brought grass and water from the fields,
the forest, or from distant lands. Indeed,
as he continued to serve in this manner, even while eating only what was left over after others had eaten, [the cow remained with him].
The fruit of serving a cow, as well as the fruit of her blessing,
was obtained by him once in the morning when Mṛtādana was impelled [by that thought]:
"Today I shall smear my house with white clay and cow dung."
Having deliberated thus with his wife, he took Sītā and the spade,
as well as two bamboo vessels,
and went to the riverbank where auspicious white clay could be found in order to fetch earth. || 44-45 ||
And with a spade, Sītā dug up the earth in a pit;
a trench one span deep was excavated on the bank, at its side and level with the ground.
Just then, a vessel of copper-colored metal, filled with gold and silver, [was discovered].
By the power of destiny, he emerged from the middle of the earth in a splendid manner.
Having quickly extracted gold rings from that dead man, he placed them in a bamboo vessel, concealed them in soil, and returned home. (47–48)
Five vessels were brought, yet no one knew of them;
they were all cast into a cavity within the house and well concealed.
Considering it to be the fruit of cow-service, he, together with his wife, continued to serve the cow.
Having placed that copper vessel back into the hole exactly as it was,
he covered it over with earth and went home; there,
using coins as required, he enjoyed all kinds of pleasures.
He enjoys food, drinks, garments, and sweets;
he consumes his earned wealth in such a way that others do not even know of it.
He also attends to guests who arrive by that same path.
He attends to guests staying in the cow-pen in places shaded by trees.
He offers fruits, sugar, and even honey-mixture (madhuparka); he gives clothing, water as required, and chickpeas and other such foods.
He gives to the virtuous food that has been cooked in ghee, cooked in oil, or even roasted over fire; food ripened by the sun or ripened by the seasons.
He gives what is appropriate and does not serve what is inappropriate to the virtuous yogi.
He serves his family, attends upon the virtuous, and listens to devotional songs.
He hears my delightful, supreme, and purifying story as told by the saints.
Non-violence is the highest dharma; one who eats the remains of the sacrificial meal (vighasa) is liberated.
The eating of meat is a great sin that leads to the city of Yama.
One who eats fish is an eater of all kinds of flesh; such a person is never liberated at any time.
Having fallen through the consumption of forbidden food, one never attains liberation anywhere.
The messengers of Yama torment and subjugate him in the abode of Yama;
they constantly cook that meat-eater in a great fire, they cut him to pieces, kill him, and cast him into hell.
Intoxicants, meat, theft, and sexual misconduct—these are defilements, terrifying and most dreadful; they must never be committed by human beings.
Indeed, this human birth on earth is obtained for the sake of liberation.
Liberation is indeed to be achieved by human beings; therefore, faults and sins must be abandoned.
(62) Even though wine, meat, and other such things have been consumed across many bodies—whether as birds or as animals—the end of that sin is not found. (63)
"In this human state, indeed, meritorious deeds that grant heaven must be performed;
devotion to Hari must also be practiced, so that liberation in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman] may be attained.
Thus did the leather-worker listen to this purifying story.
Then, through association with the virtuous, a sudden desire for liberation arose within him.
He undertook religious observances, including non-violence and the renunciation of meat and other such things;
he also practiced eating only vegetarian food and the constant service of Lord Hari.
Service to the virtuous, service to cows, avoidance of sin, giving gifts to worthy recipients as is appropriate, and likewise the chanting of the Lord’s glories;
as well as the observance of vows and festivals for the gods, and the Cāturmāsya vows.
He undertook such restrictive observances that always grant liberation.
(68) Then the virtuous Dharmaśālāyana, wandering through the forest by name, arrived naked near the house of a leather-worker. (69)
The leather-worker saw him, a yogi whose mind was fixed on yoga,
auspiciously reciting prayers with a rosary while remembering the Supreme Self;
he was sky-clad, tranquil, free from agitation, and firm in his resolve.
The matted-haired sage was of beautiful form, observing vows and observances, and free from passion.
A leather-worker, having approached him, joyfully prostrated himself before him:
"Welcome to you, O illustrious one! O holy man, may victory be yours forever! (71–72)
"Come and dwell here with me; I am a leather-worker by birth.
If you so think it right, O virtuous one, purify my home, O sinless one.
Having heard these auspicious words of the truth-speaker, Śālāyana replied:

Even the Lord of divine nature comes under the control of a devotee who is devoted to the virtuous; what then need be said of a saintly person? Even those born from the womb of a *caṇḍāla* are purifiers when they are devotees of the Lord. (74–75)
Indeed, all subjects are bound by leather;
for they are born from leather, with leather as their womb and leather as their source.
They cause them to bathe in leather and adorn them with leather.
They perform massages and other treatments with oils and the like upon the skin itself;
they even offer ornaments and garments to the body as if it were made of leather.
The entire world is composed of leather; who is not a tanner? (77–78)
Brahmā was a leather-worker, and his sons were leather-workers as well;
you, O devotee, are a leather-worker, born into the lineage of a leather-worker.
Among subjects, there is no distinction whatsoever in being a leather-worker.

Those who are deluded regarding the realm of the skin are considered to be mere leather-workers. Those who are not deluded regarding the realm of the skin are considered to be of the nature of Brahman.
The virtuous are the abodes of Brahman; they are of the nature of Brahman and are dear to the Great One (Brahman).
As long as this self exists within the body, it is a leather-worker;
when it becomes bodiless through devotion, it attains liberation and becomes a creator of Brahman.
"I am the Self, the form of the virtuous, and I indeed become the form of Brahman."
Through devotion to Hari, which consists of love, I myself become the form of Brahman.
O devotee, through the practice of the virtuous, you too become the form of Brahman.
Those who are devoted to the virtuous are themselves virtuous in form and performers of virtuous deeds.
"He whose entire wealth consists of virtuous purpose, and who indeed says 'Brahman is the Self'—
he alone is free from sin, a meritorious soul, and a purifier of the assembly.
Having spoken thus, that virtuous man then departed for his home.
The shoemaker Bhaktarāja offered him a most auspicious welcome.
He provided a beautiful seat and performed the washing of his feet;
indeed, together with his entire family, he drank the nectar of his [the guest’s] feet. (86–87)
He massaged his feet and likewise rubbed his body;
he offered him sweet madhuparka, as well as sugar and parched grain.
He also gave various kinds of excellent, ripe fruits.
He gave them water and a bed for the sake of rest.
Having fed them all—the sons, daughters, and the couple—they performed a massage of their bodies to relieve the fatigue of the journey. (3.187.90)
He attained supreme, peaceful sleep, and they all performed a massage for him,
as well as rubbing his body and fanning him with a fan to provide a breeze.
In this manner, they indeed rendered service to Dharmaśālāyana.
Having slept in the Dharma-śālā, he then woke up;
having drunk water, he sat upon his seat engaged in the recitation of mantras with a garland. And the Mṛtādana and others sat before him with a spirit of devotion. (92–93)
The saint said: "One must always practice devotion to the Supreme Self;
for the sake of liberation in this world, service to cows and service to saints must be performed.
Receive from me, along with your family, this divine mantra."
"Then you shall attain divine heaven and thereafter liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having been addressed thus, the cobbler, together with his family, then received the mantra of the saint: "Hare Kṛṣṇa Narāyaṇa."
"Oṃ, obeisances unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā!
Then, following the path prescribed by the saintly, he worshiped Bālakṛṣṇa.
Thereafter, he indeed went on a pilgrimage together with the saintly one.
He bestowed gold in many ways there as a gift for the Kuṃkumavāpikā field and the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake;
likewise, he had a temple constructed on the shore of that lake. || 98-901 ||
He constructed his own auspicious hermitage for the purpose of worship;
there he lived together with a virtuous man and his flute.
Then one day, I, Kamala, being pleased, arrived there.
He granted him his own vision, four-armed and possessing the splendor of a son.
He worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the eternal one, along with my family.
Eating the remnants of my food, he washed my feet and drank that water.
A celestial chariot, exceedingly radiant and originating from the abode of Brahmā, arrived swiftly;
there, at my command,
the deceased man ascended it along with that cow, and I brought him to my own realm.
All the rest of the family became gods in heaven.
Having enjoyed the merit resulting from the conduct toward the cow, they shall go to my supreme abode;
for such is the fruit of service to the virtuous and likewise of devotion to me.
O Lakṣmī, they shall enjoy that which is beautiful and filled with eternal bliss.
Thus, by the service of cows, the sin of eating meat has been destroyed;
and through the arising of merit, there is the company of the virtuous and the arrival of wealth.
Dwelling at sacred fords, supreme liberation— all this was attained by him.
By reading, hearing, remembering, and even reflecting upon this,
there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and the eternal state is acquired.
