Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Sins such as Meat-Eating and the Attainment of Merit for the Leather-worker named Mṛtādana through Saving the Life of a Cow, as well as His Meeting with a Holy Man, His Ascent to Heaven, and Liberation," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 187. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 188 [Author:
Chapter 189 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious story of the thief’s liberation. There was indeed a thief named Śaṅkudhara in the city of Mālava;
he made his dwelling in a thieves’ lair and served to nourish the circle of thieves.
Another remains intent on a thieving expedition at night, carrying weapons and the like;
he even assumes a different appearance and adopts a different mode of action.
Having understood the distinction regarding entry, one should act with every possible effort in accordance with that.
Having made an appointment at night, he indeed commits theft of wealth;
sometimes from a horse, sometimes from a camel, and sometimes from a long-necked donkey.
Having deposited his load of wealth, he runs away to a great distance.

Thus, having gone to another country and indeed having stolen wealth, he brings it to his own home; having divided it with his fellow-thieves, he protects his own share. He celebrates a festival, eats, consumes, and rejoices.
He must commit theft in every way; no other task exists for him.
He is intent on the effort of stealing, his thoughts are fixed on stealing, and he is devoted to the meditation of stealing.
He subsists by the belly of theft, filling the belly of his family.
Sometimes, where there might be a festival of the gods or some great occasion;
where thousands of people gather at a sacred ford (tīrtha), or at a shrine (caitya), a temple, on a mountain, at the edge of a village, or on a riverbank. (8–9)

Whether in a temple or elsewhere, this circle of thieves goes there; they search everywhere for valuables, wondering where they might be. When and where will the house of a wealthy man ever become deserted?
Where is the path for entry or exit, or where and how?
How is attainment achieved, how is one's own protection secured, and how is concealment maintained?
Thus, devoted to his own meditation, he travels with his caravan while carrying the stake.
Having committed theft in various other towns, he would carry off wealth;
once, during the latter part of the night, such a man had a dream consisting of the acquisition of boundless gold and jewels.
He perceived that the capital had formerly been located in the forest.
In that lonely, desolate forest, he saw in a dream a supreme treasury situated far away, inlaid with gold and jewels, which had previously been protected by the kingdom. (14–15)
Just as no one else knew of his secret treasury, so too,
having risen in the morning and eaten, he departed under the pretext of a stroll.
In a dream, he saw an ancient forest and path.
He saw the clusters of trees, the stones, and the earth covered with ancient grass;
he saw the former dwelling there, indicated by its old markings.
Thus did this thief see everything and gain full confidence.
Those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) sown in a previous birth that have endured for a long time will undoubtedly sprout as a lotus in another life.
This man was a thief in a former time, more than a thousand years ago.
Suhotra was the king’s treasury superintendent.
At that time, Suhotra’s city there was named after his father;
it had been built by his father Kāñcana as the city of Kāñcanī.
That treasury-guarding function indeed belonged to the kings of the Lunar dynasty (Candravaṃśīya).
Then, after some time, the treasuries were removed to another location;
they were all taken and deposited there, yet indeed through deception.
Indeed, by the treasurer named Apajāpaka,
the treasury was entirely concealed from others so that no one would know even a little of it;
he kept the gold and the jewels strictly separate.
Right there, for the sake of his own inherent purpose, he employed a stratagem.
Then, after a long period of time had passed and much time had elapsed,
he was indeed unable to lead away Guptakoṣaka through deception.
In this very way, having died there in the new city of Mālava,
he was indeed sent by the Yamas to the southern city on account of the sin of theft;
beaten with iron rods, he suffered misery in the pit.
Bound repeatedly with nooses, mallets, and staffs, he was punished like a criminal;
only after exhausting the fruits of his sins was he released there in that desolate forest.
Having become a *preta*, he was unable to leave that place.
He always delights in the forest and perceives only the treasury;
he eats all that is wild and dwells even among the trees of the treasury. In this manner, eight hundred years of his life indeed passed away. (3.188.30)
At that time, in that secluded place upon the eastern ground, a brahmin named Sumantuka arrived to perform austerities.
Having recognized in the forest that beautiful spot as a suitable place for penance, [he settled there]. (3.1)
In a place free from obstacles, abounding in trees, creepers, and thickets, and possessing excellent water sources,
the ascetic took refuge in the shade of a banyan tree not far away and performed austerities while worshipping Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī and Supreme Person. (32–33)
Then, when a year had passed, this deceased man, perceiving that the ascetic was a virtuous soul who would effect his own deliverance,
assumed the form of a Kirāta and stood before him in the shade of a banyan tree.
Bowing down, he praised the ascetic power of that great-souled one.
Sumantu, through his own ascetic power, recognized him as being in the form of a ghost;
nevertheless, he offered a welcome to him who had arrived at the banyan-tree hut.

The king of sages questioned that forest-dweller— who was dark-complexioned, emaciated, and indeed suffering— asking, "O embodied one, O forest-dweller, is it well with you here? The deceased replied, "It is well for the ascetic through his spiritual power."
The sage asked about his residence, his village, his conduct, and his deeds.
The deceased man, becoming free from deceit, related his history from the beginning:
"Formerly, I was the treasurer here, a man of hypocrisy and sin. (38–39)
Having died and gone to the city of the Yāmyas, having experienced painful torments and obtained some small remnant of the fruit of my deception,
I have been born here in this forest as a *preta*; release me out of compassion.
Thus, while observing his fast, he did not show the treasury to him at that time.
That compassionate sage, muttering the Gāyatrī, gave water to him for the sake of the deceased's liberation; and his state as a preta vanished.
However, due to his nature as a thief and his deceitfulness toward humans,
this thief Śaṅkudhara became a resident of the city of Mālava;
endowed with his former habitual tendencies, he remained thoroughly proficient in thievery.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the power of his past impressions (saṃskāra), this man devoted to theft experienced a memory of a treasury from a previous birth in a dream. Thereupon,
he went into a desolate forest to see that very treasury.
He surveyed everything marked with the signs he had seen in his dream;
then that man, who was full of greed, became delighted.
He saw the banyan tree right there at the former site of the ascetic.
There is no ascetic there at all, but an auspicious banyan tree exists.
Since Sumantu became one of divine body through his asceticism,
that ascetic of divine form remains hidden within the banyan tree.
Then Śaṅkudhara did not see that ascetic at all;
he saw only the banyan tree, for he did not bow to the tree as he had done before.
Thinking his treasury of gold had reached its full measure, he departed for his own abode.
He returned to his own home that very evening, feeling quite pleased.
Then, being alone, he reflected repeatedly within his heart:
"How indeed can I bring wealth from him here?"
Just so that others might not know,
it must be brought back secretly; having made my dwelling there in the forest,
I must always bring it here alone by means of some artifice.
Having reflected thus, and under the pretext of theft, he went alone;
having spoken to his household members and taken up weapons, he went to that forest.
And while he was digging slowly and stealthily for the sake of theft, even in the darkness—
Having dug until dawn, he went for a moment beneath a banyan tree to rest;
returning there again, he dug very slowly.
Indeed, he remained alone in the middle of the forest, fearless and without hesitation.
Just then, a sound came from that banyan tree like that of a human being.
Hearing it, he looked all around in alarm; yet he did not see any human at all, and so he became even more suspicious again and again.
He dug gradually until a stone slab, heavy with rock,
arrived there; lifting it up upon the surface of the stone,
he beheld eight copper vessels containing all manner of living beings.

Having beheld all the gold, silver, ornaments, coins, gems, and diamonds, as well as all the specific objects designated as wealth that he had seen in his dream, he attained the highest peace in every respect. (3.188.60)
Then, having covered these vessels each in its proper place, he placed a heap of grass, leaves, and other materials upon them; thereafter,
he quickly cast branches from thorny trees over the top as well.
Then, having gone back to the banyan tree, he indeed found rest for a moment (62).
Recalling what must be done at night— the theft of the wealth—
he thought through his entire plan and slept for just a moment (63).
At the end of a ghaṭikā, he arose and stood before him;
the king of yogis, Sumantuka himself, appeared in bodily form, laughing repeatedly.
Having become motionless for a moment and recognizing that ascetic as a great ṛṣi, [he remained still].
Having quickly recognized him as one seen before, she bowed down to him.
With a serene countenance, she spoke swiftly to that lord of sages, Uddhāraka: "O Teacher, I was formerly a preta. (65–66)
"In this matter, I have been rescued by you, and I am indeed a human being.
I am a thief named Śaṅkudhara, devoted to the act of stealing.
Sustaining myself through theft, I wander about as a sinner. (67)
"O best of Brahmins, O ocean of compassion, my former preceptor, grant me deliverance!
Act in such a way that I may attain both worldly prosperity and liberation.
Having heard these words from his former devotee who had come for refuge, the sage—
Filled with compassion and reflecting upon his deliverance, Sumantu said:
"I shall bring about your supreme welfare; of this there is no doubt.
O disciple, listen as I speak, and perform it with reverence."
Listen; I shall speak to you a brief instruction that is worthy of you.
In former times, you belonged to the Lunar dynasty and were a great lord of treasures.
Thereafter, having gone to the city of Yama and experienced torments there, [you have come here]. (71–72)
"Born as a ghost, you have indeed become a human being through my grace;
nevertheless, I tell you this: your state of being a thief has not been destroyed here.
Whatever treasure was dug up by you and whatever wealth may be there—"
Therefore, perform the sacrifice here, conducted through the agency of Sumantu’s hands.
I myself am that very Sumantu; I dwell here beneath this banyan tree.
All people in the world know me as an ascetic who has attained perfection in yoga.
"Sumantu shall perform the sacrifice as well; speak also to him.
Grant confidence to all your subjects.
The seers, sages, and likewise the deities will arrive. (76)
"Therefore, O Brahmins, virtuous men, and noble women present at this sacrifice, I shall spend my wealth;
I shall perform a supreme sacrifice. When this is done, your merit will be great and your highest welfare will be attained. (77–78)
Accept this purifying mantra of Kṛṣṇa, which sanctifies those who recite it:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Viṣṇu, Bālakṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī!"
"O Supreme Lord, ocean of mercy, Lord of Lakṣmī, Lord of Ramā!
Always perform such chanting day and night;
all your sins will surely come to destruction in every way."
O dear one, by my blessing, the merit of this sacrifice shall belong to you alone;
likewise, you shall attain self-purification as well as devotion to Śrī Hari, who is I.
My words shall bear fruit—of this there is no doubt.
"Both enjoyment and liberation shall belong to you and to your family as well.
Having spoken thus and knowing his mind, the sage then gave him a mantra;
the king of sages, Sumantu, sent him back to his hermitages.
Having heard the excellent news from the hermitages of the brahmins, the hermitages of the sages, and from virtuous men and women, the learned ones quickly arrived there for the sacrifice.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, the sovereign sage Sumantu [performed it] by mere resolve alone.
He constructed mountains and rivers as accumulations of all kinds of materials.
At that time, the deities beginning with Brahmā appeared there in person;
the great seers, the ancestors, the virtuous, and the noble women also arrived. (86–87)
Then the sage performed the Viṣṇu-sacrifice for seven days;
at the desire of Sumantu, Viṣṇu became manifest there in person.
At that time, the sacrificial fires themselves directly accepted the oblation.

During the *pūrṇāhuti* offering, Sumantu remembered me, the Supreme Lord. For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of his devotee, I then appeared before him; highly honored by Sumantu and the others, I partook of the sacrificial oblation itself. (3.188.89–90)
Then Sumantuka caused gifts of the materials excavated there to be given by the hand of Śaṅkudhara: ten million pieces of gold,
ten million silver coins, and likewise ten million jewels.
He caused crores of diamonds to be given away as gifts through miraculous wonders.
No one at all understood from where this wealth had come;
for they considered everything to be the work of Sumantu’s miracles.
A great cry of victory arose from the gifts, the sacrificial fees, and other offerings.
The gods, the ancestors, human beings, the supreme sages,
and indeed all embodied beings were satisfied there at that great sacrifice.
At the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*), Sumantu bathed his disciple.
There, he requested me to grant an audience to his devotee;
I [granted it] even to Śaṅkudhara, together with his family. (95–96)
He revealed his own form, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, and indeed,
at the word of Sumantu, he purified all of them,
having shaken off all the sins of the devotee and [bestowed upon him] a treasure of merit.
Having given him a vehicle for ascending to heaven and having taken hold of the two great stars,
Śaṅkhadhara,
together with his family, departed for the eternal heaven while the virtuous looked on. ||98-99||
Having attained a divine body, he quickly went to the abode of Dhruva;
for, having enjoyed the fruit of the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice in the abode of Dhruva,
he will then go to Vaikuṇṭha together with his family.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, by the power of Sumantu’s devotion,
even that thief became free from theft; and having performed an auspicious sacrifice through my grace and the favor of that best of sages, he became a supreme god.

Being honored by all the worlds, he became renowned and attained the eternal state. Thus, through association with a saintly person, even sinners and the wicked become free from sin and indeed go to the supreme abode.
"By reading and hearing this, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Sins, the Performance of Sacrifice, and Liberation through the Yoga of Sumantu and Karṣi for the Thief named Śaṅkudhara," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 188.
Chapter 189 [Author:
Chapter 190 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, the favor of Hari toward the virtuous arises only through constant service (*anuvṛtti*), and certainly not by any other means. Furthermore,
the direct vision of Hari occurs either through His grace or through service.
Through meditation that is constant, it will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
(2) Stability of conduct in the form of Hari is difficult for embodied beings to attain;
nevertheless, through the yoga of practice, it is indeed accomplished—of this there is no doubt. (3)
O Lakṣmī, my form is a wish-fulfilling gem that bestows whatever is thought of;
it grants heaven, prosperity, supreme bliss, and liberation whenever they are desired.
It also grants the vision of the Self, the vision of the Lord, and the vision of Brahman.
The vision of the liberated is divine; from that comes my own vision as well.
Whatever is fully intended is obtained through the form of meditation.
And by such contemplation, the illusion of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" surely perishes.
Even the illusory memories of one who practices meditation perish;
even Māyā, which takes the form of the three qualities (guṇas) as house, son, and wife, perishes.
Likewise, for the meditator, even that Māyā known as latent impressions (vāsanā) surely perishes.

The destruction of craving certainly occurs, and the attainment of peace arises. (8) When the devotee, through the power of meditation on Hari, becomes absorbed in Him and of His very nature, he indeed becomes one who does not rise again; then follows the falling away of the body. (9)
The separation from the modifications of the material elements occurs,
and likewise, the destruction of the subtle body comes about through the power of meditation.
The stream of consciousness within the Self alone increases as the function of meditative absorption.

This divine consciousness itself, in the form of a substance, increases. That very [consciousness], having indeed assumed the form of meditation, becomes well-united with the image. Through that yoga, however, for the living being who is conscious and whose nature is that [consciousness]— || 1.1–1.2 ||
Indeed, at the time of departure, the form of Hari becomes equal to his own form;
that conscious being himself attains it completely.
This one, whose nature is the form of Brahman, shines forth with a divine appearance.
The embodied self, whose nature is Brahman and who resembles Hari, becomes manifest.
By the will of Śrī Hari, O Lakṣmī, the most excellent among the liberated shines forth. Great affection for me is the cause of supreme bliss in Hari.
Thus, those who are always affectionate, self-possessed, great-souled, and virtuous—
these purifiers indeed purify and sanctify sinful people.
For it is through their very compassion that their activity bestows liberation.
And by my command, they accomplish that task of uplifting the fallen;
then, even sinners who have taken refuge in the virtuous surely attain liberation. Through association with the virtuous, embodied beings certainly achieve supreme liberation.
Even courtesans, violent men, thieves, those who engage in illicit sex, murderers, the fallen, the wicked, and even the hateful cross over [the ocean of saṃsāra] by association with the saintly.
Whatever respect is shown to them in the world, it is due to their repeated association with the saintly. (1.9)
If one has formed an association with the virtuous, that very pride is surely crossed over.
One should always accept the virtues of the good and always avoid their faults.
One who accepts virtues certainly crosses over, while one who accepts faults sinks down.
One should honor the virtuous but disregard one's own kin;
for the righteous deliver the one who honors them,
while those who treat the virtuous with contempt surely fall.
Having their merit consumed, they go to a lowly womb.

Those who, having observed the physical nature of a virtuous person arising from a particular state at some time, seize upon his faults and become revilers of that virtuous one, likewise fall into such a state. (23–24)
They are always born rich in faults and possess a vision focused on defects;
they constantly impute sins to virtuous people and always proclaim their shortcomings, which bring about the destruction of their own reputation.

Desire, anger, greed, pride, delusion, attachment, arrogance, envy, lack of foresight, as well as indifference toward hospitality, lack of generosity, failure to invite others, apathy, and thirst for worldly things— [these are the faults]. (26)
Arrogance, lack of restraint, and perverse vision;
attachment to possessions, greed, and external latent impressions; outward-directed activity, the quality of passion (rājasatva), the quality of darkness (tāmasatva), and lack of awakening. (27–28)
Subservience to the tongue, gluttony for the genitals and belly, unrighteousness, association with kings, possessiveness, and egoism;
ignorance, lack of fitness, sleep, and worthlessness—[these are the defects]. || 29 ||
Falsehood, untruth, deceit, guile, hypocrisy, overeating,
folly, theft, and great indolence—
these are the evil qualities which those who are hostile, slanderous, and possessed of wicked traits themselves imagine [to exist in others].
The wicked conceive evil; they become possessed by evil.
Just as they regard their own actions, so too do they regard [the conduct] of the virtuous.
And just as their own latent tendencies are, so too do they perceive those [tendencies] in the virtuous.
Just as wickedness is innate to them, so too do they instill that very same quality in the virtuous;
they cause these wicked traits to enter into others and those who have taken refuge with them. They cause people to perceive faults where none exist, and they bring about contempt. (33–34)

All the wicked and faulty actions of the virtuous incite non-cultivation and drive out their good qualities; they speak with constant fault-finding, and likewise declare their conduct and behavior to be entirely corrupt. (35)
I have quenched the wickedness and sin, just as the Daityas or Dānavas [quench the heat] of the Āsuras.
For those of demonic nature project their own demonic state upon the virtuous;
they perceive good qualities even in all their own inherent vices.
They display hatred through their eyes, and they harbor hatred even in their gait;
they show hatred in bowing and looking, and they speak hatred even with their speech.
Indeed, regarding the duty of the virtuous, they treat it as a non-duty, and even as a wicked deed.
They display quarrels to others and engage in causeless strife:
"This was done by this good man; it is not at all fitting.
This man is certainly not good, and there is no goodness here at all. (3.189.40)
Who would touch his feet, who would salute such a one,
who would bow to him, and who would serve him? Having seen many such as he,
those like you, devoid of worldly ties, regard such beings as truly virtuous.
Even those like us do not see their faces anywhere.
Thus they constantly engage in censure, seizing upon faults;
and by means of wicked rumors, they cause others who possess faults to seize them as well.
Likewise, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, listen to the demonic conduct of those asuras who have no affection for the virtuous,
and who possess the defects of lust, anger, theft, and untruthfulness.
Deceit, backbiting, and sexual indulgence constitute the state of passion (rājasī sthiti).
Those people are indeed full of faults; they are powerless to abandon those faults, and on the contrary, their minds being attached to sense objects, they remain submerged in them.
Therefore, when the virtuous attempt to eliminate those very faults,
those evil-minded ones proceed to slander the saint who is effecting that refutation of their defects. (47)
This virtuous man is ignorant of what should and should not be said; he truly does not know how to speak.
Possessing only partial knowledge, he lacks vast wisdom;
considering himself a scholar, he conducts himself devoid of true insight. (48–49)

"He does not follow me anywhere, nor does he accept what I say; being intoxicated by the excellence of his own words, he is intent on refuting us. He knows nothing of our hermitage, nor does he know our virtues. (3.189.50)

They indeed disparage the enjoyments and other such splendors appropriate for the householder's life. Therefore, they say, "This man is devoid of discernment; he is a fool. In this way, they revile the virtuous person who offers beneficial instruction. (51–52)
For those of such a nature, there can never be affection even for the virtuous;
without affection, trust in the words of the virtuous does not arise.
Without trust, there is indeed no faith that increases the knowledge of greatness.
For through lack of faith there is no practice; from the absence of practice, there is no meditation at all.
There is no service, no cultivation, and no realization of identity.
Consequently, there is no attraction whatsoever; how then could there be greatness?
He has no desire to hear stories of him, nor even to hear news of him;
he lacks enthusiasm for receiving his commands—how then could there be any deep affection?
Listen, Lakṣmī, to how you possess the notion of ownership toward me.
In you there exists only the state of being a maidservant; no distinction is found therein.
Whether beaten, assaulted, reviled, saluted, or insulted, even so, you are never contrary, but remain a servant. (57–58)
O Mistress, you always serve me with the nature of all things— through non-existence, through joy, and as a devoted maidservant who naturally embraces virtue.
In that regard, O my Sovereign, there is never any lack of humility in you toward me.

Likewise, those who possess no inclination whatsoever toward the company of the virtuous, nor even a sense of equality toward them, but rather have a disposition for superiority; those who regard greatness, divinity, and even the state of being beyond the qualities (nirguṇatva) as residing in the virtuous—[they do not attain the goal]. (3.189.60–61)
In all virtuous actions, one should cultivate the thought that they bestow auspiciousness; in every undertaking, whether good or bad, one should cultivate the thought that they bestow merit.
Those in whom these thoughts truly exist always possess true mastery over the virtuous.
When cultivated, it shall bestow divine fruits and grant divine liberation;
it shall effect the severing of the bonds of illusion, time, and the like, as well as karma and other fetters.
Just as one feels affection for one's own wife, for a son, and for one's kinsmen, [so should one feel toward all beings]. (63–64)
Just as one feels affection for one's parents, for a daughter, or for servants and maidservants,
so indeed should one act toward the virtuous.
Even a worldly feeling of affection attains a divine state when directed toward the virtuous.
Through attaining the favor of a virtuous person, every undertaking succeeds.
Just as a wife perceives no faults in her own beloved husband, nor does she perceive wicked deeds or evil dispositions, but rather perceives only his excellent qualities.
Likewise, O Lakṣmī, those among the virtuous whose vision is pure perceive even faults as being entirely virtues;
they alone, having attained the auspicious favor of the holy ones, [attain liberation].
Having received blessings, having obtained the fruit of their service,
and likewise having gained affection and the joy of self-surrender, they attain supreme delight in the Self and cross over the ocean of worldly existence. (3.189.70)
Their affection may indeed exist, and let it be even greater than that for wife and son;
such a person, purified by virtuous affection, crosses over Māyā.
Whether man, woman, or eunuch, one is liberated through affection for the saintly.
I speak this as truth, indeed as truth: I am of a virtuous form.
My greatness is known from the virtuous alone, and never from any other source.
The virtuous are my heart; my dwelling is always with the virtuous.
Satisfaction arises for me alone in pleasing the virtuous; I delight in them.
The virtuous are purifiers, their very forms sanctifying from the tips of their nails to the crown of their heads.
Listen, Lakṣmī, those who are wicked toward others truly cause distress to the virtuous.
In matters of food, drink, seating, and acts of hospitality;
in receiving guests and in service—they exhaust virtuous people.
They even compel the righteous, the elders, and the great men to serve as their slaves.
Devoid of wisdom, they thus accumulate heaps of sin through their actions;
some, regarding virtuous men as equal to their own wives,
provide them with fine food and have meals cooked for the sake of their own eating.
Some begged for a vessel and cool water for drinking;
indeed, those ignorant ones asked for both from the virtuous man just as servants do from their master.
Others asked for a ball and such, or even a seat for sleeping. (78–79)

Some ignorant people cause the virtuous to perform labor and service for their own sake, treating them as they would a slave; likewise, some cause the virtuous to provide hot water and fresh, hot food for their own benefit, treating them as they would a servant. (3.189.80)
Indeed, those who possess base knowledge recite their own inflated praises in assemblies (8.1).
They cause praise to be made for them just as from a messenger, and likewise from a virtuous man; just as from a bard, so too from a *sūta*—even so from a virtuous man (8.2).
Some, intoxicated with pride and arrogant, have the virtuous carry their own chests— burdensome with their contents— by the hands or even by the heads of those very people.
Some wicked ones even forcibly bow down humble, saintly men.
The wicked cause their own hymns of praise to be performed again and again.
Such sinners indeed, burdened by mountains of evil,
wander about here deprived of wealth and food, and eventually come to their rest.
Under the pretext of instructing the virtuous, they accomplish their own selfish ends;
devoted to their own interests, those clever men go at last to the abode of Yama.
And those proud ones who maintain their own existence among the virtuous—
Even those who engage in egoistic conduct go to the abode of Yama;
likewise, those who seek out virtuous people with sudden, malicious intent, and who falsely attribute faults and stains to the righteous. (87–88)
Those who are merciless and bring ill-repute upon the virtuous,
those haters of the company of the righteous, indeed go to the abode of Yama.
Listen, Lakṣmī, likewise those who revile the virtuous merely because of their outward appearance.
Those who never give even a tattered old rag,
yet criticize fine, high-priced garments given by others—
pure and beautifully colored— and speak of them as being "kingly" (ostentatious), [are condemned]. (3.189.90–91)
They indeed revile the bowl, the vehicle, and the mount of the virtuous; likewise, they revile the hall, the mansion, and even the hut of the holy man.
They revile his brilliance and they revile the gift that has been offered. (92)
They censure the offering of material substances and the rubbing of sandalwood paste;
they censure medicinal herbs and the like, as well as protection provided according to one's means;
and they censure wealth such as cows and buffaloes, even when acquired by righteous means.
Filled with envy, they revile acts such as helping others— a practice cultivated by the virtuous— and they likewise revile the wandering for alms and ascetic penance.
Upon merely seeing a temple or chaste women, they flare up with anger.
Even after beholding the celestial abodes blazing with splendor,
these Asura folk go at the end of their bodies to a cycle of sin within the lotus;
indeed, they are repeatedly tormented in the worlds of Yama and in miserable wombs.
Therefore, one should always worship my virtuous representative wearing my garb; perceiving him as myself, one should serve him and propitiate him with auspicious offerings.
One should likewise please him through devoted service and by surrendering all that one possesses.
Having offered devotion to Hari, one should also seek to please virtuous people;
one should constantly serve the guru and always serve one's parents; one should serve one’s husband with devotion and delight the saintly with devotion. (3.189.100)
One should worship the Lord with various sentiments and glorify Hari with faith.
One should always offer everything to the Deity and sustain one’s family. Having set aside all as an offering to Kṛṣṇa, one should eat; not otherwise.
For those who live in this manner, enjoyment and liberation are held in the palm of their hand.
(102) From reading, hearing, remembering, and even retaining this [teaching], the fruit of serving the virtuous shall be attained, and at the end of worldly experience, liberation will occur. (103)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fulfillment of All Desires through the Attainment of the Lord Cintāmaṇi by Meeting with Holy Men," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 189. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 190 [Author:
Chapter 191 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this wondrous tale:
there were a hundred devotees from the great Saurāṣṭra country who had gathered in a group [to visit] the sacred field of Kuṃkumavāpikā, Somanātha, and Raivata.

They went to Saurāṣṭra to establish such holy places as Svarṇavatī, Kṛṣṇabhūmi, and the beautiful Gopanārtha. On the way, they crossed the Mahī river and the Vāpī lake by boat, and thereafter [proceeded further].
Having crossed the Sābhramatī river, they arrived at Gopanātha; then, having performed the secret Prayāga rite, they entered the great Siṃhavana forest.
As soon as they had entered, they proceeded swiftly toward Somanātha.
Then, robbers bearing weapons arrived in the Siṃhāraṇya forest.
Among them was the leader of the robbers, Sāmāntavikrama by name,
accompanied by horsemen and joined by soldiers equipped with weapons and other gear.
Standing nearby, neither too close nor too far, Yantra and Nādānaka,
along with his followers, shouted terrifying threats;
they quickly formed a cordon around the assembly for the purpose of plundering.
In the midst [of the city], through terrifying threats, they placed a hundred men at the service of the Saṅgha.
Having brought together all the ornaments for women and whatever articles of adornment for men, those fierce men caused them to be piled up in one place.
They seized all the fine garments belonging to those in the caravan;
then the merchants, who were the leaders of the caravan, bound them with ropes.
[There were] the Padmacandra, the Śaṅkhacandra, and also the Śṛṅkhalācandra.
Those robbers bound Vanacandra and Vālicandra;
they inflicted beatings with sticks and other punishments upon the others to instill fear.
All those merchants, being terrified and tormented, became silent.
Severely beaten, they gave all their possessions to these robbers.
Among them was my devotee, the Vaiṣṇava Vanacandraka;
his wife, Sukhādevī, was also my devotee, O Rame.
From childhood, these two have been my devotees, worshipping me without interruption.
(14) These two Vaiṣṇavas, who are endowed with devotion and take refuge in Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, belong to the virtuous one named Sāyana-Āyanana through their yoga. (15)
In that time of distress, those two devotees then remembered me;
the other cowherd boys as well wept and remembered the Lord, crying,
"O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, please protect us from the robbers!"
In the forest, you are the protector of the helpless; you are Nārāyaṇa, whose protector is Kṛṣṇa. (17) You are the savior, the liberator from suffering, the guardian, and the father.
May Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the mother, the teacher, and Bāla-Kṛṣṇa protect [us]. (18)
"Since we, having committed sins, are being plundered within this forest, nevertheless, O Mādhava, grant protection to your own devotees.
We shall practice devotion to you and we shall indeed bestow gifts upon you. (19)
"O Lord Viṣṇu, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, protect all our possessions!
(3.190.20) We shall offer our wealth and other goods at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā, if you will grant us protection from these wicked plunderers. (21)
We shall offer all ornaments, whatever excellent garments there may be, silver coins, and gold coins at Aśvasarovara.
Having undertaken the vow during the month of Kārtika, we shall perform it with fruits and other offerings.
And we shall indeed constantly repeat the *Śatamālikā* hymn.
Having stayed for one month each during the month of Māgha in the monasteries of the virtuous, we shall perform service in accordance with the instructions of the saints.
Thus, Vanacandra and the others, afflicted and plundered by the robbers,
performed various acts of penance (mānatā) for the sake of liberation from the robbers.
Vanacandra’s wife, Sukhādevī, and the other women did likewise.
Whichever women were present within the assembly, they indeed entreated me:
"O Hari! O forest-dweller! O you who take delight in wandering in Vṛndāvana!
O Kṛṣṇa, hidden within the midst of the multitude of gopīs, protect your female servants! || 26-27 ||
To the weak you are strong; to your devotees you are the Blessed Lord.
To your servant-maids you are the creator of joy; O Kṛṣṇa, protect these servant-maids!
In the forest you are the one who sports with the cowherd girls; in the solitude you are the friend of Rādhā.
O Kṛṣṇa, who brings joy to Kamalā upon your couch, protect your maidservants! (29) At the time of dissolution you are served by the liberated; at the time of creation you are the Lord of the devoted;
in the Rāsa dance you are enamored of all—O Kṛṣṇa, protect your maidservants! (3.190.30)
O Lord of those distressed in calamity, protector of those who seek refuge,
remover of the suffering of enemies, O Kṛṣṇa, protect your maidservants!
You are the nourisher of the fetus in the womb, and in childhood you dwell within the stainless hearts [of your devotees].
O Kṛṣṇa, you who were the object of our love in youth, protect your maidservants!
O best of the learned, you who grant victory in battle, you who are the refuge for the helpless—O Kṛṣṇa, protect your maidservants! (32–33)
O Kṛṣṇa, may he who was formerly the demon Rohiṇāṇḍa, yet is the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, having been slain by you, protect us. O Lord,
you were formerly the beginningless Śrī Meru-Nārāyaṇa.
Protection was indeed afforded by you to Meru as it was falling downward;
[so too] in the past, protection and peace were provided by you, the beginningless Viṣṇu in the form of Nārāyaṇa, to the universe being consumed by the fire of the sun.

O Śrī Hari, in the past, you— whose self is the primordial Lord Nārāyaṇa— brought about the destruction of the demon Dhūmra and provided protection for Candra. O Anādi Yajña-Nārāyaṇa, it was by you that the sacrifices were set in motion.
In ancient times, you were indeed the beginningless Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of Rudra;
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you became the beginningless Āditya-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of regulating the abodes of the gods. O Kṛṣṇa, protect your female servants!
O Garuḍa, you who possess the form of Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the Nāgas,
you became the primordial Ārṣa-Nārāyaṇa for the sake of eternal stability; indeed,
it was solely for the purpose of the defeat of the Daityas, beginning with Śurānanda.
You are the beginningless Prājña-Nārāyaṇa, O Supreme Lord.
You are the beginningless Vīra-Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the righteous.
You are the beginningless Bhadra-Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of liberating those who have been consumed by suffering.
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you were Harinārāyaṇa, the husband of the daughter of Tuṅgabhadrāsana; protect your maidservants!
In the past, for the sake of destroying the demon named Kośasta, you became that very being.
The beginningless Śrībījanārāyaṇa is the protector of the seed.
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you became Anādiśrīvaranārāyaṇa for the sake of the liberation of the sons of Dharmavrata; may that Nārāyaṇa protect us. 44–45.
By the curse of the great virtuous Sudarśanī, the world became female in nature;
for the sake of its protection, you attained the state of the primordial male Nārāyaṇa.
You are the beginningless Śrī Jala-nārāyaṇa; [you slew] the Makara demon.
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having slain the Rakṣasas who do not protect the worlds, please protect us, your maidservants.
(47) In ancient times, you were the beginningless Śrī Śīlanārāyaṇa;
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of thoroughly protecting the dharma of the virtuous, please protect us, your maidservants. (48)
In the past, you were the beginningless Śrīvardhinārāyaṇa;
O Kṛṣṇa, protect these maidservants from tigers, fire, and other dangers.
In the past, you were the beginningless Caturmukhanārāyaṇa.
You became the bestower of desired fruits to Rādhanikā and Puṇyarāta;
formerly, you were Śrī Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa.
For the sake of purifying the holy places, you became the beginningless Tīrthanārāyaṇa. || 3.190.50-51 ||
For the sake of devotion, you became the beginningless Śrījīvanārāyaṇa;
in the sacrifice, you became the illustrious Ardhaśrīśvaranārāyaṇa;
and as the deliverer of your fathers, you became the beginningless Ardhaśrīpitṛnārāyaṇa.

Out of devotion, for the sake of instructing [the people] on liberation, you became Plakṣanārāyaṇa. (53) In the Naramedha sacrifice—O Lord of Gods, O Kṛṣṇa, having become Narāyaṇa, the primordial Person who protects his devotees, you acted; now protect your female servants. (54)
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, in former times you became Anādinārāyaṇa through King Sūryavarcas; protect these female servants.
You were indeed the beginningless Śrīrājanārāyaṇa in the past.
O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of the Asuras and peacock-emblemed one, protect your maidservants!
O Kṛṣṇa, you who were formerly the beginningless, illustrious Brahmachārī Nārāyaṇa, for the sake of protecting those committed to lifelong celibacy, protect your maidservants! (56–57)
For the sake of destroying the demon Hālaka and for the sake of restoring Śiva to life,
you formerly became the beginningless Śrī Śivanārāyaṇa;
you formerly became the beginningless Śrī Svarṇanārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of reviving Kubera, protect the maidservants.
In ancient times, You, the beginningless Lord Śrī Svāminārāyaṇa, performed the protection of the people who had been consumed by the mountain fire that was red with flames. (3.190.59–60)
In former times, you became the beginningless and protective Nārāyaṇa together with Lakṣmī, who was propitiated by the Nirvāṇika; may he protect [us].
In the past, through devotion to King Aṃśukrama, you became [the Lord] himself.
May that Kṛṣṇa, the beginningless Śrī Sādhu Nārāyaṇa, protect us.
May he who became the beginningless Śrī Bhakta Nārāyaṇa for the sake of reviving the life of the cursed Varṇiśāla protect us.
In the past, for the sake of liberating the lord of the earth who was wearing armor, you yourself became the primordial Lord Śrī Medhanārāyaṇa; may he protect us.
In the past, for the sake of destroying the great asura Anala, you [became... 64.
May that Nārāyaṇa, who became the primordial fire of Śrī, protect us.
(65) For the sake of destroying the belly of Ilā, you became Rasanārāyaṇa;
as such, O Kṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, protect your female servants. (66)
O Kṛṣṇa, O Kṛṣṇa, you were formerly the beginningless Śrī Cakranārāyaṇa, the destroyer of the Daityas; protect us, your maidservants.
You are the beginningless Satyanārāyaṇa who established the Dharma.
For the sake of establishing the unseen [truth], you were formerly the beginningless Śrī-Hiraṇyanarāyaṇa; for the sake of your devotees, you were the beginningless Śrī-Nairañjaninārāyaṇa;
and you also became the beginningless Śrī-Puṇyanārāyaṇa in the past. (68–69)
May that Kṛṣṇa, the remover of the curse of Puṇyavatī, protect us!
You became the beginningless, glorious, great Brahman Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of fulfilling the minds of the Apsarases, protect these maidservants.
In ancient times, you were the beginningless Śrī Guru Nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of bestowing the knowledge of Brahman, protect these maidservants.
You are the one who bestowed the auspicious initiation at the sacrifice of King Bṛhadharma.
May that beginningless, glorious Ācārya Nārāyaṇa protect us.
In ancient times, he was the beginningless, glorious Mahāvidyunnārāyaṇa;
he is Vidyut, the slayer of the Daityas. O Kṛṣṇa, protect your female servants!
In the past, you were the beginningless, glorious Madhu-nārāyaṇa;
O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of the Asuras who consume honey, protect your maidservants!
In the past, you were also the beginningless, glorious Nātha-nārāyaṇa.
O Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of destroying the Daityas during the Tiṣya [age], protect the maidservants;
for you were formerly Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Lord of Śrī.
O Kṛṣṇa, at the golden festival of Brahmā, protect the maidservants.
In the past, you were the beginningless Śrī Mokṣanārāyaṇa;
and now, O beloved Keśava, you are the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
O Lord of Brahmapriyā and the others, protect us from robbers!
"O Bālakṛṣṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of the beloveds, show us mercy!
Quickly grant protection from these plunderers; we have come to you for refuge.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, those women also meditated upon Hari.

I, Hari myself, having arrived there, became invisible for a moment while listening to the words of praise concerning my past deeds; meanwhile, the plunderers were gathering coins and other valuables in one place. (3.190.80–81)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Hymn by the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha when it was Harassed by Robbers," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. Chapter 191 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 191: The Arrival of the Lord of the Gods and the Liberation of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha from the Robbers. Śrī Nārada said: O great sage, having heard the hymn of praise uttered by the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, what did the Lord of the Gods do? Please tell me this. Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: O Brahmin, having heard the hymn of praise uttered by the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, the Lord of the Gods, accompanied by his retinue, arrived there. Upon seeing the Lord of the Gods arrive, the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, with palms joined in reverence, bowed down and offered him worship. Then the Lord of the Gods spoke to them. The Lord of the Gods said: O members of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, why have you come here? What is the cause of your distress? Tell me everything truthfully. The members of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha said: O Lord of the Gods, we are being harassed by robbers. We have been plundered of our wealth and possessions. O Lord of the Gods, please protect us from these wicked men. The Lord of the Gods said: O members of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, do not fear. I shall protect you all from the robbers. You need have no anxiety. Śrī Śukadeva Gosvāmī said: Having spoken thus, the Lord of the Gods took up his divine weapons and set out toward the place where the robbers were. Seeing the Lord of the Gods approaching, the robbers fled in all directions. Then the Lord of the Gods, having liberated the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha from the robbers, returned to his own abode. The members of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha, having been freed from their fear, returned to their own city and lived happily ever after. Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Arrival of the Lord of the Gods and the Liberation of the Mahāsaurāṣṭryī Saṅgha from the Robbers," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. [The Author: Chapter 192.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, Lakṣmī, both the girls and the boys were also overwhelmed with distress.
I heard what they were saying as they praised me for the sake of their own protection.
(1) He who, having liberated the divine princess Divyādevī—the daughter of Divodāsa—who was bereft of fortune from her distress, established her in his own imperishable state and led her there. (2)
May that Lord Bālakṛṣṇa protect us, O female attendants!
In ancient times, a Bhilla woman and a Bhilla attained liberation through the power of your holy man.
King Subāhu, together with his wife, [attained it] by taking refuge in a saint.
O Kṛṣṇa, in former times, through your majesty, [the sage] attained the path of liberation.
O Kṛṣṇa, you protected the maiden Aśokasundarī, the virtuous daughter of Śaṅkara, in the past; now protect us, your servants.
In the past, you assumed the form of a woman for the sake of destroying Vihuṇḍa;
as the husband of Kāmodā, may he protect us, your female attendants.
You are the one who granted liberation to Śuka; protect us, your own daughters.
There was a Khaśa named Viṣṇudāsa and his beautiful wife was Rāmaṇī;
their daughter was Līlāvatī, who was previously brought forth by you, O Lord.
O Kṛṣṇa, O All-pervading One, the sins of courtesans were indeed [purified] by you in the past.
O Lord, having performed meritorious deeds, you then created meritorious people;
in ancient times, you also made courtesans and yoginīs. You [created] the Śvapacī woman named Rakṣā, who was the wife of Sumara.
May that Lord Kṛṣṇa, the giver of liberation who is free from material existence, protect us, his servants— He who in ancient times made Kauśika, Garuḍa, and Mālava the Vaiśya,
as well as others, experts in singing.
May he who led us to the world of Brahmā protect us, O female attendants;
may he who granted liberation to the Brahmin Harimiśra protect us.
Formerly, you [O Goddess] were the wife of Jiṣṇu to the great queen Citāmbare.
Having handed over the mace, he provided protection from the Bhadraka Rākṣasa.
And may that Jīvana protect us, along with her attendants, the Raṇeśvarīs, who were made his own by him; they are dear to Brahmā and are the daughters of Gadā.
May he by whom even Nārāyaṇa was made black protect us;
may he by whom the lords of battle were likewise liberated protect us;
and may he by whom the liberation of Bindumatī, the wife of Yayāti, was brought about, protect us.
May that Mādhava protect us from the plunderers of the forest;
may this Kṛṣṇa, who possesses lovely qualities and by whom Paraśucandraka was delivered, protect his own servants.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect us— he who led the cowherd’s wife Sucandrīkā and her husband, the cowherd, to the imperishable abode.
May he, the consort of Hari, the first Manu, lead [us] along the path of Brahman toward the Imperishable.
May that Kṛṣṇa by whom Hari was brought [to us] protect us.
May that Kṛṣṇa— the Supreme Soul by whom the liberation of the vultures was accomplished in the past— Bālakṛṣṇa, Harikṛṣṇa, he, Kṛṣṇa, protect us.
May that Kṛṣṇa who granted liberation to Jīvacandra protect us;
may that very Śrī Hari by whom the sons of Śatānanda and Vinodinī were liberated protect us.
May He who grants liberation to the women of Kāśī protect us. May that Kṛṣṇa— who,
by means of his power as a bull, protected the sparrows,
and who is the beginningless Kṛṣṇa, the Black Child— protect us.
May that Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, by whom the liberation of Citraketu and Queen Mālatī was formerly accomplished, protect us;
may that Kṛṣṇa, by whom the virtuous have been made preeminent, protect us.
May he by whom the fire was made lean-limbed protect [us].
May that very Lord Kṛṣṇa, by whom the man Nara and the woman Nārī were repeatedly made to sound like broken reeds, protect his own female attendants here.
May the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, who protected Vipula and Devaśarman, protect us from this suffering; He is the bestower of liberation.
In ancient times, at the sacred ford named Gokarṇa, it was by Him that the sages were settled.
May that very Blessed One protect us from robbers. May Kṛṣṇa, who ordained the welfare of Kuvalāśva, as well as Uttaṅka, Satyavrata, and Gālava, protect us.
By whose majesty the powerful Brahmasādhu became renowned;
may that Kṛṣṇa protect us from plunderers.
And indeed, Ālambāyana, the son of Keśarinī, attained liberation.
May He by whose majesty Kṛṣṇa protected the hundred thousand virtuous men at Gokarṇa and led them to the imperishable abode—
may that dear and beloved Bālakṛṣṇa protect us, O beloveds! || 31-32 ||
May that Kṛṣṇa protect you, his attendants— he by whom the Śabara, the Rākṣasa, as well as the vulture and the outcaste were liberated from the bonds of worldly existence;
he who, seeing the head of Khyāti intent on cursing, severed it.
May that Kṛṣṇa protect us from robbers, O His own female attendants!
May He who delivered Bhāruṇḍa and Puṣkasa protect us;
may that Kṛṣṇa who released Vṛṣādarbhi protect us. (34–35)
May that Kṛṣṇa protect you, his devotees— he by whom the thief Naraśāya was liberated, he by whom the wealthy were set free,
he by whom Kundadharmā was protected, and he by whom the sacrifice of Jāṅgalāma was preserved.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, of divine beauty, protect our daughters.
May that Bālakṛṣṇa, by whom even Śambhalavāra was liberated along with his subjects, protect us, his beloved servants, here. 37–38.
Bālakṛṣṇa was born in the divine lineage of the hosts of gods;
may that very Lord protect His own servants here.
Salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; salutations!
Salutations to the one born as Śrī Kambharā, Lakṣmī, and Gopāla! Salutations!
May that very Śrī Hari, by whom the eminent brahmin Dīrghaśīla was liberated from the noose of Yama, protect his own female devotees. 40–41.
May this Lord, our Master— who liberated the Brahmin woman Brahmasatī by means of the Supreme Self— protect us, his own female servants.
[42] The great queen Kālandharā and the king named Vaivarta—
May that Kṛṣṇa, by whom Vṛṣagamana, the son of Romapāda, was liberated, protect his servants. May that Kṛṣṇa, by whom Vṛṣagamana, the son of Romapāda, was liberated, protect his servants. (43–44)
May that Bālakṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa protect us— he by whom the thief Agrabhaṅga was formerly liberated,
and by whom the wielder of the discus (Cakrin) slew the demon Bhaṇḍāsura through Lalitā.
May that Kṛṣṇa, whose splendor is dark, protect us here,
O servant girls! May that Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, by whom millions of maidens from the Mānasa-lake were accepted as his own in the past, protect you, O servant girls!
May that Kṛṣṇa, who brought liberation to the Vaiśya Lohāṅgāra and by whom Pīvarī and others were established with their desires fulfilled through his vow,
protect us from robbers, we who are his female servants.
May that Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa protect us— he by whom Vasiṣṭha and Agastya were liberated from their curse,
and by whom the cruel hunter was released along with his wife. (49–50)
May she who brings liberation even to Puṣkaravāhana protect us—
she who is the lotus-lake, the creator of the pitcher, the virtuous sovereign, and endowed with compassion. By her grace, Padminī became equal to Kamalā.

May that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect us from robbers. (5.2) He who provided protection for the brahmin Dharmatapas, and he who granted the status of a Manu to Suratha—may that Lord of Śrī [protect us]. (5.3)
By that Supreme Self, Dhanavarmā was sent to heaven;
likewise, O twice-born one, Balīśvara was established in his kingdom among men, and by him also,
Ānandavarṇin was likewise established among men.
May Kṛṣṇa protect his servants— he by whom the Śūdra Ghṛṇeṣika was established in the kingdom of Mānava, by whom Bhūti was saved,
and by whom the demon Bālaka was rescued and turned into jewels. (55–56)
May that Viṣṇu, by whom Bāṣkali was destroyed, protect us;
by Gajanārāyaṇa, Purukutsara was slain;
and by the wielder of the Śārṅga bow in his form as a fish, Pralamba was destroyed.
By him indeed Bhīmaratha was slain in the form of a tortoise;
by him Śāntaśatru was slain in the form of a swan;
and Mahākāla was destroyed by him as Hayagrīva.
May that Kṛṣṇa, the slayer of Hiraṇyākṣa, protect his own female devotees;
may Vāmana and Kṛṣṇa, the destroyers of Kālakākṣa, protect them as well.
May Hari, the enemy of Bali and the slayer of the gods, dispel all suffering.
May the Lord who destroyed the Ten-necked one protect us in the form of a woman;
may Hari, the slayer of Tāraka, protect us even in the form of a neuter;
and he by whom the Ṭiṭṭibha bird was formerly struck down in the form of a peacock.
May that wielder of the discus, by whom Śuci was slain, protect us;

likewise may Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of liberation, protect us—[he who is the protector] of Sādhubhāvāyana, of the sage Ṛṣi, and of the illustrious Anasa. May Kṛṣṇa also protect us, [the protector] of Cidānanda.
May he who liberated Sadvidyā, the wife of Yanapa, who was indeed the fruit of sacred revelation, protect us;
may he who brought about the liberation of Alarka’s mother protect us.
He is the channel for the stream of liberation and likewise the gateway to the forms of supernatural powers.
May that Śrī Kṛṣṇa protect us— he whose refuge has liberated this Ṛṣi, who was a husband with hands folded in supplication for alms and a master of wandering mendicancy;
he by whom both his mother, who sought eternal refuge, and his son Keśin were set free.
May that Great King Bālakṛṣṇa protect us here.
He by whom his mother Cāraṇī and his son Vyāghra were delivered;
he by whom his virtuous father Kūṭadeva and Śyāma were delivered. (67–68)
May Kṛṣṇa protect his servant— he by whom the supreme Bhūdeva and the Ṛṣi Devāyana were likewise liberated from distress;
he by whom the Vaiśya Virālaka was indeed uplifted along with his family.
May Bālakṛṣṇa, whose life is his beloved, protect [us] from robbers.
May he who rescued King Pṛthvīdhara and Queen Madhuvindā,
as well as the wretched Durvoḍhaka, protect [us].
May he who protected Sāgara, Śūdraka, and the king named Venapāla,
as well as Hīrukā, the wife of a Śūdra, protect us.
[Likewise,] Vṛkṇadeva, Bhāvaśūra, and the virtuous Satī.
May this very Kṛṣṇa, by whom they were liberated, protect his female servants.
May Mañjulakeśa, Bhūdeva, Pāśupateśa, Viprarāja, Bāṇāṅgaṇa, and likewise Śūdra— may he who protected them grant us protection.
May he by whom Mṛtādana, Santadāsa, Dharmaśālāyana,
Śaṅkudhara, and Uddhṛta were subdued protect his servants.
And this lord of plunderers is Sāmantavikrama by name.
O Kṛṣṇa, alas Kṛṣṇa, protect us! He is plundering our entire wealth.
We belong to you here, we belong to you here; O servant of yours, protect us!
O Inner Self, O Pervasive Self, O Infinite One, protect us here!
The children also likewise offered hymns of praise to Kṛṣṇa.
O Rame, hearing this, I suddenly assumed a hundred forms there.
Horsemen, camel-riders, armed kings, and soldiers [were present].
Having arrived from afar with a speed of fifty [yojanas] for the sake of protection, they indeed raised a loud cry:
"Let the thieves be ready!
We shall surely kill them here; let the mothers and sons perish! || 79-80 ||
Thus making the thieves hear their cries and causing them to burst with fear,
the king’s attendants, in an instant, surrounded those robbers in all ten directions with camels, horses, and other beasts;
having hemmed in those circles of thieves, the royal officers—
They went before [him] to overpower, punish, and strike;
meanwhile, having fallen into a rage and abandoned all hope for life,
they fled from the Middle Country, shouting insults and letting out bursts of laughter.
Then, O Lakṣmī, my attendants quickly discharged slingshots;
a mutual battle ensued consisting of those slings and pellets.
All those exceedingly arrogant ones were pierced by me with my own pellet-machines.
All fifty of them died there, pierced by the cow's horns.
I brought all of them, who had died, to heaven with my own hands;
then I consoled those merchant devotees whom I had liberated.
All those men, women, young girls, and children, having sought refuge,
fell at my feet as I appeared in the form of an army.
Then I bestowed upon them wealth according to their needs.
I gave away my entire possession—ornaments, garments, and all else—to each person as they deserved.
All of them became happy; I touched their beaten limbs, and they became free from pain as well as free from fear.
Then, O Lakṣmī, suddenly concealing the forms of the horses, camels, and soldiers, I alone became the four-armed Nārāyaṇa;
I caused Vanacandra and Sukhādevī to behold my own form.
Then he gave his own vision to all the others as well. Overcome by supreme wonder, they all fell at my feet;
they had all sought refuge, being devotees equal in their devotion.
Then, in that forest grove, I gave them my mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. [And:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Anādi Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa! (93)
"O Lord of the beloved of Brahmā, O Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, grant me protection!
[94] Then, O Kamalā, he bestowed the great Vaiṣṇava initiation upon her;
thereafter, he crossed over all the forests and regions. [95]
Having inquired after the welfare of all and pointed out the path to the sacred ford,
O Lakṣmī, I vanished there; they too then slowly proceeded to Prabhāsa,
from there to Raivata, and from there they arrived at Aśvapaṭṭa.
At that time, they performed all those acts of penance (*mānatā*) consisting of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), giving gifts (*dāna*), and self-restraint (*ātma-pratā*);
they took the form of offering their entire possessions (*sarvasva-arpaṇa*).
They performed my worship and likewise rendered service to the virtuous (*sat*).
All of them, being restored to health, performed devotion to me at every sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Then they went to the Golden City, Camatkārapurī;
from there they reached their own country and performed devotion to me constantly.

O Lakṣmī, those who were devoted to my devotees have been delivered and protected by me; at the end of their bodies, they have been led to my abode. Even those who were thieves and plunderers, if they knew my true nature, [attained that same state].
Indeed, I have brought them from heaven to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha at the end.
Thus, being compassionate, I protect and lead those who have taken refuge in me;
I release them from the bonds of worldly existence and uplift them.
"From reading and hearing this, there shall likewise be enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, assuming the forms of royal officers and others, slew the plunderers and protected the devotees following the praise of women and children for the sake of protection from robbers," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
