Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to this purifying story of a devotee. Formerly, there was a brāhmaṇa named Dhaniṣṭhakoṣa who possessed great wealth and other riches. (1)
He was a performer of sacrifices and rituals, a worshiper of the five deities (Pañcāyatana),
devoted to bhakti, exceedingly generous, and likewise possessed of the wealth of a thousand cows.
He was the lord of fields, gardens, and forests, endowed with industry and perseverance.
Indeed, there were always hundreds of thousands of gold and silver coins in his treasury.
Though highly honored by the king and respected in many ways by the Lord of Yuddhapura,
King Mālavasiṃha constantly offered him auspicious betel.
He bestows upon him great honor and dignity in the assembly hall within the magnificent palace;
he seeks his very approval for matters of state that are exceedingly difficult to manage.
Indeed, he honors the Brahmin as the foremost and most eminent leader.
In all festivals, monasteries, and water-stations (prapās), in assemblies,
and in every auspicious duty that was to be performed, he regarded the twice-born as his own kin.
And the affection of the subjects for him, whose treasury was most abundant, became supreme.
Indeed, for the sake of assisting his subjects,
he bestows wealth even without a written document, for truthfulness is the very price of his word.
And [he provides for] the wretched, the poor, and the helpless women.

He provided assistance with clothing, food, and other necessities to virtuous people and mendicants. He restored many dilapidated houses, numerous temples, religious rest-houses, and monasteries for holy men. (3.192.10)
He caused water-stations and food-distributions to be established like a king;
the king also provided him with assistance everywhere.
Dhaniṣṭhaka constantly worships me, the Supreme Lord.

Having bathed and worshipped me, O King, and then met with me, he thereafter bows to the five deities and others; he eats daily, and never otherwise. His entire family is my devotee and always worships me, O Rāma.

Now, the intoxication of sovereignty, the intoxication of fortune, as well as the intoxication of wealth and even the intoxication of youth, lead a person astray. So too do the violent impulses of the senses and the presence of sense objects.
The fickleness of the mind also casts the devotee into impurity.
Whether in constant dancing or yoga, or in constant assemblies of instrumental music, or in constant states of erotic passion, the quality of *rajas* increases. (15–16)
Constant engagement with sense objects and constant association with worldly things carry away the mind— just as a swift current flows downward—
just so does the conduct of this devoted person in the assembly of kings [distract him]. (17)

For by attending dances performed by courtesans and others during the nights and other such times, and through living together with female slaves and the like, the mind becomes subject to corruption. Even those women who are beautiful become lustful and delusive through the desire for wealth. (18–19)
With seductive gestures, amorous states, services, and shared dwellings, the courtesans cast my devotee— who was like a treasury of wealth— into delusion;
they gradually caused him to become immersed in most delightful sense objects.
Seized by greed, they remained before him, waiting to enjoy the wealth once it was obtained.
Although he was my devotee, having abandoned his devotion and fallen into association with the king,
he then frequently took up residence in the royal garden.
At times he would look after his own family for a long duration,
while at other times he would spend much time in the garden together with the king.
The king, too, always attended upon him as his childhood friend.
Through drinks, food, games, and the like, as well as through dancing, singing, and entertainment— thus,
when a devotee is joined with sense objects that engage the external faculties,
my worship, recitation, and meditation all gradually [occur]. (24–25)
Having suffered injury and fallen into dissolution, my devotion toward him became broken.
He occasionally remembers me, but especially women;
attended by courtesans, he remains devoted to sexual indulgence.
Then his sons and daughters, and his virtuous wife, the devoted partner named Snehalatādevī, lamented for the condition of her husband:
"My most fortunate wife worships me, Śrī Hari. (27–28)
She indeed prays for the protection of her husband’s dharma through worship, for the abandonment of unrighteousness, and for fame, glory, and birth in a noble lineage.
"Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Kṛṣṇa, Puruṣottama, Mādhava! [29]
"Quell that restlessness which exists in the mind of your devotee.
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Śrīkānta Keśava, release me from the addiction to the sexual union of my husband."
O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that the king may also become your devotee;
O Supreme Soul, act so that even the courtesans may become your devotees;
and O Kṛṣṇa, show such grace that the subjects as well may become your devotees.
"From this day forward until the end of the year, I shall observe a vow of eating but once a day;
likewise, with a concentrated mind, I shall serve virtuous women and perform your worship every day for the duration of one ghaṭikā."
During the period of birth-impurity, I shall perform worship with the sixteen types of offerings.
I shall also have a golden swing fashioned, as well as a golden image of you,
endowed with Śrī and joined by Rādhā and Ramā.

I shall likewise have a most excellent and auspicious bedstead fashioned, joined with Padmāvatī, endowed with Māṇikya, beautiful, accompanied by Lakṣmī, delightful, richly adorned, and in the full bloom of youth. (36–37)
I shall also have your implements made of gold and silver—
fans, chowries, an umbrella, sandals, and ornaments—
all fashioned from gold and jewels for your satisfaction.

I shall perform constant massage with the essence of fragrant substances and the essence of oils (39), as well as anointing with liquid unguents and worship with *tulasī* leaves; for the sake of his supreme satisfaction, I shall offer oblations of ghee and desired foods. (3.192.40)
"O beloved Keśava, I shall cause your festivals to be celebrated annually;
deliver my husband, this merchant, from his addiction to courtesans.
Here I am, having come to you for refuge, fallen at your feet. (41)
"Kindle the sins of my husband and do what is pleasing," she said.
Having spoken thus on the day of the festival of lights (Dīpotsava) dedicated to Hari, Snehalatikā performed my worship and observed the vow for an entire year.
That virtuous woman observed all the prescribed rules;
indeed, she completed the vow named Patisaṃskāraka.
On the final day, she performed the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the vow by means of a mountain of food.
On the very next day, in order to complete his vow, he had a pavilion constructed for the festival of Kṛṣṇa;
it was adorned with plantain pillars,
provided with archways and other ornaments, beautiful, and equipped with sacrificial pits and altars.
It was provided with lion-thrones and graced by Brahmins, deities, and others; it was endowed with the materials for offerings to gods and ancestors, as well as the requisites for giving;
and it resounded with the sounds of sacrificial fuel, fire, ritual acts, the Vedas, and mantras.
It resounded with the chanting and other recitations performed by virtuous men and women and devotees of Viṣṇu;
it was filled with the sounds of musical instruments, hymns, and songs, and augmented by the giving of gifts.
It was presided over by the inhabitants of the worlds such as Satyaloka and others.
It was graced by the arrival of holy bathing places (*tīrtha*) and the divine nature [of its inhabitants], adorned with the attendants of Kṛṣṇa,
embellished by the playful movements of the beloved of Brahmā, and endowed with banners and flags;
it was beautified by a preeminent maṇḍala named Sarvatobhadra, which signifies "auspicious on all sides."
Where Mādhava is worshipped with sacrificial implements such as bowls, jars, and vessels, along with gifts of beds and other articles,
and where oblations of various kinds are offered into the fire. (51–52)
Where Vedic chants and mantras are recited by the Brahmins,
where gifts consisting of gold and silver are bestowed,
and where desired foods and delicacies are enjoyed by the Brahmins. (93)
And blessings that bestow prosperity were given by those with contented minds.
Then, a stream of clarified butter was offered as the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
At that time, the aged Nārāyaṇa-Nara arrived there at the pavilion.
"O Lakṣmī, he who was I in the form of a brahmin, possessed of great splendor, is indeed that very same one.
The gods and the sages welcomed me and offered me hospitality;
they gave me an excellent seat, and Agni worshipped me as well."
There, I, a twice-born man honored by all, sat down.
"Whose sacrifice is this? I asked that wise brahmin.
That brahmin, Somāyana, replied to me with a glance of his finger.
"For this creeper of affection, there exists today a sacrifice for the conclusion of her vow;
may what is desired for her success be fulfilled here.
And I immediately said, "May it be so," at that very sacrifice.
Listen, Lakṣmī, a great marvel occurred then in that garden.
There, in the palace where the great merchant, the king, and his servants resided, that palace began to tremble as if shaken by an earthquake. (3.192.60–61)
At that time, I took no pleasure in anything other than the palace together with its gardens.
Then, by my very will, that terrifying earthquake occurred;
the palace collapsed, and by it, the courtesans were crushed to pieces.
The king and the merchant fell there upon the middle floor of the collapsing palace;
though their limbs were broken, they survived in fear.
Having fallen together, they regained consciousness and met one another. (63–64)
As they were calling out to one another, the king asked, "What is your condition, O wealthy man?
The wealthy man replied, "My foot is broken at the knee.
The king said, "My hand is broken at the elbow."
No other suffering exists here, for our lives still persist.
Indeed, death has not occurred; rather, this [state] was brought about by the Supreme Lord.
Having abandoned the path of Śrī Hari, we have followed the way of courtesans. (66–67)
This evil was grasped by her, and its fruit is this destruction;
nevertheless, through former merit or through the merit of our relatives,
we two live here within the belly, in the space granted by Kṛṣṇa.
"From this day forward, we shall indeed abandon association with courtesans;
we shall worship the Supreme Lord and observe sacred vows, so that we may escape from this wretched place where no refuge can be found. (3.192.70)
"We shall surely emerge alive from this broken middle;
let us worship Nārāyaṇa here, and he will grant us protection.
Having thus reached their decision, the two of them chanted "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa."
O Lakṣmī, those two were protected by the merit of the sacrifice of the creeper of their affection.
(72) Then, immediately after the final oblation of the sacrifice in Yuddhapura, the collapse of the royal palace was heard from the mouths of the people. (73)
The atheists declared that the result produced by the transgression in the sacrifice was real;
however, no such transgression had actually occurred in the ritual.
Indeed, that [result] arose through my will and by the sin of the merchant.
The courtesans were defiled by the falling of my food;
they died indeed through their own sin, while the devotee was protected by me.
Even the king, through his connection with the devotee, was protected by me for the sake of devotion.
Then the believers said, "The wicked have died due to their own sins;
nevertheless, because of the merit of the sacrifice, the merchant and the king have not died.
And the men, having gone quickly to the entire Kāṭamāla forest, [reported this].
Having slowly moved far away and cleared the stones and soil,
they gradually extracted the merchant and the king, who were still alive though dwelling beneath the wooden structure with broken limbs, while administering medicinal herbs.
All those courtesans were found to be composed of corpses; they were mangled and truly dead, and they entered the city of Yama.
Upon being touched by Vṛddha, the merchant king quickly regained his hands and feet, becoming whole once more.
Having heard the news of the sacrifice, the two were indeed exceedingly delighted.
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, assuming the form of an old man, touched them both with his hands; Mūḍhamāra then vanished.
All suffering vanished, and the two met within the pavilion;
they beheld the meritorious deed and heard of the woman’s vow, performed for the sake of purifying her husband and likewise for the sake of purifying the king. (83)
Then, having learned of the vow undertaken by the woman for the sake of the purity of her offspring, the subjects, the king, and all the wealthy men praised the devoted wife:
"Blessed is this woman, a devotee of Hari, seeking liberation and purifying. (84–85)
For the sake of the welfare of her subjects and others, she observed her vows for a long time; she also offered her own wealth for the sake of divine rites.
By her merit, both this king and the merchant have been well protected.
"We shall all worship Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī.
The king also spoke clearly in that pavilion,
just as the merchant and the subjects had spoken in the pavilion.
We shall abandon all calamities and sinful deeds;
we shall worship Hari, Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, the eternal one.
We shall perform expiation for the sinful acts already committed.
"We shall indeed become Vaiṣṇavas and at the end go to the abode of Hari. Thus, hundreds of thousands of spectators who had come there—
both men and women, whether for the sake of the sacrifice or having arrived by chance— [spoke].
All the people born in that kingdom, their minds transformed by the power of the aged brahmin, trembled at the sight of the Vaiṣṇava initiation.
They accepted [the teachings] from the aged brahmin and abandoned their vices.
They wore a *tulasī* garland around their necks and took my name as "Bālakṛṣṇa.
They received the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," and they indeed became the best of Vaiṣṇavas. (93–94)
They all undertook the vow for the bright fortnight of Kārttika:
"You yourself shall eat only once a day, perform my worship every day, give gifts of food constantly, and likewise devote one ghaṭikā [of time] to my service. ||95||
Then, in that pavilion, I revealed my auspicious vision:
four-armed, of divine form, accompanied by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Ramā; together with Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, and Śrī, most enchanting. (96–97)
Adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, the Kaustubha gem, and necklaces;
his face enriched by a halo of divine splendor and decorated with armlets;
he is served by divine liberated attendants and great sages.
Having seen the Supreme Lord, who is worshipped by the sacrificial fires, the deities, and the gods,
and who had arrived for the sake of fulfilling the desires of his devotees,
they honored me and drank the water from my feet.
The lords of the earth accepted the remnants of the sacrifice and partook of them;
all of them brought the sacrifice to completion and then performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Likewise, the king and the merchants bathed in the Luṇī river.
O Rame, at that time, the sins of the people blazed up intensely.
There is the Avabhṛtha, the great ablution which destroys all sins;
for those who have committed even great crimes and offenses become pure by bathing there.
The king and the merchant remembered the courtesans for the sake of their liberation;
immediately, by the power of intoxication and through the merit of the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*),
all of them were swiftly released from the abode of Yama by the king and the merchant.
The women who had been liberated by the messengers arrived there on the bank of the Luṇyā;
they drank water, bathed, and were sprinkled with water by me.
Freed from their sins, they immediately attained divine bodies. || 105–106 ||
Then, by means of celestial chariots, they all departed for heaven;
thereafter, they shall proceed to the eternal abode of Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme realm of the Supreme Self.
Thus were those subjects liberated and made devoted to Viṣṇu.
The king and the merchant were freed from their afflictions and filled with devotion by the woman.
Then, having received worship, I quickly vanished from that place.
At the end of my lifespan, [I encountered] the affectionate creeper and likewise the twice-born Somāyana.
Dhaniṣṭhaka, the merchant, King Mālava-siṃha,
and all his Vaiṣṇava subjects— these, along with those who were disciplined, endowed with devotion, and free from adultery, [attained] my imperishable state at the proper time. || 3.192.10 ||
O Lakṣmī, having purified my devotee, I lead him to liberation.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even reflecting upon this, one who has practiced sinful deeds shall become pure and go to my abode. (111–112)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of How Śrī Hari Granted Liberation to the Merchant Dhaniṣṭhaka, who was addicted to courtesans, through the performance of the vow of devotion by his own wife," in the section concerning the Dvāpara Age within the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 193. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 193.
[The Author: Chapter 194.
Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the liberation of the slayer of a Brahmin.
In a village named Vāṭāsīna, there was a king named Rājīva.
His queen was the virtuous Kunda-nadevikā by name;
she was a daughter who possessed sons, devoted to dharma, and ascetic. (1–2)
Devoted to me and to Śrī Hari, intent upon vows and meditation, she is never seen by the sun and is untouchable by other men; with her I sport at times.
Devoted to the virtue of a faithful wife, she is dedicated to the worship of the gods, ritual bathing, and other such duties.
She observed the Cāturmāsya vows and performed festivals for Hari;
she was devoted to the duty of charity and distinguished by her service to others.
Having consecrated all her possessions for the sake of honoring and serving the virtuous, she was auspicious in every way. (4–5)
She serves the poor, the helpless, and cows; she worships the Sun;
she bestows honor upon maidens; and she is intent upon my propitiation.
She provides food and clothing for guests and those who have arrived.
She was always intent on worshipping the feet of her husband and performing pilgrimages;
thus endowed with refined character, she constantly recited her rosary, delighted in beholding the deity, and was ever engaged in listening to sacred discourses. (7–8)
She indeed knows the welfare and well-being of her own subjects;
she is devoted to the dharma of non-violence and dedicated to the vow of truth.
By her merit, the kingdom truly shines and rejoices greatly.

And his subjects were free from fear and disease, possessing great prosperity. (3.193.10) Now, O Lakṣmī, just as gold does not become fragrant, so too the husband of a golden wife shall go to a low state. (11)
Her husband is a cruel king who does not acknowledge the gods;
full of arrogance, he considers dharma, ritual action, and the like to be useless. He takes no account at all of the Brahmins, the virtuous, or those who are righteous.
The undiscerning person indeed shows contempt for those worthy of honor.
He performs neither ritual bathing, nor giving, nor worship, nor even virtuous vows;
he frequents neither sacred fords, nor offers hospitality, nor does he perform any righteous deed.
The property of the gods, the wealth of Brahmins, the wealth of the virtuous, and the property of the righteous—
whatever coin belonging to another is obtained even by force—
the greedy-souled man seizes it and never relinquishes it to anyone. (15)
Through theft, force, extortion, plunder, battle, and oppression;
through fraud and deception—he considers all that which is thus acquired to be just.
He regards injustice as justice itself; such is his understanding of the duties of a king.
Whatever wealth belongs to the subjects—fields, land, houses, and so forth;
their businesses and tax shares; and the subjects themselves—that is indeed my wealth.
My sons, daughters, cows, bulls, horses, and elephants [are likewise mine].
He knows all the vehicles, mounts, and animals belonging to the king;
for the kingdom belongs to the king and no one else, whether it be inanimate or sentient, since the king is the lord of the earth and the subjects indeed belong to the monarch. (3.193.20)
"Since the king enjoys the earth, he indeed enjoys the kings of the earth,
as well as all its transformations"— thus the lord of the land thinks.
Furthermore, he possessed a particular hatred toward the brahmins from his very birth.
"Brāhmaṇas carry away sweets and sacrificial fees in vain;
likewise, their wandering for alms is in vain. Brāhmaṇas are manifest robbers.
Thinking thus, upon seeing the Brāhmaṇas, he drives them far away. (22-23)
He indeed punishes in many ways and even seizes what has been begged.
Listen, O Brahmins: once there were twenty Tīrthaṅkaras;
though they wandered extensively and were devoted to no one, they came to the abode of Vāṭa, which was filled with Lakṣmī. (24)
Then, for the sake of providing rest on the road, they were honored by the queen with food,
clothing, drink, and the like, as well as gifts and vehicles. At that time,
the king also learned that they indeed possessed wealth even before him.
The king had previously given away vast wealth under the pretext of [establishing] a sacred ford;
however, having heard of this, the monarch was seized by greed and summoned the brāhmaṇas to his presence.
Thereupon, he plundered all that wealth belonging to the brāhmaṇas as well.
And on that day, out of anger, he confined everyone in prison. (28) Then the brahmins, being greatly incensed, uttered a fierce curse:
"Your kingdom shall perish, and you shall be deprived of your family and all else. (29)
Become a forest-dweller and a hypocrite, for you are indeed a base mendicant;
having enjoyed the fruit [of your actions] for twenty years in a bestial body,
O nihilist, O merciless one, experience all manner of sufferings.

The curse was pronounced by the brahmins during the day; at night, the lord of Vaṭodara arrived with his army and seized [the kingdom] through battle. Having appointed Deśapāla to his own kingdom, he placed [the others] in fetters. (3.1–3.2)
Having liberated the brahmins and provided a livelihood for the queen,
and having protected the king’s family there,
he then indeed began to search for the lotus stalk, even though it was difficult to find.

But King Rājīva, having abandoned his own city, quickly departed by a secret path for the forest region of the Narmadā. Due to the fault of the brahmins' curse, he remained there for twenty years. || 34–35 ||
In the forest, I experienced the suffering of a beast, filled with wretchedness. Then the queen, accompanied by her sons and daughters, took refuge in me;
she was renowned by the name Kundanadevī and was devoted to Kṛṣṇa.
Even while dwelling in the forest, Rājīva was indeed distressed by his own sins.
He committed many evils, such as plundering and slaughtering animals.
Thus, while he was living in the forest, a certain Brahmin [encountered] the Narmadā river. || 37-38 ||
While going to bathe in that forest, Rājīva met him nearby; he questioned that brāhmaṇa:
"Tell me now, where are you going? What is before you? Give me everything here! || 39 ||
The Brahmin said, "I have a small amount of wealth for provisions on my journey;
I will not give it to you, O forest-dweller, as it is intended only for my own use.
As they were thus disputing, a battle broke out between them.
Struck by Rājīva and crushed in the heart with stones,
this Brahmin was born there as a ghost on the bank of the Narmadā;
he writhed against the king, the slayer of his life and a killer of a Brahmin.
Then the king, unfortunate due to the curse and further afflicted by the Rākṣasa,
wandered through the forest lands like one distracted, insane, or dull-witted.
Nevertheless, Queen Kunda-nadevī remained devoted to her Brahmanical conduct.
Once, while he was asleep in the forest, he saw him in that state of suffering—
tormented by hunger and thirst, possessed by a *rākṣasa* and driven to madness,
having adopted the conduct of a beast and followed the way of a *rākṣasa*. (45)
And [he saw him] eating a dead animal or even a bird;
likewise, he was remembering and uttering the words "Kundana! Kundana!
He was black-complexioned, hairy, and bore coarse matted locks. (46–47)
Appearing as if it were someone else, with all its true nature laid bare—
whether a Śabara, a Pāradhi, a murderer,
or a dog-cooker— it is seen as such, inspiring fear even by its very sight.
Beholding such a forest-dweller, a personification of sin, whose body was exceedingly foul-smelling, soiled, and decrepit, repeatedly uttering "Kundanā! Kundanā! (3.193.50).
For a moment she reflected, "Who might this be in a dream?
Then, overcome with fear, she asked: "Who are you in the midst of the forest?
He replied: "I am named Rājīva, the husband of Kunda-nā."
"Afflicted as I am by the sin of the curse and especially by the Rākṣasa,
if Kundanā were to rescue me, then I would attain a good state.
As long as Kundanā hears what was spoken by the king while she is asleep..."
Then the queen’s sleep departed; at dawn she awoke.
Having risen, she was overcome with grief, distressed by the suffering of her husband.
Beholding [the world] as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of her hand, she acted with great haste.
Having bathed, the virtuous woman worshipped me, Śrīpati, the remover of suffering.
With a face overcome by grief and an exceedingly tormented mind, her eyes clouded with tears, the chaste lady uttered my name and offered praise to me. (55–56)
O Lord, Your desires are already fulfilled, for nothing remains to be attained.
Nevertheless, tell me, how have You come here into this cycle of worldly existence?
If it is for the sake of fulfilling the desire of a devotee, then fulfill my own wish.

"If you consider me your devotee, disciple, or servant, then Rājīva, who was seized by the Rākṣasa, must be liberated from the suffering of the forest. If, in every way, the destruction of karma occurs through the experiencing of its fruits, [then let this be so]. (58–59)
O Compassionate One, your compassion is in vain, and your arrival is in vain;
all your devotion is in vain as well, because you have not fulfilled the needs of one who seeks every object of desire.
For I am indeed a woman seeking wealth, yet I am nevertheless your servant.
"Bring about the salvation of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa!
O Kṛṣṇa, if Your grace does not arise for the sake of this sinner, I shall give my own merit to him; by that means, You must deliver him. (61-62)

O Kṛṣṇa, if you have no compassion for me when I am being consumed by the rod of Brahmā, then having shown mercy to me, you ought to protect my husband. If the full punishment is ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, [then let it fall upon me].
Therefore, I now consider it right that you should apply that punishment to me.
For I am his wife, and as such, I seek half of his merit and demerit;
let half of the merit born of my devotion accrue to him.
"May his sin and half of my own karma also abide here.
O Nārāyaṇa, O Viṣṇu, by this justice and according to this rule, he ought to drink it even through an exchange with one who is worthy. (66)
Therefore, O Blessed One, be the slayer of the Asuras yourself and the bestower of liberation;
O Keśava, bring happiness even to Rājīva. For the sake of my peace, O Lord, grant what I have requested for my sake.
"Just as you carry off the *pārijāta* tree for the sake of Bhāmā, so am I Bhāmā; I am your servant, and I request my own *pārijāta*.
O Kṛṣṇa, in kalpa after kalpa, Bhāmā has been made content by you. (69)
"By the gift of the *pārijāta* tree, satisfy me, O Bhāmā.
Here, I shall gratify you with devotion; you, gratify me with a gift.
A woman [gratifies] a man with service, and a man [gratifies] a woman by the giving of wealth. (3.193.70–71)
O Protector, you ought to act in such a way as to grant favor in all circumstances;
for though she has a protector, you regard her condition as one of being without a protector.
Thus spoke Rājīva to Araṇyaka: "Kundanā, Kundanā! 72.
"You surely seek my rescue; therefore, deliver me and show compassion!
As long as you do not rescue me, I shall remain in a fast unto death.
Having spoken thus, Queen Kundanādevī undertook a fast, O Lakṣmī.
Seated on a single seat, without water, without food, and free from desire;
having conquered sleep and conquered hunger, she made a firm resolve regarding death.
Closing her eyes, she became absorbed in meditation within her heart.
She made me revolve incessantly upon her rosary as I chanted;
through the functions of concentration and meditation, she bound me within her heart.
Strengthened by her great momentum, I did not waver for even a moment, wherever I was.
Desiring the release of Rājīva, she became intent upon me alone.
Having understood her mind, I, remaining within her, quickly emerged from her outwardly in a beautiful form for the sake of her husband’s liberation.
Bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Ramā,
enriched with all ornaments and finery, and likewise served by his attendants;
with a gracious countenance, peaceful, and intent upon bestowing boons.
Her body was completely enveloped by a halo of radiance, and she wore divine ornaments. When I stood before her in such a form, Kundaṇā,
having been awakened within by me, quickly emerged from her meditative absorption.
Beholding me as the Supreme Self, Satī rose up quickly;
she immediately fell at my feet and embraced me closely to her chest.
By the mere touch of me, divine vision was born within her.
She gazed upon her own husband, whom she had seen in a dream, within the forest.
She quickly pointed out her husband with an outstretched hand and then requested him to rescue him, who was suffering and possessed by a rākṣasa. (83–84)
Right there, for the sake of my husband's liberation alone, I suddenly mounted Garuḍa and, taking with me the one named Kunda,
went as a bird to that forest where the rājīva lotus was located.
Then, descending from the sky, I came there and took my pleasure with her.
I sprinkled the lotus that was wandering about with the water from my own water-pot; at that, the Rākṣasa who had been leaping about fled.
Having drunk the water, he immediately became possessed of a divine body;
having praised me, he went to heaven by means of a celestial chariot through my power.
Then Rājīva also, with a composed mind and a truly radiant countenance, [departed].

Having realized that I was his own wife and likewise the Supreme Lord, she bowed at my feet and prostrated herself like a staff. Then Kundanādevikā informed him of everything that had occurred. (3.193.90)

Then, having been sprinkled with water by me once more, he became pure; he effected the destruction of his sins, and I caused him to drink water from my own hands. Having placed him upon Garuḍa, I brought him to the city of Vāṭāsana.
The queen caused the mantra to be given to the king, who, having abandoned his pride,
accepted my mantra as well as the necklace and the tulasī beads.
Thus he became a Vaiṣṇava, a devotee of the Lord, and one possessed of a faithful disposition.
All the sons, daughters, and subjects likewise attained a state of serenity. Then, having provided for their security and well-being,
I spoke these words for the purpose of my departure to the imperishable world at the end.
Having granted [the boon], he quickly vanished from the sight of King Vaṭodara;
then, assuming the form of a brahmin, I went there under the pretext of begging for alms.
Thereupon, that king named Bhāskaravikrama was indeed entreated.
"Speak, O Brahmin; I shall grant you whatever is within the scope of your desire.
He then said to me, "I request the protection of the lotus-pond," repeatedly asking that the kingdom be restored to him while he remained seated in his enclosure.

The noble King Rājeśvara, saying "So be it," quickly dispatched a messenger with a similar letter to the chief minister. He also caused the kingdom to be bestowed upon Rājīva; I too am a twice-born brahmin.
Having again granted an audience to the queen and the king,
I then vanished; thereafter, after some time,
I took delight with Rājīva, Queen Kunda-nāda, as well as their sons and daughters.
I brought that Vaiṣṇava family and their abode to the imperishable realm (akṣara-dhāma).
Thus, in the past, through my devotion and the worship of my wife,
even the sinful Rājīva, though a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, was protected by me from the forest.
The Rākṣasa was liberated, and the Rākṣasa was also set free; indeed,
the entire family of King Rājīva was delivered from sin through the power of Kunda’s vow of fasting.
And by devotion to my worship, his own kingdom was restored once again.
(104) Thus, O Lakṣmī, through devotion to me, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall be attained here;
likewise, by reading or hearing this, one shall obtain both enjoyment and liberation. (105)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Lord and Liberation from Suffering through the Supreme Devotion of Queen Kunda-nadevī—Who Was a Brahmin-Slayer, Overcome by Rākṣasas, and Deprived of Her Kingdom—King Vāṭāsīnāra," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Continuum, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 194: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā, Section 3 (The Dvāpara Yuga Continuum) — Chapter 194.
[The Author: Chapter 195.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, you who are the lotus-lake for the Lord of devotees.
The life story of Devaviśrāma, the destroyer of women’s infatuation:
There was a king named Cakradhara, the sovereign of the city of Virāma.
He had a most righteous minister named Devaviśrāma. (1–2)
He was one who brought about the prosperity of the kingdom, desiring the welfare of his subjects;
he was ever intent on the effort of protecting the realm and a constant worshiper of the gods and other deities. He was devoted to the path of dharma and dedicated to truth and righteousness.
He is devoted to the service of virtuous men, women, and chaste wives, and is an exceedingly devoted servant.
(4) Whatever individuals are destitute of wealth, they beg for a divine rest;
he grants them their desired object and indeed satisfies the mendicants. (5)
Even those who seek wealth, being well-pleased and uttering great blessings, say: "May heaven, a kingdom, and a great empire be yours!
The king, too, being ever righteous, constantly serves the Supreme Lord.

Neither thieves, nor rogues, nor the crafty, nor deceivers, nor those fond of trickery find favor with the king in his own kingdom. As is the king, so is the minister; he always metes out punishment for theft and other crimes.
Those who are devoted to malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), those who live by means of mantras, tantras, and the like,
and those who are slayers and murderers— these are not pleasing to him at all. Then once, the female servants of the mother Bahucarā...
The yoginīs, who were knowers of mantras, went out for alms in Rāma’s land.
Wherever kings were lords of charity and wherever there were people who gave, there they indeed begged for wealth, O Rāma. (3.194.10–11)
They beg for gold, silver, garments, vehicles, and even mounts;
for diamonds, rubies, and various kinds of gems;
and they also beg for ornaments, and they obtain what is requested.
In that manner, they offer up Bahucarā, the Great Goddess.
"Mother Bahucarā will grant a hundred-thousandfold reward to the donor," thinking upon these supreme words, those women accept the gift. (13–14)
Then, wherever wealthy merchants, kings, or common people give to them,
those women settle upon seats at their city gates and house doors, proclaiming [their names] in groups.
Having undertaken a vow of fasting, they perform penance against Kali.
Victory, victory, O Mother who wanders far! Victory, victory, O Mother who wanders far!
You are the giver of wealth to those who seek it; victory, victory, O Mother who wanders far!
Thus, playing the *tālī* drum, they sing aloud in the courtyard of the house;
for five or seven days they remain there and do not depart.
Then the masters of the house, having met with defeat, even give [them their freedom].
And they seize gold, silver, wealth, and so forth in many ways.
(19) Now, if they do not surrender the desired wealth and property, they resort to force and even to hunger strikes, and strive through quarrels as well. (20)
"Women do not depart by force in any other way; they must take [the wealth] and then go.
All those ten yoginīs were of such a nature. At that time, for the sake of wealth, the minister indeed employed force, and he gave the money.
Even after obtaining a hundred gold coins, they remain devoid of satisfaction;
just as a thousand gold pieces are [insufficient], so too are other riches—gems, diamonds, ornaments, and the like—even when acquired separately from a king. (22–23)
Ten thousand coins and garlands of gems and pearls—
thus equipped with such forceful persistence, they entreated him, yet he did not go forth.
Then, when seven days had passed while the thousand [coins] were being given away...
When those golden seals did not bring him satisfaction,
they then performed a foul incantation for the destruction of the minister and a malevolent spell for the destruction of the king as well.

Then the minister fell down, agitated and deeply unconscious; after a moment, however, regaining his senses, he rose up again. The king also, having reached such a state, then fell into a swoon once more.
And having risen, he performed all those rites of sorcery.
The minister, unable to endure it, and the king as well,
had her head cut off by their own soldiers, even though she was worthy of the highest honor.
Then other women, cruel and weak, fled out of fear of death;
taking only the wealth that had been given and abandoning the corpse of the dead woman,
they began to run and departed for another part of the city.
In every part of the world and among all people, the king committed the murder of women;
and his minister also committed the murder of women, so that an ill repute arose.
[He was accused of being] one who sets fires, one who administers poison, one who raises weapons, and one who employs spells and malevolent incantations.
These women are assassins, givers of curses, and likewise givers of enmity;
there is indeed no fault in their destruction, for she who takes away life deserves to be slain.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, there is no blame at all in the destruction of one who possesses such a form.
Nevertheless, public rumors arise concerning the killing of women;
all such things bring ill repute to the world, for the ways of people are diverse. The subjects censure both that minister and the king as well.
Indeed, without even knowing the cause— such as malevolent magic— they falsely proclaim their ill repute, saying, "The king is a killer of women" or "He is a treacherous minister.
Then King Cakradhara spoke these auspicious words to his minister:
O high-minded one,
how can the washing away of the stain of one who speaks ill of what ought to be done be accomplished so as to remove that blemish and bring satisfaction among the subjects? (37–38)
"Even though there is no sin in the killing of a woman who practices malevolent magic (*abhicāra*),
nevertheless, one should perform a vow for the pacification of her ill-repute.
O minister, having reflected upon this, tell me what is auspicious and brings happiness."
"Whatever religious duty ought to be performed should be done accordingly. The minister said, "O King, summon a splendid assembly and announce your intention there to the elders of the people."
Having heard this, the king acted accordingly; and there, men who were elders of the subjects arrived in their assembly by the thousands, both men and women.
Then, the most virtuous family priest was pointed out by the minister.
Learned in the scriptures, accomplished in the treatises, and a master of the Vedas;
knowing the law and discerning the proper place and time, he— urged by the words of the ministers and acting on the king’s command— proclaimed the duties in the assembly.
May the venerable assembly, as well as the elderly women and men, listen;
I shall declare the characteristics of Dharma according to the scriptures:
Dharma is characterized by injunction, it accomplishes worldly ends, and it also bestows liberation. (45)

That which causes misfortune, possesses contrary meaning, leads to an evil rebirth, and is not a "bull" (vṛṣa) [of virtue]—that which the noble ones indeed praise when it is being observed is truly a "bull";
but that which people censure is proclaimed to be unrighteousness (adharma). ||46-47||
That by which the support, nourishment, and protection of the worlds are provided,
and through which happiness, security, and well-being arise— that is called Dharma. Furthermore, that conduct which is established according to place, time, and worthy recipients is indeed Dharma.
That which bestows happiness is dharma; that which bestows suffering is adharma.
Through dharma, fame arises, as well as constant happiness and peace, along with prosperity, advancement, heaven, and eternal liberation.
That alone is the dharma by which a king makes his subjects happy:
worship of the gods, as well as charity, religious observance, compassion, and sacrificial fees.
Constantly helping others—this is the dharma for all embodied beings.
Bathing, recitation of mantras, salutation of the gods, as well as dedication to the gods;
honoring the elderly and honoring the king—this is dharma.
Right conduct is indeed the primary dharma; its opposite is adharma.

Dharma is indeed the conduct of the virtuous, but not so that of the wicked. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, the vow of celibacy, austerity, and self-restraint—this alone is declared to be the supreme dharma; even service to the elders is difficult to find.
Service to the virtuous and association with the good are proclaimed as the supreme dharma.
Helping living beings according to one's ability is considered the bull of dharma;
making others joyful is dharma, for joyfulness itself is indeed difficult to attain.
Lack of faith, as well as agitation, lack of assistance, failure to serve,
violence, falsehood, forcible seizure, and association with the wicked—
these constitute unrighteousness itself; they should always be abandoned by people.
A gift given with faith is indeed considered to be righteousness;
but that which is taken by force is unrighteousness, for it is the act of a plunderer.
If a rite performed with mantras should result in the destruction of living beings, it would be sorcery (abhicāra).

For kings, unrighteousness itself is [the cause of] the destruction of life, and even such destruction is unrighteous; likewise, the killing of a preeminent person through malevolent magic is unrighteous. Furthermore, violence committed at the wrong place, at the wrong time, toward an unworthy recipient, or with a wicked intention is likewise unrighteous.
Furthermore, the act of an assassin is proclaimed to be indeed unrighteousness (adharma).
When such unrighteousness manifests in the form of an assassin toward a man, a woman, a boy, or even a young girl, [it must be countered]. || 61-62 ||
Unrighteousness, as well as the unrighteous person, must indeed be dealt with by means of weapons and other such tools;
an assailant must be struck down by all possible means for the sake of protecting one's life.
Indeed, he who does not strike back when an assailant attacks him [is likewise at fault].
Therefore, an assailant must be slain swiftly; he who acts as an aggressor deserves to be killed.
This very nature of dharma has been declared by me before you.
Furthermore, here is the worship of women who are devoted to many wandering [sages].
Although they had offered thousands of gold coins according to their respective means, the women, firm in their resolve, forcibly and by sheer persistence sought to take [the king] away;
they then performed malevolent rites against the king and his minister, causing a great mortality.
Therefore, those Mārikās, like Pūtanās, are said to be Rākṣasīs who are harmful and characterized by tamas; they are knowers of mantras and practitioners of malevolent rites against enemies. (67–68)
"They must indeed be slain; there is no fault here, for such is the established law of dharma.
All of them were worthy of death, yet one among them was spared.
Compassion was shown, not cruelty; that is dharma, and nothing else."
For in that case, what appears as the killing of the wicked is indeed Dharma;
since for living beings, the destruction of those who take life is itself Dharma.
There is no fault in the killing of a woman; it is precisely like the slaying of Pūtanā. (3.194.70–71)
There is indeed no fault in the destruction of a *kṛtyā*; understand that to be the law (*dharma*).
Likewise, there is no compassion for a lioness, a female elephant, a female snake, or a female scorpion;
nor is compassion approved for a life-taking *rākṣasī*. (72)
For this very reason, people should never show compassion toward a lethal [weapon].
When it is engaged in the destruction of life, one should by no means show compassion;
when it is engaged in that which does not destroy life, indifference toward it is appropriate.
Such is the nature of those who lead their subjects; therefore,
whatever you may say here regarding the destruction of this sorceress—
whether it be sin, or merit, or neither, or both— that shall come to pass.
Having heard this, those venerable members of the assembly spoke most righteously:
"There is no fault in killing an assassin, nor in the killing of one who has killed;
and there is no fault found in killing one intent upon malevolent magic."
"However, for the sake of purifying the statement that 'the woman has been struck,' a Viṣṇu-sacrifice must be performed, which brings peace to all slander.
Such is our opinion; let the King perform this meritorious deed.

O Lakṣmī, the words of the subjects were honored by the king and accepted by the minister in the assembly for the sake of complete purification. Then, having taken an auspicious moment, he performed a sacrifice. (3.194.80)
The pavilion, the excellent sacrificial pit, the installations of the deities,
the worship, the gifts, the feasts, and the clarified butter;
likewise, various priestly fees, oblations, and sacrificial fuel.
The king, his ministers, and the subjects offered to Viṣṇu garments, suitable food, wealth, and other articles for worship;
then they performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), at which time [it was realized] that "I am indeed Nārāyaṇa. || 82-83 ||
Then, having become an outcaste, I went there and requested food;
the minister gave me that meal from afar, while I was delighted.
At that time, I, who purify those at the dining row, ate the food.
He made a handful of water and likewise performed the washing of his hands;
as soon as he had drunk the water,
a blackish-grey smoke emerged from the king's body and entered the mouth of the minister.
From the body of the minister, Kṛṣṇā emerged as a sinful woman;
that yoginī, having died, indeed became a woman in the form of a murder.
Drawn away by a dog-cooker (śvapaca), she vanished within that dog-cooker.
From the head of that outcaste, who had been consumed by fire, she suddenly emerged in the form of lightning;
having attained power, she quickly ascended into the sky.
Possessing a divine form, she praised me, Śrīpati, the Lord of Ramā.
"O Blessed One, you have arrived here at this sacrifice for the sake of my liberation from this unchaste woman,
and for the fulfillment of both the sacrifice and the king’s purpose.
Even a killing committed through the hand of a devotee leads to liberation."
Even my sinful act of killing has, through your grace, granted me heaven;
it shall surely grant me liberation, and now merit is born within me.
O Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bāla Kṛṣṇa, Śrīpati, Supreme Lord! || 91-92 ||
"Deliver me, your servant, who has wandered much for the sake of your power.
Having spoken thus, she quickly attained the heavenly state by the glance of the Blessed One.
In the course of time, that virtuous woman went to Vaikuṇṭha through devotion to Hari.

Then the king, his family, the ministers, and even the subjects, having recognized me as the Supreme Lord Hari, worshipped me. At that moment, I suddenly assumed a four-armed form upon my auspicious seat at the sacrifice.
Having been seated, he sat down and then granted me his favor.
To everyone, he gave the form of gold contained in the sacrificial vessel (caru), and they too accepted it.
Indeed, by my arrival, they all became completely purified.
Thus, indeed, the stain of the murder of those two was destroyed by me;
the liberation of the Yoginī named Kāṇḍikā was accomplished through the granting of boons to the king and his minister for the sake of heaven and final release. (97–98)
Having joined them with blessings and established them within their families,
I then, in the course of time, made those two dwellers of heaven partakers of liberation;
thus, O Lakṣmī, I made the two followers of the king destined for final release.

Thus, out of compassion, I performed everything subsequent to the sacrifice. I then vanished from the sacrificial ground while causing even their minds to behold me; then those men and women who remembered Me went to that imperishable abode.
"Thus, O beloved, have I destroyed the sin of killing a woman.
Both the reader and the listener of this shall attain worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(102) Thus ends the [account of] the sin of the Kāṇḍikā-Yoginī’s murder by the minister named Devaviśrāma, at the command of King Cakradhara, in the sacrifice performed by Śrī Hari, in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
The one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination that [Worldly] Cessation Has Been Accomplished," Chapter 194.

[Author: Chapter 196.
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this story that destroys all sins.
In Saurāṣṭra, at the city of Māyūra, on the bank of the river Matsyā— || 1 ||
In that great garden lived its keeper, Mālī, who was a householder named Harṣula;

he was a devotee of Hari, dedicated to righteous deeds, and devoted to bathing, worship, giving, and other such acts according to his ability. (2) He remained intent upon these practices to the best of his capacity.
Hṛṣula had a wife named Vidrumavallakī.
She too was a devotee, yet she was childless and filled with grief.
[She sought remedies] through the application of medicinal herbs as well as auspicious mantras and other such means.
Due to many kinds of pride, she did not become beautiful with child.
When she became hopeless because old age was approaching,
her husband then abandoned that hope and [took] another auspicious woman.
By the decree of fate, he made his wife one who was half-impregnated.
She became pregnant and was named Citrapallavā;
Harṣula, filled with joy, was absorbed in thoughts of his future son.
Out of a desire for a son, he performs acts of charity, religious duty, vows, and meritorious deeds;
he honors the virtuous and offers them hospitality with fruits and food.
In every way, he also pays reverence to those who arrive as guests.

Endowed with faith and desiring a son, he accepts the blessings [of the deity]. (9) With a devoted heart, he daily brings fruits and other offerings from his own garden to the temple, and he serves the shrine and its surroundings. (3.195.10)
Vidrumavallakī was likewise possessed of variegated foliage;
she was devoted to her husband and filled with fear of sin.
Vidrumavallakī indeed constantly experienced sleep and humiliation at all times.
For she reflects upon her childlessness, especially because of her old age.
But Citrapallī, who is pregnant, deserves respect in every way;
for great sorrow has come upon Vidrumā due to her co-wifehood.
There too, perceiving the intense suffering of her co-wife who possessed a son, she constantly worried that a miscarriage might occur.
She [avoided] foods that were pungent, sharp, hot, or fresh.
Having prepared ten thousand such [medicines], he indeed gave them to the pregnant woman.
Nevertheless, no miscarriage occurred; consequently, he further administered a medicine for inducing miscarriage in her food.
The miscarriage did not occur; the months were complete for the birth.
The birth of a son took place; Mālī became joyful and attained great delight.
Citrapallī became serene, and the withered coral lute was restored.
Harṣula also gave gifts to the twice-born according to his ability (18).
He bestowed gifts of fruits, flowers, garments, gold, silver, and roots, as well as the gift of cows and food, upon a worthy and virtuous man (19).
Overwhelmed with love, he performed the birth-rites and other ceremonies for his son.
From that time on, he joyfully constructed a small hut in the garden for every guest who arrived there;
indeed, whenever a visitor came, he would build one for him.
He serves a guest who is virtuous and good with food, fruits, and other offerings.
In his old age, he indeed cultivates the company of the righteous and attains sons.
He constantly delights in chanting and likewise sings the praises of Hari.
He indeed worships my form with devotion using fruits, flowers, and other offerings.
In this way, a year passed for the son, entirely auspicious.
Vidrumavallakī, however, was angry and afflicted by grief due to intense burning heat.
Filled with envy for her son, she reflected thus:
"Having dug up the root of poison and extracted even a small amount of its juice, this wicked woman gave it to him in his milk to drink for the sake of the child's destruction. (24-25)
Then I, the Blessed Lord, who am the protector of my devotees,
assumed the form of a holy man and manifested my divine glory there;
I went to the garden in the house of Harṣula like a guest.
Harṣula honored me with offerings of honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as fruits, water, and other items;
he welcomed me with sweet foods, auspicious meals, seats, and so forth.
Citrapallī, being gracious and filled with joy, also served me.
But one Vidrumavallikā knew about the drinking of milk;
she thought, "The child will die because the juice from the root of a poison has been given.
With a gracious mind, she became devoted to the service of the virtuous. || 29 ||
"When will the sinful death come for my child? [she wondered].
While the child slept peacefully after drinking milk, his mother realized this; therefore, O virtuous one, she remained for a long time in service to him. (3.195.30–31)
The boy became unconscious due to the onset of the poison;

indeed, no one else knew of Hari except for those who were entirely devoted to the service of the virtuous. (32) When they had all become intent upon serving the holy ones, [the poison was neutralized].
Nandā, that coral-creeper-like woman, went there for the purpose of purification.
Having taken a dead lizard there,
she then brought it to the side of her son’s cradle and cast it upon the ground.
Then, so that others might not know, she slowly cast it aside;
but then, seizing a staff, she cried out with great force:
"Run here! Run here! This son of yours has been bitten by a lizard!"
"O husband, this lizard is being beaten here by me with blows from a staff!
O sister, come quickly; the son has been bitten by her here!
Thus she strikes even the dead lizard with a stick. (35–36)
He raised a great outcry so that others might hear it;
hearing that immense clamor, they falsely accused him of murder.
Then all the virtuous men, running together, rushed toward the son's dwelling.
Just as they had gone forth under the power of their life-breaths upon hearing and seeing their son dead,
all of them wept; and their mother, like a female osprey,
was even more overwhelmed with grief than they were for being deprived of her son.
Immersed in grief due to the loss of her son, the virtuous woman was overwhelmed by sorrow;
her father, too, having fallen into grief, wept aloud with an unrestrained voice.
Nearby in that garden, there were many farmers and others.
For they arrived, afflicted by grief upon hearing of their son's death;
suddenly beholding his corpse, they were submerged in an ocean of sorrow.
And I recognized Vidrumavallakī, who was engaged in a deception.
She too became afraid, thinking: "This man is a virtuous and powerful one;
if he should discover the poison given by Vidrumavallī, then my husband will surely bring about the destruction of my life."
Thus overcome with fear, she grasped the feet of the virtuous man;
then, by means of a sign, she slowly made the gesture of massaging, and through the touch of her fingers, she indicated: "This is my fault."
She informed him for the sake of protection: "Do not make this public.
She was then addressed by me: "I am indeed a virtuous person who acts for the benefit of others;
here, I shall act solely for the welfare of all, free from any sin."
"Let the servants of the virtuous not grieve over the death of their son.
Indeed, I am entirely capable of dispelling their sorrow by restoring the dead child to life through the *sañjīvanī* vidyā. (48–49)
"I am able to do this; therefore, let those who are dear to the virtuous not weep.
I shall also restore the iguana to life; let them indeed find happiness here.
Having said this, I suddenly took water in my hand.
Having consulted [with them], I placed [the mantra] into the mouth of the dead child in my name.
By the mere touch of water, he indeed became endowed with breath;
the child was suddenly restored to life and became free from poison.
The iguana, too, through contact with the water, was restored to life.
Then, having paid homage to me,
that divine iguana ascended a celestial chariot arrived from heaven and departed for the auspicious realm of the gods.
Beholding this great wonder, Harbulā and the others regarded both the Lord and me as their supreme refuge;
they offered their devotion and received the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (94–95)
They approached me with their whole being and then begged for my forgiveness;
they all held a supreme festival in the presence of that saint.
For a day and night, I remained there as a holy man known by the name Sañjīvanāyana.
He dwelt in that beautiful house, attended in a magnificent garden.
That joyful man served me for the sake of increasing his son’s lifespan.
I bestowed this word upon him: "May he live for a hundred thousand years."
For a hundred thousand years, his son was named Sañjīvana;
he obtained longevity from me, for my grace toward a devotee is indeed infinite.
And Citravallī, being well-pleased, served me again and again.
Through the service of massaging his body, she was exceedingly joyful at the prospect of her son’s long life.
Then, when midnight had passed, that wicked coral-creeper came to me in secret and said, "Lift me up; have mercy! (3.195.60–61)
Indeed, a great sin—the killing of a child—has been committed by me as a woman out of jealousy and the feelings of a co-wife; forgive me and do not cast me out.
O Lord of the World, destroy my secret sin.
Having spoken thus, she performed a foot massage and a body rub.
Out of compassion for her, both for the sake of destroying the devotee's sins and for my own sake,
I looked upon her with a divine form and a divine vision.
As soon as she was touched on the body with my two arms,
the personified sin of child-murder emerged trembling from her body;
I quickly consumed it with the gift of water, and it went to its destruction.
Vidrumavallikā quickly became free from fear.
Thus, my devotees Lakṣmī, Citrikā, and likewise Vidrumā,
as well as Harṣula his son, and Godhā were indeed delivered from sin.
"Protected, guarded, nourished, and satisfied by you, I have now risen at dawn and received hospitality and food. While I am still desiring to depart, this devotee has become exceedingly joyful. (68)
He asked, "O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, what should be done for your sake? And there, he instructed both him and the two women:
"One must seek the company of the virtuous, and likewise, Hari must be served. (3.195.70)
Even when place and time are adverse, Janārdana protects;
I am the beginningless Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa. Whenever dharma is indeed impaired, I provide protection for my devotees.
Even for a devotee who possesses faults, I shall count those faults as nothing;
(72) but for my servant who has attained the company of the virtuous and who knows my greatness, I do not count his faults in any way whatsoever. (73)
From association with the virtuous, merit indeed arises that destroys sin;
therefore, one should always cultivate association with the virtuous followers of Śrī Hari.
Likewise, my incarnations too should be remembered by people at all times.
The birthplaces of His divine sports should be remembered for the removal of sins.
(75) Furthermore, at the time of death, or even when there is adversity regarding place and time, the remembrance of Sat and the others destroys sin and bestows liberation. (76)
Indeed, one who cannot endure the excellence of others should never practice envy;
through envy, all harm and sin arise, as does censure and death.
Consequently, even the journey to the regions of Yama becomes a source of suffering.
Therefore, both male and female devotees should diligently abandon envy.
They should always maintain a cheerful disposition, for it bestows happiness even upon those who excel them. I indeed become pleased with one who performs service for others.
Rivalry between co-wives should be made to yield happiness, and likewise, that which must be practiced should be made to yield happiness.
One must act in a way that is pleasing to the husband; by that alone am I truly satisfied. Therefore, that evil trait must be abandoned by the devoted man and the devoted woman.
My form, served by Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and others, should be meditated upon.
(81) Even if it cannot be seen while being meditated upon, it should nevertheless be meditated upon repeatedly with faith within the heart; I always bestow my grace upon such a person. (82)
I become subject to him alone and grant whatever he desires;
that indeed should be understood as discernment (*viveka*)—the perception of virtues in devotees, the observation of one's own lack of virtue, and even the quality of being receptive to virtues. (83)
The virtuous Hari said: "That which is beneficial must indeed be accepted.
Thus instructed, the devotee attains great stability;
and the functions of the senses become intent on the service of Śrī Hari and the virtuous.
For whomever they may serve, the grace of Hari quickly becomes theirs;
through the association with Śrī Hari, all their principles become purified,
and millions of sins and other evils are destroyed.
My devotion increases, and from that, one attains what is desired.
Therefore, the senses should be directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa and toward Me and the saintly; association with the saintly should always be practiced for the sake of achieving purity and liberation.
One should never engage in harmful or malicious association at any time,
nor should one ever practice criticism upon observing the physical actions of the virtuous.
By doing so, one’s vision becomes divine and love for Kṛṣṇa increases.
When [these] exist, affection increases, merit is gained, and one attains liberation.
Indeed, once the direct union with Hari has arisen, one should not contemplate any incompleteness;
for firm devotion toward Me in human form must be maintained within one's sphere of experience.

Indeed, by means of seeing me and so forth, the self should be contemplated as one whose desires are fulfilled; my association should be sought in every way for the increase of devotion. For such a devotee, I fulfill their heart's desires.
"I forcibly bestow my own supernatural sovereignty even upon one who does not desire it.
(93) Therefore, having attained Kṛṣṇa as one's visible beloved husband and lord, and having served him, the goals of human existence are to be accomplished through Hari. (94)
As long as there is no destruction of passion and hatred, nor the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā),
so long will there be no state of exclusive devotion toward me, the Supreme Self. Indeed,
that desire for pleasure which exists through the impulse of the senses [persists].

That [desire] must always be destroyed by surrendering it indeed unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Having cultivated association with the great ones, one's latent impression (vāsanā) must certainly be slain—that by which the longing for objects other than Kṛṣṇa is destroyed. (96–97)
That devotee is indeed of the nature of Brahman; him I truly encompass.
He is my single-minded devotee, effecting the liberation of countless embodied beings.
And as the Inner Controller, I am the fulfiller of all his desires.

I am the giver of the fruits of all actions as well as of all prosperities. Since the body and so forth arise from me, and whatever karma is produced is fashioned by me, therefore, having brought that very body into existence, [the fruit] is accumulated. (3.195.100)
I bestow upon him alone, at the appropriate time, that which has been obtained;
I grant him the supreme fruit of service to me, and even more besides.
Therefore, service to me should always be performed by people endowed with faith.
I fulfill that person’s desire, even if it is something not destined by their past karma (prārabdha).
Even in times of adversity, service to the virtuous must be performed, just as it was done for me;
for such service is like a wish-fulfilling vine (kalpalatā), auspicious and the granter of all desires.
My service toward wife, children, wealth, and the like is greater;
likewise, my service toward husband, wife, and parents is indeed greater.
Through my service, every happiness in this body reaches the embodied being.
At the end of the body, he attains even my own abode, the supreme imperishable.
Whatever kind of devotion arises in one's mind toward me throughout life,
I grant him that very same state as his destination at the end.
To him who has served me directly and to her by whom my service was performed directly,
I grant that supreme state which takes refuge in me.
In every way, I provide protection for them against the obstacles of self-restraint (yama) and the other practices.
He has no fear of untimely death, nor indeed any fear of time or karma. For my devotee is truly fearless;
being well-pleased, I lead him to my own abode known as the Imperishable (Akṣara).
At the end of the body, my devotee indeed goes to my abode in every way;
whether through remembrance, or even through fainting, or through agony, he departs.
By attaining the company of the virtuous, one should know that it is surely the highest good.
For him, there shall indeed be supreme welfare both in this world and in the next.
(111) Therefore, devotion should be practiced toward me alone and toward the virtuous as well; for having abandoned affection for anyone other than me, such devotion is difficult to attain. (112)
The characteristic of a devotee is service; setting aside even one's own personal pleasure, one must always perform what is pleasing and agreeable to the Master.
This devoted attendance should be maintained, for it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
"Thus let my devotees worship me; I shall grant them everything they desire.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord, in the form of a saint, restored the life of a son and destroyed the sin of child-murder for the devotee named Harṣula when his first wife’s son was lost due to the second wife," in the Third Section (the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age) of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
*Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 195.
Chapter 196 [Author:
Chapter 197 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Thus, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, that auspicious [teaching] which bestows liberation was then instructed by me to those two women and to Harṣula.
Nevertheless, Vidrumavallī remained old, childless, and devoid of [other] progeny.
“O Hari-Kṛṣṇa, [she] asked me: ‘O beloved, please show mercy to me so that I too may become a mother of sons. By her prayer, such was the good fortune of that devoted woman. (2–3)
And through my service there, I produced a new, auspicious [son] who bestows sons. When I said, "Let it be so," she became pleased.
Furthermore, I gave them instruction that is exceedingly purifying.

Whoever possesses devotion for me, the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, who am manifest before them, their duty is to constantly abide by the word of Kṛṣṇa; and whatever task the devotees of Kṛṣṇa might say, that too should be carried out with haste.
One who desires such [a state] should await the word of Hari;
likewise, one should continuously maintain my form within the mind.
Always possessing ever-fresh faith, one should maintain it and never abandon it.
And being devoted to meditation, he should consider me as one whose desires are fulfilled;
by meditating upon my form for a long time, he then attains the supreme goal.
Or, by performing service to the virtuous, he likewise reaches that highest state.
One should grasp only the virtues of the virtuous, abandoning their faults;

one should seek out virtues even in the Supreme Lord and in the saintly, regardless of their outward appearance. One should always practice righteous conduct, which is the cause of the favor of the holy ones.
One should never entertain doubt regarding the conduct, speech, actions, yoga, and service of the virtuous; for bad association arises from doubt.
Therefore, with full confidence, one should perform what is desired by the virtuous and likewise by Hari.
That alone shall indeed bestow liberation; one shall attain victory without a doubt.
I am the deliverer of the lowly, and I uplift those who have taken refuge in me. One should serve Hari with enthusiasm, as is the way of the virtuous.
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible for enthusiastic servants.
(14) The attainment of various kinds of objects occurs through attaining Me; those who take refuge in Me are always filled with bliss by My happiness. (15)
He who completely renounces all objects of sense between himself and them,
and who always worships Me— he is liberated and he is dear to Me.
(1.6) The activities of one's own senses should be offered unto the Supreme Self.
Then all divine activities become centered upon me;
his satisfaction proceeds directly from union with Kṛṣṇa,
and through union with Hari himself, his own state becomes that of Brahman.
For one who possesses this, there remains no further duty to be performed for the sake of liberation.
Whatever all the sensory organs perceive as their own food—
that food is Lord Hari himself, and the eternal attributes of Hari.
In this way, Hari is the object of the senses, which are like servants;
for him who possesses [this realization], there shall indeed be eternal bliss in this world.
Upon attaining divine qualities and the like, everything becomes permeated by Kṛṣṇa.
In this very way, one should always act and exist here;
for the form of the virtuous is that of Hari, and likewise the taste of the virtuous is that of Hari.
The fragrance of the virtuous is that of Hari, and likewise the sound of the virtuous is that of Hari.
The touch of the virtuous and of Hari is always purifying and bestows liberation.
(23) Beholding the virtuous and Hari, touching them, serving their bodies, and even massaging their feet are always sanctifying and purifying. (24)
The residence of the virtuous in the abode of Hari, as well as the observance of His command, is undoubtedly pure and always bestows liberation.
Whatever is to be enjoyed must be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa; never otherwise.
One should offer it to Kṛṣṇa, or to the true person who is the self of the form of Kṛṣṇa. (26) What is thus offered attains divinity; its enjoyer shall go to liberation.
Through union with Hari, that reality becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa); its enjoyer likewise becomes devoid of qualities. (27)
For it immediately purifies the internal organ, making it free from the qualities (nirguṇa).
For one who is free from the qualities, bondage does not arise through experience.
Having understood this, [one should likewise understand] the five [elements] as well as other objects.
The divine [objects], which are purifying and consist of grace, should always be served.
Those not offered [to the deity] should certainly not be used; indeed, they should be avoided from afar.
For those who conduct themselves in this manner, no distraction whatsoever arises.
There shall be no bondage, and meritorious liberation will be held in one's hand;
all desires are purified, and cherished goals are always accomplished.
My abode, which bestows happiness, is forever within him.
Having discerned this, one should thus cultivate association with the virtuous and with Hari.
Association with the virtuous should always be practiced, for it bestows the supreme good;
there is no such object or substance that, through union with Me, could equal it.
One should not attain a divine state, nor should one think that it will not grant liberation;
for through my yoga, everything—whether superior or inferior—is pure.
Knowing this, one should offer everything, including this very physical body, unto Me.
Indeed, I become the refuge for such a person who has taken refuge [in me],
who is established in the Self that is Brahman, who is endowed with the dharma of the guru, who is free from passion toward all things, and who possesses affection for me alone. (25–36)
Even in his abode, there exists my entire sovereignty— belonging to me, who am the knower of majesty, and to me, whose treasure is grace.
Sovereignty is obtained through my favor, and it is by means of that [favor] that it is acquired.
From constant association with the virtuous, one should grasp the perfected dharma (siddhadharma).
Indeed, the perfected dharma bestows liberation; one should acquire it by taking refuge in the virtuous.
I, Hari, am the dharma to be accomplished (sādhyadharma), and I am attained through perfection.
Even for one who has the direct attainment of Hari, direct union with Him, constant service,
and perpetual vision of Him, if his soul still desires worldly pleasure— which is merely illusory— he remains unsatisfied and goes to hell. (3.196.40)
Indeed, he alone is to be known as devoid of wisdom who does not renounce craving.
Having attained the realization of what is real and unreal, one should then abandon the pleasure of *māyā*.
Forsaking the bliss of the Self, such a person delights in the pleasure of *māyā*.
None of his eternal duties can ever be accomplished;
however, that person who enjoys the happiness of Hari residing within himself is indeed a wise one—a liberated soul and a devotee-soul who is superior to all. (43)
Indeed, by the power of worship, he becomes Nārāyaṇa;
and the woman becomes Nārāyaṇī, just as Rādhā, Lakṣmī, and Ramā [became so].
For one who has attained the company of the virtuous, there is the realization of one's own self as the Supreme Self. 44–45.
Indeed, a divine vision truly arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
For one who possesses the company of the virtuous, there is the manifestation of the Self, and by His grace, there shall be the autonomy to behold the Supreme Self as well.
For one who exerts effort in the practice of seeing the Self, who dwells in the company of the virtuous,
and who, relying upon my majesty and establishing the internal vision,
beholds his own true nature— he beholds that which is radiant as the sun.
In the stainless self-luminous [consciousness], one beholds me directly as Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord; indeed, such a person shall possess eternal bliss.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever possesses exclusive devotion (aikāntikī bhakti) [to me], [shall attain this].
She who has surrendered all her possessions for my sake proceeds to the supreme state.
While all ritual acts are being performed, Hari himself must be contemplated and held in mind, exactly as he has been seen and exactly as he has been heard.
I am Hari, who is to be enjoyed, served, and cherished;
by Him, devotees surely proceed to the supreme, imperishable abode of Brahman.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is to be beheld for a long time with inner vision by one whose mind is tranquil.
All joys are to be attained by me, for they are of the nature of my own form.
This individual soul (jīva) resides within the bodies of embodied beings in this boundless ocean of saṃsāra, across eighty-four hundred thousand types of bodies associated with various wombs. 53–54.
Indeed, as a woman or a man, one has been born many times again and again;
men have been enjoyed by him, and women likewise have been enjoyed by him repeatedly. All milks have been drunk, and the chambers of the womb have been beheld.
Death and birth were likewise seen by him again and again.
Even though the notions of "I" and "mine" had been repeatedly cultivated toward the body and bodily objects,
he attained stability within that very body.
Indeed, all those previous bodies have been forgotten;
likewise, when this other birth is attained, they are forgotten again.
Therefore, attachment to this very body must be abandoned as is appropriate.
Egoism and possessiveness should be abandoned through knowledge, just as was done by those of old.

Having abandoned attachment to sense objects through discernment and having fixed [the mind] on me, Hari, that embodied being who remains attached [to me] becomes liberated by taking refuge in me. (3.196.60)
For the sake of liberation, for the sake of discernment, for the sake of greatness, and for my own sake as well, the holy ones—
who are eternally pure, sanctifying, and in the form of fish— should always be served. Through such service, one attains absolute devotion and divine nature.

Having attained the supreme abode, the Imperishable, through union with the attributes of the Imperishable, millions of liberated souls serve [it], just as this one serves me. Thinking, "I must stand in that row of the liberated," one should thus serve me. (62–63)
Having reflected that all other happiness is incomplete, trivial, and likewise momentary,
one should practice exclusive devotion toward Me, which knows the secret [of liberation].
One’s own mind should be made free from greed regarding the illusory objects of this world.
By that power, no greed whatsoever arises here for beautiful forms and the like;
likewise, even while traveling on the path toward the abode of Hari,
the supernatural perfections (siddhis) come to him, yet he truly feels no greed for them.
He who has taken refuge in me certainly goes to the further shore beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
Having become single-minded, he enjoys my own exalted bliss.
He in whose every action there is the remembrance of my form—
Indeed, her stability shall remain constant in every way toward her Lord.
