Whatever happiness anyone may desire, that very happiness is to be received from my presence; it is not from elsewhere, for I truly grant everything to him.
"My kingdom is the kingdom of my devotees; no distinction exists therein.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, you should always conduct yourself as a queen and never as a courtesan. Thus indeed was it instructed by me to you, O Lakṣmī.
With their minds moistened by affection, they worshipped me with supreme devotion.
Eagerly, they offered me fruits of the finest kind;
yet, they remained intent on propitiating me, who appeared in the form of a holy man.
Eager to serve, they made a firm resolve to dwell there;
then,
out of their persistence, he who appeared as a holy man indeed consented to stay with them day and night.
Day after day, they bathed him with devotion using warm water;
they offered worship with many garlands of flowers, ornaments fashioned from flowers,
floral garments, and floral cosmetics.
A crown of yellow flowers, as well as bracelets and armlets—
ornaments made of yellow flowers were fashioned by them and worn by me. Indeed, all the garments were truly composed of the seven kinds of flowers.
At that time, fragrant and variegated [garlands] were held by me.
A swing was fashioned for the branch of a kadamba tree using ropes;
it was bound and adorned with beautiful sprouts, flowers, arches, and other ornaments. || 77–78 ||
Having seated me upon a swing, those three, their hearts filled with devotion,
rocked my beloved lord, the protector of their lives.
They then caused him to drink the juice of sugarcane as well as that of oranges.
They also offered coconut water, sweet water, and fragrant water.
At night, filled with eagerness, they performed kīrtana accompanied by various musical instruments.
Thousands of people arrived there, desiring a vision [of the deity].
Consequently, they became sanctified by means of seeing, touching, and so forth;
and having received his grace, they returned to their own abodes.
Harṣula and his two wives also attended upon me during the night.

Through total surrender, with a faultless mind, and by means of divine services—(83)—now, she who was his chief wife was named Vidrumavallakī; after all had fallen asleep and past midnight, she herself [approached him] in secret. (84)
Having come there secretly and alone, she who desired a son served me, the Supreme Lord, by rubbing my body.
Silently, she placed her face near my ear.
She entreated him: "O Blessed One, O Keśava, grant me a son.
Hari, pleased in every way by the service of his devotee, said, "So be it," and touched her, saying, "May you become possessed of a son."
Her fortune having been fully restored, she became exceedingly devoted;
with even greater affection, she served me as she pleased.
While I was asleep, she then went to attend upon her husband.
Her desires fulfilled, Śobhanā likewise became pregnant.
Then, when the time had arrived, she gave birth to an auspicious boy; seeing that one radiant son, Harṣula was filled with great joy. (3.196.89–90)
Thus Vidrumavallakī, having obtained a son who was a vessel of honor, thereafter became forever beautiful with every auspicious fortune.
In this way, O Lakṣmī, that devotee was then delivered by me through her service.
Being pleased, I have delivered her from the sin of killing a child;
the child has been restored to life, and likewise, my service has been accepted.
Indeed, in this very manner, I always provide protection for my devotees.
As many living beings as there are who are joined with bodies, they all exist only with defects; yet, through devotion, they cross over.
By means of devotion, I swiftly deliver even these sinful men.
Then, desiring to depart and having been honored and saluted by them,
I suddenly vanished in an instant while still in the guise of a holy man.
Harṣula and the others meditated daily upon me, just as they had seen me.
They practiced devotion with their whole being and served the virtuous;
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, they went to the highest heaven.
Having reached a heaven even higher than heaven, they went to my imperishable abode.
Thus, through service performed without desire, they go to the stainless Brahman.
Through service, O son, a son is obtained; through service, happiness is obtained;
and through service, fearlessness as well as freedom from sin are likewise obtained.
Through service one obtains millions of enjoyments, and through service eternal happiness; through service I, Śrī Hari, who bestows the fulfillment of all desires, am attainable.
By devotion I deliver the devotees, and thereafter I accept them through their service.
I gladden all through identity with them and bestow that which is supreme.
(101) From reading, hearing, remembering, and likewise serving this, there shall indeed be enjoyment and liberation, and eternal prosperity shall arise. (102)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Lord Hari’s Instruction in the Garden of the Devotee named Harṣula and the Attainment of a Son by Harṣula’s Elder Wife," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 197 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga.
Chapter 197.
[The Author: Chapter 198.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the slayer of his father.
In Saurāṣṭra, there lived a devoted, elderly householder who was a farmer.
(1) In the village of Paṭolaka, near the city of Koṭināra, there was one named Śāṇadhara, who had five sons and many grandsons. (2)
The father of seven daughters, who possessed a garden, fields, and cattle,
worshipped both Śrī Hari and me daily during his agricultural labors.
Whatever was produced there, he would indeed offer it all to me first.
Together with his family, he partakes of new grains and other such foods;
likewise, all kinds of leafy vegetables, both cooked and uncooked grains, whatever tubers and roots are suitable, potherbs, sprouts, and excellent fruits. (4–5)
Whatever she obtains with effort— ornaments, garments, and the like, as well as milk, curd, molasses, juices, and so forth— she offers it all to me in every way;
she then consumes her own food, vehicles, mounts, and likewise all her personal requisites.
Having offered water and food to me constantly and in every way,
my devotee, who is devoted to faith and devotion, indeed accepts [the remnants].
Likewise, [he visits] the holy site of Mūlakṛṣṇapura and Prācīsārasvata.

Endowed with devotion and faith, he indeed proceeds forward, visiting the great pilgrimage site of Somanātha, the pilgrimage sites of Gopanātha and others, the holy ford of the river Svarṇarekhā, and likewise Kuṅkumavāpikā.

Whatever was performed by such a devotee in a previous life, that has been obtained in this other birth and manifested intensely in this present life. Formerly, he was a cowherd who was always devoted to the protection of cattle. (3.197.10–11)
Then, seizing those cats from the bull,
he plucked off all their wings;
having rendered all those hostile cats wingless, he indeed threw them to the ground.
All of them fell upon the ground, afflicted by hunger and thirst;
they died in extreme agony, uttering curses again and again:
"Since you have made us handless, may you likewise become miserable!"
Because of the curse [pronounced] daily upon the stinging insects as they were dying, in this very birth, a great disease arose in both the hands and the feet of that Śāṇadhara,
affecting all the thumbs and fingers. (15)
He became afflicted with a form of leprosy characterized by a foul-smelling discharge.
(16) Although very many medicines were administered by physicians, the discharging flow did not cease at all, nor was there even the slightest alleviation of the disease. (17)
Even though the gods were honored in many ways,
and acts such as giving and merit were performed repeatedly and manifoldly,
the disease nevertheless increased, and his nails gradually fell away.
The tips of his fingers were destroyed and the middle sections were falling away.
Then, all his fingers and thumbs fell off from the roots.
Due to the influence of his past karma, he experienced supreme suffering.
Having had a stable for fodder constructed in the garden field by my sons and others, my father was always kept there on a comfortable couch;
rubbing his hips again and again, he would move from side to side. (21)
There he makes excrement and urines all around;
he even spits, and no one goes near his side. The ground all around that house has become exceedingly foul-smelling. (22–23)
To such an old man, who is covered in foul-smelling filth and infested with flies and crows, his sons always cast food from afar;
unrefined, they even throw water from a distance.

The aged bearer of the curse experiences the gradual fruit of having rendered the flies wingless; his life-force does not depart from the body, and here within this very body, a dreadful hell has arrived for him to experience as his retribution. (29–26)
It cannot be cleansed by anyone at all; rather, it increases even with medical treatment.
Furthermore, the hands, feet, and hoods have been devoured by sloughing leprosy, and the disease has become exceedingly violent, reaching as far as the edge of the forearm.
O Lakṣmī, in this world, kings kill birds, animals, reptiles, beasts, and insects by an untimely death, which indeed brings great sin;
as do they kill the rat, the mongoose, the monitor lizard, the sparrow, or the frog. (28–29)
In this world, those ignorant ones obtain only cruel fruit, which brings about the destruction of all; they likewise kill the offspring of living beings,
and thus a curse upon them arises in vain for their innocent [offspring].

Indeed, even if they are engaged in their own work, they repeatedly strike their vehicles—horses, bulls, elephants, and camels—even if it be in vain. By their curse, the master's entire wealth and happiness perish. (31–32)
Women are beaten by the ignorant, and even dogs by children;
by the curse of those [women] and those [dogs], the strikers (tāḍakāḥ) are consumed.
Moreover, the sick, the wretched, and even those deprived of water and food [suffer likewise].
They are poor, destitute of wealth, and deprived of household prosperity.
Whatever action has been performed remains present in every way, whether long ago or today.
Thus, this man's own committed action has manifested in its full intensity.
Even in the midst of extreme suffering, his sons and others did not die; yet the family became broken-hearted, their desires shattered, and their hopes destroyed.
Then, with their faith broken, the sons held a consultation.
The father does not die, though he is afflicted by the disease-wind of the garden (vāṭikā).
And because of the dwelling of the sick man, the grain has become diseased in the form of food.
If one who suffers from leprosy with oozing bile should die, it would be auspicious. (37–38)
Due to the abundance of these past sins, death does not indeed come to him, nor does disease; rather, he becomes tranquil and his condition increases.
What should be done? Where should one go? Truly, no remedy appears at all.
Moreover, even if the unpleasant act of harming their father must be performed by sons—
whether he is to be killed here, cast away elsewhere into a pit,
or sent adrift upon the water while still alive— it is indeed a cruel slaughter.
"Protection is appropriate here; what need is there for this unbearable vow?"—such was the deliberation that arose among the five sons.
Among them, the youngest was suddenly filled with both righteousness and affection.
Knowing the fruit of serving one's father, he spoke indeed in the midst of his brothers:
"The father is Nārāyaṇa himself; the father is likewise the other Brahmā.
The father is declared to be the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha); indeed, the father must be served by those born of his lineage. (43–44)
"The fruit of a son's service to his father is heaven and liberation;
therefore, he should be served even if he is diseased or of ill conduct.
Having heard these words of the youngest brother, the second one also spoke thereafter.
What you have said is appropriate and brings auspiciousness, provided one remains in good health and conducts oneself well.
However, a suffering greater than death itself is seen here;
therefore, service causes him pain and increases all his ailments.
Indeed, whoever should be intent on serving him would also suffer from disease;
this affliction is contagious, arising from such modes of transmission as contact.
Therefore, even service to him is destructive to all health.
"Therefore, that service would yield evil fruit; I do not approve of it.
Then the third spoke: "In this service, let us constantly employ another person—either a male servant or a female servant—on a good salary. (3.197.50)
The fourth said: "Even though that is appropriate, neither a woman nor any man at all can be obtained even through service and wages.
Therefore, what must be done in this matter? Let that be considered. ||51||
Then the fifth son, Jīvana, who was indeed the eldest, spoke to his father:
"Various methods of entering the water at a sacred ford, in a river, or even in the ocean, as well as leaping from a precipice, have been shown in the scriptures. (52–53)
Falling from a mountain, burning in fire, plunging into water,
lying in a pit in the earth, or fasting in sacred places—
[these are the means] for those with incurable diseases, for the dispassionate, and likewise for renunciants. (54)
For those desiring heaven, such falls from the Bhṛgu cliff grant the fulfillment of their wishes.
Indeed, in the end, one must perform the ritual suicide by falling from the Bhṛgu cliff, provided that no servant is found who will not serve for wages. (55–56)
Having reflected thus, he appointed these five to the service of the younger brother; however, out of loathing, he became despondent.
His faith departed, and thereafter he appointed a servant.
Many have become servants for one day or two days;
some are servants for five days, and others for merely half a day.
Indeed, those filled with compassion do not perform service, and they depart.
"Thus, since a servant cannot be found, these five sons of yours are highly esteemed;
let the act of throwing him down from a mountain be carried out, for that is what pleases him.
When his father was thus questioned, he heard it and, being overcome by excessive passion, replied, "No."
When asked about being consumed by fire, he likewise said "no" to them.
When asked about the noose around his neck, he likewise said "no" to them.
Endowed with the sense of "I" regarding the body, he would not accept death.

When questioned, he told them, "Even so, no; casting me into a hole in the earth is not what I desire, nor is being carried away by the current of a river. Indeed, for my father, whose body is afflicted by illness, life itself is what he desires. (63)
Even in this extremely degraded body, the living self (jīvātman) possesses here a permanent substratum,
as well as affection and a sense of identity, just like that of an animal;
this occurs even for humans, gods, and the wise.
What wonder is there indeed in this for the ignorant in the cycle of existence?
Thus, even his father— having attained a state of identity with his own diseased, aged, and wasting body—
was truly unable to abandon it.
He spoke to his sons like one in distress: "I do not wish to die.
Just as food and water are given to me from afar, let them be given to me in the garden or nearby in the forest. (67–68)
"O sons, I do not desire my own death at all; great fear is seen to arise when one forcibly abandons life through excessive exertion.
I shall remember the Supreme Self; cast me far away from here."
"Only after having fully experienced the fruit of my karma do I wish to die in every way.
When he had spoken thus, those sons, full of deceit, said in private:
"So be it, father; we shall indeed cast you into the forest."
We shall provide food and other offerings there, but certainly not in the garden;
rather, first a holy site (*tīrtha*) must be established, for from that merit shall arise in its entirety and there shall be the washing away of all sins. (72)

"Having bathed our father at the Mūladvārāvatī-tīrtha, which is situated on the seashore, we shall carry him to the vicinity of the garden. We shall keep him in the forest out of fear of the transmission of disease. (73–74)
Having spoken thus, all those sons, who were indeed disguised as pilgrims,
placed their father upon a cart and went to the vicinity of the ocean.
Having reached the shore at the water's edge, they bathed him there.
"O father, they say you must remember the adorable Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Whether an object or anything else has been placed on the ground, in a pit, or elsewhere—if it is to be seen or spoken of, show it and report it. (76–77)
"Perform for me the act of throwing myself from the Bhṛgu cliff or casting myself into the waters of the ocean, which grants the attainment of heaven; fix your mind on Kṛṣṇa.
Thus addressed, his father said, "Such was my destiny (prārabdha)."
"O sons, it is not your fault that my death has occurred in such a manner.
This is the fruit of many past sins that have ripened here for me, even though I have five sons, a devoted wife, and daughters. (3.197.79–80)
"Though my death in the ocean while broken and helpless be thus,
let there nevertheless be much gold and silver coinage;
let them also know that which was previously deposited by me beneath the hearth."
"That wealth, earned over many years, shall indeed amount to more than a hundred thousand;
others do not know it at all—let only five know my riches.
Having spoken thus and meditated upon Śrī Hari, his sole kinsman and supreme protector, ||82-83||
O Kṛṣṇa, he quickly remembered me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, with his heart focused one-pointedly through all his mental functions.
Having concealed the perception of the body and withdrawn the activities of the senses, [he meditated]. (84)
Completely establishing the internal manifestation within the individual self (jīvātman)—
Sve-rūpe Saccidānanda, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī,
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Ramā, and the Lord of Māṇikī. (85–86)
When the end of her life was at hand, Padmāvatī praised with devotion her Lord— the Sovereign of Padmāvatī, the husband of Brahmapriyā, and the protector of the virtuous.
But her sons, lifting him up, threw him into the waters of the ocean.
They remained watching from the bank and bathed under his pretext;
at that time, while his father’s body was submerged in the water, his sons thought, "He is either dead or has been seized by some creature. (87–88)
There, those sons wept with a display arising from the power of affection;
for the removal of their sin, they remembered the Supreme Lord Hari and me:
"O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, forgive us this terrifying patricide."
"It was she who destroys merit, destroys heaven, destroys liberation, and causes destruction.
We have indeed cast her into the ocean; forgive us for that, O Supreme Lord.
We shall perform the Viṣṇu-sacrifice with abundant ancestral wealth."
"Provide for my father's elevation to heaven or his liberation"—
thus did they seek refuge at my feet upon their father's death.
Then seven daughters and a wife likewise undertook a fast unto death within the house.

Weak, powerless, and unable to speak of the terrible end, they understood that their father had been killed and performed the fast unto death (*anaśana*). At home, they worshipped me with the sixteen types of offerings (*upacāra*). ||93-94||
They offered hymns of praise for the sake of their ancestors and maintained the integrity of their vows;
indeed, they performed my worship with a hundred thousand *tulasī* leaves.
Then, O Lakṣmī, the Lord, the bringer of auspiciousness to his devotees, suddenly spoke.
I suddenly appeared in the ocean in the presence of my father’s body.
Having been touched by me while in the midst of the water, the sick man fell into a swoon;
yet his disease was instantly destroyed, and he was restored with his hands and feet complete with their fingers.
The old man Śāṇadhara became robust, possessing a divine body;
then, lifted by me over the water at the edge of the ocean,
he was cast down upon the shore in the presence of his sons, with his limbs restored and free from disease.

He and all his sons worshipped me with devotion as I held the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; then I quickly vanished from there. Having appeared in the house, I saw those women who were staying there for the purpose of fasting. (3.197.100)
I spoke to those women, and Śāṇadhara was restored to life by me;
unhurt, he is coming quickly with his sons.
Having performed the pilgrimage to Somanātha, they will indeed arrive here.
Thus addressed, they worshipped me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their beloved Lord.
They waited for the garden where their father’s guide had arrived;
then I vanished, and at the end of the day, my father returned home.

He arrived together with his son, bringing about a festival of joy; indeed, the entire family became exceedingly delighted, as did other people as well. They became knowers of my greatness and were filled with wonder. (104)
They say that devotion is the cause for health and for the preservation of life. (105) Now, a great sacrifice known as Vaiṣṇava was performed by my sons;
there, the gods, sages, ancestors, and I were gratified with the food offered. (106)
By means of sacrificial fees, the poor were satisfied; by food, those who bear bodies;
and through my devotion, both I and Śrī Hari became truly pleased at the sacrifice.
Thus, the protection of my father was achieved by me against those who would have killed him.
I have acted with compassion toward my devoted ones by that Great-Souled One.
Thus, at the end, they were led to liberation in my supreme, imperishable abode.
By reading or hearing this, there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Health arises and good fortune also increases;
there shall be the destruction of obstacles and even the destruction of enemies. My devotee shall obtain well-being and prosperity as well. (3.197.110)
One shall indeed obtain heaven, prosperity, as well as one's own desired life.
Being entirely pleased by devotion, I grant whatever is most sought after:
sovereignty, long life, wealth, grain, sons, and daughters.
"O Daughter of the Ocean, I give everything to my devotee and even to my devotee's devotee.
Thus, being subject to the power of devotion, I remain and I protect.

(1.13) Thus, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, in the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, [it is told how] the farmer named Śāṇadhara, who had developed the disease of galat-kuṣṭha due to his actions in a previous birth, was thrown into the ocean by his sons out of fear, and [how he was rescued] by the Blessed Lord.
The one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of Disease, Protection, and the Destruction of Sin," etc., [ends].
Chapter 197 of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age),
Chapter 198.
[The Author: Chapter 199.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, the excellent twice-born Nimbadeva—
In Saurāṣṭra, however, there lived a devotee in a small village named Sadālaya.
Endowed with righteousness, knowledge, and dispassion, he constantly worshipped me with devotion;
he was intent on benefiting others and always devoted to charity. (1–2)
He who knows the Self considers non-violence to be the supreme dharma, service to the virtuous to be superior to that, and service to Hari to be far higher still;
he also performs service to cows and appropriate service to Brahmins.
He performs service to his subjects and service to guests with great respect.
(4) Those who are truthful, virtuous women, holy men, guests, and travelers—whoever comes to his door—he serves them all with a pure heart. (5)
He has established a feast of food for the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the needy; he has established a sacrifice of animals for the benefit of the lame and the aged.
Such is Nimbadeva, who worships me day and night.
Having gone to my temple, he meditates upon Puruṣottama.
He always performs the cleansing, the offering of lamps, the offering of incense, the excellent presentation [of flowers], the offering of water, and the offering of food to me.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Hare, O All-pervading Lord! (9) Thus chanting My name, he goes forth and returns to His home.
Announcing his own home and providing water for the people,
he then became a bull in that village, protected by the villagers;
he was massive in body, exceedingly strong, well-nourished, white, and marked with footprints.
Mahākakughnī and Mahāśṛṅgī, adorned with beautiful forms,
sit on a spot shaded by a *pippala* tree during the day at the outskirts of a village;
sometimes they settle in a village, and sometimes they wander even upon the royal highway.
At night he wanders through the fields and even through the vegetable gardens;
returning again in the morning, he stands upon the village grounds. Whenever this bull sees such things as these: ||| 13-14 ||
Whether he sees Nimbadeva in the middle of the village, on the road, in a field, at a crossroads, at the edge of the settlement, in a garden, or anywhere else—
at that moment, he of fierce form rushes toward him swiftly on four legs.
Remembering his former enmity, he rushes forward out of anger toward Maraka, as if to kill Nimbadeva, to crush him, or to destroy him;
or perhaps it is for the sake of avenging that previous birth.
Thus, when many such occasions arose, Nimbadeva would quickly protect himself through his skillfulness, whether entering a marketplace or a house,
or by climbing onto an altar, a tree, or a high platform.
He always protects his own [village] and travels along the road like one afraid.
Wherever the bull stands, he indeed avoids that road;
for the sake of business outside the house, he travels by another road. (3.198.20)

On the royal highway, in a square, in a field, in a garden, at a city gate, at the outskirts, on the ground, or wherever his gaze falls— he simply does not go there. Thus, with a mind constantly filled with fear, Nimbadeva conducts himself.
The bull, too, constantly cleansed Nimbadeva.
[Thinking,] "When shall I meet him? I shall kill him," he remained ready for action.
Thus, after much time had passed, on one occasion, [he went] to the temple of the god.
Nimbadeva went out at nightfall to see [the deity], devoid of his staff; then, by good fortune and through the turn of fate,
he encountered that bull on the road while it was without weapons.
Then that powerful bull, bellowing like a cow, ran with great speed and fury to kill Nimbadeva. Afterwards, a second cart indeed arrived behind him. ||25-26||

On the narrow path, there was no space on either side to run anywhere; the bull rushed forward, even as he was caught between two snares on a path that brings death. (27) Thus it was on both sides, in a path that bestows death.
At that moment, Nimbadeva immediately remembered me, Hari.
He saw a very solid stone lying there, which could be lifted by the hand;
he quickly and forcefully raised it with his hand.
With all his might, he suddenly struck the bull on the head with his hand; he struck it so violently that he completely killed it.
Then the bull split open the forehead of its head.
From that beating, he quickly fell into a swoon and experienced two cycles of dizziness;
he collapsed there upon the ground and died in an instant.
Thus, it came to pass that there was no fault in the killing of an assailant.
One should never place trust in those with fangs, those with horns, nor likewise in those with weapons; nor in the mindless, nor in thieves seeking food and drink,
nor even in kings, courtesans, enemies, and elephants.

One should never place trust in those with claws, in those characterized by darkness (tamas), in fires, in waters, in the planets, or in those who act for their own selfish ends; likewise, one should never place trust in wicked women or evil men. 34–35.
One must never place trust in those who are aged, nor in mechanical devices, nor in entertainers, nor in those who are violent or prone to mockery;
nor in the young, nor in the sick, nor in those possessed by anger, nor even in those who are reckless. (36)
One should never place trust in beggars or fools;
(37) nor should one place trust in those of unripened intellect, the lazy, those who destroy righteousness, atheists, or those who seek only pleasure. (38)
One should never place trust in those who are unacquainted with one's circle, nor in the deceitful, the greedy, the weaponless, or the lustful. Likewise,
[one should not trust] clouds, the heat of the sun, dust, or the winds.
One must never place trust in those who are characterized by darkness (*tamas*) or who act out of darkness;

nor should one place trust in those possessed by delusion, those intoxicated with pride, those whose nature is excessively fawning, or those who seek to gain entry into one's inner circle. (3.198.40–41)
One must never place trust in travelers, in caravans that meet for a moment, in those who possess great pride and the like, nor even in independent women;
nor in wicked co-wives who are characterized by a lack of attentiveness.
One should never place trust in those who do not abide by the rules of dice;
nor should one place trust in people devoid of faith, nor in actors, dancers, and yogis, nor in those at gambling dens or on the battlefield. (42–44)
One must never place trust in barbers who lack a compassionate heart, who benefit those of a different caste, who drink liquor,
who are by nature prone to looking for flaws, who are envious, and who are negligent. (45)
One must never place trust in those who have not practiced [the arts] and are unskilled;
nor should one place trust in those whose speech is full of pleasant flattery, who act in opposition to the path of political ethics (nīti), or who do not follow the sacred scriptures. 46–47.
One should never place trust in those who claim to be mindless, who destroy their own fame and reputation, whose minds are addicted to disputation,
who subsist by the practice of plucking [hair], and who behave with falsehood and injustice.
One should never place trust even in those who guard the truth;
likewise, one should never place trust in deep ravines, forests, wildernesses, or lakes, nor in those whose sensory faculties and mental activities have been stilled. (3.198.50)
One should never place trust in those who are unsteady, tall, or short, in those who hang low, nor in the one-eyed or the lame;
likewise, not in those whose channels are constricted, nor in those who have abandoned their families.
And one must never place trust in those who have abandoned their country and subjects;
nor should one place trust in courtesans, in deceptive goods, in women who have sought refuge, or in women related to the king. (52–53)
One must never place trust in regions of excessive rain, in grassy meadows, in the earth, in mountains, or in mud;
nor in physicians whose conduct is unknown, in cremation grounds, or in those who are impetuous.
One must never place trust in unknown medicinal herbs;
one must never place trust in food provided by an enemy, nor in perfumes provided by an enemy, nor in persons sent by an enemy. (95–96)
One must never place trust in parrots that have been nourished by an enemy, birds that have been protected by an enemy, or those whose wings are marked with an enemy's seal;
nor in wives who are excessively prone to anger, nor in husbands who are excessively prone to anger. (57)
One should never place trust in those who have over-eaten (568).
Likewise, one should never place trust in dilapidated dwellings, in decrepit bodies, or in medicines that have long been stored away. (569)
One must never place trust in those who are addicted to mantras and tantras, those who are experts in elixirs (*rasāyana*), or in *āsuras* and *rākṣasas*.
For those who crave honor, there is honor here and honor there.
One must never place trust in double-tongued men, nor in those who are solitary;
one must never place trust in widowers, nor in widows, nor in deceitful women; one must never place trust in those devoid of passion, nor in those who are haughty.

One must never place trust in those who are disoriented by confusion of the directions, those possessed by *preta*s or *bhūta*s, those afflicted by wind-diseases (*vāyu-roga*), those who have fallen into the hands of a foreign enemy,
nor in reptiles, those with webbed hands, aquatic creatures, or those who move crookedly.
One must never place trust in people who are hungry;
nor should one place trust in spies, forest-dwellers, those who have entered a foreign kingdom, or even dependents who lack affection. (64–65)
One must never place trust in those deities who have been installed by the ignorant, nor in their actions which are inherently transgressive; likewise,
one should not trust the words of fools who are overwhelmed by times of calamity.
One should never place trust in people who accomplish their own selfish ends;
nor should one place trust in those who serve many households, those who attend upon many kings, those who are highly disciplined yogis, or those who have made their homes on the borders. (67–68)
One must never place trust in those who roam at night, in those who seize by force, in those who are suffering, or in those whose conduct is unknown; nor in those who are agitated,
those who are dispassionate, those under religious vows, or those who act with impetuosity.
And one must never place trust in those who are intent on external activities;

nor should one place trust in those whose lands are overgrown with moss, in those whose ships have been wrecked, in those who are high-minded, or in those who are angry one moment and satisfied the next. (3.198.70–71)
One must never place trust in those demons who are attached to their bodies, senses, and so forth; nor in the wives of others; nor in a gathering of many people;
nor in those who are jealous during a festival; nor in paramours or the wives of paramours.
In the same way, one must never place trust in the sons of concubines (upaputra), nor in stepmothers, the blind, merchants, or fallacious logicians;
nor should one place trust in those who are devoid of devotion to me. || 73-74 ||
One must never place trust in those who are diseased, wounded, inflamed, or trembling, nor in those who experience many dreams; likewise,
one should not trust those who are unknown, unheard of, unpracticed, or beginners in their actions.
One must never place trust in those who have not practiced cooking.
(76) One must never place trust in those who possess only partial practice, those whose roots are uprooted, those of boundless stature, or those who take their stand upon the sky. (77)
For in every such case, O Lakṣmī, one who places his trust [in others] inevitably encounters suffering, injury, calamity, or even death; there is no doubt about this.
Realizing this, Nimbadeva then slew the bull.
The sin of cow-slaughter clung to him;
Nimbadeva quickly fell into a state of unconsciousness, turned black, and became afflicted with leprosy.
Somehow or other, he suddenly returned to his own home.
Having summoned the Brahmins, he confessed that killing;
the twice-born ones also told him that for the sake of a Viṣṇu-sacrifice, the expiation consists of eating only one meal a day for a year and the gift of a thousand cows.
(8.1) Even so, [he performed] the giving of a thousand cows while eating but once a day.
He performed everything and gave the sacrificial fee at the conclusion of the sacrifice;
nevertheless, his dark complexion did not fade and his mental confusion did not depart.
Then he fell into despair and remembered me, Hari.
Knowing him to be a supreme devotee, Nārāyaṇa and I appeared before him;
manifesting in a divine form, he touched him with his own arm. Instantly, the devotee became white-complexioned, pure-minded, and perfectly composed.
I gave the mantra to him, and he received it with great devotion:
"Bālakṛṣṇa is Lord Hari himself, the Blessed One who grants me liberation. Thereafter, he too constantly spoke this mantra.
When the time had come, my devotee Nimbadevaka attained liberation.
Thus, indeed, the destruction of his sin of killing was brought about by me at his sacrifice.
By my power, no inauspiciousness whatsoever remains among my devotees.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in a previous birth, he was a servant of Nimbadeva.
Even after receiving his full wages and completing his work, he remained lazy, negligent, and prone to anger. (88–89)
Having died from fever, that servant indeed became a bull;
possessing the memory of his past life, he constantly beheld his master—who was ever assigning him tasks and even reviling him. (3.198.90)
Seeing [the master] again and again, he displays his enmity there;
driven by anger and rage, he runs toward his own master to kill him.
Indeed, such a bull meets his death at the very hand of his master. (91–92)
Having incurred a debt, he was born again as his son—
handsome, wise, and a performer of many deeds.
Then, in his old age, Nimbadeva gave everything to his son.
Together with his family, he worships me, the Lord, daily; thus I rejoice.
His son also worships me, known by the name Gokulavardhana;
indeed, through devotion to me, that son also attained liberation even while in the state of food.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the faults committed in this way are surely destroyed by my majesty,
as well as by devotion to me, meditation, chanting my names, and seeking refuge;
and through service to and association with the virtuous, all sins perish in every respect.
Through the service of devotees, women, and virtuous wives, as well as through their blessings, all sins are destroyed in every way;
likewise, all obstacles perish, and it is the destroyer of all calamities. (97–98)

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Sin of Cow-Slaughter was Averted for the Devotee Named Nimbadeva by the Blessed Lord," in the Third Section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 198. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 199 [Author:
Chapter 200 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, out of compassion I shall tell you that which must always be practiced by all people: the service of the true scriptures,
and specifically the study of this *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*.
This must be performed by women and by men alike, by all embodied beings.
It is the modes of devotion to me, as well as the means for liberation, the causes for attaining heaven, and the sustenance of all created worlds. (2–3)
All these many things have been spoken here by me out of compassion.
Indeed, I have declared that my auspicious devotees are those who possess exclusive devotion.
Furthermore, there are those whose intellect perceives the body as the self, as well as those whose intellect perceives Brahman as the self.

Those devoted to their own self-interest have been described as such, whereas those whose nature is divine are devoted to the interest of others. (5) But the divine ones, established in the Self which is distinct from the three bodies, worship Me directly in that Self which is supremely luminous. (6)
They behold my eternal form as the Self, which is exceedingly luminous;
within that form of the Self, they behold me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord, intensely radiant and delighting in union with the Self. (7)
These very ones, possessing divine vision, though remaining in this world,
abide in the city of Brahman, just like you who are dear to Brahman.
Indeed, the state of Brahman, which bestows supreme bliss, is to be realized by devotees through spiritual practice.
For those women or men who harbor the thought that I am their husband, let there be fear of obstacles for them, or let there be separation from me;
or perhaps, due to my absence, they might never attain my abode at all. (3.199.10)

Therefore, my devotees in this world certainly never entertain the notion of me as a mere human being; rather, they always maintain a divine conception of me. Indeed, just as they hold a divine conception of me, so too do they hold it of themselves.
One should cultivate divine contemplation, and not the contemplation of the body as the self;
for those embodied beings, the contemplation of the body as the self becomes a source of obstacles.
Brahmā himself fell into delusion upon beholding the very form of Pārvatī.
From that lapse, the great sages known as the Bālakhilyas were born.
Śaṅkara, upon seeing me in my enchanting form, became infatuated;
and Nārada, out of a sense of physical attachment, desired to marry me.
In this way, many others as well have gone, having been freed from delusion;
yet for those who possess a body, a great obstacle consisting of delusion arises.
But for those endowed with divine nature, who dwell established in the Self—
Indeed, the state of Brahman arises like that of Śuka, as did that of Sanaka and the others.
All my divine pastimes should be understood as arising from spontaneous love; through affection for me, that divine play (yoginī) surely bestows liberation. || 17–18 ||
May there be for me deep affection and intense love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa,
and may that supreme love which is eternally fixed upon my own Self remain firm.
By this affection, the illusory attachment of devotees is dissolved.
The affection for Māyā indeed provides the basis for its persistence, yet it does not exist within me. (3.199.20) Meditation upon me must always be performed constantly with affection;
the steady state of meditation is the cause of great samādhi. (21)
When one's conduct becomes firm, there shall be single-minded devotion to me, Keśava—
the Lord who is a mass of eternal bliss and the bestower of great happiness.
One should constantly establish steadfastness in me during all activities.
When such practice has arisen, the self is restrained within me;
with the internal organ and the senses, it becomes completely absorbed in me.
Thus, through the restraint of the mind, when all [modifications] are restrained, one comes to abide in me.
O Rame, the cause for that is an abundance of love, and nothing else.
Through affection, the minds of devotees become fixed upon Me;
likewise, O Rame, may My dwelling within their very selves be sudden and firm.
Indeed, through love, even my physical form becomes a direct reminder [of the Divine].
(26) Furthermore, the knowledge of His majesty increases constantly through love.
Love conjoined with the knowledge of majesty attains the state of abiding as the Self that is Brahman. (27)
He would not perceive illusion; he would perceive me, the eternal Brahman—imperishable, of divine form, and filled with existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Indeed, within that very imperishable, eternal Brahman which is one's own true self, [he perceives me].

In the all-pervading light of consciousness, which is eternally of one single flavor, he shall behold me, the Supreme Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the divine and beloved; he beholds no other form. (3.199.30)
This is the divine state of Brahman, as well as the state of supreme knowledge;
it is also the state of divine wisdom, known as the dissolution of [dualistic] knowledge.
It consists of eternal stability when Kṛṣṇa, the supreme deity, is directly realized.
O Lakṣmī, that embodied being who constantly undertakes this [practice] attains the supreme and most excellent state, just like yours;
for by him my greatness has indeed been directly realized. (32–33)
By his grace, there shall arise within his heart a corresponding measure of illumination;
he beholds that consciousness-constituted light as it increases, and likewise perceives its expanding majesty for as long as it grows. (34)
By my grace, he finds within the form of Brahman the *praṇava* of that same extent and likewise my own form of that same nature;
gradually, he beholds everywhere the fully perfected light.
He indeed hears the sweet sounds of the resonances of my names,
while being immersed in the sound of Brahman (brahmanāda) and absorbed in the eternal Self.
For one who is free from illusion and liberated, that very state is becoming one with Brahman (brahmībhūtatva).

To whatever extent one experiences my majesty in abundance, to that same extent there is the vision of me, the Supreme Self, as the state of Brahman. This occurs for one who has reached the highest pinnacle and who knows my majesty. (38–39)
Sovereignty over time, māyā, and the controllers arises [in me]; I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, and He is equal to me.
I am the sustainer of all incarnations and the regulator of time and māyā.
Transcending all qualities, changeless, the Lord of the lords of all lords,
I manifest here like a mortal by my own will for the sake of the welfare of embodied beings;
and like a mortal, I perform all actions for the sake of my devotees.
In this regard, those of deluded intellect and little knowledge, possessing only the eye of flesh,
rely upon their own experience as an analogy and project faults [upon me].
"O Lakṣmī, I am always faultless and ever like a wish-fulfilling gem."
Indeed, all the defects of the imagined enter into those who imagine;
for those who conceive of me as a lustful being become lustful themselves, and those who conceive of me as angry become angry themselves. (44–45)
Those who are themselves lecherous think of me as a lecher;
those who are themselves deceitful know me to be deceitful.
Indeed, the demonic ones of base intellect perceive me as non-divine.
Those who indeed know me as both divine and human,
they become divine; and even those deities who know me, though possessing a human form, as the faultless Lord, [they too become divine].
Even those who are possessed of faults become faultless by my power,
for he under whose control are all the external senses and the internal ones,
and under whose control is even his volition, having the firm conviction that Kṛṣṇa is directly present before him.
He alone is always considered full, blessed, and one who has achieved his purpose. As is the liberated one, so is he; as it is in the Imperishable (akṣara), so is it here for him.
As is the divine state, so shall he be here, endowed with all sovereign powers.
O Lakṣmī, he should consider his own fortune as merged with the fortune of Śrī Hari and not separate from it; indeed, he should consider himself blessed.
In this world, which is scorched by the forest fire of lust and other passions, he is truly blessed that [this fortune] belongs to me.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa met him in person.
Indeed, the saints who grant liberation and destroy all faults have gathered around him;
by their grace, I shall conquer the internal enemies such as desire and the rest. (53–54)
And by the power of my good fortune and through the grace of Śrī Hari, I shall perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa in the form of Brahmā, which bestows liberation.
Such devotees of mine as these are considered fortunate; I take delight in them.
They have indeed attained all perfect qualities and employ the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
There is no incompleteness in them; they are perfectly fulfilled by virtue of being my refuge.
For I, the Lord of Rādhikā, am present before their very eyes, having met with them.
For their merit arising from previous births is abundant,
since this great yoga of association with the virtuous has arisen, which bestows liberation.
However, if there should be any incompleteness in the devotee who has surrendered, [then...]
However, that [state] is rich with the knowledge of one's own greatness when it is established in the Self and free from what must be removed.
If the state of being established in the Self is weak, it causes suffering even during meditative absorption (samādhi).
But when sounds are heard as if they were splitting the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), [then it is not so]. (3.199.60)
But at that time, one who lacks steadfastness in the Self fears even within samādhi;
however, being fearless through the reality of the Self, he indeed attains identity with Brahman.
The meditator beholds therein the splendor that consumes the cosmic egg.
Then, being devoid of self-abidance and lacking a refuge, he fears;
or else, Hari—who is purified by love—becomes his companion on that path.
One who knows the Self does not experience fear, whether he has Hari as his companion or not.
For the knower of the Self, all latent tendencies toward sense objects shatter;
yet, through one-pointedness, the mind attains cessation within Kṛṣṇa.
The relinquishing of the flow of all the senses into Me, Kṛṣṇa, [is the means].
My devotees must remain steadfast; no obstacle shall arise for them.
When the mind of a devotee—possessing a single strength and a single function—becomes perfectly steady and fixed upon Me alone, it can no longer be drawn away. (65–66)
For that [state] is indeed free from latent desires (nirvāsana) because of its delightful objects;
it is restrained within my form and devoid of thought of anything other than Me.
In this way, the mind of the virtuous becomes truly restrained in Me.
Abandoning all else, those whose purpose is fulfilled by Kṛṣṇa perform my worship.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I am attainable through grace and am the bestower of complete desires;
for the great devotees of the Lord, being saintly, worship me in nine ways.
Those who are established in Brahman, who know the Self, and who understand my majesty—
those whose devotion is firm and whose service is constant— their [realization] increases; likewise,
being established in identity with Me, they become one with Me.
Nevertheless, one should not strive for excellence, for in excess there is the state of a burnt seed.
For the grace of Hari ceases to be fruitful when directed toward such [excellence].
Therefore, everything, including prosperity and the like, should be established in Me alone.
Intellect, mind, ego, consciousness, and the functions of the senses,
as well as the body and the qualities of the body, should all be established within me, the Lord.
May my state of being a relisher of divine rasa be fixed solely upon Hari, the infant Kṛṣṇa, my Sovereign.
One should constantly offer [all things] to the Lord of Śrī Lakṣmī and Rādhikā;
the aesthetic flavor (rasa) of the singer should also be offered to the Lord.
Kīrtana, along with gestures (hāva) and emotional expressions (bhāva), should be offered to Me, the Supreme.
If devotion were to exist as a sentiment elsewhere without being offered to Me, there would be attachment to that;
consequently, there would be a fall from the path of the highest good.
This cannot happen for the singular devotee who is a connoisseur of the aesthetic flavor [of devotion].
Indeed, there may be aesthetic relish (*rasa*) somewhere among other objects in the worlds besides Me;

yet he who finds his relish in the Word (*śabda*) that partakes of My playful qualities (*līlā-guṇa*), and not elsewhere—he alone is My beloved, the connoisseur of the Word (*śābdika-rasika*). (77–78)
That devotee who finds delight in the touch of my limbs through yoga is considered truly enamored;
he is not a connoisseur of my touch anywhere else.
He whose vision of me and of my own [devotees] is filled with aesthetic relish (rasa) [is truly mine].
He who has no desire for anything else, being a connoisseur of my beautiful form— he is mine.
He whose excellent taste finds delight in the exquisite flavors of the food, betel, and other offerings presented by me, and who finds no pleasure in anything else— he is mine.
He who finds true flavor only in smelling the fragrances and other offerings dedicated by me,
and not in any other scent or the like— he is my connoisseur of fragrance.
As for me, however, the grasping of divine objects belongs to my two hands.

His speech consists of the essence of rasa, recounting my stories and the like; through union with me, his words are filled with the true flavor of bliss and other such states arising from my yoga. (83–84) His walking is the circumambulation of my temples, and his feet are my own.

(83) [The above is the continuation of verse 83. His speech consists of the essence of rasa, recounting my stories and the like; through union with me, his words are filled with the true flavor of bliss and other such states arising from my yoga. (84)

All such things as these indeed possess flavor for my sake; the mind, the intellect, the consciousness, the ego, and even the vital breath—all these truly partake of the nature of my rasa for that devotee who possesses them. (85)
He who finds joy in my form and even in the forms of material objects,
who possesses an excellence of aesthetic relish (rasa) toward the divine devotees in every respect, and whose ultimate inclination is directed toward me alone— [he is truly devoted]. || 86–87 ||

Whether waking, sleeping, or even in a state of unconsciousness—for one who is established in the fourth state (turyā) within me alone, and for whom every aesthetic flavor (rasa) is considered to reside in me;
for that divine devotee, true connoisseurship (rasikatā) is deemed to exist. ॥88॥

In the heart of such a devotee, a connoisseur of rasa, I, Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, ever manifest in my divine form. And as he beholds my extraordinary form within his own heart, [he attains liberation]. (3.199.90)
The splendor of Brahman shines forth, and within that radiance I am the Lord;
therefore, my form should be held fast by devotees through singing and chanting.
And let the mind be established in my form, endowed with self-surrender and faith.
Wherever it may be, it cannot be entered by any other object;
for the Blessed One is capable of removing all illusory obstacles from every side, for he is indeed the Lord of all lords.
By him the terrestrial spheres were supported, and likewise the stars were held in the sky;
by him indeed the rising and setting of the sun and moon were ordained;
and by him the clouds were fashioned—those water-bearers that bestow moisture.
By him were created the seasons, which bestow trees, creepers, and fruits;
by his command even the oceans do not overstep their own shores.
From a mere drop of his seed are born embodied offspring with distinct forms. (95–96)
I am that glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, who possesses a human form; by my own will, I have established myself as the soul, which is indeed beyond the senses.
I am the Lord both externally, within the heart, and in the divine abode.
And here, the Lord is united with his devotees for their supreme spiritual welfare.
(98) Having realized me to be such, as the object of the knowledge of my majesty, my devotee should offer me devotion free from all fear. (99)
For such a wise person, the state of Brahman exists here in this world;
indeed, the illusions of *māyā* do not enter his heart.
His state becomes truly divine, for he is indeed equal toward pleasure and pain.
Whether in worship or in beating, in mounting an elephant or riding a donkey;
toward enemy or friend, gold or iron, beauty or ugliness, and in both contempt and honor—his equanimity indeed remains constant. (101–102)
Indeed, my residence is always within the heart of such a person;
even the gods and lords perform his worship.
He becomes the deliverer of worldly beings from the ocean of existence.
This [Lord] is the support of the worlds and is also endowed with sovereign power. (1.04) Endowed with countless auspicious qualities, He also bestows liberation.
My form always dwells within His form; I rejoice there. (1.05)
All my senses dwell within his senses; my entire inner organ rejoices within his inner organ.
Therefore, he is the illuminator of the eyes and other faculties of all the worlds.
Though he is capable like me due to his union with my very self,
nevertheless, by abiding in goodness, he endures even the insults inflicted by lowly creatures; for the dharma of forbearance is indeed the mark of a virtuous man.
That very Great Self is indeed patience, the supreme capacity.
Through association with such a holy man as I,
and through the offering [of oneself], all desires are fulfilled, and one attains both heaven and liberation.
"By reading and hearing this, O Rame, one shall obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari Spoke of the Brahman-absorption, Sovereignty, and other qualities of His Exclusive Devotees," in the Third Section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Chapter 200 [[Author: → Chapter 201
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of Bhāṇḍabhakta.
In the city of Bhāṇḍīya, there was indeed a Śūdra named Bhāṇḍa who was a king among devotees. (1)
Formerly, there was one named Kālīndara, skilled in singing and instrumental music. From childhood, Kālīndara was exceedingly proficient and possessed a deep appreciation for musical melodies.
He understood the art of instrumental performance as it follows the contours of vocal song.

Many musical instruments belonging to him, having arrived at the hall from afar, were even then being practiced there by the residents— [instruments] consisting of dances, songs, and rhythmic clapping, whose very essence was the rhythmic clapping of the throat. (3–4)
Many female dancers, courtesans, and young maidens also came to his hall and practiced such movements as those consisting of throat-beats, palm-claps, hip-shakes, and hand-claps.
Year after year, they then hold a great festival;
in that assembly, they present exhibitions of instruction.
Thus, there are singers and dancers who are exceedingly skilled.
Debateurs, jesters, and men and women of many forms receive excellent rewards according to their learning—
whether consisting of gold, silver, jewels, or ornaments. (8)
The musical form consisting of costumes was presented by the assembly.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, a very great festival occurs every year;
because of that, he became famous as Bhāṇḍa Kālīndara. (3.200.10)
Virtuous, truthful kings, merchants, and officials arrive at the festival as bestowers of rewards;
he honors them with hospitality according to their rank and their wealth. (11)
King Bhāṇḍīra,
being worthy, also offered due honor and a fitting welcome to the king and the others;
and in such an assembly as this, Kālīndara was the most devoted of all.
He installs my beautiful golden image, resplendent with all ornaments, upon a throne situated within the assembly hall;
it is the lovely form known as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Lakṣmī and Rādhā. (14)
In a radiant pavilion made of light, resembling the assembly hall of heaven,
you should first worship me,
and thereafter worship the kings, the virtuous men, and the chaste women who stand before you. (15–16)
Having respectfully bowed to the elders, the Brahmins, and the eminent merchants, he then first offered me this beautiful song, rich with prayer:
"Victorious is Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the cause of all! (17)
This Śrīpati, the lord of all prosperity;
this Nārāyaṇa, who has reached the further shore of the Vedas, the beloved of Rādhikā, the Lord of lords—He is victorious! (18)
Victorious is the Lord of Kamalā, the husband of the consort of Brahmā, the beloved of the pearl-like Muktānikā, the Supreme Lord!
Victorious is the Lord of Light and the Lord of Avatāras!
Kambharābālaka is Bālakṛṣṇa. Victorious is Gopālaja, the leader of the Māṇikīs, the sovereign of the imperishable, and the supreme lord.
Victorious is Kṛṣṇa Hari, the Lord of Pārvatī, the inner self and sovereign of all the worlds;
victorious is the Lord of the Gopīs, victorious is the steadfast one.
Victorious is the Lord, the King of all kings;
victorious indeed is Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Mādhava; may the Lord of the lords of lords be triumphant! 21.
May Śrī Hari, Kṛṣṇa— the protector of his devotees and the bestower of the desires of his own people— deliver me,
as well as those of the merchant class and dancing women.
May the Lord of Lords deliver the singer;
may Acyuta, the Lord who is especially the friend of the distressed, fulfill the devotion of his devotees. 22.
Kālīndara praises that Time, who is beyond Māyā, for the sake of enjoyment, liberation, and peace.
Thus, [he praises] me, the person accompanied by the female dancers, with this song. 23.
Having heard Kālīndara, O Lakṣmī, I became repeatedly pleased.
Together with Lakṣmī, Rādhā, and the others, I showed them my own vision;
for Nārāyaṇa, O Lakṣmī, is subservient to his devotees. (24–25)
There, in that assembly hall within the gathering in the pavilion, I manifested an exceedingly radiant mass of splendor born from my own form.
There, my form gradually appeared, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, a crown, bracelets, the Kaustubha gem, and other ornaments; richly arrayed in divine attire and finery; with a gracious countenance and auspicious in appearance;
accompanied by Rādhā and Lakṣmī, and joined by his divine attendants. (27–28)
For a moment there, all the women and men were bewildered; for a moment they indeed became stunned and blind by the masses of splendor.
That splendor suddenly dissolved, and I became a man wearing a dancing costume.
I was seen by them as possessing a beautiful form, yet in an instant I vanished.
Out of even slight devotion on their part, I thus displayed my form;
indeed, the entire assembly desired to behold that form again and again.
Then they all took refuge with the great devotee Kālīndara;
through their faith in me, they all became Vaiṣṇavas. They all worship me constantly and perform kīrtana every morning.
They tell my stories and perform worship for me with various articles. They all partake of the food offering, which is the very form of my grace.
Likewise, they all gather together in the evening to perform *saṃkīrtana*.
O Lakṣmī, that hall of devotees was always like a storehouse;
by my divine grace, through the practice of eating but one meal a day, there occurred a constant chanting of my praises which brought me great joy. (35)
Virtuous men and virtuous women constantly come and go there.
Likewise, Kālindara and other devotees perform my worship daily— beautifully, in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
Through constant devotion, they indeed became purifiers of the assembly.
Once, at the onset of night, my devotee Sādhu Kamalāyana went to the city of Bhāṇḍīra while performing a pilgrimage.

The great devotee Kālīndara, a prompt servant of the saintly, quickly offered water and food to the sage, Lakṣmī; he extended a welcome, presented the madhuparka offering, provided lodging, and performed service with deep devotion. (3.200.39–40)
After evening, an assembly of spectators gathered there.
Among them, Kālindara asked Sata:
"O holy man, tell me how one's own ultimate and absolute well-being may be attained. (41)
The virtuous Kamalāyanasādhu began to speak in the assembly:
"The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who is most dear to all, has out of compassion appeared here in the human lineage for the welfare of embodied beings. (42–43)
Having himself assumed a human form, he dwells indeed upon the earth;
and virtuous, compassionate people who take refuge in him also move about there.
Acting for the welfare of the worlds, they teach his qualities.
Having heard of his qualities, human beings offer devotion.
Through devotion, well-being surely arises and one attains the state of the Imperishable.
Those people who fully grasp the qualities of the virtuous Supreme Self—45–46.
They perform service to the holy ones as well as to the glorious Supreme Soul;
they worship that Lord and the holy ones, and thus they cross the ocean of worldly existence.
But those who seize upon faults fall into the ocean of worldly existence.
The latent impressions of that person increase through the sin of grasping at faults.
But those who, with divine vision, praise and grasp the virtues of the holy Hari which grant liberation, they go to the supreme goal.
Purity arises in the hearts of those who serve the virtuous.
A virtuous person is equal to a hundred Brahmins; Hari is equal to a hundred virtuous persons.
To the extent that he associates with the virtuous day and night, [to that same extent does purity arise].
In that same measure, divine nature increases toward Hari and toward the virtuous;
and in that same measure, purity and association with the good increase.
Great merit, which bestows the supreme liberation, increases.
The sins of the senses perish through association with the virtuous;
therefore, those who are adorned by goodness—the saints—should be served with total self-surrender.
Service to the saint is service to Hari, and by that, one attains the supreme state.
Wherever a saint resides, that house always bestows liberation. Wherever Kṛṣṇa resides, that temple grants supreme release.
That land bestows liberation where the saint Hari shines resplendent.
That bed is purifying upon which a virtuous and peaceful person sleeps.
That day on which one obtains the sight and service of a holy man of Hari is declared to be auspicious;
it is liberation itself, the destroyer of sins.
An assembly is a social gathering where the virtuous meet; it is auspicious. (57) Furthermore, the company of devotees destroys sin and likewise bestows liberation.
So too does the association with saintly Vaiṣṇavas and the service of chaste women. (58)
Association with the virtuous is indeed the treasury of men, for it leads to liberation.
One should always give gifts, merit, food, and so forth to the saintly;
indeed, one’s entire possessions should be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for that brings about liberation.
A wise person should achieve liberation through such services as these.
One should avoid an improper place, an improper time, and the company of the unworthy;
one should cultivate the company of the virtuous and perform righteous deeds, for by that, liberation shall be attained in this very world.
Association with the wicked is a destroyer of devotion; one should abandon it.
One should also avoid association with the corrupt, for it obstructs liberation.
Through the influence of past impressions, purity arises within the heart.
Purity arises in the heart through the awakening of past merit;
purity also arises in the heart through the grace of Śrī Hari; and purity likewise arises in the heart through the grace of the saintly. (63–64)
Through service known as *pauruṣa* toward the holy ones and Śrī Hari,
and through the act of surrendering all one's possessions, supreme purity arises.
He whose inner organ is thus purified becomes attached to the assembly of the virtuous.
Having performed service to holy men and service to Hari, [he attains] grace and favor;
having obtained the favor of Hari and the favor of the holy man,
he then receives the granting of a boon from Hari, the virtuous, and the high-souled ones.

Having attained Śrī Hari, the Lord who assumes the human drama, through right understanding; having met saintly persons who bestow liberation and formed association with the virtuous devotees of Hari;
and having received supreme knowledge from them, one attains divinity through devotion to Him.
By divine grace, the devotee goes to the supreme state.
Through association with the virtuous, there occurs the cessation of volitions, latent impressions, and illusions, as well as the attainment of liberation from Hari. (3.200.70)
The mind of those united with love for Hari Kṛṣṇa becomes absorbed in Him;
likewise, it occurs for those of exclusive devotion through sincere service.
One who is intent on service and devotion is superior, not one who is solely devoted to renunciation.
The servant seeks the liberation of countless others and has desisted from seeking his own liberation.
Since devotion toward Kṛṣṇa is greater for one who serves as a slave, he is superior by the power of that superior devotion and is capable of liberating countless beings. (72–73)
One who has turned away [from devotion] is weak and inferior, whereas by serving His devotees, one becomes strong; such a servant is considered to be firmly established in the command of Kṛṣṇa.
Even if some fault, such as harshness of speech, should occur therein, [it does not affect his status].
He is divine and cannot be grasped; what appears as a fault in Him is actually a virtue.
Indeed, that person who perceives faults is a Dānava or an Asura.
He who seeks out faults in Kṛṣṇa is merely imitating the dance of a human being.
The bestower of auspiciousness and Hari himself fulfills the desires of his devotees here;
he satisfies the longings of women and grants the cherished goals of men as well.
Thereupon, the Daityas, following their own precedent, conceive [these things] as born of karma.
In his divine deeds, which remove all evil by the mere hearing of them, [he manifests] faults such as desire, anger, and greed; yet because of these, they go to a low state.
It is not on account of this that Hari—the virtuous one who brings about the welfare of the world—[is at fault].
Even a scent of fault may arise regarding the divine Supreme Self;
however, one who perceives faults is of demonic nature, therefore one should not imagine any fault.
This applies in every way, whether toward great devotees or even those who are very small.
One should not impute even the slightest fault to Hari in any way whatsoever.
Kṛṣṇa is divine; Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes are divine and may they grant auspiciousness.
The saints are divine; likewise, the pastimes of the saints are divine and grant liberation.
The divine command of Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa prevails there;
whoever is divine in this regard is indeed considered great.
Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of Akṣara, is Śrī Puruṣottama.
"Having directly attained [this state], he who bears the human dance is the one here who sets forth the command.
Having thus resolved, the devotees abide following his word;
through their service, liberation occurs exactly according to his command.
The devotees are marked by [divine] command; they seek liberation and proceed toward liberation.
But those who are non-devotees are worldly, seeking sense objects.
For the devotees, who are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, even sense objects become [liberation].
But for those who are not devotees, the objects of the senses consist of being intent on the tasting of desires:
vulgar song, desirable forms, touch, body-born fragrance, and the eating of forbidden food—these are the objects for those who seek sense-objects. (87–88)
The path of Kṛṣṇa, the form of Kṛṣṇa, the touch of Kṛṣṇa which is exceedingly fragrant,
even the scent of Kṛṣṇa itself, as well as water, food, fruit, ornaments,
the leaf of Tulasī blessed by Kṛṣṇa, and even clothing— [all these are dear]. (89)
The splendor of instrumental music and song, amorous gestures, laughter, songs, dalliance, and dancing—these emotional expressions (bhāvas) are bestowed upon the devotees by the Blessed One.
Those who are vulgar remain outside; the true devotees abide in Keśava.
Just as village folk are unable to abandon their village enjoyments,
so too devotees are truly unable to abandon the enjoyments of Kṛṣṇa.
Even those devotees established in meditative absorption engage in the narration of the stories of Śrī Hari.
They are drawn toward the qualities of Kṛṣṇa alone, and not toward others.
(93) When one abides in sattva, meditation on Hari arises, which brings peace and happiness;
however, when one is in a state of rajas or tamas, meditation on Kṛṣṇa is difficult to sustain. (94)
If the manifestation of the object of meditation does not occur within a heart characterized by passion (rājasa) or ignorance (tāmasa),
then Kṛṣṇa— who assumes the role of a human actor— should be seen externally as one worthy of being beheld.
At that time, the holy devotees (sādhus) likewise should be beheld only externally.
The external states characterized by passion (rājasa) are to be cultivated for the sake of worldly happiness and prosperity. Alternatively, when one’s own true nature is well-considered,
then the state of ignorance (tāmasa) as well as that of passion (rājasa) dissolve through knowledge.
The mind, which is naturally restless like a monkey, must be restrained;
for if it is not restrained, one should constantly chant the praises of Hari externally.
One should perform the excellent chanting of Kṛṣṇa's names accompanied by the playing of cymbals.
By that, the volitions born of passion (rājasa) as well as those born of ignorance (tāmasa) are destroyed.
One should serve the virtuous and receive instruction from the mouths of the virtuous.
Indeed, one should accomplish peace that bestows immortality through sacred recitation (saṃkīrtana).
In Kṛṣṇa, there is an exceedingly firm refuge that brings about grace;
by means of this refuge, the impulses of the qualities are stilled for the yogi of devotion.
One should take refuge in the Supreme Self with complete trust.
The refuge of the Supreme Self should be established either for one’s own sake or out of affection for others.
Or else, the refuge of the Supreme Self should be established through knowledge.
Of these three, the former ones are indeed weak; the refuge born of knowledge is powerful.
People who place their trust in the words of the virtuous take refuge in Hari for the sake of attaining sovereignty, power, health, wealth, and so forth;
yet those people who are motivated by self-interest do so out of affection for His beauty, kindness, relationship, and love. (1.04)
Having become affectionate, they indeed take refuge [in Him] and do not endure separation.
(105) Through the power of association with the virtuous, having realized the majesty of the Supreme Self, those foremost among the wise take refuge in Hari; they possess eternal shelter. (106)
The wise, however, know Hari, the Lord of all lords, the substratum of all qualities and their absence, as well as the master of divine *māyā*;
the Lord, the all-pervading Sovereign, who is the locus of both fault and its absence, and of both justice and injustice. (107)
Minute and great, long and likewise the locus of desire and non-desire;
endowed with sovereignty and lack of sovereignty, accompanied by fear and fearlessness;
existent and non-existent, the sheath of all, and filled with whatever wonders exist. (1.08–1.09)
Action and non-action depend upon Him, as do all things, each according to its own nature.
There is no possibility whatsoever for anyone to exist without Hari;
indeed, He is the great refuge of both the unrighteous and the righteous.
Everything is indeed possible in Kṛṣṇa, who lies within the body of all;
when he is present everywhere, action occurs as it does with a physical body.
Even in his transcendence, everything is indeed possible when he is free from māyā.
That which is equal to illusion (*māyā*) is like illusion; that which is equal to the non-illusory (*amāya*) is like the self.
Therefore, no obstacle arises for one who relies upon this.
Thus, if the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa is resorted to through knowledge, [he is attained].
He shall be a treasury of all arts and the bestower of all supreme blessings. Indeed, by taking refuge in him, all spiritual practices performed become truly effective;
there is no doubt about this. Having propitiated him, one should grant liberation.
"O Kālīndara! Always recognizing this, repeatedly take refuge;
worship Nārāyaṇa Hari, the supreme abode, just as one seeks the highest state for a crop.
Having spoken thus, the saint departed toward another direction as was appropriate.
O Lakṣmī! Kālindara and the others, remaining steadfast in those words, took refuge in me.
Then, at the end of their bodies, I led those partakers of devotion—who had attained my firm shelter—to my supreme, imperishable abode.

"By reading this, by hearing it, by remembering it, and likewise by practicing it, there shall indeed be both enjoyment and liberation through my grace, O Rame, forever. (11.9) Thus ends the two-hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of the Liberation through Supreme Devotion of Kālīndarabhāṇḍa, an inhabitant of Bhāṇḍīra Village, along with his female dancers and others, and the Instruction of the Great Sage Kamalāyana," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
