Chapter 202 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of the devotee, the dancer named Rāyaṇadeva, which bestows devotion. 1.

In the great village of Ākhoṭaka, there lived a devotee named Rāyaṇadevaka together with his family; he indeed resided there and constantly worshipped me. Merit performed in a previous birth stands by one everywhere.
In a previous birth, he was a peacock living near the village gate;
he constantly dwelt upon a tree at the edge of the settlement, frequented by holy men, ascetics, and pilgrims who came there. (3–4)
Those who dwell upon the earth— whether in a garden, having reached a village,
or staying in a grove of trees for two days or so—
they perform their devotions there, cook their food, and eat.
They drink the water offered to Hari in every way.
Furthermore, they cast the leftover vessels, leaves, and food and water into the groves of trees for the sake of the birds dwelling there.
Animals, birds, insects, and other creatures eat the food remnants and drink the water; they consume it, they drink it, and they pass away.
Yet, by the grace of Hari, the peacock eats and drinks the food and water [of the Lord].
The virtuous man properly drinks and eats that which is pleasing to him.
Thus, for one who has attained such serenity, his great merit becomes powerful while his evil comes to an end; he then passed away in due time. (3.201.10)
By virtue of his merit, the bird entered the womb of Kastūrikā, the wife of the Śūdra named Hārītaka, and took birth as a human being.
After dwelling in the womb there, he remained for eight months, possessing great devotion.
The great sage Bodhāyana, who was devoted to the righteous dharma, arrived there.
Then the brahmin went to the house of Hārītaka for alms; and Hārītaka, recognizing him as a learned brāhmaṇa skilled in astrology, made a request of him.
"Accept alms—milk-rice, ghee, and likewise sugar—and remain steady here for this day; dispel my doubts.
Having spoken thus, she gave him alms consisting of sweet food, ghee, and milk.
Having cooked flour, fruits, honey, and excellent water, Bodhāyana offered them to the Supreme Self; he then partook of the prasāda and gave all that remained away. (16) 19.
Having even consumed his own family [as medicine] for the sake of the Hārītaka family, he asked that great sage in the evening, when he was established in health and steady conduct:
"Will there be a boy or a girl in my wife's womb? (17)
Tell me, what qualities will my offspring possess?
Will he be long-lived or short-lived? Will he be devoted or not? And how may devotion and faith toward the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa arise?
How is there liberation and how is there divinity? How is there refuge in Nārāyaṇa?
How is there association with the virtuous, service, and reliance upon dharma?
How is there emancipation, how is there renunciation, and how is there the destruction of saṃsāra?
"And how may there be both lordship and liberation for a householder?
Grant me all these nectars.
Thus addressed, Bodhāyana, the best of virtuous men and king among devotees, [replied]. (21–22)
He replied in the presence of his family, where a pregnant woman was present who indeed heard that most purifying discourse:
"Listen, O Hārītaka! And let your wife listen as well."
Let your family listen here as I speak these most beneficial words for your welfare.
For you shall have a son, a child who will be auspicious and a deliverer; he will be devoted to the virtuous, a devotee of Hari, and possessed of the impressions of his previous lives in this world.
He will perform all dances like a peacock;
he shall be an enjoyer of the grace of the virtuous, long-lived, and ever-devoted.
Through his devotion, he will indeed bring about the liberation of your family.

He will be a constant bestower of fortune and shall become possessed of great good luck; he will also be a devotee of Viṣṇu and a giver of Nārāyaṇa. [He shall be devoted] to Kṛṣṇa, the Lord who is higher than the highest, the sovereign treasure-house of supreme bliss.
"Indeed, from childhood, this boy shall be devoted to the practice of dance;
for in a previous birth he was a peacock. Therefore, this son of yours will become the foremost among those skilled in the art of dancing and a supreme devotee. (29)
Those people who are experts in dance, as well as others,
and all the female dancers skilled in the arts, will assemble there;
and through association with your son, they too shall indeed become Vaiṣṇavas.
Even those beings who are products of *māyā* within this world created by *māyā* will take refuge in the path to liberation and go to the supreme state;
for many among them constantly delight in dancing, singing, and amorous play.
When this world was first created by Nārāyaṇa,
he also fashioned the bond of affection for the sake of establishing the continuity of the world-process.
Bound by this affection, this entire world revolves through its various states.
The affection of men for women is innate;
through that [affection], it arises toward a son, a husband, wealth, a home, and a wife—indeed, it is born toward a daughter-in-law, a field, livestock, profit, and the family. (35)
This self, which increases all things, has been placed within the father by means of *māyā* alone.
Even those living beings who are bound by such *māyā*, though they may be experts in the arts, shall meet with your son and will indeed become Vaiṣṇavas. (36–37)
Through the power of your son, they will cultivate devotion that bestows liberation; and through the yoga of Hari, they will attain it in their dancing.
He who is the Lord beyond illusion exists on earth for the welfare of all people.
Having manifested, he shall remain forever; a child will worship him. At that time, people endowed with their former merits will worship Hari;
and so too shall the birds, beasts, and forest-dwelling animals within the grove of trees.
Those who have died here, having partaken of the food of the virtuous's grace, are reborn as humans; they exist as purifiers joined with merit.
Indeed, all of them become dancers, singers, and even instrumentalists.
Whether born in this village or in another village, those excellent Vaiṣṇavas have previously enjoyed the grace of beholding Śrī Kṛṣṇa and His [associates];
they are auspicious children born here in this village as those who possess the purificatory rites. ||42-43||
Through association with those virtuous ones and by hearing news of Hari,
their devotion to Kṛṣṇa exists and will become even firmer and greater.
And all of them, having gathered together, will perform [services] for the virtuous devotees of Hari.
Through their compassion for the virtuous, all those endowed with faith will offer service, devotion, servitude, and attendance that grant liberation;
they will attain supreme love for the holy one, the Supreme Lord. (45–46)
They will become capable of liberating both their own dear ones and others from the bonds of worldly existence, and of instilling love for Hari.
By that means, those excellent yogis will indeed abandon insignificant pleasures.
All shall become firm through association with the virtuous and utterly devoted to the company of Hari.
Free from passion, they shall all become destroyers of Māyā;
established in Brahman, they shall renounce everything that creates obstacles to devotion.
After propitiating me for some time, those of divine nature shall attain the eternal fruit—
the supreme, imperishable, and divine Brahman.
Through association with the virtuous, devotion toward the Supreme Self increases.
Through association with the virtuous, knowledge of the Supreme Self arises.
Through the realization of Hari’s majesty, faith increases constantly. Through discernment, does the divine nature within Hari not shine forth eternally? (51–52)
O Blessed One, when [the senses] are present, divine splendor also shines forth;
through discernment, one becomes firmly established in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. By taking refuge in Him, one becomes a refuge for the virtuous who seek shelter.
For one who is devoted to virtuous conduct and performs service to the saintly,
there arises the taking up of the duties of a great devotee (mahābhāgavata), such as service and so forth.
Through constant service, the compassion of Lord Hari toward the saintly is set in motion.
Through meditation on Hari, compassion, liberation, renunciation, as well as the dissolution of saṃsāra, and identity with Nārāyaṇa arise;
likewise, one-pointedness, restraint, and samādhi are born in Hari.
The enjoyment of all bliss and great bliss arises for him incessantly.
(17) Therefore, virtuous people should be fed and served with water and food;
likewise, service should be rendered like that of a slave, a handmaid, or a servant. (58)
The service of the virtuous should always be performed like that toward a wife or a son;
likewise, they should be honored like a father or a mother, and like a king. Furthermore, they should be regarded like a master, a husband, a brother, or a protector. (56)
The virtuous, who are practitioners of yoga through devotion to Hari, should always be served;
they should therefore be propitiated here, saluted again and again, constantly asked for forgiveness, and gratified like gods. (3.201.60–61)
For the virtuous are indeed worthy of worship here and should be protected like one's own sons;
by attaining the favor of the virtuous, both worldly enjoyment and liberation may be attained in this life.
Adhering to the command of the virtuous, one should indeed proceed upon the path of the righteous.
Drawing back the senses and the internal organ from every direction,
they should indeed be placed within Kṛṣṇa, so that they do not follow a wrong path.
And if they should follow a wrong path, then one must immediately draw them back again.
When the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa, who bestows happiness, is approached with force,
the internal organ (the mind) withdraws its power from external objects to the same extent that there is a deficiency in the recognition of Śrī Hari’s majesty. ||65||
To avoid deficiency, one should always maintain association with the virtuous.
One’s devotion should be directed toward Kṛṣṇa alone, while all other associations must be abandoned.
There is fear for those traveling on a wrong path, but there is no fear on the path of Kṛṣṇa.

Upon attaining Kṛṣṇa, there remains nothing further for embodied beings to attain; once one is devoted to the bliss of Kṛṣṇa, no other pleasure remains. If, having abandoned that Hari, one seeks here the acquisition of trivial happiness—

If those people who desire worldly enjoyment strive for enlightenment, they are said to be merely transmigrators; such procreators lead to hell. They subvert the word of the Blessed One and do not carry out the command of the virtuous. (3.201.70)
Those who pursue trivial objects constantly encounter suffering,
even if they are intelligent, highly learned, and skilled in reasoning.
On the other hand, even one of very little intelligence who serves Śrī Hari and the virtuous [attains bliss].
Here he takes recourse in the path of the highest good and abides in the goal of the virtuous man;
he constantly accepts the true qualities of the holy ones who are practitioners of devotional yoga, and he stands firmly upon the divine, great path of the Bhāgavata. (92–93)
He alone is declared wise who is devoted to his own true interest and liberation; he alone is called virtuous who has made a firm resolve for the sake of liberation.
But one possessed of much intellect yet indulging in worldly enjoyments shall go to hell.
Devoted to pursuing worthless objects and censuring the path of the virtuous,
that wicked atheist who reviles the qualities of Hari and of the saintly,
reaches the abode of Yama through his defiled intellect and surely incurs sin. (75–76)
Milk mixed with sugar becomes destructive if it is tainted by poison;
likewise, even when great, an intellect that is corrupted destroys one's welfare.
One joined with such [an intellect] surely falls and may become a traitor in another birth.
There shall be no good rebirth for him, nor even for one who associates with him.
Furthermore, he is not fit to be spoken to; by speaking to him, one surely causes a downfall.
For by pointing out his faults, one thereby instills defilement.
A servant of limited intellect who is endowed with devotion and fit for spiritual association,
indeed stands upon the path of the highest good when he receives words of blessing;
for he abandons pride, hypocrisy, anger, and likewise envy.
He who exists as a servant through the state of being a slave to the virtuous,
perceiving the divine nature in the virtuous and in all the activities of the virtuous— he is called a "sādhū" here, and is entirely worthy of service. (81–82)
He alone is in every way a worthy recipient of the grace of Hari and of the virtuous;
he is indeed the powerful one who effects the deliverance of those who have taken refuge [in him].
He alone shall surely be the bestower of liberation, just as the virtuous are and just as Hari is.
But another, possessing an asuric intellect, may indeed become a ghost (bhūta) or a departed spirit (preta) in this world;
or he may become a rākṣasa, a malevolent doer, or a daitya who commits evil deeds.
For such a hater of Hari and of the virtuous, there is certainly no liberation.
Through a state of enmity toward Kṛṣṇa, he may eventually become united with Him;
or, through Kṛṣṇa’s grace, he may at some point abandon his demonic nature.
Then, after a period of time, by the mercy of Kṛṣṇa, he attains the supreme goal.
Therefore, one should never at all feel attachment toward trivial objects.

(87) One should always cultivate love for Hari, for the virtuous, and practice service and devotion toward them—He for whom the entire world, gold and a clod of earth, heaven and the ground, are all equal. (88)
One should serve him, in whom everything is permeated by Brahman, like a slave;
one should serve him like a maidservant, and thus become a virtuous Nārāyaṇī.
Having thus instructed Lakṣmī, the sage Bodhāyana—
Having traveled to another land, he eventually received worship there. In time,
Kastūrikā gave birth to a divine son, a yogi of devotion,
who had heard the supreme knowledge taught by Bodhāyana while still in the womb.
Endowed with omniscience, a powerful son was born.
From his very childhood, he practiced devotion through dancing and singing;
he engaged in discourse rich in discernment and performed worship constantly.
He performed worship and chanting, making every action consist entirely of Kṛṣṇa.
Then Bodhāyana came once again to see him;
seeing that disciple, his devotee named Rāyaṇadevaka, [he was pleased]. (93–94)
The sage initiated him along with his hundred disciples, as well as Rāyaṇa together with his hundred female disciples. [He taught them the mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Having bestowed the Bhāgavata initiation and the mantra, the sage departed for the forest.
All those beginning with Rāyaṇadeva— the dancers, the virtuous ones,
the singers, and the women— worshipped me with dance and hymns of praise.
O Lakṣmī, thousands of people— both men and women— became his disciples and were born as Vaiṣṇavas devoted solely to my worship.
Once, in an assembly, he granted them his supreme vision.
I am Nārāyaṇa, the four-armed one, together with Śrī and Lakṣmī.
Honored by them, I caused them to drink the water of the *pāyasa* offering and granted them supreme liberation, the divine state consisting of Brahman.
His disciples and grand-disciples, as well as others, exist upon the surface of the earth;
they worship me, the Lord Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Thus, O Rame, through my skillful yoga, the dancer was uplifted by me.
Even the dancing girls were uplifted and directed toward the path of liberation.

(102) Thus, through the power of devotion to me and likewise the power of service to the saintly, by reading and hearing this, one shall attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation in this very life. (103)

Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Knowledge, Devotion, Vision of Hari, and Liberation of the Dancer Rāyaṇadeva while Still in the Womb through the Instruction of Bodhāyana," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 202 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) — Chapter 202.
[The Author: Chapter 203.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to [the account] of that great-souled singer.
1. [I shall tell] the delightful story of Vratardin, which is filled with my grace.
2. In the city named Nākirāla, there was a devotee of Vratardin, a Vaiśya who was highly skilled in playing all musical instruments, such as the lute and the drum.
Before him dwell many male disciples and female disciples, who, being inclined toward singing, reside there for the sake of practicing the arts of music and the like;
and from various regions and distant lands, they arrive on the day of their vow.

Having heard of the master of the science of music and having received instruction from him, they departed. (4) Now, there was a king named Puṇḍravarmā, the ruler of the city of Nimbāṭikā; he was righteous and devoted to the worship of the Blessed One. (5)
Having heard of the best of singers in Saurāṣṭra on the day of his vow,
the king summoned him to his own capital for the sake of singing.
Having gone there, the messenger delivered to that singer the king's message.
"Come to the royal festival," the best of singers said to you, "O King.
Vratardī replied thus: "I shall not perform as a singer at a royal festival;
I am a devotee of the Blessed One who has offered himself to Him. (7–8)
Without Hari, my tongue shall never sing of another;
without Hari, my eye shall never behold another;
without Hari, my mind shall never meditate upon another. (9)
"I am a devotee of the Lord's devotees, endowed with the spirit of service.
How then can I sing here of the royal qualities of this king, which are merely illusory? O messenger, tell the monarch: 'No other singer shall sing [of him]. (3.202.10–11)
The illuminator of vows is a singer of Kṛṣṇa alone, never a singer of anything else;
he remains solely a singer of liberation, yet also a singer for his devotees.
He is never a singer for those who lack devotion, nor does he ever become an illuminator of vows for them.
Having been thus answered, the messenger departed and reported it to the king.
(13) The king was suddenly delighted: "I am truly blessed, a king forever!
In my kingdom there is a highly fortunate singer of Kṛṣṇa. (14)
I too must become a devotee of the Lord for the sake of liberation; I must become a Vaiṣṇava, and thereafter I must listen to and chant the praises of the Lord.
On the day of the vow, the supreme chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s glories was performed.
"Afterwards, having become a king who is a worthy recipient (*satpātra*), you must by all means listen.
Having reflected thus, he said to the messenger: "I must become devoted;
therefore, come to my palace and cause me, the king, to take refuge [in him]."
"Having made him a devotee of Viṣṇu, then cause him to hear the *kīrtana*. Speak thus to the Lord of Devotees, and depart on the day of the vow.
Having heard this, the messenger went quickly on the day of the vow as instructed by the king.
He related everything; having heard it, the singer was pleased.
Having prepared himself, he went to the king’s palace accompanied by his attendants.
The king repeatedly honored that devotee on the day of his vow.
Then the king requested initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*) and the status of a Vaiṣṇava. Having quickly heard his vow, the preceptor took water in his hand,
gave it to the king, bestowed the mantra upon him, and promptly caused it to be recited.
"Oṃ, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord from Oṃkāra, is my master and my husband.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Master; Svāhā!
Having received this mantra, the king wore the Tulasī necklace around his neck.

The Queen, the daughters, the sons, and the royal family likewise accepted my image of Bālakṛṣṇa, which had been offered by the singers. Indeed, all the male servants and female attendants there became Vaiṣṇavas.
Water, fruit, food, and sandalwood offered to Hari were given as *prasāda* by Vratardī to the royal family. Having eaten and drunk the *prasāda*, the king then held a court assembly.
He placed the resplendent Kṛṣṇa upon the central throne.
Holding an unsurpassed umbrella for Kṛṣṇa’s service, the king stood there, as did his family, holding yak-tail whisks and fans. (27)
A cane, a cloth, an incense burner, a banner, and a small flag;
a mirror, a drinking vessel, and likewise a betel-box;
a vessel for fragrant essences, oil-essence, and sandalwood.
Holding the vessels for worship and garlands of flowers, she stood in her proper place.
Having worshipped Bālakṛṣṇa, the observer of vows performed a song of praise:
"Come, Kṛṣṇa! Come, Kṛṣṇa! O Beloved, come, come!"
O Kṛṣṇa, grant it; O Kṛṣṇa, grant the vision to this good body!
Create a new circle of devotees and a divine, noble lineage.
Abandon the latent desire for worldly birth and bestow the latent desire for the Divine Abode.
Come, Kṛṣṇa!
You alone are the liberated Lord of the virtuous; you alone are the true refuge of the abode;
you alone are the one who assumes incarnations; and you alone are the witness of all.
"Come, Kṛṣṇa!
[33] Previously you were the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), then you were the Best of Men (Narottama);
then you were Janārdana, and thereafter you are the Destroyer of All (Sarvamardana).
Come, O Kṛṣṇa!
You are one whose mind is gracious; you are the bestower of perfect prosperity;
you are the giver of the happiness sought by yourself; you are the giver of peace to your own self.
Come, Kṛṣṇa!
You are the lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī; you are the lord of Pramā and Satī; you are the lord of the Śrī of the virtuous; and you are the lord of Māṇikī.
Come, O Kṛṣṇa!
You are the husband of the beloved of Brahmā; you are the husband of the beloved of Hari;
you are the Lord of the Unborn (Aja); you are the Lord of the day of vows.
Come, Kṛṣṇa!
You are a treasury of splendors; you are a treasury of wonders;
you are a treasury of supreme joy; you are a treasury of those with supreme knowledge.
Come, Kṛṣṇa!
You are indeed the son of Vṛṣa; you are the son of Gopaja;
you are the son of Kāśyapa; and you are the son of Kambharā.
Come, O Kṛṣṇa!
O Hari, you always abide in consciousness, yet you also abide in the unconscious;
you manifest yourself, O Hari, within the circle of your own devotees.
"Come, Kṛṣṇa! Come, Kṛṣṇa! O beloved, come, come!
Give me, Kṛṣṇa! Give me, Kṛṣṇa! O fair-bodied one, grant me your vision!"—in this way, O Lakṣmī, he entreated me with auspicious songs.
There, filled with love, he remembered me and performed the vow of the lamp.
Singers and female singers also filled the air with the melodies of their songs.
Hearing them, I was drawn out quickly from the image by the cord of love.
Manifested, exceedingly handsome, captivating, and in the full bloom of youth; his form was perfectly proportioned to its beauty, with well-developed and radiant limbs.
Adorned with a necklace and a crown, he was united with Śrī Rādhā.
Delightful with all ornaments and resplendent with every grace,
his face bears a serene smile; he is illuminated by divine luster and filled with the bliss of beauty, fragrance, and affection.
Fulfilling all desires and increasing the joy of the assembly,
he remained established in me, captivating the minds of those present in the hall.
That bliss which belongs to the Supreme Self in the imperishable, supreme ether—

Overcome by compassion, he gave all of that to those present in the assembly for a moment. Immediately after that moment, O Rame, I caused my divine nature to disappear. Then those kings and others beheld me joined with Rādhā and Ramā.
They were repeatedly bewildered by my form, and they indeed placed me within their hearts;
impelled for the sake of boons, they worshipped me with all their being.
They chose supreme liberation, and I granted them service [to me], saying, "So be it."
And as he suddenly vanished, the assembly was filled with wonder.
By the power of their vows, they indeed obtained the vision of Kṛṣṇa;
with single-minded devotion, they always enjoyed my presence through divine states of being.
Then, through their devotion to their husbands, the kings and other Vaiṣṇavas sought my favor;
the devotee Parihāra rejoiced at the sight of me.
Having received his reward, he departed for his own kingdom along with his retinue.
That king indeed went from his palace to the royal residence, which was like a gateway to the abode [of the Lord].
(53) Then, when the time had arrived, he led the circle of devotees, including the king, to my imperishable abode, as well as the circle of those observing the vow. (54)
Likewise, those hundreds of thousands of people who became Vaiṣṇavas,
remembering my miracles and worshipping me incessantly—
I led them to my imperishable world, the eternal and supreme abode.
Listen, Lakṣmī: in this world there are people whose conduct is characterized by renunciation.
For one who possesses intense renunciation and dispassion, affection for me shines forth most brilliantly;
however, for the passionate person, constant remembrance of sense objects arises. (56–57)
Bound by affection for trivial objects, they do not cultivate love for Kṛṣṇa;
devoid of love for Kṛṣṇa, they certainly do not attain the fruit of liberation.
Therefore, one should always cultivate love for me, the Supreme Person.
Affection for an outcaste must be abandoned by one who knows my greatness.
Furthermore, through self-knowledge, affection for illusory objects must be relinquished.
This Self is existence-consciousness-bliss; it is distinct from the body, which is inert matter. (3.202.60)
He has no body, no mansion, no family, and no gardens;
he has no caste, no lineage, no yoga, no wealth, and no possessions.
He should always contemplate himself thus: "I am indeed free from illusion."
Realizing one's own self to be of such a nature, one should not remember the physical body.
One should not think of family members, nor of ancestors, whether from former or recent times;
for those who lack devotion to the Lord are merely causes of bondage. (62–63)
That by whose remembrance bondage indeed occurs should never be remembered;
however, at the time of a śrāddha, they should be remembered for the sake of their satisfaction and for one's own liberation.
[This applies] during sacrifice, giving, pilgrimage, religious duties, vows, and so forth.
They should be remembered for the sake of their satisfaction and for one's own liberation in the temple of Hari.
Otherwise, under the influence of passion, they should never be remembered.
Divine sages should be remembered, and my own images should be remembered. (65–66)

Likewise, virtuous women who are dear to Brahman should be remembered by those possessing knowledge and specialized insight for the sake of attaining liberation; however, kinsmen should be forgotten. For women and householders are the givers of bondage.
All sense objects and obstacles to liberation must be forgotten entirely.

(68) For one by whom all things, such as sons and so forth, have indeed been forgotten through the vision of Brahman, there shall be love for Hari and for those virtuous ones who bestow liberation. (69)
All the virtuous indeed become divine inhabitants of Brahman;
just as Hari is, so too are the virtuous to be remembered, for they are bestowers of liberation.
The holy ones and Hari alike should be constantly taken as one's refuge.
I myself, Hari, Janārdana, am directly to be worshipped by such a devotee.
For one who is thus devoted, there is no fear of time, nor of karmas, nor of Māyā, nor of King Yama, nor even of bondage. (71–72)
The will of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is indeed to be understood as *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion) for the yogi of devotion; it is not like that of a sinful soul.
Such a person is truly to be saluted and is worthy of worship by all.
Whether he be a householder or an ascetic, no distinction exists in this regard.
Even the gods and other celestial beings bear upon their heads the dust from the feet of such a devotee—one for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal. (74–75)
And every day at dawn, the gods behold him;
relying upon my majesty and remaining in his home performing devotion,
he now sets out for renunciation and will swiftly reach the further shore of the ocean.
At the end of his body, such a devotee of mine, whose form is composed of consciousness, shall become liberated in Brahman and possess a divine body; he shall abide in service within my abode.
Indeed, the sight of him destroys illusion, sin, time, and all such evils.

O Lakṣmī, I consider that person who performs all actions for my sake to be equal to me in destroying karma; for him, I am Acyuta. In every way, I remain under his control and move within his sphere of influence.
O Lakṣmī, from the very day a devotee indeed enters into the company of the virtuous,
from that time forward he practices discrimination between virtues and faults;
having acquired such qualities, he has abandoned these evil traits.
Every year, the benefactor reflects upon his progress;
through the power of association with the virtuous and by service to the Lord Hari,
all these virtues have been attained by me and those defects have vanished.
One should indeed be diligent in destroying the remaining faults;
one should be diligent in acquiring the remaining good qualities.
For one who is thus habituated to effort, these qualities shall become givers of satisfaction to me. (83–84)
There shall be a total destruction of the defects, and likewise, divinity shall arise here;
indeed, his supreme and eternal happiness of Kṛṣṇa is born.
The mind becomes free from latent impressions (vāsanā), devoid of volitional constructs (saṃkalpa), and becomes steady.
May my mind, which delights in me, constantly turn toward the many life-narratives of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
may it become filled with great peace, both for renunciants and for householders alike. (86–87)

O Lakṣmī, outwardly one should perform worldly activities merely for the sake of maintaining the body, like an actor; yet the mind should be fixed on me, Hari. One should [contemplate] the life-stories of the virtuous, of Nārāyaṇa, and of the wives of Kṛṣṇa.
The devotees of Śrī Hari should also always be meditated upon. (89) Through that, the mind becomes free from latent desires, whereby there is happiness in liberation.
One should seek the company of such people, for it yields the fruit that brings about liberation. (90)
By association with the singer Vratardana, Puṇḍravarmā, the best of kings, attained liberation, as did thousands of others.
Therefore, my devotees— who are truthful and whose latent desires have been uprooted— should be served.
They perform divine rites, are devoted to meditation, and have taken refuge in Tāraka;
they are free from obstacles and devoid of all impediments.
Having resorted to my service, they follow the divine Bhāgavata Dharma.
By providing refuge for the virtuous, by engendering clarity of mind,
and by carrying out the commands [of the Lord], the imperishable abode shall come into one's hand.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, whether on earth, in heaven, in Satyaloka, or in Vaikuṇṭha—
Those who dwell in Goloka, Akṣara, Śvetadvīpa, Śrīpura, Amṛta,
Avyākṛta, or Badarī, and who are devoted to me—
they are all liberated women, having offered their very selves to Kṛṣṇa.
Those who enjoy eternal bliss, as well as those who observe vows and sing my praises—
all of them, serving eternal bliss, have attained liberation from me.
Whosoever in this world, being skilled in the arts, offers that art to me—
By my grace, they all go to the imperishable abode; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever dharma, quality, art, or action one may have before them, let that indeed be the means for pleasing Śrī Hari himself.
Therefore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Hari, should be propitiated by men and by groups of women; likewise, the virtuous should be propitiated.
Then the body, the mind, and the inner being shall become divine.
Virtues, actions, conduct, and service—all these become divine in their entirety;
having belonged to Hari and having attained Hari, that person who offers everything rejoices.
By reading and by hearing this, O Lakṣmī, one likewise rejoices in Me.

Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vaiṣṇava Status and Liberation of King Puṇḍravarman along with his progeny through the Yoga of the Devotee-Gentleman Vratadin," in the Third Section (Dvāpara-Santāna) of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 202. [Chapter 203] *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (Dvāpara Yuga Lineage).
Chapter 203.
[The Author: Chapter 204.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious story of Vāyaka.
In the city named Dhūrila, there lived a weaver called Tūlavāyī who resided with his family, always honored by both the king and the subjects;
he was skilled in weaving fine threads and the like, as well as in the manufacture of yarn. (1–2)
With his digits and his nails, he fashions threads that are exceedingly subtle;
indeed, those fibers are like spider-silk produced by a spinning wheel.
From his digit, there arise forms that are most delicate and exceedingly subtle.
In the sky, his garment is worn, fashioned from threads;
it is not seen at all within the rays, yet thus it becomes subtle.
A cloth can even be spread out upon a golden ring.
Likewise, a lower garment, an upper garment, and a turban are produced from those very threads;
indeed, garments suitable for a queen’s attire arise from those same fibers.
This weaver [employs] the shuttle, the loom, and the joining-rod.
And indeed, one joins fine shuttle-pins to the weaving;
for there are those that are most minute, more minute, minute, and resembling the minute;
as well as those that are coarse-fine, medium-coarse, coarse, and very coarse.
Indeed, very thick threads of a dull body are produced;
various beautiful *phālikās* and *kukaṭyas* are also produced.
Furthermore, there are boxes for the threads, and cotton-spinners in the workshop.
Threads are produced by means of hands, as well as by machines, spindles, and the like; they are generated by rollers and revolving wheels. Indeed, many men and many women serve as laborers.
They produce threads of cotton and others as well—
threads with equal channels and coils according to their purpose—
neither deficient nor excessive, and free from knots or breaks. (1.2)
Free from defects such as coarseness or fineness and being auspicious,
it is well known that people, kings, and even merchants generally wear garments made from these very fibers. (13–14)
The great seal (mahāmudrā) of cotton-weaving is impressed [upon it], increasing human prosperity;
its excellence always shines forth in threads and in the garments produced from them.
Such is the cotton-weaver, the performer of vast deeds.
Nevertheless, he maintained devotion toward me in all his undertakings.
Even upon machines, in iron implements used for the practice of the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
and everywhere— even upon plowshares and sickles— he [engraved] the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

On their clothing, on the walls, and in the hall, the name of Kṛṣṇa was indeed inscribed. All the male workers and the female workers as well were chanting the name of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Tūlavāyī constantly worships me, Nārāyaṇa, himself.
Having bathed and worshipped me, he afterwards ascends to his exertion.
[He partakes of] my grace, the food offering, rice, water, fruits, and so forth. (3.203.20)
He always eats together with his family as if it were an offering to Me;
having offered me garments, vessels, seats, and so forth, he employs them for my sake.
Such a person, the best among devotees, worships Me with a concentrated mind.
Then this weaver, due to carelessness while operating the machine, lost his grip as the wheel spun rapidly;
he fell and his hand was crushed. His hand became severed from his shoulder, and my devotee-king fainted. (22–23)
He too quickly remembered me and requested protection for his heart;
and all the servants, having recognized the chanting of my name,
came to his side, and there I bestowed the medicine.
Having become a skilled king of physicians, I arrived as a healer.
Taking with me the medicinal herbs that bind wounds, stop bleeding, nourish, and restore stability, I quickly presented myself before her. (25–26)
Having poured water into her mouth with my hand, I prevented her from fainting;
I joined the base of the udder of the cow in milk (sandhinī) to her neck,
and by means of the "blood-stopping" [mantra], I caused the blood to remain steady.

Having provided nourishment to the arms and the fingers as appropriate with the *poṣaṇī* mudrā, and having established the hand in its proper position with the *sthitisthāpanī* mudrā, I made it easy to handle;
then, bestowing steadiness, I remained seated upon the throne. (28–29)
Then, beholding me in my divine form, their minds were enchanted;
they attained supreme confidence and indeed regarded me as Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
They offered hymns of praise, prostrated, performed worship, and made supplications.

They requested from Kṛṣṇa forgiveness, upliftment, liberation from the noose of illusion, association with the virtuous, devotion, and knowledge. To them I said, "So be it," and I bestowed upon them my supreme knowledge.
"O Lakṣmī, I granted divine vision of myself to all;
saying 'So be it,' I gave them enjoyment, liberation, and prosperity.
Then, I vanished from that place, and after some time..."
At the end of his body, he gradually led them all to my imperishable state.
When Tūlavāyī became old and was bound for liberation,
I again granted my own vision to Tūlavāyī.
Tūlavāyī questioned me for the welfare of the worlds:
"What is your nature in your abode? What are the millions of liberated ones like? What is your house and your splendor like? And what are even the lords like? (36)
And what are the sovereign powers (*īśvaryas*) that descend [from you], O Truth?
What are those holy ones (*sādhus*), and what are your liberations (*muktis*)?
What are your accomplishments (*siddhis*), and what am I, who have taken refuge in you? (37–38)
"O Mādhava, tell me how I shall dwell in your abode;
O Lakṣmī, I have completely stilled my desire to be fanned like cotton wool.
Listen: I shall become your devotee here, appearing before your divine eyes. (39)
Thus, I exist within that abode in every way as one possessing a divine form—
Mādhava, the visible embodiment of all liberated souls, an ocean of boundless virtue, beauty, grace, and brilliance. (3.203.40–41)
I am always two-armed, yet by my own will I assume other forms,
possessing many shapes with thousands of arms and more.
I become all tastes, all fragrances, and all forms.
I am all touch, all sound, and all bliss.
(43) I am a youth, the lord of the countless liberated souls who are dear to Brahmā; I am the lord of the countless liberated souls who are dear to Hari, possessing a robust body. (44)
I am worthy of service and the fulfiller of all desires within my imperishable state;
in that very imperishable abode dwell millions of liberated souls.
All are devoted to me as their supreme goal, divine, and possessed of forms equal to mine.
Rich in all divine qualities, possessing forms, and oceans of bliss—such are my liberated youths; they dwell here exceedingly beautiful, radiant, most charming, and captivating. (46–47)
My supreme imperishable state is the highest ether, the supreme abode, the supreme dwelling;
it is fashioned of gold and resplendent with rows of thousands of millions of pillars.
It possesses thousands of millions of domes and is filled with all prosperity and spiritual perfections.

It exists with great extent, enriched by thousands of millions of chambers. Indeed, all desires and all ritual forms exist there in their perfect manifestations. There are couches consisting of every kind of enjoyment and indeed all lion-thrones. (3.203.50)
The highly precious elephant-throne exists in my abode;
such is that supreme realm where I dwell together with the Śaktis,
accompanied by both the liberated ones and those of divine form.
From me alone manifest incarnations numbering tens of millions of Kṛṣṇas;
there are innumerable Nārāyaṇas, and tens of millions of Rāmas and men.
Sages of immeasurable splendor come into being and descend [to earth]. (52–53)
Vāsudeva and others, as well as millions of Hiraṇyagarbhas,
Vairājas, Īśvaras, Bhūmans, and Brahmās—
these Rudras and the foremost Viṣṇus likewise constitute millions of Īśvaras.
Having obtained great sovereignties from me,
millions of incarnations become lords who enjoy the excellence of pure *sattva*;
and all their powers have indeed been manifested by me.
They truly become sovereign ladies, the powers that constitute the essence of saṃsāra; they are mines of bliss, and therefore they are real.
They are virtuous women, whose very form is Brahman, and who are devoted to the practice of celibacy.
They are those who seek the goal of moral conduct and vows, as well as the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
They are indeed the incarnations, the Lakṣmīs, the Kamalās, the Śris, the Ramās, the Rādhikās, and they are also the Sampads. ||58-59||
In my sovereign abode, there are indeed maṇḍalas of such a kind;
from such worlds, my attendants (pārṣadas) come here.
Those devotees are solely intent on renunciation; they are my divine forms.
They indeed become virtuous ones who perform every kind of auspicious deed.
In the service of the virtuous, there exist liberations consisting of divine forms— namely,
those characterized by residence in the same world (sālokya), equal power (sārṣṭi), identical form (sārūpya), and union (sayogika).
Such indeed are the liberations that bestow divine bliss;
likewise, the supernatural powers (siddhis) which are all-seeing and all-hearing,
whose nature is the attainment of everything, and which consist in the realization of true desires.
They shall also be cows that milk all desires, always filled with perfect bliss;
possessing beautiful forms and complete in every way, they shall become my attendants.
Having become liberated, O Bhava, you will dwell there, O weaver of cotton! (64–65)
Day by day, a divine youth, possessing celestial sovereignty and identical in form to my own image, filled with perfect bliss, shall reside there.
For you dwelling there, there will be a supreme state free from conceptual construction.
It shall be so that no other view whatsoever remains for you. Once you have become one with Brahman, nothing other than Me will be within your range of perception;
indeed, all this is the Supreme Brahman, and there is no other vision.
Even those [objects] are not within the range of one who has attained identity with Me;
therefore, the Imperishable is the range, yet You are not even within Your own range.
You shall attain such a supreme, divine state therein.
"You shall always be immersed in my form with its manifold aspects.
In your vision, there is indeed no liberated soul, no Imperishable, and how could there be Lords?
Where is Māyā, and where are the individual souls? Everything is of the nature of Brahman for you. || 3.203.70–71 ||
O weaver of cotton, such shall be your state therein;
through my grace, your liberation will become exactly like that.
That state is considered to be free from conceptual construction, bodiless, and characterized by identity with Me.
Those among those here who are my liberated ones, who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta),

perceive māyā, as well as individual souls (jīva), the principles (tattva) in every respect, the Lord (Īśvara), all abodes, and states of meditative absorption with conceptual content (savikalpa-samādhi). (73–74)
Even while observing the illusions of time and karma,
they are neither bound nor slain, nor do they ever become attached to them.
Indeed, they move about here through the body, senses, and so forth, entirely untainted.
These indeed are my devotees who offer themselves to me;
they always practice devotion toward me, enriched with righteousness, knowledge, and dispassion.
Possessing devotion while still in the state of conceptualization, these virtuous ones are liberated here in my presence.
Likewise, householders as well as ascetics who know the Nyāya,
female renunciants, and even virtuous women free from passion—
those who abide in the state of *savikalpa* (with mental constructs)— are my ninefold [devotees]. 78.
They constantly practice devotion with love, offering their entire selves. (79) They listen to my stories, proclaim my divine sports, remember my form, and massage my feet and other limbs. (3.203.80)
The crushing of the feet and even the bodies of the virtuous;
my worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings; saluting me with words;
offering me complete service; and providing a seat near me. (81)
Indeed, the observance of all commands, service through constant attendance, friendship, a state of affection, and uninterrupted unity of action;
as well as the offering of oneself and the offering of everything that belongs to oneself—[these constitute the nature of service]. (82–83)
In every way, dwelling together like a wife, as well as service—
such is the devotion of a yogin who still possesses conceptual thought;
through being entirely absorbed in Me, it indeed bestows happiness.
That which consists of making My presence manifest through such devotion, affection, service, knowledge, and a sense of exaltation—
that is considered *upāsanā*, and it illuminates all that is divine. (85–86)
Indeed, that worship consists of repeatedly and in many ways directing the flow of all kinds of knowledge toward me,
Hari; as well as reflection, firm conviction, and the constant remembrance of me, Śrī Hari.
I am Kṛṣṇa, the divine youth, served by millions of liberated souls and others. (88) In the imperishable realm there exist my lineages—the liberated males and the auspicious liberated females.
I am Hari, endowed with every ornament and enchanting to all. (89)

Possessing an infinite abundance of sovereign power and being the locus of infinite qualities of invisibility—for one such as I, knowledge is perception; for that indeed is worship (upāsanā). Devotion, affection, service, worship, and abiding in speech [are its forms].
That embodied being who accomplishes this is called *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living).
Such a person here in this world possesses *savikalpa-samādhi* (meditative absorption with mental constructs);
thereafter, having attained the state of Brahman, he becomes attached to Me, Mādhava.
By means of the body, mind, speech, action, and the functions of the senses;
by the self, by mental cultivation, and by latent impressions such as feeling and the rest;
and also by meditation, concentration, dedication, and restraint.

That devotee who, through identity—that is, through a state of melting into oneness—becomes bodiless as it were, becomes a videhī, possessing the samādhi free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
Having attained such supreme, divine joy, he rejoices in Me. ||94–95||
"Thus I have told you everything; O weaver of cotton, act quickly!
Go swiftly to my supreme abode, which is filled with all bliss.
Having been addressed thus by me, O Lakṣmī, that weaver of cotton bowed to the Lord.
Having abandoned the body, he indeed became divine, possessing a liberated form.
Ascending a celestial chariot, he went to my imperishable abode.
In this same way, other devotees of mine as well—those who perform their duties like cotton blown by the wind—[attain the same state]. 97–98.
In due time, I have led them all to my imperishable state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, let one become a devotee, full of devotion, and a worshiper of me;
having granted him my vision, I lead him to my supreme abode.
I grant both worldly enjoyment and liberation; I provide protection in every way.
By reciting, hearing, remembering, and likewise preserving this, one shall obtain both enjoyment and liberation, and attain my supreme bliss.

Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord, through His grace, protected the weaver named Tūlavāyī, granted him a vision, and bestowed liberation upon him and his workers," in the Third Section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 204: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 204.
[The Author: Chapter 205.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the wood-gatherer.

[He gave] the beautiful [image] of my devotee named Jāṅgaladeva. (1) There was a devoted householder named Śūdra called Jāṅgaladeva, a wood-gatherer living in Niśāra village, who was exceedingly devoted. (2)
Rising every day at dawn during the hour known as Brāhma-muhūrta,
he bathed in the well, meditated upon Hari, and offered me *roṭaka* along with water mixed with sour gruel; thereafter,
he prostrated before me.
Having prepared incense of fragrant wood, gundrā grass, and so forth before me,
and having offered wild fruits, flowers, leaves, and cotton-seed products to me, this devotee, having taken leave of his wife and children, [proceeded]. || 4-5 ||
Every morning he would take his rope and axe and go to the forest;
having diligently cut various dry pieces of wood,
he would bind them into a load at midday and stand in a spot shaded by trees.
Remembering the roasted cake brought along, he eats it with his mind fixed on me.
Having finally found rest, he indeed returns to his own home when his exhaustion has subsided,
just as one carrying a load of wood on his head eventually goes home once the burden is removed.
Whenever he cuts dry wood or a dry branch from the tree,
at each instance he remembers Hari, bows to the tree, and then cuts it.
If a leaf, a flower, or a fruit is obtained, he gives it to me.
"Go to the tree, O Nārāyaṇa-yoga," he says; and he also says: "O Hare Kṛṣṇa, O Hari Viṣṇu, O Bālakṛṣṇa, Supreme Lord, Inner Controller of this tree, grant auspiciousness! (3.204.10–11)
For such a devotee as I am, who reflects upon the excellence of trees,
worships me, the Lord of Śrī and the best of men, even in the midst of the forest.
And many other wood-gatherers have likewise attained their own yoga.
Devotees of Viṣṇu, dedicated to the chanting of my names,
have fashioned my stone image upon a pedestal beneath a Pippala tree in the forest, having gathered there with wood-gatherers. (13–14)
Established there for the purpose of being seen on that auspicious day and moment,
they gather at midday, worship me, and glorify me;
they honor me as Hari with fruits, water, leaves, and other offerings.
Then, all of them eat wild tubers and go to rest.
On an auspicious day, they perform a new and ever-fresh great festival,
beautified by leaf-pavilions, archways, and flower garlands.

They dance and chant with devotion, using mṛdaṅgas and other instruments. O Lakṣmī, thus, both the dancing and the chanting of those devoted to my glorification have become dear to me, especially at the time of worship and during the performance of the dance.
And during the chanting, I remained invisible while listening;
then, having assumed the form of a holy man and becoming a mendicant, I went at that time to the sacrificial altar site on the Pippala tree within the circle of wood-gatherers.
Honored by them with words of welcome, I, appearing as a holy man, was likewise worshipped;
fed with fruits, tubers, and other foods, my feet were massaged,
and I was then rubbed on the body and saluted by the people.
While staying there, he was questioned by them:
"How indeed, O Blessed One, can the Lord Janārdana—who is formless—be perceived by the eyes? And how can liberation be attained here by these wood-gatherers who carry firewood?"
Then, out of compassion, I bestowed supreme knowledge upon Kamala there; indeed, I revealed the Vaiṣṇava light within her own heart.
Furthermore, Nārāyaṇa should be remembered even while gathering firewood.
Even when carrying firewood, one should always remember Śrī Hari;
(25) and even when tying up a load, the Supreme Lord should be remembered.
Even at the time of sale, it should be said: "May people sell Hari. (26)
"Let people sell *rāma*-fuel, *keśava*-fuel, and *kṛṣṇa*-branches; let them sell *kṛṣṇa*-fuel and black wood!"—
thus should this Nārāyaṇa be shouted at every step.

The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord who bestows liberation, is to be remembered always; the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the husband of Śrī, is the giver of liberation. He alone exists as the inner self, a treasure-house of compassion. (28–29)
The Lord is the giver of heaven, the giver of happiness, and the bestower of all prosperities;
He is the giver of eternal bliss and the one who enables crossing the ocean of creation.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, obeisance to the Master."
Let them constantly recite the purifying mantra of the Supreme Lord.
Let those who carry wood offer everything to me, the Lord;
through devotion, all this will become the merit-bestowing state of actionlessness (naiṣkarmya).
The Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa exists as the cause of all causes; Lord Hari is the bestower of light upon all luminaries. By His radiance, all this world shines and is made manifest.
At the beginning of creation, the Supreme Lord abides in the imperishable abode.
He is the Lord of Rādhā, Lakṣmī, the liberated souls, and the beloved of Brahmā;
by His own will, He brought forth both Prakṛti and the Puruṣa into manifestation. (34–35)
From those two, creation was first produced, entered by Nārāyaṇa;
from those two came Pradhāna and Puruṣa, and from those two came the Golden Being (Hiraṇyapuruṣa).
From him came Virāṭ, from him Brahmā, and from him the great seers and the gods.
From that, human beings were born, as well as animals, birds, and trees.
Thus all this was produced and fashioned by the glorious Supreme Self.
The elements, the senses, their objects, the gods, and so forth, were all infused with the Supreme Self.
Hari dwells within them according to their capacity, and He is present therein;
Hari is the impeller toward action, and Mādhava is the illuminator.
Hari, Kṛṣṇa, is the eternal companion of the individual soul in the world beyond.
Even in this world, Hari himself is the friend and witness of all people.
Having observed the karma performed by living beings, the Lord, as the bestower of fruits,
grants to those beings the rewards consisting of bodies, homes, and other forms of prosperity.
He bestows heaven or even hell according to one's karma;
understand that Lord Kṛṣṇa is thus always the witness.
Thus the Blessed Lord, possessing form, has entered into the state of being the inner controller of all.
He exists as all-pervading and yet he exists within the range of vision.
Hari himself, the Lord, exists in the form of the virtuous. By worshipping the virtuous, one performs the eternal worship of Kṛṣṇa.
The Supreme Hari, the ocean of mercy, appears indeed in the form of a saintly person;
Kṛṣṇa, the purifier of devotees, dwells among the virtuous by His grace.
Devotees intent on the service of the saintly cross the ocean of worldly existence.
The virtuous always have Brahman as their supreme goal and seek liberation for all embodied beings;
for them, this entire universe shines within their vision as the form of Brahman.
With minds free from conceptual construction, they are saviors even of the sinful. (46–47)
But those who perceive the soul, the Lord, and Māyā as one with Brahman, seeing Brahman itself—they are happy; through the bliss of Kṛṣṇa, they bring happiness to the people who take refuge in them.
Free from desire, anger, and the like, their minds are fixed on Śrī Hari.
Though they are bodiless goddesses, they move about like ordinary people.
They cause others to perform devotion to Hari and instruct the people;
they deliver all beings—men, women, and eunuchs alike. (3.204.50)
They cultivate delightful discourse, protect the most excellent virtues, and liberate beings from bondage; these virtuous ones are the very form of Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, they [bring about] the fruits of their respective actions for living beings of many species.
The virtuous who liberate those eating [from suffering] are delivered from the ocean of existence.
Wherever the holy ones dwell, Nārāyaṇa himself dwells there too,
having assumed a human form, though remaining unmanifest.
Though endowed with all forms of radiance, he undertakes the human drama; at times, by the power of his compassion, he indeed assumes the noble deeds of a superhuman being.
The virtuous, and no others, recognize him as the Lord in human form.
But others, through association with the virtuous, come to know Mādhava;
they take refuge in Him, they feel affection for Him, and they delight in the Supreme Self.
Those who do so are indeed liberated from the cycle of worldly existence and go at last to the abode of Brahman.

In Him, Kṛṣṇa, they take delight; there they play, full of joy. There they bring bliss to one another and enjoy an abundance of happiness. Whether knowing it or not, he who feels affection for Kṛṣṇa in His human form—‖57‖
Having indeed become one who has transcended the qualities (guṇātīta), he goes at the end to the imperishable state (akṣaraṃ padam).
Because Kṛṣṇa possesses a divine form, those who depend upon him through that connection— whether they themselves possess a divine nature or not—
become divine and go to Brahman.
Because Hari, the Lord of Māyā, is himself free from Māyā, even those who have taken refuge in it—
even ordinary people— cross over Māyā by the power of Hari.
As for the women of Vraja, they always [resided] with Hari through the state of desire.
Those beloved ones of Brahmā, who were all devoted to Bālakṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, having become affectionate toward the attributeless Kṛṣṇa, indeed attained liberation,
their forms now devoid of qualities. (61–62)
Out of desire, affection, merit, or self-interest, they were attached to the Supreme Soul;
their bonds perishing instantly, they immediately cast off their bodies composed of the gunas.
Mādhava is Kṛṣṇa, devoid of qualities, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Those who were devoid of qualities attained divinity and entered into union with him.
Thus, through affection for Hari, whose nature is truth, liberation becomes certain;
likewise, through affection for the virtuous, there is liberation, for the virtuous are the very forms of Kṛṣṇa.
Through association with the virtuous, they indeed proceed to the supreme, imperishable abode of Hari. The single-minded devotees of Hari desire only the service of Hari;
they do not desire heaven, nor liberation, nor even the world of the Supreme Self.
They do not desire sovereign powers, nor do they desire a form identical [to that of the Lord].
They do not desire proximity, nor ever oneness.
Those who possess such desires would be full of longing; they are indeed of the lowest order.
That [state] is indeed called *truṭi* when there is devotion consisting of the offering of everything;
for in the offering of the self, there is the surrender even of one's intention (*saṃkalpa*), since once it has been performed, they no longer form intentions for their own sake. (69)
For this very reason, those who are free from desire are indeed the most excellent of all in every way. (3.204.70) By the command of Hari, they desire service, but not by their own will.
Service is declared to be the supreme fruit; everything is fully accomplished therein. (71)
Through service to Kṛṣṇa, the fruit of serene devotion is attained;

there is no other fruit superior to this that resides in the hearts of those free from desire. What need is there for states such as *sālokya* and the rest, when the supreme goal is obtained through service?
But those who destroy the state of servitude never desire oneness [with the Lord].
For how can there be service, how can there be grace, or how can there be happiness in a state of oneness?
Therefore, indeed, the devotees who are free from desire become dear to Hari.
Kṛṣṇa thoroughly protects those devotees who are free from desire for worldly rewards;
he accepts with love their service performed out of love. Even toward devotees who do not desire anything, the gracious Lord Hari remains well-pleased.
The Lord bestows His own great sovereign powers upon the Imperishable One.
Thus, those devotees who are contented become like Kṛṣṇa in luster;
by His grace, the Lord of Māyā always sports together with them all.
They are dear to Him as He is dear to Himself; they are contented, wise, and happy.
Free from desire, those supreme devotees indeed become dear to Him.
[This applies] whether in eating, sleeping, bathing, walking, sporting, or in performing actions.
Whether in play, in speech, in recreation, in laughter, or in steadfastness—
Janārdana protects those desireless ones who dwell with Him.
Without doubt, such devotees are always dear to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus instructed by me, O Lakṣmī, all those wood-gatherers who were seeking the path of the virtuous became practitioners of the yoga of knowledge.
Then, having recognized me as the supreme saint whose very self is Nārāyaṇa—
They took refuge in him, rejoiced, and thereafter made this request:
"If through the yoga of a virtuous guru there is the vision of the Supreme Self, then we are fit to be your disciples; therefore, grant us that which bestows liberation. (82-83)
Then I said this to them: "Perform meditation indeed within your hearts;
you shall behold right here Śrīnātha, the Supreme Lord, Mādhava, Hari.
Having been addressed thus, they fixed their mental faculties upon Keśava.
At first, they beheld me, Kṛṣṇa, in the guise of a holy man;
then, from that ascetic’s dress, they beheld the Supreme Lord in his divine form with four arms—the beloved of Śrī and the beloved of Rādhikā, the Supreme Lord. (85–86)
All those wood-gatherers beheld the imperishable abode, most brilliantly radiant,
resplendent with countless millions of liberated souls of Śrī Hari;
there they saw a beautiful throne and a most excellent elephant-throne.
There they beheld me, Hari, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor— the Lord of the lords of lords, the Master who is the husband of Rādhā,
the husband of the beloved of Brahmā, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person. (88–89)
Beholding him in the form of a holy man, suddenly serving infinite, absolute, and liberated joys within their hearts,
they all then saw the ascetic standing outside once more.
Filled with affection, they suddenly gazed upon the virtuous one.
Having risen and recognized me as the Supreme Self who had arrived in the forest, they honored him,
embraced him, and then drank the water from his feet.
And having been granted grace by me, they ate with great joy;
all of them attained a divine state and prostrated themselves like staffs.
Rising again and again, full of delight, they considered themselves blessed.
They danced with rhythmic clapping of their hands and likewise performed kīrtana;
they made excellent offerings of their tongues at the soles of my feet,
and all rolled upon the ground in the dust near my feet.
Then they attained peace and paid homage to me, the eternal;
they requested service just as it had been seen in my abode.
Having uttered, "So be it," I quickly vanished from sight.
Then those who were indeed free from conceptual construction and knew how to worship me became divine devotees; and in time, casting off their bodies,
they went to my supreme abode where the Sādhyas dwell.
In this way, I rescued the wood-gatherers who were intent on devotion;
O Lakṣmī, even thousands such as Jāṅgala, Deva, and others were likewise devoted.
Those among them who possessed worldly desires were led toward heaven.
O Lakṣmī, those who were free from desire were led to Vaikuṇṭha and likewise to the imperishable realm.
Some, however, were led to the most brilliantly radiant abode of Goloka;
and others, O Lakṣmī, were led to Śrīpura, the home of Lalitā.
Some were sent to the abode of Śrī Badarī, others likewise to Śvetadvīpa;
some were brought to the unmanifest realm (avyākṛta-dhāma), and others to immortality.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, these wood-gatherers have been delivered by me.
"From reading and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will certainly be attained.

(10.3) Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of how Jāṅgala-deva and the other wood-gatherers beheld Śrī Hari in the form of a saint through their devotion and attained liberation at the end," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 204. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 205 [Author:
Chapter 206 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the supremely purifying story of my devotee named Vātsalyadhīra, who performed acts of merit. In the village of Nāgaśālāyana, there was indeed a Vaiśya who was my devotee.
Increasing through the abundance of family, wealth, gardens, cattle, fields, and so forth, he was highly honored by both the people and the king;
he was a worshiper of the Brahmins and was devoted to meditation upon me, Hari. (2–3)
Constantly devoted to worship and recitation, intent upon devotion and chanting; serving holy places, saints, and virtuous women; serving cows and serving the gods;
honoring the elderly and dedicated to the dharma of giving food.
That wealthy man gives excellent wealth year after year for the sake of sacrifice;
likewise, he also gives for the purpose of planting trees,
and he also gives for the excavation of ponds, wells, and tanks.
He bestows gifts even for the restoration of ruined temples and the like;
he also gives for the sake of assisting the helpless, children, and the wretched.
[7] He likewise provides for cows, bulls, horses, parrots, and birds such as pigeons.
The virtuous merchant gave even morsels of grass and food.
He established almshouses for food and other necessities, auspicious rest-houses, beautiful water-stations, and platforms at crossroads and other locations. (8–9)
Within his domain, he established water-stations, food-distribution centers, and shelters providing refuge;
he also instituted an excellent, continuous flow of worship for the gods.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, his wealth was constantly being expended even upon acts of charity.
The coin of affection, firm and inexhaustible, increases eternally.
(11) Such a devotee of mine performs a supreme great festival for the vow, like a king, with most precious services. (12)
He indeed causes a grand festival to be celebrated with instrumental music, singing, chanting, and other forms of praise, as well as with devotional worship, dance, and festivities;
[he honors him] with offered food and water, with desired delicacies, fruits, and milk-rice.
He indeed gratifies all those who have gathered for the great festival.
What was given previously, what is obtained here, and even what is given from that [which was obtained]—all this shall become imperishable when it is offered to Nārāyaṇa. (14–15)
Thinking thus, one should indeed give; what is given shall become inexhaustible.
It shall increase and never diminish; therefore, one should especially practice giving.
The fruit of such merit is great, and the gift leads to the supreme heaven.
There shall be clarity of mind toward Hari and satisfaction within the self.
(17) The giving of juices, food, and wealth is in every way a source of happiness, as is the giving of houses, fields, gardens, cows, and likewise milk. (18)
The gift of substances and implements is likewise inexhaustible;
it must be given in every way by those endowed with prosperity, and prosperity will accrue to them.
One never obtains what has not been given—neither women, wealth, houses, and so forth.
Everything that is given is indeed obtained, as well as all happiness born of the senses and the body.
O Lakṣmī, Vātsalyadhīra was present at every sacrifice and in every place;
he inscribed the names of Kṛṣṇa upon door-panels and at water-stations.
In huts, on walls, in vessels, and even upon garments and other objects,
he chants the name of the Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī.
For such a devotee as this, who constantly worships me—
Having become a matted-haired ascetic, I went indeed to his house.
I was invited by him to a seat of grass for the sake of a meal,
and I, being devoted, spoke to him regarding the washing of my feet.
Having filled a golden vessel with water scented with fragrances,
he affectionately washed my feet and drank the water born of his grace.
Then, the king of devotees was quickly offered [the remnants] by me once again.
Indeed, for the purpose of massaging my body with fragrant oils,
he too, with a gracious mind, massaged my limbs accordingly.
Then, being told by me, he proceeded to bathe me with warm water.
Then, full of resolve, he himself arrived there quickly with warm water;
though rejected by me, he entreated me for his wife.
Immediately, that devoted wife named Mañjulikā suddenly appeared.
At her husband’s command, that virtuous woman, free from hesitation and with a serene mind, approached me to bathe me; she offered me a golden seat, and I,
clad in nothing but my loincloth, sat down upon that auspicious seat.
That virtuous and faithful woman, full of devotion and love, repeatedly rubbed me all over my limbs with her hands and bathed me. Then,
while awake, I indeed showed her my transformed state.
Nevertheless, she respectfully bathed me;
though that devoted wife repeatedly touched all my limbs, Mañjulikā, with a serene mind, did not undergo any change [of emotion]. (32–33)
Steadfast, firm, and virtuous, she praised him with palms joined in reverence:
"Be gracious, O liberated soul, for I perform service unto you.
So that the command of my husband may be fulfilled, I shall serve you without any doubt. (34)
Nārāyaṇa is truly virtuous; he is Hari himself in a divine form.
Service to him is indeed obtained by a woman through great fortune. If you have my husband’s permission, I am yours, for I am devoted to my husband.
And having been addressed thus, O Lakṣmī, I likewise summoned her husband, saying:
"Let your wife be given to me; she troubles my mind.
Then the husband, having honored my feet, replied, "So be it," and gave her to me.
By my command, she too was born as one whose nature is devoted to me,
O Rame. Without even touching her, I then quickly became the divine four-armed one,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama.
She too, considering herself blessed, fell at her feet;
and her husband, though steadfast in his affection, was overwhelmed with love. Recognizing me as Hari in the form of a holy man, he fell at my feet.
He summoned his devotees and immediately performed service for them.
With garments, ornaments, sandalwood paste, saffron, and other such things,
he offered everything to me— food, water, and fruit.
She prepared a couch, a golden seat, and exquisite, most worthy ornaments;
she performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and then gave me a bed.
Then I, the Lord in the form of a holy man, was worshipped by all.
And the devotees made this request, while he, steady-minded with affection, replied:
"O Supreme Lord, let food be granted;
O Highest of the High, let the divine state be bestowed, and let knowledge endowed with majesty be given."

One must cultivate complete detachment from all worldly things (47). Dispassion must be protected in every way for the sake of severing the bonds [of saṃsāra].
Furthermore, there must be devotion to me, Kṛṣṇa—love, affection, and great tenderness (48).
Women and men must by all means offer themselves unto Me;

Through such affection, there shall arise within the heart an unbroken remembrance of Me, Hari.
By that means, the manifestation of my form shall always exist, bestowing happiness.
However, other conceptualizations lead only to rebirth;
indeed, when dissolved along with *māyā*, they become seedless.
The fulfilled intentions of those possessing perfect love, who are ever devoted through the yoga of bhakti, fall within my range of perception; they never become objects for others.
However, if there is a contrary state due to attachment to place, time, and so forth, then it is illusory (māyika).
If a conceptual thought (saṃkalpa) should arise, then pain would occur in the heart;

Just as a sharp blade of a spear-head, having entered the heart, would indeed cause pain. (53–54)
Just as a thought directed toward another causes pain to one who is dependent [on that other],
so too should such supreme affection be directed toward me, Keśava.
Indeed, my affection increases through the knowledge of my greatness.
And from the taking of the garland of choice (varamālā), there may also arise a natural [affection].
A necklace, a garland, and a garland of choice—these are remembered as my "choice" (vara) mantra.
Upon its acceptance, there would be affection, like that of a maiden for her beloved. ||56-57||
Affection arises even for one who is unseen, for he is the support of all and the protector; indeed, every disposition of the devotee becomes one of total self-surrender to him.
Even at the mere touch during the taking of the hand in marriage, affection increases exceedingly.

I am the Self, the conscious, the divine, having taken refuge in the Blessed One.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss; I am liberated, established in Brahman.

Thus, one who possesses discernment becomes entirely devoted to Kṛṣṇa;
free from the notions of "I" and "mine," and devoid of all attachment and the like.
"I have no mother, no father, no wife, and no wealth."
"I have no son, nor daughter, nor house, nor garden.

yet through ignorance I have forgotten them here, and likewise these [present ones]."

That is true; by it, devotees cross over, whereas worldly people, lacking discrimination, are bound in saṃsāra and do not cross over.

Taking him by the arm, she should indeed take refuge in her beloved Kṛṣṇa;

Even though he is a householder, he should be regarded as a true saint.

He who worships Kṛṣṇa, being established in such knowledge and possessing detachment—for him Hari is indeed not far off; he alone is truly a saint (sādhu). Therefore, his bonds perish; that very saint is to be served.

Moreover, even for those who have renounced everything and abandoned their homes and such, in some instances—

Thus, O Lakṣmī, I instructed that merchant-chief;

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord, being pleased by the devotion of the merchant Vātsalyadhīra and his wife Mañjulikādevī, granted them His vision, and how they both became perfected saints," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the lineage of the Dvāpara age.

Others, having worshipped that God, went to the supreme state in the past;

absorbed in Hari, the bestower of supreme bliss, gentle in form and brilliantly radiant—

Then, there within the heart of Śaṅkara, the auspicious and supremely divine four-armed form of Hari was seen together with Lakṣmī,
