Those weapons were not at all conducive to their victory.
Suddenly, a discharge of weapons occurred in their presence;
then the battle proceeded with arrows, missiles, and iron clubs.
Eka fought alone against twenty others who stood in his midst;
though wounded many times by weapons, he fought valiantly while remembering me.
Ten of Nāñja’s men, pierced by broad-headed arrows in the chest, indeed died.
Then, among those thieves, not a single thief fell to the ground from the repeated blows of their swords, as he repeatedly remembered me while in a state of swoon.
At that moment, I, a hero holding a sword, quickly went to his side at that spot. (286–287)
A great-bodied being appeared, with a body as firm as a diamond and skilled in combat;
without hesitation, he pierced the remaining thieves with his sword.
All twenty thieves there quickly met their death.
The twenty-first, however, was a lone thief who, uttering "Rāma,
Rāma," fell into a swoon and quickly lost consciousness as he went toward his death.
Then, touched by compassion, I [touched] him who was solely devoted to the name of Rāma.
Reviving that devoted man, I made him free from disease.
Then that devotee, named Mahāmaya, rose up;
moved by compassion, he earnestly entreated me for the sake of his own restoration to life.
Then, repeatedly touching him with both my hands,
I dispelled his fainting fit and raised him up, filled with happiness. And then,
having seen Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, those two [were likewise restored].
The two, filled with devotion, offered praise together so that the dead might regain their lives:
"Aho! You are indeed Nārāyaṇa, Rāma, the deliverer from the Rākṣasas;
aho! You are the Blessed One, Nṛsiṃha, the destroyer of the Daityas."
Aho! O Kṛṣṇa, O Hare, O Rāma, you are the one who raised up the elephant.
You alone, who are affectionate toward your devotees, exist for the sake of destroying the demons.
And the destruction of the sins of sinners occurs simply by the sight of you.
Indeed, sinners cross over [suffering] here through both touching and remembering you;
you abide as Viśvambhara (the Sustainer of the Universe), the nourisher and the protector.
You manifest as Saṃkarṣaṇa, Rudra, and Kāla (Time), the destroyer.
Protect, protect me, O ocean of compassion; indeed, restore those who have died here to life!
(37) Even a devotee becomes a thief through association with thieves.
I am a great sinner, a devotee who has been intent upon the act of theft. (38)

Nevertheless, O Lord Kṛṣṇa, fulfiller of the desires of Your devotees, You have protected this devotee here by means of the name "Rāma"; my protection here has arisen through that connection, not from Your direct presence. (39)
These who have attained the yoga of devotion must be protected by you, O Compassionate One.
Even if they are dead, they shall be restored to life and will worship Nārāyaṇa.
Or, if it pleases you to liberate them, do so accordingly.
Thus addressed, O Lakṣmī, I then, out of compassion, first ordained a residence in heaven for the sake of the liberation of those who had died;
and through my yoga and their devotion, I caused their sins to perish.
I destroyed all their sufferings of Yama from their heads.
Recalling the celestial chariot and assuming divine forms,
I swiftly dispatched those twenty who had died in battle to heaven.

Likewise, having repeatedly touched Mahāmaya with my hand and fed him, I restored him to health, free from disease, just as he was before. Then, once they were nourished and freed from suffering, I enlightened them both.
This saṃsāra is indeed impermanent; the body, the home, and so forth are impermanent.
All objects arising from illusion are impermanent and subject to decay.
Nevertheless, ignorant people, abandoning right conduct, wander upon the wrong path.
They constantly engage in violence, theft, and destruction;
they do not cultivate the company of the virtuous, nor do they worship the Supreme Lord.
They do not listen to the discourse of the scriptures and commit sin without hesitation.
Therefore, being punished, they experience great sufferings in the realm of Yama;
even sinful people take birth among beasts and birds, and those who act contrary to dharma encounter suffering upon suffering. (3.207.49–50)
By stealing the food of others, one is born as a mouse;
by stealing ghee, milk, and the like, one becomes a cat;
and by stealing vegetables, roots, and such, one attains birth as a peacock.
By the theft of clothing and utensils, one is born as a buffalo;
by the taking of fruits, leaves, and the like, one is born as a monkey;
and by the theft of gold, gems, and so forth, one is born as a bear. (52–53)
By stealing water for drinking and such, one becomes a ghost in a waterless forest;
by stealing a wife, children, and so forth, one attains the state of a eunuch and birth as a courtesan.
By stealing musical instruments, one becomes a jester, and likewise, by stealing [other items], one becomes an actor.
For those who betray trust, there is the state of a wolf or a chameleon;
for those who commit theft, birth as a horse;
for those who live by serving as mounts, birth as a bull; and for those who revile others, the state of being mute.
One becomes a eunuch or a bull among those who lust; a woman becomes a female demon (piśācinī).
One becomes a deceiver or a mendicant, and shall suffer the misery of poverty.
Furthermore, one becomes a dog, a crow, or a mouse, consuming the food and wealth of the gods.
A killer of a noble family becomes a mongoose; a killer of a woman becomes a *rākṣasa*.
A destroyer of dharma, devoid of fortune, is born as a boar in the forest.
A destroyer of devotion becomes a denizen of hell, childless, and a messenger of Yama.
A drinker of intoxicants becomes a urine-insect; one who consumes poison becomes a scorpion;
and when enraged, one becomes a serpent as well as a blue monkey.
Having thus understood these births resulting from karma, one should avoid them.
A human being should perform only what is auspicious with this body, and never anything inauspicious.
One should cultivate auspicious virtue, auspicious knowledge, and auspicious dispassion;
one should also practice auspicious devotion and seek the company of the virtuous, which bestows liberation.
One should always perform sincere service for Lord Hari and for the virtuous;
one should cause the temple of Kṛṣṇa, its garden, and other areas to be smeared with plaster and swept clean;
and one should perform the massaging of the feet and the rubbing of the bodies of the virtuous.
One should offer food as an oblation, meals, and drinks to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
One should offer these immediately and according to one's desire, serve the circle of gurus,
constantly listen to the sacred narratives, and perform the chanting of the Name.
One should abide in self-realization through the self that is of the nature of Brahman;
one should know me, Hari, the divine, who is free from all defects.
One should carry out my message and always maintain affection for me.
One should likewise become free from attachment toward illusions and their effects;
one should always perform auspicious service to the virtuous and keep the company of the good.
One should cultivate a lack of relish for sense objects, and the mind should be inclined toward tranquility.
One should make one's mind firm in the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
one should never at any time direct the mind toward anything else.
One should perform service and likewise adornment for Me solely out of love.
One should bear my form, whether as a human or as a deity.
One should indeed maintain affection for my devotees and nowhere else.
One should always avoid attachment and the bonds of affection toward wife, children, and so forth.

One should remain engaged only in activities related to Kṛṣṇa and, with a concentrated mind, desist from those devoid of connection to Kṛṣṇa. One should constantly perform worship of me and pray for one's own welfare.
O Nārāyaṇa, O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Master, O Supreme Lord!
Protect me from the world that follows the path of unrighteousness, and likewise protect me from the atheist.
Grant me constant communion with Your devotees and perform what is auspicious.
May there be no association with the wicked; protect me always in such a way.
Do not grant me the company of thieves, sinners, or revilers, nor the company of those who consume liquor and meat, nor of those who engage in sexual misconduct.
O Kṛṣṇa, you who are compassionate toward those who have sought refuge, do not grant me the company of those who destroy idols and ruin spiritual practice.
Act in such a way that no day passes for me without devotion. || 76-77 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, cause my mental activity to always abide in You;
likewise, act so that my mind may feel detachment toward worldly things.
O Kṛṣṇa, grant me the company of the virtuous and the sight of Your own form.
Grant me your vision for a long time and take up residence within my heart.
Whether externally or internally, may that divine vision of yours be ever present; likewise, O Kṛṣṇa, grant me the auspicious inner sight.
"O Lord, grant me that imperishable abode resplendent with Your own form;
O Kṛṣṇa, I likewise pray for liberation consisting of service to You.
In this manner, one should constantly petition me, the Blessed Lord Hari.
"Since you two have come within the range of my vision because of your devotion, may there be well-being for you both;
I am now departing for my own abode.
Having spoken thus and granted courage to the farmers, the Blessed Lord then [departed]. (82-83)
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Having bestowed this mantra upon the farmers and the two devotees, He vanished.
Those farmers, having witnessed that miracle, took refuge in me.

O Lakṣmī! Through worship and devotion, even the guardian of the field (Kṣetrapa), though possessed of great disease, suddenly became free from ailment upon meeting Nārāyaṇa; and even Añjana, though full of impurity, was freed from his impurity. (85–86)
They all constantly worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī, Rādhā, and Ramā; they performed my worship, fed me, meditated upon me, enjoyed with me, and remembered me.
They also performed my kīrtana perpetually, and after the end of their bodies, they attained that which is beyond.
Then, arriving swiftly in a celestial chariot as resplendent as Viṣṇu’s own,
accompanied by my attendants at the border of Aśvapaṭṭa,
I led the farmers, now possessing divine bodies, to my own realm.
He did not bring any other food; instead, he brought that which is free from disease.
Thus, my devotees, as well as the guardians of the field, have attained the imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, you should offer me fresh grain produced from the field.
One should offer the *cirbhaṭa* gourd, a fly, as well as leaves and flowers.
One should offer to me the bulb, fruit, stalk, sweet vegetable, bud, cluster, stem, tube, joint, or branch. (91–92)
Whether it be a grain of rice, a jujube fruit, or even a particle of purifying clay—
whosoever offers these to me with devotion, I uplift that offerer. [I accept] sacrificial fuel, a tulasī leaf, sandalwood, or a fruit-bearing tree.

Whoever offers me a blade of grass, a *darbha* stalk, or even a sprout shall partake in liberation. Whoever offers me cotton, a tuft of wool, a legume, or even a pod; or a cluster of flowers, or a water-pot—such a person shall attain mokṣa. (94–95)
One may offer sesame seeds, wheat, chickpeas, or likewise split pulses;
or nivāra rice, sārīka rice, or dates;
or sugar, turmeric, salt, or ginger. (96)

If one should offer me various kinds of fermented rice-gruel (āranāla), citron (laviṅga), areca nut (pūgikāphala), cardamom (elā), or even saffron (kesara), one shall partake in liberation. Or likewise, if one offers a seat, a vessel, a creeper, or even a cane (vetra)— [97–98]
One who offers me a vehicle, clothing, food, oil, excellent fragrance,
and ornaments becomes a partaker of liberation.
[Likewise, one who offers] milk, juice, cooked food, and cool sweet drinks.
One who offers me a fan or even a condiment shall partake in liberation.
Indeed, by offering oneself, all go to my abode, O Kamalā;
by reciting, hearing, or even remembering this, one partakes in liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of How the Lord Protected the Village Headman, the Devotee Nāñja, the Great Devotee Mahāma, and the Farmers from Thieves," in the Third Section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 208: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 208.
[The Author: Chapter 209.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of this devotee born of the Kirāta caste.
There was a virtuous man named Sāgara, a resident of the great city of Śāṭīnagarī.
Accompanied by his family, he lived in a forest on the bank of the Mahī river;
he wandered for the sake of maintaining his body and made provisions at home.
Of wild tubers and roots, as well as grains,
pulses, fruits, seeds, and juices;
in some places he eats food, fruit, or leaves, and in others he consumes tubers.
He maintains his livelihood for the journey of this body and worships me.
Sometimes he even becomes a porter for wealthy gardeners, and at times he serves as a servant to merchants. (4–5)
Acting in this way, he does not obtain food anywhere for his sustenance;
then, intent upon fasting, he worships me with great joy.
He also performs the recitation of the garland-mantra, saying "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa."
Considering that vow to be natural, he indeed keeps a vigil at night;
though afflicted by hunger and thirst, he performs kīrtana during the night.
His wife, sons, and daughters—all of them likewise observe the vow.
Once, during the bright fortnight, on the eleventh day of the month of Kamala (Kārttika), not even the slightest food was obtained for their ears;
thus, the vow born of the Ekādaśī, along with its natural observance of staying awake throughout the night, was spontaneously fulfilled.
They performed my worship and my glorification even without water.
Then, at dawn, O Rame, they all offered me a vegetable dish;
having presented water to me, they themselves ate that very vegetable dish.
"O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord! they cried as they drank water with joy, O Lakṣmī. Then I, the abode of compassion, went before them together with a cartload of wheat.

Thinking me to be a merchant and a most excellent seller, they all bowed to me, offered water, and sang for a moment for the sake of my rest. And I, having understood their words, [placed] Śakarī in the courtyard of that house.

Having tethered the two bulls and bound them to the seat prepared by him, they all sat down and massaged my feet. O Kṛṣṇa, with their minds deeply absorbed, they called out, "Kṛṣṇa! Kṛṣṇa! while performing this service.
Then, when I asked them all what their occupations were and how they made their living, they replied:
"Kṛṣṇa provides our livelihood, and thus we live.
Today, worship with water and the offering of food has been performed."
"O merchant, we have eaten our greens and drunk water; indeed, peace always dwells within us, bestowing happiness. What need is there for wealth in the tens of thousands or millions?
We worship Śrī Hari eternally, and He alone provides our food. (18)
We offer everything to Hari, who is beyond all attributes.
You are a merchant today, and there is no great wealth in our house to serve as a fitting welcome-offering for you. (3.208.20)

Then he said to me, "O Lakṣmī, this vegetable dish is pleasing to you; please accept it. Thus addressed, I then ate that vegetable with affection, and I also drank water and attained the satisfaction born of devotion.
Then I gave them a complete heap of wheat,
and I also gave them a thousand silver rings as wealth.
Thereupon they asked me my name, my village, and my family.
I say: "I am Harikṛṣṇa; I am Bālakṛṣṇa.
My village is the abode of the Imperishable (Akṣara-dhāma), and my family is the circle of devotees.
In their homes, I am present as their festival and their great honor. (20)
"The vow of Ekādaśī along with the night vigil that was performed by you—
by means of ghee and water, I have been gratified and have arrived for the sake of protection.
Out of compassion, I have come here to bestow all the wheat."
"Once these wheat grains have been touched by my hand, they shall become inexhaustible;
having placed them in a granary and covered them above, they must be drawn out through a hole, and not otherwise. (27)
"By my power, they shall indeed become inexhaustible.
May my devotees, born in succession through their lineages, be happy, even when there is no longer any worship of me here in this house. (28–29)
"Then those wheat grains bestowed by me shall reach exhaustion," he said,
and granted me the divine vision as well.
He gave me a four-armed form, endowed with splendor and captivating to the mind.
They all praised me and fell at my feet.
Overwhelmed by love, they all shed tears;
they chose protection from me, as well as liberation in the end and the supreme state.
O Lakṣmī, having spoken words of encouragement, I quickly vanished from that place along with the cart, the two oxen, and likewise [my companions].
Throughout my life, the Kirāta has been devoted to me; he provides wheat and *polikā* cakes.
Having prepared it together with his own wife, he offered it [to them].
(34) Whatever ascetics, other holy men, virtuous women, saintly nuns, and mendicants come, they receive wheat cakes along with the seasoned vegetable dish. (35)
A continuous feast of food was maintained for the ocean;
indeed, even those who had come merely as pilgrims found peace in his house.
Sāgara always obtained the great benefit of serving the virtuous.
Sāgara, who was endowed with great merit, became like the ocean itself.
In his house, sages would go to eat food provided by the grace of the gods;
even deities in the guise of virtuous men would come to eat wheat cakes.
Perceiving his divine grace, mendicants indeed come to him;
they eat the wheat cakes given by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which are equal to nectar.
These are consumed by the deities and the ancestors, who have taken the form of mendicants. (29)
The perfected ones (*siddhas*) with their divine bodies enjoy these meritorious *polikās*.
Indeed, from morning until evening, the *polikās* continue to be served;
all the wheat is inexhaustible and increases within the interior of the granary. (3.208.40–41)
The house of Sāgara became a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the world;
it became celebrated even in the three worlds as a purifying place.
Then, having heard that the food-distribution hall was inexhaustible, Durvāsas—
Accompanied by ten thousand disciples, he arrived unexpectedly in the morning.
Honored by Sāgara, who extended a respectful welcome,
he then had rows of seats prepared for the meal, arranged so that everyone would eat simultaneously.
Terrified, Sāgara reflected upon the Lord, the Consort of Śrī;
then I appeared within his house together with Śrī.
Seeing both me and Śrī, Sāgara rejoiced exceedingly.
Then Lakṣmī was commanded by me to quickly prepare polikās;
Ramā, however, suddenly prepared only five polikās.
She was cooked on the hearth by the fire and held in my hand. ||46-47||
These five [offerings] are indeed inexhaustible and never diminish;
having taken a vessel in his hand, Sāgara served them,
and ten thousand portions were presented to each individual.
In this way, ten thousand polikās were served.
A vessel was also given from the pot and distributed to everyone.
Touched by me, both the vessel and the polikās became delicious. (3.208.50)
All those followers of Durvāsas ate their fill; being satisfied, they took a mouthful of water and considered it a great wonder. Then, there remained exactly five *polikās* in the cooking pot.
Having witnessed this great marvel, Durvāsas returned home.
While he was away, Hari and I, together with Lakṣmī, vanished from sight.
Durvāsas, having repeatedly bowed down to the grain-basket and to his devotee Sāgara, [departed].
Having bestowed his excellent blessing upon her wife named Sārikā, he said:
"May your wealth be inexhaustible, may your grain be inexhaustible;
may your vessels also be inexhaustible, and likewise may your faith be inexhaustible. (54)
May your food-offering (*anna-satra*) be inexhaustible, and likewise may your merit be inexhaustible.
May your liberation be inexhaustible, and may your devotion also be inexhaustible.
May the dharma of your giving be truly inexhaustible; with these words, I shall now depart.
Having spoken thus, being honored and exceedingly gratified, he departed for the forest.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, was the ocean protected by me there.
Then, having heard this, the Vālakhilyas—the great sages and sons of Brahmā—[arrived].
Eighty-eight thousand dwarfs arrived there;
indeed, on the new moon day, they came early in the morning to eat at Prasādapolikā.
Sāgara honored them and likewise extended a welcome.
Then, for the purpose of a meal, they were invited to sit in an auspicious row;
at that time, the Ocean remembered Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu and me as well.
Immediately thereafter, Janārdana arrived there together with Lakṣmī.
And there I became a brahmin, and Lakṣmī likewise became a brahmin woman.
Having quickly made ten *polikā* cakes the size of the palm of the hand, we each gave ten to every one of the eighty-eight thousand [brahmins]. (61–62)
Having shared it out together, they gave it to him, and they ate it with great joy.
Having become truly satisfied after drinking from their cupped hands, they departed,
praising the devotion to the Ocean and the grace of Hari.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, that ocean was protected by me there along with you and our excellent companions; all the sages were fed. Then Śaṅkara, having learned that his home had become supremely sanctified, [arrived]. (64–65)
Accompanied by ten hundred thousand followers, they arrived at midday.
All of them indeed possessed the appearance of holy men, wearing matted hair and animal skins.
Recognizing that it was a supreme and inexhaustible food-distribution center, they made their request.
The food consisted of fried cakes and black lentil soup in bowls;
there, Sārikā and Sāgara were terrified and remembered me.
Then, together with Lakṣmī, I quickly arrived at their home.
Having prepared a hundred *polikā* cakes, I gave them to each individual saint;
indeed, I myself gave ten lakhs [of offerings] to the ascetics.
While assuming many forms, I remained at the end with a hundred [cakes] remaining.

Having eaten those *polikā* cakes and being satisfied, they praised Sāgara and departed for their own Kailāsa; Śaṅkara then practiced meditation and beheld the cause, Viṣṇu as Bālakṛṣṇa, endowed with splendor.
"Seeing me, who am dependent upon my devotees, he attained supreme wonder.
Thus indeed, O Lakṣmī, was the ocean protected by me at that time.
Then, having heard this, Brahmā himself approached for the sake of the *polikā* (sweetmeat).

Accompanied by ten million perfected beings (siddhas), he quickly requested a favor from Vyoman for the sake of obtaining grace. And Sāgara, for the sake of satisfying the ten million siddhas, again requested a favor from Hari regarding the production of *polikās*. (73–74)
He remembered me as his protector, and I then appeared before him,
together with Lakṣmī, together with Śrī, and together with Rādhā;
likewise, together with Lalitā, with Māṇikī, and with Ramā.
At that time, together with Padmāvatī and the beloved wives of Brahmā,
I remained in the sky accompanied by my crores and billions of consorts.
Having had a thousand *polikās* prepared, I was joined by ten million beloved ones.
I gave a thousand *polikās* to each of the Siddhas, yet a thousand remained; thus the Creator of the Universe was struck with wonder.
Then Sāgara, likewise perceiving his own supreme good fortune, [acted].

Having indeed made everything dependent upon Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, he performed the honoring and welcoming [of guests] day and night. His inexhaustible granary attained renown throughout the three worlds. (3.208.80)
Great lords from the three worlds come and go;
casting aside all supreme exertion, the ocean serves him with joy.
He did not even request the aid of another force, for he possessed divine power.
When that devotee, overcome by fear, remembers me alone, then—

having observed the disposition of such a devotee who has surrendered his very self— I became pleased with him, for he was performing service for the sake of all living beings in the three worlds. (82–83)
In particular, I reflected there for the sake of my devotees:
"I must provide him with a wish-fulfilling vessel from which countless *polikā* cakes shall constantly appear, as well as another such vessel for food. (84)
"Wherein even infinite vessels might appear, well-prepared," he reflected thus and gave him two vessels of excellent luster.
"In the very morning, having cooked them well here, there shall be *polikās* and likewise *bhājikās*. (85–86)
He constantly protects both bowls by covering them.
I said to Sāgara there: "Either you or your wife shall be devoted to her husband.
Indeed, there are infinite full bowls, as many as one desires."

You will resolve upon as many auspicious and beautiful things as you desire, and they shall issue forth from these two through mere volition alone; there will be no need for the effort of serving food, nor even the act of giving vessels. (88–89)
"They shall not have to perform [the rites], for they will naturally take their place in the row.
Having spoken thus, I was honored; and I gave him a vessel of water—such as it was, inexhaustible and full, serving as the cause for a full ceremonial pitcher.
Then, from that place, Sāgara vanished and rejoiced exceedingly. Then,
on the auspicious new moon day of the month of Bhādrapada, having realized this great marvel,
the Pitṛs numbering in the tens of billions— those born of Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya— [arrived].
Then all those embodied beings, eager for the sake of satisfaction, arrived at the will of Suprasāda and stood in rows.
Sārikā, purified by bathing, prepared vessels and *polikā* cakes.
He placed the milk-preparation fit for the *śrāddha* rite into those two vessels;
having covered them and offered them to Viṣṇu, he prepared everything as prescribed.
Sāgara, too, having performed his ablutions, approached the vicinity of the vessels.
At that time, indeed, millions,
tens of millions, and billions of vessels— countless and full— issued forth from the pair of bowls.
Each one was presented individually to every ancestor and deity.

O Rame, the vessel was filled with *polikā* cakes and milk-rice (*pāyasa*), as well as with various dishes and water-jars that provide satisfaction. Having eaten, the ancestors—numbering ten million, a hundred billion, and a trillion—were satiated and then departed. (97–98)
Empty vessels returned to their dissolution by their very nature;
likewise, that ocean-like devotee was nourished by me with great compassion during the *godhūma-satra*, acting as a benefactor to all who arrived. (99)

Indeed, Kirāta experienced [the fruits] through devotion in every way, as did Devarāta. Then, after some time, accompanied by divine attendants, I brought the couple in a magnificent celestial chariot to my imperishable abode.
O Lakṣmī, thereafter the city was named Mahīśāṭī, followed by Godhumabhājikā; likewise, it became known as Godhumasārikā,
and then that purifying land was called Godhumarā.

Thus, that great sacred site was established by me, the compassionate one, for the sake of the liberation of the couple. Subsequently, King Godhara-sūri made that Kusulā [village] his own domain, and there he cultivated wheat. || 103–104 ||
"They have become invisible, and the three vessels have also become invisible;
the food-distribution has ceased, and the miracle has vanished.
Thus did the sage Godhara behold that which was wrought by fate.
Hari always worshipped Kusula while remembering him, even though his granary was perpetually empty.
Nevertheless, that wonder which had departed has indeed returned.
O Lakṣmī, by reading or hearing this, one shall attain the divine state.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari, pleased by the devotion of the Kirāta devotee named Sāgara during the lineage of the Dvāpara age as recounted in the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā, bestowed a heap of wheat in the form of a merchant, made the grain in his granary inexhaustible, rendered his cakes, vessels, and water-pots inexhaustible, and granted him liberation," from the third section (the lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) of the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā. Chapter 209.
[The Author: Chapter 210.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇīśrī, to the virtuous story of the devotee from the Hūṇa land.
He was known by the name Sāraṅga and resided in the village of Bhūdharī.
(1) O Rame, in the forest of Bhūdharīgrāma in Saurāṣṭra, there dwells a member of the Hūṇa caste who is a devotee of mine, together with his family. (2)
Having first performed his bath and worshipped me thereafter,
he leads the herd of cows to a grassy meadow for grazing;
having wandered through the pasture forest, he returns home at evening.
In the forest there are lions, tigers, and even bears;
there are also wolves, leopards, and other predatory creatures.
Tigers and lions sometimes attack cows, buffaloes, and bulls. (4–5)
Having killed them, they devour them; for they are indeed givers of terror and givers of suffering.
There is a Hūṇa named Sāraṅga, who possesses fifty female buffalo;
he grazes these buffaloes upon his most excellent and beloved fodder.
Then, at the hour of midday,
five lions emerged from the midst of a thicket of *pārśva* trees by way of the forest path leading to Karmadrya, and approached the herd of female buffaloes who were grazing on grass. (7–8)
Suddenly and unexpectedly, five roaring lions fell [upon him]—
powerful, exceedingly well-fed, invincible, and filled with hunger.
Suddenly those female buffaloes also, having formed a line of droplets on their backs...
Having protected their offspring in the center while guarding the circle of their faces on all sides,
they formed a defensive circle out of anger for the sake of preserving their lives and out of fear; having come together and arranged themselves like a village, they took refuge on the ground.
Upon seeing the village of buffaloes and quickly becoming afraid, those lions turned back and from a distance repeatedly discharged clouds of foul-smelling wind to strike terror into the beasts. (12)
If, having emerged from their own circle, they were to disperse separately, then lions would attack them and devour them as food;
thus they roared and displayed their ferocity. (13–14)
Nevertheless, those female buffaloes did not emerge from the caravan;
remaining exactly as they were, the lions continued to roar most terrifyingly.
Hearing them, ten other lions arrived for the sake of food.
The fifteen lions were positioned around the wheel; all those queens stood as they were at each secondary wheel (praticakra). They did not flee, they did not escape, nor could they reach them.
In this very way, it became evening; the lions stayed far away. Then the Sāraṅga and Hūṇa kindled the fire, with separate piles of fuel gathered all around the female buffaloes.

Thinking that the lions would flee far away out of fear of fire, they [the deer] likewise moved to a distance; yet those cruel beasts of prey did not depart altogether. They continued to roam all around and rushed forward for the purpose of killing them. (3.209.20)
Nightfall has arrived, and there is no assistance there;
at night, the strength of lions increases when shrouded in darkness.
There will be the destruction of the female buffaloes—what should be done on this ground of calamity?
Without Nārāyaṇa Kṛṣṇa, no helper is found.
Thinking thus that the Lord alone is the protector when the great time of calamity has arrived, he indeed obtained a mantra and, absorbed in Him, recited it.
The excellent mantra which was obtained from Lomaśa by Aśvapaṭṭatīrthi,
that very mantra the king of the Hūṇa devotees formerly recited:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, he beheld Hari in the sky:
"O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, Teacher of the World!
O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, protect me, protect me here! (25–26)
O Savior of those who have come for refuge, protect me here from this lion's attack!
O Kṛṣṇa, in this forest there is no other protector to be found but you.
O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa, O Bālakṛṣṇa, come quickly and protect us!
As darkness increases, death will surely come to us; of this there is no doubt. (28) If I am your devotee, O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, protect me!
Death occurs for living beings everywhere; there is no doubt about this. (29)
But, O Kṛṣṇa, it is not my view that premature death here by the tearing of their bodies with nails is appropriate for these queens,
whose milk you, O Blessed One, drink every day.
O Kṛṣṇa, at the morning worship and during the offering of food, as well as by day and by night, I cause lamps to be lit with ghee at the onset of the evening;
if you do not protect them, are you indeed merciless? || 31-32 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, why do you not protect those for whom you consume such exceedingly sweet and thick, excellent curds?
Come quickly for our protection; otherwise, I am your devotee.
I myself shall first give up my life for the sake of the sacrificial animal.
Indeed, the protection of those who have sought refuge must always be performed by a master first;
for it is not considered right that their destruction should follow upon the master’s own ruin due to his fault.
"O Kṛṣṇa, these queens are looking toward me as their protector.
O Kṛṣṇa, residing within my heart, do you not see?
Look, look, O Hari Kṛṣṇa! These women have fallen into great distress."

"Let him be a devourer, let him remain a devourer, or even let him be a protector," having said this, O Lakṣmī, Sāraṅgahūṇa, the king of my devotees, shed tears and indeed heaved a long sigh, free from all worldly desire.
Thinking, "We have come to our death," he wept for a moment.
Lions exert their strength while remaining at a distance out of fear of fire;
yet the sarabha is stronger than fire, and it stands on all sides of the logs of firewood.
Having kindled it, and having thoroughly kindled it, he casts it down here and there.
As long as one has the strength of intellect, effort must be made for the protection of life;
thinking thus, one exerts effort, yet the will of Viṣṇu is more powerful.
Then, holding a blazing piece of wood in his hand and wandering about on all sides,
he performed intense worship for the protection of his queens,
chanting: "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī!"
"Hare Viṣṇo! Hare Jiṣṇo! Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa, O Lord of Ramā!"—thus, O Ramā, he performed my kīrtana with his neck upraised. Then, for the sake of his protection and for the protection of his wife, I spoke.
Instantly, he assumed the great form of the lion-king, the maned one, complete with a trunk, by which even lions, tigers, elephants, and śarabhas were quickly struck with fear—
how much more so ordinary deer?
Assuming the form of a great king of lions— extremely fierce, terrifying, and possessing a fresh trunk-like tail— I went forth;
making a roar like that of a cloud, I caused the beasts of the forest to tremble.
Hearing that I am a great lion, a man with eyes flashing like lightning,
the king of all species of lions, and a source of terror—
possessing a strength exceeding a hundred [lions]— the lions in the great forest were struck with fear.
Then, suddenly leaping from the forest into the very sky,
I tore through the air at a height of a hundred cubits and descended into the presence of the lion;
meanwhile, the lions, their courage destroyed by great fear, stood before me.
Suddenly, out of fear of me, all those lords of beasts fled from the mouth of that which had the form of Death; they all entered the forest.
Having suddenly put those lords of beasts to flight, I, the king of lions, [remained].
Assuming the guise of a human being, I quickly became visible;
with a serene countenance and peaceful, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
I comforted my queen, the devotee, and the devotee himself.
Seeing both Hari and me, Sāraṅga also approached closely;
having regained his life, he rejoiced and praised [us] with supreme joy.
He fell at our feet and addressed the queens with fearless cries.
He awakened all the queens, even though they were fearless;
they rejoiced and became full of happiness there from the two men.
Then Sāraṅga, the king of devotees, regained his composure.
Then Lakṣmī, having milked the milk, caused it to be drunk by me;
and I drank the excellent milk of all the queens.
Then, together with the followers of Sāraṅga and likewise with the queens—
I proceeded slowly toward that gate of the mountain fortress to address that fault.
There, until dawn, I dwelt joyfully, honored by my devotees;
I was served by the group of his wives and by other Hūṇas.
He was gratified by the chanting of his names and other such acts, by massaging his feet and the like,
by offerings of water, and by various other great festivals.
Then, at dawn, he assumed the form of a virtuous man at the arrival of the sun.
Served by all of them with food fragrant with flowers,
I was questioned by those devoted to the Hūṇas for the sake of their welfare; and for the purpose of destroying their sins, I likewise instructed them.
"Listen, all you who are my devotees, though you may possess coarse intellects;
nevertheless, by striving for the highest good, you shall become subtle-minded.
Indeed, you do possess the wisdom for liberation, for that is a subtle intellect. (63)

Those who are intent upon their own highest good are indeed possessed of very subtle intellects. (64) If they are clever in worldly affairs but not so in their own highest good, then they are considered to be always asleep, fools of dull intellect. (65)
Those who are shrouded by illusion are called dull-witted, foolish, and like beasts.
Whether one be a king, a leader, a guru, a teacher, or even one who has mastered the sciences—if such a person does not strive for their own liberation, [they remain bound]. (66)
Indeed, that very person of gross intellect is a fool who shall go to the realm of Yama.
Those men and women who abide in devotion to me are divine;
however, those who are not devoted should be understood as being like cattle, dwelling in hell.
My devotees obtain a vision of me with their own eyes;
for those eyes are non-material (aprākṛta), being eternally purified through my yoga.
Indeed, I, Hari, dwell within the heart of the devotee, which is truly divine.

The bodies of my devotees are divine, and their senses are likewise divine; their inner organ is divine, and their actions are always so. Abiding in the imperishable abode, I dwell somewhere upon the surface of the earth.
In some places here, I appear in the likeness of a devotee;
nevertheless, I am truly divine, as are you all who possess divine forms.
All the queens are divine, and the male and female devotees are divine.
I am the soul of all, the self, independent, the Lord of all powers, and the Sovereign.
I am higher than the highest, Hari, the Lord of Rādhā and Lakṣmī. I am the form of the cause of all, yet distinct within my own abode.
I myself have become this virtuous form, appearing here within the range of perception.
By my yoga, the cowherd women and the Hūṇas have attained divinity;
indeed, so too have all my external and internal faculties.
Having attained identity with Me, they see Me directly through that divine [vision].
(76) I am to be seen by one who is free from illusion, and never otherwise.
Out of compassion, I am personally accessible to the devotee, and indeed not to anyone else. (77)
All the principles of *māyā* attain divinity through contact with me;
indeed, the twenty-fifth principle, the individual soul (*jīvātman*), becomes liberated by uniting with me.
And I am the twenty-sixth, the Blessed Lord, who is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*).
I am under the control of my devotee, the cause of all incarnations.
I am free from the qualities of *māyā*, adorned with divine and auspicious attributes. Worshipped by the lords and others, I remain likewise among my devotees. (3.209.80)
Having worshipped and served me, and having realized me as the divine Nārāyaṇa,
my devotees go to the imperishable abode served by the divine attendants.
Women who have attained union with me likewise become possessed of divine forms.
Through union with me, the cows, the buffalo-cows, and the bulls attained divinity.
By my yoga, my daughters, as well as the sages and the virtuous,
and even the young cowherd boys, attained divinity equal to mine.
Furthermore, by my yoga, those beloved wives of Brahmā, as well as the trees and creepers, were transformed into divine beings equal to me;
let them therefore worship me constantly and let them offer water and milk.
Fruit, root, bulb, sweet food, and even leaves—let them perform worship at morning, at midday, and also in the evening. Day and night, in all their activities, let them remember me, Kṛṣṇa. (85–86)
May they constantly serve the virtuous with food and water,
and may they always worship and glorify me with great zeal.
At the end, I, the Lord of the Gopīs, shall grant them liberation in the imperishable realm.
"Furthermore, for those with desires, [I shall grant] skillful enjoyments of heaven that bring happiness.
Having spoken thus, and having given the great conch which always wards off faults,
he said, "The harmful ones shall depart far away," and then received worship.
O Lakṣmī, those Sāraṅga-Ḍhūṇakas vanished from the forest;
they became happy in the end and attained the imperishable abode.
Thus it is with those who dwell in the forest, or those who dwell in villages, or those with separate houses.
Whether they be poor men or women, those who worship me, Hari— I, the Lord,
being remembered alone, truly deliver them from distress. I grant them both worldly enjoyment and liberation, as well as a state of eternal bliss.

"By reading this, by hearing it, and even by remembering it, there shall be the destruction of the sins of sinners, as well as liberation and eternal protection. (92) Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of how Śrī Hari protected the Hūṇa devotee named Sāraṅga— who possessed cattle and wealth in the form of buffaloes— and granted him liberation after he had been attacked by a lion in the forest," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to another story of a devotee.
There was a Puṣkasa named Yajñarādha who lived in Virādhakheṭa.
In the region of Ānarta, on the shore of the Samudrakhaḍika,
there was a devotee where the arrival and departure of ships laden with goods occurred constantly; it was there that he performed the work of cleaning.
Appointed by the superintendent of the great ships and supported for his livelihood,
he constantly performs, together with his wife, the clearing away of rubbish from the ships and the riverbanks at various spots. (2–4)
Likewise, other ship captains, merchants, and laborers—even those who were compassionate—gave him the remnants of their food:
vegetables, leafy greens, and the like, as well as flatbread and milk. (5)

He also gives roasted grain, cooked food, clothing, and other such things. Thus, provided with this devotion as well as a fair wage, he—who is always skilled in his own work—indeed maintains himself constantly. (6–7)
Whatever is obtained there, one should first perform the supreme sprinkling with water;
then, having held a *tulasī* leaf and remembered me,
one should mentally offer it to me and then eat— thus one is protected, and not otherwise.
Every morning, at the foot of a *pippala* tree, he indeed worships Hari and me,
having remembered us with water, food, fruits, and leaves;
likewise at midday and in the evening, he eats only after remembering me.

At night, having gathered together and performed *kīrtana* while remembering Me, the devotee—whether a son, a daughter, or a wife—sleeps while rotating the rosary. For such a devotee, who constantly subsists on the remains of offerings (*vighasa*), [there is no fear]. (11)
Having given [food] to dogs, cows, crows, and those of the *puṣkasa* caste;
having given to ants, and having given in the air to the gods;
indeed, he who eats the remains (*vighasa*) after giving even to the fish—[he is a true eater of the remains].
Even that outcaste (puṣkasa) beholds Hari within all living beings;
he possesses the realization of the Self as Brahman in all things, and is thus a king among devotees and endowed with knowledge.
Indeed, the body of the outcaste is always a vessel for impurity.
Likewise, all bodies are in every respect merely vessels for impurity.
For if they are not pure in mind, they are equal to outcastes (puṣkasas). He whose mind is pure—for him, the state of being an outcaste dissolves. (15–16)
In the womb, the child is not pure, as it partakes of the impure channels;
likewise, birth itself is impure, and following birth, one remains possessed of impurity.
Thus, being eternally devoid of purity, one is perpetually impure and beset by defilement.
Possessed of mental impurity and defiled by passion, anger, and other such stains;
characterized by deceit for one's own sake and permeated by latent impressions (vāsanā), he is impure; though endowed with a body, he is full of pride, envy, and malice. (18–19)
Endowed with the notions of "I" and "mine," exhausted by negligence and delusion,
he is indeed impure, bound by his attachment to wife, children, and retinue; defiled by ignorance, passion, attachment, clinging, and other such stains.
Furthermore, this body— sustained by the sense of "I-am-ness" (asmitā) and the like, burdened with the sins of sensual indulgence,
and pursued by the great miseries of disease, affliction, old age, and death— is called a *puṣkasa*; I am the conscious self (*cidātman*), not a *puṣkasa*.
All bodies are indeed *puṣkasas*, but the Self is never a *puṣkasa*.
The Self is Brahman—stainless, peaceful, pure, devoted, and radiant;
through the majesty of the Supreme Lord, it possesses the realization of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
"I am always liberated and free from bondage; here, I partake in liberation.
O Lakṣmī, even a Puṣkasa knows his own nature thus at all times;
he always conducts himself like one who is liberated, being solely intent on meditation upon Me.

O Lakṣmī, tell me: for such a devotee who is fixed solely on the Blessed One and likewise fixed on the Supreme Self—possessing no self-interest and not even the slightest mental affliction—how could [the Lord] indeed not [grant his grace]? 26.
I provide protection, delight to the mind, and the fulfillment of desires.
O Lakṣmī, my devotees—whether they be living beings, gods, or even lords—are always equal to me;
all embodied souls here within this Māyā are indeed my own sons. (27–28)
The Brahmin, the king, the wretched person, the outcaste, the woman, the eunuch, the beast, the bird, the insect, the afflicted one, the tree, the creeper,
and even the grass— everything, down to the aquatic creature and the moth, is of the nature of my son.
But for those who worship me, being immersed in service— especially for them,
I am the father, the protector, the sustainer, the guardian, the leader to the supreme state; whereas for others, I am merely the witness and the bestower of the fruits of their own performed deeds.
Then, on one occasion, a thought even arose in the mind of Bhakta:
"How might Nārāyaṇa himself become directly visible to the eyes?
He then heard from the mouth of a virtuous man that Hari himself dwells within the virtuous.
Through service to a virtuous person, one comes to perceive the [divine] sphere.
Now, this Yajñarādha indeed seeks such service; wherever a holy man is heard of, he goes to that very place. (33–34)
Having heard [of him] in Camatkārapura, he went to the bank of the Sādhu river under the pretext of visiting a sacred site; there,
with true devotion, he bathed in the river and beheld the ascetic Sādhu at the holy ford of Nāganātha.
He saw the great seer, a sage who had reached the further shore of the three states, divine, established in Brahman, beloved of Hari;
known by the name Brahmāyana, peaceful, renounced, and absorbed in meditation upon Brahman while seated in dhyāna. (36–37)
Having gone before him, he prostrated himself like a staff;
for one *ghaṭikā* he stood motionless in front, with palms joined in reverence.
At the end of that *ghaṭikā*, the best of sages emerged from his meditation.
He saw before him his devotee Puṣkasa, the Yajñarādha.
Yajñarādha stood there having prostrated himself with palms joined in reverence. Having been addressed by the saintly one, "May it be well with you," and having been seated, he was instructed.
With great devotion, he sat down before the virtuous one;
he inquired for the sake of increasing his virtues, for the sake of attaining the company of the good,
and indeed for the sake of directly obtaining the Supreme Lord through the means of spiritual practice.
Having heard this, the sage Brahmāyana, who possessed knowledge of both the self and the supreme self, rejoiced.
Remembering me, Nārāyaṇa, he spoke and instructed him:
"Listen, O devotee, to the virtues of the virtuous—those qualities which people here indeed adopt."
These virtuous ones indeed become oceans of excellence;
the wicked, however, seize upon the faults of the good.
Through constant association with the virtuous, future excellences surely arise.

In the constant grasping of the virtues of the good and in the recognition of their greatness, one's own beautiful, auspicious, and perfected qualities—which bestow the state of accomplishment—thrive. One should never grasp at the bodily defects of the good, which arise only occasionally. (45–46)
Those who perceive faults indeed become faulty themselves, even if they possess virtues;
through great sin, their virtues perish from the root in no time at all.
Therefore, one should always accept the good qualities of the virtuous, but never their faults.
By grasping even a small, base quality, great ruin may occur. (48) Through association with the virtuous alone, millions of virtues increase;
likewise, the Bhāgavata dharmas flourish through association with the good. (49)
By serving the virtuous who are single-mindedly devoted, one attains divinity.
Through affection, the company of the virtuous arises for embodied beings in this world.
The holy ones are the givers of liberation and the destroyers of all sins.
Realizing that "the virtuous grant what is desired," one who always behaves like a servant before the virtuous shall attain association with the virtuous;
all absolute dharmas flourish through the company of the virtuous. (51–52)
Dispassion arises, as does the knowledge of both the self and the Supreme Self.
Thereafter, devotion to Hari occurs, accompanied by the knowledge of His majesty.
Furthermore, one's refuge becomes firm, and all activities are performed for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
For the devotee, the activities of both the external and internal organs indeed become permeated by the Blessed One;
thus the door to liberation is opened wide.
This becomes the most excellent bestower of the divine abode, granting progress upon the Great Path.

Attachment to the wealth of women and the like is a great bondage for the embodied soul, difficult to cast off; yet, when directed toward the virtuous, it likewise grants liberation to the embodied soul.
One should always cultivate affection for the virtuous, even more so than for wife and children.
For those who are attached to the virtuous with affection, eternal liberation occurs.
(57) Both woman and man should cultivate great faith in the service of the virtuous;
service performed with one's whole being certainly delivers even the most deceitful person. (58)
Service performed with total self-surrender makes a person successful;
when the saints are pleased, they indeed bestow the imperishable abode and divine nature.
Auspicious place and time should be resorted to, and likewise, auspicious company should be sought.

Auspicious rites should always be performed, and the most excellent auspicious mantra should be maintained. Meditation on Hari should be practiced constantly, and the virtuous should always be held in one's heart.
The initiation of a devotee (bhāgavatī dīkṣā) should be received, and refuge in Hari should be sought at all times.
For one who conducts oneself in this manner, Nārāyaṇa will indeed become manifest.
Through association with improper places and the like, the intellect becomes ruined and fallen;
through association with proper places and the like, the intellect becomes excellent and pure.
Through the conjunction of powerful merit, a person obtains a good country and other such blessings.
For him, association with the virtuous arises, and from that, divinity is born.
One whose intellect is stainless does not find fault with countries and the like. (63–64)
For whomsoever these [signs] occur here, one should consider that great evil committed in the past has arrived, by which he is impelled toward sin; or else,
it must be that he has committed an offense against the great and virtuous ones.
As a result of that, indeed, a sinful intellect was born which bestows transgression.
To destroy that, one should perform service with a sincere disposition;
furthermore, through service to Hari, one shall attain the favor of the virtuous.
Now, he who is wicked indeed commits treachery;
out of a state of atheism, he utters only base speech:
"What could possibly come of associating with the virtuous here on this earth? (68)
"For there are rogues who pose as virtuous; let them not have association with us.
Thus indeed do the wicked speak; they must always be avoided from afar.
Therefore, one should cultivate the company of the good, for the company of the good is indeed medicine. (3.210.70)
One must certainly not associate with the wicked; association with the wicked is supreme poison.
A person in distress resorts to Śrīnātha solely for the sake of destroying that distress.
One who seeks wealth does so for the attainment of wealth, while one who seeks sovereignty does indeed become [his devotee] for the sake of sovereignty.
Even one who is devoted to the self worships Hari constantly for the sake of liberation.
But the man of knowledge, being devoted to the Lord, serves the Supreme Ishvara.
One who offers himself to the Lord and is devoted to Him becomes dear to Hari. (72–73)
For one who is devoted to Hari on this earth, there shall be direct realization;
he will possess complete knowledge of Hari’s majesty in every way.
His love for Hari persists constantly and in manifold ways at all times.
Indeed, all his latent impressions (vāsanās), whether dark or otherwise, are destroyed.
By serving those who are single-mindedly devoted, all latent impressions are indeed destroyed;
therefore, having become a man of knowledge, one should practice the company of the virtuous.
One should always, through the company of the virtuous, gain knowledge of Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord of the syllables, together with his majesty;
and one's pride must always be uprooted by the assembly of the virtuous.
The divine qualities never flourish in one who is proud.

A proud person does not perform service for the virtuous, even when it is at the lowest level; he does not stand with palms joined before the virtuous, nor does he praise them with his speech. (78–79)
One should not bow before men even while living like a pauper;
pride is a great defect, for the pillar of pride is the cause of destruction. For those possessed by pride, devotion, knowledge, dispassion, and the like never increase.
But for the devotee whose pride has dissolved and whose great virtues increase, Nārāyaṇa himself dwells directly within his heart;
this occurs through constant service and attendance upon the virtuous and upon Hari. (8.1–8.2)
The pride of one who is rich in intense dispassion indeed dissolves quickly;
through devotion to the contemplation of Brahman as the Self, Hari is pleased with him. To him whose mind is pleased, the form of Hari appears truly gracious.
His form is sweet within the heart and is indeed seen externally as well.
Free from pride, he is considered the best among the kings of devotees and is empowered by the Lord.
Abandoning all pride, he worships Śrī Hari, firmly established in the Brahman that is his own self.
O Blessed One, for one whose steadfastness in the Self and steadfastness in the Lord have indeed reached maturity,
every illusory affliction dissolves right here and now.
This occurs even by merely hearing the sacred narratives and likewise through the service of the virtuous.

Through devotion to Nārāyaṇa and likewise through the worship of Hari, they attain the state of a Siddha, as well as omniscience and lordship. Such is the power of one’s own chosen deity, according to its specific nature. (87–88)
For him, such a great, divine, and supreme happiness arises;
illusory suffering is utterly destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
Those who possess a love for Lord Mādhava equal to that of the women of Vraja [attain this].
For them, nothing remains to be done except for the observance of the boundary [of conduct] toward the virtuous.
(3.210.90) Through service to the righteous, there arises firm conviction in the majesty of Kṛṣṇa;
and the perfection of their spiritual practice will swiftly become firmly established on all sides. (91)
He who exists in the supreme imperishable abode, in the realm of Goloka,
in Vaikuṇṭha, in Śrīpura, and in the unmanifest, immortal realm—
he is the Lord of Brahmā, Hari, the Lord of Rādhā, and the Lord of Kamalā.
He is the Lord of Lalitā, the Lord of Ramā, the Sovereign Lord of Śrī;
he alone is the Inner Controller, the Beloved, and the Blessed Lord himself.
He is perceived within through devotion in meditative absorption, and from without through service. 93–94.
Hari Nārāyaṇa, assuming a human form, indeed meets with even ordinary people;
among men, he becomes equal to them.
By his splendor, the imperishable Brahman and millions of liberated lords [are surpassed].
The sun, the moon, and other luminous bodies shine because He alone is that [source of light].
Indeed, when He has assumed a human form, He is perceived by means of a lamp;
in the radiance of the sun and moon, He becomes visible to human beings.
Even at the end of the body, by the remembrance of whose name a great sinner quickly becomes pure and free from sin, he is fit for the path of liberation;
he alone becomes accessible through the devotion of a sincere devotee.
Worship that Supreme Soul, the Lord of Śrī, Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa.
Recite the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," and likewise meditate upon Bāla-Kṛṣṇa within your heart. (3.210.10)
"Drink the water which is always pleasing to the sight; eat what is offered.
Remember the Lord who is the beloved husband of Brahmā; you shall attain liberation.
Having been addressed thus by that lotus-born one, the source of Brahmā, the Puṣkasa—
Having obtained this knowledge and worshipped it, he then went to his own home. He worships, meditates upon, and serves [it] according to the prescribed method;
he indeed performs service to the virtuous, and he beholds and remembers the Lord.
Once, however, near a *pippala* tree, Yajñarādhā beheld a virtuous man, rich in beauty, auspicious, and equal to Brahmā himself.
Seeing him suddenly, she prostrated like a staff and offered him a welcome and other courtesies.
And the virtuous man, feeling affection for him, also inquired after his welfare.
The devotee said: "I am well, especially because of the gain of your presence, O virtuous one. Give me your command, so that I may serve you along with my family."
The saintly one said, "Indeed, I must depart from this place for the holy site of Aśvapaṭṭasara, where Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa resides.
Please come along with me as my traveling companion. (107)
"So be it," the Puṣkasa agreed, and he departed together with his entire family and his young children. Just then,
a divine celestial chariot quickly arrived from the sky.
O Lakṣmī, moved by compassion, I myself became the giver of liberation to him.
Having made those attendants divine and placing them in celestial chariots,
I caused them to cast off their material bodies and led them to my own imperishable abode.
"Those devotees of mine, possessing divine forms, have attained your eternal state.
Thus did he bring about their welfare through the assembly of the virtuous;
all living beings who worship me become like that.
"From reading this, from hearing it, from remembering it, and even from causing others to hear it, there shall surely arise enjoyment, liberation, divine progress, and prosperity.

(11.3) Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Liberation through Devotion to Śrī Hari and Other Matters," in the section on the Dvāpara Age within the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*, concerning the meeting of the Puṣkasa named Yajñarādhana with the holy sage Brahmāyana and his family, and their subsequent attainment of liberation. (210)
