Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of a Caṇḍāla as well;
it concerns one who lived at Rāyaṇāgra, known by the name Kapikṣaya.
Indeed, there was a Cāṇḍāla named Kapikṣaya who lived with his family near Mount Raivata in Rāyaṇā; he was highly virtuous.
At first, due to the defect of his birth, he became a violent man while wandering in the forest.

Having killed the red forest-dwelling monkeys, he would devour them. (3) Consequently, having been informed by the inhabitants of another forest that he was a "monkey-destroyer," he became famous in the forest by the very name Vānaramāra ("Monkey-Killer"). (4)
Then once, seeing a great circle of monkeys situated in a grove of trees in the forest, he took up an arrow to slay them.
Before the arrow was even released, the best of monkeys—
A divine voice spoke to him: "Listen, O best of outcastes!
Having heard this, act as you desire for the sake of your journey; understand my words.
Formerly, you were a twice-born man who consorted with low-caste women and was devoted to courtesans."
There lived a brahmin named Prājñeśvara, a resident of Śṛṅkhalāgrāma, who was devoted to righteous deeds and other such duties; for even the people there were non-violent,
and by virtue of his association with them and his providing them with food, they too came to dwell in that state.
For through association with generosity and honor, your mind indeed became cruel;
and due to the absence of proper place, time, action, speech, and companions, your heart gradually became devoid of virtue and fond of sin. (3.211.9–10)
The auspicious body of this brāhmaṇa has been rendered unrighteous by you through union with a prostitute, as well as by his indulgence in forbidden foods and drinks;
thus he has become intent on petty deeds and devoted to liquor and meat. (11)

Then, in the course of time, death occurred for you; thereupon you went to the city of Yama, where you experienced the tortures of Yama. Due to the remainder of your sin, you now exist here as a Cāṇḍāla.
That prostitute, that low-caste woman, was indeed your wife here who accompanied you;
your sinful friends, sons, and kinsmen are also present here in this Cāṇḍāla womb, sinful beings bound by their own wickedness. (14)
Having committed sins in the past, you attained the state of a *caṇḍāla*.
Previously, your status as a Brahmin was defiled by you like a stain;
thus, your great merit, as well as heaven and liberation, were destroyed.
And now, moreover, you indeed subsist on the flesh of monkeys;
since you are a slayer of monkeys, you will certainly become a slayer of men. Monkeys are human beings; therefore, that sin born from the killing of men [will be yours].

O Cāṇḍāla, the very fact that you have killed a child and the certain fact that you have killed a woman will surely result in your birth again among humans, who are so difficult to attain. For you have performed acts of violence for the sake of your belly and for the sake of your family. (18–19)
Furthermore, those torments of Yama and the downward path await you again;
for the sake of those by whom you were previously cast down, you now strive once more.
What kind of preeminent fool are you? What gain do you have from these falls?
Behold, O fool, the meaningfulness of a human being’s righteous deeds!
Likewise, behold your own liberation, the happiness that destroys all sins—the sacred ford on the river Svarṇāvatī where Dāmodara-Nārāyaṇa resides. || 21-22 ||
Behold! Perform meritorious deeds and quickly abandon violence; be happy.
Become a holy devotee in this world and worship Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having bathed in the Nārāyaṇa lake, perform that which destroys all sins.
Having bathed in the Revatī-kuṇḍa as well as in the Vāmana-kuṇḍa,
in the field of Kuṅkumavāpikā and in the Aśvapaṭṭa-sarovara,
and having bathed at the holy Somatīrtha and in the Sarasvatī, may you be happy.
Bathe in the city of Mūladvāravatī and go from there to heaven;
having established an auspicious sacred site for the sake of concealment, go to Gavāyana.
O fool, worship Govinda, the Lord of Śrī, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa!
Having shown compassion, having supported the bull, and likewise having offered devotion to Hari,
go to the supreme, eternal, and everlasting world of Brahmā.
The Supreme Lord resides at the holy ford of Kuṅkumavāpikā.
He indeed possesses both divine and human bodies; he is the creator, the beloved of Brahmā, and the Lord.
He alone is the Blessed One, the creator and protector of the world, abiding within it.
He is the husband of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, the glorious Bālakṛṣṇa, the Supreme Lord.
Just as a man who is served by men and women remains [in that state],
even at the end of the body, a great sinner— merely by the remembrance of Him—
is liberated from all sins and goes to the supreme, imperishable abode. (3.211.30–31)
Go to him and worship that cowherd boy, the son of Kambharā;
take refuge in that self-possessed Supreme Lord who dwells within the heart.
[2] May there quickly arise in you knowledge of the majesty of that Lord of Rādhā and Ramā.
Therefore, liberation must indeed be directly realized; thus eternal liberation comes to pass.
Through intense affection for the Blessed One, clarity of mind arises;
by that means, liberation—which bestows the abode of the Blessed One—comes into one's grasp.
"O Cāṇḍāla, listen; I shall tell you how affection must indeed be cultivated in every way:
as one feels for a newly wedded wife toward her husband, as one feels for one's first-born son, as a child feels for its mother, and as a greedy man feels for his wealth. (35)
Just as one who is hungry has [affection] for food, and one terrified by fear for a protector;
just as aquatic creatures have [affection] for water, and a moth for fire—so too should affection always be directed toward the Supreme Lord, the bestower of happiness. (36–37)
The Lord of lords is to be touched with the skin, contemplated with the eyes,
heard with the two ears, tasted through kissing and other such acts,
and His very fragrance is to be taken in; O Hari, His form is always to be grasped.
The Blessed One should be embraced and Mādhava should be glorified;

Śrī Kṛṣṇa should be made the source of joy, and likewise, the offering of everything to Hari must be performed. Furthermore, the daily practice of recollecting the qualities of Hari should be carried out.
Affection for Kṛṣṇa arises through the knowledge of His majesty, qualities, and so forth; or rather, an innate affection arises specifically in the devotee,
just as it does toward one's wife, children, and wealth, so too toward Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Having attained natural affection, one is fit for becoming Brahman.
Those of divine intellect possess innate affection;
their divine actions are for the sake of Hari, and their affection flourishes.
If pride stands as an obstacle to the nourishment of affection,
it must be eliminated by all means, for it creates hindrances on the path to spiritual welfare.
Indeed, all evil dispositions must be destroyed with diligent effort.
Those who dwell within the body should indeed be destroyed by one seeking liberation with the mindset of an enemy;
however, if those of evil nature behave like friends, they should be eliminated through association with the virtuous when they become obstacles to liberation. (45–46)
One should always cultivate the company of the virtuous; the company of the virtuous is a great medicine.
I am the self, powerful, having Kṛṣṇa as my helper, and possessing excellent dharma. Whatever one desires, one is indeed capable of accomplishing, even liberation itself.
One who has taken refuge in Hari should uproot the impulses of passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas).
The superimposition of the self upon the body, harmful association, and the accumulation of past karma—
all of which cause delusion through Māyā— must be destroyed by the company of the virtuous.
Through discernment, the superimposition of the self upon the body must be abandoned by means of the words of the virtuous;
and through association with the virtuous, evil company must be destroyed by meeting with the good.
All the latent impressions (saṃskāras) formed in previous births that lead to sinful action [must likewise be overcome].
In this world, those [enemies] must always be slain by the great through their constant devotion.
For a man of extreme wickedness, the fruit of his sin is torment;
then, calamities arrive for the sake of his destruction.
Though you, O Giver of Wealth, run swiftly here and there in every direction,
nevertheless calamities increase and do not depart to a distance.
Then, becoming dejected in mind, one encounters people in even greater misery.
Having heard [the truth], he informs a virtuous elder of his misfortunes.
Having received the words of the virtuous one, he performs vows and worship,
as well as seeking the company of the good, devotion, service, and the remembrance of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Thus, by the power of the seed, his impurities indeed dissolve;
thereafter, his heart becomes stainless and pure.
There, Kṛṣṇa shines forth through the speech of the virtuous, becoming worthy of their devotion.
It shines forth gradually, and virtuous people are born.
In this way, even impure mental formations (saṃskāras) attain purity;
likewise, an outcaste attains the status of a Brahmin, and a wicked person becomes a good man.
Through the favor of the virtuous, even a pauper quickly attains the status of a king;
likewise, through the favor of the virtuous, a fool attains scholarship.
Through the favor of the virtuous, even a sinner finds merit and heaven.
Through the grace of the virtuous, even a wicked person becomes a purifier of the assembly.
To attain a state of extreme favor, one must always behave without guile before the holy ones,
following their conduct accordingly.
In whatever they find delight, that should be accomplished without hesitation; in whatever they find no delight, that should always be abandoned immediately.
Indeed, one should cast aside pride, worldly shame, and arrogance regarding one's virtues.
One should perform service for the virtuous, and the words of the virtuous should be held within the heart.
Whatever obstacles arise during the propitiation of the virtuous, all those negative qualities must be abandoned; only that which bestows clarity and favor should be accepted.
Those by which virtues indeed become serene are considered true virtues;
that alone is called righteousness by which serenity arises.
That which is a cause for the displeasure of the virtuous is indeed a base quality.
That very person is to be shunned by the devotee; instead, one should cultivate goodwill toward the virtuous.
For the holy ones are indeed pleased with a devoted servant who acts in accordance with their will.
By embracing the virtues of the virtuous, the faults residing within the heart are destroyed.
The virtuous and great ones should be served, for they bestow divine nature;
devotion toward the Supreme Self increases through the grasping of their qualities.
By grasping the quality of selflessness in the virtuous, one attains selflessness.
By grasping at the quality of freedom from anger in the virtuous, one shall attain freedom from anger;
by grasping at the quality of freedom from greed in the virtuous, one shall attain freedom from greed;
by grasping at the quality of freedom from delusion in the virtuous, one shall attain freedom from delusion. (3.211.69–70)
By grasping the qualities of the divine form of the virtuous, one becomes possessed of a divine and beautiful form;
likewise, by grasping the quality of the Blessed State (bhagavattva) of the virtuous, one becomes so.
Indeed, through such devotion, one becomes supreme, endowed with great sovereignty and other such attributes.
Elsewhere there is no liking for him; his interest is always in Kṛṣṇa and in saintly persons.
His affection is fixed on Kṛṣṇa and the virtuous, while a lack of attachment exists toward others. For one such as this, service to Hari and to the saintly increases.
Supreme servitude, which is ever-increasing, stainless, and rooted in love,
sometimes indeed transforms into lordship through the grace of the Lord—
just as lordship may arise through grace toward a disciple or a servant.
Likewise, the status of a servant in a slave may attain the state of being a master.
There is no partiality before Hari or before the virtuous. Even a woman, a Śūdra, or even a Caṇḍāla attains the supreme goal through devotion.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, even by that monkey, the forest-dweller Kapikṣaya was awakened; he then attained a wondrous realization and gained true understanding.
He indeed considered himself to have accomplished his purpose and to be a partaker of merit.
By whom indeed was this auspicious knowledge, which bestows liberation, obtained from the monkey?
Then he questioned the monkey: "Who are you here, who are the giver of knowledge, the giver of liberation, and the destroyer of faults such as violence? (78–79)
"You remove the defect of illusion and destroy all ignorance;
tell me truly, who are you that wanders here in the forest?
By your words, I have become blessed and fulfilled."
"Having recognized you, I shall especially become your purifier.
Having heard this, the monkey said: "We, these forest-dwellers, and those monkeys of red hue—all of us are deities from heaven."
We all become possessed of divine bodies and dwellers in heaven;
we enjoy the merit of heaven until that merit reaches exhaustion.
No new [merit] is earned there, since heaven is merely a land of enjoyment.
On this earth, which is the land of action, merit performed here shall meet [its fruition].
On Mount Raivata, in the form of monkeys, for the sake of merit, they gathered fruits, leaves, and so forth, and performed worship by offering them to the deity. 84–85.
Having partaken of this auspicious, purifying, and liberating grace,
we drink the water from the Svarṇarekhā, as well as from the Nārāyaṇahrada and the Dāmodarahrada, thereby increasing our great merit.
"Having bathed at this sacred ford, we who desire liberation seek future emancipation.
We are not monkeys, but gods in monkey form, so that after our stay in heaven, we may never again take birth in the world of mortals. (87–88)
"Let us establish a sacred ford here so that liberation may be attained by us;
you too, O consumer of fruits, should likewise establish a ford.
Together with your family, you shall attain the supreme goal."
"Go to the Aśvapaṭṭa lake and approach the yogi Lomaśa;
there, receive a mantra from Hari, and you shall become pure.
Having been addressed thus, that outcaste prostrated himself before the host of deities.
Having quickly drunk the water of the Nārāyaṇakuṇḍa, which was as clear as the sky, he went to the abode of Lomaśa; there he bowed down and spoke.
Afterwards, at the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake, he related the entire account.
Having bathed, he compassionately received the mantra from Lomaśa:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Together with his family, this devotee became mine, a devotee of Hari.
He undertook a pilgrimage to the Aśvapaṭṭasara lake and became purified;
by his devotion to me and through the shelter of Lomaśa, his sin was destroyed.
Then, when the end of his time had arrived, he cast off his body.
Then all their wives and children abandoned their bodies. Uttering "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Lakṣmīkānta, Ramāpati," they became yogis liberated while still alive, endowed with divine forms.
A celestial chariot, attended by my attendants, arrived there;
having ascended it, they all went to my beloved, imperishable abode.
Thus was the welfare of the devotee accomplished through the association with the monkey.
O Lakṣmī, it was indeed by my grace that this eternal [state] was attained by the Cāṇḍāla.
In the same way, others too, through devotion to me and through devotion to the virtuous, purify themselves; they serve both me and the virtuous, and they too attain the supreme goal. (3.211.100)

Through reading, hearing, or remembering this, those with desires attain prosperity, while those free from desire attain my supreme state. (101) Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of the Cāṇḍāla Kapikṣaya along with his Family through Devotion to Hari by Means of Instruction from a Monkey-Formed Deity," in the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā. (211)
← Chapter 211 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā/Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 212 [[Author: Chapter 213 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the iron-smith named Nālīka, my purifying devotee. 1.
My devotee Nālīkara lived in the city named Vakranadā;
he was indeed an iron-smith residing there together with his family.
[He made] long chains of clods of earth, as well as small pegs and the like.
He also makes silk cloths, earrings, ribbons, and leaf-shaped clay ornaments;
many clay vessels and even iron implements; as well as carts and the ritual requisites for the planets. (3–4)
While moving the bellows, during inhalation and exhalation, one should remember Śrī Narāyaṇa; while raising the iron-beater,
lowering it, and pressing the iron,
as well as during the work of joining iron and so forth, one remembers me, Narāyaṇa.
Regarding Ramādevī as a bellows, Narāyaṇa as the fire,
and the moving staff as a rosary, he always worships me, Hari.
And having contemplated Māyā as a forge for iron— that is, a forge for the mass of one's sins— he [worships me].
Perceiving clods of earth as mere illusions, he strikes them for the sake of liberation;
and he regards the sounds arising from the striking of iron as the sacred syllable *praṇava*.
Thus, the devotee Nālīkara, possessing self-knowledge through the vision of Brahman, [attains his goal].
He conducts himself with devotion and also worships my image.
Having bathed in the morning, he bows to the image at home and offers incense;
having lit a lamp, he also presents me with a garland of flowers and sandalwood paste. (3.212.10)
Having offered me the essence of fragrance, the food offering of milk and sugar,
and having presented cakes, as well as water and betel-leaf;
and having offered [these] to me and requested forgiveness, he then eats and drinks.
In the very same way, having gone from there to the iron foundry, he remembered Mādhava, paid homage, offered incense and a lamp,
as well as a garland of flowers, sugar, and other excellent fruits. (12–13)
Having delivered [the materials] at the proper time, he then performs his work;
with a pure mind and devotion, he carries out my iron-work.
Once, such a devotee had this reflection:
At night, one should always perform worship together with many people.
Worship performed by a community is the means for the liberation of many.
Thus, with a virtuous mind, [one should include] the people of one's own village and kinsmen.
He spoke in order to establish a circle of devotion, and even then they, with great joy, formed an excellent circle of devotees.
Men and women, having gathered at the onset of night for two ghaṭikās, [performed the rite].
They constantly began the auspicious chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s names.
(18) All the people living in the city, having heard of and seen this virtuous deed, offered their assistance there and joined the circle of devotees. (19)
Thousands of people, filled with enthusiasm, perform devotion through all the festivals of Śrī Hari with instrumental music, dance, and the like; likewise,
they are eager with adornments, worship, and vigils.

And they perform [these rites] at the proper time, O Lakṣmī, being intent upon their own spiritual welfare. Beholding their devotion, I then became pleased with that devoted blacksmith, who was a promoter of devotion unto me.
Once, for the sake of increasing their devotion, I manifested an exceedingly brilliant and radiant splendor from the forehead of my own image; it was shown to them in its dazzling glory,
and I quickly quelled it with that [splendor], whereby they became filled with the weight of devotion.
Especially manifesting devotion toward me with deep inner feeling,
they became knowers of me as I abide in my form bearing the Śārṅga bow;
indeed, they constructed a temple for Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
There they performed a continuous stream of worship and other rites according to their means.
"O Daughter of the Ocean, I dwell within this image together with you;
I remove the sorrows and calamities of all beings day by day. (26)
They perform these meditations which destroy the suffering of disease;
they destroy all afflictions— those arising from the self, from divine agencies, and from other beings— and they indeed become established in well-being.
They worshiped me with intense devotion, praising my wondrous deeds and other such virtues.
Then one day, she became a female ascetic wearing the garb of a *tāpasī*,
and I, having become a yogi ascetic, arrived at the onset of night.
Observing the circle of devotees in the area near the temple,
you appeared like some wretched, destitute beggar who has emerged; likewise, you were one of humble mind, a female mendicant devoid of vows.
Just as a common woman, though unworthy of bathing in the Dharma and devoid of its purification,
remains soiled, even so am I defiled, yet captivating to the minds of those who behold me. Indeed, [I am like] a single small child covered with a little filth, urine, and the like.
Having assumed the form of a young Garuḍa, I stood before them in their belly.
Seeing this triad thus, and seeing me arrived at the front of the temple begging like one in distress, they then became filled with compassion.
Having summoned them, they seated them comfortably upon the altar and offered them food produced from the grace of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
filled with devotion, they also gave milk for their offspring.
Having partaken of food and drink, O Lakṣmī, we remained at ease;
we sat upon the raised platform and performed the chanting of the Lord’s names.
Then, in the courtyard, they began the Rāsa dance with rhythmic clapping and beautiful dancing.
Indeed, countless men and women, full of devotion, offered their worship;
and while they were performing *kīrtana* and taking a moment’s rest,
I rose up there in that courtyard along with you.
Accompanied by cymbals and anklets, I performed kīrtana with dance.
Then, seeing both you and me, they were filled with supreme wonder;
being pleased, they repeatedly questioned the peaceful me for the sake of their welfare.
"O holy one, please show us compassion and tell us something that bestows auspiciousness here.
O Lakṣmī, having heard this, I then imparted knowledge to them;
indeed, I explained the cause of love for the Blessed One and His own majesty.
Furthermore, trust in love that is accompanied by knowledge of His majesty is also a cause [of liberation].
One should take refuge in Hari, the controller of Māyā, Puruṣa, and Kāla, as well as of the insentient and sentient principles—the modes of nature and their functions. (42–43)
One should take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the independent creator of all, the cause of all incarnations, and the bestower of all powers;
a person who possesses knowledge of His majesty should take refuge in the Supreme Self with love.
Having served that Lord with devotion, one should acquire the supreme abode.
Indeed, being possessed of discernment, one should effect the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) in every way.
Whatever taste or desire I have for worldly objects— || 45–46 ||
Having analyzed how much [of it] there is, that [impurity] must indeed be removed from there.
Or rather, how much pure desire or will exists toward Hari?
Whether it be equal to, less than, or even greater than that which exists toward Māyā.
Having discerned [the truth], one should always strive diligently to increase [virtues] in Hari;
and one should laugh at Māyā until it is completely uprooted. For that which pertains to Māyā possesses perishability, the quality of bestowing suffering, and the power of bondage. 48–49.
Having understood that [attachment] arises toward the multitude of objects, one should abandon it;
one should renounce attachment to illusory things, which binds even those who are liberated. Indeed, from this lack of relish, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) occurs very swiftly.
Through association with the virtuous, through connection with Kṛṣṇa, and through chanting the praises of Kṛṣṇa,
a taste for Kṛṣṇa certainly arises— especially through direct yoga. In this way, by means of the yoga of practice, love for Kṛṣṇa increases.
For one who has tasted the nectar of the Lord, there is a swift destruction of attachment toward worldly enjoyments— whether they be pleasant or otherwise, whether illusory or like impurities.
To him, the divine world consisting of Brahman shines as being of the very nature of Nārāyaṇa.
For one whose devotion is fixed on the Blessed One, the supreme dharma is the state of Brahman.
That is the ultimate abiding of the great Bhāgavata, which brings joy;
it is free from the conceit of *māyā* and is adorned by the state of being the Blessed One. (54–55)
For the sake of destroying latent impressions (vāsanā), for the sake of love for Hari,
and likewise for the sake of attaining self-abidance (ātmaniṣṭhā) and supreme detachment (vairāgya),
one should cultivate the knowledge of the excellence of Kṛṣṇa’s majesty and the complete surrender of oneself.
One should accomplish the goal established by the Blessed One and associate with the virtuous.
(57) One should diligently perform service to the virtuous who are established in the self free from latent desires;
having attained the grace of the virtuous, one shall conquer māyā and go to the Supreme. (58)
Through knowledge, one attains supreme steadfastness by taking refuge in the Supreme Self;
through the assistance of the company of the virtuous, the steadfastness of the good becomes firm in Hari.
Likewise, through devotion united with self-abidance, there arises stability in steadfastness.

For the steadfast one who has attained the state of liberation, obstacles do not arise at all. Even supernatural powers (*siddhis*), which take the form of hindrances to devotion, do not approach him;
for such powers come only to test the ripeness of one's devotion.
By the command of Śrī Hari, they repeatedly attempt to entice him who has taken refuge [in Him];
nevertheless, he does not look upon them, and having conquered them, he goes to the supreme abode.
For such a devotee, Kṛṣṇa himself becomes submissive.
Hari is always pleased with one who is devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of *māyā* and has dedicated everything to Kṛṣṇa;
indeed, Śrī Hari sometimes [manifests] from the heart of a devotee who possesses supreme love for Kṛṣṇa. (63–64)
One whose armor is bound by the cord of love becomes unable to go [into the world].
For him alone the Blessed One is the protector, the master, the beloved, and the bestower of liberation;
He dwells entirely within his heart, removing the suffering of illusion.
Indeed, such a devotee possesses divine qualities. All virtues, such as truthfulness and purity, arise from taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa;
they are born even in one who possesses devotion through Kṛṣṇa’s divine wisdom.
Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa Mādhava is the controller of time, karma, inherent nature, illusion, the individual soul, and even the lords. He is the Lord,
the Consort of Śrī, the creator, the nourisher, and the destroyer of all creations.
There is that cowherd boy; he dwells in the hearts of all.
That Lord, the sovereign of Rādhā, Ramā, and Pradhā, remains untainted.
Having realized this, he established a firm connection with Hari Kṛṣṇa. (3.212.70)
Even the divine qualities belonging to that Śrī Hari manifest in every way as all forms of sovereignty for the devotee;
just as the eye, by association with a lamp, acquires the quality of light.
In whatever way, through union with Hari, virtues enter the devotee. By the grace of Kṛṣṇa, he becomes independent and equal to Kṛṣṇa;
endowed with perfection, he becomes capable of doing everything and is born eternally perfected.
Just as Indra, driven away by the host of Apsarases— specifically by the presence of Urvaśī— came to Narāyaṇa-Nara to cause an interruption of his asceticism,
so too are those possessed of supernatural powers (siddhimantaḥ) cast out by one who has attained supreme perfection (susiddhinā).
Even primordial illusion (mūlamāyā) is cast aside by the power of Hari through devotion.
The gods indeed become devotees endowed with the qualities of the Blessed One;
the asuras are never born possessing the qualities of the Blessed One.
But when sinners enter the vast ocean of compassion of the great saints, their virtues indeed manifest at some point through devotion to the Lord.
For the saints, being pleased by service, destroy all evil qualities.
They destroy the state of being an asura and bring about a divine nature.
But he who, out of pride, disregards poor people who are his devotees—
he too, by the mass of that sin, though formerly divine, shall fall into the state of an asura.
One who is cursed becomes as if consumed by a Brahmin’s wrath; virtues do not enter him.
Therefore, one must never at any time show contempt for the wretched. One should stand before the wretched as if one were wretched oneself; by that, Kṛṣṇa is well-pleased.
The Blessed One never shows compassion toward those who are arrogant.
Auspicious qualities never arise in those who are hostile.
By being hostile toward a humble, devoted, and wretched person, one’s merit is destroyed.
There is no doubt that this occurs; for the weak are not to be despised.
Though they may appear filthy on the outside, their hearts possess pure intentions.
Devoted to the Lord, those holy ones (sādhus) are indeed worthy of honor and bestowers of liberation.
In their hearts the Blessed Lord, the Antaryāmin, shines resplendent (84). The Protector of the wretched, the Guardian of the helpless, dwells there together with them;
for Mādhava becomes enraged by the insult of his devotees (85).
One who treats [the devotee] with contempt quickly brings about his own destruction;
yet, being subservient to the devotion of the wretched, he swiftly causes [destruction] to be wrought by another.
O you who act like a reed! We are miserable, soiled, and swarmed by flies.
"Those who came here for the sake of food were filled with fear and dejected in mind;
yet you did not treat them with contempt, but instead showed them honor. Therefore, we are now pleased in heart and endowed with happiness. (87–88)
"You are devotees of the Lord, truthful and servants free from pride;
therefore, if it pleases your minds, ask for a boon.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, when I had bowed to my own form, I said:
And as he desired to go far away, the boy produced excrement;
Nālīkara carried the water and gave it to his wife.
That woman, named Kundaṇikā, received the offering from his hand.
With deep devotion, he washed away the impurities of that child;
indeed, my own joy became especially great.
He then granted his own divine and wonderful vision to his devotees.
O Lakṣmī, I likewise showed you my beautiful form as the glorious Śyāmasundara, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
and I also displayed my true nature as a child and in the form of Garuḍa. 93–94.
Then the devotees, having fulfilled their purpose, were born within their hearts;
having beheld [the Lord], they danced and, full of longing, worshipped him. At that time, they requested a boon for the sake of liberation, and nothing else.
Having granted the boon, saying "So be it," I vanished in an instant and entered the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa along with you; and at that very moment,
Garuḍa suddenly entered the form of the bird.
Having thus given them my own vision, I bestowed upon them supreme happiness.
Then, as time passed, due to the iron-workings of Nālīka,
a disease of the breath arose in his chest, such that the movement of breath was entirely obstructed.
Afflicted by the disease known as *damā*, the king of devotees was unable to perform his duties;
he prayed to me who had assumed a physical form.
Suddenly manifesting myself, I caused him to drink milk with my own hand.
Having touched his heart with my hand, the disease was destroyed.
Then, quickly vanishing, I always dwell and take delight within his form.
[Even so,] when one's lifespan is exhausted, there is no escape from the lotus-like woman.
I brought Kuṇḍanikā by means of my celestial chariot to the supreme, imperishable abode.
In this same way, I have also led other devotees to the imperishable realm—
those who worship me with devotion and likewise accept my qualities.
They serve the virtuous in every way with a spirit of love;
having attained the favor of the virtuous, they shall go to my abode.
By reading, by hearing, by remembering, and even by serving [this], [they attain that goal]. 104.
"Enjoyment becomes liberation itself; such is the supreme goal attained according to one's desire.

Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of Nālīka the Blacksmith’s Vision of Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Garuḍa through Devotion and His Liberation," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
← Chapter 212 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā/Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 213 [[Author: Chapter 214 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious story of the leather-worker named Maṅgala, which is filled with devotion to Me. 1.
In the city of Droṇikā, there was a devoted and most loyal leather-worker named Maṅgaladeva; he was a householder who performed his work in leather.
[He possessed] buffaloes, cows, deer, and likewise lions.
He purifies the hides of dead tigers, elephants, and other species of beasts with ritual consecrations; indeed, he sells those consecrated hides for high prices. (3–4)
Having prepared seats made of various skins and purifying materials,
he also gave them to the virtuous— both to the deer and to the lions of the forest.
Having gone daily to the monastery of the virtuous, he constantly sought the company of the holy ones.
He performs the sweeping of the courtyards and other areas around the gate-towers and similar structures.
(6) Having taken the dust from the feet of the virtuous upon his head, heart, face, and body, he bathes with that dust and even rolls about in the very powder. (7)
"Oh, what fortune! O leather-worker, I bathe in the dust of the merit of the virtuous.
Having obtained the favor of the virtuous, I shall go to the supreme state.
Speaking thus, he even drinks the water from their feet, which possesses such greatness.
He eats the food left over by the virtuous, served upon a bed of leaves.
Though his body was that of an impure leather-worker, it became pure through the grace of the virtuous;
all my sins were destroyed, and my state as a leather-worker vanished. (3.213.9–10)
"Oh, how blessed are the saintly! Oh, Kṛṣṇa! Oh, my birth here!
Though born into a low caste, I am indeed most fortunate through this service.
Knowing His greatness in this way, he remembers Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa.
He even writes the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa upon hides;
he gives gifts to the virtuous and seeks his own welfare as well;
and having fashioned other various implements made from hide, [he employs them]. (12–13)
He sells [his possessions] after writing down the name Śrī Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa;
he writes Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa upon the courtyard of his house and upon the archway.
O Rame, for that devotee, everything consists of Kṛṣṇa.
He also established a shop called the Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa-āpaṇa;
it was decorated on all sides upon the walls, doors, archways, and floors with [the names]:
"Rādhākṛṣṇa, Hare, Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, Ramāpati. (15–16)
O Beloved Lord, Consort of Kamalā, Śrī Kaṃbharāja;
O Gopāla-bālaka, glorious Nārāyaṇa, Supreme Sovereign!
O Blessed One, destroyer of sins, bestower of merit, who dwells within! 17.
In this way, everywhere with these names and likewise with images and so forth,
the entire marketplace was decorated and the house was similarly adorned.
Such a devotee of mine, having bathed, performs my worship.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as food offerings and fruit,
he presents betel leaf, water, and the like, and then performs the ritual dismissal.
Having eaten the food obtained as grace, he indeed proceeds with his daily activities.

All his laborers and servants, having performed my worship, constantly carry out their tasks; I delight in this. And at night, gathering together, they engage in conversation and even perform kīrtana.
They sing my verses and rejoice in festivals;
if it is the day of the vow, they remain awake until dawn.
In the morning, having gathered together, they perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) of the vow.
They feed and honor many devoted leather-workers,
and they also honor with gifts others who have arrived in their own city, whether they be virtuous practitioners or others who are worthy. (24–25)
To those who come to them, they even give footwear;
thus indeed do they perform service in many ways with conscious devotion. And the virtuous, being pleased, become bestowers of blessings upon them.
May my devotees be happy, and may their devotion bear excellent fruit without obstacles.
May they live long, be pure, and be free from all misfortunes; and may the servants of virtuous women and the righteous be endowed with merit. (27–28)
Thus, through the grace of the virtuous, they receive blessings. Then once, on the full moon day of Āśvina,
when the moon had reached the sky complete with all its digits, there was a great festival.
Those leather-workers indeed fashioned an image of Hari on the Kaumudī night;
having placed it upon a beautiful seat, they worshipped it in the moonlight with sandalwood paste,
lovely garments, and splendid ornaments.

They performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and other rites; they offered oblations (naivedya) consisting of flattened rice (pṛthuka) mixed with sugar and immersed in milk, which they presented to Viṣṇu.
Having placed that prasāda uncovered in a large vessel, they [offered it]. 32.
Eagerly, they performed the *rāsa* dance before the Blessed One. With the rhythmic clapping of their hands and feet, they chanted the praises of Acyuta;
immersed in love, they moved in a circular formation.
They circumambulate me, Hari; eager to leap, they sing my praises;
they converse with rhythmic claps and bound about in various ways.
They sit down, stand up, wander about, roll on the ground, and rise again to move forward.
They take up the cymbals and play them, facing one another and facing back to back.
(36) In this way, my servants enjoy great joy and bliss, O Lakṣmī, when the ground in the middle of the night shines like the milk of the moon. (37)
Then I, the Lord Viṣṇu, being greedy for the elixir of devotional love, became single-mindedly intent on the rāsa dance; I saw and I heard them.
Yet, just as those embodied forms did not see me at all, so it was with me.
I became gracious and bound by love for my dear Lord.
Listen to what happened there: a serpent, greedy for the song, approached and remained still in a corner of the house. (3.213.40)
Having heard the song filled with the essence of the *rāsa*, having heard the rhythmic chanting,
having smelled the auspicious *pṛthuka* grains in the vessels along with milk and sugar,
and having seen those [places] situated in solitude, he went toward them very slowly.

Having tasted the milk with his tongue and drunk its sweetness again and again, he was purified by grace; yet, filled with fear, he quickly retreated a short distance. Then, finding rest at the conclusion of the *rāsa* dance, he remained there to obtain further grace.
All those devoted people served the poisoned *pṛthuka* grains in rows before the thousand embodied beings.
Having eaten the *pṛthuka* grains, those people who knew his greatness—

All of them, from children to the elderly, having eaten food and drunk water tainted by the venom of black snakes, slept for a moment in the courtyard; many of them fell into a toxic stupor and were on the verge of death. (45–46)
They became scorched by the poison and were deprived of their bodily luster.
Then others, touched by the diminished venom, suffered intensely;
they experienced the aggravation of the poison in others and the dizziness of their own heads.
The rays of their eyes possessed the luster of orange, blue, and green waves.
They quickly performed an examination and indeed recognized the poison;
all the children, afflicted by the venom, declared it openly.
Then, having been eaten, a fainting spell that brings death indeed set in.
For the sake of neutralizing the poison, they all quickly drank ghee. Vomiting occurred for them, which brought about the removal of the poison.
Moreover, many devotees there were as if dead from poison;
other people entreated me to restore them to life.
Many women, sons, husbands, and kinsmen wept there.
They remembered me, the Supreme Lord, the giver of life who dwells within; and seeing their state of distress, their weeping, their devotion, their vows,
and their piety, I was pleased and quickly manifested myself before them.

Having heard the account of those who caused my grief, I remained there in the guise of a virtuous man, carrying a basket of medicinal herbs for the stomach ailment [of the king]. Having quickly reported the news and having indeed filled a jar with water, I stood there. (54–55)
There, having cast medicinal juice and offered water for rinsing the mouth into the mouths of those who were unconscious and in a state resembling death,
they suddenly became free from fainting through the contact of the water with their palates.
They became immortal and attained the movement of supreme knowledge. All of them suddenly rose up like those awakening from sleep;
established in their own nature, they recognized their own calamity there as if it were a dream.
Even poison attained the state of nectar through the water of the sage’s medicinal herbs.
Then, having all gathered together, they gave food to the sage;
at the end of the night, they also provided delightful drink and a seat for his rest.
Those people, having returned to life, massaged his feet.
Immersed in their service, they asked that virtuous man:
"O Blessed One, how does an obstacle arise for those who have attained steadfastness?"
Then the saintly one said to him: "Indeed, an obstacle arises by the will of Kṛṣṇa for the purpose of testing;
it is certainly not considered a true obstacle.
From this, there shall arise firmness in the grace of Kṛṣṇa and firmness in devotion."
He comes in person and effects the destruction of all obstacles.
(63) In times of adversity, there shall be remembrance of Śrī Hari by his devotees;
when a miracle is displayed, their devotion shall become exceedingly firm. (64)
"Aha! This Blessed One exists as the remover of all suffering.
His service should be performed; it is auspicious, bestowing liberation and happiness.
Such are the thoughts that constantly arise upon beholding his sovereign majesty.
Then, while Kṛṣṇa was imitating the human dance in his observation of lack of sovereignty, [Satyabhāmā] felt distress, thinking: "This is not the Blessed Lord;
for a long time I have performed service here, yet it has been fruitless. (66–67)
Just as I am weak, powerless, and dependent on others,
so too is he weak, incapable, and dependent on others.
Just as desire, anger, greed, delusion, and fear reside in me, [so do they in him].
Likewise, desire, greed, anger, delusion, and fear indeed exist in Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, he is certainly not the Blessed Lord, but a human being.
Thus, possessing a material intellect regarding Kṛṣṇa, one perceives him as an ordinary mortal. (3.213.70)
One whose divine disposition has perished imagines faults in others as if they were his own;
therefore, one should always contemplate Hari with a mind empowered by divine disposition.
One should consider oneself to be perfect, thinking: "Nothing is to be attained by me apart from Hari."

Nothing further remains for me to accomplish; the means to attain Hari is complete. Indeed, Hari himself is present here in person; that supreme state is right there. The abode of Brahman is also there, and the liberated souls dwell there as well. (72–73)
While Hari is present here, everything—earth and all else—is supreme;
the assembly is divine, the devotees are divine, and the men and women are divine.
Through their union, my bliss exists as being composed of the Blessed Lord.
I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose, since Hari dwells here.
The Blessed Lord exists here in the form of a virtuous man and in embodied form.
Such are the thoughts that arise in the heart of a devotee who knows the Self.
The gods and the lords who have attained liberation are happy through His abundance;
that very Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), shines here.
He is the imperishable, all-pervading abode of Brahman, higher than the highest.
Devoted to that [purpose], the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa has come here.
The great king has met me; there is no end to my good fortune.
Indeed, through the union with that Kṛṣṇa, our life is truly restored.
In the divine, eternal, and supreme abode, Śrī Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent,
worshiped by countless great liberated souls who are equal to Himself. Indeed, it is by the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa that those divine liberated souls [attain their state].
In each single hair there is a brilliance resembling ten million times ten million suns.
The entire radiant brilliance of such innumerable liberated souls merges into a single hair; such is that Imperishable.
The divine abode of Brahman indeed exists, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
likewise, all such abodes and even the splendors of those abodes are dissolved into a single hair-pore of Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (83)
Such is the manifestation of the Supreme Self that proceeds;
such is the Lord Kṛṣṇa, the all-powerful and most great Hari, who, endowed with every potency, is moved by compassion for the welfare of embodied beings. (84–85)
Having assumed a divine human form, he is born among men like an ordinary man; though concealing his great sovereign powers, he exists in human guise.
Through devotion to him, all sufferings come to an end.
There is no bondage for him by time, by karma, or by illusion.
Through service to that Śrī Hari, his protection is always secured,
just as protection has indeed been provided here for you by me while I am present.
In the same way, Kṛṣṇa causes His own protection to be performed through the agency of the virtuous.
All devotees, living beings, conscious entities, and whatever principles of *māyā* there may be—all these indeed constitute His body; they are pervaded by Him and remain under His control. (89)
Everything indeed becomes subject to the will of this Great Soul.
Within all those principles (tattvas), even among the liberated ones and the lords of the imperishable,
Kṛṣṇa exists as the pervasive one, even within those consisting of Māyā and individual souls.
Kṛṣṇa is the impeller of all, independent, and the controller;
endowed with all sovereignty, he is the supreme remainder of all, the Lord who bestows auspiciousness.
Manifesting on earth in the likeness of a man, he performs the dance of humanity.
O men and women who possess divine nature, you should indeed serve that Hari;
all of them shall surely attain the entire sovereignty of Śrī Hari.
Those who serve Hari with love, possessing the form of Brahman and the state of Brahman, [attain this].
Even in the world of Brahmā, those of such a nature serve the Supreme Lord.
Therefore, here in this world, Hari—who appears in the form of a saintly person—is to be served as the supreme protector.
Within the saintly person, Nārāyaṇa himself resides, personally fulfilling the desires of his devotees.

Thus, O Lakṣmī, Maṅgaladeva and the others were described by me at that time. Some perceived Kṛṣṇa within me, while others perceived me as Kṛṣṇa; they then worshipped my virtuous form again and again with intense devotion.
Satī, the wife of Maṅgaladeva, named Vibhāvarī,
served me with great devotion by massaging my feet and other such services.
Then, I was repeatedly entreated by them for the sake of their liberation.
"So be it," I said, and I revealed my own divine form:
a youthful, radiant being with a dark and beautiful body, possessing a form more exquisite than ten million Cupids, adorned with a crown and holding a lute. (3.213.100)

Having shown me such a form as this— the Lord of Śrī, who is saluted by Rādhā and others, served by the beloveds of Brahmā, and attended by millions of liberated great *mahāmuktā* maidens— within a moment...

But when You vanished from their sight, those who were devoted to the Great Wonder danced and sang hymns upon seeing Kṛṣṇa directly before them. Thus, they constantly worshipped You with supreme devotion at all times.
When the time had arrived, I brought them by means of a celestial chariot to that supreme and transcendent abode of divine syllables, and I established them there among the liberated ones— namely,
my devotee Maṅgaladeva, as well as his wife Vibhāvarī.
I protected my feet while serving on that ground of letters;
thus, O Lakṣmī, I then provided protection for the shoemakers. Overcome by compassion, I, appearing in a virtuous form, gave them a mantra.

"Oṃ, obeisances unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master; svāhā! By chanting, hearing, remembering, and even serving this [mantra], they chanted, worshipped, remembered Me, and went to My supreme abode. (1.07) By reading, hearing, remembering, or even serving this [mantra]...
"Through worship, one obtains prosperity, the divine realm, and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord, having appeared in person through the devotion of the leather-worker devotee named Maṅgaladeva, removed his poison," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
