Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious account of the chariot-maker who dwells in the village of Sutāra—an account rich with devotion to me. 1.
On the bank of the Raṅgamayī river, there lived in the city of Sutāra a very pure chariot-maker who was my devotee and had a family.
He manufactured all kinds of wooden vehicles, including carts and wagons.
He manufactures all kinds of wheel-less vehicles, wooden seats, and couches;
he produces grass mats, stools, beds, and screens;
as well as beautiful wooden vessels and wooden male and female figurines.
The preeminent artisan indeed constructs boats, elephants, horses, cattle, and bulls,
as well as various other implements, by means of his own skill;
he also makes chests, caskets, and beautiful four-sided pavilions.
In all his undertakings, he would even write the name of Hari;
moreover, having first written his own name as "Haridāsa," he would then write "Hari" upon all objects.
And in his house, within a wooden hall, he drew an image of the Lord Śrī Hari;
through the lattice of the house, he installed a wooden statue of the Supreme Soul,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
In the morning, he worships this beautiful image of mine with Śrī,
using flowers, leaves, sandalwood paste, unbroken grains of rice, saffron, ornaments,
garments, liquid offerings, incense, lamps, food offerings, and water. (3.214.9–10)
Having thus worshipped daily, one then consumes the *prasāda*;
furthermore, after distributing it to others, one proceeds with one's duties.
During times of exertion, one should remember the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.

Haridāsa, the king among true devotees, [sought] Hari-Kṛṣṇa, Bāla-Kṛṣṇa. (1.2) Then, on one occasion, a reflection occurred to him regarding the realm of the gods and others: "Abandoning all other exertion, let me undertake the service of the Image. (1.3)
For those whose meditation becomes divine in nature for the sake of creative activity,
and who likewise maintain constant remembrance of the gods during the performance of forms, colors, and other rites;
for them, there shall be perpetual chanting and the offering of worship embodied in iconic form.
Having reflected thus, Haridāsa, eager for the sake of Hari, began with devotion an endeavor consisting of the form of Hari. He fashioned a most beautiful image of Puruṣottama. (15–16)
The form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa adorned with a *maṇikī* gem, the couple Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa, and both Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
Vāsudeva together with Śrī, and Viṣṇu joined with Kamalā. (17)
He fashioned Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Nārāyaṇa reclining upon Śeṣa;
Śrīpati seated upon Śrī-Garuḍa, [Viṣṇu] seated upon an elephant, and [Śiva] seated upon Māṇikī;
and he fashioned [them all] seated in celestial chariots and chariots, possessing divine splendor. (18–19)
The Lord who destroys suffering, accompanied by Śrī and the cows;
likewise, the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Kapila, and Hari;
Vāsudeva, Rājarāja, Pṛthu, Datta, and Nṛsiṃhaka.
Haṃsa, Ṛṣabha, Paraśudhara, Yajña, and Vāmana;
Rāma, Kumāra, Vyāsa, Hayagrīva, and Nārada;
Bālakṛṣṇa, Buddha, Kalki, and the Lord of Nārāyaṇī.
Hara and Satī, Brahmā and Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, Prajñā, Pārāvatī, Durgā, Gaṅgā, and likewise Kālikā;
Sūrya, Vahni, Candramas, Gaṇeśa, and Kālabhairava.
He fashioned auspicious images of Nanda, Sunanda, and the Liṅga;
indeed, from wood of various species, including the *savana*, *anāma*, and *sāga* trees, as well as from *vaṭa* and *śiṃśapā* trees, he created beautiful idols. (24–25)
He indeed fashions various [images]— small, medium, and large—
adorned with colors and ornaments, consecrated, and marked with signs;
constantly chanting the name of Hari while performing worship, he always creates these images.
But for those whose forms shine within his heart, he does not [behave] in that way;
rather, sitting in a secluded place and remembering me, he maintains my form. With single-minded focus, he becomes one with my very body within his own heart.
The dissolution of all the functions of the senses indeed occurs within me;
in whatever manner he strives like a yogi and meditates with steadiness,
half a day or even a full day passes for him as if in samādhi.

Nevertheless, immersed in love, he does not emerge from his meditative absorption (samādhi). Since Mādhava’s form is like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), the desires held within it become fulfilled by its very presence.
Thus, for Haridāsa, who was possessed of such certainty,
as long as the form consisting of his duty did not arise in any way,
so long did he remain steadfast in samādhi upon my image, absorbed in me.
Desiring to see a new form, worthy of being fashioned and most beautiful— then,
when by my grace a form of the embodied [deity] arises, having seen and held that form intended for the image, again and again; || 33–34 ||
Having practiced this, the devotee then emerges from it, and not otherwise.
Whatever form was seen [in meditation], such indeed is the form of the *sādhya*-deity;
[the practitioner] brings forth that beautiful form from wood by means of artistic skills.
Gentle, with a smiling face, and equipped with all suitable weapons;
richly adorned with appropriate ornaments, he thus elevates the wooden form—such a beautiful wooden image as was envisioned in the heart. (36–37)
Having made such an arrangement, he sells it beautifully adorned. In this way, having made [such arrangements] for all the gods, for the great ascetic yogis like Hanuman,
for virtuous women, and for the deities, he performs the sale.
She meditates upon all the deities, and especially upon her beloved;
she meditates upon Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Therefore, because I am her image, I fulfill even that which is desired by her.
He became famous in the world as Haridāsa, the very body of Hari;
even kings indeed had their chosen deities fashioned by him.
And Haridāsa, having made them, would surely give away those most auspicious images.
Haridāsa made this vow:
"Except for Nārāyaṇa, and except for an image of a human being that is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, I shall never under any circumstances create a material image that is contrary to true devotion. (42–43)
An image of a human woman should never be made for those who harbor base thoughts;
likewise, an image of a human woman should never be made for those who lack devotion.
However, for the devoted, it should be auspiciously fashioned, joined with their chosen deity.
Thus, he constantly guarded his self-surrender.
Therefore, O Lakṣmī, being pleased, I approached him for the sake of a test;
having become a sovereign emperor, I traveled along the road under the pretext of visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Accompanied by elephants, horses, and chariots, and joined by an army of more than a thousand soldiers; attended by thousands of queens, female and male servants;
adorned with jewels, diamonds, necklaces, and other ornaments, and graced by the royal parasol.
Seated upon the back of a great white elephant accompanied by a golden female elephant,
fanned with yak-tail whisks, honored with shouts of "Victory!",
and surrounded by warriors bearing missiles and weapons; ||48-49||
Saluted and served by the preceptor, ministers, chiefs,
and others, you, Lakṣmī, are my queen, sovereign, and most excellent beauty,
adorned by a multitude of thousands of beautiful young female attendants.
Protected by female servants dispatched by me and honored by my attendants,
you likewise arrived seated upon a celestial vehicle rich with great gold and jewels; indeed,
you came together with me, having been previously sent forth by me.
Being such as this, O Emperor, I indeed went forth ahead toward a grove of trees on the bank of the Raṅgamayī river under the pretext of a pilgrimage to sacred sites.
[There I reached] the excellent bank of a sacred site known by the name Mahāśālagrāma-tīrtha.
Relying upon them for the sake of stability, I descended from my elephant;
accompanied by my army, I dwelt there with my mind intent on bathing, worship, and other rites.
Then, the subjects residing in the city named Sutārā arrived.
The preceptors, the Brahmins, and the mendicants, filled with curiosity and desiring sacrificial fees, as well as those wishing for a glimpse [of the king],
all arrived at the city to see the monarch.
Nevertheless, that king of devotees did not come, knowing it to be illusory.
Then, having performed a pilgrimage according to the prescribed rites and having given many gifts, I heard about the auspicious images.
He also saw images established on the banks of the holy ford.
He questioned the men who had gathered there concerning the preeminent artisan.
They replied, "O King, there resides in this city a master craftsman."

"Though summoned by me through messengers, even Haridāsa did not come," he said. "Except for a holy devotee of the Lord, except for Nārāyaṇa Hari, and except for another devotee of Hari, he does not go into the presence of anyone else. (3.214.60–61)
Then I spoke my name as Kṛṣṇadāsa:
"O best of artisans, I am Śrī Kṛṣṇadāsa, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa;
come at my request for the sake of the image. (62)
The messengers went and spoke to him accordingly; having heard this, he indeed approached.
Taking garlands of flowers, he placed them upon the king's chest.
Knowing the king to be a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, he did not bow down with great devotion.

The king, being highly discerning, also bestowed honor upon him. The artisan was questioned by the king regarding the creation of the images, and he was likewise asked about the price for purchasing those images. (65)

He too gave me an image of Kṛṣṇa together with Rādhā, along with a thousand silver coins, as well as Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa. Having received these, I gave him a ring and furthermore a hundred pieces of gold.
Having given him a reward as well, I said to him on my behalf:
"Fashion one image of me and one image of my queen.
I shall give you as much gold, gems, and diamonds as you desire. (68)
He said, "O King, I am a devotee, solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
I always fashion images of the manifestations of Nārāyaṇa, as well as of Nārāyaṇa himself, and of the gods and the deities. (3.214.70)
I shall certainly not perform a human *māyā*, nor shall I perform an illusory *māyā*.
[That is,] I shall never entertain the thought that one whose mental activity is fixed upon such a fabrication would not contemplate Nārāyaṇa.
And I shall never, at any time, even remember a puppet made of *māyā* or of something illusory.
"O King, if I were to fashion a doll for your queen, it would indeed result in my loss of human memory, and there would be a diminution of my devotion.
Therefore, I shall certainly not make a doll for you; please forgive me."
Although you are indeed a great devotee, you are nonetheless of a rajasic nature;
this great deluding power (mahāmāyā) of the King persists as a source of infatuation for you.
Therefore, I shall not direct my remembrance toward anyone other than Narayana and Lakshmi.
If it pleases you that both of us remain together in service— just as Lakṣmī remains with the King and you with Mādhava—
then I shall create an image of myself together with the Lord of Śrī.
"I shall not accept anything exclusively for myself, nor do I desire a reward.
Salutations to you; please forgive me as well, for the king is to be honored by his subjects.
Having spoken thus, O Lakṣmī, Haridāsa, the king of devotees, went home.

"I am a king," he said, "and having thus tested my devotee from behind, I reached his house on foot; the people were filled with wonder. Out of discernment, that king of devotees gave me a wooden seat."

He gave and showed me the food and water offered to Śrī Hari; he sat down for the purpose of meditation before all the images. Disregarding my fear and maintaining the auspicious composure of Hari, [he remained there].
Then, immersed in samādhi within my heart, I became present in his heart. Lakṣmī appeared in the form of the queen and I in the form of the king, each according to our respective roles.
Having recognized me as Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī, he quickly arose.
He welcomed me and performed a circumambulation like one prostrating with a staff;
he suddenly began chanting and danced, overwhelmed with joy.
Then, as for the other people who were there as spectators at that time—
Having seen this great marvel and having heard what was uttered by Bhakta, they all [exclaimed]:
"Indeed, Nārāyaṇa himself has come to my house as a sovereign emperor, and the Great Queen Lakṣmī has arrived; I am truly fortunate! (84–85)
Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune for the inhabitants of the village of Sutāra!
Oh, what supreme auspicious fortune for my wife, the illustrious Mānavī!
And what fortune for my family, for my servants, and for the wives of my servants!
Today, indeed, is the most excellent fortune, that Hari, the Beloved, is in our home;
that Śrī, the beloved queen of Hari, has arrived in the form of a royal consort.
May this bring welfare to the noble Avyā and liberation to the servant of Hari.
Oh, what a fruit for the maker of the image! Lord Hari is visibly present in the house.
Oh, what a gain for one who has offered oneself! The Lord Himself is visibly present in the house.
My art has become true art; my life has become a true life.
"Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Śrī, has been directly attained by me.
Upon hearing this, the people also worshipped the King, the Lord of Śrī;
they prostrated themselves like staffs, and the devotee fell at His feet.
O Lakṣmī, meanwhile my own supreme four-armed form, divine and enchanting, was revealed by me along with you,
Lakṣmī; and at that very moment, the entire army that was on the riverbank—
Then, that great wonder was concealed there.
Having granted me his direct vision in my home, the Blessed One then accepted my worship, bestowed a boon, and transmitted the tradition for the sake of liberation. (93–94)
Having offered my devotion, I then stood for a moment with you and said:
"To this devotee who knows the Self, and to him who worships me in this manner, I shall certainly act on his behalf in every way. (95)
I am like a wish-fulfilling creeper; I fulfill all desires.
Those artisans who, devoted to meditation upon me, create my image—being free from greed and self-interest and possessing pure intentions—[shall likewise attain their goals]. (96–97)
"I shall grant them liberation, just as you have done here, O King of Devotees.
Having spoken thus, she vanished from within the house where her own form had been established for worship by Kṛṣṇa and Lakṣmī.
Then, although he was my devotee, even as he constantly meditated upon and remembered me,
when the appointed time had not yet arrived, I appeared at his house by means of a celestial chariot;
I beheld his illustrious wife and likewise that servant of Hari.
Having caused those two to ascend [to heaven] and having made them divine, I led them to my imperishable abode;
and in the same way, over time, I led others as well to my imperishable realm.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the chariot-maker and his devotees were indeed delivered by me.
From reading and hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall certainly be attained.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How Liberation Was Granted by the Blessed Lord to the Chariot-Maker named Haridāsa and His Family through Devotion," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
*Chapter 214: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga)*
Chapter 215 [Author:
Chapter 216 → Puruṣottama said:

Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of Śilāhāra as well. Formerly, in the city of Sudāma, there lived one named Dāmaśila, who resided there with his family, engaged in the business of mining and selling stone.
Indeed, hundreds of people act as laborers there, exerting themselves;
they extract massive, long stones from the surface of the earth and send them to foreign lands for the purpose of building the abode of the King of Gods. (2–3)
Variegated peaks and palaces of diverse kinds arise—
divine structures made of white stone, adorned with the excellence of artistic craftsmanship;
fashioned from that very stone through the skills of the most eminent artisans.

For the excavation of stones during the day on the surface of a quarry is performed constantly by those skilled therein who are directed by the *dāman*. Indeed, the *dāma*, the *śilāda*, the *pramātṛ*, and likewise the *mūlyakṛt* are the overseers. (5–6)
He conducts inspections at the proper time over the mines and the ground;
the laborers strive in the extraction and the hauling, with carts,
wagons, and an abundance of various implements.
There, Dāmaśilāda indeed gave to those who had come seeking for the purpose of purchase (8) auspicious stones of appropriate value,
suitable for [divine] images, highly precious, and likewise fit for palaces (9).
Suitable for houses, suitable for walls, and others suitable for floors—
she gives them to the seeker with various prices and qualities.
Her servants load them onto a cart from the stone-pavilion.
They draw the beautiful chariots with bulls, camels, excellent elephants, and likewise with yaks,
buffaloes, and mechanical animals;
for the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa himself provides protection everywhere.
She performs [these actions] in ascending and descending, in extending [the limbs],
in rising up and withdrawing, in turning over and tearing asunder.
Among them, some can carry a hundred bhāras, while another is even more heavily burdened.
Half of those and half again of those are constantly being excavated.
Indeed, in some places, due to the excessive weight of the rocks, the cart breaks;
for when the cart is crushed upon the surface of the rock, it turns into mere debris.
Lord Hari indeed protects one from sudden calamities and the like;
having thus reflected upon his karma-servants, Śilāda chose the Supreme One.
"O Hari! O Nārāyaṇa! O Master! O Beloved! O Lord of Śrī! O Hari!"
In this way, he constantly taught worship, the chanting of the names of Hari, and the loud proclamation of Him— by means of which He Himself grants protection and liberation;
He performs worship Himself and causes His servants to do so as well.
Upon the stones he inscribed the names of Kṛṣṇa, which possess great merit:
the stone of Kṛṣṇa, the stone of Rāma, and likewise the stone of Nārāyaṇa;
the stone of Lakṣmī, the stone of Ramā, the stone of Rādhā, and the stone of Hari.
The *devopalā* is a stone from a temple; the *mūrtyupalā* is a stone for an image, such as a stone of Satī. (3.215.20) There are also the *viṣṇuśilā*, the *brahmaśilā*, and the *parameśaśilā*.
Furthermore, there are the *devīśilā*, the *sūryaśilā*, the *tīrthaśilā*, and the *gurūpalā*. (21)
The Mokṣa-śilā, the Ātma-śilā, and likewise the Muktī-śilā;
similarly the Avatāra-śilā and the Goloka-prastara.
The Vaikuṇṭha-śilā, the Cakra-aśman, and likewise the Śālagrāma-śilā. (22)
He also made stone slabs for the Blessed One, known as the Janārdana stone;
by these names— Yoga-stone, Jñāna-stone, and Dhyāna-stone—
he created groups of stones for the propitiation of Nārāyaṇa.
"O men, I shall proclaim the name of Nārāyaṇa through the application of the *śilā-yoga*;
they shall take up that auspicious name, which is supreme and destroys all evil.
Having thus intended these well-composed names of Hari, [he spoke].
Indeed, by that Dāmaśilāda, [the names] which grant liberation were inscribed upon the stones.
Even men take up the purifying names of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) under the pretext of these stones,
as well as the names of his circle of attendants and the merchant-princes.
Thus, through his devotion, true devotion consisting of kīrtana was performed;
even common men and women were purified by the holy names.
Great merit, characterized by a state of spiritual clarity, arose within him.
Indeed, my form of grace increases incessantly.
O Rama, hearing of the devotion of that devotee, men come to his house;
virtuous devotees, righteous people, travelers, and mendicants all arrive there. (3.215.30)
Having gathered together, they perform my worship and my glorification;
indeed, having installed an image of me made of *śilājatu* in their home,
they always worship it with devotion, through great festivals and excellent offerings.
They perform singing, dancing, and chanting in the *rāsa* dance before me.
Having offered me incense, lamps, and the like, as well as food offerings and water, they receive my grace and then depart. (32–33)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the assembly of the virtuous truly attained nourishment in the palace of Dāmaśilāda; at that time, I became especially pleased and remained constantly present within the image.
"I accept the service rendered and shall provide protection in every way.
(35) Then once, while the devotee was at home, the servants were indeed at the quarry; they were all engaged in extracting stone at a distance of one krośa. (36)
Long, massive boulders were dragged out by them and placed upon a cart,
but that cart was quickly broken.
The servants and laborers who were standing beside the cart—
Among them, two or three indeed fell from the cart onto the surface of a rock.
Then, alas, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the people there;
they truly began to beg for water to drink.
Then they gave water, but they fell into a swoon, on the verge of death.
Then others remembered me, Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Protector;
with great effort, they quickly acted to relieve the burden that oppressed them.
Having gathered together with other men, they lifted up both the cart and the stone;
yet two or three of those laborers were cast out, rendered motionless,
their strength gone, facing death, and deeply distressed.
While they were still occupied thus,
Dāmaśilāda, who was devoted [to me], having been informed by the laborers, went quickly to his home;
then, remembering me, Nārāyaṇa, he returned to the mine.
At that time, disguised as a virtuous ascetic, I came from the forest to the pit;
seeking food as a mendicant, I begged for water. Seeing those who had acted so wickedly, I was filled with the utmost wonder.
I remained motionless for a moment, while they entreated Acyuta:
"O Hare, O Kṛṣṇa, friend of the distressed! Revive these wretched men!
Protect us so that the sin of killing a human being does not fall upon this devotee. || 46 ||
You are the dispeller of the protection of the wretched; you are the fulfiller of the desires of your devotees.
You are the remover of all suffering; protect your own people.
There would be no medicine capable [of healing] when the bones have been reduced to powder. 47–48.
In this body, when the blood has been exhausted, there is no life without you;
indeed, without wonder and without accomplishment, they have no life at all.
These animals are as good as dead, for there is no one other than you, O Yogi.
"Another is capable of renewing, equalizing, and effecting a reconciliation.
Hearing those who were speaking thus, the virtuous man took water in his hand and gave it to them for sipping (ācamanīyaka) into their mouths.
Having established a protection and placed the ashes within his belly, he held them in both hands and diligently rubbed them all over the bodies of those who were broken;
at that moment, they regained their composure, their bones were set, and they were freed from pain.
They became filled with blood just as they had been before;
then, like those awakened from a dream, they rose and prostrated before the true yogi.
Having regained their life-breath, they found rest for a moment in the presence of the Holy One.
The virtuous one accepted alms and then ate food with water;
they all likewise properly partook of my grace.
Then, serving at his lotus feet, they remained there in peace.
They asked me for the supreme means that destroys sin,
as well as the knowledge of Nārāyaṇa and his most excellent embodied form.
I indeed related all of that to them exactly as it is.
Service to the virtuous, devotion to Hari, and likewise the visiting of sacred pilgrimage sites—
these become destroyers of sin through the grace of the Lord.
Only through association with the virtuous does the realization of Śrī Hari arise.
Through the study of authentic scriptures and by listening to discourses, knowledge of Hari arises by the power of past impressions;
and through the practice of yoga, there is the sudden destruction of impurities. (3.215.59–60)
Through the path of the yogi and the path of Brahman, the form of Kṛṣṇa shines forth.
Within the physical body (piṇḍa), there exists a beautiful arrangement, exactly as it is;
furthermore, in the Vairāja [state], it likewise exists as both subtle and gross, due to their non-difference.
In the human body, however, the channels (nāḍīs) are the rivers in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). In the body, the cavities (kukṣayas) exist as the oceans in the cosmic egg.
The soles of the feet are the netherworld (pātāla), the head is the realm of truth (satyaloka), and the waist is indeed the earth (bhūḥ).
The channels of the senses within the body have as their causes the channels of the cosmic senses (vairāja); therefore, these [channels] attain a state of oneness.
Those devoted to the practice of yoga reach the tip of the tongue through meditative absorption (samādhi).
Then the yogis behold the end of the tongue of Vairāja. In this way, through meditative absorption (samādhi), they reach the limit of all the senses;
then the yogis behold the end of the senses of Vairāja.
The Suṣumṇā runs through the center of this body, ascending from the navel toward the head;
the Iḍā is always situated on the left, while the Piṅgalā remains on the right.
Having reached the head at the end of the Suṣumṇā, one beholds the Vairāja state.
That [channel], long from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), reaches the Vairāja yoga.
Indeed, in the form of rays of light, it extends from the Vairāja up to the Puruṣa;
from the aperture of the Mahāpuruṣa, it is designated as the "rays of light. (68–69)
Because she has attained identity with the Imperishable (akṣara), she indeed resides within Hari;
having reached identity with the subject (pramātṛ), she exists as the nature of rays.
Therefore, by means of the path of the Suṣumṇā, the yogi goes to the supreme state.
The ray emanating from Hari is that which enters into all incarnations;
for it exists pervasively among both lords and individual souls.
That is Brahman, that is consciousness, and that is indeed pure being and light. (71)
By its light all this shines forth, endowed with the radiance of knowledge.
And through an excess of affection for such a person, their splendor increases.
Whether one is awake, asleep, or in deep sleep, whenever [this occurs]...
One should go to that person in whom there is absorption in Hari through affection;
likewise, by the resolve of Hari, and also by the power of Hari—
namely, by the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will of Hari.
Living beings, endowed with action, proceed while knowing;
all living beings are under the sway of karma and are certainly not independent.
Indeed, they possess action, desire, and knowledge only through the knowledge, action, and desire of Hari.
The Blessed One is in every way the bestower of the fruits of actions.
Those powers of Hari impel the knowledge and other faculties of men according to their respective karmas; by that means, creation proceeds. (76–77)
Indeed, through the practice of meditation upon Hari, the living beings of creation become divine;
they truly possess divine vision, and then [they behold] the Sudarśana of Brahman—
that radiant, attribute-less Brahman which is devoid of the qualities of Māyā and the like.

The great-souled ones, who have obtained the true fruit of association with the virtuous, attain the eternal Supreme Brahman— the Lord of all, the Supreme Self, the Transcendent Reality, endowed with His own divine attributes. (3.215.80)

These yogis go to Him who has a human form yet possesses a divine body— the Lord of Śrī, the protector of the virtuous, the supreme Self of divine form. Many become divine, equal to Him, and take on the nature of Brahman.
Just as the divine Brahmāpriyā, and as the countless liberated ones (muktas),
just as Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Satī, and Sarasvatī,
so too do men and women become divine when they have merged with the Supreme Self. //82-83//
Therefore, Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa is indeed to be worshipped as the protector;
he is the bestower of liberation and heaven, and the one who grants attainment of the path of Suṣumṇā.
In the pit, Janārdana Nārāyaṇa should be constantly remembered.
"Lord Hari dwells within the form of the virtuous; He is to be served by the virtuous, for He is their refuge.
Having spoken thus, I then made them fearless and gave them this mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (85–86)
Then, O Lakṣmī, regarding me as their guru, they led me— who possessed the form of a saint and was a source of wonder to people— back to my own abode;
they fed me most abundantly and made me drink what was pleasing to me.
They respectfully partook of milk-rice mixed with sugar;
they also offered worship and then begged for forgiveness.
They drank the nectar-like water from my feet, and I likewise [drank] that at that time.
"Endowed with blessings and made objects of my grace through compassion,
may enjoyment and liberation indeed arise for you always as you desire.
Then, O Lakṣmī, I was desirous of departing from you at that time.
Desirous of beholding Kṛṣṇa and seeking the direct vision of him, they entreated me;
and I, having been directed by the thought "so be it," stationed myself there.
They beheld me as Hari, bearing the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
Having attained supreme wonder like those who have realized yoga directly,
they then quickly manifested as divine beings of celestial form;
they danced, sang, and rejoiced with exceeding joy.
They worshipped me, the Supreme Brahman, the protector, the guardian of their very lives.
(94) Then, while they were looking on, I vanished from that image.
From that time forward, they too have remained devoted to the worship of the image. (95)
In every way, thousands of devotees offered themselves to Him.
Then, when the time had arrived, [He accepted] the devotee Dāmaśilādaka,
his many devoted servants, and likewise his wife named Kalā.
By means of this celestial chariot, I have brought you to my supreme, eternal, and imperishable abode. Thus, O Lakṣmī, protection has been afforded by me, devotion has been instilled,
knowledge and power have been granted, and auspicious liberation has also been bestowed.
In this way, I grant liberation at the end for my devotees;
through devotion, I am also attainable, and I bestow divine nature as well.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even praising this [account], [one attains these fruits].
"Enjoyment indeed becomes liberation, and likewise the desired goal bestows auspiciousness;
the beloved Śrī Guru is my master, lord, and sovereign, and I am the refuge for all. (3.215.100).

Thus ends the fifteenth [chapter] of the Third Section, the Dvāpara Cycle, in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, titled "The Description of how the Blessed Lord protected the servants of the devotee named Dāmaśilāda, who subsisted on stone, and brought about the final liberation of Dāmaśilāda and the others."
