[Author: Chapter 217.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of those who are skilled in the arts of craftsmanship.

[He was] named Sañjayadeva, my devotee; [I shall describe his] auspicious [life]. (1) A devotee of me, Nārāyaṇa, he resided in the city of Kutarka. Together with his family, he constantly worshipped me, the Lord of Śrī. (2)
He knows the artisan in its many forms—those born of wood, stone, and minerals; trees, creepers, and clusters of blossoms; gods, sages, and humans;
as well as beasts, birds, snakes, insects, and so forth, along with their essential principles.
He understands every kind of thing exactly as it is, through his subtle power.
In every kind of artistic craft, Sañjayadeva indeed depicts me, Hari, within [the work],
in my most subtle form and essential nature.
He performs that which is indispensable so that others may not know it;
he provides the primary craft, the intermediate craft within it, and the auspicious "Me" within that,
because he remembers Me as the artisan endowed with seed-syllables (sabīja).
O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, that which is offered to You becomes divine, like the excellent yoga of Kṛṣṇa.
(7) Thus, the devotee always performs the offering to Kṛṣṇa as being composed of Me;
every craft is of My nature, adorned by fruitful endeavor. (8)

Within himself, the devotee perceives devotion as being composed of His own essence— that devotion in which I, Nārāyaṇa, am fashioned and brought forth. And in all the arts and crafts, he perceives me, Nārāyaṇa, Hari.
He gazes, meditates, performs [rites], bows, and even worships.
Having risen daily at dawn, he meditates and performs my worship:
the bathing of the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), likewise bathing with holy waters (tīrtha), and the offering of water for honor (arghya).
They always offer me ornaments, cosmetics, and garments;
likewise, incense, lamps, food offerings, betel, and water;
as well as the essence of fragrant oil and a costly seat or couch. (12)
Having bowed down and prostrated like a staff, he offers praise to me;
he constantly petitions for welfare both in this world and the next—
for association with the virtuous, service to Kṛṣṇa, and the chanting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s glories.
At the onset of night, Sañjaya constantly performs dancing, singing, and listening to stories of Kṛṣṇa’s wonders within his home, together with his wife Keśavatī and his son Suradeva. (15)
He prepares auspicious offerings as a gift for the temple;
having partaken of the consecrated food, he thereafter always remains engaged in service.
Thus, Sanjayadeva indeed abides steadfastly in devotion to me. (16–17)
Other artisans and laborers abide under his command;
they too, through the yoga of their service, worship the Supreme Lord.
(18) Now, once upon a time, there was a king named Khaḍgavarman, the ruler of Vihāra.
He summoned him for the construction of his own new palace.
(19) Within the chambers of that seven-storied mansion, in every corner and at every spot, he intended to install statues of all the most famous species [of beings]. (20)
The king issued the command, demonstrating magnanimity even in the expenditure of wealth;
bestowing gifts and satisfying the artisans, he showed his generosity.
This devotee, filled with great joy, accepted the king's command.
Having worshipped the auspicious earth according to the proper rite,
he had it excavated there and performed the consecration with the hand of the king.
Indeed, a seven-storied palace was completed, resembling the abode of Indra.
In various places, they installed even very large, beautiful, diverse, gentle,
and captivating images of Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Rādhā, and Śrī.
And [the images] of Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Māṇikī, and the wives of Brahmā;
also the auspicious forms of the incarnations of Śrī Hari and of the lords, as well as the images of the goddesses, the great sages, the gods, and the yogins. || 25–26 ||
Of goddesses and gods, of humans and birds, of wild animals and domestic creatures—of all embodied beings;
likewise, of purifying, auspicious, and renowned images. (27)
He also showed him the lovely sights of plants that sprout from the earth, as well as rivers,
mountains, planets, lightning moving through the sky,
clouds, and oceans. (28–29)
Having constructed such a great mansion at various locations,
he established me, the subtle and infallible Nārāyaṇa, within it.
With a serene mind, that devotee offered the dwelling to me.
The king summoned the Brahmins and had them perform the consecration of the site (vāstupūjā). He caused sacrificial offerings, feasts, and acts of worship to be performed;
the king bestowed gifts, ritual fees, and rewards.
To the artisans, he gave an elephant adorned with golden ornaments;
he also gave five villages, as well as male and female servants.
And to the craftsmen, the king gave wealth and other gifts according to their merit.
Then, as Sañjayadeva was proceeding toward his own home mounted upon a decorated lordly elephant,
at that very moment the elephant suddenly became frantic and overcome with excessive rut on the road.
Invincible and exceedingly powerful, he moved about with a distracted and frenzied mind;
though beyond discipline, he became a source of great delusion and transgression.
Unrestrainable even by elephant-keepers, he was inaccessible and likewise terrifying.
Causing great nourishment and possessed of a great forceful flow, it ran uncontrolled along a wrong path;
indeed, men fled in fear solely for the sake of protecting their lives. (37–38)
Indeed, no one remained there where the elephant went;
Ambālikā, along with the driver's box, was overturned and fell to the ground.
Sañjaya, the mahout, also fell and collapsed.
The elephant, seizing my devotee Sañjayadeva with its trunk, suddenly flung him a great distance; the devotee fell into a pit.
Indeed, in the midst of that pit which was devoid of any exit, he fainted from the agony of the fall.
There, the elephant remembered me, Hari, the protector of devotees, within his heart. As soon as the elephant had gone far away,
men came from all sides to dig there and to search for him for his protection.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, I went to the side of that devotee;
touching him with both my hands, I dispelled his fainting fit and his pain.
I granted him the vision of myself as Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa.
Taking him by the hand, I drew him out from the pit;
the devotee became healthy, free from disease, and devoid of all affliction and suffering.
Indeed, while wandering in the forest, he was deluding men by making them worship me.
The Blessed One said: "He has indeed come here for my protection.
By his hands, I am free from disease and I remain here without affliction.
Thus, let everyone worship Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord."
Having said this, he pointed with his finger at me standing before him—
Kṛṣṇa, who had assumed the form of a brahmin, his excellent body pervaded by splendor.
They prostrated before me and Hari, who possessed a divine human form.
They prayed for what is auspicious, and I also instructed them:
"Auspiciousness arises through devotion to Kṛṣṇa and by serving the virtuous. Therefore, one should perform every purposeful action solely for the sake of pleasing Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (3.216.50)
The favor of the virtuous is to be obtained, and likewise their qualities are to be attained.
The virtuous, who are always superior even to the gods, are auspicious and worthy of honor by those seeking liberation.
They are to be worshipped like Viṣṇu and served like Viṣṇu.
The command of the virtuous must be obeyed, and their words must be held in the mind.
One should behave before the virtuous without guile, like a servant.
Upon seeing the virtuous who are equal to Kṛṣṇa, one should bow down before them.
The virtuous, who are embodiments of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, should be contemplated within one's own heart;
they are great, capable, divine, auspicious in every respect, purifying, the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, free from transformation, and supreme. (54)
There are those who have gone beyond illusion, and I am among them.
Indeed, the destruction of my illusion will come through service to the virtuous;
all the sins of me, a commoner, shall go to their exhaustion.
In this way, one who perceives the virtues of the virtuous shall become an ocean of merit in this world.
But those wicked people in the world who revile holy yogis,
who speak among themselves of their censure and the description of the faults of the virtuous—
Just as these virtuous ones, being truly devoid of discernment, do not know how to stand, eat, drink, or speak in this world;
nor indeed do they know how to wear clothing or give a gift. (58–59)
They do not even know how to offer a welcome to one who has arrived as a guest;
yet those who give counsel strive only to proclaim their own greatness.
Desire, greed, passion, and anger exist within them just as they do in me. (3.216.60)
"This person is not virtuous; he is a liar"—thus do they seize upon faults.
Such people, who possess only the eyes of their skin, become inhabitants of hell;
after death, they are born here as servants of Yama, suffering in misery. (61–62)
Never do those who are virtuous and facing toward liberation arise;
rather, they should be known here as demonic beings who harbor malice toward the righteous.
You, however, are indeed knowers of arts and crafts, and Sañjaya especially so.
As long as he maintains my form in all its parts within the arts,
my devotion toward him and toward those objects is total.
Through such a yoga of devotion, Janārdana appeared in the form of a brahmin.
I have arrived as your protector, pleased by my service.
Having served Hari, let the virtuous go to liberation, the supreme state. The image of Kṛṣṇa is to be worshipped like Kṛṣṇa himself; it is to be honored and served like Kṛṣṇa himself.
Likewise, the virtuous (santaḥ) are to be worshipped, honored, and served just like Kṛṣṇa.
Kṛṣṇa, the great ones, and the virtuous are all endowed with sovereignty and other perfections;
they are the protectors of all, omnipresent, and possessed of power.
They enter the bodies of others and protect them from calamity and misfortune.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa, having entered the form, remains there for the sake of protection;
having entered the form directly by his own will, he shines forth.

Just as it is directly before me, so too must this boundary always and in every way be observed out of respect—both in the presence of my form and in the presence of the virtuous. Indeed, having entered directly and in every way into the hearts of the virtuous, [I abide there]. (3.216.70–71)
Therefore, I always abide [by this principle]; indeed, the virtuous are to be served.
The standard of conduct must certainly be maintained, for it is equal to my own embodied form.
Those men, however, who consider the image of the virtuous to be merely stone—
Considering virtuous men to be ordinary, the nihilists revile them.
My words and the words of the saints—which grant even liberation—they, being deluded by illusion, treat as false and meaningless. (73–74)
The revilers and sinners will surely go to the suffering of hell;
in them, no knowledge of the self, the supreme self, and so forth arises.
No certainty regarding Kṛṣṇa arises for one who has resorted to my form.

Indeed, for such as these, there is never any auspiciousness at all; their wickedness is indeed manifest in their very forms. But among the virtuous, such [qualities] exist in that same way toward their own chosen deities. (76–77)
Due to a lack of control over their own destiny and other such factors, great sinners develop atheism;
they do not believe in the incarnations of the Lord at all,
nor in Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Śrīpura, or the imperishable abode.
Those wicked people do not consider the state of Brahmā to be a source of prosperity.
Through association with the wicked, wickedness arises; likewise, wickedness indeed arises through the connection with prior sins and the like. (3.216.80)
Through association with the words and discourses of nihilists,
as well as through the defects such as lust, anger, and pride, wickedness arises.
O Hari, the disposition of the virtuous does not abide in the heart of a wicked person.
Therefore, in this world, men who desire liberation must never associate with a wicked person who is like a donkey or similar beast. Instead,
they should listen to the divine and auspicious stories of Hari, which bestow divine awakening.
The divine pastimes of the holy ones must always be heard by their servants;
association with the holy ones and with Nārāyaṇa must also be cultivated.
The divinity of the holy ones must be understood, and my own abiding presence within their forms must be understood.
My greatness is to be known by me, and one like me is to be understood by the virtuous.
(85) I provide protection in every way for such a devotee, just as protection was granted here by me to Sañjaya in the pit. (86)
"Abiding within the image, I shall provide supreme protection so that they may worship me;
through non-violence, I, Kṛṣṇa, dwell within all living beings.
My devotees here must conduct themselves in every way with compassion. (87)
Non-malice is a powerful dharma; bringing joy is the supreme dharma.
One should bring joy through the disposition of offering one's all, and never cause harm—whether by body, speech, mind, action, or service. (88–89)
One should please me and the virtuous; from that, one shall attain heaven and liberation.
For anger, egoism, pride, and other such faults are injurious and must be avoided. One should always abide in tranquility and worship Janārdana.
"The virtuous ones, who possess the true essence of the Lord's feet, are to be venerated.
(91) Having spoken thus, he gave to my devotees the mantra centered upon me:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (92)
Having accepted the worship offered by the devotees, I quickly vanished.
The elephant, however, was captured with great effort by the king’s men;
once pacified by soothing treatments, they then handed it over to Sañjaya.

Then, O Lakṣmī, when my prosperous devotee’s lifespan was complete, I, Acyuta, appeared in person at his house for the purpose of granting him liberation. Taking that devotee, as well as others, upon the elephant-vehicle, I departed.
Having displayed my divine power, I quickly brought the king together with his army to the supreme,
eternal, and divine abode; likewise, I led other skilled artisans, men,
and devoted women to that highest realm.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have provided protection;
even when cast into a pit, my image is fashioned by those skilled in the arts, and they worship me.
Possessing divine natures through their devotion, they go to my supreme abode.
In whatever kind of *śālagrāma* stones I may dwell,
and among virtuous, chaste, and holy yogis—
I abide in all places, as well as in consecrated images. (99)
I remain especially established as the fulfiller of the minds of my devotees.
Wherever my residence may be—whether in wood, on a wall, or upon a stone slab—everything becomes divine through association with me, who am divine. (3.216.10–101)
Through my yoga, women, men, trees, and so forth become divine;
by my yoga, they always become divine and bestowers of liberation.
Faults indeed arise as virtues, and the insentient truly become sentient.
"By my yoga, whatever divine things may arise [come forth].

(103) Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Blessed Lord Protected and Liberated the Elephant through the Devotion of Sañjayadeva, the Artisan," in the third section, the Dvāpara Age, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. (216)
← Chapter 216 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā/Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) Chapter 217 [[Author: Chapter 218 →
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the auspicious and purifying story of my devotee named Saṃbharadeva, as told by Citrakṛt. 1.
In the village of Mahāgrāma in Saurāṣṭra, during the Nimbaka period,
there lived a devotee named Saṃbhara-deva, who was skilled in the art of painting. He was an independent creator and the very embodiment of all forms of art.
Just as there is the state of being for a human, a beast, or even a bird;
and for insects, trees, creepers, and the elements such as earth and water—just as their form, color, nature, visibility, and activity [are distinct]. (3–4)
Just as her radiance, her smile, her gestures, and her postures were,
so too did she suddenly manifest them all through the brush upon the paintings,
and likewise upon cloth scrolls, on walls, in dramatic performances, and in statues. (5)
In palaces, temples, and in every kind of chamber of white-plastered mansions;
and upon walls, wooden panels,
and in all manner of statues, that painter brings forth the various qualities and characteristics of ordinary life.
Endowed with such arts, he worships me incessantly;
indeed, among all wonders, he creates my subtle form.
Having made himself exceedingly subtle, he truly perceives that his purpose is fulfilled.

That painting in which Hari is not present is a painting of fruitless action. That painting in which the form of Hari is present is a painting of fruitful action. In this way, his very activity was always permeated by Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (3.217.10)
Her livelihood was always devoted to painting and centered on Kṛṣṇa;
even in her dreams, while engaged in painting, the Lord, the Consort of Śrī, appeared before her.
Rising in the morning, He would address her by name, saying, "O Nārāyaṇī! (11).
"Rādhākṛṣṇa! Harikṛṣṇa! Śrīmatkṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
(12) Having thus remembered and called out, he then bathes and worships the Lord with all available offerings, and offers incense and lamps. (13)
Having offered the food offering, water poured like a staff, the waving of lights, and circumambulation,
and having requested forgiveness, he partakes of the excellent prasāda;
then he proceeds to the picture gallery and engages in the painting of pictures.
Many other painters were also there;
they too, as laborers, devoted themselves with great devotion to me alone—the Supreme Self, Śrīnātha, the son of Kambharā. (15–16)
The cowherd boy, the beloved lord of Brahman, the husband of Māṇikī, the lord of incarnations, the lord of the liberated, and the destroyer of suffering—
meeting together at night, they all glorify the Lord of Ramā.
They dance before the form and likewise sing songs.
Then Sambharadeva also, impelled by the circle of devotees,
offers a description of the form for the sake of attaining meditation upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
"Let the painters listen to me: Hari shines within my heart.
I shall describe Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, Hari, as I have seen him—the Lord of the Imperishable, the husband of the beloved of Brahmā, possessing a divine human form. (3.217.20)
Pervaded by a halo of splendor, possessing the brilliance of ten million times ten million suns,
illuminated by all his excellent limbs which exude nectar,
he has a height of fifty-five and a quarter finger-breadths and possesses golden hair.
The Lord has golden hair and a golden form, consisting entirely of gold;
his face bears a serene smile, and he has a long, round face.
His eyes extend as far as his ears, and he is as beautiful as ten million gods of love.
His eyes were filled with love, possessing divine and direct vision;
his forehead was broad and elevated, marked with a mole at its center,
and adorned with a mole situated above the hairline on the right side of the brow.
In the upper corner of the right side and in the upper corner of the left side,
his forehead is radiant, adorned with black sesame seeds of equal size;
on the hairline of the upper part of the left side, there are two tiny sesame seeds.
On his left cheek, which possesses the beauty of a deep curve at the corner of the eye, he bears a sesame mark;
on his right cheek, he is endowed with four minute sesame marks;
and above each of his two ears, he is endowed with a single minute sesame mark. (27–28)
His divine eyes were as beautiful as sesame flowers and captivating to the mind;
he was adorned with two ears graced by long earlobes, and his teeth shone like jasmine buds, enriched with a fine, white luster. (29)
Resplendent with a pair of lips shining like ripe bimba fruits;
with a full face, a beautiful chin, and fine, reddish-brown hair;
bearing a saffron tilaka on his forehead and a crescent-shaped mark of kunkuma in the center.
His forehead is adorned with a long line extending to both edges,
and it is graced by a central line resembling a half-moon.
A fine mole shines upon his left neck above the collarbone.
In the hollow of the throat, a black sesame seed shines forth auspiciously.
The tongue resembles a red land-lotus and is the abode of Sarasvatī;
and below the hollow of the throat, at a depth of one finger-breadth, there is a sesame seed.
On the right shoulder there is a very small sesame seed, and below that another sesame seed;
and below that on the arm, there is indeed a third sesame seed as well.
And below that, a fourth auspicious sesame seed is also present.
The fifth *tila* is located on the upper arm near the elbow;
the sixth *tila* is on the upper arm above the elbow joint.
Furthermore, at the joint of the elbow, there is a subtle group of five *tilas*.
A sesame mark exists on the upper back portion above the elbow;
there is a fine sesame mark on the palm, and a sesame mark is also present on the back of the hand. On the back of the hand, there is a beautiful cluster of six ball-like marks (laḍḍukas).
Upon her palms there are lines in the form of a fish, a bow, a banner, a trident, and arrows;
likewise, there are lines of the svastika and the wheel, all red upon her moon-like radiance.
Her fingers are tender and endowed with red, elevated nails. (38–39)
The lines of hair are auspicious and shine with a golden hue;
there is a conch-mark at the tip of the middle finger, and discus-marks on all four fingers.
There is a barley-corn mark on the forefinger, and the hand is as radiant as the moon.
On the left shoulder, at the base of the clavicle, a dark mark shines beautifully.
Below that, near the arm, there are three tiny moles.
On the back of the shoulder, there is also a very minute mole of red color.
A single mole shines beautifully on the left side of the belly, near the flank of Nala.
Furthermore, the navel is deep and sunken, and the belly is radiant.
Three folds shine upon the navel, and the belly is well-proportioned.
Three *tilaka* marks shine beautifully on the right side of the abdomen;
one *tilaka* on the right back, and two *tilakas* on the right flank. The nipples are dark-colored, hairy, and endowed with beauty. (44–45)
His chest is broad and elevated, marked with the Śrīvatsa sign;
below the chest, there is a fine mole upon the upper part of his abdomen.
On his left arm, by the side of his flank, there indeed resides a beautiful mole.
On her left arm there is a very beautiful tilaka mark (47).
Likewise, at the joint of the left elbow there are two small tilakas;
on the forearm there is a fine tilaka, and the nails of the fingers of her hand are auspicious (48).
On the middle fingers there are lines like conch shells, and on all four [fingers] there are wheels;
the palms of the hands and likewise the nails are red, resembling land-lotuses.
They are radiant, with a steady luster and form that is utterly enchanting.

A divine form, beautiful as ten million gods of love, shines forth, filled with the fullness of youth and capable of shattering the fortitude of women. Adorned with a sacred thread, she is further graced by a radiant necklace upon her neck.
In her hand she holds a rosary, and in another a pen;
her form shines forth, endowed with weapons such as the discus and accompanied by the sacred narrative.
On the hip of Bālakṛṣṇa, the form of Lakṣmī shines resplendent.
Indeed, two sesame seeds shine upon the upper and lower parts of the center of the linga.
Two beautiful sesame seeds reside on the right hip,
and two sesame seeds shine on the lower part of the right thigh.
Her two knees are exceedingly beautiful and likewise shine, being perfectly rounded.
On the lower part of the right knee, on the calf, there is a sesame seed mark;
likewise, in the middle of the inner side, a black sesame seed mark shines most beautifully.
On the joint of the left thigh, an excellent mole shines beautifully.
Beside that, on the part of the thigh, there is indeed a large mark of a wound;
furthermore, on the left hip, there is a very fine mole.
Upon his left thigh sits Śrī, resembling the full moon;
she is invisible, radiant, divine, and the fulfiller of all desires.
The shanks of the Supreme Self are as thick as an elephant’s trunk.
The two hands of Śrī Ramāpati hang down as far as his knees.
Indeed, a single mole exists on the lower part of the left forearm;
it is auspicious, located near the ankle and close to the base of the foot.
A second auspicious mark, a subtle tilaka, is present upon the line;
moreover, three ankle-bones are found on each outer side of the foot.
The soles of the feet resemble *kammānika* flowers and are as delicate as the *śirīṣa*.
And upon his reddish palms, the lines are adorned with rows of hair (62). Indeed, on the upper joints of the fingers and thumbs there are golden hairs;
likewise, all his nails shine like the moon and are elevated (63).
On the palms of the feet of the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) are the divine marks;
on his form, the subtle marks described by Samudra are also present.
The nine-fingered blossoming liṅga of the Supreme Self exists there.
And on his two feet, auspicious upward-pointing lines appear, O knower of Brahman.
The voice of Hari is always sweet, like the flowing of nectar;
and in Bālakṛṣṇa, there exists supreme generosity and beauty.
Compassion, beauty, and the possession of auspicious qualities;
|| 66 || the imperishable valor of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa exists.
All sovereignties are indeed present, as well as all powers. || 67 ||
All the splendors of adornment and all wonders come to pass;
all marvels exist within the wealth of this sovereign of kings.
Indeed, all his fortunes possess the quality of attracting [all beings].
Indeed, all states of sweetness and all oceans of bliss exist here in the Supreme Self;
all festivals and all joys are present in Him. He is the fulfillment of all desires and the inner ruler of all. (3.217.70)
Like Hari, he possesses the state of being more beloved than all that is beloved, as well as the quality of giving everything;
he always possesses omniscience and the capacity to assume all forms.
Standing by his side are Śrī Rādhikā, Padmāvatī, Māṇikī, and Ramā.
Nārāyaṇī, Sukhadā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Kamalā, and others— these beloveds of Brahmā, as well as the liberated ones, the Sāṃkhya-yoginīs, the Kumāris,
and the Gopīs who are dear to Hari— all serve Him in this manner. (72–73)
The liberated attendants, as well as their mounts and weapons,
serve his sovereign powers and his manifestations which are equal to him.
For the sake of the liberation of all living beings, he exists within the human state of birth.
He alone possesses a divine form, whether he be human or non-human.
He is the Lord himself present here in human form, accompanied by his own splendor as well as by liberated attendants and others. (75–76)

The sphere of activity of the Supreme Lord proceeds with his entire retinue; there is no distinction whatsoever between his human and divine states. Wherever Kṛṣṇa is, there reside the abode, the liberated souls, and the powers.
All [of them] are divine, embodied, possessing form, and resemble Kṛṣṇa.
Those men and women become divine in form and liberated.
You all, indeed, are divine yogins of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Let them worship here the eternal Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī, the son of Gopāla and Kambharā, who holds a flute in his hand; let them constantly chant the name of the Lord of Śrī and meditate upon the Consort of Kamalā.
"May those who serve the Beloved of Māṇikī attain supreme bliss!"—
thus does my devotee, standing in the midst of the circle of devotees, constantly instruct his fellow devotees with these words that bestow auspiciousness. (81–82)
The devotees regard Sambharadeva as their own teacher and master; they honor him, worship him, offer devotion, and serve him.
Then, on one occasion, I became pleased on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha.

Having observed the worship of the Guru and the worship of the deity performed by them in that house, I quickly assumed the auspicious form of Saṃbhara-deva. [Thinking: "Saṃbhara-deva is in the house, while I am in the courtyard. (84–85)
Beholding those two deities, Saṃbhara and Deva, all the people who were their worshippers and the painters alike fell into a state of confusion mixed with wonder;
going again and again, they looked at them both in the courtyard and in the house. (86)
"How can there be two distinct forms of the Guru, each being real?
(87) Then they conducted an investigation at home and then in the courtyard; they performed the *ārātrika* rite for both of them simultaneously. (88)
The radiance within the body of the householder became obscured,
whereas the light of the lamps situated at the crossroads was unobscured.
They perceived [the Lord] within the midst of the body and concluded that Hari was at the crossroads.

They said that in the house he was in the form of the Guru; therefore, O Śrīguru, from the house Sambhara quickly went outside to the sacrificial altar to meet Hari. While everyone looked on, Hari quickly became merged within Sambhara.
Considering this to be a most great wonder, they, filled with longing, offered praise:
"O Hare, Kṛṣṇa! O Hare, Viṣṇu! O Lord Nārāyaṇa, O Master!
Grant us Your grace so that we may behold You directly once again. (62)
They danced before their guru and performed recitations;
they offered various kinds of worship to both the guru and the image.
Then, at the time of midday, on the auspicious occasion for the offering of the food oblation (naivedya), [they performed these acts].

Then, O Rame, I myself appeared there once again in the form of a Guru. Then they beheld me, the Guru Hari, in a divine form—four-armed, marked with the discus and other signs, and the Lord of Śrī. ||95||
Resplendent and wearing a crown, marked with the signs described by the Guru;
adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, head-ornaments, rings, and the like;
distinguished by garments and ornaments enriched with chains and precious gems. (96–97)
They brought food and fed me, and likewise performed the nightly lamp-offering (ārātrika).
They indeed gave me water, betel-leaf, and excellent fragrances.
Men and women alike massaged my feet in every way.
They offered words of blessing to me, and I bestowed upon them the gift of liberation. The painter quickly spoke of his worship and vanished from the image.
All of them, with joyful hearts, worshipped me in the form of their guru.

[He came] to Hari, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Śrī. Then, when another period of time had arrived and the lifespan of Saṃbhara was nearly exhausted, He of the divine form came together with an elephant to lead [him away]. (101)
He showed his own elephant to Saṃbhara-deva;
then he revealed his own true form, the divine Īśvara.
Thereafter, he granted a vision of himself to Saṃbhara-deva.
Having thus fashioned that devotee Sambhara with a divine body, and having likewise fashioned his wife, named Citrasarit, with a divine form,
he placed them upon a golden elephant and took them to Ambalika.
He led him to the most excellent imperishable abode, as well as others whose devotion had reached its fruition.
(105) Thus, O Lakṣmī, the artisan Citraka was uplifted by me as my follower.
From reading or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation will surely be attained. (106)

Thus ends the two hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of How the Lord Granted a Vision and Liberation through Devotion to the Painter named Saṃbhara-deva," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 218 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 218.
[The Author: Chapter 219.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, listen to the story of the remover of the charcoal.
Of the one who dwells on the slopes of Jharaṇā, the devotee Mauktikeśin—
Mauktikeśin is my devotee, a sovereign friend of the Pārtha lineage,
who always illuminates the mines and the peaks of his family. 1–2.
There, by the thousands, people working with charcoal in the mine dig up the black *pārtha* wood of excellent quality day and night.
Having eaten his morning meal, he then proceeds toward the mine.
For a moment, he causes my servants there to perform worship for me.
Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare Hare!
O Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Śrī, Hare Hare!
Having thus prepared and caused the vessel to be fashioned,
he quickly enters the mountain cave together with his workmen;
they then bury the black stone fragments and charcoal within the cavern.
They worship me, the Blessed One, the Lord of Śrī, at the moment of their exhaustion.
Having eaten at midday, the ritual practitioners rest;
then Mauktikeśī awakens the people with divine consciousness, just as she does.
Without the worship of Kṛṣṇa, this profound and vast cycle of worldly existence—bottomless and composed of latent desires—cannot be crossed by anyone at all.
Countless millions of births, deaths, old age, and diseases are its crossing-places. (9)
Likewise, there are various levels of karma there that impel one toward different activities.
Without devotion to Hari alone, a person does not attain the end [of suffering].
One who is unattached and associates with the virtuous attains the final goal through dispassion.
These two exist in the heart, opposed to one another and having different spheres of activity:
one leads one into illusion (māyā), while the second leads one to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
One says, "I shall enjoy illusory objects."
The second says, "I shall certainly not eat these illusory things.
In that case, there is one which is the mind alone, illusory and directed toward illusory objects;
the second is the self named the living soul (jīva), which always performs the act of negation.
Having thus discerned, one should know the Supreme Lord by means of the self;
one should abandon other objects here that obstruct liberation.
The latent impression (vāsanā), joined with the mind, is the impeller even toward sense-objects.
Arising from words concerning worldly objects, she even says, "Eat! (16).

But arising from the context of the discourse of the virtuous, that [consciousness] dwelling within the self through cultivation indeed issues the prohibition, "Do not eat," regarding illusory things. (17)
Worldly talk should be cast out, and the nectar of the discourse of the virtuous should be retained.
Father, mother, friend, kinsman, sister, brother, maternal uncle;
son, wife, queen, cow, horse, clothing, house, and wealth—[all these are transient]. (18)
"‘This is mine’ and ‘this is yours’—such are the worldly latent impressions (vāsanās).
Caused by the notions of ‘I-ness’ and ‘mine-ness,’ they cast [beings] into the abyss;
they wander through the ritual sections of the Vedas and are born again and again. (3.218.20)
Having indeed taken to heart the words of the virtuous who bestow auspiciousness:
"Neither father, nor friend, nor kinsman, nor brother, nor maternal uncle, nor sister;
nor son, nor wife, nor queen, nor cow, nor horse, nor clothing, nor house, nor wealth [are truly one's own]. (21)
This is not mine, nor is this yours; rather, it belongs to the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is my father, mother, friend, kinsman, and husband;
I, however, am the eternal servant of Śrī Hari, a conscious being.
My father and mother are indeed the givers of liberation; I am their servant, possessed of great devotion.
For me there is no bondage, no *māyā*, no ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*), and nothing that belongs to "mine" (*māmaka*).
Pure by nature, a devotee of Hari, I am liberated through the company of the virtuous.
Indeed, latent impression (*vāsanā*) is bondage; liberation is the dissolution of latent impression.

In this worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) abounding in suffering, true happiness exists only in the state of Kṛṣṇa. The words of the world are the words of the wise; they contend as bringers of awakening. (25–26)

For those who possess great strength in that knowledge called discernment (*viveka*), which is constantly engaged in battle within the heart, victory shall indeed belong to them alone. Where Nārāyaṇa resides, and where the holy ones who grant liberation dwell— there [victory lies].
In that very place resides victory, while the power of illusion (māyā) becomes fruitless.
Kṛṣṇa dwells in the hearts of the virtuous, and victory always belongs to the virtuous—those in whose hearts the saints, who are the very embodiment of instruction, reside. (28–29)
Through the medium of sacred narratives, Kṛṣṇa remains ever-present in the hearts of those for whom he dwells;
for them, strength and victory arise that bestow the attainment of liberation. However, internal virtuous beings flourish through association with external virtuous ones.
Through association with external non-virtuous beings, internal non-virtuous states flourish.
(31) In those that have flourished, power increases; in those that have not flourished, there is decay.
Therefore, the virtuous should be nourished, but never the non-virtuous. (32)
To whatever extent the virtuous may become pleased, to that same extent one’s livelihood is secured;
the satisfaction of the virtuous is nourishment, and through that, the favor of Kṛṣṇa is attained.
When this occurs, victory indeed arises for the individual soul.

One attains even the kingdom of liberation and the great bliss of service to Kṛṣṇa (34). For the devotee who strives for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and for the sake of serving the saintly, the Lord, the self-sovereign, becomes a witness as he fights (35).
If death occurs only in battle, the Lord will certainly be pleased.
In battle, there is both death and victory; the Lord is pleased with him [who dies].
He knows that "this one has gone to his death out of a desire for what is dear to his master."
One who has never turned his back [in battle] truly deserves victory;
for his master surely grants him a reward even greater than that of the victor.
Therefore, one should fight against the strong with chest forward, facing the enemy in the pursuit of victory.
One should die facing the enemy with one's chest forward for the sake of pleasing one's master;
one should die with devotion and righteousness, with the Lord who bears the Śārṅga bow present before one's heart.
One should die by serving the virtuous, with the Lord who wields the discus present within one's body.
Through devotion to Hari in his human form, one must proceed to the depths of the cave.
Bad association must be abandoned in every way, while good association must certainly be cultivated.
The stories of the virtuous should be heard, and Kṛṣṇa should always be held within the heart.
One should go for refuge to Hari solely for the sake of immediate supreme bliss;
certainly not for the sake of bodily comfort, nor even for the acquisition of wealth or sons.
Nor should one go for refuge to Hari out of greed for kingship or similar worldly gains.
One should go for refuge to Hari with a disposition free from desire,
because a disposition characterized by desire arises as an obstacle to liberation.
Since the taking of refuge must be abandoned when desire is frustrated, that [desiring disposition] is not appropriate here.
That which is preceded by desire should be grasped, but that which is preceded by the absence of desire should also be grasped;
for liberation arises with certainty through that which is thus to be grasped.
Those possessed of desire, however, worship Hari with devotion for the sake of attaining their desires.
When their desires fail, they utterly abandon even their spiritual cultivation (bhāvanā).
They completely reject the awakening of the virtuous; what need is there to mention [their rejection of] the state of the Blessed One?
On the contrary, they even practice atheism and engage in slander.
Those who are motivated by their own self-interest fall indeed into the hells;
therefore, one should serve the Lord Hari with a desireless disposition.
For even though He fulfills the intentions of those with desires out of His compassion, [one should not seek Him for such ends].

The Lord, who takes account of what has been done, surely bestows upon His devotees who have sought refuge the fruit born of taking refuge in devotion—a fruit of infinite qualities. Yet, being under the control of His devotee, He reduces even the great suffering of that devotee to something very small. (3.218.49–50)
Indeed, the boundary of karmas was bound by that very wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
Hari, remaining within, always bestows the fruit according to one's prārabdha,
with equal treatment, yet especially out of compassion.
The Supreme Lord is independent, the creator of all, and the regulator.
Even those who have committed extremely wicked deeds would become [liberated] if they [worship] this true Lord;
for out of compassion, Śrī Hari [destroys] even their very many karmas.
Those things which are to be enjoyed over a long period of time, yet are harmful and bring suffering,
he indeed makes them enjoyable for only a short time and of little value.
He completely wards off the pain of a thorn by means of a stake.
The giver of food and clothing wards off the suffering of extreme poverty.
Devotees alone recognize this grace of Hari, and no others;
for those who are not devotees of Hari even imagine faults where there are no virtues.
Having cast aspersions on his lack of sovereignty, they even abandon those who rely upon him; they revile those equal to themselves and call them "inarticulate babblers.
[Thinking], "I have regarded him as my lord and have expended my wealth in every way," [they speak thus]. (57)

Although the virtuous have been honored by me through the surrender of all my possessions, nevertheless, not even a slight bit of my suffering has been removed by him. Furthermore, I did not recognize his service to me; what will he do for me in the future? (58–59)
Therefore, I have abandoned this which bears the meaning of the word Nārāyaṇa;
having thus abandoned it, one surely goes from there into the hell of Māyā. Therefore, devotion to Kṛṣṇa must indeed be practiced with a desireless mind.
O Lakṣmī, service to [Mādhava] is for one's own spiritual welfare and never for the attainment of desires.
Mādhava does not accept the service of a devotee who possesses desire;
the state of having desires in a servant is a defect characterized by greed. (61–62)
Thirst, desire, and longing are indeed but different forms of transgression. A devotee of Hari should never harbor longing for Him in any way.
If such longing remains unfulfilled, it constitutes an offense against the Supreme Self.
Indeed, there is a great offense against Nārāyaṇa that constitutes betrayal.
He does not tolerate betrayal, suffering, censure, the description of faults, the disparagement of virtues, or the false attribution [of defects]. (64–65)
Hari does not forgive even the slightest offense committed against Him or His devotee; therefore, such an offense must never be committed under any circumstances.
This includes the disparagement of the form of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
The disparagement of those possessing virtues and the refutation of the virtuous are indeed great offenses that bestow great hells;
they must never be committed, whether knowingly or unknowingly, even when engaged in a dispute. (67–68)
In the supreme divine world, in his own imperishable state,
the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), dwells with a divine form. He, the Lord of Māṇikī, is served by countless divine liberated souls (brahmamuktas).

Out of compassion, that Lord exists here in human form. (3.218.70) Just as the divine is seen here in a human, material body, yet he does not remain material but is divine, like the Imperishable. (3.218.71)
That which is our physical eye is the object of perception for Him, just as He is for it;
by His very grace, Hari indeed reveals Himself here to us. Just as one is devoted, so is He perceived by him, for He exists under the sway of compassion.
He alone, possessing a divine form, is to be understood by the assembly of devotees.
There is nothing higher than Him, nor even anything else to be attained or known.
Yet, if His own devotee desires to behold the abodes of prosperity, [He grants that vision]. (73–74)
Then the compassionate Blessed One reveals it in every way;
that divine and imperishable abode exists together with Him.
Through His majesty, there are also sovereign powers shared with Hari.
Accompanied by his retinue, the Imperishable One (Akṣara) dwells upon the earth in his own abode;
he is perceived by the eyes of men.
His imperishable abode appears like a human being, and his qualities are identical to those of worldly activity.
Their liberated states are equal to those of humans, and their activities are like those of ordinary beings;
between those established in the celestial abodes and those on earth, not even the slightest difference exists.
Those who possess the eyes of divine samādhi perceive the most sublime realms.
Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is His abode, and there are the liberated Śaktis.
All of them accept the food, water, clothing, wealth, prosperity, houses, and so forth offered by devoted human beings, just like ordinary men. (3.218.80)
Nevertheless, being free from desire, they accept those divine [offerings] for the sake of the welfare of their devotees;
by association with them, these [devotees] become divine.
The donors, however, attain that divine form in the imperishable state.

Thus, the majesty of Kṛṣṇa, as well as that of his devotees and the virtuous, is always to be known; for it bestows divine liberation. Indeed, no calamities befall one who is endowed with the majesty of Kṛṣṇa.
Even a destitute person who is a devotee of Kṛṣṇa must never be treated with contempt;
for one who despises a pauper suffers destruction due to the resulting affliction of Kṛṣṇa residing within him.
All the activities of Kṛṣṇa are indeed divine in every respect.
Those [pastimes] of His devotees should also be considered divine by one who understands devotion.
Hari delights with human devotees for the pleasure of the minds of His devotees;
He also delights through desire and likewise delights through laughter.
He delights with women who resemble him in their gestures;
nevertheless, his state of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) amidst ten million women is a source of wonder.
Śrī Hari, assuming ten million forms, bears those women who have destroyed their lust and pride.
Assuming a human form for the sake of his devotees, he performs actions like a human being.
At times he displays desire, anger, fear, greed, delusion, grief, and envy; yet all of that is indeed for the welfare of men. (88–89)
Everything heard, spoken, seen, meditated upon,
and even rejoiced in regarding the life of Śrī Hari bestows liberation upon human beings.
Indeed, Śrī Kṛṣṇa in human form shall fulfill the hearts of men.
Through the state of being of the same nature as [the Lord], the duty of service toward Hari arises for men.
(91) By that means, one shall attain the supreme good from Him who is served and propitiated.
Even a pauper, even one in the state of servitude, even a female servant, and even one devoid of qualities—(92)
For one who has taken firm refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, there shall always be joy:
"The supreme good has been attained by me; my companions shall be liberated.
I have achieved my purpose; those who follow my words have achieved their purpose. (93)
The peaceful ones are my very selves, and I am always the seer of the Self.
There is nothing other than Hari that is to be seen by me as being composed of Māyā.
Thus, my dwelling is here upon this earth, yet also in the supreme, imperishable realm.
"There is no doubt in this matter; knowing this, worship him.
The Blessed One will provide protection both in this world and in the next.
Having thus instructed them and having heard [this], they went to the mine to perform their work.

To test them, he caused water to flow from the wall of the mine into a pit in the form of a great river; indeed, due to the breach in the wall caused by the excavation, it flowed like the current of a mighty stream. (97–98)
A torrent suddenly arose there in that abyss.
All of them, satisfied by knowledge, were freed from the fear of death.
O Rame, remember me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

The water in that abyss became indeed like a lake. Those devotees who were broken and submerged, yet remained devoted to me, the Lord of Ramā— those wise ones established in the Self— held me as their firm refuge within their hearts.
May those who rejoice in meditative absorption perceive me as their inner self;
may my devotee Mauktikeśa remember me while digging the earth.
May the exceedingly devoted one, submerged in water, [remember] Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, within the womb of the earth.
Then, for those who were free from suffering and devoted as my servants,
I appeared there in the midst of the water within that pit as the Subduer of Waters (Varuṇa).
With my Sudarśana discus, I dried up the all-pervading water.
In a mere instant, indeed in a moment, I even blocked the current;
my devotees became truly at ease upon seeing the Sudarśana discus.
Having seen me, they were submerged for a moment in eternal bliss.
Then they worshipped me and prayed for the imperishable abode for the sake of liberation alone. I said to them,
"So be it," and after instructing them on the firmness of devotion, I then quickly vanished from that place.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. Thus Mauktikeśī, the lord of the mine, gave this mantra to them.
By the mere recitation of it, they all became possessed of divine knowledge.
Then, after some time,
he brought Mauktikeśin and other men by means of a celestial chariot to my abode, the imperishable supreme state.
Thus were the Kulasānas, who had been dug up from the earth, examined.
"O Lakṣmī, they have been protected and liberated by me, drawn by my compassion.
Through the recitation and hearing of this [work], there shall be both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

(111) Thus ends the chapter titled "The Examination and Liberation through Devotion of the Bhakta named Mauktikeśin, the Lord of the Stone-Coal Mine," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the hunter as well.
There was a hunter named Cakradhara, devoted to violence, who lived in the village of Piñjala;
he was of the Śūdra caste and a thief who supported his family. (1–2)
Even one who is great becomes a thief of animals belonging to their owners;
likewise, he is a slayer of wild animals such as hares and the like.
Driven by cruelty, he commits violence for the sake of satisfying his own life-force. (3)
Then once, drawn by an intense longing for deer, he went into the forest. There,
amidst a thicket of trees, pillars, and bamboo groves, he saw the great seer Pautimāṣya in the form of a deer, as well as his wife in the form of a doe.
Seeing those two beautiful deer— named Sāma and Kṛṣṇa— who were in the form of does,
who subsisted on leaves, flowers, and grass, and fed upon fresh sprouts and fruits,
the hunter drew his arrow.
Then the sage, having looked upon him, vanished along with the doe.
Cakradhara, too, being filled with doubt, went quickly through the grove of trees where the two had gone, following their tracks step by step.
Then, by a voice from the sky, the great sage said to that hunter:
"O sinner, do not fix your mind here in vain upon one who is full of evil.
I am no deer; I am Pautimāṣya, a great sage who subsists on forest fare."
"Accompanied by my wife, I wander here in this forest constantly, established in happiness. Go elsewhere, O great sinner; you have fallen from liberation.
Having attained a human body, why do you not desire liberation?"
Having heard this, the hunter said: "I am always desirous of sense-objects; I eat meat here for the sake of nourishing my lust. Then Pautimāṣya said: "Lust brings you to hell."
For where there is violence, there is indeed unrighteousness, consisting of the killing and devouring of living beings.
"Your residence shall always be in hell"—do not speak thus.
Cast this human existence into desire and carry it to hell! (13–14)
Listen, hunter, if it pleases you, I shall tell you this for your benefit; for association with the virtuous is indeed a savior.
This passion is a defect born of the body, arising from food, drink, and the like.
The gross portion of *vīrya* arises as the constituent of the body.
(16) Throughout the entire body, particles of *vīrya* exist that provide nourishment;
these indeed constitute the gross, material form of Kāmadeva. (17)
Then the internal mind, which always resides within the *manovaha* [channel],
having moved from moment to moment through all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*),
conceives of virility and draws it into the wombs.
At the root of the *sivanī* channel, it arises concentrated as one;
accompanied by the mind, it attains non-differentiation.
Having become pervaded within the mind, it is endowed with the subtle form of the mind. (2.219.20)
By means of causes and the force of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [semen] flows from the penis through the power of action (*karman*).
Therefore, desire is threefold and always exists in three bodies.
The subtle cause, consisting of latent impressions, is of the nature of the mind.
The gross [body], however, consists of the form of semen; it is illusory and does not belong to the Self.
(22) The Self exists as the nature of Brahman, the controller of all the senses, and is distinct from hair, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and sinews. (23)
Vīrya possesses the nature of the six sheaths; the seventh is the carrier of enjoyment (bhoga).
It dwells at the impure gate and exits through the impure gate;
it is the binding of the impure body and the bestower of the city of Yama for one’s sins. (24)
From desire arise violence, anger, delusion, latent impressions, and impure thoughts.
Birth, action, death, suffering, and likewise agitation—all these arise from that evil desire; therefore, having abandoned it, conduct yourself according to dharma. (25–26)
The seasonal gift should be bestowed; this is the eternal dharma.
One should not seek excessive enjoyment, for it creates an obstacle to the path of liberation.
The virtuous sages and true women are devoted to renunciation.
Immersed in the bliss of the Self, they abandon desire far away.
(28) Through the practice of yoga, they protect the bodily constituents in every way;
constantly restraining the mind, they uproot latent impressions. (29)
Those lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) are born with upward-directed vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*);
they are free from the flow of perspiration and devoid of nocturnal emissions. Immersed in the bliss of the Self that is Brahman, those stainless ascetics (*yatayaḥ*) are born.

Indeed, they become as capable as Īśa, as masters of prosperity as Viṣṇu, and as creators of emanation as Vedhas—these lords of the supreme state. For those devoted to celibacy, however, fire and wind arise upon their rising from their seats. (31–32)
Those who possess great majesty approach in embodied form to welcome him.
At the end of his enjoyment, the supreme Brahman is to be attained by one who follows the dharma of Manu.
There is no end to craving through enjoyment; rather, craving increases within enjoyment.
Therefore, renouncing enjoyments, worship the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Seek refuge in Hari, the wielder of the discus; indeed, seek refuge in the wielder of the discus.
Having shattered the wheel of illusion, become established in the wheel of Brahman.
Thus addressed by the sage, O Lakṣmī, the noble-minded Cakradhara’s mind was indeed transformed by those instructions;
he then desired a vision of his preceptor, Pautimāṣya.
And the Guru, assuming a human form, requested an audience;
he granted him his vision, made him drink water,
gave him the water from his feet, and utterly destroyed his sins.
"Oṃ, obeisances to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā.
Having given this Vaiṣṇava mantra, he caused him to perform worship with the leaves of Vṛndāvana.
From that time forward, even the hunter took refuge in Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.

Having gone home, purified by the sacred ford, he caused his wife to be purified as well. Always abandoning violence and theft, they both worshipped me, the Supreme Lord. He constantly worships me, Kṛṣṇa, within the Tulasī tree.
Even while undertaking a pilgrimage with offerings of wild fruits obtained through divine grace,
he has since then performed the service of the virtuous constantly with such wild fruits;
indeed, appearing as a holy man, he became one who wears matted hair.

His wife wore matted hair and smeared herself with ashes; she was a worshiper of Tulasī, perfected in her vows, and contented with eating the remains of offerings. Thus, with a pure mind and through devotion, I [acted] according to the desire of the sage. (43–44)
When the time for his liberation had arrived,
I, Hari, appeared before him in a divine form; he and the woman beheld me,
and bowing down, they fell at my feet, covered in dust.
Eager for the sake of liberation, the two of them, overwhelmed with emotion, offered me a welcome;
immersed in love, they quickly presented me with wild fruits, O Gaja.
Then, casting off their bodies, they immediately ascended [to heaven] in divine forms.
O Rame, sent by me, those two went to Vaikuṇṭha.
Thus was liberation granted to the hunter through the association with a true guru.
In the same way, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of those who are devotees of the virtuous [are likewise purified].
They perish and the mind also becomes eternally pure.
Desires, anger, and other defects, as well as whatever sins there may be, vanish; through the grace of me and the virtuous, they become divine in form. (2.219.50)
They go to the supreme Brahman, O Lakṣmī, which bestows eternal bliss.
From reading or hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall come to pass.
