Chapter Two Hundred and Nineteen (219):
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age),
Chapter 220.
[The Author: Chapter 221.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to [the account] of that indeed treacherous devotee.
In the city of Sambhala, there was a devotee named Vāṭadhara who served the king and offered himself [to him].
He was a servant of the lord of the earth named Sutārasiṃha. (1–2)
He was skilled in statecraft and clever in pleasing the king; he had exerted himself in legal procedures and in the sciences of exchange and commerce.
He was a favorite of the king and a recipient of the queen’s esteem.
Devoted to the royal family, he rises above the commoners of his own station;
he perceives with sharp intellect, acts with wisdom,
deliberates with knowledge, and counsels with discernment.
Intellect (*buddhi*) is the faculty that ascertains objects; thought (*mati*) has the senses as its domain;
knowledge (*jñāna*) is the clarity of discrimination; wisdom (*prajñā*) is fresh intuition;
and consciousness (*vijñāna*) resides thus in the knower, just as it does in a skilled artisan. 6.
But for a task that is impossible to accomplish, he certainly seeks a pretext;
therefore, he brings a task to completion when dealing with kings and others—just like an elder, a minister, a judge, or a teacher. (7–8)
Although this Vāṭadhra is thus endowed with excellent conduct,
nevertheless, being under the sway of his own nature, he occasionally practices slander.
[He reports] the Queen’s words to the King, and the King’s words to the Queen and the Minister.
The minister, however, [should speak] to the subjects, the queen, and sometimes to the king,
in such a way that it remains undisclosed so that others do not know it;
thus he speaks so that the listener alone may understand.
Then once, on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), the queen gave abundant gifts to brahmins, the destitute, and virtuous men, including food and other provisions;
she also secretly gave jewels, gems, and the like, such that the king did not know of it at all.
The Queen of Dvīpa gave away wealth as a gift from her own hand. Appointed by the Queen to give, Vāṭadhara understood [the procedure];
after the gift, the Queen also gave auspicious food to the virtuous.
The virtuous who have taken refuge in Hari partake of the desired foods that are to be eaten;
among them, there was a certain ascetic named Ghaṭīyantra who was detached from worldly things.
He would stay in one place for only a single ghaṭikā and no longer than that.
While his meal was being served there in rows,
a full *ghaṭikā* passed; having risen and abandoned the food,
he went to another tree and stayed there for another *ghaṭikā*.
Having drunk water, he indeed went from there to another place;
having stayed for just one *ghaṭikā*, he repeatedly went to yet another spot.
Seeing him thus restless and having abandoned his food, the gatekeeper [reflected].
Having swept the ground in the evening, he quickly reached the place where he was sitting.
Having gone there, bowed down, offered fruit, and performed a salutation, he asked the reason for his agitation while bowing repeatedly. (3.220.20)
Ghaṭīyantra then said to him: "O Lakṣmī, the cause of your instability is this:
staying for no more than a single *ghaṭikā* in one place is your true virtue.
No bondage occurs anywhere, nor does attachment arise anywhere. (21)
Possessiveness never arises, and dispassion shall be constant.
Even non-possessiveness is a vow, and by it one is protected.
Long-term residence leads to bondage; therefore, one should not dwell for long.
Whether in water, on land, or among trees, long-term residence is fraught with danger for holy men.
Their sitting should be stable for only as long as it takes to milk a cow or for a single *ghaṭī*.
Sitting for a *ghaṭī* is appropriate in the realm of *māyā*, but in Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there is eternal sitting.
Having understood this through discernment, my discipline is to restrain restlessness.
From attachment arises affection; from affection, the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatā) comes into being.
Through that [sense of mine-ness] comes obsession, and through that, latent impressions (vāsanā) arise repeatedly therein.
Co-residence is indeed bondage; separation is the supreme liberation.
Latent impressions (vāsanā) must be abandoned in every way, and attachment must be renounced by the high-souled one.
One who possesses discernment should attain a state free from latent impressions through dispassion (vairāgya).

O Blessed One, through being intent on the ultimate goal and intent on the Self, and by perceiving suffering and its defects, one becomes free from latent impressions (*vinirvāsanatā*). [One realizes:
"I am the Self, a devotee of Hari; I do not belong to *māyā* nor to karmas. (28–29)
I am of the nature of Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss; I am distinct from the perishable body.
I am firmly established in the refuge of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Imperishable.
I have no attachment to Māyā, nor any taste for the objects of the senses.
"I dwell within the internal Śrī Vāsudeva and I rejoice [in Him].
(3.1) Thus, for the discerning one who possesses constant and firm dispassion, the sprout of attachment does not arise even when engaged with the most excellent objects. (3.2)
Even while dwelling in delightful divine enjoyments, he remains detached in mind;
remaining unattached and indifferent, he is considered one who is free from latent desires (nirvāsanaka).
Furthermore, they should adopt the virtues of the wise and recognize their divine nature.
They too shall always be rich in divine qualities and victorious over illusion.
But those who seize upon the faults and vices of the virtuous—those very desires and so forth—they indeed come to be enveloped by desire and the rest. (34–35)
Afflicted by desires and other such passions, they wander about in extreme misery;
they obtain neither liberation, nor a good heaven, nor even worldly prosperity.
Indeed, those who are revilers, sinners, and wicked men fall into the hells.
Those men and women who, in the company of the virtuous, perceive their own divinity,
go to the supreme Brahman, their divine nature having been fully cultivated;
indeed, their senses then become blunted by Māyā.
Whether he be a king or a householder, even one who is prosperous and possessed of enjoyments,
having attained such knowledge as this, he conducts himself above the realm of sense-objects;
by the force of his previously commenced merit, he remains even while situated in the midst of sense-objects.
Nevertheless, he remains like a virtuous man, free from attachment like a yogi.
For even while eating, he is truly a non-eater, just as a lotus leaf remains untouched by water;
and he performs the act of chewing chickpeas with a mouth that has no sense of sourness.
Likewise, one who is unable to grasp objects does not give rise to latent impressions (vāsanā); for one whose [intellect] is blunted, the illusory (māyikī) impression dissolves.
He who knows even a slight taste of Māyā has no latent impression at all.
The essence of illusion departs from the heart; therefore, one should abandon it.
In the directly perceived form of the Lord, one should recognize all-encompassing perfection.
By that alone, all the undertakings of the yogi of devotion are accomplished.
Having engaged in the company of the virtuous, one must understand this very point:
for one who knows thus, Hari surely accomplishes every desire. And for one who offers their mind to Hari, all latent impressions (vāsanās) perish in this world.
For one who has offered their mind to Kṛṣṇa, every moment spent apart from Kṛṣṇa feels like an eon;
in separation, there arises a great burning within the heart.
When Kṛṣṇa is attained, peace occurs, and the desire to behold him increases day by day.
Upon hearing of Kṛṣṇa’s majesty, one’s affection shall become exceedingly great;
toward activities related to Kṛṣṇa, one’s inclination shall become preeminent;
and there shall always be a state of constant devotion to the performance of Kṛṣṇa’s commands. (48)
Even though such a person remains far away, he dwells in the presence of Mādhava.

But one who transgresses commands, who is devoid of love, and who has not offered himself—even if standing right beside him, he should be understood as being far away; for a wicked lord is self-interested. (3.220.50)
Therefore, just as the Lord Mādhava dwells within one’s own heart,
so indeed should His residence be established by oneself in the imperishable state.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Thus, recite this mantra constantly and worship the infallible Lord:
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Bālakṛṣṇa, Nārāyaṇa, O Lord of Ramā!
Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Lord of the Universe! (52-53)
"Thus, cause the wise king, his ministers, and the subjects to hear this constant worship of Śrī Hari; by that, their highest good shall be attained.
In this manner, he gave the instruction on Lakṣmī to Vāṭadhara.
Dhaṭyayana was a virtuous servant of Hari, adorned with excellent qualities.
Even though he was a mere gatekeeper, he went home and performed worship as instructed;
he constantly engaged in the service of Hari, chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" at all times.
Ghaṭyayana, however, departed for another village while remembering Hari;
Vāṭadhra became a great devotee who brought about liberation.
He indeed bestowed upon the king, the queen, and the subjects the mantra that grants liberation.
He caused him to perform the recitation of "Hare Kṛṣṇa" in every way.
Indeed, for one endowed with devotion in this world, virtuous qualities do arise;
nevertheless, the innate nature of his birth—his inherent wickedness—does not cease.

Even if one were as great a devotee as Garuḍa himself, his inherent nature as a serpent-eater does not perish; it is a quality of his very birth. And though the monkeys are devotees of Rāma, they do not abandon their animal instincts.
Even though he was a devotee of Pārvatī, the lion did not abandon his predatory nature;
even though he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, that Kṣatriya did not abandon the battle;
and even though he was a devotee of Viṣṇu, the Kirāta did not abandon his forest-dwelling ways.
The cow and the devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa do not abandon grazing;
this sky-dweller, a devotee of Viṣṇu, does not abandon his crookedness.
Whether it be the property of another, or that which belongs to an enemy, or anything else consisting of virtues and faults— [he does not abandon it]. (63)
That which ought to be spoken in secret is indeed considered backbiting (piśunatā).
Whatever fruit arises from it—whether it be affliction, war, quarrel, or even mental distress, agitation, anger, or even destruction—that is its result. (64–65)
Therefore, one should never engage in backbiting against anyone;
instead, one should look for virtues rather than looking for faults.
One who perceives virtues attains happiness and becomes a possessor of merit.
One who seizes upon faults becomes miserable and is even born as a sinner.
Backbiting brings about ruin, whereas instruction bestows virtue.
One should never engage in backbiting; rather, one should occasionally offer instruction.
If there is indeed such fitness, then instruction may be given, and not otherwise— whether to one's father, mother, brother, sister, sister-in-law,
wife, husband, kinsman, disciple, daughter, or son. (69)
One should never speak slanderous words to a wife, an elder, or a child;
nor indeed should slander ever be spoken to a king, a queen, a minister, or a prince, nor to the subjects at any time, O King. (3.220.70–71)
Due to the fault of his low birth, he once committed slander,
reporting to the king that the queen had given a gift;
[specifically] that she had secretly given diamonds, gems, and other valuables to a brahmin.
"He gave food and ornaments to the virtuous.
Then the king, realizing that his hidden wealth had been given away in charity, summoned the queen and asked: "Tell me, where was the wealth and so forth that was given?"
Whatever was given without my command, or whatever was done that was not desired by me—that was indeed done improperly.
All your wealth was kept hidden; it was always preserved for your own sake.
That gift was certainly not for the purpose of charity; therefore, what was given was not appropriate.
A woman must not do anything at all without having obtained her husband’s permission.
O Queen, let her go to her father; a wife who is not beloved [by her husband] is not truly beloved. She who spends money in secret is one who will eventually bring about total ruin.
"O Goddess, such a beloved wife as this should not have been born of me to be protected at home;
go to your own father and dwell there for a long time in happiness.
Having been addressed thus, that beautiful woman was overcome with great grief and wept.
Then the king, for the sake of Khavāsa— who was like a gateway—
inflicted a punishment that stripped him of all his possessions and placed him in fetters;
for the one who acts, the one who causes another to act, and the one who approves, are all equal in this matter.
Thus the king imposed a fine and confiscated his house and garden;
he even seized the wealth and property of the gardener Bhakta.
Though bound in fetters, the gardener worshipped Hari with great humility.

Deprived of honor and deprived of food in her own palace, the queen, a devotee of Viṣṇu, quickly became established in a vow, desiring indeed to die. "In the practice of charity there is no sorrow; how then has this sorrow arrived? (82-83)
"May Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the remover of suffering, take away my pain"— thinking thus,
she remained standing before my image, having undertaken a fast.
Even while bound in shackles, Vāṭadhra likewise remained steadfast in his fast.
Thinking of Hari, there should indeed be no punishment regarding the matter of giving.
Having reported the suffering that had arisen, he meditated upon the Lord within his own heart;
yet that account spread even openly among the subjects and others.
Grief suddenly entered the subjects, the classes of brahmins, the virtuous, and the women; for the king had not done what was appropriate.
Thus, news praising his generosity spread everywhere.

"Indeed, charity is the duty of kings; what is performed by the queen is a virtuous deed. "There is no depletion whatsoever of the king's wealth, for he enjoys the fruits of his kingdom. Such exceedingly auspicious talk prevailed among the subjects. (88–89)
For the sake of destroying the queen's sorrow and for the peace of Vāṭadhāra,
the subjects, having remembered Hari, gave blessings that bestow happiness.
When the seven-day fast had passed there, Mādhava appeared at night.
I, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, went to the prison and likewise to the palace of the queen to protect my devotees;
adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, crown, and necklaces. (91–92)
Having granted her his own vision, I gave the gift of drinking milk to the queen;
thereafter, I likewise gave the gift of drinking milk to Vāṭadhra.
Having offered him consolation as well, I proceeded to the royal palace.
In the form of a brahmin, exceedingly radiant and the best among those who know the treatises on dharma,
he offered me a royal seat; and when questioned by me regarding my well-being,
he told me that my family was free from affliction and at peace.
The king related the account and the cause of his distress.
Then [the sage] instructed the king: "A woman is independent regarding her own property;
even in that regard, specifically concerning gifts, she is fit to perform meritorious deeds. (96)
Indeed, a virtuous wife who is devoted to her husband crosses over [the ocean of suffering].
The gift of cows, the gift of jewels, and the gift of ornaments truly deliver one;
the gift of the best [of things] delivers even a king, her husband, though he be a great sinner. (97–98)
"Therefore, O King, honor a virtuous woman as is fitting,
and also honor Vāṭadhra here, who performs deeds of goodness. Having said this, I myself manifested my own form, pervaded by light.
He gave Rūpa to the king, and the king fell at his feet. He begged for forgiveness and for liberation in the abode of Nārāyaṇa, saying,
"I became invisible after receiving the worship he performed."
The king honored the queen and his own attendants with respectful offerings;
he likewise caused a festival to be held and performed auspicious acts of charity.
He pacified the quarrel through affectionate words and gifts.
By means of these returns, he likewise established honor even for Vāṭadhra.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, that queen was protected by me at that time;
though she desired death and had fainted from hunger, she was given milk to drink. || 103-104 ||
The gardener, too, was my devotee and was protected from royal punishment.
Then, when the time had arrived, I took the king— who recognized his devotion—
as well as the queen and the gardener, in my own celestial chariot.
This is the imperishable, supreme abode, free from all malice.
By reciting, hearing, or remembering it, one’s sins are destroyed;
one attains worldly enjoyment, liberation, heaven, and one's own desired supreme delight.

Thus ends the two hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Protection and Liberation by the Blessed Lord of Vāṭadhara Piśunakhavāsa and Queen Dvaipī from the Punishment of King Sutārasiṃha," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 221 Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga) – Chapter 221
[The Author: Chapter 222.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the housebuilder.
In the city of Takṣaśilā, there was indeed one named Śivajaya. He was a devotee, skilled in the construction of palaces, an expert in building temples and houses,
knowledgeable in the layout of cities, and a builder of shrines and other edifices.
The preeminent artisan, by his own intellect alone, brings about the creation of artistic wonders;
he is the builder of the royal palace who has manifested novel architectural innovations.
He fashions new forms and occupies himself with new chambers and other such works.
With innumerable jewels, he constructed palaces resembling those of the gods.
(4) Once, a sage named Vṛṣaparvan approached him;
he was a great devotee of the Lord, a worshipper, virtuous in conduct, and well-restrained. (5)
Rising suddenly, Śivajaya offered a welcome;
full of devotion, he gave the sage *argha* and *madhuparka*.
He seated him upon a beautiful, pure seat and offered water.
He performed the massaging of the sage's feet and the rubbing of his limbs.
With a joyful mind, the sage inquired after his welfare; he too, upon his arrival there, told him, "I am well. (7–8)
That house where the feet of a holy man are worshipped with faith is indeed divine; any other is a cremation ground.
Today all my well-being has vanished, and my misfortune remains.
"I am blessed; today the god-like man truly shines in my house.
Having said this, he observed a vow of silence and spoke to Vṛṣaparvan:
"Tell me that which is your supreme welfare, for I have come to you for refuge."
Then, O Lakṣmī, having remembered the beginningless Nārāyaṇa, Vṛṣaparvan instructed her in many ways for the sake of Śiva’s victory and for liberation.
"O Śivajayā, listen: affection for Kṛṣṇa indeed bestows liberation."
Furthermore, through the perception of Māyā as inferior and so forth, one becomes devoid of affection for it;
however, affection for Kṛṣṇa arises from the perception of His excellence.
His excellence is such that He is Himself the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord.
Savitṛ, the lord of all abodes, the master of the virtuous,
the lord of all liberated souls, the lord of all sovereignty, and the lord of Ramā—
Kṛṣṇa is the Blessed One among the Blessed Ones, the most supreme Lord. (15)
And above all is the Inner Self, the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
(16) He is the Inner Controller, within whom nothing whatsoever exists independently; for without His will, even the powerful wind cannot move a single dry leaf. (17)
He indeed does not act for the sake of movement; he is the impeller himself.
That very Lord dwells here on earth in the form of a saint, assuming whatever form he desires, fulfilling the minds of his devotees.
Divine, possessing divine conduct, and in every way of divine form—indeed, even all his bodily actions grant liberation. Such is the greatness of Hari that dwells within his heart. (3.221.20)
The kinsmen and family members of that devotee— ten from before, ten from after, and twenty-one including himself— indeed rescue him.
They would certainly grasp the virtue of that devotee if it exists in every respect.
"Oh! A devotee of Kṛṣṇa has indeed been born in our family; he is truly a purifier.
(22) By him, our great fortune will lead to our deliverance, and through the merit of his devotion, we, his family members, shall also attain it. (23)
Those who possess such qualities as these cross over [saṃsāra]; of this there is no doubt.
Others who possess such qualities also become partakers of merit.
They indeed cross over saṃsāra and proceed to the imperishable abode.
Those who proclaim virtues are indeed those who perceive virtues. Those who receive words of praise for Kṛṣṇa go to His abode.
Discourse on devotees, singing of the virtues of devotees, and the salutation of a devotee—[these lead to the same goal]. 25–26.
Praising devotion, bestowing grace upon the devotee, and granting liberation—these are the duties [of the Lord].
But those relatives and others who harbor hatred toward the devotee, whoever they may be, go to hell, driven by the messengers of Yama. (27)
The wrathful, the envious, the proud, the deceitful, the lustful, the hateful,
and the slanderous— these certainly go to hell.
But those people who, having completely abandoned these faults, worship Janārdana, [attain the highest state].
Devoted solely to love for Kṛṣṇa, they proceed to the abode of Hari;
filled with love for the Lord and intent on the service of the Lord,
they indeed become endowed with excellent qualities equal to the qualities of the Lord.
A devotee endowed with the qualities of the Blessed One becomes the one who grants liberation to those who have taken refuge [in him].
(31) Thus, protecting his own dharma, achieving freedom from passion, established in the Self and established in Hari, the affectionate one attains the supreme state. (32)
Whether in an auspicious place or time, or at the beginning of waking and so forth,
or in an inauspicious or contrary state, the devotee who casts off the body,
being favored by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, surely attains the supreme abode. (33)
One who is not a devotee of Hari, one who hates Him, one who hates the virtuous, one who is a reviler,
and one who is indeed devoid of dharma and other virtues— even if in an auspicious place and so forth—
upon casting off the body, always goes to the terrible abode of Yama.
Whatever state of mind one has practiced will become one's destination at the end;
whether death is auspicious or inauspicious is not the cause of a good or bad rebirth.
For the devotee there is upward progression, but for one who is otherwise, there is a miserable fate.

The all-seeing Guru Kṛṣṇa-Narāyaṇa, the Lord of Mercy, leads his own devotee to the imperishable abode; of this there is no doubt. Or else, by the power of the worship of his own Narāyaṇa, the devotee [attains that state]. (37–38)
Worshipping Kṛṣṇa, he becomes independent and goes to the imperishable abode himself;
like the Lord, he is capable of the dissolution and creation of universes.
What difference does it make whether he maintains or abandons this body?
Indeed, such a devotee as this is truly rare upon this earth. (40) One should become such a devotee in whom there is no deficiency;
one should become such a wise person whose affection is not directed elsewhere. (41)
One who possesses such vows shall attain devotion to Lord Hari;
one who possesses such qualities shall attain the state of the Imperishable Brahman;
and one who possesses such divinity, whose vision transcends the world of Māyā, [shall attain the supreme goal]. 42.
In Mukta-koṭi, there shall be a dwelling that rains down eternal bliss.
That alone is auspicious; everything else is inauspicious.
Listen to all that is auspicious, and having heard it, practice it.
He for whom the time of day is for the sake of Hari— whether morning or evening—
and in whom there is the worship of Kṛṣṇa, he is indeed skilled in the proper timing.
In whose house, shop, temple, or on the earth there is an image of Hari...
Whether in the field, the garden, or in active exertion, that place is considered skillful.
But whatever action is for the sake of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, for the sake of the goal, for the sake of the gods, for one’s own self, or for the sake of liberation— that action is considered skillful.
That association which is indeed with the virtuous brings about the happiness of knowledge of the Dharma; it destroys latent impressions, generates love for Kṛṣṇa, and is truly beneficial.
That mantra which destroys delusion, bestows realization, and illuminates the heart—||48||
Indeed, that divine initiation, joined with the name of Kṛṣṇa, is the destroyer of sins and is truly auspicious.
That initiation which bestows the state of Brahman, is purifying and the annihilator of sin; it produces knowledge and grants devotion to Kṛṣṇa—it is indeed auspicious. (3.221.50)
That meditation which bestows peace, destroys the agitation caused by the suffering of illusion and so forth,
grants eternal bliss, and bestows a divine state— that indeed is the wholesome [practice].
Likewise, the Guru is the one who bestows divinity and likewise effects the destruction of defects.
He is indeed a savior, a purifier, a benefactor in liberation, and one who is skillful.
(52) That mother who causes one to drink the nectar-milk of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who nourishes devotion, reveals liberation, and is truly skillful—she is indeed [the true mother]. (53)
He who is a father, training one in the exertion required to protect dharma, duty, and so forth,

and who is indeed skillful in guarding the great path to the world of Brahmā— he is truly a father. He who is a brother, who sustains and even causes others to perform actions that grant liberation— [he is truly a brother].
That skillful woman also gives him a divine, radiant garment that bestows liberation.
(55) That sister who gives food to her brother which has been offered to Brahman is indeed skillful;
she bestows the liberation of Brahman and grants blessings. (56)
That wife who bestows the yoga of Śrī Hari,
who is a servant, who binds Kṛṣṇa, and who bestows prosperity, is considered auspicious. That son who, through vows and devotion to Kṛṣṇa, delivers his own father—
He who wins the favor of his father is considered skillful.
That husband who, being full of devotion, bestows the bliss of Brahman and causes [his wife] to drink the nectar of Brahman which grants liberation—he indeed is skillful. (588–589)
Those householders who cause others to abandon the deceptive, bitter, and sorrow-inducing [world] and who bestow liberation upon them are always virtuous.
Likewise, those such as subjects and kings who are assistants toward liberation [are likewise virtuous].
But all those who have turned away from non-liberation are considered virtuous (kuśala).
Those qualities which bestow happiness, provide service to the holy, grant Hari, and bestow other joys that lead to liberation—they are considered virtuous. (61–62)
Those prosperities which are for the sake of the Lord, for the sake of the virtuous, and which bestow the yoga of merit;

those which are for the sake of helping others and for the sake of attaining [spiritual] gain—these are considered auspicious and granters of liberation. But those riches which are for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of the gods, and which bestow the dharma of giving—[these are also auspicious]. (63)
Those cows which are for the sake of the devotees and for the sake of the guru are always divine and auspicious.

Cows, buffaloes, bulls, horses, elephants, vehicles, and female slaves—those who possess these for the sake of Kṛṣṇa and for the sake of the virtuous are indeed auspicious and granters of liberation. (64–65)
Whatever body, mind, speech, senses, or riches one may possess—those which are for the sake of Hari and are virtuous, they indeed grant liberation; for they are truly auspicious.
Even those beds that are very soft, as well as golden vessels and diamonds—[these too are for His sake].

Jewels, silver, gems, and wealth are beneficial when they serve the purpose of Kṛṣṇa. Those joys, enjoyments, festivals, and pleasant associations which are for the sake of Hari, for the sake of the virtuous, and which grant liberation—verily, they are auspicious. (67–68)
Those practices, arts, sciences,
and specialized knowledges that are for the sake of Hari, as well as those manifestations intended for the virtuous— these indeed are skillful.
Furthermore, income and expenditure intended for Hari and intended for the virtuous belong to those on the path to liberation.
Those two divine ones, Māyā and Bandhakṣapaṇaka, are considered skilled [in these].
Generosity, vows, observances, conduct, worldly consensus, the stages of life (āśramas), and the path—all these are for the sake of Hari; indeed, they are the means to skill. 3.221.70–71.
Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—those who always offer these to Hari find that they take on the form of the goals of human life for him; being virtuous, they always bestow liberation.
[Yet for others] there is instruction, wretchedness, poverty, and wandering in the forest.
May you be well; may your activities for the sake of Hari have their dwelling in the great palace [of the heart].
May you be well; may your activities for the sake of Kṛṣṇa be directed toward the goals of virtue throughout waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
And may you be well; may your activities for the sake of liberation find their purpose in the fourth state (turyā) and in the liberation that is Brahman.
For one who possesses exceedingly affectionate and virtuous people, as well as Lord Hari,
and whose undertakings are directed toward liberation, all is well in every respect.
He in whose house, heart, and toward his family members there is always devotion—
May there be well-being in every respect for that virtuous person on the path to liberation.
(76) In whose house there is worship of Hari, as well as a hospitable welcome for the saints, for the gods, and for chaste women—for him there is well-being in every respect. (77)
In whose house there is the constant prasāda of Hari as food, for him the state of eating vighasa is supreme; he is virtuous in every respect.
He who has dedicated all his possessions for the sake of Hari is one who has offered himself to Him.

For him who possesses desireless devotional yoga, there is well-being in every respect. (95) For him who has no perception of Māyā and whose divine vision is ever auspicious, there is well-being in every respect through his constant appreciation of virtues. (3.221.80)
Faith in the words of Hari and the words of the virtuous, the preservation of that [faith],
and every effort for the sake of liberation— this is his well-being in every respect.
Faith, choosing [Hari], surrender, humility, and steadfastness toward Hari [constitute this].
For one who possesses service to the Rucya [deity], there will be well-being in every respect.
Now I shall describe those unwholesome qualities here which are indeed destructive:
atheism, unrighteousness, being devoid of devotion, and the violation of vows. (82–83)

Censuring others, committing acts of malice, and violence are indeed unwholesome deeds; so too are eating forbidden food and drink, spending one's days in vain, associating with the wicked, and being possessed by delusion, pride, and arrogance. (84)
Indeed, causing suffering to others is always unwholesome;
likewise, lust for another's wife, longing for another's wealth, backbiting, and deceit are always indeed unwholesome. (85–86)
Lack of devotion to the Dharma, being devoid of self-discipline, ignorance, illusory delusion, and indeed constant unwholesome acts;
as well as thirst, envy, fear, greed, and the avoidance of virtuous deeds. (87)
Unwholesome deeds always lead to a state of bondage to karma.
Knowing this, O Śivajaya, constantly perform wholesome deeds and abandon the unwholesome; you shall attain liberation.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā.
Recite this mantra and chant the name: "Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Hare.
Having crossed over Māyā, you shall go to the world of Brahmā, the supreme abode.
Having spoken thus, Vṛṣaparvan accepted the worship and departed for the forest.
Śivajaya took refuge in me, Acyuta, the Supreme Person, O Lakṣmī;
he performed every auspicious act and abandoned all that was inauspicious.
He became a great devotee of the Lord, intent upon meditation, dedication, and worship.
Other eminent artisans also worshipped Mādhava in his home;
they cultivated the company of the virtuous and performed the most excellent vows and festivals. (93)
Then once, on the twelfth day, after the morning observance,
they performed my worship at night following the ritual vigil;
they likewise performed the concluding rite (udyāpana), as well as chanting and dancing.
There I appeared, possessing divine splendor and four arms.
Seeing me as Hari, the beloved of Śrī, they all rejoiced;
they then worshipped me with objects born of their hearts, anointed with love.
They requested liberation from him, and having said "So be it," he vanished.
Then, after some time, Śivajaya, accompanied by his devotees,
cast off his body and went to the imperishable abode, escorted by my attendants.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, my devotees go to my imperishable abode through worship, adoration, self-surrender, and communion;
indeed, by association with the virtuous, they attain the divine, supreme state. (99)
Even those who possess a good reputation and those who recite [the scriptures] attain the highest well-being.

(3.221.100) Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Liberation of Śivajaya, the Builder of the Temple, through the Yoga of the Sage Vṛṣaparvan," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā. (221)
