Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the story of the spider-weaver;
the weaver used to sport on the bank of the river named Kamalā.
In that monastery, he became a maker of fish-traps and nets;
he devised snares for the feet of birds and for the horns and feet of beasts—
such nets as would ensnare fish and other creatures within their very bodies.
He makes and sells cords made of thread everywhere.
By means of the wealth produced from that, he indeed maintains his livelihood.
Known by the name Saṅgarayādaska, he resides in the city of the creator.
Having purchased nets together, those possessing nooses bind aquatic creatures, tree-dwellers, and forest-dwelling beings from this conflict.
Once, having placed the nets upon his shoulder during that struggle with the water-beings—
He went to the city to buy [nets], crying out loudly, "Buy nets! carrying a small bundle at his waist for the purpose of making them heard. Then his time arrived; it was midday and he became hungry.
Having purchased food from the market, he indeed came outside the city;
having gone to the bank of the Kamalā, he ate and drank water.
Just then, a beggar arrived, desiring to beg for alms.
By name Śuklāyana, he was a virtuous man wearing a garland upon his neck and hand;
chanting the names "Hare Kṛṣṇa" with his mouth, remembering Kṛṣṇa in his heart, upholding the dharma of non-violence, and reflecting upon discernment. (3.222.10)
Carrying only what was necessary for his journey and free from the pairs of opposites,
he approached him; he first recited, "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," and afterwards sat down near him.
Though his clothes and body were soiled, he was radiant within;
with a gentle gaze, he looked upon him, drawing his mind toward himself.
Then, as if desiring to maintain silence, he remained firm, having resolved upon it.
Seeing the detached yogi, who was steadfast and deeply inspiring confidence, the spider, though not impelled by fate, felt as if impelled and said:
"Salutations to you, O holy man; from where do you come, how have you arrived, and what do you desire?"
The virtuous man said, "Salutations to the Inner Controller; is all well with you?
"I desire some food accompanied by a drink of water.
The spider, with a gracious heart, gave him parched rice grains. (15–16)
"May you also have roasted chickpeas seasoned with a little salt;
may there be for you constant auspiciousness, freedom from disease, and an abundance of happiness.
Through my offering of rice and chickpeas, may you have peaceful sleep."

Having spoken thus, remembering Śrī Hari and offering [the food] to the inner self, he ate rice and other items; having drunk [water], he then attained satisfaction. At that time, he indeed inquired about the occupation of the spider-catcher.
The fisherman explained his occupation with the net exactly as it was.
Having heard this, the saint meditated upon Kṛṣṇa for a moment and then gave him instruction:
"Listen, Saṅgarayādaska; I shall tell you what is beneficial for you in every respect."
There are eighty-four lakhs of wombs for embodied beings here;
among them, the human body alone is truly fit for liberation.
Indeed, after many births, through heaps of merit, one attains the human state.
Through merit, the embodied soul indeed attains a body and then heaven;
through devotion, liberation; through one's own duty, prosperity; and through discernment, happiness.
A human being should always accomplish virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
One should avoid a life that is like that of cattle and characterized by violence.
Through violence, one obtains the realm of Yama, suffering, and residence in hell;
likewise, through violence, sin, malice, and misfortune arise. (24–25)
Confusion arises, as well as poverty and the destruction of people;
for those who commit violence, there occurs a downward course and the state of going to hell.
For those violent ones, such as hunters and thieves, the sin of killing is produced.
For even by one who constructs a net, the sin of harming living beings is produced.
(27) The killer, the eater, the one who approves, the assistant, the giver of weapons, the giver of snares, and the giver of nets shall share an equal portion [of the sin]. (28)
For one who makes nets, the sin of violence inevitably arises;
indeed, the embodied beings caught in the net seem to hiss at the net itself.
May those who hold the net and those who make the nets be cursed and remain in suffering.
Therefore, for your own happiness, I shall instruct you well in this matter:
merit has the preservation of life as its fruit, and the fruit of that is supreme bliss;
sin has the injury of living beings as its fruit, and the fruit of that is intense suffering.
Abandoning the work of weaving and the craft of the loom, prepare garments;
through garments suitable for covering, evil does not arise anywhere.
Having attained the means for self-realization, perform what is beneficial for yourself.
Having performed bathing, meditation, worship of Hari, service to others, and self-surrender;
having served the holy ones and attained merit, go to heaven.
Having worshipped the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa with devotion, [go to heaven].
Having performed vows, festivals, and acts of charity, proceed to the supreme heaven;
do not, however, construct a snare that causes harm and brings about sin. Make human life meaningful by attaining liberation and other such goals.
Having always heard the discourse of the scriptures, worship Nārāyaṇa.
Having known Nārāyaṇa alone, proceed to the supreme state.
Remember Nārāyaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Śrī, the Consort of Kamalā.
He is the Lord of the Imperishable, the Lord of Māṇikī, the Lord of Rādhā, and the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He alone, the Blessed One, is present here upon this earthly realm of men;
as the manifest Lord of the Divine Abode, he takes birth in human form.
Whatever deeds he performs, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
they indeed become divine; they are truly to be contemplated as bestowing liberation, granting great peace, and yielding virtue.
Desire, anger, fear, sorrow, joy, victory, and defeat;
hunger, thirst, action, and sleep—all that is auspicious for him.
Whatever his deed may be—whether censurable, blameworthy, base, or cruel—that too belongs to him.
Everything that bestows auspiciousness should be understood as pertaining to Hari; no fault exists in Hari.

Because Hari is devoid of material qualities (nirguṇa) and because He is divine among the virtuous—those who have attained a connection with Hari—He possesses both the state of being beyond qualities and divinity.
Realizing that [the virtuous] act in this way, one should indeed serve the saintly;
having attained affection for the saintly and having established affection for Hari, and having abandoned attachment to anything else, one shall attain steadfastness in the Supreme Lord. (44)
Thus, through constant practice, the latent impression (saṃskāra) becomes powerful.
By that, an exceeding affection for Kṛṣṇa arises repeatedly;
and so it remains for the devotee even in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
The vision of the divine form of Śrī Hari arises;
likewise, through great affection, the virtuous women behold Hari,
and through intense longing, the wives— the gopīs— behold Hari.
The Daityas beheld Hari through excessive hatred;
the gods repeatedly beheld Viṣṇu through excessive self-interest;
and the yogins beheld Brahman through the yoga of extreme identification.
Through supreme knowledge, the wise perceive Brahman in every way;
likewise, through service in the form of servitude, one perceives Kṛṣṇa.
Through the dharma of constant devotion, grace from Hari is attained.
Through compassion, there arises at all times the vision of the illustrious Hari; likewise,
when there is complete purity through the benedictory words of the virtuous,
there is the vision of Hari everywhere— in the hearts of devotees and externally.
Indeed, for one who possesses partiality toward the devotees of Kṛṣṇa just as he does toward his own family members, that association with the saintly is eternal.
For such a devotee, millions of faults are destroyed.
Latent impressions perish and the virtues of the virtuous arise.
Without affection for Hari, association with the virtuous is as if its very root has been destroyed.
But he who is free from pride, desirous of liberation, and possesses divine vision— ||415||
Recognizing the greatness of Hari, of the saintly, and of the wives of the devotees,
let association with the virtuous always remain firmly rooted as that which must be understood.
And the Lord, unable to endure the separation from such devotees, [remains ever present].

Though established in the Imperishable and beyond the senses, he assumes a human form by his own will out of compassion for the sake of the highest good and moves upon this earth. One should constantly conduct oneself by following his example.
Unwavering devotion is the means for propitiating Hari’s grace;
he who possesses Hari’s grace finds favor with the virtuous.
For the sake of attaining such favor, one must renounce the comfort of the body.
Association with the virtuous should be nourished by one's body, one's form, and even by one's mind.
(3.222.60) This is the manifest Lord Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of the world, the incarnate Supreme Brahman, the glorious son of Gopāla. (3.222.61)
These virtuous devotees of Hari are residents of the imperishable realm (akṣaravyoman);
all of them here are liberated, even the women who are equal to Lakṣmī.
By virtue of Bālakṛṣṇa’s yoga, this earth is indeed the imperishable abode.
We are all liberated souls by virtue of our association with Nārāyaṇa.
Where Kṛṣṇa is, there is His abode, and likewise the liberated souls and the gopīs.
This meeting with divine beings is a great fortune for us.
Dwelling together with these, everything becomes divine for me;
for Hari is to be served, and indeed the virtuous are to be served.
Their commands must be obeyed, and thereby the state of divinity is attained.
Indeed, the qualities of the virtuous come to one through the observance of the command of the virtuous.
One should constantly serve the virtuous like a god and likewise like Kṛṣṇa;
meditation on Kṛṣṇa is the supreme task to be performed, and devotion should be practiced in manifold ways.
One should abandon evil, which is of a wicked nature, by serving the virtuous;
one should increase the power for spiritual welfare and conquer the internal enemies.
Whether in one's presence or in one's absence, Kṛṣṇa should be kept aware of one's actions in his own proximity.
The direct witness, omnipresent everywhere, assuming many forms;
the inner self, the supreme self, the lord of Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Māṇikī—he, the supreme Lord, perceives everything directly and exists everywhere. (3.222.70)
It exists in the stationary and the moving, in the gross and the subtle, as well as in others;
yet the powerful wind does not move a leaf without its desire.
Holding everything, it remains as the bestower of the fruits of all actions.
He indeed possesses the power of supporting the earth, as well as that of the water;
he possesses the power of satiation and likewise the power of upholding the sky.
That Supreme Lord is the giver of the light of the moon, the sun, and fire.
Indeed, such a capable human being as this exists here;
Kṛṣṇa, Hari, the son of Kaṃbhārāśrī, grants his own vision.
Thus, Lord Hari should be contemplated incessantly in the mind.
For he alone indeed dispels the sufferings of those who have taken refuge in him.
He is capable of providing protection and exists possessing a divine nature;
yet at times, through human forms, he even endures hardship.
He fears, he desires, he forgives, and he even cries out at times;
for here, all actions performed toward Hari are indeed auspicious and purifying.
The holy devotees of that Lord are as dear to Him as His own self.
"Aha! This Blessed One exists here as one who is subject to his devotees.
By His power, His devotees bring about auspiciousness; they are holy men who grant us liberation"—in this way, one should cultivate [an understanding of] His majesty. (78–79)

One whose intellect regarding Hari is always extraordinary, like that of the virtuous, should constantly cultivate it and never a base intellect born of worldly association. One should perceive the defects inherent in one's own nature and practice divine familiarity.
By that, the defect of false impressions departs from the heart.
One should increase true devotion performed by the body, senses, and mind— that devotion which consists of the surrender of all one's possessions and bestows the state of supreme liberation.
Service to the saintly is considered the primary means for attaining liberation, the very state of the Lord.
Indeed, even in times of calamity, one must constantly serve the virtuous.
To destroy sin, one should listen to the stories of the saintly and the news of Hari.
For the sake of liberation, one should offer everything—the body, the home, wealth, and so forth—to the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the husband of Śrī Māṇikī;
one should know him as the Supreme Self, the Lord of Śrī, and the husband of Rādhikā. (84–85)
The Vyūhas such as Vāsudeva and others, the Mūrtis such as Keśava and others,
and the Avatāras such as the Fish and others indeed belong to Bāla-Kṛṣṇa.
Having thus attained this greatness, she should resort to her Lord like a virtuous wife.
Just as a wife finds refuge in her husband, so may a person obtain both worldly enjoyment and liberation from Kṛṣṇa.
O Śaṅkarayādava, having thus abandoned the work of weaving nets, you should instead engage in the weaving of cloth, mats, and the like. (87–88)
"Worship Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman; obtain liberation and the highest state.
Go to the divine, imperishable, and eternal abode, you who are possessed of true devotion.
Thus spoke the virtuous Śuklāyana as he sat upon the riverbank.
Having bestowed his blessing upon him and made that devotee of Viṣṇu a servant of devotion,
Saṅgara suddenly vanished,
like a long tube of dye breaking apart once it has reached its destination within a house.
Having done so, he kept [the image] in his house and abandoned its concealment behind a lattice.
Together with his family, he worshipped me and caused many devotees to perform worship.
O Lakṣmī, my worship and adoration grant liberation just as they do for others.
From that time forward, he observed the duty of non-malice in every respect.
And he brought me within the range of his perception through his devotion as a servant, his affection, and other such qualities.
Then, when the time had arrived, Mādhava came with his chariot.
I went to that house to lead Rūpāvatī,
her husband Saṅgara, and their divine bodies to my imperishable abode; having seated them in the chariot and granted them celestial forms, I departed for that eternal realm.
Other hosts of devotees as well, led by me, have gone to the Supreme.
O Rame, I have consumed all the multitudes of sins;
out of compassion, I have established purity within my devoted and virtuous devotees.
Even those who are sinful, associated with the wicked, ignorant, and attached to sense-objects,
become purified through association with the virtuous and partakers of the bliss of Brahman.
Even women, animals, the dull-witted, or even the impure [attain this].
Having attained the service of the virtuous, they become purifiers of the assembly.
(99) Neither Brahmins, nor gods, nor cows; neither vows, nor observances, nor restraints;
nor sacred fords are as excellent, nor even as supremely excellent, as the virtuous. (3.222.100)
Indeed, her entire divine and purifying form, from her toenails to her crest,
is truly like Nārāyaṇa himself, and Nārāyaṇī is like Lakṣmī.
The grace of the virtuous is divine, and the touch of the virtuous is likewise supreme.
Indeed, service to the virtuous bestows happiness, destroys suffering, and grants Hari.
(102) From reading, hearing, remembering, and even reflecting upon this, there shall be the destruction of sin, the attainment of merit, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation. (103)

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of How the Holy Śuklāyana Caused the Attainment of the Lord by Making Jālaka Abandon His Work for Saṅgara-Yādaska," in the Third Section, the Continuation of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 223: *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (The Continuation of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 223.
[The Author: Chapter 224.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of Ajapāla as well.
In the city of Nandipattana, near the river Candraprabhā, there was a goat-herd named Udyamaśrī who possessed goats as his wealth. He owned five hundred goats and likewise a hundred cows. (1–2)
He possessed five hundred rams, a hundred donkeys,
ten dogs, and twenty female buffaloes;
he also had ten servants for his menial tasks.
He has six wives and seventy sons and daughters.
[This land] is bounded by rivers, situated on riverbanks, in forests, and on grassy plains rich in fodder;
it is beautified by dense medicinal herbs and possesses an abundance of lush grass.
It dwells not far from Nandipura in Suvṛttika,
where there is a settlement of cattle-herders belonging to other Bharadvājas;
it consists of a hamlet whose inhabitants subsist on forest-grown food and such.
The glory of his exertion is great, as is his fame and his longevity;
(7) and by reason of his livestock, wealth, family, and hospitality toward guests, many forest-dwellers come frequently to his abode. (8)
He also welcomes them all with water for their feet and other offerings.
Holy men, ascetics, perfected ones, and yogis arrive;
virtuous women also come repeatedly to his house, intent on service.

He honors everyone and gladdens them with food, with gifts and marks of respect, with proper hospitality, and by massaging their feet and other services. His wives, sons, daughters, and even his servants are always [devoted] to him. (3.223.10–11)
They serve saintly persons and saintly women with great devotion,
regarding the saints as Lord Hari himself and offering their very selves to them.
For Hari dwells directly within the saints, and Ramā herself dwells within the saintly women.

For the gods also sit among guests, since they are indeed worthy of worship. While he was thus performing service to me, his Lord, twenty virtuous women who were established in Sāṃkhya and Yoga arrived at his house.
There were elderly Vaiṣṇava female ascetics who were devoted to the Lord; with milk and other offerings, as well as gifts of forest-grown food,
he honored them, welcomed them, and gave them lodging in a leaf-hut.
Those women, devotees of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa,
divine and endowed with divine qualities, bathed in the river and worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa, their lord of life, the glorious Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa. (16–17)
Then, having offered food to the Supreme Soul, they ate;
and having taken rest, they performed the evening congregational chanting (saṃkīrtana).
They performed the lustration rite (ārātrika) and those skilled in narration told stories of His divine exploits.
Thousands of cowherd women, boys, and girls came from all sides to hear the story, knowing it to be a supreme assembly of virtuous ladies;
those mothers were always immersed in their conduct within the form of Hari. (3.223.20)
They worship and sing praises of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, their beloved Lord.
Among them, one who had attained the status of a preceptor was named Satīśvarī.
This virtuous woman recounted the stories of Hari, which the Gopī women listened to.
And likewise, all the cowherds, with faith and a spirit of devotion,
[listened to] the beautiful and virtuous story from the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, which bestows excellent liberation and burns away sins. (22–23)
By him whose mind is fixed on Kṛṣṇa, the world is indeed conquered;
for that mind is truly conquered which is fixed upon the Supreme Self.
The senses move toward their objects along with the mind.

But when the mind has gone toward an object, that very mind is indeed unconquered. Having turned back the movement of the mind from the objects of the senses toward Hari, one should fix that mind; then the senses are truly conquered.
Upon the destruction of passion, dispassion arises; by that, the mind becomes conquered.
Through love for Hari, the mind would not go elsewhere; thus, the mind becomes conquered.
By abiding in Brahman, passion, desire, and the like are indeed destroyed.
The notion of enjoyment shall perish, and by that, the mind will be conquered.
(28) But for one who is immersed in the divine bliss of Śrī Hari, the Lord of Śrī, and who is endowed with the knowledge of His majesty—for him, the mind will be conquered. (29)
For one whose state of pure consciousness persists through the destruction of the existence of the body,
his dull and despondent mind becomes conquered.
There is eternal satisfaction from Hari, and a turning away from that which is illusory.
His mind is considered to be eternally satisfied and steady, and his intellect ever-conquered.

(3.1) Through the destruction of the identification with the body, through the strength of abiding in the Self, and through the total abandonment of the latent impressions of passion, the mind shall become eternally conquered. (3.2)
The mind is said to be in the form of a woman, and the individual soul (jīvātman) assumes the form of a man.
When the mind abandons its enjoyment, the mind becomes naturally conquered.
I am the conscious Self, the woman; the Supreme Self (paramātman) is my man.
My husband is my enjoyer and giver of happiness; there is no other supreme provider of enjoyment for me.
He is Kṛṣṇa manifest, Bālakṛṣṇa, Hari, the beloved of Śrī, the protector, the sustainer, the creator, my dear one, the lord of my life, and my husband. (34–35)
He is the Master, the Radiant One, and the Desireless One, overflowing with all-bliss;
this Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is my beloved, the bestower of bliss upon me,
and the ruler of lords and of those who descend as incarnations.
This very Lord of Goloka has attained the state of being the Master of the cowherd girls (vallavīs).
This very Lord of Vaikuṇṭha is the Master of the female attendants (pārṣadāṇīs) and the Lord of the liberated women (muktānikās); Kṛṣṇa shines resplendent in the imperishable abode (akṣaradhāma).
In the unmanifest, immortal Śrīpura, he is the Lord of Śrī, Lakṣmī, and Kamalā;
the Lord of Lalitā and Māṇikī; the Lord of Prabhā and Padmāvatī;
the Lord of Brahmapriyā, and he is also the Lord of Haripriyā.
He is the Lord of Viśālā and Badarī, the supreme husband of Śvetadvīpa;
the Lord of the autumnal moon over the Ocean of Milk, the husband of Sītā, and the husband of Satī.
He is Kṛṣṇa, the husband of all virtuous women, and indeed the husband of Kumbhakārī.
The Lord of all those who are liberated, the Lord of the perfected ones, the Lord of all friends, the Lord of all maidservants, the Lord of even his own life-breath—
the Supreme Person. Having understood this, one should worship Hari, the beloved, who is the refuge of all happiness.
If his mind becomes attached to Kṛṣṇa, that indeed is considered victory.
And this Blessed Lord dwells within my heart, in my very self;
He, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, shines forth among saintly men and women.
The illustrious Gopālabāla shines in the imperishable field;
he is the personified treasure-house of all happiness, Vāsudeva himself.
[He is the goal] of men, gods, ancestors, and perfected yogis.
Whatever exceedingly great joys belong to millions of incarnations of lords,
and whatever joys indeed belong to the liberated ones dwelling in the abode of Brahman—
all those belong to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā.
If such a Lord exists even at the tip of a single hair,
He who is our met master Kṛṣṇa, the treasury of all happiness—
then compared to the splendor of His abode, whatever splendors and pleasures there may be [elsewhere] are indeed nothing.
Of all the hosts of world-protectors possessing sovereign splendor, of the planets, the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, and even the two Aśvins;
of the Sādhyas, their wives, the Rudras, and the other dwellers of heaven. (3.223.49–50)
The abodes of the suns, of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, as well as of other celestial dwellers,
are indeed hells compared to the station of this Supreme Self.
Having abandoned this beloved Lord of Śrī, who is designated as the ultimate goal, they instead resort to what are called hells.
"How may I, O Supreme Goddess, regard others as being of the nature of happiness?
Having thus understood this majesty, the virtuous woman endowed with divine disposition should abandon delusion, which leads to hells; her mind is forever victorious.
Then, the illusory latent impressions (vāsanās) constantly go to their dissolution.
Such desire for the body and desire for enjoyment, which are illusory, are forever burnt away;
having arisen, they are indeed uprooted. (54)
She who does not recognize such greatness as Hari's in this world—her disposition toward men, even toward ordinary ones, will be driven by desire;
her affection for sons, friends, wife, husband, and so forth, is likewise a bondage. (55–56)
The mind of that woman, dwelling in the pursuit of her own self-interest, may abandon the Supreme Self when she is dragged away by affection for her family;
or she may abandon Him due to the affliction of disease and the like, or through the failure to obtain the objects of the senses. //57//
Her mind, however, always wanders toward Keśava for the sake of sense objects.
But in the absence of those objects, she becomes a commoner;
she surely falls from devotion to Hari and does not find the path to liberation.
Therefore, one should cultivate a love for Hari that is natural and devoid of self-interest;
it should certainly not arise from form, nor from desire, nor from greed, nor from gain,
nor should it be performed for one's own sake, but rather it must be natural.
One should always cultivate affection for Him, from whom arises the knowledge of the majesty and wonder of His divine qualities—an affection whose destruction never occurs.
In Hari reside divine qualities such as truthfulness, purity, and bliss. (61–62)
Furthermore, his affection is boundless, as are his sweetness, excellent character, friendship, compassion, love, pity, tranquility,
forbearance, delight, joy, beneficence, endurance, divinity, and steadfastness. (63)
Magnanimity, eternal bliss, and protection by the Refuge—these qualities come even to devotees through service;
indeed, these qualities manifest even by hearing the true teachings. //64-65//
Affection for devotees endowed with such qualities arises in Kṛṣṇa;
therefore, service to Hari should be performed through body, mind, and speech. Furthermore, one should conduct oneself with the physical form in accordance with the pleasure of Hari.
Austerities and other practices should be performed according to one's own inclination toward Hari.
(67) One should always serve Hari, the virtuous, the yogis, and saintly women with faith; thus, firm affection for Kṛṣṇa shall arise. (68)
Harsh speech should not be spoken; rather, one should speak that which is truthful and beneficial.
One should neither engage in dispute with the great, nor seek victory over them. One should speak words that are free from pride and gentle, characterized by humility and moderation.
One should speak words that are excellent and accept the authoritative commands of Hari with respect;
indeed, even harsh words from Hari should always be received with reverence.
Even a command from Hari that is impossible to carry out or seemingly unworthy of performance must certainly be accepted.
In this way, there arises love for Hari, and likewise love for the virtuous.
In beholding, hearing, meditating upon, worshipping, and serving Hari,
as well as in the presence of the form of Śrī Hari, one-pointed concentration brings about the attainment of all desired goals.
Just as one might repeatedly behold something ever-new and extraordinary,
so too should one make that vision firm and enduring for a long time, and at that moment indeed see nothing else;
such a vision is truly the cause of love for Hari.
Whether externally or internally, such a sight is the cause of affection;
for the Lord of the Śārṅga bow, love does not arise at all for one whose gaze is flickering.
Nor indeed would there be affection among the virtuous for one who looks elsewhere.

Whether toward a man, a woman, an animal, a painting, or a door with moving panels, the gaze is made flickering by a mind that flows in many directions. By means of that gaze, one does not go elsewhere, nor does pleasure for that [object] arise. (76–77)
Just as a lustful man gazes upon a woman of desire with single-minded intent, so should one gaze upon the Lord, one's husband, with a state of being entirely absorbed in love.
Not even the slightest thing that may arise in the interval should be taken into account.
Just as a bride’s first sight of her husband at the very first moment is ever-new,
providing firmness of form and stability while bestowing a radiant thrill,
so too is that vision of Him eternally new, the very cause of divine love. (3.223.80)
Indeed, one must practice such single-minded concentration while listening to the narrative;
for through hearing his life-story, the Lord, the creator of all beings, becomes manifest.
Whether it be the eye, the ear, or even the mind among all the senses—
These [senses] are indeed especially fickle and must be restrained;
for the organ of desire is even more restless than they.
Having restrained the mind, desire too must be restrained along with the mind.
Otherwise, during meditation on or worship of Śrī Hari, worldly forms and sense objects—
which cause affliction and create obstacles— may manifest. Indeed, if the mind is powerful, it will surely enter through the linga, the eyes, or the ears.
But at that time, one must exercise discernment regarding vulgar sense objects.
There is no gain whatsoever in abandoning Hari to go toward other objects,
because all sense objects bestow suffering and are the causes of bondage through illusion.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī, is the embodiment of bliss;
one should remain there for the sake of attaining eternal bliss.
This is the state of perfection, the divine state, a treasury of joy and supreme delight.
Everything indeed arises from Kṛṣṇa; therefore, obtain great happiness.
For one who strives elsewhere, there may be some small pleasure, but that is mostly full of suffering and likewise bestows hell.
Therefore, listen to the narrative, behold Kṛṣṇa, and contemplate him in every way.
Go indeed to that bliss which comes from Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved, and not from any other.
Thus, through love established in Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain the desired perfection.
Through devotion to Him, one attains all opulence, prosperity, beauty, and the Lord Śrī Rādhāmāṇikī,
who is equal to Viṣṇu and Nārāyaṇa. Whether with the body or after death in His abode, everything is attained in every way.
Therefore, one should always abide in Hari with the eye, the mind, the speech, the ear, the heart, the desire, and even with the very self.
Indeed, for one who possesses love for Kṛṣṇa through such constant devotion, [there is no doubt]. ||93||
Or, by means of a woman full of love, there may be the state of being an object of Kṛṣṇa’s affection. From that, his divine status would become like Kṛṣṇa’s, or she would become like Lakṣmī;
there would be no deficiency in him compared to Hari, nor any inferiority in her compared to Śrī.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, the great virtuous Satīśvarī instructed the cowherd women and the cowherds who were affectionate toward the Lord for the sake of liberation.
The cowherd women, the cowherds, as well as the Bharavāṭas and others—
Udyamaśrī and the others received supreme devotion.
(97) They received from Satīśvarī the mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā," as well as the supreme name. (98)
"Bālakṛṣṇa! Hari! Kānta! Lord of Rādhā! Lord of Ramā!
Bestower of liberation! Beloved! Granter of all desires! Supreme among men!"—thus they took up these names and performed kīrtana with reverence.

The virtuous women, having performed their worship and eaten breakfast, departed for another village; and the Bharavaṭas and Bharavaṭīs likewise went repeatedly. They always performed worship and adoration of Bālakṛṣṇa.

Indeed, through their devotion, the Blessed One suddenly appeared together with Rādhā, Ramā, Māṇikī, and Śrī. Seeing Him in His four-armed form within the house during that great festival, [they rejoiced].
On the twelfth day (dvādaśī), the day of the vow, at the very dawn in the temple,
thousands of people then attained supreme wonder;
for [the Lord] granted them His own vision as well as the auspicious *prasāda* of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Having granted the boon for the sake of liberation, the Lord vanished. O Lakṣmī, when that time arrived, I [manifested] the people who possess the glory of exertion—
namely, the Bharavāṭas, the foremost devotees, and the Gopīs who were overflowing with love.
I led them to my own abode, the eternal and supreme Goloka.

Thus, through their association with the virtuous woman, the Bharavāṭyas and the cowherds were delivered from the world of illusion by the compassionate Lord, by means of their affection and devotion.
In this way, those women and men who worship me with total dedication shall all go to my supreme abode, where they serve their Beloved.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even following this [work], [they shall attain that state]. 108.
"Enjoyment, liberation, and great bliss—may these be offered by me.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Devotion and Liberation through the Service of the Chaste Satīśvarī by the Cowherds, including Udyamaśrī and Others," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*. (223)
← Chapter 223: Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā – Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga), Chapter 224 [[Author: → Chapter 225
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī; on the earth of Maru, there was a camel-herder named Dīrgharaṃbha in the village known as Citrordhva. (1)
He possessed more than a hundred camels that fed upon *śamī* trees;
he was a dweller in high lands, a seller of wool, a dealer in camels, and likewise a trader in grain.
(2) He was a seller of camels and an operator of the grain trade.
He was one who transported grain from one place to another;
for the most part, he lived in the forest as a protector of camels.
He dwelt in the forest at night together with ten camel-herders.
In the exceedingly vast Śamī forest, camels were wandering everywhere;
having built a fire there, Dīrgha,
Raṃbha, and others sat down upon woolen blankets and sang the praises of Rāma.
And having gathered together, they likewise engage in conversation and songs concerning the gods.
Having offered the milk of camels into their hearts as an oblation to the Lord,
they eat *roṭakas* (flat cakes) prepared with *śamī*, chickpeas, and sour gruel.
If any travelers happen to come upon the forest path,
they give them milk, flat cakes, and other provisions with due respect.
One should perform acts of service for others by giving food, blankets, and similar gifts.
Thinking thus, they offer even the finest woolen blankets.
Or, virtuous people who have undertaken pilgrimages meet on that path;
to them they offer food and water, and perform the rites of welcome and so forth.
Always desiring meritorious and virtuous deeds, they serve the assembly of the virtuous with devotion according to their wish, through the very thought of Rāma.
Then, on one occasion, for the purpose of making a pilgrimage to Arbuda, [they went] to Tripuṣkara.
They arrived at the maṇḍala of the virtuous men and women, and on the way they chanted with the sounds of musical instruments: "Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Janārdana!
Narasiṃha, Hara, Viṣṇu! Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta! (12–13).
Having seen them, Dīrgharaṃbha went to meet them and prostrated;
he gave them milk, *roṭaka* cakes, and water at midday.
In the evening, those virtuous ones, full of eagerness, found rest there.
At night, all the camel-herders attended upon the virtuous people;
they likewise heard the chanting of His names and discourses on Rāma.
Then [they heard] that best of holy works called the Rāmāyaṇa, the supreme Vaiṣṇava scripture.
Bowing low, he asked how his own welfare might be attained;
then the narrator of the Rāmāyaṇa replied with the means for achieving that welfare:
"The service of the virtuous and the auspicious chanting of the name of Rāma. (17)
Indeed, [he taught] the ninefold devotion to Viṣṇu and the means for attaining auspiciousness:
constant salutation to Rāma, worship with many articles,
and daily worship within the heart through mental offerings.
And meditation is the means for accomplishing what is auspicious; it is the contemplation of Rāma.

With his body bristling with horripilation due to love, his speech faltering with choked words, and his mind focused solely on His true nature, the devotee should thus be intent upon the worship of Hari.
Whether one performs external worship or practices internal adoration,
this person— esteemed by all devotees— is indeed distinguished above all others in terms of devotion.
However, one who lacks single-minded concentration and is devoid of affection is not praised.
He who possesses abundant faith in worship and service,
and especially who possesses faith and reverence for the sacred narrative and its glorification; he whose greatness is supreme and who maintains a spirit of true friendship toward his devotees.
For one for whom even a long duration of time becomes like a single moment when engaged in the worship of Rāma and other such practices;
for whom the ninefold service of Hari is performed freshly every day; and for whom this service is never secondary nor ever anywhere become stale—[such a person attains the goal]. (24–25)
He whose faith and devotion are constant, ever-new, and ever-bright—he is liberated here, and she too is liberated; for on this earth, he is truly a man and she is truly a woman.
Even such devotees who remain at a distance are as if standing in the very presence of Kṛṣṇa.
If those standing by one's side are not of such a nature, they are considered as far away as if they were distant.
Therefore, one must strive constantly for the attainment of the arising of love through hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and divine vision.
The story of Hari should be heard from the mouth of a saint who has attained identity with Kṛṣṇa; it should be accompanied by the remembrance of Śrī Hari and it sustains the purpose.
Furthermore, there must be reflection upon the meaning heard, which is repeated inquiry.
It should be performed together with the form endowed with love, which removes all latent impressions (vāsanā).
Thereafter, one should perform pure recollection born of mental refinement (saṃskāra), namely meditative concentration (nididhyāsana), with faith and affection; Mādhava will then be pleased with him.
By this means, there should be a spontaneous and constant manifestation of Hari within;
upon that manifestation, there shall always be a direct realization of the divine form of Hari.
In this way, love for Hari should be cultivated, and through that love, the love of Hari shall arise.
From that, identity arises between the two who possess mutual affection.
(33) Celibacy, steadfastness in the Self, dispassion, hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, and taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa—these are declared to be the causes of direct realization. (34)
Reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) bestow the fulfillment of the desires of devotees;
hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone does not directly grant the fruit of realization.
Indeed, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) do not perish without meditative absorption.
The knots of the heart are destroyed through uninterrupted contemplation of Kṛṣṇa (36).
For one who is engaged in profound meditation and is a direct seer of reality, there exist fullness of desire and bliss; but these do not belong to anyone else (37).
For one who perceives Kṛṣṇa as external and likewise harbors resentment in the heart,
Keśava does not swiftly manifest His form constantly to the rememberer;
this is so even for one who does not behave in such a way, provided he has not made such an effort.
The Lord, the divine self and soul of the universe, does not manifest at all within the heart.
Therefore, the means for the direct realization of Kṛṣṇa within the heart are said to be hearing, reflection, meditative absorption, and love. (3.224.40)
Hari manifests like a beloved lover through a love that is constantly maintained;
therefore, one should practice the reflection upon Hari—both as heard and as seen—in such a way that it is accompanied by remembrance, joined with love, and endowed with faith. (41)

Upon that, love for Hari arises, which effects union with His effulgence. As long as the identification of the individual soul with the body persists, one must recognize that [attachment to the body] is a great obstacle to love for Kṛṣṇa, causing rebirth in the cycle of worldly existence. ||42-43||
Therefore, the realization that this Self is distinct from the body and so forth must be attained by the discerning person from a true guru and from the scriptures; furthermore,
the delusion of identity between the inert body and the Self must be destroyed.
The essential natures of both the insentient and the sentient, as well as their attributes in every respect, must be understood so that the distinction between these two may manifest;
thereby, the delusion of identity shall perish along with its very root. (45–46)
Inert, consisting of suffering, diseased, perishable, and deformed;
subject to decay, pervaded by saliva, urine, and impurities, and possessed of birth, death, and old age;
bound together by joints, existing in many states, illusory, material, and composed of the elements. (47)
This body always exists as a mass of many forms that undergo diminution;
indeed, all the senses are qualities of the subtle body, and they likewise produce suffering, defects, agitation, and anxiety. (48–49)
I am not such as this; I am of the nature of consciousness, possessed of bliss, free from disease, eternal, changeless, and devoid of decay.
I am of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, transcending birth, death, and old age.
I am indivisible, stable, one, divine, and free from illusion;
I am non-material, devoid of the elements, luminous, and free from laughter;
I am of a single form, stainless, unattached, the witness, and immortal.
"My divine powers are the impellers of the sensory faculties;
such indeed am I—the conscious one, possessing the nature of liberation.
Thus one should properly contemplate the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self.
Having learned of that [Self] from the mouths of the wise or from the scriptures, one should practice it.
When knowledge has matured, there is no longer any confusion between the attributes of the body and the attributes of the Self.
Through that, one becomes established in the Self; thus, one is also said to be established in the Blessed Lord.
In this state, the human being becomes one whose form is that of Brahman and whose form is that of liberation.
For such a person, neither latent impressions remain, nor delusion, nor torments. This discrimination between the Self and the non-Self must be firmly established by him.
Driven by delusion, he is afflicted by the bodily attributes such as suffering and the like;

(57) as long as his practice remains lax, so long shall he remain under the sway of the notion that the body is the self, behaving like a beast with bestial conduct characterized by the sense of "I" and "mine. (58)
Consisting of the identification with the body, senses, and so forth, it deludes through desire and volition;
it is filled with attachment to the juices of male and female wealth, and with the thirst for suffering and sin.
Like one who eats sweet food mixed with poison, this [identification] brings suffering even when the self is gladdened.
By that mode of life, he indeed goes to illusory hells.
Therefore, one should strive so that there may be no going to hells at all;
one should achieve steadfastness in the Self through service to Hari and to the virtuous.
With love and an awareness of his greatness, one should abandon attachment to the body;
with faith one should serve the virtuous, and with devotion, Janārdana. One should also remain constantly within the command of Hari and the saintly.

One should protect the duties prescribed by the scriptures and acquire knowledge of His majesty. (63) In this way, freedom from latent desires arises; moreover, through love for Kṛṣṇa, that occurs swiftly.
Devotion toward Kṛṣṇa increases when it is accompanied by knowledge of His majesty. (64)
For one devoid of knowledge of the Lord’s majesty, the qualities born of devotion perish;
for one endowed with knowledge of His majesty, those qualities become sources of auspiciousness.
Indeed, all [virtues] come to dwell within the heart, just as they do in the case of the saintly.
Upon the arrival of virtues, all latent impressions (vāsanās) quickly perish.
If death occurs for a devotee who is practicing while a residue of latent impressions still remains, his birth will be radiant among the gods and other celestial beings.
Therefore, it shall indeed bring about prosperity and enjoyment in the home of devotees;
then, having attained the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), liberation will become certain.
For a devotee who has destroyed their latent impressions, there is no journey to the realm of Yama.
The fruit of devotion is considered to be either the world of the gods or the world of the Lord.
Having become a devotee, one may become a great universal emperor (mahācakravartin) and then go to the Imperishable (akṣara).
Kṛṣṇa, whose compassion is boundless, is the supreme goal of the devotee. (3.224.70)
Having rendered that [world] devoid of latent impressions, he protects his own devotee;
for even the illusory glories of Kṛṣṇa’s abode appear as nothing but hells to those who know the Self. ||71||
Having eaten and then abandoned them, they proceed to the imperishable state (akṣaraṃ padam).
Chanting the name of Rāma, touching Kṛṣṇa, and beholding Nārāyaṇa,
one becomes divine, stainless, and of the nature of Brahman, and attains the supreme state (paraṃ padam).
He goes to the abode of yogis, the supreme state of the liberated;
standing in the midst of the circle of the virtuous, he enjoys great bliss in the Imperishable.
Whether they be devotees or non-devotees, [they all obtain] the direct vision of Hari.
Those who perform touch and service indeed become divine.
If those who are not [yet] devotees, yet possess minds and serve with hearts full of love,
then they, having abandoned their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), proceed to the supreme state.
Even those devotees who serve the Lord, the Master of Śrī, without a mind [for worldly things],
will eventually attain His state in a future birth.
For the Lord is most proximate to those whose devotion is characterized by intense spiritual urgency.
For those whose devotion is characterized by weak spiritual urgency, Janārdana remains most distant.
Chanting the name of Hari without a focused mind, as well as seeing, touching, serving, and so forth, will never yield its full fruit in any circumstance. (78–79)
However, that meditation which is devoid of mental focus would be lacking in spiritual radiance;
therein, the form of Nārāyaṇa would never manifest at all.
Therefore, devotees should worship in both ways—both externally and internally.
With a state of mind characterized by love and one-pointed concentration, they should cultivate the Great Lord.
By the power of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, at the end of their bodies, they immediately go to the beautiful Goloka; liberated, they possess divine forms.
Others, however, having attained merit, will reach that state after undergoing rebirth through devotion and other means, once they have fully completed that merit.
But for those whose service consists of offering their very selves, as was the case with the gopīs—
Touching, beholding, and chanting—these three forms of ritual service established [by Vyāsa]—those who perform them quickly attain the divine liberation whose essence is Kṛṣṇa.
Everything performed without mindfulness is fruitless; it does not bestow liberation.
O camel-herders, sirs, perform that very thing with love, affection, and a devoted mind, offering everything from the depths of your hearts.
Serve, glorify, and touch Śrī Hari, who belongs to the virtuous. (86)
For those whose devotion is rich with intense affection, liberation will come swiftly.
(87) For forest-dwellers, chanting, service, and devotion are the means to liberation;
for Brahmins, the six duties and ninefold devotion lead to liberation. (88)
For the virtuous, meditation is the desired bath, and likewise, service is the worship;
detachment, steadfastness in the Self, and steadfastness in Kṛṣṇa lead to liberation.
For women, service filled with affection through the state of being a beloved leads [to the same].
"Total surrender and devoted service as a servant to Hari lead to liberation.
(3.224.90) Recite the supreme mantra: "Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā," and even chant aloud the name of Bālakṛṣṇa. (91)

"Performing mental worship of the Supreme Self, let them contemplate His deeds; through that, may they attain liberation. Having spoken thus, O Rame, all the holy ones, beginning with the *Rāmāyaṇa*, [proceeded].
Having been honored and fed, they took their leave;
then Dīrgha, Rambhā, and all the others followed the path of the saintly teachings and took refuge in the Lord,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Beloved of Śrī.
"Hare Kṛṣṇa, Hare Rāma, Hare Viṣṇu, Hare Prabhu! O Bālakṛṣṇa, Hare, Lord of Sītā, Lord of Rādhā, All-pervading One!
In this way, those camel-herders performed worship of You both in the forest and at home.
O Lakṣmī, having always gathered together with affection and devotion toward me, my Lord;
then, after some time had passed, he arrived in a divine form with four arms in order to lead Dīrgharambha and the others to liberation. ||96-97||
Rāma, the lord of Vaikuṇṭha, resplendent together with Sītā,
brought him and the others by means of a divine celestial chariot;
he also caused those gifts of camels which had been given to the virtuous to be conveyed.
Taking birds that possessed divine forms, I approached;
taking beautiful birds of golden hue adorned with every ornament, and making them sound with the tinkling of small bells, I arrived. (3.224.99–100)
Having transformed those various camel-herders who were my devotees into divine beings and having mounted them upon celestial camels, I, whose abode is divine, led them to me.
Thus were the camel-herders liberated through the context of the Rāmāyaṇa.
O Lakṣmī, all these divine [mantras] have been composed by me with devotion out of compassion.
From the recitation, hearing, remembering, and even the contemplation of this,
there shall arise enjoyment, liberation, as well as desired prosperity and wealth.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Dīrgharava and the Other Camel-herders through their Association with the Holy Man named Rāmāyana," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
Chapter 224. Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā—Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Yuga).
Chapter 225 [Author: Chapter 226] → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the auspicious story of the devotee named Ratnaprabha, the protector of the Khara clan, which bestows the state of liberation.
On the bank of the Lūṇī river, in the city of Lūṇī, there was a most excellent Kṣatriya.
And there was one named Ratnaprabha, the protector of a thousand asses.
With long ears, he would indeed carry away grains and other goods from one country to another country,
and from one village to another village, again and again.
For the merchants, kings, and others, he performs their business by means of donkeys,
both bringing and carrying goods for a wage earned through labor.
In this manner, he gathered many grains, vessels, and likewise sacrificial fuel from the forest, from fields, from threshing floors, from the city, and from other towns. (5)
He indeed causes [the goods] to reach another village or the center of the village by means of donkeys;
having taken the wage for the labor, he certainly provides the journey home. (6)
Then once, having loaded two thousand measures of wheat onto the backs of donkeys,
he departed from the village of Lūṇī.
Accompanied by forty fierce guards as his servants,
he proceeded fearlessly toward the capital city of Yuddhapurī on a day of scorching sunlight.
As he was traveling on the road, he became exhausted by the heat;
perceiving that the donkeys were likewise exhausted, he too succumbed to fatigue. (9)
Indeed, for two ghaṭīs he stayed there beside a water-channel in a grove of trees;
there resided a community of virtuous men, abundant with forest produce.
Ratnaprabha and the others, having thus given water to the donkeys—
Having eaten flat cakes and other foods, they went before the holy men (sādhus).
Having bowed and uttered "Victory to Śrī Rāma," they stood before them.
Then the sādhus offered a welcome and bestowed blessings upon them.
Having repeatedly understood the fatigue born of activity in going and coming,
they spoke for the sake of [others'] welfare of this auspicious refuge in Nārāyaṇa through their discernment.
He is the best of holy men, known as Narasiṃhasvāmī, and is served by the virtuous.
He instructed everyone for just a moment regarding the Imperishable (Acyuta).
"Alas! All that has been done in this world—if service to Kṛṣṇa has not been performed—then it is indeed fruitless, like the body of an embodied being still within the womb. || 14-15 ||
Just as a donkey laden with a burden of sandalwood perceives only the weight and does not perceive its fragrance— thereby being devoid of joy—
so too in this world is one who is intent on toil but devoid of devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
He is called a bearer of the burden, but not one who experiences his own pleasure. ||17||
For there is no difference perceived between a donkey and a human insofar as both are carriers of burdens; indeed, such a human is just like a donkey. (18)
Like donkeys and other beasts, potters fall under the sway of laziness;
they fall under the sway of their own past actions like other animals.
Devoid of devotion, devoid of dharma, and bereft of human effort— ||19||
But those men who are devoid of the merit of generosity are like donkeys. ||20||
Those men who are devoid of visiting sacred fords, who are bereft of ritual bathing and worship, and who lack service to the virtuous, are like donkeys. (21)
Devoid of their own true welfare and attached to flavors and the like, men in this world who are greedy for genitals and bellies are just like donkeys. (22)
Bearing the burden of their families yet devoid of the path to the highest good, men who consume the fodder of sense-objects are like donkeys. (23)
Those men who tread paths devoid of moral boundaries, who are bereft of service to their parents, and who lack the realization that all beings are the Self, are like donkeys. (24)
Exerting effort only for the sake of food and devoid of asceticism and vows, these men—covered in ashes yet naked—are like donkeys. (25)
Those men who are devoid of even a trace of devotion to the five deities, who are atheists, and who lack reverence for their guru, are like donkeys. (26)
Even householders who are devoid of faith, who avoid sacrifices and offerings, and who are devoted to sexual indulgence and greed, are like donkeys. (27)
Having four legs, a tail like a fool's, and coils that wind around their dwelling places, yet devoid of the remembrance of the Divine, householders are like donkeys. (28)
Hearing the vulgar, they have long ears; crying out in distress, they run after the objects of the senses like household donkeys. (29)
Unpeaceful, wandering among objects of the senses like illusory travelers,
householders waste their lives in vain like donkeys,
even though they have bathed at holy fords and are eloquent in the chatter of the scriptures. (30)
And those ignorant ones who do not know its majesty wallow in the ashes of their sins. //31//
Even when there are seven sons, the female donkey remains a bearer of burdens; even when there are many excellent stars, housewives remain bearers of burdens.
Even when there are seven sons, the burden of the camel is not lessened.
Even when there are six sons as householders, the burden of the father does not diminish.
(33) Just as even a decrepit camel runs for a hundred *krośas*, so too an old man runs for a hundred *ākrośas*. (34)
The donkey wanders in the village; the man wanders in the house.
He wanders nowhere in Hari; what difference is there between the donkey and the man? 35.
A man with a long neck is always like a camel;
when it comes to eating, what difference is there between a man and a camel who both lack devotion to their food? (36)
One is constantly beaten with clubs, while the other is [beaten] with words; since both are indifferent to the removal of suffering, what difference is there between a human and a donkey? (37)
The sense-objects are "kha," and he who bestows (*rāti*) those upon the senses (*khara*) is indeed *Khara*.
The word "nara" signifies Nārāyaṇa; he who bestows (*rāti*) that [Nārāyaṇa] is remembered as *Nara*. (38)
If a man, having abandoned Nārāyaṇa, falls into hell, what difference is there between that man and a donkey, other than the fact that one is born with nails and the other with hooves? (39)
Since the movement of both the donkey and the man is unrestrained, and their actions lack all bounds, what indeed is the difference between the donkey and the man? (40)
If a man bathes [at sacred sites] and yet never chants the name of Hari, he is indeed a donkey; he is truly that very donkey.
Therefore, having risen early in the morning and bathed, one should chant the name of Nārāyaṇa;
one should worship the Supreme Self and feed the Lord, the Consort of Śrī.
Then one should eat that meritorious food and drink the water of His grace.
One should serve virtuous people and always worship Śrī Hari. 43.
One should indeed practice the chanting of the Name;
one should contemplate the form of Kṛṣṇa during dreams, while awake, and even in sleep. (44)
When the senses possess outward activity, that state is proclaimed as waking.
At that time, the form of Hari and the saintly persons (sādhus) should be perceived externally;
indeed, the sādhus must be served with all external efforts. (45)
In the waking state, which is dominated by the quality of sattva, these [states] should be cultivated with discernment. ||46||
Even through delusion, those whose waking state is dominated by *rajas* should be served;
those whose waking state is dominated by *tamas* should be served during times of grief, fatigue, and the like.
The functions of the senses, however, reside in the heart and the throat.
The cows have not yet arrived; this indeed is the state of sleep while one is actually sleeping. ||48||
At that time, in a dream characterized by discernment, one should serve the virtuous;
at that time, in a dream dominated by the quality of goodness (sattva), one should serve Hari. 49.
In a dream dominated by *rajas*, one should serve [the deities] with a deluded intellect;
in a dream dominated by *tamas*, they should be served through grief, fatigue, and the like.
When the mental states (*vṛtti*) dwell slightly within the heart, that is the state of half-sleep (*ardhasuṣuptikā*).
Indeed, for a moment, one should perform equal service toward all beings while they are asleep. 51.
For a moment, service characterized by wandering [in distraction] should be performed during the Rajasic sleep;

for a moment, service characterized by surrendering into absorption (laya) should be performed during the Tamasic sleep. By implication, absorption is also directed toward Kṛṣṇa, while wandering is likewise performed among His devotees.
At that time, the perception of Hari exists only among the virtuous (sādhus) and not elsewhere among those who are illusory (māyika).
Then, in the Supreme Self, there is the dissolution of all things; this is the state of deep sleep (suṣuptikā).
Furthermore, the oneness of the self with Śrī Hari is the fourth state (turyapada), which is the state of deep sleep. ||52-54||

The enjoyment of that, delight in that, and the surrendering of one's consciousness therein; likewise, the surrendering of bliss, the surrendering of the individual soul (jīva), the surrendering of the vital breaths (prāṇa), and the surrendering of all latent impressions (saṃskāra). ||55||
The offering of all enjoyments is that perfect deep sleep which is always directed toward Hari.
This must be practiced by the devotees of the Lord, wherein lies the great bliss of Brahman—the destruction of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," and the dissolution of agency and possessiveness. (56–57)
When one offers oneself to Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, then Hari—
the Supreme Brahman, the inner witness, the observer of karma—
becomes the seer abiding within the self; for that is indeed the supreme state of the Fourth (turya).
There too, the Blessed One is to be served, as in the fourth state [turyaka] within meditative absorption (samādhi).

For the virtuous are to be served in that manner; indeed, they are absorbed in the fourth state through the vision of the abode, the power of the abode, the senses of the abode, and its splendor. || 59–60 ||
The Blessed One is to be served by one's own self through the rites of the *dhāman*;
the Supreme Brahman is to be served as the Brahman-self in the supreme state.
Then, in the fourth state (turya), Nārāyaṇa is to be served by Śrī with her own self through her divine, single-flavored, and spiritual body.
This is the state of liberation here, wherein the abode is conjoined with liberation.
O Kṛṣṇa, that [devotion] is to be made a source of bliss for Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-vallabha.
All states of existence are to be offered to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord;
childhood, youth, and old age are to be surrendered to the Supreme Self.
Femininity or masculinity must indeed be bestowed upon the Supreme Self;
likewise, virginity, boyhood, the state of being husband and wife, and womanhood [must be bestowed].
Ascetic practice and even death must be offered to Mādhava;
likewise, deliberation, the *bindu*, the *nāda*, the resonance (*dhvani*), and the words;
as well as the supreme (*parā*), the intermediate (*aparā*), the visionary (*paśyantī*), the middle (*madhyā*), and the articulate (*vaikharī*) [speech].
All those born of Brahman, who are embodiments of Brahman, should be offered unto Hari. ||67||
The supreme speech is that which consists entirely of the description of Brahman;
it is the discourse of the virtuous concerning Kṛṣṇa, consisting of recitation and song,
the description of the pastimes and deeds of Hari, and the description of devotion.
And there is a description of the incarnations, as well as praise for those who are virtuous. (69)
The description of devotees is also called the supreme speech;
that which bestows liberation and consists of divine sounds is proclaimed as entirely supreme. ||70||
That [devotion] which is offered to Hari is also pleasing to Hari and brings happiness; whereas other [forms of devotion] directed toward worldly objects merely engage one in mundane affairs. (71)
That speech which is true to its meaning, of the nature of truth, yielding the fruit of *ṛta*, and bestowing merit—such speech, ever perceiving [the Truth], should always be offered to Hari. (72)
That [devotion] is always considered [the highest] among lords, gods, and sages;
it reveals the quality of purity (sattva), bestows happiness, and should be offered to the Supreme Lord. //73//
Furthermore, that which is intent upon another purpose, consisting of censure or praise, aimed at achieving one's own worldly ends, and arising from a portion of delusion or error; ||74||
That speech which is moderate, yielding both merit and demerit as its fruit, or even fruitless, should be offered in every way to Hari Kṛṣṇa by one endowed with devotion. (75)
Furthermore, other speech that is devoid of meaning, or which causes agitation through faulty meaning, or which is base or vulgar, as well as cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), are fruitless in both respects. (76)
That *vaikharī* speech, which is devoid of fruit for both the listener and the speaker, devoted solely to disintegration, and accompanied by mere affliction, is always the lowest. (77)
That [speech] too should be offered to Kṛṣṇa, provided it arises according to the requirements of place and time;

furthermore, there is another kind which has a single determined meaning, and yet another which has many meanings; moreover, speech is fourfold: that with unclear meaning and that with clear meaning. (78)
Therefore, it should always be offered to Kṛṣṇa, for it is divine and bestows liberation. ||79||
The categories, sentences, and means of valid cognition should be imparted regarding the Supreme Self; those whose nature is established by logic should be imparted regarding the Supreme Self. (80)
The principles of the elements and their derivatives are to be offered into the Supreme Self;
the triad of the object of meditation, the act of meditation, and the meditator are to be offered into that Supreme Self. (81)
The categories of the object of enjoyment, the enjoyment, and the enjoyer should be offered into the Supreme Self;
devotion, which is the act of worshipping, should be offered to the illustrious Supreme Lord. 82.
O Indra, one's powers and those worthy of being offered should be dedicated to Mādhava;
whether it be gentleness or harshness, they should be cast into the Lord Hari. (83)
Having then become divine, she would manifest as the nails among people;
for that Nārāyaṇa, the divine sky is indeed the imperishable ether.

"In that regard, one should cultivate delight in the [spiritual] act of lovemaking (*ratā*), not in the [physical] act of scratching with the nails (*nakharatā*). Thus were Ratnaprabhā and the others instructed at that time by the virtuous Lord Narasiṃha, the yogi Hari.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā! 86.
Having been given the mantra, they were made pure, devoted to Viṣṇu, and intent upon my worship; then, regarding their guru as the god Lord Nṛsiṃha, they [proceeded]. (87)
They honored him exceedingly and fed him with great respect;
and from them, he received blessings that bring about well-being. (88)
Having bowed to the virtuous, the donkey-herders went to another village;
indeed, in their own home, they worshipped Hari according to the aforementioned method, crying out, "Hare! Hare! (89).
Through their devotion, their service, their knowledge, and their attendance upon their guru, I quickly became well-pleased with the keepers of the donkeys. (90)
Once, having made Garuḍa into a donkey and standing upon that donkey, I went along the road and met them first in front;
I was bearded, dressed in the attire of a Kṣatriya, and appeared splendid as if eager for a journey. (91)
To them, I reminded the illustrious Puruṣottama by these names: “Victory to Kṛṣṇa! Victory to Rāma, Janārdana!
Victory to Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu! Victory to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa!
Having quickly dismounted from the donkey, he offered his salutations;
and they too, hearing the name of Hṛṣīkeśa, became joyful and licked me with their tongues, just as beloved kinsmen, sons, or parents [would treat their child]. (94)
Having restrained me and made me sit down quickly upon a woolen seat,
they, being exceedingly joyful on the road, gave me water, fruit, and likewise food;
they even asked about my home, my arrival, and my activities.
Then I showed him my supreme divine abode in the highest ether,
as well as the account of the deeds known as Nārāyaṇa and the arrival for the sake of visiting the sacred ford.
Having heard this, O Lakṣmī, they became exceedingly devoted to me, Nārāyaṇa; and knowing me to be their supreme devotee, they served me with heart-felt massages of the body.
And considering me to be the best of holy men, they prostrated themselves before me like a staff.
Then, on that very path, I quickly granted them a vision of the four-armed Lord together with Garuḍa;
I bestowed my grace upon them, and whatever fruits and such they had eaten [were transformed]. || 99–100 ||
Clad in woolen blankets, carrying staffs in their hands,
and wearing leather sandals on their feet, they danced with great excitement.
With long cloths draped over their heads and wearing clean jackets, they danced with excessive joy and repeatedly rolled upon the ground. ||102||
Grant me liberation, grant me Your state, O Hare, whose vehicle is the donkey!
Grant us Your divine abode, O Kṛṣṇa, whose vehicle is Garuḍa! 103.
Having uttered this, they suddenly placed the dust of my feet upon their faces; then, as if in meditative absorption, those charming ones fixed their gaze intently upon me.
Then, O Lakṣmī, they vanished; and in another moment, having regained their radiance and describing me, they considered themselves to be of blessed fortune. (105)
There on the path, they constructed an altar for Nārāyaṇa;
they constantly performed devotion always on the bank of the Luṇī river. ||106||
When the time was ripe, O Rame, even those who were thousands in number, I gradually led to my own abode, the imperishable state of liberation, by means of Garuda.
Thus indeed have the devotees been uplifted by me through the practice of yoga.
From reciting or hearing this, enjoyment and liberation shall become certain.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Devotee Ratnaprabha, the Donkey-herder, Attaining the Lord and Liberation through the Holy Yoga of Lord Nṛsiṃha," in the third section, the Dvāpara Cycle, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.
