Chapter 226 [[Author: → Chapter 227.
Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, on the bank of the Ājīvanī river in Saurāṣṭra, there was a physician named Gadārdaneśvara. (1)
Having made his residence in Jīradurga and knowing the essential secrets of medicinal herbs,
the brāhmaṇa, together with his family, established his own shop in Jīradurga and there performed medical treatment for the sick using those medicines.
Indeed, he became renowned as one who possessed the skill to destroy diseases.
To the surrounding clusters of villages and throughout the people of the land,
the subjects came to his house for the removal of their ailments.
He too, having remembered Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, administers the medicine;
that indeed becomes highly effective, virtuous, and a remover of disease.
It should be combined with sacrificial ashes and sugar as a divine favor.
Medicines derived from wood and minerals, enriched with powdered *tulasī* leaves; ashes and other substances; juices processed by fire that alleviate autumnal fevers;
as well as fermented liquors (*āsava*) that destroy phlegm and cure chronic fever. (6–7)
Purgatives, pills, digestive stimulants, and those that destroy wind; seeds of trees that bestow power and nourish the bodily tissues;
powdered insects and husks derived from roots that remove diseases.
Whether derived from leaves, flowers, or even from the powders of bark, it certainly destroys all diseases for the patient in every way;
it also swiftly removes poison arising from the venom of snakes and other creatures. (3.226.10)
In the laboratory of such a physician, ten men perform grinding, as well as kneading, cooking,
the extraction of essence, powdering, and constant incineration. (11)
They diligently prepare medicines as is appropriate.
At the onset of the rainy season, Gadārdana himself goes to the field on the riverbank,
taking vessels made of crystal and other materials to that place teeming with living beings.
Having caught reptiles, copper-colored insects, indragopas, ants,
and creatures that cause redness to swell, he places them in a vessel;
by the thousands, they perish through those cruel means of killing.
In order to prepare stimulating oils, the king of physicians captures lizards from holes and other places, places them in glass vessels, and deprives them of life;
mercilessly, for the sake of his own profit, he destroys the lives of others. (15–16)
Though a Brahmin, he indeed adopted the nature of a Rākṣasa, becoming intent on the path of violence;
through greed for coins and by his craving, he became a perpetrator of harm.
Thus, Gadārdana, from time to time, became a destroyer of living beings.
For the sake of medicine, he became a killer who destroyed ten million living beings.
Even those creatures, fainting and tormented, cursed that twice-born man:
"May even other creatures take away the life-breaths of you, the destroyer of our lives! (18–19)
"Having repeatedly encountered suffering like ours throughout eighty-four hundred thousand births, go again and again to your death.
Thus was that physician cursed with many curses of intense force.
In the course of the ripening of his karma, he gradually became afflicted with fever.
To cure the fever, he suddenly employed medicinal pills and other remedies;
yet the fever did not subside, but rather increased all the more. (21–22)
For an obstacle that has arisen from one's past karma (*prārabdha*) is not destroyed even by ten million means;
likewise, great suffering arising from a curse does not dissolve through other means.
[This applies to] the physician, King Yama, the god, and the bull.
What need is there to speak of a capable human being?
[A person] is liberated only by the grace of the one who wields the curse, and not otherwise.
In this matter, those creatures have perished; from where could they obtain grace? (24–25)

Indeed, chronic fever has acquired power over the physician; constantly devoted to the destruction of diseases, it withers him away as if he were an inanimate object. (26) Then, for the sake of dispelling it, he drinks medicinal decoctions daily.
When decoctions that have not been properly prepared are destroyed, they become contrary [to their intended effects]:
they cause the loss of blood, increase heat, and even create minute perforations in the channels and masses of flesh. (27–28)
Then all those decoctions that caused wounds ceased their action;
even the blood portion flowed out through his urine, excrement, and spittle.
Although the physician had applied the most excellent treatment, he himself became more afflicted than the patient.

Neither intelligence, nor strength, nor wealth, nor skillful applications prevail against great sin when it has arisen, even for those who are proficient. O Lakṣmī, [this applies] even to one who is a renowned physician and has exerted effort toward healing. (3.226.30–31)
Other physicians also arrived from afar for the sake of treatment;
having performed a root-therapy, they administered medicine.
Nevertheless, not even a trace of recovery was seen in this man, who was struck by sin.
Having their hopes shattered, they return to their own homes.
Indeed, the flow of blood from the physician has not ceased at all;
rather, O Lakṣmī, by the medicines he applied there, it has only increased further. (33–34)
Thus a year passed for him, suffering like a denizen of Yama’s realm;
then the physician himself consumed the ashes that had arisen from his mother.
She too, having undergone a transformation, broke out with pustules all over her body.

The body became filled with pus, foul-smelling, and cracked all over; it oozed from the sides and was moistened, becoming like a hellish cauldron. No one could approach his side; the physician wept as he suffered from the piercing pain.
Afflicted by the bites of insects and creatures that have arisen [within him],
he cries out in extreme agony, his flesh being devoured by those creatures.
O King of Physicians, O Rama, you have experienced such great suffering.
"The suffering man constantly resorts to me solely for the destruction of his misery.
Indeed, I am not capable of destroying the misery of a curse;
for at that time, I was dwelling within the heart of the one who uttered the curse and was tormented by it. (3.226.40)
"I am indeed the giver of the curse; how then could I be the remover of it?
Without that curse, I have no power to bring about the liberation of a living being.
Even for such a physician as myself, who worships me..."
Suffering ceases entirely; neither death nor birth occurs.
He takes food that sustains life, which is easily digested by his stomach fire.
Consequently, the vital breaths do not depart, as they are bound by the continuity of experiencing the curse.
The king of physicians also performed many meritorious acts of charity;
yet his vital breaths, possessing a radiance equal to the city of Yama, did not leave their place.
Through the application of medicinal herbs, a slight recovery of health was observed.
For a month, health is seen and the flesh and marrow increase;
yet again, thousands of creatures are born there,
and insects bite in many ways, just as in the hell-pot of Yama here.
Thus, by the power of the curse, this physician remains in such a state again and again.
Ten years indeed passed for this patient in this manner;
for as many living beings as he had killed, for that very same duration did it last.
Suffering arose here directly, and yet the realm of Yama remained [as the destination].
O Lakṣmī, in the meantime, his six sons, due to association with sinners and excessive diarrhea, gradually met their death one after another. (48–49)
The six daughters of Gadārdana became widows and were deprived of offspring due to the fault of their association with him;
indeed, all of them became widows because of the sins of their father.
Sin is transmitted among people through sitting, lying down, clothing, eating, and joint labor;
through procreation and the division of inheritance. Just as there is fear for those householders when living beings are killed, [so too is the sin transferred]. (51–52)
And likewise, due to his curse, there was suffering for his family members;
all this intense and swift-flowing misery has arisen right here.
Thus, having reached the state of being without offspring, only his wife remains.
She too, overcome with anxiety, summoned her own brothers and gave them all her wealth; consequently, the house became as if empty.
Both his wife and his brothers were likewise bound by the snare of wealth.
All those who consumed wealth for their own enjoyment quickly became afflicted with disease and died;
indeed, due to their attachment to sinful wealth, they became utterly destitute.
Therefore, one must not eat the food of a physician, for by doing so, one becomes liable to perform penance.
O Lakṣmī, the physician is indeed like a *śataghnī* weapon; his food is considered to bestow sin.
Behold, physicians are truly merciless, always like the messengers of Yama, engaged in cutting, killing, inflicting death, and attending to corpses.
By practicing with a naked corpse, by gazing upon a naked corpse,

by constantly beholding corpses that are naked, foul-smelling, infested with insects, or putrefying; and by performing the funeral rites for the sick, or by habitually indulging in cooking and the like— (59)—
Physicians who are impure and who take the lives of others are like messengers of Yama.
Those who act without personal experience are sinners and snatchers of life;
one must not eat the food of such people, for that food brings about ruin. (3.226.60–61)
Indeed, not everyone in this world is equal to Dhanvantari.
If those who know the truth were meritorious, non-violent, and purifying,
they would always be considered worthy of worship, like the sons of Aśvinī.
For those who act for the welfare of the world and have abandoned the path of violence,

who apply medicinal herbs according to need with great devotion, who are free from injury to living beings, and who employ substances such as wood and minerals [for healing], [are not considered killers]. (63–64)

Those physicians of the gods are difficult to find, yet their worship bestows merit. Now, O Lakṣmī, after some time had passed, that wife of Gadārdana, named Mukundinī, became afflicted with the disease of consumption (kṣayaroga).
Devoted to Viṣṇu and faithful to her husband, she was endowed with the qualities of faith and pure disposition.
From her childhood, she had been a devotee of Hari, performing ritual ablutions and worship;
she was full of devotion, virtuous, and dedicated to the duty of a devoted wife.
She constantly performs vows, charity, and austerities; she serves the virtuous and is devoted to the stories of Kṛṣṇa; she is adorned by purity and contentment;
and through her body, mind, speech, and actions, she serves the holy ones.

Constantly devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa and endowed with the ninefold devotion, she prepares offerings such as necklaces, food, and incense; she is a worshiper of Viṣṇu, one who has surrendered her self, a great Bhāgavatī, and a beloved of Hari. (3.226.70)
Devoted to virtue and truth, virtuous, endowed with righteousness, and firm in her self-discipline;
divine, possessed of celestial qualities, O Blessed One, she is eternally steadfast.
She is devoted to meditation and intent on offering her very self to me, Hari.
O Lakṣmī, though she is such a devotee, she is deeply distressed by [worldly] association.
Indeed, half of all that belongs to a husband is enjoyed by his own wife;
thus, being overcome by grief and afflicted, she remains devoted to me.
When her year had passed and she was emaciated, her husband died.
Dependent on others and widowed, she wept like a female osprey;
beholding her husband’s miserable fate and remembering her daughters, sons, and other kin.
Remembering her deceased brothers and her own miserable fate, she,
like one afflicted by consumption, lost her fortitude and wailed with loud lamentations.
Hearing that outcry, the gods then stood motionless for a moment.
The seasons and the elements also became momentarily inert.
Then, O Lakṣmī, I, the inner self, suddenly felt my own approval;
dwelling in the heart of Mukundinī, I became affectionate and sorrowful.
The inner self granted her fortitude, and I too did so through right reflection. Having attained spiritual knowledge and taken hold of her courage, she repeatedly remembered me, Hari:
"O Lakṣmī, O Lord, O Lord, have mercy! (78–79)
Show compassion toward this devoted woman who is suffering and widowed;
be kind to her who remains, having lost all her possessions.
There is no limit to my sorrows; rescue me from the ocean of worldly existence.
"First kill me, and then kill my husband.
For one who is with her husband there is a destination, but for a widow there is no destination.
Here I am; having kindled the fire, I shall indeed burn while still alive."
Chastity is always appropriate; widowhood is terrifying.
Have mercy, come here, and restore him to health.
If you do not, then grant death to both of us simultaneously.
Having spoken thus, my devotee meditated upon me within her heart for a moment.
Meanwhile, I dispatched my attendants toward her husband—
to him who was being led away by the messengers of Yama, sorrowful and seeking refuge.
My attendants, having gone quickly, were separated from me by those seeking Yama;
they were seized, brought back, and made to enter my body once more.
Suddenly, the body, though bound with fetters, rose up of its own accord.
Seeking the corpse, they stood motionless, filled with great wonder.
Some said: "The experience of suffering for sinners is not yet complete;
he has returned to undergo further punishment for his sins, for he was not protected by the messengers of Yama. (87–88)
But others then said, "Due to the devotion of his truthful wife,
he shall indeed become free from disease through her great devotion.
Others said, "This sinful man is surely possessed by a *vāsana*."
"One does not go to the next world alone, leaving behind one's own wife.
But others then said, "The lines of karma are indeed difficult to overcome.
Thus they desisted and ceased their persistence toward him. (3.226.90–91)
Then, O Lakṣmī, by the power of my wife’s devotion, I appeared before her in a divine form, embodied and accompanied by my attendants.
I was the Lord Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, four-armed and possessing a celestial body. (92)
And I said to Mukundinī, "Choose a boon before me.
She too, rising suddenly, fell at my feet.
Gadārdana also, seeing me, slept as if free from illness.
Rising up, they quickly fell upon the ground at my feet;
and being commanded by me to grant a boon, those two said:
"O Ocean of Compassion, Supreme Lord, Consort of Ramā, grant us liberation! (95)
Everything has been brought to its end by Time; indeed, we two have been rendered homeless.
Mahākāla is the physician of physicians, and the Supreme Lord is his physician.
Summoned by Yama, we have been driven away here in every way by your attendants.
"O Supreme Lord, grant us liberation or assign us whatever task you desire.
To those two who were thus entreating him, he replied, "So be it," and having placed them upon a celestial chariot,
he sent them to the highest heaven by means of his attendants.

Then, by the power of her devotion to Satī, the virtuous Mukundinī abandoned heaven and quickly went to the world of Satī along with her husband. My attendants indeed [saw] that Mukundinī together with her lord. (3.226.100)
Having established the world of the virtuous, they indeed departed for my abode.

For a husband receives half of the merit performed by his wife.
Vows, gifts, and other acts of devotion—everything reaches half [the merit] to the deceased.
Likewise, relatives, sons, wives, friends, and others perform meritorious deeds even in the name of the departed; that merit reaches the deceased.
Therefore, people perform acts of faith, sacrifice, and charity only after [attaining] devotion. O Rama, there is indeed no other means for granting liberation equal to devotion;
by reading and hearing this, both worldly enjoyment and liberation shall surely come to pass.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sufferings of the Physician Named Gadārdaneśvara Due to His Sins, and the Liberation of His Wife Mukundinī through Devotion," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī; I shall tell you another story.
In the city of Pārvatī, there was a devotee named Harṣadharma who was a barber. (1)
He lived there with his family, engaged in the work of serving the king.
There, the ruler was a king named Svarṇadhanvā.
This barber, along with his family, performed service for him.

The barber had a wife named Nigamikā, who was virtuous, devoted to her husband, dedicated to the worship of Viṣṇu, and deeply righteous. She was intent on vows, charity, and the chanting of prayers, and she took delight in Nārāyaṇa.
Constantly devoted to the service of the virtuous and always possessed of a divine disposition,
she had five sons and five beautiful daughters.
All of them were devotees of the Blessed One, Vaiṣṇavas endowed with devotion.
They cry out to me, Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the cowherds and the Consort of Śrī.
(6) They also constantly worship me in their homes with offerings and presentations; they always honor me with the sixteen modes of service. (7)
Abiding always in their form, I accept their worship with joy.
Even the barber, having always bathed and performed my worship,
and then having offered me the food offering (naivedya) and eaten it himself, goes to the king’s palace.
For a servant indeed serves the king with his whole soul, not a barber.
Likewise, the sons and daughters of the barber serve the members of the royal family as is appropriate, having performed my worship and other rites. (3.228.10)
Every day, that barber’s wife, Nigamikā, would rise first in the morning, bathe, and clean the house and its surroundings;
then, having prepared warm water and bathed Keśava, she would attend to him. (11)
Having worshipped both Śālagrāma and me with all kinds of offerings—
fruits, grain, sweetmeats, flat cakes, curd, milk, and auspiciously prepared warm, thickened food— he indeed presents them to me.
Then, having performed the ritual waving of lights (nirājana) and offered the customary gifts, she rises and bathes her husband; likewise, having drunk the water used for washing her husband’s feet—
and indeed the water from Kṛṣṇa’s feet— she honors her husband as well.
And afterwards, she offers whatever is desired and required by her husband.
Then she gives food and water as appropriate to guests, virtuous people, and the destitute, and even to the cow. (1.9–1.6)
Having offered water to the Sun and presented the *arghya* offering to Viṣṇu,
and having thereafter given flour to the swarm of ants,
one should likewise give to the ancestors whatever remains that is pure.
Then, having offered food and water to the husband,
she likewise offers food, water, and fruit to her daughters and others; finally,
the Nigamikā herself eats the remaining prasāda.
"In every morsel, I offer it to Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa";
thinking thus, she eats, and likewise she drinks water.
In between, there are a dog, a mongoose, a monkey, a parrot, a sparrow, a cow, and a bull.
Even a female cat would come [to beg], and having given [something] to them, she eats; it is not otherwise. Such a devotee is like a maidservant of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
having completed her household duties, she is very swift in the very morning. || 21-22 ||
The exceedingly virtuous Nigamikā proceeded to the queen’s quarters;
there she gently massaged the limbs and rubbed the feet of the queen named Pañcadevī as she lay sleeping upon her bed. || 23 ||
For the sake of the queen, he quickly prepares warm water, as well as tooth-cleaning powder, mouthfuls of water for rinsing, and so forth;
he performs her cleansing and other rites, and bathes her with waters. (24–25)
The rubbing of fragrant unguents, as well as the cleansing of the body; the grooming of the hair, and the beautifying of the hair-dress and so forth;
the wearing of elegant attire, ornaments, and the like, and the application of collyrium and ointment. (26)
Having duly offered lac-dye for the coloring of nails, lips,
and so forth, and having honored her just as one would Lakṣmī,
the giver of wind pleases the Great Queen with a fan. (27–28)
The barberwoman performs all the household tasks beautifully,
including the midday and evening services such as massaging and so forth,
up until the presentation of betel leaves to the queen. (29)
She constantly spreads out a bed rich with flowers and perfumes.
The queen sleeps happily while the barber-maiden massages her feet;
the queen indeed falls into a deep sleep while the barber-maiden continues her work.
Having gone home, she performs service for her husband, consisting of massaging his feet, and indeed sleeps there constantly; meanwhile, the barber,
having performed excellent service for the king, [goes home] at the end of the latter part of the night.
He comes to their house constantly and serves them; therefore,
O Lakṣmī, blessed is the faith of those servants who serve there,
and even more so that of the women whose souls are endowed with devotion to their husbands.
This world is bound by karma; indeed, it acts under the sway of karma.
Yet, one who is subject to the state of desirelessness—a sovereign among devotees—acts [freely].
Both the barber and the king understand the bondage of karma.
Service to the king is a bond of karma; this exertion is for the sake of acquiring wealth. (36) Indeed, without the acquisition of means, the maintenance of the body cannot be accomplished at all.
Food, wealth, and clothing are obtained through service to the king. (37)

Nevertheless, those two, being full of devotion, perform service to me out of a desire for eternal bliss, rather than through false service and the like. Indeed, the embodied soul must perform actions for the sake of the body, senses, and objects, under the power of karma. (38)
One who desires liberation should perform actions for his own sake through knowledge;
however, one with a resolute disposition should perform them for the sake of Śrī Hari by means of total surrender.
Thinking thus, those two always perform service to me. (3.228.40)
In Rājagṛha as well, those two always perform worship of me;
they also repeatedly sing my *gopīgīta* (the song of the cowherd girls),

Having heard that, the queen and the king, their minds fixed on Kṛṣṇa, remained asleep;
yet they continued to worship Him and others in this manner, even while causing devotion to be performed.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Master, svāhā! (42–43).
O Kṛṣṇa, as they both repeatedly chanted "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" while reciting prayers,
such was the constant discipline of those two devotees in their service to the King.
Once, however, in the evening, when the barber had departed from the house, [the King went out].
While remaining in the house for the service of that very king,
at the moment of his departure,
ten other virtuous men and ten virtuous women of great honor arrived.
Through great fortune and great merit, holy men arrive;
indeed, for the sake of welcoming the holy, everything should be done with reverence.
Abandoning even a hundred tasks, one should practice service to the holy.
Hospitality toward guests is always considered the highest duty for householders. Furthermore, for the sake of virtuous and noble women, this is regarded as the supreme dharma;
it is certain that they must set aside everything else and remain devoted to service.
The human body exists for the sake of liberation, and on this earth, saintly persons exist for the sake of liberation.
Therefore, people should swiftly offer their entire being to them in yoga;
otherwise, what benefit is there in the human body without such service?
That house where guests arrive and are satisfied with a welcome and other courtesies shall always be purifying and worthy of being the abode of Lakṣmī.
But that house where guests indeed depart with disappointed minds— [shall never be so].
A house where [guests] are treated with disrespect and dissatisfaction is considered as if it were burnt;
it surely becomes devoid of merit and bereft of fortune and prosperity.
However, that house which provides refuge for holy men, renunciants, ascetics, and yogis [is otherwise].

That house is the abode of the gods, a divine and supreme sacred site at all times. But that house where there are no virtuous people and no service rendered to guests is declared to be a cremation ground; indeed, impurity (sūtaka) always resides therein.
In that house where virtuous people reside, the deities dwell;
all obstacles are warded off, and spiritual accomplishments abide there.
Even sacred pilgrimage sites come to such a place out of a desire for the feet of the virtuous.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa shines resplendent there.
Wherever Nārāyaṇa is, there are Rādhikā, Kamalā, and Ramā;
there the liberated ones dwell, possessing divine bodies and beloved by Hari.
That family upon which a saint bestows compassion becomes like Videha;
indeed, it is considered divine, a remover of sins, possessing liberation,
most excellent, Vaiṣṇava, and a bestower of mokṣa.
In whosever home the steadfast sages eat and drink,

All indeed become liberated through the attainment of the company of holy and virtuous people;
for service to the holy is an inexhaustible treasury, whereas any other is subject to depletion.
Therefore, having served the holy ones and likewise having fed them, [one attains liberation].
"Having laid him down and obtained his permission, I shall indeed depart from there.
Having thus resolved, "I am here solely for the sake of serving the Queen," the barber offered a welcome to the virtuous one and joyfully presented the *madhuparka* offering.
She gave them seats and offered fuel for the fire and water;
likewise, having prepared sweet food and warm fruit, she joyfully gave it to them.
Then she fed all those virtuous men and women.
She also massaged the bodies of the virtuous women and the holy men.
With steadfastness, she remained devoted to her task even as the holy men spoke of it;

Everyone—the virtuous men and women, as well as the barber—was asleep;
however, the barber’s wife, being very eager to perform service for the queen, felt a slight anxiety.

Then, although the time had passed, the barber’s wife did not arrive;

"Tomorrow I shall surely seize all the property of this barber, who has been entrusted to me by another."
"I shall expel her from the village, or I shall place her in fetters"—thus she became enraged; indeed, the Lord himself knows this.
O Lakṣmī, at that time, during the first watch of the night, I, the Blessed One, [acted] swiftly.

Assuming the most beautiful form of another devotee, that woman came for the sake of service and to pacify the angry queen. Reflecting thus: "That devotee of mine serves virtuous men and virtuous women," [he went to her].
"The enraged queen will destroy the livelihood of my devotee;
let that not happen to my devotee, my servant, who is likewise virtuous.
This righteous devotee of mine must be protected by me."
"Indeed, that entire family must be protected with devotion.
Having reflected thus, I, the protector of my devotees, assumed the form of a barber and went quickly to the queen's palace during the first watch of the night. (75–76)
All services were performed by me, acting skillfully in the form of a woman, for the queen during the night—namely, the preparation of ornaments, food, and the like;
the cleaning of vessels, as well as drinks and fragrant delicacies. (77)
The preparation of a delightful bed, as well as the offering of betel leaves and other refreshments;
the thorough massaging and rubbing of the queen's body;
the fanning with a fan to provide a breeze, and engaging in pleasant conversation. (78–79)
"O Lakṣmī, listen to that very instruction which I myself gave at that time during the night; I performed all the instructions and so forth.
Indeed, the discourse of the scriptures is to be heard, and the Guru is to be honored in every way."
Likewise, charity should be given by the Queen with faith, she who is the consort of Dharma.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa should always be served with the intellect.
The notions of "I" and "mine" must be abandoned, and pride should never be displayed under any circumstances.

One must protect the distressed; one should not show anger toward a servant. One should show compassion toward female slaves, and even when wounded, one must not take [their] food, wealth, or house, nor even their service at any time. (83)

The Supreme Self is to be worshipped by that queen; upon her, Hari’s grace is always present. By that, liberation in the Imperishable occurs, and she becomes a stainless, great liberated soul, equal to Kṛṣṇa.
She is not bound by auspicious or inauspicious karmas like Lakṣmī;
yet, through excessive affection, she attains oneness with Hari, just as Lakṣmī does.
Or rather, remaining distinct as his wife, she serves him with devotion.
By the grace of Hari, she always becomes independent in her activities;
established in Brahman and possessing the character of Brahman, she attains liberation in the Imperishable.
But that queen who is devoted to worldly enjoyment and devoid of service to Kṛṣṇa— ||87-88||
Having died and gone to heaven, she enjoys [its fruits] and is then born here again in the mortal world.
Thus, through many births, one who is perfected by devotion shall be liberated;
and by the grace of a holy guru, she will ultimately attain the imperishable state.
By the grace of Śrī Hari, indeed, all latent desires (vāsanās) here come to an end.
By engaging in the company of the virtuous and by worshiping the Supreme Lord, one should make this human birth meaningful, bestowing the eternal kingdom of liberation upon the self.
"This self is of the nature of Brahman; one should indeed perceive Kṛṣṇa within it.
Having thus instructed Queen Lakṣmī and having served her, I made her sleep as if she were awake, and then I departed from her abode.

At that moment, at midnight, the barber's wife arrived there, trembling and filled with fear, to serve the great queen; having approached the place of the bed, she bowed down and begged for forgiveness. (93–94)
"A great deal of time has passed for me in the course of this glorification.
O Great Queen, please forgive me; I did not come because I was occupied with service.
Having heard this, the queen was struck with supreme wonder and fell into doubt.

"How indeed has this very servant, who departed after having served you, returned again and begs for forgiveness without any offense? Having reflected thus, he said to her: "O nurse, how have you come back again? (96-97)
"You have arrived; tell me, how is it that you ask for forgiveness?
Having just now completed all my service to you during the night and so forth, you go to your own home—how indeed can you ask for forgiveness?"
The barber’s wife said: "I have certainly not come to attend upon you today.
Why do you speak to me as if I were deluded, saying 'I have arrived at this very moment'? O venerable lady, do not joke in this way; I was not present here. (3.228.100)
"Could it be that service was rendered to him by some other woman?
Upon hearing this, the queen fell into a moment of delusion; then, after a brief interval, she felt at ease. Having dismissed the barber woman, that sovereign of the people went to sleep.
Then, as soon as that barber’s wife was returning to her own home,
she saw a woman in her house who possessed many forms; at that moment, she appeared identical to herself in beauty, age, and dress.
For a moment, overcome with wonder, she asked the beautiful, smiling woman:
"Who are you, how and from where have you come here to my house, O lady equal to Kamalā?
Then I, Lakṣmī, having withdrawn my own beautiful form—
I revealed the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa Viṣṇu to you.
For your sake, having assumed the form of a barber, I served her;
however, while you were serving her, the queen then became enraged.
She resolved that everything must be taken from you through non-service.
Assuming your form, I served that mistress of creatures.
O Lord, I am your devotee, and I have come for the sake of your welfare.
"You are always accompanied by my husband, sons, daughters, and so forth.
You must constantly practice meditation upon me alone within the range of your perception.
I shall lead your family, who are within your sight, to my supreme abode."
Having spoken thus, I was detained by her and remained upon the bed for a moment;
having bestowed supreme bliss upon me, she vanished in the next instant.
In my dream, O sons, there were barbers, daughters, and virtuous women as well.

They all indeed beheld me and woke up in the morning. They engaged in a mutual description of the form of Hari, which was like a vision, and they considered their good fortune supreme because of this vision of Brahman.
Then, having bathed again in the morning and eaten, those virtuous ones departed for another village; and that divine housewife followed after the barber and his family.
"The barber worships me, and his entire family worships him."
Then, after some time, by means of excellent celestial chariots, I led them all to my supreme, imperishable abode. O Lakṣmī, Hari, moved by compassion,
and the king along with the queen and others, indeed came to understand my conduct.
Having ascertained that he was divine, they, together with their progeny, indeed took refuge in him;
and in the course of time, they too went to my supreme, imperishable abode.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have the devotees been delivered by me, the compassionate one.
Even under the pretext of serving the virtuous one named Kalyāṇadhāman, O Rame, by the grace of this [work],
through its recitation and hearing, may there be both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
and may my every desire be fulfilled.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of how the Lord, being pleased by the devotion of the barber’s wife named Nigamikā— who remained engaged in service to the saintly Kalyāṇadhāma and others— manifested in the form of Nigamikā and performed service to the queen, and protected and liberated the family of the barber," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to this story concerning the birth of a devotee.
There was a cowherd woman who was my devotee, residing in the city of Ārdraśṛṅga.
In the tiger forest— a place filled with lions, tigers, and predatory beasts—
dwells the goddess named Rūṭāṇakī, purified by her past impressions.
Listen, Lakṣmī, I shall relate to you this great wonder concerning that devotee.
In a previous birth, that virtuous woman was a Śūdra fisherwoman on the bank of a river (3).
She lived as a fisherwoman’s wife upon his boat,
always residing on the land situated at the confluence of the Śatruñjaya and the ocean (4).
With her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, she indeed carries those men traveling to the great pilgrimage site of Gopanātha across every shore by boat;
that virtuous woman receives with true devotion all the holy men who arrive there.
Indeed, even without taking any material offering, he leads one to the further shore;
yet at other times, having taken a material offering, he leads others to the further shore.
Once, there was a holy man named Śrī Haricaitanya, a king among yogis. (6–7)
To reach the further shore,
that perfected one, the best of holy men, indeed proceeded upon the water by means of his sandals.
By the power of his own perfected asceticism, he travels sometimes through the sky as well.
Nevertheless, wandering at his own will along the bank of a river upon the earth,
he arrived there by chance; and seeing him,
that fisherwoman indeed paid him homage and earnestly requested him to come onto her boat.
The best of yogis, for the welfare of the best of wise women, boarded my boat and, gratified by her devotion, gave her this instruction there:
"Worship Kṛṣṇa; worship Nārāyaṇa, the glorious Puruṣottama."
Associate with the virtuous and the chaste women; you shall attain a noble state.
(1.2) This body is of the nature of a fisherwoman, while your self possesses the nature of pure consciousness.
Indeed, this body always remains under the control of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). (1.3)
Just as the boat is under your control, so too is the body under your control.
Just as the boat is the object of sight while you are the seer and the impeller,
so too the body is the object of sight while the Self is the seer and the supreme impeller.

The body is pervaded by suffering and the like, while the seer is devoid of suffering and the like. (15) In that regard, another certain omniscient being shines forth within the seer; he impels one toward wholesome action and forbids one from unwholesome action. (16)
The inner self, whose nature is that of a witness, is indeed the Lord Hari;
he is the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the noble one, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa.
(17) Worship Him alone, who is honored by the lords of yogis and by virtuous men and women.
Worship him with single-minded devotion consisting of pure love.
Always behold that Lord, the beloved Kṛṣṇa, within your heart; constantly perform meditation upon the Lord of the Gopīs, who is endowed with his own divine form.
Abandoning external objects, behold Mādhava within your heart; offer all the senses unto that Kṛṣṇa. Turning back the functions of the senses, employ them in that Kṛṣṇa.
Accumulate great bliss from the mass of existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda).
Always become equal to Ramā, the enjoyer of Kṛṣṇānanda.
Through the attainment of the enjoyment of Kṛṣṇa, other worldly enjoyments become like poison.
In that way, they shall indeed become so; therefore, enjoy Kṛṣṇa as your husband and lord.
Always chant with devotion the divine and human exploits of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, which truly bestow both heaven and liberation.
Constantly remember all the wondrous deeds of the Lord of Ramā;
remember all the activities of the Lord of Śrī, including his acts of desire, his martial endeavors, and his festivals. (24–25)
Whether worldly or transcendental, whether inferior or superior—
all those divine exploits of the Lord of Ramā,
Hari, can make the insentient sentient and the sentient insentient. (26)
Always maintain the company of Hari, who is capable in such a manner.
Abandon negligence, great indolence, great delusion, and pride.
Having abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine," always remain established in the nature of the Self.
To cross the ocean of saṃsāra, remain steadfast in the company of the virtuous.
Having become devoted to Hari, always worship Hari as your husband.
Abandoning the state of the body, take refuge in the state of Brahman.
Offer all enjoyments, both gross and subtle, to Hari Kṛṣṇa.
Reflect thus: "I am the Self, not the body. And carry out your divinity by thinking, "I shall offer myself to the Lord of Śrī."
Having thus attained solitude, strive with persistence through your actions;
abandon the sin born of identification with the body, and abandon the path to the realm of Yama.
Having worshipped the Lord of Śrī and finally beheld the divine Lord of Ramā, [you shall attain liberation].

Go with that celestial chariot to the realm of divine syllables. Abandoning the state of a fisherwoman, assume the excellence of wisdom. Through association with me, the virtuous one, become truly supreme and devoted to Viṣṇu.
"Go to the Imperishable either in this birth or in the second;
thus, O Lakṣmī, that fisherwoman was instructed by the virtuous man.
Having attained supreme awakening, she indeed became wise. (35)
Having reached the opposite shore and disembarked,
the king of holy men went to the sacred ford after bestowing unsurpassed knowledge upon the boatman’s wife;
thereafter, she chanted the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa day and night.
By the power of destiny and through the course of time, that fish-eating woman died and was born as a human— a cowherd woman possessing many buffaloes.
Once again, that virtuous woman became a highly devoted follower of the Lord (mahābhāgavatī).
A servant of the virtuous from her childhood, she was devoted to celibacy;
she never entertained a desire for marriage, and even though her youth had arrived, her longing was burnt away so that she remained as if in old age. (3.229.40)
By the power of her past impressions, that yoginī remembered her former births;
by her very nature, she became devoted solely to the realization of the Self.
Known by the name of the goddess Ruṭāṇakī, she was dedicated to divine knowledge.
That virtuous woman, devoted to the service of the holy, was always a practitioner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
offering herself to the Self, possessing renunciation and endowed with dispassion, she incessantly performed the rotation of the rosary and the chanting of the praises of Hari. 42–43.
Having always prepared the milk of buffaloes so that it is wholesome and sweet,
she indeed feeds it to him with devotion in the form of *pāyasa*.
Having bathed in the morning, having worshipped Hari-Kṛṣṇa, and having offered the *arghya* water—
Having offered the *arghya* water to the Sun and having performed the dedication to the ancestors,
she then offered the *śrāddha* with milk-rice, cooked grains, fruits, and water;
thereafter, that virtuous woman caused the holy men and likewise the virtuous women to partake of a meal.
She always eats what is pleasing and conducts herself as one who purifies the assembly;
just as Lakṣmī, just as Gaṅgā, and just as the goddess Sarasvatī,
so indeed does that Ruṭāṇakī, whose supreme essence is Brahman, shine forth.
For in whosever home virtuous men always arrive, and virtuous women also come, having recognized their devoted service;
they perform kīrtanas, rāsas, and auspicious great festivals. ||48-49||
Thus, while the servant Bhajamānā was at home,
when midnight had passed and all embodied beings were asleep,
a certain Daitya with iron earrings arrived from the forest.

With a body as tall as a palm tree, dark in complexion, and excessively hairy, he was a youth, strong and well-nourished like another banyan tree. With great agility, he seized that sleeping, most virtuous woman. (91–92)
Having taken her, he traveled by way of the sky and arrived at a great forest;
there, with agility, he descended into a dense thicket of trees.
Having gently set that beautiful Ruṭāṇakī upon the ground, he departed.
The Daitya awakened her, and as soon as she had regained consciousness,
she saw herself in the middle of the forest,
brought there by a forest-dwelling Daitya named Āyasakuṇḍala, who had brought her under his control.
Moreover, she was a great devotee, courageous, virtuous, and a sovereign lady; indeed, she was a Vaiṣṇavī goddess equal to Durgā,
possessing the power of Kṛṣṇa, and being chaste, she did not feel even the slightest fear.
She remembered in her heart Kṛṣṇa, her beloved, the Lord of the universe, her husband:
"If I am your devotee, and if I have been made your own by you;
if I abide in my devotion to you alone, being equal to Śrī herself. (57–58)
And I am indeed one who has surrendered her very self to you, a practitioner of Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
for my hand has been taken forever by you as my lord.
And if I have served the virtuous and those worthy of attainment, [then let me be yours].
"If I am dear to you, having surrendered all my possessions for your sake, then come to me, O Viṣṇu; O Kṛṣṇa, appear before me quickly.
Come in person and protect me from this terrible demon."
"If I am not born to you, or if I have become devoid of devotion, then let the demon Bali touch you, if it pleases you.
O beloved, do as you wish; do as you desire with your own life."
"O Blessed One, exert yourself or practice indifference.
Having spoken thus, she then offered worship into my heart;
and the Daitya, in turn, delighted her with his speech through many expressions of affection.
Though eager, he indeed incited her to engage in various kinds of conversation;
nevertheless, having fallen silent and with her mind fixed on me, she did not speak at all.
The demon danced repeatedly before her, performing many jests.
Nevertheless, with her mind fixed on Kṛṣṇa, she did not direct her thoughts outward at all.
(66) Then, even while asleep in their homes, everyone—including the virtuous men and women, the saintly, and the great dignitaries—became as if insentient. (67)
Ruṭāṇakya’s father, named Durvāraṇa, was also asleep;
his mother, named Khaṭamiṣṭādevī, was likewise fast asleep. All the other villagers were then in a deep slumber. (68)
By some it was not perceived that Ruṭāṇakī had been carried off in that darkness;
for those queens were like beasts, their vision limited to scent, and though they were awake, they remained as if in a deep sleep, perceiving only the scent of the Daitya.
The queens indeed perceived that the Daitya had arrived;
they saw him taking the goddess Ruṭāṇakī away through the dark sky, and they raised a great outcry, crying out "Raṇakāṭa! and "Rambhaṇa! and wailing like animals.
Having heard that danger had arrived, they all remained awake;
out of fear of a tiger, they placed fires around the logs on every side.
Indeed, they made loud, long-drawn-out sounds all around.
Fearing him to be a lion, all the Daityas did not recognize him at that time;
thus an hour passed even though they were guarding him on all sides.
Their queens did not become calm, but remained agitated as if roaring.
But one queen, Rūṭāṇakī, quickly went to the throne;
taking the throne with her two horns, she began to wander about.
Then everyone called out, "Rūṭāṇakī! Rūṭāṇakī! (75–76).
"Where has she gone, and why does this queen even destroy her own seat?
For when summoned, that passionate woman did not reply;
she is nowhere to be seen among the people, nor even within the house amidst the virtuous and faithful women."
Then the little girl, having become a source of anxiety, was taken away by someone. Thereupon, all were distraught and wept while searching for her;
they went out everywhere around the boundary, but did not see her anywhere.
Their hopes departed, they returned and remembered me, the Supreme Lord;
all the virtuous women and men performed the chanting of my names:
"O Anādi-Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Arya-Kṛṣṇa-Mādhava! (3.229.80).
Then, accompanied by my discus and Garuḍa, I went into the forest.
With great agility, I cut down that dancing king of the Daityas;
having drawn his splendor into myself and placed him upon Garuḍa, [I departed].
Having gladdened her with affection, I quickly led her to her home;
by the mere touch of me, that virtuous woman became most divine.
O Lakṣmī, she was like you, possessing divine sovereignty, for she was indeed your equal.
Thus, having established her in the house at Ārdraśṛṅgapura by way of the sky-path,
and having granted my divine, radiant vision to all the devotees, I remained there for more than a ghaṭikā.
Having accepted the service rendered by the virtuous men and women—
consisting of milk-rice, food, worship, water for drinking, betel-leaf, and so forth—
and when I, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, was ready to depart after having partaken [of these offerings], ||| 86 ||
Then the devotees, immersed in love and filled with longing, made this prayer:
"O Kṛṣṇa, take us along with him, if we are indeed your most devoted servants.
The saintly men and women of Rūḍhāṇakī likewise entreated him in the same way. (87–88)
O Lakṣmī, I then gave them my auspicious mantra:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā. I also then gave them water from My feet, prasāda, and milk-rice (pāyasa). ||89||
Having instructed the immature men there to perform acts of devotion,
she likewise [instructed] the mature, virtuous, and holy people, as well as Ruṭāṇakī, that chaste woman,
her mother, her father, and even the queen.
Having granted divine bodies to the liberated souls and likewise to the Muktānikās,
and having placed them upon the back of Garuḍa, I led them to my imperishable abode.
As for others who were not yet mature, I led them to the supreme Vaikuṇṭha in due time.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have indeed provided protection for the women of the Ābhīras. She has become Muktānikā, a beloved of Brahmā in my imperishable syllable;
today she exists in your realm by the name Rūpeśvarī.
"This young woman is my wife; behold her, wedded to me.
Here are ten other virtuous young women who are my wives—these ladies here, beginning with Mandāra-kalikā, are your friends."
In the sacred field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, my beloveds are dear to Brahmā;
only those with divine vision know this story, and no others.
This divine wonder of mine has been told by me as I sport. ||96-97||
In this way, I always protect my devotees in every manner;
I also grant liberation to those who have matured and bestow upon them the imperishable abode.
Those who constantly worship me with the disposition of offering their very selves—
For they and I are indeed interconnected;
I always and in every way protect those who have surrendered to me from time,
Yama, karma, the senses and so forth, and from all defects.
"From reading, hearing, reflecting upon, or even speaking of this, there shall surely be enjoyment and liberation; my attainment bestows happiness.

(101) Thus ends the account in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, concerning how in a previous birth, the fisherman’s wife Rūṭāṇakī—a devotee of the Ābhīra caste—and the virtuous women were protected and liberated from the demon by Śrī Hari.

Śrī Puruṣottama said: Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, you who dwell in Matsyapattana.
Nevertheless, for that fish-eating fisherman who was full of devotion,
[he related] the story arising from the company of the virtuous,
which effects liberation, purifies sinners, and likewise destroys the delusion of Māyā. (1–2)
There was a fisherman named Dhīraparva in Matsyapattana,
who was always the master of a hundred boats at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā river and the ocean. His boats, manned by servants, used nets to catch fish.
From the hour of Brahmā until sunrise, this occurs constantly:
a net always catches hundreds of thousands of fish—both small and large, very long, and possessing various qualities and body sizes. (4–5)
For them, a sinful nature characterized by violence arises during the festival of the wise.
Even though Dhīraparvan possessed a lifespan of one hundred thousand years,
through excessive violence his life was constantly diminished until it was measured at only a hundred days.
Within two years,
seventy thousand years of his lifespan were cut short by sins due to the curse of Matsya.
After thirty years had passed, he devoted himself to the occupation of a fisherman.
Having thus passed thirty-two hundred thousand years,
in the final month of that thirty-second year, during the rainy season, there was a downpour of rain.
For seven days it fell continuously throughout all the regions of Kṛṣṇa.

Likewise, O Lakṣmī, in the regions of the Tuṅgabhadrā, there was a constant downpour of rain resembling the flow of a ploughshare. At that time, the waters of the rivers did not subside due to their full force.
Abandoning the paths of the cities, many men there, as well as forest-dwellers and even holy men, fled to the paths of the earth and the wilderness;
even beasts and birds were carried away by the floods of water. (12)
Many among them died in those floods, dragged far away;
all who were without support perished, while those with support clung to wood, and others within the city who clung to trees and such remained alive. (13–14)
At that time, seeing living beings even in the great waters at the confluence of the Matsyapaṭṭa and the Kṛṣṇasāgara,
Dhīraparvan arrived with his servants to protect them using mechanical boats.
He commanded all the captains of the hundred ships:
"Do not catch fish or crocodiles as long as there is danger from the river; instead, capture living men from the midst of the flood."
In every way, the gift of life—indeed, merely sustaining the breath of living beings who are carried away by the current during this dissolution—is what must be performed here;
as well as providing food, such as dry grain and roasted chickpeas and the like. (18)
Blankets, garments, and other items for warding off the cold should be given.
Thus indeed was protection ordained there by the wise Parvata, through the provision of wealth, food, clothing, boats, and so forth, by means of his servants and men. (3.230.20)
Men, women, children, or the elderly, whether clinging to wood,
attached to bamboo poles or great trees, hanging from branches,
stuck in straw baskets and the like, or taking refuge in corpses and such; ||| 21 ||
Indeed, thousands of men—ascetics, virtuous men and women, those free from passion, and even Vaiṣṇavas—were devotees dedicated to Nārāyaṇa; they were protected while still alive. (22–23)
From the great ocean of merit obtained through their blessings,
there also arose the emergence of the great merit of the gift of life;
for merit and sin cannot be exhausted without experience.
Within seven days of the exhaustion of his lifespan, this conjunction occurred.
Indeed, life is diminished by sins and increased by merits;
the former is the experience of what was done previously, and that which follows is the experience of what was done later.
The fruit arising from actions such as violence and killing is indeed repeated death;
by that very act of slaughter, the executioner shall suffer it in the abode of Yama.
O Bali, the karma born of slaughtering fish is characterized by intense momentum.

Previously, he was indeed obtained for the sake of enjoyment, bound by the noose of Time, and joined with the messengers of Yama, [reaping the fruit] born from the slaughter of ten million fish and other creatures.
At the end of seven days, on that day when the force of the rains had diminished... (28–29)
Seated upon a mechanized boat,

attended by his servants and accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, he went out onto the water to behold the shore at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and the ocean, where the great current flowed with immense speed.
As he traveled upon the great waters of the ocean for a distance of one *krośa*,
there suddenly appeared beneath the ship’s deck a wondrous tossing of tree branches;
an unexpected and towering whirlpool of water arrived.
And even when a great flood arises unexpectedly,
should two great walls of water collide with one another,
[the practitioner] leaps with great speed from the front of a large ship into the sky. (33)
As far as the bow had descended into the great waters,
so far was the stern lifted up by force into the sky; then,
the prow of the ship was driven downward into the depths of the water by the two walls of water on either side.
Then, overturned by the waters of the great current at its side,
she sank for a mere moment into the waters of the ocean;
having reached the bottom of the earth, she was left without support and without companions.
Dhīraparvan and all the others died, having fainted in the waters.
Those sinners were swiftly led to the world of Yama by the messengers of Yama.
Their corpses were devoured by fish, and their wealth was seized by the servants and men.
The boats were carried away by the sailors, but the life-breaths were taken by the attendants of Yama;
the merits and sins were carried away by those deceased family members,
just as provisions for a journey travel together with the person themselves.
And at the appropriate time, they were led by messengers toward the abode of Yama.
There, Citragupta recited their sins in the presence of Yama;
however, the King of Dharma did not punish them all according to their deeds.

Then he cast the fish-killers into the Kālasūtra hell for a long time; thereafter, he cast them into the hell known as Galapāśa (the Noose around the Neck). After that, he cast them into the Kṣārakardama (the Slime of Alkali) hell for a very long duration.
Then he cast them, along with their weapons, into the sacrificial pit of slaughter;
thereafter, he cast them for a long time into the Forest of Sword-Leaves;
and then he cast them into a fire-pit filled with great flames.
Then he threw them into that pit there, which was teeming with living creatures;
therein scorpions, chameleons, and other venomous stingers bit them.
Thereafter, King Yama cast them into the Lālāmukha hell.
Then, in the pit for fish and other creatures known as the Salt Ocean,
he cast them into a boat-net under the oppression of his soldiers;
there, those fish became food for the great fish and others.
They were torn apart by fish and devoured again and again;
yet, having been restored to life once more, they underwent further sufferings.
Then, after a long period of time, they were all expelled from the pit.

At the end of their punishment for all their sins, by the command of Dharma, they became hungry ghosts (pretas) suffering in a vast, parched forest. After a thousand years, having endured those torments of the hungry ghosts, [they were released]. (3.230.50)
Fish born in the salt ocean at the confluence of the Black Sea were caught by fishermen using nets and machines, and were subsequently eaten. Thus,
they experienced the end of their suffering through the exhaustion of the fruits of those committed sins.
Then, the even greater merit born from the gift of human life was attained.
All those [children] became the fine sons of Vaiṣṇavas, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and ship-owners in the city of Matsya. (52–53)
Those who, by means of ships, carried out the trade of goods belonging to many countries—
engaging in that most excellent, wealth-bestowing enterprise rather than violence—
had such sons as these, auspicious and endowed with devotion.
In whosever house there is an abundance of wealth and grain, they shall be endowed with happiness wherever they may be.
They will be devoted to Brahmins and devoted to the virtuous, intent upon the dharma of non-violence,
dedicated to the worship of the gods, charitable, and eaters of the remains of sacrificial offerings.
They were devoted to the service of cows, worshippers of virtuous men and women,
full of faith in the service of temples and other sacred sites, and endowed with prudence.
Indeed, they had a temple of Nārāyaṇa constructed there.
There, Hari was installed along with Lakṣmī by the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites.
(58) Then, a devoted Brahmin named Nirvāṇanāvika, having completely renounced the life of a householder, entered the stage of renunciation. (59)
Having become a virtuous priest, he always resided there in that temple;
he was the supreme Vaiṣṇava ascetic named Nirvāṇāyana,
who performed service to the deity, service to his devotees, and service to the righteous.
He performs divine Vaiṣṇava festivals and causes them to be performed as well.
In the evening, he narrates sacred stories, and men and women come from all directions to hear them; indeed, the city became a center for the Vaiṣṇavas.
Once, drawn by his devotion and overcome with compassion,
I became a saintly Vaiṣṇava and went there to hear the discourse. Seeing that I had arrived as a guest, he seated me upon an auspicious seat.
That virtuous and auspicious one even offered me a welcome and other courtesies.
Then, following the narrative of the *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*,
Hari compassionately taught it there to the members of the assembly.
Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa is pleased by the hearing of this narrative;
for that Kṛṣṇa whom the narrative describes becomes manifest here in person.
Indeed, the fruit of the narrative is love for Hari, which arises from the knowledge of His majesty.
O Blessed One, there is steadfastness in the Self, steadfastness in the Lord, and liberation in His abode;
the destruction of the delusion of Māyā, constant service to Hari, and likewise a divine state forever filled with eternal bliss. (67–68)
The fruit of that [devotion] is said to be this: the story should thus be heard with reverence.
For a devotee full of love, a single ghaṭikā does not pass without Kṛṣṇa;
he would not be able to remain at all without the sight of Kṛṣṇa.
He exists as one possessed of knowledge, devotion, and detachment.
A firm and imperishable stability in Hari arises within him;
even for the goddess Śrī, her love for her beloved remains unswerving.
She is exclusively and fully devoted, always charmingly absorbed in Hari;
intent upon accomplishing her own purpose, she seeks nothing other than Kṛṣṇa.
Her mind never goes elsewhere; it dwells eternally in Hari alone.
She certainly accomplishes her own purpose as well as the purpose of Kṛṣṇa through devotion.
As the beloved of Kṛṣṇa and a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, she should always be devoted to Hari;
abandoning her own self-interest, she should accomplish every task for Kṛṣṇa.
She should possess the disposition of offering her all and remain eternally surrendered to Hari.
Thus do women become truly charming, devoted, and fully surrendered.
For them, Kṛṣṇa is their husband in three ways; He is their deliverer from the great ocean [of worldly existence].
For their welfare, Kṛṣṇa is born as a human husband;
indeed, for the sake of grace, Hari is born as King Ramaṇa, the bestower of liberation.
For the welfare of the virtuous, he is born as the ascetic sage.
Those who take refuge in Him as the King, the Holy One, the Lord, and the Master,
become divine and liberated in tens of millions.
With divine vision, they know Hari-Kṛṣṇa as the Supreme Lord.
[They worship] the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of the Lord of Lakṣmī.
(79) Just as embodied beings drink the water of the ocean of sweetness, they satisfy themselves according to their bodies, according to their capacity, and according to their strength. (3.230.80)
All embodied beings, from ants up to the great fish,
nevertheless never reach the far shore of the ocean; likewise, from gnats to Garuḍas, they cannot transcend the sky.
Indeed, having attained happiness according to their capacity, they perform flight;
yet they do not reach the end, for the sky is said to be boundless.
In the same way, no one at all reaches the limit of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra.
Just as an embodied being on the ground perceives the moon as a mere plate, yet when he has reached its proximity, he perceives it as vast; so too,
a person situated within the moon perceives the moon as boundless.
Likewise, a devotee who remains close attains the boundless Kṛṣṇa.
Indeed, the power of worship when it is slight is said to be like that of a lamp; however, when that power becomes greater, it truly arises like a forest fire. (889–890)
That [light] is even greater than that, like the fire of the great elements;
that which is even greater than that is considered equal to the abode of Brahman.
Filled with the splendors of Brahman, the devotee finds Mādhava.
The great liberated one, whose nature is Brahman, serves the Supreme beyond the supreme— the shoreless, most divine, dark-hued, lovely,
and heart-stealing Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beginningless Master and Lord of Ramā. (88–89)
By the power of devotion and practice, a woman attains the Lord of Māṇikī—
the Lord of the virtuous, the Lord of the liberated, the Lord of Brahman, the Great Sovereign.
Just as an increase occurs in affection, illumination, and so forth, so it is here.
Having attained liberation, he obtains the great, divine bliss of Kṛṣṇa.
With Kṛṣṇa as his soul, with Kṛṣṇa as his form, and overflowing with the bliss of Kṛṣṇa, that man or woman who has offered themselves becomes the most excellent among the liberated. (91–92)
Through the power of devotion and practice, even oneness with Kṛṣṇa arises—
eternal and imperishable, like Lakṣmī, Rādhikā, and Māṇikī.
Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, is to be worshipped eternally.
O Hare, O Śrī Bālakṛṣṇa, O Lord of Śrī, O Lord of Akṣara, O All-pervading One!
(94) "Oṃ namas śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā"—let the servants of Nārāyaṇa indeed chant this mantra daily. (95)
"May those who offer themselves be intent on every resolution for the sake of Kṛṣṇa.
Having said this at the conclusion of the discourse, I indeed became four-armed,
adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, jewels, crown, and earrings.
O Lakṣmī, he was resplendent with all his splendors and hailed with cries of "Victory!
(97). He was honored by hearts with devotion and with waters of sandalwood;
saluted for the sake of their own liberation, I said to them, "So be it" (98).
Suddenly attracting their minds into the ether of consciousness (*cidambare*),
when the time arrived, I led them to my imperishable abode (*akṣara-dhāma*).
Some I brought to heaven, others to the realm of truth (*satya*), and still others to the station of Vairāja.
He likewise led others to Śrīpura and another to Amṛta;
he caused those devotees— the ferrymen who protect living beings— to reach Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, the unmanifest, and the supreme abode.
O Lakṣmī, those who protect the virtuous, protect the chaste women, and protect children;
those who bestow the gift of life upon their devotees, who are born of a second birth—
such great sinners as these may, at some time, [attain liberation] for the sake of the Blessed Lord.
For the sake of virtuous women, for the sake of the virtuous, and even for the sake of cows,

I lead those who perform meritorious deeds— even those who are merely virtuous practitioners— to the unchanging, supreme state, the abode of the highest, upon the arising of their merits in due course of time.
From reciting, hearing, remembering, or even contemplating this,
there shall surely be enjoyment and liberation, and one’s desired goal will be attained.
Even the sins of the sinful are destroyed by the mere remembrance of Śrī Hari.
And by singing the glories of the devotees, all their sins are purified in every respect.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of how Dhīra, Parva, and the other fishermen who were fishers in their previous birth—after undergoing the torments of Yama due to their former meager merit—were born as boatmen, performed worship there, and attained liberation," in the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*, within the third section, the *Dvāpara-santāna*.
*Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa-Saṃhitā*, Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*). Chapter 230.
