Chapter 232 → Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī,
to the story of this Jallāda, known by the name Tārakādarśaka, who was impaled upon a stake.
In the city of Cambāvatī, indeed, on the banks of the Rāvī river—

In that great fortress-prison which inflicts the punishment of the trident, he was appointed as the overseer of the stars, the one who impales [criminals] upon the trident. Those great offenders who had been punished by royal decree were there. (2–3)
Killers of women, killers of cows, killers of children, killers of men, and destroyers of images—
those who ruin temples shall all be punished with the stake or the staff.
Tārakadṛśi subjects them to mounting the tip of a stake.
In the city of Cambā, there was a great king named Supathānaka.
He protected the trident-wielder (Śiva) known as Tārakādarśaka and Jallādaka.
In the midst of the fortress stands a stake upon which those who move through the air (the Siddhas) always reside.
Winged creatures, desiring to eat flesh, indeed fly about; upon remembering her, a trembling of the hair arises even in one possessed of fortitude,
and upon seeing her, even a weak person experiences a paralysis of the heart.
Upon hearing of the punishment, even virtuous people remember the Supreme Lord.
Even sinners remember the Master, crying out, "O Lord of Lords, protect me!
For them, that place is as terrifying as the abode of Yama.
There, in that fortress, he lived day and night in a state of wretchedness;
he received a meager wage from the kingdom and sustained his life by it.
He stood before the executioner who wields the spear and staff, at the very moment of being sentenced to punishment for his wickedness.
He indeed causes the names "Kṛṣṇa" and "Nārāyaṇa" to be heard.
"O Mādhava, O Govinda, protect me! Protect me again from sin!
Here I am, surrendered to Kṛṣṇa in the form of the stake. || 11-12 ||
"I alone shall experience this fruit of my own sin; no one else here bears a share of the fault.
If I am to be liberated from this evil, I shall never again commit such a transgression.
Let all people listen: by virtue of my own karma, I now ascend [the funeral pyre]. (13)

Let them not grieve at my destruction; rather, let those of evil deeds alone grieve. Let my kinsmen, fathers, mothers, relatives, sons, and daughters not commit sins, nor let them suffer upon the stake. (14–15)
"And those friends and the people of the world who behold me here—
let them uphold my dharma and say nothing else.
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā."
Having thus uttered all of that,
they bound the eyes of that man wearing the staff with a cloth, lifted him slowly by his attendants,
and placed him upon the sharp-edged tip of the spit, with his back resting on the base.
When the back pain gradually subsides in the middle part of the spine and the sharp ache in the back enters the arm as it is raised upward,
then the devotee Jallādaka chants "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa" indeed.

"O Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa-Kṛṣṇa, you make the sinner hear [your name]. When the destruction of sin as well as liberation arises, or else when a virtuous birth occurs for the sinner, [it is through you]. (3.231.20–21)
At the time of his final breath, while uttering the name of Hari, they give water mixed with *tulasī* to that sinner; meanwhile,
the king’s attendants play various musical instruments there in many ways.
Indeed, one would never hear the sounds of suffering, such as cries and insults;
rather, once the vital breath has departed, they remove the corpse from the stake and cast it into a fire-pit, or else give it to a relative. (23–24)
By the king's command, he indeed gives [the property] to the householder exactly as it is;
in this same way, that Tārakādarśa sends even the offender either to the world of Yama or to heaven upon proclaiming the name "Kṛṣṇa. (25)
I know that Hari-Kṛṣṇa is indeed within me; I delight in that. My devotee Tārakādarśa is engaged in the chanting of the Name.
Having performed this act of penance, he then bathed and [wore] a garland.
Holding [the image] in his hand, he even recites the *Kṛṣṇakṛṣṇa* mantra a thousand times;
likewise, he performs seven days of fasting as an atonement.
He begs forgiveness from Kṛṣṇa, saying, "Forgive me for the sin of the trident."
Then, having bathed at the auspicious ford on the Rāvinī river in the region of Jambū,
he indeed gave as a gift the wages earned that day;
he constantly served holy men and performed the remembrance of Hari.
Constant meditation upon Hari, as well as His worship and devotion;
likewise, the offering of food, and the offering of betel-leaf and water;
incense, lamps, prostrations, the waving of lights (nīrājana), and hymns of praise.
Having performed even the request for forgiveness, he performs the dismissal with "namas.
Then, having eaten the prasāda that was offered,
he stands humbly before [the deity] as one appointed to his own service.
Whirling a rosary in his hand and chanting "Nārāyaṇa," he sees devotees and offers salutation to the Inner Self;
regarding everything as the abode of Brahman, he remains indeed immersed in it.
Such was my devotee Jallāda, whose vision was like that of Tāraka.
Having attained firmness in devotion to me, he would call together men and women to his own courtyard in the evening and perform kīrtana at the onset of night.
"O Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa Viṣṇu, O Victorious One, Lord of Rādhā and Ramā! O Govinda, Mādhava, Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of Śrī!
Thus they cried out together with the people for two ghaṭikās.
At the conclusion of the *kīrtana*, he performs my worship as well as the *ārārtrika* ceremony;
he distributes the *prasāda* offered to me to all the devotees, and at night, having placed the *mālā* around his neck, he indeed goes to sleep. (38–39)
I am indeed named Bālakṛṣṇa-Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
Thus, being pleased by his devotion, I appeared before him;
though remaining invisible, I indeed heard his kīrtana and other devotional acts.
I see his worship and always accept it with affection.
Then, on one occasion, I thought of delivering my devotee:
"Food, water, and clothing must be given by me to him constantly. (41–42)
This man must be liberated from the procedure of impalement;
he is my devotee and is entirely free from attachment to the act of impalement.
Nevertheless, he performs it for the sake of sustaining his life or for the sake of wages.
Violence is indeed a sin, and the stake is its instrument.
My devotee trembles at that and performs penance;
therefore, he must be released from the authority of the act of impalement.
Having reflected thus, O Lakṣmī, I then became the superintendent of the prison. Assuming the form of a prison warden, I went toward the king and reported to him the conduct of Tārakādarśa.
Listen, O King, I shall tell you what I say; then do as you please.
This man, Tārakādarśaka, has indeed been appointed by you on a salary to wield the trident for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon the wicked. (47–48)
This devotee, endowed with compassion, performs penance;
he regards the impalement upon a stake as a sin for the embodied being deserving of punishment.
Chanting "Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa," he does not eat for seven days.
Gentle-hearted and compassionate, he is in some respects subject to the power of mercy. It appears to me that he might indeed disregard commands at times;
for this reason, one of such a mild nature is not fit for that task. (3.231.50–51)
In that matter, another person who is always capable and cruel should be appointed—one in whom there is complete trust and from whom no fear arises.
However, I perceive a danger from this [other person]; therefore, you must remove him.
"Grant him protection for the forest where there is no violence;
[grant it] such that there shall be no fear for him, nor for his authority, nor for his governance.
Having spoken thus, he issued a formal edict of command right then and there accordingly.
Having caused [the document] to be written and having made the forest my place of refuge, I vanished;
meanwhile, by the king's command, a letter arrived at my abode through a messenger.
Even the sight of that star was considered a favor from Hari.
"By the will of Kṛṣṇa, my departure from this sinful place is indeed certain.
Lord Hari, the protector of his devotees, does what is appropriate.
Thinking thus, and disregarding the Lord’s desire, he quickly abandoned the site of Śūlin.
He quickly took charge of the forest region with high salaries;
endowed with great happiness,
he dwells in the forest tract together with his family, constantly on the auspicious bank of the Rāvinī river.
With wild fruits, tubers, leaves, legumes, and seeds;
with grains, auspicious medicinal herbs, cooked foods, juices, and likewise with honey—he indeed sustains his livelihood through these fresh provisions, which result in happiness. (3.231.59–60)
Having recognized my greatness, he serves me even more intensely;
mounting his camel at night and by day with his soldiers,
he surveys the great forest and always conducts himself like a king.
The forest-dwelling people offer honor with milk, curd, iron, and bricks;
they present sweet foods, sugar, and the like, as well as edible offerings consisting of newly grown grain. (62–63)
The lords of the fields and groves, as well as those authorized to guard the boundaries, [honored him];
just as someone who has been released from hell or from prison might receive a royal consecration, even so did he attain happiness.
Thus, by the power of compassion, Tārakādarśa became happy;
he indeed attained growth in devotion, meditation, worship, and service.
He constantly performs a thousand rounds with a rosary.
How could I not worship Mādhava, who has bestowed happiness upon me through his own self?
Thinking thus, my devotee especially worships Nārāyaṇa for the sake of well-being and prosperity,
honoring me in many ways through acts of devotion.
In his own hermitage, he fashioned a beautiful image out of clay.
Black antelope skins were well-applied there as garments, and two black spots were joined as eyes by means of two matted locks of hair. (68–69)
Then two clusters of flowers were placed as ear-ornaments upon her ears;
likewise, a garland made of lotus seeds and a garland of *guñjā* berries were offered.
Crystals were fastened as armlets on her upper arms, and auspicious ornaments were placed upon her forearms.
They fashioned rings from darbha grass and cords from muñja grass;
they subsisted on fruits and wore garments of bark,
as well as woolen blankets, deer skins, and flower ornaments.
Just as they had appeared at the proper time, those very [weapons] were offered to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
his four-armed form held the conch, discus, mace, and lotus,
and likewise by his side was the auspicious Lakṣmī, a young woman beautifully adorned.
She was adorned with all kinds of ornaments made from wild materials,
and she was beautifully decorated in their proper places with saffron, lac, and other pigments.
Her vessels were made of wild leaves, and her hut was constructed from bamboo and similar materials.
Forest offerings were prepared by that practitioner of devotion;
for the sake of the Blessed One, he protected cows that were well-nourished in the forest due to the abundance of grass, fodder, and other provisions. (76)
Having thus bathed every morning and worshipped the Lord Ramā with flowers,
garlands, and other offerings, having properly adorned her with sandalwood paste and the like,
and with honey, sweet roots, the essences of trees, fruits, and so forth; 77–78.
One should offer sweet juices, sweet tubers, as well as food offerings (naivedya),
water, betel leaf, a lamp, incense, circumambulation, and hymns of praise;
[then] the forgiveness of offenses, prostrations, obeisances, and handfuls of flowers.
He provides a remedy; he always acts in this manner:
at midday he takes his meal, in the evening he performs worship, the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and the eating of food;
having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, he always engages in kīrtana. (3.231.80–81)
His wife, Kṛtaśalyā, rising every morning and bathing daily, would bring flowers and fashion garlands and other offerings;
she would then present them to Kṛṣṇa and bow down to him hundreds of times.
Then, having offered an apology and bowed to her husband, she performed her household duties;
likewise at midday she provided him with a meal,
and in the evening she offered him sweet sacrificial food (naivedya).
Having removed the ornaments, dress, and other finery from the Lord Śrī,
she puts on suitable attire for herself and puts him to sleep at night.
In the morning, she dresses him in a new, most excellent, and beautifully adorned costume.
Whatever was cooked or prepared, he offered it all to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow;
by His grace, his family—including sons, daughters, and others—daily ate food, water, and vegetables mixed with *tulasī* leaves. (86–87)
While Tārādarśa was conducting himself in this manner,
I, having assumed the appearance of a guest and become a matted-haired ascetic, went to the forest.
In the evening, my family received me with affection.

Having recognized that the virtuous Śrī Narāyaṇa was performing his recitation, I was fed, honored, given water to drink, and my limbs were massaged by him. In the morning, I was laid to rest on a bed, awakened, and saluted. (3.231.89–90)
Having been bathed, honored, fed, and presented with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
and having been properly entreated for his favor as well as for liberation,
he was addressed with the words "So be it" and dispatched by those who were exceedingly devoted.
Then I was transformed into a divine form with four arms;
endowed with splendor, pervaded by divine lusters, and filled with serenity, I—
subdued by the devotion of my devotee— bestowed a blessing for the sake of liberation.
Having offered their devotion and flower garlands to the family of ten,
they suddenly beheld a disappearance within that very image;
they attained a state of great wonder and acquired divine vision.
From that time forward, they behold me in my divine form, joined with Lakṣmī and bearing the Sudarśana discus,
eternally and directly, just as parents [behold their child].
And by my divine grace, they have indeed become fulfilled in all their purposes.
Then, when the time had fully arrived, by means of a most radiant celestial chariot,
I led them to my imperishable abode, O Lakṣmī, which is higher than the highest.
Thus, indeed, has liberation been granted by me, the compassionate one, to this devotee.
I am especially present in the hearts of those seeking liberation for the purpose of protecting them.
Even sinful men—those of evil conduct and those who associate with the wicked—should take refuge in me or in the most excellent of holy men out of a desire to destroy their sins. (98–99)
Having completely shaken off their sins and bestowed merits upon them in every way,
and having purified those embodied beings and granted them divine bodies,
I lead them truly to heaven, to Śrīpura, or to the immortal realm.
Whether it be the indeterminate Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, or the imperishable abode—
the supreme station, beautiful as the king of kings— I cause you to attain it; there, I grant you eternal service at my feet.
“O Rame, from the reciting, hearing, touching, or even the mere turning over of this [text],
enjoyment, liberation, divine progression, and final release arise.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled “The Description of the Prosperity and Liberation through Devotion of Śūlīprada, Tārakādarśa, and his wife Kṛtaśalyā,” in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of Agnidasa as well. There was a Śūdra named Jvālāprasāda who was a forest guard. (1)
Formerly, on the bank of the river Kālindī in the Vṛtraprastha forest,
he lived with his family in that woodland. There, he subsisted on wild roots and fruits and was likewise engaged in the work of wood-gathering.
Likewise, for the sake of sustaining his life, he engages in the business of fodder, creepers, grass, stalks, and medicinal herbs;
yet even while intending no harm, he reduces useless pieces of wood into charcoal. (3–4)

Having gathered heaps of wood, he places fire upon them; from that, charcoal is produced—extinguished fires of great value. He always sells half-burnt pieces of wood, such as *maṭṭhī*, *sthān*, and *kulasā*.
And with those riches, that wealthy man lives performing meritorious acts of giving.
He knows that when wood is burned, countless species of living beings are consumed therein;
yet he commits this great sin of mine by piling it up.
For the sake of its pacification, a gift amounting to one-twentieth part [of the income] should be bestowed;
religious duties should be performed, and the service of virtuous women and holy men should be attended to.
Festivals for Lord Hari should be celebrated, as well as worship and the observance of vows.
That which is to be given should be bestowed upon a temple; that which is to be given should be given to one who has no protector or body [to sustain].
It should be given to one who is without support, it should be given to a dweller at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
It should be given for the sake of helping others, and likewise, it should be given to a performer of sacrifices (makhin).
Then, indeed, the purification of sin occurs, and never otherwise;
having realized this, one should surely offer one's own things and personal wealth with faith to a virtuous person who is a worthy recipient.
To those who arrive for the sake of visiting sacred fords, he gives food;
likewise, he gives gifts of clothing and offers medicinal herbs grown in the forest. He also provides fuel to virtuous men for the purpose of maintaining the sacrificial fire.
He constantly worships Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the beloved of Rādhā and Lord of Ramā;
he worships Hari, the Lord of Kamalā, the Lord of Prabhā, and the husband of Śrī Māṇikī.
He bathes daily in the Yamunā and offers arghya to the Sun.
He offers water, performs the *śrāddha* rite for his ancestors, and gives fruit and food;
he bestows what is appropriate upon guests and also gives to mendicants.
Now, this man has fashioned a wooden image of me, Śrī Hari. (15–16)
Shining together with the goddess Śrīmāṇikī, she possessed a brilliant luster;
her face was serene, she was peaceful, and she was adorned with the beauty of erotic passion (śṛṅgāra).
She was complete in all her limbs and decorated with divine ornaments.
Every morning, having risen and bathed, he indeed serves her—
who is seated upon a beautiful wooden throne and attended by her associates—
with water for the feet, respectful offerings, water for sipping, a ritual bath, and anointing with oil and other unguents. (18–19)
With cow’s milk, ghee, curd, rich sugar, and honey,
he performs the bathing and the consecration upon his big toe;
likewise, he performs the wiping with a cloth, the cleansing of the teeth, and the rinsing of the mouth.
Having had ornaments and such fashioned, as well as divine garments,
he gives me all manner of erotic adornments, sandalwood, saffron, flower garlands, crowns, and floral attire. (21–25)
He offers me incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of excellent and desirable fruits;
water, milk, milk-rice, curd, and the finest cooked foods;
as well as betel-leaf and the most excellent mouth-freshener.
He performs circumambulation, prostration like a staff, the waving of lights (ārārtika), bowing, and hymns of praise;
he requests forgiveness for his offenses,
offers self-surrender, and having waived the formal worship, he partakes of the offered food (niveditānna).
He and his wife, the goddess named Prabhāvatī, as well as their sons, daughters, and others, eat only that very prasāda; thereafter, they proceed to their respective endeavors. (26)
Even at midday and likewise at night, they perform worship for me;
they offer food offerings, drinking water, the waving of lights, and hymns of praise, as well as the chanting of the names of Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu, the Lord of Bālakṛṣṇa and Ramā. (588)
O Lord Rādheśa-Māṇikīsvāmin, O Śrīpati, O Lord of Kamalā!
Having performed their playful jests, they lead me before You;
thereafter, they sing beautiful songs and fall asleep.
Thus they all continued to worship him constantly.
Then one day, a great yogi named Narāyaṇāyana, accompanied by hundreds of virtuous men and women, arrived at his residence.

Prabhāvatī and Jvālāprasāda likewise offered a welcome to the virtuous; they both performed a hospitable reception for the holy women and the preeminent saint. They provided seats, water, sweet drinks, delicious foods, and fruits.
Greatly delighted, they gave honey and juices, as well as bulbous roots, legumes, and cucumbers;
roasted grains, dried foods, parched grain flour, and chickpeas;
and various vegetables along with leafy greens. || 33-34 ||
Then the virtuous men and women were serene, satisfied, and happy;
they performed their evening baths, meals, drinking of milk, and worship of Śrī Hari with instrumental music, singing, and excellent rhythmic accompaniments. || 35 ||
At that festival, many people indeed gathered there at night.
(36) Thousands of men and women, longing for the sight of the virtuous one, as well as the subjects of the city of Vṛtraprastha, also arrived. (37)
The forest on the banks of the Yamunā became like heaven because of the people;
at that time, men remained there after having beheld the holy ones, and they sat in the assembly hall, eager to hear their discourses. (38)
There, Nārāyaṇāyana indeed instructed him for his benefit, out of affection and through the yoga of devotion toward Kṛṣṇa and toward those who are virtuous;
by serving chaste women, by the worship of images, and by the adoration of deities. (3.232.40)
Through service, there shall be purity, divinity, and likewise liberation;
indeed, the direct attainment of the Supreme Lord occurs through service.
Through devotion, the presence of the Supreme Self arises, and through affection, [He is attained].
In this state, the destruction of illusion occurs and the person gains divine vision.
He perceives Govinda directly, both within and without,
and becomes free from the veil of illusion, just like the Lord himself.
From this [state], one beholds Goloka, Vaikuṇṭha, and the imperishable abode (akṣara-pada).
Therefore, saintly persons, virtuous women, and likewise Lord Hari must be propitiated through service.
By the blessings of the gracious saints, Lord Hari becomes manifest.
Among the virtuous, Nārāyaṇa abides, bestowing the bliss of liberation from the cycle of rebirth.
For the sake of attaining divine bliss, the holy ones as well as Hari should be served.
With faith and discernment, one should cultivate the highest association with the virtuous.
Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and service to the virtuous—these grant liberation.
All these auspicious qualities should be acquired. A seeker must never hastily place trust in the wicked.
That being so, vices such as craving and the like always increase.
A mortal who possesses a state of atheism is like saline soil; in such a place, the seed of affection and devotion does not sprout, but rather undergoes combustion.
For association with the wicked is indeed the cause of one's downfall; great evil arises from the company of those who are ill-acquainted.
Association with the virtuous is a treasure-trove of all merits and the destroyer of sin.
Those who do not understand the value of association, who act contrary to human purpose, indeed cultivate bad company;
because of that, they fall into a degraded state. Through quarreling, disputes, sleep, and sinful deeds, [they decline]. (51–52)
Furthermore, those afflicted by their own faults die through the performance of improper deeds;
they undergo rebirth, death, hell, and even a downward course. Subjected to tortures there, they reach the city of Yama.
But the discerning person in this world, having understood that the body is inert,
and having realized that the senses, the mind, and the intellect are composed of illusion (māyā),
as well as the three qualities (guṇas), primordial nature (prakṛti), and various latent impressions (vāsanās); ||54–55||
Knowing that they bestow bondage upon the living soul, one should become free from attachment;
for one who is devoted to constant practice, latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like perish.
For the renunciant, these impressions do not arise again, being deprived of their root.
The beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa resides within the hearts of these [devotees]. He does not allow faults to enter the hearts of His devotees.
To one possessed of identification with the body, the Lord does not manifest in the heart. (57–58)
In the heart, which is a manifestation consisting of darkness, Māyā increases; through that,
the notions of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" attain nourishment,
and from them, latent impressions (vāsanās) are produced in many ways, so that the thread of craving grows ever stronger.
"Furthermore, sins arise through craving for sense objects.
(3.232.60) "Therefore, I am the conscious self, the controller of the body and its adjuncts;
a devotee of Kṛṣṇa whose abode is Brahman—thinking thus, one should abandon craving. (61)
One who desires happiness should always remain vigilant and discerning;
one who seeks his own welfare must constantly strive for the sake of Hari’s happiness.
Faults shall not afflict him, for they perish by the power of Hari.
Latent impressions and the like do not overcome a person who is established in the Self.
Faults do not prevail over one who seeks the service of the virtuous, who is free from deceit, devoted, and humble; for those faults are shattered by the grace of the virtuous.
A wicked nature is indeed destroyed from its very root through association with the virtuous;
therefore, the defects of embodied beings who associate with the virtuous shall dissolve.
From childhood itself, one should cultivate association with the virtuous and devotion to Acyuta.
One should indeed cultivate affection for the devotees of Hari, for they are the bestowers of Hari.
By means of that [affection], firm devotion toward Hari shall arise even during youth;
and by the power of such devotion, desires and the like will certainly not afflict the embodied soul.
One should always serve the virtuous who are peaceful and free from mental disturbances;
thus, mental disturbance shall go to dissolution and youth shall be preserved.
One should never harbor any ill-will toward virtuous people.
In one who imagines faults, faults arise from sin.
Indeed, through lack of discernment, one is afflicted by those very imagined faults.
Therefore, one should behold the holy ones as divine, having Nārāyaṇa as their very self.
If anyone were to perceive a fault in those who are truly virtuous, then that fault would belong to himself.
This is not a fault; rather, it is a divine quality, of this there is no doubt.
Thus, one should conceive of the divine, and in that way, one’s own divinity will be realized.
One who perceives faults becomes faulty; one who perceives virtues becomes virtuous.
(72) Considering the three bodies to be distinct, one should serve a peaceful and holy person.
Through such service, one attains eternal peace belonging to the Supreme Lord. (73)
One should practice unfeigned devotion to Hari, which brings auspiciousness to the virtuous;
through the attainment of Hari’s grace, the devotee attains the very nature of Hari.
Firmness in knowledge and firmness in love for Hari grant liberation to the virtuous.
Service arises from affection, for constant mindfulness comes through love. Indeed, absorption in that [Reality] occurs only when there is vision throughout the three states.
But once direct realization has arisen, nothing further remains to be done.
In the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, who has assumed a human form:
first there is perception in the body, then indeed perception in the senses;
thereafter, perception occurs in the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇas), and finally, perception in the individual soul (jīva).
Thus indeed the Blessed One dwells as divine within the body, the senses, and the self. (78) He who, having observed the bodily nature of Kṛṣṇa, recognizes His divinity, and he who,
having understood His mental nature, likewise perceives His divinity— (79)
Having cultivated one's own meditation, one should likewise contemplate divine nature;
one should conceive that all divine pastimes of Kṛṣṇa are bestowers of liberation.
Thus, through yoga with Kṛṣṇa, both the internal and the external [are realized].
For the instruments, the body, and all else indeed become divine.
By means of the divine, the divine Lord is perceived by the yogi of devotion;
Hari cannot be grasped by that which is non-divine, even if one is born as a human being.
Therefore, all the devotees of the divine Yogi Kṛṣṇa are divine;
their regulations are divine, and even their desires and so forth are divine.
Indeed, everything belonging to a devotee that is dedicated for the sake of Kṛṣṇa is divine.

For the welfare of living beings, the Lord Kṛṣṇa, out of great compassion, takes birth here on earth from the world beyond the Imperishable (akṣara). He causes people to engage in His own true association for their ultimate well-being. 84–85.
Though possessing a human form, he performs worldly activities like a man;
yet let men understand that even these are his divine pastimes. May all those who behold them truly experience the bestowal of auspiciousness.

In this way, the Blessed One grants his own vision and association exclusively to his devotee, who has been fashioned by his own will from his divine essence. Therefore, the senses and other faculties of the devotee indeed attain the state of Kṛṣṇa.
Due to their connection with divine Kṛṣṇa, [the devotees'] illusions are not divine;
for as Kṛṣṇa is indeed divine, so too are the saintly persons divine.
Indeed, even those devotees who do not perceive faults are divine, just like the saintly.
Men and women who are always divine and do not perceive faults [are truly virtuous]. (3.232.90) Association with the virtuous is indeed divine; the virtuous are divine, and so is Hari.
All are faultless, bestowers of liberation, and devoid of the effects of *māyā*. (91)

The intellect of one who harbors a sense of fault toward them was indeed previously cursed by their parents, and thereafter by the virtuous. Through the transgression against the virtuous, his mind becomes corrupted by that curse. (92)
The virtuous, who are dear to the Lord, are like children and are weak.
At the very moment they are oppressed, Hari himself, residing within their hearts, becomes oppressed;
therefore, the mind of one who has been cursed is firmly bound by that curse.
Indeed, the wicked person is burned, for they grasp at faults and are not pure;
one should always strive to destroy that [wickedness] by serving the virtuous with body, mind, wealth, senses, and prosperity at all times. (95)
One should be devoted to service for the sake of obtaining the grace of the holy man.
By serving with the disposition of offering all one's possessions, he indeed attains purity, freedom from curses, divinity, and the capacity to perceive virtues. (96–97)
Having propitiated Kṛṣṇa, one attains purity from that and shall go to the imperishable state;
and by propitiating the virtuous, one shall attain the divine hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
Therefore, for the sake of liberation, one should always serve virtuous people.
"Having consumed this world with the fire of knowledge, offer yourselves into the fire of Brahman.
Having thus instructed them, O Rame, He gave them the mantra of Hari:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (3.232.100)
He gave them the nectar from his feet for us, O Nārāyaṇa. O Lakṣmī, virtuous people, having rested at night and bathed in the morning,
worship their own feet and the Self, and then eat fruits and drink water.
Having spoken words of blessing to the devotees, the saintly ones departed for the sacred ford.
Those devotees, purified by the grace of Jvālā, constantly served me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the beloved of Kṛṣṇa, with great affection.
Then, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika, when the night of the eleventh day had passed and dawn was breaking, they held a festival;
while they were dancing and chanting praises, [the Lord] appeared before them in the courtyard.
Four-armed, accompanied by Māṇikī and Śrī, and adorned with divine ornaments—
having received all that worship offered by them, I vanished in an instant; yet,
bound by the noose of love, I dwelt eternally within that very image.
When the time had come, I brought my abode, Jvālāprasādaka,
as well as his wife Prabhāvatī and thousands of devotees.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, have I rescued this devotee from the ocean of worldly existence.
"By reading or hearing this, one shall obtain deliverance.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of How the Lord Granted Liberation to the Devotee Named Jvālāprasāda— who had been reduced to charcoal by fire— through his devotion and meeting with the saint Nārāyaṇāyana, as well as the liberation of his wife and thousands of other embodied beings," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya-Saṃhitā*.

→ Chapter 234
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the liberation even of the poison-giver.
In the delightful region of Kāśamitra, in the city of Śrīnagara which brings great happiness—1.
On the bank of the Jhillīmāsā river lived a devotee named Lavādana.
He was a preeminent brāhmaṇa, possessed of a family, learned in the scriptures, and highly righteous.
Of renowned lineage and great honor, he was respected by the lord of Śrīpura.

There was a king of Śrīnagara named the illustrious Āneśvara. He was constantly honored by him, treated as the foremost in the assembly, held in the highest esteem in the court of justice, and regarded with great respect by the subjects. (3–4)
Then another king, Lavādana, conducts himself like a sovereign;
having achieved all the prosperity of a kingdom, he is skilled in the administration of instruction, as well as in military stations and administrative affairs. (5)
Thus the wise man conducts himself, being highly honored even by the queen.
Such is this chief minister, who is indeed the king’s preceptor;
he performs all the affairs of the kingdom as well as those of the realm.
Perceiving harm to the king, the subjects, the army, or the kingdom, he—
free from doubt and equal in intellect— averts that harm.
He protects the king, the subjects, and the armies when they have fallen into calamity.
In this world, that believer exists as a vessel of honor for the gods.
He is always worthy of worshipping the Sun, Hara, Viṣṇu, the Moon, Brahmā, Fire, Indra, Suvarṇa, Māyā, and the Jīva. (3.233.10)
Devoted to the ten sense-bases (āyatana), he also performs ten types of religious duties:
the gift of water, the gift of leather, and the gift of fortune in many ways;
likewise, the offering of medicinal herbs, the offering of ornaments, and the offering of clarified butter.
He performs the gift of bows, the gift of gold, the gift of daughters, and the offering of sacred stories;
he likewise performs other appropriate duties,
and even the bestowing of houses, fields, dwellings, groves, and gardens.
This great being is capable of both expending and acquiring royal fortune;
such a devotee serves the ten deities.
Though he is possessed of knowledge and is righteous in soul, at times he exhibits a tamasic disposition.
He performs great acts of punishment characterized by violence, which are of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
Whether it be a king, a prince, his own son, or another,
he inflicts punishment upon those deserving of it in accordance with the treatises on dharma (dharmaśāstra).

Then, as time passed, the king—mature, youthful, and exceedingly royal—gradually became intent upon hunting and sexual intercourse; indeed, he forcibly indulged in sexual union with his subjects. (17)
Because of that, among the subjects of this lord of men, there arose constant reproach as well as fear, due to the oppression of the people. The king had five sons and twenty daughters.
There were also seven queens who were young women, yet he,
dragged by the power of desire, was constantly engaged in sexual intercourse;
consuming wine, spirits, and meat, he became devoted to extreme wickedness.

Then, indeed, for the sake of his restraint, the subjects repeatedly entreated him to consume [the demon] Lava and to administer the rod of righteous punishment. Lava, however, grieved, thinking, "In that way, it would become an act of treason against the king."
"If I do not punish him, it would be an act of treachery toward my subjects; what should I do in this matter?
While he was reflecting thus, the path gradually became clear to him:
"The kingdom must be given to the crown prince; the king is now useless."
He will become one who must be instructed by his own lack of devotion.
(24) But once, while [the king] was established in courage, Lava reported to the king this auspicious speech from a circle of wise men, which brings about welfare. (25)
Indeed, saṃsāra is devoid of essence; its essence is liberation.
Through service to the virtuous, or else by taking refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the destruction of sin and likewise liberation arise for embodied beings.
When the end of life has arrived, neither kingdom, wealth, nor kinsmen protect even a great king who is a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Dharma alone protects that which is performed; adharma never protects anything at all.
In the world beyond, it is *dharma* alone that, when practiced, serves the person;
whereas *adharma* afflicts one here and in the world beyond like an enemy.
Having attained renunciation (*nivṛtti*), the Blessed One should be venerated by one who desires their own welfare.
Having entrusted the burden to a worthy son, one who seeks happiness should strive for liberation.
There is no limit to desires; they increase along with craving.
They cause one to fall into hell, tormenting and burning one with flames.
Having abandoned the desires residing in the heart, one should practice dedication to Nārāyaṇa;
for worldly activity, devotion, and desires cannot coexist.
One who possesses the goal of virtue (dharma) should abandon desires while performing worldly activity for the sake of devotion.
"Therefore, the kingdom should be given by you to Prince Śānteśvara;
it will be a splendid thing for that worthy eldest son.
Upon hearing this, the king was consumed within as if by a flame of fire.
O Lotus-born One, for one who is possessed by craving, everything—even nectar—becomes poison;
there is no doubt that even words of benefit and words of renunciation turn into poison.
He, however, spoke with policy to his own preeminent and supreme teacher.
"O Guru, what you have reported to me is indeed appropriate;
nevertheless, at the end of some time I shall grant it accordingly. For my son’s fitness has now ripened, and he shall likewise attain the kingdom. (36–37)
"Then, through practice, I shall grant you the kingdom; there is no swiftness [in this matter].
Thus addressed, the preceptor attained silence and bowed to the king.
The king, for his own purpose, constantly reflected upon the deception.
"This current preceptor is the royal preceptor, the chief, and the presiding officer of the assembly.
He must indeed be removed from his position, and another preceptor must be installed;
then there will be security for me and well-being at all times. (3.233.40)
Having reflected thus, at the end of three months, he removed him from his position;
Lavādana, too, recognizing it as the will of fate, abandoned his own office.
Having attained cessation, he indeed constantly worshipped those ten deities.
The king indeed increased excessively in his sexual intercourse with his own subjects;
having forcibly taken beautiful young women from among the people, he indulged his desires with them and, once his purpose was fulfilled, let them go. (42–43)
Out of extreme rage, verbal abuse toward the subjects alone increased:
"This king must indeed be destroyed; he is the banisher of the chief.
Indeed, a single cry was heard among all the subjects in every way.
A king who is addicted to sexual misconduct with his subjects must indeed be destroyed;
otherwise, a great calamity will surely befall the subjects.
Having thus decided, all the foremost of the subjects [prepared] for the slaughter of Lava.
Driven by fate for the destruction of King Mimi,
they indeed went toward the commander-in-chief, accompanied by Lava,
and reported that Sūryakānta had also become a transgressor of his vows.
If he does not resort to righteousness, there will surely be the destruction of the king. You, though the teacher of the subjects, must likewise adhere firmly to the policy of statecraft;
this king must certainly be removed from his royal position by all means.
Having heard these words to the core, Sūryakānta replied, "So be it.
Then they all went to the crown prince Śānteśvara.
[The prince said: "This king remains on a wrong path; he is not worthy of your feet."
"You too must be dismounted from your vehicle and established [in your place] by the subjects with respect.
Know this for certain: otherwise, a great calamity will befall you.
Then the prince likewise spoke thus to the queen: "Let it be so."
All of them declared this conclusion regarding Śreṣṭhottamā;
and she, the discerning woman, likewise said, "So be it," by the power of destiny.
Then, a great assembly was convened by the subjects for the sake of a decision.
There, the queen, as well as the other queens, the princes who were the best of subjects,
the commander-in-chief, and the chief minister, arrived for the sake of reaching a decision.
They presented their case for a decision to the new chief minister.
But Gartamanī, though the chief, did not approve of the decision;
rising up, he departed and reported the unfavorable matter to the king.
With sudden anger, the king spoke to Gartamanī.
Let the commander place the prince in prison.
Having heard from Gartamaṇi that the queen, the subjects, the former chief minister, and likewise the enemies were [hostile], the king’s soldiers acted by the king’s command. ||57–58||
Then, hundreds of the king’s soldiers rushed from all sides to swiftly place those who opposed the king in fetters;
many were seized there and indeed bound in chains.
Then Lavādana, having approached the queen, the prince,
and the commander-in-chief there, and having arranged a consultation,
took an extremely potent poison and went for refuge to the king.
Then she placed a garland of flowers containing poison around the king's neck.
Having inhaled its fragrance, the king gradually fell into a swoon;
he died instantly, and then Garta-maṇi slipped from his feet.
Lavadana was honored by the subjects in the position of the chief minister. All those held in prison were released by Lavadana. Prince Shantishvara was consecrated upon the royal throne. (63–64)
It was proclaimed among the subjects that the lord of men had died;
those queens and the princes performed the funeral rites for the king.
That son of Lava, Yajña, performed a sacrifice for the sake of the king’s purification.
The Brahmins, the helpless, the virtuous, and likewise the maidens;
the subjects were fed and gratified with gifts of gold,
as well as with gifts of cows, gifts of houses, and gifts of daughters for the young boys.
Through his religious acts at the sacrifice, the king, upon dying, was joined with merit;
yet in the city of Yama, there are many painful torments such as the glowing iron pillar (sūrmi).
After experiencing heaven through the merit of the sacrifice, the king indeed departed [from that state].
The prince became king, and he indeed administered a righteous kingdom.
He was constantly devoted to the virtuous and solely dedicated to Nārāyaṇa; a thousand virtuous men always ate at his court.
He ruled a righteous kingdom, approved by Lava and Anala.
Then there was a most excellent saint named Kiṃśukāyana, a true guru who was established in the Self and devoted to the Lord; he [was] the guru of Lava and Anala.
Then the commander-in-chief instructed King Śānteśvara, Sūryakāntaka, and the foremost of his subjects in that which is beneficial and brings about welfare:
"In this world, embodied beings are born and pass away according to their actions. (72–73)
Dharma consists of knowledge, detachment, devotion to Hari, and devotion to the virtuous;
whatever merit has been earned through service and charity indeed accompanies one [to the next world].
A righteous king is like a father, but an unrighteous one is to be punished like an enemy.
The welfare of the subjects should always be ensured by the king, who is the possessor of dharma.
Indeed, a king who practices service toward the virtuous shines among his subjects;
however, one who behaves like a cat or a crow is despised by the people.

But that king whose heart is stainless, who is devoted to the service of Kṛṣṇa, who has conquered his senses, and who protects his subjects, prospers through the blessings of the virtuous. Someone may practice the dharma of the saintly in childhood, but act contrary to it in youth.

Even one who is wicked in childhood may become righteous in youth. Through association with the virtuous, however, from childhood until the end of life, an embodied being is born as a truly noble person, always established on the path to the highest good. (78–79)
Through association with the wicked, an evil man increases in wickedness alone—
due to living together, social interaction, and sharing food, drink, and insults. (3.233.80) In a child, and especially in a youth, virtues appear as vices.

Through the power of merit in childhood, one may become a practitioner of dharma even in youth. (8.1) Through tranquility of mind comes peace, and through the taming of the external horses [the senses] comes self-control.
By means of these two, all defects such as desire, anger, and the rest are to be eliminated. (8.2)
Both of these are beneficial for renunciants and householders alike;
however, for those devoted to the service of the virtuous, faults are destroyed at their very root.
A living being skilled in discernment shall destroy the entire circle of defects.
Kṛṣṇa, the witness and the inner self, shall lead [the devotee] to the supreme abode.
For the welfare of living beings on earth, the Blessed Lord, the beloved of Śrī, manifests in an auspicious form; by serving Him, one is liberated.
Although Śrī Hari, while remaining in His own abode, is indeed capable of bestowing liberation, nevertheless, for those men and women who are lovers of Him and who reside here,
their separation from Hari [is what they desire]. (86)
Yet, for the sake of their destruction, he assumes a form that is unbearable even for a mere moment, according to what is appropriate;
out of devotion to them and in order to fulfill the desires of his devotees, he assumes here a form filled with supreme bliss and other qualities. (87–88)
Having bestowed yoga, he fulfills all the heart's desires of his devotees;
for he indeed becomes one of their own kind solely for the sake of increasing their love.
That very compassion of Hari should be understood as manifesting in the birth of those who belong to the same class as the devotee.

Filling the minds of men and women with his countless divine, excellent qualities, sovereignty, majesty, and splendor, he remained under their influence as a son, a husband, a well-wisher, and a friend. (3.233.90–91)
He conducts himself as a father, a mother, and a virtuous wife;
he acts as a disciple, a teacher, and a king.
Having brought them happiness according to their desire, his supreme task is the establishment of Dharma.
Simultaneously bringing about the destruction of the asuras as a secondary effect,
the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the son of Śrī Kambharā, withdraws from the sight of his devotees by his own will after their satisfaction has been achieved. (93–94)

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who was once a cowherd boy, should be accepted with devotion. Having abandoned lust, anger, deceit, greed, pride, envy, and malice, and having burned away all sins, one should worship Him, the Lord of Māṇakī.

Through devotion and service to the virtuous, that Lord becomes fully pleased. By serving Kṛṣṇa, the sin of one who sets fire to dwellings, one who administers poison, or one who commits the murder of a woman— even the sins of the virtuous— are destroyed.
The sin of one who serves Kṛṣṇa—whether it be the sin of killing a child, the sin arising from the slaughter of a cow, the destruction of a king, or likewise the sin of matricide—is dissolved.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; svāhā."
"Recite the mantra constantly, and purification from sin will occur.
Having said this, Kiṃśukāyana bestowed the mantra upon Kamalā;
right there, he made all those hundred thousand subjects excellent Vaiṣṇavas.
Indeed, they all took refuge in me, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa;
then Lavādano worshipped me, Puruṣottama, along with the ten gods, while all others— the kings, subjects, and so forth— worshipped me especially.
Those who had surrendered their very selves took refuge in me, Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
Then the saintly ones indeed departed for Badrīnārāyaṇa;
there, he was pleased by their service during his old age, which lasted but a moment.
O Lakṣmī, I appeared before him with a divine form;
having shaken off the great sin of the poison-giver by means of that celestial body,
I assumed a divine, liberated form and led him to my imperishable abode.

He led all the queens, as well as the commander-in-chief and the new king, with devotion; being satisfied by this, he led them all step by step to the imperishable state. And he led the subjects, who were endowed with devotion, to the purifying state.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, all of them were liberated by me through the agency of the saintly; freed from the bonds of illusion, they were established in the supreme, imperishable Reality.
The great sin of administering poison has entirely dissolved through devotion.
In this way, through devotion, all sins are dissolved in every respect, O Rame;
by the power of my worship, they surely attain worldly enjoyment and liberation.
By reading and hearing this, there shall always be enjoyment and liberation.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Liberation of King Garada—the Chief of Lavādana—through Devotion to the Lord and Service to the Holy Sage Kiṃśukāyana, as well as the Liberation of His Queens and Subjects," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the story of the wielder of weapons.
Formerly, there was a man named Vikhaṇḍalavarman who bore arms;
he was a Kṣatriya living in the village of Nāndala on the auspicious bank of the Mahī river,
a great ruler over the forest-dwelling Kirātas and the thieves.
He was the punisher of robbers and likewise a wielder of bow and arrow;
he was the protector who ensured safety on the road for married couples.
He was also the guardian of processions traveling for the purpose of marriage.
He is the protector of those whose minds are distracted by worldly affairs, and he bears the name [of the Buddha] everywhere.
(4) Upon hearing that name, thieves always flee far away.
Thus, the Teacher is the one who inspires fear, yet he is the punisher of those who punish. (5)
But a devotee, indeed, having taken recourse to the path of righteousness in his heart,
maintains himself solely by that very wage provided through protection by merchants and kings, and not otherwise. (6)
In appearance he was like a messenger of Yama; in compassion, he was always like Dharma;
in protection, he was like a king; in the path of policy, he was like Śukra;
in wisdom, he was equal to Bṛhaspati; and in devotion, he was like Garuḍa. (7–8)
He who knows the Self conducts himself with the spirit of offering all things;
yet, having encountered a person intent on unrighteousness, he inflicts punishment. He always punishes the wicked and the deceitful man according to what is appropriate.
"Or indeed, by the force of a weapon-strike, he kills one who is exceedingly wicked.
(3.234.10) Thus, the thought "the sin of killing and so forth will surely occur" arises constantly in his heart; while performing worship, he asks for forgiveness. (11)
Having bathed in the morning and performed the worship of my image with the sixteen articles,
having offered the waving of lights (nīrājana) and presented sweet food as an offering,
one should then give water for sipping and mouth-freshening betel leaf.
Just as one might cast down a weapon before me and beg for forgiveness, [so it is said:
"I am neither cruel nor a killer; I am neither self-seeking nor a libertine.
May my weapon not prove wicked upon falling upon you who are free from fault. (13–14)
May it not fall upon one who follows the right path, a devotee, or one who is exempt from punishment;
O Lord, may my weapon, through ignorance, never be touched by fault.
And in the chastisement of the wicked, may this [weapon] never suffer defeat.
May I not be tainted by sin arising from conduct that transgresses moral law.
Even though this is so, if at any time sin should indeed assail me due to human ignorance or through some humble transgression, [may it be removed]. (16–17)
"O Kṛṣṇa, I am to be punished in every way; if I am to be forgiven, then let me be forgiven.
Thus does this devotee of mine constantly offer swords, arrows, and other weapons before me, and thereafter, having eaten that which is produced from my grace— ||18|| —he speaks.
Having drunk the nectar of his feet, he goes for the purpose of protecting that which is to be protected.
In the village, the forest, the threshing floor, the courtyard, or the field, Indra joyfully protects all things that must be guarded in every way. (3.234.20)
At midday, he always eats the food and the prasāda offered to me;
in the evening, having returned from the boundary, he performs worship at home with flowers,
incense, lamps, food offerings, and excellent water.

Having offered me the *nīrājana* rite, hymns of praise, betel-leaf, and fragrant scents, and having even laid down his weapons before me, he constantly entreats me again and again: "Forgive, indeed, this sin born of ignorance. (22–23)
"I am yours; I am your servant; I am your devotee, though still subject to darkness.
Having attained identity with you, I become your remnant (śeṣa).
Thus, O Lakṣmī, always entrusting me with the weapon and the task," [he said].
Having indeed entrusted me to his bed, he falls asleep while remembering me.
His wife, named Harasatī, also serves him;
she is a great devotee of me, Bālakṛṣṇa, the glorious Lord Narāyaṇa.
When he beholds me as Nārāyaṇa in his husband, he perceives nothing else;
while I am present within the form of his husband, he performs all service toward me.
He performs separate service to my image as if it were distinct from me, his lord.
Bathing, adornment, ornaments, and the like; the waving of lights, a sumptuous meal, drink, betel-leaf, the gift of a fan, and being rocked upon a swing;
likewise, songs arising from my sweet throat that are full of my divine play. (28–29)
She also proclaims the abandonment of sleep; thereafter, the beautiful woman performs her own daily duties. In this way, the devotee, exceedingly affectionate, worships me incessantly.
Virtuous men and virtuous women also go to that purifying house;
having eaten, drunk, and cast off their fatigue, they depart for the supreme sacred site (tīrtha). Then, on one occasion, a virtuous man named Nirmohanāyana arrived.
Honored, fed, and having had his feet massaged by them at night,
he instructed them in the supreme means for attaining liberation—
the weapon of forbearance, which is a weapon against others, auspicious, and bestowing all peace. (33)
Forgiveness is the splendor of the spirited; forgiveness is the austerity of the ascetics.
(34) He who forgives all oppressions is indeed considered Nārāyaṇa.
Forgiveness always exists in the earth and in the mother of all embodied beings. (35)

Forgiveness, whose nature consists of divine qualities, is always found among the virtuous. Indeed, it bestows victory in this world and is an aid to heaven and liberation. Forgiveness is the weapon that destroys all calamities.
For forgiveness indeed bestows peace in desire, anger, intoxication, greed, and pride.
Forgiveness is a weapon for the weak, just as it is a weapon for the discerning.
For the virtuous, forgiveness is a weapon that both disciplines and delivers.
For those who are forgiving, Kṛṣṇa always dwells within as the inner self;
by His very grace, He provides protection for them especially.
Indeed, it is held by people that a weapon is called a "protector" only because it chastises.
"O Teacher, that is indeed true because of the fear of illusion and the fear of karma.
But it is not at all true that the body is governed by a weapon in its literal sense;
nor is it truly the case that the senses are so governed. (3.234.40–41)
The body and the senses are the effects of *māyā* and are perishable;
even if their protection is attempted in ten thousand ways, they surely perish at the time of dissolution.
Indeed, the protection of things that are subject to destruction is futile and serves only its own immediate purpose.
Thus, weapons are indeed useless, and effort is a burden devoid of fruit.
The forest is indeed subject to destruction, and the boundary is likewise;
indeed, everything such as fields, gardens, and so forth, proceeds toward destruction.
Thieves are subject to death, and so too are the crops;
likewise, you, the Teacher, though embodied, are likewise subject to destruction.
That which is subject to death is taught by those who are subject to death—this is a matter of wonder.
Indeed, it is better not to touch the mud at all than to wash it off later.
Therefore, weapons are certainly not the means for liberating the body;
rather, those weapons that grant liberation must be guarded with every effort.
These divine weapons of mine, O Vikhaṇḍala, which must be guarded, retained, and employed for the sake of liberation—listen now to them.
Indeed, youth is the form of the enemy; the weapon against it is the acquisition of vows.
Desire is the great enemy there; the weapon against it is celibacy (brahmacarya).
Latent tendencies are the maternal foe; the weapon against them is self-abidance. Discernment is the knowledge of distinctions; the constant practice is devotion to Śrī Hari.
Renunciation, detachment, and constant indifference toward external objects—
these indeed are the weapons that destroy illusion (māyā).
Seeking eternal refuge in Śrī Hari and associating with the service of the saintly are likewise essential.
The ninefold devotion to Śrī Hari and worship with supreme feeling; (52) serving saintly persons who are free from deceit by offering them everything one possesses;
meditating on Śrī Hari within the heart; and surrendering one's own self through the body. (53)
Constant reflection with the mind, perpetual manifestation through the intellect of Hari,
and the dedication of all activities such as bliss to the Lord of All;
the tasting of aesthetic flavor (rasa) and so forth should be directed toward the grace of Kṛṣṇa alone, and not otherwise.
Sound, touch, and all other objects belong to Kṛṣṇa alone, and not to others.
By these weapons, there occurs the destruction of illusion as well as the dissolution of karma;
through desireless action, peace arises for one who is free from craving.
Those whose undertakings are free from desires and conceptualizations and are indeed devoid of the qualities (guṇas),
attain through that association with the virtuous a divine state characterized by freedom from the qualities;
yet, through the attainment of Hari, they reach divinity, and through direct yoga, liberation.
In one endowed with knowledge of His majesty, affection for Hari arises.
(58) For one who is attached through affection for Hari, the imperishable manifestation of Hari proceeds;
thereafter, even the senses become of that same form. (59)
The internal organs indeed arise as the temples of Kṛṣṇa;
the self becomes the throne of that Nārāyaṇa.
By means of that [throne], the self rejoices, rests, eats, exults, and delights.
Consisting of the state of Brahman, he brings joy through states of identity [with it].
Abiding everywhere in worldly activity while contemplating Brahman, he is liberated from the bondage of karma; he is indeed Brahman—of this there is no doubt. (61–62)
One who is divine, whose mind is steady, who is Brahman itself, and who is absorbed in Brahman—having firm refuge in Kṛṣṇa, he delights in Kṛṣṇa; of this there is no doubt.
Kṛṣṇa, the deliverer of the lowliest, accepts him who has been offered unto his shelter.

Mādhava purifies even one who has fallen and sports with him in affection. He surely grants the true goal to those devoted to him; one attains the ultimate state of supreme bliss when everything is offered to Mādhava.
When all effects of *prakṛti* dissolve into the abode of the Imperishable (*akṣara-dhāman*),
the splendor consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*) shines forth for the devotee.
Within that splendor resides the Lord, the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
He shines forth as the internal regulator of both the conscious and the unconscious.
Possessing a divine form, divine raiment, and the splendor of divine ornaments, he is served by innumerable liberated souls who have become one with the Great Brahman. (67–68)

He alone bestows service upon his own feet for the one who serves Him— service performed by those such as Rādhā, Ramā, Muktānikā, and others, who possess infinite powers and grant the bliss of performing worship and massaging His feet. (69)

He alone exists on earth as Kṛṣṇa, the husband of the beloved of Brahmā; for the ultimate welfare of the worlds, he has assumed a form for the sake of divine qualities. Having reflected thus, one should take refuge in Puruṣottama, the Supreme Brahman.
Then those who have taken refuge and reached maturity perceive Him directly;
those with subtle vision see the subtle Inner Self within,
while those with gross vision see that Lord in His gross form within the gross.
When Māyā, unconfined by the body, is merged in equilibrium within the Imperishable (akṣara), then it is subtle;
then Kṛṣṇa is perceived here in his subtle form.
And when the conscious powers (cetana) are merged, devoid of any other principles (tattva), [then he is perceived]. || 73–74 ||
Then, when they are subtle, Kṛṣṇa is perceived there in a subtle form;
but when Māyā is in its uneven state, and likewise when conscious beings are engaged in action,
then they are gross, and Kṛṣṇa is perceived within them in a gross form.
For those possessing divine vision, the sight of Kṛṣṇa is endowed with divinity;
for those who do not possess divine vision, the sight of Kṛṣṇa is merely ordinary,
just as all the powers of Hari— both subtle and gross— are likewise perceived.

But all the powers of Māyā, whether conscious or unconscious, along with their attributes, manifest either individually or together— whether with qualities or without qualities— within subtle and gross objects deposited by the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
All those riches indeed belong to the beginningless Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa;
the devotee who has surrendered all his possessions, the most excellent of the Bhāgavatas, enjoys them. The one devoted to the Lord attains all sovereign powers. (3.234.80)
In Lord Hari, the Lord of gods and Master of liberation, only His own state remains;
the Lord bestows everything else belonging to Himself upon that devotee.
Great and eternal affection is a weapon that brings even the Master under one's control.
By that very weapon of affection, Hari should be disciplined within the heart;
he should be bound by the snares of affection so that he does not wander far from the heart.
This alone is the imperishable liberation for embodied beings, and this is their divinity in this world.
That state which is the enjoyer of the bliss of the divine enjoyment bestowed by the Lord must first be attained here on earth through the Guru, who is Kṛṣṇa manifest before one's eyes;
thereafter, abiding in the City of Brahmā (the heart), it shines forth.
That enchanting love for Hari always bestows great bliss.

Wherein there is ever-present happiness in Hari, even for tens of millions of crores of Cupids—one who has attained the state of identity with Him obtains that [bliss] in the Lord, the Master. (85–86)
He obtains infinite pleasure for the eyes and infinite pleasure from touch;
he attains incomparable bliss through kissing in his mistress, the Sovereign;
and he attains the great bliss of embracing in the Supreme Self.
He likewise obtains the divine essence of all the senses, as well as the tasting of the directions;
and he attains a divine festival of joy and delight,
as well as divine gladness, peace, coolness, and that which is mixed with nectar.
One obtains [all this] in Śrī Hari, the beloved, the Lord, the Master, and the Sovereign. Indeed,
whatever joys belong to the twenty-four principles,
and whatever joys exist within the three creations— [all these one attains].
One obtains all those [perfections] within the form of the Lord, the Supreme Self, O Lakṣmī.
Having thus given this instruction for the sake of dispelling delusion, and having spent the night there, he, being well-honored, departed for another sacred site (tīrtha). || 91-92 ||
In the morning, Vikhaṇḍala performed the devotion as prescribed,
accompanied by knowledge; his wife also, who was of the nature of Brahman,
offered such devotion, full of affection and ever-increasing.

Indeed, in the worship of the image, they both performed everything as was appropriate. (94) Pleased by their devotion, I appeared before them, as the divine four-armed Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, exceedingly beautiful. (95)
Laughing, I accepted all the most excellent offerings presented to me; having partaken of the *naivedya*, I gave them the *prasāda*.
Having eaten with joy, the two of them drank the nectar-like water.
Then they both became divine in form, equal to me;
free from delusion, they both prayed for liberation.
Taking those two divine beings upon my celestial chariot, I led them to my own imperishable abode.

Fulfilling their resolve along with his attendants, he brought about their liberation; thus, through association with the saintly, those two, his own followers, now eternally abide in the imperishable abode of Kamalā. 99.
By reading or hearing this, O Lakṣmī, one shall attain liberation.
Or, being devoted to me, one obtains heaven, or Satyaloka, or a kingdom, or the sovereign station, or whatever enjoyment or liberation one desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Lord and the Liberation of the Weapon-Bearer named Vikhaṇḍala and His Wife Harasatī, Occurring in the Context of the Righteous Nirmohanāyana," in the Third Section, the Lineage of the Dvāpara Age, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (*Dvāpara-yuga-santāna*) — Chapter 234.

Chapter 236 → Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Śrī Nārāyaṇī, to the virtuous story of Jīrṇodbhava. In the city of Ārāma, on the vast bank of the Vīṇā river,
there lived a great and industrious farmer named Jīrṇodbhava.
He had a hundred sons and a hundred servants; he was powerful and the husband of twenty wives.
(2) He was the father of a woman who had a hundred sons, and he was adorned by four hundred grandsons.
He resided in a magnificent mansion that was graced by two hundred granddaughters. (3)
Thus, Kṛṣīvala was born into a family of noble lineage; he was exceedingly pure, constantly devoted to the gift of dharma, and dedicated to the service of cows and other such duties.
He possessed five hundred head of cattle as well as two hundred buffaloes.
He possesses a hundred horses and eight hundred bulls.
(5) He also owns fields, orchards, great gardens, lands for crops, forest pastures for fodder, and extensive tracts of land. (6)
A yojana from here, on the bank of the river Vīṇā, lies his land;
there he performs agriculture, sowing seeds according to the season.
Various kinds of grain and all types of food are produced there.
Split pulses, tubers and roots, flowers, and leafy vegetables;
fruits, ears of grain, pods, and *veṣavāra* seasoning; knots, stalk-seeds, potherbs, and likewise *bhājikā*—these constitute the greens. (8–9)
All kinds of fermented gruel and whatever is bitter or pungent grow in every way for him in great fields such as those of vāṭī;
even various medicinal herbs grow there when they are sprinkled with water.
Men and women, devoted to the exertion of agriculture, strive diligently.
By sowing seeds, they produce many kinds of edible grains. From all that which is produced, they pay a full twentieth part as tax. || 11-12 ||
For the sake of Dharma, he indeed gives gifts in acts such as charity and worship.
In his house, which is ever-restored from decay, homeless holy men, twice-born brahmins,
mendicants, travelers, virtuous women, and the destitute eat their meals.
They consume curds that are indeed thick and milks that are sweet;
clarified butters endowed with nourishment, as well as sugar and molasses;
and they eat honey, most delicious sweets, and the finest foods. (14–15)
Day after day, they offer me ripe foods for Hari.
Thus, through the practice of dharma, his riches increase;
indeed, by the power of merit, they do not diminish even while being enjoyed by the virtuous.
Then his fortune indeed became exceedingly prosperous (verse 17),
such that five sacrifices were always performed in his house by the twice-born.
At one of his sacrifices, a virtuous man arrived, named Caitanyakāyani (verse 18).
The illustrious Jīrṇodbhava, a supreme devotee endowed with renunciation and detachment, arrived; he offered him a welcome and,
bowing down, presented him with water, an auspicious seat, and sweet *madhuparka*.
He gave him lodging in the temple hall and performed service for him.
At night, having performed the worship of the deity and eaten,
Caitanyakāyani engaged in the chanting of the pastimes and other qualities of Anādikṛṣṇanārāyaṇa.
He proclaimed the birth of Hari within the fifty-third year of this Brahmā,
as well as the liberating divine sports performed therein;
thereafter, he offered hymns of praise which all the farmers heard.
He who is the Supreme Brahman, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Beloved and the Master, shines in the imperishable, supreme ether, served by the liberated souls;
from whom, indeed, manifold manifestations arise during creation. (23–24)
This very son of Śrī Kambharā, the cowherd boy, resides in Saurāṣṭra at the sacred site of Aśvapaṭṭasāra, in the field of Kuṅkumavāpī,
where the venerable Lomaśa dwells and the beloveds of Brahmā reside. (25)
All sacred fords, the gods, the lords, and the manifestations of power;
Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Padmāvatī, Śrī, Māṇikī, Pradhī, and Haripriyā—these wives of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Brahmā dwell here. (26–27)

Salutations to Him who is the dancer among men, the inner controller of all; salutations to Him where countless holy sages dwell, self-luminous by nature, divine seers who take refuge in Him as their protector. (28)
Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Soul, who Hari provides protection from virtuous inner beings,
as well as from the miseries pertaining to the self (ādhyātmika) and likewise from those pertaining to the divine (ādhibhautika and ādhidaivika).
Homage again and again to the protector from the hardships of elemental spirits and other such dangers;
by whom the merchant Vanacandraka, his wife Sukhādevī, and [their] subjects were protected from cruel plunderers. (31)
They were liberated by the meeting with Sāyanāyanasādhu.
That Kṛṣṇa exists as the protector; salutations again and again to him!
