salutations to Śrī Hari, that Kṛṣṇa who, on the occasion of the Vṛṣaparva festival, liberated Gṛhakāra Śivajaya.
And Hari liberated Yaśaskara from his bonds and the net-maker, and through his service to the sage Śuklāyana, he [obtained] the beautiful wife Rūpavatī;
likewise, by his birth, he [obtained] Bharavāṭa, named Udyamaśrīti.
I bow to that Lord Hari, the beloved Master, who rescued Satīśvarī, his wife, and the cowherd women; and who, on the occasion of Rāmāyaṇa, rescued the camel-herder Dīrgharambha.
Through the grace of Lord Nṛsiṃha, Hari Nārāyaṇa rescued Kharapāla, who was radiant with jewels; I bow down to him.
[I also bow to] Gadārdaneśvara, the physician, and his wife Mukundinī.
I bow to that Lord of Men who indeed liberated [the king] from saṃsāra.
I truly bow to him who brought about the liberation of the monkey and the mongoose, of Deśyāvana,
and of his wife Purikā.
The Lord [met] the barber named Harṣadharman and his wife Nigamikā;
the king Svarṇadhanvan and his queen Pañcadevikā—
these he encountered through the arrival of the virtuous Kalyāṇadhāman.
I indeed bow to that Hari Nārāyaṇa who rescued the goddess Rūḍhāṇakī,
the daughter of the Ābhīras, who had been oppressed by the Daityas;
he protected her, the mistress of beauty, in the midst of the beloved wives of Brahmā.
The illustrious Lord likewise created Mandārakalikā and others of divine form as his wives; I bow to that Janārdana.
Through the yoga leading to liberation, he [established] Dhīra-parvan as a fisherman.
I bow to Kṛṣṇa, who, having performed a purifying act, liberated him;
he who rescued Tārakādarśaka from being impaled on a stake,
restored King Supathānaka, and healed Śūlyaṅganā who had been pierced by a dart.
Having become one with matted locks, the son of Hari and Śrīkṛṣṇa rescued him;
I bow to that Kṛṣṇa, the beloved son of the cowherd.
[73] To the one named Jvālāprasāda, the giver of fire, and to Prabhāvatī—
I bow to him who, through the practice of yoga, liberated Nārāyaṇa.
[74] Furthermore, the illustrious one appointed Lava as the governor, Garada as the king, Aneśvara as the prince, Śānteśvara as the crown prince, and Sūryakānta as the commander-in-chief. [75]
I bow to that Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Teacher who dwells within the hearts of devotees, who by means of the Kiṃśuka-āyana yoga rescued Indra, the wielder of weapons, along with his wife Satī.
||76|| I bow to him who [rescued] Indra, the wielder of weapons, and his wife Satī.
"Salutations to you who, through the yoga of the path that removes delusion, do not grant liberation.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, Sādhu Caitanyakāyani then performed this hymn of praise to Hari, who dwells within all and surrounds everything.
Having heard and seen this, those farmers were struck with supreme wonder.
Jīrṇodbhava, the leader of the farmers, bowed down and questioned that sage:
"By whom has such protection and liberation been granted to these people by the Supreme Lord?"
"Tell me the reason for this, O Caitanyakāyana.
Having heard them, the sage spoke the mantra of Nārāyaṇa to me:
"Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya svāmine svāhā. (3.235.80–81)
Let other seekers of liberation constantly recite this mantra;
indeed, enjoyment and liberation shall be attained, and one shall become Nārāyaṇa himself.
In times of calamity, the Supreme Lord shall provide great protection.
Having spoken thus, he ceased; remembering me, he fell asleep.
The farmers were also sleeping while muttering that very mantra.
Then, having risen in the morning, the virtuous man bathed and worshipped me.
Having eaten the offered food and received worship, he departed for the forest.
Those farmers constantly recite the supreme mantra;
they worship me as Hari and even celebrate great festivals.

During the four-month period, they performed various vows for me. Then, in the month of Āśvina, in gardens, fields, forest lands, wild jungles, and thickets, they [gathered] stalks, grain, and grasses. (86–87)
When all the trees bore fruit and the ears of grain were entirely filled with an abundance of grain and were fully ripened,
that land, four yojanas in extent, was indeed resplendent with crops. (88)
And with medicinal herbs having ripened leaves, it shines with a golden hue.
Then, indeed, by the turn of fate, through the force of the wind,
fire was drawn from the upper region at the boundary toward the farmer’s hearth.
And having been cast down by the wind, he suddenly rose up and spread everywhere over the fields of grain,
the dry grass, and then over all the crops.
Then he pervaded the fields on all sides with ears of grain amidst the standing corn.
Like a forest fire, it spread across half a *krośa* and surged forward.
Then, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose among the farmers; indeed, thousands of men ran forth to extinguish the fire. (92–93)
But, soaring again and again by the force of the wind, he went far away;
having become like the sky, he moved through another enclosure and into another field.
Indeed, that terrifying one could not be restrained at all as he continued to advance.

Aiming to destroy the grain that had already grown and burning all the grass and other vegetation, it spread in every direction, taking the form of one who brings about famine; at that time, all people, despite their efforts, became hopeless. (95–96)
They recited the protective mantra obtained through the Caitanya lineage;
as long as they remained steadfast, repeating each individual bead of the rosary, they remembered me, the destroyer of suffering, who acts as their protector within their hearts. (97)
Indeed, for the sake of protection, I quickly thought of a plan in the sky:
having conjured a cloud accompanied by lightning and thunder,
I brought down rain within the span of a single ghaṭikā, and thus the fire that threatened the crops was extinguished.
Within a distance of just one krośa, everything there was indeed reduced to ashes in every way;
yet, specifically for the sake of the abundance of crops,
I brought down rain there once more, so that the grain, the grass, and the ears of corn might flourish.
They were born just as before, following the proper seasons.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, at that time the fire was indeed extinguished by me through rain;
thereafter, all the farmers produced a fresh heap of grain.
In the ninth year, all desired foods, whatever vegetables there may be,
boiled rice, split pulses,
various saline foods, roasted grains, and other delicious, savory, and excellent delicacies [are provided].
All kinds of cooked foods, smeared with nectar, and excellent milk-rice offerings were presented to me in that vast palace. There,
within the image, I became manifest together with Lakṣmī.

The four-armed Lord himself partook of all kinds of foods— those to be chewed, those to be eaten, those to be licked, those to be sucked, as well as drinks and betel leaves— and having eaten, he bestowed his grace-born gifts.
Having received the lustration ceremony (*nīrājanā*) and worship in that manner, I quickly vanished from sight.
All the Vaiṣṇavas attained a wonder born of my grace;
they partook of the divine [food] and became purified.
All those members of my family have always maintained devotion toward me. Then, when the time arrived,
O Rame, I drew the farmers to my own divine and imperishable abode, in due order and as was appropriate.
Indeed, all these hundred maidens, devoted to their husbands,
having served me and given birth [to sons], have become dear to Brahmā and have taken refuge with you;
they are these very ones, beginning with Devamaṇikā, now in your abode.
The cowherd girls of Vṛndāvana have become divine beings in every respect;
others, O Rādhā, have attained liberation through my worship.
Thus, O Lakṣmī, those farmers were liberated by me at that time.
By reading, hearing, remembering, or even practicing this [text], people become like those who are liberated;
they enjoy my bliss, have all their desires fulfilled, are not inferior to me, and are of my very nature. (1.13–1.14)
Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O Hari, O Lord, O Husband, O bestower of all happiness, O object of my affection!
How may I, your devoted wife, become beautiful for the sake of your pleasure? (1.15)
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
A woman who desires to become beautiful in all her limbs should perform my supreme vow called Janmajayantī on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
She may subsist on fruits, or consume milk, curds, and so forth;
with whatever offerings she obtains, that virtuous woman should worship me, who am endowed with splendor.
To obtain a face like the moon, she should offer me a golden moon.
One should offer three gold leaves for the sake of beautifying the eyes, eyebrows, and forehead.
For the sake of the excellence of the cheeks, ears, nose, and lips, one should indeed offer golden leaf-sprouts, excellent flowers, and bimba-fruit ornaments. (118–119)
Likewise, for the sake of teeth with a beautiful fragrance, one should give golden *kunda* flowers during the vow;
and for the sake of sugar, filaments, saffron, and so forth, one should give them during the vow.
For the sake of beautiful breasts, one should give pomegranate and other fruits, as well as gold, during the vow.
One should offer a golden sugarcane stalk for the purpose of beautifully adorning the hands;
one should offer golden pitcher-shaped plaques for the sake of the beautiful sides, belly, and chest, and indeed, one should give gold and silver plates which bestow beauty. (121–122)
One should give two jars for the sake of a slender waist and for the sake of the hips;
one should give gold ornaments for the sake of a delicate vulva, as well as golden rings and pearls,
and likewise a golden cowrie, a chain, and a pearl-shell.
One should give a vessel made of gold for the sake of hairless hips;
one should give musk, diamonds, and the like for the sake of health of the womb;
and one should give two silver plantain trees for the sake of beautiful thighs. (124–125)
One should offer plantain fruit for the sake of the feet, shanks, and beautiful limbs of one's chosen deity;
sandals made of gold for the vehicle; and pearls for the sake of [attaining] the dust [of the deity].
By propitiating Lakṣmī, Nārāyaṇa, and a virtuous woman, one shall obtain everything.
On the day following the vow, one should feed the virtuous and shall obtain the fruit [of the rite].
(127) Thus everything has been told to you, which fulfills all desires. May all women obtain their wish through this vow or through giving. (128)
Thus have I truly related to you my own life stories,
which indeed protect my devotees, occurring during my sixteenth year;
you have heard them all, for they were truly desired by your mind.
Endowed with the greatness of the virtuous and bestowing great liberation,
O Rāma, these have been spoken by me out of mere compassion for the welfare of those who remember them,
for the liberation of those who meditate upon them, and for the removal of the sins of those who recite them.
For those who practice the yoga of identity with them, they bestow great bliss;
for women who have surrendered their all, they grant the state of being beloved by Brahman;
and for men who have surrendered their all, they grant the liberation of Brahman.

For those with desires, they fulfill all desires and grant happiness; for those without desires, by my grace, they bestow equality with me. O Lakṣmī, my divine pastimes are divine, and so too are my divine yogis and human beings.
My entire divine field on earth consists of the supreme abode;
sixteen years have passed, overflowing with great bliss.
Indeed, the seventeenth year will swiftly arrive on my birthday.
"A great festival will take place here, initiated by Lomaśa and others (1.36).
And I shall cease even from the exhaustion of all my wives.
Om, obeisance to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Lord; Svāhā! (1.37)."

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vision of the Lord and Liberation of the Farmer named Jīrṇodbhava through his Union with the Holy Caitanyakāyani, and the Narration of the Vow that Bestows Beauty upon Women," in the third section, the Dvāpara-santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*. Chapter 236 *Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā* — Section 3 (The Lineage of the Dvāpara Age) — Chapter 236.
[The Author: Chapter 237.
Śrī Puruṣottama said:
Listen, O Nārāyaṇī Śrī, to the great festival of the seventeenth day.
On my birthday, the Caturvyūha will perform [the ceremony].
Vāsudeva, as well as Saṃkarṣaṇa, Aniruddha, and Pradyumna—
all of them are thus lords and great seers.
"Having arrived tomorrow at the divine and most glorious field of Kuṅkumavāpikā, they will dwell there; let the attendants be ready.
They have been summoned for the seventh day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika."

All the Lakṣmīs, the wives of Brahmā, undertook their respective endeavors. The goddesses of the assembly halls quickly fashioned the assembly hall itself and all the locations within it, wherein the reflection of the entire creation was established.
The Śṛṅgāradevis created divine ornaments;
the Dhāmadevis made [their] splendors manifest, and the Vanadevis [created] forests. The Tarudevīs created gardens, while Māyā made [all these] visible.
The goddesses of taste produced all flavors; the goddesses of fragrance produced sweet scents;
Sarasvatī produced songs; Night produced heaven; and Annapūrṇā produced the most excellent and delicious foods. (7–8)
The Kalpalatās produced flowers, leaves, and petals;
the Kalpamaṇis produced ornaments, and Vahni produced gold.
Bhūdevī provided delightful beds, and Vāyu indeed provided vehicles.

The Rasa-halls, such as Kamalā and others, and the drinking-halls of Vāruṇī were present; Lalitā, Śrī, Mahālakṣmī, and Dāsikā brought lotuses. Viṣṇu, however, brought his own servants, the liberated souls (mukta-pārṣadas).
Yajñanārāyaṇa quickly constructed the sacrificial pavilions;
all kinds of medicinal herbs and fuel-sticks were swiftly brought forth.
The Gandharvas brought along singers accompanied by musical instruments.
Dancing girls, kinnaris, and apsarases also arrived swiftly.
Then the lords of lords, the supreme masters,
and the great generals of Śiva, such as Śāṅkara and others, arrived for the purpose of welcoming him.
The great seers returned with enthusiasm and gathered together;
the manifestations of Vāsudeva and others, as well as the Nārāyaṇas, arrived there.
The Rudras, the unborn ones, the Siddhas, and the Viṣṇus also came to that place.

All the female lords (*īśvarāṇyaḥ*) and liberated women (*muktānyaḥ*), as well as all the *ramā*s, arrived; the friends of Rādhā, the friends of Ramā, and the friends of Brāhmī also arrived. The *vairāja*s, the *hiraṇyapuṃsa*s, and the *māyātattva*s also arrived. (16–17)
The gods, goddesses, and ancestors, the guardians of the quarters and protectors of the worlds,
the sages, human devotees, and the descendants of Kaśyapa all arrived.
Righteous, virtuous, truthful, and endowed with the character of Brahman, they assembled together.
The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas arrived, as did the supreme sacred fords (tīrthas).
Famine, Fortitude, Auspiciousness, and Power—the wives of the Vedas—arrived together.
The oceans and the wives of Kṛṣṇa, including Rādhā and others, also arrived. (3.236.20)
All the Yoginīs belonging to Śaṅkara and all the Gaṇas also arrived;
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and other ascetics came there as well.
Forests, groves, and even entire regions of the earth arrived.
The sacred shrines, the seasons, and the times beginning with the year all arrived.
Even the month of Puruṣottama came, sounding its great drum,
bringing auspiciousness and bestowing every blessing upon the imperishable field.
Yogis arrived; sacrifices arrived, accompanied by their sons who were acts of devotion.
There was no end to the celestial chariots, nor likewise to the elephants and birds.
There was no end to the vehicles, nor to the bodies of the bards and panegyrists.
On the night of the seventh day of the bright fortnight, all embodied beings arrived at the place of the bards of many forms who provide entertainment;
the goddesses and gods offered them a most excellent welcome.
The virtuous attendants, who were dear to Brahmā, acted as well;
they became his father, mother, sister, and brothers.
Likewise, all the disciples and the sages themselves became lords.
The sages headed by Lomaśa and the virtuous ones headed by Lālāyana offered a welcome, as well as food and drink; likewise,
all the wish-fulfilling cows then gave their milk.
All the maidservants and servants there performed the service of honoring the earth; indeed, at midnight, nothing whatsoever was lacking.
And having risen in the morning, O Lakṣmī, I, Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, said:
Having performed my ablutions and adorned myself with ornaments, accompanied by my beloveds,
and having been honored by my mother and father, I went quickly to the assembly hall.
At that time, musical instruments were played, as well as those of Vāsudeva and others.
The incarnations and the male lords, as well as all the female goddesses, and the liberated gopīs and gopas came to my pavilion;
and having performed worship of me as I sat upon the divine lion-throne, they [remained there]. //33//
They all performed the *ārārtrika* rite, offering unbroken grains of rice (*akṣata*) and crescent-shaped marks of saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
The Brahmins and great sages uttered words of blessing and sang hymns.
There were millions of abodes, millions of lords, and millions of celestial sages and ancestors.
His wives likewise honored me with unbroken grains and flowers.
All human beings, all sacred fords, the principles of reality, the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
the Sarasvatīs, the Śāradās, and all the Lakṣmīs performed my worship.
They performed every kind of offering for me and presented divine gifts upon the floor of the assembly hall. (37) In this manner, a most magnificent worship continued there until midday;
everything that arrived there I gave away as a gift. (38)
Then, meals were indeed provided for the honored guests;
exemptions were granted, and auspicious sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) were bestowed.
Rewards were given in the form of gifts according to each person's merit.

During the night, there was the great sound of musical instruments, singing, dancing, and festivities until the end of midnight, after which there was a cessation. And on the ninth day, the great men were honored and likewise fed.
Having been honored and sent off, they departed for their own abodes.
Thus, on the eighteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, on the seventeenth year from my birth,
I rejoiced in the festival of my own birthday.
This fame of yours shines forth throughout the three worlds;
yet, regarding my own wonder here in my sixteenth year,
it has indeed been described by me during this third succession of the Dvāpara age.
I am the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Lord; I am the ordainer, the creator, the speaker, and the recorder of these narratives. Whoever performs the recitation of this third section—
He shall possess manifold prosperity and his lineage shall become extensive.
(46) Having fashioned a golden Garuḍa, one should offer it along with the book of the Dvāpara age;
by that act, the gift of the entire earth is indeed bestowed—of this there is no doubt. (47)
Whatever is offered during a moment of this narrative, even if it be very small,
shall become multiplied infinitely and shall bestow the great heaven.
Whether it be the gift of a cow, the gift of a garden, or the offering of gold and jewels—
The gift of a maiden, the gift of a house, the gift of an elephant, and the offering at a sacrifice—the fruit of all such gifts arises from this very gift.
Likewise, the gift of a celestial chariot, the gift of a city, and the offering of a forest [yield their fruits]. (3.236.50)
By means of giving, the offering of all one's possessions arises for him;
the gift of Brahman, the gift of the Vedas, and the supreme gift of liberation [arise].
By means of giving, the surrender of one's self arises for him.
The ancestors also cross over and become dwellers in the divine abode.
Through this gift, the bestowal of universal sovereignty itself arises for him;
diseases and obstacles perish, and misfortunes diminish.
Misfortunes perish through the gift of the *Dvāparakhaṇḍa*.
One should cause it to be recited for seven days, or for a fortnight, or even for a month.
Furthermore, one should feed virtuous Brahmins—both the listeners and the speakers—according to one's wealth.
She should feed virtuous women and widows, as well as all the poor and destitute. She should cause the reciter to be carried around the city in a palanquin by women;
and likewise the Brahmins, the kings, the merchants, and the common people.
Likewise, maidens with water-filled coconut jars, pearls, and *āsini* flowers, well-attired, should cause [the deity] to be circumambulated;
as well as married women with songs, unbroken rice grains, flowers, and saffron.
One should worship it, cause it to increase, and likewise carry it in procession through the city.
(58) They should also bestow great gifts upon the high-souled reciter;
indeed, they should give whatever is necessary so that the holy man may be well-pleased. (59)
Through hearing this, one attains enjoyment and liberation, as well as divinity;
there shall be the destruction of latent impressions and the dissolution of impurities.
There shall be the eradication of the threefold suffering, and there shall be eternal peace.
Desiring a son or a daughter, one should perform the gift of the Dvāparakhaṇḍa,
accompanied by a new cloth and provided with gold coins.
By that, one is indeed freed from enemies, and fear of the king does not arise.
Through this gift given with sincere devotion, he shall be liberated from prison;
even that which is impossible shall become possible for him through hearing [this teaching] here.
Furthermore, omniscience arises for him in many ways through such hearing.
May the beloved noble one, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Lord, the Great Master;
the husband of Rādhā and Lakṣmī, the husband of Padmāvatī and Śrīmāṇikī;
and the eternal husband of Prajñāmuktā—shine forth within his own heart through hearing [of His glories]. (64–65)
One shall indeed meet Him face-to-face at the end of a year; one should listen to Him constantly.
The Soul of the Universe will meet one in secret, and one will meet Him even in a dream—of this there is no doubt.
He shall protect one in times of calamity through the recollection of the Dvāpara-khaṇḍa.
This image of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is indeed mine;
this fragment of the Dvāpara age is within my belly.
By touching, meditating upon, and serving my form, one attains the imperishable state.
"Whoever—whether men or women—should have a desire for Me, who am directly present within their hearts, they and they alone shall listen to My discourse and chant My mantra:
'Oṃ namaḥ śrīkṛṣṇanārāyaṇāya pataye svāhā'. (69)
Having come, I shall indeed grant you my vision and happiness according to your desire.
This mantra bearing my name shall be perfected by one hundred thousand recitations;
a fire-offering (homa) consisting of one-tenth that number must be performed, and it should be meditated upon within the lunar day (amā).
Adorned with the Kaustubha gem and a crown, decorated with all ornaments,
with a gracious countenance, the beloved of Lakṣmī, as beautiful as Kandarpa—
there is no object in the three worlds that I do not give away. (72)
In all the three worlds, there is nothing that I do not bestow upon my devotee.
(73) Likewise, the lion-throne, the lap, the abode, the imperishable state which is my own seat—I grant all my sovereign powers to the one who recites the mantra. (74)
O Lakṣmī, this is my heart; it is my compassion and my grace.
I shall indeed grant everything as desired to one who recites the mantra of identity with Me.
Those known as the wish-fulfilling trees, the cows of plenty, and the wish-granting creepers—[all these belong to Me].
World-axles, wish-fulfilling gems, and inexhaustible vessels;
the lotus-mark, wonders, and all the supernatural powers (siddhis) come to exist within the heart of one who recites the mantra through identification with it. (76–77)
He hears the lineage of the Dvāpara age and recites my mantra;
for him there is eternal merit and perpetual success in his ritual practice (kalpasiddhi). Indeed, his movement is unimpeded and his vision is unobstructed.
Through the perfection of mantras, one indeed attains [these states] by my will; of this there is no doubt.

Whether it be divinity, or the state of a sage, or the state of a perfected being (siddha), or even lordship, or even the status of an incarnation—one may obtain these simply by hearing [this] during the Dvāpara age.
One may obtain the state of the earth, the state of auspiciousness, and likewise the golden state,
or the abode of the Great Person, by hearing [the glories] of Dvāpara;
provided one fixes the mind steadily upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa while listening.
One should listen with great festivity, for it bestows the four goals of human existence.
One should constantly give fruits, grains, garments, and ornaments, as well as all items of daily necessity, while listening to the narrative.
Having abandoned fear of revilers, as well as fear of atheists, and having abandoned fear of adversaries, one should indeed listen within my refuge.
Wherever I am, there is victory; wherever I am, there are festivals.
Wherever I provide protection, there indeed is fear in my absence.
Having heard this again and again, let your intellects become perceivers of aesthetic flavor (rasa), for they are within the range of my vision as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. ||85-86||
I, Kṛṣṇa, am the deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence for those who, with concentrated minds, shall hear even a single chapter or a single verse;
this applies even to those who are sinful, of low birth, or performers of base deeds.

Just as those of improper conduct become pure in every way through union with the virtuous, so too, by hearing this, sinners are purified; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, through my yoga, all listeners become free from the qualities (nirguṇa).
In this regard, those who possess human forms are considered liberated souls (muktas), and their consorts are considered liberated women (muktānikās).
However, my abode, which is the imperishable locus of discourse, should be understood as non-illusory.
The speaker of this [truth] is my own form; I speak it myself, without a doubt.
O Lakṣmī, in every verse here I have showered down my grace.
Even those who approach Hari, their beloved, with even a slight degree of devotion—
I approach them every day with joy a hundredfold.
If, after all sacrifices have been performed, one wards off any misfortune, one should remember me and repeatedly recite my mantra of identity (*tādātmya*).
All calamities will perish; this is the promise proclaimed by me.

Merely hearing this fragment of the lineage of the Dvāpara age would bring about the destruction of calamities; or it may happen through the mere formation of a resolve. On one side are all the stories together, and on the other side is my Manu alone. (94–95)
O Lakṣmī, Manu is already distinguished; how much more so one who is engaged in his discourse!
May there be welfare for you from even a drop of the compassion of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa. May the Teacher, the son of Kambharā, be auspicious; may the Son of Gopālā be auspicious.

May there be peace for you from Śvetavyāsa and the others, up to Vyāseśvara Hari—the one who is satisfied, endowed with the gentle splendor of his younger brother, wisdom, and omniscience; the all-knowing, the all-perceiving, the inner self of all, and the cause of all. 97–98.

The refuge of all dharmas, the abode of all, possessing the excellence of all goals; may he who is enriched by every excellence, the sovereign lord of all mines, and the foremost leader, grant you prosperity!
Indeed, it is by his residence that Saurāṣṭra attains its status as Saurāṣṭra.
May He— both manifest and unmanifest— grant you eternal well-being.
In the sacred field of Akṣarakuṅkumavāpī, frequented by Lomaśa, may Hari, the Lord of the gods and the Great Brahman, ever grant you peace.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Festival for the Seventeenth Birth Anniversary of the Beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, the Greatness of Hearing the Narratives of the Dvāpara Lineage, the Giving of Gifts, and the Recitation of Mantras," in the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter 237 *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*, Section 3: The Dvāpara-Yuga Lineage.
Chapter 237.
The author writes: Śrī Nārāyaṇī Śrī said:
O beloved of my heart, O life-breath, O lover, O ocean of bliss!

O compassionate Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, I have been purified by hearing the divine and auspicious sacred narratives of Your Lordship. Indeed, all these beloved wives of Brahmā, as well as these other beloved wives of Hari, [have likewise been purified]. 1–2.
By hearing your stories, all the hosts of gopīs have attained the state of supreme purification;
they are all forms of Ramā, Lakṣmī, Śrī, and Strī,
as well as Īśvarīs, Siddhas, Devīs, and even Mānavīs.
The Kāśyapīs and Talinīs have accomplished their purpose under Hari.
Oh, what fortune, what fortune for the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas,
that here we possess maidens whose very soul is the beloved Kṛṣṇa!
Oh, how great is the compassion and how great is the grace of the glorious Supreme Soul!
The wives are the listeners, the husband is the speaker, and the speaker himself is Śrī Puruṣottama. O Lord, the good fortunes of these women have been severed or indeed shattered.
Indeed, those women whose lotus-faces are darkened shall not hear the nectar of his story for even a moment.
Many other women and men will hear this nectar of his tale;
therefore, provide a summary of the story for those of limited intellect.
Puruṣottama said:
O Narāyaṇī, for the sake of recollection by those who have acquired faith in even a very brief moment, I shall relate the seeds of the narrative of this section; listen attentively.
The chapters of this section are two hundred and thirty-six,
and the verses amount to twenty-five thousand and more.
The chapters for the Satya, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages are indeed twenty-six.
Likewise, O Rame, one hundred and one thousand verses grant liberation.
The verses of the three sections amount to one lakh and twelve thousand one hundred; they bestow the joy of the face of Bhūmi (the Earth).
This enumeration is to be understood here in the world of humans, and not otherwise;
this extensive compendium was already described to you previously.
Here, at the beginning of the Dvāpara age, the praise performed by Śrī is recounted.
Then, from that time, the calculation of the period of creation was proclaimed for the Creator (Brahmā).
Thereafter, the cycles known as *kalpas*, numbering fifty-two years, were described.
Then, for the sake of destroying the demon Rohiṇa, Hari, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa of the celestial realm, [manifested].
Then Merudhārta is celebrated as Merunārāyaṇa;
Viṣṇunārāyaṇa is described as the one who caused the destruction of Ravi.
And for the sake of destroying the demon Dhūmra, the Lord Devanārāyaṇa appeared.
He is celebrated as Yajña-Nārāyaṇa, the originator of sacrifices;
thereafter he is called Brahma-Nārāyaṇa, the teacher of Rudra;
and then Āditya-Nārāyaṇa, for the purpose of regulating the abodes of the gods.
The Teacher Nāga, Śrī Garuḍa, and Nārāyaṇa are described;
then there is Ārṣa Nārāyaṇa, who bestows stability and firmness.
Then follows Thurānanda Praśāstā and Śrī Prājña Nārāyaṇa.
The virtuous Naiṣṭhika-vīranārāyaṇa was described;
thereafter, Mokṣada-bhadranārāyaṇa was also praised.
Then, the festive wedding of Lakṣmī, the daughter of Tuṅgabhadrāsana, took place.
The incarnation known as Anādi-Śrī-Harinārāyaṇa has been described;
after him came Bīja-Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the seed.
Then Hari was born as Vara-Nārāyaṇa in the house of Dharmavrata.
He who brings about the release from the curse for all those who had assumed the forms of women due to the curse of Sudarśanī is celebrated as Strīpuṃnārāyaṇa. Then,
for the sake of destroying the Mākara demon, he became Jala-nārāyaṇa.
Then Śīlanārāyaṇa appeared for the purpose of establishing the dharma of the virtuous;
then Vārdhinārāyaṇa appeared for the purpose of destroying the demon Vyāghra;
and thereafter Kṛṣṇa was described as Caturmukha, resembling the Creator.
Śrī Puruṣottama descended into the house of Rādhanikā, who was a mass of merit; thereafter, O Ramā, this story was told. Then Tīrthanārāyaṇa, the purifier of holy places, was proclaimed.
Then Jīvan-Nārāyaṇa was described as the promoter of devotion;
after that, O Rame, Ardha-Śrīśvara-Nārāyaṇa was extolled;
and then Ardha-Pitṛ-Nārāyaṇa and Plakṣa-Nārāyaṇa.
In the human sacrifice (naramedha), he was then proclaimed as Puṃs-Nārāyaṇa.
Then Śyāma-Nārāyaṇa was mentioned along with Vaṭaśrī.
After that, for the sake of destroying the demon Māyūra, he became Rāja-Nārāyaṇa.
After Kāmabhasmottara comes Brahmacārinārāyaṇa;
then Śambhūjjīvaka is mentioned, followed by Śivanārāyaṇa.
Kuberojjīvaka and Svarṇanārāyaṇa are also described.
Then there was Svāminārāyaṇa, the performer of burning with flames;
after him, Śrīsāvananārāyaṇa in the house of Nirvāṇika;
and also Sāghunārāyaṇa, who appeared together with the female ascetic Lakṣmī.
The Lord Bhaktanārāyaṇa, who revives the minds of those wearing the ochre robe,
appeared once more for the protection of King Varmadhara, who had become a horse; likewise,
the Lord Medhanārāyaṇa arose together with the goddess of intelligence, Lakṣmī.
Then Vahninārāyaṇa appeared for the purpose of destroying Analāda;
then Rasanārāyaṇa appeared for the purpose of destroying Ilodara;
thereafter Śrīcakranārāyaṇa, the slayer of Daityas, was proclaimed.
Then Satyanārāyaṇa, the establisher of truth and dharma;
then Hiraṇyanārāyaṇa, for the sake of the stability of the mountains;
and then Nairañjaninārāyaṇa, together with the glory of absolute poverty.
Then Śāpanārāyaṇa [appeared] for the pacification of Puṇyavatī’s curse;
Brahmanārāyaṇa for the fulfillment of the Apsarases’ hearts;
and Gurunārāyaṇa for the illumination of the knowledge of Brahman. (38–39)
Then the Lord Ācārya-Nārāyaṇa, together with the glory of his consort Ācāryāṇī, bestowed the auspicious initiation upon King Bṛhaddharma.
After that, Vidyun-Nārāyaṇa appeared for the purpose of destroying Vidyut-srāva and others.
Then, for the sake of destroying Madhubhakṣa and the others, Nārāyaṇa with the honey (Madhunārāyaṇa) was proclaimed;
likewise, the slayer of Daityas, Śrīnāthanārāyaṇa, and Vibhunārāyaṇa together with the goddess Vibhvī at the golden festival (Svarṇotsava). 41–42.
Then there is Mokṣanārāyaṇa, accompanied by Muktiśrī;
then Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, joined by Śivarājīśrī. The Lord is described as the beloved of hundreds of millions, billions, and trillions of consorts.
The *Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa-dvandva-dvādaśordhva-sahasraka* (44),
the hymn of praise to the Couple (*dvandva-nāma-stava*) which destroys all sins,
and the manifestation of Nara-Nārāyaṇa as the form of the Supreme Brahman (45).
Then follows a description of the duties of household women who are obedient;
likewise, the virtuous conduct of young brides, the qualities to be protected by a bride, and the strength of chastity and truth;
and finally, the yoga of devotion that is beyond the material modes.
The Puruṣottama-yoga and that which pertains to the Supreme Brahman;
the identity with that which transcends the Imperishable (akṣara), the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow,
the greatness of the Guru, and thereafter the liberation of the divine goddess.
The story of King Subāhu regarding the gift of food and water,
the story of Nahuṣa, and indeed the story of the parrot Kuñjala;
the story of Kāmodā has been told, and after that, the story of Cyavana.
The disclosure of the guru’s secret, the description of virtuous conduct and so forth;
through the union with the Ṛṣi Dharmarṣi, the supreme state of being beloved by Brahmā;
and the narrative concerning Līlāvatī, Suśīlā, and the other female companions.
Then follows the narration of the liberation of the Rākṣasa horse-herder;
thereafter, the Guru’s identity as Hari, followed by the hymn of total self-surrender (sarvārpaṇa-stava).
Then, regarding the status of being the best of Vaiṣṇavas, there is the illustration of Kauśika and others.
Thereafter, the acquisition of musical instruction by Nārada was told;
after that, the attainment of the state of Garuḍa by Ulūka was described;
and following that, indeed, the marks of a great devotee of the Lord were explained. (53–54)
Thereafter, the examination by Queen Citrāmbarā was described;
then, the protection performed for the queen by the goddess Gada was recounted.
Furthermore, the superior power of the sciences, mantras, and gurus was proclaimed.
Then there is the service of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇasevā*), followed by the *vrata* known as *damanaka*.
On separate lunar days, the worship of Hari in various forms is proclaimed.
There is the narration of the majesty of devotion (*bhakti-māhātmya-kathana*) and the secret concerning the devotion of the bride (*vadhū-bhakti-rahasya*).
Then the entire essence of Hari’s grace was described;
thereafter, the secrets of the great mantras along with their meaningful nyāsas were revealed.
Furthermore, the Gāyatrī, the vertical sectarian marks (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and so forth, as well as the knowledge of their hidden meanings, were taught.
The manifestation of the three quarters and the divinity of the single quarter were thus desired.
Then the power of Yayāti was described through devotion to his names, followed by a description of the means for propitiating Hari. (3.237.59–60)
The story of the miser, the fruit of [the tree] that bears different results, the company of the virtuous,
the means for attaining the state of one most devoted to Brahman, as well as the accounts of chaste wives and sages;
and the wonderful narrative concerning the cowherd woman Sucandrikā has been told.
Then the story of Manu’s wife Brahmaprathā was told;
the means for attaining long life, namely the release of a hundred vultures, was described;
and thereafter, the abandonment of a hundred sons by Vinodinī was recounted.
In connection with Vātsyāyana, the liberation of courtesans has been discussed;
the causes for their virtuous conduct have been stated, and the means to liberation have been proclaimed.
By Vṛṣāyana, Carakā was saved from the hawk; thus it was declared.
The fruit of serving the virtuous through Citraketu and Mālatī has been declared.
From the example of Viṣṇu, it is stated that the saintly are superior to the brahmins;
and from the example of Durgā, those who share the same religious duties have been described. (65–66)
The hells have been described through the illustration of the farmer;
likewise, those going to heaven and the executioners have been described.
Holy men are said to be a moving shrine that purifies everyone.
The son of a Brahmin with emaciated limbs, though born of a Śūdra woman,
attained the state of one most devoted to Brahman and the nature of fire through his austerities by virtue of a boon from Indra.
There are many such examples of the various transformations of births.
There is also the example of King Bhaṅgāsvana’s transformation into a woman,
and the example of the yogin Viśvāmitra through the power of Brahmanical yoga.
[Likewise] there is the destruction of the demon Lomaka by Kapardaka, and the taming of Vṛṣa by Ruci.
The defeat of Indra and the gratification of the Guru are described;
then follows the rescue of Gokarṇa-tīrtha submerged in the ocean.
Thereafter, the story of Kuvalāśva and the narrative of Triśaṅku are told. (71–72)
The discourse on Brahman by Praṇat was likewise delivered as a narrative by Kaśyapa;

the means for attaining liberation are the company of the virtuous and strength [derived therefrom]. Furthermore, through association with the saintly Ālambāyana, there occurred the liberation of a hundred thousand [beings].
Furthermore, there is the liberation of the vulture, the outcaste, and the Śabara;
the abiding of Lakṣmī among the virtuous, and from that, the manifestation of Śrīvāsa.
Then, regarding the incarnation [of Viṣṇu], the curse of Bhṛgu is declared, as well as its cause, which is his own will.
The gift of a cow (godāna) and the vow of propitiating the cows have been described, as well as the rescue of the bhāruṇḍa birds, which is a cause for the liberation of the deceased;
and there is the illustration of Vṛṣādarbhi and Sūrya regarding the recipient of a gift.
By the virtuous Śrī Cakrabhāsa, liberation was granted to the thief Naraśaya; the wealthy were awakened to the Brahma-sacrifice;
his wife was wedded, and the root of all dharma was demonstrated. (77–78)
In this regard, the example of Jāṅgalāmakhani is proclaimed:
the liberation of the son of the barber of Śambhalavāra, who was a virtuous devotee, along with his various sons, daughters, husbands, and wives. (79)
Then follows the examination of service with auspicious devotion;
thereafter, the manifestation of Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa upon the earth is proclaimed, and the *Śrī Puruṣottama Sāman* along with the description of the thousand names is recounted. (3.237.80–81)
And the fruit of the Puruṣottama-sāman is the attainment of the Imperishable;
likewise, the fruit of the gift of land and so forth, as well as the fruit born from the gift of food and so forth [are described].
Between the two, the one named Dīrgha-śīla who is an āstika and the one who is a nāstika—
Indeed, the instruction through the gate of Yama and the subsequent liberation were recounted;
then follows the illustration of the offering of the body by the Yoginī Brahmasatyā, and the rebirth of Devarāta in the wife of King Vaivarta. (83–84)
Then the liberation of Romapāda Paśupati was recounted,
as well as the protection of the thief named Nagnabhaṅga through the company of the virtuous;
and furthermore, the restoration to life brought about by the saintly Bhāgavatāyana.
Even for one who has been consumed by a forest fire, such wonder arises [at the sight of her]:
the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, who had arisen from the ashes produced by Kāmadeva, and likewise the battle between her and the armies of Lalitā, Śrī, and Mahālakṣmī. (86–87)
Then follows the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura and the Lalitāśrīstava;
thereafter, the distribution of rewards and the sixteen temples.
[88] Therein is the service performed by female attendants residing in the Cintāmaṇi palace.
The two-fold nature of Mahālakṣmī in the city of Kāñcī has been declared;
likewise, the procedure for initiation and the residence of the three deities have been proclaimed. [Therein are] one hundred and thirty-five names of Lalitāśrī. (3.237.90)
The gift that bestows the attainment of a son and the vow have been proclaimed;
thereafter, the vow of service to the virtuous is declared the supreme vow.
Also, the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa and the gift of the Hiraṇyagarbha.
The gift of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-dāna) and the gift of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa-dāna) have been proclaimed.

[92] The great gift of a thousand cows (gosahasra-mahādāna), the offering of the golden wish-cow (svarṇakāmagavā), the great gift of a golden horse (hiraṇyāśva-mahādāna), and the gift of a golden chariot (hiraṇyaratha-dāna). [93]
The gift of a golden elephant-chariot, the gift of five ploughs,
the great gift of the golden earth, and the offering of the Viśvasudarśana [image];
the gift of the garland-wheel (mālācakra) is likewise proclaimed as a gift of ornaments.
The gift of the Great Kalpalatā tree, the bestowing of wish-fulfilling trees,
the granting of desire-yielding trees, the offering of teachers, deities, and so forth,
the dedication of temples, and likewise the gift of the seven oceans. (95–96)
The gift of the great elements (mahābhūta) and the gift of prosperity (lakṣmī) are proclaimed [as meritorious],
as are the pacification of the planets, their worship, and the like, as well as the recitation of mantras ten million times and more.
The pacification of the planets serves as an illustration for a Vaiśya who possesses iron and charcoal.
Then, two hundred names of Mahālakṣmī were indeed recited;
likewise, there is the image of Mahālakṣmī and her mandala.
Through the hymn of names, the daughters of the Pitṛs obtain their own desired fruits. (98–99)
The Lakṣmī-Saubhāgya-Śayana-vrata and its procedure have been declared;
likewise the Ghaṭalakṣmī-vrata and the Sarvamaṅgala-vrata;
the Sāṃkhya-yoga-vrata, the Rasa-kalyāṇa-vrata, and the Lalitā-vrata.
The Ārdrānandaramā-Nārāyaṇa-vrata is proclaimed;
the Śāradeya-vrata is also mentioned, as well as the Kalyāṇī-kamalā-vrata.
Likewise, the Viśoka-lalitā-dvādaśī-vrata has been declared.
The vow consisting of the playful fondling of Kṛṣṇa by Vibhūti has been described,
as well as the illustration of King Puṣkaravāhana.
Furthermore, the instruction regarding the sixty-one vows has also been proclaimed.
The sacred ford (tīrtha) consisting of Kuṅkumavāpikā effects liberation for sinners.

For the pacification of the power of untimely death, the performance of mantras, worship, and so forth has been described; likewise, the religious duties and rites appropriate for men of the Dvāpara age have been shown.
The distinction between the duties of the various ages (yugas) and so forth, the rite for pacifying portents, the rite for pacifying bad dreams, as well as the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña),
auspicious dreams and omens, and the rite for pacifying inauspicious [omens] have thus been declared. (106)
The lineage of Hanumān and Manu has been described,
as well as the primary means for the destruction of great sins and other evils; thereafter follows the description of the lineages of Dharma and Adharma.
The residence of Duḥsaha and so forth, as well as the calamities that befell his lineage,

the discernment between what ought and ought not to be done, and [the effects of] the lunar mansions and other astrological factors, have been proclaimed. Furthermore, the fourfold widowhood of Sarojinī and Kumbhakartṛ has also been described.
Through service to Satīśvarī, one attains the state of Padminī and the state of Ramā.
Following that, the lineage of the fourteen Manus and their progeny is described,
as well as the narrative of the Prajāpati Ruci.

The sporting of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Brahmapriyā and others, on the Himālaya mountains has also been described. Furthermore, the origin of diamonds and other excellent gems from the Bala-rākṣasa is recounted. 11.2.11-2.12.
Then follows the fall of Bala’s attendant due to a curse (11.3);
the transformation into a Daitya, the emergence of gems from that body, and the qualities and characteristics of all types of jewels are proclaimed (11.4).
The fourteen incarnations of Hari among human beings,
the procedure for the *jīva-śrāddha*, the cessation of *saṃsāra*,
the *vyapohana* [mantra], the hymn of praise, and the giving away of daughters and other gifts at a sacrifice.

Indeed, when the cause of death is destroyed, there is the illustration of the path of becoming (bhāvāyana). (1.16) Furthermore, the investigation of the illustrious Śrī Acidānanda Yogin is presented;
and in the Dharma of Liberation, the causes for the attainment and dissolution of the body are declared. (1.17)
The cause of that which is called Māyā, as well as the attainment of the supreme abode;
the question and answer regarding the wife Sadvidyā and her son, and concerning *naiṣkarmya*;
the experience of auspicious and inauspicious [results] and so forth, and consciousness—these are proclaimed. 118.
The discernment of the dharma of liberation and the discrimination of the inner self (adhyātma) and so forth;

the wandering for alms by the great seer, the state of the self as devoid of qualities (nirguṇātmatā) while in the householder stage, and the deliverance of his son—who was eternally dependent—through devotion, have thus been described. (3.237.1–20)
The destruction of leprosy for the leper named Vyāghra has been declared;
the liberation of Uttama, the village priest, has been proclaimed.
Likewise, the destruction of pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman) and the deliverance of Virāla have occurred.
The restoration of sight to Andha, the son of Pṛthūdharā;
the healing of the broken feet of the Śūdra Sāgara;
the removal of the mutilation of Vṛkṇadeva; and the liberation of Bhāva. (1.22–1.23)
Then follows the story of the liberation from the curse of the Pāśupata Śiva-brahmin;
Bāṇāṅgaṇa, a liquor-seller, was liberated through the company of the virtuous;
and Mṛtādana, a leather-worker who served cows, attained liberation.
Through the practice of *sumantukarṣi*, even Śaṅkudhara attained liberation.
(1.25) The community of Mahāsaurāṣṭra was protected from bandits;
the merchant Dhaniṣṭhakeśava was delivered from sexual misconduct. (1.26)
The liberation of a Rākṣasa through devotion by a king who was a slayer of Brahmins;
the liberation from the sin of killing a woman by Devaviśrāma through the Kāṇḍikā weapon;
and the restoration to life of the deceased son of Harṣula’s devotee.
The destruction of the disease of leprosy and its protection for Śāṇadhara;
the warding off of the sin of cow-slaughter for the devotee named Nimbadeva;
and the sovereignty, devotion to Brahman, and so forth of the single-minded devotees are recounted. (1.28–1.29)
The liberation of Kālīndara through devotion to Bhāṇḍa has been declared;
likewise, while Rāyaṇadeva was still in the womb, he became a knower of dance and accumulated a store of knowledge.
Furthermore, liberation through the instruction of Bodhāyana has also been proclaimed in that same manner.
The Vaiṣṇava nature and subsequent liberation of King Puṇḍravarmā, who was learned in the Gāyatrī mantra and observances along with his subjects, were proclaimed;
and the liberation of the cotton-carder and the weaver has also been described. 131–132.
The release of the wood-carriers, headed by Jaṅgaladeva;
the virtuous conduct of the devotee Vātsalyadhīra together with his wife;
and the liberation of Tilakaraṅga, the forest-guardian—these have been illustrated. (13.3)
The protection of those devoted to the *añja* and those devoted to the *mahāmaya* was ensured;
the protection of farmers from plunderers was proclaimed; and an inexhaustible granary was established for the Kirāta named Sāgara. (1.34–1.35)
The protection of the queen of Sāraṅgahūṇabhakta was performed;
thereafter, the attainment of liberation by Yajñarādhapuṣkasa occurred.
Following that, the liberation of the outcaste named Kapikṣaya is narrated.
The liberation of Nālīkara and the blacksmith was described;
the warding off of poison by Maṅgala, the deity, and the leather-worker was proclaimed;
and thereafter, the liberation of Haridāsa and the chariot-maker was described.
The protection of Śilāhṛd, Dāmaśila, and Adabhṛti was accomplished;
likewise, the artisan Sañjayadeva was rescued from the elephant.
Thereafter, the liberation of the painter Sambharadeva is recounted.
The liberation of the lords of the pearl-oyster beds, the stone mines, and the charcoal pits;
the destruction of the sins and other evils of the hunter named Cakradhara;
and the release of the treacherous Vāṭadhara and Khasa.
The liberation of the daughter of Dvaipīrājñī from the punishment of King Siṃha; the release of Śivajaya, the builder of the temple;
and the vision of Kṛṣṇa by Jālakṛt, the son of Saṃgara.
Then there was the liberation of Udyama, Śrībharu, Vāṭa, and others;
through the application of the practitioner (sādhuyoga), the camels and their keepers were liberated by Dīrgharava.
Furthermore, the liberation of Ratnaprabha was also declared to have occurred through the application of the practitioner.
Hari liberated Gadārdana, Īśavaidya, and Mukundī;
he also brought about the release of Deśyāvana and Kīśasvāmin. Hari assumed the forms of Nigamikā, the barber, and others.
Thus he performed service for King Svarṇadhanvan and his queen.
Following that, their liberation was also proclaimed.
Furthermore, it was told how in a previous birth Hari [rescued] the fisherman's wife from the demon Ābhīra.
He performed the protection and liberation of Ruṭāṇakya;
then followed the torments of Yama for Matsya, Māra, Dhīra, Parva, and others.
After that, his births as a boatman and his subsequent liberation were narrated.
Then there was the liberation of Tārakādarśaka, the wielder of the trident;
the release of Aṅgāraka, known as Jvālāprasāda; and the release of Garada, the chief of those who administer poison. (3.237.150)
Then, the liberation of the wielder of the weapon named Vikhaṇḍala was described;
likewise, the liberation of Jīrṇodbhava, who had been made a farmer, through the application of a *sādhuyoga*.
[This occurred] from my birth as the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa.
In the seventeenth chapter, the Jayantī festival on the anniversary of the Lord’s birth is described (152).
Furthermore, the greatness of listening to this section of the Dvāpara-santāna-khaṇḍa,
as well as the greatness of giving gifts and the recitation of mantras, has been proclaimed (153).
Then, the essence of the stories concerning the Dvāpara age was proclaimed:
"O Lakṣmī, Rādhā, Ramā, Kṛṣṇa, Padmāvatī, and Māṇikī;
O Nārāyaṇī, beloved of Brahmā, Kamalā, Amṛtā, and Ramā. (154)

All those who are dear to Hari have been made to hear my own Self by me. All stories consist of me; you are established within them. Men are consciousness and women are bliss; I am the essence of both.
These three collections of discourses, whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss,
are indeed you yourselves— you who are the Brahman, the virtuous ones, the seekers of Brahman, and those established in the intellect.
And between those two principles, I am the Supreme Lord, Bliss itself.
These very realized souls are my power of consciousness (cicchakti) and my primordial nature (prakṛti).
Mūla-māyā is the divine Rādhā, and I am her bliss.
All realized beings are my incarnations, and their consorts are my consciousness.
Of those two, I am Puruṣottama, the source of bliss.
"Sat" is the cause, which is all; "cit" is the object of consciousness, which is the effect. Of these two, I am the giver of bliss, the Lord of All, the Supreme Lord.
I am of the nature of differentiation, and yet I am the underlying continuity of consciousness. Dwell­ing within the interval between those two, I am blissful and possess the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Such as I am, I am everywhere simple; though difficult to attain, I become accessible through the power of grace. 161–162.
In all creations, I myself become the object of vision for those devoted to me;
indeed, throughout all the universes, I assume innumerable forms.
Yet, in every respect, there is no difference between my forms, my essential nature, and my activities.
Or perhaps, in some instances, there exists an internal enumeration and such a measure [of my devotees];
yet, for my devotees, there is no counting of their numbers, nor of their deeds,
nor indeed is there ever any reckoning of my stories within the universes.
Whatever nectars there are, whatever ambrosias,
and whatever elixirs exist in this world— all of them are surpassed by her;
likewise, all the loves and affections directed toward devotees do not equal her.
O Rame, all the means of attainment, all the causes, and all the instrumental factors that yield fruit are contained within this section [khaṇḍa] as the grace of Hari; indeed,
their purpose here is centered upon Him.
Whatever fruits belong to efforts, whatever fruits belong to births,
and whatever fruits belong to devotion— all those have here borne fruit in every way.
Whatever purity belongs to the liberated and whatever purity belongs to the yogis— [all that has been attained].
That very purity which belongs to his own devotees belongs likewise to those who serve him.
O Lakṣmī, just as Kṛṣṇa possesses intensity in the destruction of the sins of sinners,
so too does the lineage of Dvāpara possess intensity.
Devotees indeed cross over by devotion, the affectionate by their love for Mādhava;
sinners cross over by yoga, and the virtuous by service through grace.
Even the wicked, the asuras, and the daityas [cross over] through direct union with Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then, through the hearing of the lineage of Dvāpara,
all those perfections that exist among the gods, the Daityas, the mantras, and the perfected yogis—
those perfections belong to this listener, the speaker, and the one who rejoices. (173–174)

The celestial chariots of liberation, the mounts such as elephants that carry one across, and the Siddha goddesses who act as guides— all these come to resort to him by virtue of his refuge [in truth].
All this is the fruit of the dharma of Truth, as is the fruit of the dharma of the Tretā age.
Indeed, by merely hearing this [text], men attain the state of Nārāyaṇa and women the state of Nārāyaṇī;
both attain the very appearance, ornaments, and so forth of him, through the mere hearing of it. (176–177)
The grace of Hari, the grace of the saintly, and the grace of Lakṣmī are firmly established in the embodied soul who takes refuge in the lineage of Dvāpara.
All supreme merits, as well as those residing in the highest abodes, [are attained by him]. 178.
Indeed, for this listener, there arise ever-increasing floods of bliss.

Even that which is difficult to attain, difficult to traverse, difficult to abide in, and devoid of hope—by hearing this, it indeed becomes easy to attain, easy to traverse, easy to abide in, and full of hope. (3.237.180)

"Salutations to the beginningless Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, the Incarnate One; salutations to Him whose body consists of both consciousness and the unconscious, the Inner Controller of all. (181) By this single verse alone, one obtains the fruit arising from the Dvāpara-khaṇḍa.
Even a helpless embodied being, while dying anywhere, may obtain [this teaching];
or he for whom there is not even a moment to hear it in the forest—even he is liberated by mere remembrance, so what need is there to speak of hearing it? (182–183)
Thus, O Lakṣmī, I have described to you in every way the supreme majesty of the lineage of Dvāpara, which is greater than all others.
Then, a white man appeared, four-faced and four-armed.
The four-footed one, who was not of the same name [as before], being pleased, spoke to Puruṣottama:
"I am the Satya-yuga; I have been made worthy of liberation by you. By means of the connection with the Kṛta lineage, people shall attain liberation. (185–186)
Then Pītapumān arrived—he who had three necks, three arms, and three feet; laughing, he bowed to Śrī Puruṣottama. He said:
"I am the Yuga and the Tretā; by your grace, I have become worthy of liberation."
"Through the conjunction with the lineage of Tretā, embodied beings shall attain liberation.
Then there arrived a man with two legs, two arms, and two faces;
he was red in color and full of joy, yet he did not bow to Śrī Puruṣottama.
Accompanied by a loud laugh, he said: "I am Dvāpara.
By you, who are the progeny of Dvāpara, I have been made a bestower of liberation.
Indeed, embodied beings shall attain liberation through my progeny."
Then, O Lakṣmī, he arrived from there looking dejected and frail;
his heart was unexpanded, devoid of happiness and joy, dark-complexioned, sorrowful, and like another man utterly wretched. (191–192)
Suddenly shedding tears, he repeatedly prostrated himself like a staff;
like a sinful soul who is impure and has been banished by people, he spoke, making known his own state: "I am a defiled Kali age. (193)

Indeed, I have no place among the gods nor among the great seers; likewise, O Blessed One, I never have a place among the perfected ones, the virtuous women, or the holy beings. I am miserable here in this creation of yours; deliver me!
Just as the three brothers attained liberation through yoga, so too may embodied beings attain liberation through my yoga.
Welcome to me and to the gods; may your grace be upon me, O Mādhava.

"By whose association with you I, who am a sinner, may become meritorious here—I bow to that gracious Lord, the illustrious Dayālu. Thus addressed, I, Kṛṣṇanārāyaṇa, overcome by compassion, spoke: || 198 ||
"Having composed the Tiṣyasaṃtānaka Khaṇḍa for you as well, I shall make you equal to my three brothers; be joyful!
O Lakṣmī, having heard this and bowed down, the four brothers departed together like the [four] Yugas.
Therefore, after this, there will be one born of the lineage of Tiṣya,
who is the Supreme Person, the Great Brahman, higher than the highest,
and who is greater than all the liberated incarnations.
May that Puruṣottama, who on earth was the son of Kambharā as Bālakṛṣṇa, and who is saluted in the heart by Īśas and Jīvas alike, protect you here externally as well. (20.1)
May He who is the beloved of all, the son of Gopāla and Kṛṣṇa,
who assumes incarnations such as the creation of all souls, and who is the source of all incarnations, protect us constantly. (202)
Twenty-five thousand, one hundred and sixty-two verses were composed by Śveta in the lineage of Dvāpara.

(203) Thus ends the description of the subject matter of the Dvāpara lineage, the specific majesty of the Dvāpara lineage, the direct revelation of the lineages of the four ages, and the prayer for the eligibility for liberation during the Kali age, in the third section, the Dvāpara Lineage, of the *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā*.
Chapter Two Hundred and Thirty-Seven, titled "The Discourse on the Lineage of Tiṣya and the Benediction.
Thus ends the third section, the Dvāpara-Santāna-Khaṇḍa, of the glorious *Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa Saṃhitā*. Om.
May this be offered unto the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord.
