72. By means of the recitation of the mantra containing the name of the Blessed One, through the power of Yayāti, all his subjects attained devotion to Viṣṇu and other virtues.

73. Thinking that Yayāti had gained greater devotion on earth than he had while in heaven, Indra bestowed Bindumatī upon him for the purpose of making him renounce the earth; subsequently, the king obtained youth through his son, and at the end, the king along with his subjects attained Vaikuṇṭha, and so forth.

74. A description of the means for pleasing Hari through recounting the greatness of a devotee of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa; and how the miserly Brāhmaṇa Paraśucandraka obtained infinite fruit from a very small gift, and so forth.

75. The manifestation and disappearance of fire; the attainment of various fruits through various means; the majesty of the saintly; and the attainment of Śrī Hari by me through association with the saintly, and so forth.

76. The means for attaining the state of being most devoted to Brahman and goodness; the means for reaching the divine abode; the means for the path of passionlessness and truth; and the yoga of Hari, such as divine charity and other practices. 77. A description of the realization of the supreme limit of devotion to the husband among virtuous and chaste women.

78. An account of the wonder of the chaste, concerning how the cowherd woman named Sucandrikā, through her devotion to her husband and her devotion to the chastity of Hari, went with her husband to heaven, Satyaloka, Vaikuṇṭha, Goloka, and the Akṣara-dhāma.

79. Regarding the duties of a virtuous woman (*sādhvī*), such as worship and giving; and how the virtuous Brahmaprathā, the wife of Hariprathamanu, after residing in heaven, attained the abode of the Imperishable (*akṣaradhāma*) as the fruit of serving virtuous men and women.
80. Means for bestowing long life and means for liberation, such as service at the holy places of the virtuous (*sādhutīrtha*).
81. Through association with the virtuous, the liberation of a hundred vultures, the liberation of the worm Jīvaṭa, the attainment of virtue by Vinodinī and her five hundred sons, and so forth.
82. Regarding women who are independent, lustful, unchaste, or courtesans, there is liberation after the destruction of sin through the meeting with the virtuous Vātsyāyana in Kāśī, and so forth.
83. Concerning the state of being virtuous, there are various instrumental causes and so on, as well as the fruits of praising or not praising the virtuous.
84. Even for one devoid of the company of the virtuous, there are means to liberation; [this section covers] the attainment of the virtuous, the attainment of virtue, its various types, and so forth.

85. Nārāyaṇa is the foremost dharma of the virtuous (*sādhu*); by him, one attains the state of being virtuous. Through devotion to Nārāyaṇa, the virtuous Vṛṣāyana protected the sparrows by giving his own flesh, which was the weight of the sparrows, to the hawk, and so forth.

86. Regarding the supreme welfare of those such as Citraketu, who were intoxicated by wealth, pride, strength, arrogance, and sovereignty, the examples of Mālatī and others demonstrate the fruits of the power of the virtuous.

87. In the sense that the virtuous are in every way most excellent compared to brahmins and householders, there is the illustration of Viṣṇu and the illustration of Durgā’s service to the virtuous, and so forth.
88. A description of the nature of dharma and how, in the absence of dharma, one goes to hell, and so forth.

89. An illustration of the hells perceived through direct perception; by means of the examples of the farmer and the servant, it is demonstrated that wealth and other such things are hells perceived through direct perception, as well as heaven perceived through direct perception, and so on.
90. Those who go to heaven; those who are slayers even without having killed; gradual deliverance through compassion; deliverance through service to the virtuous, and so forth.

91. The sanctifying power of those who have committed violence through their connection to sacred fords (*tīrtha*); the fact that virtuous people and others constitute a "mobile ford" (*jaṅgama-tīrtha*); and how, in ancient times at Lake Aśvapaṭṭasara, a Brahmin woman’s son—who was emaciated, born of a Śūdra, and even a Cāṇḍāla—attained the state of being most devoted to Brahman (*brahmiṣṭha*) and became like fire (*kṛśānu*) through his austerities and a boon from Indra, and so forth.

92. Even for those of other castes, a change of caste and the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood occurs through the application of virtues, vows, conduct, initiation, boons, curses, planetary alignments, and so on; regarding this matter, there are numerous illustrations, such as the example of King Bhaṅgāsvarana attaining womanhood.

93. The victory of the disciple named Vipula, who was established in yoga, over Indra—the power of whose Brahman-yoga surpasses all other powers—due to his protection of the virtue of Rucibrāhmaṇī; the destruction of the Rākṣasas Lomamarṣaṇa and Kapardaka; the teacher’s favor and blessing; and the honor accorded to his saintliness, and so forth.

94. The recovery of the Gokarṇa Tīrtha, which had been submerged in the ocean, by Paraśurāma while residing in Siṃhāraṇya; Kuvalāśva’s attainment of the status of Dhundhumāra through the grace of Uttaṅka; and Triśaṅku, known as Satyavrata, ascending to heaven in his own body through the grace of Viśvāmitra—such are the glories of the virtuous.

95. Regarding the majesty of holy men who are worthy of worship and salutation: through the blessing and service of the saint named Praṇada Brahmā, Kaśyapa and Aditi attained the status of being the progenitors of the gods alone, and the status of being the progenitors of all creation.

96. Regarding the Lord, virtuous persons, dharma, saintly women, liberation, and its means such as devotion, the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is as follows: the company of the virtuous is a strong means of valid cognition, and direct experience (*camatkāra*) is the strongest, and so forth.

97. Even for those engaged in worldly exertion, liberation is attained through association with the virtuous; likewise, even for those afflicted by suffering, it is so—such as the attainment of liberation at Gokarṇa by hundreds of thousands of men through their meeting with the holy sage Ālambāyana, and so forth. 18. Even for one fallen into calamity, association with the virtuous brings about welfare—such as the subsequent liberation from hell and the attainment of heaven by the vulture, the outcaste, and the Śabara, and so forth.
99. Prosperity always dwells among virtuous persons, and they are the very abodes where prosperity resides.

100. The narrative concerning the manifestation and arrival of the incarnations of the Blessed One, the cause being either divine grace or the curse of Bhṛgu; the twelve battles with the Daityas; the prior history of the family of the goddess Pārvatī and her consort, and so forth. 101. The greatness of the cow and related matters, such as how the gift of a cow (*godāna*) is the means for the liberation of a deceased spirit (*preta*) who lacked the yoga of the virtuous.

102. The vow named *Gavārādhana*; the abiding of Lakṣmī within cow dung and urine; the various fruits of the gift of a cow; those [deeds] which effect the deliverance of the *bhāruṇḍa* spirits; and how taking refuge in the virtuous is the liberator of all, and so forth.

103. Liberation of hungry ghosts (*preta*) occurs through various kinds of gifts; the worthy recipient (*dānapātra*) is the excellent virtuous person—such is the illustration provided by Vṛṣādarbhi and Sūrya at the outset.

104. In the *Gārhasthyadharmasāra*, liberation is attained through the divine fortune (*divyalakṣmī*) resulting from the union with a virtuous practitioner (*sādhuyoga*), even for a man who has stolen the wealth of others; furthermore, there is the liberation and the realization of the *Brahmasattra* for those who were previously wealthy, and so forth.

105. A wedded wife is the root of all religious duties and actions; this is the marvel regarding the shared duty (*sahadharma*) of Kundadharmā, the wife of the Kṣatriya Jāṅgalāmakhā: [the discussion of] fitness for giving a daughter in marriage, fitness for a bridegroom, fitness for inheritance, purity of seed, and so forth.

106. There are various sons, various wives, and various husbands; liberation through the yoga of the saintly (*sādhu-yoga*); and the liberation of Śambhalavāra, a member of the Sūta caste who was devoted to the saintly, after he had attained a kingdom, sons, cattle, birds, and so on, by means of his devotion and penance, together with his progeny.
107. An examination of the service of Kalyāṇadevānīka, who was devoted [to Him], and a description of the lineage and succession of the root of the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa dynasty, and so forth.

108. A presentation of the Thousand-Name Hymn (Sahasranāma Stotra) of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, known as the Śrī Puruṣottama Sāma, which destroys all obstacles and grants all desired objects, and so forth.

109. After enjoying the fruits of his gifts, the donor experiences the fruit of chanting the Puruṣottama Sāma, which consists of eternal bliss residing in the imperishable abode (Akṣaradhāma), and so forth.

110. [The fruits of giving to a worthy recipient (dānapātra), the fruit of the gift of land, the fruit of the gift of food, the fruit of the *puruṣottamasāman*, and so forth. 111. For one who gives water, gives land, performs various kinds of gifts, recites the *puruṣottamasāman*, possesses long-standing virtue, and is a believer (*āstika*), there is instruction on the gate of Yama and liberation; and likewise for one of long-standing virtue who is even an atheist (*nāstika*). 112. In the description of the fruits of the gift of a cow, the gift of a cow equal to the earth, and the performance of various vows and conducts, there is the illustration of the gift of the body by the Yoginī Brahmasatyā, her liberation, and so forth.

113. The fruits of various types of austerity; how those very same austerities grant liberation when joined with devotion; the absence of a destination for King Vaivarta due to his atheism, followed by his rebirth through his wife as Devarāta, and subsequently his attainment of liberation through theistic rites and devotion, and so forth.

114. The liberation of Romapāda, the cowherd, by taking refuge in a saintly person; the protection of the thief named Namabhaṅga from the fear of the king through meeting a saintly person; and the revival of mango groves, trees, and other plants scorched by forest fires through their association with the saintly sage Bhāgavatāyana, and so forth.

115. Description of the preparation of the army of Lalitā-Mahālakṣmī, who appeared at the sacrifice of the gods who had come to the region of Indraprastha for the purpose of destroying the demon Bhaṇḍāsura, who had arisen from the pride of his own desires.

116. Mahālakṣmī’s armies set forth for the destruction of Bhaṇḍa; the counsel of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura; the destruction of Bhaṇḍa’s forces; and Bhaṇḍa’s recollection of Kaikasā and others. 117. Following the destruction of Bhaṇḍa’s forces by Mahālakṣmī’s armies, the destruction of the demon Bhaṇḍāsura and subsequent events.

118. The worship performed for the sake of the victory of Śrī Lalitā Mahālakṣmī; the *Mahālakṣmī-stotra*; rewards and other honors for those who are victorious; the various forms of Kāma; the sixteen palaces of Mahālakṣmī; and descriptions of the beauty, power, and service therein, and so forth.
119. Service rendered by divine attendants residing in the Cintāmaṇi palace; the mantra of Mahālakṣmī, its recitation (*japa*), its fruit, and so forth.

120. Another mantra of Mahālakṣmī; the dual form of Mahālakṣmī in the city of Kāñcī; the residence there of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa; the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā), and so forth. 121. One hundred and thirty-five names of Lalitā-Mahālakṣmī; the greatness of the Guru-tīrtha, and so forth. 122. The giving away of a daughter (kanyādāna) for the sake of obtaining a daughter; the gift of Lakṣmī (lakṣmīdāna); the vow of a daughter (putrīvrata), and so forth.
123. The supreme vow among all vows consists of service to the virtuous and a humble disposition.
124. Regarding pleasure, pain, and so forth, there is the vow of serving the virtuous, the gods, and others, as well as humility and the like.
125. Within the sixteen great gifts (*mahādāna*), the procedure for the gift of the *tulāpuruṣa* (the person on the scale) is described.
126. An exposition of the rules for the great gifts of the Hiranyagarbha and the Brahmāṇḍa. 127. An exposition of the rules for the great gift of the Kalpavṛkṣa and the great gift of a thousand cows.
128. An exposition of the rules among the great gifts for the great gift of the Golden Wish-Cow, the great gift of the Golden Horse, and the great gift of the Golden Chariot.
129. An exposition of the procedures for the great gifts of the golden elephant-chariot, the great gift of the five-ploughed field, and the great gift of the golden earth.

130. A description of the great gift of the universal Sudarśana great wheel, the great gift of the garlanded great wheel, the gift of the protector, and the great gifts of rings, finger-rings, armlets, bracelets, chains, fetters, bangles, necklaces, and so forth.

131. A description of the gift of the Mahākalpalatā-golden creeper, the gift of Kalpapriyā, the gift of Svarṇakāntā, the gift of merit, the gifts of fearlessness and so forth, the great gifts to the Guru, the gods, and the goddesses, and the great gifts of temples, sacred fields, gardens, ornaments, and the like. 132. A description of the great gift of the seven oceans, the great gift of the jewel-cow, the great gift of the vessel of the great elements (Mahābhūtakalaśa), the great gift of Lakṣmī, as well as other great gifts. 133. An exposition on the most auspicious days and an exposition on the propitiation and worship of the planets, etc.

134. The procedure for reciting and offering oblations one hundred thousand times or ten million times during a planetary sacrifice (*grahamakhā*); the recovery of all possessions by a merchant named Lohāṅgāra after their loss, through the pacification of the planets (*grahaśānti*), and so forth.

135. The two hundred names and forms belonging to Mahālakṣmī as spoken by Dakṣa Prajāpati; the propitiatory worship (*śāntipūjā*) in the Lakṣmī-sacrifice; and the image of Mahālakṣmī, her mandala, and so on. 136. The attainment of one’s desired fruits by the daughters of the Pitṛs and others through the recitation of the two hundred names of Lakṣmī; the procedure for the *lakṣmī-saubhāgya-śayana-vrata*, and so forth.
137. An exposition of the Ghaṭalakṣmīvrata performed by Agastya—the Lakṣmīvrata which is the most auspicious of all auspicious things—and the Sāṃkhyayogalakṣmīvrata.
138. An exposition of the Rasakalyāṇalalitāvrata, the Ārdrānandaramānārāyaṇavrata, the Śāradeyavrata, and the Kalyāṇīkamalāvrata.

139. A description of the *viśokalalitā-dvādaśī-vrata* and the *vibhūtilalitā-kṛṣṇalālana-vrata*, along with the example of the sovereign king Puṣkaravāhana of Puṣkaradvīpa, the marks of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and so forth.
140. A brief description of the sixty-one miscellaneous vows (*prakīrṇaka-vrata*).
141. The liberation of even sinners through the remembrance, sight, and other acts related to the sacred site (*tīrtha*) of Kuṅkumavāpikā, and so forth.

142. An exposition of the nature and power of timely death, the recitation of specific mantras for the purpose of conquering it, and the methods for worshipping the Supreme Lord and others. 143. An exposition of the nature of the dharma of the Dvāpara age and the presentation of mantras and other means for the liberation of human beings of that kind.
144. An analysis and investigation of the transitions between the dharmas of the various ages.

145. In the *Saṃkīrtana*, there is an exposition on the scales (*svaras*), musical modes (*grāmas*), and modulations (*mūrchanās*) of the *saṃgītikā*; the vision of the divine *saṃgīta* hall of Lakṣmī, and so forth. 146. An account of various rites for pacifying portents (*utpātas*) originating from the gods, the atmosphere, and the earth.
147. A detailed description of the pacification rituals and other measures for various kinds of portents.
148. The determination of the propitiatory rites for planets (*grahayajña*) and so forth, for the purpose of pacifying the afflictions caused by bad dreams and similar portents.
149. Auspicious omens, dreams, and the like during a journey or expedition; and, for the sake of averting adverse signs, worship, pacificatory rites (*śānti*), sacrifices (*yajña*), and so forth.
150. The determination of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other rituals pertaining to the *Hanuman-mantra*.
151. An exposition of the means for destroying all great sins and the like, as well as the expenditure of wealth regarding the nine treasures (navanidhi).
152. A description of the lineage of Dharma and a description of the lineage of Adharma; therein, the dwelling places of Duḥsaha and the calamities and so forth of the lineage of Duḥsaha.

153. The fruits—whether favorable or unfavorable, and whether actions should be performed or avoided—based on specific asterisms, yoginīs, lunar days, yogas, planetary periods (daśā), omens, hiccup, locations, ascendants (lagna), and specific ghaṭikās.

154. Due to the sins of her previous birth, Sarojinī, the daughter of a potter, went to the hermitage of the holy Satīśvarī after the death of her four husbands; there, through service to her guru, devotion to Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, and ascetic penance, she was freed from the defects of the planets and physical ailments, and subsequently attained the state of being a *kamalinī* creeper—the abode of Śrī Lakṣmī—as well as the status of a lotus-lake goddess (*padminī-rāmā*), and so forth.
155. A description of the births and other details of the eight Manus.
156. A description of the births and other details of the nine Manus beginning with the ninth up to the thirteenth.
157. Ruci’s vision of his ancestors, their praise, his life as a householder, and so forth.
158. The narrative of the fourteenth Manu.
159. Anādi Śrī Kṛṣṇa Nārāyaṇa, accompanied by Brahmapriyā and others, traveled by celestial chariot across the earth, beholding it, and arrived at the home of Himālaya, and so forth.

160. Having received the worship performed by Himādri, [the Lord] visited Kedāra, Kailāsa, Mānasasaras, Mount Nūmata, Kāśī, Vindhya, Saptapuṭa, Bhagukaccha, Gopanātha, and others; then He proceeded to Hari’s Kuṅkumavāpī, where He observed the desire of the beloveds of Brahmā to know about the origin of diamonds and other minerals from the physical elements.

161. The attendant named Bala fell from his abode in Śrīpura due to a mutual curse with his companions Jayā and others; furthermore, during the sacrifice of the Daitya Bala, jewels were produced from the bodily constituents of the sacrificial fuel (*samidh*). And so forth.

162. An examination of the origin, value, and excellence of diamonds (*vajramaṇi*) and pearls (*muktāmaṇi*). 163. An examination of the origin, qualities, and other characteristics of gems such as ruby (*padmarāga*), emerald (*marakata*), sapphire (*indranīla*), lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*), topaz (*puṣparāga*), karketana, bhīṣma, pulaka, ruby (*rudhira*), crystal (*sphaṭika*), and coral (*vidruma*).
164. An examination of the purposes and nature of the fourteen incarnations (*avatāra*) of Hari throughout the fourteen *manvantaras*.
165. An examination of the ritual procedure for the *śrāddha* performed while the deceased is still alive (*jīvacchrāddha*).
166. An exposition of the poisons of *saṃsāra* and the means for their removal. 167. The *Vyapohana-stotra*, intended for the destruction of all calamities, sins, bonds, and so forth.

168. That the giving away of a daughter in marriage, the dedication [of acts] to Kṛṣṇa, the taking of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), the propitiation of Vināyaka, and the worship of persons who are sinful, miserable, or happy, yield great fruit.
169. The causes that bring about death, the means for their destruction, and the example of the sage Āyanara who attained saintliness, and so forth.
170. In the *Muktidharma*, there is the instruction on the various abodes [of the soul], such as the mutual manifestation of the glorious *Saccidānanda-yogin* and others.
171. In the *Muktidharma*, there are the causes for the destruction of the body, the causes for the attainment of a body, the causes for liberation from the body, and so forth.
172. In the *Muktidharma*, there is the means for the dissolution of *māyā* and the attainment of the abode of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahma-dhāma*), and so forth.

173. In the *Muktidharma*, regarding the question posed by the sage Sadvidyayana—husband of Śrutiphala and husband of Apatni—concerning the departure to the world of Kava and other matters, the answer is given that one attains the world of the Supreme Brahman through the method of renunciation (*naiṣkarmya*) and the surrender of all actions (*sarvasamarpaṇa*), and so forth.

174. In the *Muktidharma*, [the topics include] the attainment of a body according to [one's state], the experience of auspicious and inauspicious results, the realization of Brahman, the foundation of karma, the offering of fruits, the acquisition of divine stature, eternal liberation, dwelling in the Imperishable (*akṣara*), and the comprehension of [liberation] such as *sārūpya* (likeness), and so forth.
175. In the *Muktidharma*, there is a description of the knowledge for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra and related matters.
176. An exposition of the qualities of those who possess the dharma of liberation in brief, as well as the qualities of the body and those beginning with the illusory (māyika).
177. An exposition of the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), the celestial (adhidaiva), the divine (daiva), the supreme-divine (adhideva), and so forth.

178. The liberation of the sage Bhikṣāyana through acts such as offering everything to Lord Hari even while in the householder stage—despite having no wife, begging without asking, and subsisting on handfuls of grain—as well as the majesty of alms-gathering, and so on.

179. The vision of Śrī Hari and the liberation of Keśin, the son of that devoted woman who was without a protector and whose constant refuge was He; and so forth. 180. The destruction of leprosy for the gold-thief named Vyāghra, a devotee of the wandering singers (cāraṇas); the destruction of dropsy for the village-priest Brahmin named Uttama, a devotee; and the vision of the Lord, liberation, and so forth. 181. The story of the previous birth of the Vaiśya named Virāla; his attainment of Śrī Hari at the sacred site of Kuṅkumavāpikā; the destruction of his pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman); liberation, and so forth.
182. The account of the previous births of the son of King Pṛthvīdhara, who was blind from birth, and how he was granted the power of sight by the Blessed One, and so forth.
183. The account of the Śūdra named Sāgara, whose feet were broken, and how his feet were made free of pain by the Blessed One, along with his previous history, and so forth.
184. The destruction of the mutilation of the devotee Vṛkṇadeva through his devotion, the liberation of King Bhāvaśūra through the yoga of devotion, his previous birth, and so forth.

185. The Lord liberated from his curse and granted liberation to the Brahmin named Pāśupateśa, who had fallen into a state of madness due to the curse of a devotee Brahmin named Mañjulakeśa, and so forth.

186. Through association with a holy man (sādhu), the Lord granted liberation to the liquor-seller named Bāṇāṅgaṇa; [the Lord also bestowed] divine manifestations upon the body of that holy man, and so forth. 187. By saving the life of a cow, the leather-worker named Mṛtādana was freed from sins such as meat-eating, attained merit, met with holy men, and obtained heaven and liberation, and so forth.
188. Through the application of yoga, the thief named Śaṅkudhara—who was dragging away Sumantu—experienced the destruction of his sins, performed sacrifices, attained liberation, and so forth.
189. Through association with the virtuous and the attainment of the Lord Cintāmaṇi, there was the fulfillment of all desires and other such benefits.
190. A hymn of praise for the Great Saurāṣṭra community, which had been plundered by bandits.

191. For the sake of protecting [the people] from robbers, Hari, assuming the form of a royal soldier and others, slew the robbers after first praising women and children; thus, his devotees were protected, and so forth. 192. Through the devotion and the observance of vows performed by his own wife, Śrī Hari brought about the liberation of the merchant Dhaniṣṭhakaśa, who was addicted to courtesans, along with the king of Yuddhapura; and so forth.

193. [The account] of King Āsīna of Vāṭa, a slayer of Brahmins who was overcome by Rākṣasas and deprived of his kingdom; how, through supreme devotion, he beheld the Blessed Lord and was liberated from all suffering, and so forth.

194. [The account] of how, at the command of King Cakradhara, the Blessed Hari brought about the prevention of the sacrificial rite of the minister named Devaviśrāma, who was burdened by the sin of killing a woman who was a *kāṇḍikā*-yoginī, and so forth.

195. When the son born of a second wife was lost to a devotee named Harṣula due to his senior wife, the Blessed One, assuming the form of a holy man, restored the son to life and destroyed the sin of child-murder; and so forth. 196. Instruction given to Harṣula and others, as well as the obtaining of a son by the senior wife, and so forth. 197. A farmer named Śāṇadhara, who had contracted leprosy due to actions in a previous birth, was cast into the ocean by his sons out of fear; the Blessed One then cured his disease, protected him, and destroyed his sin, and so forth.
198. The sin of cow-slaughter committed by the devotee named Nimbadeva was averted by the Blessed Lord, and so forth.
199. By Śrī Hari, the state of being established in Brahman, sovereignty, and other qualities were described for His exclusive devotees.

200. Through supreme devotion, the liberation of Kālīndarabhāṇḍa—who resided in the village of Bhāṇḍīra along with his dancers and others—and the instruction of the great sage Kamalāyana, and so forth.

201. Through the instruction of Bodhāyana, the dancer Rāyaṇadeva attained realization while still in the womb, as well as devotion, the vision of Hari, liberation, and so forth. 202. By means of yoga, the singer-bhakta named Vratadinna brought about the Vaiṣṇava state and the liberation of King Puṇḍravarmā along with his progeny, and so forth.
203. Through his devotion, the Blessed Lord protected the weaver named Tūlavāyi, as well as his workers; having granted him a vision, He led him to liberation, and so forth.

204. The forest deities and others who were wood-gatherers beheld Śrī Hari in the form of a holy man through their devotion, and were liberated at the end; and so forth. 205. The Lord, being pleased by the extreme devotion of the merchant Vātsalyadhīra and his wife Mañjulikā, granted them a vision; they both became perfected saints (sādhus), and so forth. 206. Through the devotion taught by Śiva in the form of a holy man to the forest-guardian named Tilakaraṅga—a devotee of Śiva—and through the worship of Nārāyaṇa, he attained supreme liberation; and so forth.
207. The Lord provided protection for the field-guardian Āñjabhakta, the great devotee Mahāmaya, and the farmers from plunderers, and so forth.

208. Being pleased by the devotion of the Kirāta named Sāgara, Śrī Hari, appearing in the form of a merchant, bestowed upon him a heap of wheat; He made it inexhaustible while stored in the granary, and likewise made his cakes, vessels, and water-pots inexhaustible, and granted him liberation, and so forth.
209. The protection by Śrī Hari and the liberation of Sāraṅga, a Hūṇa devotee who possessed a wealth of buffalo cattle, after he had been struck down by a lion in the forest, and so forth.
210. The attainment of liberation through the company of the saintly sage Brahmāyana and through devotion to Śrī Hari for Yajñarāta, a Puṣkasa, along with his family, and so forth.
211. The liberation of the Cāṇḍāla named Kapikṣaya, along with his family, through devotion to Śrī Hari upon receiving instruction from a deity in the form of a monkey, and so forth.

212. Through the devotion of Nālīka, the blacksmith, the devotee obtained a vision of Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and Garuḍa, and was liberated; and so forth. 213. Through the devotion of the devotee Maṅgaladeva, the shoemaker, the Lord Himself came and warded off poison for him; and so forth. 214. Through the devotion of Haridāsa, the chariot-maker, the Lord brought about the liberation of him along with his entire family; and so forth.
215. The Lord protected the servants of Śilāhāra—the devotee named Dāmaśilāda—and brought about their liberation at the end of Dāmaśilāda’s life, and so forth.
216. Out of devotion, the Lord protected and liberated the artisan Sañjayadeva from an elephant, and so forth.
217. Out of devotion, the Lord granted a vision to the painter named Saṃbharadeva and brought about his liberation, and so forth.
218. The Lord granted liberation through His grace to the devotee named Mauktikeśin, who was the master of a mine of stone-coal, and so forth.

219. Through his meeting with the sage Pautimāṣya, the hunter named Cakradhara’s sins, such as violence, were destroyed; subsequently, through devotion, he attained liberation, and so forth. 220. The Lord provided protection and liberation from the punishment of King Sutāra-Siṃha for the devotee Vāṭadhara, whose dwelling was Piśunakhava, as well as for Queen Dvaipī, and so forth.
221. Through the power of Vṛṣaparvan’s forbearance, Śivajaya, the builder of the palace, was liberated, and so forth.
222. Having caused Jālakārya, who was devoted to Saṅgarayāda, to abandon [his former ways], the virtuous Śuklāyana brought about his attainment of the Blessed One, and so forth.
233. Through association with the virtuous Satīśvarī and other holy women, Udyamaśrī and the others from Bharavāṭa developed devotion to Kṛṣṇa and were liberated, and so forth.
224. The liberation of Dīrgharava and others, who were camel-herders, through their association with the virtuous one named Rāmāyaṇa, and so forth.
225. The liberation and other benefits for the devotee named Ratnaprabha, a donkey-herder, through his connection with Lord Narasiṃha, and so forth.
226. The sufferings caused by sins for the physician named Gadārdaneśvara, and the liberation of his wife Mukundinī through her devotion, and so forth.
227. Through the connection with the merchant Sudhāmarasādhu, who was a protector of monkeys and a forest-dweller, there was his liberation, and so forth.

228. The Blessed One, being pleased by the devotion of Nigamikā—the wife of Harṣadharman, a barber in the service of King Svarṇadhanvan—and by her steadfastness in serving holy men such as Kalyāṇadhāma, assumed the form of Nigamikā and served the queen; he protected and liberated the family of the barber, and so forth.
229. In a previous birth, the protection and liberation from a demon of the virtuous women, as well as of Ruṭāṇakyā, a fisherwoman devoted to the Ābhīras, and others.

230. In a previous birth, the subsequent births as ship-captains for Dhīraparva and others who were fishermen, their devotion [to the Lord] therein, and their liberation due to former merit, and so forth.
231. Through devotion, the prosperity and liberation of Tārakādarśa, the giver of the trident, and his wife Kṛtaśalyā, and so forth.

232. Through devotion to the Blessed One and by means of the practice of the holy Nārāyaṇāyana, the Blessed One brought about the liberation of Jvālāprasāda—who had been turned into charcoal by fire—along with his wife and thousands of other embodied beings, and so forth. 233. Through devotion to the Blessed One and by serving the holy Kiṃśukāyana, [the Blessed One] brought about the liberation of the king named Lavādana, who was a poisoner, as well as his queens and his subjects, and so forth.
234. Through the association with the saintly Nirmohanāyana, the vision of the Lord and the liberation of the one named Vikhaṇḍala, who bore weapons, as well as his wife Harasatī, and so forth.

235. The liberation of the farmer named Jīrṇodbhavana through the company of the saint Caitanyakāyani, and the description of the granting of vows that bestow feminine beauty and other such blessings, and so forth.

236. The festival celebrating the seventeenth birthday of the beginningless Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Nārāyaṇa, and the greatness of hearing the stories of the lineage of Dvāpara, the giving of gifts, and the chanting of mantras, and so forth.

237. A summary of the subject matter of the Dvāpara lineage, the specific majesty of the Dvāpara lineage, the direct scriptural testimony regarding the lineages of the four yugas, the prayer for the eligibility of the Kali age for liberation, the introduction to the Tiṣya lineage, the benediction, and so forth.
Thus ends the table of contents for the chapters of the third section, consisting of the Dvāpara lineage, in the Śrī Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇīya Saṃhitā.
(Chapters: 237; Verses: 25,162).
